title: Hong Kong port needs a new lease of life in value-driven era

content: Hong Kong’s surging exports amid recent global trade shifts and tariff measures are reason to celebrate. However, they have not reversed the decline in the city’s port’s container throughput, which hit 12.99 million 20-foot equivalent units in 2025, down 5.1 per cent year on year. To address public doubts over the city’s standing as an international shipping centre, Hong Kong’s first five-year plan seeks to transform the maritime hub from being throughput-driven to value-driven. The policy emphasis falls on cultivating a commodity trading ecosystem and advancing high-value services, ranging from shipping finance and marine insurance to ship management and maritime dispute resolution. As Hong Kong pivots towards maritime services, there are fundamental questions about the strategic purpose of the city’s physical port in a value-driven era. How should the port evolve so physical cargo flows power Hong Kong’s high-value service ecosystem instead of lagging behind? As maritime value compounds on operational scale, high-value maritime services cannot exist in a vacuum. A thriving port provides the essential foundation, real-time data and practical exposure needed to build top-tier maritime services. Dockside operations generate the intelligence required for marine surveying, vessel inspection, risk assessment and claims settlement. Furthermore, port calls are indispensable for high-margin strategic initiatives such as green marine fuel bunkering and trading. Every vessel docking creates an immediate commercial opportunity for bunkering, which in turn refines local practices, builds liquidity in green fuel trading and yields associated service fees. Without sufficient traffic, the operational feedback loop breaks. This erodes the city’s ability to price risk, structure complex maritime products or maintain its service edge over competing regional hubs. However, aiming for the throughput levels seen 10 or 20 years ago is unrealistic. Hong Kong must accept the reality that its role as the sole gateway for mainland trade is history. Rather than accepting a self-defeating narrative of lost competition, though, the new pathway includes Hong Kong as a member of the Greater Bay Area port cluster. The fate of Hong Kong’s port is key to the competitiveness of the cluster. It requires Hong Kong to view the cluster as a collaborative network of ports with distinct roles rather than a collection of competitors. The city should find its unique value propositions and development direction rooted in comparative advantages. While mainland ports excel at massive industrial scale and primary inland cargo aggregation, Hong Kong’s competitive edge lies in its international connectivity, free port status, common law judicial infrastructure and financial prowess. By coordinating feeder networks, establishing green energy corridors and standardising cross-boundary digital customs data across the cluster, the Greater Bay Area becomes an integrated, positive-sum ecosystem. In this framework, physical cargo flows across neighbouring ports directly feed into Hong Kong’s high-value maritime services financial architecture. Realising this collaborative vision requires overcoming institutional hurdles rooted in Hong Kong’s port governance model: port ownership, planning and development. Unlike Singapore’s PSA – a public entity fully owned by Temasek – or state-owned mainland port groups, the Kwai Tsing Container Terminals are fragmented across five private operators with distinct corporate structures and commercial priorities, operating under private land leases that run until 2047. Furthermore, the Marine Department lacks any legislative authority to regulate, guide or mandate Kwai Tsing port planning and infrastructure development. Without legislation, the Transport and Logistics Bureau’s road maps and policies could face limited compliance and cooperation. This governance vacuum stands in stark contrast to the mainland’s Port Law, which empowers municipal port authorities to issue legally binding port planning master plans. It also compares poorly to Singapore’s Maritime and Port Authority Act, which uses statutory licensing conditions to require licensees’ compliance with any direction given by the authority, which can be revoked or modified. This institutional reality manifests in three acute market failures. First, industry adoption of smart logistics solutions has remained piecemeal, fragmented and slow as uncoordinated private terminals rely on legacy, proprietary operational systems. Second, it creates chronic confusion and friction regarding financial responsibilities for infrastructure serving the public good. While the government expects private operators to capitalise long-term decarbonisation assets, private terminal operators might argue that the public benefits of emissions reduction justify direct public financing. Third, private fragmentation breeds collective action problems. Without a single statutory voice, individual terminal operators lack the unified mandate or incentive to negotiate cooperation with state-backed mainland port authorities. To bridge this gap, Hong Kong must establish a dedicated statutory port authority equipped with clear regulatory levers, operational licensing oversight and master planning powers over terminal land and operations. A centralised port authority is essential to ensure port operator alignment, coordinate public-private investments in smart and green infrastructure and enter legally binding strategic alliances across the Greater Bay Area. By replacing fragmentation with central leadership, Hong Kong can ensure its waterfront remains a dynamic, world-class engine driving the region’s premier maritime services hub.

title: Can Prabowo’s economic nationalism save Indonesia from potential MSCI downgrade?
description: In the wake of Indonesia’s worst stock-market rout since the 1998 Asian financial crisis, President Prabowo Subianto’s administration has turned to appeals to economic nationalism to shore up confidence, urging citizens to rally behind the country’s battered stock market. content: In the wake of Indonesia’s worst stock-market rout since the 1998 Asian financial crisis, President Prabowo Subianto’s administration has turned to appeals to economic nationalism to shore up confidence, urging citizens to rally behind the country’s battered stock market. The government has promised reforms in response to warnings from global index provider MSCI that Indonesia could be downgraded from emerging-market to stand-alone-market status. But analysts say its patriotic appeals will do little to restore investor confidence without concrete steps to improve market transparency and governance, while potentially exposing retail investors to further losses. After the Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) plunged 11 per cent on Friday, further sell-offs followed in the ensuing days, prompting a defiant Prabowo to address the market turmoil at a cabinet meeting five days later. “MSCI wants to scare us, but I say to them: Indonesia fears no one and will not be intimidated!” Prabowo also claimed Indonesia’s dispute with MSCI was among the “hurdles and obstructions” continuing to harry his administration. “But the nation has the strength, courage and willingness to make the necessary sacrifices.” The president’s defiance was accompanied by calls from senior figures in his administration and allies in the business community for Indonesians to support the domestic stock market. Sufmi Dasco Ahmad, deputy speaker of the House of Representatives and a senior leader in the ruling Gerindra party, launched a Buy Indonesia campaign on Tuesday, urging citizens to buy domestic shares to prevent further declines. “Through collective pan-Indonesia efforts, we can turn our bourse around. Buy Indonesia!” Dasco said on social media, reaffirming his confidence in the resilience of the local economy. He was among the first officials to visit the Jakarta Stock Exchange on the day of the October 16 crash. Mufti Nurlatifah, a lecturer in the Department of Communication Science at Yogyakarta’s University of Gadjah Mada, said while Dasco’s public appeal attempted to maintain optimism about Indonesia’s economic future, “it’s hardly enough without giving the public concrete reasons and measurable indicators why they should remain upbeat”. She said it would be a grave error to conflate citizens’ patriotism with indiscriminate investment in Indonesian stocks. Indonesian tycoon Jusuf Hamka, recently made one of Prabowo’s presidential advisers, also tried to support the market by announcing on Sunday that he was setting up a consortium to inject 5 trillion rupiah (US$277 million) into the bourse. “Our blue chips can yield between 8 and 9 per cent annually, higher than term deposits,” he claimed. Hamka described MSCI’s downgrade threat as a “shakedown” by a foreign force seeking to destabilise Indonesia, and urged local entrepreneurs to “step up and defend our sovereignty by buying up our domestic stocks”. Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of Jakarta-based think tank the Centre of Economic and Law Studies, called the patriotic appeals made by Dasco and Hamka “dangerously misleading”. “They could put retail investors in jeopardy as stock prices could tank further if and when institutional investors take a hike,” he said. An MSCI downgrade could remove Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracking emerging markets, potentially prompting funds that follow those benchmarks to reduce their exposure to the country. To calm market nerves, the Indonesia Stock Exchange met MSCI on Monday and outlined further measures to improve transparency, including identifying affiliated shareholders and excluding highly concentrated stocks from the JCI’s calculation. Authorities have also pledged broader capital-market reforms. MSCI has said, however, that investors want evidence of the measures being consistently implemented and having a meaningful impact. MSCI’s consultation on Indonesia’s proposed reclassification remains open until April 30, 2027, with a final decision expected by the end of June that year, giving the government time to demonstrate progress on the reforms. Bhima argued that the central issue was how the Indonesian stock market was administered, rather than a lack of patriotic support for domestic shares. “Instead of enacting the necessary reforms in the capital market, the government and its cohorts have opted for a narrative steeped in economic nationalism.” For Vedi Hadiz, a political sociologist at the University of Melbourne, the market turmoil also reflected tensions arising from Prabowo’s efforts to recentralise political and economic power. These include the creation of Danantara, a sovereign wealth fund designed to consolidate management of state-owned enterprises, and plans to channel exports of key commodities such as coal and palm oil through a single state-owned company, giving the government greater control over the movement of resources and capital. “His efforts to change the rules of the game to suit his own political and economic agenda will inevitably cause problems for established business groups who have to adapt to his agenda,” Hadiz said. Dasco’s Buy Indonesia plea also exposed the tensions emerging from Prabowo’s bid to bring big businesses under tighter political control, Hadiz said. “But an appeal based on economic nationalism glosses over these tensions by suggesting that everyone shares the same interests.” Hadiz observed that patriotic appeals have featured in previous administrations’ responses to economic turmoil, often with limited results. He cited former president Joko Widodo’s 2015 appeal to Indonesians to buy local products to counter rupiah depreciation. In January 1998, amid the rupiah’s collapse, presidential daughter Siti Hardijanti Rukmana launched the Love the Rupiah Movement and tried to set an example by publicly selling US$50,000 of her own money. Her initiative failed to arrest the currency’s slide, with the rupiah reaching almost 17,000 to the US dollar in June 1998, Bhima noted. “It happened because the appeal was made when the government had lost all public credibility and trust.” For investors, the concerns extend beyond the immediate MSCI dispute. Ricky Ho, chief investment officer and portfolio manager at Jakarta-based family office Four Capital, said he remained “bearish on Indonesia”. In his assessment, the Indonesian equity market faces a daunting combination of headwinds, including higher global discount rates, a stronger US dollar, expensive oil, weaker purchasing power among the middle class, continued pressure on banks’ asset quality, uncertain commodity margins and the unresolved MSCI issue. “That is simply not the environment in which I’d want to take large risks,” Ho said. For Hadiz, however, the stock-market turmoil did not in itself demonstrate that big businesses were resisting Prabowo’s economic agenda, often referred to as Prabowonomics. “Resistance can take the form of lobbying, holding back investment, demanding concessions or pushing for changes in policy.” The upheaval nevertheless presents a dilemma for the president. “Prabowo wants to exercise greater control over the conglomerates, yet still needs their investment and cooperation to make his economic and political agenda work,” Hadiz said.

title: Indonesians turn to eco-art as haze sparks anger and diplomatic tension
description: As wildfires rage across Sumatra and Kalimantan, frustrated Indonesians are turning to performance art to call for greater government action and draw global attention to the destruction of both the country’s rainforests and rich cultural heritage. In South Sumatra, local art collective Jaga Api recently launched a project titled Tarian Kehancuran Budaya (the Dance of Cultural Destruction), using traditional performance to convey the human and environmental toll of the fires, as reported by The...
content: As wildfires rage across Sumatra and Kalimantan, frustrated Indonesians are turning to performance art to call for greater government action and draw global attention to the destruction of both the country’s rainforests and rich cultural heritage. In South Sumatra, local art collective Jaga Api recently launched a project titled Tarian Kehancuran Budaya (the Dance of Cultural Destruction), using traditional performance to convey the human and environmental toll of the fires, as reported by The Straits Times. Filmed in a scorched forest outside the provincial capital of Palembang, one viral video shows a dancer wearing a gas mask and Aesan Paksangko – South Sumatra’s ceremonial bridal attire. Against a backdrop of burnt trees and ash, she performs the tari tanggai, a traditional welcome dance whose usual celebratory symbolism takes on a more sombre meaning amid the destruction. The video has over 3,500 likes and 820 re-shares on social media, reflecting the attention the performance has received online. View this post on Instagram “The tanggai dance is usually used for welcoming,” Jaga Api wrote on social media. “There is no welcome for officials who allow corporate land [clearance] through barbaric ways, leaving bruises and shattering culture with grief.” Other creative protests have taken place across Indonesia. In Ketapang, West Kalimantan, Zwageri Generation – the youth wing of the non-profit conservation organisation Yiari – performed a similar dance, according to The Straits Times, attracting over 25,400 likes on social media. “When words can no longer stir the conscience, allow us to speak through art,” the group said in a post online. “We give voice to the wounds of the forest and the cries of life that are slowly being destroyed by greed.” Many users have expressed solidarity in the comment sections of these videos. However, some have questioned whether art can actually influence decision-makers. “Will these loud, classy protests reach those in power?” asked one user. Another added: “Is Wowo watching or not?” – referring to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto by his popular nickname. Public frustration over the wildfires has intensified as toxic haze spreads across Southeast Asia, triggering health warnings and political friction across borders. Student-led demonstrations were held across several Indonesian cities on Tuesday, with protesters blaming the government for incompetence and corruption in managing land clearance and putting out the fires, CNA reported. Some Indonesians have also urged neighbouring governments, including Singapore and Malaysia, to sue Jakarta over the haze crisis. However, Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan ruled out legal action on Friday, as reported by The Straits Times, saying that Kuala Lumpur would instead resolve the issue through diplomacy and Association of Southeast Asian Nations channels. But Singapore has taken a stronger legal stance. Its National Environment Agency has issued legal notices to 10 companies operating plantations in South Sumatra and Kalimantan under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, The Straits Times reported. In response to growing domestic and international pressure, President Prabowo has directed cabinet officials to mobilise “all available resources”, expanding deployment orders to include additional personnel from the military, police and forestry agencies. Jakarta says it has deployed more than 60,000 personnel across six provinces. Despite the scale of the fires, Jakarta continues to decline offers of foreign aid from its neighbours. Indonesia’s Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs said on Monday that national authorities remained fully capable of putting out the fires on their own, CNA reported.

content: Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung received a share of the profits her ex-husband made from investing in luxury watches, the model’s murder trial has heard. Chan Leong-hang, an employee of Aristo Watch & Jewellery in Tsim Sha Tsui, said on Thursday that Alex Kwong Kong-chi sold upmarket timepieces to the shop and asked that the shop transfer part of the proceeds to Choi via bank transfer. Chan said the company transferred HK$6 million (US$764,580) to Choi’s bank account after her ex-husband sold a watch to the shop in October 2021. He also recalled Kwong selling a Richard Mille watch worth HK$10.5 million and asking for part of the profit to go to his former partner. The witness described Kwong as a “smart consumer” who would compare prices at different shops, prompting Chan’s company to negotiate a lower price with him to close the deal. Kwong, 31, his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial for allegedly murdering the 28-year-old influencer in February 2023, following a bitter family dispute over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat in Ho Man Tin. The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, is also contesting a charge of preventing the burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to the charge before the trial began last month. Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, previously alleged that the Kwong family had been living off her family’s wealth in the lead-up to her daughter’s killing. She also called her former son-in-law a jobless “brute” who lied in court about financially supporting her over the years. Alex Kwong’s legal counsel, Andrew Raffell, sought to prove that his client had earned substantial sums by reselling watches to high-end customers in mainland China and that he had given part of the profits to his ex-wife. During cross-examination on Thursday, Chan confirmed that Alex Kwong had introduced “clients” on numerous occasions, although he did not realise at the time that the defendant was making a business out of the purchases. Raffell suggested that Alex Kwong had once referred friends of his former mother-in-law to the shop to buy watches, but Chan said he had never heard anything like that before. The defence lawyer also highlighted an incident in around 2020 and 2021 in which Alex Kwong asked the watch company to prepare a cheque using his remaining credit at the shop and give it to his father to settle outstanding management fees for the Kadooria flat. Chan said he understood the encounter had been an unhappy one, as Kwong Kau allegedly snatched the cheque from the shop’s workers while they were still confirming that he was indeed Alex Kwong’s father. Choi’s alleged murder came to light after parts of her dismembered remains were discovered at a 600 square foot rental flat on the ground floor of a three-storey house in Tai Po’s Lung Mei village on February 24, 2023. Hui Yan-yan, the landlady at the time, said Kwong Kau agreed to rent the property for HK$10,000 a month on February 2 and signed the tenancy agreement at the premises three days later. Asked why he wanted to rent the flat, Kwong Kau allegedly told Hui that he wanted a place to spend time with his wife after retiring. He also claimed that his son, daughter-in-law and their children were returning from Australia and would be living at his supposed residence in Mong Kok, the court heard. “He said that because he and his wife were old, they could rent somewhere further away and retire there. He said the environment here was comfortable,” Hui told the court. She also noted that Kwong Kau had specifically asked whether there were surveillance cameras installed inside the rental flat on the day he signed the agreement. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: Safety of Australian women MPs in focus after man with nunchucks threatens staff

content: A man has been charged with threatening an Australian lawmaker’s staff with nunchucks, police said on Thursday, days after another legislator was critically injured when a man repeatedly hit her with a car. The incidents are heightening concerns about female politicians’ safety and raising concerns about security in a country where lawmakers are highly accessible to the public. Police say that a 56-year-old man entered Western Australian state government minister Hannah Beazley’s electorate office in suburban Perth on Wednesday, brandishing nunchucks and making verbal threats. Beazley was not in the office at the time. Nunchucks are a weapon used in martial arts consisting of two sticks or rods connected by a rope or chain. The man was detained and charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear and with threatening to perform an unlawful act. He spent the night in police custody and would appear in a Perth court later on Thursday, police said. There was no allegation the man’s behaviour was connected to the driver who hit federal lawmaker Helen Haines with his car in the east coast state of Victoria on Monday. Haines’ alleged attacker, Brendan Nugent, appeared in a court on Wednesday charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official. He did not enter pleas and remains in custody. Police are still searching for a motive. Haines, a 65-year-old independent lawmaker, remained in critical condition on Thursday in a Melbourne hospital where surgeons had amputated both her legs, a health department statement said. Safety fears Both the Haines and Beazley incidents have raised concerns about the safety of female politicians, who account for a growing proportion of lawmakers in Australian parliaments. Just under 50 per cent of federal lawmakers and a majority of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s cabinet are women. Australian lawmakers are some of the most accessible in the world and political violence has traditionally been rare. But there are fears that increasingly toxic public debate driven by social media creates additional risks for elected women. Albanese said the fact that the threat to Beazley came so soon after the alleged attack on Haines was “just heartbreaking”. Beazley is the daughter of Albanese’s former federal colleague, Kim Beazley. “We can have debate and disagreement, but do it in a way without descending into the sort of violence that we have seen in too many parts of the world,” Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corporation. “It’s certainly not who we are as Australians.” Albanese attended an online security briefing this week for women lawmakers in his centre-left Labor Party. Security agencies addressed misogynistic threats directed at them. Male and female federal lawmakers agree that women are facing the worst of the online abuse. “Of course people are concerned. They’re anxious,” Albanese said. “There has been a normalisation of behaviour that can be very aggressive in a way that wasn’t happening a couple of decades ago.” Beazley said she was in the state parliament when the man entered her electorate office demanding to see her. She said two members of her staff had been “rattled”, but had remained safe behind a security screen. “We don’t know his motives at all,” she told reporters on Wednesday. Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who is only the second woman to ever serve as the British monarch’s representative in Australia, said that she was abused on social media for speaking at a press conference on Wednesday alongside Haines’ husband, Phil Haines. “Like any woman who has stepped up into any position across any part of our society, there is a unique and pernicious form of attack that comes our way,” Mostyn told ABC. “Women across the country know that there are certain things that are reserved for women in that attack that go to our gender and they are often vicious and just despicable.”

title: Hong Kong watchdog joins global agencies to warn of web scripting hack risks
description: A Hong Kong information security watchdog issued an “extremely high risk” warning on Thursday morning over two critical flaws in a widely used web programming language that could allow hackers to execute code remotely and take control of servers. The warning followed similar alerts from governments and cybersecurity agencies overseas, which urged website operators to install updates to fix the vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language. content: A Hong Kong information security watchdog issued an “extremely high risk” warning on Thursday morning over two critical flaws in a widely used web programming language that could allow hackers to execute code remotely and take control of servers. The warning followed similar alerts from governments and cybersecurity agencies overseas, which urged website operators to install updates to fix the vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language. The Hong Kong Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre said a remote attacker could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code on a targeted system. The government-funded group advised organisations to install the patches immediately. “If immediate patching is not feasible, organisations should consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until the security fixes are applied and verified,” the centre said. The South China Morning Post has contacted the Hong Kong government’s Digital Policy Office to ask whether authorities have taken corresponding action. OpenAI said in a post on social media on Wednesday that its artificial intelligence models had helped researchers discover the PHP flaws. The PHP development team urged users to update the programming language immediately to fix the two critical vulnerabilities, each given a severity rating of 9.2 out of 10. Francis Fong Po-kiu, honorary president of the Hong Kong Information Technology Federation, said WordPress, the world’s most widely used content management system, relied heavily on PHP, as did various e-commerce and enterprise portals. He said the flaws could affect popular websites used by the public. Fong explained that when a user clicked a button, filled in a form or logged into an account, PHP running on the server processed the data, connected to databases and generated webpage content in real time. He urged website administrators to install the patches immediately. “If exploited, hackers can gain direct control of servers, posing a severe security threat to both enterprise and personal websites,” he said. The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on Wednesday strongly urged organisations to address the problem immediately, noting that while it “has not observed exploitation of these vulnerabilities as of the time of publication, they pose a risk to organisations if left unpatched”. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Cyber Division also urged organisations to install the updates immediately. “If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommended that organisations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated,” it said. Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre also recommended updating to the latest version of PHP and continuing to monitor for updates. The Cybersecurity Service for the Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies – the cybersecurity service for the European Union – also “strongly recommended” an update. Finland temporarily shut down the government’s public web services, while the Netherlands’ cybersecurity agency said it was taking its own website offline because of the vulnerabilities, according to the BBC.

content: Australia and East Timor signed a defence deal on Thursday to boost cyber and maritime security as Canberra seeks to curb China’s influence among its island neighbours. Australia is East Timor’s largest defence and security partner and the agreement will significantly increase defence exercises, Defence Minister Richard Marles told reporters. “This is a time to double down on friendship, to double down on family,” he said in East Timor’s capital Dili. Australia will provide A$62 million (US$44 million) for cybersecurity, maritime security, infrastructure, disaster relief and training, under a defence framework signed on Thursday by Marles and East Timor’s Prime Minister Xanana Gusmao, according to a statement from Canberra. East Timor, around 700km (440 miles) northwest of Australia, gained independence from Indonesia in 2002. Australia has expressed concerns over the rapid expansion of China’s navy and the presence of Chinese police in several Pacific Island countries. As part of Thursday’s agreement, Australia will also give East Timor three additional police vessels, according to Marles. Gusmao told reporters the agreement would help East Timor fight organised crime and illegal fishing. Euan Graham, an expert associate with the Australian National Security College, said Canberra was facing difficulty “matching its recent cut-through in the Pacific” in Southeast Asia. East Timor is situated close to the northern Australian city of Darwin, which hosts a rotating force of US Marines, and is “a key location for the security of Australia’s northern approaches”, according to Graham. “It is vital for Canberra to ensure that Dili, at very least, does not provide strategic access to China,” he said. China’s defence ministry said in August its Defence Minister, Dong Jun, had met East Timor’s leaders in Dili and offered to “take military-to-military relations to a new level”. East Timor’s Foreign Minister Bendito dos Santos Freitas visited Moscow for talks this month. Australia has recently struck a series of defence and economic agreements with Pacific Islands including Vanuatu, Fiji and Papua New Guinea, designed to limit China’s security role. The A$500 million Vanuatu agreement states no foreign military base or infrastructure can be built there and Australia is the archipelago’s main policing partner. But Vanuatu’s police minister rejected on Wednesday that the deal would require Chinese police to be “phased out”, and Vanuatu’s police force published images on social media of Chinese police training officers to use surveillance drones.

title: Falling child vaccination rates raise concern as Hong Kong flu deaths rise
description: A senior Hong Kong health official has warned of a higher risk of influenza infection as vaccination rates fall and the city’s summer flu season stretches on, following the death of a second unvaccinated child from the virus. Centre for Health Protection controller Edwin Tsui Lok-kin issued the warning as Hong Kong’s current flu season, which began in June, showed no sign of easing. He said authorities were monitoring possible changes in how the virus spreads after two consecutive summer flu...
content: A senior Hong Kong health official has warned of a higher risk of influenza infection as vaccination rates fall and the city’s summer flu season stretches on, following the death of a second unvaccinated child from the virus. Centre for Health Protection controller Edwin Tsui Lok-kin issued the warning as Hong Kong’s current flu season, which began in June, showed no sign of easing. He said authorities were monitoring possible changes in how the virus spreads after two consecutive summer flu seasons. “Since September 17, we have administered more than 900,000 doses of the flu vaccine. Compared with the same period last year, when we had given one million doses, there has been a slight decrease of about 10 per cent,” Tsui said. “Last year, the flu season was pretty much over by week 18. We are now at about week 16, with no sign of it waning. So I expect this year’s season to be longer than last year’s,” he said, attributing the change to a shift in the virus strain. Tsui said he was particularly concerned about lower vaccination rates among children attending nursery, kindergarten or primary school, and among those aged two to 11. Their vaccination rate is about five percentage points lower than last year’s. “The rate among elderly people living at home has fallen by about 1.8 percentage points, while the rate among those living in care homes has risen by three percentage points,” he said. Hong Kong’s flu seasons were traditionally concentrated in winter, and summer outbreaks occurred in only about half of the past 10 years. But the city has now experienced summer flu seasons for two consecutive years. “This change in the flu virus’s transmission patterns after the Covid-19 pandemic is something we need to examine with more scientific data,” Tsui said. On Tuesday, a 12-year-old unvaccinated girl became the second child to die from influenza A in Hong Kong during the current flu season. She first developed a fever, cough, and diarrhoea on Saturday, followed by vomiting. She was subsequently admitted to a paediatric intensive care unit after suffering a cardiac arrest, from which she was resuscitated. The girl, who had underlying health conditions, was diagnosed with influenza A infection complicated by septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure. In August, a seven-year-old boy who had previously been in good health also died. He had received the 2025-26 seasonal influenza vaccine, and his respiratory specimen tested positive for influenza A(H3). His clinical diagnosis was influenza A infection complicated by shock and encephalopathy.

title: China moves to set global standards for brain-computer interface technology
description: China has taken a major step in spearheading the standardisation of brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies, as it now chairs the secretariat of a subcommittee jointly overseen by two key international organisations and lists the technology applications as a national development priority. content: China has taken a major step in spearheading the standardisation of brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies, as it now chairs the secretariat of a subcommittee jointly overseen by two key international organisations and lists the technology applications as a national development priority. The China-led subcommittee, known as ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 43, was set to formulate global standards regarding the communication and interaction between brains and computers that are applicable across application areas, according to abstracts on both websites of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC). The committee, chaired by Yu Yuntao, a technical director with the China Electronics Standardization Institute, has already published several standards, including the BCI vocabulary, data format for non-invasive brain information collection, reference architecture and use cases. “The [Chinese] government is betting on this industry, among others, as one that has the potential to become the next EV sector,” said Xiaomeng Lu, director of geo-technology at Eurasia Group. ISO is “the de facto global industry standard with major commercial implications”, according to Lu. This was “a very meaningful step for Chinese and global BCI companies”. BCI is an emerging technology that translates neural signals into commands for external computers, allowing humans to steer technology using thoughts. BCI is one of six industries of the future under China’s 15th five-year plan and this year was included for the first time in the government work report delivered to the National People’s Congress. On Wednesday, two of the highest policy authorities in China – the General Office of the Central Committee of the Communist Party and the General Office of the State Council – released a joint call to accelerate the industrialisation and commercialisation of BCI as a key frontier technology. “China’s BCI sector needs access to overseas markets, especially for its most advanced products, approved invasive and non-invasive brain devices,” said Altynay Junusova, an analyst at the Berlin-based think tank MERICS. “Chinese policymakers want to help the industry to scale up, ahead of the US and Europe,” Junusova said, adding that China’s leadership on the ISO document would help it “secure the terms on which everyone else’s BCIs are built.” Lu said the Chinese government, with a few exceptions, mirrored Elon Musk’s research road map in its own technology investment plan. “A group of Chinese companies are fast followers,” Lu said. Musk co-founded the leading BCI company Neuralink. “My theory is that the Chinese government views Elon Musk as a tech visionary,” Lu said. In July of this year, Shanghai-based Neuracle Medical Technology completed the world’s first commercial surgery using BCI. “Washington has not paid a lot of attention to this industry yet,” Lu said. “Their attention is concentrated on more visible and mature technologies such as semiconductors and AI models.” A US delegation also took part in the drafting of the ISO’s BCI standards document. China’s BCI market was projected to be valued at 6.14 billion yuan (US$919.88 million) by 2028, with a compound annual growth rate of 17.7 per cent from 2024 to 2028, according to the China Centre for Information Industry Development.

title: Haze forces Malaysian fitness groups to swap outdoor runs for shopping mall laps

content: Runners in Malaysia are swapping their usual routes through parks and city streets for laps around shopping malls, commandeering air-conditioned corridors to keep up their training as a stubborn blanket of haze makes exercising outdoors increasingly hazardous. The switch comes as smoke from forest and peatland fires continues to foul the air across parts of Southeast Asia, with Malaysia’s capital Kuala Lumpur and its surrounding districts among the hardest-hit areas. By 9am on Thursday, 15 of Malaysia’s 68 air quality monitoring stations were recording unhealthy pollution levels. Readings reached 163 in Negeri Sembilan, while parts of Kuala Lumpur and neighbouring Selangor remained above 150, according to data from the Department of Environment. At Atria Shopping Gallery in Petaling Jaya, just outside Kuala Lumpur, dozens of runners spent Wednesday evening weaving through the mall’s upper-floor corridors, clocking up laps past shops and escalators in a workout that would ordinarily have taken place on the streets. The free event, organised by fitness studio The Active Chimp with the mall’s approval, attracted nearly 200 registrations – far exceeding the 50 to 60 participants organisers had anticipated. “We were actually expecting the first run to attract around 50 to 60 people, but it was actually overwhelming,” The Active Chimp founder Keith Tan said. Organisers eventually limited participants to around 150, with running coaches setting the pace along a roughly 500-metre circuit and helping participants avoid shoppers. Tan, 40, came up with the idea after struggling to find somewhere to run without exposing himself to the haze. He approached the mall’s management after noticing how much space was available during quieter hours. “I was watching, I was teaching classes, and I was like, ‘Oh, the mall’s so empty,’” he recalled. “I was wondering, can we actually run inside the mall when there’s not so many people?” He pitched the idea to management, arguing that runners needed somewhere to train while the air outside remained hazardous. “It’s hazy and no one can run outside,” he said. The mall agreed, moving benches to widen the route and providing security personnel to help manage foot traffic. Tan’s coaches also tested the circuit at different times of the day before launching the first organised run. The fitness entrepreneur, who has worked in the industry for more than a decade, wants the runs to become a regular fixture if the arrangement proves manageable. “I know the treadmill is a choice, but running on a track is different,” he said. “Personally, it’s my own pain because I wanted to run and I had nowhere to go.” Retail ‘run’ therapy Fitness groups across the Klang Valley, which includes Kuala Lumpur and its surrounding cities, have also begun organising indoor mall runs as the haze disrupts outdoor training. At The Starhill, an upscale shopping centre in Kuala Lumpur’s bustling Bukit Bintang district, the Worst Pace Run Club held its first indoor mall run on Wednesday, promoting the event on social media with a cheeky declaration: “The haze can have the streets, we’ll take the mall!” Other events advertised this week include a mall run at United Point in Kepong, a session at Sunway Square Mall on Saturday and a 3km (1.9-mile) indoor run at 1 Utama on Sunday, according to running community directory runclubs.my. These makeshift running tracks follow a similar experiment across the border in Singapore, where the worst haze since 2015 has disrupted outdoor exercise and forced the cancellation of sporting events, including the Great Eastern Women’s Run and the Singapore Half Marathon. Last Saturday, about 15 runners from X-Run Singapore took over sections of Marina Square shopping centre before opening hours, covering distances of between 9km and 21km with permission from management. Back in Malaysia, Amirul Hakim, 32, was among those who signed up for the Atria run after missing his usual outdoor routine. “We haven’t been able to run like we used to for a long time,” he said, explaining that the opportunity to try something new encouraged him to join. “It won’t be the same as running outside because the surface can be slippery … but at least we can have fun and work up a sweat.” With his office nearby, Amirul said he would consider joining future sessions if the mall allowed them regularly. No clear skies Malaysia’s Ministry of Health has urged the public to avoid outdoor exercise when the air pollutant index exceeds 100, warning that fine particles in the haze can penetrate the respiratory system and pose serious health risks. It has recommended N95 masks for those who must venture outside. The prolonged pollution has also disrupted school activities, with education authorities suspending outdoor sports in affected areas and ordering temporary closures when air quality deteriorates. Under government guidelines, educational institutions must close when the API exceeds 200. The transboundary haze remains a perennial diplomatic headache in Southeast Asia, where smoke from forest and land-clearing fires regularly drifts across national borders. Malaysia and Indonesia were exploring closer cooperation on fire prevention and hotspot monitoring, Deputy Minister of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Syed Ibrahim Syed Noh told parliament on Wednesday. “Malaysia and Indonesia will continue to work together through the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution,” he said, outlining plans to strengthen regional prevention and monitoring efforts. For 50-year-old Steven Ho, who works in Kuala Lumpur’s KL Sentral district, completing an estimated 5km around Atria on Wednesday proved surprisingly challenging due to the air conditioning. “When we run outside, our body temperature will go up because it’s outside. But here it’s a bit cold,” he said. “I probably need a few more laps to warm up.” Still, Ho sees great potential in the concept. “Malls that are a bit empty, or floors that are a bit more empty, could open up space for people to run, especially during the haze,” he said. The coming monsoon season offered another reason to keep the corridors open, Ho added, given how frequently heavy downpours interrupt outdoor running towards the end of the year. Organiser Tan is already looking beyond the two sessions at Atria, noting that around 180 people had signed up for the next event by the time he spoke to This Week in Asia. But turning shopping centres into regular running venues will require more than just enthusiastic participants – especially when regular shoppers are going about their day. “We cannot just accommodate the runners and neglect the shoppers. We have to find a balance,” Tan said. “If safety, traffic and all the benefits can be secured, hopefully it gives the confidence for the mall to actually allow people to run here.”

title: What is the ‘cadaver skin jab’ beauty trend and does it really work?
description: A growing interest among Hong Kong women in an anti-ageing injection containing human tissue has prompted a recent crackdown by health authorities, as the product, widely known in Chinese as the “cadaver skin jab”, has not been registered for use in the city. The South China Morning Post examines why the injection has become a new beauty trend, what it claims to do and the risks involved. 1. What is a ‘cadaver skin jab’? The “cadaver skin jab” refers to Elravie Re2O, a cadaver-derived skin...
content: A growing interest among Hong Kong women in an anti-ageing injection containing human tissue has prompted a recent crackdown by health authorities, as the product, widely known in Chinese as the “cadaver skin jab”, has not been registered for use in the city. The South China Morning Post examines why the injection has become a new beauty trend, what it claims to do and the risks involved. 1. What is a ‘cadaver skin jab’? The “cadaver skin jab” refers to Elravie Re2O, a cadaver-derived skin injection marketed as an anti-ageing skin booster. It is commonly known by that Chinese nickname on social media. Developed by South Korean biotech company L&C Bio and distributed by Humedix, the product was launched in November 2024. According to the distributor, it contains human acellular dermal matrix – material derived from processed human tissue obtained from deceased donors through United States tissue banks. The company claims the product improves skin condition by supplying structural proteins such as collagen and elastin. It describes the treatment as a form of “structural replenishment” for aged or damaged skin, rather than a traditional booster that provides only temporary stimulation. 2. Why is it under scrutiny? Over the past week, Hong Kong health authorities seized 20 vials of Elravie Re2O – said to contain human tissue – during raids on four premises offering beauty services. In a joint operation with police, a 38-year-old woman was arrested on suspicion of unlawful commercial dealing in human organs, as well as unlawful possession of Part 1 poisons and unregistered pharmaceutical products. Dr Fung Ying, controller for regulatory affairs at the Department of Health, said the injection was classified as a “regulated product” under the Human Organ Transplant Ordinance and as a “pharmaceutical product” under the Pharmacy and Poisons Ordinance. She said authorities had received an application for an exemption for the regulated product, but none had been granted. No application had been received to register the injection as a pharmaceutical product. Fung warned that the product lacked clinical safety data and posed potential public health risks. 3. Where are people getting the treatment? The Department of Health seized the 20 vials from beauty-service premises in Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui. It is not yet known whether any customers received the injections locally. However, an SCMP check found that the injection is available and approved for use in Singapore, Taiwan and South Korea. Some beauty clinics market it in Chinese, comparing it with Rejuran, another popular skin-booster injection. Some influencers have shared their experiences of receiving the injection on social media and praised its skin-enhancing effects, although it is unclear whether those endorsements were sponsored by clinics. Some medical professionals have also reported treating patients who suffered severe skin complications after the injections. 4. What do experts say? Dr Peter Pang Chi-wang, a specialist in plastic surgery, warned that products containing human tissue could carry unknown pathogens. He said that even if a product was claimed to have had all its cells removed, that did not mean it was free of bacteria, stressing that its clinical safety had yet to be proven. Pang added that it remained uncertain whether the product worked, noting that records showed injections of medical substances or saline solution, as well as microneedling, could also improve skin condition. Nelson Ip Sai-hung, founding chairman of the Federation of Beauty Industry, said there had been more discussion about the use of Re2O recently, but few operators were offering it because it was difficult to source. He urged people to be cautious when trying new beauty treatments. “It is not a bad thing to observe a bit. There must be a reason why the product has not yet been registered in Hong Kong,” Ip said.

title: Malaysia’s TuJu app struggles after Anwar suggests switching from Waze
description: Malaysia’s highway authority is working to resolve technical disruptions affecting its TuJu navigation application following a sharp increase in users. In a statement on Thursday, the Lembaga Lebuhraya Malaysia (LLM) said the matter was being resolved together with the application provider Prosignal Consortium. content: Malaysia’s highway authority is working to resolve technical disruptions affecting its TuJu navigation application following a sharp increase in users. In a statement on Thursday, the Lembaga Lebuhraya Malaysia (LLM) said the matter was being resolved together with the application provider Prosignal Consortium. LLM said the surge in users came after Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim suggested that the public consider using a locally developed navigation application instead of Waze. “We apologise for the inconvenience caused, and efforts are under way to identify the cause of the disruptions, restore system stability and improve the application’s capacity to accommodate more users,” the statement added. LLM said feedback on navigation functions, route information accuracy and the overall user experience was also being taken into account. “Improvements will continue to be made to ensure that TuJu provides a more stable, accurate and user-friendly service,” it added. TuJu, introduced on November 26 last year, is a highway navigation application developed by Prosignal in collaboration with LLM. Besides travel information, the application provides updates on traffic conditions, highway facilities and emergency help to support motorists during their journeys. LLM said efforts to strengthen the application would go beyond system stability to include improvements to navigation functions, information accuracy and its ability to meet users’ needs. It added that, in line with the government’s focus on strengthening cybersecurity and national digital sovereignty, LLM would continue to work with the Works Ministry, the National Cyber Security Agency and relevant parties to strengthen the local navigation ecosystem. “This would include addressing security and data governance concerns. We thank the public for their patience and feedback, and we assure users that the issues raised would be taken seriously,” it said. “Further updates on the recovery and improvement efforts would be shared through LLM’s and TuJu’s official channels.” Users can submit complaints or feedback about the application via email to feedback@prosignalconsortium.my. The government is encouraging the public to use TuJu as an alternative for road navigation needs. Anwar had proposed the alternative due to security risks concerning information and data on citizens’ movements, given that Waze is subject to the laws of the Israeli government. This article was first published by The Star

title: Russia and Ukraine trade major attacks as Trump touts progress

content: Russia and Ukraine traded attacks overnight, with seven killed on the Ukrainian side, authorities said on Thursday, shortly after US President Donald Trump’s envoy held talks with Russian leader Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg. Trump sought to strike an optimistic tone after US envoy Steve Witkoff’s meeting with Putin on Wednesday, saying negotiators were “maybe now the closest we’ve been” to ending the war. The Kremlin indicated it was “in principle” open to the resumption of trilateral talks involving the two sides and the United States. But attacks did not let up in the wake of the visit. Moscow’s mayor Sergei Sobyanin said two people had been wounded in huge barrages of 630 drones fired towards the region, 163 of which were approaching the Russian capital. The governor of nearby Tula region said Russian air defences had destroyed 70 drones. Another man was wounded in the Lipetsk region, its governor said. In Ukraine, the attacks killed one man in Sumy and a woman in Kharkiv, both in the northeast, as well as three people in southeastern Zaporizhzhia and two in the eastern region of Donetsk, authorities said. Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko said on social media strikes had wounded 15 people in the Ukrainian capital. He said the strikes had damaged metro infrastructure at the Pivdenny Bridge, which officials said had restricted traffic between parts of the city. Ukraine’s air force posted a warning in the early hours of “more ballistic missiles towards Kyiv” and instructed residents to stay in shelters. Witkoff had flown to Russia from a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, which was aimed at smoothing over a bitter rift between Trump and the Ukrainian leader. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner also took part in the talks with Putin remotely. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters that Russia was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral talks in mid-November – after the US midterm elections – and that the Kremlin wanted them to focus on post-war security. Zelensky said Ukraine also backed resuming trilateral talks. Ushakov said Witkoff briefed Putin on “some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv” from the Oslo meeting, but that “there wasn’t really much substance in them”. A summit between Putin, Trump and China’s Xi Jinping was also being prepared in Shenzhen for next month, Ushakov said, calling it “the first such meeting in history”. During their three-hour meeting, Witkoff praised Putin for granting Trump’s request to free US citizen Stephen Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had been detained for fighting for Ukraine – charges he denied. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian – you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff said. Witkoff said on social media the talks with Putin were “constructive” but that “there is still important work left to do”. Discussions would continue between the United States, Ukraine and Russia at the technical level, he added. Trump returned to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours – but more than a year of US-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough. In recent days, a frustrated Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war. Trump also delayed the imposition of sanctions on Russia’s war machine – a decision he defended on Wednesday as necessary to secure Hubbard’s release. “If you would’ve put those sanctions on … you could forget about him. You’d never see him again,” Trump told reporters at the White House. Witkoff told Putin Washington was “grateful” for the diesel deal, which sparked outrage in Kyiv and across Europe. The war, Europe’s worst since World War II, has killed tens of thousands of people since Russia’s February 2022 invasion. Putin has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.

title: What border warnings by Kim Jong-un’s sister reveal about inter-Korean tensions
description: The two Koreas appear to be coming closer to an armed clash along their poorly marked military dividing line after a series of increasingly hostile warnings from the North, observers say. Back-to-back statements on Wednesday and Thursday by Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, appear aimed at building a case for blaming Seoul for any future exchange of fire, they say. “The two sides appear to be edging closer to accidental armed clashes,” said Oh Gyeong-seob, a...
content: The two Koreas appear to be coming closer to an armed clash along their poorly marked military dividing line after a series of increasingly hostile warnings from the North, observers say. Back-to-back statements on Wednesday and Thursday by Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, appear aimed at building a case for blaming Seoul for any future exchange of fire, they say. “The two sides appear to be edging closer to accidental armed clashes,” said Oh Gyeong-seob, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification. “The South Korean military has no other alternative but to respond with warning shots as North Korean troops keep intruding across the military demarcation line, while the North vows to retaliate strongly.” Seoul says North Korean troops, accelerating efforts to fortify the border ahead of winter, have been encroaching south of the line in some areas. Under existing rules of engagement, South Korean troops first issue loudspeaker warnings when North Korean soldiers appear to be crossing the military line. If they step across, South Korean forces fire warning shots to compel them to return to the North. “Once the North sets up its new walls even a few metres south of the MDL, there would be no means to roll it back. That’s why the South has to respond sternly,” Oh said. In a statement on Wednesday, Kim warned that the North Korean military would “mercilessly” retaliate if South Korean troops threatened the safety of its personnel. “If the enemy’s provocative warning shots go beyond warnings and threaten the actual security of our territory and the safety of our servicemen, our border troops will mercilessly deal with the armed thugs who have lost their reason,” Kim was quoted as saying by North Korea’s official Korean Central News Agency. Kim visited several frontline fortification sites early on Tuesday. Hours after the visit, she said the border had been “clearly blocked off and is becoming increasingly fortified”. She said her brother had stressed that the border should become a permanent divider and that sharing a border with what he termed the world’s “most despicable and vile enemy” was a “terrible tragedy”. Kim, who claimed that the South Korean military had issued 2,870 warning broadcasts and fired 201 warning shots between August 1 and October 17, accused South Korean troops of broadcasting warnings and firing warning shots at North Korean soldiers at “at least two places” on Tuesday. On Thursday, she issued another warning. “Should a ‘mistake’ – whether intentional or unintentional – occur, even for a fleeting moment, driven by a pathological bravado, those responsible must be prepared for the consequences,” she said. “Everything will be shattered, broken, and brought to ruin,” Loudspeaker politics Kim’s statements also revealed a shift in the timing of the North’s planned loudspeaker operations – which she has called “the most justifiable measure and an appropriate response”. On Wednesday, she said Pyongyang would activate broadcasts along the entire border by the end of the month. But on Thursday, she appeared to soften the immediate threat, saying the loudspeakers intended would be placed in a state of operational readiness within the coming days. North Korea’s propaganda loudspeakers fell silent after Seoul stopped its own broadcasts in 2024. A defining feature of Kim’s recent statements was her repeated accusations that Seoul was engaging in hostile and provocative acts, said Yang Moo-jin, a distinguished professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul. “This repetition may amount to an indirect admission that South Korean warning broadcasts and warning shots are unsettling North Korean troops and making it difficult for them to carry out border fortification work smoothly,” Yang said. This interpretation is supported by her recent inspection of the frontline construction sites, accompanied by Marshal Pak Jong-chon, one of North Korea’s highest-ranking military officials, according to Yang. During the visit, the two sought to reassure troops by arguing that completing the fortifications would eliminate the risk of military clashes along the frontier. “Our military is accomplishing a great undertaking despite the enemy’s persistent threats,” Kim said. “A peaceful and great history will soon begin.” The fact that the inspection was not reported in the Rodong Sinmun, the ruling Workers’ Party newspaper aimed at domestic audiences, might reflect an effort to prevent signs of anxiety among troops and their families from spreading, Yang said. Kim’s remarks that completing the fortifications would reduce the risk of inter-Korean military clashes further reinforced this interpretation, he added. “Pyongyang’s underlying message appears to be an indirect appeal for restraint from Seoul: if South Korea refrains from taking actions that North Korea regards as provocative, Pyongyang would have less need to maintain heightened response postures or prepare to reactivate its loudspeakers.” He called on the two Koreas to “sit down together and seek a practical solution through dialogue”. Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies, said the North Korean leader’s decision to send both his sister and his top military official to the fortification sites showed his determination to turn inter-Korean relations into a permanently hostile relationship. The move was also intended to reinforce the message that his orders must be carried out without fail and boost morale among the troops, Lim said. “Because Kim Jong-un personally issued the order, there appears to be no room to revise or adjust it, despite shortages of resources at the construction sites, difficult conditions or the risk of accidental clashes between the two Koreas,” he said. “If the warning shots continue, there is a chance that the North would use this as a pretext for reinforcing the front lines with additional weapons capable of using tactical nuclear weapons.” On Thursday, South ⁠Korea’s defence ministry urged the North to discuss measures to ease tension at the ⁠border and prevent ‌any accidental military clash.

title: Could China’s 100-channel single-photon detector enable broadband quantum internet?
description: Chinese scientists have developed a 100-channel single-photon detector, a breakthrough promising to pave the way for broadband quantum networks. State-of-the-art single-photon detectors – essential components underpinning photonic quantum technologies – could previously support a maximum of 32 detection channels for photon signals. Now, a newly developed interconnect scheme by a Shanghai-based team has broken this bottleneck, supporting more than 100 detection channels while maintaining accurate...
content: Chinese scientists have developed a 100-channel single-photon detector, a breakthrough promising to pave the way for broadband quantum networks. State-of-the-art single-photon detectors – essential components underpinning photonic quantum technologies – could previously support a maximum of 32 detection channels for photon signals. Now, a newly developed interconnect scheme by a Shanghai-based team has broken this bottleneck, supporting more than 100 detection channels while maintaining accurate and stable operation. “This work establishes a robust and scalable infrastructure, paving the way for large-scale quantum photonic applications,” the authors said in their paper. Achieved by researchers at the Shanghai Institute of Microsystem and Information Technology (SIMIT) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the breakthrough was published in the peer-reviewed journal Laser & Photonics Reviews in late September. Advances in photonic quantum technologies are accelerating their transition from laboratory demonstrations to practical applications in fields such as quantum computing, communications and metrology. The scaling of these systems urgently requires large-scale, parallel single-photon detection capabilities. Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors – high-end optoelectronic devices that use the extreme sensitivity of superconducting materials to detect individual photons – represent the most advanced technology available, boasting a detection efficiency approaching 100 per cent, the paper said. Owing to advantages including high detection efficiency, fast response speeds and high time resolution, they are widely used as core components in photonic quantum technologies, light detection and ranging (lidar), and single-photon imaging. However, scaling these systems up has long been a technical headache. Temperature poses a major challenge. Such detectors rely on cooling an ultra-thin superconducting nanowire film to a cryogenic environment approaching absolute zero. A cable is then used to connect it to a room-temperature environment to transmit the detected signals externally. Coaxial cables are traditionally used and relatively thick, and their metal materials are highly thermally conductive. Heat from the room-temperature end continuously conducts down the cables into the cryogenic chamber, a phenomenon known as thermal load. When the number of detection channels – independent, dedicated informational routes for receiving, processing and outputting photon signals – expands to dozens or hundreds, the massive bundle of cables introduces a heavy thermal load to the cryogenic environment. This dramatically increases the system’s size and cooling power consumption. Previously, standard set-ups could only support about 32 channels. To overcome this, the Shanghai team undertook a comprehensive redesign. They developed ultra-thin, specialised flexible materials known as “high-density multi-core microstrip lines”. The new material and structure are highly thermally insulating. According to the team, the heat leaked into the system is just one twenty-first of that generated by traditional thick cables. The researchers also achieved stability and miniaturisation for this large-scale parallel design through a series of architectural innovations. Under typical cooling power, the system comfortably supports more than 100 independent detection channels while maintaining long-term stability. During a continuous seven-day 24-hour test, the cryogenic platform’s temperature remained steadily below 2.1K – an extreme low temperature extraordinarily close to the physical limit of “absolute zero” (0K, or -273.15 degrees Celsius). Test results also showed that all channels achieved a system detection efficiency exceeding 80 per cent, coupled with incredibly low signal false alarm rates. To prove the platform’s abilities in real-world scenarios, the team built a five-user, fully connected quantum entanglement distribution network. The set-up formed 10 two-way quantum links among the five users, with each user receiving entangled photons via the newly developed channels. Test results revealed that the communication fidelity – how well a quantum channel preserves information – exceeded 90 per cent across all 10 links.

title: Tai Po fire inquiry submits final report, singles out 4 government bodies
description: Four government bodies have been singled out for accountability over Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades, according to a landmark inquiry report handed to city leader John Lee Ka-chiu, a source has said. The judge-led independent committee investigating the tragedy, which killed 168 people, said on Thursday that it had submitted the two-volume report to Lee. “With the evidence and materials received as the factual framework, the committee has completed its inquiry work on the matters set out...
content: Four government bodies have been singled out for accountability over Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades, according to a landmark inquiry report handed to city leader John Lee Ka-chiu, a source has said. The judge-led independent committee investigating the tragedy, which killed 168 people, said on Thursday that it had submitted the two-volume report to Lee. “With the evidence and materials received as the factual framework, the committee has completed its inquiry work on the matters set out in its terms of reference, and prepared the report accordingly,” the committee said. Lee thanked the committee members for their efforts, saying the panel had provided a comprehensive review of the fire and recommendations on large-scale building maintenance and renovation projects. “The government will make comprehensive reforms in areas including the supervision of building maintenance works, building management and the regulation of fire service installations,” he said. “We will carefully study the committee’s report, actively follow up on its recommendations and shortly announce plans for comprehensive reforms and pursuing accountability.” The government said it would seek legal advice on how best to publish the report at the “earliest possible juncture” without prejudicing the court proceedings. The source told the South China Morning Post that the report contained more than 10 chapters detailing the committee’s findings on the causes of the fire. The report singled out four government bodies for accountability – the Fire Services Department, the Buildings Department, the Labour Department and the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit – as well as some civil servants named during the hearings, the insider said. The source added that the report also included recommendations on construction material standards and measures to combat bid-rigging. The fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on November 26 last year killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000 residents. The blaze engulfed seven of the estate’s eight buildings and was Hong Kong’s deadliest fire since 1948. Lee ordered the establishment of the committee after the fire, tasking it with investigating the causes of the blaze and problems in the city’s building maintenance sector. Chaired by High Court judge David Lok Kai-hong, the panel held 30 public sessions from March, calling about 80 witnesses, including residents, workers, fire services installation contractors, firefighters, government officials and experts. The committee’s lead counsel, Victor Dawes, identified six “human failures” that led to the tragedy. These included the use of non-fire-retardant scaffolding mesh, the widespread installation of combustible polyfoam boards over windows, the deactivation of the fire alarm system and the suspension of the fire hosepipe reel system. The other failures involved temporary openings in emergency staircases, where fire-rated windows had been replaced with movable boards, and workers’ smoking habits. At the final hearing, the committee’s legal team presented a 627-page closing statement, blaming the “litany of failures” for the disaster. The statement said the government bore “unshirkable responsibility” for the tragedy and singled out the four government bodies. The SCMP previously reported that the government would address the report’s submission “shortly” and begin disciplinary proceedings. A redacted version of the report could be made public next week at the earliest.

title: Why Chinese pundits say France’s riots could reshape European politics

content: The social unrest roiling France is being closely watched for a possible spillover effect beyond the country’s borders that could reshape European politics, Chinese analysts said. The crisis is a major stress test for French politicians as they navigate deep-seated economic and societal tensions in the run-up to the country’s presidential election in April next year, according to the analysts. A critical question was whether the riots would subside quickly or escalate into prolonged instability, they added, with political parties across the spectrum exploiting the upheaval to advance their electoral gains. What happens next could also define the legacy of President Emmanuel Macron, who has led France for nearly a decade. According to Cui Hongjian, director of European Union studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, the friction between ordinary citizens and the government has reached a tipping point. “Even a minor local incident can trigger widespread rage,” Cui said. Weeks of student protests over deteriorating school conditions in France escalated into nationwide riots over the weekend as peaceful demonstrations led to looting and arson. The movement has since expanded into a broader unrest fuelled by public anger over spending cuts, rising living costs and deepening dissatisfaction with the government. Since the demonstrations began in France, more than 550,000 protesters have taken to the streets, resulting in over 2,000 arrests and at least two reported deaths. Macron faces intensifying political, economic and social turbulence as his second term nears its end. This week, he directed the government to convene students, educators, parliamentarians, labour organisations and business representatives to develop “concrete proposals” to resolve the crisis. Demonstrators will return to the streets this Saturday, prompting French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to put authorities on high alert. Lecornu promised a massive police presence and said new curfews would be imposed if necessary. The French government is struggling to contain public debt, which sits at nearly 120 per cent of GDP. Facing a persistent budget deficit projected to hit 5.4 per cent in 2026, market pressures have driven the 10-year government bond yield near 5 per cent. In addition, France’s fiscal crisis has increasingly squeezed domestic budgets for social programmes, forcing the government to cap general spending, freeze public wages and implement below-inflation increases for education. Song Luzheng, a France-based researcher affiliated with Fudan University’s China Institute, described the demonstrations as appearing on the surface “to be about stagnant economic growth, rising prices and declining purchasing power”. “But the cause is the declining competitiveness of France and Europe in the post-Cold War period due to high costs, low efficiency and weak innovation,” he said. Song argued that Europe was paying a devastating price externally for “geopolitical miscalculations”, ranging from the Russia-Ukraine conflict to Middle East tensions. He said globalisation, financialisation and automation had eroded Europe’s middle class, providing fertile ground for the emergence of political polarisation. The rapid escalation of the protests reflected how fiscal belt-tightening had created cascading effects across society, Song added. The turmoil has unfolded as France prepares for its presidential election in April next year, with China featuring in debates over economic sovereignty, market protection and geopolitical rivalry. In recent years, Europe’s trade deficit with China has widened and Chinese competitiveness in strategic sectors like electric vehicles has intensified. Macron’s centrist government faces a fractured parliament divided between Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally and Jean-Luc Melenchon’s hard-left coalition. Polling suggests National Rally holds a strong position ahead of the election. Le Pen has framed the unrest as a “profound crisis of trust and authority” under Macron, reiterating her emphasis on security and public order. Meanwhile, Melenchon and his party, La France Insoumise, have criticised the government’s crisis management and voiced strong support for the protesters. Both Cui and Song said French political parties were weaponising public anger to advance their electoral ambitions ahead of next year’s presidential vote. Far-right parties and figures had positioned themselves as champions of popular discontent, Cui said, exploiting flashpoint issues such as immigration and fiscal discipline to “intensify confrontation between the public and mainstream parties”. “Whether this unrest quickly subsides or turns into prolonged instability will shape France’s political landscape, which will inevitably influence broader European political change,” Cui said. Economic development and social justice must “be coordinated properly”, he added, noting these were challenges confronting many other countries. Indeed, rallies are being held in multiple countries, including Italy, Spain, Belgium and Portugal, although grievances differ depending on the location. As for what was happening in France, the stakes extended far beyond its borders, Song said. He warned of a starker situation if far-right forces were to triumph in both France and Germany, considered the European Union’s twin pillars. Song said the far-right forces’ shared agenda of opposing immigration and challenging EU integration would raise existential questions about the bloc’s future. “Europe’s future is likely to be filled with uncertainty and turbulence,” he added.

title: Malaysian teen arrested after live-streaming axe attack on teacher in class
