content: Malaysian police have arrested a 16-year-old student after he live-streamed an attack on a teacher with an axe at a private school in Kuching, the capital of Sarawak state. CCTV footage shows the teenager entering a classroom at around 7.50am on Wednesday, hitting the female teacher with an axe before leaving. He re-enters through a second door and swings the axe at students as they flee the room. As the teacher tries to intervene, he attempts to hack at her again but is subdued by two male students and has the axe taken away. Viral clips circulating online appear to show the teenager preparing for the attack inside a toilet with a mobile phone strapped to his head to live-stream the assault. Shaky footage believed to be from his live broadcast was briefly posted online before being taken down. Sarawak acting police commissioner Saifullizan Ishak said in a statement that officers received an emergency call at 8.03am telling Kuching district police that a student had brought firecrackers to school and injured a teacher with an axe. “The victim reportedly sustained a cut to her hand,” he said, as reported by local newspaper The Star. The student was arrested and is being held in the psychiatric ward of Sarawak General Hospital, according to the New Straits Times. Police are investigating the case under Section 324 of the Penal Code for voluntarily causing hurt with a dangerous weapon, as well as Section 6(1) of the Explosives Act 1957 regarding the possession of explosives. Tunku Putra-HELP School, where the attack occurred, told news portal Borneo Post that the teacher was recovering well and had suffered no critical injuries. The school said it immediately activated emergency response protocols, with staff acting quickly to intervene before emergency services arrived. “Students in the affected classroom managed to evacuate the area, and no other injuries were reported,” the school said, adding that the teenager was no longer enrolled at the school. “The matter remains under police investigation, and the school will continue to cooperate fully with the relevant authorities.” Three ancillary police officers have since been stationed at the school, where security checks will also be carried out on anyone entering the campus. Sarawak’s Education Department said it had contacted the school to offer psychosocial support for students, teachers and staff. The live-streamed attack has raised concerns across Southeast Asia, coming just two months after a similar incident left a student dead before the attacker died by suicide at a private school in the Philippines. During the August 18 attack in the Philippines, ninth-grader Mohammad Mael Jalani used a body camera to film himself shooting at teachers and students at Ateneo de Zamboanga University. “He entered and started indiscriminately firing, hitting a Grade 10 student on the fourth floor,” Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla told reporters. “He showed this on Facebook Live starting [from] when he was climbing the stairs, but there were only snippets.” Philippine authorities have stepped up online monitoring following another fatal school shooting in Banga, South Cotabato, last month. “The trend has changed. Incidents are now more on the internet, in cyberspace,” regional police director Allan Manibog said, according to the Philippine Inquirer. “We really need to strengthen our anti-cybercrime unit, not only in the [police] but also in other law enforcement agencies with the same mandate to look into this kind of problem.”

title: South Korean publishers raise alarm over bulk book buys linked to AI training
description: South Korean publishers are calling for stronger copyright protections and compensation as bulk book purchase requests suspected of being linked to artificial intelligence training raise concerns over intellectual property theft. Publishing groups are investigating suspicious orders and seeking a coordinated response. However, authors and publishers face a fundamental obstacle: they often cannot know for sure whether their books are being used to train AI systems. Kyobo Book Centre, a bookstore...
content: South Korean publishers are calling for stronger copyright protections and compensation as bulk book purchase requests suspected of being linked to artificial intelligence training raise concerns over intellectual property theft. Publishing groups are investigating suspicious orders and seeking a coordinated response. However, authors and publishers face a fundamental obstacle: they often cannot know for sure whether their books are being used to train AI systems. Kyobo Book Centre, a bookstore chain in South Korea, said on Wednesday that 10 overseas companies, including businesses in the United States and Britain, had approached it since early this year, each seeking only one copy of roughly 100,000 titles. “Many introduced themselves as book wholesalers,” a Kyobo representative was quoted as saying by Yonhap News Agency. The representative added that some denied an AI training purpose but identified data-related companies as the final recipients. The bookseller declined the request because it could not rule out the use of AI training. Yes24, another bookstore, also reportedly received an inquiry from a US distributor in late August about buying used books in bulk. The two sides held one meeting, but discussions stopped after the distributor ceased responding. Last week, the Literature Translation Institute of South Korea said it notified local authors after identifying 21 of their books on a compensation eligibility list associated with a US copyright settlement involving Anthropic. The AI company faces a class-action lawsuit by authors over allegations that it illegally downloaded copyrighted works for model training. In Japan, bulk purchases of second-hand books on philosophy, history and medicine have also fuelled suspicions of AI developers acquiring material for scanning. This week, the Korean Publishers Association has begun surveying bookstores, distributors, second-hand booksellers and publishers about potentially AI-related bulk orders. An association official said publishing organisations should form a joint body after the survey that will aim at establishing compensation arrangements and legislation. The Korean Publishers Society, meanwhile, issued an appeal demanding fair compensation when publications are used for AI training. Over 240 publishers and organisations, along with 702 authors, translators and illustrators and publishing professionals, joined the appeal as of Wednesday. Cho Han-na, head of publisher Prunsoop, said individual rights holders could not effectively confront large overseas technology companies alone. Publishers also argue they lack information about where AI companies obtain book content and how they use it. Park Jung-in, a copyright specialist and professor at Duksung Women’s University’s AI DynaInfo institute, said information gaps made it difficult to negotiate licensing terms or prove suspected infringement. “The core problem is a structure in which rights exist but are difficult to exercise in practice,” Park said, calling for procedures that would allow rights holders to check the sources and use of training data. This article was first published by The Korea Times

content: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] For many of Hong Kong’s high-flying executives and entrepreneurs alike, Central is already part of their working day. That proximity is part of the reason why OCBC has chosen the prime location of 35 Queen’s Road Central for its Central Branch. Here, clients can access wealth management services close to where they work or spend their time, in a cosy, private setting, while eligible Premier Private Clients can also access health and wellness support available in the same building. Fewer separate journeys can leave more time for work, family and life outside both. The opening also comes as the role of the brick-and-mortar bank branch is now very different from what it was even less than a decade ago. As everyday transactions can now be handled easily and securely through digital channels, the value of physical branches increasingly lies in conversations that benefit from professional advice, privacy and trust. For affluent clients, that can mean discussing investments, succession or other important financial needs face to face. OCBC’s Central Branch is taking an early lead in this direction, combining private advisory and meeting spaces with hospitality, lifestyle offerings, while selected wellness services are available to eligible Premier Private Clients. Reimagining the branch experience Held on September 29, the grand opening was attended by senior management, government and business leaders, partners and singer-songwriter Hanjin Tan. The occasion also marked the introduction of its new Premier Private Client Centre and the unveiling of a 3D LED display wall on the building façade. With the addition of its newly opened second and third floors, the expanded premises give OCBC considerably more room to rethink what eligible Premier Private clients can do during a branch visit. The approach also draws on OCBC’s Singapore origins and long presence in Hong Kong. That relationship is expressed in its latest campaign, “A Tale of Two Cities, For Your Wealth and Beyond”, which presents the two financial centres as complementary bases for serving clients whose business, wealth and families may increasingly cross borders. A façade inspired by the Hong Kong spirit A 3D LED display wall on the branch façade introduces an original cast of animated characters inspired by qualities associated with Hong Kong people. A cat shopkeeper represents innovation and entrepreneurial spirit, while the “Wong Choi” dog embodies trust and reliability, and the “Kong Jr.” monkey represents adaptability and an ability to recognise opportunities.Reflecting the spirit of the Twin Hubs, the characters give wealth planning ideas a more playful expression. Seeking opportunities, protecting accumulated wealth and preparing for the future are represented by personalities encountered on Queen’s Road Central instead of being confined to a banking brochure. There is an Instagrammable side to the campaign, too. Until October 31, visitors can photograph the display from a designated location outside Loke Yew Building at 50–52 Queen’s Road Central, with at least one of the cat, dog or monkey characters visible. After posting the photos on Facebook, Instagram, WeChat or Xiaohongshu with the specified campaign hashtags, visitors can redeem a limited-edition OCBC character blind box at the Central Branch, subject to terms and conditions. The installation gives passers-by a reason to interact with the branch even without a banking appointment, while the blind box turns the digital characters into something tangible. A Hong Kong story with Singapore roots The same two-city idea is explored through music in OCBC’s new advertising campaign. Hanjin Tan has a tale of two cities of his own. Born in Singapore before establishing his career in Hong Kong, the singer-songwriter and Hong Kong Film Award winner embodies the connection at the centre of the campaign. He appears in the TVC and also composed and wrote its theme song.Inspired by the spirit of Hong Kong, the campaign follows aspirations at different stages of life. Creating wealth may dominate earlier years; preserving it can become increasingly important as responsibilities grow; later, succession and preparing for the next generation can become a priority. Tan’s career has crossed the same two cities that OCBC uses for its regional proposition, allowing the campaign to talk about wealth through personal ambition, family and long-term planning instead of financial products alone. “The sense of being at home, the trust, and the peace of mind are what OCBC Premier Private Client offers,” said Tan, who is also an OCBC Premier Private Client, at the Central Branch grand opening. Embedding wellness into the wealth journey The new Premier Private Client Centre occupies the second and third floors of the Central Branch, with Singapore-inspired interiors, private meeting areas and a garden terrace. Through its “Navigating Your Wealth & Wellness Together” proposition, OCBC offers eligible Premier Private Clients access to personalised wealth management, wellness privileges, regional banking, lifestyle experiences and legacy planning services. Through a partnership with Fullerton Health, eligible Premier Private Clients can access personalised one-to-one nutritionist consultations at a dedicated consultation room conveniently located within the same building, as well as cross-border medical referral services and regional healthcare support, subject to applicable terms and conditions. [Premier Private Client Centre] Commenting on the grand opening of OCBC’s Central Branch and the soft launch of its new Premier Private Client service in Hong Kong, Mr. Wang Ke, Head of Greater China of OCBC and Chief Executive Officer of OCBC Hong Kong, said, “Hong Kong remains a key wealth management hub in Asia and an important market for OCBC. The opening of our Central Branch and the soft launch of Premier Private Client mark an important milestone in our growth journey in Hong Kong. Mr. Sunny Quek, Head of Group Consumer Financial Services, OCBC, added, “OCBC Premier Private Client is a key offering of our wealth franchise, supporting our customers’ increasingly sophisticated wealth needs. We are now extending the experience to Hong Kong as we strengthen our Singapore-Hong Kong twin wealth hubs to capture rising Asian wealth flows. Ms. Josephine Lee, Head of Consumer Financial Services, OCBC Hong Kong, said, “Hong Kong’s affluent customers are increasingly seeking trusted advice that extends beyond investment returns to address wealth preservation, liquidity management, retirement planning, healthcare needs and legacy planning for the next generation. By bringing together personalised wealth management, wellness support and regional connectivity, OCBC Premier Private Client aims to support customers’ financial, family, lifestyle and wellness aspirations through different stages of their wealth and life journeys. This reflects our purpose to enable people and communities to realise their aspirations.” OCBC’s new Premier Private Client Centre combines private advisory and meeting spaces with a health and wellness proposition for eligible Premier Private clients.Explore OCBC Premier Banking Open an OCBC Premier Banking account and enjoy welcome rewards, including a preferential time deposit rate of up to 3.5% p.a., and investment, insurance and securities rewards of up to HK$73,000. For more information about OCBC’s Premier Banking offers, click here. Investment involves risk. Promotion period valid till 31 October 2026. Terms and conditions apply. Customers must fulfil all relevant reward requirements. Specific offers are subject to limited quota on first come first served basis.

title: Could US advances in drone command give it an edge over the PLA in a Taiwan conflict?
description: From the cockpit of an F-22 fighter to an aircraft carrier sailing in the Pacific, the US military is showing new ways to command uncrewed aircraft over vast distances. The United States disclosed two tests this month as Washington seeks to outpace Beijing in a technology contest that could redefine air and naval power in the region. Illustrating US military advances and their potential significance for a Taiwan conflict, an F-22 pilot controlled an autonomous YFQ-44A combat drone during flight,...
content: From the cockpit of an F-22 fighter to an aircraft carrier sailing in the Pacific, the US military is showing new ways to command uncrewed aircraft over vast distances. The United States disclosed two tests this month as Washington seeks to outpace Beijing in a technology contest that could redefine air and naval power in the region. Illustrating US military advances and their potential significance for a Taiwan conflict, an F-22 pilot controlled an autonomous YFQ-44A combat drone during flight, while operators aboard USS Ronald Reagan aircraft carrier remotely operated an MQ-25A refuelling drone at a facility more than 3,380km (2,100 miles) away in Illinois. Experts say these technologies could help US forces track and strike targets while keeping manned platforms beyond the reach of enemy defences. They warn, however, that Chinese jamming and anti-satellite attacks could disrupt the communications links needed to command the drones. China is pursuing similar capabilities, having showcased its GJ-11 stealth attack drone flying in formation with crewed combat jets. The latest US tests highlighted ways to command uncrewed aircraft. In the F-22 demonstration, disclosed on October 16, the pilot assigned tasks to the YFQ-44A, while the drone’s software carried out manoeuvres without the pilot steering every movement. The trial also showed the US expanding the types of drones able to work alongside its fighters, a year after an F-22 pilot commanded a General Atomics MQ-20 Avenger drone. The navy’s test, meanwhile, focused on long-distance communications. On Monday, the service announced that operators aboard USS Ronald Reagan used satellites to command an MQ-25A at Boeing’s Illinois facility, which could eventually allow carriers to steer drones far beyond direct radio links. Other trials have involved a pilot in an F-35 on the ground issuing orders to an airborne drone, and a drone autonomously adjusting its mission plan as conditions changed. Together, the tests illustrate both the growing variety of ways of controlling drones and the increased freedom granted to these assets to carry out tasks. Analysts say these developments offer combat advantages. For Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, the value lies partly in protecting expensive aircraft and warships. Drones could serve as “scouts, shields or decoys”, carry “different sensors or targeting arrays” or take on enemy drones while crewed aircraft focused elsewhere, he said. That could force the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) to track more aircraft and distinguish real threats from decoys. Drones sent ahead might also locate Chinese warships or missile launchers without exposing US pilots, while others could draw fire from air defences, forcing Chinese forces to reveal radar positions or expend valuable missiles. Timothy Heath, director of the defence consultancy Perceptum, said a pilot near the fighting could also change a drone’s orders as the situation unfolded, allowing more “flexible and responsive actions”, from scouting ahead to potentially striking a target. Yet the type of drone matters, too. Peter Layton, a retired Royal Australian Air Force group captain, said sophisticated aircraft such as the YFQ-44A drone were intended to make crewed fighters “more survivable and lethal”, rather than overwhelm defences through sheer numbers. Layton, now a visiting fellow at the Griffith Asia Institute, said these drones could carry “additional missiles” for fighters to use against Chinese radars and air-defence weapons. Rather than briefly overwhelming those defences, destroying them could make later American attacks harder to stop. Whether these advances give Washington an edge will also depend on how far China has progressed. In November 2024, Chinese aircraft maker AVIC said its two-seat J-20S stealth fighter could team up with drones in combat. Details on how the PLA is applying these concepts, however, remain scarce. In November 2025, the PLA Air Force released footage of a GJ-11 stealth attack drone flying alongside a single-seat J-20 and a J-16D electronic warfare aircraft, without revealing whether either jet was commanding the drone. A June assessment by the US Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI) suggested the PLA Air Force’s 9th Aviation Brigade, also known as 9th Fighter Brigade, had helped validate J-20 tactics involving drones as part of efforts dating back to 2024. Bosack said this could mean China was further ahead in bringing the technology into service, although there was little public evidence of what its systems could actually do. Earlier research identified hurdles in those efforts. In an August 2025 study, Rand researcher Shanshan Mei found the PLA was still developing ways to incorporate crewed-uncrewed teaming into combat – a key challenge, as advanced aircraft and drones require seamless coordination in rapidly changing situations. A separate CASI study from April also highlighted related obstacles in operator training, multi-drone coordination and maintaining communications under enemy interference. Even if the PLA overcomes these challenges, it may have less need for fighter-drone teaming in a Taiwan conflict, experts say. Heath argued that the PLA “can project power” using missiles, aircraft and drones on the nearby mainland. Such concepts could instead prove more vital farther from the mainland China coast, including in the South China Sea. For both militaries, however, a fundamental weakness remains: the communications links carrying orders to drones. Layton said satellite-controlled drones – which could face Chinese “electronic warfare, cyberattacks or disruptions to satellite communications” – would be more exposed to interference than systems operating near fighters. Bosack said that made alternative command links essential and stressed the need for “redundant satellite capabilities” alongside reliable direct and longer-range communications. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Chinese public urged to stay confident in domestic innovation after Tesla flying-car debut

content: Tesla’s “flying” Roadster stunt has set social media alight worldwide, turning a car launch into a debate about technological innovation and China-US rivalry. At an event in Texas on October 15, Tesla unveiled its redesigned sports car, the Roadster, with stunts including a takeoff from a steep, curved ramp and a leap over parked cars. Pre-orders are open in China with a deposit of 332,000 yuan (US$50,000) for the street-legal, two-seat “Performance” package. The flying-car reveal quickly turned Tesla into a meme machine, inspiring viral user-generated content across social media. Chinese netizens created AI-generated memes showing the Roadster soaring off elevated highways or leaping over traffic jams and toll booths. Brands joined in, too. McDonald’s Taiwan playfully posted: “Drive-thru is not currently open to flying cars,” while Ikea shared an image of a toy car on a U-shaped track with the caption: “Safety tested. Suitable for kids.” The spectacle captivated the internet, but also divided public opinion. Critics dismissed it as a marketing gimmick to prop up stock prices, calling the Roadster’s flying capabilities “impractical” because nobody would dare sit inside. Supporters saw it as a display of ambition and execution. One commenter noted that coachmen mocked Carl Benz in much the same way when he invented the automobile. William Li, founder of Chinese EV maker Nio, also praised the reveal: “Incredible. We genuinely don’t have anything like this. Hats off to Tesla.” An op-ed in Zhejiang Daily called the launch a “wake-up call” for Chinese carmakers, warning against treating EVs as “fast-moving consumer goods” and sacrificing quality for rapid growth. Although the wording was later quietly edited, the piece fuelled concerns about whether China is losing its lead in the EV market. On October 21, People’s Daily urged readers to take a more measured view of Tesla’s milestone, framing it as a catalyst for global competition rather than evidence that Chinese technology is falling behind. The commentary highlighted China’s strength in the sector, noting that more than one-third of global automotive patents originate in the country. It cited key breakthroughs in top speeds, ultra-fast charging, autonomous driving and flying cars – including BYD’s record speed of 496.22 km/h, CATL’s six-minute full-charge battery and XPENG’s Land Aircraft Carrier, a modular flying car. Ultimately, the article encouraged the public to turn tech anxiety into confidence, emphasising that China’s auto industry welcomes healthy competition, as it did when Tesla first entered Shanghai. Ying Jie, a Chinese military influencer with 1.1 million followers, made a similar argument from the perspective of industrial technology. In his view, much of what the Roadster showcased relies on traditional aerospace technology. On attitude control, he said, China is already among the global leaders, citing examples ranging from unmanned cargo spacecraft to high-speed, precision docking at the Tiangong Space Station, which orbits at an altitude of 400km. “While the US slowly leaks aerospace tech into consumer goods, China easily adapts military tech – like gallium nitride chargers – for daily life, though our scientists stay quieter about it,” Ying said. On international social platforms, the discussion increasingly shifted to the Roadster’s underlying commercial viability. After the reveal, Gene Munster, managing partner of Deepwater Asset Management, posted that the Roadster “was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers.” Another analyst, however, argued that the Roadster’s value lies in its “halo effect”: inspiring family-car buyers to want a Tesla. A third observer described the launch as a “global talent magnet” that could attract engineers eager to push technological boundaries under Elon Musk’s leadership.

title: Hong Kong student gets 10 years for sexually assaulting 4 underage girls

content: A Hong Kong tertiary student convicted of sexually assaulting at least four underage girls has been sentenced to 10 years in prison, with the judge slamming him as a “very sick individual” who showed no remorse. High Court Judge Andrew Chan Hing-wai on Thursday noted from the assessment reports that Fan Chi-yuen, 22, had shown no remorse or empathy towards his victims. They included a 14-year-old girl who was so distressed after Fan attempted to rape her that she subsequently committed suicide. The court heard that Fan, an associate degree student in psychology, met the girl through RedNote, a popular Chinese social media platform, in August 2023. He arranged to meet her at a hotel a few days later, where he molested her in the room. Two weeks later, the girl took her own life. Her mother later discovered messages between the girl and her friend in which the victim revealed she had been sexually assaulted. Following a police report, investigators searched the defendant’s phone and computer, discovering evidence that he had engaged in sexual activity with at least three other underage girls in hotels between June 2022 and September 2023. From the child pornography material retrieved from the devices, there were up to nine victims in total, though some could not be identified. Citing the psychologist and psychiatrist reports, Chan noted that Fan admitted he had dated these girls “just for a short-lived relationship with sexual intention behind [it]”. The reports revealed that Fan enjoyed manipulating the girls to gain their trust before engaging in sex within a short time frame. He specifically targeted teenagers looking for romance and relationships. Mental health professionals concluded the defendant posed a high risk of reoffending, as he failed to realise his behaviour was wrong and showed no empathy towards his victims. Addressing the defendant, the judge said: “You are a very sick individual. You prey on young ladies.” The judge added that Fan showed a complete lack of respect for his victims, referring to them as “chicks” during assessment interviews. Furthermore, when told by a psychiatrist about the 14-year-old girl’s death, Fan displayed no emotion. Chan described the hotel assault on the girl as “carefully calculated and orchestrated”. He sympathised with the girl’s mother, saying the death must have caused the family “indescribable pain and sorrow”. “I fail to see a case with more serious consequences than the present one. Given the fact that the defendant kept looking for a young girl to satisfy his sexual gratification and caused such a serious consequence, the present one calls for the maximum sentence to be imposed,” he said. Fan had earlier pleaded guilty to 12 charges, including attempted unlawful intercourse with a girl under 16, which carries a maximum sentence of five years’ imprisonment. Noting the charges only involved four victims, Chan said the present proceedings only represent a fraction of Fan’s overall sexual encounters. The court heard that he attempted to rape another 14-year-old girl in 2022 whom he met through an online game in 2022. The rape was unsuccessful only because the girl managed to resist him and run away from the hotel room. The defendant had also molested that same girl on the upper deck of a bus and, on a separate occasion, secretly filmed her showering while repeatedly demanding sex. Judge Chan handed down a seven-year sentence for the series of assaults involving the second victim, ordering parts of the sentences for the third and fourth victims to be served consecutively, bringing the total term to 10 years. He stressed that the 10-year prison sentence was imposed after taking into account the severity of the crimes and the critical need to protect young people. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Missing lift fire door frames confined to Taizoom, Hong Kong authorities say

content: Inspections into lift safety across Hong Kong have found no missing fire-resistant door frames among contractors other than Taizoom Elevator, authorities said on Thursday, after 338 buildings served by the firm were confirmed to lack the crucial components. The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department offered an update on the checks on Thursday after the government pledged to expand the inspection scope to cover lifts handled by other contractors as well to check whether the problem existed across Hong Kong. Citywide inspections of lifts serviced by Taizoom were launched on October 16 after fire-resistant door frames were found missing from 48 newly installed lifts at two public housing estates. The department eventually found that 338 buildings under Taizoom’s service lacked crucial components designed to prevent flames and smoke from entering the shaft in the event of a fire. It also required other registered lift contractors to carry out the same inspections on lifts they had installed over the past 10 years and submit reports to the department, which then conducted sample checks. According to the latest results, none of the 20 buildings within housing estates and 70 single-block buildings with lifts installed by contractors other than Taizoom was found to have missing door frame components. “As inspections to date show that all cases of missing lift door frame components are related to Taizoom, the department will at this stage focus its resources on installing lift door frames for these buildings as soon as possible,” he added. According to the spokesman, the property management companies, owners’ corporations and residents of all inspected buildings have been notified of the inspection results, regardless of whether the lift door frame components have been installed as required. He said that the installation works would be supervised by the department, with the costs borne by the contractors, and spot checks conducted upon completion. Police last Friday arrested a Taizoom director and two registered lift engineers on suspicion of deception over safety certificates allegedly stating that the work had been fully completed.

title: EU gives top human rights award to ICC after Trump sanctions
description: Facing US sanctions, the International Criminal Court was on Thursday awarded the European Union’s top rights prize, in a show of support that risks upsetting President Donald Trump. “The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” said European Parliament chief Roberta Metsola in announcing the award. content: Facing US sanctions, the International Criminal Court was on Thursday awarded the European Union’s top rights prize, in a show of support that risks upsetting President Donald Trump. “The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” said European Parliament chief Roberta Metsola in announcing the award. The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize “at a time when the court and its officials face unprecedented challenges”. “Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” ICC president Tomoko Akane said. This month, the United States announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. Trump’s administration has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick”, furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza. The win comes after ex-ICC judge Navi Pillay, who also served as UN rights chief, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this month – a choice Trump slammed as “disgraceful”, arguing the award should have gone to him. The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the US sanctions – which will come into force in six months – and has said it is “ready to take any necessary measures” to make sure the court can keep working. Set up in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organisations to recognise their fight for human rights or democracy. The ICC was among three finalists this year, alongside Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, representing those prosecuted by the Iranian government. The nominees are put forward by the political groupings in the EU and the winner is chosen by senior lawmakers. An award ceremony will be held in December. Lissu, head of Tanzania’s opposition Chadema party, was detained in April 2025. He faces a possible death penalty if convicted of treason for allegedly inciting the public to boycott last year’s election. Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 21, have respectively been sentenced to death and 36 years in prison for having taken part in anti-government protests in Iran. Other recent high-profile winners of the Sakharov Prize have been Venezuelan opposition chief Maria Corina Machado, deceased Russian Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny and the people of Ukraine.

title: Ahead of Communist Party plenum, Xi Jinping warns that China faces a ‘new Long March’

content: A strong and united party leadership is vital to victory, Chinese President Xi Jinping said in a keynote speech on Thursday marking the 90th anniversary of the Long March. Speaking days before an important Communist Party meeting known as the fifth plenum, Xi said the party managed to turn the tide of defeat into a path to victory 90 years ago because it rallied around the leadership of Mao Zedong. By linking the Red Army’s historic endurance with today’s geopolitical struggles, Xi said China today faced a “new Long March” and had to learn how to navigate complex geopolitical pitfalls and fight for its interests. At a high-profile commemoration marking the 90th anniversary of the Long March’s victory in Beijing, Xi stressed that the historic survival and ultimate triumph of the Red Army hinged on establishing a firm political core – a historical lesson he framed as “indispensable” for China’s modern trajectory. “The great victory of the Red Army’s Long March was forged through the correct leadership of the party,” Xi was quoted by state news agency Xinhua as saying, invoking the 1935 Zunyi Conference as the pivotal turning point. During that critical retreat, the party “began the formation of the first generation of central collective leadership with Comrade Mao Zedong at its core”, he said. The move “opened a new phase in which the party independently solved the practical problems of the Chinese revolution and saved the party, the Red Army and the Chinese revolution at the most perilous hour”, he added. History proved that establishing a strong central leadership core was the “decisive factor” in overcoming internal divisions and external obstacles, Xi said. The Long March was a strategic retreat by the Communist Red Army from 1934 to 1936 to evade Nationalist forces during the Chinese civil war, when they travelled about 10,000km (6,200 miles). The party frequently invokes the event as a symbol of its endurance, discipline and political unity. Xi delivered his address just days ahead of the fifth plenum of the 20th Central Committee, scheduled for October 26 to 29 in Beijing. The committee is the party’s top political-executive organ. The prominent political meeting is expected to focus on tightening party governance, internal discipline and political loyalty. The present 205-member Central Committee has drawn unprecedented anti-corruption scrutiny. Of its full members, 35 have been either placed under investigation or stripped of their legislative seats, with many cited for disloyalty to the committee, according to the South China Morning Post’s calculations. On Thursday, framing modern national ambitions through a historical lens, Xi defined the “new Long March” as China’s present-day journey towards becoming a fully modernised socialist power and achieving the “great rejuvenation” of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernisation. Transitioning from historical reflection to present-day challenges, Xi warned that the path ahead would not be smooth. He called on the party, military and public to prepare for severe external headwinds. “On the new journey, facing complex international and domestic situations, we must dare to fight and be good at fighting,” Xi said. He also called on the entire country to bolster its resolve and prepare to withstand “high winds, raging waves and even dangerous storms”, emphasising a need to balance national development with national security. He issued the warning against a backdrop of escalating global turmoil and sustained friction with Western powers. Sino-US relations remain tense amid trade disputes, tech decoupling pressures and strategic volatility across the Taiwan Strait and the South China Sea. For its part, Beijing has increasingly promoted self-reliance and internal solidarity. On Thursday, major state media outlets went all out in publishing commentaries echoing Xi’s central message. Party mouthpiece People’s Daily said that centralising authority around the party’s core – a political foundation known as the “two establishes” – was the fundamental guarantee for maintaining political stability, driving economic reform and advancing Chinese modernisation through turbulent international waters. Meanwhile, PLA Daily’s editorial urged the armed forces to uphold absolute party control over the military, ramp up combat readiness and execute military modernisation targets ahead of the army’s centenary in 2027, when Beijing aims to transform the military into a world-class force. Across the country, local government authorities and cultural institutions marked the 90th anniversary with commemorative events, thematic exhibitions and public educational activities. In Beijing, the Military Museum of the Chinese People’s Revolution launched a major exhibition featuring rare historical artefacts, interactive digital displays and archival documents from the 10,000km trek. Similar memorial rallies, youth symposiums and red-tourism cultural festivals were hosted across historical sites along the Long March route, including Zunyi, Yanan and Yudu, drawing hundreds of thousands of visitors to honour the historic milestone, according to Chinese media reports.

title: Indonesia haze: why Jakarta won’t declare wildfires a national disaster
description: Indonesia’s government has resisted mounting calls to declare widespread forest and land fires a national disaster, insisting it can handle the crisis alone as residents report worsening health impacts and disaster experts warn that a broader, coordinated response is needed. Critics suggest the reluctance may stem from concerns that a national declaration could force Jakarta to redirect funds from other political priorities, while exposing the administration to greater scrutiny over its disaster...
content: Indonesia’s government has resisted mounting calls to declare widespread forest and land fires a national disaster, insisting it can handle the crisis alone as residents report worsening health impacts and disaster experts warn that a broader, coordinated response is needed. Critics suggest the reluctance may stem from concerns that a national declaration could force Jakarta to redirect funds from other political priorities, while exposing the administration to greater scrutiny over its disaster response. The dispute intensified on Tuesday – the second anniversary of President Prabowo Subianto’s administration – when student protesters across the country demanded a national disaster declaration, the restoration of damaged ecosystems and action against both the rising cost of living and the perceived erosion of democracy. A similar demand was included in a class-action lawsuit filed by civil society and indigenous groups in West Kalimantan last month, though the government maintains the fires do not warrant such a designation. “If a national disaster is declared, there will inevitably be those who exploit the situation. Disaster management is now nationally mandated, no longer the responsibility of regional governments,” Dudung Abdurachman, Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs, told reporters on Wednesday. “These fires are not just caused by ordinary people – corporations and certain parties from outside are deliberately creating [these] conditions.” In a speech on Wednesday, President Prabowo warned against “countries that like to insult” Indonesia over wildfires and transboundary haze, adding that “when the time comes, we will reveal the companies involved”. While Jakarta appreciated foreign aid offers, Dudung insisted external help would not solve the problem. “Japan, Malaysia and Singapore have offered assistance. Japan even arrived with a Chinook helicopter, but they still weren’t able to extinguish the fires,” Dudung said, adding that the government “has tried its best”. Dudung said on Monday that Malaysia had offered three helicopters and 52 firefighters, but pointed to logistical challenges on the ground. “There are many obstacles [in the field], such as fuel distribution. This isn’t necessarily about the equipment and personnel provided. For now, we can still cope,” he said. But satellite data shows the scale of the destruction. The blazes burned through more than 1.9 million hectares (4.7 million acres) of Indonesian forest between January and late September this year – a 38 per cent increase compared with the same period in 2019 – according to deforestation monitoring site Nusantara Atlas, as cited by Agence France-Presse. The true scale was likely higher, the organisation said, as the figures excluded individual burn scars smaller than 6.25 hectares. ‘Selfish’ move Edy Kurniawan Wahid, a lawyer with the Indonesian Legal Aid Foundation, alleged that fiscal and political motives were behind the administration’s hesitation. “While disaster occurrences have risen sharply over the last five years, the national budget allocated for disaster management has actually decreased,” Edy said. Jakarta allocated 400 billion rupiah (US$22.1 million) this year for the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB), a sharp drop from 2 trillion rupiah last year. “The government may be concerned that if this is declared a national disaster, the consequences will be a refocusing of existing budgets, including those for free nutritious meals and Prabowo’s other ambitious projects.” Edy currently represents victims of last year’s flash floods and landslides in Aceh and Sumatra, who filed a citizen lawsuit in May over the government’s handling of that crisis. “In the trial process, the government’s legal counsel said that one reason why the disasters [in Aceh and Sumatra] were not declared a national disaster was that they were worried that this would disrupt the macro economy and fiscal policy,” Edy said. On the ground in hard-hit regions such as Central Kalimantan, residents lamented Jakarta’s position as daily life under the blanket of toxic smog became increasingly grim. “We deeply regret that this statement was issued, considering that there are already quite a lot of victims in Central Kalimantan, especially those suffering from acute respiratory infections,” said Janang Firman Palanungkai, executive director of environmental group Walhi in Central Kalimantan. “The local government is no longer capable of handling this situation. The haze is getting thicker every day. Even if this isn’t declared a national disaster, how exactly is the central government handling it? To this day, that remains unclear.” Janang said health facilities in the province were “overwhelmed”. On October 10, local media reported that a six-month-old baby in Central Kalimantan died from pneumonia after suffering from shortness of breath and convulsions. Between August 20 and October 20, the Ministry of Health recorded 21,607 cases of respiratory disease in the province, including 5,133 involving toddlers. Janang added that vital medical supplies like N95 masks and oxygen tanks had become scarce and “very expensive”. “A national disaster declaration would ensure an increased budget, especially to help medical personnel and firefighters,” he said. “The central government is [being] selfish.” Coordination and international aid A national disaster declaration could help unite government ministries and state agencies under a single, coordinated response, according to Avianto Amri, chairperson of the non-profit Indonesian Disaster Management Community. “We must approach forest and land fires like Covid-19, as the threat is constantly evolving – unlike floods and landslides, which end when extreme weather is over, allowing us to focus on recovery,” Avianto said. “The current situation is even more dangerous and critical because response efforts require intensity, and the risk of spread remains high.” The Covid-19 pandemic was the last state of emergency designated a national disaster in Indonesia. Avianto said a formal declaration would also streamline foreign help from regional partners via established mechanisms, such as the Association for Southeast Asian Nations Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance on Disaster Management. “If the government gives its blessings and accepts foreign aid, it will help civil society access foreign funding to help extinguish these fires,” he said.

title: China expands tax workforce as tougher enforcement moves into spotlight

content: Beijing’s plan to recruit more tax officers next year is drawing attention from businesses and wealthy families as tax compliance rises up the policy agenda and authorities intensify enforcement efforts. China’s 2027 national civil service recruitment plan includes 24,013 tax-related positions, accounting for more than 67 per cent of all vacancies, up from over 65 per cent a year earlier. Most of the vacancies are at the State Taxation Administration’s local branches, which are recruiting staff to collect and administer taxes, social security contributions and other levies, according to the recruitment catalogue. The national civil service examination will be held in November. “There is the potential for an increase in disputes involving high-net-worth families and their trusts,” said Emma Holland, a partner in the trust and probate litigation team at UK disputes law firm Stewarts. “Our team, which has experience working with clients in China, believes the changes could expose previously undisclosed trust interests, disrupt existing arrangements for managing family wealth and create new opportunities for litigation.” Beijing regulators have rolled out tougher tax enforcement measures. In the first half of this year, at least 80 listed Chinese firms were ordered to repay corporate income taxes and late-payment fees to local authorities, according to financial data provider Wind. Companies in the pharmaceutical, new materials, chemicals, environmental protection, agriculture and information technology sectors accounted for most of the cases. The latest focus is offshore trusts. Earlier this week, the State Taxation Administration said taxpayers with offshore trust income must file and pay individual income tax on trust gains. A 90-day grace period applied, with no late-payment surcharges for settlements completed by the October 22 deadline. Cai Chang, a professor at the Central University of Finance and Economics’ School of Public Finance and Taxation in Beijing, said tax administration was becoming increasingly important. “Recruiters are now seeking candidates with more diverse backgrounds in computer science, artificial intelligence, law and public administration, rather than just finance, taxation and accounting,” Cai said. “The tax service faces structural labour challenges. Many senior staff are retiring, while a considerable number of employees have left for private-sector positions at listed companies and law firms, triggering a notable outflow of talent from the civil service.” He added that demand for tax officers could decline in the coming years as AI becomes more widely adopted. Many listed companies were already using big-data tools to monitor and review their own tax compliance, Cai added.

title: Hong Kong pay growth slows as Guangdong accelerates, survey finds
description: Hong Kong workers received smaller pay rises this year as Guangdong’s wage growth picked up, with the starting salaries of university graduates edging closer to those of sub-degree holders, an annual survey has found. Hong Kong’s Baptist University released the findings of its 2026 Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area Pay and Benefits Survey on Thursday. It showed that companies in Hong Kong and Macau slowed pay rises this year. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s unemployment rate rose by 0.1...
content: Hong Kong workers received smaller pay rises this year as Guangdong’s wage growth picked up, with the starting salaries of university graduates edging closer to those of sub-degree holders, an annual survey has found. Hong Kong’s Baptist University released the findings of its 2026 Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area Pay and Benefits Survey on Thursday. It showed that companies in Hong Kong and Macau slowed pay rises this year. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s unemployment rate rose by 0.1 percentage points to 3.9 per cent between July and September, the highest since the period from November last year to January, the government revealed. The figure was 3.8 per cent in the previous three-month rolling period, between June and August. But Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun said the labour force and total employment had risen further amid “a continued influx of fresh graduates and school leavers into the labour market”. According to the university’s survey, the average pay increase for employees in Hong Kong fell from 2.5 per cent last year to 2.3 per cent, while Macau’s wage growth slowed from 1.6 per cent to 1.1 per cent. In contrast, Guangdong’s average increase rose from 1.8 per cent in 2025 to 2 per cent this year. Guangdong also expects a higher average pay rise next year, forecast at 3.8 per cent, while companies in Hong Kong and Macau forecast an average increase of 3.1 per cent. “Salary increase forecasts for 2027 have rebounded in Hong Kong, Macau and cities across Guangdong province,” Ray Leung, president of the Hong Kong People Management Association, said. “This reflects the fact that, although businesses continue to face challenges from the external economic environment and cost pressures, they remain confident about their future development and talent needs.” The survey, conducted between July and September, covered 78 companies in Hong Kong, 38 in Macau and 105 in the nine cities of Guangdong province, representing more than 270,000 employees in total. Participating companies submitted employee pay data from July 2025 to June 2026 through an online questionnaire and provided forecasts for next year’s pay trends. The study was jointly conducted by Baptist University, South China University of Technology, the Hong Kong People Management Association and the Talent Development and Management Association of Guangdong. It also found that the average starting salary for Hong Kong university bachelor’s graduates remained unchanged at HK$19,500 (US$2,484) this year, showing no upwards trend. The average starting salaries of recent bachelor’s degree graduates in Hong Kong edged down to between HK$17,500 and HK$23,000. The gap between the starting salaries of bachelor’s degree and sub-degree graduates narrowed by 17 per cent, or HK$500, from HK$3,000 last year to HK$2,500 this year. Sub-degree graduates’ average starting salaries ranged from HK$15,500 to HK$20,500 this year. In terms of bachelor’s degree graduates’ pay, engineering graduates were offered the highest average starting salaries, earning HK$23,000 on average, up from HK$21,500 last year. Other sectors reported declines, including information technology, where bachelor’s degree graduates’ starting salaries fell from HK$20,500 to HK$19,500 this year, and finance and accounting, where they dropped by HK$1,000 to HK$19,000 this year. Looking ahead, 41 per cent of surveyed Hong Kong firms expected an average pay rise of 3.1 per cent in 2027, while one anticipated a pay freeze. The remainder did not provide forecasts. This year’s survey also included a new study on artificial intelligence (AI). While 78 per cent of bay area companies have begun piloting generative AI tools, exploring process automation and applying AI across various business functions, only 15 per cent have yet to establish formal AI policies, according to the survey. Cecilia Tam, director of the Centre for Human Resources Strategy and Development at HKBU’s School of Business, noted that about one-fifth of companies had seen a reduction in junior administrative and support roles. But she said companies were not simply replacing employees with AI. “A common trend is that companies increasingly value people who can effectively use AI,” Tam said, adding that future competitiveness would depend not merely on attracting AI specialists, but on empowering every professional to use AI effectively.

content: Across Paris’ toniest shopping districts, luxury boutiques bear the scars of a weekend of rioting that filled social media feeds around the world. Now they are bracing for the possibility of another round. On the avenue Champs-Elysees, Louis Vuitton’s flagship store has metallic grates protecting its windows that are not there at quieter times, as does the Christian Dior Couture emporium on avenue Montaigne, a nexus of high-end shopping in Paris’ eighth arrondissement. Both stores escaped serious damage last weekend, even as shops elsewhere were less fortunate. Boarded up windows and doors line the rue Saint-Honore, not far from France’s presidential palace, where mobs on Saturday broke into and looted shops including those of Burberry, Christian Dior perfumes and Guerlain. All three boutiques remained closed on Wednesday, as did a Salomon sportswear store on the nearby boulevard de la Madeleine that was similarly ravaged. An Hermes boutique on avenue George V, close to the Champs-Elysees, suffered broken windows. The brand’s store in Marseille fared far worse and “won’t reopen any time soon” after being ransacked by rioters, chief financial officer Eric du Halgouet told reporters on a call on Thursday. Hermes has since boosted security measures, he said. The violence followed protests last Saturday that drew more than half a million people across France. As night fell, roving bands of hooded and masked rioters hit hundreds of shops, smashing windows, destroying equipment and running off with merchandise. The turmoil abated after curfews and transport restrictions were imposed on Monday, but protesters’ call for another day of unrest this Saturday has residents, authorities and shopkeepers on edge. The brazen attacks and ineffectual police response prompted an outcry from retailers, among others, and led to a profit warning from Carrefour, one of the country’s largest grocers. About 50 of its stores were hit on the first day of rioting, with many looted and damaged, CEO Alexandre Bompard told financial analysts on Tuesday. The unrest is hurting consumer confidence, dissuading shoppers and driving up costs for security and logistics, Bompard said. Carrefour expects a hit to profitability of as much as €200 million (US$225 million). Laurent Milchior, who heads lingerie brand Etam, told BFM Business that the destruction over the weekend represented €1 million in lost sales and another €500,000 from stolen goods and damage to its stores. “If it’s a one off, it’ll work out, but the issue is if it lasts,” he said, referring to repeated days of protests that degenerate into violence. He called on President Emmanuel Macron to mobilise the army to deal with these events as anti-riot police and other forces were outmatched. Thierry Guibert, the CEO of Lacoste owner Maus Freres, urged the state in a social media post “to mobilise without delay all legal means it has to put an end to the violence, protect our citizens, our police officers, our workers and our companies”. Galeries Lafayette, after suffering damage and looting at locations including boulevard Haussmann in Paris and in Bordeaux, said the material and economic consequences will be significant. In response to the attacks, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu promised “massive” security measures around this Saturday’s protests in remarks to the National Assembly. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez is scheduled to detail those plans on Thursday. The impact of the rioting is likely to ripple across the tourism industry, particularly if it carries on. Images of violence have led to cancellations at high-end Paris hotels, according to Christophe Laure, who heads UMIH Prestige, which represents four- and five-star hotels. Well-heeled guests of those establishments often tend to shop at the local luxury stores. “It’s too early today to assess whether this will have an impact on foreign tourist clientele in coming weeks,” Hermes’ du Halgouet said. With demand for luxury goods in China already weak and the wider industry in a slump, an extended drop in tourist purchases in France would come at a difficult moment. That is especially the case with the Christmas shopping season just getting under way. Milan, another European luxury shopping destination, also experienced looting in the past few days. Two prominent events likely to lure foreign visitors are still going ahead this weekend. The Art Basel Paris fair, at the Grand Palais, said it “has extensive protocols in place” for the show and “works closely with a private security company and, where necessary, the Paris police”. On Sunday, the National Football League will hold a game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the New Orleans Saints at Stade de France, the stadium in the suburbs of Paris where a Champions League finale in 2022 ended in scenes of chaos and violence as local individuals assaulted football fans. Security will be heightened for the game, Associated Press reported. Not everyone has been deterred by the unrest. On the Champs-Elysees on Tuesday, Dallas resident Keegan May and his girlfriend stepped out of the Louis Vuitton store after buying a bag costing €2,200. May has spent a month in France, mostly working in the town of Vannes, in Brittany, and came to Paris for a holiday. He was on the left bank when the riots took place and saw little of the mayhem. Asked if the turmoil had soured his desire to return to Paris, he answered: “We’ll come back, but we’ll aim to stay in places like Vannes, which is lovely, quieter, and generally less stressful.”

title: Chinese students stand by France study plans despite widespread civil unrest
description: Social unrest in France is not deterring some Chinese students from pursuing studies there – at least for now. Despite nationwide demonstrations over the rising cost of living and declining public services escalating into violence over the weekend, prospective applicants said they remained committed to their academic plans. A 30-year-old woman from Guangdong province who gave only her family name as Wang said she had obtained a student visa and planned to proceed with a language programme in...
content: Social unrest in France is not deterring some Chinese students from pursuing studies there – at least for now. Despite nationwide demonstrations over the rising cost of living and declining public services escalating into violence over the weekend, prospective applicants said they remained committed to their academic plans. A 30-year-old woman from Guangdong province who gave only her family name as Wang said she had obtained a student visa and planned to proceed with a language programme in Montpellier, starting in January. The language school is away from the areas most affected by the unrest. “Even in Paris, I think you can avoid joining the protests,” she said. “The main inconvenience is school strikes and closures.” However, she was concerned that a prolonged crisis could disrupt her studies and daily life, complicate visa and residence procedures, or push up living costs ahead of next year’s presidential election. An advertising agency employee in Beijing who called herself Zhouzi is preparing for admission in autumn next year. She saw the crisis as temporary and said the unrest was unlikely to affect her application, although she was keeping her options open. “It doesn’t make much difference to me. I don’t think this will persist long term,” she said, adding that she did not want news about the protests to dim her view of studying in France. “Since I have made up my mind [to apply], I can decide whether to go, or [I can] defer enrolment after I am admitted.” France is a major destination for Chinese students. According to data released by Campus France, the country’s official agency for international student mobility, 26,327 Chinese students enrolled in French higher education in the 2024-25 academic year. That figure is down 3 per cent from the previous year but still makes China the country’s third-largest source of international students. The wave of demonstrations began with students protesting over education conditions before drawing in rioters who looted shops and attacked public buildings in cities such as Limoges and Paris. The unrest prompted police to ban gatherings near key landmarks. It comes less than a year before France’s presidential election. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading polls, while incumbent President Emmanuel Macron cannot seek a third term because of term limits. Macron has called for a clear distinction between peaceful demonstrators and those destroying property. On Monday, China’s foreign ministry and its diplomatic missions in France renewed safety warnings, advising citizens to avoid demonstration zones. Among the prospective students in China exercising caution in light of the protests, 23-year-old Momo said she was considering postponing her plans or choosing another country because of the protests – even though her course in France was not soon. Momo, who is planning her master’s studies for autumn 2028, said her main concerns were “personal safety, France’s political situation and the budget”. For those already on the ground, the impact appears to be immediate, yet tolerable. A 20-year-old exchange student at Paris Nanterre University who called himself Muye said his campus had not held in-person classes since October 2. “From October 2 to 15, we received daily emails telling us whether there would be class that day,” he said. He said Chinese students around him were mainly discussing safety and the disruption to their studies. Some worried about living in areas affected by the violence, while others expressed sympathy about shops that were damaged, according to Muye. “Nobody wants to suspend their studies or return home early,” he said. “But one classmate said that, had they known this would happen, they might have flown home for a month-long holiday.” He said the unrest had not changed his own view of France as a study destination. “France continues to attract international students with its relatively low education costs compared with Britain and the United States, as well as close cooperation among universities,” he said.

title: India seeks to expand navy’s reach with 4 amphibious warships

content: India’s planned acquisition of four large amphibious warships would strengthen its ability to support naval logistics and humanitarian missions across the Indian Ocean, with security experts saying their value depends on how the navy could effectively utilise them during a crisis. The Indian Navy has invited bids for four landing platform docks (LPDs), each with a displacement of more than 30,000 tonnes. Indian Navy Vice Chief Vice Admiral Ajay Kochhar said at a media briefing on Monday that a request for proposal had been issued to shortlisted shipyards the previous week. The four LPDs will be built in India, with their electric propulsion systems being developed under an India–UK defence partnership. The latter was announced during a meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then UK prime minister Keir Starmer in Mumbai in October last year. With a length of 220 metres each, the ships are estimated to cost nearly US$5.3 billion in total and can accommodate up to 900 fully equipped army personnel, vehicles, tanks and artillery. They will feature specialised landing craft to ferry troops and equipment ashore, two heavy-lift helicopters and 12 helicopters for special operations, as well as onboard workshop facilities. Walter Ladwig, a senior lecturer in international relations at King’s College London, said the ships would significantly improve the Indian Navy’s ability to deploy and sustain its forces across distant waters. “These ships could evacuate civilians, deploy peacekeepers and provide logistical support to friendly states,” he said, adding that their helicopter decks, medical facilities and landing craft would be useful to respond to natural disasters and other emergencies. Given the complexities of modern conflicts, the LPDs would require substantial support from other naval assets to deal with threats from submarines, drones and anti-ship missiles, he added. The ships would not be effective for amphibious assaults, said Ladwig, noting that the last major amphibious campaign that took place during a conflict against a conventional military was the Falklands War. The LPDs are set to be the second-largest India-made combat ships after INS Vikrant, India’s 45,000-tonne aircraft carrier. The navy currently operates one LPD, INS Jalashwa, acquired from the United States. With one LPD currently, the Indian Navy could not maintain a continuous amphibious operation, according to Ladwig. The Navy could do so in future with one LPD if it were to acquire four such vessels, with the other three on standby for other missions, he added. C. Uday Bhaskar, director of the Society for Policy Studies think tank and a former Indian naval officer, said India’s geographical circumstances made the acquisition important. India needs to boost its amphibious capabilities to protect its island territories, including the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep, while the LPDs could also support humanitarian missions across the Indian Ocean, stretching from the east coast of Africa to Southeast Asia, according to Bhaskar. He added that the LPDs would help the Indian Navy react quickly to an emergency. “Navies acquire capabilities and hone their professional skills so they can respond when the need arises. The December 2004 tsunami is a classic example of how the Indian Navy responded at short notice.” However, India has faced setbacks in acquiring LPDs in past years. A 2011 proposal stalled over accounting issues between Indian and foreign manufacturers, while a 2013 tender was scrapped in 2020 after the navy’s requirements changed. Bhaskar said India would need a more disciplined approach to avoid a repeat as it explored foreign partnerships with domestic shipyards to build the LPDs. “Delays in decision-making and awarding contracts, and time-cost spillovers in shipyards are systemic challenges that will have to be surmounted,” he added. Atul Kumar, a fellow at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation’s strategic studies programme, said the Indian government needed to cut through red tape to accelerate the launch of the LPDs. Their acquisition is important to India’s ability to respond to a changing regional security environment in tandem with its expansion of commercial and security infrastructure across its island territories, according to Kumar. China’s growing naval power has made the activation of LPDs in nearby waters a key consideration for India, he said. “Safeguarding these remote outposts against an external power requires robust power projection. Given the exponential growth of China’s Navy, four of these multirole ships represent the bare minimum for India to maintain a credible deterrent,” Kumar added. Dongkeun Lee, a policy fellow at the Asia-Pacific Leadership Network, said the LPDs’ primary value for India was their deployment for humanitarian missions rather than amphibious battles. Referring to the INS Vikrant and INS Vikramaditya, a former Russian aircraft carrier acquired and modified by India, Lee said: “The purposes of acquiring LPDs and aircraft carriers are quite different. Aircraft carriers are designed to project air power, primarily for sea control purposes, whereas LPDs are intended to support amphibious operations, which involve projecting land power ashore. Although both types of ships are relatively large, their operational purposes are fundamentally different.” Ultimately, the LPDs could extend the Indian Navy’s regional influence across vast distances, Lee added. “Given their non-combat nature, such missions could be conducted across a much broader geographical area of the Indo-Pacific, encompassing both the Indian Ocean region and Southeast Asia, allowing the Indian Navy to expand its naval presence while also supporting its naval diplomacy objectives.”

title: Super Typhoon Champi: Hong Kong airlines cancel at least 12 Taiwan, Japan flights
description: Airlines in Hong Kong have cancelled or rescheduled more than a dozen flights to and from Taiwan and Japan due to Super Typhoon Champi, with further disruption expected in the coming days. Four other flights serving Taichung and Kaohsiung have been postponed until Saturday. The airline said it was notifying affected passengers...
content: Airlines in Hong Kong have cancelled or rescheduled more than a dozen flights to and from Taiwan and Japan due to Super Typhoon Champi, with further disruption expected in the coming days. Budget carrier HK Express announced it would cancel 10 flights between Hong Kong and Taiwan on Friday, with six serving Taipei and two each serving Taichung and Kaohsiung. Four other flights serving Taichung and Kaohsiung have been postponed until Saturday. The airline said it was notifying affected passengers by email. HK Express, Cathay Pacific Airways’ low-cost carrier, said affected passengers could rebook free of charge, with change fees and fare differences waived, provided their new departure dates were within two weeks of their original bookings. Passengers could also request full refunds for unused flight segments without cancellation charges. All requests must be submitted before the original scheduled departure times. Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific has also introduced special ticketing arrangements for passengers travelling to and from Taipei on Friday and Saturday. Rebooking and re-routing charges will be waived for tickets issued on or before Wednesday. Passengers must make changes before Saturday and complete their journeys by December 31. Any fare or tax differences will remain payable. The airline said it was closely monitoring the weather and would rebook passengers on the first available service if their flights were cancelled. Hong Kong Airlines, meanwhile, revealed further cancellations of six flights between the city and Taipei, originally set to take off on Friday. This followed the airline’s earlier announcement that it would cancel two flights on Thursday to and from Okinawa – the outbound HX658 and return service HX659. The operator also warned flights between Hong Kong and Shanghai Pudong scheduled for Saturday or Sunday could be cancelled. It said rebooking, re-routing and refund fees would be waived for passengers with confirmed bookings on the cancelled Okinawa flights. Greater Bay Airlines said its flights were operating normally but warned of possible changes to services to and from Taipei and Okinawa because of the typhoon. The airline urged passengers travelling on Friday and Saturday to check their flight status before heading to the airport. According to the Hong Kong Observatory, Champi was centred about 590km (367 miles) southeast of Taipei at 4pm on Thursday, and was forecast to move northwest at about 14km/h (9mph) towards waters east of Taiwan. The forecaster said the super typhoon had maximum sustained winds of 195km/h near its centre at 2pm. The Observatory expected Champi, named after the Lao word for the frangipani flower, to move towards waters east of Taiwan on Thursday and Friday before potentially turning north across the East China Sea towards Japan and Korea. It added that the storm could still skirt the coasts of Taiwan and Zhejiang province. Despite the storm, Hong Kong was expected to remain generally fine and dry over the next couple of days, with temperatures reaching 32 degrees Celsius (90 Fahrenheit) on both Friday and Saturday. The Observatory said sinking air associated with Champi’s outer circulation would bring very hot weather to parts of Guangdong later this week. A fresh to strong northeast monsoon was expected to affect the southern China coast early to mid-next week.

title: Canadian publisher drops Thelyson Orelien, says he used AI to write novel
description: The publisher of top-selling Haitian-Canadian writer Thelyson Orelien said Wednesday it had confirmed that he used artificial intelligence to help write his novel It Was Either That or Die. But on Wednesday, Boreal said it had conducted a further investigation into the allegations. “New information, confirmed over the past few days,...
content: The publisher of top-selling Haitian-Canadian writer Thelyson Orelien said Wednesday it had confirmed that he used artificial intelligence to help write his novel It Was Either That or Die. Orelien has denied allegations that he used AI on his breakthrough novel and, last week, Canadian publisher Boreal said it was standing by the 38-year-old writer. But on Wednesday, Boreal said it had conducted a further investigation into the allegations. “New information, confirmed over the past few days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process” of the novel, a Boreal statement said. The publisher announced it was “ending its professional relationship” with Orelien. Boreal said it did not know the extent of AI’s use in the writing process “and we will likely never have a definitive answer”. It said it gathered all the working versions of the novel and hired an outside party to analyse the various drafts. “The results obtained this week revealed traces of AI tags in the metadata of certain documents,” Boreal said. Before conducting this analysis, the publisher said it had tried to work with Orelien to gather the evidence necessary to prove his innocence. That effort was inconclusive, and Orelien “subsequently announced that he would not provide any further information,” the publisher said. The novel about migration, known by its original French title C’etait ca ou mourir, had been scheduled for translation in more than 20 countries. The book was shrouded in suspicion and withdrawn from the shortlist for France’s top book prize, the Goncourt, after tests with AI detector Pangram indicated a 100 per cent probability it contained computer-generated text. In a statement earlier this month, Orelien called the allegations “slander and heresy”. “Here and there I did use tools for research, particularly for foreign idioms,” he said in a statement sent to Agence France-Presse. “But not a single sentence in this book was created by a machine, nor the meaning or the structure of a story that comes from my gut.” He stood firm on Wednesday, telling the French newspaper Liberation he used AI “in the creative process” for “historical research”. “I’ve explained everything to those close to me, but at the moment I don’t think my words count for anything,” he said, adding that what he is currently experiencing has “gone way too far”. Orelien said he started writing the book in late 2017 “on the corner of a table” and completed a first draft in 2019 of more than 300 pages, several years before the advent of AI services such as ChatGPT. The author fled his native Haiti following a 2010 earthquake that struck the Caribbean island, already ravaged by poverty and unrest. In response to separate allegations of plagiarism, Orelien admitted to making “unacceptable mistakes” in the past in his writing, without mentioning specifics. “I was just over 20, I was probably a little too impatient, without really understanding how much I still had to learn. I wanted to write, I was reading a lot,” he wrote. “But admiring someone does not give you the right to take, to claim as mine texts that are not my own.”
