title: Asean wants a single digital economy. Will different state laws hobble its goal?
description: Southeast Asian nations are seeking to make it easier for businesses and consumers to operate across borders in the digital economy, but achieving the goal will depend on whether governments can align their domestic laws under a proposed pact, according to analysts. Targeted to be signed during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila in November, the Asean Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) is aimed at improving compatibility between rules and systems governing...
content: Southeast Asian nations are seeking to make it easier for businesses and consumers to operate across borders in the digital economy, but achieving the goal will depend on whether governments can align their domestic laws under a proposed pact, according to analysts. Targeted to be signed during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila in November, the Asean Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) is aimed at improving compatibility between rules and systems governing digital payments, data flows and online commerce across the region. However, its draft text is yet to be published. In an interview earlier this month, Philippine President and current Asean chairman Ferdinand Marcos Jnr said he hoped Singapore, which will chair the 11-member bloc next year, would help advance the agreement then. In June, Asean announced that its officials had resolved all outstanding issues arising from a meeting in Manila in May, adding that DEFA was expected to play a transformative role in unlocking the full potential of the region’s digital economy. Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation think tank, said the text could be released some time between the coming Asean summit and 2027. This would depend on how much “legal scrubbing” by the bloc’s members was needed before signing the pact, she said. “We are therefore left to speculate about what might or might not be included in DEFA.” A 2024 preparatory study on DEFA, prepared by the Boston Consulting Group with support from the Australian government, identified differing payment standards, fragmented digital payment requirements, restrictions on data sharing and transfers, cybersecurity gaps and insufficiently connected trade infrastructure as barriers to increasing digital trade within Asean. More than 2,000 micro-, small- and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) across the 10 Asean members at the time, as well as corporate and government representatives, were interviewed or surveyed for the study. Elms said a major risk for companies was that governments would pursue different domestic regulatory approaches without coordination at the Asean level to finalise DEFA. Members could, for instance, introduce different privacy requirements for various types of data, leaving businesses to navigate multiple legal regimes, according to Elms. DEFA was intended to encourage coordination and regulatory alignment, but businesses would need clarity on how interoperability would operate in practice, Elms said. “They will be required to create interoperable rules. But absent clear criteria for how to make this happen, firms might discover that interoperability on offer is not actually making a difference on the ground,” Elms said. These difficulties, she suggested, might first emerge in payment systems or rules governing data flows. To bridge these gaps, Hafidzi Razali, founder and CEO of public affairs advisory firm Strategic Counsel, argued that Asean should adopt a flexible DEFA to accommodate domestic legal amendments by its members. “At Asean level, a principle-based approach can guide member states to achieve consistency in addressing the different facets of interoperability,” Hafidzi said. “The challenges presented by the rise of AI present a good case study, where it’s still early but not too late to mitigate the unintended effects.” Elms predicted that DEFA could entail implementation barriers similar to those encountered by the bloc for its existing Agreement on Electronic Commerce, which was signed in January 2019 and came into force in December 2021. “It is worth remembering that Asean already has an active E-Commerce Agreement that covers many of the same topics,” she said, adding that much of the earlier agreement had not been implemented or had been implemented unevenly. “This is not unusual for Asean, as the institution prizes flexibility and implementation is always the challenge,” she said. The 2024 preparatory study for DEFA recommended staggered timelines and commitments to accommodate member states’ different starting points, alongside mechanisms to help countries move towards higher levels of commitment. It also called for continued private-sector engagement and updates to policies and standards as business needs and technologies evolved. Farlina Said, director of cyber and technology policy at Malaysia’s Institute of Strategic and International Studies, said Asean’s ambitions required greater cross-border data flows and transactions, supported by compatible approaches on trusted credentials, privacy and security. Institutions would also need greater capacity to manage increased digital activities and the accompanying cybersecurity challenges, she said. “While DEFA advances conversations on cross-border data flows, there can be bottlenecks to implementation,” Farlina said. While the agreement sought to position Asean as a digital market and encourage its population to participate in the digital economy, constraints on access and connectivity could affect the pace at which its benefits spread across different communities in the region, according to Farlina. “While some communities may advance quickly, others may just be slightly slower to benefit from the agreement,” she said.

title: Chinese influencer ‘reborn’ from 35-storey fall returns to social media

content: A Chinese influencer has sparked heated online discussions after posting about her remarkable recovery from a fall from the 35th floor nearly a year ago. On October 12, the influencer, who uses the handle @wananan, returned to her account after an almost 17-month hiatus, saying she “had been reborn through adversity”. The 27-year-old woman from Hunan province in central China said she had almost fully recovered from the fall, which happened more than a year ago. It was previously reported that she accidentally fell in June last year and was immediately rushed to the Third Xiangya Hospital of Central South University. She suffered multiple bone fractures, an intracranial haemorrhage, injuries to her cervical spine and organs, and the loss of her lower right leg. Her life was saved after 14 hours of emergency surgery. She spent 50 days in the intensive care unit (ICU). Her doctor, Xing Wei, said the treatment was successful beyond expectations. Apart from the amputation of her lower leg, her other organ functions have basically recovered, Xing said. In addition to the efforts of the medical team that made her survival possible, @wananan was also said to have been lucky: she hit a tree and then some bushes, which cushioned her fall and helped prevent a fatal outcome. The influencer previously had around 100,000 followers, who admired her looks and her singing voice in cover songs. She also said she was lucky not to have suffered serious injuries to her face or hands. Her comeback video had received 1.7 million likes and 100,000 comments at the time of writing. Her follower count on the platform had also risen to 250,000. She does rehabilitation exercises every day and plans to be fitted with a prosthetic limb soon. Speaking about her future, @wananan was optimistic: “I can still walk to the places I want to go, and if I can’t walk, I’ll just call a taxi.” She said her life no longer belonged only to her, but also to the many people who had helped her. She would live it beautifully as a way of thanking them. She recalled having difficult days after the fall, especially while suffering from severe pain “everywhere” in her body as her injuries healed. But the experience helped her realise that “suffering is not meant to destroy me, but to forge me. Life is not about being glamorous, but about the courage to face the broken pieces and piece them back together.” She also encouraged her audience to focus on what they gain rather than what they lose. “What is lost will not be lost again,” she concluded. “It is a wonder that she survived after falling from the 35th floor,” one person said. “You are very lucky. Wishing you peace and happiness in the future,” another commented under her post. The hospital’s official account also commented, saying it was delighted to see her “rebirth” and thanking her for “sharing the power of life.”

content: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] For two weeks in September, Samarkand was the capital of world chess — and when the pieces were finally swept from the boards, it was the home team standing at the top. Uzbekistan won the Open section of the 46th World Chess Olympiad, the largest in the event’s history with a record 397 teams from 205 federations, sealing gold with a final-round victory over Ukraine in front of packed stands. It is the country’s second Olympiad title after Chennai 2022: the team finished two points clear of the field, with India taking silver and Germany bronze. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev hailed the players as heroes of New Uzbekistan and a golden generation, singling out their wins over defending champions India, over China, and over the world’s top-rated team, the United States, on the road to the title. A new presidential decree on the development of chess, he added, will lay the foundation for even greater success. Shortly before, FIDE had named the Chess Federation of Uzbekistan the best federation of 2026 — recognition of a rise that has been both deliberate and backed by the state. Javokhir Sindarov was also named Best Male Player. The tournament belonged to the players who, in just four years, have turned Uzbekistan from underdogs into champions. On top board, Nodirbek Abdusattorov went unbeaten against the strongest player of every opposing team, taking individual gold with the best performance of the entire Olympiad. The team was led by Rustam Kasimdzhanov — a former world champion himself — and it was reserve Mukhiddin Madaminov, also undefeated, who sealed the title on the final day. “I think we can now say with confidence that Uzbekistan has no equal in the world of chess,” Abdusattorov said after the victory. “I believe we played this tournament at the very highest level,” added Sindarov. In a field of almost 2,000 players, the hosts settled the question on the board. But Uzbekistan’s biggest chess moment of the year is still to come — and it belongs to 20-year-old Javokhir Sindarov, who played his part in the Samarkand gold. In late November, he travels to Geneva to play for the World Championship — the ultimate prize in chess. His opponent is the reigning champion, India’s Gukesh Dommaraju, who took the crown in Singapore in 2024 at the age of eighteen, winning 7½–6½ over fourteen games. Both players are 20, making the forthcoming contest the youngest World Championship match in the history of the game. Sindarov’s road to the match reads like a modern fairy tale. In 2025 he won the FIDE World Cup in Goa, becoming, at nineteen, the youngest winner in the event’s history. This spring he won the Candidates Tournament in Cyprus with an unbeaten score of 10 out of 14, earning the right to face Gukesh across the board. FIDE chose Geneva as a neutral venue — a city with a long tradition of bringing nations together. The first game is scheduled for 24 November, and the match will run until mid-December over a maximum of fourteen classical games. The total prize fund stands at US$2.5 million. Both players arrive in Switzerland having just tested themselves in the same playing hall in Samarkand — Sindarov with Uzbekistan’s gold, Gukesh with India’s silver. It was their final rehearsal before the title is decided. The stakes are matched only by the intrigue. Magnus Carlsen, the world’s highest-rated player, has called Sindarov the clear favourite, pointing to the champion’s inconsistent recent form. For Uzbekistan, this match is more than a sporting event. “We all expect great victories from Sindarov,” said President Mirziyoyev, addressing the young grandmaster directly and assuring him that he is more than capable of achieving them. Only four years ago, Uzbekistan was just announcing itself as a chess power; today it is a champion that has welcomed the whole world on home soil. From Samarkand, the ancient crossroads of the Silk Road, the country now sends a single player to Geneva: 20-year-old Sindarov carries the hopes of an entire nation — and a chance Uzbekistan has never had before, to call the reigning world champion its own. The first game is now just weeks away. Official Olympiad website: chessolympiad2026.fide.com

title: Receivers to sell indebted Shimao’s 2 Hong Kong hotels to Malaysian developer

content: Receivers of the Sheraton Hong Kong Tung Chung Hotel and the Four Points by Sheraton have agreed to sell the dual-branded complex, which together comprise the city’s third-largest hotel by room count, for HK$2.7 billion (US$344 million), Shimao Group announced on Thursday. In a filing to the Hong Kong stock exchange, the distressed mainland Chinese developer said the buyer was Oceanfront Hong Kong Limited, which is controlled by Malaysian property developer ParkCity Group. The complex was seized by receivers after Shimao failed to sell it despite slashing the asking price to about HK$4.5 billion in late 2024 – down from at least HK$6 billion a year earlier. “The sale price was well below the property’s valuation, meaning the banks would also take a loss on the disposal,” said Glen Ho, Deloitte’s Asia-Pacific contingency planning and insolvency leader. “This shows that Hong Kong is now a buyer’s market, with foreign investors seeing opportunities to enter after property prices have adjusted.” Una Ge, a partner and managing director at AlixPartners and one of the receivers, said ParkCity was Oceanfront’s majority owner. ParkCity also has projects in Vietnam. According to Companies Registry records, Oceanfront’s directors are Joseph Lau, who holds a Malaysian passport, and Keoy Soo Lik, who holds a Hong Kong ID card. It was incorporated on September 29. Lau is the CEO of ParkCity. This will reduce the overall indebtedness of the group and strengthen its financial position Shimao Group Shimao said the sale was expected to be completed by the end of the year, with the net proceeds to be used to partially pay off a loan taken out by the group in 2020. “This will reduce the overall indebtedness of the group and strengthen its financial position, consistent with the group’s ongoing efforts to address its liabilities in an orderly manner,” Shimao said. Savills arranged the bidding process for the 1,219-room property on Lantau Island, near Tung Chung MTR station and Hong Kong International Airport. The receivers launched a global tender on June 23 and closed bidding on August 31. The HK$2.7 billion consideration is subject to adjustment and covers both the hotel properties and their operating business. The property, completed in 2020 and registering a gross floor area of around 610,000 square feet, was estimated to cost more than HK$10,000 per square foot to develop. Savills said no floor price had been set for the tender. AlixPartners’ Ge said the transaction was structured as two “interconditional” asset-sale agreements rather than a share transfer, allowing the buyer to acquire the hotel properties and operating business without taking on the indebtedness remaining in the borrower company. Ge said Shimao’s management had been cooperative throughout the receivership, providing information to facilitate the sale. Lenders to it had also supported the process, she said, adding that the sale was expected to be completed by the end of the year, subject to the buyer securing funding and the finalisation of transfer arrangements. AlixPartners and complex operator Marriott said in a separate statement that Marriott would continue to operate both hotels under their existing brands after the sale. A ParkCity spokesman described the acquisition as “a rare opportunity to own one of the largest hotel properties in Hong Kong, at the gateway to the Greater Bay Area”, and said it was being viewed as a “long-term investment”, citing the hotels’ proximity to the airport, the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge and planned developments. The hotels recorded a blended occupancy rate of about 85 per cent in the first quarter of this year. They also house one of Hong Kong’s largest event venues, featuring a 13,300 square foot column-free grand ballroom, function rooms and an outdoor garden, making them a destination for weddings and big events. Should the deal be completed as scheduled, it will be another in a string of Hong Kong commercial real estate acquisitions by Southeast Asian buyers this year. “We are seeing interest from both overseas and mainland Chinese investors in Hong Kong commercial properties, although buyers remain selective,” said Kelvin Li, director at Midland Commercial. “The attraction is not just pricing following the property market adjustment. Interest in Hong Kong’s stock market and broader investment opportunities is also encouraging investors to take a fresh look at the city, with commercial property among the asset classes they are considering.” By the middle of last month, Hong Kong had seen HK$30.36 billion worth of commercial property deals for properties selling for more than HK$50 million, according to data tracked by Savills. Southeast Asian investors contributed HK$3.37 billion – or more than 11 per cent – of the total value, Savills said. Mainland buyers contributed HK$1.75 billion, or 5.8 per cent, while Hong Kong-based capital accounted for HK$25.25 billion, or 83.2 per cent. Thomas Chak, head of capital markets and investment services at Colliers, said: “International capital is becoming increasingly active in Hong Kong’s investment market, where it contributed 30 per cent of total transaction value in the third quarter, the highest share since the fourth quarter of 2022, signalling renewed appetite for Hong Kong commercial real estate following the significant repricing of the market. “We are particularly seeing interest from Southeast Asian investors, including Singapore-based capital, as investors look beyond their home markets for assets offering attractive entry prices and longer-term upside.”

content: Hong Kong has ranked 24th in a global rule of law index, despite slipping slightly in the fundamental rights and criminal justice categories. The index, released by the World Justice Project on Wednesday, showed the city remained among the world’s top 10 for “absence of corruption” and “order and security”, rising to seventh in the latter category. The organisation said the global erosion of the rule of law slowed in 2026, but the overall decline continued, with 62 per cent of the 143 jurisdictions surveyed recording falls. The index assessed jurisdictions across eight aspects of the rule of law, scoring each on a scale of zero to one. Hong Kong’s overall score fell by 0.01 from last year to 0.71. Its score has declined steadily since peaking at 0.78 in 2016. The city remained sixth in East Asia and the Pacific. Responding to the ranking on Wednesday night, the government said: “Hong Kong’s scores in most of the aspects are similar to those of last year, and its overall ranking continues to be ahead of some Western countries, which often unreasonably criticise the rule of law and human rights situation of Hong Kong.” It added that the implementation of national security laws had better protected the city’s security and maintained “an excellent environment” for business and investment. Hong Kong remained 63rd globally for “constraints on government powers” and 20th for “civil justice”. Its score of 0.54 for constraints on government powers was its lowest across the eight categories, while its highest was 0.92 for “order and security”. The city slipped one place in each of the “absence of corruption”, “open government” and “regulatory enforcement” categories, ranking 10th, 29th and 16th respectively. Hong Kong’s largest declines were in the “fundamental rights” and “criminal justice” categories, with the city slipping two places in each – to 69th and 23rd respectively, from 67th and 21st in 2025. The government said it would continue to safeguard the rights and freedoms residents enjoyed under the law and step up its publicity and explanatory work. It also pledged to continue upholding the rule of law and safeguarding national sovereignty, security and development interests.

title: An AI apocalypse? Hong Kong’s real challenge is much less dramatic
description: For many of us, artificial intelligence (AI) started out as something to play with. We asked it to write poems and arrange our calendars; we shared its more entertaining mistakes. Then it became something to believe in: an escape from drudgery, an assistant to every profession, even perhaps the start of a new industrial revolution. Now it is something to fear. The progression has been astonishing. Governments are scrambling to draw up AI strategies, companies are reorganising operations and...
content: For many of us, artificial intelligence (AI) started out as something to play with. We asked it to write poems and arrange our calendars; we shared its more entertaining mistakes. Then it became something to believe in: an escape from drudgery, an assistant to every profession, even perhaps the start of a new industrial revolution. Now it is something to fear. The progression has been astonishing. Governments are scrambling to draw up AI strategies, companies are reorganising operations and investors are financing the infrastructure. The world seems to be mobilising at warp speed to join the AI rush, although there is rather less agreement about where we are going. Hong Kong’s sensitivity to this race was illuminated by a recent report that the Monetary Authority had questioned a major bank about its decision to establish its AI centre in Singapore and hire over 100 AI specialists there. The competitive anxiety is understandable. Attracting the investment, however, is not the same as preparing for the risks that accompany it. This gap should concern all of us. Investors may tolerate uncertainty, provided their AI investments deliver financial returns. A regulator cannot. Bringing AI into a business is one decision, but understanding what it may affect is another. The second decision is the one most easily skipped in a rush. Alongside this rush came the warnings from leading AI developers about the dangers of the technology they are advancing. There is an obvious irony. Some of those most concerned about the technology’s advance are also doing the most to advance it. Their businesses benefit from making their products more capable. While the conflict of interest is worth noting, it does not dispose of the argument. A warning can be self-serving without being wrong. But hearing a warning is not enough. For Hong Kong, the useful question is what companies should do. If companies adopt overseas tools carelessly, they risk importing someone else’s account of the problem along with the technology. This is where the government can step in to provide guidance. It is important to note that a model that helps an attacker has not, by that fact alone, defeated any organisational defence. The attacker still needs to identify the vulnerabilities and the opportunity to act. But some threats are not so forgiving. Familiar safeguards cannot be assumed to remain adequate simply because the threat sounds familiar. Fraud is old; the means of making it convincing are not. Besides, AI tools are improving by leaps and bounds, and while AI did not invent identity fraud, it can make age-old deception far more scalable. A case reported by the Hong Kong police last month illustrates the point. Investigators alleged that a syndicate used identity-card images, photo-editing software and AI tools to create false documents for online account applications. Most were automatically rejected, but some slipped through. The problem is not confined to bad actors. Last month, it was reported that unrepresented litigants were making error-strewn legal references, including citing non-existent ordinances – mistakes thought to be due to the use of generative AI. There was no malice but the risk to trust is real. The court was not fooled but those without legal training might have been easily persuaded. The danger is not merely that the machine gets something wrong. It is that users wield the tool irresponsibly. A large-language-model assistant on a phone can make expertise look deceptively easy, but true professional qualifications often require years of training. The time experts have to spend separating the wheat from the chaff is only part of the cost; others may act on the errors before anyone catches them. Hong Kong’s government is examining the legal implications. The Department of Justice is leading an interdepartmental review of legislation to support wider AI use, while government policy also addresses AI-enabled crime, liability and the management of AI agents. That is welcome. But the law is one thing; equipping people to understand it is another. Hong Kong’s judicial guidance on generative AI, for example, stresses the importance of understanding the technology’s limitations and verifying its output. If even the legal profession requires such supervision, what hope has the layman? “Human oversight” is a reassuring phrase, but it means little if the person supposedly in charge is kept in the dark about how the system reached its conclusion. Oversight is meaningful only where the person can actually interrogate the result, and that capacity matters most in high-stakes domains. None of this requires us to treat every application as dangerous. Translating a routine document is not equivalent to approving a loan. Where AI accelerates an existing threat, augmented defences may suffice. However, where AI changes the chain of authority, something new is needed. For example, AI agents may be handy, but what happens when an agent acts on faulty instructions? Suppose an AI agent wrongfully signs a contract on a principal’s behalf. Would that bind the parties? The question is no longer hypothetical. Talk of an AI apocalypse attracts attention because it is dramatic. The challenge is less theatrical: preventing the gradual transfer of judgment to systems whose answers are easier to accept than to challenge.

title: Beijing hits out after Taipei bans mainland travel for Sun Yat-sen anniversary
description: A fresh dispute has erupted between Beijing and Taipei over commemorations for Sun Yat-sen, a Chinese revolutionary hero who is revered on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. Beijing on Wednesday lashed out at Taipei’s move to ban Taiwanese officials from attending events in the mainland Chinese capital marking the 160th anniversary of Sun’s birth on November 12. Sun brought an end to more than 2,000 years of imperial rule when he founded the Republic of China (ROC) in 1912, and he also founded the...
content: A fresh dispute has erupted between Beijing and Taipei over commemorations for Sun Yat-sen, a Chinese revolutionary hero who is revered on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. Beijing on Wednesday lashed out at Taipei’s move to ban Taiwanese officials from attending events in the mainland Chinese capital marking the 160th anniversary of Sun’s birth on November 12. Sun brought an end to more than 2,000 years of imperial rule when he founded the Republic of China (ROC) in 1912, and he also founded the Kuomintang (KMT). After the civil war ended in 1949, the KMT government fled to Taiwan and the People’s Republic of China was established on the mainland by Mao Zedong and the Communist Party. Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the mainland’s Taiwan Affairs Office, condemned the travel ban by Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) as a “betrayal of history” that would “heighten cross-strait confrontation”. Beijing last year said it would host a grand celebration for the 160th birthday of Sun. President Xi Jinping delivered a speech at the 150th commemoration for Sun a decade ago and is expected to do so again this year. It is the first time the DPP has formally blocked Taiwanese from taking part in mainland Chinese events honouring Sun, who died in 1925. Sun remains one of the few historical figures claimed and honoured by both Beijing and Taipei. Last week, Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council said it would reject travel permit applications from Taiwanese officials seeking to attend the official commemorations in Beijing. It urged “all sectors” to refrain from travelling to mainland China, Hong Kong or Macau to take part in related events. High-ranking retired defence and security officials were also reminded of the island’s statutory rules prohibiting participation in political events hosted by mainland authorities. At least 32 retired Taiwanese military officials and several retired senior KMT figures were among the 3,000 attendees of the 150th anniversary event at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing a decade ago. The Mainland Affairs Council accused Beijing of distorting historical facts surrounding Sun and claimed the Communist Party used commemorative events as propaganda tools to advance its “anti-independence, pro-reunification” narrative. In Taiwan, Sun is venerated as the founding father of the ROC, which remains the island’s official name after the ROC relocated its seat of government there in 1949. In mainland China meanwhile, Sun is officially celebrated as the “Great Forerunner of the Democratic Revolution” and Beijing invokes his legacy as part of its narrative of national reunification. Zhang emphasised this point on Wednesday, saying Beijing’s commemorations aimed to “unite all Chinese people – including Taiwan compatriots – to firmly counter ‘Taiwan independence’ forces, reject external interference, and work together towards national reunification and revitalisation”. During his 2016 speech, Xi delivered a stern warning to pro-independence movements, saying: “We will never permit anyone, any group or any political party to split any portion of Chinese territory from the nation at any time or in any form.” Sun’s political lineage is another point of contention between Beijing and Taipei. At the 2016 event, Xi claimed that members of the Communist Party were “the most faithful successors of Sun Yat-sen’s revolutionary cause”. His statement drew immediate pushback from the KMT. Its officials countered that the Kuomintang remained the legitimate successor to Sun’s founding ideals, calling it an “undeniable historical fact that stands beyond debate”. For the DPP, with its emphasis on local identity, issues surrounding Sun pose a dilemma. DPP lawmakers have repeatedly introduced legislative amendments to end mandatory requirements for displaying Sun’s portrait in government spaces and school auditoriums, though these bills have stalled. Taipei’s travel ban also reflects a broader policy stance that has limited exchanges between the two sides. Similar restrictions were enforced last year when the DPP prohibited current and former officials from attending Beijing’s high-profile military parade in September. Taipei said it did not want to validate Beijing’s political framing. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons. Despite the tensions across the Taiwan Strait, Sun is also an enduring historical bridge. The KMT frequently invokes Sun’s legacy during cross-strait exchanges to emphasise shared cultural and historical bonds. During a trip to mainland China in April, KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun visited the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum in Nanjing, invoking his spirit to foster cross-strait peace and reconciliation. Responding to the DPP travel ban, KMT caucus secretary general Hsu Yu-chen said the party welcomed anyone commemorating Sun’s legacy. But she said any cross-strait exchange or joint commemoration must be conducted on the basis of parity, dignity and explicit recognition of the ROC’s existence.

title: Prabowo warns regional critics Indonesia won’t be ‘insulted’ over haze
description: Indonesia’s president railed against “countries that like to insult” his nation over wildfires that have razed vast areas, spewing toxic haze into neighbouring countries. The Southeast Asian giant has for months struggled to contain fires that Nusantara Atlas, an independent monitor analysing satellite data, said had consumed more than 1.9 million hectares (4.7 million acres) in the nine months to September. The haze has sent air pollution levels surging to dangerous levels not only at home, but...
content: Indonesia’s president railed against “countries that like to insult” his nation over wildfires that have razed vast areas, spewing toxic haze into neighbouring countries. The Southeast Asian giant has for months struggled to contain fires that Nusantara Atlas, an independent monitor analysing satellite data, said had consumed more than 1.9 million hectares (4.7 million acres) in the nine months to September. The haze has sent air pollution levels surging to dangerous levels not only at home, but also in Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor, prompting the Asean regional bloc to call a meeting over the crisis. “As for certain countries that like to insult the Indonesian nation, when the time comes, we will reveal the companies involved,” Prabowo Subianto told a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, claiming that “many corporations bear responsibility” for the crisis. He did not name names or nationalities. The leaders of Indonesia’s neighbours have offered help while steering clear of overt criticism at the highest diplomatic level. With public anger growing, however, a Malaysian MP last week called for Indonesia to be treated as an “outcast” in the region. “Indonesia is a polite and patient nation. Our country is often insulted, but believe me, our nation does not want to be insulted all the time,” Prabowo said. The president said he had asked for investigations into the cause of the fires which he insisted was “not purely natural”. Experts say Indonesia’s wildfires can be blamed in large part on slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that result in the destruction of fire-resistant forest cover and drained peatlands. This year, the blazes were intensified by a severe drought fuelled by the El Nino weather phenomenon. “I am asking the police, the Attorney General’s Office, the Ministry of Forestry, with the support of the Armed Forces and intelligence services, to investigate,” Prabowo said. “The people have also caught various individuals who deliberately set fires – this is something we can regard as environmental terrorism.” The president, who marked two years in office on Tuesday with record-low approval levels, said deliberate fire-setting amounted to “a crime against humanity, because what they have done endangers the health of millions of our citizens”. Once the evidence is in, he added, “we will revoke all licenses of companies that violate the law”. Lawsuit in Pontianak Residents of Indonesian Borneo have urged the government to do more to combat the wildfires. They spoke out as a court in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, began hearing arguments on Wednesday into the admissibility of a case brought against the state by residents in the province of nearly six million people. “The issue … is not merely about burning forests and land; it is also closely tied to public health, air quality, economic activity, education and the safety of residents,” resident Achmad Mundzirin, 36, said. “This lawsuit serves as a means to demand that the government be held accountable for its handling of forest and land fires.” Lawyers have filed a class action case claiming “negligence, omission and failure” on the part of the government that has resulted in “a massive public health crisis” in West Kalimantan. It singles out Prabowo and 26 officials from the national, provincial and local governments, as well as police and emergency services. Glorio Sanen, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, told reporters the community was suffering. “The president must directly lead the handling of this smoke disaster so that our aspirations, our hope for fresh air, blue skies and sunshine can return here in West Kalimantan,” he said. For Pontianak resident Andi Fachrizal, 54, the court case held “important meaning for the environmental struggle”. “This legal process is a moment to reaffirm that the public’s right to a good and healthy environment is not merely a norm enshrined in laws and regulations, but a right that must be protected and fulfilled by the state,” he said.

title: Hong Kong raids spark health warning over beauty jabs using dead people’s skin
description: Experts have warned of the infection risks associated with an anti-ageing beauty treatment known as “cadaver-derived skin injection” amid growing interest in the treatment, as authorities crack down on beauty premises offering services with unregistered products. The warnings came a day after the Department of Health revealed it had seized vials of an injectable product called Elravie Re20, which claims to contain human tissue, following raids on four beauty premises in the city on Friday and...
content: Experts have warned of the infection risks associated with an anti-ageing beauty treatment known as “cadaver-derived skin injection” amid growing interest in the treatment, as authorities crack down on beauty premises offering services with unregistered products. The warnings came a day after the Department of Health revealed it had seized vials of an injectable product called Elravie Re20, which claims to contain human tissue, following raids on four beauty premises in the city on Friday and Tuesday. A 38-year-old woman was arrested during the operation. Health authorities said the product, carrying Korean packaging, was classified as a “regulated product” under the Human Organ Transplant Ordinance, as well as a “pharmaceutical product”. The department had also referred other cases involving the products contravening the ordinance to police, which on Wednesday confirmed they were following up. The department had received an application for an exemption of a “regulated product” and was still processing it, but had not received any application for it as a “pharmaceutical product”. According to Humedix, the Korean distributor of Elravie Re20, the product contains materials called human acellular dermal matrix, which is derived from processed human tissue. The company claims the product can help improve skin blemishes and pores. Korean beauty clinics have also set up webpages in Chinese making claims about the product’s anti-ageing effects. But Dr Peter Pang Chi-wang, a specialist in plastic surgery, warned that products containing human tissue could carry unknown pathogens. “The product is claimed to be acellular, meaning all cells have been removed and suggesting it’s sterile. But are bacteria found in cells only?” he said. “The safety of the product has not been proven yet.” Pang also said the claimed benefits of the product remained uncertain, as there were records showing that injection of medical substances or saline solution, or purely microneedling, could also help reduce pores and tighten skin. Dermatologist Dr Kingsley Chan Hau-ngai also warned of possible infection risks when using unregistered injection products. “Cadavers are not that clean, how can they ensure the pathogens are removed?” he said. “Also, how are the products stored? If they have been stored for a long time, there could also be bacteria, fungi or virus growing.” Chan added that the product sounded like a gimmick and not a product supported by strong evidence. Dr Fung Ying, controller of regulatory affairs at the department, warned on Tuesday that the product lacked clinical safety data and could pose public health risks. The South China Morning Post reporter posing as a customer contacted the Korean Aesthetic Surgery Centre Hong Kong, a local medical beauty clinic that claims to be the only authorised distributor of Re20 in Hong Kong, to ask whether the injection was available. A staff member said the injection was not yet available as it had not been approved by the government. On social media platforms, posts from users believed to be in Hong Kong and Taiwan discussed Re20. In a statement released last month, the clinic claimed that the product was made from donor skin from the United States. Each donor was also thoroughly evaluated, including their cause of death, medical history and blood and microbiology tests. Nelson Ip Sai-hung, founding chairman of the Federation of Beauty Industry, noted discussion about Re20 had increased recently. “It is a trending topic recently … Many people were talking about it and saying how magical it is,” Ip said. But not many of his peers were offering the product, he said, adding that it was difficult to source. Ip urged consumers to exercise caution when trying new beauty treatments. “It is not a bad thing to observe a bit. There must be a reason why the product has not yet been registered in Hong Kong,” Ip said. “When you are not clear about a new product, is there a need to be impulsive and try?”

title: China’s Unitree unveils ‘guardian’ robot that can disarm attackers, lift cars
description: A knife-wielding intruder is confronted. A car is lifted to free a trapped victim. A pedestrian is pulled from the path of an oncoming vehicle. The scenes described are not from a Hollywood blockbuster, but a promotional clip for a new “guardian” robot created by the Chinese technology firm Unitree Robotics. The footage for the H2-X model, released on Wednesday, underscores a wider shift in strategy by the Hangzhou-based firm, as it focuses on finding practical, real-world uses for its athletic...
content: A knife-wielding intruder is confronted. A car is lifted to free a trapped victim. A pedestrian is pulled from the path of an oncoming vehicle. The scenes described are not from a Hollywood blockbuster, but a promotional clip for a new “guardian” robot created by the Chinese technology firm Unitree Robotics. The footage for the H2-X model, released on Wednesday, underscores a wider shift in strategy by the Hangzhou-based firm, as it focuses on finding practical, real-world uses for its athletic robots. Unitree shot to fame with a series of viral stunts – with its robots performing martial arts routines, dances and somersaults – helping the company raise massive amounts of capital. But China’s robotics industry is now coming under growing pressure to deliver commercial returns. Unitree recently signalled a pivot towards practical capabilities. Last month, the company announced that its UnifoLM-X2-1.0 artificial intelligence model allowed humanoid robots to spar autonomously by punching, blocking and dodging. The H2-X – dubbed “Kung Fu Legend: Guardian” – builds on Unitree’s H2 model, a full-sized humanoid standing 1.8 metres tall and weighing about 70kg. According to its product description, the earlier model had 31 degrees of freedom and a maximum leg-joint torque of 360 newton metres – though Unitree did not confirm whether the H2-X would retain these specifications. The company said the newer model could operate for about eight hours while standing, but did not disclose when the robot would go on sale, how much it would cost, or provide detailed technical specifications. Unitree also did not clarify whether the actions shown in the promotional video were performed autonomously or were choreographed in some way. Nor did it say whether the H2-X could independently identify threats and respond safely in unscripted environments. Unitree concluded the video with a warning against dangerous modifications and unauthorised uses, advising customers to maintain a safety buffer of at least two to three metres from the unit. When contacted for comment on Wednesday, a company representative declined to provide additional details, stating that “everything is subject to the official announcement video”. The new robot’s unveiling comes as Unitree and its peers face heightened scrutiny from investors demanding clear paths to sustainable revenue growth, technological moats and viable deployment scenarios. Unitree’s shares closed down 2.1 per cent at 515 yuan on Wednesday, snapping a three-day rally that had seen the stock gain nearly 30 per cent. The stock is down about 39 per cent from its debut price of 845 yuan, achieved during its listing on Shanghai’s Star market in August. In a regulatory filing on Tuesday, the company said it was unaware of any undisclosed information driving a recent unusual stock price movement.

title: Takaichi remains popular with Japanese public. Can she maintain her grip on LDP?
description: Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has marked one year in office still riding relatively high in public opinion polls – a heady position that few political analysts anticipated despite geopolitical tensions and persistent inflation. A poll by the conservative-leaning Yomiuri newspaper published on Monday indicated that Takaichi’s cabinet retains the support of 57 per cent of the Japanese public, down two percentage points from the previous survey on September 18 and significantly lower than...
content: Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has marked one year in office still riding relatively high in public opinion polls – a heady position that few political analysts anticipated despite geopolitical tensions and persistent inflation. A poll by the conservative-leaning Yomiuri newspaper published on Monday indicated that Takaichi’s cabinet retains the support of 57 per cent of the Japanese public, down two percentage points from the previous survey on September 18 and significantly lower than the 73 per cent recorded in December and February, but still a figure that her predecessors would have envied. Takaichi has certainly hit some bumps on the political road over the last year, including firing her agriculture minister last week over allegations that he refused to fund municipalities that did not support him. Analysts, however, agree that Takaichi has shown remarkable resilience. The question is how long she can retain support from both the electorate and her ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), where discontent is simmering within some factions. “It has been extremely surprising,” said Hiromi Murakami, a professor of political science at the Tokyo branch of Temple University. “She has managed to keep a relatively high support rate when her predecessors saw their support decline very rapidly [in their first year].” Murakami believes that part of Takaichi’s success has been her consistency in communicating what she is trying to achieve. “Her biggest achievement has been stability in her support, which has allowed her to stick to her policies,” Murakami said. Murakami added that conservatives were delighted with two pieces of legislation that Takaichi had passed – making defacing the hinomaru national flag a crime and revising the Imperial Household Law, which effectively makes it impossible for a woman to ascend to the Chrysanthemum Throne. “I still find it puzzling that even though we have a weak yen, rising interest rates, inflation and other economic issues, these have not really hurt her standing with the public.” Takaichi, who marked a year in office on Wednesday, is pushing legislation through the Diet that will cut the 8 per cent consumption tax on basic food items for two years to tackle the cost of living crisis, even though economists say the reduction would have a limited impact. “It is odd that until now she has not made changes that positively affect people’s lives but she still has support,” Murakami said. “The only explanation I can suggest is that people believe she is trying her hardest and they still have high hopes.” Toshimitsu Shigemura, a professor of politics at Tokyo’s Waseda University, also admits to being surprised at the resilient public support for Takaichi, which he attributes partly to her gender. “Her support rate among women has fallen slightly, but it is still relatively high. I think that is in part because Japan has only ever had male prime ministers in the past and a lot of female voters have reached the conclusion that they are all liars who say one thing to get elected and then immediately go back on their word when they are in power,” Shigemura said. Female voters also like the consumption tax cut, which will help with household budgets, and they can relate to Takaichi’s frequent remarks on being a hard-working woman in a man’s world, according to Shigemura. Takaichi has said she sleeps just a few hours each day because of her responsibilities as prime minister and that she still has to do household chores and put on her make-up before work. Still, analysts agree that Takaichi may find the year ahead trickier to navigate on the domestic and international fronts than her first year in office. Relations with China are at a low, with little indication that they may improve any time soon, and this poses serious security and trade challenges for Tokyo, according to Murukami. Ties with North Korea remain tense while the previously stable relationship with Moscow has worsened in recent months, particularly over the Ukraine conflict. And it remains to be seen if Takaichi can maintain her rapport with President Donald Trump following the US midterm elections. “Lots of challenges appear to be piling up for the prime minister now, and if the economic situation at home does not begin to show signs of improving, I wonder how long the people who are still supporting her will remain patient,” Murakami said. “She has made promises, and now she really needs to start delivering or public opinion could turn quite quickly.” For now, Takaichi is untouchable as LDP’s leader, even though the party’s “old guard” are reportedly bristling at her independence after they agreed to Takaichi becoming prime minister on the assumption they could control her, according to Murakami. The key threshold for Takaichi is at least 40 per cent public support ahead of the next party leadership election in one year from now, and she may yet again surprise political pundits with her staying power, Murakami said. “She is safe now, but as soon as her support rate starts to decline, I think there are factions within the party who will turn on her.”

title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi strikes shake kingdom
description: The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and family members to depart ‌from its missions in Saudi Arabia and plans to withdraw family members from a number of other US missions in the region, US officials said. The order came as attacks in Saudi Arabia killed at least one person and injured eight others at a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people were killed in a drone attack on an oilfield. US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a post on social media ⁠that the...
content: The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and family members to depart ‌from its missions in Saudi Arabia and plans to withdraw family members from a number of other US missions in the region, US officials said. The order came as attacks in Saudi Arabia killed at least one person and injured eight others at a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people were killed in a drone attack on an oilfield. US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a post on social media ⁠that the department ordered the departure of “non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only” amid attacks ‌by the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen on civilian targets in the country. Washington had returned some diplomatic personnel to the region in recent months after many were pulled out when Tehran launched ‌attacks on US facilities after the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February. “Iranian-supported Houthis have ⁠increasingly engaged in hostilities against ⁠Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” Pigott said. Four US officials said that US missions in other Gulf states would also be ordering family members to leave. Pigott did not address changes to other missions outside Saudi ‌Arabia. The relocations also appear to extend beyond diplomatic staff. NBC News reported Wednesday that American military personnel were being pulled out of bases across the Middle East due to regional threats, citing unnamed US officials. When asked about the report, US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a US Central Command spokesman, said: “We regularly move US service members and assets to optimise mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons”. The latest ‌withdrawals follow an escalation of the fighting in Yemen, opening another front in the regional conflict triggered by the ‌US-Israeli war on Iran. The wider conflict has snarled global energy trade and hurt Gulf economies. After the departure order, ⁠Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority reported an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam that killed one person and ⁠injured eight others. Earlier in the day, two people were killed after Saudi air defences intercepted a drone that was attempting to hit a facility at Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield, the energy ministry said. The US ‌embassy in Riyadh issued a ‌security alert on Wednesday about possible further attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia, after recent deadly strikes including on Riyadh’s airport. The embassy and a CIA station hosted there came under attack by drones in early March, as Iran began launching attacks across the region. Across the Gulf late on Wednesday, signs of fresh volatility emerged as Iranian state media reported the sound of explosions in the southern Hormozgan province overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, breaking a spell of relative calm. “A few minutes ago, the sound of several explosions was heard in the Karpan area of Sirik, in Hormozgan Province,” the official IRNA news agency said. It added that “local sources have not yet disclosed the nature of these explosions”. The strikes launched earlier this year by the United States and Israel killed Iran’s supreme leader along with senior military commanders, touching off months of retaliatory exchanges. Iran has attempted to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, demanding all ships seek its authorisation to cross. In peacetime, the strategic waterway carried around a fifth of the world’s oil supplies. In retaliation, the United States has imposed a counterblockade on Iranian ports and ships. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse and Bloomberg

title: Could Hong Kong’s student housing boom lure property giants off the sidelines?
description: Hong Kong’s largest landlords and developers could get their first formal route into the rising student accommodation market after the government announced plans to tender land for a purpose-built student hostel this quarter, according to analysts. Development Secretary Bernadette Linn Hon-ho announced on Thursday last week the inclusion of a 1,100 square metre (11,840 square foot) site for student accommodation as one of two land tenders in the October to December quarter. The plot – at the...
content: Hong Kong’s largest landlords and developers could get their first formal route into the rising student accommodation market after the government announced plans to tender land for a purpose-built student hostel this quarter, according to analysts. Development Secretary Bernadette Linn Hon-ho announced on Thursday last week the inclusion of a 1,100 square metre (11,840 square foot) site for student accommodation as one of two land tenders in the October to December quarter. The plot – at the junction of Yuen Shun Circuit and Yuen Hong Street in Siu Lek Yuen, Sha Tin – is expected to provide 600 hostel places. “The tender of a dedicated PBSA [purpose-built student accommodation] site could be an important catalyst for Hong Kong’s major developers to take a closer look at the sector,” said Kathy Lee, head of research and retail consultancy at property consultancy Colliers in Hong Kong. “If the tender terms and land premium allow for commercially viable returns, we believe it could encourage joint ventures between established local developers and experienced PBSA investors or operators, as it involves new-build development.” Hong Kong could face a shortfall of 100,000 student beds in the 2027-28 academic year, Colliers estimated. Education-related assets, including student accommodation and education-facility transactions, were the main driver of investment demand in Hong Kong’s property market in the third quarter of 2026, accounting for 43 per cent of the HK$10.7 billion (US$1.36 billion) of deals completed during the period, according to Colliers. Recent transactions included Singapore-based Wee Hur Holdings’ acquisition of One Bedford Place, an 18,141 square foot office building in Tai Kok Tsui, for HK$748.8 million in June. Wee Hur said it planned to convert the property into a 500-bed student housing project. Meanwhile, Centurion Holdings had provisionally agreed to buy Yan Wo Building in North Point for HK$364 million, according to Land Registry records dated August 25. The company reportedly planned to convert the property into student housing. While the sector has emerged as one of the most attractive segments of Hong Kong’s property market, major developers have yet to make significant investments. Nicholas To, senior associate director for investment at property consultant Savills Hong Kong, said the lack of large-scale deals did not reflect a lack of interest. “Several big players are actively looking into the student housing segment, but they just haven’t found anything that is suitable for them,” said To. “Many of the properties converted into student housing were worth only a few hundred million Hong Kong dollars and, for big players, those [deals] were too small. This is why big developers and other big groups have not really invested in the sector.” To also said he expected that the Sha Tin tender could finally open the door for major developers to enter the student housing sector, even as investment yields had moderated to about 5 per cent from 5.8 to 6 per cent previously. “In recent years Hong Kong has seen several student hostel transactions, so yields have slightly declined,” he said. “For new investors, it is less attractive.”

title: “Talent in, Impact Out”: Inside The Education University of Hong Kong's vision for an interconnected world of talent and expertise
description: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] The Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) pursues a dual internationalisation strategy: attracting talented students, scholars and researchers from around the world while exporting educational and research expertise to communities beyond Hong Kong. “We live in an interconnected world that goes beyond the West, and it should be viewed as a highly connected whole,” says EdUHK President Professor John Lee Chi-Kin....
content: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] The Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) pursues a dual internationalisation strategy: attracting talented students, scholars and researchers from around the world while exporting educational and research expertise to communities beyond Hong Kong. “We live in an interconnected world that goes beyond the West, and it should be viewed as a highly connected whole,” says EdUHK President Professor John Lee Chi-Kin. “When we welcome students and scholars from diverse backgrounds, they bring different approaches to learning, teaching and research, and help cultivate global citizens who respect every culture.” “Partnerships are not one-off events but sustained, ever-growing relationships,” he adds. “As we mark the 10th anniversary of the University’s retitling, our next decade is about education with impact: attracting and nurturing talents who contribute to social good in Hong Kong SAR, China, and the world.” The journeys of three faculty members bring this vision to life. Bringing international expertise to Hong Kong Professor Andrew Mark Edwards joined EdUHK in 2025, among a growing number of international scholars drawn to the University. He now serves as Associate Dean (International Engagement) of the Faculty of Liberal Arts and Social Sciences (FLASS). He previously held senior academic positions in the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand, and is internationally recognised for his research in exercise physiology and psychophysiology. “I was drawn to Hong Kong by its ambitious and highly supportive higher education environment. Higher education is deeply valued here, and the opportunities to make an impact through research and teaching are strong,” he says. “EdUHK offers a distinctive focus on education while embracing interdisciplinary research and innovation. Within my first year at EdUHK, I secured a competitive General Research Fund grant. The University has been highly supportive in helping me establish my research programme, including supporting an international PhD student from the Netherlands to join my research group.” The University's commitment to building international networks and fostering global collaboration left a strong impression on Edwards. Shortly after joining EdUHK, he was invited by the President to help the Head of Department organise a major international conference. "Shaping the Future: Sport, Health and Education 2026", which will be held in November. As Associate Dean (International Engagement), Edwards is also helping to advance a wider programme of international engagement across FLASS, covering staff mobility, international partnership development and global impact initiatives. “What impressed me most was its openness to new ideas and international collaboration. The University provides a supportive environment where academics can exchange ideas, expand global networks and create research with real-world impact,” he notes. A strategic focus on Belt and Road countries EdUHK actively promotes international educational collaboration, with a particular focus on Belt and Road countries. One notable example is its longstanding partnership with Kazakhstan, which includes the establishment of the EdUHK-Kazakh Academy of Education in Almaty, and a major student recruitment initiative. Dr Artem Zadorozhnyy, now an Assistant Professor in the Department of English Language Education at EdUHK, first encountered the University at a recruitment talk promoting its PhD programmes at Nazarbayev University in Astana, Kazakhstan, while he was pursuing a master's degree in multilingual education. Inspired by the opportunities available, he chose to undertake his doctoral studies at EdUHK under the highly competitive Hong Kong PhD Fellowship Scheme. After completing his PhD, he secured a grant under the RGC Postdoctoral Fellowship Scheme, placing him firmly on the path towards becoming a promising early-career researcher. The appeal of EdUHK lies in its generous support, world-class research environment and strong reputation in technology-enhanced language education, Zadorozhnyy explains. “I found an inspiring academic community at EdUHK, where scholars are engaged in rigorous, collaborative, and socially meaningful research. What particularly appealed to me was EdUHK’s emphasis on interdisciplinary collaboration, where fields such as language education, digital learning and computer science intersect to generate innovative research,” he says. Exporting research expertise and creating global impact Integral to EdUHK’s internationalisation strategy is the export of expertise through international research partnerships and capacity-building projects that create tangible benefits for communities worldwide. One example is the work of Dr Deng Wenjing, Acting Head of the Department of Science and Environmental Studies and Associate Professor at FLASS, who has built an international research collaboration from a project examining environmental risks in schools. Aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, the initiative demonstrates how EdUHK translates research excellence into practical solutions while informing policymaking in several Belt and Road countries. “Our team was the first in Hong Kong to identify endocrine-disrupting chemicals in indoor school environments,” Deng says. “By working closely with international partners, we have transformed research findings into practical tools, STEM learning programmes and school-based interventions that help create healthier learning environments across Belt and Road countries.” Deng’s team has developed monitoring technologies, educational resources and policy-support tools that help schools better understand environmental health risks and respond effectively. “Because environmental challenges vary across regions, we work with local universities, schools and education authorities to co-create solutions tailored to each community’s needs,” she explains. Through portable air-quality sensors, hands-on monitoring activities and STEM learning resources, the team empowers local educators and students to improve their own environments. “Through initiatives in Sri Lanka, Nepal, Malaysia, Indonesia and Guangxi, Chinese Mainland, we have reached more than 3,000 students and educators.” “The success of this work demonstrates how international collaboration, built on local ownership and co-creation, can generate lasting impact,” Deng adds. Deng’s achievements also reflect EdUHK’s commitment to fostering an inclusive academic ecosystem that provides opportunities for talented and dedicated scholars regardless of gender or background. “I am grateful for the many opportunities at the University. I think I have made a mark as a woman in science,” she says. EdUHK’s internationalisation strategy demonstrates how Hong Kong serves as a welcoming, dynamic and globally connected education hub, where scholars from diverse backgrounds and at different stages of their careers can thrive, contribute and create meaningful global impact.

title: Unvaccinated girl, 12, becomes Hong Kong’s second child flu death this season
description: A 12-year-old unvaccinated girl has become the second child to die after suffering from influenza A since the current flu season began in Hong Kong in late June, the Centre for Health Protection has said. Centre controller Edwin Tsui Lok-kin said on Wednesday that local influenza activity remained at a high level. “I urge the public not to take influenza lightly, and to take appropriate preventive measures, including receiving [a vaccination] as early as possible in order to build an immunity...
content: A 12-year-old unvaccinated girl has become the second child to die after suffering from influenza A since the current flu season began in Hong Kong in late June, the Centre for Health Protection has said. Centre controller Edwin Tsui Lok-kin said on Wednesday that local influenza activity remained at a high level. “I urge the public not to take influenza lightly, and to take appropriate preventive measures, including receiving [a vaccination] as early as possible in order to build an immunity barrier in the community and reduce the risk of severe illness and death,” he said. The girl, who had underlying health conditions, developed a fever, cough and diarrhoea on Saturday, followed by vomiting. Her condition deteriorated on Monday evening and she was taken to the accident and emergency department of Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital in Chai Wan, the centre said. She suffered a cardiac arrest and was resuscitated, then admitted to the paediatric intensive care unit for treatment. Her respiratory specimen tested positive for influenza A (H1) virus. Her clinical diagnosis was influenza A infection complicated by septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure. The girl died on Tuesday. A preliminary investigation found that she had no travel history during the incubation period and had not received the 2026-27 seasonal influenza vaccination. One of her household contacts recently developed mild upper respiratory symptoms, but did not require hospitalisation. The centre will continue to investigate the case, which will be referred to the coroner. Since the city entered the flu season in late June, 25 cases of severe paediatric influenza infection have been recorded, the same as during the same period last season. Twenty patients recovered and have been discharged from hospital. One was in a serious condition, two were in a critical condition and two died, including a seven-year-old boy in August. The boy had previously been in good health and had received the 2025-26 seasonal influenza vaccination. His respiratory specimen tested positive for influenza A (H3) virus. His clinical diagnosis was influenza A infection complicated by shock and encephalopathy. The rate of severe complications or death following influenza infection was around five times higher among unvaccinated children than among vaccinated children, according to the centre’s data last year. Among unvaccinated residents aged 65 years or older living in care homes for the elderly, the rate of severe complications was around four times higher than among vaccinated residents. Since the new academic year began in September, nearly 460 influenza-like illness outbreaks have been recorded in schools, affecting about 2,800 people. Schools and parents have been urged to remain vigilant and take preventive measures. The centre said it expected influenza activity to continue fluctuating at high levels in the coming weeks. Tsui warned that children with influenza could deteriorate rapidly. Parents should pay close attention to the condition of their children and visit an accident and emergency department immediately if they develop symptoms such as shortness of breath, wheezing, blue lips, chest pain, confusion, a persistent fever or convulsions.
