content: Hong Kong police are investigating after two local media outlets received suspicious letters containing white powder – believed to be crushed oatmeal – sent from the United Kingdom. Police said that at around 3pm on Wednesday, online media outlet HK01 received an airmail letter delivered from the UK at its Kwai Chung office. Staff at the office in Tower 1 of Ever Gain Plaza opened the letter and found suspicious white powder inside. They subsequently called police. The police force deployed officers from its explosive ordnance disposal bureau while the Fire Services Department sent its hazardous materials team to handle the letter. The force’s Counter Terrorism Response Unit also arrived at the scene. The Kwai Tsing district crime squad is investigating the case. HK01 later issued a statement strongly condemning all despicable acts that attempted to incite panic or intimidate journalists and interfere with editorial independence through the use of hazardous items or threatening letters. At about 6.21pm, the Ta Kung Wen Wei Media Group’s Aberdeen office at Hing Wai Centre also received a letter containing suspicious powder. Dot Dot News, the group’s online media outlet, confirmed on its website that its staff had received the letter and heard the sound of powder when shaking it. They subsequently called police. The outlet strongly condemned any acts attempting to interfere with normal journalism through improper means. Both cases were classified as a “request for police assistance”. A police source said initial investigations indicated that both envelopes contained crushed oatmeal sent from the United Kingdom. No credible chemical, biological or radiological agents had been found so far. The letters were taken away for testing, with the results pending.

title: Hong Kong semi-private schools admit 20 more non-local students under expansion scheme
description: About 20 more non-local students have been admitted to Hong Kong semi-private schools under a government scheme to boost the city’s status as an international education hub, with a principal urging authorities to do more to promote the initiative to prospective pupils. Education authorities said on Wednesday that the non-local students holding student visas this year came from countries including Thailand, South Korea, Singapore, the United States and several European nations. Ida Lee Bik-sai,...
content: About 20 more non-local students have been admitted to Hong Kong semi-private schools under a government scheme to boost the city’s status as an international education hub, with a principal urging authorities to do more to promote the initiative to prospective pupils. Education authorities said on Wednesday that the non-local students holding student visas this year came from countries including Thailand, South Korea, Singapore, the United States and several European nations. Ida Lee Bik-sai, deputy secretary for education, wrote on the bureau’s blog that 170 non-local pupils holding student visas had enrolled in Direct Subsidy Scheme (DSS) schools on a self-financing basis, up 13 per cent from last year. The schools cover both primary and secondary levels. The figures imply that there were about 150 such non-local students in the last school year, before the roll-out of the new expansion scheme, which drew around 20 more pupils this year. “This school year, non-local students holding student visas come from a wide range of countries, including Thailand, South Korea, Singapore, European countries and the US,” Lee said, describing the pilot scheme as having had a “good start”. She added that besides the seven DSS schools that had admitted non-local students for two consecutive years, seven more DSS schools had admitted overseas students this school year. Under the expansion scheme introduced in last year’s policy address, DSS schools that were already admitting non-local students with student visas can apply for dedicated additional places to take in more such students. DSS schools in Hong Kong are allowed to offer non-local curricula, such as the International Baccalaureate and international A-levels. Non-local students do not receive government subsidies, unlike local ones, and their intake will not affect local students’ chances of securing a place at those DSS schools, according to the policy. Lee said a total of 48 DSS schools had been approved to add classes or places for non-local students on a self-financing basis under the scheme. She added that the bureau would support the DSS sector in formulating a code of practice for operating student hostels”, setting standards for accommodation, hygiene, safety and warden arrangements in future. Samuel Cheng Kin-tak, principal of United Christian College (Kowloon East), said his school had also admitted non-local students under the new scheme. Students must pay tuition fees of about HK$110,000 to HK$120,000 (US$14,015 to US$15,290) this year, as well as accommodation fees of about HK$52,000. He said the additional 20 students were in line with expectations, as some overseas parents had said they did not know Hong Kong schools could admit non-local students. He attributed this to a lack of promotion and financial support from the government. Cheng said the government had offered insufficient support for promotion work, adding that DSS schools had to pay for and conduct their own promotion. His school, for example, had promoted the scheme in Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia after the government announced the initiative. “All schools promoting the ‘Study in Hong Kong’ campaign have no difficulty admitting students, and our waiting lists are very long. We do it because we support the government’s policy,” he said. “But we also hope the government will support us financially in our promotion work, or our school managers will question why we have to pay for it.” He suggested that the government establish official scholarships during the scheme’s initial launch phase, rather than relying solely on private donations driven by the Direct Subsidy Scheme Schools Council. He noted that other countries used government resources to fund scholarships for international students, which offered larger financial awards and sent a stronger official signal that attracting non-local students was government policy. He said some non-local students were eyeing Hong Kong’s universities and even hoped to work in the city in the future, but the school had rejected some applicants because of their poor English proficiency.

title: Hong Kong to tighten media access to land records, triggering concerns
description: Hong Kong lawmakers and the media industry have raised concerns about the authorities’ plan to tighten arrangements for journalists searching land records, with some legislators urging the government to explain operational details and streamline the application to support investigative reporting. The Hong Kong Journalists Association voiced objections on Wednesday, after the government tabled eight pieces of subsidiary legislation, including the Land Titles Regulation that covers land record...
content: Hong Kong lawmakers and the media industry have raised concerns about the authorities’ plan to tighten arrangements for journalists searching land records, with some legislators urging the government to explain operational details and streamline the application to support investigative reporting. The Hong Kong Journalists Association voiced objections on Wednesday, after the government tabled eight pieces of subsidiary legislation, including the Land Titles Regulation that covers land record search arrangements, at the Legislative Council for negative vetting. Negative vetting involves enacting the law first and scrutinising it later. Most provisions, including the tightened search arrangements, will take effect in the first half of next year. The association said authorities had not justified the changes and had not consulted the public beforehand, stressing that the arrangements would weaken the public’s power to monitor the property market. “We call on the government to withdraw the provisions tightening land searches and to restore the long-standing position that existed before the amendments, under which land records could be inspected without any restriction,” the association said. The new search arrangements are the government’s latest move to tighten thresholds for public access to information, after it imposed restrictions on access to the vehicle registry and Companies Registry. The government said Hong Kong currently did not restrict who could access land records and documents, and the new arrangements were aimed at protecting privacy while ensuring the system’s transparency and efficiency. Under the new regime, only land record searches for nine specific purposes can be used to obtain essential information, such as the names of current and former owners, purchase prices, registration dates, encumbrances, application forms and supporting documents for current entries. Specific purposes include property valuation, due diligence for transactions, building management, legal proceedings, conducting academic and market research and conducting inspections in the public interest. The registrar will consider applications filed based on public interest individually, considering how the records would be used to serve the interests of society, if they outweigh the right to privacy and whether the documents would be misused, among other factors. Meanwhile, historical records, such as documents relating to previous property transfers or building orders that have been complied with, can only be accessed by 15 types of people. The list does not explicitly include journalists, but does allow those who declare that the applications are made in the public interest, current or former owners and professionals. The association doubted whether media outlets could secure approval from authorities, as most reporting could only establish links to the public interest after obtaining the records. “The new rules shut the gate before any evidence of public interest exists and require applicants to produce proof of public interest in order to have it opened, putting the cart before the horse,” it said. The association also expected land searches to be obstructed, as only one of the 17 applications made by media for vehicle registration particulars was partially approved after considerable delay. Lawmaker Rebecca Chan Hoi-yan, a former news editor at Now TV, urged the government to help media reporting under the new system. “Press freedom must be respected. When the public interest is involved, it is necessary for the media to conduct land record searches,” Chan said. “Is there a faster mechanism to get approval?” Chan cited the example of using a standardised application form endorsed by the news outlet’s management and collecting applications through the Information Services Department, the government’s communication agency for the media sector. Roundtable lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung also urged authorities to set clear criteria for assessing media applications. “Media needs to safeguard the public’s right to know, such as whether lawmakers have failed to declare conflicts of interest [on land matters],” he said. “At least the operational details should be clearer, including the assessment details and some objective guidelines.” Election Committee lawmaker Andrew Lam Siu-lo, a town planner, said that while the changes would tighten the rules, there was still room for the media to conduct land searches if their reasons were deemed valid by the government. He said he supported the establishment of a bills committee to discuss the details of the amendment. Lawmaker Julia Lau Man-kwan, who represents the architectural, surveying, planning and landscape sector, explained that the subsidiary legislations were intended to streamline arrangements for agricultural land. She added that the mechanism offered news outlets to apply based on public interest.

title: Star Ferry fares to rise by up to HK$1.80 from January
description: Star Ferry fares are set to rise by as much as HK$1.80 (23 US cents) from January after Hong Kong authorities endorsed the operator’s application for an increase, taking the cost of a weekend cross-harbour trip to up to HK$8.30. The operator, which last raised its fares in 2023, applied in March to increase charges on its two franchised routes by between 80 HK cents and HK$2 per journey. Under a proposal approved by the Executive Council last Tuesday and announced on Wednesday, fares for the...
content: Star Ferry fares are set to rise by as much as HK$1.80 (23 US cents) from January after Hong Kong authorities endorsed the operator’s application for an increase, taking the cost of a weekend cross-harbour trip to up to HK$8.30. The operator, which last raised its fares in 2023, applied in March to increase charges on its two franchised routes by between 80 HK cents and HK$2 per journey. Under a proposal approved by the Executive Council last Tuesday and announced on Wednesday, fares for the Central-Tsim Sha Tsui and Wan Chai-Tsim Sha Tsui routes will rise from January 25 next year. After the adjustments, fares on the two routes will increase by 60 cents to HK$1 per trip on weekdays, and from HK$1 to HK$1.80 at weekends, capping adult tickets at HK$6 on weekdays and HK$8.30 on weekends. The monthly ticket price will remain unchanged at HK$190. Passengers covered by the government’s HK$2 fare concession scheme – residents aged 60 or above using JoyYou Cards and eligible people with disabilities – will continue to pay HK$2 per journey. A government spokesman on Wednesday justified the need for Star Ferry to raise its fares. He noted that Star Ferry had recorded “heavy accumulated losses” of more than HK$100 million between 2018 and 2023 because of factors including the Covid-19 pandemic, forcing it to rely on debt financing to operate its franchised services. “While the company recorded marginal profits in the past two years, it will continue to face severe financial pressure in the coming years and is expected to record losses again starting from 2026 due to slow patronage growth, limited room for cost-compression and continuous increases in operating costs and debt-related interest expenses,” the spokesman said. “Therefore, there is a need for Star Ferry to adjust its fares.” According to a Transport and Logistics Bureau paper released on Wednesday, tourists and local passengers, respectively, accounted for over 60 and about 40 per cent of the firm’s patronage. It noted Star Ferry had invested resources in upgrading its electronic payment system, crowd control measures, vessel deployment, maintenance of pier facilities and fleet, to refurbish its service and operational standards. Despite noting the need for the fare bump, the government said the rise should be “moderated to cater for the need of passengers.” “After the fare increase, Star Ferry is still the most affordable means of cross-harbour public transport, with fares about 30 per cent to 50 per cent lower than MTR or franchised bus fares,” it said. A single adult MTR trip from Admiralty or Central across the harbour to Tsim Sha Tsui costs HK$12.50, or HK$10.60 if paid with an Octopus card. For franchised daytime cross-harbour bus routes, single trips typically charge at least HK$12.20, depending on where the passenger boards. The government said it would continue to encourage Star Ferry to improve its long-term financial viability not only through fare adjustments but also other revenue, to preserve a historical landmark “filled with memories for Hong Kong”. “Running cross-harbour ferry services since 1898, Star Ferry is a key icon of Hong Kong,” the spokesman said.

title: Hong Kong tours avoid France protest areas as schools cancel planned trips
description: Tour operators have changed itineraries and pulled Hong Kong travellers away from protest hotspots in France, while some school groups have cancelled planned trips to the country following the issuance of an official travel warning. EGL Tours chairman and executive director Steve Huen Kwok-chuen said one of the company’s tour groups had encountered protests at the Louvre in Paris on Saturday, with police helping clear a route for their coach to return to the hotel. “Our tour group happened to be...
content: Tour operators have changed itineraries and pulled Hong Kong travellers away from protest hotspots in France, while some school groups have cancelled planned trips to the country following the issuance of an official travel warning. EGL Tours chairman and executive director Steve Huen Kwok-chuen said one of the company’s tour groups had encountered protests at the Louvre in Paris on Saturday, with police helping clear a route for their coach to return to the hotel. “Our tour group happened to be there that day when there were protests and unrest at the Louvre,” he said. “They boarded the coach, and police cleared the way so they could return to the hotel safely.” The group returned to the museum on Sunday without problems, Huen said, adding that the travellers had since left Paris. Hong Kong authorities on Tuesday issued an amber outbound travel alert for France, following weeks of protests that began as student demonstrations over poor school conditions, before widening into a broader movement against rising living costs and worsening public services. Heavy looting and clashes have been reported in major cities such as Paris, Lyon, Marseille and Nice. The Security Bureau’s amber alert asks travellers to monitor the local situation and exercise caution while travelling. Others on the list include Thailand, over adverse weather and border clashes, and Nepal, due to the latest floods. Sunflower Travel Services assistant general manager Moon Yau Moon-yee said the company had no tour groups in France at present and would continue to monitor the situation closely. “For coming tours, we will adjust itineraries flexibly or change the timing of visits to affected areas as needed,” said Yau, who is also vice-chairman of the Tourism Industry Employees’ General Union. “The safety of our tour members and frontline staff will always be our top priority.” About 20 teams from Hong Kong’s universities and secondary schools have signed up to join the iGEM Grand Jamboree, dubbed the “World Expo of Synthetic Biology”, in France this year, scheduled to run from November 13 to 16 at the Paris Convention Centre, according to Samuel Cheng Kin-tak, principal of United Christian College (Kowloon East). Cheng said his school also planned to send nine students to join the competition, but would now prefer submitting their work online instead of travelling to France as in previous years. “The turning point was when the Hong Kong government issued an amber outbound travel alert for France. As it is an official warning from authorities, everyone has to think carefully about whether they really need to go. We have to put students’ safety first,” he said. He said the competition’s organiser had reassured the school sector last week that protests were common in France and that the venue is located far from any demonstrations. Cheng added that he had not heard of any schools that still planned to go ahead with the trip following the alert. He noted that his students were disappointed, as the most valuable elements of the competition were presenting to judges in person and engaging in on-site exchanges with participants from around the world. A spokeswoman for the Education Bureau said it reminded schools to make safety the top priority for outbound study tours. She said schools must ensure the safety of all participants in study tour activities, make appropriate adjustments in response to the situation at the visited region and maintain communication with stakeholders. Hong Kong-born, Paris-based radio and television host Sony Chan said Paris had “temporarily quietened down” following a curfew. “As a foreigner, I can only view as an onlooker and treat it as an experience,” Chan said. Online personality Chong Kung-sum, a Hongkonger who moved to France over a decade ago, explained in an online video why students were protesting, drawing many positive comments praising her in-depth explanation. Speaking from her experience in the French education system, she said that the students faced absent teachers, a lack of resources and opaque university entrance procedures, among many other long-standing problems. “The students, the teaching unions and parents have been complaining about them for years,” she said.

title: Hong Kong’s Election Committee race: should you care? Here’s what you need to know
description: Nominations have closed for Hong Kong’s Election Committee election, setting the stage for the November 22 poll. The poll, the second since Beijing overhauled the city’s electoral system to ensure patriots rule Hong Kong, will return 1,500 members who will nominate and vote in next year’s chief executive election. Here’s all you need to know about the 2026 Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections, now that nominations have closed: from the hopefuls’ line-up and the heavyweights in the...
content: Nominations have closed for Hong Kong’s Election Committee election, setting the stage for the November 22 poll. The poll, the second since Beijing overhauled the city’s electoral system to ensure patriots rule Hong Kong, will return 1,500 members who will nominate and vote in next year’s chief executive election. Here’s all you need to know about the 2026 Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections, now that nominations have closed: from the hopefuls’ line-up and the heavyweights in the race to what happens next. 1. What is notable about the line-up? The 1,500-member electoral college comprises 40 subsectors across five major sectors, each representing different interest groups in society. A total of 1,115 hopefuls signed up to run for the 982 elected seats, while designated bodies submitted nominations for 161 individuals. When nominations closed, 31 of the 36 elective subsectors received more nominations than available seats and will go to a competitive poll. That is a sharp increase from the 13 contested subsectors in 2021, and follows comments by some politicians that Beijing “encouraged competition” to foster a stronger electoral atmosphere. But competition overall is not considered intense, with an average of 1.14 candidates vying for each seat. The social welfare and medical and health services subsectors face the fiercest contests, with 25 and 23 candidates respectively competing for 15 seats in each. 2. How many nominated John Lee in 2022? About 60 per cent, or 587, of the Election Committee members elected in 2021 are seeking re-election. The re-election rate is highest in the committee’s fourth sector, which comprises lawmakers and district representatives. Of the 1,276 nominations, roughly one in four – 336 individuals – previously nominated John Lee Ka-chiu in the 2022 chief executive election. The proportion is highest in the Heung Yee Kuk, finance and Employers’ Federation of Hong Kong subsectors, where nearly 90 per cent of hopefuls had nominated Lee. Lee was elected unopposed in May 2022, winning 99.2 per cent of ballots cast by Election Committee members. 3. Who are the hopefuls and what are they pushing for? The line-up includes former senior government officials, prominent lawmakers and business figures. Notable candidates include former secretary for justice Rimsky Yuen Kwok-keung, who stepped down in 2018 and is running in the legal subsector; former Legislative Council president Andrew Leung Kwan-yuen, contesting the industrial (first) subsector; and former secretary for food and health Sophia Chan Siu-chee, running in the medical and health services subsector. From the business world, Henderson Land chairman Martin Lee Ka-shing and CK Asset executive director Justin Chiu Kwok-hung are running in the real estate and construction subsector. Billionaire Richard Li Tzar-kai, younger son of Hong Kong’s richest tycoon Li Ka-shing, has signed up for the Employers’ Federation of Hong Kong subsector. Meanwhile, dozens of hopefuls – mostly in the district subsectors – have published campaign platforms on social media. Their most common pledges are to facilitate Hong Kong’s integration with the mainland, accelerate development of the Northern Metropolis and improve residents’ livelihoods. 4. What happens next? The election will proceed in stages before polling day on November 22. All 1,276 nominations will first undergo a two-week vetting process by the Candidate Eligibility Review Committee, which takes advice from the Committee for Safeguarding National Security. In the five uncontested subsectors – labour; education; associations of Chinese fellow townsmen; representatives of Hong Kong members of relevant national organisations; and sports, performing arts, culture and publication – valid candidates will be declared elected automatically once vetting is complete. For the 31 contested subsectors, the Electoral Affairs Commission will hold a candidate briefing on November 3 at Queen Elizabeth Stadium. Chaired by commission chairman Justice David Lok Kai-hong, the session will explain the electoral guidelines and key rules for the campaign period. 5. What happens on polling day and beyond? Only 5,757 registered voters are eligible to cast ballots on November 22, with voting primarily conducted by corporate bodies. The election will return 982 elected members, who will join 362 ex-officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies to form the full 1,500-member Election Committee. The new committee will take office for a five-year term on February 1, 2027. Its central role will be to nominate and elect Hong Kong’s next chief executive in early 2027, as well as to nominate candidates and elect 40 of the 90 lawmakers in the 2029 Legco election.

content: Sun Hung Kai Properties (SHKP), one of Hong Kong’s largest developers, has sold out the latest batch of flats at its Sierra Sea project in the New Territories, where units were offered at discounted prices ahead of a possible US Federal Reserve interest-rate increase by year-end. By 5.40pm on Wednesday, SHKP had found buyers for all 128 flats offered at listed prices in Phase 2C(2) of the development in Shap Sze Heung, between Sai Kung and Ma On Shan, according to agents. Sales began at 2pm. “Developers will continue to launch new flats in an orderly and steady cadence in the coming weeks,” said Derek Chan Hoi-chiu, head of research at Ricacorp Properties. “Strong sales results in mid-October and recent sales brochure releases confirm that developers are capitalising on current buyer demand to roll out their pipeline systematically.” SHKP sold all 142 flats offered at Sierra Sea in a separate batch on Saturday. Alongside Wednesday’s 128 flats offered at listed prices, SHKP made another 24 available by tender, with a further 19 flats to be offered by tender from Saturday. The latest batch includes two- and three-bedroom units ranging from 418 to 679 square feet (38.83 to 63.08 square metres). The flats offered at listed prices sold at discounted rates starting at HK$12,714 (US$1,620) per square foot, with individual units costing about HK$5.47 million to HK$9.87 million. Centaline Property Agency said long-term investors accounted for 60 per cent of its clients buying flats on Wednesday. “Centaline recorded more than 10 groups of buyers intending to purchase more than two units, with the largest bulk buyer planning to spend nearly HK$30 million to acquire four units for rental investment purposes,” said Louis Chan, Asia-Pacific vice-chairman and CEO of the property agency’s residential division. Chan said the prospect of the US Federal Reserve raising interest rates in the coming weeks or months had encouraged developers to fast-track launches. “It is expected that primary market transactions this month could top 2,000 or even reach 2,200 units, hitting a six-month high,” he added.

title: Attitudes shifting in Hong Kong’s favour as city reaps Apec benefits: Paul Chan
description: Hong Kong has reaped the benefits of the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting, with foreign political and business leaders expressing renewed confidence in the city and supporting cross-border digital finance infrastructure development, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po has said. Following the conclusion of the two-day milestone meeting on Wednesday, Chan said senior officials and representatives had discussed macroeconomic, fiscal and financial policy, as well as young talent, in a sincere and...
content: Hong Kong has reaped the benefits of the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting, with foreign political and business leaders expressing renewed confidence in the city and supporting cross-border digital finance infrastructure development, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po has said. Following the conclusion of the two-day milestone meeting on Wednesday, Chan said senior officials and representatives had discussed macroeconomic, fiscal and financial policy, as well as young talent, in a sincere and open manner. The overall feedback from delegates was positive, Chan added. He said the meeting enhanced their understanding of Hong Kong’s unique role and its attractiveness as a platform to tap not just mainland China but also the broader Asian market. “A more important implication of this event is the attitude and understanding of foreign business and foreign political leaders about Hong Kong,” he said. “I’m very confident that in my conversations with them in the past two days, they all felt very positive about our development and the economic direction.” Chan said they were impressed that foreign investors were active in the city, as about 35 per cent of capital flows came from the United States, Europe and the Middle East and another 25 per cent or so came from the mainland. For the first time, Hong Kong hosted the gathering with the support of Beijing, which will be followed by the Apec leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen next month. About 500 representatives and senior officials from Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economies visited Hong Kong for the meeting, with many joining the event’s social programme to experience the city’s culture and dynamism. Chan said the delegates and representatives had reached a consensus on a number of areas that would result in further cooperation. For example, they were interested in digital infrastructure investments, for which Hong Kong could provide financing solutions, he said. Chan cited Project CargoX, a strategic fintech and trade finance initiative by the city’s de facto central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, designed to leverage real-time cargo and supply chain data to help small and medium-sized enterprises access bank loans. He added that delegates felt positive about Hong Kong’s positioning in Beijing’s development plan by having its own first five-year plan. He referred to Hong Kong’s “four centres, one hub” strategy in Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s economic blueprint up to 2030. The strategy aims to reinforce Hong Kong as an international financial, maritime and aviation, and trade centre, while developing it into an international innovation and technology centre and high-calibre talent hub. “So this gives them the indication as to which areas we may cooperate more [on] and work more together and where the potential is,” Chan said. Shirley Kwong, board secretary of the Hong Kong committee of the world’s largest business organisation, the International Chamber of Commerce, said advancing digital infrastructure would be a game changer for global trade financing. She said the local committee would press ahead with development by collaborating with industry stakeholders such as banks, fintech firms, logistics firms and companies to discuss pain points and identify what needed to be done for cross-border data exchange. “The finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong is a stamp of approval for us being the regional and global trade finance centre,” Kwong said in an interview after attending the meeting earlier in the day. “We should be more involved in discussions in the international arena on this aspect, adding our expertise so that we can take the world to the next level.” Peter Burnett, co-chair of the Pacific Basin Economic Council, a Hong Kong-based international business association, noted a regional shift in trade trajectories. “China is very big in the room,” London-based Burnett told the South China Morning Post after attending the meeting earlier in the day. “During the last few years, this region has moved from an east-west to a north-south trajectory.” As host city for the 21-member bloc’s event, Hong Kong projected renewed confidence even though it remained under the geopolitical spotlight. “There’s a great deal more confidence,” Burnett said. “A lot of talk about the Northern Metropolis. A lot of talk about financial services and professional services ... A lot of talk about maritime capabilities.” With Beijing seeking to raise Hong Kong’s profile as an international financial centre, Burnett suggested the city was outperforming its rival London in areas such as stock trading and its role in helping mainland companies go global.

title: ‘Nothing is set in stone’: Peak lighting project suspended amid tree damage fears
description: A controversial lighting project along a walking trail on The Peak “is not set in stone yet”, authorities have said, with the South China Morning Post learning that related works have been suspended amid mounting complaints that the installations are damaging the environment. The project’s future remains uncertain after residents accused the Tourism Board of removing trees and flowers to make way for the installations, while a lawmaker said a district councillor from the city’s largest political...
content: A controversial lighting project along a walking trail on The Peak “is not set in stone yet”, authorities have said, with the South China Morning Post learning that related works have been suspended amid mounting complaints that the installations are damaging the environment. The project’s future remains uncertain after residents accused the Tourism Board of removing trees and flowers to make way for the installations, while a lawmaker said a district councillor from the city’s largest political party had not been involved in the initial consultation. Lugard Road and Harlech Road were quiet on Tuesday, with no workers in sight. The lighting installations remained in place behind barriers that blocked parts of the trail, with a few security guards stationed nearby. Near a park on the Harlech Road and Lugard Road circular walk, a large stretch of grass had been fenced off and fitted with lighting installations. Some sections had been dug up. A security guard at the site told an SCMP reporter that installation work had been suspended for three days from Wednesday. “The work had not stopped until today,” he said, adding that “workers were still laying and fixing wires on the grass last night”, pointing to a toolbox left on a flower-shaped lighting installation. “We were told originally that this project should be ready and open to the public before October 24, and it had already gone through some rounds of testing last week. But now we have to wait for the result of the government consultation during the suspension.” Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said on Wednesday that the Tourism Board and the Tourism Commission were gathering public feedback and would visit the relevant sites with district councillors. “As the project is still under way, nothing is set in stone yet,” Law said. “It is still too early to talk about advancing the project. We are still listening to opinions and may make modifications.” The installations were planned for selected locations along the walking trail as part of a new light show for the forthcoming Hong Kong WinterFest. Law said the board could only confirm later whether the installations would form part of the light show at Christmas. “For future projects, we have to carefully strike a balance between tourists’ experience, residents’ needs and the ecological environment,” she said. Spotlights and light boxes lined the railings along parts of the trail, while some lighting devices and tangled wires hung from tree trunks. Transparent light strips arranged in flower shapes cover sections of grass and are connected to electrical installations shaped like the centres of flowers. Although tourism authorities said the project was designed to “further enhance the appeal of Hong Kong’s nighttime tourism”, some visitors passing the site expressed little interest in the light show. Wendy Wang, a master’s student at the University of Hong Kong, was walking along the trail with a friend from Beijing who was visiting the city for five days. “We don’t think the light show will be attractive for us. Such shows are quite common now, while The Peak trail is most famous for its natural scenery.” Lawmaker Chan Hok-fung said he was following up on the issue with fellow Democratic Alliance for the Betterment and Progress of Hong Kong member Shih Jan-noel, a Central and Western district councillor. Chan said he had relayed residents’ comments to the tourism minister. Chan stressed that Shih had not been involved in the Tourism Board’s initial consultation and had learned of the issue only when residents emailed him for help. “Comments in the past said that tourism had concentrated on either side of the Victoria Harbour and could not boost spending in other neighbourhoods with hopes to promote it elsewhere. The idea is worth pushing for,” he said. “But whether to do this on The Peak, it’s an experience this time around. People seem to [care] a lot about the natural environment. Rick Mesquita, a tourist from Britain who had arrived in Hong Kong the previous day for a three-day visit, said he was seeking some peace and quiet with a walk along the trail. “We’re not interested in light installations,” he said. “I chose to come here to get away from the noise and bustle of the city, so the less artificial, the better.” Man Kwok, a quality regulator who lives on Hong Kong Island and hikes up to The Peak every couple of months, visited with a friend on Wednesday morning. “I don’t know why they chose this spot. This is a walking trail, not an artificial attraction,” he said. “It takes around 20 minutes to walk here from either end of the trail. I don’t understand why people would walk so far just to see a light show.” The Tourism Board said it had consulted tree experts “on tree protection and the installation of light fittings”, although some professionals remain doubtful. Jim Chi-yung, a research chair professor of geography and environmental science at The Education University of Hong Kong who is widely known as the “Tree Doctor”, said installing a lighting project in a natural setting was “incongruous” and “a mismatch”. He likened the fittings attached to trees to “strangulation”, explaining that they compress the cambium and phloem beneath the bark – the thin tissue responsible for transporting food to the roots – thereby disrupting the trees’ growth. “When water accumulates around the installations, there will be rotting as well. Moisture at the interface between the installation and the tree will cause decay and attract pests, which harms the tree,” he added. The installations were planned to operate from 7pm to 10pm on a 12-month trial basis, according to tourism authorities. “If you strangle a tree for a year, its leaves will start to drop, some branches will begin to dry out and rot, and may even snap and fall, causing secondary impacts and raising safety concerns,” Jim said. “A year is absolutely unacceptable.” Jim further explained that nighttime lighting can “mess up the plant’s biological clock”. Additional reporting by Ambrose Li

title: Queen Elizabeth visits Hong Kong for the last time in 1986 – from the SCMP archive
description: This article was first published on October 22, 1986. ‘Our thoughts will always be with you’: Queen confident on HK future Hongkong gave Queen Elizabeth a warm and enthusiastic reception yesterday (October 21, 1986) when she arrived for her long-awaited visit. And in return she gave the people a message of confidence in the future. Fresh from her triumphant tour of the mainland, the Queen told a welcoming ceremony in City Hall that the Sino-British agreement over Hongkong’s future had made...
content: This article was first published on October 22, 1986. ‘Our thoughts will always be with you’: Queen confident on HK future Hongkong gave Queen Elizabeth a warm and enthusiastic reception yesterday (October 21, 1986) when she arrived for her long-awaited visit. And in return she gave the people a message of confidence in the future. Fresh from her triumphant tour of the mainland, the Queen told a welcoming ceremony in City Hall that the Sino-British agreement over Hongkong’s future had made possible her trip to China, the first by a British sovereign. She said the visit symbolised the new relationship between Britain and China, a relationship in which the agreement over Hongkong had played a significant part. “You have been promised in that agreement that in the institutions, traditions and way of life so important to the people of Hongkong will be preserved. “The agreement, and the firm commitment to the governments of the United Kingdom and China enshrined it will, I trust, be an assurance and encouragement to you as you face the challenges of the future.” She recalled that on her first visit to Hongkong in 1975, the first by a British sovereign, times “were not altogether easy” because of a recession. “However, I felt the determination and commitment of the people and the Government to overcome those difficulties, to build a better city and a better society,” she said. “No one sailing into Hongkong Harbour, as I did this morning, could fail to be impressed with what that determination and that commitment have achieved. “The people of Hongkong, with imagination and hard work, have created a unique city and a unique society. And this has earned you respect and goodwill throughout the world.” She said Hongkong had profited from both Chinese and British traditions in surviving the rapid changes of the past. “The pace of change distinguishes Hongkong from most other parts of the world. Much that we saw in 1975 has gone, much that is new has taken its place. Because you have profited from your two traditions you have been able to adapt to this rapid progress where less adaptable folk may well have succumbed.” Hongkong would be able to draw on these two strains in the future. She concluded: “As you move towards a new phase in your development, our thoughts will always be with you.” As if to symbolise the harmony of views over Hongkong, the monarch was met at Queen’s Pier not only by the Governor, Sir Edward Youde, but also by China’s top representative here, Mr Xu Jiatun, director of the Hongkong branch of the New China News Agency. Later, at lunch, she spoke at length with Mr Xu, but officials could not say what they discussed. For most people, however, thoughts of the future took second place to the genuine enthusiasm the Queen’s visit generated everywhere. The eventful day began when the Royal yacht Britannia led a stately procession down the harbour. Exactly on schedule the Queen stepped ashore to a cheering, flag-waving crowd. After the welcoming ceremony before more than 1,000 dignitaries in City Hall, the Queen and Duke of Edinburgh laid a wreath at the Cenotaph, and then visited the Legislative Council chambers and the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank headquarters. After lunch at Government House, they travelled across the harbour to the Hongkong Polytechnic, and then returned to the island to lay a foundation stone for the Convention Centre in Wan Chai. Months of meticulous planning had gone into making the day a success and it paid off handsomely. Even the weather co-operated, and the Queen was able to see the territory she last visited 11 years ago at its sun-drenched best. In the evening, the Queen travelled to Tsim Sha Tsui, where huge crowds were waiting to greet her. The mood was festive, the evening air balmy, and the short trip to Hongkong Coliseum for a Youth Spectacular with a cast of 6,000 young people, was made to cheers and applause. The performance, which included the national anthem played on Chinese instruments – much to the delight of the Queen and the Duke – was a fitting finale to a day marked by a good deal more spontaneous warmth than the Queen received in some parts of China. It was a day when Hongkong was able to forget tomorrow and rejoice in the present.

title: Abby Choi’s ex-father-in-law pocketed HK$7 million rebate on flat purchase: court

Property agent Marco Wong Tak-sing told the High Court on Wednesday that Kwong Kau had requested a share of the agency’s profit from the 2019 sale of the luxury flat at the Kadooria development in Ho Man Tin. The court previously heard that Choi issued two cheques and bought two cashier’s...
content: The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung received a cash rebate of nearly HK$7 million (US$891,900) after buying a HK$72 million flat using the model’s money, a court has heard. Property agent Marco Wong Tak-sing told the High Court on Wednesday that Kwong Kau had requested a share of the agency’s profit from the 2019 sale of the luxury flat at the Kadooria development in Ho Man Tin. The court previously heard that Choi issued two cheques and bought two cashier’s orders to cover the flat’s HK$60 million purchase price, which later allegedly became a flashpoint between the 28-year-old and her former in-laws. Wong said his agency received HK$8.18 million in commission from the developer for the sale, of which HK$6.97 million was returned to Kwong, the flat’s registered owner. He said Kwong had separately paid HK$3.09 million in stamp duty for the purchase, but he was unsure where the money came from. Kwong, 68, is standing trial for allegedly enlisting his two sons to help kill his former daughter-in-law following a bitter family dispute over the flat’s proposed sale in 2022. Prosecutors said Choi registered the Kadooria flat in Kwong’s name to avoid paying HK$9 million in double stamp duty, but she never intended to give it to her former in-laws. Kwong pleaded not guilty to a joint count of murder, as did his sons, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, and Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, who is Choi’s ex-husband. The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, also denied preventing the burial of Choi’s body. His two sons admitted the offence before the trial began last month. Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, earlier testified that her daughter had given Alex Kwong more than HK$70 million for investment, including flipping luxury watches, but she stopped financing him after he failed to make any profit. Chan Leong-hang, an employee of Aristo Watch & Jewellery, confirmed that Choi had made 31 deposits into the shop’s bank account, totalling more than HK$26 million, to pay for the timepieces her ex-husband bought over the years. Chan said Alex Kwong had also sold watches to the company and asked that the proceeds be temporarily kept at the shop so that he could use them to buy watches on the next occasion. He said before he first met Alex Kwong in person in July 2022, he did not realise that “Damon”, his supposed assistant who would collect the merchandise for him, was in fact his elder brother, Anthony Kwong. At around 4pm on February 21, 2023, Alex Kwong asked Chan to return to him a Patek Philippe watch that he had bought but left in the shop’s possession and HK$1.4 million, which was the profit from a watch the defendant had sold to the shop, the court heard. Two days later, after Alex Kwong collected the valuables from Chan, he allegedly called the watch shop employee again, asking in what Chan described as a “very sad” voice that he delete all of their messaging records on his device. Alex Kwong was arrested at Tung Chung Development Ferry Pier on February 25. The alleged murder came to light after parts of Choi’s dismembered remains were discovered at a 600 square foot rental flat on the ground floor of a three-storey house in Tai Po’s Lung Mei village on February 24, 2023. Cho Chin-to, who lived at the flat above at the time of the incident, said the flat’s windows were completely sealed with black material from around the middle of that month, and that people outside the premises could not see what happened inside. Cho said he noticed the sound of heavy objects being carried into the flat at around 3pm on February 21, before he heard electric saws and noise that appeared to come from renovation work. He added that a “very nice aroma” resembling a typical radish and carrot soup came out of the ground-floor flat at around 7pm and lingered for a long time that night. Defence counsel Oliver Davies, representing Kwong Kau, argued there was never any noise of electric saws coming from the flat, noting that a nearby surveillance camera was unable to record any unusual sound during the period concerned. Davies further suggested that Cho fabricated his testimony about the smell of the soup based on what he subsequently read in the news. The witness rejected the lawyer’s claims. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: ‘How much longer?’ Chau Tin-yu’s father hits out at last-minute delay to doctor’s hearing
description: A high-profile disciplinary hearing for a doctor accused of leaving a girl in a vegetative state six years ago has been adjourned pending a coroner’s inquest, a decision the girl’s father learned of just a week before proceedings were due to begin. The Medical Council informed Eddie Chau, father of Chau Tin-yu, on Tuesday night that the hearing, originally scheduled to start on October 27, would be postponed until after the inquest. The decision leaves both proceedings in limbo. Just last month,...
content: A high-profile disciplinary hearing for a doctor accused of leaving a girl in a vegetative state six years ago has been adjourned pending a coroner’s inquest, a decision the girl’s father learned of just a week before proceedings were due to begin. The Medical Council informed Eddie Chau, father of Chau Tin-yu, on Tuesday night that the hearing, originally scheduled to start on October 27, would be postponed until after the inquest. The decision leaves both proceedings in limbo. Just last month, the Coroner’s Court told Chau it would wait for the Medical Council inquiry to conclude first, to avoid a scheduling clash. “The council did not say when the hearing will begin and we do not know when a coroner’s inquest will happen … now I have no idea how much longer I need to wait,” Chau, who has advanced-stage cancer, said. “The hearing has been delayed for a long time and they had long known a coroner’s inquest would happen. Why did they choose to make such a decision at the last minute?” Chau said the council claimed it would write to the Coroner’s Court on Wednesday to notify it of the decision. The complaint against the anaesthesiologist involved in the surgery was lodged with the medical watchdog in April 2021. In May this year, the council decided the hearing would take place between October 27 and 30. The court told Chau in February that an inquest would be held, but did not provide a date. Chau also launched a civil lawsuit against the Hospital Authority, which was settled in 2023. Tin-yu was four when she underwent surgery to remove a rhabdomyosarcoma tumour, a rare form of cancer, after chemotherapy and radiotherapy shrank it to an operable size. But during surgery at Queen Mary Hospital in Pok Fu Lam in May 2020, a blood transfusion was delayed by 48 minutes and her heart stopped beating for 52 minutes. She emerged from the operating theatre in a vegetative state. The girl spent four years in that condition before dying in March 2024, aged eight. Alex Lam Chi-yau, a patient rights advocate and member of the council, said it was uncommon for a disciplinary inquiry to be postponed for this reason. However, Lam said it was reasonable for a death inquest to precede a disciplinary inquiry against a doctor, because the inquest’s investigation was far more comprehensive and had the authority to compel witnesses to testify. Evidence gathered by the court could therefore be used by the council in disciplinary proceedings. Lam also said it would be “ridiculous” if both sides told a complainant that they would wait for each other. “In death inquests, the Department of Justice has the role of presenting evidence, while in a Medical Council disciplinary inquiry, the department acts as the legal officer,” he said. “It is hard to imagine when the department is involved on both sides.” Lam said both the department and the council should explain why this had happened. “A complete complaint handling mechanism should have reasonable time frames and procedures, so that people can have reasonable expectations. Even if, through due process, the doctor is found not guilty, the due process must be visible to people.” The Medical Council secretariat said on Wednesday that after the case was referred to the inquiry panel for a hearing and scheduled accordingly, it was notified that the Coroner’s Court had also decided to hold an inquest into the patient’s death, although a date had not yet been fixed. Given that further evidence and relevant factual details may be disclosed during the coroner’s inquest, which would help the panel conduct a more comprehensive inquiry, the panel chairman decided to adjourn the disciplinary hearing. It will resume in accordance with the law and established procedures after the conclusion of the death inquest. An amendment to the Medical Registration Ordinance is under way to diversify the council’s composition with more lay members and speed up complaint handling, including by requiring the council to set time frames. The proposed changes to the watchdog’s operations followed a 15-year delay in its handling of a complaint against Dr Sit Sou-chi, who was accused of a blunder that left a boy permanently disabled in 2009. The case was terminated last year on the grounds that the procedural delay prevented a fair hearing, but the council reversed its decision and resumed the inquiry in April after a public outcry. The doctor was subsequently found guilty of professional misconduct and suspended from the General Register for nine months. Additional reporting by Simpson Cheung

title: Hong Kong police arrest 4 teenagers over viral back-alley assault video
description: Hong Kong police have arrested four boys on suspicion of inciting another person to become a member of an unlawful society and assault causing bodily harm, after a clip of a back-alley dispute in the early hours on Monday went viral. A police spokesman said on Wednesday that officers arrested four local boys aged 13 to 17 the day before, following an investigation based on a clip of a suspected attack in a back alley in Sai Wan Ho that had circulated online. “All arrestees are under custody for...
content: Hong Kong police have arrested four boys on suspicion of inciting another person to become a member of an unlawful society and assault causing bodily harm, after a clip of a back-alley dispute in the early hours on Monday went viral. A police spokesman said on Wednesday that officers arrested four local boys aged 13 to 17 the day before, following an investigation based on a clip of a suspected attack in a back alley in Sai Wan Ho that had circulated online. “All arrestees are under custody for investigation,” the spokesman said. In the clip seen by the South China Morning Post, four boys were seen attacking another boy by punching him, slapping him in the face, swearing at him and encircling him in a back alley between two buildings. Towards the end of the video, one of the alleged attackers was heard telling the victim, “Remember this, I am your real boss”, before the four boys left the scene. The case is now being investigated by the anti-triad team at the eastern police district. Under Hong Kong law, the minimum age of criminal culpability is 10 years old. Defendants under the age of 14 and those aged above 14 but under 16 are generally handled in a specialised juvenile court. No child aged between 10 and 13 can be sentenced to imprisonment, while a young person aged between 14 and 15 should not be sentenced to imprisonment if their sentence could be dealt with in any other way. Sentencing options for young offenders thus include detention centres focusing on physical labour and strict discipline for male offenders aged 14 to 24, training centres focusing on vocational training for offenders of all genders from 14 to 20 years old, as well as rehabilitation centres for offenders aged 14 to 20 whose offence warrants a short custodial sentence. The maximum punishment for inciting someone to become a member of an unlawful society is two years’ imprisonment and a fine of HK$50,000 (US$6,370). The highest penalty for assault occasioning actual bodily harm is three years’ imprisonment.

title: Why is Hong Kong so hot in October and will winter be warmer than usual?
description: Hong Kong’s exceptionally warm October weather is being driven by a combination of a super typhoon, El Nino and global warming, a climate expert has said, warning that higher-than-usual temperatures are likely to persist through the winter. The warning came as autumn temperatures across the city topped 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit) over the past few weeks. Professor Amos Tai Pui-kuen, of the earth and environmental sciences department at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, explained on...
content: Hong Kong’s exceptionally warm October weather is being driven by a combination of a super typhoon, El Nino and global warming, a climate expert has said, warning that higher-than-usual temperatures are likely to persist through the winter. The warning came as autumn temperatures across the city topped 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit) over the past few weeks. Professor Amos Tai Pui-kuen, of the earth and environmental sciences department at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, explained on Wednesday that El Nino had altered typhoon paths and weakened the northeasterly winds that typically reached the city in autumn. “A ‘super’ El Nino means that paths of typhoons would move more northerly … if and when typhoons do hit Hong Kong, because of the high sea level temperatures, there will be more heat and steam evaporating, which contributes to a stronger typhoon, too,” he said. He added that El Nino had changed atmospheric circulation, weakening the autumn northeasterlies and reducing heat dissipation, leaving Hong Kong hotter. Another factor was a super typhoon near Manila, Tai said. He explained that an anticyclone had formed over Hong Kong as part of the typhoon’s outer circulation, causing air to sink and winds to weaken, with sunshine becoming “particularly abundant”. He added that global warming had also raised baseline temperatures. A local green group and a leading meteorologist warned in July that Hong Kong should prepare for stronger storms and a warmer, wetter winter, as the current El Nino was likely to intensify into a super event. Tai said temperatures would gradually fall as winter approached, but the season was likely to be warmer than in previous years because of the lingering effects of the “super” El Nino, which could last until spring. Five hikers fell ill in separate incidents across Hong Kong on Monday as hot weather gripped the city on the final day of the Chung Yeung Festival long weekend. Some were airlifted to hospital by the Government Flying Service. Conditions were hot and dry that day, with the maximum temperature reaching 32 degrees Celsius at the Hong Kong Observatory’s urban headquarters and several degrees higher in parts of the New Territories. The Observatory forecast temperatures would reach 33 degrees on Friday before gradually falling below 30 degrees later the following week.

content: Only 3 per cent of Hong Kong companies have fully integrated AI into their workflows, with many facing hurdles including resistance to organisational change and outdated digital infrastructure, a survey has found. Consultancy Accenture, which polled 150 companies and released the results on Wednesday, said the survey suggested businesses had a strong desire to adopt artificial intelligence (AI) in their work but many struggled to put it into practice. “Hong Kong really has strong AI ambitions and strong interest, and frankly, the right ingredients in place now. However, few enterprises have really scaled AI across the business,” said Robert Hah, the consultancy’s Hong Kong office lead. Hah pointed to government initiatives to promote the AI industry and upskill the city’s workforce, as well as Hong Kong’s robust capital markets, as favourable conditions for companies’ adoption of AI. But resistance to change in operational and organisational models, as well as outdated digital core infrastructure within companies, was delaying AI adoption, he noted. The survey, titled the “Hong Kong AI Index”, was launched this year. It evaluates respondents’ AI readiness across 10 dimensions, divided into two categories: foundational capabilities and new AI and data essential capabilities. The first category assesses whether the respondents have baseline capabilities in AI strategy, digital infrastructure, data governance frameworks, ethical safeguards and overall employee AI literacy. The second focuses on whether they can industrialise AI applications at scale. These include large language model operations, modern database structures, data source diversity, management of AI models and products and specialised talent upskilling. On a scale of 0 to 1, Hong Kong respondents reported an average score of 0.42 in the former category and 0.47 in the latter. But Hah cautioned against directly comparing the city’s performance with other economies, saying each market had its own unique circumstances. The survey found that business leaders in Hong Kong had set ambitious goals for AI adoption. The companies on average expected to deliver a 15 per cent increase in productivity, a 14 per cent uplift in revenue, a 14 per cent improvement in customer experience and an 11 per cent reduction in costs over an 18-month period with the help of AI, the poll showed. In contrast, only 12 per cent of the respondents’ AI initiatives had currently expanded across an organisation to deliver impactful outcomes, while only 3 per cent of the organisations could fully integrate AI into their business strategies, highlighting an ambition-operation gap. “I truly believe in today’s environment, the biggest issue with [AI] deployment has nothing to do with technology. It really is about people, mindset [and] operating models,” Hah said. The survey found that 45 per cent of firms had identified stagnant operating models as a barrier to their wider AI adoption. Other common obstacles included resistance to organisational change and an inability to anticipate challenges and opportunities. According to Hah, rather than blindly introducing AI to existing workflows, companies should instead re-engineer their operations through the lens of AI. Hah cited the example of using AI to make PowerPoint slides, which he said could be time-consuming as users had to repeatedly refine their prompts to produce slides consistent with their needs. “You need to rethink: does this process even need to exist in the future, given how Gen AI works? Is it really a linear process like it is today?” he said. A successful example cited in the report was Hong Kong’s flagship carrier, Cathay Pacific Airways, which attached great importance to experimentation, making it quick to test and prove emerging ideas of AI adoption. Proven use cases then moved into the next phase focused on outcomes, integration and accountability, the report added. This measure had enabled the carrier to quickly identify AI initiatives that could bring value to its operation, the report said. Hah said human resources departments should rethink the talent needed in the AI world, while IT departments should rewire their digital infrastructure to make use of the unstructured data of their organisations’ operations. Beyond that, a sound governance framework would also be needed to ensure the responsible use of AI, he said. The development of technology, especially AI, has taken a centre stage in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and the latest annual policy address, with the government working to refine the governance and legal frameworks for the technology, subsidise enterprises in adopting AI and upskill the labour force amid the AI era. Hah said these moves had set a good policy environment for companies and that it was time for them to review their governance structure to leverage the technology’s value.

title: From ideas to impact
description: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] The HKUST-SINO One Million Dollar Entrepreneurship Competition and Impactathon take different approaches to helping promising ideas move from early concepts to practical applications in businesses and communities. Across these initiatives, Sino aims to connect innovators with communities, universities and businesses at critical stages when feedback, practical experience and industry connections can help their ideas gain...
content: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] The HKUST-SINO One Million Dollar Entrepreneurship Competition and Impactathon take different approaches to helping promising ideas move from early concepts to practical applications in businesses and communities. Across these initiatives, Sino aims to connect innovators with communities, universities and businesses at critical stages when feedback, practical experience and industry connections can help their ideas gain momentum. Supporting ideas at an earlier stage Launched in 2011, the HKUST-SINO One Million Dollar Entrepreneurship Competition gives aspiring entrepreneurs access to training, mentorship, investors and industry contacts as they develop technologies and business models. Support after the competition continues through HKUST InnoBay 1M PLUS, which gives promising teams access to real-world application scenarios, industry networking, partnership matching and proof-of-concept opportunities as they progress from technology validation towards market adoption. Smart City will be its first theme. According to David Ng, Deputy Chief Executive Officer of Sino Group, this initiative seeks to connect young ventures with partners across government, industry, academia and the community, as well as businesses and investors that can help promising ideas progress towards application. “Through the HKUST InnoBay 1M PLUS programme, we hope to connect promising teams with start-ups, industry partners and investors, opening up more opportunities for collaboration, application and commercialisation,” he said. Partners include Samsung Electronics, Cyberport, Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation and the Smart City Consortium. Companies from the competition’s mainland regional contests will also gain access to Hong Kong’s industry, investment and business networks. The finalists this year showed why young companies can require different kinds of support. Refined Motor Company, which won the Platinum Award in the HKUST Track, has developed proprietary modular powertrains for converting existing petrol and diesel vehicles to electric power. Its solution is Hong Kong’s only approved EV conversion technology, allowing existing vehicles to be retained rather than scrapped.Singapore-based Waveity is at another different stage of development. The International Student Track Silver winner has developed a manta ray-inspired offshore system that uses floating modules to generate electricity from wave motion. For Waveity, the immediate challenge is putting the technology into a full-scale operating environment. “Our first priority is full-scale deployment because we still need to validate the idea under real-world conditions,” the team said after the competition. “After that, we can potentially look at Hong Kong infrastructure and try to implement the technology here.” Prof Carrie Ling, Director of the HKUST Entrepreneurship Centre, said early-stage companies often need time to establish customers, refine products and produce evidence that investors can assess. Her advice is to engage potential users early. “Try early and talk to the customers early. You need to understand the market first and then work out what solution is needed,” she said.Learning from real users The need for support does not end once a technology leaves the university or competition setting. The next challenge is often seeing whether it works for the people it was designed to serve. Impactathon addresses that stage by matching start-ups with community organisations in the Northern Metropolis, enabling them to test their solutions with residents and refine them through direct feedback. More than 50 partners participated in the five-month programme, including the Northern Metropolis Co-ordination Office (NMCO), Social Ventures Hong Kong (SVhk), over 10 start-ups and six local universities. More than 1,000 residents and stakeholders were engaged, while seven community partners helped identify local needs before start-ups worked directly with the people their technologies were intended to serve. Hong Kong healthtech start-up GOFA had developed a solution using AI to screen older people for fall risk and provide exercise training, intervention and ongoing monitoring. What the team had lacked was direct access to its intended users. Through Impactathon, GOFA was paired with the Chinese YMCA of Hong Kong and invited 28 older people to try its solution. Their experience prompted changes to the product. Text was enlarged, animations were simplified and access to exercise instructions was made easier. After the adjustments, the proportion of participants able to complete training independently at home rose from about half to around 90 per cent.The team also added a check-in function to encourage older people to walk outside and interact more with their communities. The developers added new features after seeing how older people actually used the AI assessment tool. After refining the solution through the community trial, GOFA received both the Grand Prize and Most Innovative Award at Impactathon. For start-ups such as GOFA, direct user feedback can reveal design and usability issues that are difficult to identify during development alone. Melanie Kwok, Deputy General Manager for Sustainability and Innovation at Sino Group, said: “What is most important is that the business sector can provide an application setting.” She added that feedback gathered from operating properties or customers can help start-ups refine their products, while industry connections may open doors to more opportunities. Beyond community-based trials, Sino’s property portfolio has also served as a testing ground for emerging technologies, while Sino Inno Lab provides a platform for proof-of-concept development and pilot projects. Established in 2018, Sino Inno Lab has engaged more than 800 innovators and supported more than 140 technology solutions. As a start-up matures, it may need university guidance, industry contacts, community trials and investment at different stages. Access to these networks, user feedback and real-world testing can help promising technologies progress towards wider adoption. Through the HKUST-SINO One Million Dollar Entrepreneurship Competition and Impactathon, young ventures are given opportunities to take these next steps towards practical application.

title: Why foreign companies are still betting on Hong Kong’s culinary reputation
description: Despite a downturn in Hong Kong’s food and beverage sector, foreign enterprises are still betting on the city as a fine-dining destination, with a South Korean hydroponic ginseng grower and a 123-year-old Japanese confectioner choosing it for their first overseas ventures. Jack Kwon, founder and CEO of Seoul-based Biofx, signed a deal with Hong Kong hydroponics firm Farm66 last Thursday to grow Korean gourmet ginseng in the city and sell it to local consumers and restaurants.
