content: Despite a downturn in Hong Kong’s food and beverage sector, foreign enterprises are still betting on the city as a fine-dining destination, with a South Korean hydroponic ginseng grower and a 123-year-old Japanese confectioner choosing it for their first overseas ventures. Jack Kwon, founder and CEO of Seoul-based Biofx, signed a deal with Hong Kong hydroponics firm Farm66 last Thursday to grow Korean gourmet ginseng in the city and sell it to local consumers and restaurants. The deal marks the first time the Korean company has expanded hydroponically grown ginseng operations overseas. Hydroponics is an indoor cultivation technique in which plants are grown not in soil but in mineral- and nutrient-infused water under LED lights, typically using a method that allows crops to be planted vertically on shelves to optimise space. “We had several choices: Japan, Singapore, Vietnam and so on, but we made the decision to go to Hong Kong because Hong Kong is the number one fine dining market in Asia,” Kwon told the South China Morning Post. The group also hopes to use Hong Kong as a springboard to other markets in the region, such as Singapore, Vietnam and Japan, he said. He added that the process of opening a company in the city for his international ambitions was also the most flexible and that he had strong relationships with an accounting firm in Hong Kong, which provided support. Kwon said all of the ginseng plant, including the stems and leaves, could be turned into products, unlike traditional ginseng harvested just for the roots. He aimed to bring that expertise, as well as marketing materials, to a Hong Kong urban farm. Kwon said he had used ChatGPT in August last year to find Farm66 for his first overseas venture. The company will provide infrastructure and technologies for his operation in Hong Kong. Gordon Tam Chi-ho, founder and CEO of Farm66, said his firm was currently looking for a site to house a container farm for hydroponic ginseng, and was confident that it could secure a place within a year. “We learned a lot from them because from their research, the leaves are higher in nutrients and could also become products,” Tam said. The leaves could be harvested every two months and used to make pesto, served in salads or brewed as tea, he added. Victoria Wang, the farm’s chief information officer, said Farm66 used cameras linked to artificial intelligence and real-time data analytics, allowing Kwon to keep a close eye on the plants in Hong Kong while he was in Seoul. Wang added that manipulating the LED lights could also help grow more, larger leaves, with adjustments done electronically. Bringing in foreign capital has been a top priority for Hong Kong. The city’s investment promotion arm, InvestHK, has helped set up or expand 516 overseas and mainland Chinese companies in the city in the first eight months of the year, Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah told the SCMP in an interview earlier this month. He believed they tapped the Hong Kong market because the city was “stable, safe and free”. The investment came despite restaurant receipts and purchases remaining flat, with 0.8 per cent growth in value offset by a 0.1 per cent reduction in volume in the first six months of this year, compared with the same period last year. Another newcomer to Hong Kong is Okaman Honpo, a 123-year-old producer of wagashi, or Japanese confectionery, from Tokushima. The company recently launched its first overseas outlet in Hong Kong in collaboration with local brand Master Gift, owned by 78-year-old Hong Kong chef Wan Tat-kong, who has lived and worked in Japan for more than 30 years and whose food has received accolades there. Kenji Okada, the 79-year-old fourth-generation owner of Okaman Honpo, said he had not thought about expanding the company beyond Japan but decided to do so after being persuaded by Wan, a friend. The pair jointly developed wagashi that combined Chinese and Japanese influences for the Hong Kong market, in a project initially planned to run for five years. “There is a limit to the [amount of] ingredients we have, such as sugar from cane, because we grow them on our farm, and cannot scale too much. So the company will focus on its Hong Kong business first,” Okada said through an interpreter. Okada said he would have retired had it not been for Wan’s proposal to collaborate. But now he hopes that whoever takes over the family business will continue with the joint venture. Wan said he would visit Okada’s workshop in Japan three to four times a year to jointly produce the wagashi, which would be delivered to Hong Kong at a more affordable price than what was currently available on the market. “This is also a form of people-to-people cultural exchange between two countries,” Wan said. Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, a senior economist at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank, noted that both businesses had partnered with Hong Kong firms to enter the market, adding that such synergy benefited both local and overseas enterprises. “If the economy were great, perhaps they [foreign businesses] could just set up here on their own. In reality, it’s not as easy to do so, so this allows them to share risks and achieve a win-win scenario,” Ng said. These collaborations demonstrate that businesses are exploring new growth avenues, from creating tailored products to reach customers more effectively to offering fresh dining choices, according to Ng. Ng also pointed out that the target market segment for both the Japanese and Korean businesses, though smaller, appeared to be more premium and niche, which could present unique opportunities in Hong Kong. Another factor prompting Korean and Japanese businesses to venture overseas is weakness in their domestic markets, even as specific sectors – such as semiconductors in South Korea and tourism in Japan – continue to perform well. As a result, many enterprises were looking to export products to sustain growth, and Hong Kong presented targeted opportunities for those seeking expansion, Ng said. Vera Yuen Wing-han, a lecturer in economics at the University of Hong Kong, noted that despite shifting consumption patterns, with many local residents heading across the border to mainland China for food and entertainment, the city still retained strong spending power. “If there are special enough offerings, Hongkongers are willing to pay a premium,” Yuen said. “If it’s a concept backed by good promotion, a rich story, quality, and unique selling points, it can become very popular.” She pointed out that Hongkongers’ penchant for all things Japanese and Korean significantly boosted market receptivity for products from the two countries while frequent cultural exchanges and tourism further facilitated business collaborations. “It’s more special when these are brands from overseas, not affordable products or those that you could secure from the mainland, as many people already have access to those by spending time across the border,” Yuen said.

title: Another World drawn by hand and heart: A key animator's seven-year craft
description: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the design industry, where speed and efficiency have become the norm. But the Hong Kong animated film Another World took a different path. Entirely hand-drawn over seven years, it was selected for the 2025 Annecy International Animation Film Festival in France — hailed as the “Oscars of the animation world” — and won Best Animated Feature at the Golden Horse Awards...
content: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the design industry, where speed and efficiency have become the norm. But the Hong Kong animated film Another World took a different path. Entirely hand-drawn over seven years, it was selected for the 2025 Annecy International Animation Film Festival in France — hailed as the “Oscars of the animation world” — and won Best Animated Feature at the Golden Horse Awards last year.One of the film's key animators is Hilary Tang Yin-ting, a graduate in fine arts with a focus in animation and visual effects from Hong Kong Metropolitan University (HKMU) in 2020. She believes animators must feel a character's movements in their own bodies to bring them to life. “The work is gruelling,” she says, “But I stay focused, and then hand audiences a surprise — That joy keeps me moving forward.”A bold first step into the industry Hilary's love of illustration drew her to HKMU. During her studies, she interned at the company that later produced Another World. When the project was about to begin, she put herself forward before graduating and rose to become a key animator. Once a storyboard is completed, production is divided between background and animation teams, with key animators responsible for the characters' main actions. Hilary recalls long days drawing for Another World, often until nightfall. “Animation takes an enormous amount of time,” she says. “A piece I spend weeks — sometimes a month — drawing is often just a blink on the screen.” During the seven-year process, Hilary admits there were moments when she felt lost, but found fulfilment through perseverance. “There is a touch of the ‘craftsman's spirit’ in this work,” she says. “I check my drawings frame by frame before submitting them. That's something the audience never sees.” A craftman's spirit Creating animation demands not only creativity but also mental, physical and emotional resilience. Drawing day after day took a toll on Hilary's wrists. “You need your 'three treasures' — eye drops, painkilling patches and a wrist brace — and proper self-care,” she says. There was a weight on the mind as well. Early on, seeing colleagues’ refined work, she felt pressure to deliver, fearing she might otherwise hold everyone else back. Luckily, teamwork eased the burden. After hours, the team would trade ideas to solve problems and improve efficiency, and mealtimes sometimes became a chance to air their frustrations. This deepened her appreciation of collaboration. Acting it outHilary has a preference for 2D animation, though she admits it is far from easy. “Think about how to draw a strand of hair floating in the air,” she says. To make a character come to life, Hilary boils the secret down to one rule: “Do it yourself.” She adds, “Animation, after all, springs from life.” Many times, she acted out movements in front of a mirror, filming herself as a reference for her drawings. In Another World, Goran flees after her family is torn apart. To capture the frantic, off-balance feeling, Hilary filmed herself racing on a treadmill until she tumbled off. For a scene of a soul passing through a waterfall on its way to rebirth, she spent a month swimming to study how the body moves through water. As AI hits one industry after another, Hilary remains convinced that the human hand still holds value. “At this stage, AI is only a tool. The fine work of tuning a character's movements still has to be done by humans,” she says. “It's a person's eye for beauty and judgment that decides how high a work can stand.”Her studies at HKMU built a strong foundation for her career. “Our lecturers walked us through so many of the fundamental principles — the logic of cinematic storytelling, the language of the camera, and the like — which helps you tell the good from the bad and choose the most fitting shots.” Practice beyond the classroom Hilary says her programme at HKMU guided her through the animation production process and have proved helpful in her work. She looks back fondly on Drawing and Life Drawing. “Sketching from life, with the model changing poses every five minutes, is a real test of your ability to capture movement and set it down on the spot,” she recalls. Hilary enjoys returning to her alma mater to share her experience and gain perspectives from students' questions. She hopes Hong Kong animation goes from strength to strength. “Don't give up easily,” she offers some advice for those who hope to enter the field. “There is no denying that audiences often decide how far an animation can go, but that is not the whole story. You will accumulate experience and become better at what you do. Follow your heart and keep pushing forward,” she says.

title: Second land tender at Hong Kong’s border tech hub draws 9 bids

content: A second batch of land at Hong Kong’s flagship tech hub at the border with mainland China has drawn nine bids, with frontier technology firms and major conglomerates among the tenderers. The Loop Hong Kong Park Company, which operates the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park (HSITP), revealed the results on Tuesday, nearly two months after six bids were received from conglomerates and hi-tech firms for its inaugural land tender at the end of August. Tuesday’s tender covered three land parcels mainly for laboratory and office use in the park’s first phase of development. One is eligible to be paired with a talent-accommodation parcel. “The participating bidders include frontier technology enterprises, enterprises with park operation experience, and major conglomerates, reaffirming the industry’s confidence in the future of the Loop Hong Kong Park,” the company said. It said the results of the first two tender rounds would be announced by the end of the year. The company said the parcels offered across the two tender rounds would complement the first batch of eight buildings due to be completed soon, including Loop Academy One, the flagship project of the Northern Metropolis University Town. “Upholding the tripartite mission anchored by academia, with R&D a core part, and underpinned by technology, the building will convene top-tier universities and R&D institutions from the mainland, Hong Kong and overseas, injecting a powerful momentum into frontier scientific research across the park,” it said. The company said it would closely monitor market conditions and development needs, and continue to release land in a well-ordered and progressive manner. In his policy address last month, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said more than 100 innovation and technology (I&T) firms had moved into the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park. He also revealed that about 10 AI and biotech companies would be the first to access cross-border data flows under a new pilot scheme expected to roll out this year, while a “white list” to facilitate cross-border movement for more than 1,000 workers would be ready by the middle of next year. The government said earlier that it would set up dedicated boundary control facilities at a western bridge linking the parks in Hong Kong and Shenzhen to serve people on the white list. Working with the San Tin Technopole and surrounding industrial spaces, the park was building a comprehensive I&T industry ecosystem spanning R&D, commercialisation and mass application, the company said. The company earlier described the response to the inaugural tender, which covered four land parcels in the park, as “enthusiastic”, with six bids submitted. According to a source, five companies submitted six bids. Of these, three specialise in cutting-edge technologies including chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum technology. The remaining two are conglomerates with AI, data and medical research departments or subsidiaries. These sites are earmarked for laboratories and talent accommodation, with a combined gross floor area exceeding 76,000 square metres.

title: Hong Kong-based IOMed settles more disputes as body marks its first year
description: A Hong Kong-headquartered intergovernmental mediation body has successfully settled an infrastructure dispute in Malaysia and received “more than a dozen” inquiries, its head has revealed on the organisation’s first anniversary. Teresa Cheng Yeuk-wah, secretary general of the International Organisation for Mediation (IOMed), told a reception marking the body’s first anniversary that it had wrapped up a case on Tuesday and was handling another. “Our ambition is not simply to build a successful...
content: A Hong Kong-headquartered intergovernmental mediation body has successfully settled an infrastructure dispute in Malaysia and received “more than a dozen” inquiries, its head has revealed on the organisation’s first anniversary. Teresa Cheng Yeuk-wah, secretary general of the International Organisation for Mediation (IOMed), told a reception marking the body’s first anniversary that it had wrapped up a case on Tuesday and was handling another. “Our ambition is not simply to build a successful institution, but to foster a culture where mediation becomes a natural and trusted choice to resolve international disputes,” Cheng said. Inaugurated on October 20, 2025, the organisation now has 48 signatory states, compared with 37 last year. The number of contracting states also rose from eight last year to 18. These states span Asia, Africa, Latin America, Oceania and Europe. Contracting states, which have ratified their membership, include Nicaragua, Pakistan, Kenya, Myanmar, Cambodia and Serbia. Signatory states include Kyrgyzstan, Morocco, Vanuatu, Angola, Cuba and Kiribati. “The growth reflects the international community’s confidence in and aspiration for mediation, and we hope, also of the work of the International Organisation for Mediation,” Cheng added. The body had previously disclosed that it had successfully handled a maritime dispute involving parties from mainland China and Singapore in May. Cheng said on Tuesday that the body had resolved another dispute at its Wan Chai headquarters within a day. The case concerned an infrastructure project in Malaysia, and was brought about despite the lack of a prior agreement between the disputing parties to use this alternative form of dispute resolution. Cheng said the body had also been handling another case, which it was conducted online. “With the consent of the parties, we are disclosing as much information as we can to let everyone know about our development,” the secretary general said. Cheng added that IOMed had received “more than a dozen” inquiries from parties interested in conducting mediation at the body. Speaking at the anniversary reception, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu called the growth in signatory and contracting states “encouraging”, saying the body had been gaining trust quickly over the past year. “In short, IOMed is fast emerging as a trusted intergovernmental body, committed to resolving international disputes through mediation, and doing so based on mutual respect and understanding,” Lee said. He highlighted that the government remained committed to supporting the intergovernmental body to promote Hong Kong as a global hub for mediation. These efforts included a measure announced in the policy address last month to include IOMed mediation as a dispute resolution option in government contracts and agreements. Lee said he hoped to work with the body to encourage young professionals to contribute to international peace and cooperation. Cui Jianchun, commissioner of the Chinese foreign ministry’s office in Hong Kong, said separately in his congratulatory remarks at the reception that IOMed's development had been a “pioneering journey”, pledging continued support from the nation. “As both initiator and host country, China remains fully committed to supporting the development of IOMed,” Cui said. He said the growth in signatory and contracting states has shown broad international representation, while its success with two settlements has proven its value as a dispute resolution platform.

title: Hong Kong child sex sentences remain far below maximum life, report finds
description: Average sentences for Hong Kong’s gravest child sex crimes have remained below 10 years over the past three decades, far below the maximum penalty of life imprisonment, prompting a call for a sentencing council to issue clearer judicial guidance. Citing data from 401 publicly available judgments between 1990 and 2025, University of Hong Kong law professor Puja Kapai on Tuesday said her research found six offences – including rape, buggery, and unlawful sexual intercourse – carried average prison...
content: Average sentences for Hong Kong’s gravest child sex crimes have remained below 10 years over the past three decades, far below the maximum penalty of life imprisonment, prompting a call for a sentencing council to issue clearer judicial guidance. Citing data from 401 publicly available judgments between 1990 and 2025, University of Hong Kong law professor Puja Kapai on Tuesday said her research found six offences – including rape, buggery, and unlawful sexual intercourse – carried average prison terms ranging from four years and six months to nine years and eight months. Kapai and her team also found that four of the six gravest sexual offences involving children showed a downward trend. This trend was especially pronounced for unlawful intercourse with a girl under 13, where average sentences fell from 10 to 12 years in the mid-2000s to under five years in recent years. While acknowledging that judges were bound by precedent and had already taken a range of factors into account, the report found that sentences for the six offences “consistently fell in the low to medium range, far below the statutory maximum”. Under Hong Kong’s common law system, appellate judgments provide sentencing guidance, setting starting points that judges may adjust upwards or downwards after considering aggravating and mitigating factors. The associate professor remarked that while lower sentences were not a matter of judicial bias, “I would say that it’s fair to describe the attitude as fairly conservative”. She said judicial officers were not obliged to adopt a “trauma-informed approach”, which should include not only the assault itself but also the mental burden of navigating court proceedings. The report did not include all cases of sexual offences involving children as it only included judgments in the public record and excluded cases resolved through guilty pleas and other procedures. Kapai’s team singled out six sexual offences involving children that warrant the maximum penalty of life imprisonment under the Crime Ordinance: incest by men, rape, non-consensual buggery, homosexual buggery with or by a man under 16, buggery with a girl under 21, and intercourse with a girl under 13. Rape and non-consensual buggery carried average prison terms of 9.8 and 9.5 years respectively, according to the report. They were also the crimes that had shown rare spikes and “comparatively harsher” penalties within the period. Describing a sentencing council as a “support aid” to the judicial system, Kapai said such a body could help establish more “principled, transparent and consistently applied” sentencing guidelines for these crimes. In the United Kingdom, for example, an independent public body called the Sentencing Council develops guidelines, monitors their implementation and evaluates the impact of potential penalties on victims. Kapai said Hong Kong lacked an equivalent body, leaving victims facing uncertainty even after perpetrators were convicted. She added that judgments rarely explained clearly how various factors shaped the final sentence. “Recognising that a lack of certainty, inconsistency, or even perceptions around inconsistency, can be damaging to criminal justice outcomes as public interest,” she said. If guidelines were in place, complainants would have a clearer sense of the likely penalties perpetrators could face if they decided to file a complaint and pursue legal proceedings, she added.

title: Contested subsectors double in Hong Kong’s Election Committee poll
description: The number of contested subsectors in Hong Kong’s powerful Election Committee has doubled compared with 2021, in a move observers said reflected Beijing’s push to foster healthy competition within the pro-establishment camp and strengthen the legitimacy of the body responsible for selecting the city’s next leader. The two-week nomination period ended on Tuesday, with 1,115 hopefuls signing up to run for 982 elected seats across 36 subsectors on the Election Committee. The poll will be held on...
content: The number of contested subsectors in Hong Kong’s powerful Election Committee has doubled compared with 2021, in a move observers said reflected Beijing’s push to foster healthy competition within the pro-establishment camp and strengthen the legitimacy of the body responsible for selecting the city’s next leader. The two-week nomination period ended on Tuesday, with 1,115 hopefuls signing up to run for 982 elected seats across 36 subsectors on the Election Committee. The poll will be held on November 22. A total of 31 subsectors will hold contested elections, up from 13 in 2021, the first poll since the “patriots-only” electoral system shake-up. Elected members will join 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies to select the chief executive next March and elect 40 of the Legislative Council’s 90 members in 2029. Contested subsectors include all 18 under the industrial, commercial and financial sectors, which will hold contested elections, breaking with their long-standing practice of coordinating within subsectors to avoid competition. Among them, the commercial (second) and industrial (second) subsectors, representing the Chinese General Chamber of Commerce and the Chinese Manufacturers’ Association of Hong Kong respectively, will stage contested polls for the first time. Social welfare and medical and health services face the fiercest contests, with 25 and 23 candidates respectively vying for the 15 seats in each. The five uncontested subsectors are labour, education, associations of Chinese fellow townsmen, representatives of Hong Kong members of relevant national organisations, and sports, performing arts, culture and publication, accounting for 259 elected members. All nominations will be subject to vetting by the Candidate Eligibility Review Committee to ensure national security. Excluding uncontested subsectors, only a small pool of 5,757 voters is eligible to cast ballots, including designated representatives from pro-government groups, corporate bodies named by authorities, and government-subsidised NGOs. Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said a more competitive election would improve members’ performance and bring in fresh blood. “If everyone is re-elected uncontested, how can others come forward to compete? This does nothing to help nurture politicians,” he said. “With competition, those who are elected will have to work diligently … If they run uncontested, they may be unmotivated.” Lau stressed that the body must demonstrate broad representativeness. Active participation by elites from different backgrounds would help ensure the elected chief executive and lawmakers fairly serve the interests of various sectors, while also raising public awareness of and support for the poll, he added. Lau said the Election Committee’s expanded role after the “patriots-only” electoral system shake-up – which included nominating Legco candidates and choosing lawmakers – had encouraged more elites and business figures to join. The body also served as a platform for them to enter politics and demonstrate their expertise, while the political experience gained would benefit their future development, Lau noted. Veteran political commentator Sonny Lo Shiu-hing said the trend was in line with the Legislative Council and District Council elections after the electoral system overhaul, with no seats left uncontested. He said the central government aimed to encourage healthy competition within the pro-establishment camp and expand the patriotic front by attracting more elites to take part under the “patriots administering Hong Kong” principle. “Beijing wants to win the hearts and minds of more Hongkongers to the patriotic front,” Lo said. “If the patriotic front is limited to the same group of people, it is unable to enhance its legitimacy and the breadth and depth of their participation.” Lo added that Beijing hoped a competitive election with a more robust electoral atmosphere would further improve the Election Committee’s legitimacy. However, he cautioned that competition remained confined to the elite, while the public largely stayed apathetic or even cynical about politics. “I believe the public holds a ‘wait-and-see attitude’ … there is a discrepancy between the elite political culture and the mass public,” Lo said. “Some of the public are just spectators watching.” The coming election will also see the absence of opposition-leaning candidates. The only centrist Election Committee member, Tik Chi-yuen, who stepped down as a lawmaker last year, has not sought re-election in the social welfare sector. A growing number of former senior government officials have submitted nominations to run, including former justice minister Rimsky Yuen Kwok-keung, former health minister Sophia Chan Siu-chee and former innovation and technology secretary Alfred Sit Wing-hang. Major developers such as billionaire Pacific Century Group chairman Richard Li Tzar-kai, Henderson Land Development chairman Martin Lee Ka-shing and Sino Land chairman Daryl Ng Win-kong have also entered the race. The committee comprises five sectors representing 40 subsectors, with four consisting only of ex officio or nominated members, including the religious subsectors, representatives of associations of Hong Kong residents on the mainland, Legco members and deputies to the National People’s Congress and members of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference. The full list of nominations can be seen here.

title: Scathing Tai Po fire report expected to be submitted on Thursday
description: An independent committee investigating the deadly Tai Po fire is set to submit its final report to the Hong Kong government on Thursday, with the judge-led panel expected to largely endorse the scathing closing submission of its lead counsel, sources have said. A redacted version of the committee’s report, which may withhold some information to avoid prejudicing criminal proceedings related to Hong Kong’s deadliest residential fire in decades, is scheduled for public release next week at the...
content: An independent committee investigating the deadly Tai Po fire is set to submit its final report to the Hong Kong government on Thursday, with the judge-led panel expected to largely endorse the scathing closing submission of its lead counsel, sources have said. A redacted version of the committee’s report, which may withhold some information to avoid prejudicing criminal proceedings related to Hong Kong’s deadliest residential fire in decades, is scheduled for public release next week at the earliest, the South China Morning Post has learned. “The committee will leave it to the administration to decide who to hold accountable and when to take disciplinary actions,” a source familiar with the arrangement said on Tuesday. Another insider added: “[Disciplinary procedures] will not take long as seasoned administrative officials with experience working in the Civil Service Bureau were reshuffled to prepare the groundwork earlier this month.” The panel – led by Justice David Lok Kai-hong – investigating the inferno at the Wang Fuk Court housing estate last November that claimed 168 lives did not dispute the major arguments put forward by lead counsel Victor Dawes SC, the sources said. The final report, which will be submitted to Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu, will closely align with the closing submission delivered by Dawes, although it will be shorter than the 627-page document. Dawes argued that the blaze at the estate – which was undergoing extensive renovation work at the time – resulted from systemic failures and a blatant disregard for safety. One insider said the issue of bid-rigging was expected to be addressed in the final report, although it would not be a “major focus”. In his final submission, Dawes said the government bore an “unshirkable responsibility” for the tragedy, explicitly naming four bodies for failing to properly heed fire risks: the Fire Services Department; the Buildings Department; the Labour Department; and the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit. Dawes also said that the contractors’ actions merited the committee’s “strongest condemnation” for using non-flame-retardant materials and deceiving authorities to cut costs in the estate’s HK$336 million renovation. The sources said that the committee would issue a statement on Thursday announcing the submission of its final report, without holding a press conference, mirroring the arrangement in 2013 when a commission of inquiry into the deadly Lamma Island ferry collision submitted its report to then chief executive Leung Chun-ying. Upon receipt of the report, the Department of Justice would review it and redact parts of it when necessary to avoid prejudicing criminal proceedings, one insider said, while stressing that the redactions were expected to be relatively “insignificant”. The source added that names of civil servants involved in various departments would not be redacted as they had already been disclosed during public hearings. The Tai Po fire has led to 25 criminal charges against seven individuals and two companies, including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, money laundering, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion. The defendants include directors and a registered inspector from the project consultancy firm, Will Power Architects, and directors from the main contractor, Prestige Construction and Engineering. In the 2013 report on the Lamma tragedy, which claimed 39 lives when two vessels collided, all parts relating to the responsibilities of the two captains were redacted. That was done because the government wanted to ensure a fair trial as manslaughter charges had already been laid against them. The independent committee investigating the Wang Fuk Court fire concluded its inquiry after holding six rounds of public evidential hearings from March to July, spanning 30 days. Some 80 witnesses were called upon to give evidence. A third government insider said the timing of the report’s submission and public release in late October was “carefully calibrated”, after Lok “largely finished” compiling it earlier this month. The source said senior officials sought to avoid having news of the report overshadow the Apec meeting of finance ministers being held in Hong Kong on Tuesday and Wednesday. Meanwhile, Lee’s team was also aware that the government should publicly address the submission of the report “shortly”, preferably “next week” at the earliest as planned, to begin any internal disciplinary actions. “The government has been sensitive not to publish [the report] close to the first anniversary of the fire, as that might aggravate public distress and residents’ grief,” the source said. Lok, who also chairs the Electoral Affairs Commission, needed to conclude the inquiry early and move on to oversee the procedures for the Election Committee election on November 22, the source added.

title: Hong Kong issues amber travel alert for France as school protests turn violent
description: Hong Kong has issued an amber outbound travel alert for France after weeks of protests over school conditions spread across the country, triggering clashes and damage in major cities. The alert – the lowest of three levels in the Security Bureau’s outbound travel alert system – advises residents travelling to France to exercise caution in response to signs of a threat to personal safety. “Due to persistent protests across many places in France, which have resulted in clashes and damage, the...
content: Hong Kong has issued an amber outbound travel alert for France after weeks of protests over school conditions spread across the country, triggering clashes and damage in major cities. The alert – the lowest of three levels in the Security Bureau’s outbound travel alert system – advises residents travelling to France to exercise caution in response to signs of a threat to personal safety. “Due to persistent protests across many places in France, which have resulted in clashes and damage, the government advises residents who intend to visit France, or are already there, to monitor the situation, exercise caution, attend to personal safety, pay attention to local announcements and avoid large gatherings,” a government spokesman said on Tuesday. The bureau said it would continue to closely monitor the situation. Residents requiring assistance may call the Immigration Department’s 24-hour hotline on (852) 1868. France endured a turbulent weekend as weeks of high school student protests over poor study conditions were hijacked by violent looters in major cities, amid anger over rising fuel prices and the cost-of-living crisis. While the movement, which began on September 17, drew hundreds of thousands of largely peaceful protesters, clashes over the weekend led to chaotic scenes, with hundreds of shops looted and the historic city hall in Limoges burned down.

title: Hong Kong to focus on infrastructure monitoring in first phase of ‘AI city brain’
description: Hong Kong authorities will focus on incorporating infrastructure monitoring into the first phase of their AI-powered urban management system, while exploring its expansion into public services in later stages. Officials also told a Legislative Council meeting on Tuesday that government arms were encouraged to develop their own databases before connecting them to the “AI city brain”. Undersecretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Lillian Cheong Man-lei said authorities would prioritise...
content: Hong Kong authorities will focus on incorporating infrastructure monitoring into the first phase of their AI-powered urban management system, while exploring its expansion into public services in later stages. Officials also told a Legislative Council meeting on Tuesday that government arms were encouraged to develop their own databases before connecting them to the “AI city brain”. Undersecretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Lillian Cheong Man-lei said authorities would prioritise incorporating several databases monitoring city infrastructure conditions into the AI city brain system. These include the Lands Department’s geospatial database and its underground utilities system that maps water, natural gas pipes and electricity grid conditions. The Buildings Department’s system that transforms two-dimensional building plans into 3D models, alongside information systems on highways, weather and landslide monitoring, would also be connected, she added. “Our objective is to build a smart decision platform to collect, share and analyse interdepartmental data, with the aim of enhancing the government’s capability in resource allocation and decision-making, as well as prediction and alerts, ultimately improving our urban resilience,” she said. The meeting was a joint session between the subcommittees on artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics development and “new quality productive forces” – referring to productivity led by technological advancement – to discuss industrial applications of these technologies. The initiative stems from Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s latest policy address, in which he announced the government would develop the AI city brain system to consolidate databases maintained by different government arms and create an intra-government data-sharing environment. A task force chaired by Chief Secretary for Administration Eric Chan Kwok-ki will steer the programme. In an earlier interview with the South China Morning Post, Chan said the project aimed to provide a “full picture” of Hong Kong, and the authorities would launch a pilot version focusing on extreme weather response before typhoon season next year. The first phase is expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2028, with HK$200 million (US$25.48 million) earmarked for this stage’s development. During Tuesday’s meeting, several lawmakers asked whether the government would connect public service databases, such as the Labour and Welfare Bureau’s welfare recipient records, to the AI system to expand its functions beyond city management. Acting Commissioner for Digital Policy Daniel Cheung Yee-wai said while the early stage of the project would focus on urban management and emergency response, authorities were in parallel exploring scenarios for later incorporation. “We encourage various policy bureaus to work on databases within their respective purview and use AI platforms provided by the Digital Policy Office for analysis,” he said, adding that the Labour and Welfare Bureau has already been developing a system to identify vulnerable cases warranting more help. “Ultimately, the AI city brain will connect these data sets for interdepartmental data analysis,” he added. The meeting also discussed authorities’ plan to commission the government-owned Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation to develop the Hong Kong Innovation and Technology Application Scenario Promotion Centre. The initiative, also announced in the latest policy address, aims to provide a targeted list of public and private sector scenarios where the tech industry can apply innovative solutions. Cheong told lawmakers that another objective of the centre would be to facilitate trials of technological application and empower enterprises to better attract investment. “In the Northern Metropolis … we expect to launch some new trial scenarios for new technologies, and the government will also provide policy packages such as subsidising public organisations to try these technologies,” she said.

title: Abby Choi did not have enough cash in year before death, murder trial told

Choi’s former chauffeur, Chin Kei-shun, said on Tuesday that the influencer appeared to have run into cash-flow difficulties after she and her partner incurred a HK$5 million (US$637,090) debt during a leisure trip to Macau in August 2021. Chin said Choi would usually carry a substantial amount of cash in her handbag when she went...
content: Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung did not have enough cash to cover her expenses in the year before her death, her former driver has told her murder trial. Choi’s former chauffeur, Chin Kei-shun, said on Tuesday that the influencer appeared to have run into cash-flow difficulties after she and her partner incurred a HK$5 million (US$637,090) debt during a leisure trip to Macau in August 2021. Chin said Choi would usually carry a substantial amount of cash in her handbag when she went out, but appeared to have insufficient cash from February to the middle of 2022. She would ask him to pay for her expenses first and repay him later, Chin added. The former chauffeur also said Choi appeared to have sought HK$600,000 from her ex-brother-in-law, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, because of her financial difficulties. Kwong, 35, is standing trial in the High Court on a joint count of murder alongside his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and his younger brother, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, Choi’s ex-husband. The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, is also contesting a charge of preventing the burial of Choi’s body, an offence to which his two sons pleaded guilty before the trial began last month. The court heard that Anthony Kwong served as the 28-year-old model’s stand-in chauffeur after Chin resigned in November 2022. He remained in the role until Choi’s killing came to light on February 24, 2023. Chin said Kwong had asked him to take unpaid leave because the Kwong family would be away on a two-month trip. He said he resigned after his request to be placed on half pay was rejected. Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, previously alleged that Kwong’s mother, Jenny Li Sui-heung, used various excuses to remove Chin from the job so that her elder son, who was unemployed at the time, could succeed him. Li allegedly tried to persuade Choi to dismiss Chin by accusing the driver of theft and having financial problems. She also allegedly told Chin that he could take a few months off while her family travelled. Chin admitted on Tuesday that he had two drug-related convictions in the past, but said no one had ever questioned his integrity during his employment. Asked whether he had committed theft or had a gambling habit, the witness said: “I also want to know what I allegedly stole.” Prosecutors contend that Anthony Kwong played a part in Choi’s murder, noting that he accompanied his father when the latter sourced items used to dispose of the socialite’s body after her killing. Kwong Kau earlier admitted that he had visited a kitchenware supplier in Yau Ma Tei on February 8, 2023, where he bought a commercial meat mincer, a 14-by-14-inch soup pot, a wooden chopping board and a frying sieve for HK$8,700. A saleswoman at the shop, whose name was withheld from open court at her request, said the elder Kwong also asked about the price of an industrial-grade bone grinder after buying the mincer. She added that when she said a bone grinder would cost about HK$35,000, a younger man – whom prosecutors said was Anthony Kwong – told Kwong Kau the device was too expensive, and the pair left the shop. Prosecutors suggested the alleged murder arose from a family feud over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat at the upmarket Kadooria development in Ho Man Tin. Kwong Kau, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the flat and enlisted his two sons to help kill the influencer. The defendants previously acknowledged that Choi covered 99 per cent of the flat’s HK$60 million purchase price. Property agent Marco Wong Tak-sing said Kwong Kau submitted the required tender documents for the flat’s purchase in 2019, but it was Choi who paid a HK$3.74 million deposit. Asked about the purpose of the purchase, the elder Kwong told Wong that his “daughter-in-law” wanted the flat for the convenience of her children going to school. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: Luxury homeowner fined HK$255,800 after eighth prosecution over illegal renovations

The Buildings Department said on Tuesday that the owner of a Beaulieu Peninsula detached house on Yu Chui Street in Tuen Mun was convicted and fined at Tuen Mun Court last Friday. It was the eighth time the owner had faced...
content: The owner of a luxury house in Hong Kong has been fined HK$255,800 (US$32,600) for persistently failing to comply with a statutory removal order even after previously being prosecuted seven times for illegal site works and unauthorised structures found at his property. The Buildings Department said on Tuesday that the owner of a Beaulieu Peninsula detached house on Yu Chui Street in Tuen Mun was convicted and fined at Tuen Mun Court last Friday. It was the eighth time the owner had faced prosecution for ignoring the removal order, which was issued in 1993. “Failing to comply with the removal order, the owner had been prosecuted by the Buildings Department seven times and was fined and sentenced to four months’ imprisonment, suspended for two years, upon convictions by the court,” a department spokesman said. “As the owner persisted in not complying with the removal order, the owner was prosecuted for the eighth time.” According to the department, the unauthorised building works included site formation works for constructing an unauthorised platform of about 122 square metres (1,292 square feet) on a slope adjoining an approved garden. Unauthorised structures were also found that extended the floors at different levels of the block, amounting to a total floor area of about 57 square metres. The remaining unauthorised works were the erection of a floor slab over a space near an approved dining room and removal of parts of the house’s external walls. The owner had not sought prior approval and consent from the department for those alterations. Under the Buildings Ordinance, the Buildings Department can issue statutory orders to owners and require them to remove unauthorised structures. Failing to comply with a removal order can result in a maximum fine of HK$200,000 and a year in prison, and a further fine of up to HK$20,000 for each day of non-compliance. The department said HK$155,880, or 61 per cent of the total fine that the court imposed on Friday, was for daily penalties. According to supplementary information provided by the department, it first inspected the property in April 1992 and issued a removal order on nine unauthorised building works in February 1993. In 2019, the owner appointed an authorised professional to handle the order, but the professional had not submitted any proposal before resigning in 2021. The owner later appointed another professional in the same year. The department inspected the property in August 2024 and found at least five of the nine items had yet to be rectified. The professional resigned in December of the same year. The owner subsequently hired other professionals, who submitted a preliminary slope remedial report to the department in January last year. Five months later, the department told them to submit a slope demolition and restoration proposal. In December 2025, the department’s inspection found that at least six of the nine items had yet to be rectified, including the site formation works and the extra floor spaces. Beaulieu Peninsula was among the luxury estates inspected by authorities after landslides triggered by a heavy downpour in September 2023 exposed unauthorised structures at Redhill Peninsula in Tai Tam. According to the latest available information, the department reportedly initiated prosecutions against owners of 25 houses in Beaulieu Peninsula, as of mid-2025. Following rampant flouting of building laws, the Development Bureau proposed to amend the ordinance by increasing relevant penalties, reducing the prosecution threshold and introducing new offences. The government plans to submit proposed amendments to the Legislative Council by the end of this year, alongside proposals to strengthen oversight of renovation works raised in the wake of the Wang Fuk Court fire last November. The deadly blaze tore through all but one of the Tai Po estate’s eight towers, killing 168 people and displacing about 5,000 others.

title: Pakistan and the US factor as China looks to sell its J-35 stealth jets

The Pakistan Air Force is also the only declared interested buyer of China’s J-35 stealth fighter, a generational leap in technology. The Chinese jet first flew at the Zhuhai...
content: Last month, the US published the fine print of a US$686 million upgrade deal for Pakistan’s F-16 fighter jets. The deal is for data link systems, new encryption gear and a refit that keeps the jets flying until 2040. The notice says Pakistan can protect the technology to “substantially the same degree” as the US government. The Pakistan Air Force is also the only declared interested buyer of China’s J-35 stealth fighter, a generational leap in technology. The Chinese jet first flew at the Zhuhai air show in 2024, and may well appear again when the biennial event returns in December. Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC) has been pitching it as a cheaper F-35 – America’s stealth fighter jet. In June last year, a Pakistani government social media post listed a Chinese offer of 40 J-35s, KJ-500 early-warning planes and HQ-19 air defences. It was taken down soon after. This May, the air force said it had signed an “initial collaborative agreement” to buy the J-35 but gave no details. Last year, Defence Security Asia reported that the first J-35s would arrive by early 2026. None arrived; Pakistan Air Force sources dismissed online claims that some had. Neither government has announced a delivery, but the same site now says timing depends on how many jets can be spared after fulfilling domestic orders. Then there is the money. Pakistan’s defence budget for this financial year is 3.01 trillion rupees (US$10.7 billion). The air force gets 573 billion rupees, and that has to pay salaries too. And all of it sits under a US$7 billion International Monetary Fund loan. When Pakistan bought advanced American F-16s after September 11, the deal came with minders. Washington made Islamabad host and pay for a US technical security team at the Shahbaz and Mushaf airbases where the jets were to be deployed. Because Pakistan also flies the JF-17, which it builds with China, those F-16s must be kept apart from other aircraft, with access tightly controlled. The programme still has money behind it. In February 2025, the Trump administration spared US$397 million for it from previously frozen foreign aid. Washington takes this seriously. In July 2019, it threw Turkey out of the F-35 stealth jet programme for buying Russia’s S-400 air defence system. The US said the jet could not coexist with a Russian system that would be used to learn about it. As Ellen Lord, then the Pentagon’s acquisition chief, put it: “Turkey cannot field a Russian intelligence collection platform in proximity to where the F-35 programme makes repairs and houses the F-35.” In July this year, US President Donald Trump said the US would lift sanctions on Turkey and consider restoring its participation in the Joint Strike Fighter programme. However, this month US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a sale can’t go ahead until the S-400 issue is settled. Pakistan has kept its fleets apart so far. Its Chinese-made J-10CEs, which first arrived in 2022, are kept at the Minhas airbase, well away from the F-16 bases. The situation is more complicated when it comes to stealth jets. There is speculation that Pakistan’s air force, looking to eventually replace its ageing F-16 fighter jet fleet – the oldest ones turn 50 from 2030 – could turn to China’s J-35 stealth fighters. Pakistan’s F-16 deal would see it fly the upgraded jets until 2040, keeping the US and Pakistan air forces closely linked for at least another decade. Pakistan is likely to keep the F-16s and J-35s separate as it has done with the J-10CEs. But that arrangement has slipped once. After the 2019 clash with India, the US State Department rebuked Islamabad for moving F-16s to unapproved bases. Beijing would want guarantees of its own, and neither government has said where the J-35 will go or under what rules. Pakistan’s aircraft complex at Kamra builds 58 per cent of the JF-17’s airframe and keeps the fleet flying. Yet the first jet to need a major overhaul had to go to AVIC in Chengdu in 2017. Buying complete Chinese systems leaves Pakistan less room for its own work on data links, weapons and integration. With the J-35, the details that matter have not been published: who overhauls the engines, who gets into the software and who controls the mission data the sensors rely on. Other buyers are likely to face the same test. China showed the J-35A at the Dubai Airshow last November, and the United Arab Emirates’ air force already flies China’s L-15 trainer jet. The UAE has been here before: it shelved an F-35 deal in 2021 after Washington doubted it could protect American technology while working so closely with China. In December, the UAE’s Al Fursan aerobatic team is set to perform at the Zhuhai air show. Selling to the UAE would mean Beijing deciding to trust its stealth secrets to an air force that nearly flew America’s F-35. By selling first to one of its closest partners, Beijing avoids that decision.

title: Why US Secretary of State Rubio is skipping New Delhi for an Indian oil refinery

content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India’s Jamnagar this week – home to the world’s largest oil refining complex – signals energy cooperation as the anchor for bilateral ties even as broader policy friction frays relations, according to analysts. On Tuesday, Rubio indicated that India’s largest private company, Reliance Industries, which owns the Jamnagar oil refinery complex, will buy more Venezuelan oil. “India is a refining superpower. They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They’ve done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, it’s something they can do,” he told reporters in Mumbai, the country’s financial capital. Rubio met Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar on Tuesday in Mumbai as both sides sought to deepen energy cooperation and move closer to finalising a broader trade deal, following an interim framework reached in February. An India-US trade deal has stalled over legal uncertainty surrounding American tariffs, New Delhi’s demand for preferential rates compared with competitors like Vietnam and Washington’s push for market access for its politically sensitive agriculture and dairy sectors, analysts said. “We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement,” Rubio told reporters. Broader ties between the two countries have suffered in recent months over issues such as Washington’s clampdown on professional visas, which has hit Indian technology workers and firms. Rubio’s itinerary during his October 20-21 visit – choosing to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar while skirting India’s capital, New Delhi – reflects a shift in Washington’s approach. “Rubio’s trip to Mumbai and Jamnagar, which hosts the world’s largest single-site oil refinery complex processing 1.4 million barrels per day, is a purely commercial visit unlike a traditional business-led diplomatic one,” said Soumen Ray, a former Indian diplomat. Given the condition of Russian refineries following Ukrainian attacks, this visit may be construed as a last-ditch US effort to find succour to bail them out before the midterm elections,” Ray added. US President Donald Trump has publicly blamed Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries for surging domestic fuel prices. US petrol prices have risen by roughly US$1.26 to nearly US$1.50 per gallon since the start of the war with Iran in late February 2026, pushing the national average to between US$4.30 and US$4.40 per gallon as global oil and refined product supplies tighten. The US secretary of state’s visit comes days after Elon Musk accused Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani, chairman and managing director of Reliance Industries, of blocking Starlink’s entry into India. Ray said that Rubio’s visit showed how the US administration had sought to distance itself from Musk’s “derogatory and highly objectionable remarks”. Policy shift “I see Rubio’s itinerary as reflecting the transactional character of India–US relations under this Trump administration,” said Uday Chandra, a political science professor at India’s Ashoka University, highlighting the financial weight of both Mumbai and Jamnagar. “The focus is, therefore, on investment, energy security and commercial deals. We should not read the absence of Delhi as a diplomatic snub,” Chandra said. India’s foreign ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal told a media briefing on Friday that foreign dignitaries had previously been hosted outside Delhi, including in Vadodara and Ahmedabad. Chandra added that Rubio’s visit showed how energy cooperation could become a defining feature of the US-India relationship. “India needs secure, affordable energy supplies, while the US seeks large markets for its oil and gas and greater investment in its energy infrastructure. There are obvious complementarities here, especially amid disruptions to global energy markets,” he said. India is the world’s third-largest oil importer and has emerged as a key exporter of refined petroleum products, including to Russia following Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian processing facilities. Srinivaasan Balakrishnan, director of strategic engagements and partnerships at Delhi-based think tank Indic Researchers Forum, highlighted that Reliance Industries had invested at least US$100 million in Texas-based start-up America First Refining. The deal was originally framed by Trump in March 2026 as a US$300 billion partnership to build the first major new US oil refinery in 50 years at the Port of Brownsville. “Now the real conversations are happening around capital, refining capacity and specific deals rather than in the political capital. Skipping Delhi keeps the focus on execution and private sector interlocutors who can move money and projects faster than formal inter-governmental machinery,” Balakrishnan said. He added that the sequence of events, combined with Rubio’s trip, pointed to a “practical bargain” over American commercial presence in India alongside Indian refining scale and access to crude oil from diverse sources, including Russia. Last week, Trump temporarily suspended and waived a threat of up to 100 per cent tariffs on major importers of Russian oil – including India and China – via an executive order. The decision was a big relief for India, which is a major buyer of discounted Russian oil. “It is transactional rather than strategic, but in a period when the older political pillars of the relationship have thinned, energy and investment flows are among the few things both sides can still usefully discuss without requiring perfect alignment,” Balakrishnan added.

content: A Gen Z jet-setter in the Philippines has been named commissioner for the urban poor, raising eyebrows over her qualifications for a position dealing with issues such as food and housing insecurity. Zofia Canlas took her oath as commissioner for the Presidential Commission for the Urban Poor (PCUP) on Monday, but drew widespread attention for social media photos depicting a fashion-forward lifestyle and lavish getaways, such as posing in front of the Eiffel Tower in Paris, and other trips around Europe and the United States. Canlas, 27, graduated from De La Salle University Manila with a medical biology degree in 2024. She ran as a nominee for the Batang Quiapo party-list in the 2025 midterm elections but lost, before becoming chief of staff at the PCUP in July that year. She is the daughter of Jose Marcell Canlas, who reportedly serves as an assistant secretary under the Office of the Executive Secretary, according to the Office of the President’s website. The appointment has raised questions about Canlas’ credentials for a role that champions the rights and welfare of the urban poor and pays an annual salary of 2 million pesos (US$31,580). “You graduated with a degree in biology in 2024, and now you are the face of an agency that serves as the voice of those being driven out of their homes. Meanwhile, community leaders who have been devoured by demolitions for decades cannot even be given a seat in the waiting area,” said political youth group Akbayan Youth. The group pointed out the irony of Canlas’ feed filled with trips to Italy, Spain and France, while urban poor families struggled in relocations to areas without water and power. “We do not accept a new nepo baby. Not now, not tomorrow, and not ever, especially for the seat of the genuine poor,” the group said. This Week in Asia has reached out to the PCUP to contact Canlas. Her social media pages have been unavailable since Tuesday. President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s administration on Tuesday defended Canlas’ appointment, saying her age and background would not hinder her role. “The president has always emphasised this: regardless of your status in life, whether you are rich or poor, if you can work and serve the country, that is the No 1 priority for the president – to have someone sincere and dedicated to serving the nation,” said palace press officer Claire Castro. Canlas had been with the PCUP “for a long time” as chief of staff since 2025, making her no stranger to the agency, Castro added. “She has been with the [commission] for quite some time; perhaps you just haven’t noticed. So she is already familiar with the agency’s mandate.” Castro said judging how Canlas would perform in her new role was difficult since she had not yet been seen working. “Let us see first, and if she commits a mistake then that is when we criticise,” Castro said. The PCUP often intervenes as a direct link between urban poor communities and the national government, especially in terms of policy formulation and programme implementation regarding housing. The agency is also often present when informal settlers are evicted from public land. Castro also said Canlas did not need a law degree to be qualified for the role. “Removing someone from office, filing a case, and handling a case require a lawyer. But negotiating on behalf of our fellow Filipinos who belong to the marginalised sectors of society does not require a lawyer. What is needed is dedication and a genuine commitment to one’s work,” Castro said. Nathaniel Candelaria, assistant professor in the University of the Philippines Diliman’s political science department, told This Week in Asia there were several factors behind the public’s concern. “Apart from the lavish lifestyle projected online, connections play a role in this,” Candelaria said, noting that Canlas’ appointment could have given the impression that one could “simply bypass hard work” while others had to sit for a civil service examination to qualify, thereby sparking public outrage. Candelaria said it was important to hire the right people for an urban poor commission “since they will help steer the government’s actions to address poverty”. While young people such as Canlas could contribute to society, the commissioner position “requires certain skill sets which people with more experience can perform better”, Candelaria said. These include an understanding of political and economic forces that shape urban poor conditions, as well as a sense of humility and empathy, according to him. The appointment process must also be meritocratic, Candelaria said. “Not recognising merit in political appointments will definitely be noticed by the people. Given how unpopular the current administration is, people will definitely scrutinise every political appointment, including this one,” he said.

title: For Filipinos, virtual assistant trumps doctor as ‘dream job’. But what’s the reality?
description: When Mark Ifurung left his 18-year career as an IT professional in May, he was happy to ditch his two-hour commutes from his home in Cavite province south of Manila to his office in Makati City. So for his fresh start, the 40-year-old father of four wanted something that would allow him to work from home. “After being unemployed for five months, I decided to explore freelancing,” he said. “With my background in IT operations and application support, I realised I already have transferable skills...
content: When Mark Ifurung left his 18-year career as an IT professional in May, he was happy to ditch his two-hour commutes from his home in Cavite province south of Manila to his office in Makati City. So for his fresh start, the 40-year-old father of four wanted something that would allow him to work from home. “After being unemployed for five months, I decided to explore freelancing,” he said. “With my background in IT operations and application support, I realised I already have transferable skills that I can offer to clients.” While job hunting online, he came across information on the “virtual assistant” industry and was lured by the idea of flexibility and attractive pay. Ifurung is one of a growing number of Filipinos gravitating to virtual assistant work, a booming sector of the Philippines’ offshore labour industry that has steadily risen post-pandemic. Virtual assistants provide administrative, technical or creative services to businesses and individuals, often overseas. Unlike traditional office workers, they typically work from home and may serve multiple clients on a freelance basis – handling tasks ranging from scheduling and customer support to social media management and IT services. VA Masters, a virtual assistant placement agency, estimates there are more than 1 million virtual assistants in the Philippines. Filipinos make up about 38 per cent of the global market, often for clients and companies based in the US, the UK and Australia, according to the agency’s estimates. A survey based on online job searches from May 2025 to May 2026 by remittance agency Remitly found that the role is now the top “dream job” among Filipinos, overtaking doctors. “Virtual work in the Philippines is a fast-rising source of employment for Filipinos,” said Verna Dinah Viajar, an assistant professor at the University of the Philippines School of Labour and Industrial Relations. Viajar said virtual assistant work had attracted Filipinos branching out from the business process outsourcing sector, after AI replaced many tasks in IT and communication such as call centres. “With adequate skills in IT communications, many [business process outsourcing] workers have shifted to VAs,” she said. Work from home, earn abroad Many virtual assistants in the Philippines are independent contractors who are not tied full time to a particular employer. This allows them to take on several clients at once and increase their income potential. Erica Marie Ebrona, 29, manages seven clients from her home in Dumaguete City in central Philippines. “I work as a social media and content strategist, handling content planning, captions, strategy and analytics. I have flexible hours, so I can choose when I work as long as I meet deadlines,” she said. Ebrona started as a virtual assistant in 2023, transitioning from human resources, and earned her first client through a referral. While her monthly income varies, she earns at least 100,000 pesos (US$1,580) a month – over five times the minimum wage in Metro Manila. Virtual assistant work, she said, “offers flexibility and opportunities to work with international clients”. Phu Huynh, a labour analyst for the International Labour Organization (ILO), said the strong interest in virtual assistant work “reflects the appeal of relatively accessible remote work that can connect Filipinos directly to international clients and potentially higher earnings without having to migrate abroad”. A young, digitally connected, and English-speaking workforce made the Philippines an attractive location for outsourced labour – but did not necessarily guarantee decent working conditions, he added. The industry’s unregulated nature leaves many workers open to abuse, according to experts. Most have no contracts, no social protection benefits, and are vulnerable to health issues due to working in different time zones. This lack of regulation could make some assistants “work like slaves in the cyberworld”, Viajar said. Their geographical location also means they do not have redress from the head office. “Being in remote work, it is difficult to follow up work grievances, and their isolated work formats … robs them of the opportunity to exercise their rights as workers,” she said. Most people are drawn to virtual assistant work because of “the prospect of building a better livelihood while remaining connected to their families and communities”, according to Alistair Mercado, CEO and founder of Kasama Connect, a technology platform focused on transparent agreements, payments and accountability for remote work. But the dream should not stop there, he added. “It should include getting paid reliably, developing expertise and having a meaningful say in the terms of your work.” To protect independent contractors, “we need to stop treating ‘be careful’ as a worker-protection system”, he said. “Professionals have responsibilities, but clients, platforms, intermediaries and government have responsibilities too.” AI intervention Artificial intelligence is another challenge to the industry. “[The] work is exposed to AI because many routine tasks such as scheduling, data entry, drafting and basic customer support can increasingly be automated through AI technologies,” Huynh said. “However, ILO research suggests AI is more likely to transform many jobs than eliminate them entirely.” Virtual assistant roles may shift towards more complex tasks requiring judgment, problem solving, managing client relationships and the ability to use AI effectively, he said. “The challenge will be ensuring workers are well equipped with these complementary skills.” Viajar said that AI has become a necessity for virtual assistants. “AI can easily replace tasks that are repetitive but if the work still requires human cognitive abilities, AI becomes a tool for higher productivity and precision work,” she said. Virtual assistant Dani Gregorio, 25, does not see AI fully replacing her job just yet. “I can definitely see why people are worried. We’ve already seen how AI is changing the way different industries operate, and some roles … are being automated or reduced,” she said. “But I also think we need to look at what AI can actually replace and what it can’t fully replicate … You can automate certain processes, but managing people, building trust, understanding human behaviour, and making decisions that consider the bigger picture require more than simply generating an answer. Emotional intelligence and accountability matter, too.” Not everyone would have such skills – “and that’s OK”, Gregorio said. “We shouldn’t romanticise one kind of work just because it looks good on social media.”

title: Malaysia bars civil servants from using Waze, citing Israel’s control of app
description: All civil servants in Malaysia have been banned from using Waze, following a warning by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim of security concerns over the Israeli government’s control of the mobile navigation app. The government announced the decision after a National Cyber Security Committee (NCSC) meeting chaired by Anwar on Tuesday, according to an official circular. “In this regard, all ministry secretaries-general and heads of department must make sure this decision is communicated to all officers...
content: All civil servants in Malaysia have been banned from using Waze, following a warning by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim of security concerns over the Israeli government’s control of the mobile navigation app. The government announced the decision after a National Cyber Security Committee (NCSC) meeting chaired by Anwar on Tuesday, according to an official circular. “In this regard, all ministry secretaries-general and heads of department must make sure this decision is communicated to all officers under their supervision, including agencies and related departments for immediate implementation,” said the circular dated October 20 and issued by the chief secretary to the government. Waze, which evolved from an earlier project called FreeMap Israel, was acquired by search giant Google in 2013 for US$1.15 billion but remains headquartered in Israel’s economic and tech hub of Tel Aviv. Its business operations are governed by Israeli law, according to the app’s terms and conditions. In an earlier statement on Tuesday, Anwar said the NCSC had discussed security risks linked to information and movement data of Malaysian Waze users, given that the app fell exclusively under the jurisdiction of Israeli law. Security concerns over Waze usage were part of a broader discussion on Malaysia’s preparedness to deal with potential threats stemming from rapid advancements in post-quantum cryptography and autonomous artificial intelligence, the prime minister said. “The use of local [navigation] application TuJu, developed by the Malaysian Highway Authority, is encouraged as an alternative,” Anwar said. Waze told This Week in Asia it operated under strict privacy policies to protect user data and comply with global legal data protection standards. “Claims that Waze collects sensitive government information or allows any entity to exploit personal user data are completely false,” a Waze representative said on Thursday. However, the ban would be unlikely to do much to stop any potential cyberthreat outlined by the prime minister, said Benjamin Loh, a communication and media studies lecturer at Monash University Malaysia. Loh said the justification for the ban was weak unless the government was sure that data from Malaysian civil servants who used Waze was being sent to Israel – similar to the reason used by the US to ban Chinese tech giant Huawei. “Commercial apps are not involved in that kind of power play, and the government should provide evidence that national safety is being compromised if it exists, as this affects regular Malaysians who are still using the app,” Loh said. The ban on Waze is the latest move by Malaysia to restrict businesses and activities linked to Israel, which Anwar has repeatedly accused of committing genocide after it launched its war on Gaza on October 7, 2023, in retaliation for a deadly assault in southern Israel on the same day by the Palestinian militant group Hamas, the latter of which killed around 1,200 people. Anwar is seen as Southeast Asia’s most vocal critic of Israel and its closest ally, the US, over the Gaza war, which has killed at least 74,000 people – mostly civilians – and injured nearly 176,000 others, according to the latest data from Gaza’s health ministry. Malaysia has no diplomatic ties with Israel. In August, Malaysian authorities detained several Israel-bound shipments at the Port of Tanjung Pelepas in Johor state, as part of continued enforcement of a December 2023 decision to ban Israeli logistics giant ZIM Integrated Shipping Services and all Israeli-linked ships from using Malaysian port facilities. “We will not allow our country to be used as a conduit for any shipment that supports or contributes to Israel’s military capabilities and its atrocities against Palestinians and other innocent lives,” Anwar said in a statement that month. In July, Malaysia shut down a start-up academy in Johor launched by crypto investor Balaji Serinivasan following claims that Israeli students were studying there. The Malaysian government said then that it would deport any Israelis with dual citizenship found in the country, triggering an outcry from several US lawmakers who urged the US administration to re-evaluate its ties with the Southeast Asian nation.

title: ‘Mourning run’ or clout chase? South Korea divided over runner’s death tributes
