content: South Korean social media posts displaying users’ running records to honour a local woman who died at a Seoul marathon have raised debate over the appropriateness of the gesture for mourning. Yoo Ji-won, a 25-year-old graduate student at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science Technology, collapsed just 500 metres (1,600 feet) from the finish line of the 2026 Seoul Race half-marathon on October 11, local media reported. The cause of her death has not been disclosed. Yoo was a running influencer, who often shared achievements and training snapshots under her Instagram account, mta1n_0ne. In the days following her death, some runners took to social media to post “mourning run” photos. One user showed a certificate of a 25km run finished in two hours and 29 minutes, alongside a memorial image of Yoo. “We will run the remaining 500 metres for you. May you rest in peace,” the post read. Others also posted the distances and times of their own runs on social media, captioned with hashtags such as “mourning run” and “memorial run”, The Korea Herald reported. The posts drew criticism from other users, who questioned the sincerity of acts. Some were doubtful that running was an appropriate way to grieve someone who died in a race. “I don’t understand why you would post it on social media when you could just mourn quietly on your own,” one user commented under the post. Another likened it to “going to a shooting range to mourn victims of gun violence”. However, some runners defended the practice, calling it “a runner’s way” of paying tribute. When Memphis resident Eliza Fletcher was killed during her early morning run in 2022, 30 people in the US city held a memorial run in her honour, ABC News reported. Likewise, an annual community run has been held in Manchester since 2023 to honour Mike Dunne, a running enthusiast who died that year due to cancer, according to Wythenshawe FM. South Korea has been experiencing a running boom, with more than 10 million people considering themselves regular runners, according to The Korea Times. With no special requirements for equipment and venues, the sport has attracted busy urban workers, especially after the Covid-19 pandemic lured people away from crowded indoor gyms to the outdoors. The number of marathon events in South Korea has risen rapidly in recent years – increasing from 19 in 2020 to 49 in 2021, 142 in 2022 and 205 in 2023, the Asia Business Daily reported, citing data police submitted to the National Assembly last year. A total of 254 events were held in 2024, with more than 1 million participants. In response to Yoo’s death, the Korean Medical Association urged the government to strengthen safety management for large-scale sporting events at a briefing on October 15, according to the Jeonnam Ilbo. “The government must ensure that emergency medical preparations, such as the deployment of medical personnel and automated external defibrillators, are specifically included in the safety management plans for running competitions,” the association said. It added that runners should stop running if they detected symptoms such as chest pain or shortness of breath, and ask for help. “Those with heart disease, those who have experienced chest pain or fainting during exercise, or those with a family member who died suddenly at a young age should consult a doctor before participating in competitions,” the association urged.

title: Singapore hits back over claims it rigged Indonesia’s stock market crash

content: Singapore’s state investors Temasek and GIC have denied involvement in Indonesia’s looming MSCI reclassification, following accusations that the city state’s sovereign wealth funds were pulling strings behind the scenes for their own gain. On Wednesday, Fock Wai Hoong, head of Asia-Pacific at Temasek Global Investments, said the claims had “no basis” and were “patently untrue”. GIC also dismissed the allegations. Former Indonesian trade minister Muhammad Lutfi on Monday claimed that both firms were working behind the scenes to push for a downgrade of Jakarta’s market status. “No one from Temasek – neither the institution nor the individuals working for the institution – has ever reached out to MSCI in order to influence any decisions they have ever made around any exchange across the region. We will leave it at that,” Fock said when asked about the allegations at the launch of the e-Conomy SEA Report 2026, jointly published by Google, Temasek and Bain & Company. A GIC spokesperson said the sovereign wealth fund’s investment decisions were driven by company- and asset-level fundamentals, and not index classifications or top-down views of a market. “We have been invested in Indonesia for over 30 years across asset classes and will continue to invest where we find good, bottom-up, risk-adjusted opportunities.” Lutfi said Singapore’s state investors aimed to create market panic to acquire Jakarta’s assets at discounted prices. “The fall of our stock index this week was no coincidence, but the culmination of a well-designed scenario,” he said on social media. ⁠Indonesia’s ⁠President Prabowo Subianto told his cabinet ‌on Wednesday that MSCI was trying ⁠to “scare us”, adding ‌that the country was “not afraid” ‌and would not ⁠buckle, Reuters reported. MSCI announced last Friday it was launching a formal consultation to decide whether to downgrade Southeast Asia’s largest economy from “emerging market” to “stand-alone market” status. The Jakarta Composite Index plunged 11.6 per cent on Friday – making it one of the world’s worst-performing benchmarks and wiping out around US$85 billion in market capitalisation. It fell a further 3.64 per cent to close at 4,996.60 on Monday, a six-year low. The global index provider cited persistent concerns over structural issues in Indonesia’s market, including opaque ownership structures, highly concentrated shareholdings and coordinated trading practices. A final decision is expected by June 30 next year. Lutfi’s comments sparked a strong reaction online, with many Indonesians urging their government to address core issues such as corruption and strengthen market fundamentals before pointing fingers at other states. One user questioned the logic of the claim, coining it a “conspiracy theory” which insinuated that a country “as small as Singapore” could dictate the MSCI. Another user said that while the former minister’s comments appeared to defend the sovereignty of Jakarta’s stock market, they needed to be backed by actions to eliminate practices that undermine transparency and credibility. “Patriotism does not mean turning a blind eye to the collapse of the market itself.”

title: Does Singapore’s tougher stance on haze mark an inflection point?
description: Singapore has warned it will go after companies responsible for the forest fires in Indonesia causing the regional haze, but cross-border challenges remain stumbling blocks to solving a problem that has plagued the city state for decades. content: Singapore has warned it will go after companies responsible for the forest fires in Indonesia causing the regional haze, but cross-border challenges remain stumbling blocks to solving a problem that has plagued the city state for decades. Analysts point to long-standing obstacles hampering the country’s decade-old haze legislation, such as complex corporate ownership and opaque transboundary supply chains. To date, no company has been prosecuted under the law. Beyond legal threats, greater accountability is needed from corporate boards and investors, observers add. The renewed push has reignited tensions over state ownership, with a former Indonesian minister challenging Singapore to take hard action against companies with business links to the city state. On Monday, Singapore’s Coordinating Minister for National Security K. Shanmugam told local media the country would use “every legal and regulatory lever” at its disposal to “exert pressure where it matters – including on [companies’] bottom lines, including on their access to financing, and including on their standing with investors”. Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister, said the city state would change or introduce laws on an urgent basis to ensure further cooperation. “Companies cannot claim to be environmentally responsible while refusing to subject themselves to scrutiny. Their claims must be backed by evidence, not just words. They cannot greenwash their behaviour,” he said. Companies would not be able to simply wait for the haze to clear and return to business as usual, he added. “We will pursue this matter for as long as it takes.” As of Monday, Singapore sent notices under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act (THPA) to 10 companies with plantations in South Sumatra and Kalimantan. Felicia Liu, a senior lecturer in sustainability at the University of York, called the issuance a “significant step”, but said “the real test is whether this translates into meaningful investigations and enforcement where accountability can be established”. THPA, which came into force in 2014, allows authorities in Singapore to hold companies responsible for causing or contributing to haze pollution in the city state even if the activities take place overseas. It allows the state to require a person to provide documents or information, and can issue preventive notices. Citizens or businesses badly affected by the haze can also hold the haze-linked companies to account under the Act. If found guilty, firms can be fined up to S$100,000 (US$78,245) a day, capped at a total of S$2 million. But an increasingly complex structural setting and the ambiguity of accountability made it fundamentally difficult for Singapore to take action, said Lawrence Loh, director of the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at the National University of Singapore Business School. “Responsibility attribution is made even more difficult when there are subsidiaries, special-purpose vehicles, nominee ownerships, joint ventures and independent suppliers,” he said. No company has been fined or sued under the law. In 2015, Singapore issued notices to six companies under THPA and subsequently closed two cases. In response to queries, the National Environment Agency said investigations into four companies – Bumi Andalas Permai, Bumi Mekar Hijau, Sebangun Bumi Andalas Woods Industries and Rimba Hutani Mas – remained ongoing. Tan-Soo Jie-Sheng, director of the Institute for Environment and Sustainability at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, underscored Singapore’s inherent limitations in tackling the haze due to its cross-border nature. “Even within national boundaries, pollution crossing state or provincial borders can be difficult to address,” he said. Other challenges include identifying forest fires, the companies behind them, and establishing that pollutants from the blazes contributed to the haze in Singapore, he said. “Quantifying the damages attributable to each company introduces further complexity.” Loh said it was challenging to implement the THPA, acknowledging that it was hard to gather evidence across borders. “It is even more difficult to enforce the law as external parties in other countries cannot control investigations and legal processes in the country where forest-burning occurs,” he said. Shanmugam said in his press conference that manufacturing giant Asia Pulp and Paper (APP) bought from three of the companies that received notices. This Week in Asia has contacted APP for comment. The minister also noted that some of the fires or smoke-source points seemed to be associated with Singapore-listed palm oil producers First Resources and Bumitama Agri, and First Borneo Plantations, and said authorities would be asking more questions of these companies. Former Indonesian trade minister Muhammad Lutfi addressed Singapore leaders in a social media post on Tuesday, saying: “Don’t write letters just to make your constituents and voters happy.” He noted that of the seven companies listed, Bumi Andalas Permai, Bumi Mekar Hijau, SBA Wood Industries and Bangkanesia were “suppliers to conglomerate groups with massive corporate holdings and listings” in Singapore and urged authorities to take action against those with offices in the city state. “Singapore has no jurisdiction in Indonesia, and you know it. So, if you truly believe you have jurisdiction over these groups, then just charge them. No need to threaten and announce at a press conference. Prosecute their headquarters in Singapore and show us what Singapore is really made of,” Lutfi said. His remarks struck a nerve among Singaporean social media users, with many accusing him of shirking responsibility and pushing blame to the city state. Calvin Cheng, a former Singapore nominated member of parliament, fired back on social media that Indonesia was “turning the narrative” onto Singapore. “Indonesia officials use Singapore as the bogeyman whenever something bad happens.” Loh said the perennial problem was less a policy inadequacy than a failure in business incentive and corporate governance. “Boards of directors and senior management must play critical roles beyond passive oversight,” he said. “Statements are not enough and they do not absolve the companies from responsibility in the forest burning and haze situation.” Liu said while Singapore’s individual efforts were not sufficient to solve the systemic crisis, it had an “important opportunity” to lead in corporate environmental accountability. “The Transboundary Haze Pollution Act alone will not improve accountability in the agroforestry sector overnight,” she said. “Singapore’s financial sector must also step up on its demands for disclosure and accountability in investment chains to ensure that Singapore, as the region’s financial hub, is not bankrolling haze.”

content: A monthly trip to Costco has become routine this year for Kim Eun-young. The 42-year-old mother of two living in Seoul’s Gwangjin district used to pick up what she needed at a nearby supermarket, but rising prices prompted her to change her shopping habits. She said buying groceries and household essentials in bulk seemed more economical, at least for her family of four. “The bill is bigger each time, but buying in bulk works out cheaper for the same amount. I mainly buy food we eat regularly and everyday household essentials, and divide the food into meal-sized portions for storage.” Kim’s changing habits reflect a growing appetite for warehouse shopping as South Korean consumers seek relief from high prices. According to market tracker WiseApp Retail, combined estimated card spending at Costco and Emart Traders totalled a record 1.45 trillion won (US$1.1 billion) in September. The estimates are based on a sample of South Korean consumers’ credit and debit card payments. They exclude cash and bank transfers and therefore differ from the retailers’ reported revenue. Warehouse retailers keep prices competitive by buying a limited selection of products in large quantities. Concentrating on popular goods, rather than carrying numerous brands and sizes, helps them secure lower purchasing prices. Selling large packages and displaying merchandise in boxes or on pallets further reduce operating costs. Private labels also help keep prices down. By developing goods with manufacturers and selling them under their own brands, retailers reduce distribution and marketing expenses and pass on savings to shoppers. Costco’s Kirkland Signature range spans groceries, dietary supplements, apparel and household supplies. The retailer takes part in product development and oversees aspects of manufacturing to control costs while maintaining quality. Traders works with manufacturers throughout product development, from initial planning to launch, for its T Standard brand. Savings on design and promotional spending help the chain offer lower retail prices. The growing appeal of warehouse shopping is also reflected in financial results. Costco South Korea’s revenue rose 12.1 per cent to a record 7.32 trillion won in the 2025 financial year from September 2024 through August 2025. That followed sales of 6.07 trillion won in the 2023 financial year and 6.53 trillion won in 2024. Traders has likewise recorded gains in both sales and profit. Its annual gross sales rose from 3.37 trillion won in 2023 to 3.55 trillion won in 2024 and 3.85 trillion won in 2025. Sales grew 14.2 per cent over the two years, while operating profit more than doubled from 58.1 billion won to 129.3 billion won. “Spending at warehouse retailers is growing among major retail formats, including hypermarkets, department stores and convenience stores,” an industry official said. “Their focus on bulk products appears to be attracting grocery shoppers trying to manage the burden of high prices.” This article was first published by The Korea Times

title: What’s behind the quiet US diplomatic thaw with Myanmar?
description: Fresh from walking down red carpets laid out by his Southeast Asian neighbours, Myanmar’s ex-military chief Min Aung Hlaing appears to have a new diplomatic feather in his cap: re-engagement with the United States. content: Fresh from walking down red carpets laid out by his Southeast Asian neighbours, Myanmar’s ex-military chief Min Aung Hlaing appears to have a new diplomatic feather in his cap: re-engagement with the United States. Washington slapped sanctions on Min Aung Hlaing just 10 days after his February 1, 2021 coup and the ensuing bloody crackdown on pro-democracy protesters. Waves of subsequent sanctions targeted military-linked companies and cronies. Yet since last month, two rounds of talks with US officials have taken place. While details have yet to be made public, experts say Myanmar’s rare earths are likely on the table. The State Department under Donald Trump’s administration appears set for a course change – part of a wider retooling of US foreign policy that critics say prioritises pragmatism over principle. Reuters confirmed at least two meetings between White House officials and Myanmar representatives in recent weeks. The first round, held last month in the capital Naypyidaw, secured the release of US businessman Adam Castillo and touched on protecting American citizens from the scourge of cyber scam centres operating in Myanmar. Castillo’s release was a symbol of “friendly relations” between the two countries, Myanmar state media later reported. The substance of follow-up talks in Tokyo in early October – reportedly led by Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance – remains unconfirmed. Describing the talks as “exploratory”, Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia Programme director at the Australian think tank Lowy Institute, said the US might in part be supporting Myanmar’s “peaceful return to democracy”. But “the more dominant objective at the moment appears to revolve around exploratory talks with [an] emphasis on access to rare earths and cooperation to eradicate cyber scam operations”, Marston added. Myanmar is among the world’s largest producers of rare earth ores and is China’s main import source for these critical minerals, which are essential for everything from electric vehicles and wind turbines to defence technology and robotics. As artificial intelligence fuels rising energy and hardware demands, the White House is determined to secure long-term access to rare earth stockpiles wherever possible. Washington has signed supply deals globally to curb its reliance on China, which dominates global production. But securing access to Myanmar’s known deposits is a daunting challenge. Buried in the mountainous borderlands near China and Thailand, many of Myanmar’s mineral-rich areas are beyond central government control. Northern Kachin state – rich in dysprosium and terbium critical to advanced military technologies – is administered by the Kachin Independence Army (KIA), an ethnic armed group fighting the junta. “Unless the KIA is at the table, it seems exceedingly unlikely that the US will be able to get the types of deals it may have in mind,” Marston said. “Short of a new front in the war to retake territory in Kachin, the military seems unable to deliver those types of wins for the United States.” Optics and lobbying Diplomatic life has also become a lot easier for Min Aung Hlaing since April, when he swapped his military fatigues for civilian clothes to assume the presidency. That followed elections widely denounced as a sham – held only in government-controlled areas – designed to offer a veneer of civilian legitimacy. In recent months, neighbours including Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Laos and Cambodia have all hosted Min Aung Hlaing in his capacity as president. China, Russia and India have also welcomed him. Thailand has been a driving force within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to reintegrate Myanmar. A visit to Malaysia earlier this month, where Min Aung Hlaing was warmly received by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, added fresh momentum towards bringing Myanmar back into top-level Asean summits, from which it has been barred since the coup. Min Aung Hlaing was previously shunned internationally for jailing political rivals – including democracy champion Aung San Suu Kyi – and plunging the country into a devastating civil war that forced countless young people to flee abroad or take up arms. Under the Biden administration, Washington worked with the UK and EU to impose fresh sanctions on the junta. Under Trump, however, there have been signs that a gradual rollback could be under consideration. Some Myanmar watchers attribute the junta’s shifting fortunes in Washington to the hiring of veteran Republican strategist Roger Stone in April. Stone is said to draw US$50,000 monthly as a consultant for the Washington-based lobbying firm DCI Group, which signed a US$3 million contract with Myanmar in July last year. But Marston warns against overstating the lobbyist’s role. “My guess would be Roger Stone and DCI Group have had relatively little influence over the modest change in approach,” he said. There are other signs of a change in tone from Naypyidaw – long notorious for ignoring outside opinion. On Monday, Myanmar government officials posted a rare photograph of 81-year-old Suu Kyi receiving a package sent by Britain’s King Charles. Min Aung Hlaing also gave a rare interview to Western media for a profile feature in Time magazine.

title: India’s voter roll overhaul fuels citizenship fears: ‘what if they ask us to leave?’
description: Laddli Khatun pulled one document after another from a yellow bag, desperately hoping one would be enough to keep her name on India’s electoral rolls. As the world’s largest democracy overhauls its voter lists, millions like Khatun are scrambling to re-establish their credentials, despite having voted before. Critics and opposition parties say the exercise risks mass disenfranchisement, and those removed fear wider citizenship repercussions. More than 133 million names – including 28 million...
content: Laddli Khatun pulled one document after another from a yellow bag, desperately hoping one would be enough to keep her name on India’s electoral rolls. As the world’s largest democracy overhauls its voter lists, millions like Khatun are scrambling to re-establish their credentials, despite having voted before. Critics and opposition parties say the exercise risks mass disenfranchisement, and those removed fear wider citizenship repercussions. More than 133 million names – including 28 million listed as dead – have been cut from rolls, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings. Protests have rocked New Delhi, with demonstrators demanding the chief election commissioner’s resignation, alleging the overhaul is designed to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission of India, a constitutional body, denies wrongdoing and says the revision complies with the law. The special intensive revision requires voters to link themselves – directly or through their parents or grandparents – to electoral rolls from 2002-03, the last time such a rigorous review took place. Khatun, 39, was not of voting age at the time. So she must now prove that at least one of her parents or grandparents featured on those rolls. “My parents died when I was a baby,” said Khatun, who lives in a Delhi slum. “They were poor unlettered people who left no documents behind.” Many face Khatun’s predicament. “Women, minorities, people living at the margins and the poorest are the worst hit by this exercise, because they find it very difficult to produce documents which can prove their citizenship,” said transparency activist Anjali Bhardwaj. The Election Commission previously sought to enrol eligible voters through door-to-door visits, guided by its motto: “No voter to be left behind”. Critics say the exercise shifts the “burden of proof” onto voters. “The methodology followed has been of physical door-to-door verification,” former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa said. “It was never that you asked people wholesale to establish their eligibility all over again … after they have been admitted to the rolls through the prescribed due process.” Surajmukhi, made homeless when an eviction drive demolished the slum where she had lived for 30 years, was removed from Delhi’s draft rolls and marked “untraceable”. “I have no document to link myself to the 2002 voter rolls, because at the time I was not enrolled as a voter, and my parents are long dead,” she said, standing in the rubble of her home. “But I have voted multiple times since – the officials themselves came to our home and enrolled us as voters. What has suddenly changed?” Officials on the ground acknowledge the difficulties the exercise poses for poorer voters. “Mapping yourself to the 2002 voter lists is not easy for those who are not educated and technologically savvy,” said Mukesh Khanna, a booth-level officer in a Delhi suburb with a large population of working-class migrants. Special camps have been set up to help voters, but many still struggle to navigate the process. ‘Logical discrepancies’ Millions have also been flagged for additional checks after the Election Commission used automated systems to identify what it calls “logical discrepancies” – including mismatched names and inconsistent family details. Independent analyses suggest Muslims have been disproportionately affected. In Delhi, an analysis by The Hindu newspaper found Muslims accounted for around 20 per cent of voters flagged, compared with 13.6 per cent of the electorate. The disparity was even starker in West Bengal, according to the Kolkata-based policy think tank Sabar Institute. Street cleaner Shahida, 42, received a notice because her mother was only 15 years older than her – an age gap the software flagged as “suspicious”. “What am I expected to do – go back in time and ask my dead grandparents why they got my dead mother married so young? The reality is child marriages were common among the poor at the time.” National rugby player and actor Aslam, 24, who uses one name, said his voter registration was flagged as “suspicious” because six other people were linked to his deceased father. “It is clearly targeted against voters who don’t vote for the BJP,” said Aslam, a Muslim with six siblings. “It almost feels like the idea is to create a category of second-class citizens.” It almost feels like the idea is to create a category of second-class citizens Aslam, national rugby player and actor Modi’s Hindu-nationalist BJP, which strongly backs the revision, has long alleged that undocumented migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh – particularly Muslims – have fraudulently entered electoral rolls. The Supreme Court has said exclusion from electoral rolls does not establish that someone is a foreign national. However, Indian media have reported cases in West Bengal in which people excluded from voter rolls were accused of being undocumented migrants from Bangladesh, detained and, in some instances, pushed across the border. For Khatun, the prospect of such an outcome hangs over an already gruelling ordeal. “I have provided document after document, everything that I have,” she said. “But what if they still ask us to leave the country?”

title: Malaysia’s border chief charged with assaulting police in viral airport clash
description: Malaysia’s border control chief pleaded not guilty on Wednesday to two charges of assaulting junior police officers at the country’s main international airport last month, after a video of the confrontation went viral. Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain, director general of the Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency, was filmed confronting two men at Kuala Lumpur International Airport on September 28. He previously linked the incident to an operation against airport touts following complaints about...
content: Malaysia’s border control chief pleaded not guilty on Wednesday to two charges of assaulting junior police officers at the country’s main international airport last month, after a video of the confrontation went viral. Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain, director general of the Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency, was filmed confronting two men at Kuala Lumpur International Airport on September 28. He previously linked the incident to an operation against airport touts following complaints about smuggling syndicates at the airport. The former national criminal investigation chief entered his plea before magistrate Khairatul Animah Jelani at the Sepang Magistrate’s Court. According to the charge sheets seen by This Week in Asia, Shuhaily, 54, was accused of voluntarily causing hurt to two junior officers, Lance Corporals Muhammad Ekmal Sofwan Dirman and Mohamad Faiz Saman, between 1.27pm and 1.35pm on September 28 near Counter J on Level 5 of Terminal 1. View on Threads Both charges were brought under Section 323 of Malaysia’s Penal Code, which carries a maximum penalty of one year in prison, a fine of up to 2,000 ringgit (US$490), or both, upon conviction. “I pleaded not guilty and claimed trial to the charges,” local media reported him as saying. Only selected media organisations were allowed into the courtroom on Wednesday because of limited space. The court granted Shuhaily bail of 1,500 ringgit per charge – totalling 3,000 ringgit – with one surety, and set November 25 for the next case management. His lawyer, Rosal Azimin Ahmad, told reporters prosecutors had initially sought bail of 5,000 ringgit per charge before the court allowed the lower amount. Rosal played down the severity of the charges, describing them as akin to a “petty offence” despite carrying a possible jail term. “This is a compoundable case. It is not a serious case,” he told reporters, referring to provisions under Malaysian law that allow certain minor offences to be settled out of court. Asked whether Shuhaily would continue leading the agency while facing trial, Rosal said his client would remain in post for now. “As a civil servant, I believe he will continue carrying out his duties until told otherwise,” he said. National police chief Mohd Khalid Ismail confirmed earlier this month that two officers had filed reports alleging physical assault during the airport encounter. Investigators recorded statements from 25 people – including police and border agency personnel, airport auxiliary police, baggage handlers, medical officers and independent witnesses – according to Khalid’s statement. Police also obtained CCTV footage and medical records as evidence. At an October 1 news conference, Shuhaily said his officers and airport security had detained a suspected foreign tout and brought him to a baggage inspection room for questioning. According to his account, two unidentified men entered the room and began filming without permission. His officers brought the men forward and instructed them to delete the recording. Shuhaily acknowledged reprimanding the pair but declined to comment on whether physical contact occurred, English-language daily The Star reported. His agency also lodged a police report over the circulation of the footage, which he suggested could have been an attempt to damage the agency’s reputation and his own. Ahead of his court appearance on Wednesday, Shuhaily thanked the public for their messages of support that he said had given him strength. “I will let the court conduct due process,” he told reporters. Shuhaily took charge of the border agency in July 2025 on a two-year appointment after leading the police’s Criminal Investigation Department. The agency, which operates under the Home Ministry, was established to tighten security at Malaysia’s entry and exit points and combat cross-border smuggling. In May, the agency intercepted 3.3kg (7.3lbs) of cocaine at Kuala Lumpur International Airport, and in July seized cannabis worth 1.69 million ringgit intended to be smuggled out of Terminal 1. Soon after taking office, Shuhaily proposed tougher recruitment procedures and dismissal for officers implicated in smuggling or abuse of power.

title: Stinking rich: Malaysia eyes land routes to boost durian trade in China
description: Malaysia is negotiating with Thailand, Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia to establish overland transit routes for fresh durian exports to China, according to Agriculture and Food Security Minister Mohamad Sabu. The minister said the move would reduce transport costs and improve access to the lucrative Chinese market. “Durian is a favourite among Chinese consumers, but they sometimes find it difficult to get the fruit at a more affordable price,” he said during parliament’s question and answer time on...
content: Malaysia is negotiating with Thailand, Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia to establish overland transit routes for fresh durian exports to China, according to Agriculture and Food Security Minister Mohamad Sabu. The minister said the move would reduce transport costs and improve access to the lucrative Chinese market. “Durian is a favourite among Chinese consumers, but they sometimes find it difficult to get the fruit at a more affordable price,” he said during parliament’s question and answer time on Wednesday. Transporting durians by land could take three to four days, offering a potential alternative to costly air freight, he said. Mohamad said his ministry was working with the Foreign Ministry and Transport Ministry to facilitate negotiations with the four Asean countries. In 2025, Malaysia exported 18,370 tonnes of durian products to China, with fresh durian exports alone valued at about 150.6 million ringgit (US$37 million). In the first half of this year, Malaysian durian exports to China reached about 124 million ringgit. Discussions on transit arrangements had been ongoing since July 20, Mohamad said, although negotiations were challenging as the four countries also exported durians to China. Malaysia was also exploring sea freight as an alternative, but the longer transit time made it less suitable for consumers seeking fresh durians. “Chinese consumers want fresh durians. That is why we are discussing air and rail transport intensively,” he said. Mohamad said the government was seeking to expedite arrangements to enable Malaysian durians to reach Chinese consumers more efficiently. The proposed routes could give local exporters more efficient access to the Chinese market and enhance the competitiveness of Malaysia’s premium durian exports, he added. This article was first published by The Star

title: Singaporean parents jailed after 8-month-old son dies from severe abuse
description: A Singaporean couple who regularly abused their first child after he was born, resulting in his death at the age of eight months, were sentenced to jail on Wednesday. Chloe Gan Ci Xuan, 23, and Neo Jia Ming, 27, were sentenced respectively to 15 years and three months’ jail and 16 years’ jail for various charges over the death of their son, Trevor Neo Yu Hin. Gan pleaded guilty to three charges comprising causing the death of a child, ill-treating a child and permitting such ill-treatment. Neo...
content: A Singaporean couple who regularly abused their first child after he was born, resulting in his death at the age of eight months, were sentenced to jail on Wednesday. Chloe Gan Ci Xuan, 23, and Neo Jia Ming, 27, were sentenced respectively to 15 years and three months’ jail and 16 years’ jail for various charges over the death of their son, Trevor Neo Yu Hin. Gan pleaded guilty to three charges comprising causing the death of a child, ill-treating a child and permitting such ill-treatment. Neo pleaded guilty to four charges: allowing the death of a child, ill-treating a child, permitting Gan’s ill-treatment of Trevor and domestic abuse of his wife. The couple had married in August 2023, after Gan became pregnant with Trevor around April that year. After giving birth, Gan initially lived with her parents and a confinement nanny before moving to live with her husband and his uncles. From February 2024, the couple hired a nanny who cared for Trevor during the day on weekdays. Other relatives helped look after him on weekends. Gan soon realised she could make her baby stop crying or faint by shaking him vigorously. She had seen her husband do this. They shook Trevor frequently to stop him from crying, and later began covering his nose and mouth or smothering him. For about seven months of his life, Trevor was assaulted by his parents and left with bruises. His father would slap him so hard he left bruises, or pinch his fingers forcefully to see his reaction. Neither parent intervened when they saw the other abusing the infant. There were two instances of medical intervention. In January 2024, Trevor was hospitalised at KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital (KKH) for about a week after losing consciousness when Gan shook him. No injuries were found on him. The second occasion was in early April 2024 when a nanny saw bleeding under the child’s tongue and insisted he see a doctor. The couple then took their son to KKH on April 2, 2024, where a doctor noted local trauma under the child’s tongue, with redness. The couple left the hospital with the child, and Neo told Gan that he had dug around in the boy’s mouth to stop him from crying, causing the bleeding. Smothered to stop crying In May 2024, Gan’s mother noticed bruises on the child and warned her daughter to stop hitting the infant. Around early August 2024, Neo told his wife not to hit the infant at all until after a doctor’s appointment, or the doctor would see the bruises and accuse them of abuse. Trevor died after repeatedly being smothered by his mother in early September 2024. His father was in the same room playing a game on his phone. Neo was found to have no mental illness, while Gan was found not to be suffering from any postpartum psychiatric disorder around March or April 2024. However, the court previously heard that she could have been suffering from an adjustment disorder which could have had a minor contributory link to the offence. The prosecution had sought 14 to 15 years’ jail for Gan and 15 to 16 years’ jail for Neo. Gan’s lawyers, Josephus Tan and Cory Wong from Invictus Law, had asked for not more than 12½ to 13 years’ jail, stressing Gan’s youth and mental condition. Neo’s lawyers, Eugene Thuraisingam, Johannes Hadi and Seraphine Loh from Eugene Thuraisingam Asia, sought seven years and seven weeks’ jail. The penalty for causing the death of a child is a jail term of up to 20 years and a fine or caning. For ill-treating a child where death is caused, an offender can be jailed for up to 14 years or fined up to S$40,000 (US$31,000), or both. If death is not caused, the maximum penalties are eight years’ jail or a fine of up to S$8,000, or both. This article was first published by CNA

title: Inside scorching Pakistani factories making clothes for global fashion brands
description: Machines whirred around Siddiqui as her vision blurred and her heart hammered. The garment factory on the outskirts of Karachi was sweltering. The room was packed with sweating fellow workers and huge industrial equipment that radiated heat. The air felt thick with the humidity of this summer’s monsoon. Siddiqui, who asked to be identified only by surname, felt like she was suffocating. Concerned colleagues called over her supervisor. “The supervisor said, ‘Just complete this work,’” the...
content: Machines whirred around Siddiqui as her vision blurred and her heart hammered. The garment factory on the outskirts of Karachi was sweltering. The room was packed with sweating fellow workers and huge industrial equipment that radiated heat. The air felt thick with the humidity of this summer’s monsoon. Siddiqui, who asked to be identified only by surname, felt like she was suffocating. Concerned colleagues called over her supervisor. “The supervisor said, ‘Just complete this work,’” the 28-year-old said. “Suddenly darkness came before my eyes.” Exhausted by the heat, she collapsed. Extreme heat – intensified by climate change – is creating dangerous conditions for factory workers in Pakistan. From blue jeans to homeware, these factories produce goods for global companies that have pledged to protect workers’ safety. But experts and labour rights advocates say those promises remain unfulfilled, as temperatures rise and workers pay the price with their health and safety. Of the more than a dozen workers interviewed in Karachi, all described scorching workplaces, absent heat protocols and negative health effects, including fainting. They spoke on the condition that their identities be protected out of fear of retaliation by their employers. All but one said they lost wages when heat-related illness forced them to miss work. Ten of the workers made goods for global brands sold in the United States and Europe. For workers like Siddiqui, extreme heat – temperatures at or above 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit) combined with high humidity – is not just a workplace hazard. Living with her six children in a small room with no air conditioning on the outskirts of Karachi, temperatures routinely exceed 37.8 degrees during heatwaves. Inside the garment factory where she stitches clothes for Spanish brands like Zara and Mango, it is even hotter. Huge machines churn heat into the air. There are fans, but they’re often broken or small. Windows are slitlike and set high, or even closed to deter theft, further trapping the heat, workers said. “Smoke, heat, you face it,” said a 34-year-old male factory worker. Silent killer Extreme heat is a silent killer. It can show few outward symptoms while causing severe internal damage and worsening conditions, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes and asthma. Studies have linked it to dehydration, heatstroke, organ failure and death. “The longer you work in the heat, the less that you’re protected from it and the health risks rise,” said Andreas Flouris, the founder of FAME Lab, which researches heat’s impact on health. The number of people exposed to extreme heat is growing exponentially due to climate change. Heat stress is a leading cause of weather-related deaths, according to the World Health Organization. Studies by World Weather Attribution say that climate change has also drastically increased the frequency, intensity and risks of extreme heatwaves in Pakistan. Workers interviewed described temporary muscle paralysis, swollen limbs, blood pressure swings, breathing problems, blurred vision and exhaustion that peaked in the hottest months. One worker showed scaly skin rashes on her arms from routine chemical exposure, saying how the pain intensified during summer. All said they had seen colleagues faint from the heat. Several said they had fainted themselves, some multiple times. Those who fainted were often offered only a short break or sugary drink before being told to resume work. They said complaining to supervisors led to no changes. Only one worker had paid sick leave. The rest said that missed hours – even from fainting on the job or from heat-related illnesses – meant slashed wages. Siddiqui wept on the floor of her home as she described fainting and being sent to the hospital. As she earned 15,000 rupees (US$54) a month, the hospital visit cost, which her employer refused to pay, left her unable to buy food for her children. “Sometimes they eat one meal, sometimes they don’t eat a meal,” she said, adding that the younger children sometimes cry from hunger. “The older ones have gotten used to it.” There are simple, scalable and economically feasible measures factories can take to protect their workers from extreme heat, including accurately measuring temperature and humidity inside workplaces, providing cold drinking water and allowing workers breaks, according to Flouris. Other solutions include installing barriers to block radiant heat from machinery, installing quality ventilation and cooling systems and painting rooftops white to deflect sunlight. “We’re talking about some very simple strategies,” he said. Simple solutions, none taken Factory workers said that almost none of these measures were taken in their workplaces. Several said their factories’ metal roofs made the summer heat unbearable, yet they received no extra water or breaks. All the workers said there were no heat sensors installed. Only one worker said a ventilation system was installed at their workplace, but that it was turned on only when auditors visited the factory for inspection. The workers said water was provided by their employers, but that it was rarely cold and they were not sure if it was clean. “Sometimes it smells like dead rats,” the 34-year-old male worker said. Pakistan has national and provincial laws as well as constitutional protections meant to shield workers from such conditions, according to Farhan Haider, a programme manager at the Pakistan Institute of Labour Education and Research in Karachi. Some companies supplied by the factories, including Inditex – Zara’s parent company – and Mango have signed legally binding agreements to protect workers or have their own company safety pledges. The most concrete is the International Accord for Health and Safety in the Textile and Garment Industry, which in 2025 announced it would treat heat as a workplace safety risk and develop heat stress protocols, which are under review but not yet in effect. Representatives from the Pakistan Accord, a country-specific safety programme that operates as an extension of the broader International Accord, did not reply to a request for interview or comment. Brands had a responsibility to ensure their suppliers are held accountable for worker safety, including extreme heat, said Cara Schulte, a researcher at Climate Rights International who published a report last year about worker conditions in Pakistan. Inditex said in an email the company was strengthening efforts to address heat stress in its supply chain through updated factory audits, guidance and training for suppliers and collaboration with industry initiatives. Mango called worker health and safety a “non-negotiable priority”, citing its supplier code of conduct, which was “strengthened this year to explicitly address extreme temperatures and heat stress.” A government spokeswoman for Sindh province, where Karachi is located, acknowledged implementation remained an issue. “The government is making efforts to enforce these regulations, but given the province’s vast size and the presence of numerous industrial zones, complaints are inevitable,” said Sadia Javed, who is also a member of the provincial assembly. For workers like Siddiqui, complaints remain ignored as temperatures continue to rise. “If you feel too unwell, [supervisors] say, ‘This is an everyday problem. Women cry and complain a lot, but the work still must be done,’” she said.

title: In Japan, Takaichi’s first-year leadership style threatens hold on power
description: With her government entering its second year on Wednesday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi may face growing questions over whether her leadership style, oft-described as assertive, could fuel discontent within her Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). Bolstered by high public approval ratings and an overwhelming majority in the House of Representatives, Takaichi has pushed through divisive legislation and made personnel appointments heavily tinged with her will. Political analysts warn that...
content: With her government entering its second year on Wednesday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi may face growing questions over whether her leadership style, oft-described as assertive, could fuel discontent within her Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). Bolstered by high public approval ratings and an overwhelming majority in the House of Representatives, Takaichi has pushed through divisive legislation and made personnel appointments heavily tinged with her will. Political analysts warn that Takaichi’s confrontational governing approach – driven by popularity among voters, not necessarily by a solid factional power base – could prompt a backlash from within and potentially threaten her administration’s stability should public support weaken further. “It was a year in which the deliberative process of parliamentary democracy was significantly hollowed out,” said Ikuo Gonoi, a political science professor at Takachiho University. After becoming Japan’s first female prime minister on October 21, 2025, Takaichi, seen as a security hawk and fiscal dove, led the coalition of the LDP and its junior ally, the Japan Innovation Party, to a landslide victory in February’s lower house election. The bloc secured about 350 of the chamber’s 465 seats, comfortably exceeding the two-thirds majority needed to override the rejection of a bill by the Senate, the less powerful upper house where the ruling camp falls just short of control. Armed with that parliamentary strength, Takaichi has advanced a series of controversial initiatives, which she says could “split public opinion”, despite doubts cast by opposition parties about their necessity and implications for civil liberties. Among them were legislation to establish the National Intelligence Council and to penalise desecration of Japan’s national flag. Also citing the limited time Takaichi spent answering questions in the Diet, Gonoi said the prime minister had failed to adequately explain the bills and had instead “increasingly dismissed opposing views”. Signs of discontent within the LDP became visible over the government’s plan for a two-year consumption tax reduction on food and beverages from 8 per cent to 1 per cent from April as well as September’s reshuffle of the party leadership and cabinet. In August, Yuko Obuchi, known for emphasising fiscal discipline, resigned as a senior member of an intraparty tax panel, apparently in protest at the tax cut. Growing tension In the party leadership reshuffle, the replacement of Junichi Ishii with Kazuhiko Aoki as LDP secretary general in the Senate drew attention as Ishii was seen as an influential figure in the party’s upper house caucus who maintained ties across party lines. Takaichi had reportedly grown frustrated with Ishii’s handling of Senate deliberations – especially after parliament failed to enact the initial budget for the 2026 financial year before its start on April 1. Ishii’s removal prompted some criticism, with Senator Shoji Nishida openly complaining about the decision, calling Ishii a “central figure” behind the passage of government-sponsored bills during the previous Diet session. Mikitaka Masuyama, a professor at the National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies, said the episode highlighted growing tension between Takaichi and parts of the party establishment. Further questions about Takaichi’s government emerged with the resignation last week of Kazuo Yana as farm minister, after she defended him for about two weeks following media reports on his past remarks. Yana came under fire over remarks in May implying municipalities whose mayors backed his rival in the February election received less funds for their road budgets. “Regardless of whether the remarks were true or not, it raises broader questions about whether local government leaders and assemblies feel compelled to align themselves with those in power” – and such concerns could be decisive in next April’s nationwide local elections, which come every four years, Masuyama said. Support for the administration has begun to soften. A two-day phone survey conducted by Kyodo News from Saturday, after Yana’s resignation, showed the approval rating for Takaichi’s Cabinet at 49.1 per cent, down from 53.4 per cent a month ago. It marked the first time her cabinet’s approval rate had dropped below 50 per cent. It had maintained relatively high ratings, at one point reaching almost 70 per cent. Experts say Takaichi’s popularity with voters – her greatest political strength – may ultimately become her biggest vulnerability if public support continues to erode. “A further decline of the cabinet approval ratings could lead the administration to face a tough time, and growing dissatisfaction within the ruling camp could energise anti-Takaichi forces,” Masuyama said. He also said such opposition could emerge among liberal members and fiscal conservatives in the LDP, suggesting that former internal affairs and communications minister Yoshimasa Hayashi could rally them ahead of next fall’s LDP leadership race. Hayashi, viewed as a moderate, was defeated in the five-way LDP presidential contest a year ago and was left without a cabinet or party post in September’s reshuffle. Meanwhile, LDP Vice-President Taro Aso, an influential former prime minister, and Secretary General Shunichi Suzuki, his brother-in-law whom it was rumoured could be replaced due to a reported lack of communication with Takaichi, remained in their positions. Aso and his group have not broken with Takaichi, “presumably because her approval ratings remain high”, Masuyama said. “If the ratings fall, however, it may become impossible to stop anti-Takaichi forces from jumping on the bandwagon.”

title: Southeast Asian families tying house move to top schools spur privilege worries
description: Singapore’s recent parliamentary debate over primary school admissions has put a familiar parental strategy in the city state under the spotlight – parents moving house to improve their children’s chances of getting into popular schools. Speaking with This Week in Asia, property agents say some families in Singapore have been approaching them with the intention of buying or renting particular residences at least two years before their children’s primary school admission. Living close to a...
content: Singapore’s recent parliamentary debate over primary school admissions has put a familiar parental strategy in the city state under the spotlight – parents moving house to improve their children’s chances of getting into popular schools. Speaking with This Week in Asia, property agents say some families in Singapore have been approaching them with the intention of buying or renting particular residences at least two years before their children’s primary school admission. Living close to a sought-after school does not guarantee entry, however, as a family might still face balloting for a particular school if it is oversubscribed. The debate comes as Singapore prepares to widen admission to 12 schools in predominantly private-housing neighbourhoods, in a bid to encourage greater social mixing. Beyond Singapore, the school admissions systems in Malaysia and Indonesia also factor residential addresses, albeit with different criteria taking into account socio-economic conditions. Planning years ahead Joyce Foo, a property agent in Singapore, said some families accepted living in smaller homes to improve their children’s school admission chances. She recalled one family who moved from a five-room to a four-room public housing flat to be nearer their preferred school, with a parent also volunteering there. When advising her clients, she would consider past balloting results, housing budgets and potential sale of the properties they are eyeing 10 years later. “They want to make that move, but they also don’t want to lose money,” she said. Those calculations now need to be considered alongside recent changes to Singapore’s school admission framework. From next year, for registration of children starting Primary 1 in 2028, most schools will reserve 60 places, up from 40, for Phase 2C, which does not factor in school ties. At the 12 schools located in neighbourhoods dominated by private houses, Phase 2C places will be split equally between applicants living within 2km and those farther away. Priority admission for children of primary school alumni remains. Foo said some alumni parents were now considering renting, rather than buying near their former schools, or looking at alternatives with better prospects of success. “Many parents come to inquire because they want to have that certainty that their kid will be placed.” However, she had not seen a surge in customer inquiries following the announcement. Based on her 13 years’ experience in Singapore’s property market, Foo said the data she had analysed showed that sales demand and rental premiums were not necessarily correlated with properties within 1km of popular schools. Jason Tan, an associate professor at Singapore’s National Institute of Education, said the admissions framework encouraged parents to strategise because certain conditions depended on what they could do, including alumni connections, volunteer work and residential addresses. “Most of the criteria have nothing to do with the individual child,” Tan said. Giving priority to children living near schools made sense because of their young age, Tan said. But better-off families have a clear advantage as they can choose whether to move closer to a preferred school, according to Tan. Family income matters In Malaysia’s Klang Valley, senior sales manager Neo Wee Liem and his wife also linked preferred school admission for their son to house-hunting criteria as they wanted their eldest child to have a grounding in Mandarin. After returning from Singapore and renting in Petaling Jaya, the Neos shortlisted three Chinese-medium primary schools, taking into account their housing budget, living space and transport convenience, before making a final decision. “We were not really picky on which Chinese school it was,” Neo said. In Malaysia, Chinese- and Tamil-medium primary schools sit within the national education system alongside Malay-medium primary schools. Private and international schools are also options for parents who can afford them. Noor Azimah Abdul Rahim, an education advocate who is a co-founder of Malaysia’s Parent Action Group for Education, said such housing calculations were a source of concern. “When families contemplate paying additional rent, changing their living arrangements or reorganising their daily lives just to secure a school place, it raises questions about the fairness and accessibility of the system. Shakira Teh Sharifuddin, a PhD candidate at University College London’s Institute of Education and an economist at a public policy body, said the priorities of families varied across locations, income groups and educational stages. What parents living in more urban areas look for in schools for their children differed from their peers living in rural communities or less-developed districts, such as Chinese education, she said. For some Malay families, whether from urban or rural areas, they do not need to buy a house near top secondary schools or selective boarding schools to secure a place, according to Shakira. Nonetheless, the financial position of different families would still play a role in determining their attitude towards school selection, she said. “Lower-income and more rural families could find themselves basically just taking what the system gives to them, because there are fewer options.” Falsifying residential addresses In Indonesia, families also make housing decisions based on preferred schools for their children. In a 2019 CNN Indonesia report, a father rented a house in East Jakarta and changed his residence details so his child could apply to a secondary school under Indonesia’s old zoning policy. Last year, Indonesia revised its school admission policy under which a family’s residence address is a key consideration. Local governments have the flexibility to designate housing areas for school admission. At least 70 per cent of public primary-school places are allocated based on a family’s residential address. At least 15 per cent are set aside for students from low-income families and those with disabilities. Ubaid Matraji, the national coordinator of the Indonesian Education Monitoring Network (JPPI) watchdog group, said such a principle of school admission was fair, but varying degrees of school quality continued to be a major concern for families. “On paper, this system is fairer because everyone has the same opportunity to attend the school nearest to home. But it becomes a problem because the quality of schools is not the same,” he said. Some parents used their work or business address, “rented” addresses of relatives or falsified residence documents to improve their children’s chances of getting into popular schools, Ubaid added. His comments indicate that the problem has not disappeared even with Jakarta’s latest school admission policy. Explaining its rationale for the reforms last year, Indonesia’s education ministry identified false housing addresses as one of the key problems under the old system. Under the national framework, local governments can work with private schools to accept pupils when the capacity of public schools is insufficient and provide financial help for those from lower-income families. Ubaid, however, said the authorities should ensure that there were enough public-school places for children seeking admission. As for families who have missed out on public-school places, private schools are not a feasible option because of higher costs, such as registration and development fees, according to Ubaid. For Noor Azimah, whether it is in Malaysia, Indonesia or elsewhere, school access should not be determined by the ability of families to pay for houses. “A child’s educational opportunity should not become a property-market privilege,” she said.

title: ‘Poster child’: why more Chinese firms have Thailand in their expansion plans
description: With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter. A subtle shift is taking place among Chinese businesses as they adopt a “China plus one” outlook and redirect domestic investments to neighbouring economies – a...
content: With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter. A subtle shift is taking place among Chinese businesses as they adopt a “China plus one” outlook and redirect domestic investments to neighbouring economies – a strategy largely designed as a hedge against tariffs and geopolitical risks. Vietnam, popular for much of this period, is beginning to lose some favour as firms look to Thailand as another alternative destination. The latter country has gained the edge on its competitor in the post-trade war 2.0 era, attracting billions of US dollars in outlays last year. But the influx has also made Bangkok more mindful of risks, particularly those related to US measures intended to limit Chinese transshipment. “Thailand is hailed as a new poster child of the ‘China plus one’ strategy of the new era,” said Donald Low, professor of public policy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. As tech-intensive Chinese manufacturers flock there while the sun sets on export re-routing via Vietnam, the Land of Smiles may gain further ground over its neighbour. “Thailand has a reasonably mature, sophisticated manufacturing base that is more advanced than Vietnam’s,” Low said. From Vietnam’s perspective, “manufacturing saturation” and a perception change – aggravated by US trade scrutiny, including punitive tariffs of 40 per cent on Chinese goods found to have been diverted through the country – mean it may have run its course as a popular destination, the scholar added. Thailand in, Vietnam out? In 2025, Thailand attracted US$5.33 billion in Chinese investment, compared with Vietnam’s US$2.46 billion, according to data from the Chinese Ministry of Commerce. Thailand’s location and established industrial infrastructure have allowed China-funded factories to plug straight into supply chains that are being extended from China to members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), Low said. “For tech-intensive manufacturing – like electronic components and machinery, electric vehicles [EVs] and solar panels – Thailand has the requisite capabilities to attract investments. BYD, for instance, runs an EV plant there,” he said. In a success story now touted by Thai officials, the first EV made by BYD in Thailand rolled off the production line in 2024 in Rayong, the location of a US$490 million factory with an annual capacity of 150,000 units and a Thai workforce of 10,000. On the other hand, BYD’s plan for a similar factory in Vietnam, unveiled in 2024, remains stuck in the slow lane, with construction delayed. “Even before the US imposed tariffs on transshipped goods, there were already signs Vietnam was ‘saturated’ with manufacturing from China, especially in assembly,” according to Low. “It was becoming less attractive to assembly manufacturing due to infrastructure bottlenecks and rising labour costs … American levies added to the pressures facing Chinese firms there.” Some again see Thailand as the next Vietnam … They need a ‘Made in Thailand’ label Thai trade official Perception in Vietnam is also becoming less favourable towards Chinese investment. “A growing view is that Vietnamese domestic manufacturers weren’t benefiting from Chinese firms investing there for avoiding US tariffs,” Low said. “There was little technology transfer, the investments weren’t helping the economy upgrade and worse, they may also squeeze out Vietnamese firms.” In contrast, Thailand is anticipating a growing influx. In the first half of 2026, Thai authorities approved 321 mainland China-funded investment projects for government incentives, representing one-quarter of the total. These projects brought in 45.7 billion Thai baht or 9.7 billion Chinese yuan (US$1.4 billion), according to Thailand’s Board of Investment (BOI). Between 2021 and 2025, total investments from mainland China reached 132.5 billion yuan, with an average year-on-year growth of 56 per cent. Thailand has also entered the top four recipients of Chinese foreign direct investment in Asean, alongside Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia. Thailand not becoming another Vietnam Though more Chinese firms are making their way to Thai shores, their motives may still differ substantially, according to a trade official with Thailand BOI’s office in China, adding that some still sought only to divert exports. “Some again see Thailand as the next Vietnam … They need a ‘Made in Thailand’ label,” she said, declining to be named as she was not authorised to speak to media. The official said Bangkok’s relatively favourable trade ties with Washington presented an opportunity for companies looking to establish themselves in Thailand – as well as less scrupulous exporters searching for tariff loopholes. She pointed to Bangkok’s 17 free trade agreements covering 24 partner economies, which would enable “broad export access”, as well as Bangkok and Washington’s reciprocal trade agreement, which included possible zero-duty treatment for certain products. This stands in contrast with Vietnam’s higher US duty exposure, thanks to stricter transshipment rules and its trade surplus with the US – two times the size of Thailand’s. Thailand, though also subject to rules of origin verification, experiences “relatively lower US scrutiny”, the official said. These considerations are likely to have influenced Chinese manufacturers’ plans. In a December stock exchange filing, Shandong Bailong Chuangyuan Bio-tech, one of China’s largest food ingredient producers, said it had raised 748 million yuan to expand its Thai operations. “This is a strategic move … The Thai facility will not only boost profitability by leveraging low-cost raw materials and tariff advantages there … It can also circumvent trade barriers,” said the company. Some analysts warned that a rush by Chinese manufacturers into Thailand could eventually turn the country into another Vietnam, with those seeking a new tariff haven getting squeezed all over again. “With tools like Section 301 probes, Washington is looking through the map,” said Dan Martin, a Vietnam-based international business adviser with global consultancy Dezan Shira & Associates. “Other countries like Thailand can also come under scrutiny, just like Vietnam. Exporters should stop hunting for the next loophole.” But Thailand is not sitting idle, and appears to be heeding lessons from Vietnam’s experience over punitive measures targeting transshipment and “origin fraud”. Minimal processing or simple relabelling before re-exporting has been under heavy scrutiny by the Thai Department of Foreign Trade, with the department heightening monitoring for products of Chinese origin and formulating watch lists for sectors vulnerable to tariff circumvention, according to Thai media reports. To avoid US retaliation and access restrictions, and to protect legitimate local producers, Bangkok is collaborating with Washington to inspect suspected supply chains and mandate strict rules of origin certification. Last year, Thailand’s Anti-Dumping and Subsidy Consideration Committee said it had determined certain Chinese steel pipe imports were slightly altered or transshipped through the country to bypass tariffs, a practice it deemed an evasion of anti-dumping rules. In February, the US Department of Commerce also determined imported pipes, completed in Thailand but using steel billets from China, circumvented anti-dumping duties. Thailand still beckons As Bangkok takes steps to combat re-routing and other tariff avoidance practices, Thai diplomats in China stressed their country still “fully embraces” Chinese investments, adding that Bangkok was committed to helping companies tap Thailand’s potential. Siwadee Suksawate, commerce consul with the Thai consulate in Guangzhou, said there were immense opportunities for Chinese firms who “invest local and sell local”. “We have a huge domestic market of 66 million people. In areas like electronics and automotive, especially EVs, we are positioned to attract manufacturers seeking diversification and localisation,” she said. “Rather than viewing Thailand as [only] for export, more Chinese firms now have long-term commitment and localised production and management.” Unlike many in Vietnam, prominent Thai voices are continuing to call for infusions of Chinese capital. “Thailand is not wrong to welcome Chinese investment. The capital is real, the factories are being built, and the technology is arriving,” read a May editorial by the Thailand Business News. “For a developing economy seeking to industrialise rapidly, that is not a relationship to squander.” New era, new playbook Underpinning their warmer economic ties after last year’s peak tariff levels, Beijing and Washington have extended their trade truce and pared back tensions, particularly after this year’s summits between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump. New Chinese investments coming to Thailand are lured by our real advantages, less likely for transshipment Siwadee Suksawate, Thai commerce consul The US has agreed to identify US$30 billion worth of “non-sensitive goods” from China, like toys, fireworks and daily necessities, for tariff exemption under the new Board of Trade mechanism. Beijing has agreed in principle to a similar exemption. Officials and business leaders from Thailand, Vietnam and China said the friendlier atmosphere could reduce the incentive to divert exports. “This means new Chinese investments coming to Thailand are lured by our real advantages, less likely for transshipment,” Suksawate said. One type of Chinese investment being courted heavily is in hi-tech electronics, she said, adding that Bangkok had optimised tax and other incentives for them, particularly for those setting up shop in Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor, a special economic zone close to the Chinese border. Liu Quanlei, chairman of the Chinese Enterprises Chamber of Commerce in Thailand, observed a similar shift towards local sales. “Notably, more [Chinese firms] are going local, prioritising sales in Thailand and Asean … This is particularly evident in the tech and digital sector, led by Huawei and ZTE, in the home appliance sector represented by Haier, Midea and TCL, as well as EV makers like BYD and Chery,” Liu said at a business seminar held in September at the 23rd China-Asean Expo in Nanning. He added some Chinese investors were shipping finished products and components back home, including rice, rubber and non-ferrous metal. Liu said this demand was expected to bring more positive spillovers to Thailand, Vietnam and other countries in China’s periphery, including Chinese producers based there, in the form of more imports. Though Thailand has gained a considerable lead on Vietnam, it is not all gloom in Hanoi, even as the momentum wanes for export re-routing. “Vietnam is no longer a low-cost, low-income economy. It’s naturally looking to upgrade industrial structure and technology capabilities, rather than attract low-end manufacturing,” Low said. At the China-Asean Expo in September, Vietnamese exhibitors occupied 170 booths spanning 3,000 square metres (32,290 square feet). While attending the expo, Vietnam’s deputy prime minister Pham Gia Tuc made no reference to export re-routing, but said Hanoi would welcome Chinese trade and investment in artificial intelligence, smart manufacturing and industrial estate development. Meanwhile, China’s launch of the massive river-to-sea Pinglu Canal in September, a waterway connecting southwest China with the Gulf of Tonkin – and several nearby Vietnamese ports – could again redraw trade in Hanoi’s favour. The canal is expected to slash tens of billions of yuan in annual logistics costs and spur more two-way flows between China and Asean, potentially positioning Vietnam as the beachhead for trade between the bloc and the world’s second-largest economy.

title: US troops in South Korea must be ready for missions beyond peninsula, commander says
description: The commander of the US Eighth Army in South Korea said his troops must be ready for deployment outside the Korean peninsula if ordered, arguing that it would be “irresponsible” to focus “myopically” on threats there. Lieutenant General Joe Hilbert said that while his command’s focus was on fulfilling US commitments under its mutual defence treaty with Seoul, the Eighth Army’s location did not limit the missions it could undertake. It would be “irresponsible to focus myopically” on threats on...
content: The commander of the US Eighth Army in South Korea said his troops must be ready for deployment outside the Korean peninsula if ordered, arguing that it would be “irresponsible” to focus “myopically” on threats there. Lieutenant General Joe Hilbert said that while his command’s focus was on fulfilling US commitments under its mutual defence treaty with Seoul, the Eighth Army’s location did not limit the missions it could undertake. It would be “irresponsible to focus myopically” on threats on the Korean peninsula alone, he told the South China Morning Post by email, or to “suggest that we cannot do other things simply because we are in Korea”. Describing the Eighth Army as part of a “global force” that trains for “readiness so that we can deploy where needed by our national command authority,” Hilbert cited the Eighth Army’s participation in multinational exercises across the Asia-Pacific as an example of its activities beyond the peninsula. “We view readiness as largely threat-agnostic. If we have a trained, ready force capable of executing the Army’s assigned missions, we can apply that force against whatever threat is required,” said Hilbert. “So, we train every day with our Korean allies against our principal threat, while also ensuring we remain available and ready for whatever the nation may require.” Hilbert’s comments reflect the Trump administration’s push to place greater responsibility on allies for their own defence while increasing the strategic flexibility of United States Forces Korea (USFK), allowing American troops to be deployed beyond the Korean peninsula for contingencies elsewhere in the Asia-Pacific. Headquartered at Camp Humphreys in Pyeongtaek, south of Seoul, the Eighth Army commands US ground forces in South Korea. It is the only US Army stationed on the Asian continent in the Asia-Pacific region and the sole permanently forward-deployed American field army. As part of the roughly 28,500-strong USFK, the Eighth Army has traditionally focused on deterring North Korean threats rather than preparing for contingencies elsewhere, such as in the Taiwan Strait. But the Trump administration has signalled a shift towards a broader regional role. The national defence strategy, published in January, instructed that Washington aim for “strong denial defence along the first island chain,” while calling for Seoul to take “primary responsibility” for deterring Pyongyang with “critical but more limited US support”, noting that the “shift in the balance of responsibility is consistent with America’s interest in updating US force posture on the Korean peninsula”. The first island chain refers to a string of islands and archipelagos running from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines and the South China Sea. The Korean peninsula falls within this line. During a press briefing in August last year, General Xavier Brunson, commander of USFK, said that “strategic flexibility” will be at the centre of the “alliance modernisation” between Seoul and Washington in responding to the “threat” that nuclear-armed China, Russia and North Korea pose to a “free and open Indo-Pacific”.
