A more reciprocal US-South Korea alliance Lami Kim, Korea chair in advanced technologies, national security and defence at the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, said that the nature of the alliance is shifting towards a “more reciprocal partnership,” instead of Washington’s primarily “one-directional” responsibility to defend Seoul. “Both countries are expected to contribute to each other’s security and South Korea assumes greater responsibility for its own defence,” said Kim. “I think this is a natural evolution that reflects South Korea’s significantly enhanced military capabilities – a far cry from its position in the 1950s, when the alliance was first established.” Troy Stangarone, a visiting senior fellow at the Korea Economic Institute of America, said that the broader trend in US-South Korea defence ties has been towards Seoul taking on a larger role, while growing its domestic defence industrial base, and the US seeking “greater flexibility” to utilise US forces for other contingencies. “The United States has already moved forces and equipment off the Korean peninsula to support US operations, both in the recent Iran war and the Iraq war in 2003. I would expect it to continue to do so as conditions require,” said Stangarone. Seoul’s enhanced military capabilities were reflected in its weapons’ recent integration and partnership with the US military. In August, the US Army awarded a contract worth up to US$260 million to South Korea’s Hanwha to deliver prototypes of its K9 Mobile Howitzer for its new Mobile Tactical Cannon programme – a first case of a South Korean weapons system acquired by the US military. US defence contractor General Atomics also showcased a scale model of the Mojave short take-off and landing (STOL) drone at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition last week. The drone was co-developed and co-produced with Hanwha Aerospace under a partnership agreement signed last year. Keeping US forces supplied in the Pacific Speaking at a panel discussion during the AUSA Annual Meeting, Brunson said the US Army is trying to “change” the “depot mindset” of maintaining US weapons and equipment by travelling back and forth between the continental US and the Asia-Pacific region, which often consumes several days and weeks for those systems to be delivered. He said partnering with South Korea, which he described as having “an absolutely premier industrial base”, can achieve “admirable endurance” and keep US forces with an “enviable posture” within the first island chain. “What’s going to be important in the future, in particular in a fight in the Pacific, is our ability to endure, whether that be able to protect the things that we’ve placed forward, or whether that be the ability to stay there because we can sustain ourselves inside the first island chain from Korea,” said Brunson. Brunson’s remarks follow Hilbert’s earlier proposal at the Land Forces Pacific symposium in Hawaii in May, where he said partnering with South Korea’s advanced manufacturing base would reduce the need to cross the Pacific and increase “strategic flexibility” for the US Joint Forces. Kim said that as the alliance becomes “increasingly reciprocal”, it is becoming more difficult for Seoul to expect Washington to “maintain its security commitments without making meaningful contributions in return”. “South Korea would likely provide logistical support to US forces in the event of a regional contingency,” said Kim. “If the conflict became prolonged, South Korea’s defence industrial base could also play an important role in replenishing American weapons stockpiles and sustaining US military operations.” Stangarone said that South Korea, as a logistics hub, plays a “critical role”, as it is the only US ally in the region with the defence industrial base capable of supporting US forces in the case of a contingency. “Despite periodic calls for South Korea to commit forces to any contingency in the region, it has long been clear that its primary role is a supporting role providing needed munitions and armaments,” said Stangarone. “South Korea shares interests and capabilities with the United States in the Indo-Pacific. While deterring North Korea needs to remain the priority, Seoul can and should play a larger role in US strategy in the region in recognition of its own growing capabilities.”

title: First Quad leaders’ summit after 2 years in Manila next month, Rubio confirms
description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed on Tuesday that the leaders of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue would meet in the Philippine capital next month, marking the group’s first summit in more than two years, just days before US President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. “It’s been agreement now that we’re going to do it; we’re going to do it in Manila, at the Asean conference,” Rubio said in an interview with Indian news channel CNN-News18. “We don’t...
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed on Tuesday that the leaders of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue would meet in the Philippine capital next month, marking the group’s first summit in more than two years, just days before US President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. “It’s been agreement now that we’re going to do it; we’re going to do it in Manila, at the Asean conference,” Rubio said in an interview with Indian news channel CNN-News18. “We don’t have the specific date yet, but that’s going to happen, and we’re very enthusiastic about it.” The Philippines chairs the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) this year and will host the leaders’ summit and other multilateral meetings from November 16 to 18. The Quad, an informal grouping that includes the US, Japan, India and Australia, is widely seen as a mechanism to counter China’s influence in the strategically vital region. The last Quad leaders’ summit was held in September 2024 in Wilmington, Delaware, the hometown of then US president Joe Biden. India was due to host the Quad leaders’ summit in 2025, but the meeting was repeatedly delayed as relations between New Delhi and Washington deteriorated over US tariffs, oil sanctions and visa restrictions. Australia is the rotating chair for this year. However, the bloc continued to convene at the foreign ministers’ level, with the most recent meeting held in Manila in July, where all four countries reaffirmed their commitment to a “free and open Indo-Pacific”. During a meeting in May, the grouping announced several new initiatives on maritime and economic security, including the US$20 billion Quad Critical Minerals Initiative Framework. On Tuesday, Rubio said that Quad foreign ministers would meet again in late October on the sidelines of a Group of 20 (G20) gathering of top diplomats in Atlanta to make final preparations for the leaders’ summit. He recalled that his first meeting as secretary of state was with Quad foreign ministers. “As soon as I was sworn in, I went upstairs, and we did it,” he said, referring to the January 2025 meeting. “And the leaders' level meeting, we look forward to being a part of that at Asean here in just a few weeks.” Rubio is on a two-day visit to India that bypasses the capital, New Delhi. He held talks with Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in Mumbai and called for “increased energy trade” between the two countries. The Quad leaders’ summit announcement comes amid shifting priorities under the Trump administration in the Asia-Pacific region, and concerns among partner countries about Washington’s long-term security commitments and its approach to countering China’s growing clout. In June 2026, the US renamed Indo-Pacific Command to Pacific Command, reversing a change made in 2018. In August, Trump ordered the annual US-South Korean military exercise cut from 11 days to five. His administration has also pressed regional allies and partners to shoulder more of their own defence costs. Meanwhile, Trump has met the Chinese leader twice this year and will hold their third bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen in late November, before capping the year with their fourth meeting at the G20 summit in Miami.

title: India’s record US$108b Jio IPO tests market faith as Musk rivalry heats up
description: The coming launch of India’s largest-ever initial public offering (IPO) will test investor confidence in the country’s leading telecoms operator, Jio Platforms, the digital arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries. Jio’s public share offer on Wednesday comes close on the heels of an escalating row between Ambani and Elon Musk. The SpaceX founder has accused the Indian industrialist of using monopolistic influence to block Starlink’s entry into India – a charge Reliance has denied,...
content: The coming launch of India’s largest-ever initial public offering (IPO) will test investor confidence in the country’s leading telecoms operator, Jio Platforms, the digital arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries. Jio’s public share offer on Wednesday comes close on the heels of an escalating row between Ambani and Elon Musk. The SpaceX founder has accused the Indian industrialist of using monopolistic influence to block Starlink’s entry into India – a charge Reliance has denied, saying it has never feared competition. Ambani’s US$3.2 billion Jio Platforms listing has already drawn strong interest from institutional investors, including Singapore’s GIC, BlackRock and Fidelity, reportedly generating bids totalling nearly 30 times the quota reserved for anchor investors. Targeting a valuation of over US$108 billion, the IPO comes at a sensitive juncture, as soaring oil prices caused by the Middle East conflict continue to weigh on global trading sentiment. “It is a mega listing and there is tremendous interest in the IPO despite geopolitical concerns,” said Pranav Haldea, managing director of market data firm Prime Database, referring to the Middle East conflict and the broader uncertainty it has wrought on financial markets. Reliance Jio is India’s leading telecoms provider, holding close to 80 per cent of the domestic market alongside competitor Bharti Airtel, according to data from the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India as of August this year. The listing has drawn international attention not only because it is the largest in Indian history but also because it coincides with foreign investors pulling tens of billions of dollars out of India’s stock market amid rising global interest rates, high energy costs and a shift towards artificial intelligence assets. However, Haldea said secondary market capital flight was unlikely to derail Jio’s debut. Foreign investors have continued to invest in India’s primary market – where companies issue new shares – showing a sustained appetite for individual companies despite broader withdrawals. Steady and substantial domestic inflows into secondary markets via mutual funds had largely cushioned the market against heavy outflows by foreign portfolio investors, further insulating Jio’s share offer from adverse impacts, Haldea added. Analysts say a successful IPO is likely to bolster Reliance Jio by increasing cash flow and allowing it to pay down debt, even though none of the capital raised is earmarked for expanding terrestrial telecoms services or launching satellites. “Nine rupees in 10 will go to repaying debt. None of it is ring-fenced for satellites. The boost is real, but indirect,” said Raj Kapoor, chairman of the India Blockchain Alliance. Debt repayments could lower Jio’s annual interest burden by 20 billion to 25 billion Indian rupees (US$211 million to US$264 million), Kapoor estimated. “That frees up cash flow, and a listed share gives Jio a currency it can use to raise capital again,” he added. Space ambitions and Starlink competition Jio currently operates a massive nationwide mobile network and land-based high-speed broadband infrastructure. The operator upended India’s telecoms landscape in 2016 by offering free voice calls and cheap data, rapidly expanding to become the country’s largest mobile operator. The company has set its sights on satellite connectivity, planning a constellation of 1,600 low earth orbit satellites supported by 23 ground stations. The technical architecture has already received approval from India’s space regulator, IN-SPACe. Jio has not confirmed a launch date for the satellite constellation, but industry estimates suggest deployment could take two to three years. Reliance Jio has stated its intention to keep the entire value chain within India – from design and engineering to testing and launch. “That is a strong sovereignty pitch, but it is also India’s biggest constraint, because domestic launch capacity has never handled anything at this scale,” Kapoor said, adding that Starlink already operates over 10,000 satellites. “Jio is entering a race in which the leader is roughly six times its planned size and years ahead in operating experience,” he added. Satellite-based internet is considered critical for reaching remote and mountainous regions where traditional terrestrial fibre and cellular infrastructure are impractical to deploy. Investors see the IPO as a barometer of market demand for Jio’s broader telecoms and digital services – spanning mobile services, broadband, cloud computing, entertainment and AI – alongside its future offerings. “The Jio IPO strengthens the balance sheet, settles a [firm] valuation and tests foreign [investor] conviction. Whether it wins the space race against Musk will be decided by launch schedules and [regulatory] licences, not subscription numbers,” Kapoor said. He added that satellite connectivity poses little immediate threat to Jio’s core business in the near term. “Sat[ellite] com[munications] is a last-mile tool, not a tool for disrupting the mass market. Jio’s real advantage is distribution: both Jio and Airtel are positioned to bundle satcom with terrestrial services,” Kapoor said. “Starlink has no retail footprint or customer base in India. Jio has more than 500 million subscribers.”

title: As Indonesia faces MSCI downgrade threat, officials vow reforms to ease fears
description: As the threat of a reclassification by MSCI that could relegate Indonesia to an investment hinterland looms, the country’s financial regulators and stock exchange officials have vowed to address systemic concerns, including removing stocks with concentrated ownership. The global index provider announced on Friday it was launching a formal consultation to decide whether to downgrade Southeast Asia’s largest economy from “emerging market” to “stand-alone” status, similar to countries such as...
content: As the threat of a reclassification by MSCI that could relegate Indonesia to an investment hinterland looms, the country’s financial regulators and stock exchange officials have vowed to address systemic concerns, including removing stocks with concentrated ownership. The global index provider announced on Friday it was launching a formal consultation to decide whether to downgrade Southeast Asia’s largest economy from “emerging market” to “stand-alone” status, similar to countries such as Argentina, Zimbabwe, Ukraine and Russia. MSCI cited persistent concerns over Indonesia’s market dysfunction, including opaque ownership structures, highly concentrated shareholdings and coordinated trading practices. Its final decision is expected by June 30 next year. On Monday, officials from the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) held an online meeting with MSCI representatives, where they laid out measures to reform the country’s problematic stock market. “First, we will include a description of whether 1 per cent shareholders are affiliated or unaffiliated [with the company] when publishing the names. Second, to provide a more credible and integrated price index, we will remove all high shareholding concentration [HSC] shares from the Jakarta Composite Index,” IDX CEO Jeffrey Hendrik told reporters. “We hope these two initiatives will provide greater transparency and greater market data integrity.” HSC refers to a market situation in which a huge percentage of a company’s shares – in some cases above 95 per cent – are owned by a small number of shareholders, with a very small free float available for public trading. According to Hendrik, HSC shares currently account for 18 per cent of JCI’s total weighting. Such shares had been excluded from Hong Kong’s benchmark Hang Seng Index, he added. Hendrik said the new measures followed previous steps taken by the Indonesian bourse to improve transparency, such as setting 15 per cent as the minimum requirement of free float, or the proportion of a company’s shares readily available for the general public to buy and sell, and expanding the number of investor categories from nine to 39, among others. The JCI plunged 3.64 per cent at the close of trading on Monday to a six-year low at 4,996.60. After MSCI issued its warning, the benchmark index plunged 11.6 per cent on Friday, making it one of the world’s worst performers and wiping out around US$85 billion in market capitalisation. On Tuesday, the index rose 5.65 per cent to close at 5,278. A downgrade to stand-alone market status could trigger US$5.6 billion in passive fund outflows, with another US$2.7 billion fleeing if FTSE Russell – a leading global provider of benchmarks – were to take similar action, Goldman Sachs warned in a note on Sunday, as quoted by CNBC. As of Sunday, the proportion of foreign ownership of Indonesian stocks was 25 per cent, down from 27 per cent in January, while the value of foreign holdings had dropped to US$130 billion from US$250 billion in January, the investment bank said. Over the weekend, the Financial Services Authority (OJK) in Indonesia and IDX sought to steady the nervous market by declaring a fine of 2.1 trillion rupiah (US$116.4 million) on three firms alleged to have manipulated trading of their shares. Two of the firms, Barito Renewables Energy and Petrindo Jaya Kreasi, belonged to a group owned by conglomerate Prajogo Pangestu, while another, Dian Swastatika Sentosa, is part of the Sinar Mas conglomerate. More fixes needed While economists welcomed the measures by IDX, they said regulators still needed to impose firm law enforcement to help Indonesia avoid reclassification by MSCI. “The key to adjusting the perception of Indonesia needs to come from strict enforcement of IDX and OJK rules and regulations and the imposition of sanctions, including significant fines and even imprisonment. This is criminal behaviour after all,” said Angus Mackintosh, an Asean specialist at Aletheia Capital in Singapore. “Forthright statements from the top are required to ensure that actions are taken to their logical conclusion, even if those market abusers are closely connected to the government.” Bhima Yudhistira, executive director at Jakarta-based think tank Centre of Economic and Law Studies (Celios), said that the disclosure of 1 per cent shareholders “must be accompanied by an investigation into their ultimate beneficial ownership, as many companies use the names of other companies, or nominees, as their shareholders”. The market was also rattled by an effort by state wealth fund and investment agency Danantara to acquire shares of the IDX, which would “ultimately lead to a decline in the independence of the stock exchange”, Bhima added. The IDX is currently undergoing a demutualisation process, which will see it become a limited liability company owned by shareholders. IDX is currently owned by its members, including 90 securities companies. Dipo Ramli, an economist with the Centre of Reform on Economics Indonesia, said that IDX was still facing “a decline in market confidence,” which could “indirectly influence” the assessment of the Indonesian economy by rating agencies. Earlier this year, Fitch and Moody’s downgraded Indonesia’s rating outlook from stable to negative due to concerns relating to economic governance by President Prabowo Subianto’s administration. Martyn Terpilowski, a British investor in Indonesia, said that “foreigners are unlikely to buy” the charm offensive by regulators to lure them back into the market. “What you find in Indonesia, a lot of the deals are off-market transactions. That’s because the actual real price of the stock is heavily inflated and the insiders know that,” Terpilowski said. “It’s just not a transparent market that people can invest into.” He also questioned the authorities’ promise to make the market more open to investors. “It’s a difficult one because the economy will be hurt if US$40 billion flows out of the economy. The question is, if they open the floodgates to allow a better system, will that hurt the oligarchs more?” Terpilowski said. “The problem you’ve got in Indonesia is pretty similar to the United States now, as the business leaders are all very close to the government leaders.” Wider economic crisis? Bhima argued that the current pressure on the Indonesian bourse could lead to an economic crisis similar to one in the late 1990s. “There’s a disconnect between the government’s claims of economic success and the actual state of economic fundamentals. There is damaged governance in the stock exchange, as well as the declining independence of Bank Indonesia,” Bhima said. “This could lead to a financial crisis, similar to the 1998 model, due to distrust over policy credibility. The issues are already intertwined between the [government] fiscal and financial sectors.” Mackintosh, however, said the wider economic crisis would not occur as long as regulators continued overhauling the local stock market and making it transparent. “IDX and OJK need to show their teeth in dealing with these problems and sanction those companies which are connected to share manipulation activity and market abuse. The brokers involved should also be sanctioned, heavily fined and disbarred from trading,” Mackintosh said. “There is a good deal of scepticism around the move by the MSCI in that it has impacted the whole stock market, bringing about a significant correction and destruction across the board, when the vast majority of companies maintain high-quality governance standards.”

title: In Malaysia, viral air purifier test fans flames of anger over haze

content: As haze from forest fires in Indonesia continues to shroud Southeast Asia, Malaysians have taken to social media to air their grievances, with a video of an elevated outdoor reading from an air purifier among viral content marking public frustration. The clip, posted by user syahierarafie, shows a device detecting an Air Pollutant Index (API) of up to 318 in Gelang Patah, a suburban town in western Johor Bahru which borders Singapore. The video has drawn over 990,000 views as of Tuesday. “Today, my office staff did an IPU experiment outside. IPU 300++ wow. It is very unhealthy,” the post read, referring to API by its Malay name, Indeks Pencemar Udara. Many online users chimed in, with some posting pictures of their own air purifiers registering similar readings of high API levels. Some complained that Malaysia’s official website for API reported a lower reading than what people were experiencing. The API classifies a reading above 300 as “hazardous”, the highest level of the five-level scale. Readings of 201-300 are “very unhealthy”, 101-200 “unhealthy”, 51-100 “moderate” and 0-50 “good”, according to the Malaysia Environmental Quality Management System. View on Threads On Wednesday, when the viral video was posted, the API registered in Gelang Patah was 121, putting the air quality in the “unhealthy” category, according to Accuweather. Air purifiers typically measure air quality using a built-in laser sensor to detect the scattering of light by small particles passing through, such as PM2.5 and PM10. The numbers refer to the diameter of the particulate matter, measured in micrometres. Based on an image reverse search, the purifier used in the video appears to be a Xiaomi Smart Air Purifier model. Xiaomi says its air purifiers are equipped with laser sensors to detect particles in real time. In comparison, API is calculated from six major pollutants: PM2.5, PM10, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide and ozone, according to the Malaysian Medical Gazette. The official system does not measure pollutants in real time. Instead, each pollutant is measured based on an average period of one to 24 hours. PM2.5 and PM10 – among the most dominant pollutants during the haze – are measured based on a 24-hour average. That means official readings may be lower than what is shown on air purifiers or different commercial weather platforms. Malaysia and Singapore are experiencing severe haze as Indonesia grapples with its worst fire season in more than a decade. Blazes across Sumatra and Kalimantan have sent thick smoke across the region. The ongoing haze has spiked demand for air purifiers across Southeast Asia. Regional electronics retailer Courts told The Straits Times that air purifier sales have increased by 600 per cent from September 28 to October 12 compared to last year. Singapore-based retailer Gain City also reported “a significant increase in air-purifier demand”, according to the newspaper. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim defended the government’s handling of the haze on Thursday. “We have done everything we can,” he said, in response to allegations that Putrajaya had not been proactive enough in pushing Indonesia to resolve the issue. Foreign minister Mohamad Hasan said the same day that Malaysia would not pursue a legal action against Indonesia to “safeguard the close relationship between the two countries”.

title: Malaysia’s opposition bloc declared invalid, but limited gains for Anwar
description: Malaysia’s main opposition coalition lost its registration on Tuesday, just 11 days before nominations for a state election, drawing accusations that Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government is using state powers to cripple its rivals. The decision leaves Perikatan Nasional (PN) – already fractured by a bitter dispute between its Islamist anchor, the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS), and estranged partner Bersatu – fighting to preserve its electoral identity ahead of Melaka’s November 14...
content: Malaysia’s main opposition coalition lost its registration on Tuesday, just 11 days before nominations for a state election, drawing accusations that Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government is using state powers to cripple its rivals. The decision leaves Perikatan Nasional (PN) – already fractured by a bitter dispute between its Islamist anchor, the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS), and estranged partner Bersatu – fighting to preserve its electoral identity ahead of Melaka’s November 14 vote. National elections are due by February 2028, although Anwar has indicated an earlier vote could be considered. Analysts identified his federal governing partner, the United Malays National Organisation (Umno), as a potential beneficiary of the decision as it negotiates an electoral pact with PAS against Anwar’s own alliance in Melaka. The Registrar of Societies found that explanations submitted by PN on October 12 failed to rebut grounds for deregistration outlined in a notice issued last month. “The reasons given could not refute the grounds for cancellation of registration … nor provide a strong justification for maintaining the organisation’s registration,” the agency said. Registered organisations must comply with the law and their own constitutions, it added, pledging to enforce those requirements “firmly, fairly and in accordance with the law”. The dispute stems from a complaint by Bersatu that it was excluded from a July 16 meeting of PN’s supreme council following months of friction with PAS. Bersatu Secretary General Azmin Ali on Tuesday blamed the PAS-led leadership for violating the coalition’s constitution by denying his party the right to participate. “Unlawful action can cause immense harm and destroy the future of Perikatan,” he said in a statement. Azmin also accused PAS and its allies of portraying themselves as political victims to win sympathy ahead of the Melaka election. Meanwhile, PN Secretary General Takiyuddin Hassan questioned why the registrar acted just two days before the Kuala Lumpur High Court was scheduled to hear PN’s application for a stay against the initial suspension notice. “A government that respects the rule of law should allow the court space to decide the application, and explain why it could not wait even two days,” he said in a statement. According to Takiyuddin, the court granted permission for a judicial review on October 13 and fixed the stay hearing for October 22, but PN’s written request for authorities to hold off pending that hearing went unanswered. “The cancellation of PN’s registration exposes a government that is increasingly desperate and fearful of the people’s growing support for PN,” he said. Fractured alliance PN emerged from the political defections that brought down the Pakatan Harapan (PH) government in 2020 and installed Bersatu President Muhyiddin Yassin as prime minister. It was formally registered that August. Muhyiddin resigned in August 2021 after losing his parliamentary majority. PN subsequently backed his successor, Ismail Sabri Yaakob – who belonged to Umno rather than a PN member party – before moving into opposition after the 2022 general election brought Anwar to power. Deregistration leaves its component parties able to contest under their own banners, although they have yet to settle on a logo for Melaka, according to Takiyuddin. PAS is pursuing cooperation with the Umno-led Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition, which remains part of Anwar’s federal administration while preparing to challenge his PH coalition at the state level. BN Chairman and Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi last week insisted his coalition would defend the 21 seats it won at the previous Melaka election, leaving the remaining seven state seats open for negotiations with PN’s component parties. For PAS and Wawasan – the party led by former Bersatu deputy president Hamzah Zainudin – losing PN’s banner meant surrendering a recognisable electoral identity, according to Adib Zalkapli, managing director of political consultancy Viewfinder Global Affairs. “The Perikatan Nasional brand has been well received among Malay-Muslim voters outside the traditional PAS strongholds,” Adib said. PAS could fall back on its established name and moon symbol, while the relatively new Wawasan might have to contest under PAS or BN’s banner, he added. “The real beneficiary is BN,” Adib said. “With PN out of the picture, BN – and especially Umno – is in a stronger position in the seat negotiation process with PAS and Wawasan.” Aziff Azuddin, research director at Iman Research, a Kuala Lumpur-based sociopolitical think tank, was sceptical that deregistration would significantly alter the electoral equation, given that the parties could still cooperate and PAS remained a familiar name among voters. “A pre- or post-election agreement can still happen with or without the PN vehicle,” Aziff said. “PN as a brand worked to sell the idea of a collective Malay-Muslim coalition, with Bersatu and PAS being its most prominent components. The question for the polls is whether the PAS brand is effective with Melaka voters.” He cautioned against assuming the decision would substantially help Anwar’s coalition, given its rivalry with its own federal partner. “We’re talking about PAS as though they are an active threat to Pakatan when Umno, their governing partner, has been the one antagonising them at the state polls,” Aziff said.

content: Two Singaporean men lost their positions in the armed forces after they were convicted of having sex with a 15-year-old boy. Former army captain Chaw Chia Jun, 41, was sentenced to 17 months’ jail on Tuesday, while his co-accused Owen Toh Wei Song, a former navy cook, was jailed for 12 months on September 22, according to CNA. Singapore’s Ministry of Defence has confirmed that both were suspended after their arrest in 2024 and were no longer in the military. “The Singapore Armed Forces holds its service personnel to high standards of discipline and integrity. Service personnel who commit offences will be dealt with in accordance with the law,” it said in a statement. The court heard that the Secondary 4 student had contacted Toh, now 26, on Telegram after finding his profile on an online forum around April 2024. He told Toh he was a secondary school student about to take his N levels exams that year. Both began discussing sexual topics, including niche acts. Toh said he was not experienced in the area but that his ex-boyfriend, Chaw, was and suggested all three meet, The Straits Times reported. Toh and Chaw were in a relationship between 2021 and 2022 but remained in contact after breaking up. The teenager agreed. Two months later, Toh picked up Chaw and the teen and drove to a multi-storey carpark. After parking the car on the empty uppermost deck, Toh asked the teen to strip and performed a sex act on him while Chaw filmed them on his phone. Chaw also undressed and asked the teen to perform a sex act on him. The teen refused but agreed to do it on Toh instead. All three later got dressed and left. At Toh’s request, Chaw sent him a copy of the video. Chaw continued meeting the teen after the incident. On one of the occasions, on June 5, 2024, they had sex in a disabled toilet at a shopping centre while Chaw videoed the act. He kept all the videos on his phone, later describing his record of sexual activities with others as his “personal collection”. The acts came to light when the victim’s mother and sister grew concerned about his behaviour and the gifts he was receiving from an adult man. When they confronted him, he told them what had happened and lodged a police report on October 23, 2024. On Tuesday, Chaw pleaded guilty to three charges of sexual penetration of a minor, causing a minor to perform sexual penetration and producing child abuse material. The maximum penalty for each offence is 10 years’ jail, a fine or both. The child abuse material charge also allows for caning. Toh pleaded guilty last month to a charge of causing a minor to perform sexual penetration, with another two charges taken into consideration. Chaw’s lawyer, Mark Yeo, said his client “genuinely but mistakenly” believed that the victim was of age. He also highlighted that the victim had lied about his age and sent a fake photo of someone else in a Telegram chat. While acknowledging this, District Judge Kenneth Chin pointed out Chaw did not take further steps to ascertain the victim’s age. It also did not matter whether the victim was an active participant or initiator, he added, as the objective of the offence was to protect minors from exploitation. “Absence of coercion is a neutral factor and is not a mitigating factor,” Chin said.

title: Energy shock could spark Asia’s next debt crisis

content: A country need not run out of money to find itself in a debt crisis. It only has to run short of US dollars to pay for its energy. At the recent International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, the IMF, which expects global economic growth of 3.1 per cent this year and 3.4 per cent the next, cautioned that energy-importing and lower-income economies face a harder road, even as those riding the artificial intelligence boom fare relatively well. According to the World Bank’s International Debt Report, between 2022 and 2024, low- and middle-income countries paid US$741 billion more in debt repayments and interest than they received in new external financing. As buffers drain, the next energy shock could push vulnerable economies over the edge. Past financial crises have taught policymakers to watch for failing banks and collapsing currencies. An energy shock follows a different path. It begins at the fuel terminal, not in a bank vault. By the time stress surfaces in the banking system, the damage to a country’s external position is done. The IMF has warned that rising borrowing costs and currency pressures can worsen the impact of such disruptions. Asia is particularly vulnerable. Its net oil and gas imports amount to about 2.5 per cent of gross domestic product, and it buys 80 per cent of the liquefied natural gas (LNG) passing through the Strait of Hormuz. That exposure does not necessarily lead to default, but rising energy costs can drain foreign exchange reserves and make debt repayments harder to manage. How hard that collision lands depends on the cushion each country holds. India, despite being a major oil importer, held US$682 billion in reserves at end-May, enough to pay for about 11 months of imports. Indonesia, which both produces and imports energy, had a smaller financial cushion with reserves of US$146.3 billion at end-September. Vietnam is more vulnerable, with the IMF predicting its current reserves would cover only around two months of imports. None of these countries faces an imminent sovereign debt crisis, but a prolonged rise in energy prices could test their ability to meet external obligations in very different ways. The risks become more apparent in South Asia’s smaller economies. Bangladesh is an early warning. Its reserves were US$26.7 billion for the year ended June 30, 2025, covering just 3.8 months of imports. In May this year, the World Bank approved an additional US$350 million in financing for Bangladesh’s LNG imports. Since then, rising energy import and subsidy costs have added further pressure. Pakistan has the narrowest margin. The IMF, which puts Pakistan’s reserves at US$21.5 billion, projects its external financing needs at US$21.2 billion for the current financial year. Sri Lanka has reserves of US$6.85 billion as of September, enough to cover about three months of imports, but has little time to strengthen its finances as its energy bill continues to rise and larger repayments on its restructured foreign debt are set to resume next year. Seen side by side, the same oil-price rise that India can absorb could shake refinancing confidence in Bangladesh, Pakistan or Sri Lanka. Debt surveillance should reveal that difference before markets do, and three steps would help. First, the IMF and World Bank should build a joint “energy-to-debt stress test” for vulnerable importers. A standard exercise could model oil at US$20 a barrel above the baseline and a temporary doubling of spot LNG prices, then trace the effect on the import bill, current account, reserves, exchange rate, state-owned energy companies and foreign-currency debt service over 12 to 24 months. The aim is to pinpoint when an energy shock becomes a refinancing problem. Second, the test should trigger faster temporary liquidity, such as from the IMF’s Rapid Financing Instrument or the World Bank’s Rapid Response Option. Third, prevention means financing the exit. The World Bank’s Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency already uses portfolio guarantees to support renewable generation and battery storage projects. For energy importers, verified future savings on fuel imports should carry explicit weight in concessional finance and guarantee decisions. This is not only climate investment; it is also balance-of-payments insurance. Each step needs guardrails. Emergency liquidity should not subsidise permanently cheap fuel, so access should require transparent reserve data, disclosure of state energy companies’ liabilities, cost-reflective pricing where feasible, targeted cash support and hard sunset clauses. Broad price caps can become unaffordable and losses at state energy firms can migrate onto the public balance sheet. A debt crisis that begins at the fuel terminal will not look like a banking collapse until late in the story. By then, the foreign exchange reserves may already be depleted. The lesson of the Bangkok meetings should be simple – stress-test the energy bill before it becomes a sovereign balance-sheet crisis.

title: How a Malaysian coffee shop menu became latest political battleground
description: Calls to boycott a Malaysian Chinese-owned coffee-shop chain over its omission of Malay text from its menu have reignited arguments over race and national identity, as political parties jostle to court the country’s majority ethnic group ahead of the next general election. The Oriental Kopi boycott marks the latest saga fuelling ethnic grievances that politicians have been seen to capitalise on by portraying themselves as defenders of Malay identity. It comes ahead of the November 14 election in...
content: Calls to boycott a Malaysian Chinese-owned coffee-shop chain over its omission of Malay text from its menu have reignited arguments over race and national identity, as political parties jostle to court the country’s majority ethnic group ahead of the next general election. The Oriental Kopi boycott marks the latest saga fuelling ethnic grievances that politicians have been seen to capitalise on by portraying themselves as defenders of Malay identity. It comes ahead of the November 14 election in Melaka, where Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s multiracial alliance Pakatan Harapan (PH) will face off federal partner Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition. The Umno-led coalition won sweeping victories in Johor and Negeri Sembilan earlier this year, contesting alone in the former and cooperating with the Islamist party, Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS), and its allies in the latter. BN has agreed in principle to cooperate again with PAS for the Melaka state poll. The national election is due by February 2028, although Anwar said last month that calls for an earlier vote would be considered. Oriental Kopi, a Malaysian chain known for egg tarts, coffee and local dishes served in the tradition of Chinese coffee shops known as kopitiam, came under criticism after photographs of its English and Chinese menu circulated on social media last week. The company listed on Bursa Malaysia’s ACE Market on January 23 last year, as it pursued expansion at home and overseas, having opened its first Singapore cafe through a joint venture. One online user questioned why a business celebrating its Malaysian identity had omitted the national language while others called for a boycott until it was included. “This is Malaysia, not China,” one wrote. The cafe’s defenders responded with their own taunts. “All [Malays], please boycott Oriental Kopi so next time I don’t have to queue,” one said. Some questioned why comparable menus elsewhere had escaped scrutiny. Founder Calvin Chan apologised on Wednesday and said a redesigned menu including Malay was already being prepared. “As a brand born in Malaysia, we have always respected Malay as our country’s national language. We apologise for this shortcoming,” he wrote in Malay on Threads. “We are already in the process of introducing a new menu design that also includes Malay. We humbly ask for a little time to make these improvements.” Chan said the chain welcomed customers from all communities. “Oriental Kopi is for all Malaysians, regardless of race and background.” Wooing the majority Malays account for 58.4 per cent of Malaysia’s estimated population of 34.4 million, with ethnic Chinese making up 22 per cent and Indians 6.5 per cent, according to official figures. Other indigenous communities make up most of the remainder. Anwar has previously said supporting Malays should not come at the expense of other communities. Late last month, he pledged to advance Malay interests while rejecting views that belittled others or denied their rights. “I want to help the Malays because they are my people. I’m proud of their culture, their heritage,” he said, as quoted by local media. Politicians usually stood to gain from prolonging such disputes rather than settling them, said Syaza Farhana Mohamad Shukri, an associate professor of political science at the International Islamic University Malaysia. It is easiest to continue with racial rhetoric to hold on to the Malay political imagination Syaza Farhana Mohamad Shukri, a political science professor “In the absence of clear policy debates and having politics be about mature debates, it is easiest to continue with racial rhetoric to hold on to the Malay political imagination,” she said. “At the end of the day, the Malays would say they expect [the] government and politicians to defend their identity, so it is a political issue.” But Anwar should resist chasing voters firmly opposed to him or his coalition, she added. Instead, he should address the complaint with a practical solution that could appeal to undecided voters. “Anwar should focus on the middle ground voters, those who are still rational and not partisan,” she added. Political scientist Wong Chin Huat said the controversy reflected “ethnic protectionism”, describing it as a continuation or revival of the Buy Muslim First campaign of 2019. “When halalness cannot be questioned, language becomes a convenient tool to ignite what is part of a larger culture war,” he said. Competition among Malay parties encouraged nationalists to use cultural disputes to stir insecurity and rally voters behind calls for Malay unity, the Sunway University professor said. But he questioned whether this particular boycott would deliver much electoral benefit. “Oriental’s Malay clientele is likely bilingual or Anglophone,” he said, suggesting that ethnic and religious appeals might already have reached their limit beyond the urban middle class.

title: Malaysian student who called out Najib’s donation drive fires back at trolls
description: Universiti Malaya student Ummi Umairah Bakhit, who went viral recently for questioning the donation of money to former Malaysian prime minister Najib Razak, has spoken out against what she described as cyberbullying, political obsession and emotional loyalty. The youth stood by her criticism of donating money to the former prime minister, saying she would not apologise for raising the issue. In a social media post, Ummi Umairah said the response to a question she raised at the International...
content: Universiti Malaya student Ummi Umairah Bakhit, who went viral recently for questioning the donation of money to former Malaysian prime minister Najib Razak, has spoken out against what she described as cyberbullying, political obsession and emotional loyalty. The youth stood by her criticism of donating money to the former prime minister, saying she would not apologise for raising the issue. In a social media post, Ummi Umairah said the response to a question she raised at the International Young Future Leaders Summit sparked a national conversation, but maintained that her stance on corruption and in support of integrity, equality and justice remained unchanged. “I stand by my question. I will never apologise,” she said. She said much of the reaction focused on her choice of words and the mention of Najib, while overlooking her broader points about corruption, feudalism, facts and data. She said her activism had not been selective, citing her participation in a demonstration against Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission chief Azam Baki and her criticism of unequal opportunities at her university. Ummi Umairah urged more people to speak out on corruption and integrity without fear, adding that the criticism she received would not change her position. On Sunday, Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil condemned the bullying and threats against Ummi Umairah over the views she had expressed. He said berating and threatening the student, including threats to track her down, should not have occurred simply because there was a difference of opinion. “We can have different views, that’s not a problem. In Ummi Umairah’s case, she expressed her views and we know that university students have the right to speak up,” Bernama reported him as saying after attending the Smart Parents Inter­active Hub Programme in Selangor. “So, we should welcome this because she has not violated any laws, nor has she committed any criminal offence. She only add­res­sed matters concerning the crime of corruption.” Last month, Najib’s Umno launched a fundraiser to help pay his 50 million ringgit (US$12.3 million) fine that will allow him to spend the rest of his jail sentence under house arrest after the former leader secured a conditional pardon from Malaysia’s king. Najib was jailed in 2022 after failing to overturn a conviction for stealing 42 million ringgit from a former unit of the troubled state fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad. This story was first published by The Star

title: Malaysia’s Anwar promises ‘full disclosure’ as ‘corporate mafia’ scandal grows

content: Malaysia’s government will publicly release the findings of a special task force on corporate malfeasance in three months, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Tuesday, as his administration seeks to appease public anger over its perceived failure to clamp down on corruption. Anwar is facing a reckoning in the final stretch of his term after his ruling Pakatan Harapan coalition was handed bruising defeats in three state elections over the past year. Former supporters have accused the coalition of abandoning its promised reforms in favour of a political compact with former ruling party Umno. Public discontent has been compounded by allegations of a so-called “corporate mafia” involving officers from the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC), who were alleged to have coerced stake sales and corporate takeovers. The MACC and Azam Baki – who was chief commissioner at the time and was himself accused of holding stocks well above government-mandated limits – have denied the allegations, which were first reported by Bloomberg in February. Anwar said he had instructed the Attorney-General’s Chambers to form a special task force on corporate crime made up of representatives from the central bank, the police, the MACC, the Securities Commission and other relevant agencies. “The task force will prepare a report within three months. This report will be a government report, and I have asked that the report be presented to the public,” Anwar told parliament in a question and answer session. Anwar’s assurance comes months after allegations emerged that individuals close to him and his party were linked to “corporate mafia” dealings. The controversy followed disclosures by prominent investor Victor Chin Boon Long, who accused former Anwar aide Farhash Wafa Salvador Rizal Mubarak of using enforcement agencies to force a boardroom takeover at IT firm NexG. NexG currently holds 2.5 billion ringgit (US$612.3 million) worth of contracts to supply passports and national identity cards to the government. Farhash denied the allegations, saying he had no knowledge of any campaign to take control of the company. Chin also alleged that he had paid 9.5 million ringgit to a lawmaker from Anwar’s People’s Justice Party, whom he identified only as “Mr R”, on the promise that the politician would help settle a problem with the “corporate mafia”. Human Resources Minister Ramanan Ramakrishnan later denied that he was the individual in question and challenged Chin to reveal the identity of “Mr R”. Anwar said at no point had his administration attempted to cover up any wrongdoing, even when it involved members of his own party. He pointed to the case of his former political secretary, Shamsul Iskandar Mohd Akin, who was charged last December for allegedly receiving some 240,000 ringgit in bribes. The prime minister added that the government had frozen or seized assets and shares worth around 5.3 billion ringgit and issued 1.1 billion ringgit in compound fines for offences related to corporate crime. The public release of the task force report would serve as further proof of his administration’s commitment to transparency, Anwar said. “This will show that there is no one that is protected. Be it Azam Baki, Farhash, Victor Chin … we will allow for full disclosure,” he said.

content: Filipino seafarer Jay was on lookout duty aboard a vessel passing through the Strait of Hormuz one evening in August when drones swarmed overhead, darting past his ship and two others it was following. Within seconds, an explosion rang out from a tanker ahead. “That was traumatic for me when I saw that the tanker ahead of our vessel had been hit,” said Jay, whose real name has been withheld to protect him from possible employer retribution. The 29-year-old and his fellow crew members made it through the strait unscathed, but the experience stayed with him. “We never talked about what happened; it was done. We would move on and proceed to the next voyage,” he said. For sailors like Jay, however, the danger does not end when a voyage is over. As conflict threatens the Strait of Hormuz and other maritime chokepoints in the Gulf region, these Filipino workers face a difficult choice: risk sailing through dangerous waters or refuse a voyage and potentially jeopardise their livelihoods. The Philippines is the world’s leading supplier of seafarers, with more than 468,000 Filipino seafarers deployed last year, according to data from the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW). In March 2024, DMW issued a memorandum setting out the right of Filipino seafarers to refuse to sail through high-risk areas, particularly the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and surrounding waters, following an increase in piracy, hijackings and armed attacks on civilian ships. Under the rules, Filipino seafarers who refused to sail through these areas are entitled to protections including repatriation help and two months’ basic wages. Recruitment and placement agencies also cannot bar them from future contracts or employment. The memorandum was issued after Houthi rebels attacked a commercial vessel in the Red Sea that month, killing two Filipino seafarers and injuring three others. Nearly 1,500 Filipino seafarers had exercised that right over the past three years, according to the DMW. In September, 10 Filipinos who refused to sail through the Strait of Hormuz returned safely to the Philippines. Since the Iran war began in February, five Filipinos had died and one remained missing, Secretary of Migrant Workers Hans Cacdac confirmed in September. Protection problem Manila generally assesses potential threats to overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) and issues corresponding alert levels, according to Arnold de Vera, director of the workers and employees programme at the University of the Philippines Law Centre. “The worst cases justify a ban on deployment and, for those already there, mandatory repatriation,” he said. However, much of their protection still depends on the recruitment agencies and foreign employers that hire them. “Our system of regulatory protection for OFWs relies heavily on the statutory provision imposing a solidary liability between the foreign employer and the local recruitment and placement agency. By making them solidarily liable, the local agency can be made to answer to the liabilities attributable to the foreign employer,” de Vera said. Many seafarers are also covered by collective bargaining agreements negotiated by unions and shipowners, which provide another layer of protection, according to de Vera. Implementation remains a challenge, though, particularly when disputes end up in litigation. The division of responsibility for worker safety can leave seafarers in situations where exercising their right to refuse becomes complicated. After Jay’s ship docked in Al Jubail, Saudi Arabia, he decided to exercise his right to refuse to sail, knowing that he would again have to transit the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, both designated high-risk areas. “I sent an email to my company informing them that I would exercise my right to refuse. I also emailed the DMW and other concerned groups,” he said. However, he and his fellow crew members were not allowed off the vessel. “It is very hard to be poor. My company said that it had filed for financial losses because its other ships had been attacked. We asked our company to increase our compensation if we would not be sent home but they failed to meet our demand … we continued to sail even after we exercised our right to refuse.” In September, the family of a Filipino seafarer killed aboard an oil tanker attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz said that he had not been informed in advance that the vessel would transit the strait. The DMW said that same month it was examining compliance with regulations. This Week in Asia also contacted the department for comment. Jay said his employer had failed to address the psychological toll of the experience, focusing instead on completing the voyage. “They don’t even care about the mental health of their crew that has experienced this trauma. What they told us is [there will be] no crew change and [to] deliver the cargo,” he added. He feared that his agency might not rehire him when his contract ended because his email to the DMW had included the name of his vessel and its route. Family obligations The prospect of losing future work was also a factor for Filipino seafarer Ronald Allan Ruiz, who transited the Strait of Hormuz despite the risks. “In the Red Sea, what we deal with is the pirates, the Somalis … the conflict between Iran and the US, and the nearby tensions, that is what changed things,” Ruiz said. He and his fellow Filipino crew members had agreed to the voyage because of their families’ financial needs back home. They were also offered incentives for transiting high-risk areas, he said. “Even though you have the right to refuse to sail, [the financial need] doesn’t go away for our colleagues either. Maybe the office won’t rehire you – because, of course, the company deals with a big business.” Although Ruiz felt his recruitment agency and employer had treated him fairly, he remained concerned about the uncertainty he might face if he returned home. “There’s also what we call ‘if the price is right’. So sometimes even when you’re afraid, you also think about your family,” he said. “If you go home, they might not rehire you right away, you could be without work for a long time.” Advocacy groups say escalating tensions have become a serious concern for seafarers and their families. “Every ship attacked puts more seafarers at risk. Their families send them off to work, not to face the deadly consequences of wars fought for the interests of powerful countries. How many more lives must be put in danger before our government takes a clear stand?” said Edwin Dela Cruz, president of the International Seafarers Action Centre. Yet for seafarers such as Ruiz, the need to provide for their families means the risks can be difficult to avoid. “Every Filipino here is here because of the job, because of the money. So [even if] deep down, we don’t want to sail through danger … sometimes people have a lot of financial obligations, or we just tell ourselves bahala na [come what may].”

title: Singapore, Hong Kong take different paths in race for stablecoin dominance. Who will win?
description: While Hong Kong is betting on its established banking network to bring stablecoins into mainstream finance, Singapore is seeking to make regulated digital currencies easier to use. content: While Hong Kong is betting on its established banking network to bring stablecoins into mainstream finance, Singapore is seeking to make regulated digital currencies easier to use. Both approaches reflect different priorities in the race to build global cryptocurrency centres: Hong Kong is linking stablecoins to its existing financial system, while Singapore is looking to strengthen the infrastructure for circulating and settling tokenised assets. Analysts said the ultimate test would be whether either regulatory framework could support practical, commercially viable uses. HSBC, one of Hong Kong’s largest banks, revealed the name of its stablecoin, RedCoin, last month. The Hong Kong dollar-pegged token is expected to launch in the second half of this year and be integrated into the bank’s mobile banking platforms. Ramkishen Rajan, an economics professor at the National University of Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, said both frameworks favoured cautious expansion. “One concrete difference concerns banks. Hong Kong has licensed HSBC itself, while Singapore proposes that banks issue MAS-regulated stablecoins through separately licensed non-bank entities,” he said, referring to the Monetary Authority of Singapore. Stablecoins are a type of cryptocurrency token designed to maintain a steady value by being pegged to a reference asset, typically a fiat currency such as the US dollar. They have become more prevalent as traders use them to hedge against major price swings and businesses adopt them for cross-border payments. In April last year, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority granted stablecoin issuer licences to HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial, a joint venture led by Standard Chartered, reflecting the territory’s stringent requirements and bank-centred financial ecosystem, observers said. MAS suggested legislative changes last month that would distinguish between regulated and non-regulated stablecoins, and introduce safeguards to protect customers. The proposed amendments to the Payment Services Act 2019, which establishes the regulatory framework for payment services and stablecoins in Singapore, would also allow multi-jurisdictional issuance and the recognition of a limited number of foreign stablecoins. As tokenisation gains traction, a framework with clear guardrails and high standards of value stability and governance is crucial, according to MAS deputy managing director Ho Hern Shin. “Trusted and well-regulated stablecoins can serve as a credible settlement asset in tokenised financial markets, while mitigating risks to users and the broader financial system,” she said. Competition among financial hubs had increasingly extended beyond traditional markets into digital and tokenised finance in recent years, said Tsang Cheng-Yun, an associate professor of law at Monash University, adding that both systems allowed the issuance of fiat-referenced stablecoins and emphasised financial stability. “The line between Hong Kong and Singapore is not sharp and is not mutually exclusive,” he said. “Nevertheless, their institutional contexts and emerging commercial priorities suggest somewhat different pathways to developing digital financial infrastructure.” Singapore’s proposed amendments could be interpreted as an effort to strengthen its position as a global hub for the circulation and settlement of digital assets, Tsang said. As Hong Kong stood to benefit from its established banking network and position as a gateway between mainland China and international markets, “its framework makes it easier to bring trusted settlement assets into the existing financial system”, he added. David Lam, an associate fellow with the regional economic studies programme at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, said Hong Kong had taken a more stringent approach, laying the foundation for channelling digital asset use towards appropriate applications. Its monetary authority does not allow retail investors to trade non-licensed stablecoins – such as Tether, a leading US dollar-backed token. Front runner? The different approaches do not necessarily make one hub a clear winner, observers say. Hong Kong appeared to be further along in putting its rules into practice with the licensing of HSBC and Anchorpoint, Rajan said, but “it is too early to judge either framework superior for growth”. Singapore’s proposal to recognise foreign-issued stablecoins had particular merit for cross-border businesses, provided all parties could cooperate effectively during a crisis, he added. Tsang cautioned against using quantities to gauge the success of either framework. “I would not judge either framework simply by the number of licences granted, the volume of stablecoins issued or the speed of market adoption,” he said. According to the experts, success in scaling stablecoins would ultimately depend on how regulatory credibility translated into commercial use – including whether businesses could make payments more cost-efficiently and reliably. Lam said risks such as speculation and illicit finance needed to be appropriately mitigated for stablecoins to be channelled towards productive uses, such as wholesale payments and tokenised real-world assets. Hong Kong, for example, restricts stablecoin transfers to verified blockchain accounts unless issuers can demonstrate that they can effectively prevent money laundering. While stringent requirements could bolster business confidence, costly compliance obligations could dampen competitiveness and make services uneconomic, Rajan said. “It’s a balancing act.” Regulators must also look beyond the activities and risks of individual issuers, according to Tsang. “In the end, I think financial centres will increasingly compete on who can build trusted, liquid and interoperable settlement infrastructure for the next generation of financial markets.”

title: Australian police charge man after attack on MP Helen Haines

content: Australian police said they charged a man on Tuesday for what they allege was a “targeted” attack on lawmaker and former midwife Helen Haines, who suffered critical injuries. Brendan Nugent, 43, was charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury, as well as the federal crime of harming a public official, Victoria police said. Nugent, from nearby Tarrawingee, was in custody and would face court on Wednesday, police said. National broadcaster ABC and The Sydney Morning Herald reported Haines had lost a leg. Nugent’s father released a statement on Tuesday describing Haines as a “deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community”. “Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” Rod Nugent said, adding that he would cooperate with police. Earlier, Australian barber Ricky Jefferies was hailed a hero ⁠for running out of ⁠his store to detain the suspect after the incident in the small town of Wangaratta. Jefferies had just finished haircuts for a family on Monday when he said he heard a “loud bang” outside his shop and realised the ‌driver of a Toyota LandCruiser had struck Haines, leaving her badly injured. “It was crazy, I just ran out the front to see what was happening,” he told reporters on Tuesday. He said he ran to assist the well-respected local MP, grabbing a knife from the alleged attacker’s pocket and pulling him out of the car. “He did have a knife. He didn’t pull it out. I just wasn’t comfortable with ⁠his movements, and so I basically just took it out of his pocket and threw it away,” he ‌said. Jefferies said he then held the man down until police arrived. “I just leaned over him and once he was on the ground and he was no longer a ‌threat, I just stood with him and I told him that he can’t leave,” he said. Independent politician Haines, ⁠65, was airlifted ⁠to hospital where she underwent surgery overnight. She remains in a critical condition. Early investigations suggested the driver performed ‌a U-turn before hitting Haines as she was loading or unloading things from the boot of her car, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. Counterterrorism ‌authorities were among ‌multiple agencies involved in the investigation. While police have given no motive for the alleged attack, the ‌involvement of counterterrorism investigators has raised alarm that it could have been an act of political violence, which is ⁠rare in Australia. Barber Jefferies, whose shop is next door to Haines’ electorate office around three hours’ drive northeast of ⁠Melbourne, described the former midwife as a “genuine, kind person”. Albanese praised Jefferies’ intervention, calling him a hero. “At this dark and terrible time, an element of light is the fact that a Good Samaritan, someone ‌rushed to Helen’s defence in Wangaratta, ‌put themselves potentially at risk by doing so. And that person is a hero today,” Albanese said in an interview with the Nine network’s Today show. Jefferies downplayed the praise. “I don’t think I’m a hero. I think that I just was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way,” he said. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Thailand, Cambodia seek to calm escalating dispute over US$300 billion seabed
description: Thailand and Cambodia have agreed to dial down the rhetoric and use a hotline between their navy commanders to avoid flashpoints over a vast contested patch of energy-rich seas in the Gulf of Thailand, according to a UN-backed mediation panel at The Hague tasked with helping to settle the dispute between the neighbours. content: Thailand and Cambodia have agreed to dial down the rhetoric and use a hotline between their navy commanders to avoid flashpoints over a vast contested patch of energy-rich seas in the Gulf of Thailand, according to a UN-backed mediation panel at The Hague tasked with helping to settle the dispute between the neighbours. The Southeast Asian countries have also squabbled for decades over the demarcation of their 800km (500-mile) land border, where clashes last year killed scores on both sides and froze cross-border trade worth billions of dollars. While an uneasy ceasefire agreed in December holds along the frontier, relations between Bangkok and Phnom Penh have plunged to a nadir, with both accusing the other of targeting civilians during the conflict and intermittent breaches of the truce. Amid the rancour, competing claims have escalated over the Gulf seabed which holds oil and gas reserves worth an estimated US$300 billion. Thailand scrapped a bilateral channel with Cambodia in May governing the claims to the waters. That triggered Cambodia’s request to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea’s conciliation commission, hosted in Singapore last month, to start the mediation process over control of the lucrative waters. A second round of talks at the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) was held last week at Peace Palace at The Hague over the claims to 27,000 sq km (10,400 square miles) wedge of sea. The PCA late on Monday said both sides showed good faith towards the peaceful resolution of the dispute and agreed to confidence-building measures as the process continued. Those included a commitment to approach “public statements on the maritime boundary and on their relationship with one another with a view to creating space for constructive engagement, rather than to generate pressure on the other party or foreclose options”. Equally, “both Parties will undertake to exercise restraint in public communications and statements that could contribute to negative public sentiment or heighten tension between the peoples of the two countries” and “guard against misinformation and disinformation that could undermine the conciliation”. It is a small but significant step forward in relations that have been dogged by mistrust since the vicious battle over the land border erupted last July. While the physical conflict has eased, a social media battle has raged between the public of both countries, with nationalist feuds flaring over everything from Thailand’s alleged encroachment onto Cambodia’s land to Cambodia’s apparent co-option of traditional Thai clothing claimed as its own. In addition, the PCA said the commanders of both nations’ navies will use a hotline set up “for the prompt notification and management of maritime incidents, so as to avoid misunderstandings and tensions that could have negative impacts on the conciliation proceedings”. During the PCA’s first meeting in Singapore in September, foreign ministers of both countries painted the other nation as the aggressor and a disingenuous negotiating partner, as they jostled for the moral – and legal – high ground in the talks, which are only the second time in Unclos’ history that the conciliation process has been used. The first, initiated by East Timor against Australia in 2016, took nearly two years to resolve. The five-member conciliation commission is chaired by Australian lawyer and diplomat Katrina Cooper. The process is not legally binding. After the second round of discussions, Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the confidence-building measures would act as “guidelines to foster an environment conducive to progressing discussions under the conciliation process”. “In moving forward, the Thai side hopes that both sides will advance these [the measures] in earnest,” the ministry added in a statement late on Monday. Cambodia’s foreign ministry echoed the sentiments, reaffirming “its full support for the conciliation process that it initiated”. “International law provides the pathway for peaceful resolution of disputes between States,” it said in a statement.

title: South Korea’s Seoul wants to put brakes on taxi overcharging
description: As South Korea seeks to attract more visitors to tap into the global popularity of K-pop, a lawmaker has warned that taxi overcharging of foreign tourists could tarnish the country’s image, with official figures pointing to a perceived lack of punishment against offenders.
