content: As South Korea seeks to attract more visitors to tap into the global popularity of K-pop, a lawmaker has warned that taxi overcharging of foreign tourists could tarnish the country’s image, with official figures pointing to a perceived lack of punishment against offenders. Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Mo Gyeong-jong cited Seoul city government data on Sunday showing only 204 of 6,481 complaints of taxi overcharging involving foreign tourists between 2021 and August this year resulted in administrative measures. Mo told reporters that a city scheme offering a reward to people whose overcharging complaints led to penalties against errant taxi drivers has yet to pay a single cent. The problem came under scrutiny in June when a Taiwanese tourist sparked an online controversy after alleging that he had been charged nearly 10 times the expected fare for a taxi ride from eastern Seoul to Incheon International Airport. After returning home, the tourist said on the social media platform Threads that the driver had charged him 690,800 won (US$520) for a trip initially estimated to cost 70,800 won. Posting a photograph of the receipt, he said: “At that price, it would be like travelling all the way from South Korea to North Korea.” He warned others against taking taxis in South Korea unless they were prepared to pay exorbitant fares. Officials at the Seoul Metropolitan Government told This Week in Asia that the tourist was subsequently refunded, but they declined to disclose the disciplinary measures imposed on the 79-year-old driver who ferried the tourist. The driver claimed he had accidentally entered an extra zero when manually processing the fare. In another case reported in June, an Australian tourist said a taxi driver demanded 75,000 won for a trip from the Busan Port International Passenger Terminal to a hotel in Yeongdo-gu. Deeming the fare excessive, the tourist got out and took another taxi, paying just 9,000 won for the journey. Last year, Seoul received 898 complaints from foreign tourists, a 67 per cent increase from the previous year, including 309 related to taxis, according to the city government. An official in Seoul, who declined to be named, said persistent complaints of taxi overcharging had prompted the city government to introduce tougher penalties, along with a public awareness campaign targeting foreign visitors. “Repeat offenders were suspended in the past following an initial warning for the first offence. But starting from last month, they will be suspended for up to 30 days for the very first offence and subject to tougher punishments if they repeat,” the official said. The city has also introduced a QR-code-based reporting channel, with cards distributed at Incheon and Gimpo international airports since June linking to surveys in English, Chinese and Japanese that allow tourists to report suspected overcharging, unmetered rides and refusals by taxi drivers to take passengers. Upon receiving such reports, officials cross-check submissions against vehicle records and fare details to establish whether a violation has occurred, while tourists can also call Seoul’s 120 helpline to lodge complaints. “Keeping the receipt or other material evidence is important to get refunded,” the official said. An official at the Seoul Taxi Association advised foreign visitors to check estimated fares using Naver Map, a popular navigation service in South Korea, to reduce the risk of overcharging. Passengers can also look for a notice attached inside the taxi displaying the driver’s name, vehicle registration number and a phone number for lodging complaints. However, questions remain over whether the city’s measures are leading to effective enforcement. Mo said 67.4 per cent of the 6,481 complaints received between 2021 and August this year had been closed without administrative action, citing official data. The most common reasons included complainants withdrawing their reports, mistaken complaints, failure to meet reporting requirements and investigators unable to establish that a violation had occurred. Kim Hyung-joon, an aide to the lawmaker, said: “Lawmaker Mo is especially concerned that overcharging of taxi fares for foreigners unfamiliar with standard fares would deal a blow to the country’s reputation as the home of K-pop.” The city’s award scheme over such cases has also failed to gain traction. Under an ordinance revised in 2013, Seoul can award 500,000 won to people whose complaints about taxi overcharging involving foreign tourists lead to administrative penalties. Foreign tourists who have been overcharged are also eligible if they file a complaint. No one has applied for or received a reward despite the 204 cases resulting in administrative measures between 2021 and August this year, according to the data. Under the rules, anonymous reports are ineligible, and applicants must provide their names, addresses and telephone numbers. Payments are made only after the period for appealing against a penalty has expired, and the application has been reviewed. However, the rules do not specify how short-term foreign visitors can apply for and receive rewards after leaving South Korea. Mo said the reward scheme was introduced with “good intentions”, but it had not taken off because foreign tourists were unaware of it. “Procedures must be put in place to protect both complainants and taxi drivers, so that the vast majority of drivers who work honestly are not unfairly viewed with suspicion,” he added.

title: Japan’s dilemma over frosty ties with Russia deepens after reporter’s arrest
description: The arrest of a Japanese journalist in Russia has finally woken Tokyo up to the fact that Moscow is playing hardball in their diplomatic relationship, and the country’s apparent unwillingness to push back with commensurate force could encourage the Kremlin to test its neighbour’s resolve, analysts say. Japan lodged an official protest with the Russian ambassador in Tokyo on Wednesday, a day after Moscow announced the arrest of Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun Press on suspicion of espionage....
content: The arrest of a Japanese journalist in Russia has finally woken Tokyo up to the fact that Moscow is playing hardball in their diplomatic relationship, and the country’s apparent unwillingness to push back with commensurate force could encourage the Kremlin to test its neighbour’s resolve, analysts say. Japan lodged an official protest with the Russian ambassador in Tokyo on Wednesday, a day after Moscow announced the arrest of Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun Press on suspicion of espionage. He was taken into custody in Russia’s far eastern Sakhalin region, with Moscow accusing him of obtaining details of mobilised Russian soldiers in the region. Russia has released footage of Imai’s arrest and his transfer to Lefortovo Prison in Moscow. An official of the Japanese embassy in Moscow has been refused access to speak with Imai. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has denied that the journalist was conducting espionage for Tokyo, a position echoed by his employer. The detention comes after a fraught few months in bilateral relations. In August, Russian President Vladimir Putin visited an island off the north of Japan, which was part of the disputed Kuril chain of islands seized by Soviet forces soon after Tokyo’s surrender in 1945. Tokyo still claims sovereignty over the four southernmost Kuril Islands, known as the Northern Territories in Japan. Japan was also incensed about the unveiling of a statue in the Russian city of Khabarovsk in September to mark the end of World War II. The statue depicts a Soviet soldier smashing an imperial-era border marker bearing the chrysanthemum motif of the Japanese monarchy. Russia has also stepped up air and naval operations off northern Japan, announcing that it would be carrying out live-fire air drills over the disputed island of Etorofu from October 13. It has also demanded that Tomoko Akane, the Japanese head judge of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, be handed over to Moscow because a Russian court had indicted her. James Brown, a professor of international relations specialising in Russian affairs at the Tokyo campus of Temple University, believes the schism in relations can be traced to the start of this year. “In the spring, Japan announced that it was going to contribute to the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List [PURL] to support Kyiv and also that it was sending Self-Defence Forces personnel to Nato headquarters in Wiesbaden,” Brown said. “Russia views Nato as its principal enemy and saw this as a provocative step by Japan,” he said. When Russia piled pressure on Japan with its subsequent moves, it was surprised by Tokyo’s inaction, Brown added. “Putin went to the disputed islands. There was the statue issue and the ICC issue. And now Russia has taken what is effectively a hostage. And what has Japan done in return? Nothing of note,” he said. “And if that is going to be Tokyo’s response, why would the Russians not continue with more similar steps?” Yakov Zinberg, a professor of international relations at Tokyo’s Kokushikan University who is originally from St Petersburg, said Moscow seized the Japanese journalist with the aim of a prisoner swap in mind. “Russia is in the habit of taking somebody to exchange for one of their people,” he said, pointing to the case of an alleged cyber hacker named Vladimir K, who was arrested in Japan in May for being a suspected member of the Qilin crime organisation and later handed over to authorities in Germany, where he was on a wanted list. “I think this Japanese journalist was in the wrong place at the wrong time and Russia needed someone for an exchange,” he said. Zinberg said Moscow had become more “frustrated” with Tokyo’s actions in recent months, including its support for European Nato members that were providing Kyiv with military equipment and intelligence. “But there is also an element of propaganda for a domestic audience in all this,” he added. “The economy in Russia is not good, the war has dragged on for many years, more and more men are being killed. Arresting a Japanese ‘spy’ and accusing Tokyo is designed to make [Russian] people think about something other than the bad news.” Zinberg said Moscow was likely monitoring public unrest in France and Italy over the rising cost of living and that Putin would hope to see similar unrest in Japan, he added. Yoichi Shimada, professor emeritus at Fukui Prefectural University, said Takaichi might have hoped to build a close working relationship with Putin, mirroring the ties between the Russian leader and the late former Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe when he was in office. Abe’s priorities then regarding Moscow were the return of the disputed islands and an increase in bilateral trade, particularly in energy, according to Shimada. “It was a sensible approach and would make very good economic and strategic sense for Russia and Japan to be allies and partners, although that is obviously impossible at the moment,” he said. “I think that Takaichi is still playing the long game and looking beyond the end of the war.” Brown noted that Japanese leaders before Takaichi took a tougher stance on Russia after it began invading Ukraine in February 2022. Soon after revelations about the massacre of Ukrainian soldiers and civilians in the city of Bucha came to light, then Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida expelled eight Russians whom Tokyo described as “embassy staff” but were likely intelligence officers. Tokyo has the options to effectively counter Moscow’s “bully tactics”, according to Brown. For instance, Japan could reduce its energy imports from Russia and seek alternative sources, increase sanctions against Moscow or express stronger support for Ukraine, Brown said. “And let’s not forget that there are plenty of real Russian spies in Tokyo at the moment, and there is no reason why Japan should not show them the door,” he said.

title: ‘Comrade Raul’: Beijing defends Cuba’s ex-leader over Florida murder warrant
description: China on Wednesday condemned an arrest warrant issued in the US state of Florida for former Cuban president Raul Castro over the 1996 downing of two civilian planes, accusing the United States of using the courts to pressure Havana. Foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning was asked about the warrant by the state-run Global Times at a regular briefing in Beijing. She referred to the 95-year-old as “comrade Raul Castro”, a “venerated” leader held in high international esteem. Mao said China opposed...
content: China on Wednesday condemned an arrest warrant issued in the US state of Florida for former Cuban president Raul Castro over the 1996 downing of two civilian planes, accusing the United States of using the courts to pressure Havana. Foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning was asked about the warrant by the state-run Global Times at a regular briefing in Beijing. She referred to the 95-year-old as “comrade Raul Castro”, a “venerated” leader held in high international esteem. Mao said China opposed the “abuse of judicial measures to pressure Cuba” and called on the US to “immediately stop its blockade and any other form of coercion and pressure against Cuba”. A state judge in Miami signed the no-bond warrant on Friday, charging Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced plans to issue the warrant on Monday. The charge relates to the February 1996 attack on two Cessna aircraft flown by Brothers to the Rescue, a Miami-based exile group that searched for Cuban migrants lost at sea. The incident killed all four men on board the civilian aircraft, including three US citizens and a US legal resident. The warrant is separate from a federal indictment unsealed in May. It charged Castro, Cuba’s defence minister at the time, and five former military officers with conspiracy to kill US nationals, destruction of aircraft and four counts of murder. Federal prosecutors allege that Cuban fighter jets fired air-to-air missiles at the two planes over international waters without warning. According to the indictment, Cuban agents who infiltrated the group passed details of its flights to Havana before the attack. Because the planes were downed outside US territory, Florida prosecutors built the state case on that espionage. The affidavit says Cuban spies transmitted flight data and monitored the naval station in Key West, which prosecutors argue is enough to establish that the conspiracy took place in Florida. “Raul Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy,” Uthmeier said in a statement. Uthmeier acknowledged that Castro was unlikely to travel to Miami. He said the charges would still restrict the former leader’s movements, since a trip to any country with a US extradition treaty could lead to his arrest. Cuban president calls warrant a ‘pathetic Miami circus’ Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel called the warrant a “pathetic Miami circus” with an electoral motive. Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez described it as a “sterile manoeuvre” by anti-Cuban politicians in South Florida. Havana has long maintained that Brothers to the Rescue, a Miami-based exile group, repeatedly violated Cuban airspace and that its forces acted in defence of national sovereignty. The announcement fell on the first day of early voting in Miami-Dade County for the US midterm elections. Uthmeier faces Democrat Jose Javier Rodriguez in the November race for lawyer general, and his rival said the charges were politically motivated. Beijing has pledged to do what it can for Cuba as a US oil blockade imposed in January, on top of the decades-old trade embargo, leaves the island short of fuel. The shortage has also disrupted Air China’s Beijing-Havana route, which has struggled since Cuban airports ran out of jet fuel in February. The Chinese embassy in Havana arranged an extra flight this week for passengers stranded by cancellations. The UN General Assembly is due to vote next week on Cuba’s annual resolution calling for an end to the US trade embargo. Last year it passed by 165 votes to seven, with China among those in favour.

title: China says it allowed Philippines to resupply warship amid diplomatic tensions
description: China has allowed the Philippines to resupply a grounded warship on a disputed South China Sea reef, the coastguard said on Wednesday, as tension remains high over the Chinese ambassador’s controversial comment. The Philippines delivered necessities to its warship BRP Sierra Madre grounded at the Second Thomas Shoal on Wednesday, “with permission from the Chinese side”, the China Coast Guard said in a statement. “The China Coast Guard conducted confirmation checks and maintained full supervision...
content: China has allowed the Philippines to resupply a grounded warship on a disputed South China Sea reef, the coastguard said on Wednesday, as tension remains high over the Chinese ambassador’s controversial comment. The Philippines delivered necessities to its warship BRP Sierra Madre grounded at the Second Thomas Shoal on Wednesday, “with permission from the Chinese side”, the China Coast Guard said in a statement. “The China Coast Guard conducted confirmation checks and maintained full supervision throughout the operation,” CCG spokesman Jiang Lue said, adding that China would continue to carry out rights-protection and law enforcement activities in the area. The Second Thomas Shoal, known as Ren’ai Jiao in China and Ayungin Shoal in the Philippines, is one of the major flashpoints in the South China Sea. Manila maintains a small military garrison aboard the BRP Sierra Madre, a rusted World War II-era ship it intentionally grounded in 1999 to bolster its claim, while Beijing frequently attempts to block Philippine resupply missions. This mission came amid heightened diplomatic tensions following controversial remarks by China’s ambassador to Manila, which Philippine officials interpreted as “conveyed a threat”. Ambassador Jing Quan told a forum last week that China could “easily win” a war between the two countries but instead chooses peace. “If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force and we love peace,” he said. Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro summoned him on Monday to express “serious concern and strong objections” over his “provocative and unacceptable” language. After the meeting, Jing denied he was making a threat, saying in a statement that he had been advocating for peace between the two countries. The tension between China and the Philippines over disputed South China Sea reefs has escalated in recent months, with multiple stand-offs and clashes reported at several hotspots. These include the use of water cannon in July and an interception involving a Chinese fighter jet and a Philippine aircraft in October both near Scarborough Shoal, a collision between two coastguard vessels in September near Sabina Shoal, and repeated incidents near the Second Thomas Shoal. On July 20, Chinese coastguard personnel allegedly struck a Philippine sailor repeatedly on the head with a wooden baton during a confrontation near Second Thomas Shoal, in one of the most serious recent clashes. Beijing blamed the Philippine side for aggressive manoeuvres and attacks on Chinese officers. The latest reported confrontation over the BRP Sierra Madre resupply mission occurred on September 24, with China’s coastguard saying it had warned and monitored Philippine vessels, while Manila accused Beijing of obstructing the mission and conducting dangerous manoeuvres. Earlier this month, the Philippines accused the China Coast Guard of using water cannons and tailing Philippine vessels during a medical evacuation mission near Second Thomas Shoal, delaying the evacuation of an ailing Filipino naval personnel stationed aboard BRP Sierra Madre for nearly 10 hours before the patient was eventually evacuated. China disputed the Philippine account, saying China had immediately allowed the medical evacuation on humanitarian grounds, permitting the transfer by small boat and providing necessary help while handling the operation in accordance with Chinese laws and regulations.

title: Top Democrat says chip restrictions are ‘key lever’ for US AI edge over China
description: Just two weeks before the US midterm elections, Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said he did not believe America would maintain its lead over China in frontier AI indefinitely, describing restrictions on advanced chips as Washington’s key leverage. “I don’t believe for one second that we’re going to maintain a lead over Chinese frontier models forever. But we should for as long as we can,” said Himes at a Brookings Institution event in Washington. “And the one...
content: Just two weeks before the US midterm elections, Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said he did not believe America would maintain its lead over China in frontier AI indefinitely, describing restrictions on advanced chips as Washington’s key leverage. “I don’t believe for one second that we’re going to maintain a lead over Chinese frontier models forever. But we should for as long as we can,” said Himes at a Brookings Institution event in Washington. “And the one real lever we have there, of course, is just slowing the dispersion of advanced chips into China.” Himes is a member of the “Gang of Eight”, a bipartisan group of congressional leaders briefed on classified national security matters. His comments come ahead of the midterm elections next month, with recent polls suggesting Democrats could regain control of Congress. A Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Monday found Democrats lead Republicans 47 per cent to 35 per cent on the “generic ballot”, which asks participants the party they would vote for if the congressional elections were held today. Himes was speaking at the event titled “AI on the ballot: Data centres and the 2026 midterms”, which examined local opposition to data centres and global expansion of AI infrastructure. A panel of experts at Wednesday’s event also discussed how chip constraints could shape the ongoing AI race between the US and China. Whether China can produce enough chips to meet domestic AI demand and also compete abroad remains the “big question”, said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “In the near term, we are not competing with China for building AI data centres abroad,” he said. “China is constrained by their chips, by their own chip production capacity.” In the medium to long term, however, he sees several Chinese companies gearing up for broader global expansion, including offering cloud and AI services abroad. If China’s chip production ramps up, Chan said, Chinese firms could be poised to offer “package deals with the models, the hardware, maybe even the energy to go along with that, in a kind of repeat, in some ways, of the Belt and Road Initiative, China’s plan to grow global trade, but for AI”. The two countries face different challenges: the US has an energy bottleneck, and China a chip bottleneck, according to Chan. “In the US it’s always about connecting to the grid, getting new power to power all these data centres and these chips. In China, they complain constantly about not having enough compute, not having enough chips themselves,” he said. “What’s interesting is for China, they do see compute as part of their national infrastructure, and they’ve been working hard to kind of build out their data centre capacity.” Elsewhere in the conversation, Himes addressed allegations that foreign adversaries were amplifying opposition to data centres in the US. Data centres have become increasingly contentious in the US, with communities weighing up whether they want such facilities built in their backyards. “There’s a tonne of allegations out there that the Chinese and two or three other people are putting out lots of inflammatory stuff about data centres,” he said, while conceding he did not know if this was true. Among those attributing community pushback against data centres to foreign influence from China is US President Donald Trump. “A big part of it is China,” Trump told Fox News in August.

title: US colleges scale back cooperation with Chinese institutions after Pentagon’s push
description: Virginia Tech is accelerating the closure of a joint undergraduate programme with China’s Xidian University, bringing forward the end of a partnership that it had previously planned to keep running until 2029, according to a university spokesperson and a copy of an official letter reviewed by the South China Morning Post. This decision comes as the Pentagon’s push to tighten oversight of US universities’ research ties with China has led to more than 80 termination-related actions across 30...
content: Virginia Tech is accelerating the closure of a joint undergraduate programme with China’s Xidian University, bringing forward the end of a partnership that it had previously planned to keep running until 2029, according to a university spokesperson and a copy of an official letter reviewed by the South China Morning Post. This decision comes as the Pentagon’s push to tighten oversight of US universities’ research ties with China has led to more than 80 termination-related actions across 30 American colleges, with some schools scaling back academic partnerships with Chinese institutions. Margaret Ashburn, Virginia Tech’s associate director of media relations and deputy spokesperson, shared a copy of the school’s letter to the Pentagon and told SCMP that the university had recently decided to accelerate the closure of the joint programme with Xidian University. “The programme noted in the letter will officially terminate after the current academic year,” she said. In the letter, the school said it had previously decided in 2025 to wind down the programme and stopped admitting new students, but enrolled students could continue until 2029. It remains unclear how the accelerated shutdown will affect students currently enrolled in the programme. SCMP has contacted Xidian University for comment but has not received a response. To address security concerns before the complete shutdown, the letter also said Virginia Tech had introduced significant mitigation measures for the programme, including research security briefings before and after travel for faculty members visiting Xidian University. Additionally, addressing another flagged relationship, Virginia Tech clarified that recent joint publications with Shandong University – added to the US blacklist in July 2026 – stemmed from earlier work, noting that active collaboration had already been discontinued in 2019. The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Beijing has consistently opposed the restrictions. Liu Chang, a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy, previously accused the US of overstretching the concept of national security and politicising academic exchanges. Liu said scientific research required openness, that restricting normal exchanges would also harm American researchers and institutions, and urged Washington to abandon its “Cold War mentality” and ensure a fair and open environment. Pentagon’s audit In August, the US Department of Defence ordered 30 universities to audit their foreign research ties, including partnerships with Chinese institutions on its blacklist, or risk losing federal funding. The blacklist, formally known as the Section 1286 list, contains 130 foreign organisations, mostly Chinese but also Russian and Iranian, that Washington deems national security risks. Many leading Chinese civilian universities, including Fudan University, are on the Section 1286 list. The August announcement did not name the universities, but media reports citing a US official said the 30 included some of the country’s most prestigious institutions, such as Harvard, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Cornell University. The Pentagon announced on Monday that the 30 universities had completed initial audits of their foreign research ties and addressed relationships flagged as potential security risks. It also named seven universities for their swift actions in compliance with the audit: Oklahoma State University, Pennsylvania State University, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, the University of South Carolina, the University of Southern California, the University of Texas at Austin and Virginia Tech. The department did not provide further details about the termination-related actions. Emil Michael, undersecretary of defence for research and engineering, said institutions that failed to meet research security standards were on notice and would not receive taxpayer funding if their partnerships endangered US troops or the country’s technological edge. “Our work will continue,” Michael said. “The department commends the institutions that took decisive action to mitigate relationships that could expose American research to foreign exploitation.” There has been pushback elsewhere, too. According to The Washington Post, a Pentagon official asked Southern Illinois University Carbondale this summer to audit its ties with nine Chinese entities. The university initially saw no need to cut ties but later ended an agreement with Shenyang Aerospace University, which had recently been added to the blacklist, at the department’s insistence. Drake University in Iowa said in September that the government had raised concerns about its joint degree programme with Qingdao University, which Drake said was not on the list. The audits are not the end of the effort. The department said it would continue working with Congress, including the armed services and appropriations committees in both chambers, as well as the House Select Committee on China.

title: Taiwan’s Iran-style attack drone could swamp PLA air defences: analysts
description: A flight-tested attack drone similar to Iran’s Shahed model that its Taiwanese maker says could reach military targets in mainland China is meant to swamp PLA air defences, analysts said. Drawing on battlefield lessons from Ukraine and the Middle East, military experts broadly agree on the utility of such low-cost systems, but differ on how the drone could be deployed in a conflict with Beijing should it enter service. While some see greater value in targeting People’s Liberation Army forces in...
content: A flight-tested attack drone similar to Iran’s Shahed model that its Taiwanese maker says could reach military targets in mainland China is meant to swamp PLA air defences, analysts said. Drawing on battlefield lessons from Ukraine and the Middle East, military experts broadly agree on the utility of such low-cost systems, but differ on how the drone could be deployed in a conflict with Beijing should it enter service. While some see greater value in targeting People’s Liberation Army forces in the event of a landing on Taiwan, others point to strikes against airfields and ports on the mainland. The weapon at the centre of the debate is Thunder Tiger’s Papa Delta PD-136, which the company showcased at the Association of the United States Army defence exhibition in Washington earlier this month as it sought international defence-industry partners. Visually, the PD-136 adopts a familiar strategic silhouette: its delta-wing airframe and rear-mounted propeller closely resemble Iran’s Shahed-136, a munition drone extensively deployed by Russia in Ukraine. The design also mirrors the US Low-cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System (Lucas) – itself developed by reverse-engineering a Shahed-136 obtained by the United States, according to a Pentagon official cited by ABC News. Notwithstanding the design similarities, the PD-136 would carry a smaller payload than the Shahed-136, which the Centre for Strategic and International Studies estimates at 20-50kg (about 44-110lbs). Thunder Tiger says the attack drone is designed to carry a 10-15kg payload over a distance of more than 300km (186 miles), potentially putting areas of Fujian province on the Chinese mainland within reach, with defence outlet Army Recognition reporting a range target of about 500km. Powered by a proprietary 250cc two-stroke engine, the PD-136 completed a catapult launch and flight test in Yunlin county in Taiwan on October 2. The advertised range has not been publicly demonstrated. Major technical details remain undisclosed, including the drone’s guidance system, resistance to electronic warfare and operational warhead specifications. More significantly, Taiwan’s military has yet to announce an order for the PD-136. Despite these uncertainties, Taipei’s interest in attritable strike platforms reflects lessons from recent conflicts. “Taiwan has very likely taken lessons from the Russia-Ukraine war and the US war with Iran, both of which have shown the importance of drones,” said Timothy Heath, founder of defence consultancy Perceptum. However, the PD-136’s slow speed could make it vulnerable to interception when targeting mainland Chinese radars and sensors, Heath said, adding that the drone might be more useful against PLA troops and equipment after they had landed on Taiwan, where mainland Chinese forces would have less time to react. That assessment aligns with Taiwan’s broader military priorities. In an April briefing to lawmakers, the island’s defence ministry outlined plans to acquire more than 210,000 drones, focusing on autonomous navigation, coordinated operations and systems intended to strike enemy landing forces, armoured units and transport vehicles. The PD-136 could support such a high-volume approach if produced cheaply. Built around a simple piston engine and a stamped-aluminium airframe, the drone is intended for low-cost mass production, though Thunder Tiger has not disclosed a unit price. Both experts said low-cost drone attacks could force defenders to spend heavily on interception. According to Peter Layton, a visiting fellow at the Griffith Asia Institute in Australia, massed attacks would almost certainly combine weapons like the PD-136 with other drones as well as cruise and ballistic missiles. “The principal concept is to launch very large numbers and overwhelm the air defences,” said Layton, who is also affiliated with the Royal United Services Institute. “Most of the drones will be shot down, but in so doing use up many expensive air-to-air missiles and surface-to-air missiles.” Heath echoed that assessment, noting that low unit costs could allow Taiwan to invert the attrition ratio in a conflict with Beijing. “The drones are far cheaper than cruise or ballistic missiles yet can be highly effective,” he said. “This could be a way for Taiwan to put the cost ratio in its favour in a war with Beijing.” While both analysts saw advantages in launching inexpensive drones in large numbers, they differed over the best targets. Heath said that attacking PLA forces after a landing on Taiwan would be more effective, while Layton pointed to airfields and ports on the mainland, arguing that large numbers could compensate for their “mediocre accuracy”. However, Layton cautioned that such drones would be “ineffective against hardened targets such as buried facilities, hardened aircraft shelters or runways”. Beijing has already trained against massed drone attacks. In January, state broadcaster CCTV showed a PLA Navy unit using shipborne missiles and other defence systems against simulated swarms of suicide drones. Nevertheless, Layton suggested, Beijing might need additional countermeasures, including radar-controlled 30mm anti-aircraft guns and low-cost interceptor drones similar to those deployed in Ukraine. He said the PLA would be “very effective against individual drones” but warned that, when launched in large numbers, “some will get through”. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Is China a Russia-allied Arctic threat to Europe or a potential polar partner?
description: Europe should work with Beijing to develop shipping through the Arctic rather than trying to advance its transatlantic security alliance by framing China as a threat linked to Russia. That was the assessment of Chinese analysts following the release of the European Union’s Arctic policy on Tuesday. In addition to identifying Russia as its main threat, the policy warns of Beijing’s growing strategic ambitions in the European Arctic through its deepening alignment with Moscow. “With our new...
content: Europe should work with Beijing to develop shipping through the Arctic rather than trying to advance its transatlantic security alliance by framing China as a threat linked to Russia. That was the assessment of Chinese analysts following the release of the European Union’s Arctic policy on Tuesday. In addition to identifying Russia as its main threat, the policy warns of Beijing’s growing strategic ambitions in the European Arctic through its deepening alignment with Moscow. “With our new strategy, we are investing in stronger security, resilient infrastructure and economic opportunities,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said. While the policy document does not detail the scope of Beijing’s ambitions, cooperation between China and Russia in the region centres on polar navigation. China launched its first regular container shipping service through the polar zone in August, as conflicts in the Middle East added to the appeal of shipping in the region. Northern Arctic routes can cut transport times between Asia and Europe and are becoming more viable as climate change makes the area passable throughout the year. Wang Yong, director of the Centre for International Political Economy at Peking University, said Brussels should be more constructive and less defensive about the benefits for Europe of a shorter passage to and from Asia. “Europe has done far too little to pioneer Arctic shipping routes and European enterprises should instead partner with China to jointly develop these corridors,” Wang said. Although several major European shipping lines have publicly ruled out Arctic transit on environmental and safety grounds, the EU’s new policy signals an interest in their long-term potential – Brussels plans to produce a strategic foresight study on Arctic shipping, but discussion would be with “like-minded partners”. The blueprint maintains support for scientific collaboration and environmental coordination in the Arctic, but Wang warned that the shift towards security reinforcement was concerning and detrimental to healthy global governance. Xu Guangmiao, associate professor and deputy director of the Centre for Russian Studies at East China Normal University in Shanghai, had similar concerns. She said China’s activities in the Arctic region were modest, yet the idea of “Sino-Russian militarisation of the Arctic” still dominated policy discussions. “If we conflate perception with reality, we risk oversecuritising areas where cooperation remains possible, and we may ultimately undermine the very stability that all parties claim to seek,” Xu said. She noted that Brussels’ effort to bundle China and Russia into a joint threat was mainly a bid to reinforce Nato’s operational relevance and solidify the EU’s link with the United States. This concern is reflected in the EU’s proposed “Pan-Arctic cable” project, a subsea fibre-optic network designed to link Greenland directly to Europe, with planned extensions to Canada and Japan. The plan highlights Brussels’ growing anxiety about how relations among China, Russia and the United States will evolve. Europe feared that its interests could be sidelined and Russia’s advanced by major-power coordination on a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire, Xu noted. By anchoring critical subsea infrastructure alongside Canada and Japan, the EU aimed to rally those countries with similar security pressures, she said. In its updated strategy, the EU anchors this approach as “Northern Neighbourhood”, calling for closer cooperation among member states, Arctic partners and other allies, including the US and Nato. The EU continued to list the US among the key neighbours it needed to work with, noting that the two sides had “long-standing cooperation in the Arctic”. Emphasising its commitment to transatlantic engagement, the policy added that the agreement signed between Greenland, Denmark, and the US – which expanded Washington’s military footprint on the Arctic island – “strengthens [the] common security in the Arctic”. However, Wang warned that Brussels was clinging to a legacy mindset of relying on Nato and Washington for Arctic security – hopes that could fall short given US President Donald Trump’s recalibration of US strategy towards Europe and closer ties with Russia.

title: China’s offshore tax crackdown could inadvertently fuel a digital dollar boom
description: From October 22, China’s grace period for the disclosure and settlement of certain offshore-trust tax liabilities ends. For the Chinese government, this deadline highlights its desire to affirm control over capital outflows, while for Chinese high-net-worth families, it serves as a reminder that it is now harder to keep international assets beyond the reach of the government. The deadline sits against the backdrop of China tightening scrutiny around cryptocurrency, stablecoins and real-world...
content: From October 22, China’s grace period for the disclosure and settlement of certain offshore-trust tax liabilities ends. For the Chinese government, this deadline highlights its desire to affirm control over capital outflows, while for Chinese high-net-worth families, it serves as a reminder that it is now harder to keep international assets beyond the reach of the government. The deadline sits against the backdrop of China tightening scrutiny around cryptocurrency, stablecoins and real-world asset tokenisation. The authorities have reaffirmed that all cryptocurrency-related activities remain illegal, while also imposing strict limits on yuan-pegged stablecoins both within and outside the country and on tokenised-asset activity outside approved financial infrastructure. Furthermore, on September 28, China’s Ministry of State Security warned that virtual currencies can be used for criminal purposes, calling digital assets a “haven” for hackers and spies, and “accomplices” to espionage. An interesting contradiction is unfolding: the Chinese government’s efforts to restrict some private paths to global finance are making offshore diversification, and subsequently dollar-linked digital assets, more appealing due to their portability. Digital assets have been a key tool for wealthy Chinese looking to preserve their capital independently of government regulations. The government’s firm stance on the illegality of cryptocurrency means those caught engaging in digital asset transactions face severe penalties, putting themselves at risk of prosecution and their assets at risk of seizure. Earlier this year, in June, a court in Shanghai jailed five people for up to six years each for facilitating over US$29 million in illegal cross-border transactions using cryptocurrency. They were marketing their services to wealthy Chinese looking to diversify their international holdings. Despite the risk of enforcement, demand for financial flexibility remains among wealthy Chinese. China’s crackdown on offshore-trust tax liabilities actually highlights the system’s weaknesses, particularly that of a governance model built around controlling where capital is held and how it moves. While it is obviously not the government’s intention to accelerate capital flight, an unintended consequence of its tax crackdown could be to make the portability of digital assets more attractive to those determined to diversify their holdings, particularly the extremely wealthy. China’s desire to internationalise the yuan is well known. The government has developed alternative infrastructure to reduce its reliance on the US dollar. There is the digital yuan, which plays an increasing role in domestic transactions and in limited cross-border pilots. And there is the Cross-border Interbank Payment System, China’s own financial market infrastructure designed to clear and settle yuan-denominated cross-border transactions. Institutions like China Development Bank and Export-Import Bank of China also play a significant role. As these government-backed organisations encourage development financing and infrastructure investment, they promote yuan internationalisation. Projects such as the Belt and Road Initiative develop this effort, with yuan-denominated financing and investment being offered to countries to reduce reliance on the US dollar while also strengthening China’s integration into global financial networks. As partner countries become more connected to China, they gain incentives to adopt the yuan in trade, reserves and financial transactions. This enhances China’s capital flow globally and boosts the country’s reputation as a premier source of development and investment funds. However, the tension between Chinese government’s restrictions and high-net-worth individuals’ demand for flexibility could have lasting consequences beyond China’s borders, potentially entrenching the dollar’s internationalised role. For one, dollar-pegged stablecoins offer a digital means of holding and transferring dollar-denominated value. About 99 per cent of stablecoins globally are dollar-denominated. This makes them attractive to individuals seeking access to global markets without relying exclusively on conventional banking channels. Furthermore, tokenised financial assets denominated in dollars could broaden access to investment and settlement networks, while still being subject to custody, identity, tax and securities regulations. If Chinese restrictions increase the perceived value of financial portability, they could indirectly sustain demand for dollar-linked instruments, even as Beijing seeks to limit their use. This is ironic, particularly for a government intent on preserving monetary sovereignty and reducing vulnerabilities to foreign financial influence. Hong Kong serves as the principal gateway for Chinese wealth moving to international markets, with the Boston Consulting Group noting that Hong Kong manages roughly US$2.9 trillion in offshore wealth, with this being primarily driven by mainland capital outflows. Countries like Singapore, Japan and South Korea have also benefited indirectly from Chinese capital outflows. China’s deadline for offshore-trust tax liabilities points to a broader contest between the government’s desire to preserve control over private wealth and the growing ability of digital financial networks to move value across borders. While the Chinese government has legitimate reasons to guard against illicit transactions and capital flight, it is these very restrictions that could encourage high-net-worth investors to see offshore access as essential to protecting their assets. This results in an interesting paradox, with the Chinese government seeking to consolidate financial sovereignty while indirectly reinforcing the appeal of dollar-linked alternatives.

title: Chinese mathematician Sun Zhiwei proposes 1,000 problems to challenge AI
description: In an age of AI-induced answers to complex mathematical problems, Chinese mathematician Sun Zhiwei maintains that curiosity and asking good questions are more important then ever. Over a career spent probing the edges of number theory, Sun, a 61-year-old professor at Nanjing University’s department of mathematics, has built a vast landscape of problems – more than 1,000 and counting – for the global research community to tackle. While traditional mathematical training emphasises mastering...
content: In an age of AI-induced answers to complex mathematical problems, Chinese mathematician Sun Zhiwei maintains that curiosity and asking good questions are more important then ever. Over a career spent probing the edges of number theory, Sun, a 61-year-old professor at Nanjing University’s department of mathematics, has built a vast landscape of problems – more than 1,000 and counting – for the global research community to tackle. While traditional mathematical training emphasises mastering existing formulas and proving established theorems, Sun said true progress relied on using intuition to discover new questions and using logic to solve them. “If a discipline has no conjectures, people no longer know what to do and the field approaches a standstill,” Sun told China Science Daily. “[Artificial intelligence] cannot solve every mathematical problem. Mathematicians need not panic. Instead, they can free up time to focus on tasks where AI falls short, such as developing new methods and establishing new theories. “I view AI as a highly knowledgeable, diligent and intelligent graduate student. When setting it to tackle difficult mathematical problems, I provide appropriate guidance and, when necessary, prompt it to adjust its strategy,” he said, adding that he would cut off the AI’s internet search access so it could not discover that the problem remained unsolved and refuse to work on it. Sun said that, in his early career, he was a traditional problem solver and made key advancements on Hilbert’s Tenth Problem posed in 1900. But a 2005 visiting professorship at the University of California, Irvine, marked a turning point when he met an American professor who was adept at using mathematical software to uncover patterns, a technique that was new to Sun at the time. After helping the professor resolve a conjecture that had remained unsolved for years, Sun said he realised mathematical tools were undergoing a qualitative leap forward. In 2009, he started to teach himself how to use the Mathematica program for technical computing. Using computers enabled him to validate thousands of cases, a task that previously demanded painstaking and often unfeasible manual calculations. “From that year on, I suddenly had an epiphany and all sorts of whimsical ideas started coming to me,” Sun recalled. This year, Sun compiled a collection of problems more than 400 pages long, containing 1,000 unsolved conjectures that he had proposed. His academic homepage also features a collection of conjectures paired with cash prizes for their proofs, funded using his salary. Many of his problems push beyond classical milestones. For example, Sun introduced new constraints to French mathematician Lagrange’s two-century-old four-square theorem, which states that every natural number can be expressed as the sum of four integer squares, to formulate new conjectures. “We simply state that a given theorem is ‘beautiful’, and once the proof is complete, we consider the matter closed. We never discuss whether the theorem is strong enough or it has limitations,” Sun said. “Textbooks often only talk about greatness, not flaws.” As AI reshapes scientific discovery, Sun said the role of AI should be welcomed in advancing mathematics in the pursuit of truth. “If you pursue mathematics solely for fame and fortune, you might worry about AI taking your job, but if your goal is the pursuit of truth, you should welcome the way AI advances the field,” he said. He said he dubbed some of his most difficult problems “alien conjectures” – problems that he said “Earthlings definitely cannot solve.” When asked about the point of proposing unsolvable problems, Sun said: “My motive is not whether you can solve it or not, I am just pursuing the truth. As for whether modern tools are enough, that is another matter.”

title: Beijing’s top Taiwan official meets US think tank to reaffirm red lines
description: The director of Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO), Song Tao, has held a rare meeting with a delegation of US scholars, pledging to push for the peaceful development of cross-strait ties. During the meeting in Beijing on Tuesday with a delegation from the National Committee on American Foreign Policy (NCAFP) led by its president and CEO, Susan Elliott, Song spoke of a broader diplomatic context following summit meetings between Chinese and US leadership. “President Xi Jinping elaborated on...
content: The director of Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO), Song Tao, has held a rare meeting with a delegation of US scholars, pledging to push for the peaceful development of cross-strait ties. During the meeting in Beijing on Tuesday with a delegation from the National Committee on American Foreign Policy (NCAFP) led by its president and CEO, Susan Elliott, Song spoke of a broader diplomatic context following summit meetings between Chinese and US leadership. “President Xi Jinping elaborated on China’s principled stance on the Taiwan question during his recent summit with the US leadership, emphasising that China firmly safeguards national sovereignty and territorial integrity,” Song said, according to a TAO statement. “We urge the US side to adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’ and handle the Taiwan question with utmost prudence.” Song said Beijing would continue expanding economic and cultural exchanges across the Taiwan Strait to deepen integrated development while “resolutely” countering foreign interference and separatist activities. In response, Elliott cited a critical need to maintain robust communication channels during volatile global conditions. “Maintaining close communication between the United States and China is of vital importance, and cross-strait exchanges and integrated development contribute to peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait,” she was quoted as saying on behalf of the delegation. “The [committee] will continue, as always, to play a bridging role in promoting the peaceful development of cross-strait relations and contributing to constructive strategic stability between the US and China.” Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Taiwan has been a focal point during recent presidential summits and high-level working channels. In these exchanges, Beijing reiterated its red lines regarding Taiwan, while Washington highlighted the importance of peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait alongside ongoing bilateral security cooperation. The meeting on Tuesday continues a Track 1.5 diplomatic engagement model used in recent years. However, it is not common for the TAO – Beijing’s main official agency on its policies towards Taiwan – to engage with US groups. Between 2008 and 2015, former TAO directors Wang Yi and Zhang Zhijun regularly conducted official working trips to Washington and New York to meet White House and Department of State officials. Following an escalating trade war in US-China dynamics during Liu Jieyi’s tenure (2017-2022) – friction that was compounded by pandemic-era travel disruptions – direct TAO trips to the US were largely paused. In their place, Beijing-hosted meetings with influential non-governmental institutions such as the NCAFP have become the main conduit for Chinese policy architects to communicate strategic red lines directly to American foreign policy circles following major bilateral summits. In 2024, Song hosted Elliott and the NCAFP delegation in Beijing shortly after the Apec summit in Lima – where Xi met then US president Joe Biden – to clarify strategic baselines following head-of-state meetings.

title: China’s Type 051C gets a refit as the PLA Navy’s legacy warships near retirement
description: China’s Type 051C destroyer Shenyang has been spotted undergoing sea trials after a reported refit, as the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) begins phasing out legacy warships following the commissioning of a massive wave of new vessels. Witness photographs circulating on social media appear to show the Shenyang, hull number 115 and lead ship of the Type 051C class, with its Russian-made hardware replaced by domestic air defence systems. While precise details have yet to be independently confirmed,...
content: China’s Type 051C destroyer Shenyang has been spotted undergoing sea trials after a reported refit, as the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) begins phasing out legacy warships following the commissioning of a massive wave of new vessels. Witness photographs circulating on social media appear to show the Shenyang, hull number 115 and lead ship of the Type 051C class, with its Russian-made hardware replaced by domestic air defence systems. While precise details have yet to be independently confirmed, the apparent changes raise questions about the future operational role of the Type 051C class, which once served as an important component of China’s regional air defence capabilities. The Shenyang’s Russian 30N6E1 Tomb Stone phased-array radar and six 8-cell S-300FM long-range air defence missile vertical launch systems (VLS) reportedly have been removed in favour of four HQ-10 short-range systems, similar to those on smaller Type 054A frigates. Such a reconfiguration would represent a substantial downgrade to the ship’s air defence capabilities, reducing both its ready-to-fire missile load and engagement range. The Russian interceptors are capable of handling six targets simultaneously, over a maximum range of around 150km (93 miles). The substitute HQ-10 is a point-defence platform with a range of around 9-15km. While the apparent reduction in capability has surprised many military observers, the class’s inherent design disadvantages, combined with an estimated remaining service life of just 10 years, probably make comprehensive modernisation economically unviable. The PLA Navy commissioned two Type 051C destroyers – Shenyang and its sister ship Shijiazhuang – in 2006 and 2007, respectively, to serve as an interim long-range air defence solution, particularly in the waters off northern China. They were built around the Russian-designed naval variant of the S-300 air defence system – including the 30N6E1 radar and the revolver-type VLS launchers for 48 surface-to-air missiles. China’s indigenous shipborne phased-array radar and advanced air defence systems have since matured and the 7,000-tonne Type 051C’s legacy foreign equipment can no longer be easily integrated into the navy’s modern data links and fleet air-defence architecture. The large Russian missile-launching system occupied too much deck space, forcing the Type 051C designers to omit a conventional helicopter hangar, significantly limiting its aviation support and anti-submarine warfare capabilities. The steam-turbine propulsion system is less efficient than the gas-turbine or combined diesel-and-gas systems on most modern destroyers, with slower start-up times and higher fuel consumption. Sustaining the ship’s imported radars, launchers and missiles is also likely to have become increasingly difficult because of Russia’s strained supply chains and stockpiles. Meanwhile, China’s world-leading shipbuilding capacity has enabled it to rapidly expand its fleet of modern destroyers and frigates, securing its position as the world’s largest navy by number of vessels. The surge in construction has meant that the Chinese navy has enough advanced assets to make it possible to phase out some of its legacy ships. In August, the PLA Navy formally decommissioned the Type 052 destroyer Harbin, hull number 112, which entered service in 1994. Despite representing another major landmark in China’s domestic development of modern surface combatants, the Harbin’s relatively small 4,800-tonne hull, lack of a VLS and outdated armaments severely limited room for meaningful modernisation. In retirement, the Harbin has been designated for use as a national defence education site. Its sister ship, the Qingdao, hull number 113, commissioned in 1996, is also approaching the end of its service career. Chinese naval commentators have suggested the names and hull numbers of the Harbin and the Qingdao are likely to be reassigned to the latest batch of Type 055 destroyers, the PLA Navy’s largest and most powerful surface combatants.

title: Can China turn national power into world leadership?
description: As turbulence grows in many countries, it is tempting to ask if there is a global hegemon that can sort everything out fairly. US President Donald Trump has threatened that his country would not defend Nato allies if they failed to spend enough on their defence. Together with new trade barriers, his words suggest that the US is scaling back its ambitions for global leadership and concentrating more on its own region. Our latest projections of national strength for 2027 take into account...
content: As turbulence grows in many countries, it is tempting to ask if there is a global hegemon that can sort everything out fairly. US President Donald Trump has threatened that his country would not defend Nato allies if they failed to spend enough on their defence. Together with new trade barriers, his words suggest that the US is scaling back its ambitions for global leadership and concentrating more on its own region. Our latest projections of national strength for 2027 take into account resources, territory, economic strength and military power. They still put China in first place, with its lead over other countries widening. But when might China move beyond leading the ranking to exert decisive influence over the world’s trouble spots and become a global arbiter? To explore that question, we should first look at how states have assessed national power. Ancient rulers counted people, revenues, troops, ships and resources but these were separate assessments, not a single measure of national power. A more systematic approach emerged in the late 17th century. Economist William Petty’s political arithmetic compared England with France and Holland through territory, population, trade, shipping, public revenue and the ability to support armed forces. It was an early attempt to assess a country’s strength by considering several factors together. Today, computing power and better tools for analysing data make it possible to assess many dimensions of national strength across countries at once. A national strength index is like a state’s dashboard. One gauge shows the fuel level, another the speed, a third the condition of the engine. A driver needs the whole panel: each gauge tells only part of the story. Gross domestic product shows the size of an economy, while defence spending shows how much a country devotes to its armed forces. Overall strength also depends on territory, resources, population and science, and on how these assets work together. Among the 193 countries in our index, China ranks first, the US second and Russia third. China’s lead rests mainly on the scale of its economy and industrial production. Its large domestic market, workforce, infrastructure and extensive supply chains provide a strong base. They help China develop its scientific and technological capacity, strengthen its armed forces and increase its influence on the world economy. Our calculations show a gradual decline in America’s relative strength and share of the global economy. Structural imbalances, slower growth and rising debt pressures are part of the picture. The US pays more than US$1 trillion in interest on federal debt every year. The components of our index reflect how a state works. Each has its role, but also supports the others. In our assessment for 2027, the economy carries the most weight, followed by the armed forces. The economy is the military’s material base. Defence spending becomes real power through factories, design centres, testing grounds, repair facilities, transport, energy supplies and skilled workers. In a long confrontation, the ability to produce weapons and ammunition at scale, repair equipment and raise output quickly becomes crucial. Economic capacity thus shows the depth of a country’s reserves and its ability to sustain a military effort. Large defence orders can also support the economy. Long-term contracts give factories steady work and a reason to invest in equipment. Mass production creates demand for metals, chemicals, electronics, machine tools, transport and software. Training builds engineering skills, while research can produce technologies with civilian uses. New plants and infrastructure can expand a country’s productive capacity for years to come. Military spending trends show that major powers see defence capacity as a long-term priority. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, global military expenditure has risen significantly. The three biggest spenders, the US, China and Russia, accounted for about US$1.48 trillion, or 51 per cent of the world total. Their concentration at the top broadly matches our national strength ranking, although the order and gaps differ. Military spending matters, but overall strength rests on all the components. Europe saw particularly rapid growth: military spending reached US$864 billion last year, up by 14 per cent. Germany increased spending by 24 per cent to US$114 billion, while Spain raised it by 50 per cent to US$40.2 billion. But military protection is only part of the picture. It is one response to the fragmentation of the global economy into macro-regions, a trend noted by many international organisations. Fragmentation may be only the first stage of this change. The next could be “fractalisation”, a process in which large regional economies reproduce some of the functions of the former global system within their own networks. They connect markets and build supply chains, transport routes, payment systems, technology platforms and standards. They continue to trade with the wider world, while making sure essential functions can keep working if particular external links fail. Chinese President Xi Jinping’s proposals last month for a Brics special economic zone, a digital platform and closer industrial cooperation may be early signs of this process. Our calculations for 2027 put China first in national strength. But a ranking cannot tell us whether other countries will accept its leadership. That depends on whether the links China offers work beyond its closest partners, and whether others find them reliable and beneficial. If stronger regional systems begin to connect more closely, they could lay the foundations for a new phase of globalisation. Only then will we see whether China can play a leading role in shaping the next world order.

title: Strongest storm of the year barrels towards Taiwan and mainland China

content: As Super Typhoon Champi – now the strongest storm of the year worldwide – barrels towards eastern China, authorities are planning evacuations and urging those in its path to prepare. Airports in major Chinese cities could be affected by the storm, including Wenzhou Longwan, Fuzhou Changle, Ningbo Lishe, Hangzhou Xiaoshan, Shanghai Hongqiao, Shanghai Pudong and Xiamen Gaoqi, according to aviation data platform VariFlight. Travellers are bracing for potential disruptions, though there have been no large-scale delays or cancellations announced yet. Champi is expected to make landfall along the eastern coast of Taiwan around Saturday as a strong typhoon, according to China’s National Meteorological Centre. It could then pass through the island and make a second landfall in the mainland province of Fujian with diminished force as a severe tropical storm or typhoon. Alternatively, it may turn northeastward over the waters northeast of Taiwan while gradually weakening. Super Typhoon Champi has become the world’s strongest storm of the year in terms of wind speed. As of 8am on Wednesday it was packing winds of up to 245km/h (152 mph) near its centre. Moving at a speed of 20km/h, the storm is currently approaching waters to the east of Taiwan. The national forecaster has maintained a blue typhoon warning for Champi, the lowest level in China’s four-tier system. While its path is uncertain, Champi is expected to bring heavy rains and strong winds across China’s southeastern seas and the coastal provinces of Zhejiang and Fujian, as well as Shanghai, the country’s economic powerhouse. Emergency authorities have urged the public to stay alert to real-time updates, prepare their home defences and make sure outdoor structures are secured, and to avoid mountain and river valley areas that could be prone to landslides and flash floods. Authorities in Zhejiang started their typhoon emergency response at 8am on Wednesday, according to Chinese media reports. The province plans to evacuate vulnerable residents in the path of the super typhoon including the elderly, sick, disabled and pregnant women. Meanwhile it is preparing to suspend group outdoor activities, classes, work, business operations and public transport if needed. Zhejiang authorities are also conducting inspections for hazards along drainage channels, and are set to evacuate workers from fish farms and offshore construction sites, while coastal tourist attractions are being shut down. As of 8am on Wednesday, 36 passenger ferry routes had been suspended and 223 marine construction projects halted in Zhejiang. In neighbouring Fujian province to the south, all fishing vessels have been ordered to seek shelter in nearby ports by Wednesday, with crew members to return to shore by Thursday.

title: Terracotta warriors were mainly built by women and children, batch fingerprints show
