Now, a new study shows that a portion of the terracotta warriors was largely made by adult women and minors, not solely by men as previously...
content: Some 5 metres (16.4 feet) underground near one of China’s oldest cities lies the life-size army of thousands of terracotta warriors. The purpose of the army, located 35km (22 miles) northeast of historic Xian, was to protect China’s first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, in the afterlife. The Terracotta Army was buried with him after his death in 210BC. Now, a new study shows that a portion of the terracotta warriors was largely made by adult women and minors, not solely by men as previously thought. “These findings challenge the long-held assumption that Terracotta Army production relied exclusively on adult male labour, providing the first quantitative biological evidence for a diverse workforce including women and children,” Shen Jingyi wrote in the paper published on October 13 in the peer-reviewed Journal of Cultural Heritage. Shen, the corresponding author of the paper, is an associate professor at the school of archaeology at Shandong University. The researchers’ model estimates that men accounted for about 45 per cent of the total fingerprints, women for nearly 32.7 per cent and the remaining 22.3 per cent came from children under 15 years old – the legal threshold for adulthood under Qin dynasty law. Previously, archaeologists believed that large-scale handicraft production during the Qin dynasty (221-207BC) was undertaken only by adult males. However, there was a lack of direct evidence regarding the creators of the Terracotta Army. State broadcaster CCTV reported last year that, using modern scientific instruments, researchers at the Emperor Qin Shi Huang’s Mausoleum Site Museum had found over 100 fingerprints on more than 40 unearthed terracotta warrior figurines. While it was the first time minors’ fingerprints were discovered, it was still believed that the artisans’ fingerprints were mostly those of adult males. Shen’s team took a different approach. She analysed 79 well-preserved fingerprints found on 36 terracotta warriors in Unit T23 of Pit 1 of the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor. To distinguish between males and females, researchers used a Bayesian mixture model, which could analyse an entire group of fingerprints at once, rather than attempting to classify each trace. The researchers also compared ancient fingerprints with modern fingerprint data of different ages and sexes. Each ceramic warrior bore between one and five distinct fingerprints. They were distributed across the figures – the head, arms, armour, hands, collar and even the feet – apparently left unintentionally during production. Of these, 73 fingerprints were left during the shaping, moulding and assembly processes, and six were formed when pre-made decorations, such as armour rivets and belts, were pressed onto the surface of the terracotta figures. Scientists photographed the fingerprints and measured the mean ridge breadth, which increases with age. Artefacts unearthed in other regions and legal documents such as Qin dynasty bamboo slips also support Shen’s viewpoint. Anthony Barbieri-Low, a professor of Chinese history at the University of California, Santa Barbara, wrote the book Artisans in Early Imperial China in 2007, which provides a detailed account of the artisan groups of that era. During the Qin dynasty, lacquerware inscriptions were unearthed, including da nvzi (adult woman), xiao nvzi (young woman) and xiao nanzi (young man), indicating that women and children took part in craft production under state supervision. According to the book, xiao nanzi is a male under 1.5 metres (4.9 feet) tall. Xiao nvzi is a female who is no taller than 1.43 metres. Xiao nvzi could not sign her name on handicrafts like da nvzi, and could do only simple or subservient work. The findings of Shen’s team suggest this batch of pottery figures may have been made by female and underage artisans, although it may not reflect the distribution of artisans among all terracotta warriors. “Unit T23 represents only a localised area of Pit 1, so the results may reflect the labour structure of a specific phase or production group rather than the entire project,” Shen wrote at the end of the paper. However, this archaeological evidence and research suggest that the Terracotta Army may have been made by a greater number of female and underage artisans than traditionally assumed. The terracotta figures have lain underground with Emperor Qin Shi Huang for more than 2,200 years. In 1974, they were discovered by several villagers while digging a well, and later became known to the world.

title: China builds the world’s smallest wearable brain monitor with a cortex-wide view
description: Chinese scientists have developed what they say is the world’s smallest wearable mini brain monitor that can track the activity of thousands of neurons at the same time. Weighing in at one gram (0.35 oz), the wireless “Airscope” is the lightest device of its kind and enables researchers to track a wider range of brain activity in untethered laboratory animals. The device was jointly developed by scientists from Tsinghua University and the Chinese PLA Medical School, and detailed in a paper...
content: Chinese scientists have developed what they say is the world’s smallest wearable mini brain monitor that can track the activity of thousands of neurons at the same time. Weighing in at one gram (0.35 oz), the wireless “Airscope” is the lightest device of its kind and enables researchers to track a wider range of brain activity in untethered laboratory animals. The device was jointly developed by scientists from Tsinghua University and the Chinese PLA Medical School, and detailed in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature on Monday. “This microscope will push optical brain-computer interfaces towards more precise neural detection,” said Dai Qionghai, the paper’s corresponding author from Tsinghua’s automation department. In a social media post by Tsinghua University on Tuesday, Dai noted that the technology’s potential extended far beyond brain research. “In the future, its application is expected to expand from neuroscience to fields such as immunology and oncology, enabling the complete tracking of the disease development process,” he was quoted as saying. The Airscope is a mesoscope, a high-end optical instrument designed to observe biological tissues, such as cortical neural activity, at an “intermediate” level. It plugs the gap between a microscope and a macroscope, enabling researchers to observe cell activity over a wide field of view. For years, scientists have sought to clearly observe how brain neurons regulate complex behaviours during natural, group interactions – a crucial step in understanding the nature of intelligence. To do this, they must track a relatively large area of animal tissue while still distinguishing the activity of individual cells. Previously, devices that could do this required animals to have their heads fixed in place or be tethered by cables. And, devices small enough to allow free movement typically had a restricted field of view, often less than 1mm (0.04 inches). Dai’s team shrank the volume of their device by nearly five orders of magnitude compared to conventional benchtop microscopes, with “comparable” quality of recorded neural signals. They also used a two-megapixel image sensor that compresses data, enabling the wireless transmission of megapixel-grade images. The whole project meant optimising optical, illumination, electronic and wireless transmission systems. The team used artificial intelligence to design the lenses and developed a computer vision model that can identify and continuously track individual subjects from video footage, preventing target loss or confusion. Using the Airscope, the team studied neural signal changes across various mouse behaviours. The team fitted their devices to mice and allowed them to roam a custom-built micro-habitat featuring ramps, tree holes and shelters. The mice were able to burrow and climb freely because the entire set-up was light enough not to interfere with the mice’s natural behaviour. While the animals explored their surroundings, researchers used the ultra-lightweight headset to record the activity of more than 8,500 individual neurons in a single mouse’s cerebral cortex, all at one time. Their findings include identifying how cortical activity patterns in dorsal brain regions influence an animal’s social competitive advantage. The team hopes to use this technology to further investigate the neural mechanisms underlying social behaviour and emotional states, potentially providing vital clues for research into conditions such as depression. According to the Tsinghua article, Dai’s team has been researching mesoscopic imaging technology since 2013. In 2024, Dai’s team from Tsinghua announced the development of a super intravital microscope that could clearly image the entire three-dimensional interactions of a large network of cells. The microscope – called the RUSH3D system – features subcellular resolution over a field of view that is centimetres-wide. It is capable of high-speed 3D imaging at 20 frames per second, allowing for many hours of continuous observation. The development, published in the journal Cell in mid-September of that year, was listed as one of China’s biggest science advances of 2024.

title: Taiwan admits paying for retired US general to observe largest annual war games
description: Taiwan’s defence ministry has confirmed for the first time that it has allocated funding for the US Indo-Pacific Command to send a retired general and other personnel to observe the island’s largest annual war games. The disclosure sheds rare official light on military exchanges that Taipei and Washington have traditionally kept out of public view, as security cooperation between the two sides deepens amid growing pressure from Beijing. According to a defence ministry report submitted to the...
content: Taiwan’s defence ministry has confirmed for the first time that it has allocated funding for the US Indo-Pacific Command to send a retired general and other personnel to observe the island’s largest annual war games. The disclosure sheds rare official light on military exchanges that Taipei and Washington have traditionally kept out of public view, as security cooperation between the two sides deepens amid growing pressure from Beijing. According to a defence ministry report submitted to the legislature last week, NT$82.4 million (US$2.5 million) has been allocated for a programme covering the Han Kuang exercises in 2026 and 2027, including NT$41.219 million this year. The Annual Assessment by Senior Observers and Exchanges programme pays for a retired American general to serve as a senior observer during the exercises, as well as a delegation of military professionals and civilian personnel organised by the US Indo-Pacific Command. The American observers assessed the drills according to their training objectives and gave recommendations on improving the Taiwanese military’s joint operational capabilities, the ministry said. Their findings are incorporated into the final Han Kuang exercise report and used as a reference for the military’s force development and combat preparations. The details were disclosed after opposition Kuomintang lawmaker Ma Wen-chun questioned the programme’s implementation, the seniority of personnel being sent to Taiwan and its expected benefits. Lawmakers froze NT$1 million of the funding and required the ministry to submit a written explanation before it could be released. Reports of American military personnel observing Han Kuang are not new, but the defence ministry has previously avoided confirming details of their participation. During the 41st Han Kuang exercise last year, local media reported that retired US Army four-star general Robert B. Abrams, a former commander of US Forces Korea, had served as a senior observer and adviser to Taiwan’s chief of the general staff, Admiral Mei Chia-shu. The ministry declined at the time to comment on individual cases. According to Max Lo, executive director of the Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, a Taipei-based think tank, the significance of the latest disclosure lay less in Taipei paying for the programme than in its acknowledgement that retired senior American officers were involved. “There have long been reports that the US sends personnel to Taiwan to observe the Han Kuang exercises, but the defence ministry has always declined to comment,” Lo said. “This is the first time the defence ministry has confirmed that senior US observers participate in Han Kuang.” Lo said the acknowledgement suggested that Taipei and Washington were becoming less reluctant to disclose sensitive military exchanges that would previously have been kept under wraps. “This is mainly because Taiwan-US relations have become increasingly close while tensions across the Taiwan Strait have also risen,” he added. “By making these military exchanges public, they can send a message to mainland China that the United States remains firmly supportive of Taiwan.” Lo said Beijing had previously lodged strong protests over such military exchanges, but its reactions recently appeared less forceful. “[US President Donald] Trump has repeatedly said that Xi Jinping would not attack Taiwan while he is in office,” Lo continued, referring to the Chinese president. “This could mean that the two leaders have reached some degree of understanding about the possibility of conflict in the Taiwan Strait.” He suggested this might be an additional factor behind Trump’s repeated delays in approving US$14 billion worth of arms sales to Taiwan. Lo said a greater willingness by Taipei and Washington over the past two years to disclose such exchanges could be intended to test Beijing’s reaction. “If mainland China does not react strongly, Taiwan and the US could move towards deeper military exchanges, ultimately testing where Beijing’s bottom line lies,” he added. According to Chieh Chung, a research fellow at the Association of Strategic Foresight, the American observers also served an important practical purpose. “Taiwan has increasingly adopted US recommendations in areas including military training, modernisation of its ‘kill chain’ and special operations, making direct observation necessary for Washington to determine whether its advice is producing the intended results,” he said. The visits allowed the US side to identify the strengths and shortcomings of its recommendations and military exchanges with Taiwan, as well as make subsequent adjustments, Chieh added. One particular focus was assessing the results of American help in training Taiwanese instructors, he said, especially in reserve mobilisation and training. Taiwanese officials have acknowledged increasingly close military cooperation with Washington while remaining reluctant to disclose operational details. Defence Minister Wellington Koo Li-hsiung said in August that Taiwan was drawing on US combat experience to improve its forces’ operational capabilities. Asked about the presence of US personnel – sometimes euphemistically referred to in Taiwan as “American English teachers” – Koo said those visible to the public represented only part of the exchanges. The latest disclosure comes amid signs that other previously discreet areas of Taiwan-US defence cooperation are becoming more visible. Earlier reports said the Pentagon was preparing to station representatives from its policy office and experts from the non-profit Institute for Defence Analyses inside Taiwan’s defence ministry under a separate NT$470 million cooperation programme. Analysts said such moves could serve both operational and strategic purposes: allowing Washington to more directly assess Taiwan’s military preparations while signalling US security commitments in the Indo-Pacific to Beijing and American allies. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Burnham’s Britain can learn from Trump in engaging with China
description: Getting relations with China right is widely seen as Britain’s epoch-defining challenge. It is also one it is woefully unprepared to face. content: Getting relations with China right is widely seen as Britain’s epoch-defining challenge. It is also one it is woefully unprepared to face. So concluded a recent audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC), which highlighted that top negotiators lacked basic Chinese language skills. More critically, it exposed a deeper deficit: a poor grasp of China spanning political elites and the public alike. This is rooted in a desk-bound classroom sinology rather than a nuanced appreciation and lived immersion. Yet IPAC’s audit will do little to fix this deficit. Indeed, its ideological framing will deepen it. The report depicts China as a neo-totalitarian state seeking to engineer the souls of its citizens. It alleges that this coercive ambition extends globally, that Beijing seeks to upend the liberal world order to usher in an era favourable to authoritarian imperialism. Relations are thus framed as an ideological clash – Beijing an existential threat to the British way of life; every micro-engagement shadowed by a suspicion that Chinese interlocutors are party-programmed actors. Such hyperbole reads like a direct lift from political theorist Hannah Arendt’s study of totalitarianism, poisoning perceptions long before genuine engagement can occur. Nevertheless, while IPAC’s audit fails to illuminate modern China, it gives insight into contemporary Britain. While China is drawn as a totalitarian threat, Britain is cast as the defender of liberal values – the primary role it has claimed to project relevance in its post-imperial era. As the former US secretary of state Dean Acheson observed, Britain lost an empire and failed to find a subsequent role. To compensate, London continually re-enacts the script of its 1940s “finest hour”, framing antagonists from Gamal Abdel Nasser, Saddam Hussein, Slobodan Milosevic and Vladimir Putin as Hitler returned. Opposing authoritarianism thus becomes less about effective statecraft than about proving Britain’s relevance. IPAC’s audit is simply another exercise in post-imperial reflex, with China framed as the next existential threat Britain must resist. Tellingly, IPAC co-founder and co-chair, Iain Duncan Smith, has claimed that compared to Nazi Germany, “China is even worse”. If Britain is to successfully engage with Beijing, it must disentangle itself from this ideological script. Lessons here can be drawn from US President Donald Trump. Upon taking office, Trump discarded American exceptionalism, the century-old ideology morally compelling Washington to spread liberal capitalism while overcoming evil authoritarian dictators. In its place, he adopted a transactional “business-minded” framework in which international rivals are not existential threats to be vanquished, but counterparties to strike a bargain with. While critics dismissed Trump’s summit last month with Chinese President Xi Jinping as more pageantry than substance, the meeting established functional channels of collaboration and dialogue on the economy and, notably, artificial intelligence. Pageantry in statecraft should also not be so quickly dismissed. Western media bemusedly noted that, while labelling his domestic enemies “communists”, Trump flew the five-star flag from the roof above the Oval Office. Internationally, such symbolism carries immense weight. Beijing has long resented Western states adopting postures of moral superiority that frame China as an untrustworthy state characterised by Oriental despotism. This resentment reached a peak during the Covid-19 pandemic, especially in relation to the United States and Britain. A high-level reception treats China like a peer power rather than an immoral adversary and threat, a prerequisite for sustained, constructive diplomacy. Tellingly, Chinese state media welcomed the US gesture, with the Global Times praising the “unusually warm reception” as a foundation for a new historical starting point. Since taking power in 2024, Britain’s Labour government has similarly gravitated towards a more pragmatic stance – despite former prime minister Keir Starmer’s tendency to entrap himself in the role of a liberal vanguard. The pivot crystallised last year through visits to China by both the chancellor of the exchequer and the chief of defence staff to establish functional dialogue on shared economic and security interests. This trend is likely to continue under Andy Burnham’s much-expected pragmatism: a prime minister likely to be more focused on ensuring buses run on time than lecturing the world on liberal values. This shift has resonated in Beijing. State media praised Burnham’s “Manchesterism” – interpreted as a turn away from Westminster orthodoxies to address the pragmatic economic concerns of working class and regional Britain – as a solid foundation for bilateral relations. Manchesterism is especially appealing due to the established connections between Manchester and China, Wuhan in particular being a sister city, which Burnham maintained and developed during the worst lulls in UK-China relations. While calling Burnham to congratulate his ascendancy to the prime ministerial office, Xi stressed this narrative, stating his belief that the two men could rise above their different political systems to embrace greater commonalities and shared concerns. Again, Manchester was raised as a linchpin of relations, the conversation recalling Xi’s trip to the city in 2015. Here lies the profound irony in the IPAC report: an audit calling for “China literacy” whose own ideological posturing blinds it to the reality it seeks to understand. It exposes a British world view trapped between classroom sinology and the geopolitical textbooks of the 1940s. The world has moved beyond such ideological impasses; Trump’s business-minded stance pioneers a transactional approach that does not reduce Beijing to the totalitarian other. Britain would benefit from a similar pragmaticism disentangled from ideology. Burnham is ideally placed to deliver this. His Manchesterism offers a road map for bilateral relations based on tangible pragmatic engagements grounded not in a clash of civilisations but a history of connectivity and mutual encounters.

title: Brazil’s family farming backbone embraces Chinese AI to reverse vital sector’s decline
description: The family farmers who produce the lion’s share of Brazil’s staple foods are opening their arms to cutting-edge Chinese artificial intelligence in a bid to modernise operations and secure their future. Brazil and China agreed to a five-year cooperation programme in September aimed at giving smallholders – the backbone of the Brazilian agricultural sector – an AI boost after a decade of declining employment and limited access to affordable technology. Representatives of the Brazilian Agricultural...
content: The family farmers who produce the lion’s share of Brazil’s staple foods are opening their arms to cutting-edge Chinese artificial intelligence in a bid to modernise operations and secure their future. Brazil and China agreed to a five-year cooperation programme in September aimed at giving smallholders – the backbone of the Brazilian agricultural sector – an AI boost after a decade of declining employment and limited access to affordable technology. Representatives of the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation (Embrapa) and four Chinese institutions signed the memorandum of understanding in Nanjing, capital of Jiangsu province. The Chinese parties were the state-owned Sinomach Digital Technology Corporation, Nanjing Agricultural University, the Jiangsu Academy of Agricultural Sciences and the International Association for People’s Cooperation. The agreement includes the establishment of the Brazil-China Cooperation Centre for the Application of AI in Agriculture, aimed at strengthening this key sector of the Brazilian economy by developing new technologies and tools. “The idea is to combine complementary skills from both countries … to develop and adapt technologies to Brazilian production, social, and environmental conditions,” said Luciana Romani, a researcher at Embrapa Digital Agriculture. According to Romani, these complementary skills include “agronomic knowledge, artificial intelligence, computer vision, automation and smart agricultural machinery”. The World Bank has reported that family farming accounts for around 77 per cent of Brazil’s five million rural establishments, producing 87 per cent of the country’s cassava and 70 per cent of its beans – a foundational and essential staple of the Brazilian diet. Family farms are also responsible for 60 per cent of Brazil’s milk, half of its poultry and 34 per cent of its rice. In its 2017 census of agriculture, the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) found that family farms employed around 10.1 million people – 67 per cent of the agricultural workforce and around 5 per cent of the total population. Cristhiane Amancio, general head of Embrapa Agrobiology, said “an important milestone is expanding access to digital technologies that reduce arduous labour in the production of healthy and sustainable food. That is an important step to help keep workers in rural areas as well.” Under the agreement, Smart Agricultural Machinery Centres will be established in pilot family farming areas of Brazil where small and medium-sized machines, sensors, Internet of Things devices and AI will support crop monitoring and management. “The technologies integrated into agricultural machinery have evolved significantly in recent years and are being adopted in Brazil,” said Jayme Barbedo, another researcher at Embrapa Digital Agriculture. However, he noted that in many cases “those machines are too expensive or have dimensions that do not suit the conditions found in family farming”. According to Romani, China and Brazil will work together “to identify needs, develop technology and validate artificial intelligence solutions and other digital technologies aimed at family farming”. However, the Chinese technologies identified as offering potential applications in Brazil were developed for specific agricultural conditions and must be proven, tested and adapted to Brazil’s diverse production systems and local environments, she said. Amancio added that Sinomach in particular “has an integrated platform that supports decision-making at different management levels, adding value for both farmers and managers within associations, cooperative unions or in the public sector”. Romani also highlighted the expertise of the Brazilian research team in artificial intelligence, computer vision and automation, which will be essential to testing and adapting the technologies to local conditions in Brazil. The initial phase is expected to include an assessment of equipment and systems already being tested at the Brazil-China Centre of the University of Brasilia, alongside technical exchanges with Chinese researchers. Romani said potential applications included “artificial intelligence-based systems for pest and disease diagnosis, crop monitoring, decision-making support, more efficient use of inputs and natural resources, as well as the integration of those tools with smart agricultural machinery and equipment”. The history and tradition of China in developing technologies for smallholders and medium-scale farmers, together with its advances in automation and robotics, were an important factor in choosing Chinese partners for the project, she said. “This knowledge complements what has been developed in Brazil and fits very well with the current needs of smallholders and midscale farmers.” The researchers said the cooperation was intended to go beyond technology transfer, establishing a continuing process of joint development, adaptation, validation and knowledge exchange to deliver practical solutions for family farming. According to Barbedo, the use of AI does not represent a new model of farming. Instead, it will “play a central role as a tool to support decision-making, automation and the adaptation of technologies to real family farming conditions”. By combining data from sensors, machines and other digital tools, these technologies could be used to interpret, identify patterns, optimise resources, support the diagnosis of agricultural problems and improve the use of inputs and natural resources, he said. “Artificial intelligence should not be seen as an end in itself, nor as a substitute for agronomic knowledge and the experience of farmers, but as a technology that can expand such capabilities.” According to Barbedo, the project will focus mainly on adapting existing AI models rather than developing new ones. The researchers will need to account for Brazil’s diverse production systems, crops, environmental conditions and producer profiles. “Consistent data collection, adjustment, testing and validation efforts will be essential, ensuring that each developed solution is reliable and suitable for real-world use,” he said. Romani added: “The project aims to transform advances in AI and automation into concrete, affordable and reliable tools with the potential to increase efficiency, reduce costs, improve sustainability and expand the management capacity of smallholders and midscale farmers.” The project will also need to consider how to make these technologies affordable. “One possible approach is the involvement of farmers’ associations and cooperative unions to allow for quicker adoption,” Barbedo said. Silvia Massruha, Embrapa president, said that “if we don’t digitally include smallholders and midscale farmers in family agriculture, the gap between them and large-scale farmers will grow”. Family farming in Brazil declined by 9.5 per cent between 2006 and 2017, according to the IBGE, while employment in the sector decreased by around 2.2 million people. Over the same period, employment in non-family farming increased by around 703,000. Embrapa Agrobiology’s Amancio highlighted the importance of South-South scientific and technological cooperation in strengthening national capabilities and autonomy as well as supporting economic and social development. The cooperation is also expected to include scientific and technical exchange, training and capacity-building activities, such as giving Chinese scientists the opportunity to learn more about the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation’s experience, while gaining a better understanding of the sociocultural conditions of family farming. “Raising awareness of the importance of investing in science and technology to promote national development is fundamental so that partnerships like this one can increasingly qualify Brazilian scientists and strengthen both the national industrial and agricultural sectors,” Amancio said. title: China close to matching US spending on ‘new way of war’, Republican senator warns
description: The United States is lulling itself into a “sense of false security” over its military rivalry with China, according to a Republican senator who called for more spending on modern warfare systems and closer cooperation with allies. Speaking at the Hudson Institute after a recent trip to Japan and South Korea, Dave McCormick, a Pennsylvania senator and West Point graduate, claimed up to 90 per cent of US defence spending funded decades-old equipment and technologies. “We convince ourselves; we...
content: The United States is lulling itself into a “sense of false security” over its military rivalry with China, according to a Republican senator who called for more spending on modern warfare systems and closer cooperation with allies. Speaking at the Hudson Institute after a recent trip to Japan and South Korea, Dave McCormick, a Pennsylvania senator and West Point graduate, claimed up to 90 per cent of US defence spending funded decades-old equipment and technologies. “We convince ourselves; we lull ourselves into a sense of false security,” he said. Although China’s total defence budget was significantly lower than the US one, McCormick said China’s spending “on the new way of war … is much more comparable”. McCormick gave drone production as an example, saying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told him, “10,000 drones a day are manufactured in Ukraine”. “I don’t think we manufacture more than 100,000 drones a year in America,” he added. The senator told the conservative think tank: “Cheap drones and autonomous systems are decisive battlefield technologies, and China dominates the world’s drone supply chain today.” “If you’re shooting down US$10,000 drones with US$4 million Patriots, that’s not sustainable in the long run,” he added. He also said AI-related energy projects were the single most critical national security issue facing the US Congress, adding that while the US took five to six years to permit energy projects needed to power AI compute, China completes the process in under six months. In a conversation with Mike Gallagher, a fellow at the think tank, McCormick said the US needed to work with allies such as South Korea and Japan to outcompete China in hi-tech fields. “Japan and Korea are world leaders in robotics, batteries and chips, and for that reason, we need to work hand in hand with them on our joint national security objectives,” McCormick said. “We have to stand with our allies on training and planning, and fighting as one military force, one military capability.” McCormick said his home state was already benefiting from investments from US allies, citing the South Korean shipbuilder Hanwha’s US$5 billion investment in the Philly Shipyard with a target of building 15 to 20 ships a year. Meanwhile, Japan’s Nippon Steel will invest US$14 billion in US Steel to fund Pennsylvania’s first new mill in 50 years. South Korea has also pledged US$25 billion in US military equipment purchases. But recent media reports have cast doubt on the viability of Hanwha’s investment in Philadelphia, with The Chosun Daily citing high labour costs, limited production capacity and questions about the ability to attract new clients. “There is a huge gap between the announced investment amount, actual production expansion, and profitability,” The Chosun Daily report said. McCormick also argued that Washington must abandon old assumptions that trade would liberalise China. He called for the revocation of China’s Permanent Normal Trade Relations status, which was granted in 2000 and allows the two countries to align their trade relationship with World Trade Organization rules. McCormick cautioned that winning the strategic contest with China required not only external military and economic strength, but also national values – an area where he believes America is currently faltering. The senator made claims that America’s young people are now turning to socialism over capitalism, citing a recent Gallup poll. Released in September, it found that among those aged 18 to 34, 57 per cent view socialism positively, compared to 43 per cent who view capitalism positively. “Beijing’s glad to help using fake American voices to turn Americans against their own country and the principles that have made America America. So we have to make the case for freedom again, for liberty again with confidence, starting here at home,” he said.

title: Will Xi, Trump, Putin meet at Apec? First, they must agree on an agenda
description: While US President Donald Trump has said he is open to sitting down with Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at the Apec summit, it remains far from certain that the three leaders will actually meet in a few weeks. Observers said much would depend on whether the countries could agree on an agenda, with one expert describing this as a “critical lever”. Russia was set to gain most if the trilateral meeting took place, experts said, as the summit would be a potent symbol...
content: While US President Donald Trump has said he is open to sitting down with Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at the Apec summit, it remains far from certain that the three leaders will actually meet in a few weeks. Observers said much would depend on whether the countries could agree on an agenda, with one expert describing this as a “critical lever”. Russia was set to gain most if the trilateral meeting took place, experts said, as the summit would be a potent symbol that the country’s international isolation was ending and of its great-power status. While Trump would get to show he could deal with the other powers, this could unsettle US allies. Speculation has been building over whether the three leaders, who are all expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, will hold an unprecedented sit-down on the sidelines. Putin earlier said he was “all for” a trilateral meeting but added that the agenda had to be clear. “[A trilateral meeting is] certainly possible. To a large extent, this will depend on China as the host of the event,” he said. On Monday, Trump also signalled he was open to such talks. But he said it would be “not so much for Ukraine” and that such a meeting would have to be “based on denuclearisation”, an issue Beijing has long resisted negotiating. His comments followed a Wall Street Journal report on Monday that said Putin floated the three-way talks as a way to negotiate an end to the Ukraine war, now in its fifth year. The South China Morning Post understands that Chinese officials have privately welcomed the idea of three-way talks, but have not pushed aggressively for them. There has also been little substantive discussion of an agenda or preparations. When asked on both Monday and Tuesday to comment on the possibility of a trilateral meeting, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she had no information to provide. Wang Wen, dean of the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University, said the agenda would set the tone for any summit and determine its success. “The agenda is the critical lever for whether a meeting can actually take place,” Wang said. “If the three parties harbour conflicting private agendas or if their proposed topics are fundamentally misaligned, the meeting is highly unlikely to happen. “Only when the agenda focuses on areas of consensus while steering clear of ‘red lines’ … can a dialogue become a viable possibility.” Denis Simon of the Quincy Institute, a Washington think tank, agreed, arguing that the three countries had “overlapping interests” but did not share a “common strategic vision”. He added that while the nuclear issue offered the most obvious potential starting point, Ukraine, trade, Taiwan and the broader international order would inevitably enter any conversation. Hemant Adlakha of Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi said that “without a clearly agreed-upon agenda, the possibility of the trilateral [talks] happening in Shenzhen is rather remote”. He suggested that, in the absence of a formal meeting, the three leaders might instead opt for a more informal encounter, perhaps a “stroll together or a cup of tea”. Lyle Goldstein of Defence Priorities, a Washington think tank, said the agenda might determine whether the potential gathering was “short and symbolic or alternatively lengthy or substantive”. He argued that Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin had been “helpful overall in cooling world tensions”. Wang said Beijing would be keen to discuss issues that were global, constructive and mutually beneficial, such as the risks inherent in major-power relations, the global economic recovery, food and energy security and climate change. But Beijing would resist any pressure to align with a particular bloc as well as “unfair proposals” such as “forcing China into US-Russia nuclear arms control negotiations”. “[China is] open to discussing mutually beneficial cooperation, but issues concerning [its] sovereign rights are off the table, and any demand to ‘take sides’ is a non-starter,” he added. Beijing has long refused to join trilateral arms control talks with Washington and Moscow, arguing that its nuclear arsenal does not match up to those of the US and Russia. China is thought to have hundreds of warheads, while the Russian and American stockpiles are in the thousands. Cui Hongjian, head of European Union studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, said the thaw in Washington’s ties with both Beijing and Moscow had laid some groundwork for a meeting, but that stability would need to be maintained for talks to go ahead. He pointed to uncertainty over the Ukraine war, which he said was weighing on the US-Russia relationship, and to the trade tensions between Washington and Beijing. “To bring about a three-way meeting, I think an important precondition is that each of the bilateral relationships stays stable, with no major reversals or changes,” he said. Cui said the political will of the three sides would also be decisive. The Trump administration, in particular, would first need to weigh how a meeting fitted its domestic politics, including the looming midterm elections, before committing fully to talks on the agenda, he said. Sergey Radchenko, a Chinese and Russian foreign policy specialist at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, said a meeting of the three powers would give Russia a chance to “separate the US from its European allies” and hand the Kremlin political leverage while bolstering its status as a great power. He expected Ukraine to be on the agenda if a meeting took place, with Russia pushing for an end to the war. He also said China’s presence could open the door to talks on security guarantees that would bind Beijing to any settlement. But he doubted that Xi “will necessarily be enthused by the idea of such a summit”. “He and Putin have previously cooperated in trilateral formats. However, this is a proposition of a completely different order, and perhaps it is a format that Xi will find difficult to handle,” he said. Simon offered a more granular reading of the three leaders’ incentives. Trump, he said, would see the meeting as “an opportunity to demonstrate his ability to deal directly with the world’s other two major powers, without being constrained by traditional alliances”. For Putin, simply sitting at the table would be a diplomatic victory, ending Russia’s isolation and giving him a platform to discuss Ukraine, whereas Xi is likely to be the most cautious, according to the Quincy Institute’s Simon. “Xi would welcome the recognition of China as an indispensable global power, but would be cautious about becoming part of an arrangement that legitimises American and Russian spheres of influence at China’s expense,” he said. Cui suggested that if the meeting went ahead next month, it would send a positive signal that the three major powers shared a desire to promote global stability and development. Beijing, as host, would stand to gain by showing its sense of international responsibility, he said. “Objectively speaking, this meeting offers China primarily symbolic value, with substantive gains playing a secondary role,” Wang added. “Symbolically, this is where its greatest value lies. It reaffirms China’s status as a global hub, demonstrating that no major international issue can be advanced without China’s participation. It underscores China’s role as a core force for balancing relations between major powers and stabilising the international order.” But such a meeting could unsettle US allies, including European countries and Japan, according to Wang. He said a trilateral dialogue would deepen “strategic anxiety” in Europe and Japan since both had long shaped their foreign policies around the US’ stance in great-power rivalries. If such talks became regular, he said, it would mark the end of a “global order defined by bloc-based confrontation” and could potentially leave US allies such as Europe and Japan in “a state of strategic disorientation, compelling them to re-evaluate their own positions on the global stage”. However, Goldstein argued that seeing the trilateral as “bad news” for Japan and Europe amounted to a “zero-sum worldview”, and that having such meetings regularly could inspire other sets of three-way talks, including between Europe, Russia and the US or alternatively China, Japan and the US. Also, Adlakha said, the trilateral meeting might “severely” test China’s efforts to maintain a careful balance between supporting Putin and preserving ties with Europe. But Wang played down expectations, suggesting that a meeting would at most produce a crisis communication channel to prevent strategic miscalculation, a basic consensus on global issues and clearer “red lines” for each side. “Any expectation that such a meeting could resolve the Russia-Ukraine conflict or fundamentally reshape the global order is entirely unrealistic,” he said.

title: Chinese scientists find neurons may act as minicomputers that help decision-making
description: Chinese scientists have found evidence that individual neurons can act like powerful minicomputers that enable flexible behaviour such as making decisions. Scientists do not have a complete understanding of how our brains adapt to changing contexts to respond appropriately to sensory information. But by studying mice, the team obtained the first experimental evidence that dendrites – branchlike structures attached to neurons – can integrate learned rules with incoming sensory inputs to drive...
content: Chinese scientists have found evidence that individual neurons can act like powerful minicomputers that enable flexible behaviour such as making decisions. Scientists do not have a complete understanding of how our brains adapt to changing contexts to respond appropriately to sensory information. But by studying mice, the team obtained the first experimental evidence that dendrites – branchlike structures attached to neurons – can integrate learned rules with incoming sensory inputs to drive flexible choices. These new insights into the cognitive process could also help in the design of more adaptable and efficient AI systems modelled on the human brain, the researchers said. “These findings indicate that a single cortical neuron can perform a cognitive computation for flexible behaviour,” the team wrote in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Science on October 15. Neurons are specialised nerve cells that form the building blocks of the brain and nervous system, while dendrites are their branched extensions that receive incoming electrochemical signals from other neurons. In the past, individual neurons were seen as simple units that acted as basic switches or summation points, with complex cognition assumed to emerge from their interactions in a vast network. However, the findings by the Chinese Academy of Sciences team suggest single neurons are far more sophisticated, with dendrites carrying out complex computations before sending information to the neuron cell body. “This is equivalent to work that would otherwise require multiple computers networked together being accomplished by a single ‘dendritic’ supercomputer,” Xu Ninglong, the study’s lead author and a researcher at the academy’s Institute of Neuroscience, told the official Science and Technology Daily. Intelligent behaviour needs both sensory inputs and an understanding of changing abstract rules, a process that depends on the brain being aware of the context in which it is operating. The team illustrated this with the example of a ringing phone, which people would answer at home but know to silence it in situations such as a meeting. “Decision-making involves transforming sensory inputs into appropriate motor outputs in a context and state-dependent manner, where the same sensory input may be mapped to different motor outputs depending on the environmental state or task rule,” the team wrote. Although this ability is a key part of cognition, the team said that how individual neurons carry out such flexible mapping had been poorly understood. “Theory has long held that these dendrites integrate distinct streams of information within a single cell, yet direct evidence linking dendritic processing to flexible cognition has been lacking,” the researchers said. They added that most decision-making studies had treated each neuron as a single point and overlooked dendritic computation. The researchers focused on the role of cortical pyramidal neurons, the most common signalling neurons in the mammalian cerebral cortex, which is the part of the brain involved in complex sensory, cognitive and motor functions. These have two main types of dendrites: apical dendrites, which form a single trunk that extends upwards from the cell body, and shorter basal dendrites that sprout directly from its base. To study dendritic computation, the team trained mice to carry out a flexible categorisation task. The animals were played tones of different frequencies and had to lick either a water port to their left when a lower-frequency tone was played or a port to their right for a higher frequency. The rules determining which frequencies belonged to each category periodically switched, and the mice were rewarded with water when they were correct. The mice had imaging windows fixed to their heads, which the team used to record the activity of apical dendrites and cell bodies in the auditory cortex, which controls hearing. They then suppressed dendritic activity and found that had impaired rule-dependent choices – which in turn suggested that dendritic activity in the cortical neurons actively drove flexible behaviour. “These findings reveal a single neuron-level computation based on dendritic compartmentalisation and integration that supports flexible, rule-based decision-making,” they wrote. As well as advancing understanding of the cognitive process, the team’s finding may also help find new ways to design more flexible, brain-like AI systems. “More broadly, this form of within-neuron computation expands the capacity available to cortical networks during flexible behaviour and may inform the design of more-efficient artificial systems,” the study said.

title: Chinese military vessels and spy drones track Keen Sword war games off Japan
description: Japan says it has spotted PLA aircraft, spy drones and warships, including a supply ship that could support the Liaoning aircraft carrier, in recent days as Tokyo and Washington started drills focused on a potential Taiwan contingency. Three People’s Liberation Army military aircraft – two drones and a reconnaissance plane – flew through international airspace between Japanese islands into the Pacific before heading back towards mainland China on Monday, prompting Japan to scramble fighter jets,...
content: Japan says it has spotted PLA aircraft, spy drones and warships, including a supply ship that could support the Liaoning aircraft carrier, in recent days as Tokyo and Washington started drills focused on a potential Taiwan contingency. Three People’s Liberation Army military aircraft – two drones and a reconnaissance plane – flew through international airspace between Japanese islands into the Pacific before heading back towards mainland China on Monday, prompting Japan to scramble fighter jets, the Joint Staff Office of Japan’s defence ministry reported the same day. The aircraft included a BZK-005 reconnaissance drone and a Y-9 intelligence-gathering aircraft, which flew in from the East China Sea, passed through the Miyako Strait between Okinawa’s main island and Miyako Island, and continued into the Pacific before returning towards mainland China, the Joint Staff Office said in a post. In addition, a TB-001 reconnaissance and attack drone passed between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan, flew northeast as far as waters off Amami Oshima, then turned back and passed through the Miyako Strait towards mainland China, the post said. The aircraft movements coincided with Monday’s start of “Keen Sword”, a biennial joint military exercise between Japan and the United States running until October 29 across multiple locations in Japan. The exercise will involve about 45,000 Japanese Self-Defence Forces personnel and 12,000 US troops, making it one of the biggest drills ever conducted by the two allies. The exercise will include the deployment of US anti-ship missile systems, known as the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS), to Yonaguni, Japan’s westernmost inhabited island, about 110km (68 miles) from Taiwan. Japan’s long-range Type 25 surface-to-ship guided missiles will deploy to a training ground in southern Kyushu during the exercise. It will be the first time the missiles have been deployed outside their garrison in Kumamoto prefecture since arriving there earlier this year. The vehicle-mounted missiles have a reported range of about 1,000km, potentially putting parts of China’s coastline, including Shanghai, within reach from Kyushu. From Okinawa, the Taiwan Strait and mainland China’s southeastern coastal provinces would be within range. Tensions between Beijing and Tokyo have been running high since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in November that Japan could intervene militarily in the event of a conflict over Taiwan, angering Beijing and pushing bilateral ties to a new low. Japan’s defence ministry also reported the recent movements of seven Chinese naval vessels in a series of four other posts on Monday. Among them was Yuhengxing, a Chinese navy intelligence-collection ship with hull number 798. Japan said the vessel began sailing east through the Osumi Strait towards the Pacific Ocean on Saturday. Another intelligence-collection ship, Kaiyangxing, hull number 796, was spotted on the same day travelling south through waters about 80km northwest of Kumejima in Okinawa prefecture before continuing through the Miyako Strait towards the Pacific. Earlier on Friday, Japan detected two other vessels: the Chinese navy guided-missile destroyer Qiqihar, hull number 121, and the Hulunhu combat-support ship, hull number 901. The two vessels were observed passing through the Osumi Strait on Saturday as they headed towards the Pacific Ocean. The Hulunhu, with a displacement of about 45,000 to 48,000 tonnes, is one of the world’s largest naval replenishment ships. Chinese state media and naval enthusiasts have referred to it as the “super nanny” or “carrier mother” because of its role in supplying aircraft carrier strike groups. On October 14, the Liaoning carrier began its second series of drills in the western Pacific this year. Although Beijing did not disclose the carrier’s location, Japan reported on Wednesday that the Liaoning and three accompanying vessels had passed southeast through the Miyako Strait towards the Pacific. Japan’s defence ministry reported about 10 take-offs and landings by carrier-based fighter jets and helicopters that day. Japan continued to monitor the carrier group’s movements on Thursday, subsequently reporting that the four Chinese navy vessels had been confirmed sailing towards the South China Sea. It remains unclear whether the Hulunhu will join the Liaoning in the Pacific, but the two vessels will be closely watched during the US-Japan exercise, which will run until the end of the month. Meanwhile, a US carrier strike group led by the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived at Yokosuka, Japan, on Friday and is scheduled to take part in the Keen Sword exercise, according to the US Navy. It adds to the concentration of military activity along the first island chain, which stretches from Japan, to Taiwan and the Philippines, in the coming days. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: PLA Navy followed US vessel on patrol in South China Sea hotspot, Beijing says
description: China on Tuesday accused a US naval vessel of undermining regional stability by entering waters near the South China Sea’s disputed Spratly Islands. Early on Tuesday morning, the USS Charleston “illegally intruded” into the waters around Sabina Shoal “without approval”, said Yin Gang, spokesman for the People’s Liberation Army’s Southern Theatre Command Navy. The Chinese navy monitored and followed the Charleston, Yin said. China holds “indisputable sovereignty” over the Spratly Islands and the...
content: China on Tuesday accused a US naval vessel of undermining regional stability by entering waters near the South China Sea’s disputed Spratly Islands. Early on Tuesday morning, the USS Charleston “illegally intruded” into the waters around Sabina Shoal “without approval”, said Yin Gang, spokesman for the People’s Liberation Army’s Southern Theatre Command Navy. The Chinese navy monitored and followed the Charleston, Yin said. China holds “indisputable sovereignty” over the Spratly Islands and the US action was “detrimental to regional peace and stability”, he added, demanding Washington immediately cease such activities. Vincent Trinidad, a spokesman for the Philippines’ military, denied that the Charleston trespassed into Chinese territory and said “no single nation has the authority to require prior permission for lawful transit through international waters”, the Bilyonaryo News Channel reported. The encounter followed a collision last month between China and the Philippines near Sabina Shoal, known as Xianbin Jiao in China and Escoda Shoal in the Philippines. The Charleston’s alleged incursion came ahead of a planned visit by US President Donald Trump to Manila for an Asean meeting next month. The Charleston is an Independence-class littoral combat ship currently deployed to Southeast Asia under Destroyer Squadron 7, a Singapore-based command under the Seventh Fleet. The Seventh Fleet did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Sabina Shoal, about 145km (90 miles) northwest of the Philippine island of Palawan, has been a major flashpoint between Beijing and Manila since 2024, when the Philippines stationed a coastguard vessel there for five months amid concerns over possible Chinese land reclamation. The vessel withdrew in September 2024 following a series of confrontations, including collisions between Chinese and Philippine coastguard ships. While the encounter on Tuesday appeared to be the first time this year that China has publicly accused a US warship of entering disputed waters in the South China Sea without permission, similar incidents have occurred before. In 2020, Beijing said it warned the USS Montgomery to leave what it said were Chinese waters around the Spratly Islands. Tensions in the South China Sea have escalated in recent years as China and the Philippines have repeatedly clashed over disputed reefs and shoals, with encounters involving coastguard and naval vessels, collisions and the use of water cannons. Washington, a treaty ally of the Philippines, has stepped up joint naval patrols and military exercises with Manila while challenging what it considers to be Beijing’s excessive territorial claims. A joint statement released after the 12th US-Philippines Bilateral Strategic Dialogue in February reiterated that the 1951 United States-Philippines Mutual Defence Treaty extended to armed attacks against either country’s armed forces, aircraft and public vessels – including those of their coastguards – anywhere in the Pacific, including the South China Sea.

title: Chinese air force reveals Y-20B tanker-transport variant in official training image
description: China’s military has published what appears to be the first official photograph of a Y-20B heavy transport aircraft in PLA Air Force livery fitted with aerial refuelling pods, suggesting that the multi-role tanker-transport (MRTT) configuration has entered service. An image published by the PLA Daily newspaper on October 14 shows the four-engine aircraft painted in standard military grey, with refuelling pods beneath its wings and its rear cargo ramp open as a truck carrying equipment is behind...
content: China’s military has published what appears to be the first official photograph of a Y-20B heavy transport aircraft in PLA Air Force livery fitted with aerial refuelling pods, suggesting that the multi-role tanker-transport (MRTT) configuration has entered service. An image published by the PLA Daily newspaper on October 14 shows the four-engine aircraft painted in standard military grey, with refuelling pods beneath its wings and its rear cargo ramp open as a truck carrying equipment is behind it. The caption said an unnamed air force unit was conducting loading training in mid-autumn. While the PLA Daily did not identify the aircraft, state broadcaster China Media Group and China Military Bugle, a PLA News Media Centre social media account, both identified it as a Y-20B on Monday. In the same October 19 report by China Media Group, military commentator Fu Qianshao said the Y-20B carried enough internal fuel to refuel medium or heavy fighters without additional tanks in the cargo compartment, allowing it to retain space for personnel or equipment. A Chinese military commentator had already concluded in an October 13 opinion piece that the MRTT version had formally entered service, citing photographs showing the aircraft in PLA Air Force livery with refuelling pods fitted. The October 14 photograph provides official evidence of the configuration during PLA Air Force unit training, although it does not establish when the aircraft became operational as a tanker. The latest evidence follows confirmation by China’s CCTV state broadcaster in August that the Y-20B, an upgraded version of the Y-20A transport fitted with domestically developed WS-20 engines, could be converted into a tanker using removable refuelling equipment. Such flexibility could allow the PLA Air Force to supplement its dedicated YY-20A tankers by assigning transport aircraft to refuelling duties, potentially supporting sustained combat operations farther into the western Pacific. During a Taiwan conflict, additional tanker capacity could help People’s Liberation Army fighters remain airborne longer or operate farther from mainland bases. Andreas Rupprecht, an aviation analyst specialising in Chinese military aviation, previously told the South China Morning Post that observers had tracked the capability since a Y-20B prototype appeared with refuelling pods in January 2022. A military-grey Y-20B was spotted in April 2023 with tanker alignment markings but no refuelling pods. Rupprecht estimated that around 90 Y-20A-family transports and tankers were operational by August 2025, while about two dozen Y-20Bs were in service or awaiting delivery. The Y-20B also represents an engine upgrade over the original Y-20A, which uses Russian D-30KP-II turbofans. The WS-20 offers greater thrust and better fuel efficiency than the D-30, although reliable public figures quantifying the resulting gains in range or payload are not available. Beyond aerial refuelling, the Y-20 platform is also being adapted into the KJ-3000 airborne early-warning and control aircraft, which has been undergoing flight testing. Together, these variants could give the PLA greater capacity to move forces, sustain combat aircraft and coordinate operations far from mainland China.

title: Student sent back to China over Japanese rising sun flag incident in Russia
