It remains a symbol of Japanese militarism and aggression in China and other parts of Asia. Moscow State University made the decision after the student was criticised by...
content: A Chinese student who draped himself in the Japanese rising sun flag in a Russian university classroom has been expelled and asked to leave the country, according to state-run newspaper Global Times. The flag was used by the Japanese military during its imperial expansion and is still used by Japan’s Maritime Self-Defence Force. It remains a symbol of Japanese militarism and aggression in China and other parts of Asia. Moscow State University made the decision after the student was criticised by Chinese Communist Party mouthpiece People’s Daily as well as the People’s Liberation Army, which said his actions had glorified Japanese militarism. The South China Morning Post has contacted the university for comment. A People’s Daily commentary on Monday said such acts of “promoting militarism betrayed national conscience and violated the shared human value of cherishing peace, and deserved serious criticism and disciplinary action”. It also warned against provocations by a small number of people it labelled jingri, or “Japanese in spirit” – a derogatory Chinese term for people perceived as identifying with Japan. On Sunday, Jun Zhengping, a social media account run by the PLA, said in a post: “Regardless of which country or campus one is in, advocating for militarism is an explicit offence against human conscience and is held in contempt by all.” Global Times reported on Monday, citing sources, that the history faculty at Moscow State University held a meeting on Monday and said it would soon announce its decision to expel the student, reportedly surnamed Chen. The faculty initiated procedures on Friday for Chen to leave Russia and he had since left the country, according to the report. That came after several Chinese students in the department signed a petition calling on the university to take action against Chen. One Chinese student who attended the meeting told the newspaper that the department agreed that the historical consensus on opposing fascism must not be desecrated. The report quoted acting dean Lev S. Belousov as saying during the meeting that Russia and China had fought alongside each other in World War II, and the friendship between the two countries had a long history. He said the university’s position on the shared anti-fascist historical consensus was fully aligned with that of China and Chinese students in the department, according to the report. The incident took place during a history class at the university on Wednesday last week, according to an earlier Global Times report, which cited sources. The sources said Chen had brought a Japanese military cap from the 1930s to the classroom and draped the rising sun flag over himself. According to the report, the student was allegedly from Nanjing, the city where Japanese troops committed one of the most notorious atrocities of the war in China when it was still known as Nanking. Japan’s wartime history has been a persistent source of friction in China-Japan ties, which have been strained for nearly a year over Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks last November that a crisis in the Taiwan Strait could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, potentially prompting a military response from Tokyo. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: China protests UK border searches, phone seizures amid growing espionage tensions
description: China has lodged a formal representation with the UK after British border authorities subjected Chinese citizens to extended questioning and seizures of personal electronic devices, including mobile phones. According to a statement from China’s embassy in Britain, multiple Chinese nationals – including trade delegates, tourists and people visiting relatives – have experienced long delays, as well as questioning by Border Force officers and confiscation of phones and other devices. The embassy...
content: China has lodged a formal representation with the UK after British border authorities subjected Chinese citizens to extended questioning and seizures of personal electronic devices, including mobile phones. According to a statement from China’s embassy in Britain, multiple Chinese nationals – including trade delegates, tourists and people visiting relatives – have experienced long delays, as well as questioning by Border Force officers and confiscation of phones and other devices. The embassy said that British border officials claimed their actions were carried out in accordance with relevant provisions of the United Kingdom’s Counterterrorism and Border Security Act 2019. “China expresses serious concern over this and has lodged solemn representations with the British side,” the embassy said, noting that it would continue to urge Britain to stop the arbitrary detention and questioning of Chinese citizens. The embassy urged Chinese travellers to protect their personal property and privacy, stay informed of relevant British regulations and practices and seek consular help if necessary. A similar advisory was issued by the embassy in December, when it warned Chinese nationals that British border control might invoke counterterrorism laws to arbitrarily search documents, mobile phones, computers and smartwatches, along with prolonged questioning upon entry or departure. The latest warning comes around a week after Ken McCallum, MI5’s director general, named China in his annual threat update, accusing it of conducting “espionage, coercion or democratic interference”. In his briefing last Tuesday, McCallum disclosed that MI5 had issued an espionage alert to the British academic community, warning about a specific Chinese entity posing as a conventional research body. According to McCallum, the organisation was being used by Chinese intelligence services to fund projects in Britain relating to areas such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to bolster Beijing’s spying capabilities. “We shouldn’t be astounded by attempts to spy on us,” he said. “The UK is an innovative nation with many strengths, including in science and research. It would be odd if others weren’t trying to steal some of our advantages.” The Chinese embassy pushed back on the same day, describing McCallum’s allegations as “pure fabrication and malicious slander,” which Beijing firmly opposed and strongly condemned, it said. “China strictly adheres to the principle of non-interference in internal affairs, poses a threat to no country and has no interest in meddling in the UK’s domestic affairs.”

title: China’s new 0.1-nanometre electron microscope ready to challenge US and Japan
description: China is ready to commercialise a 200-kilovolt transmission electron microscope with an information resolution down to 0.1 nanometres that could introduce a new challenger into a market long dominated by the US and Japan. Developed by Hefei-based manufacturer CIQTEK, the microscope features a point resolution of 0.25nm and an information limit of 0.1nm – on par with leading workhorse models on the market. This marks a shift for the country’s expanding advanced electron microscopy industry from...
content: China is ready to commercialise a 200-kilovolt transmission electron microscope with an information resolution down to 0.1 nanometres that could introduce a new challenger into a market long dominated by the US and Japan. Developed by Hefei-based manufacturer CIQTEK, the microscope features a point resolution of 0.25nm and an information limit of 0.1nm – on par with leading workhorse models on the market. This marks a shift for the country’s expanding advanced electron microscopy industry from research and development to commercialisation, according to a report by the official ministry newspaper Science and Technology Daily on Monday. It also represents the latest achievement aimed at reducing the country’s reliance on imports of the technology used in vital advanced industries like chip manufacturing. On Sunday, CIQTEK officially launched its 200kV field emission transmission electron microscope – the TEM-F200 – during the 2026 National Conference on Electron Microscopy held in Nanjing. He Yu, CIQTEK’s chairman, described the new model as capable of supporting high-resolution imaging and defect analysis for advanced materials and semiconductors. “Through continuous research and development, the TEM-F200 has achieved mass production and delivery capabilities,” He said, according to Science and Technology Daily. Wu Aihua, secretary general of the China Instrument and Control Society’s analytical instruments branch, told the ministry newspaper the model could also be used in fields like biomedicine and would enhance the country’s self-sufficiency in analytical testing technologies. The development of light microscopes throughout the 17th century enabled the magnification and capture of objects beyond the capability of human vision. However, the resolution limit of conventional light microscopes is about 200 to 250nm, making the devices unable to visualise some of the smallest structures on Earth, including viruses and genetic building blocks. In the early 1930s, German scientists built the first working electron microscopes, unlocking the ability to visualise even smaller structures. Electron microscopes send focused beams of electrons rather than light at or through specimens. Detectors then capture these particles to build an image, allowing us to view details near or down to the atomic level on a display. Modern universal workhorse electron microscopes typically operate at a 200kV accelerating voltage, which helps balance trade-offs between resolution and sample damage. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM), one of the most common forms, uses a broad electron beam that passes through a thin sample to project an image onto a detector, according to US supplier Nanoscience Instruments. Many modern TEM models are also capable of scanning transmission electron microscopy, which adds a tightly focused beam that scans point by point, making it easier to build high-contrast atomic images and map the composition of materials. It has become a major part of fields like materials science, life science, as well as nano- and atomic-scale manufacturing, such as the production of chips. The global market for commercial TEM is dominated by a handful of companies based in the US and Japan. This includes market leaders Thermo Fisher Scientific – an American research supplier that produces its transmission electron microscopes in the Netherlands – and Japanese precision instrument developer JEOL. Both companies produce widely used flagship 200kV transmission electron microscope models with information limits of about 0.11 to 0.12nm. Other major players include Japanese manufacturer Hitachi and American manufacturer Bruker, whose acquired Nion series includes dedicated scanning transmission electron microscopes with world-leading resolutions. The point resolution is the finest detail that can be directly interpreted from a microscope image. The information limit is the greatest detail the microscope can actually capture, which can be brought out using processing software. For decades, China relied on imported TEM technology to meet its research and industrial needs. High-quality machines can cost anywhere from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. In recent years, China has made major leaps in electron microscope technology, achieving a series of firsts over a short time span to break its reliance on imports. In 2024, Guangzhou-based research institute Bioland Laboratory built the country’s first commercial field emission TEM, a 120kV model called the TH-F120 that is manufactured and sold by CIQTEK. Last year, Suzhou Bozhon Instrument Technology unveiled China’s first commercial 200kV TEM model, the BZ-F200, according to a Science and Technology Daily report. In May, the Chinese Academy of Sciences announced Aeye-1, calling it the world’s first artificial intelligence-driven TEM system. China is also now producing its own cryo-electron microscopy technology – a specialised TEM technique for building three-dimensional structures of biomolecules like proteins, an important tool in drug discovery. On Monday, CIQTEK announced that it had released a 120kV model called the TEM-F120, saying it could be used for life sciences and materials research.

title: Cell publisher investigates editor accused of soliciting bribes from China
description: Cell Press, one of the world’s leading scientific publishers, has launched an investigation after prominent Chinese biologist Rao Yi accused the editor-in-chief of a top medical journal of soliciting bribes from mainland authors. “Several important international academic journals have seen editors, and even editors-in-chief, soliciting and accepting bribes,” said Rao, a tenured chair professor at Peking University who stepped down as president of Capital Medical University last year, in a social...
content: Cell Press, one of the world’s leading scientific publishers, has launched an investigation after prominent Chinese biologist Rao Yi accused the editor-in-chief of a top medical journal of soliciting bribes from mainland authors. “Several important international academic journals have seen editors, and even editors-in-chief, soliciting and accepting bribes,” said Rao, a tenured chair professor at Peking University who stepped down as president of Capital Medical University last year, in a social media post last Tuesday. “Chinese scientists should collectively boycott such editors,” he added. Rao’s post singled out Steve Mao, the Chinese-born editor-in-chief of Cancer Cell – a peer-reviewed medical journal published by Cell Press – in the bribery allegation. “Organisations and various assessment bodies in China should be aware that many people believe Steve Mao has serious issues,” Rao said. According to publicly available information, Mao graduated from Peking University in 2002 and later obtained a PhD from the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Centre. Mao undertook postdoctoral research at Cold Spring Harbor and Harvard University before entering the academic publishing industry. He has served as editor-in-chief of Cancer Cell since 2020 and been director of editorial and strategic initiatives for China and the Asia-Pacific region at Cell Press since August last year. The South China Morning Post reached out to Mao seeking comment on the matter. Last Friday evening, Cell Press announced on one of its official social media platforms that it had “initiated the relevant procedures and commissioned an external, independent third party to conduct a comprehensive investigation”. “While the investigation is ongoing, we will not be making any further comment on this matter,” the publisher stated. Separately, a spokesperson for the publisher told the mainland magazine China Newsweek that Cell Press took the integrity of its editorial process very seriously. The publisher was reviewing the matter in accordance with established procedures and contacting Rao to request any supporting evidence he might have, the spokesperson said. According to mainland media reports, Mao was originally scheduled to attend an academic conference co-hosted by Cell Press and Westlake University in early November but had recently been replaced by a colleague. Rao alleged the matter was not an isolated instance, saying “a considerable number of journals and individuals are implicated”. In a social media post the day before he mentioned Mao, Rao said he had heard from Chinese scientists that “some editors at international academic journals demand personal financial payments in exchange for helping Chinese researchers publish their papers”. He broadly referred to a case in which he claimed a clinician had “bribed” an editor to secure publication in a journal. According to a source whom Rao said had disclosed the matter to him, the journal editor in question gave the clinician submitting the manuscript a quote: “An initial payment of 2 million yuan (US$299,000), with more [fees] potentially required later.” According to the post, Rao sent an email to the accused editor, writing: “Multiple sources have mentioned you as an example of an editor who has requested personal payment for publishing with journals you have served as an editor.” Rao said the editor in question had rejected the allegations, dismissing them as “completely false and baseless”. “This is completely false and baseless. I demand you immediately retract this false statement. I have preserved all evidence and reserve all rights. I will not engage in further debate here,” the editor said in reply, according to Rao’s post. The SCMP could not independently verify Rao’s claims and reached out to Rao seeking further details regarding the allegations. According to a veteran Chinese professional in the international academic publishing sector, spending hundreds of thousands or even millions of yuan to open a possibility of securing publication was a “tacitly understood” phenomenon, particularly in top-tier medical journals. Speaking on condition of anonymity, citing the sensitivity of the matter, the insider explained that this practice served to increase the probability of publication. For instance, a direct submission was highly likely to be rejected outright in the first round. However, once an internal relationship was established, journal editors might grant the author more opportunities and provide specific guidance for revisions. “I have heard of some journals already disciplining certain editors internally over such transactions, but these incidents mostly just circulate within the circle,” he added, without providing details of any confirmed cases of the practice. As to why authors would be willing to spend massive sums to bribe journals, the industry insider said it was primarily because the incentives and rewards associated with prestigious publications in China “are too high”. “It is essentially an investment,” he said, noting that once a paper was published in a top journal, “all sorts of academic titles, resources and research grants follow”. A growing number of professionals in the scientific community are dedicating themselves to monitoring and exposing academic misconduct in China, an effort that has already prompted government action in some cases. In recent years, Geng Hongwei, a high-profile blogger and PhD dropout better known as ‘Student Geng’, has emerged as China’s most prominent online whistle-blower for academic misconduct. In late August, four mainland academics lost their posts at leading universities and came under official investigation after Geng flagged their research for misconduct.

title: The evolution of China’s active defence doctrine
description: The British Army’s miraculous escape from Nazi Germany’s encirclement at Dunkirk is considered by some to be the greatest military retreat in modern history and a prime example of snatching victory from the jaws of defeat. Yet years before Dunkirk, the military retreat by the Chinese Red Army, known as the Long March, was more impressive and consequential. While the Dunkirk evacuation remains in Hollywood fare and a staple of World War II folklore, the Long March is taught at military academies...
content: The British Army’s miraculous escape from Nazi Germany’s encirclement at Dunkirk is considered by some to be the greatest military retreat in modern history and a prime example of snatching victory from the jaws of defeat. Yet years before Dunkirk, the military retreat by the Chinese Red Army, known as the Long March, was more impressive and consequential. While the Dunkirk evacuation remains in Hollywood fare and a staple of World War II folklore, the Long March is taught at military academies worldwide as a foundational case study in asymmetrical warfare, insurgency and strategic political-military integration. It was a baptism of fire that did more than resurrect Mao Zedong’s political career and mark his ascent to primacy. It also firmly established “active defence” as the Chinese Communist military’s core doctrine, which continues to guide the nation’s strategic planning to this day. Under this doctrine, the Red Army evolved from a near-shattered force of around 8,000 survivors at the end of the Long March in October 1935 into a formidable military that defeated the larger, better-equipped Nationalist forces. As the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) approaches its centenary, how it adapts and modernises the doctrine of active defence will matter far more to its future than its fleet of aircraft carriers and stealth fighters. A common Western view often attributes Chinese military success to an extraordinary tolerance for hardship and sacrifice, alongside “human wave” tactics that rely on sheer numbers. A careful study of its campaigns reveals that, in truth, the PLA often fought at a numerical disadvantage or, at best, on equal footing. Even in the Korean war, the number of Chinese soldiers deployed was comparable to, or only slightly higher than, that of the coalition forces, which had superior firepower and modern logistical support. Instead, Chinese commanders relied heavily on stealth, infiltration and rapid concentration of force to secure decisive local advantages – all of which are core components of active defence. Neither is active defence merely a synonym for guerrilla warfare, a concept popularised by the Spanish during their fight against Napoleon in the early 19th century. While guerrilla tactics are frequently employed under active defence, they do not constitute its entirety. Guerrilla warfare dictates that when facing an overwhelmingly superior adversary, one must avoid direct confrontation, disperse forces, establish base areas behind enemy lines and wage small battles of attrition. Mao was a master of this, but he also recognised that guerrilla operations alone could not decide the ultimate outcome of a war, as he articulated in his 1938 treatise, Problems of Strategy in Guerrilla War Against Japan. At the operational level, the true essence of active defence is mobile warfare. This doctrine dictates that the key to victory lies in creating battlefield opportunities through swift, unexpected movement, concentrating absolute local superiority against an isolated segment of the enemy and executing a battle of annihilation before withdrawing to safety to await the next operational window. Mao understood that while guerrilla tactics can preserve strength and wear down an opponent, final victory requires a regular army capable of executing large-scale mobile operations and pitched battles to destroy the enemy’s main force. These operational considerations, however, are merely execution. The heart of active defence lies in its strategic orientation, which synthesises more than two millennia of Chinese military philosophy. In essence, it is the integration of a “strategic defensive posture” with “aggressive operational manoeuvring”. The emphasis is not on capturing or holding territory for its own sake but on seizing the initiative through movement and creating advantageous conditions for decisive engagements. The objective is to control time and space through manoeuvrability rather than attacking with brute force. By maintaining a defensive posture at the political and strategic levels, it secures political legitimacy and moral justification while luring its adversary into underestimating its resolve. Simultaneously, the military identifies the enemy’s weakest points and waits for the other side to make the first move. When the enemy attacks, it avoids static defence but, by skilfully manoeuvring, exposes the opponent’s weaknesses. It then quickly concentrates its forces to deliver precise and devastating strikes. Once you achieve your goal, quickly withdraw to protect yourself. The objective is not to amass overwhelming strength everywhere but to selectively target vulnerabilities to achieve an asymmetrical advantage. Crucially, Chinese military thinkers view the armed forces as a direct instrument of politics, whose missions must strictly serve broader grand strategy. Capturing territory holds no intrinsic value if it fails to advance overall political objectives or preserve long-term strength. This contrasts with the American experience in Vietnam or the Soviet campaign in Afghanistan. In China’s conflicts with India and Vietnam, Beijing withdrew its troops once its limited political objectives were achieved, recognising that holding occupied land would dissipate military strength and prolong conflict unnecessarily. In this sense, active defence reflects the philosophy of weiqi, or go, which prioritises outmanoeuvring an opponent through careful control of space, positioning and tempo rather than obsessing over capturing individual pieces as in chess. Today, warfare is undergoing profound transformation amid technological disruption, yet active defence remains the PLA’s guiding doctrine. Its development of integrated air-sea battle capabilities, hypersonic missiles, aircraft carrier strike groups, nuclear submarines and stealth aircraft is explicitly built around this concept. The strategy often termed “anti-access/area denial” by Western analysts is defensively oriented in purpose, acting far from China’s shores to deter foreign military intervention. This creates strategic depth and enables mobile warfare under modern, hi-tech conditions. Whether the PLA can synthesise a modernised combat system aligned with this tradition will be the true benchmark of its progress as its centenary approaches, a challenge that extends far beyond acquiring advanced hardware. Ninety years ago, the Red Army pulled off an astounding feat that crystallised active defence; today, the PLA must execute a modern Long March to ensure this doctrine remains decisive in an era of artificial intelligence and hypersonic warfare.

title: US sanctions 5 Chinese entities over ex-Google engineer’s AI trade secrets theft
description: The US State Department announced on Monday that it was imposing sweeping sanctions under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act (PAIPA) on five Chinese entities suspected of stealing trade secrets from American companies. The targets include Shanghai Zhisuan Technology, founded by former Google software engineer Ding Linwei, venture capital firm MiraclePlus and three related entities. Ding was convicted of seven counts of trade secret theft in January. A federal judge subsequently...
content: The US State Department announced on Monday that it was imposing sweeping sanctions under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act (PAIPA) on five Chinese entities suspected of stealing trade secrets from American companies. The targets include Shanghai Zhisuan Technology, founded by former Google software engineer Ding Linwei, venture capital firm MiraclePlus and three related entities. Ding was convicted of seven counts of trade secret theft in January. A federal judge subsequently acquitted him on seven additional counts of economic espionage, finding insufficient evidence that he knew or intended at the time of the thefts that his conduct would benefit the Chinese government. The theft convictions remain in place. According to the original indictment against Ding, he stole confidential code related to Google’s AI supercomputing infrastructure, including technical details of tensor processing units (TPUs), graphics processing unit (GPU) systems and networking components used to train and deploy large-scale AI models. The technology is strategically important to China’s AI industry. With high-performance chips subject to export controls, efficiently coordinating and scheduling thousands of chips for large-model training has become one of the biggest barriers to developing super intelligence (SI). Google’s software can significantly improve the utilisation efficiency of large computing clusters. A superseding indictment in February 2025 said Ding applied to a talent programme in Shanghai. His application material stated that his product “will help China to have computing power infrastructure capabilities that are on par with the international level”. Ding joined Google in May 2019 as a software engineer and mainly worked on software development for Google’s supercomputing data centres, giving him access to the company’s core technology assets. According to the superseding indictment, he secretly uploaded more than 1,000 unique Google files to his personal cloud account from May 2022 to May 2023. While employed at Google, he secretly founded technology companies in China without notifying the company and pitched his “mastery of Google’s computing platform technology” to attract investment. Ding resigned from Google in late 2023 and booked a one-way ticket from San Francisco to Beijing. The FBI arrested him in March 2024. In January this year, a federal jury in San Francisco convicted him on 14 counts, including seven counts of economic espionage and seven counts of trade secret theft. In August, federal District Judge Vince Chhabria ruled that prosecutors had not presented enough evidence to prove that Ding “knew or intended” that his conduct would benefit the Chinese government, and overturned all the economic espionage counts while upholding the trade secret theft convictions. On September 1, Ding was sentenced to 12 months minus one day in prison and ordered to pay about US$198,000 in restitution. The State Department’s sanctions list under PAIPA comprehensively cut off the company Ding founded and the capital network behind it. The sanctioned entities include Shanghai Zhisuan Technology, which Ding founded in 2023. The company claimed to have experience with Google’s TPU Superpod, which clusters up to 9,600 chips into a single logical network, and explicitly said it could replicate Google’s SI infrastructure technology. They also include MiraclePlus, a well-known start-up incubator and venture capital firm that provided seed funding in exchange for equity in Shanghai Zhisuan and gave it a platform to showcase itself and attract follow-on investment. “Ding, using the stage provided by MiraclePlus to present his company, Zhisuan, touted his connection to Google technology and his ability to replicate its technology to fit China’s national conditions,” the sanction statement said. The list further includes two venture capital funds managed by MiraclePlus – Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase I Venture Capital Centre Limited Partnership (Phase I) and Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase II Venture Capital Centre Limited Partnership (Phase II) – and Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Zhiyuan Enterprise Management Centre Limited Partnership (Zhiyuan Enterprise), a corporate management entity wholly owned by the Phase I fund. The five entities will face a series of financial and commercial measures, including asset freezes, a ban on transactions with US individuals and entities, and restrictions on financial services and foreign-exchange licenses. The companies did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: US-China negotiators race to nail down concrete deals as Shenzhen Apec looms
description: The US and China are racing to secure concrete investment deals ahead of their leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen next month, even as both sides engage in a contest over leverage in extending their broad trade agreement. Multiple sources told the South China Morning Post that intense negotiations would continue in coming weeks, with Washington and Beijing still facing hurdles to finalising a complex package of institutional frameworks and economic agreements. The sources, who spoke on condition of...
content: The US and China are racing to secure concrete investment deals ahead of their leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen next month, even as both sides engage in a contest over leverage in extending their broad trade agreement. Multiple sources told the South China Morning Post that intense negotiations would continue in coming weeks, with Washington and Beijing still facing hurdles to finalising a complex package of institutional frameworks and economic agreements. The sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said negotiators had made considerable progress on the Board of Investment discussions since President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump met last month in Washington. The two leaders will meet again on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China’s southern tech hub in November – their second meeting in two months and third this year. The investment board, a key announcement from their May summit in Beijing, stalled because of political opposition in the US over potential Chinese investment, particularly from the car manufacturing sector. The issue was discussed again during the Chinese leader’s state visit last month, but the two sides failed to reach an agreement, although the similar Board of Trade was institutionalised after the talks in Washington. According to one source, the negotiating teams are following the model of the recently launched trade forum to formalise the structure of the investment forum and define its mandate. The trade board has a specific mandate, a defined leadership structure and a meetings schedule. It is led by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, alongside Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng. Last week, the Chinese embassy in Washington said the Board of Investment would provide an “institutionalised communication platform for both sides”, adding that economic and trade teams were “conducting regular dialogue on potential investment opportunities and barriers”. A similar process is under way to identify potential investment opportunities in both countries but the focus remains on deals in the US, given the political sensitivities surrounding Chinese investment, the SCMP has learned. Multiple sources said negotiators were discussing a shortlist of projects for potential Chinese investment in non-sensitive sectors in the US, with electric vehicles, battery storage and power equipment infrastructure among the sectors under consideration. Two of the sources said these areas could still be politically sensitive and commercially risky for Chinese companies, leaving open the possibility that the negotiating team could settle on investments in consumer goods instead. Another source added that the investment board continued to face opposition from US business leaders concerned about exposing domestic industries to greater competition from Chinese firms. The source said that most “low-hanging” fruit had already been plucked and the current set of issues was “difficult” and had “major gaps”. The SCMP reported last month that differences between Washington and Beijing over potential investment announcements played a role in the exclusion of Chinese business leaders from the White House state dinner and meetings in September. Despite opposition from US car manufacturers and lawmakers, Trump has repeatedly floated the idea of allowing Chinese companies to set up shop there. “If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I’d be OK with it,” he told Fox News last month. Two sources said that large-scale, long-term Chinese investment in the US was unlikely, regardless of the sectors involved, given the political realities of the bilateral relationship and uncertainty over Washington’s policymaking. Beyond the investment track, extending the trade truce is another key item on the bilateral agenda. The expansive deal, signed in Busan, South Korea last year, was extended by just two months, to January 2027, during Xi’s visit in September. Three sources said that both Beijing and Washington were seeking to exploit leverage points – rare earths for China, jet engine and aircraft parts for the US – to maximise gains in extending the Busan trade agreement. The original deal reduced US tariffs on some Chinese goods and put additional American restrictions on Chinese-affiliated companies on hold. It also suspended certain Chinese rare earth export controls and reversed the suspension of US export licences for jet engines and other aircraft components supplied to China. One source told the SCMP that while neither side was currently threatening to restrict access to rare earths or aircraft components, each wanted to keep reminding the other of the leverage they held. Two sources said China was “dismayed” by the two-month extension but viewed the shorter time frame as an opportunity to strengthen its bargaining position on purchase commitments, particularly for Boeing aircraft. Meanwhile, Washington saw it as a chance to press Beijing further on expanding flows of rare earths and push for increased Chinese purchases of agricultural products, they added. During Trump’s visit to China in May, Beijing agreed to buy 200 Boeing aircraft but the deal has yet to materialise. A source said that while the discussions surrounding the agreement were moving in a “positive direction”, an announcement at Apec seemed to be less likely. Another source added that Beijing was using the Boeing order as a bargaining chip in trade truce talks. Another source noted that Beijing was also reluctant to increase critical mineral supplies, viewing them as its “most effective economic weapon”. However, both sides recognised there was no alternative to an extension, three sources noted. Negotiations may not conclude in time for an Apec announcement and could spill over into the G20 summit in December, they said. Last week, the Chinese embassy observed that last month’s temporary extension gave “both sides room to take stock of and assess the implementation of the joint arrangements”. “It is believed that the two sides will continue their efforts and seek a positive solution on a further extension through high-level economic and trade interactions before the end of the year,” the embassy added. Additional reporting by Dewey Sim and William Zheng

title: US orders DeepSeek removed from federal systems, citing national security risks
description: Citing national security concerns, the US government has ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products and any third-party services developed using the Chinese artificial intelligence model from their information systems. In a notice made public on Monday, the Department of Homeland Security also barred agencies from acquiring DeepSeek products and services, including those developed by affiliated entities. The notice said that using the company’s products “may result in the...
content: Citing national security concerns, the US government has ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products and any third-party services developed using the Chinese artificial intelligence model from their information systems. In a notice made public on Monday, the Department of Homeland Security also barred agencies from acquiring DeepSeek products and services, including those developed by affiliated entities. The notice said that using the company’s products “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to ‌the PRC if used by US government employees or ⁠vendors”, adding that the models “themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities”. The underlying order was signed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on July 24. On Tuesday, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said that “China consistently opposes overstretching the concept of national security and politicising tech and trade issues” when asked about the DeepSeek ban. “We will resolutely safeguard Chinese businesses’ lawful rights and interests,” she added. DeepSeek shook up global markets and the AI industry in 2025 with the release of its R1 model. US President Donald Trump called the breakthrough a “wake-up call” for America’s tech sector. The start-up has since faced scrutiny from Washington policymakers who see its Chinese ownership as a threat to America’s national security. The House Select Committee on China published a report in April 2025 claiming DeepSeek represented a “profound threat to our nation’s security”. In June 2025, US lawmakers introduced the “No Adversarial AI Act” that sought to restrict the federal use of China-linked artificial intelligence tools such as DeepSeek. “We are in a new Cold War – and AI is the strategic technology at the centre,” said committee chairman John Moolenaar after the act was announced. At the time, Liu Pengyu, a spokesperson for Beijing’s embassy in the US, told the South China Morning Post that Congress’ allegations of Chinese technology theft were “nothing but slander and smears”. “China actively promotes innovation in artificial intelligence, and places high importance on AI safety and ethics,” Liu said in an emailed response. A separate bill, called the “No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act”, was also introduced in the House of Representatives in February 2025. A Senate version followed later that month. The bipartisan legislation seeks to ban DeepSeek from federal government devices. Monday’s announcement is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to restrict Chinese technology as the two countries compete for global AI leadership. Several other federal agencies, including the Department of Commerce and the Navy, have restricted the use of DeepSeek on government devices. Meanwhile, DeepSeek topped a “trending software vendors” list from New York-based corporate spending platform Ramp in June 2026, as US businesses seek more affordable alternatives to expensive American AI providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic. “In probably the biggest sign that companies are looking for cheaper alternatives to OpenAI and Anthropic, some are willing to use cheaper, Chinese models, sending US data back and forth from China-hosted servers,” said Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp Economics Lab, at the time.

title: US-China AI talks must ensure safety of both tech and business
description: In New York last month, US-China talks on artificial intelligence opened up a path of cooperation. This was affirmed by the Xi-Trump summit in Washington where both presidents agreed to establish a formal AI dialogue and hotline. With the next AI meeting set to happen in November, it is imperative that both countries further cooperation. The AI ecosystem is in flux. American tech companies are draining their coffers as they commit vast sums to chips, data centres and energy before the revenue...
content: In New York last month, US-China talks on artificial intelligence opened up a path of cooperation. This was affirmed by the Xi-Trump summit in Washington where both presidents agreed to establish a formal AI dialogue and hotline. With the next AI meeting set to happen in November, it is imperative that both countries further cooperation. The AI ecosystem is in flux. American tech companies are draining their coffers as they commit vast sums to chips, data centres and energy before the revenue model is even settled. Trillions of dollars are being committed to the AI buildout. While this exposure is not the same as the overleveraging in the mortgage market that triggered the 2008 global financial crisis, a sudden bursting of the AI bubble could have far-reaching consequences. Much of US economic growth this year has been from AI or AI-enabling companies. Yet, only 38 per cent of Americans saw “more benefits than drawbacks” in AI products and services – well below the global average – against 85 per cent in China, according to the Ipsos AI Monitor 2026. In May, the Ipsos Consumer Tracker found that most Americans would oppose a data centre in their community. The surge in AI capabilities has raised concerns. Rogue AI agent behaviour has gone from attempting to delete an entire email inbox to escaping sandboxes to launch cyberattacks. In July, during an isolated evaluation, OpenAI agents circumvented their restrictions to launch autonomous attacks on developer platform Hugging Face. That same month, Calif, a small US security company, created WeWorm to exploit a zero-click vulnerability in WeChat’s calling system, enabling it to seize accounts and spread between phones without the recipient answering. In India, cybersecurity researchers at Hacktron used Anthropic’s Claude models to break into OpenAI, compromising employee accounts and reaching potentially sensitive software systems. Both hacking incidents were conducted under friendly auspices and caused no damage – Tencent Holdings and OpenAI were quickly alerted and patched the bugs. But they portend the threat of AI-enabled cyberattacks, both from poorly managed AI and actors empowered by the devolution of yet more cyberwarfare capabilities into private hands. Encapsulating the moment is the increasingly urgent call for safeguards by leading AI developers and scientists. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposes opening up leading laboratories to permanent independent evaluators and coordinating safety standards across companies and governments, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is committing its models to third-party evaluation, and Google DeepMind chairman Demis Hassabis is backing pre-deployment testing of frontier systems. Last week, an open letter by at least 420 scientists across the globe called for urgent measures to prevent an AI fallout, including the creation of an international body to record and track containment failures. These concerns provide an agenda for the coming US-China AI dialogue. Talks, however, should extend beyond managing incidents and developing safeguards towards building a sustainable business case for AI. Given its increasingly self-sustaining AI ecosystem, China has plenty to contribute. First, it is clear the US and China ecosystems possess different pieces of the same business case. American developers need applications capable of converting their frontier performance into sustained revenue. China offers one of the world’s largest environments for testing, refining and commercialising applications across manufacturing, logistics, medicine, education, public services and embodied AI. While China’s industry could benefit from investment and research at the cutting edge of frontier model development, its capabilities in coordinating data centres and power supply could help take the strain off US compute capacity. Cooperation on efficient models, cooling and energy management could help both countries meet rising demand while reducing the costs borne by consumers and communities. A healthy ecosystem has room for both American frontier models and efficient Chinese open-weight models. Chinese open-weight models offer lower costs per token, making them economical companions to American frontier models. Companies can use them for routine, high-volume tasks and reserve frontier models for problems that warrant their capabilities. This high-low mix can make American frontier capabilities more economical to deploy within a wider workflow, strengthening the business case for both countries. To sustain this cooperation, both countries must also confront AI risks and manage them together. The United States and China established one narrow principle two years ago when they affirmed that people, not AI, should decide on the use of nuclear weapons. I propose going further to adopt a reciprocal no-first-use commitment covering AI-enabled autonomous weapons. The final AI issue that must be discussed is institutional. Fragmented governance risks building walls of incompatible standards and duplicated infrastructure. The US-led Pax Silica initiative and China-led World AI Cooperation Organisation should not be posed in opposition to each other. Instead, both countries should place their global AI governance and interests under a shared UN-linked umbrella, giving countries that use AI a voice alongside those that develop it. Finally, an annual US-China AI summit would serve as a strong foundation, bringing governments together with laboratories, scientists, universities, companies and civil society organisations. For now at least, it is still ultimately people who decide what moral value our technology has through what we choose to do with it.

title: Asian-Americans’ trust in Trump fading as economic woes increase, survey finds
description: Asian-Americans are laser-focused on the economy and healthcare costs and increasingly disenchanted with US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party leading into the highly consequential November 3 midterm elections, according to a survey released on Monday. While the general trend among Asian-American and Pacific Islanders (AAPI) mirrors the broader US electorate, the minority community’s views are frequently more pronounced, seen in part because they have been the object of more raids,...
content: Asian-Americans are laser-focused on the economy and healthcare costs and increasingly disenchanted with US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party leading into the highly consequential November 3 midterm elections, according to a survey released on Monday. While the general trend among Asian-American and Pacific Islanders (AAPI) mirrors the broader US electorate, the minority community’s views are frequently more pronounced, seen in part because they have been the object of more raids, detention, visa denial and deportations under the Trump administration. “The ranking of issues is similar. But the level is certainly elevated among Asian-Americans,” said Karthick Ramakrishnan, founder and executive director of AAPI Data, which conducted the data poll with AP-NORC. “Even if people think, ‘Oh, Asians generally are better off economically than the US average,’ this is where even immigration leads to economic insecurity.” Many Asian families also have strong trans-Pacific family ties that have been undercut by Trump’s immigration policies. According to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) data analysed by the Deportation Data Project and Stop AAPI Hate, ICE arrested 21,078 Asian individuals between January 2025 and August 2026, a 436 per cent increase over a similar earlier period, while detentions rose 512 and deportations rose 1,103 per cent. Indians accounted for 29 per cent and Chinese 26 per cent of these arrests. Monday’s survey, conducted from September 8-15, found that nine in 10 AAPI considered the economy central to their midterm voting choice, compared with 73 per cent for healthcare. This comes as consumer confidence declines sharply, inflation accelerates and gas prices rise even as the Iran war that the US president started with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu drags on. Asked how they felt in general about the upcoming election, 18 per cent of respondents said they were “excited”, roughly 40 per cent said they felt either “interested” or “frustrated”, and 27 per cent said they were “fearful”. This compared to 29 per cent of AAPI who felt excited and 37 per cent who felt fearful leading into the 2024 presidential election. The Republican Party’s support has also declined among Asian-Americans, Monday’s survey suggested. In March 2025, AAPI adults were roughly split on whether Republicans or Democrats would better handle the economy and immigration. Now, nearly twice as many said they trusted Democrats to handle these two key issues more than Republicans. “If you look at what the Asian-American community was expecting after the 2024 election, Trump enjoyed a little bit of a honeymoon period. It lasted two months,” said Ramakrishnan. “Asian-Americans thought that they were going to get common-sense policies on border security and strengthening the economy, especially in terms of job creation. “But once he started implementing his day-one executive orders, you started seeing the decline,” added Ramakrishnan, a research director at the University of California, Berkeley. “So it’s not just Democrats who never really liked him and are now even more motivated.” The survey found that around one quarter of AAPI adults have a favourable view of Trump or approve of his job as president, compared with around 33 per cent of overall US voters. According to a report released last week by activist group Stop AAPI Hate, expressions of anti-immigrant hostility rose 50 per cent among 1,825 reported Asian hate incidents between January 2023 and June 2026. The survey found that around one quarter of AAPI adults have a favourable view of Trump or approve of his job as president, compared with around 33 per cent of overall US voters. According to a report released last week by activist group Stop AAPI Hate, expressions of anti-immigrant hostility rose 50 per cent among 1,825 reported Asian hate incidents between January 2023 and June 2026. These “increasingly echo the anti-immigrant rhetoric and policies of the second Trump administration”, the group said. “People are told to ‘go back where they came from’, called ‘spies’ and ‘invaders’, and threatened with deportation.” On other fronts, some two-thirds of AAPI adults said they saw foreign government attempts to influence the US election as a major concern, while over half said the same about domestic rejections of valid ballots or eligible people not being allowed to vote. About half also expressed concern about fake or false candidate information, legal challenges to election results, violence after the election and threats of violence at the polls. During his second term, Trump has tried to restrict mail-in voting, access confidential voter records, require proof of citizenship and claim widespread fraud without proof. And despite several legal setbacks, he has touted these as necessary for election integrity, even as civil rights groups and election scholars frame them as moves to restrict access by his political opponents.

title: Trump says he’s open to meeting Xi and Putin in China for nuclear talks
description: US President Donald Trump said on Monday he was open to a three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to China next month, with nuclear weapons on the agenda. “We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation,” Trump told reporters outside the White House before travelling to Kansas. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it.” Trump said the proposed meeting was his suggestion and linked it to his November...
content: US President Donald Trump said on Monday he was open to a three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to China next month, with nuclear weapons on the agenda. “We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation,” Trump told reporters outside the White House before travelling to Kansas. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it.” Trump said the proposed meeting was his suggestion and linked it to his November visit to China, but no date or agenda had been agreed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last week that such talks would be beneficial. “If we can do denuclearisation, I will have done the world a big, big favour,” Trump said, without explaining the scope of any potential nuclear agreement. His comments came after the Kremlin said the three leaders could meet on the sidelines of next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China and that a potential meeting had come up in talks. Asked whether he would meet Xi and Putin without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky present, Trump said he would pursue talks if they could help end the war in Ukraine. “Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody’s there or not, whatever I can do to end the war,” he said. Separately, Trump expressed uncertainty about a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un during his November trip to Asia. “I don’t know,” he told reporters when asked whether a meeting could take place. “I’m not sure that anybody’s asking for a meeting, but my relationship with Kim Jong-un is very good.” Trump also stepped up his criticism of Zelensky, suggesting someone else should negotiate for Ukraine. “Maybe it’s time for Zelensky to get somebody else to negotiate,” he said. Asked about criticism that he was supporting Putin by waiving sanctions, Trump replied: “I’m supporting stopping the war between Russia and Ukraine.” He went on to question Zelensky’s willingness to end the conflict, without providing evidence. “Frankly, Zelensky is not helping matters much. I think he doesn’t want to stop it, but I want to see people not die,” Trump said.

title: China’s flag carrier scrambles to fly stranded passengers out of fuel-starved Cuba

content: Dozens of Air China passengers stranded in Cuba by successive cancellations were due to fly out on an extra flight on Monday, as a US oil embargo deepens the island’s energy crisis. The disruption has hit one of Cuba’s last direct air links to Europe, the Chinese carrier’s twice-weekly route between Beijing and Havana via Madrid. Air China added flight CA590 for travellers whose regular CA866 service was cancelled before October 10, the Chinese embassy said in a notice on Sunday. The flight was due to leave at 10.30pm local time, and seats were limited, it said. The embassy had warned on October 10 that flights on the route faced frequent schedule changes and temporary cancellations for “technical reasons”, without giving details. The route has been hard to operate since February, when Cuban airports ran out of jet fuel. Official notices extend the shortage at 10 airports, Havana included, until November. Unable to refuel in Havana, Air China has stopped in Nassau, in the Bahamas, on its return leg to Madrid since March, according to the Cuban independent outlet 14ymedio. A passenger whose flight was cancelled on October 10 told the outlet that airline staff at Madrid-Barajas airport blamed runway repairs in Nassau. The Bahamian airport began rehabilitating one of its two runways in August and expects to finish by October 31. Neither Air China nor the embassy has publicly linked the cancellations to the fuel shortage or to the works in Nassau. The disruption has fallen hardest on Cubans living in Spain, who favour Air China over Spain’s Air Europa, the only other direct carrier between Madrid and Havana, because of its lower fares. Air China relaunched the route in May 2024, and fifth-freedom traffic rights allow it to sell tickets on the Madrid-Havana leg. Passengers in Madrid said they waited more than 15 hours at the airport with little information and struggled to claim refunds or the €600 (US$673) in compensation promised by the airline. Pressure on Havana Air China is one of the few foreign carriers still serving Cuba after at least 11 airlines, including Air Canada, Air France and Turkish Airlines, suspended flights this year as the fuel crisis deepened. That crisis began in January, when the US cut off Venezuelan oil shipments after capturing Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro. Later that month, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order describing Cuba as an “unusual and extraordinary threat”. The pressure has since spread across the economy, and a total collapse of Cuba’s power grid in September left millions without electricity. Havana estimates the US embargo cost the island US$8.1 billion between March last year and February, a figure that excludes the energy restrictions. UN experts warned in August of a growing risk of disease outbreaks on the island. Trump told the UN General Assembly in September that Secretary of State Marco Rubio was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”, although Havana has reported no progress. He also called the island a failed state that “will fall”. The State Department had sanctioned five Cuban state entities and a grandson of former leader Raul Castro earlier that month. CBS News later reported that the US Army Reserve was assessing whether to send units to US Southern Command, in planning officials said was aimed at Cuba. Legal pressure on the Cuban leadership grew on Monday, when Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced a state arrest warrant for Castro. The 95-year-old is accused over the 1996 downing of two civilian planes flown by the Miami exile group Brothers to the Rescue, for which federal prosecutors indicted him in May. Beijing has responded with aid and diplomatic backing, and Chinese President Xi Jinping approved US$80 million in emergency assistance and 60,000 tonnes of rice for Cuba in January. A Chinese vessel delivered 15,000 tonnes of the rice to Havana in May. Speaking at the General Assembly four days after Trump, Vice-President Han Zheng said “the relevant country” should stop threatening Cuba with force and lift the blockade in full. Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said two days later that China would “firmly support” Cuba in safeguarding its sovereignty. Chinese support has also reached Cuba’s crippled transport system, with the embassy in Havana donating 80,000 bicycle spare parts last week. Ambassador Hua Xin said the parts would ease the daily difficulties Cubans face in getting around. China donated parts to repair 100 Havana buses last year. Cuba is due to put its annual resolution against the US embargo to a vote at the UN General Assembly on October 28.

title: Honduras targets Chinese shops, state builder as President Asfura sits on Taiwan pledge

Migration...
content: Honduran migration officials have summoned or placed under review 41 Chinese nationals after inspecting shops in the capital and a hospital being built by a state-owned contractor from China in the south of the country. Teams from the National Migration Institute, working with police and intelligence officers, interviewed 86 Chinese citizens at 54 shops in Comayaguela, Tegucigalpa’s twin city and main commercial district, and told 25 of them to report for further document checks. Migration officers also went to Choluteca, in the south, where China’s SFECO Group is building a regional hospital, and found that 16 of the 128 Chinese workers on site were in an irregular situation. The institute has not said what was wrong with their papers or whether any of them will be deported. The inspections come nine months into the presidency of Nasry Asfura, who campaigned on restoring relations with Taiwan, which his predecessor Xiomara Castro dropped in favour of Beijing in March 2023. Asfura has since ordered a review of the agreements Castro signed with China, but in June his foreign ministry denied holding any official talks with Taipei. Banners reading “Tegucigalpa and Comayaguela say no to Chinese shops” went up along the capital’s commercial avenues during a holiday week in early October, and it was unclear who put them there. Days later, city hall opened its own inquiry into 70 Chinese-owned stores, after Honduran shopkeepers complained that their rivals sold goods below cost. Fredy Casasola, the municipal police judge running the checks, told broadcaster TSi that “around 68 to 70 per cent of these businesses are operating irregularly” and that those which failed to regularise could be shut temporarily or for good. Neither city hall nor the migration institute has said whether the shops visited by migration officers are among the 70. Mayor Juan Diego Zelaya, whose administration is running the inquiry, said nationality played no part in the checks. “We will not allow those who comply with the law to be at a disadvantage against those who may be operating outside it,” he said. Hospital contract signed under Castro Part of the state-owned Shanghai Construction Group, SFECO signed the hospital contract in October 2024. The project is worth more than US$100 million and was due to be finished in November last year, but it is still under construction. Its workforce has been under scrutiny since last year, when El Heraldo newspaper obtained health ministry records showing that Chinese nationals made up a third of the staff on site, about half of them carpenters, rebar workers and bricklayers. “There were specific conditions for the Chinese staff who came to work to be specialised personnel that we did not have in Honduras,” Deputy Health Minister Jose Castillo said in March, adding that he had seen Chinese workers laying bricks during inspections. Wilson Paz, who headed the migration institute under Castro, has said the workers entered the country legally. A resolution passed by Congress in May told state agencies to audit Chinese shops for taxes, imports and the migration status of their staff. Its sponsor, National Party lawmaker Mario Perez, said three years of ties with Beijing had brought retail stores rather than large industrial investment. Migration chief Carlos Cordero later told lawmakers that 24,837 Chinese nationals had entered Honduras irregularly since 2014, with a spike in 2023.

content: The US State Department has added a “wrongful detention” warning to its travel advisory for China, alerting Americans to the risk of being detained arbitrarily under Chinese law. On Monday, the official China travel advisory added the “D” risk indicator for wrongful detention, while maintaining the country’s overall advisory level at Level 2, or “Exercise Increased Caution”. The advisory urges Americans travelling to mainland China to exercise caution due to the “arbitrary enforcement of local laws, the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of wrongful detention”. The move comes as Washington and Beijing seek to maintain an improving bilateral relationship following a warm welcome for Chinese President Xi Jinping by US President Donald Trump during the September visit to Washington. The two leaders are expected to meet twice more this year. A US State Department spokesperson told the South China Morning Post that the department remained committed to providing accurate information to American travellers, and the Trump administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans. “The US Department of State takes seriously its commitment to provide Americans with clear, timely and reliable information about destinations across the globe so they can make informed travel decisions,” the statement said. “The [department] has determined that Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention in China.” Hong Kong is also rated Level 2, while Macau is at Level 3, meaning travellers should reconsider their travel plans. US news outlet Semafor first reported the planned change on Friday, citing sources who said it was related to the detention of two American scholars in China, Chen Youlin and Min Zin. Both have been designated by the US government as wrongfully detained. Chinese authorities have accused Chen of espionage, likely linked to his seismic research, and Zin of espionage and endangering China’s national security. The Chinese embassy in Washington rejected claims of wrongful detention, and said the country’s judicial authorities handle cases in accordance with the law. “China firmly opposes the US side’s attempts to discredit China by citing so-called wrongful detentions as a pretext and updating its travel advisory accordingly,” an embassy spokesperson said. “The US side should promptly withdraw its inaccurate travel advisory, stop disrupting people-to-people exchanges between China and the US, and do more to promote friendly exchanges between the two peoples.” Beijing also accused the US of harassing and interrogating Chinese nationals entering the US, especially Chinese students who were refused entry and sent back. Monday’s move reinstates the “D” indicator, which the State Department removed from its China travel advisory in 2024 after Beijing released several detained Americans. The James W. Foley Legacy Foundation says 12 Americans are currently wrongfully detained in China, including some subject to exit bans. It has assessed 42 cases since 1998, though the total number of Americans caught up in China’s legal system may be higher. Rong Yufang, whose husband, Chen, has been detained since 2024, thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their continued efforts to secure his release. She said Trump had raised Chen’s case with Xi twice when the two leaders met in Beijing in May and Washington in September. “Chinese officials have left the US no choice but to publicly call them out by warning Americans that it is risky to travel to China,” Rong said in a statement. “I am also hopeful that the State Department will raise the travel risk level for China from a 2 to a 3.”

title: Rubio pitches US business in Central Asia, says China ties need not suffer
description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Washington wanted to compete for business in Central Asia without asking countries to stop working with China, as the United States and five regional governments outlined proposals to deepen cooperation on minerals, transport and technology. Speaking in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, Rubio was asked what Washington could offer as Beijing expanded its presence in the region. “I mean, look, it’s competition, right? content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Washington wanted to compete for business in Central Asia without asking countries to stop working with China, as the United States and five regional governments outlined proposals to deepen cooperation on minerals, transport and technology. Speaking in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, Rubio was asked what Washington could offer as Beijing expanded its presence in the region. “I mean, look, it’s competition, right? We have products, we have companies; they make things. And we just want fair competition and an opportunity,” he said. “This is not about coming here to say, ‘Stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country.’” Rubio’s remarks came during a visit for the C5+1 ministerial meeting, which brings together the United States, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. Chinese Premier Li Qiang concluded a two-day visit to Uzbekistan on Sunday, during which he called for closer cooperation in several of the same sectors. Central Asia’s mineral resources, including manganese, titanium and cobalt used in advanced manufacturing, have made the region a focus of competition as Washington seeks to diversify supply chains and Beijing pursues deeper economic ties. In a joint statement on Monday, the six C5+1 governments set out ambitions to expand mineral extraction and processing, improve transport connections and develop regional supply chains. They also pledged to exchange expertise on geological data and promote higher-value products made in Central Asia. The statement highlighted further development of the Trans-Caspian Trade Route, alongside improved customs procedures and regional industrial cooperation, as ways to expand trade and investment with the United States. It also called for digital cooperation using “secure and trusted technology” and expanded opportunities for Central Asian enterprises to invest in and operate in the US market. Much of the document outlined aspirations rather than specific projects. It did not name China or identify funding totals, specific mineral projects or implementation deadlines. Rubio said almost 300 American businesses were accompanying him, with the opportunity to sign agreements worth billions of dollars. Some companies had already reached agreements that would be announced later, he said, without identifying them in the remarks. Uzbekistan wanted economic relations with a range of countries, Rubio added. “We just want to identify opportunities on things we can work together on, and we’re here to do that,” he said. “And that’s not a negative action against any other country.” In bilateral talks, Rubio and Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov agreed to deepen cooperation on critical minerals, according to the State Department. Rubio also welcomed Uzbekistan’s interest in US civil nuclear technology and discussed opportunities for American companies in its space sector. Saidov signed the Artemis Accords, making Uzbekistan the 77th country to endorse the US-led framework of principles for peaceful space exploration. Rubio witnessed the signing. The signing adds a space dimension to Washington’s outreach to Uzbekistan, coming just after Li called for closer aerospace cooperation between Beijing and Tashkent. The accords establish principles for civil space activities; signing does not itself commit Uzbekistan to a particular mission. The American outreach follows Li’s talks with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Prime Minister Abdulla Aripov, during which the Chinese premier urged closer cooperation in energy, minerals, finance, connectivity, artificial intelligence and aerospace, according to Xinhua. Li also backed implementation of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, intended to connect China and Europe through Central Asia while bypassing Russia. Chinese and Uzbek officials signed agreements covering trade, education, customs, healthcare and poverty reduction. Washington had signalled its commercial ambitions before Rubio’s arrival. Sergio Gor, the US ambassador to India and special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs, said last week that American companies wanted to compete for opportunities in the region’s mineral sector.

title: Is China building a fleet of drone motherships to extend its naval reach?
description: A second unusual Chinese vessel suspected of being designed to launch and recover large underwater drones has appeared in Guangzhou, raising questions over whether Beijing is developing a fleet of specialised motherships to extend its undersea operations beyond coastal waters. The smaller vessel, seen under tow on the Pearl River in images circulating online, resembles a ship about 200 metres (660 feet) long seen at a Shanghai shipyard last month that has since been launched. Both feature...
content: A second unusual Chinese vessel suspected of being designed to launch and recover large underwater drones has appeared in Guangzhou, raising questions over whether Beijing is developing a fleet of specialised motherships to extend its undersea operations beyond coastal waters. The smaller vessel, seen under tow on the Pearl River in images circulating online, resembles a ship about 200 metres (660 feet) long seen at a Shanghai shipyard last month that has since been launched. Both feature conspicuous vertical structures at the stern that naval analysts believe could be used to lower large underwater drones into the water and recover them. If confirmed as military motherships, the vessels could enable the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Navy to deploy and recover large uncrewed underwater vehicles (UUVs) far from Chinese ports, potentially expanding its ability to conduct undersea surveillance, seabed mapping and other military missions in the western Pacific, including waters east of Taiwan. However, neither ship’s intended purpose nor operator has been confirmed. The US-based defence news website TWZ said satellite imagery taken on October 2 showed the second vessel at the Guangzhou Shipyard International facility on Longxue Island before its launch. The Naval News website also identified the Longxue Island shipyard as a possible builder, but said further imagery was needed to confirm the vessel’s origin and where it would be fitted out. The media outlet said images of the vessel came from two short videos originally circulated on the Chinese social media platform Weibo, and that the authenticity of the footage remained unconfirmed. The images show tugboats moving the vessel near Guangzhou’s Panyu district. Scaffolding remained on the ship, while sensor and communications equipment had yet to be fitted, according to Naval News. Naval News estimated the Guangzhou vessel’s length at about 150 metres, compared with slightly more than 200 metres (656 feet) for the Shanghai vessel. Although their hull shapes differ, both have raised deckhouses towards the bow, hangar-like spaces and large openings at the stern. The Guangzhou vessel has six tall vertical posts near its stern, compared with 12 of varying heights on the Shanghai ship. Thomas Lim, an associate research fellow with the Military Studies Programme at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, said the vessels appeared to be able to carry multiple underwater drones, with the rear openings and ramps supporting the mothership hypothesis. However, he cautioned that the imagery offered only a “partial fit” and that confirming their intended role would require evidence of completed supporting facilities, including cranes and docks, as well as “proof of concept in deployment or tests”. Neither ship has been observed deploying underwater drones. In a Naval News report on September 15, analyst H.I. Sutton assessed the Shanghai vessel under construction at Hudong-Zhonghua shipyard as a possible mothership for very large underwater drones. An experienced military imagery analyst who reviewed the same September 10 imagery for the South China Morning Post said he could independently identify the apparent stern launch-and-recovery system. A cradle positioned behind the vessel seemed narrow enough to pass through its rear opening, the analyst added at the time. The construction of the suspected motherships comes as China has been testing two very large underwater drone prototypes measuring an estimated 35 and 45 metres long in Hainan, according to Sutton. So far, floating docks have been used to carry these craft out to sea for testing and recovery afterwards. If built for that role, the two vessels could offer greater flexibility by transporting underwater drones towards distant operating areas, recovering them after missions and providing facilities for maintenance or preparation between deployments. Peter Jones, a retired Australian vice-admiral, said the smaller vessel might be intended to support “a different class of UUV” or reflect “another base ship design”, potentially one familiar to its builder. He said that if underwater drones proved effective, more motherships would be needed as their numbers increased. That could require modifying existing vessels or adapting established designs to allow “multiple shipyards to meet the demand”. Lim, however, noted that the differences in size could reflect “variety” within the same design or requirements for “different operational theatres”, rather than evidence that China was moving beyond experimentation towards a broader underwater drone capability. While the vessels might still be for civilian purposes, they face risks in contested waters if deployed militarily. In the SCMP’s report on the Shanghai vessel in September, China military analyst Timothy Heath warned that such a large support ship would be a vulnerable target, better suited to operating relatively close to China in less hostile conditions.

title: Taiwan coastguard wards off 16 mainland ships as Beijing turns up the pressure
description: Taiwan’s coastguard said it warded off 16 mainland Chinese vessels in one day after they sailed into the island’s self-defined restricted waters in a coordinated, multi-pronged operation that experts say points to a shift in Beijing’s maritime pressure tactics.
