The vessels – 12 coastguard and research ships, as well as four fishing boats – operated simultaneously on Sunday in waters east of Hualien, south of Pingtung, southwest of Kaohsiung and around the Taiwan-controlled Dongsha Islands,...
content: Taiwan’s coastguard said it warded off 16 mainland Chinese vessels in one day after they sailed into the island’s self-defined restricted waters in a coordinated, multi-pronged operation that experts say points to a shift in Beijing’s maritime pressure tactics. The vessels – 12 coastguard and research ships, as well as four fishing boats – operated simultaneously on Sunday in waters east of Hualien, south of Pingtung, southwest of Kaohsiung and around the Taiwan-controlled Dongsha Islands, according to the Coast Guard Administration (CGA). “The CGA monitored the maritime situation throughout the operation and immediately dispatched coastguard vessels to forward positions, where they closely monitored the mainland vessels and broadcast warnings ordering them to leave,” it said in a statement on Sunday. The agency described the activities as “hybrid warfare” intended to expand Beijing’s jurisdictional claims. It accused Beijing of pursuing “law enforcement in name, expansion of authority in reality” to create the impression that it exercised jurisdiction over the waters. The operation comes amid growing concern among security experts that Beijing is increasingly using coastguard, maritime law enforcement and research vessels to apply pressure around Taiwan, rather than relying predominantly on the People’s Liberation Army. Ma Chen-kun, a professor of PLA affairs at National Defence University in Taoyuan, said Beijing’s focus had gradually shifted this year from navy-led grey-zone operations towards asserting jurisdiction through coastguard, maritime patrol and research vessels. “For Beijing, such measures produce more concrete results than conventional military grey-zone operations,” Ma said. He described the approach as a strategy of “leaving the islands but taking away the surrounding seas” – gradually squeezing the waters around Taiwan and its outlying islands without provoking an outright military conflict. Ma said the approach, already evident in the South China Sea, was increasingly being seen in waters east of Taiwan as well as around Quemoy, Matsu, Dongsha and the Taiwan-controlled Taiping Island in the South China Sea’s Spratly archipelago. Quemoy is also known as Kinmen. His assessment broadly echoes an October 8 analysis by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, which said Beijing had stepped up law enforcement, maritime surveillance, fisheries and research activities east of Taiwan since June. The London-based think tank described the proliferation of mainland Chinese actors as a significant development in Beijing’s grey-zone strategy, potentially aimed at establishing a more complex system of maritime governance around Taiwan involving military and civilian agencies. The increased activity has also raised questions over whether Taiwan can sustainably respond vessel-for-vessel without straining its own coastguard resources. Dennis Blair, a retired US Navy four-star admiral and former commander of the US Pacific Command, said in a video address to a maritime security conference in Taipei last week that Taiwan should not automatically shadow every mainland ship or aircraft. Taipei should instead allocate its limited resources according to the level of threat, retain operational flexibility and strengthen maritime surveillance, law enforcement and self-defence capabilities, he said. Taipei has increasingly looked to learn from the Philippines and its policy of “active transparency”, under which Manila has publicised confrontations with mainland Chinese vessels in the South China Sea. Taiwan’s coastguard plans to send a vessel carrying about 100 officers and students to the Philippines next October, its first such visit in 53 years. Taipei also donated a retired patrol vessel to Manila last month. Taiwan’s National Security Council deputy secretary general Lii Wen has called for greater technological and maritime law enforcement cooperation between the two in areas including maritime domain awareness, unmanned systems and less-lethal weapons. Sunday’s operation was the latest in a series of encounters this month. Taiwan’s coastguard said it had driven mainland coastguard vessels away from waters around Dongsha on 11 occasions this year, involving 14 vessel appearances before the latest operation. Since the start of this month, it has warded off 29 mainland coastguard, research, survey and fishing vessel appearances, including 16 from Sunday. In a more serious incident on October 1, a Taiwanese coastguard vessel used a water cannon to drive away a mainland fishing boat that refused to leave restricted waters near the Dongsha Islands, prompting a strong protest from Beijing. For Ma, the broader significance lies in Beijing’s apparent effort to turn repeated peacetime activity into assertions of jurisdiction – pressure that remains below the threshold of armed conflict but could gradually reshape practices in waters surrounding Taiwan. Blair warned that the threshold would change sharply if Beijing escalated pressure by intercepting or boarding commercial vessels, forcing them to change course or imposing an effective blockade. Such actions, he said, would move beyond grey-zone coercion and amount to acts of war. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Local golfers briefly top Hong Kong Open     leaderboard in strong start on day one
description: Matthew Cheung and Isaac Lam are the first two city players to lead the standings in the tournament’s 67-year history.
content: In the 67 years the Link Hong Kong Open has been in existence, the leaderboard has never featured two local players at the top – Matthew Cheung and Isaac Lam briefly changed that on Thursday. Out among the morning groups, the pair carded matching six-under-par 64s, a score South Korea’s Kim Mink-yu also posted, to sit one-stroke clear of a bunched chasing pack at Hong Kong Golf Club. The trio were later overhauled by Jazz Janewattananond and Poosit Supupramai, who shot 63s, while Anirban Lahiri and Kevin Yuan upstaged everyone with rounds of eight under. “I did a good job of keeping it in play,” Lahiri said. “I made a few more putts today from outside 10 feet, nothing crazy, but I gave myself a lot of looks. I know I made nine birdies, but there were another five or six inside 15 feet that didn’t go in, so that’s a really solid round.” The early pace setters ultimately found themselves in a four-way tie for fifth, with Japan’s Yosuke Asaji joining them on six under. And a day of low scoring ended with just three shots separating the next 18 players from the leaders. Gusting winds aside, all those on the right side of par made the most of the generous pin positions, and eagles were not the rarity they often are. Janewattananond had two of the 21 registered throughout the day, going back-to-back on 13 and 14. Lam holed out from the fairway on the par-4 sixth for his eagle, sending a six iron 170 yards into the cup. “I was really struggling in the wind last week in Macau,” said Lam, who alongside Cheung missed the cut at the SJM Macau Open. “So, I just really worked on flying the ball well with my coach John [Wallet], and then had quite a good number, 170 yards, six iron, 10 per cent of wind, and then tracking right on line, and then just got lucky and dropped in the hole.” Cheung, meanwhile, captured his eagle at the par-5 13th during a remarkable opening to his round, which began at 11 and included birdies at 12, 14 and 15. Dropped shots at the first and ninth were the only blips in a round that also saw the 31-year-old birdie two, three and 10. “It was a bit of a blur, honestly,” Cheung said of his flying start. “I hit a lot of good shots, it was very gusty this morning, so it was actually tough to judge the wind out there. I hit a lot of good putts which just happened to hit the hole and go in. “So, you know, I’m just really happy and blessed with that stuff.” Of the other Hongkongers in the field, amateur Jeffrey Shen was next best placed on four under, with Jason Hak Shun-yat two shots further back on 68. Taichi Kho and Leon D’Souza, a late replacement for Max Lee Chieh-po, finished with 69s, while amateur Juan Tian went around in level par.

title: European EV production drive sees China’s lithium-ion battery exports to EU surge
description: Customs data also shows Chinese inverter exports to bloc rose despite exclusion from publicly funded projects.
content: China’s lithium-ion battery exports to the EU surged in the first three quarters of this year, as Chinese carmakers rush to build factories in Europe amid a tightening of import restrictions on electric vehicles (EVs). Power inverter exports to the bloc’s members also grew strongly despite EU efforts to exclude Chinese products from publicly funded energy projects. Shipments of Chinese lithium-ion batteries to the EU were worth US$31.2 billion in the first nine months of the year, up 46 per cent year on year, according to Chinese customs data released on Tuesday, and accounted for just under 40 per cent of China’s total lithium-ion battery exports. The value of lithium-ion battery exports to Austria surged by 241 per cent year on year, with Bulgaria recording a 178 per cent increase, Hungary up 156 per cent and Poland witnessing a jump by 132 per cent. China’s total exports of lithium-ion batteries in the first three quarters were worth US$78.8 billion, up 42.2 per cent year on year. Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief Asia-Pacific economist at French investment bank Natixis, said the increase was “closely tied to the ramp-up of Chinese battery and EV production in Central and Eastern Europe”. “Broader demand from Chinese carmakers’ local assembly – and their European supply chains – in these markets is likely contributing, alongside continued strong European demand for both EV and energy-storage batteries,” she said. With the EU imposing additional tariffs on Chinese EVs, Chinese carmakers have been accelerating their localisation efforts in Europe, a trend made more urgent by the recently reached agreement between Beijing and Brussels on import quotas for Chinese-made hybrid vehicles. Trade tensions and de-risking policies will keep pressure on pure exports of finished goods Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Natixis Xpeng has a production line in Europe in partnership with a contract manufacturer in Austria, and BYD has said its plant in Hungary will begin operations in the fourth quarter of this year. At this month’s Paris Motor Show, state-owned Changan Automobile announced plans to increase its production capacity in the EU in the next four years. “Trade tensions and de-risking policies will keep pressure on pure exports of finished goods,” Garcia-Herrero said, adding that she expected component and intermediate shipments to support EV production in Europe would remain solid. In the clean energy sector, power inverters have also become a point of contention between China and the EU. The devices convert renewable energy into grid-compatible electricity. In May, the bloc barred Chinese inverter suppliers from EU-funded projects, citing cybersecurity and dependency concerns. However, Chinese customs data showed that China’s inverter exports to EU rose 34.5 per cent year on year to US$1.7 billion in the third quarter of the year. Exports to countries including Ireland, Portugal, Poland and Romania more than doubled, while the value of shipments to Slovakia surged by more than 400 per cent year on year. Garcia-Herrero attributed the continued export growth to Chinese manufacturers’ significant advantages in costs and technology, adding that commercial, industrial and residential demand remained robust, with the bloc’s restrictions on Chinese inverters only applying to EU-funded projects. Chinese companies dominated the European inverter market last year, supplying more than 80 per cent of the region’s inverters, according to report issued by British energy research firm Wood Mackenzie in July. In the third quarter of this year, the value of China’s global inverter exports rose 31.9 per cent year on year to US$4.5 billion.

title: Meet Alan Bersten, who stepped in for Val Chmerkovskiy on Dancing with the Stars
description: The pro dancer waltzed with Jenna Dewan after Chmerkovskiy was pulled from the show for a week over a social media post defending his wife, Jenna Johnson.
content: Dancing with the Stars’ Val Chmerkovskiy did not accompany Jenna Dewan on the stage for the show’s “Dedication Night” this week. This came after he was suspended for making an inappropriate reference to Will Smith’s infamous Oscars run-in with Chris Rock while defending his wife, Jenna Johnson, from judge Carrie Ann Inaba’s critiques. “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night,” Chmerkovskiy, 40, wrote in a now-deleted TikTok story. The professional dancer was seemingly alluding to the 2022 incident at the Academy Awards ceremony, where Smith slapped Rock on stage after the comedian made a joke about his wife Jada Pinkett Smith. Chmerkovskiy’s post came after his wife, Johnson, who is also a pro dancer on the show, was criticised for her performance by Inaba. BBC Studios, which produces DWTS, later announced Chmerkovskiy was pulled from the show for a week. “Val’s social media post was inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show. As a result, he will not participate in next week’s show,” the company said of Chmerkovskiy’s suspension, the first in the show’s history. Chmerkovskiy responded to the ban on Instagram, saying his remarks were made “in a moment where my instinct was to defend my wife”. “I made a poor decision to reference a meme to ‘keep my wife’s name’ out of the conversation, without stopping to think through what else that reference could imply, which was genuinely never my intention,” he wrote. “Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was. “The last thing I want is to become a distraction from an important week or from the incredible work my dance partner Jenna Dewan is putting in. Please send Carrie Ann, Jenna, and the whole DWTS family lots of love during Dedication Night. I’ll be watching and cheering everyone on!!” he added. During his absence, Dewan danced alongside Alan Bersten on October 20. Bersten had been eliminated earlier this season. In response to Dewan and Bersten’s performance, Chmerkovsky left a comment under the pro-dancer’s Instagram post to thank him, saying: “Thank you for stepping in and doing such an amazing job. Jenna looks so good and most importantly happy. You’re my new favourite follow.” Here’s everything you need to know about Alan Bersten, who replaced Chmerkovskiy during his one-week absence on DWTS. What is Alan Bersten’s background? Alan Bersten was born in May 1994 and hails from Minnesota. He is of Russian heritage and reportedly started dancing when he was only seven after his parents encouraged him and his two siblings to pursue the sport. In an interview with Mpls St Paul magazine, a monthly lifestyle magazine focusing on the Minnesota twin cities of Minneapolis and Saint Paul, Bersten revealed that his parents even opened a dance studio for him and his siblings. “My parents wanted me and my brother and sister to start dancing, but they had never danced in their lives,” he told the magazine. “They found a ballroom dance studio, but it really wasn’t good enough. So they took a weird risk and opened a dance studio for us.” His professional dancing career Despite growing up dancing, Bersten told the Mpls St Paul magazine that he had never imagined making a career out of dancing. In 2013, the ballroom dancer appeared as a contestant on Season 10 of Fox network’s So You Think You Can Dance. “I made it to the Top 20. At that point I was like ‘wow, maybe I could do this, I could pursue this as a career,’” Bersten said. Bersten joined DWTS as a professional partner in 2017. Who is Alan Bersten dating? Bersten is currently dating fellow DWTS pro Emma Slater. The pair announced their relationship during a performance for the DWTS tour in 2025, where they kissed mid-routine. Slater was previously married to Sasha Farber, also a pro dancer on DWTS, from 2018 to 2023. Meanwhile, Bersten had been romantically involved with his former celebrity partner, Alexis Ren.

title: From New York to Jeju Island: an American joins South Korea’s famed female free divers
description: Kylie Genter embraces her life as a Jeju Island haenyeo, free diving with her older colleagues and adapting to a changing sea.
content: By Lee Hae-rin For American Kylie Genter, a day at the beach is no longer a day off for sunbathing and swimming. Instead, it is a place where she prays for her safety before diving into the waters to gather abalone and shellfish for a living. What others see as a holiday destination has become, to her, a workplace and a landscape of possibilities. Since she began diving as a haenyeo – female divers who harvest seafood by hand – in January 2024, the work has changed how she sees the sea. Finding her place Genter, now in her mid-thirties, arrived in South Korea as an English teacher in 2012. She moved to Jeju Island in 2016. While working as a tour guide, she received many questions about haenyeo, and that prompted her to enrol in a diving school in 2018. She eventually took up the work after learning that Youngrak village was recruiting younger divers. “When I first started, they didn’t really know my name,” she says. The veterans would call her “Hey” or “American kid”. Within that circle, Genter found her role as an extra pair of strong hands. Struggling at first to understand the local dialect, she decided to contribute through physical work. Since her first day on the job, she has arrived early to sweep the changing room, wash dishes and help carry the catches ashore, a practice called mulmajung. Relatives traditionally provided that assistance, she explains, but as their family members aged or moved away, divers increasingly did the work to help one another. “You want to be careful because you don’t want to hurt their pride,” she says. Their community is small enough for one person’s absence to change its mood. Eight haenyeo were working there when Genter joined; four retired earlier this year. Each remaining veteran, or samchun in the Jeju dialect, brings something distinct. Hong Bok-nyeo, 80, leads on shore and underwater, and recently brought in almost twice anyone else’s catch. Jwa Bok-hee, 70, helps bridge the generations, explaining the dialect and recalling a more abundant sea. Kim Won-ok, 79, knows how to tie equipment securely and repair torn diving suits. When Jwa Young-ja, 88, practised saying Genter’s name with the younger divers until she could say it easily, the gesture surprised and touched her. Choi Jung-yoon, one of the younger divers, says Genter sets an example for younger recruits, putting the veterans first and helping without pulling rank. “She always takes the initiative and quietly helps,” Choi says. As diving partners, they watch each other descend and resurface, checking whether older colleagues look tired or need help getting ashore. Hong, who has been diving for 63 years, describes Genter and Choi as “first-rate haenyeo”, praising their skill and courtesy. Lessons from summer camp Genter’s preparation for the work began, unexpectedly, in rural upstate New York. She spent her first four years living at the summer camp where her father worked. Childhood meant playing in the woods, taking swimming lessons and, later, lifeguarding. Even making friendship bracelets proved useful, as preparing diving equipment requires knowing how to tie knots. “So everything is from that summer camp,” she says, laughing. Her father supported her decision to become a haenyeo. Her mother initially worried about the danger, but began proudly telling others about her daughter’s work after reading books and articles about the divers. Her young nephews found another reason for excitement: after spotting an octopus at Costco, during a family call they asked her how to catch and cook one. Diving into the future For the next generation of haenyeo, continuing the tradition means earning enough to keep diving while adapting to a changing sea. Away from the water, Genter runs a pet boarding business and gives talks about haenyeo. Choi performs and organises stand-up comedy shows and secured a government grant for a village show that brought divers together to perform. Their overlapping commitments help them continue diving, but demand a delicate balance. “You need to have other jobs to make money, but it can’t be something that takes up too much time that you can’t dive or can’t be available,” Genter says. That effort makes portrayals of haenyeo as a disappearing figure particularly frustrating. To Genter, those accounts overlook younger women working multiple jobs to enter and remain in the profession. “They have like two jobs, three jobs, four jobs,” she says. “They’re all working really hard to be able to achieve this goal.” Hong’s concern is what will remain for them to harvest. The sea is profoundly different from the one she knew in her youth, she says. With the decline in vital marine species, she wonders how long newcomers can continue to dive and harvest. Genter believes future divers will need to adjust to changing species, harvesting methods and rules while preserving resilience and caring for one another. “Different things will come, and we will have to adapt to whatever new things are coming,” she says. She hopes the sea will be different rather than empty – and that younger haenyeo will be recognised as people shaping the tradition, not simply inheriting its decline. For Genter, that future rests on the collective life surrounding each dive: bathing together, eating together and looking out for one another. Her sense of kinship extends beyond Youngrak village to younger divers elsewhere whom she follows online. “If I see any haenyeo on Instagram, I automatically follow them. You are my sister, my comrade,” she says. “Every success that another haenyeo has is a success for all of us.” Read the full story at The Korea Times.

title: Meet Victoria’s Secret model Barbara Palvin’s sister, Anita, who planned her wedding
description: When the Hungarian supermodel married Dylan Sprouse in 2023, her older sister helped plan the celebrations – but who exactly is she?
content: On October 18, Hungarian supermodel Barbara Palvin walked the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show runway, just six weeks after giving birth to her first child with husband Dylan Sprouse. The 33-year-old reportedly welcomed daughter Sylvie on September 7 and had a “great night with [her] newborn” before returning for the VS show in Los Angeles, she told People. “I’m going to be six weeks postpartum tomorrow, which is, I think in the US, most people have to go back after six weeks. So it’s not that big of a deal,” she added. The new mother, who also walked in the show last year, flexed her muscles on the runway while her 34-year-old husband cheered her on. Speaking to People, she described motherhood as a “roller coaster”, but added that she was “feeling great”. “I think it’s very empowering that the Victoria’s Secret team is having me at the show and we’re supporting women,” Palvin said. Away from the runway, one woman who has always been in the model’s corner is her older sister, Anita Palvin. So, who is Anita Palvin? What is Anita Palvin’s background? Anita Palvin was born on March 15, 1990, in Budapest, Hungary, to parents István and Ágnes Palvin. She keeps a low profile, and there is little information about her childhood, but Barbara shared in an interview with W Magazine that she grew up in an “average family”. The sisters seem to be very close, and the model shared in a Yahoo Beauty interview that she got her first Kindle from Anita. What does Anita Palvin do? According to Anita Palvin’s LinkedIn, she attended the hospitality management school Glion Institute of Higher Education in Montreux, Switzerland. In her 2016 Yahoo Beauty interview, Barbara spoke about starting an event planning company with her sister. Anita’s current occupation is unknown, but her sister shared in a 2024 People interview that they were both in Los Angeles at the time. She planned Barbara and Dylan’s wedding View this post on Instagram When it came to planning her wedding, Barbara Palvin tapped her older sister. “We didn’t have a planner, so Barbara and her sister [Anita] planned most of it. They told me my only job was to show up and say the right name,” Sprouse told Vogue. The couple made their vows in the same church in Albertirsa, Hungary, where Barbara’s parents were wed 34 years ago. The celebrations took place at Hungary’s Harlekin Birtok estate, which is owned by the Palvin family and is known for hosting events. Barbara told People she was “very proud” of the wedding. “It was just my sister and me doing everything. It was everything I wanted and more,” she recalled.

title: How Stockport County became ‘bigger than Manchester United’ in China
description: President Steve Bellis will lead an 11-day tour from Saturday, after quarter century of romance, rickshaw races and life-changing cash gifts.
content: Around six years ago, during one of his 105 visits to China, Steve Bellis was approached by a Scotsman at a British Council function. “He said, ‘Remind me to tell you my Stockport County story before I leave’,” Bellis said. “I said, ‘Hang on a minute, I do the Stockport County stories around here’.” The president of the high-flying League One club, which he first joined 37 years ago, Bellis does indeed boast an endless stream of tales about his beloved Stockport. The man from Glasgow’s was another for the canon. “He studied Mandarin and had taken a gap year teaching English in a remote part of Xinjiang,” Bellis said. “He walked into a classroom of about 60 kids, and one was wearing a Stockport County shirt. The guy asked the child how he’d got it, and he looked terrified and said it was his brother’s. “Nobody had an answer, but … he went into a bar in Urumqi and there was a Stockport County scarf on the wall. The manager told him we’d been there years earlier, and that there was evidence of Stockport everywhere”. What was born from a chance encounter in Yang Sing restaurant in Manchester’s Chinatown 25 years ago has matured into a strong bond between a mid-sized northwest outfit that had “built itself up by being creative in the shadow of two of the biggest clubs in England” and a global superpower of 1.4 billion people. In 2004, Stockport attracted more fans to a match in China than either Manchester United or Barcelona managed around the same time. “I used to do a talk called ‘Bigger than United’,” Bellis said. “Admittedly, bigger in Yingkou, and not anywhere else.” Stockport’s multiple trips to China have spawned tales of rickshaw races, romance, feng shui masters, the club’s 50-year-old manager dusting down his boots to play, and cash handouts to stunned strangers. Bellis is set to lead an 11-day tour from Saturday, with former players Mike Flynn, after whom the president’s dog is named, and Kevin Francis in tow. “When we first went in 2001, the players thought it was an inconvenience,” Bellis said. “The current lot are all nagging us to go, because they’ve heard the stories.” Bellis joined Stockport as commercial manager in 1989, when the club had spent years “rooted towards the bottom of the Fourth Division [today’s League Two]”. Employing a number of community initiatives, Bellis helped to swell attendances by 600 per cent and establish the “youngest paying audience in professional football”. By the turn of the century, Stockport were in the second tier and competing with Manchester City and Wolverhampton Wanderers. “The chairman said to me, ‘We’re selling out our corporate spaces and magazine advertising; you’re the corporate guy, what do we do now?’” Bellis said. “I thought we should share the experience of our growth with emerging markets.” He would soon stumble across businessman Peter Gao, “a Chinese guy with a beautiful British accent”, in Yang Sing. Gao mentioned China falling in love with football, after the national team had qualified for the 2002 World Cup. Bellis said: “Thinking quickly, I replied, ‘We’ve been looking at China in terms of helping an emerging [football] market’.” Which was how Stockport home matches would come to host “coachloads of Chinese people from Manchester Business School”. “We gave them a nice meal and got a few drinks down them, so they didn’t realise how bad the football was at times,” Bellis said. “We treated them like VIPs.” Concluding that “China would be an exciting place to be involved”, Bellis recognised that “we weren’t a big enough brand to start pushing ourselves into Beijing, Shanghai or Hong Kong”, instead choosing to take the club to “provinces that people hadn’t seen”. The groundbreaking 2001 postseason tour visited Wuhan, Sichuan and Shaanxi, with Stockport using 75 per cent of their match fees to cover three months’ UK education and coaching for 25 underprivileged Chinese footballers. One of them, Zhang Xiaobin, stayed on Stockport’s books for two years, while becoming “romantically involved” with a Chinese female from the local university to whom the club had introduced him. He would eventually play for Beijing Guoan, via New Zealand and Australia. “People started saying we were a dating service as well as a football club,” Bellis said. The host at Stockport’s first dinner in China related how, explaining his belief that an economic policy should be judged only on its results, former vice-premier Deng Xiaoping said: “It doesn’t matter if a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice.” “Afterwards, one of the players said, ‘Steve, where’s the cat?’. I said, ‘What do you mean?’ He said, ‘he’s going on about this black and white cat’. I told him to forget it.” Bellis recalls two players jumping on rickshaws in Chengdu for a race back to their hotel, with the winning driver receiving the equivalent of around three months’ wages. Stopping on the way to a match, because chairman Brendan Elwood felt queasy on the speeding coach, the Stockport party found itself in “stereotypical Chinese countryside”. “We were in the middle of paddy fields, there was a guy carrying a bamboo pole with two baskets on his back, and we had a whip round for him. It came to about £280 [US$365]. “He was still staring down at this money as we drove off. Someone told us he wouldn’t have earned that in six months. He must have been thinking, ‘All I did was have my picture taken’.” In December 2003, Stockport purchased half of Liaoning Tiger Star, renaming the Chinese second-tier side Stockport Tiger Star and appointing John Hollins, the former Chelsea boss, as manager. They redrew the club’s badge in honour of Stockport’s design, replacing the English club’s two lions with a pair of tigers, and manufacturing £10,000 worth of kit. “We were on the way to the Chinese media launch in the chairman’s [Zhou Shu Yuan] old Mercedes, and he said they’d spoken to their feng shui master, who said you can only have one tiger in any kingdom, so we couldn’t use the kit,” Bellis said. “There are times you have to think on your feet. I said, ‘Chairman Zhou, you’ve not understood this … the tiger on the left has a yellow collar, because it’s female and British, the tiger on the right has a red collar, because it’s male and Chinese. Together, this is the marriage of English and Chinese football’. “He said, ‘The feng shui master will love it’. I thought, ‘Ten grand saved’.” When Stockport travelled to play their Chinese equivalents in 2004, manager Sammy McIlroy saw the 22,000 crowd and said: “I’ve got to play.” “He was 50 and got man of the match,” said Bellis, whose brother Martin, the father of Aston Villa defender Taylor Harwood-Bellis, performed his ‘Vernon Bear’ mascot role for the trip. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Steve Bellis (@steve.bellis65) Following a takeover by Brian Kennedy later that year, Bellis left because he “did not want to hang around while everything we’d built was destroyed”. His new ventures, Lynx International, then Kick Worldwide, maintained the China link, sending players to English clubs and creating the TV show “Soccer Prince”, which attracted 130 million viewers and earned winner Jin Hui, who would play for Beijing Baxi, a place in Everton’s academy. Languishing in National League North seven years ago, Stockport begged Bellis to return as director. “Lots of responsibility and no money, but it’s the club I love,” he said. Under the altruistic ownership of lifelong fan Mark Stott, Stockport have climbed back to League One, where they currently sit top. In 2024, Bellis relaunched the China tours, although the senior team are yet to return, despite players being keen to follow their intrepid predecessors. Last year, 7,000 people watched a Stockport team draw 2-2 with Foshan’s La Liga United in Guangdong. “It had been 100 years since some British missionaries played there and they made a big deal of it,” Bellis said, adding that the visits would soon become biannual. The latest visit will include stops in Beijing and Chengdu. “We always used to say to the Chinese that we were copying their ping pong diplomacy that broke that down diplomatic barriers with America,” Bellis said. “This is football diplomacy.”

title: China’s Gulf oil imports forecast to approach pre-Iran war high as shipments rebound
description: Imports from the Middle East rose for a third straight month in September and could be set for a further boost this month, analyst says.
content: Chinese crude oil imports from the Gulf region are rebounding amid months of disruption from the US-Israel war on Iran and a sharp decline in domestic inventories. Shipments from the Middle East rose 25.7 per cent month on month to 13.8 million tonnes in September, marking a third consecutive monthly increase, according to Chinese customs data. Xu Muyu, a senior crude oil analyst at data intelligence firm Kpler, said demand for Middle Eastern crude was likely to remain strong amid record drawdowns, also pointing to renewed interest in Saudi shipments. “China’s increased buying [of Saudi crude] is mainly driven by a sharp rise in Saudi supplies to Asia and an aggressive pricing strategy that makes Saudi barrels highly competitive in the market,” Xu said. Chinese refiners had been actively bidding for crude from Abu Dhabi and Iraq through spot tenders, she added. The country’s imports from the region were on track to exceed 5 million barrels per day in October, Xu said. That would mark a sharp increase from 3.5 million barrels per day in September and approach the pre-Iran war level of 5.6 million barrels per day recorded in February. Several Middle Eastern producers, including Saudi Arabia and Iraq, have cut the official prices they charge Asian buyers to keep their crude competitive, as shipping disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea have sent freight costs soaring. Saudi Arabia has also restored oil flows through its critical East-West pipeline following attacks by Yemen’s Houthi militant group last month. Meanwhile, China’s onshore crude oil inventories fell by about 1.6 million barrels per day in September, the fastest pace on record, Kpler data showed, though the rate of decline had since slowed to about 400,000 barrels per day so far in October. “China’s seaborne imports have recovered significantly this month,” said Xu, adding that she expected them to keep rising as demand from Chinese refineries increased. Shipments from Russia, China’s biggest foreign supplier of crude oil, fell 11.4 per cent by volume in September from the previous month, dragging overall imports down 2 per cent, customs data showed. Xu said the fall in Russian shipments was likely caused by seasonal maintenance on the country’s pipeline network last month, rather than a deliberate decision by Chinese refiners. “China’s demand for Russian crude remains solid, but future flows will largely depend on supply availability and the economics of Russian barrels,” Xu said. Despite the monthly decline, China’s crude oil imports from Russia remained 20 per cent higher in September than a year earlier, marking a third consecutive month of year-on-year growth. The increase came even as an earlier buying spree slowed after global energy shocks from the Iran war drove Russian crude prices higher.

title: After Tai Po fire, children use play therapy to make slow, steady recovery
description: Trauma-informed interventions are helping 153 pupils affected by the deadly Wang Fuk Court blaze last year build psychological resilience.
content:
Almost a year after a catastrophic fire tore through Hong Kong’s Wang Fuk Court, 11-year-old Jackey* still remembers the home he lost.
“I sometimes think of Wang Fuk Court and the things I left behind,” the Primary Six student said. “I wanted to go back and get them, including the gifts my mum gave me.”
Now living with his parents in a transitional housing flat, Jackey turns to the two calm-down bottles he made himself: transparent containers filled with water, glue and glitter. When distress builds, he shakes them, watching the glitter swirl and slowly settle.
“I shake them and watch them, which makes me calm down,” he said.
The psychological toll of the blaze still lingers. The fire, which broke out at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on November 26 last year, raged for 43 hours. It killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000 residents.
Yet affected residents, including children, are finding ways to cope and rebuild their lives.
Siu Ting, principal of Tai Po Baptist Public School, said students and parents had made progress in their recovery, with families taking part in school activities. “They are actively trying to pull themselves together,” she said.
Jackey, who attends the school, made the bottles during trauma intervention therapies organised by Save the Children Hong Kong for those affected by the fire.
The NGO, together with a research team from Hong Kong Shue Yan University, has provided trauma-informed interventions to 153 affected children across seven Tai Po schools and Trackside Villas, a transitional housing project.
This includes play therapy, comprising six weekly 90-minute sessions in which staff guide pupils through games and role play to express their feelings, relieve anxiety and rebuild a sense of security.
There is also expressive arts therapy, comprising eight weekly sessions, that uses media such as drawing and percussion to help pupils identify and express emotions and improve mental resilience.
Wong Shek-hung, director of the Hong Kong programme at the NGO, said some children were still recovering from the fire. They reacted to sounds of alarms or sudden noises and struggled with painful memories.
Parents, meanwhile, faced pressure to rebuild their homes and uncertainty about their economic and housing prospects, she said.
“We see that children still need time to recover,” she said. “We are not talking about three months or a single term. Some children might take five or six years.”
But Wong said proper mental health support could help speed up the recovery, reduce anxiety and improve psychological resilience.
A study of 51 children who took part in play therapy and 23 who joined expressive arts therapy found that their anxiety levels fell by 85.7 per cent after play therapy.
Distress caused by relocation, loss of familiar surroundings and life changes fell by 65.4 per cent. The study also found that post-traumatic stress symptoms fell by 31.1 per cent among children who underwent play therapy and by 61.2 per cent among those who underwent expressive arts therapy.
Researchers said the findings showed that timely, professional mental health support could mitigate the impacts of trauma on children.
“There was a significant reduction in trauma, whether through the play therapy or the expressive arts therapy – this was the area we most wanted to improve,” said Bess Lam Yin-hung, who was involved in the study. She is an associate professor at Hong Kong Shue Yan University’s department of counselling and psychology.
To extend support to affected children, the NGO said it would continue providing the therapies while making a series of policy recommendations.
These included incorporating children’s mental health recovery into the disaster response mechanism and establishing preventive and early mental health intervention systems in schools.
The NGO urged the government to promote a family-centred mental health support policy. Measures would include increasing interventions, enhancing parent training and emotional support, developing family mental health educational tools and incorporating parent support into regular funding scopes.
It further called for long-term community recovery support systems and diverse, child-friendly mental health intervention models.
“What we need is the support of society as a whole, so that children can keep moving forward,” Wong said.

title: Hong Kong stocks fall most in 7 months as chance of strong stimulus from Beijing shrinks
description: Hang Seng Index caps biggest decline since March and mainland China’s CSI 300 Index enters bear market after 20 per cent pullback.
content: Sell-offs in Hong Kong stocks deepened on Thursday, with the benchmark gauge capping its steepest decline in seven months, as hopes faded that Beijing would implement more meaningful stimulus policies, following latest economic data indicating the annual growth target was within reach. The Hang Seng Index sank 3 per cent to 22,934.68 at the close, its worst single-day performance since March 23. The Hang Seng Tech Index plunged 5 per cent, finishing at a level not seen in two years. Tencent Holdings and Alibaba Group Holding, the most valuable constituents on the city’s benchmark gauge, fell at least 2.9 per cent, as China’s sluggish consumer spending dimmed the earnings outlook of the nation’s biggest internet platforms that remain reliant on e-commerce as their major source of revenue. Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) extended its decline spurred by its interim report showing a slowdown in profit growth. Artificial intelligence model developer MiniMax fell below its initial public offering price for the first time since its debut in January on jitters about stiffer competition. The Chinese mainland’s market fared no better, as the CSI 300 Index slid 1.8 per cent, technically entering a bear market after a 20 per cent pullback from a high on June 22. The chip-centric Star Market 50 gauge retreated 2.8 per cent. Stock traders accelerated the unwinding of equity positions after Wall Street firms made the call that China would withhold major stimulus policies this year, compounding growth concerns. The nation’s economy grew by 4.6 per cent in the first three quarters, slightly above the low end of the government’s goal for the year. While overall growth held up, the divergence of different parts of the economy widened last month, with domestic demand languishing and exports remaining robust. Beijing’s piecemeal stimulus measures disappointed investors, who said that a recent mortgage interest subsidy programme was intended only for buyers of low-priced homes in smaller cities. “In China and Hong Kong, weak domestic demand, limited policy support and continued capital outflows weigh on sentiment,” said Kelly Chung, chief investment officer for multi-assets at Value Partners. “China’s limited stimulus measures disappointed market expectations. Investors have consequently largely priced out the possibility of further near-term stimulus. Near-term market sentiment is likely to remain weak.” A recent speech by the chief of the China Securities Regulatory Commission also fell short of investors’ expectations, concentrating on the approach to fostering long-term market stability rather than any immediate rescue measures that could prop up stocks. The pullback in mainland Chinese and Hong Kong stocks was part of a global unravelling of the AI trade, in which investors have started to question the rationale for huge spending on data-centre buildouts and demand solid evidence of justified returns. Elevated US Treasury yields also reined in risk appetite by compressing equity valuations. “Hong Kong stocks aren’t getting much support fundamentally at this level, amid persistent overseas disruptions,” said Chen Meng, an analyst at Soochow Securities. “Even if there’s a rebound, the upside will be limited and caution should be exercised over the Hong Kong market.” Tencent Holdings, which has an 8.05 per cent weighting on the Hang Seng Index as its second-largest constituent, lost 2.9 per cent to HK$382.40. Alibaba, the third biggest with 7.96 per cent, plunged 6.1 per cent to HK$97.35. Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post. CATL tumbled 7.2 per cent to HK$338.40, extending an 11 per cent decline a day earlier after third-quarter profit growth for the lithium-ion battery maker more than halved from the preceding three-month period. MiniMax, which is a member of the Hang Seng Tech Index, slumped 6.5 per cent to HK$160.70, breaching its offer price of HK$165 in its initial public offering. Elsewhere, Chinese toymaker Bloks Group tumbled 21 per cent to HK$54.60 after its chairman sold a 1.6 per cent stake for HK$250 million (US$31.9 million), a reduction that investors suspected was linked to the purpose of paying a new income tax levied by Beijing on offshore assets held by the wealthy.

title: 5 of the best things to do in Hong Kong this weekend, October 23-25
description: This pre-Halloween weekend offers fantasy art, mushrooms matched with Chinese wine, a Lululemon wellness event and, of course, a scary movie.
content: As we inch closer to the end of October, the city is ready to embrace the spooky and cosy ambience of the season – though the sweltering weather means we cannot ease into an autumnal mood just yet. Whether it is trying dishes with seasonal ingredients or checking out a new movie, here are five things to do in Hong Kong this weekend. 1. M+’s Myths and Monsters As the first major survey exploring two centuries of Asian fantasy visual culture, the latest exhibition at M+, “Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia”, spans four thematic sections that reveal how artists use fantastical storytelling to navigate shifting sociopolitical realities. Featuring more than 400 cross-disciplinary works across fine art, architecture, fashion, video games and film, the display highlights everything from 19th century folklore to Asian surrealism and iconic pop culture phenomena such as Godzilla and Ghost in the Shell. Complementing the exhibition are public lectures, interactive digital experiences, companion film screenings at M+ Cinema, an official co-published research book and exclusive themed merchandise. “Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia”, West Gallery at M+, West Kowloon Cultural District, 38 Museum Drive, Kowloon, until April 4, 2027. General admission tickets cost HK$190 for adults and HK$100 for concessions. Visit the official M+ website for more information. 2. Yunnan Mushroom Harvest Dinner On Friday, October 23, Hong Kong-based natural wine importer Purple Rain is hosting a one-night-only Yunnan mushroom feast at The Mushroom in Central. At this “Harvest Dinner,” guests can enjoy a sharing menu and five drinks from winemaker FARMentation – ranging from sparkling pear cider to high-altitude Medo Syrah – with FARMentation winemaker Yuchen Luo sharing insights. Dishes include Yunnan steam pot chicken with morel mushrooms; tree tomatoes mixed with cucumber flowers; and braised old Kunming abalone with crispy beef. Prices include tables of six for HK$6,888, tables of four for HK$4,888 and shared-table tickets at HK$1,280 per person. Message Purple Rain on Instagram for bookings. The Mushroom, 7/F, California Tower, 30-32 D’Aguilar Street, Central. 3. Lululemon ‘Space to Feel’ If you plan to celebrate Halloween weekend to the fullest, relaxing with a “recovery series” this week might be the ideal way to prepare your body in advance. The Lululemon “Space to Feel” Recovery Series takes place on October 24 and 25 at the Ocean Terminal Deck in Harbour City, Tsim Sha Tsui. Set against the backdrop of Victoria Harbour, this outdoor wellness event runs from 8am to 8.30pm and brings together movement, mindfulness and community connection. For HK$450, attendees can join one of 10 ambassador-led movement classes spanning yoga, dance and functional training, alongside guided harbourfront audio meditations and aroma-and-sound sensory journeys. Each ticket includes a HK$200 Lululemon Harbour City shop voucher, healthy refreshments and a HK$100 donation supporting mental health charity Mind HK. More details can be found at lululemon-spacetofeel.hk. Harbour City, 3-27 Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. 4. Nana Jacqueline pop-up View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jessica Jung (@jessica.syj) In Nana Jacqueline’s first Hong Kong pop-up, the Los Angeles-based womenswear label will be at Lane Crawford in IFC Mall until November 29. The brand is known for blending West Coast ease with Parisian glamour, featuring romantic silk dresses, tweed outerwear and velvet pieces. Those who missed Jessica Jung’s visit to Hong Kong a couple of weeks ago may be happy to learn that the pop-up features a six-piece capsule by the K-pop star. Lane Crawford, IFC Mall, 8 Finance Street, Central. 5. Clayface From Venom and Morbius to Birds of Prey and The New Mutants, elevating side characters to centre stage in Marvel and DC comic-book adaptations rarely takes flight. Clayface, however, is an exception. Set in the Gotham underworld, the new film features no sign – or even mention – of Batman, but no matter. A grisly but delicious tale of Hollywood excess, this DC thriller is part crime, part horror and certainly not one for the squeamish. Tom Rhys Harries (Suspicion) stars as Matt Hagen, an American actor whose career is soaring – before his face is sliced to shreds by gangsters. What unfolds is a vengeance-fuelled descent into body horror that will make you shriek. Read the full review here. Clayface is in cinemas now.

title: Ancient Chinese warrior queen; how to prevent osteoporosis: 7 Lifestyle highlights
description: From how AI transforms microdramas to designer Kim Jones’ affinity for Hong Kong, here are seven stories from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven Lifestyle stories from the past seven days that resonated with our readers. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. This ancient Chinese warrior queen led huge armies and stole a king’s heart Fu Hao is one of the earliest documented female military generals in history, yet relatively little is known about her. Most of the information gathered about her life is from her tomb. 2. How to prevent osteoporosis, from training to eating calcium-rich food Osteoporosis is a stealthy condition. The disease, which weakens bones by making them thinner, less dense and more likely to break, advances slowly and silently, says Dr Edith Lau, founding president of the Asian Pacific Osteoporosis Foundation (APOF), and for most people the first sign is a broken bone. 3. How AI is reshaping microdramas as video format takes a ‘generational jump’ Paddy Ma Wendi, a director of vertical dramas since 2023, has had a front-row seat to how fast and hard artificial intelligence has affected the mobile-first entertainment genre in 2026. 4. ‘So excited’: Kim Jones on choosing Hong Kong as his fashion label’s home One might not expect British fashion designer Kim Jones, a figure synonymous with modern luxury, to highlight reptiles as one of his earliest memories of Hong Kong. 5. A missionary’s stories of the Kowloon Walled City live on at a new exhibition St Stephen’s Society looks more like a contemporary art gallery than a rehabilitation facility. At the non-profit Christian charity’s compound in Hong Kong’s New Territories, there are corridors lined with sketches, canvases and photography and a wall of art supplies. 6. ‘It’s never hurt less’: Chinese runner’s knee pain fades on 20,000km trek When Ria Xi set off on her 20,000km (12,400-mile) endurance challenge, she had no idea what the impact on her body would be. But she was curious to find out. 7. French toast, egg sandwiches: Hong Kong comfort food highlighted in Lucas Sin’s cookbook When people think of Cantonese food, buttery scrambled egg between slices of soft white bread may not be the first dish to come to mind. For Lucas Sin Lok-yeung, this quintessential Hong Kong classic is the first recipe in his inaugural cookbook, Cha Chaan Teng: Comfort Food from Hong Kong’s Iconic Diners – listed as the “Perfect Scrambled Egg Sandwich”.

title: France’s borrowing costs reach 24-year high as riots deepen budget worries
description: Riots, political deadlock and a looming ratings review are fuelling concerns over the country’s fiscal outlook and growth.
content: France’s 10-year borrowing cost topped 5 per cent again in early Paris trading on Thursday, a day after touching that level for the first time since 2002, as the country recovers from its worst urban riots in years and braces for more clashes to come. Analysts expected market pressure to persist in the near term amid uncertainties at home and abroad, but noted that the situation remained far from turning into another euro-zone crisis. The spread between 10-year French and German bonds widened to 1.57 percentage points on Wednesday, edging towards the recent peak seen on October 2, when the market last fretted over France’s ability to pass its 2027 budget amid political deadlock. “Markets are adjusting very rapidly to sentiment, and I think sentiment will deteriorate,” said Stephane Colliac, senior economist at BNP Paribas. “What we observe on the market is a clear demonstration of its consequences.” Polls conducted before last weekend’s riots already showed that French people were not optimistic about the future, with the latest Banque de France business climate indicator pointing to an increase in uncertainty sentiment. The unrest was likely to have a further negative impact, according to Colliac. “Over the next weeks, it is likely that we will remain in this landscape,” he said. “In terms of rates and spread, it is very likely that we will see these kinds of levels again.” Further protests have already been called for this Saturday and the following weekend, with a general strike set for November 5. Moody’s is set to review France’s sovereign credit rating on Friday, with a negative outlook already attached to it. An initial estimate from research firm Morningstar published on Tuesday put the insured cost of the latest unrest at below €1.2 billion (US$1.35 billion). But Charlotte de Montpellier, senior economist at ING, said in a note published on the same day that past experience suggested the true cost would likely exceed insured losses. A report by the French National Assembly after the 2018 yellow vest movement found that while insurers paid out €217 million for property damage, the unrest cost shopping centres €2 billion and hotels, restaurants and cafes €850 million, with a 2.5 per cent drop in tourism numbers during the first quarter of 2019. It also took away 0.1 percentage points off France’s gross domestic product growth in the last quarter of 2018. The unrest, together with rising borrowing costs and weaker confidence, was likely to place further downward pressure on France’s economic outlook, de Montpellier wrote. Growth could come in below the already modest projection of 0.3 per cent in 2026 and 0.6 per cent in 2027, Montpellier added. The situation is also complicating efforts by France’s hung parliament to pass the 2007 budget, as opposition parties blame the government for its handling of the unrest. That political uncertainty was a key driver of the latest rise in yields, according to Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at French investment bank Natixis. Nevertheless, Colliac said both the government and the opposition parties had strong incentives to ensure a budget was passed ahead of next year’s elections. “What is quite reassuring is that the other [non-government] parties in parliament, even if they may not like the budget, will need one in place in order to modify it after the elections, whoever wins,” he said. France’s troubles were also unlikely to trigger another euro crisis any time soon, according to Garcia-Herrero. The European Central Bank had ample manoeuvring room and France’s economy was far larger than Greece’s, meaning that swift interventions would take place if needed. Greece triggered the euro crisis in late 2009 when it revealed it had under-reported its massive government deficits, shattering market confidence and forcing the country to accept multiple international bailouts tied to severe economic austerity.

title: Asian Para Games: mayor sorry for ‘painful’ mistakes after playing wrong national anthems
description: There have been three incidents this week, with one broadcasting South Korean music for about five seconds, instead of the Chinese one.
content: Officials at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya played the wrong national anthems three times this week, prompting the mayor to apologise just weeks after the city hosted the mishap-plagued Asian Games. The Asian Para Games are taking place in the central Japanese hub city through Saturday, featuring around 4,000 athletes and officials in 18 sports. Nagoya mayor Ichiro Hirosawa apologised on Wednesday for the latest error, which occurred despite officials’ pledges to implement steps to prevent mistakes, including playing the correct national anthems. “These things happened during the Asian Games, so of course the operations were reviewed and examined based on the lessons learned. The fact that it happened again is really just unacceptable,” the mayor told a press conference. On Monday, a Chinese Taipei athlete won a men’s para taekwondo competition, but the Iranian anthem was played in its entirety, according to Nagoya officials at the mayor’s press conference. Officials realised their mistake after the ceremony, they said. On the same day, the Iranian anthem was played again during a women’s para taekwondo ceremony, where a Mongolian competitor was receiving the gold medal, according to the city. The incorrect music was stopped after the Mongolian delegation pointed out the error. Organisers then played the Mongolian anthem after the music was provided by the delegation, Nagoya officials said. Separately on Monday, officials broadcast the South Korean anthem for about five seconds, instead of the Chinese one, before a sitting volleyball match between China and Iran. “It is unacceptable, or rather, it’s painful. I am very sorry about it,” the mayor said, adding that he felt the tournament was otherwise progressing smoothly. The Asian Games, which concluded in early October, faced heavy criticism for shortcomings ranging from inadequate accommodation for athletes to the playing of wrong national anthems.

title: Websites pulled offline worldwide as AI finds critical security flaws
description: Vulnerabilities in code powering 70 per cent of the internet allow passwordless server takeovers, sparking a global race to patch.
content: Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites as they raced Thursday to protect themselves from hacks after artificial intelligence uncovered critical flaws in a widely used programming language called PHP. Wiz, one of the cybersecurity firms that found the two flaws, estimated that PHP code helps run about 70 per cent of the world’s websites – from online stores and news outlets to government services. It called the flaws “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”. PHP programmers released a fix on Wednesday, and the US National Security Agency told organisations to patch their sites immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline. Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed. Many large platforms are built on other programming languages or use operators that could install the fix quickly and were able to stay online. Rahat Masood, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the University of New South Wales, Sydney, called the discovery “quite devastating”. It could allow “attackers to get into your servers without any authorisation, without any username or password,” she said. “Once they are in the servers, they can do anything they want” – from stealing sensitive information to modifying website content – she added, urging institutions to “take it seriously”. Increasingly powerful AI models can spot weak points in computer scripts that have gone unnoticed by humans for decades. That has heightened fears over cybersecurity risks, with the number of software vulnerabilities found worldwide in 2026 on track to roughly double last year’s record total. Government-run sites in countries from Australia to the Netherlands were among those that went dark, while insurance firms, transport operators and media outlets were under emergency maintenance. Japan’s prime minister advised businesses to act to protect themselves “with great urgency”, while South Korea’s government also instructed organisations’ tech departments to update their software. “If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now,” the PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post. Volker Dusch, a security engineer at the foundation, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem PHP had faced in more than a decade, comparing it to Heartbleed, a 2014 flaw that set off a worldwide rush to patch. Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model, as part of an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP’s code. OpenAI said on X it considered the flaws “one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory”. The discovery “marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact,” it added. Wiz, which is owned by Google, said it found them independently weeks later with help from AI models including Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol. Ethan Mollick, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School who studies AI, said companies he talks to were struggling to keep up with the pace of patches needed to guard against AI-driven cyberattacks. “Now consumers are going to have the same experience of getting everything updated often and fast,” he wrote on X. The flaws had been reported privately to PHP’s developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared. Details leaked online Tuesday, a day before the planned release of the fix, prompting the rush to take sites offline before hackers could exploit them. In France, local government websites, including one for the Paris police, were made inaccessible at the request of the French National Cybersecurity Agency, the interior ministry said. The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs Wikipedia, warned users they could see outages on its sites while it addressed the flaws, and said it had deliberately taken many of its supporting services offline until they could be safely patched. Popular apps, including a Pokemon sleep tracker, were also temporarily taken offline while the fix was implemented.

title: SOTY 2025/26: Grand Prize finalist explains the importance of social responsibility
description: Hazel Choi, a graduate of St Paul’s Convent School, shares how adaptability and empathy helped her become a better leader.
content:
In an industrial building in San Po Kong, Hazel Choi Hai-tung discovered a reservation‑only art exhibition that sparked an idea. The teen realised that Hong Kong had many excellent but undiscovered artists and exhibitions. The real problem was access, not interest.
“I wanted to build a practical platform to connect audiences with local arts and cultural heritage,” the 18-year-old recalled. “I sketched an app prototype to help users find lesser-known shows, reserve visits and discover community exhibitions that bring people from different backgrounds together.”
Choi learned basic coding to build the Art Tracker prototype. She entered it into the 2024 Nomad Awards Tech Competition, where she won first runner-up.
She is still testing the app. The process has shown her the power of using technology to address social issues.
“Testing it with peers at school and seeing them use it reinforced my belief that small, well-targeted tools can expand cultural access and strengthen community ties,” said the St Paul’s Convent School graduate who is now studying law at the University of Cambridge.
Choi’s leadership journey began after the Covid-19 pandemic, when she could finally return to campus life. She took the opportunity to try new activities.
“I explored mock trial and debate and discovered the power of words and storytelling. Training and competitions sharpened my public speaking [skills] and confidence, turning curiosity into a sustained interest in advocacy,” she recalled.
When Choi became the head prefect in Form Five, she saw it as a way to make a positive impact and give back to the school community.
“It was fulfilling to contribute to the place that nurtured me,” she said.
The experience helped her learn that leadership involved personal growth as well as responsibility for others and for the events that shaped her school community.
“Leading large-scale occasions like the anniversary gala, family fun day and a joint variety show required balancing big-picture planning with everyday duties,” Choi explained. “That steady, itemised approach helped me monitor progress and remain calm because I always knew what came next.”
Communication and empathy were central to her role: “Much of my work involved mediating between students and school authorities, anticipating stakeholders’ concerns during the preparatory stage and identifying the hardest parts of each project to tackle first,” she explained.
Cooperation and delegation were also key to her success, she said.
“Clear, timely exchanges kept everyone aligned … I assigned tasks according to each team member’s strengths – some handled design and backstage work, others managed outreach or performer networks.”
As president of the Young Investors Society, Choi worked to make topics related to finance and artificial intelligence (AI) more accessible and relevant.
“For young people, financial literacy should emphasise risk management and safe, legal investment practices rather than quick profit,” she said. “I believe AI literacy is essential because workplaces will inevitably adopt smarter tools; the real risk is being outpaced by those who know how to use AI effectively. AI literacy means using these tools smartly, safely and ethically.”
Through workshops, mentorship and project‑based activities, the group encouraged students to practise prompting and apply concepts in tangible pitches. Choi and her teammates equipped their peers with the skills and confidence to navigate a future where finance and AI are intertwined.
Outside school, Choi has also found opportunities for leadership and empathy.
In 2025, she served as the operations officer for a 22‑member team at JA Company, a youth entrepreneurship project. The team focused on educating the public about endangered local animals through board games, card games, keychains and tote bags.
“That experience taught me adaptability, the value of distributed responsibility and how teamwork and clear communication turn simple ideas into social impact,” she explained.
Volunteering with Run Hong Kong, a local NGO for asylum seekers, Choi worked with refugee children and teens in bridging programmes, which taught her patience and empathy. Many participants had experienced trauma and needed time to build trust; they also faced cultural and language barriers, she explained.
“Using play, field trips and workshops, I adapted my communication [style] for different ages,” she said. “Meeting a Somali former midwife who was eventually resettled in Canada showed me how legal support and training can transform lives and deepened my commitment to service.”
Choi’s ability to transform empathy and curiosity into meaningful projects was recognised when she was named one of the Grand Prize finalists at the 2025/26 Student of the Year Awards, organised by the South China Morning Post and sponsored by The Hong Kong Jockey Club.
“My advice to young people is simple: put your idea into words … and step out of your comfort zone,” she said. “Small beginnings lead to [collaborations] and opportunities that help scale your work. Be proactive in seeking chances and building relationships.”
Now a university student in Britain, she hopes to help create a better world.
“I am studying law to help build a more inclusive, sustainable society, focusing on regulatory issues around technology, AI, and corporate social responsibility,” she said. “The goal is to design rules that protect consumers and the environment while keeping pace with innovation.”

title: China edge past US at gymnastics world championships to win first gold in 20 years
description: Japan finish third in the Netherlands and all three countries secure direct passage to the Los Angeles Olympic Games in 2028.
content: China denied the United States an eighth consecutive women’s team title at the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships on Wednesday to win their first gold medal in 20 years. The quartet of Du Siyu, Ke Qinqin, Qiu Qiyuan and Zhang Qingying combined to score 165.764 points, just ahead of the United States and Japan, who finished with 165.531 and 164.063 points respectively. All three countries secured direct passage to the Los Angeles Olympic Games in 2028. Winning their first title since 2006, China trailed following the vault and uneven bars after the US posted the highest points in both events, scoring 42.633 and 42.766 respectively, to stay 1.967 points ahead. But China turned the contest around on the balance beam. Zhang scored 15.066 points, followed by compatriot Ke, who finished with 14.400 points. Despite adding only 13.900 points, Qiu ranked sixth overall as China finished with 43.366 points. The US scored 39.199 points to rank fifth among eight countries, meaning China moved ahead by nearly two points heading into the final rotation, the floor exercise. The US, who triumphed in seven consecutive editions between 2011 and 2023, again finished top of the table in the final apparatus with 40.933 points. But a combined score of 38.966 points from the same Chinese trio who shone on the balance beam was enough for China to claim gold by 0.233 points. “I’m 24 years old now. [I have won an] Asian championships gold medal, Asian Games gold medal and today I finally won the world championships gold medal too!” Du said. “What a perfect year! We are all champions. Our veterans are still persevering because this result truly deserves it.” “This gold medal marks our return to the women’s team championship podium after 20 years, which is incredibly hard-won. It’s the result of everyone’s hard work, and all the difficulties were worthwhile,” captain Qiu added. “We all share a common belief and goal: to raise the national flag and play the national anthem. So it’s a result of everyone being of one mind and united as one.” By finishing third, Japan snapped a run of 60 years without a medal at the world championships. On Tuesday, Japan took the men’s team title, pipping Russia and China. The championships in the Netherlands continue with the men’s all-around final on Thursday and the women’s all-around final on Friday, followed by the apparatus finals over the weekend.

title: Thai artist blends history and gaming in an installation that puts visitors in control
description: For his Chanel Gateway Commission at Dib Bangkok, Nawin Nuthong combines historical research with his passion for video games.
content: Growing up, Thai artist Nawin Nuthong loved playing video games, especially Civilization, where players can create empires as historical leaders. Drawn to playing as King Ramkhamhaeng, who ruled the Sukhothai Kingdom from 1279 to 1298 in what is now Thailand, Nawin soon became interested in how history is constructed. The 33-year-old now combines his twin passions for history and video games through his multimedia practice, which examines how new technology shapes and advances societies. His latest work, Project 147 (2026), inspired by the Thai folk epic poem of love and tragedy Khun Chang Khun Phaen, questions the cosmological principles, knowledge systems and myths that have shaped the region’s consciousness. The Chanel Culture Fund commissioned the installation to be the inaugural Chanel Gateway Commission at Dib Bangkok, a contemporary art museum in the Thai capital that opened in December 2025. It is also part of Dib Bangkok’s second major exhibition, “Giving Life”, which features 33 artists and their works that “come alive” in the presence of viewers. Diving into Project 147 Project 147, combining sculptures, digital screen images and games, is something of a highlight. Visitors play six-player console games inside what looks like a whimsical gaming arcade, which Nawin describes as a cross between a “crime scene and an archaeological site”. Around them, sculptural objects represent relics yet to be discovered. Red curtains section off screens and consoles, adding drama. An intriguing mix of artworks features on the walls or between the gaming areas, from a low table stacked with plastic cabbages to a sculptural relief of temple columns wrapped in traditional silk-like material, nodding to religious hierarchies in Buddhism and Hinduism. The game centres on a child protagonist who enters a forest and asks the trees, “What is history?” While awaiting answers, the child explores their surroundings, encountering mythic creatures, deities and artefacts – more than 600 – that offer clues or interpretations of history and immortality. Together, the elements explore how time is manipulated through varying narratives and power structures, and “is shaped by cultural forces such as monarchy, animism, mythology and now, game narrative”, Nawin says, adding that this was his first time properly developing a game and working with a team to realise a project on this scale. The visual and narrative language of video games Nawin’s deeply conceptual approach to “What is history?” appeals to Miwako Tezuka, the director of Dib Bangkok. “It’s related to how we’re thinking about the history of Dib Bangkok and institution building,” she explains. As a new institution, one of Tezuka’s challenges is considering the many different viewers when making programmes – especially those less familiar with contemporary art. Nawin’s practice, steeped in digital video aesthetics, provides a new entry point: gaming. “Video games have their own visual and narrative language, which is globalised,” Tezuka says. “It’s how a lot of people communicate, and therefore creates an easier access point for new audiences into contemporary art.” Picking up on intergenerational friction, particularly in Thailand, is what makes Nawin an interesting artist for Yana Peel, the president of Arts, Culture and Heritage at Chanel. “I see building the future with fragments of the past and thinking about these themes – for which the artist is a spiritual conduit – as an interesting and recurring theme here,” Peel observes. “What we loved about [Dib’s] selection is the homage to tradition and the focus on the tension between tradition and disruption, heritage and modernity.” Nawin’s commission is part of the Chanel Culture Fund’s growing cultural presence in Asia. Other supported projects include Palme d’Or-winning director Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s virtual reality installation A Conversation with the Sun (2025) at the 7th Bangkok Experimental Film Festival in 2025 and its ongoing partnership with M+ museum in Hong Kong, where it supports film restorations, the Asian Avant-Garde Film Festival and exhibitions as the museum’s lead partner. ‘Build their own history’ Another work by Nawin, Play_ (2026), is on view at M+ and features an interactive maze built out of cartoons, video games and short animations. Viewers can use the joystick to navigate a small child through various zones, where they encounter different kinds of games. When it comes to video games, one major attraction is the opportunity they provide for world-building. Many popular video games – think The Sims, Minecraft, Spore and Civilization – allow players to create rules and systems and construct universes, imparting a sense of control that might be lacking in the real world. For Nawin, contemporary art is fertile ground for speculation: “By the act of exhibiting, curating and distributing, it’s working with questions that you don’t have the answers to.” This is what drew Nawin to video games and also what he wants viewers to take away after experiencing Project 147: a sense of control over determining their own histories. “I want audiences to play the game and customise it the way they see fit – it’s a chance for them to build their own history.” “Giving Life”, including Nawin Nuthong’s Project 147, is on view at Dib Bangkok, 111 Soi Sukhumvit 40, Phra Khanong, Khlong Toei, Bangkok, until May 3, 2027. For more information, visit dibbangkok.org. Play_ (2026) is on view at M+, West Kowloon Cultural District, 38 Museum Drive, Kowloon, until January 10, 2027. For details, go to mplus.org.hk.

title: Haze-hit Singaporeans call for school classroom air con
description: Hit by regional haze and worsening air quality, parents are urging the city state’s schools to install full-time air conditioners.
content:
Salon manager Alice Pang is among several parents who are increasingly worried about the open-air classroom environments in Singapore amid the transboundary haze fuelled by fires across Indonesia.
Pang said her 10-year-old daughter had already been suffering from a sinus infection. Her classroom does not have air conditioning, and the worsening haze plaguing the city state has been making her child’s eyes water.
She would prefer that her Primary Four daughter stay home as the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) climbs beyond 200 in some areas, but the child is in the middle of exams.
“They have an air purifier in the classroom, but she says it isn’t working. It’s also too hot for the students. I think the government needs to step up and take action,” Pang said.
Earlier this month, the PSI one-hour reading reached a high of 288 in western Singapore.
The same day, Singapore began distributing N95 masks to vulnerable people, including children aged between seven and 16, and providing air-conditioned rooms in shelters in community clubs and some residents’ committee centres.
