Education Minister Desmond Lee said in a social media post that lessons and national examinations would continue in enclosed venues with air purifiers. However, his ministry might consider school closures if forecasts entered the hazardous range with a 24-hour PSI exceeding 300.
Across the 1km causeway in Malaysia, schools in several states had been shut. On October 16, Malaysia’s Ministry of Health said all educational institutions, including schools and childcare centres, must be closed if the Air Pollutant Index (API) reading exceeds 200.
Lawrence Ng, a general practitioner in Singapore, said that common conditions triggered by haze included upper respiratory infections, bronchitis, conjunctivitis, allergic rhinitis – known as hay fever – and asthma.
“Children have smaller airways, which are more susceptible to airway narrowing from pollutants,” Ng said.
When asked whether implementing air conditioning in classrooms was being considered to tackle the haze, Singapore’s Ministry of Education directed reporters to its haze management measures.
These include avoiding physical activity when the PSI is between 200 and 300, placing students in an enclosed indoor space with air purifiers, and temporarily placing those who are unwell in an air-conditioned room with an air purifier before they receive medical attention.
Politician Kenneth Tiong, who reiterated his call to provide air-conditioning in classrooms, told reporters he was not saying that air-conditioning should be on all the time, but that classrooms should have the option when needed. He has previously advocated for air conditioning to help students and teachers cope with the heat.
“The recent haze makes it more urgent. It has been very difficult for the kids: many are coughing, and I can see the toll it is taking on their health,” Tiong said.
In March, then senior minister of state David Neo said Singapore had been careful not to rush into air conditioning, as it was not very energy-efficient. Instead, the city state relied on passive cooling solutions, such as cool paint and more breathable uniforms.
Neo stressed the need to balance other considerations, such as long-term heat resilience, acclimatisation, energy consumption and environmental impact.

title: Mouthing Off | Hong Kong’s Stanley, once packed with tourists, is now dead. What happened?
description: The seaside town went from drawing weekend crowds to boarded-up bars and restaurants. How did it get like this, and is it good for residents?
content: With summer’s heat dissipating in Hong Kong, I decided to do a country walk last weekend and ended up in Stanley, a coastal neighbourhood in the south of Hong Kong Island. What we found there shocked us. It had been a few years since I visited the area, mostly because it was always packed with tourists. In all previous Stanley outings, hordes of visitors, whether from mainland China or Western countries, packed the side-street market and the main beach promenade. On this recent hike, a trail led us down behind Murray House. The historic building, relocated from Central, once housed a plethora of restaurants across its three floors. When we arrived in the early afternoon, there was nobody around other than a couple taking wedding pictures and a few stragglers. Hoarding blocked off much of the structure, which has been sitting empty for more than a year. Behind Murray House, the piazza had some families and kids playing, but nothing resembling the frenzy of the weekend craft markets of days past. Even more depressing was Stanley Main Street. The bars and restaurants along the water used to have tables spilling out onto the pavement filled with hungry and thirsty guests. Even on a sunny weekend, the strip felt like a ghost town. I used to feel sorry for the folks having to live among the crowds in Stanley every weekend. Now every other shopfront is deserted. I wonder whether the residents prefer the relaxed vibe or think it is worse with less buzz and fewer businesses. At Stanley Plaza, the little mall run by the Link Reit group, the ground-floor fast-food outlets attract a trickle of customers, but the retail tenants on the higher levels tell a different tale. On the top deck, next to the bus stop, a branch of Mercato Gourmet sells fine Italian products and fare, while the second floor is home to a 3hreesixty supermarket, the upscale cousin of Wellcome. The luxury home furniture boutiques that once drew more affluent shoppers are gone. In their place are a coin-operated claw machine depot and discount household supplies shops. The mall seems unable to decide whether to go high-end or appeal to the residents of the nearby Ma Hang Estate public housing blocks. I assume those lower-income families are not splurging on Mercato’s imported burrata cheese or M5 Wagyu rib-eye steaks. Is anyone visiting Stanley any more? And is it better off this way? Some probably think a calm and serene Stanley is ideal. The tranquillity and lack of bus tours make the area more liveable than ever. But sages always warn one should be careful what one wishes for. Stanley is now not just quiet; it is dead.

title: Starbucks China rolls out buy-before-seating rule after reversing open-door policy in US
description: The coffee chain is ending free seating across its mainland stores amid fierce competition in China’s growing coffee market.
content: Starbucks China says it will roll out its “purchase before seating” rule nationwide starting Thursday, with corresponding signs put in stores, following a similar policy it introduced at its North America stores last year. The Seattle-based coffee chain would prioritise helping visitors in need, such as pregnant women and people with limited mobility, and would continue to foster its stores as so-called third places, it said in a statement on Wednesday. The policy has sparked widespread discussion online, with some commenters saying the rule was reasonable and common sense, and Starbucks should have introduced it earlier in China, according to posts on Chinese social media platform RedNote. China’s coffee market has been expanding fast, and competition among operators has intensified. The country now has over 550 million coffee drinkers, according to data platform Canyin88’s research arm. Starbucks China plans to invest more than 300 million yuan (US$44.9 million) to upgrade its store facilities and experiences in its 2027 financial year beginning on September 28. The chain finalised a joint venture deal in April with Chinese private equity firm Boyu Capital, as it looks to further expand its footprint in China. Boyu Capital holds a 60 per cent stake in the new entity that runs Starbucks’ retail business in China. The seating policy may not be relevant to Seattle headquarters. The joint venture now operated some 8,000 Starbucks stores on the mainland, with an ambition to expand the network to 20,000 outlets over time, it said earlier. By comparison, domestic chain Luckin Coffee operates over 36,000 stores in China, including Hong Kong, making it the largest player among coffee chains operating in the country. “Free-seat hogging is only the visible issue. The bigger challenge is that shoppers willing to pay extra for Starbucks’ third-space experience are being drawn away by competitors,” said Fu Yifu, a special research fellow at Su Merchants Bank in Nanjing in China’s eastern Jiangsu province. “Still, raising the seating threshold alone is an operational improvement. To tackle broader competitive pressures, it’s important for Starbucks to pair this with stronger products, in-store experiences and distinct value,” Fu said. In the third quarter of its 2026 financial year, revenue from Starbucks’ international segment fell 34 per cent year on year to US$1.3 billion. The drop was primarily driven by the conversion of its China retail business into a joint venture, which drove company-operated store revenues lower, it said in its latest quarterly earnings. Starbucks had already moved to tighten seating access in North America. It announced in January 2025 that it would reverse its open-door policy that it introduced in 2018. The rule had allowed anyone to use store facilities, including seating areas and restrooms, without making a purchase. The change comes as Starbucks grapples with soft sales in North America and aims to improve the in-store environment in the region. The coffee chain did not launch similar seating rules in other countries but posts a code of conduct on its official website.

title: Letters | Young Westerners are wondering whether democracy delivers real change
description: Readers discuss the insecurity facing young people in democracies such as France and Britain, and the Trump administration’s immigration policy.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Student protests in France prompt me to reflect on a wider problem in Western politics: although democracy promises representation and equal citizenship, many young people feel excluded from economic security and political influence. On October 6, students, teachers and parents marched across France, while protesters blockaded hundreds of high schools. Beginning in disadvantaged Parisian suburbs, the demonstrations spread nationwide amid anger over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating buildings. Meanwhile, the government faces debt and rising borrowing costs. The crisis exposes a conflict between stronger provision of public services and fiscal discipline. This conflict extends beyond France. Young people in Britain face similar difficulties, with prices having almost tripled since 1990. While average weekly earnings reached £756 in July 2026, inflation-adjusted wage growth remained below 1 per cent; real median earnings in 2025 were lower than in 2008. Higher salaries provide limited security when housing, food and transport costs continue rising. Young people can vote but have little control over the conditions determining their independence. Weakening welfare systems deepen this frustration. In France, almost 10 per cent of teaching hours in public secondary schools went untaught in 2024-2025. Wealthier families can purchase private schooling or tutoring, while poorer families remain dependent on overstretched public services. Economic inequality therefore becomes inequality of opportunity. Political access also appears unequal. Between 2014 and 2016, Uber held discussions with Emmanuel Macron, then France’s economy minister. A parliamentary inquiry later described their relationship as “opaque but privileged”. Although governments must consult businesses, such access may suggest that corporate connections carry more influence than ordinary democratic participation. A vicious cycle has emerged. Young people protest against rising costs and shrinking services, prompting governments to promise concessions. Investors may react to tax increases, regulation or borrowing, creating instability. Higher borrowing costs then restrict welfare spending, producing further anger and protests. Western democracies ought to break this cycle through fair, financially sustainable policies. Young people are not rejecting freedom; they are questioning whether democracy can deliver meaningful change. Their trust will survive only if political rights are accompanied by economic security, equal opportunity and genuine hope. Lau Chi-yuen, Ma On Shan The US’ government problem President Donald Trump should be lauded for his persistence in rendering America increasingly hostile to foreign students. After the proposed US$100,000 levy on H-1B visa applications from individuals residing outside the United States was blocked by federal judges, his administration proposed strictures to render it virtually impossible for foreign students to contribute to the US economy. On October 7, the administration proposed a rule that would require schools to pay at least US$70,000 for each F-1 foreign student seeking to work in the US through the Optional Practical Training (OPT) programme. Historically, OPT is a vital pipeline for international talent. It is also a fundamental selling point of US postgraduate programmes, given that US salaries are generally higher, thereby justifying the high tuition fees. Much has been said on the societal ramifications of Trump’s aggressive immigration policy. Here, I wish to explicate how it accentuates the deficiencies of America’s constitutional arrangements. The US government is divided into three branches: executive, legislative and judicial. Although the executive can make laws, such are used to effectuate – not override – legislative goals. In recent years, the executive has frequently resorted to legislating for partisan ends, effectively usurping the role of the legislature. Where the people cannot express their opinions through their appointed representatives, they turn to the courts for relief. Federal courts are increasingly inundated with cases and entrammelled by partisan politics. Since federal judges are nominated by presidents, their decisions – albeit in strict compliance with the law – are often interpreted as a reflection of their political beliefs. This is unsustainable. As Alexander Hamilton argued: “The judiciary…has no influence over either the sword or the purse; no direction either of the strength or of the wealth of the society; and can take no active resolution whatever.” The courts are designed to be referees, not quarterbacks. The president must speak to the people effectively to liaise a way forward. This would eliminate traces of the very monarchy which America was liberated from. Alexander Clevewood Ng, New York

title: How Gab Waller sources sold-out luxury for the likes of Hailey Bieber and Rosie Huntington-Whiteley
description: From rare Phoebe Philo-era Celine coats to viral UGG boots, Waller’s sourcing business tracks down fashion’s hardest-to-find pieces.
content: Anyone who’s seen the dreaded words “sold out” while navigating the endless scroll of online shopping – or worse, heard those very same words after hours spent queuing outside a store – should have Gab Waller on speed dial. Where some may see those words for what they are, Waller sees an invitation to dig even deeper to find the coveted item you want, whether it’s the hottest accessory this season – she recently cited Alaïa’s Le Teckel suede clutch and Dior’s Médaillon belt as new must-haves – or a Phoebe Philo-era Celine coat like the one she famously found for model Rosie Huntington-Whiteley back in 2019. The self-described fashion sourcer is now widely credited with coining that term in the first place. Sourcing was not a well-established career path when Waller started her business in 2018, but sourcers are now everywhere, especially on Instagram – London-based Erica Wright and New York-based Jennifer Nisan are just two names that have accumulated sizeable followings for their businesses. Born in Australia and now based in Los Angeles, Waller was once just a shopping fanatic, working a government job before eventually pivoting to styling. Thinking she might move there to style clients, Waller visited LA in 2017 and the rest is history. Wowed by boutiques on Rodeo Drive, she not only fell in love with her future home but also, noticing how little luxury stock there was in Australia in comparison, stumbled upon her next career move. “[Luxury brands] follow consumer demand,” the 32-year-old Waller explained in a recent interview at the Fashion Asia Hong Kong Fashion Challenges Forum in September, when the now globally renowned sourcer was invited to speak about her work. “Where is the consumer buying? Being a smaller country from their perspective, Australia, unfortunately, doesn’t get as much stock allocated to them.” Waller notes that Australia also ends up being one of the last markets to receive their allocation – part of her job is to know things like who is getting the most stock and when. “It’s unfortunate Australia doesn’t even have some luxury boutiques. Same with Los Angeles. LA doesn’t have a Miu Miu or Alaïa boutique and I’ve always questioned, why is that? The response has been, ‘we don’t see that same demand we see in say, New York or even Orange County.’” All too familiar with those common pain points inherent to luxury fashion – wait-lists, VIP sales and other exclusionary and often elitist practices – especially for someone coming from Australia, Waller has since made it her mission to change the industry from the inside out and is now armed with all she needs to know to do so. She first called herself a personal buyer, then a shopper, before realising the designation of sourcer was better suited to describe what she does for a living. The former label, as she touched on during her Hong Kong panel discussion, aligns more with those who shop for clients who don’t know what they want, while sourcers handle specific requests from clients who do. To this day, most of Waller’s requests come via direct messages to her Instagram account, @gabwallerdotcom. “The challenge back then was I wasn’t a VIP client to begin with – I was a mid-twenties girl going into these stores I’d never shopped from before, saying, ‘Hey, can I start shopping the hardest pieces to get?’” Waller says of her early sourcing days, adding that building relationships with sales assistants on the shop floor, rather than upper management, was most important. “Some brands were arms wide open. Others, I really had to prove myself first, and understandably. They didn’t know who I was.” The initial idea was to source hard-to-find items for Australian clients internationally, and maybe even in the process bring some domestic wares to international clients, but the aforementioned Celine coat found for Huntington-Whiteley in 2019 made Waller’s business suddenly global. Demand for her services exploded around the trending hashtag, #sourcedbygw, and she’s since become a sourcer to the stars, counting Hailey Bieber, Sofia Richie Grainge and Lori Harvey – and their stylists – among her dedicated clients. Not only has Waller connected thousands of clients with the luxury items of their dreams, from A-listers looking for vintage pieces from foreign countries, to everyday buyers trying to bag a pair of UGG boots, she’s an industry pioneer rewriting the rules of fashion and entrepreneurship in the process. Having hired a team of sourcers around the world to help procure pieces in places from Paris to Hong Kong, she’s now launched an app, Sourced By, which her team uses to streamline requests, and is authoring a book about sourcing on the way. “I was like, if I don’t build this tech now, I don’t know how much longer the business can survive because of the amount of requests that were being missed and forgotten,” says Waller. “We were logging into an Excel spreadsheet back then and you can’t scale with this.” Waller clarifies that she has no plans to make the technology consumer-facing any time soon. “When I pulled back the curtain and looked at the business as a whole, the struggles were happening on the back end. But [at] the front end, clients are happy. They love being able to DM or email [requests].” Waller is adamant sourcing “is the future of shopping”, noting that a new wave of requests has come from shoppers in their early twenties disillusioned by in-person experiences. Knowing personally how debilitating luxury shopping can be, Waller remains committed to democratising access to her services, and luxury fashion in general. No deposit is charged upfront for any item she sources, and there’s no obligation to purchase once the item has been found. The process is also radically transparent. Waller charges a flat-rate fee capped at US$350 per item, tacked onto the retail price of the item, the cost of shipping and a credit card fee, if applicable. There are no hidden fees, mark-ups, or additional surcharges. “I know what it feels like to walk into a boutique and feel intimidated, to feel like I don’t belong there, and that’s something I’ve always wanted to eliminate,” Waller remarks. On that point, Waller draws a line between sourcers and resellers, who she says specialise in “buying a heap of stock” upfront with the sole purpose of reselling on their own platforms. “Brands don’t like resellers,” she clarifies, adding that the resale market opens up a whole other ball game. “Other sourcers can buy from their sourcers, almost like third-party dealing to find the item for said client, and the more parties are involved, the higher the price. Everyone wants a cut. Team Gab Waller doesn’t source from other sourcers because I want to get the best price for my clients and I never want to upsell.” Now that Waller has all the brands at her fingertips, navigating luxury’s notorious red tape behind closed doors, the media has her on speed dial, too, tapping into her connections and database. She compiles The Hot List, a monthly column of seasonal fresh finds for Vogue, and is regularly consulted for her take on brand and consumer behaviour. Are luxury shoppers, for example, really going crazy over Matthieu “Blazy-mania” at Chanel? Waller continues to see huge demand for the brand, but concedes that the hype around all luxury brands – and their tendency to say “sold out” – is often engineered. “That really came into effect post-Covid,” she adds. “Pre-Covid lines were almost non-existent. You could go into any boutique. Then came Covid and appointment-only came into effect. Brands were like, this is good for us, because naturally when you walk past a line you want to know what’s there.” Sometimes, says Waller, brands like The Row end up back-pedalling on the overexposure. Or, like Celine, see demand grow to a point where production can’t keep up. “No one has access to the data I have,” Waller concludes. “There’s been times where I’ve wanted to [tell] brands, ‘you need to put this item back into production because there’s many clients ready to purchase’.” For their part, she notes, brands also pay attention to customers who dare to hit the “notify me” button when items go out of stock. Waller might seem like fashion’s fairy godmother, making wishes come true by peering into her crystal ball and snapping her fingers, but sourcing is more challenging than people think. Ultimately, her hope is that more people consider it a legitimate career. “I’ve designed, shaped and moulded the perfect job for myself,” she muses. “With sourcing and my business in particular, everyone is welcome. Everyone should feel like a VIP. You should not have to have a minimum spend to have access to [pieces by] X, Y, Z.” Three sourcing experts on our radar Erica Wright Fashion PR & communications veteran Erica Wright isn’t just a sourcing expert, she’s the founder of a tech platform which connects average users to fashion sourcers worldwide. London-based Wright launched Sourcewhere, a marketplace for shoppers trying to track down specific hot-ticket items, in 2022. Popular requests include the Hermès Kelly handbag and the Cartier Baignoire watch. Elyse Berson US-based fashion sourcer Elyse Berson has accumulated more than 250,000 Instagram followers on her business account, @sourcedbyelyse. Raffia Alaïa ballet flats, New Balance x Miu Miu sneakers and a Margaux bag by The Row are just some of the many luxury wares Berson has sourced and shared on her page. Kelly Levian Kelly Levian started sourcing in New York in 2021 and soon launched The Coveted, now a global sourcing and styling concierge service with 120,000 followers and counting on Instagram. The company now serves shoppers beyond the US, and counts celebrities like Khloé Kardashian and Simone Biles among its clients.

title: How Hong Kong cocktail bars design for service, ergonomics and success
description: Top mixologists from Bar Leone, Dead Poets and The Savory Project explain how smart bar design can drive great hospitality and keep guests happy.
content: “You can tell in about 30 seconds whether a bar was designed by someone who’s worked a busy shift or by someone who drew a nice picture,” says Nikita Matveev. Ask mixologists what they notice when they walk into a bar, and they won’t mention the menu or the mood board. Matveev, head bartender of Dead Poets and The Old Man, counts the steps – how far bartenders must reach for ice, trash and stock, and whether they’re bumping into each other. Lorenzo Antinori sees light first: how it falls on the tables, where guests are seated and the warmth of a room. Ajit Gurung watches the service flow before he ever looks at the setup. All three run celebrated local bars – Antinori’s neighbourhood space Bar Leone, which has topped regional and world rankings; Gurung’s umami-focused The Savory Project; and Matveev’s barber shop by day, cocktail bar by night, Dead Poets. Their venues could hardly be more different. But they share a conviction that rarely occurs to most guests: a bar is a workplace first, and its design determines how well it works. A poorly designed bar wastes staff’s time and energy, wearing them out and slowing service – and guests feel every bit of it. “A well-designed, ergonomic bar allows bartenders to move fluidly without looking down or hunting for gear,” Antinori says, “keeping their heads up to make eye contact, engage [with customers] and maintain a high-energy, welcoming atmosphere.” His rule is that the cocktail station, or “cockpit” – the ice well, speed rail, water source, trash and glass rack – must be reachable within one or two steps. “Reaching, twisting, or bending repeatedly over a 10-hour shift drains productivity and physically wears down the team,” Antinori says. The cocktail station should be fixed from day one. Everything else – the backbar layout, furniture, lighting, shelving – can and should evolve with experience and guest traffic. All three agree on the importance of the cockpit, that the central operating area should have as much as possible to hand. But beyond that, there is no single correct setup – only that setups should match the space and concept. With Bar Leone, Antinori bet that Hong Kong was ready for a relaxed, high-volume aperitivo bar. Its long counter is built for speed and theatre: the bartenders face the room, the gear sits within arm’s reach, and the whole operation reads as effortless. When Gurung and his partner Jay Khan opened The Savory Project in 2023, after years of success at Coa, which runs a similar long-bar style, they chose something different. The result was a central island where guests and staff could share the workspace – an unconventional anchor for an unconventional, umami-focused concept. The island is adjustable, Gurung notes – configured for a bartender’s height or handedness, and seating guests as service demands. “Bars are becoming very personal,” he says. “Just as a bartender’s job is to find the drink according to our guest’s preference, it is also our responsibility to find the right setup according to the needs of the bar.” Dead Poets operates with a constraint no other bar in the city faces: by day, the space operates as Sauce, a barbershop. “The design had to hold two things at once,” Matveev says, “keep the energy of the Sauce brand and still read clearly as Dead Poets, and the dead artists concept, the moment the light changes for the evening.” Supporting the team behind the counter is what enables great hospitality in front of it Lorenzo Antinori, Bar Leone The solution was a single working station rather than a long bar, with most of the stock pre-batched in a separate lab. For Matveev, this means fewer steps per drink, keeping elaborate prep work out of the guest-facing space and improving overall hygiene. “When there’s no long bar between you and the guest, the interaction changes,” Matveev says. “They’re closer to the work, they ask more questions, and they read the drink as something being made for them rather than handed over.” These setups are ergonomic decisions as much as aesthetic ones, and mixologists say such choices should be made at the design stage – not patched later. Kate Gerwin, founder of Happy Accidents in Albuquerque and runner-up on Netflix’s Drink Masters, made the case on a recent episode of the Pre-Batch Podcast that bars should be built to minimise reach and reduce bending, whether the motive is ergonomics or revenue per square foot. “[Gerwin] is right to push this,” says Matveev. “It’s the least discussed part of bar design and the part your body pays for.” Concentrating everything into one station, as both Dead Poets and The Savory Project do, cuts the walking and twisting that cause most wear on a long shift. The Savory Project’s island is built high enough that bartenders never bend or hunch as they might at a lower traditional bar. Antinori and Matveev also advocate custom sink heights, waist-level bays and draft towers, and proper floor matting to reduce trip hazards and fatigue. The payoff is human before it is financial: “If a bartender isn’t physically exhausted or in pain by hour eight of their shift,” Antinori says, “their energy stays high, their interactions remain genuine, and staff retention improves dramatically. Supporting the team behind the counter is what enables great hospitality in front of it.”

title: A Hong Kong duplex regains light and space after renovation restores a 5.8-metre ceiling
description: A Repulse Bay home renovation restored a double-height ceiling, flooding the interiors with light and putting the views centre stage.
content: Holding on to a newspaper cutting for years reminded Sarah and Jeff Lee of whom to contact when the time came to renovate their 3,100 sq ft (288 square metre) 1980s Repulse Bay duplex. Several years ago, designer Peggy Bels answered that call. The couple, who have lived there for two-plus decades, told Bels they admired her work. They described their home as a place where conversation-fuelled dinner parties stretch well into the night and house guests are frequent. How could Bels improve it? Four bedrooms and two bathrooms were grouped on the upper floor, with a fifth bedroom, kitchen, living/dining areas and powder room below. Given the couple’s need for only two bedrooms plus a study, Bels, founder of Peggy Bels Interior Design, suggested repurposing one bedroom to expand the couple’s private domain, and eliminating another as a key design element of the remodel of the flat – restoring height. The eight-month-long renovation began in 2023 with the removal of a false ceiling in the living area, added by the previous owner, in addition to the small bedroom above it, which dramatically expanded the vertical volume of the space. In doing so, the developer’s original intent of a 5.8-metre (19-foot), double-height ceiling was restored. This intervention completely changed the perception of the room, according to Bels. “The increased ceiling height brings a greater sense of space, light and openness, while allowing new, taller glazing to become a defining architectural feature,” she says. “Natural light now travels much deeper into the interior, strengthening the connection with the terrace and surrounding views.” The new volume also creates an opportunity for statement lighting – a quintet of long hanging glass pendants – and gives the living room a generous, contemporary character. More light was introduced by changing the brown balustrade glass on the balcony to clear. To showcase the scenery as if a living artwork, Bels framed the new windows in black, as opposed to their previous white, a theme repeated in the dining area. The neutral interior provides a calm backdrop to the changing colours of the sea, mountains and vegetation outside Designer Peggy Bels To maintain the ambience of their dinner parties, the Lees wanted to keep the kitchen enclosed, but asked Bels to make it more functional. Again, this involved a sacrifice, in the form of built-in cabinetry. Before, the floor-to-ceiling storage was abundant, but not entirely practical. Likewise, a breakfast table hogged space in the middle of the room. By eliminating hard-to-reach cupboards and shelves, Bels was able to tuck a banquette into a corner and replace overhead cabinetry with deep, pull-out drawers, making the pantry supplies and appliances more easily accessible. In doing so, she also brought those working in the kitchen a wonderful gift (see Tried + Tested). The couple were happy to pare back years of accumulation, cherry-picking what they hold dear. Along with adding a dressing room to the main bedroom, they took the opportunity to have the bathroom they had always wanted – a glass-encased Japanese-inspired wet room with immersion tub and hand shower. And as considerate hosts wanting hotel-style privacy for their staying guests, the couple had the other upstairs bathroom converted to a second-bedroom en suite. Design-wise, the material language is consistent throughout, restrained in terms of the number of finishes, but packing character through contrasts. “Walnut furniture and natural oak flooring bring warmth to the space, while concrete walls and black metal elements give it a more contemporary, architectural feel,” Bels says. “The irregular texture of concrete catches the changing natural light and gives the space depth, without relying on decoration.” This restrained palette was also chosen to complement the home’s exceptional setting, she adds. “Rather than competing with the views, the neutral interior provides a calm backdrop to the changing colours of the sea, mountains and vegetation outside.” While the secondary en suite has been, Jeff says, “a game changer for our guests”, Sarah adds that the social-zone upgrades have elevated their entertaining to a whole new level. “Our new sitting room is so beautiful, we thought we’d all adjourn there after dinner,” she says. “But we tend to linger at our so comfortable dining table, eating, sipping and conversing.” Not all Hong Kong homeowners would sacrifice a room to open up a ceiling – let alone part with precious kitchen storage to put in a window. But where possible, Bels says, it is an idea worth considering. “As this project shows, doing so allowed us to gain something just as valuable: volume, light and a much stronger sense of space.” Dining room Vintage armchair reupholstered in Jane Churchill fabric from Altfield. Solid walnut Hakama dining table from CondeHouse. Wing Lux chairs and sideboard from Out of Stock. Bert Frank pendant lights from Olson + Baker. Wall lamp from H.Isle. Artwork by Zhang Shi Pei. Balcony Outdoor tiles from Hop Hing Lung (tel: 2511 3013). Living room Cassina Carrara marble coffee table from Atelier A+. Velvet armchairs and Artisan’s Latus sideboard from Nature Evolution. Rug from Staunton & Henry. Handmade Marc Wood Studio crystal pendants from Archetypal. Main bedroom Ceiling fan from El:ar. Thomas Bina bedside tables from Nature Evolution. House Doctor bedside lamps from Nedgis. Main bedroom en suite Victoria + Albert bathtub from Colourliving. Taps and shower fittings from E.Bon. Wall light from Aromas del Campo. Mirrors designed by Peggy Bels Interior Design. Wall lamps from Aromas del Campo. Granite countertop from Sing Fai Marble (tel: 2511 8375). Powder room Mirror designed by Peggy Bels Interior Design. Hanging light from Nature Evolution. Vanity top in Calacatta marble custom-built by Sing Fai Marble. Axor tap from E.Bon. Breakfast nook Banquette designed by Peggy Bels Interior Design. Yoyo pendant light from Aromas del Campo. Tried + tested To make the most of the spectacular sea views, designer Peggy Bels added two internal windows – one in the kitchen, another in the guest bedroom above. Recessed into the double-height textured concrete wall of the living area, the glazing introduces daylight and scenery into previously dimly lit spaces. While uncommon in Hong Kong, these atelier windows are widely found in Europe, she says, adding: “The irregular composition of the black-framed glazing lends the atelier windows a subtle art deco character, turning a practical intervention into a graphic architectural feature.” Woodblock print by Ralph Kiggell (1960-2022).

title: KPop Demon Hunters’ Ejae weds Samuel Kim in Seoul, but what do we know about him?
description: The ‘Golden’ singer walked down the aisle in a Danielle Frankel bridal gown, with her co-stars Audrey Nuna and Rei Ami among the guests.
content: South Korean songstress Ejae, who found global fame after lending her voice to Netflix’s 2025 animated film, KPop Demon Hunters, recently tied the knot with her long-time partner, Samuel Kim, on October 17. Ejae, whose real name is Kim Eun-jae, wore a custom Danielle Frankel bridal gown for the ceremony, while her groom wore a classic tuxedo by Bhambi, a New York City-based custom tailor. The newlyweds’ nuptials were featured in Vogue and were reportedly held at Stage 28 in Seoul’s Gangdong district, where her grandparents lived. “My grandparents lived in the house at the venue when I was a little girl,” Ejae told Vogue about the wedding venue. “I spent much of my childhood exploring the garden and walking with my grandfather in the hills behind the house.” Ejae’s KPop Demon Hunters co-stars Rei Ami and Audrey Nuna were among the guests at the wedding. Kim is reportedly also in the music industry. Here’s everything you need to know about Ejae’s husband, Samuel Kim. What does Samuel Kim do? Samuel Kim is reported to be an American-South Korean singer and producer. He collaborated with Ejae for one of KPop Demon Hunters’ biggest songs, What It Sounds Like. “There’s a lot of layers, lots of harmonies, lots of crowd,” Ejae said in an interview with The 92nd Street Y, New York this February. “His [Kim’s] voice is in there if you listen really closely.” In her 2025 interview with Vulture, Ejae revealed that while Kim still produces music, he has since “switched to coding”. How did Ejae and Samuel Kim meet? Ejae met Kim through mutual friends for a songwriting session at his home studio in 2017, she said in an interview with Vogue. What started out as a collaboration between two musicians slowly turned into romance, and the two began dating after Kim confessed his feelings during a night out. The couple dated for over eight years and eventually moved to Brooklyn, New York. Ejae has previously revealed that she and Kim took a “healthy, intentional break” five years into their relationship. “‘It was kind of a moment of like ... ‘If we were to part ways, how would I cope with that?’”Ejae said during an appearance on 104.3 MYfm in November 2025. “For me it was thinking, ‘OK maybe in this lifetime it wasn’t meant to be, but maybe in another life, in another world, it would have worked out.’” “It wasn’t that [Sam was] the issue. It was that just this current lifetime, that I had to deal with the trauma that I was dealt with in this life, it just wasn’t working for us,” she continued. Fortunately the couple found their way back to each other and Kim popped the question in June 2025 with a “surprise” proposal, although Ejae told Vogue that she’d “caught on about a week before”.

title: Heep Hong Society urges more SEN support for ethnic minority preschoolers
description: The charity is seeking an expansion of inclusive, multilingual early support, highlighting language and cultural barriers.
content:
A non-profit group in Hong Kong is asking officials to increase support services for children from ethnic minority backgrounds who have special needs. A pilot project showed that more than 95 per cent of participants made progress with support services.
Heep Hong Society said ethnic minority families face many problems when finding help for kids who have special educational needs (SEN). These include language difficulties and not having enough money. They may also have beliefs that make it hard to ask for help.
Government-funded centres help preschool-aged SEN children. But students need to have a diagnosis from a doctor. This can take a long time and even be costly.
The Social Welfare Department said the number of non-Chinese-speaking children getting help for special needs at preschool centres increased to 968 in the 2025-26 school year. This is up from 741 children in 2023-24.
Heep Hong Society ran a programme called Project Embrace from 2023 to 2025. It helped ethnic minority kids aged six and below through SEN assessments and support services. Oxfam Hong Kong’s study found that 95.7 per cent of participants improved in many ways.

title: In Focus | China is moving past a GDP-first mindset. Can local officials get with the programme?
description: Cadres at lower levels are juggling a complex set of priorities from Beijing – while still searching for new sources of growth.
content: Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the first part of this series, Frank Chen and Alice Li track the ways top-level policy decisions flow down to local officials – and the challenges those officials face in balancing a wide set of priorities. When many took time off to enjoy China’s National Day holiday earlier this month, stories from media outlets in the eastern province of Jiangsu showed the region’s Communist Party chief, Xin Changxing, hard at work. He started the day by conducting a safety inspection at a metro station, then visited local shops to see how sales were faring over the holiday. Later, he observed a fire drill before spending the rest of the day checking in on crowd control measures at major tourist hotspots. As China’s economy continues its transition to an era of lower absolute growth figures but greater sophistication, Beijing has expanded its to-do lists for local officials like Xin who are on the front lines of implementing policy. Once tasked almost solely with stimulating economic growth, these political cadres are now juggling a set of increasingly complex – and sometimes competing – priorities. To name a few, officials are taking steps to fight corruption, maintain national security, improve public safety, reduce debt, create jobs, nurture China’s home-grown tech and keep the economy growing. But under the weight of weak domestic consumption and a tepid property market, gross domestic product figures have been fluctuating. Earlier this year, Beijing said it would aim for 4.5 to 5.0 per cent GDP growth for 2026 – the lowest target since 1991. Caution wins over initiative ... A mistake could cost them more than doing nothing Alfredo Montufar-Helu, Ankura While concerns grew about meeting that benchmark after a 4.3 per cent growth rate was reported in the second quarter, a 4.5 per cent rate recorded in the third quarter suggests the lower end of that range remains in sight, pushing the rate up to 4.6 per cent for the first nine months of the year. All eyes are now on the fifth plenum of the party’s Central Committee, to be held from October 26 to 29. The meeting comes roughly one year before the party’s twice-a-decade national congress, a session expected to feature an extensive personnel reshuffle, including the formation of a new decision-making Politburo. The plenum is an occasion for Beijing to clarify its policy goals. But analysts said the focus of this edition of the high-stakes gathering might be on the party’s self-improvement and strengthened rule. Some observers expressed worries that Beijing’s shifting, sometimes contrasting priorities could divert local officials’ attention away from growth. Alfredo Montufar-Helu, China managing director at consulting firm Ankura, said while economic development still mattered, Beijing’s definition of it had changed. “Growth [is] increasingly judged by its contribution to security and tech self-reliance,” he said. Local officials, typically risk-averse, would be paying close attention to the party’s signals, Montufar-Helu added. “Caution wins over initiative,” he said. “A mistake could cost them more than doing nothing.” Broadening priorities While the policy juggling act expected of local officials is not a new phenomenon, analysts said more targets are being set. “Every day, they might have different orders cascade down to them,” said Zhu Jiangnan, an associate professor of politics at the University of Hong Kong. “So what are the real priorities? Those emphasised more by the topmost leaders would become the ones to work on.” But what localities are told to prioritise today is drastically different from the growth-centric mandate handed down decades ago. Then, the binding principle was “economic construction”, shaped by China’s paramount leader Deng Xiaoping after he came to power at the end of the 1970s. Successive leaders such as Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao largely adhered to a similar policy. But Xi Jinping, Communist Party general secretary since 2012 and president since 2013, has broadened what Beijing viewed as critical, analysts said. First, there was his instruction to “coordinate economic development and security”, enshrined into the party constitution at its 20th national congress in 2022. At the previous congress in 2017, he coined the term “high-quality development”, introducing another overarching principle to inform decision-making and indicate growth was no longer the only benchmark at play in policy work. China’s intensifying rivalry with the US has also prompted Beijing to make self-reliance in tech another high-level mandate as it seeks to break the West’s chokehold on advanced products and components, with localities urged to coalesce their resources in this effort. After Xi visited Shanghai twice this year – trips that were centred around tech – the city’s government gazetted two documents to supercharge basic research and innovation and promote the use of artificial intelligence, observers noted. To help cadres at all levels tackle the new priorities, Beijing has been pushing to install a “correct” understanding of what constitutes good performance among officials since February, eyeing a strong start to its 15th five-year plan. The move was seen as a pivot away from focusing on raw GDP growth and “at-all-costs” development as the sole criterion for promotion, placing the debt, fraud and vanity projects that sometimes resulted from this mindset in the crosshairs. “Nowadays, the focus is on politics and party doctrine,” said the head of a government agency in Zhejiang province who declined to be named. The official, who oversees financing for small and medium-sized enterprises, said she and her colleagues were beginning to make decisions with more caution, weighing the political dimension alongside the economic realm. “We study political theories and top leaders’ directives and apply them to our work,” she added. Growth not out of focus However, this shift in perspective has not left the problems plaguing the economy without a response. When momentum appeared to be waning in the second quarter despite a strong start to the year, Beijing held a succession of meetings, seminars and inspections dedicated to diagnosing and tackling the most pressing issues. Larry Hu Weijun, chief China economist at Macquarie, said Beijing tended to take a dynamic and adaptable approach. “Having multiple goals doesn’t mean growth is not important,” he said. “Rather, the importance of growth diminishes once the target is within reach, but rises sharply when the target is under threat.” Recent actions bear this logic out. Last month, policymakers unveiled a series of measures in quick succession to resuscitate the economy: cutting policy interest rates, offering mortgage interest subsidies for homebuyers and unlocking 550 billion yuan (US$82.18 billion) in local debt quotas to boost investment. At a meeting of the party’s Politburo in July, Beijing pledged to accelerate the pace of fiscal spending, promptly roll out incremental policies and speed up the transition of growth models for the remainder of the year amid rising volatility in global markets and the second-quarter GDP downturn. Among these efforts, top economic planner the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Finance and the People’s Bank of China have set up a 100 billion yuan fiscal-financial coordination fund to boost domestic demand. Policymakers have resisted letting loose a stimulus “flood”, saying their intent has been to focus on countercyclical adjustments and the precise targeting of priority areas, including private and small-scale enterprises, domestic demand and the green energy transition. Putting officials on notice However, local officials are frequently reminded on what their priorities are – and how they must deliver. Beijing is unafraid to name and shame as it admonishes deviations in the understanding and implementation of its directives. One area that has been given extra attention in recent years is public safety, particularly in the wake of several natural disasters. Central authorities have stepped up scrutiny of local governments this year over safety issues and tightened accountability. Since September, over 400 officials across four regions – Hainan and Jiangsu provinces, as well as the Guangxi Zhuang and Xinjiang Uygur autonomous regions – have been held responsible for safety risks and lapses in local oversight following evaluations by central government inspectors. Beijing has also taken a closer interest in localities that have been instructed to fire up their economic engines, examining the results of their efforts in detail and doling out penalties for ill-fated or extravagant projects. In June, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection – the party’s chief anti-corruption organ – named and shamed officials in Jiangxi, Sichuan and Hebei provinces, as well as the Guangxi and Inner Mongolia autonomous regions, for chasing development that increased debt risks and using public funds for projects that did not return a profit. Businesses get reality check As local officials work to navigate Beijing’s shifting requirements, they may in turn alter their practices as they deal with businesses, particularly the private and foreign firms operating in the country. While some firms have acknowledged the need to curb debt and move away from a GDP-first mindset, others have voiced concerns about mixed, even conflicting signals and structural mismatches in policy implementation. The American Chamber of Commerce in China flagged some of these issues in its annual white paper. “Central directives prioritising hi-tech self-reliance and domestic national security controls often clash directly with local-level efforts to rebuild foreign business confidence and revive consumer spending,” the chamber wrote in April. The business advocacy body called on policymakers to create a “proportionate, predictable balance” between national security and economic openness, warning sudden shifts or conflicting signals could lead multinationals to defer long-term investments. A heavier focus on national security and public safety has been cited by some business figures as complicating their operating environment. One common complaint, for instance, centres on frequent safety inspections and red tape disrupting firms’ normal operations and adding to their costs. A report published last year in an online content platform run by the Chongqing municipal committee of the Chinese Communist Party noted that some companies were subjected to four or five safety inspections in a single week. Ankura’s Montufar-Helu said Beijing’s increasing emphasis on security and party discipline has made local officials more risk-averse as they choose which projects and businesses to support with incentives. “Local governments will steer resources towards the sectors Beijing has flagged as strategic and away from anything that looks risky … Officials will be slower to back projects that could draw scrutiny, including those involving foreign and private companies,” he warned. “For them, getting things done with local authorities is likely to be harder.”

title: China’s stabilisation pledge did not lift stocks. Why are investors praising it?
description: Speech by chief securities regulator signals a much-needed shift from short-term firefighting towards long-term stability, brokerages say.
content: A slew of market-stabilising measures unveiled by the head of China’s securities regulator this week has won praise from investors, despite the fact that mainland stock prices did not roar back over the following days. The focus on supporting stocks and investor confidence over the long term, rather than deploying contingency actions to deal with short-term market turmoil, signalled a much-needed shift in Beijing’s strategy, industry players said. Wu Qing, chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), pledged at a financial forum on Monday to attract fresh funds to Chinese markets through further opening-up policies and the approval of new exchange-traded funds (ETFs). The regulator would also closely monitor the risk of contagion spilling over from overseas markets and encourage stock buy-backs by listed companies, he added. While Wu’s speech did little to provide an immediate boost to stocks, with the benchmark CSI 300 Index falling more than 1 per cent this week, brokerages said the measures marked a shift in the regulators’ approach to managing market declines. While direct state intervention remained an option, it might now be a tool that Beijing only turned to in extreme circumstances, they said. “We can see from this round of market-stabilising efforts that the regulatory mindset has shifted to building up a regular system and away from resorting to short-term contingency measures,” said Cheng Qiang, an analyst at Topsperity Securities. “Looking forward, inflows of fresh capital look certain, but that may take place at a measured pace rather than rapidly.” Wu said at the forum that the CSRC had approved 18 actively managed ETFs for the first time, a move that domestic media said would channel about 2 billion yuan (US$299.5 million) of fresh capital into the market. Mainland China ETFs now have a total value of nearly 5 trillion yuan – bigger than actively managed funds in 2024. Foreign ownership in China’s onshore stock market might also increase gradually over the coming quarters, Cheng said, as the CSRC was expected to further open up Asia’s largest stock market to global investors. Real estate investment trusts and Hong Kong’s yuan-stock trading counter would be added to the cross-border Stock Connect programme, Cheng said, adding that the CSRC would keep fine-tuning policies to facilitate the Qualified Foreign Institutional Investor scheme. China’s stocks traded near a 14-month low on Wednesday, as sentiment deteriorated after the latest economic data pointed to persistently weak domestic demand and a lingering downturn in housing prices. US Treasury yields rising to multi-decade highs also helped fuel the sell-off by squelching the multiples of Chinese technology stocks. Wu highlighted the fresh risks from offshore leveraged products linked to underlying yuan stocks trading on mainland Chinese exchanges, indicating that the CSRC was more attentive to external shocks now and would strengthen cross-market oversight to mitigate the fallout of overseas turbulence. He said the CSRC would also set up a new unit dedicated to monitoring the operation of the fund industry, broadening the scope for its risk management of investment tools. The unit would be responsible for registrations of private hedge funds, information collection and risk monitoring of mutual funds. Those moves “would curb short-term volatility from external shocks and stabilise the risk appetite”, said Wei Chunze, an analyst at Shenwan Hongyuan. “Over the medium- and long-term horizon, it’s a continuation of pushing forward the comprehensive reform of the stock market by enlarging long-term capital and optimising the market-stabilising mechanism.”

title: Trump faces fresh questions over ties to Putin after envoy’s ‘humanitarian’ praise
description: Lavish praise from envoy Steve Witkoff underscores the unusual alignment between the American and Russian leaders.
content: US President Donald Trump’s pivot away from Ukraine has triggered fresh questions about his attachment to Russian leader Vladimir Putin, the man a top American envoy flattered on Wednesday as a “humanitarian”. Trump has cast his dealings with Putin as part of a mega-deal that has secured the release of American detainee Stephen Hubbard – and which Trump says will end Russia’s war on Ukraine. At the same time, he has repeatedly berated Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and called for him to be replaced. “I do things that nobody else can do,” Trump told a reporter in the Oval Office on Tuesday when asked about Hubbard. But for Trump’s critics, it is the latest example of his willingness to sell Ukraine down the river, especially as he seeks a deal before difficult US midterm elections in November. His ties to Putin have long been under scrutiny. Trump still complains of what he calls the “Russia hoax” following an investigation in his first term into whether his 2016 election campaign colluded with Moscow. Last week, Trump announced a huge agreement under which he said Russia would release diesel to ease prices sent soaring by the Iran war – and temporarily eased sanctions on Moscow. Trump insisted on social media that there was “no ‘swap’ necessary” for Hubbard’s release. Yet in another post minutes later, he admitted that if he had not paused the sanctions targeting Russia, “those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt”. The US president has also appeared to give diplomatic rewards to Putin – who masterminded the Ukraine war and has pushed his maximalist goals for more than four years of grinding conflict. In St Petersburg on Wednesday, Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff told Putin: “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian – you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that”. Republican Senator Thom Tillis, a frequent Trump critic in recent months, reacted with astonishment. “WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian’,” he said in a social media post. Trump earlier this week confirmed that he was ready to hold a three-way summit with the Russian leader and Chinese President Xi Jinping during which Ukraine could be discussed. Moscow then announced on Wednesday it would restart three-way talks with Kyiv and Washington. Yet previous rounds of talks, including a Trump-Putin summit in Alaska in August 2025, have produced no breakthroughs. Ukraine insists it must be included in any talks. But Trump’s response was to again blame Zelensky – whom he berated in the Oval Office in February 2025 – for not accepting a deal. “Since Donald Trump has come into office, we have seen some gravitational pull towards the arguments of the Russian president,” said Liana Fix of the Council for Foreign Relations. Many of the voices that once pulled Trump back towards Ukraine are also now silent, said Fix. Staunchly pro-Kyiv US senator Lindsey Graham died earlier this year, and European leaders are dealing with their own problems at home. Putin is “exploiting Trump’s nervousness ahead of the midterm elections, and he’s playing that very well”, Fix added. Trump has been desperately seeking ways to bring down oil prices, as voters angered by the cost of living look set to punish his Republican Party in the November 3 midterms. Fears have also mounted that Trump is looking to punish Ukraine. He has blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries – and not his own war with Iran – for high oil prices. Kyiv complained that Washington had briefly halted the sending of intelligence to help counter Russia’s missile attacks and reduced speeds in the military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite system. “Sometimes I wonder if folks here in the US understand, truly understand, that Kyiv is fighting an existential war against the Russian aggressor,” said Gian Gentile, a retired US Army colonel and former director of the military history programme at West Point. Ukraine has also complained of hold-ups in the supply of vital interceptor missiles. “There’s no question that these actions are intended to hurt Ukraine,” said Mark Cancian, a retired US Marine colonel and senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

title: Macron takes veiled shot at Trump, Netanyahu over ‘stupid’ France riot remarks
description: The French president said some leaders were influenced by fake videos generated by artificial intelligence about the unrest.
content: President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday criticised world leaders for making “stupid” comments about the rioting on the sidelines of protests in France, in an apparent swipe at US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Macron said the leaders were taking aim at France in the context of coming elections in their countries and added that they had been influenced by fake videos generated by artificial intelligence about the riots. Some of the worst urban violence to hit France in years erupted on Saturday on the fringe of nationwide protests over the rising cost of living. “There was foreign manipulation of information which led to unacceptable and even stupid comments by many, including foreign leaders,” Macron told reporters in Doha after a trip to the Gulf. He did not mention Trump or Netanyahu by name. But the US leader faces key midterm election in November while the Israeli prime minister will fight for his political life in this month’s election. Macron said that the leaders campaigning for elections had repeated “sometimes with credulity” material generated by AI. Netanyahu on Tuesday said France had been hit by an “invasion of extremist Islam” while Trump has declared “what’s happening in France has to do with immigration”. Trump hailed Marine Le Pen, the far-right front runner in France’s presidential election next year, as a “conservative voice”. Macron emphasised he did not see “foreign interference” in what unfolded in France at the weekend. But he warned: “We saw images generated by AI which showed scenes that never took place in France. “We had people who explained that we had been ‘invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists’, which is totally false.” “In these moments you see who likes France and who does not. All the people who speak badly of us now do not like our country,” he added. Macron was criticised in some quarters at home for undertaking a visit to the Middle East at such a time and also for an address to the nation on Sunday which critics said lacked a clear path forward. But, before returning home, he insisted he was in control. “There must be no sign of febrility,” he said. “I am fulfilling my role. I am at my post.”

title: Riots unnerve France’s US$80 billion tourism sector: ‘it’s catastrophic’
description: ‘Honestly, we were not certain that we’d keep our stay,’ a tourist in a pricey Paris hotel says.
content: The images of France’s riots posted and broadcast around the world have cast a pall on the country’s important tourism sector, with many fearing worse consequences if violence returns. “The surge of violence in the centres of Nice, Paris, Lyon – it’s catastrophic,” said Christelle Cassagne, head of the ADN Tourisme body covering the country’s tourism institutions. “When you book a hotel for a week, it’s not so you stay stuck in the hotel,” she said. The scenes of clashes with police, public buildings on fire, shops being looted and masked young men roaming the streets have, since last weekend, shocked and fascinated news audiences internationally. The violence has usurped the usual curated footage of genteel cafes favoured by influencers, who have suddenly taken to asking “Is Paris safe?” – many using AI on thumbnails or even in their videos to boost click-through rates. The closure of the Louvre in Paris on Monday because of a small group of student protesters at the entrance also frustrated many visitors who had the museum on their list of highlights. The uncertainty has made some hesitant about visiting the City of Light. “Honestly, we were not certain that we’d keep our stay,” an Indian businessman in a pricey Paris hotel said, declining to give his name. Already, hotel reservations are weakening in major cities such as Paris, Lyon and Marseille, according to Didier Arino, head of the consulting and research firm Protourisme. For a country used to welcoming 100 million visitors a year – and the more than €70 billion (US$80 billion) they spend – it is a concern. Arino and other observers said the overall picture for France’s tourism industry would depend on whether new violence broke out in the coming weeks. “The impact of a day of rioting and urban violence in the heart of Paris caused around 1 per cent cancellation rate for the monthly count in the days following, and the same for the following weeks,” Arino said. “For the 42 million hotel nights forecast for 2026, that’s not major. But watch out you don’t underestimate the effects from repeated incidents.” “The further away the clients are, the more sensitive they are to safety risks, and the stronger the impact,” Arino said. Visitors from farther-away countries, particularly the United States and some Asian ones, often spend more than Europeans during their stay. The downward pressure on reservations comes as several countries, including the US, China and Germany, issued travel advisories for their citizens in France. Laurent Abitbol, head of the executive board of travel agency group Selectour, said: “If this lasts two weeks, that’s not so serious. However, if this continues for several months it will be catastrophic.” “When you watch CNN, or Fox News, BBC, all that, you’d believe that France is at war. That’s not good.” Another firm, MKG Consulting, said that, since last weekend, Paris hotels have lost potential bookings for the next six weeks. Its data showed bookings had weakened sharply within a day. Between October 19 and 20, the share of rooms booked for stays from October 20-29 fell from being 1.0 percentage point above the level recorded for the same period in 2025 to just 0.2 percentage points higher. For stays between October 20 and 25, the increase over 2025 levels also narrowed significantly, dropping from 3.5 percentage points to 1.9 points. “This slowdown is especially notable for near-term and high-end stays,” it said, drawing a parallel with a period in December 2018 when Yellow Vest street protests raged in the capital’s streets.

title: Editorial | Holiday rush at Huanggang Port should catalyse improvement
description: The massive queues at the revamped border crossing during the Chung Yeung Festival long weekend call for a comprehensive review.
content: The first holiday test of the revamped Huanggang Port demands a thorough review. The newly opened checkpoint was meant to showcase Hong Kong’s readiness for deeper integration with the Greater Bay Area under the latest national drive. Instead, its first major holiday rush showed that a modern building is no guarantee of travel convenience. The authorities must urgently review what went wrong, fix the weaknesses and ensure the facility delivers the seamless cross-border travel that was promised. Last week’s official opening was preceded by extensive preparation. Officials conducted pressure tests and large-scale drills. The new facility was presented as a key piece of infrastructure for strengthening Hong Kong’s role as a gateway between the city and the mainland, promising travellers smooth clearance as quickly as about five minutes. Yet the first Chung Yeung Festival long weekend exposed a gap between experience and expectation. Outbound passenger flow rose sharply from about 11am on Sunday. Between noon and 2pm, roughly 19,000 people left for the mainland, an 835 per cent increase compared with the corresponding period at the former Huanggang/Lok Ma Chau control point. In the peak hour between 1pm and 2pm, 9,728 passenger trips departed, almost nine times the previous comparable level. Travellers felt the consequences. The Security Bureau issued a “busy” alert at about 1.45pm, warning of waiting times of up to 45 minutes for departing passengers. While the government said crowd diversion at level two took 30 to 45 minutes and waiting within the level five departure hall was kept within 30 minutes, some travellers reported waits of around two hours or more. In contrast, the operations of the seven other land crossings, including Lo Wu, Lok Ma Chau Spur Line and Shenzhen Bay, remained “normal” throughout the morning and early afternoon, with clearance times as short as five minutes. Be it two hours or 45 minutes, the wait at the revamped Huanggang Port was much longer than the five minutes promised. Those who experienced standing in a long immigration queue may have felt like the clock was ticking slower as they waited for their turn. Some stranded travellers complained that they received little real-time information at the scene. The authorities apparently responded to the best of their abilities. Immigration officers opened all clearance channels and counters, and crowd-control and diversion measures were in place. The outbound peak began to ease from about 2pm. By 3.30pm, the port’s status had returned to normal. The relatively quick recovery is welcome. Meanwhile, inbound crossings during the height of the return period on Monday also remained smooth. Given the crowds on the previous days, Sunday’s crunch was not entirely unforeseen. Indeed, officials had said that the Chung Yeung Festival long weekend would be the real test following the smooth opening last week. According to Immigration Department figures, the new port recorded more than 92,000 crossings on Friday and the figure further grew to over 130,000 on Saturday. The number peaked at 152,000 on Sunday. The stakes extend beyond one inconvenient Sunday. Huanggang Port has been touted as a game-changer for closer economic, social and family ties across the Greater Bay Area. If residents and visitors cannot rely on smooth crossings during holidays, the port will fall short of its strategic purpose. This episode should be turned into a catalyst for improvement so that the checkpoint can become a model of efficient cross-border mobility. The review must be swift and comprehensive. It should cover a wide range of relevant issues, including staffing and deployment, crowd control contingencies, transport connections as well as real-time dissemination of information. Authorities on both sides of the border have invested heavily in the revamped facility. Evidently, the increasingly heavy cross-border travel means bottlenecks are to be expected from time to time. Effective contingency measures are therefore essential. Ultimately, Huanggang Port’s success will be judged not by its hardware but by its overall performance. The first holiday rush has provided a valuable, if uncomfortable, lesson that should be acted upon.

title: Ramaswamy faces firestorm over US political ad featuring Democrat rival’s estranged mother
description: Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton has not spoken with her mum since childhood, when she accused her stepfather of sexual abuse.
content: Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for Ohio governor, faced a firestorm of criticism Wednesday over an ad featuring Democratic rival Amy Acton’s estranged mother, whose husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child. Acton has not spoken with her mother, Donna Arthur, since her childhood, when she accused her then-stepfather of sexually abusing her for years. In the ad, Arthur says her daughter has “lied her entire life”. “Don’t let her become your governor. If you think she’ll make your life better, you’re fooling yourself,” Arthur says. On Tuesday, Acton issued a statement saying she and her brother “endured abuse, hunger and neglect” as children. “Between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me,” 60-year-old Acton said of Arthur. Arthur’s husband fled before he could be tried on the sexual assault charges and is now dead. Acton said she had not seen Arthur since 1978. Acton said it was “sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain”. Ramaswamy, a billionaire biotech entrepreneur who ran in the 2024 Republican presidential primaries, is facing off against Acton, a medical doctor by training and former state health department director, in the race to be Ohio’s next governor. The contest is deemed a toss-up by Cook Political Report. In an open letter to The Columbus Dispatch newspaper, the city’s former mayor Michael Coleman called the ad “the most vile, disgusting and lowest point I have ever seen in 35 years of political engagement”. MK Pritzker, the wife of Illinois’s billionaire Democratic Governor J.B. Pritzker, immediately announced a US$500,000 donation to Acton’s campaign. “Bad men gain power when we refuse to stand up and fight,” she said in a statement. Ramaswamy, who has reportedly planned to spend US$4 million airing the ad, enjoys the support of US President Donald Trump, who opted only to weigh in by saying Arthur had gone “very rogue on the daughter”. “The mother is a witness to things also. So, who knows?” he said. On the campaign trail on Wednesday in Ohio, his home state, Vice-President J.D. Vance defended his “good friend” Ramaswamy. “Now the media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is, and calls Amy Acton a liar,” Vance said. Republican strategist Jeanette Hoffman, however, said the ad was already backfiring for Ramaswamy. “A lot of times, political ads that are negative, they work. But to work, they have to have credibility behind them,” Hoffman told NewsNation, calling the ad “horrific”. “This ad is so outrageously offensive it is backfiring on Vivek because you’re making Amy Acton the victim, and Vivek is looking like the villain because Amy Acton is a victim here. She’s a victim of sexual assault.” Acton’s campaign ran a video featuring her brother Phil Stearns, who said: “She was 11 and 12 years old, and to think that that’s somehow a talking point. Shame on Vivek.”

title: Pope Leo doesn’t need further treatment for lung cancer, doctors say
description: Follow-up tests show the pontiff’s disease has not spread after he had surgery to remove part of his lung.
content: Pope Leo needs no further treatment for lung cancer after follow-up tests confirmed the disease was localised, the Vatican said in a statement on Wednesday. Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed last week in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. He left the hospital on Saturday, four days after surgery and well ahead of the week-long hospital stay the Vatican had initially anticipated. The pope’s personal doctor, Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement that results of the final post-operative tests on tissue removed during the pope’s surgery confirmed the initial diagnosis and that the cancer had not spread. “A subsequent oncology assessment confirmed that no further treatment is necessary,” the doctors said. The pope had the lower section, or lobe, of his right lung removed to try to ensure that all the cancer was removed. Additional treatment is offered in such cases if follow-up testing finds signs that the cancer has spread or has certain other signs that it might be particularly aggressive. Surgery often can be enough when tumours are caught very early, such as when someone has an X-ray or other scan that shows a spot long before it is large or causing symptoms. The pope appears to have had one of those “incidental findings”, a nodule in his lung spotted during another exam. In an interview with Vatican News, Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, confirmed that the nodule was found by chance during routine abdominal examinations. The pope carried on business while in hospital, including a call with Russian President Putin, and has appeared strong in two public appearances at the Vatican since his surgery: the traditional Sunday blessing from a window overlooking St Peter’s Square and Wednesday’s longer audience, when he greeted the faithful from all over the world. His next major engagement is an ambitious November 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Margaritora was quoted by Vatican News as saying that there was “no clinical reason” to prevent the trip, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and high altitude stops. The pope revealed that a nodule had been found and would be surgically removed during the traditional Sunday blessing on October 11, in an unusually transparent disclosure.

title: Meta to pay New Mexico a historic US$25 billion in Cambridge Analytica Facebook case
description: The company was accused of lying to Facebook users about its privacy policies and how it handled their data in the wake of the scandal.
content: Meta Platforms was ordered to pay a groundbreaking US$25 billion civil penalty to the state of New Mexico in a consumer deception case spurred by the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The fine issued by state court Judge Francis Mathew is among the largest verdicts issued in US legal history. The award comes after a jury in Santa Fe determined that Meta had violated the state’s consumer protection over 43 million times based on widely viewed deceptive statements made by the company and its top executives about how it handled hate speech and user data. Under New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act, Mathew could issue penalties of up to US$5,000 per violation. The two-week trial in the First Judicial District Court of New Mexico centred on claims by Attorney General Raul Torrez that Meta had lied to Facebook users about its privacy policies and how it handled their data in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica leak almost a decade ago. The attorney general also advanced claims that the company deceived the public about content moderation decisions and its hate speech policies, pointing to evidence that certain high-profile accounts were not subject to the same scrutiny as ordinary users. Jurors saw video deposition testimony from Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg and former chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg. Meta has been willing to pay large sums to settle cases involving the Cambridge Analytica leak, which involved a political consulting firm using ill-gotten data on millions of Facebook users to target voters for Donald Trump before the 2016 election. The Menlo Park, California, company paid out US$5 billion to settle with the Federal Trade Commission in 2019, and signed a US$725 million settlement in 2022 to resolve a consumer class action. Meta paid US$459 million in an agreement this summer to resolve cases from 46 states and two territories. But New Mexico has been an especially costly thorn in the side of Meta, opting out of state AG coalitions prosecuting the company and instead going it alone.
