The penalty award for New Mexico comes months after the state became the first in the nation to win a jury verdict against Meta over claims that Facebook and Instagram harm teen mental health and foster child sexual exploitation. That trial from earlier this year saw a US$375 million civil penalty followed by an additional US$567 million payment Meta must make to the state to set up programmes to combat the youth mental health crisis.

title: Review | Clayface review: DC spin-off delivers a grisly, vengeance-fuelled body-horror thriller
description: Tom Rhys Harries stars in this grotesque tale of Hollywood ambition, betrayal and revenge, which puts a Batman character in the spotlight.
content: 3.5/5 stars From Venom and Morbius to Birds of Prey and The New Mutants, elevating side characters to centre stage in Marvel and DC comic-book adaptations rarely takes flight. Clayface, however, is an exception. Set in the Gotham underworld, the new film features no sign – or even mention – of Batman, but no matter. A grisly but delicious tale of Hollywood excess, this DC thriller is part crime, part horror and certainly not one for the squeamish. Tom Rhys Harries (Suspicion) stars as Matt Hagen, an American actor whose career is soaring. Fresh off an Oscar nomination, he is out celebrating when he meets – and sleeps with – the girlfriend of ruthless mob boss Markos Szabo (David Dencik). In retaliation, Markos’ goons slice his face to shreds. Nobody will talk, and those who do trash Hagen in the press, leaving his career in ruins. He gets a sliver of hope when he meets Dr Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), a well-meaning scientist working on radical nanotechnology designed to aid those with degenerative diseases. Desperate, Matt begs her for help; she eventually agrees – and this is where the fun starts. At first, his grotesque scars miraculously heal, but the treatment is not stable; soon, his face is melting like plastic over an open flame. What unfolds is a vengeance-fuelled descent into body horror that will make you squirm and shriek. One scene features Matt using nail scissors to try to cut away skin that has grown over his eyes, in the bathroom of a turbulence-rocked plane. Smartly mixing visceral prosthetics and CG throughout, this film truly understands the joy of repulsion. Helmed by British director James Watkins, who previously directed the chilling 2012 film adaptation of The Woman in Black, Clayface boasts a faultless genre pedigree. The script is bolstered by co-writer Mike Flanagan, who recently released his television adaptation of Stephen King’s Carrie. Harries also convinces as the mutilated star, getting to explore method acting in a highly unusual fashion. Watkins’ take on Gotham is not as noirish as The Batman – that film’s director, Matt Reeves, is a producer here – and there is something rather cartoonish about Markos and his cronies. The addition of Rob Brydon as a chat-show host impersonating Al Pacino also does not gel. But with a story that touches on betrayal, corruption and vanity, it feels of a piece with the broader Batman mythos. From alluding to films such as Brian Yuzna’s Society (1989) and Troma’s The Toxic Avenger (1984), to featuring an unexpected and hilarious dance sequence in Markos’ club – intercut with some truly twisted shape-shifting – Clayface moulds its elements into something original and often horrifying. That is a feat few other spin-offs have managed. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Washington’s DeepSeek ban may deter US firms from adopting Chinese AI models: experts
description: Ban may ripple beyond government agencies, influencing how software firms, cloud providers and other businesses choose models.
content: The US government’s latest ban on Chinese artificial intelligence start-up DeepSeek could have a chilling effect on the wider American business community and deter companies from adopting low-cost Chinese AI models, industry experts say. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products and third-party services built on the Chinese AI model from their IT systems, according to a directive signed in July and published on Monday. The department also barred agencies from procuring such products, citing national security concerns. China on Tuesday criticised the ban, accusing Washington of politicising trade and technology under the guise of national security. Foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said Beijing opposed the overextension of national security concepts, while the commerce ministry called the ban a discriminatory measure that undermined fair competition, urging Washington to revoke it and warning that China would take necessary steps to protect its interests. DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. While the DHS order explicitly targeted federal civilian agencies, its impact could extend to private companies that served both government and commercial clients, according to industry watchers. Industry veteran Xiang Ligang, founder of Chinese telecommunications industry portal c114.com, acknowledged the need for government agencies to address security concerns, but warned against expanding the restrictions to the broader US market. “DeepSeek is highly cost-efficient and the US should not shut it out, as doing so would be detrimental to the US economy and AI development,” Xiang said. Making the DHS order public sent a clearer signal to companies beyond the federal procurement system, prompting software developers, cloud providers and systems integrators to assess whether their use of DeepSeek could jeopardise government business, according to an independent Chinese geopolitical and tech policy analyst who declined to be named. The disclosure risked turning an internal government procurement restriction into a broader market signal, influencing how American companies designed their products and chose AI models, he said. “This could change the cost calculations for American businesses when choosing AI models,” he added. The move comes as US lawmakers seek to extend restrictions on Chinese AI models to private-sector suppliers serving government customers. The growing regulatory burden is forcing American software developers to weigh the benefits of low-cost Chinese models against the risk of losing access to federal contracts. The implications could extend beyond DeepSeek, according to the geopolitical and tech policy analyst, as the national security concerns cited by the DHS could in theory also be applied to other Chinese AI systems. Washington was pursuing a multipronged strategy to counter the rising popularity of Chinese open-weight AI models, using procurement bans, defence supply chain rules and congressional scrutiny to raise compliance costs and political risks for American adopters, he said. Those measures threaten to undercut the appeal of Chinese models, which have gained traction among US developers and businesses due to their competitive performance, low operating costs and flexibility for deployment on private infrastructure. American firms have increasingly turned to Chinese-developed AI models to curb the soaring costs of deploying generative AI. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky has said the company uses Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen models, citing their speed and affordability. Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post. Other prominent US tech players – including AI coding start-up Cursor, which was recently acquired by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, legal tech firm Harvey, and conversational engine Perplexity AI – have integrated models from DeepSeek or Moonshot AI. For smaller developers, the savings can be particularly significant. A US-based developer told online tech publication Rest of World earlier this year that a coding task costing around US$10 using Anthropic’s Claude could be completed for less than 50 US cents using DeepSeek. Beijing is also moving to tighten oversight of its own AI technologies flowing overseas. China last week proposed new export controls covering advanced AI technologies and models amid rising security concerns, with some domestic industry figures calling for tighter restrictions. Wang Yuquan, founding partner of venture capital firm Haiyin Capital, urged Chinese AI developers to shift towards closed-source models, arguing that open-weight releases exposed developers to foreign regulatory risks while allowing overseas platforms to profit from their technology. Transitioning to proprietary models would help domestic developers retain control over deployment, reduce exposure to foreign bans, and build sustainable revenue streams, Wang was cited as saying in an interview with local media outlet Huxiu earlier this month.

title: Tesla signs deal to integrate Alipay into its cars as China competition heats up
description: The deal will enable Tesla drivers to pay for parking from their in-car touchscreens, with more features to follow, Alipay says.
content: Tesla has agreed a deal to integrate Chinese fintech giant Ant Group’s Alipay digital payment software into its vehicles in China, as Elon Musk’s firm steps up efforts to offer localised smart features amid intense competition in the Chinese market. The agreement, signed on Tuesday, will see Tesla roll out an Alipay-powered smart parking service across its Chinese fleet, according to the fintech firm. Neither side revealed a launch date or which car models would receive the feature, though Alipay said it would be rolled out via a “forthcoming software update”. The feature would allow drivers to pay parking fees directly from their in-car touchscreens, Alipay said, adding that additional features for “in-car lifestyle scenarios” were currently in development. Ant Group is an affiliate of Alibaba Group Holding, which owns the South China Morning Post. The partnership marks Alipay’s latest push to deepen its foothold in the automotive sector. Launched in 2024, its smart assistant connects Alipay’s vast service ecosystem with driving scenarios, designed to enable users to book tickets, order meals and perform other tasks via voice commands. Last year, the assistant was launched as an integrated app on software systems for domestic electric vehicle maker Li Auto, covering its Mega, L-series and i-series models. The feature allowed drivers to access Alipay mini-programs and payment functions to order coffee or track parcel deliveries, among other features. The assistant has been deployed across a total of 66 models from 16 carmakers – including BYD, Xpeng, Nio, Geely and Dongfeng Motor – reaching more than 10 million vehicles, according to Chinese media reports. For Tesla, the collaboration comes as an intense EV price war in China continues to squeeze profit margins. In September, the US carmaker offered discounts on its Shanghai-made vehicles for the first time since late 2024 to counter sluggish domestic demand. In the first seven months of this year, Tesla’s Shanghai Gigafactory – its largest production hub globally – delivered 266,204 vehicles to mainland Chinese buyers, down 12.4 per cent year on year, according to data from the China Passenger Car Association. Tesla has also faced delays in securing full regulatory approval to roll out its Full Self-Driving (FSD) driver-assistance system in China. Although a “supervised” iteration of FSD was launched in May for eligible test vehicles, the company is still trying to navigate stringent data localisation and driver monitoring requirements to secure a nationwide roll-out.

title: Tesla’s ‘flying car’ draws public concern in China – and an official response
description: The People’s Daily highlights recent innovations by Xpeng, BYD and CATL and defends competition as a driver of innovation.
content: The Communist Party’s flagship newspaper has urged the public not to underestimate China’s technological achievements after Tesla’s “flying car” demonstration sparked concern in some quarters that the country may be falling behind in the global auto race. The People’s Daily commentary, published on Wednesday, followed the American electric vehicle giant’s unveiling last week of a second-generation Roadster fitted with thrusters developed with SpaceX, the rocket company led by Tesla CEO Elon Musk. Footage showed the sports car climbing a curved ramp, flipping upside down in mid-air and landing on its wheels. Tesla said it planned to begin production in 2028. The showcase prompted online debate in China about the country’s position in the global auto race. Some expressed concern that the country was losing ground, while others dismissed Tesla’s “flying car” as little more than a glorified toy. Responding to the debate, the People’s Daily said there was “no need to belittle ourselves” or “dismiss the achievements of our new energy vehicle industry”. “Regulations, potential use cases and safety certification all remain unknown,” the commentary added, noting that the vehicle resembled a “polished concept showcase” rather than a car designed for daily use. Cui Dongshu, secretary general of the China Passenger Car Association, echoed that assessment, describing Tesla’s “flying car” as more of a stunt than a vehicle for daily commuting. The car’s ability to leave the ground briefly did not amount to sustained flight and regulatory requirements for road vehicles and airspace would limit public use, Cui said. Cui described the technology as an engineering experiment and distinguished it from China’s efforts to develop electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft for low-altitude urban transport. The People’s Daily commentary also pointed to broader developments in China’s auto industry, citing Chinese manufacturer Xpeng, which had received more than 7,000 pre-orders by April for its “Land Aircraft Carrier” flying car, a six-wheeled vehicle with a detachable passenger aircraft. Other examples cited included BYD’s Yangwang U9 Xtreme supercar, which reached a record top speed of 496.2km/h (308.3mph), and CATL’s third-generation Shenxing battery, which can be fully charged in six minutes at room temperature. The commentary noted China’s 35.6 per cent share of global automotive patent publications as evidence of the country’s capacity for innovation. It also defended the benefits of competition, pointing to Tesla’s entry into Shanghai and saying its factory had encouraged domestic manufacturers to make progress. “Technological breakthroughs accelerate through competition,” the commentary said. “China’s open automotive industry has never shied away from competing on the global stage.”

title: Germany wants to avoid China trade war despite EU ‘kill switch’: Merz
description: German chancellor says Beijing must address bloc’s concerns over subsidies and overcapacity, as Brussels prepares new trade powers.
content: Preparing for war is meant to prevent war – an idea with deep roots in ancient Chinese strategic thought that may have just found an echo in Berlin. The EU’s proposed “kill switch”, intended to swiftly cut off market access for third countries including China, was put forward by France and Germany and unanimously endorsed by member states. But ideally it would never have to be used, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Wednesday, stressing that Berlin was seeking “a new balance in trade” with Beijing rather than a trade war. “We are having instruments, we are opening the toolbox, we are showing the toolbox, but we do not want to make use of our toolbox,” Merz told an audience at the Berlin Global Dialogue annual summit. Europe, he stressed, was not following the playbook of US President Donald Trump. While Washington chose to close off its market to Chinese products, Europe chose to engage in dialogue, Merz said. “This is not the beginning of a trade war with China. We are looking for peaceful solutions, but the level for that is fair trade,” he stated. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told journalists on Friday that Brussels would develop a new instrument, based on the Franco-German proposal, that could quickly restrict access to the European market. Merz acknowledged that part of China’s advantage came from its competitiveness, innovation and strength in clean energy. But Europe and Germany, he said, also had to address what they regarded as unfair practices, such as subsidies and an “artificially undervalued” yuan. The European Union and China, which Merz called a reliable partner, needed to discuss Beijing reining in its currency, industrial overcapacity and subsidies if it wanted to prevent Brussels from using the tool, he warned. “We want to have a fair trade with China, in our joint and mutual interests; that is our goal, not to create a conflict,” he said. “But at the same time, we need to be ready to defend ourselves, to defend our industry.” Beijing, meanwhile, has pushed back against what it views as a European attempt to extract concessions through pressure. The Ministry of Commerce denied that a recently agreed cap on Chinese hybrid car exports amounted to Beijing giving in to Europe. In a statement published on Friday, it urged Brussels to “harbour no illusions about extracting concessions through pressure, still less underestimate China’s determination and ability to defend its own interests”. While Berlin and Paris are forming a united front on trade with China, Germany is also watching the political, financial and social turmoil across the Rhine with concern. Scenes of violence and looting featured prominently across major German media. Public broadcaster ARD reported on what it called “France’s vicious cycle”: a self-feeding loop of high debt and spending, pressure to cut spending, social tensions, protests and weak government. During a press conference on Monday, German government spokespeople expressed Berlin’s concerns about the scenes of violence but insisted that it still viewed France as an important and reliable partner.

title: Chinese athlete Wu Yanni reveals health struggles over past year, vows to keep competing
description: In series of interview videos, veteran hurdler addresses accusations of being ‘high-profile’, ‘talking big’, chokes up over online trolls.
content: Veteran Chinese hurdler Wu Yanni has responded to renewed public criticism following her bronze-medal finish in the 100m hurdles at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, revealing recent physical health struggles and vowing to continue competing for as long as her body allows. In a series of interview videos released on Tuesday and Wednesday, the outspoken athlete addressed accusations of being “high-profile” and “talking big”. “My mother thinks I talk too big, but I don’t think I do,” Wu said. “Because in Chinese women’s 100m hurdles, I have broken the 13-second mark many times – more than 20 times. Looking at that depth of consistency, I feel I am undoubtedly very strong.” She explained that as a professional athlete, she had to validate herself to remain competitive, while questioning advice that she should be more modest. “Why should I be humble and low profile on the track?” she asked. She noted that over the past 1,092 days, only she knew what she had endured. “I’ve gone through troughs, suppression and self-doubt,” Wu said. “Fortunately, I held on. Fortunately, I pushed through the final hurdle. It’s always ‘fortunately’.” Reflecting on her bronze medal at the Asian Games, Wu confessed she had never expected to reach the podium, often joking with team leaders to not hold high expectations. “I am 29 years old now, which is quite old for an athlete. I’m considered a veteran,” she said. Wu disclosed that she suffered a series of physical breakdowns over the past year. “Both my haemoglobin and serum testosterone levels dropped drastically,” she explained. “I used to power clean 90kg, but this year I couldn’t lift even 70kg. It was pretty devastating – for the first time, I felt utterly useless.” While her training intensity indicated times of 12.6 or 12.7 seconds, her competition results failed to reflect them. After clocking 13.25 seconds in the Asian Games trial final, Wu suffered a mental breakdown. She revealed that her mental state deteriorated during her Asian Games preparations, requiring daily visits to a sports psychologist for a full week before the event, including therapy on the eve of her departure. Asked if her current psychological distress stemmed from her false start at the previous Asian Games, Wu said she was unsure. “I feel like wherever I turn, there is no way forward. Public commentary has trapped me here,” she said. “If I had won gold, it would have been a fruition and people would have dispersed. But because I didn’t win gold and because I false-started, people gradually closed in on me, using words to attack, suppress, slander and abuse me.” Wu affirmed she would not retire as long as she could run, recalling her mindset at 20 when she was fearless: “Regardless of anything, just go for it.” Wu’s mother also appeared in one of the video clips, attributing her daughter’s position as a lightning rod for public attention to her personality. “Her personality is too distinct and self-centred, overturning traditional impressions of athletes,” her mother said, noting that critics questioned where she found the time to style herself. Her mother added that Wu’s make-up habits were influenced by her, but she encouraged her daughter: “The more they talk about you, the prettier you should dress yourself up.” Later in the interview, Wu choked up and wept when discussing how online trolls attacked her pre-race routine of commemorating her late grandfather before the starting gun. “I usually let most attacks slide, but netizens attacking my grandfather is something I cannot accept,” Wu sobbed, adding that the intense scrutiny since 2023 had “worn away all my sharp edges”. She added: “I don’t think it’s just me – many athletes are going through these public opinion issues. But I heard the country will introduce anti-cyberbullying laws and regulations by the end of the year, so I believe the environment will improve.” Some criticised her media presence, with one user commenting: “Low-profile results in world competitions, but extremely high-profile marketing at home.” Another suggested: “Being a bit lower profile might actually make you more popular!” Conversely, supporters defended her stance. “She is high profile because she has the track record to back it up,” one fan wrote. Another observer noted: “You’ve invested heavily in things far beyond competition and training.”

title: Putin says Russia to restart peace deal talks with US and Ukraine
description: Moscow also freed retired US teacher Stephen Hubbard following a meeting between the Russian leader and Trump’s envoy Witkoff.
content: Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, the Kremlin said on Wednesday, after Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in Washington’s latest push to stop Europe’s bloodiest conflict since second world war. The talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia – the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher held in Russia. President Donald Trump confirmed the release in a social media post, saying the United States was not required to give anything in return. Hubbard was first detained in April 2022 and was later sentenced to six years and 10 months on charges whose veracity his family and US-based lawyer question. Wednesday’s encounter unfolded ‌amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the US is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine’s military communications. The latest talks also came more than two years ‌after Trump promised in his successful election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours. The Kremlin said the new three-way peace talks, which would be at a technical level, could take place in Abu Dhabi and would be focused on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended. They could begin sometime on or after November 10, it said. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the US and Israel launched a war against Iran. The Kremlin was less upbeat, however, about the outcome of talks Witkoff had held a day earlier in Oslo ⁠with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the leaders of Finland and Norway and European and Nato representatives. Witkoff told Putin the talks had been characterised by “some degree of momentum” and a US official said Ukraine had brought new ideas and proposals. “These ‌nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us,” Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the St Petersburg meeting, which lasted nearly three hours. Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, but Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to strike some kind of a deal. He said on Tuesday it was ‌time for Ukraine to end the war or face “a very bad thing”. Putin also used Wednesday’s talks to offer to help Trump deal with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran which it has repeatedly offered ‌to leverage to address US concerns about Iran’s nuclear programme. Putin told Witkoff it was possible and necessary to get a deal with Tehran, the Kremlin said. Russia could also supply large quantities of fertiliser to the US to help US farmers, the Russian president told Witkoff. A potential meeting in China next month with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was also discussed. The Kremlin said Beijing was already preparing what it said would be the first meeting of its kind in history. Putin has shown few signs of compromising on his central ‌war aims, which ‌include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, no Nato membership for Kyiv and an overall peace deal rather than a temporary ceasefire. Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special investment envoy, was also present at the meeting with Witkoff and the Kremlin said that major joint economic projects had been discussed, including some that were close to being realised. Witkoff said he ‌had brought some documents with him containing various ideas for a potential peace deal for Putin to review, and that Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, also wanted to convey some ideas to Putin. Kushner later joined the meeting remotely by phone. Zelensky said he hoped to discuss major issues about how ‌to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin ‌and Trump. The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelensky meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared in advance by aides to make it worthwhile. US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month to help lower prices in the US. High fuel costs since he launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans ahead of November’s legislative election. Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence-sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelensky ⁠said that Tuesday’s Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues. Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk had last week ordered ‌the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Musk has said any such decision is taken by the US military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated on Wednesday that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv’s ability to access Starlink.

title: Hong Kong working to boost global banks’ use of yuan trading tools
description: The city is encouraging more foreign banks to join the Central Moneymarkets Unit, deputy financial secretary says.
content: Hong Kong has vowed to engage more international banks in a debt securities clearing system, as part of a wider push to develop the city into a leading global yuan trading hub. “Hong Kong is actively promoting a number of measures to advance the city’s offshore yuan market to higher and deeper levels,” said Michael Wong Wai-lun, the city’s deputy financial secretary, during a Hong Kong event related to the Financial Street Forum on Wednesday. On the infrastructure side, Wong said the government would encourage more foreign banks in Hong Kong to join the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU), further enhancing the efficiency, security and resilience of the city’s cross-border settlements. The CMU – set up by the city’s de facto central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, in 1990 – is the city’s central securities depository and clearing house for multicurrency bonds and money market instruments. China’s Ministry of Finance started to issue yuan-denominated sovereign bonds to institutional investors via the CMU tendering platform in 2010, with plans to issue 84 billion yuan (US$12.6 billion) worth of bonds this year. Around 200 financial institutions are currently members of the CMU. But many lenders based outside the region have not yet engaged in the Bond Connect, which is a cross-border link between mainland China’s and Hong Kong’s bond markets. Besides boosting yuan bond participation, Wong said Hong Kong was working to enhance offshore yuan liquidity, widen the variety of offshore yuan products, and proactively explore new markets from the Middle East to Central Asia. “We believe that Hong Kong has the capability to make significant contributions to promoting the internationalisation [of the yuan],” Wong said. Hong Kong remained the world’s largest offshore yuan liquidity pool with more than 1 trillion yuan in bank deposits. The issuance scale of offshore yuan bonds in the city has also reached 1.1 trillion yuan last year. At the same event, officials from Beijing and London pledged to continue to deepen financial communications to support yuan internationalisation and market opening-up. “As the global economic and trade landscape is undergoing a profound restructuring, the diversification of the international monetary system has noticeably accelerated, leading to an increased demand among economic entities to actively use yuan,” said You Jun, vice-chairman of the Standing Committee of Beijing Municipal People’s Congress, via video link. “We should think about the international use of the [yuan] not as an end in itself, but as a tool to support trade, to support investment and to support the real economy,” said Peter Wilson, the British Ambassador to China. Meanwhile, the state-run Bank of China plans to keep Hong Kong in a core leading role and work together with other key markets including London and Singapore to attract global institutions to invest in yuan assets, according to Zhang Hui, the bank’s president.

title: Opinion | Amid positive growth forecasts, let’s not forget our devastating losses
description: The distance between the old economic forecasts and where we are now highlights our shared economic loss since 2020.
content: Each autumn, the world’s economics teams come together for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. Last week’s gathering in Bangkok included the launch of the IMF’s World Economic Outlook (WEO). Led by IMF economists, the international economic community’s collective wisdom on the world’s economic prospects was made public. Remarkably, they expect steady growth in a time of so much uncertainty and strife. “This steady growth is the net result of two big opposing forces: an energy shock, hurting growth, and an AI boom, lifting it,” IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said. In the fragile balance of this moment, it is easy to forget the series of major crises we have all gone through since the beginning of this decade: the Covid-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, the fuel and affordability crisis, the Sudanese war, the violence in Gaza, the tariff disputes and the war in Iran earlier this year. It is also easy to forget how often the collective economic wisdom about the world is announced each fall, only to quickly unravel by the following spring. In October 2019, for example, we expected the world economy to grow the following year by 3.4 per cent; instead, it shrank by 2.3 per cent. In October 2021, we thought consumer prices worldwide would increase by 3.8 per cent in 2022; they surged by 8.6 per cent instead. In Ukraine, 3.6 per cent growth was expected in 2022; it plunged by nearly 29 per cent instead. In Sudan, 2.6 per cent growth was projected for 2023; instead, the economy crashed by 23.5 per cent. How much of this year’s expected growth will endure and how much of it will be drastically revised next spring in this turbulent decade? In our private lives, we might grieve following each devastating personal loss. We pause, find comfort and consolation among the people closest to us and take stock of what we have lost. What has been the equivalent of this grieving in the global economic community? The release of new WEO data can tell us something about our immediate economic future. At the same time, comparing historic data with prior economic forecasts, the latest WEO data can also tell us something about this extraordinary decade we are in. The old forecasts were not “wrong”; instead, on the eve of multiple crises, they were our best collective guess as to what our economic future looked like. They were the “old normal” – the immediate likely economic pathway – and their distance from where we are now reflects our shared economic loss since 2020. Combining two databases, the WEO Historical Forecast Database and the latest WEO Database, can quantify this loss. As an example, I can use the multi-year gross domestic product forecast data from the 2019 and 2021 fall announcements, just before the pandemic and the war in Ukraine, respectively, and compare them with actual GDP corresponding to the forecast years. Using the actual economic data for that fall (in billions of US dollars), I apply the projected real GDP growth and actual real GDP growth through subsequent years. The gap between the two series is an approximation of the economic loss, which has been staggering. The foregone world economic growth from the pandemic amounted to more than US$5 trillion in the first year of the pandemic and about US$3 trillion a year in the years after through 2024. This is equivalent to more than all of the world’s foreign aid (US$214.6 billion), foreign direct investment (US$883 billion) and remittance flows (US$685 billion) to low- and middle-income countries combined that same year. It is also equivalent to more than a fifth of the US economy in 2020. This loss has not been uniformly distributed around the world. Advanced economies have experienced much sharper recoveries relative to their pre-pandemic forecast than emerging markets and developing economies. For example, the pre-pandemic forecast for advanced economies was 1.6 per cent growth in 2021; instead, actual GDP growth after the pandemic was 6.2 per cent, a difference of 4.6 percentage points. Among emerging markets and developing economies, the corresponding numbers were 4.8 and 7 per cent, also a sharp recovery from the pandemic but only a 2.2-percentage point difference. In Ukraine, meanwhile, the war has meant an annual GDP loss of more than US$60 billion, equivalent to about a third of the country’s pre-war GDP. Because of the war in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s economy alone is on track to lose the equivalent of US$32 billion this year. We could argue and say the gap between the two GDP series is a measure of many things. It is a measure of the world’s leading economists’ forecasting errors, showing the shortcomings of economic models in an uncertain period. It is a measure of policy errors and the ineffectiveness of the global community’s response to shocks and the failure to coordinate. It is a measure of data errors, drawing as they do from information collected by national agencies in the middle of lockdowns and crises. We can also say this loss is severely underestimated as it fails to measure the lives lost from these crises and conflicts. The gap is all these things. It is also arguably a measure of the economic future that we all anticipated but never came to pass. As we take stock of the latest economic wisdom and as the expected steady growth provides some measure of relief, a second of silence for the old normal and all that we lost might be fitting.

title: Asian Para Games: Hong Kong boccia player secures first gold as athletes boost medal haul
description: The main area of success is on the boccia court, but swimmers and fencers also contribute to tally on action-packed day in Nagoya.
content: Hong Kong delivered a strong medal haul at the Asian Para Games on Wednesday, with the city winning their first gold after boccia player Vivian Lau Wai-yan beat teammate Cheung Yuen in the final in Nagoya. City athletes also won four silver and four bronze medals during an action-packed day in Japan. The main area of success for the city’s men and women was on the boccia court, where Hong Kong enjoyed a dominant outing, eventually claiming one gold, three silvers and one bronze. Lau and Cheung set up an all-Hong Kong final in the women’s (BC4) individual event after overcoming rivals from China and Malaysia, respectively, in the semi-finals, guaranteeing the city gold and silver. In the final, Lau put in a commanding performance to defeat Cheung 7-2. Yeung Hiu-lam took silver in the women’s (BC2) individual final after falling to her opponent from Indonesia, while Leung Yuk-wing also secured silver in the men’s (BC4) individual final against his Thai rival. John Loung edged out his Indonesian opponent 6-5 in the men’s (BC1) bronze-medal match to earn his first individual medal at the Asian Para Games. In the pool, Ng Cheuk-yan added a silver, clocking 40.75 seconds in the women’s (S7) 50m butterfly final, finishing behind Japanese rival An Nishida. Hung Wing-long clocked 1:09.96 to take bronze in the men’s (SB14) 100m breaststroke final, finishing behind winner Naohide Yamaguchi of Japan and Thailand’s Nithikorn Jeampiriyakul, who secured silver. Alison Yu Chui-yee pushed South Korea’s Kwon Hyok-yeong to a 14-14 tie in a tightly contested women’s épée (Category A) semi-final before Kwon scored the decisive touch to win 15-14. With no bronze-medal match scheduled, Yu automatically finished third. Tong Nga-ting added another bronze in the women’s (Category B) épée individual event, securing her medal after a 15-6 semi-final loss to South Korea’s Cho Eun-hye as there was no third-place play-off. Hong Kong athletes featured in two 100m finals. In the women’s (T36) 100m, Yam Kwok-fan clocked a season-best 15.76 seconds to finish fifth, while teammates Katie Wong Wing-hei and Yu Chun-lai placed sixth and seventh in 15.81 and 18.28 seconds, respectively. China’s Shi Yiting claimed gold in 13.56 seconds. In the men’s (T35) 100m final, Bao Chui finished sixth in 14.96 seconds. Hong Kong also enjoyed a strong start in the table tennis doubles group stage. Ho Ka-sing and Wong Chi-yin secured back-to-back 3-1 wins over Iraq and Kazakhstan in the men’s (MD18) category, while Chiu Kan-shan and Wong Yue-ching swept both of their group matches in straight sets against South Korea and Kazakhstan, winning 3-0 in both women’s (WD14) ties. Hong Kong now have a total of 21 medals: one gold, eight silver and 12 bronze.

title: The EU will ‘pull its punches’ on China despite growing trade war talk: analysts
description: European leaders are talking a big game on China, but will avoid a full-blown trade war due to internal division and fear of retaliation: analysts.
content: The European Union is likely to avoid a full-blown trade confrontation with China due to internal divisions in the bloc and fear of retaliation, according to a prominent research firm. The projection comes amid speculation that the two sides are on the brink of a trade war, with European policymakers raising the alarm about a looming “China shock 2.0” and pushing for stronger measures to protect domestic producers from Chinese competition. But the bloc would “continue to pull its punches” in any confrontation with Beijing due to a lack of consensus among and within Europe’s member states, the London-based Capital Economics said at an event in Hong Kong on Wednesday. The EU also had “concerns over retaliation” if it stepped up trade tensions with China, the research firm said, and held “lingering hopes to save the rules-based global trading system” that had helped Europe in the past. “At least on the Chinese side, there’s some concern that Europe is going to be more aggressive towards restricting exports from China, but our view is it will continue to follow a cautious approach,” said Marcel Thieliant, head of Asia Pacific for Capital Economics. “Europe is very dependent on China for lots of goods including critical minerals, and there’s a clear … concern about retaliation.” Responsibility for trade policy in Europe remains “split” between the EU itself and the governments of its member nations, the firm said in an outlook report circulated at the event. The EU decides tariffs, for example, while member nations chart investment policies, according to Thieliant. China and the EU struck an agreement earlier this month to restrict Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe, a deal that was widely seen as an attempt to take the heat out of rising bilateral trade tensions. The deal will reportedly involve hybrid car exports being capped at 350,000 vehicles per year, with the quota then rising by 6 per cent annually over the next four years. That represents a sharp reduction in shipments, with the EU originally projecting imports of 800,000 Chinese hybrid cars this year. Tensions between the two sides have been growing mainly due to a stark trade imbalance favouring China: the EU’s trade deficit with China ran at over €1 billion (US$1.12 billion) per day last year, according to European Commission data, and has continued to rise this year. The bloc has increasingly hit Chinese producers with tariffs and trade probes over the past two years, with some warning that European industry could soon be decimated unless the EU takes more urgent action. China will remain an avid exporter nation until 2030 because it sees that direction “as evidence of policy success” at a time of cutthroat price competition and weak demand at home, according to the outlook report. Capital Economics also forecast on Wednesday a 50 per cent probability of a “crisis” erupting within two to three years if China continues to gain export share, including in Europe, and if “populist and nationalist policies” emerge in the West over increased competition with China.

title: Apec finance ministers reach consensus on AI, digital financing in Hong Kong
description: Agreements on AI, digital infrastructure and financial services to help shape discussions at next month’s leaders’ summit in Shenzhen.
content: Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) finance chiefs reached a consensus on economic policy coordination and cooperation on financing technology and artificial intelligence at a landmark two-day gathering in Hong Kong, according to China’s finance minister. Lan Foan said the outcomes achieved during the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting would help shape discussions at the leaders’ summit in Shenzhen next month. “China will work with all member economies to implement the important consensus reached at this meeting in Hong Kong and make positive contributions to the Apec economic leaders’ meeting in November,” Lan said in closing remarks on Wednesday. More than 500 participants, including finance ministers from Apec’s 21 economies, travelled to Hong Kong for the meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday. The gathering served as a precursor to the leaders’ summit on November 18 and 19, when President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet for the third time this year. Lan said the meeting completed all agenda items and delivered a package of practical measures to address global uncertainties and promote digital infrastructure financing across the region. “The international landscape is intertwined with volatility and uncertainties. Spillover effects of geopolitical conflicts are spreading, and global economic growth faces multiple challenges,” Lan said. “Meanwhile, a new round of technological revolution and industrial transformation, represented by AI, is bringing fresh opportunities for global common development.” Lan said members had in-depth exchanges on a wide range of issues, reaching consensus in three key areas and issuing the 2026 Apec Finance Ministers’ joint statement and a policy statement on enhancing cooperation in digital infrastructure financing across the region. The first area was strengthening coordination on macroeconomic policy to cope with external risks and challenges, including promoting household consumption, boosting domestic demand and improving productivity, he added. “Our members agreed that we should enhance the soundness of our macroeconomic policies,” Lan said. “At the same time, we should fully unlock the potential of emerging technologies such as AI to raise productivity, cultivate new growth drivers and inject new impetus into Asia-Pacific economic growth.” The second major outcome was enhanced regional cooperation on digital infrastructure financing, Lan said. “On digital infrastructure financing, members encouraged the public sector to focus on creating a favourable policy and supervisory environment,” Lan said, adding that members also supported the private sector and multinational development banks jointly financing the digital infrastructure. The third area focused on expanding access to financial services for individuals and businesses. “Members agreed that financial services should meet the diversified needs of individuals, households and enterprises, especially SMEs [small and medium-sized enterprises], and stressed the importance of sharing experience and best practices among Apec economies,” he said. Lan also said the meeting agreed to launch a programme to support experience-sharing among young financial professionals. “We also held a retreat where participants discussed promoting Asia-Pacific economic growth in a world in flux and reached consensus,” Lan said. A working lunch was held between finance ministers and the Apec Business Advisory Council to discuss ways to mobilise private capital for digital infrastructure projects, which yielded positive results, he added. Analysts said the two-day Apec meeting had strengthened the role of Hong Kong as a fundraising hub for digital infrastructure in the Asia-Pacific region. “The Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting has reached consensus on how to maintain economic stability in the region and to meet the demand for fundraising in the trend of digitalisation,” said Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of the Our Hong Kong Foundation and executive director of the Public Policy Institute. He noted the ministers had agreed on how to mobilise private capital to finance digital infrastructure, which was vital for Hong Kong. “Hong Kong is playing a unique role in this area, as the city is connected with mainland technology players and international investors, while the city is also a hub for international investors to invest in many Asia-Pacific infrastructure projects to support digitalisation in the region,” Shui said. Some analysts believe Beijing’s decision to hold the finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong is a calculated move to bolster the city’s standing as an offshore renminbi hub and present it as a safe harbour amid lingering geopolitical tensions. “The Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting brings together many key decision makers and government officials representing different economies,” said Robert Lee Wai-wang, a lawmaker for the financial services sector and chairman of Grand Finance Group. “It also showcases Hong Kong as an international finance centre and its ability to host globally important forums to discuss collaboration and [future] challenges.” Lee said the move was also important for integrating Hong Kong with mainland cities in the Greater Bay Area (GBA). “With Shenzhen hosting the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting next month after the Hong Kong meeting this week, it shows the potential and synergy of cities within the GBA in organising important events like this,” Lee said.

title: Peruvian tenor Juan Diego Florez on Hong Kong debut, Pavarotti’s regret and singing food
description: Juan Diego Florez joins the Hong Kong Philharmonic for a night of bel canto arias and songs from Spanish zarzuela musical theatre.
content: Before Juan Diego Florez became one of the most celebrated opera tenors of his generation, he was on his way to being a pop star. Music was always part of family life. His father, Ruben Florez, was a respected singer of Peruvian criolla folk music; his mother, Maria Teresa Salom, managed a Lima pub with live music. As a boy, Juan Diego Florez would sometimes be asked to stand in and perform with his guitar. That early exposure gave him his first taste of being on stage, and by his teens, he was writing his own songs. In 1989, he won a singing competition, which was broadcast on TV nationwide. “Then I began to become famous in Peru,” he says. At 17, he entered the national music conservatory in Lima intending to sharpen his skills as a singer and pop composer. But once he got a taste of classical music training, everything changed. “I discovered it, and I said, ‘Wow, I like this, and I want to do this,’” he says. Today, at the age of 53, Florez is widely considered one of the top tenors of his generation, famed for his dazzling vocal agility, his mastery of the bel canto style and his effortless high notes. He has sung at New York’s Metropolitan Opera, La Scala in Milan and London’s Royal Opera House, and his diary remains packed with upcoming engagements at the Vienna State Opera and Paris’ Opera Bastille. He finally makes his long-awaited Hong Kong debut on October 22, as part of his Asia tour. The gala with the Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra has been designed as a showcase of his diverse musical influences: from Rossini and Donizetti – the 19th century Italian bel canto arias that launched his career – to his relatively recent interpretations of heavier-voice roles such as Massenet’s Werther, and songs from the Spanish-language zarzuela musical theatre tradition. A career of nearly three decades has brought plenty of change, he says. As his voice has matured and deepened, roles once beyond his reach have opened up. “I never thought I was going to sing Werther,” he says. “Now I’m singing it, or Hoffmann, or Romeo. I have always loved those roles. My voice now permits me to sing them. That’s the nice thing about ageing.” He will also bring his acoustic guitar on stage for some Peruvian music, he says. “That takes it back to my beginning,” he says. “I always do that now, because the audiences are not happy if I don’t do it.” It is always a challenge to get more young people into theatres Juan Diego Florez His attachment to his home country extends well beyond the concert programme. Fifteen years ago, Florez founded Sinfonia por el Peru, a music-education organisation inspired by Venezuela’s El Sistema, which works with vulnerable children and young people. “We have always managed to keep it going and to benefit many thousands of children, and also their families,” he says. “It is a net of protection for young people and children who are in difficulty.” The project has also changed Lima’s cultural life. “Because of Sinfonia por el Peru, we have more orchestras now and a bigger musical market,” he says with evident pride. But home – for a music superstar constantly on the road – is Vienna, “the city of music”, he says, where he lives with his wife, son and daughter. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Juan Diego Flórez (@jdiego_florez) Travelling usually offers little more than the drive from hotel to concert hall, he says. This time, he plans to see Hong Kong. “It’s the first time I get to visit,” he says. “I remember [Luciano] Pavarotti saying that one of the things he regretted was that he was in many cities and never got to know them.” Florez will not be sampling too much of the local cuisine ahead of the Hong Kong concert or the one in Guangzhou on October 24, also with HK Phil. “Some years ago I decided to just have quinoa with salad and avocado before concerts,” he says. “It keeps you light, and it has protein. That’s my singing food.” His current tour has taken him to Taipei and Shanghai – where he starred in the opening programme of the Shanghai Grand Opera House – and he is more convinced than ever that opera has a bright future in Asia. “It is always a challenge to get more young people into theatres,” he says. “There are cities that have more success and I see a lot of young people here in Asia. So I think this is the future, the audiences here in Asia, for me.” “Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra: Juan Diego Florez Opera Gala”, Concert Hall, Hong Kong Cultural Centre, October 22, 2026, 7.30pm. For tickets, visit hkphil.org.

title: Meet Willa Lou Deary, Keri Russell’s daughter who joined her at Paris Fashion Week
description: The Diplomat actress attended the Louis Vuitton spring/summer 2027 show with her teenage daughter, whom she shares with ex-husband Shane Deary.
content: The Diplomat actress Keri Russell’s 13-year-old daughter Willa made a rare public appearance earlier this month when she accompanied her mother to the Louis Vuitton spring/summer 2027 show during Paris Fashion Week on October 6. Russell, 50, wore a white blouse with a high collar paired with a structured black miniskirt. Meanwhile, Willa opted for an all-pink look featuring a tweed jacket and matching skirt set. Here’s everything you need to know about Keri Russell’s mini-me daughter, Willa Lou Deary. She is Keri Russell’s middle child Willa Lou Deary was born in December 2012 in New York City to Keri Russell and Shane Deary, who married in 2007. Willa has an older brother, River, born in 2009. Russell split from Deary in 2013 after nine years of marriage. The actress – known for her roles in Felicity and The Americans – went on to have a long-term relationship with actor Matthew Rhys. She became a mother for the third time when she welcomed her son Sam with Rhys in 2016. Russell and Rhys have been together for around 13 years, and she has stated that they have no plans to tie the knot. What does Willa think of her mum’s work? Despite her high-profile Hollywood career – with roles in films including Star Wars - The Rise of Skywalker, Dawn of the Planet of the Apes and Mission: Impossible III – Russell has kept her family largely out of the public eye, so it’s no wonder that the mother of three has spoken sparingly about her children. In 2023, Russell opened up about her relationship with her teenage daughter during an appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live!. “My daughter about a year ago – she’s kind of mature for her age, and she was bored one day – I said, ‘Hey, Willa, I did this show about this college girl, and you might think it’s cool. It’s really sweet,’” Russell recalled, referring to her role in TV series Felicity (1998-2002). Unfortunately, Willa was less than impressed. “After about 15 minutes, she turned it off, and she went, ‘Ugh, Mom, it’s so cringy. Why would you think I’d want to watch your college experience making out with weird boys and stuff?’”

title: Chinese star Fan Zhendong lashes out after fan posts videos of him on social media
description: Posts on Tuesday by self-proclaimed ‘superfan’ were taken last month while table tennis player was embarking on a private trip at an airport.
content: Chinese table tennis star Fan Zhendong has again condemned secret filming after photos of a private trip were leaked online. On Tuesday, a self-proclaimed “superfan” uploaded two photo-slide show videos of Fan onto social media, captioning them: “No more hiding, let’s share.” The images showed Fan walking alone through Shanghai Pudong International Airport wearing a mask and hat, showing his movements on escalators and boarding. In one photo taken from just behind him, the poster claimed Fan was “within arm’s reach”. In the comment section, the poster admitted hoarding the files for “a very, very long time”, revealing they were taken during Fan’s private trip from Pudong to Frankfurt on September 20. “I didn’t even dare show them. Can you imagine how excited I was when I saw him?” the poster wrote, adding they hesitated to publish out of fear of criticism and being immediately recognised by Fan. “But then I thought, if he remembers me this way, that brings me joy too. Then again, I was worried he’d be unhappy if he saw I posted them.” The “superfan’s” profile contains multiple posts featuring “chance encounters” with Fan. The user had previously claimed in the comments to be an airline employee, a statement later denied. The secret filming post and the user’s account have since been set to private. On Wednesday, a day after the photos circulated widely online, Fan took to social media to condemn the secret filming and express his frustration. “Do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself,” Fan wrote at the start of his post, quoting an ancient maxim from the Confucian classic the Book of Rites. He went on to ask if anyone, if put in his shoes, would genuinely be willing to be filmed without consent. “Regardless of the identity, mindset or purpose of the person secretly filming, it cannot alter the nature of such behaviour as disrespecting others and infringing upon their privacy, even if done in the name of love, and even if published with a delay,” Fan wrote. Emphasising that “having strong boundaries is not equivalent to being cold”, Fan noted that rational fans or friendly passers-by did not greet him while holding up phones with cameras recording, adding he was always happy to respond to genuine greetings. However, when confronted by people filming while shouting out to initiate contact, he added: “I am truly unable to distinguish whether they are fans who appreciate and support me, or traffic-seekers operating self-media accounts.” He concluded his post with another famous line, from the Confucian philosopher Mencius: “He who respects others will be constantly respected by others.” Online response was overwhelmingly supportive of Fan, with many calling for a stand against intrusive behaviour. “We should leave private space for athletes who bring glory to the country,” one commenter wrote. However, others argued against extreme reactions, with one noting: “As a public figure, how can you not be photographed?” This is not the first time Fan has spoken out on privacy issues. In April 2023, Fan reported a stalker who illegally entered his hotel room, subsequently halting “any form of personal contact, including accepting letters”. Less than a year later, he condemned the online leak of his national ID and phone numbers, warning offenders not to cross legal red lines after suffering harassment.

title: Former IMF executive says China and the world need an internationalised yuan
description: Zhu Min, also a former deputy governor of the People’s Bank of China, makes call as central bank upgrades digital-yuan infrastructure.
content: Both China and the world need an internationalised yuan in a multipolar global economic environment, a former senior Chinese official has urged in an article that was published as Beijing upgraded its digital-yuan infrastructure to bolster efforts to reshape the US dollar-dominated global financial system. Wider use of the Chinese currency, also known as the renminbi, would support China’s high-quality growth while offering an alternative that could help stabilise the international financial system amid intensifying geopolitical risks, said Zhu Min, a former deputy governor of China’s central bank, in an article published in Communist Party press organ the People’s Daily on Wednesday. China’s economic and trade strength and the yuan’s growing acceptance gave the world a credible alternative store of value, and China also had the payment systems, liquidity tools and banking networks to support wider yuan use, said Zhu, also a former deputy managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF). “These factors form the foundation for the yuan’s stability and credibility, and are exactly what the world needs for economic and financial development,” he said. On Wednesday, the People’s Bank of China announced two upgrades to its digital yuan infrastructure service system that focused on its back-end system for the digital yuan and a “smart-contract” framework for programmable digital-yuan payments. State news agency Xinhua described them as two major achievements from the central bank’s digital yuan operation and management centre in Beijing, which was established a year ago. The bank had earlier opened an international operations centre for the digital yuan in Shanghai, whose key responsibilities include building and operating the digital yuan’s cross-border and blockchain infrastructure. In Wednesday’s article, Zhu wrote China had a “historic window of opportunity” to accelerate its push for the yuan’s internationalisation. He said that in a changing global landscape, rising geopolitical risks and structural shifts in the world economy were being accompanied by the rise of Global South countries, with China accounting for roughly one-sixth of the world’s economic output and more than 14 per cent of global goods exports. The currency’s overall footprint overseas remains limited Zhu Min Zhu said those trends were accelerating multipolarity and creating pressure for reform of the international monetary system. For China, he said greater international use of the yuan would support its high-quality growth agenda, which involved technological innovation, advanced manufacturing, services upgrading, green transition and outbound corporate expansion. From a global perspective, China’s economic scale, long-term growth fundamentals and perceived monetary stability positioned the yuan as a usable “value anchor”, and strengthening that role would also benefit the rest of the world, he said. Zhu acknowledged that the yuan’s global status still lagged its economic weight. “The currency’s overall footprint overseas remains limited, and its functions as a unit of account, payment medium, investment vehicle and reserve asset still require further development,” he said. Citing Bank for International Settlements data, he noted that the yuan now accounted for 8.5 per cent of global foreign exchange trading and had a 12.28 per cent weight in the IMF’s Special Drawing Rights currency basket. Vina Cheung, HSBC’s global head of renminbi internationalisation, said corporate clients and institutions still had concerns over the yuan’s limited convertibility, financing costs after conversion into US dollars and unstable offshore liquidity, while acknowledging progress in the currency’s internationalisation. “Renminbi basically is now a treasury currency that can help the business in terms of cash and treasury management, managing the cost, the liquidity and the risk,” she said at the Bund Summit in Shanghai on Wednesday. “Five years ago, our clients were asking, ‘Can I pay in renminbi?’ And today they will ask, ‘Can I invoice, fund, swap, hedge, pool and invest in renminbi across [my] supply chain?’” She added that the next phase of yuan internationalisation would hinge on digital innovation, deeper capital markets and closer integration between China’s onshore market and Hong Kong’s offshore market – with the latter providing “execution certainty” and giving international businesses the confidence to use and hold the currency.

title: China AI researcher rises to Xiaomi’s top level in 10 months, talks work-life balance
description: I am like a snail who does not pursue the fastest move, but my every step is clearly visible, Luo says of her character.
content: Beijing-based smartphone and electric vehicle giant Xiaomi announced in mid-October that it would promote 31-year-old Luo Fuli to its highest-level position, once again putting the “AI prodigy” at the centre of heated discussion. The move came 10 months after Luo joined the company as head of its large language model (LLM) unit. Luo attracted significant public attention in late 2024, when Xiaomi founder and CEO Lei Jun said during a live-stream that he hoped to hire her at an annual salary of 10 million yuan (US$1.5 million), the 21st Century Business Herald reported. At the time, Luo was little known to the general public. But she had shot to fame in the computer science community in 2019, when, as a master’s degree candidate at Peking University (PKU), she was listed as an author on eight papers presented at the Association for Computational Linguistics’ (ACL) annual meeting. After graduating from PKU, Luo joined Alibaba Group Holding’s global research institute, Damo Academy. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. She was later hired by Chinese hedge fund High-Flyer Quant, which owns DeepSeek, where she worked as a deep-learning expert. Luo’s role as a core contributor to the development of DeepSeek-V2 is believed to be what Lei values most. While domestic media and internet users have celebrated Luo as an AI prodigy, she has rejected the label and turned down all media interview requests over the past two years. “I beg the cyberspace to give me a quiet environment so that I can focus on my job. I am not a prodigy, but only hope to quietly do challenging but correct things,” Luo wrote on social media last year. Luo was born into a rural family in Yibin, southwestern Sichuan province. Her father is an electrician and her mother is a teacher. She has a younger sister who is a doctor. She has said that although her family was not wealthy, her parents fostered an atmosphere of “love for reading”. While Luo was studying at Yibin No 1 Middle School, a key school in the region, her teachers described her as “not top smart, but extremely hard-working” and someone who tended to plan everything in advance. She was admitted to prestigious Beijing Normal University (BNU) to study computer science, thanks to her high score in China’s gruelling national university entrance examination, known as the gaokao. Her excellent academic performance at BNU enabled her to enter PKU as a master’s degree candidate without taking an entrance exam. Luo once described herself on social media as having a “low starting point in the computer field”. During her first year at BNU, she was among the lowest-ranked students, partly because she had no prior knowledge of computers. Luo said that while her classmates could solve a problem in just three minutes, it would take her three hours. However, thanks to her persistent effort, Luo became one of the top students in her class in less than two years. Luo said she had shown the same trait since childhood: starting as an average student in an unfamiliar environment, then rising to the top of the group. Several years ago, Luo approached a Bilibili influencer known as Liang Zi to arrange an interview about herself as a birthday celebration. In the interview, Luo said she would never be satisfied with her current work because she aspired to keep “growing”. She also said she aimed to maintain a balance between “growth in career and a happy family”. Luo’s husband also works in the hi-tech industry, but details about him have not been made public. “I am like a snail who does not pursue the fastest move, but my every step is clearly visible,” Luo said of herself.

title: Meet Nathan Fielder, who co-directed the Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything
description: The Canadian filmmaker, who was in an improv group with Seth Rogen while in secondary school, once hosted his own show on Comedy Central.
content: If there’s one name Hollywood cannot stop raving about this autumn, it’s Nathan Fielder. The 43-year-old Canadian comedian is behind the hit new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything, released on October 16, which earned an impressive US$15 million at the North American box office in its opening weekend. Fielder co-directed the A24 production with Lance Oppenheim after the disgraced Theranos founder and CEO and her long-time partner, Billy Evans, invited them to their rented Del Mar, California, property, granting them access to their private lives in the days leading up to her imprisonment for defrauding investors. “I’ve never done something like this before,” Fielder, who also stars in the documentary, told Wired, describing the experience as “freeing and fascinating”. He also revealed that Holmes had called him from prison recently to tell him, “I trust you”. Here’s everything to know about Nathan Fielder. What is Nathan Fielder’s background? Fielder was born on May 12, 1983, in Vancouver, Canada. His parents were social workers and enrolled him in a Jewish primary school that focused on Holocaust education, per Vulture. When he was 13, he moved to a public school and became interested in magic, thanks to a friend who came from a family of magicians. During his time at Point Grey Secondary School, he joined an improv group with Seth Rogen. “It was not even on the table that he would act like he was burning in lava,” the Superbad star recalled of Fielder’s unpredictability during warm-ups. How did Nathan Fielder get into comedy? Fielder graduated from the University of Victoria with a business degree and briefly worked at a brokerage, per Vulture. Unhappy with his profession, he moved to Toronto in 2005 and enrolled in Humber College for its comedy programme. He also joined the Laugh Sabbath comedy collective, presenting experimental short films at weekly shows that earned him unexpected laughs. “There was a transition where I went from trying to hide the embarrassing parts to appreciating the things about myself that I hated before,” Fielder told Vulture. These home-made videos eventually landed him a job as a correspondent on CBC Television’s satirical news show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, where he got his own segment called “Nathan on Your Side”. What is Nathan Fielder known for? Fielder’s entertainment career took off with Comedy Central’s Nathan for You, a reality comedy series where Fielder assisted struggling businesses with increasingly unconventional marketing strategies. His HBO docu-comedy show The Rehearsal earned him two Primetime Emmy nominations and a Peabody Award. Fielder also wrote, executive produced and appeared in the miniseries The Curse, starring Emma Stone and Benny Safdie.

title: China’s youth unemployment rate edges down slightly but jobseekers still doing it tough
description: Weighed down by weak domestic demand and fierce competition, job creation remained sluggish in September.
content: China’s youth unemployment rate edged down slightly in September as some graduates secured jobs, but young jobseekers still face a tough market as employers increasingly look beyond academic qualifications for candidates with relevant work experience. The unemployment rate among people aged 16 to 24, excluding students, fell to 18 per cent in September from 18.9 per cent in August, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday. With around 12.7 million university graduates having entered the job market this year, a record high, the youth unemployment rate in August matched its level a year earlier, equalling its highest point since Beijing revised its calculation methodology in 2023 to exclude students. Weighed down by weak domestic demand and fierce competition, China’s job market remained sluggish last month. Tang Qi, who holds a bachelor’s degree from Fudan University and a master’s degree from the University of Hong Kong – both top universities – completed internships in accounting, advertising and human resources before looking for a job in advertising in July. She has received few interview callbacks. “I thought interning in different industries would help me figure out what kind of work I wanted to do, but when it comes to job hunting, I’ve realised this is a weakness, as employers prefer candidates who have completed several internships in the same field,” the 24-year-old said. “Companies seem intent on getting the most out of new hires, expecting them to hit the ground running so they can avoid spending time and money training them from scratch.” Tang also said employers frequently questioned her decision to take a gap year after graduating from university. “I was worried they would see it as a sign that I wasn’t resilient enough,” she said. With employment, a key indicator of economic health, under sustained pressure and advances in artificial intelligence further fuelling concerns, Beijing unveiled an “employment-first” strategy for 2026–2030 in June, pledging to harness AI to create jobs and promote entrepreneurship while developing emerging industries, including the marine sector, as new engines of employment growth. As competition in the job market intensifies, some university graduates are turning to short-term vocational programmes to learn practical skills such as AI data labelling to secure a job, while others are taking up gig work as traditional career paths narrow. In September, the unemployment rate for those aged 25 to 29, also excluding students, stood at 7.4 per cent, compared with 7.5 per cent in August. China’s overall urban jobless rate declined to 5.2 per cent in September, from 5.3 per cent in August.

title: China’s pharmaceutical stocks gain favour amid ‘greater’ progress in innovation
description: The nation’s innovative drug out-licensing deals reached US$130 billion by the end of September, almost matching 2025’s full-year level.
content: Chinese pharmaceutical companies are ramping up global expansion and the sector, expected to sustain rapid growth in coming third-quarter earnings releases, could see a further lift in market sentiment, analysts said. In the first three quarters, domestic innovative drugs accounted for 80 per cent of all innovative medicines approved in China, according to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. “Research progress has been made across multiple therapeutic areas including oncology, psychiatry, anti-infectives, gout and rare diseases,” said Wang Weiming, chief engineer of the ministry, during a press conference on Tuesday in Beijing. The country’s innovative drug out-licensing deals reached about US$130 billion in value by the end of September this year, nearly matching the full-year level seen in 2025, according to the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC). “The sector is expected to gain greater global competitiveness. The core policy support and commercial profit delivery remains intact, and the sector’s risk-reward profile is becoming increasingly favourable,” Sun Yuanyuan, an analyst of Industrial Securities, wrote in a research report on Saturday. In the latest deal, Hong Kong-listed Hansoh Pharmaceutical Group, a domestic biomedical company, said its wholly owned three subsidiaries had reached a collaboration agreement with Swiss healthcare company F. Hoffmann-La Roche, the Chinese company said in a filing to the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing on Monday. The collaboration covers a broad portfolio of antibody-drug conjugate programmes and this is the second cooperation between the two sides. Hansoh will lead the early development of the programmes up to the completion of global phase 1-A clinical trials, while Roche will be responsible for further developing the programmes globally outside China. Hansoh will retain all rights to develop, register and commercialise the programmes in mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan, the statement said. Hansoh will get an upfront payment of US$400 million and a US$110 million first-anniversary payment and is eligible for over US$15 billion in development, regulatory approval and commercialisation of the programmes, as well as tiered royalties on future product sales. The deal lifted Hansoh’s share price on Tuesday, closing 8.32 per cent higher at HK$34.38, while the innovative drug sector in the A-share market also saw active trading. Shanghai and Hong Kong dual-listed Joinn Laboratories jumped 8.06 per cent on the A-share market, while Shanghai and Shenzhen-listed peers, including Guizhou Sanli Pharmaceutical, CSPC Innovation, Shanghai Obio Technology, Chengda Pharma and Sunshine Guojian Pharmaceutical, also rose on Tuesday. Last week, China issued a public consultation on revisions to the catalogue of technologies prohibited and restricted from export, proposing to add 40 key technologies and carry out interim registration management for the export of relevant technologies, according to a guideline by the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology. They include five biomedicine technologies covering cell and gene therapy, small nucleic acid therapeutics and pathogenic microorganisms. Sun of Industrial Securities said the policy would not affect the growth trend of the sector. The restrictions do not cover routine business development and CXO (Contract X Organisation) businesses. For cell and gene technologies and small nucleic acid technologies, only outbound ownership transfers of platform technologies are banned. Out-licensing deals and outsourced R&D and manufacturing services that do not involve ownership transfer fall outside the regulation. Technical processes necessary for R&D, testing, production, quality control, launch and compliance for business development work on a single product pipeline are not subject to regulation. China Merchants Securities said in a Monday note that the third-quarter earnings catalysts for innovative drugs firms were approaching, adding that the market favoured the innovative drug chain and names with earnings delivery.

title: French toast, egg sandwiches: Hong Kong comfort food highlighted in Lucas Sin’s cookbook
description: Lucas Sin’s Cha Chaan Teng cookbook celebrates Hong Kong comfort food – think scrambled egg sandwiches, baked pork chop rice, French toast.
content: When people think of Cantonese food, buttery scrambled egg between slices of soft white bread may not be the first dish to come to mind. For Lucas Sin Lok-yeung, this quintessential Hong Kong classic is the first recipe in his inaugural cookbook, Cha Chaan Teng: Comfort Food from Hong Kong’s Iconic Diners – listed as the “Perfect Scrambled Egg Sandwich”. Sin, 33, has been a staunch advocate of Hong Kong cuisine for more than a decade, starring in a long list of YouTube videos – from explaining claypot rice for Bon Appetit to teaching Food52 viewers the art of Hong Kong’s scrambled egg sandwiches. Sin may be based in New York, but his work remains tightly bound to Hong Kong. In November, he will launch his debut cookbook dedicated to the city’s beloved local diners and the comfort food they serve. “The part that I’m excited about is representing Hong Kong, especially internationally,” Sin says. “I think Hong Kong cuisine is the best food in the world.
