It deserves a lot of respect.” Born in Ontario, Canada, and raised in Hong Kong’s North Point neighbourhood, the chef attended Chinese International School before moving to the US to study cognitive science at Yale University. His desire to cook for others has been part of his personality since he was 16, when he opened a private kitchen called Bo Zai, serving 13-course tasting-menu dinners for fun in an abandoned newspaper factory in Chai Wan on the east side of Hong Kong Island. After moving to New York, Sin kept cooking, joining the university’s student-run pop-up restaurant concepts before joining the team at Junzi Kitchen, a fast-casual modern Chinese chain, and co-founding other pop-up concepts. Now, more than a decade later, the chef remains an advocate for his hometown across platforms, whether through his coming cookbook, YouTube videos or cooking in person. For his latest project, he and his wife, Camden Hauge, run a pop-up called Lok Kee, which takes over New York’s M Star Cafe, the city’s oldest cha chaan teng, in the evenings. The pair are in the process of inheriting the restaurant, and will eventually transform it into a permanent Lok Kee, Sin shares. For now, they serve refined cha chaan teng plates such as white curry pork chop, stir-fried macaroni and black pepper brisket cooked in a claypot. “A lot of [the dishes are] inspired by the recipes in the book,” he says. Dishes such as Hong Kong-style French toast or curry dishes, a big part of cha chaan teng repertoire, may not be familiar to outsiders. Understanding the city’s East-meets-West cuisine requires a dive into history; when the British ruled Hong Kong for 156 years starting in 1841, they influenced the city’s language, trade, laws and everyday cuisine. A window into Hong Kong’s heritage For Sin, cha chaan teng food is a window into Hong Kong’s heritage. “It deserves the treatment that a lot of other cuisines get, too,” he says. “People need to try to understand even the simplest, everyday Hong Kong cuisine can give us an understanding of where that cuisine comes from.” That “perfect” scrambled egg sandwich is an example. While most cha chaan teng in Hong Kong have a version of it on their menu, it is rarely a signature item. Sin’s recipe, however, is modelled on one of his favourite spots – Australia Dairy Company in Jordan, famed for its fluffy egg sandwiches and milk puddings. “Australia Dairy’s [perfect] scrambled egg is a combination of an accident but also [diners and operators] asking for a higher standard,” Sin says. “The creaminess of that egg doesn’t come from the addition of milk despite the name of the restaurant. It comes from recognising that a lot of the egg whites go into their desserts. “Using all those egg whites in desserts means that they have extra egg yolks, and these extra egg yolks get fed back into the scrambled egg mixture for breakfast. “As a result, I think we have achieved, in my opinion, the best scrambled eggs in the universe,” he says. “I think of it as a type of refinement that happens in Hong Kong and can only happen in Hong Kong.” Sin does not stop at scrambled eggs. In his cookbook, he dedicates an entire section to eggs, since many cha chaan teng allow diners to choose their preferred egg style, from the humble omelette filled with sliced ham and sunny-side-up eggs to the fried egg. Then comes an entire page on toast, where he explains how different toasters affect the bread’s char, before diving into his ideal bread specifications: square, crustless, with varying thickness depending on the dish the bread is for. “In the last 60, 70 years in Hong Kong’s culinary history, we’ve really taken a lot of the food that has come into our borders up a notch,” Sin says. “Whether that means refining it in a more fine-dining context or refining it by doing it over and over again and tweaking it every single day [until] it gets to something that we think is now a classic.” A team of Hongkongers To bring this cookbook to light, Sin made sure every part of the project reflected Hong Kong authentically; his team were also all Hongkongers. “I told [the publisher] that I didn’t want to write a book about me,” Sin says. “This book in general is not an attempt to put forward what Lucas Sin’s thoughts on Chinese or cha chaan teng food are. It’s not really like my take on cha chaan teng at all.” Instead, Sin consulted Samuel Lai Dic-sum, a cha chaan teng academic currently doing his PhD in anthropology at SOAS University of London, focusing on Hong Kong food culture. As part of his research, the academic previously worked in cha chaan teng himself; these connections helped Sin to get into many of the city’s local kitchens. “You don’t really convince [cha chaan teng to let you work]. You just sort of like show up,” Sin says. “Gold Garden [in Cheung Sha Wan] was a place I owe the most gratitude for because I worked there the most and the cooks there have taught me the most.” To prepare for the book, Sin worked on and off at the diner for a year. “[It was] obviously in exchange for me not telling anyone that I was working there, so that [the restaurant] wasn’t overwhelmed [with fans],” he jokes. Lai led the research and fact-checking for this cookbook, pulling from his academic research and even his personal cha chaan teng memorabilia collection, which features odd items he collected from now-closed cha chaan teng or sourced through local memorabilia groups. “I do have some artefacts which [Lucas] took pictures of, and then he put them into the book,” Lai recalls. “For example, a particular oven that some cha chaan teng used to use. It’s a composite oven which both toasts and boils tea at the same time.” In March 2025, the book began to take physical shape. Sin brought on Gloria Chung Wing-han, a Hong Kong-born prop and food stylist and journalist; photographers Nicholas Wong Wai-kin and Mario Chui Wai-chung; and his best friend and graphic designer, Justin Au Chun-him. “The shooting took three weeks,” Chung, 42, recalls. “We were stuck in that studio for three weeks.” Chung was tasked with securing a professional kitchen, designing a cha chaan teng set and sourcing props ahead of the cookbook shoot. To make sure every detail was right, Chung looked high and low for the right coloured props and even ordered a large sheet of glass to imitate a cha chaan teng tabletop. The team came up with creative ways to make the glass look worn-in and natural. “Every day, we were trying to make it as old as possible,” she says. “So we ate there, we scratched it, we did everything on the table so that it looks like a real cha chaan teng table.” Focusing on his New York restaurant Bringing Sin’s vision to life required specificity, too. “Lucas is a very cheffy, geeky person,” Chung says. “So if he wants to have a toast, I have to order from the same bakery. He would ask me the thickness of the toast or where it comes from,” she adds, recalling how she had to register as a vendor to get the bread delivered. With recipes spanning breakfast, rice, baked dishes such as Sin’s favourite pork chop rice, afternoon tea and more, the book draws directly from the diners and cooks whom Sin spent years researching. “The most difficult work for the book was trying to represent cha chaan teng,” Sin says. “That means that the recipes, the bread, the props – everything inside of the book – is something that we’ve borrowed and taken from the cha chaan teng in Hong Kong. “I guess the right word in this case is authenticity, but getting the originals right was really, really important for the book.” Now that the book is ready, he is focused on running Lok Kee with his wife. While details are to be confirmed, the couple aim to start renovations by the end of the year and officially reopen as a permanent restaurant next year. “I think [opening a cha chaan teng wasn’t] so much of a dream as it became like a compulsion,” Sin says. “It just makes sense. There’s nothing to do except run a cha chaan teng after spending so much time thinking about it via this book. “One day, my goal, my hope is that people will know what a cha chaan teng is all over the world.” Cha Chaan Teng: Comfort Food from Hong Kong’s Iconic Diners, by Lucas Sin, will be published by Artisan on November 17, 2026

title: Hong Kong sees last-minute IPO cancellations amid increased regulatory checks, weak market
description: At least three companies have now shelved their listings in the city after launching share sales since the start of July.
content: Hong Kong’s tougher oversight and weak investor demand have put many mainland China issuers in a dilemma, forcing many small-cap non-technology firms to delay their fundraising plans or even cancel them at the last minute, according to industry players. On Tuesday Jiangsu Slender West Lake Culture and Tourism (SWL Tour) became the latest such case, when the state-owned aquatic tourism service provider postponed a HK$227 million (US$28.93 million) listing. The company attributed the decision to “several factors, including the prevailing market conditions,” it said just hours after closing its order books. “Institutional investors are now more cautious about small-cap stocks with limited fundamentals and growth prospects,” said Roy Lo Wa-kei, managing partner at the accounting and consulting firm SW Hong Kong. The SWL Tour deal did not bring in any cornerstone investor, according to its prospectus, and with the firm opting for the city’s so-called Mechanism B, which caps a public tranche at just 10 per cent, leaving allocation and pricing power more dependent on institutional buyers. Lo emphasised that weak overall sentiment remained the primary deal breaker, with investors turning rational after numerous listings fell below offer price. The Yangzhou-headquartered tourism company saw strong retail demand, attracting HK$69.5 billion in margin orders, making its HK$22.69 million public offer over 3,000 times oversubscribed, according to data from several brokerages. Originally scheduled to list on October 23 with Everbright Securities International as sole sponsor, SWL Tour stated it remained committed to completing the initial public offering when conditions permit. At least three companies have now shelved listings after launching share sales in the second half of this year. The other two – Southeast Asian container yard operator EKH Limited and fintech solutions provider Shenzhen Forms Syntron Information – both cited “market conditions” for their decisions to postpone. This wave of delays coincides with the Securities and Futures Commission’s stepped-up enforcement against artificial IPO demand and IPO-rigging schemes. Kenny How Sze-ming of the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Professionals Association believed that the tighter regulatory environment was having a strong deterrent effect on the broader market. “‘Grey-area money’ that may have existed in some small-cap offerings in the past has nowhere to hide under strong supervision,” he said. “As such money and active speculators exit, some placing projects that relied heavily on this kind of funding naturally face order shortfalls, prompting issuers to suspend listings to avoid risk.” No evidence linked SWL Tour’s delay to regulatory investigations. Twenty-three of 31 companies listed in the third quarter – or 74 per cent – were trading below their offer prices, as of September 30.

title: Former PBOC governor warns of potential crisis from AI investment, urging preparation
description: The former head of the central bank urges preparations to mitigate risks and warns of exposure to potential failed AI investments.
content: Former Chinese central bank governor Zhou Xiaochuan has warned that failed artificial intelligence investments could trigger financial turbulence and urged preparations to mitigate risks amid concerns over a potential bust of the AI investment bubble. “Consider[ing]... such a large amount of the investment going to the AI facility; if a part of it goes to failure, it causes financial turbulence, and this may create a crisis,” Zhou said during a panel discussion at the Bund Summit in Shanghai on Tuesday. “It needs a very large action to bail out our economy [and] some of the financial institutions.” He called for more research and preparation, as well as tools to mitigate the potential fallout from failed AI investments. Zhou’s comments come amid concerns over excessive investment in AI-related sectors, with a sell-off in AI stocks on Wall Street last week. Sonali Jain-Chandra, deputy director at the Asia and Pacific Department of the International Monetary Fund, said Asia was vulnerable to a potential downturn in AI-related investment, given the region’s exposure across the technology supply chain, from advanced chipmaking to data centre construction. “Asia is exposed. And it’s not just the countries that you would think first about in terms of being the leaders in AI. It’s all along the supply chain,” she said during a press briefing in Shanghai on Tuesday. “This is why we have to say that now is the time to build buffers ... to make sure that if there is a downturn, whether it comes from AI or any of the other risks, policymakers have space to be able to respond.” At Tuesday’s panel, Zhou also weighed in on the debate over AI distillation, arguing that the technology and broader AI applications could boost productivity and generate returns for investors. Washington has accused Chinese firms of improperly distilling US frontier models, an allegation Beijing has repeatedly rejected. “For many people, this distillation may have a concern of the infringing intellectual property right,” Zhou said. “But actually, distillation means that your knowledge, your intelligence, is upgrading from the intelligence in the past generation. You get simplified, precise concepts which are established under existing knowledge and intelligence.” Additional reporting by Emma Ma

title: ‘He is my driving force’: how a Hong Kong-born mother built a legacy for her disabled son
description: Made homeless at 15, Georgina Tang overcame childhood trauma to build a successful career, before launching a skincare business at 52.
content: Georgina Tang’s childhood was deeply unhappy. Growing up in poverty in Hong Kong’s New Territories in the 1960s, as one of eight children born into an arranged marriage, her first memories are of physical abuse at the hands of her jealous mother. “When they were forced to marry at the age of 21, my father was in love with another woman, whom he never quite forgot about,” says Tang, now 63. “It drove my mother crazy. It made her furious that I was my father’s favourite – she hated me because he was affectionate towards me.” Tang recalls her mother beating her with a bamboo stick until it splintered, and worse. “She would starve me and send me away while everyone else was eating,” she says. A thin and sickly child, Tang was frequently ill but rarely taken to see a doctor or given medicine. Her father was, she recalls, “a weak and quiet man” who rarely intervened and left Hong Kong for the UK to find work in the restaurant trade when Tang was eight years old. Tang survived her mother’s wrath, partly because of her paternal grandmother’s care. She would step in, once carrying Tang on her back at night to the doctor when she had a soaring fever. When Tang’s father eventually saved enough money to open a Chinese takeaway in Enfield on the outskirts of London, her mother and brothers joined him. It gave Tang a few years of respite, living with her grandmother and sisters. “During that time we learned how to fend for ourselves,” Tang says. “We grew vegetables and, aged 10, I was taking them to the British army barracks to sell. It taught me the value of money. I had nothing, so I valued every penny.” In 1976, when Tang was 13, her grandmother died, and she had to join her parents and brothers in the UK. The years had done nothing to mellow her mother’s fury. The abuse continued, and when Tang was 15, her mother kicked her out of the family home. I do feel lucky and blessed despite everything, because I’ve always had someone to help me when I needed help Georgina Tang Finding a new path Tang was enrolled at the local state school, where she was able to ask for advice. To keep Tang from being sent into social care, her school careers officer helped arrange a job with a family in the north London suburb of Golders Green, where she cooked, cleaned and cared for the children. “I do feel lucky and blessed despite everything, because I’ve always had someone to help me when I needed help,” Tang says. She had managed to save £1 running errands at her father’s takeaway – where she was paid 10 pence an errand – enough to cover the commute to her new job. She worked as a live-in mother’s help for two years and saved diligently, then moved into a share house and did a stint in a hospital ward before taking a job washing dishes at a pizzeria. A hard worker, chatty and likeable, she was quickly promoted to waitressing, a role she balanced with studying for A-levels at night to prepare for higher education. She went on to earn B grades and got accepted into Liverpool John Moores University, where she studied psychology and sociology. A £2,000 student maintenance grant helped cover her living costs, and she continued to work part time. After graduating, she stepped into the corporate housing sector, pursuing foundation and postgraduate degrees in housing while working in graduate management positions. Super saving pays dividends “I don’t drink or smoke, I don’t go on holiday or go out, I make my own clothes, so I was able to save plenty and started buying stocks and shares,” Tang says. Between 1984 and 1990, when then-British prime minister Margaret Thatcher was privatising UK state utilities, telecommunications and banks, Tang bought as much equity as she could. “Everything that was going, I bought,” she says. Alongside these growing investments, her career continued its upward trajectory. She took a job at a Chinese community centre in Liverpool and worked her way up over the years, becoming head of housing and deputy CEO of a housing trust at 39. “I was incredibly thrifty,” Tang says. In her late twenties, she bought a car using cash, then a few years later, cashed in her shares to afford the £20,000 deposit on her first house. She married her Italian boyfriend Andrea – whom she met while working at a restaurant – in 1994 in Liverpool. She made her own wedding dress out of Chinese silk. Fighting for Alessio’s survival At 40, Tang gave birth to her son, Alessio – and entered the hardest fight of her life. Alessio was born with multiple severe forms of epilepsy, autism, muscle weakness and chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux. He also suffered from frightening, uncontrollable nosebleeds. Doctors warned he would not survive past his first birthday. Alessio did survive. At 10, he was diagnosed with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, a type of childhood autoimmune disorder in which the immune system attacks the joints, causing inflammation, pain and stiffness. He was treated with chemotherapy and developed severe psoriasis with cracked and bleeding skin as a side effect. His hair also fell out in clumps. None of the steroids and creams dermatologists prescribed worked. Tang, who had taken a free workshop on how to make bath products at a community centre two years earlier, created her own shea butter balm for him at her kitchen table. To her amazement, the balm brought immediate relief to his raw skin. She also developed a shampoo and conditioner to soothe his scalp and support hair regrowth. Alessio was then put on a trial biologic drug known as a TNF inhibitor, which works by blocking the proteins that drive chronic inflammation. Now 23 years old, Alessio’s severe psoriasis and many of his other symptoms are well under control. He hasn’t had a seizure since he was three years old, and he no longer takes epilepsy medication – a remarkable turnaround Tang says astounded his doctors. He can enjoy life more, although he still suffers from arthritis, severe autism and learning difficulties – and wears special headphones that dampen harsh background noise. An adult must accompany him wherever he goes as he has no sense of danger. He also has many fears and phobias, particularly around electrical equipment and in medical environments. His father is essentially Alessio’s carer, getting him ready to go to a day centre on weekdays, and waiting at home for his return if Tang is out working. A business born of necessity Tang started sharing her products with other parents and cancer patients, and then began selling them. In 2015, at the age of 52, she established her skincare and hair care company YNNY – standing for “Yours Naturally, Naturally Yours”. It now sells more than 50 products, handmade in a laboratory near her home in Liverpool. They are suitable for cancer patients, and the company offers a discount for customers who have undergone or are currently undergoing chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Alessio is Tang’s focus and driving force, and she hopes to leave a legacy for him when she and her husband are no longer around. Despite the cruel treatment her mother meted out to her, when she reached out to ask for forgiveness in 1983, Tang gave it. She also helped her mother to get treatment when she was sick. She died in August 2024. “She felt ashamed of what she did to me, and without hesitation, I helped,” Tang says. “I’ve been to hell and gone through it. My secret? I never look back and don’t dwell on the past or in sadness and negativity. I only look forward.” Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Ukraine Starlink access up to Musk, not White House, Rubio says
description: US top diplomat frames battlefield satellite throttling as a private commercial decision, despite conflicting reports of administration involvement.
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that decisions regarding Ukraine’s access to Starlink were up to SpaceX and Elon Musk, not the White House, comments that suggested ‌Musk may have restricted Kyiv’s access to the service. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink that Ukraine relies on to defend itself against missile attacks from Russia. The Journal cited one source saying that Musk, President Donald Trump and White House officials discussed the matter beforehand, and two sources saying that Musk and the president discussed the matter in the days after the slowdown. “I’m not aware that we knew about this decision ⁠beforehand. But that’s irrelevant,” Rubio told reporters during a trip to India. “The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract ‌as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at.” Musk and SpaceX did not respond to Reuters requests for comment. Reuters has cited two US officials ‌and a Western official briefed on the matter saying the decision ultimately came from the White House. This version ⁠was also asserted by Ukrainian President ⁠Volodymyr Zelensky, but denied by the administration. Rubio’s comments are likely to intensify concerns in Washington regarding Musk’s singular ability to influence US foreign policy. They also represent ‌an apparent shift in position for the administration. Trump has publicly said he believed neither he nor Musk were behind the slowdown. Departing for a trip to Uzbekistan and India on Saturday, ‌Rubio ‌had said no one ordered the slowdown, an assertion that drew criticism from lawmakers in both parties. “I’m not sure Zelensky knows ‌what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate,” Rubio said at the time. “We have nothing to do with that. I don’t – the ⁠United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it’s been restored,” Rubio said. Speaking ⁠to reporters on Tuesday, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth also portrayed the Starlink cut-off as a commercial matter. No US official has publicly said, however, that they have pushed SpaceX to reverse any cutoffs. “There are terms of service that ultimately ‌need to be complied to, and that’s ‌where Starlink has the option to make those decisions,” Hegseth said. One significant point of confusion relates to the difference between SpaceX’s Starshield and Starlink products. Starshield is essentially a military-grade version of Starlink developed for the Pentagon. Rubio suggested on Saturday that Ukraine never had access to Starshield in the first place, while Zelensky has said that both Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine have been disrupted.

title: Sushi, seafood, tea: where the founder of Qipology goes in Hong Kong for dim sum and more
description: Qipology’s Julie Liu lists a Hong Kong restaurant for dim sum, where to find Japanese-Chinese fusion and her favourite spot in Shenzhen.
content: Born in the US, raised in Hong Kong and educated in the UK, Julie Liu is the founder of the contemporary qipao brand Qipology. She spoke to Andrew Sun. My diet is typically Chinese: home-cooked meals, rice, vegetables, steamed fish and soups. Nothing fancy, just everyday Cantonese food that shapes your palate without you noticing. That is probably why I gravitate towards simpler food rather than anything too elaborate. I eat out a lot for work, so when I choose for myself, I lean towards places that feel calm and consistent rather than trendy. For lunch, I am a regular at T/EA (Shop H107, Block B Hollywood, PMQ, 35 Aberdeen Street, Central. Tel: 9531 0069). The modern teahouse reinterprets traditional tea culture with a contemporary approach, serving sparkling tieguanyin, cold teas and tea-based drinks alongside dumpling noodles and light bites such as rose cake. I also love Kikusan (B13-B16, Landmark Atrium, 15 Queen’s Road Central, Central. Tel: 2521 3344). It is a modern Japanese-Chinese spot, the kind of place where you can get everything from dim sum and ramen to sushi and rice bowls, all done well without fuss. The vegetable curry rice and stir-fried cauliflower dish are personal favourites. For dinner, I love Francis (4 & 6 St Francis Street, Wan Chai. Tel: 5216 8318) and Francis West (42-44 Peel Street, SoHo. Tel: 9039 0969). They are Middle Eastern and North African spots, respectively, the kind of places where the food is made for sharing, so you end up ordering half the menu without realising it. Francis West leans more into Maghreb flavours: Tunisian grilled salads, spiced lamb sausage and raw tuna with argan oil and gazpacho. Both have warm, intimate atmospheres. The knafeh dessert is one thing I order every time. For dim sum, I go to City Hall Maxim’s Palace (2/F, Low Block, City Hall, Central. Tel: 2521 1303). I enjoy the harbour views and the classic trolley service. I love My Cup of Tea (6 Spring Garden Lane, Wan Chai. Tel: 2386 0007), a proper Hong Kong-style milk tea shop, which gets the basics right – strong tea and the right ratio of milk. I will take visitors to Yau Ley Seafood Restaurant (Lot 359, Sha Kiu Tsuen, Leung Shuen Wan, Sai Kung. Tel: 2791 1822) for lunch. It is not just a meal – it is a full-day experience. The restaurant sits on High Island, and you can take a boat or sampan, or hike, if you are up for it. It makes the whole trip feel like an adventure, not just lunch. The family-run spot has been open since 1999, and the seafood is as fresh as it gets – caught daily by local fishermen. The deep-fried calamari is a stand-out. For dinner, Vilavilla Gourmet (51 Yi Chun Street, Sai Kung. Tel: 2788 3080) is a Hunan restaurant with bold and spicy flavours. Think sizzling beef and spicy potatoes loaded with garlic. It is casual and welcoming. You can sit outside on cooler nights. A good contrast to Cantonese, and it is anything but a tourist trap. On weekends, I will pop over to Shenzhen for lunch at Yong Fu Xiao Xian (Shop SL617, MixC World Shenzhen, 9668 Shennan Boulevard, Nanshan district. Tel: +86 755 8670 3301). The ingredients are fresh and the food is so delicious. The crab vermicelli pot is really tasty. It is also fun, as you have to go to this area to order with a scanner, which makes you feel like you are gaming in an arcade.

title: France to deploy troops for planned protests after riots and looting
description: Leaders concede intelligence and tactical lapses as Paris prepares massive security operation.
content: France will reinforce police with troops and mount a huge security operation for more protests planned on Saturday, the government said, acknowledging failures in its response to last weekend’s violence. “The deployment next Saturday will be massive,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Tuesday, adding that the immediate priority was to restore order after rioting and looting swept Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities on October 17. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the military would be deployed alongside police, while the government pledged ‌to overhaul tactics after widespread criticism that city centres had been left vulnerable. Framing the crisis as a choice “between violence and the Republic”, Lecornu blamed the unrest on far-left groups, who in turn have accused the government of underestimating public anger over high living costs and declining public services. The turmoil shocked France because of both its scale and the apparent inability of police to contain it, inflaming tensions ahead of presidential elections next year with candidates from the far-right and hard-left performing strongly in polls. Protests in other European countries, including Italy and Albania, have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading around the continent at a time when many nations, including France, are struggling with budget woes. Relative calm in France has followed targeted curfews imposed ⁠in several areas affected by the chaos, which the government said had helped reassert control. The localised curfews, some directed at children and teenagers under age 18, were extended to Tuesday night, police said. Lecornu acknowledged shortcomings in ‌the state’s response at the weekend, saying there had been intelligence failures, while police deployments had been too static and authorities had erred by not cancelling planned police leave. Nunez apologised for the mistakes. “I deeply regret what happened. I accept my share of responsibility,” he said. Parliament is setting up a commission ‌of inquiry to establish the causes of the unrest, while authorities have assigned 200 investigators to identify and track down those involved in the street violence. Police arrested on Tuesday a man ⁠suspected of starting a blaze that destroyed a ⁠historic town hall in the central city of Limoges during the rioting. Officials said he had been on a security watch list and belonged to an ultra-left group. Sylvain Maillard, a Renaissance deputy for Paris, said some apps had become “a walkie-talkie system for rioters and looters”. Underscoring ‌the broad impact of the crisis, French borrowing costs rose further on Tuesday as investors fretted about the prospect of more unrest, with the yield on benchmark 10-year government bonds touching its highest level in 24 years. Supermarket chain Carrefour said it had lost tens of millions of euros ‌through theft ‌and damage, warning that it faced an “unprecedented situation” because of the disorder. France’s main student union UNEF has called for further protests on Saturday, pledging to maintain pressure on Macron’s government over what it says is a ‌deteriorating and underfunded education system. “We carry on,” it said on social media. Separately, groups identifying themselves as Gilets Jaunes (Yellow Vests) called for protest actions over rising fuel costs. The Yellow Vest movement, largely inactive in recent years, sprang up in ⁠2018 during Macron’s first term over plans to raise petrol taxes. Traffic blockades continued for months until the government made costly concessions it can ill afford now. Northern Italian ⁠cities, including the financial capital Milan, were also hit by riots last weekend. Though not on the scale seen in France, the unrest nonetheless jolted Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government. On Tuesday, Rome introduced new security measures aimed at curbing violent youth demonstrations. A government decree calls for the deployment of an additional 500 soldiers to Milan through the end of the year, while requiring parents to pay for damage caused by minors and making it easier to prosecute offenders over age 14. Defence Minister Guido Crosetto described the disturbances as a form of “hybrid warfare” conducted through social media platforms such as TikTok, YouTube and other ‌online networks. “The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy ‌are fundamentally different from those seen in other eras,” Crosetto wrote on X. “The West has yet to realise this or take any meaningful action in response.” In Milan’s central Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, sportswear retailer On and a Levi’s store that were targeted during the unrest had reopened on Tuesday but remained boarded up. Luxury stores had restored merchandise to window displays after temporarily removing it for security reasons. Concerns over online-driven contagion also surfaced in Albania, where protesters took to the streets of Tirana for a seventh consecutive day against the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Demonstrators have repeatedly clashed with police as months of protests escalated, driven by fresh demands for better university conditions and anger over corruption. On Tuesday, Rama repeated earlier accusations that “foreign actors” were exploiting the unrest, having previously accused Russia and Iran of stoking online disinformation. “This has now been recognised and is becoming a major issue across Europe,” Rama said during a visit to the education ministry. “It is a hybrid war that gains traction precisely because it is rooted in genuine grievances, not mere fantasy,” he added, citing the rising cost of living, housing shortages and anxiety over the future. Rama hinted at a possible ban on social media for children under 16, and flagged plans to lower the age of criminal responsibility. Additional reporting by Associated Press and Agence France-Presse

title: Liberty, equality, tear gas: no nation does mass protests quite like France
description: When the French take to the streets to revolt, they aren’t just venting – they’re practising centuries of political theatre.
content: When the French fight high fuel taxes, they don yellow vests and march. When angry farmers want better pay, hundreds of them drive tractors down the Champs-Elysees. And when museum workers want better tourist management, they strike and shut down the Louvre. Passionate public protest is as French as “La Marseillaise”, the 1792 anthem that enshrines the collective duty to fight tyranny in the country’s national identity. But this month, the most violent demonstrations in years – and tough policing – have raised concern about riots overshadowing hundreds of thousands of peaceful demonstrators marching against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. On Saturday alone, at least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France clashed with police, set cars on fire, stormed public buildings, looted stores and engulfed a historic city hall in flames. More protests could be in store. “How can French people do this to France?” outgoing President Emmanuel Macron asked on Sunday. Nothing justifies the destruction, he added. “We all feel anger and shame.” But any student of French history would know that the nation’s proud, loud and colourful protest culture has sometimes turned violent – starting with the beheadings of King Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette during the revolution that overthrew the monarchy in 1789. A protest culture is born Historians say the revolution was where the modern-day French tradition of civic engagement as a duty was born. The idea is that voting is not the only way to drive change; demonstration is considered a bedrock value, a way to make elites hear the populace and to defend freedoms. The moment a child becomes an activist is seen as a generations-old rite of passage. The right to protest is even constitutionally protected. “It’s a way to build collective identity and political community,” said Magali Della Sudda, research director in political science at the French National Centre for Scientific Research in Bordeaux. France’s post-revolution history is not a solid story of protests and reforms, but of cycles of popular uprisings, repression, mobilisation and political concessions. The tradition has turned tragic; in 1871, government troops cracked down on the new Paris Commune, or municipal government, reportedly killing thousands. In some ways, collective action won – as in 1968, when student demonstrations and a general strike forced the government to grant concessions like an increase in the minimum wage. In more recent history, the “Yellow Vests” – Gilets Jaunes in French – demonstrated against a proposed fuel tax increase, and that broadened into protests over other issues like living costs and inequality. Some demonstrations in 2018 and 2019 featured burning cars, looting and confrontations with police. It’s not uncommon for French violence on the fringes to mar otherwise peaceful marches. Likewise, the student protests over the weekend expanded from education to other grievances – and featured dramatic scenes of looting and clashes with police. It’s not clear how many of those who were ransacking shops had turned out to join the day’s protest, which drew tens of thousands, or were mere opportunists. Authorities have responded with nightly curfews; there were calls for more protests later in the week. Police violence blamed for mistrust Some of the forces driving protests for the last month owe to more recent French tradition, according to political scientist Fabien Jobard, who has studied the history of protest and policing. Since the 1990s, the country has seen recurring waves of what the French call violences urbaines and Americans would call riots, Jobard said. They are often sparked by police violence: nationwide unrest erupted in 2005 after two teenagers died while fleeing police, and again in 2023 after an officer fatally shot a 17-year-old during a traffic stop outside Paris. “For young people from the suburbs, the riot is one of the traditional forms of collective expression,” he said. Government critics and human rights campaigners have alleged that police tactics in the last month have been unnecessarily violent. Much of the criticism focuses on rubber-bullet launchers, known in France as LBDs, and stun grenades, which critics blame for serious injuries to protesters. And Della Sudda noted that the nearly 8,000 arrests in the weeks leading up to October 17 dwarf the few dozen detained during a 1998 protest of 500,000 students against teacher shortages and dilapidated schools. The feeling of not being heard also is part of it, she says. Rather than listen to protesters and negotiate, Della Sudda noted for example, the government tried to appease “Yellow Vest” grievances through a digital platform, which translates to “the great national debate”. Anti-government protesters panned Macron’s plan. “As a result,” Della Sudda wrote, “mistrust is growing”.

title: Why has October been so hot in Hong Kong?
description: Global warming, El Nino and super typhoon all combine to create higher-than-usual temperatures.
content:
A climate expert has said that Hong Kong’s exceptionally warm October weather is being driven by a combination of a super typhoon, El Nino and global warming, warning that higher-than-usual temperatures are likely to persist through the winter.
The warning came as autumn temperatures across the city topped 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit) over the past few weeks.
Professor Amos Tai Pui-kuen, of the earth and environmental sciences department at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, explained on Wednesday that El Nino had altered typhoon paths and weakened the northeasterly winds that typically reach the city in autumn.
“A ‘super’ El Nino means that courses of typhoons would move more northerly … if and when typhoons do hit Hong Kong, because of the high sea level temperatures, there will be more heat and steam evaporating, which contributes to a stronger typhoon, too,” he said.
He added that El Nino had changed atmospheric circulation, weakening the autumn northeasterlies and reducing heat dissipation, leaving Hong Kong hotter.
Another factor was a super typhoon near Manila, Tai said. He explained that an anticyclone had formed over Hong Kong as part of the typhoon’s outer circulation, causing air to sink and winds to weaken, with sunshine becoming “particularly abundant”.
He added that global warming had also raised baseline temperatures.
A local green group and a leading meteorologist warned in July that Hong Kong should prepare for stronger storms and a warmer, wetter winter, as the current El Nino was likely to intensify into a super event.
Tai said temperatures would gradually fall as winter approached, but the season was likely to be warmer than in previous years because of the lingering effects of the “super” El Nino, which could last until spring.
Five hikers fell ill in separate incidents across Hong Kong on Monday as hot weather gripped the city on the final day of the Chung Yeung Festival long weekend. Some were airlifted to hospital by the Government Flying Service.
Conditions were hot and dry that day, with the maximum temperature reaching 32 degrees Celsius at the Hong Kong Observatory’s urban headquarters and several degrees higher in parts of the New Territories.
The Observatory forecast temperatures would reach 33 degrees on Friday before gradually falling below 30 degrees later the following week.

title: A 2027 turning point? Goldman, Citi see stabilising signs in China’s housing market
description: Encouraging holiday sales and shrinking supply point to recovery for country’s property sector, according to Goldman Sachs and Citi.
content: As China’s housing market downturn enters its fifth year, global investment banks including Goldman Sachs and Citi say they expect the sector to pivot as soon as 2027, with expectations fuelled by signs of shrinking supply and robust sales over the National Day holiday in early October. Citi holds a positive view on the sector and saw 2027 as a pivotal year for home price recovery in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. Home prices in China hit their lowest point in June 2024, according to Citi. Shanghai became the first city to post positive year-on-year growth in secondary home prices in September, with prices rising 0.8 per cent, according to the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday. “While we need further confirmation before declaring a sustained recovery, the evidence increasingly points to stabilising and potentially rising home prices in top cities, with most tier-two cities likely to lag,” said Griffin Chan, an analyst at Citi Research, in a report on Tuesday. Chan noted strong sales in core cities during “golden week”, and said that policy packages had lifted home price expectations and unlocked demand for upgraded housing. HSBC also highlighted encouraging sales momentum over golden week. In a report earlier this month, the bank said robust secondary market transactions alongside persistent price pressure suggested that genuine demand remained resilient, although buyers remained price sensitive. Its outlook came ahead of a similarly positive stance from Goldman Sachs on Tuesday. The investment bank forecast four pivot points for China’s housing market through to 2035, driven by a new sales model introduced by the Chinese government on August 28. The guideline from national housing, land and financial regulators instructed local authorities to prioritise completed home sales on newly sold land. Goldman Sachs also said in the Tuesday report that the supply of saleable primary market housing estates in China was set for a sharp drop in 2028, and was likely to continue material decline in the years ahead. Land sales were projected to see an accelerated decline starting in 2031. New housing starts and property fixed-asset investment were expected to see a turnaround in 2032, while the decline in structural demand was set to accelerate from 2030 onwards, it added.

title: Mariah Carey wins dismissal of US$20m defamation lawsuit filed by brother Morgan ... so who is he?
description: Morgan Carey sued his sister over claims made in her memoir, The Meaning of Mariah Carey, which alleged that he was a violent drug dealer.
content: Mariah Carey has just won a dismissal in a US$20 million defamation lawsuit filed by her brother, Morgan Carey, over her 2020 memoir, The Meaning of Mariah Carey. The “Emotions” singer’s estranged brother sued her back in 2021, claiming that she lied about him in her book where she alleged that Morgan – whom she refers to as an “ex-brother” – was violent in the family and dealt drugs in the 1980s. “More often, I felt I had to protect myself from him, and sometimes I would find myself protecting my mother from him too,” she wrote. She added that he once “slammed” their mother Patricia into a wall. “Next thing I knew she was totally limp, as if her bones had melted, folding onto the floor,” she stated in her book. Morgan has vehemently denied the claims, saying they are “false and defamatory”, the New York Post reported. Mariah’s late sister, Alison, also previously sued the pop star over claims that she’d “pimped” her out and “drugged” the singer when she was 12. Judge Leslie Stroth of the New York State Supreme Court dismissed the case on Monday, writing: “[Morgan] has not sufficiently pleaded actual malice on the part of [Mariah]. “[Morgan] fails to provide any proof that [Mariah] made such statements with knowledge of their falsity or with reckless disregard for the truth. While [Morgan] alleges that [Mariah] demonstrates ill will towards her brother, such statement is insufficient, and [Morgan] has not satisfied the pleading requirement for actual malice.” Following the ruling, Mariah’s lawyer John Rosenberg told People magazine that the songstress “is gratified that the court recognised that her memoir addresses significant issues of public interest and dismissed her brother’s defamation claims in their entirety”. Here’s what we know about Mariah Carey’s brother Morgan and their complicated relationship: What is Morgan Carey’s background? According to People magazine, Morgan is nine years older than Mariah. They share one sibling, Alison, who tragically passed away on the same day as their mother, Patricia, in August 2024. The siblings grew up on Long Island, New York, and their parents split up when Mariah was three. In 2020, Mariah opened up about her relationship – or rather, lack thereof – with her siblings over the years in an appearance on The Oprah Conversation. “We don’t even really know each other … we didn’t grow up together, but we did. Like, they were on their journeys, by the time I got into the world, they had already been damaged, in my opinion,” she said. “But again, I wasn’t there. I was dropped into this world and I literally felt like an outsider amongst my own family.” What does Morgan Carey do? @pinkprincesshoo Mariah (Carey) has a sibling named Morgan (Carey) and Mariah The Tautologist has a sister named Morgan too https://t.co/ebdzkIXeEA — Romeo S (Reloaded) 🇩🇴🥇 (@PaIIahAbdul) April 14, 2026 Morgan has had careers as a music producer, fitness trainer and model, per Page Six. “He was strikingly handsome and occasionally worked as a model,” Mariah wrote in her memoir. “He was well known and well liked.” He helped Mariah in her early career According to Mariah’s book, Morgan lent her some support when she was just starting out. The Daily Mail reported that Morgan was the one who introduced his sister to Gavin Christopher, with whom she worked with, and Ben Margulies and Chris Toland. She shared that Morgan gave her US$5,000 to launch her self-titled debut album in 1990, and she ended up paying him back, per Page Six. When did Morgan and Mariah Carey become estranged? The siblings have been estranged since 1994, after they got into a big argument, the Daily Mail reported. It seems like the feud didn’t end there. After Alison was put into a mental hospital in 2016, Morgan told the British outlet about his frustrations with Mariah, stating that he believed she could’ve financially helped Alison amid her addiction issues. “The worst is yet to come and Mariah has it in her power to at least ensure a soft landing and avoid a lifetime of regret about missing this opportunity to forgive and help her only sister,” he told the publication. “I would be hopeful, although I am not encouraged by the past, that Mariah would step up because she’s in a position to step up.” Is Morgan Carey married? 🚨 Mariah Carey and her brother Morgan Carey in 1987 on live TV. He was a fitness coach. Via TMZ pic.twitter.com/mCOSasgTCr — Dannyijbol (@Dannyijbol) April 29, 2026 Morgan is married to Ilaria Negrini Carey and they live in Italy. Unlike his mega-famous sister, he maintains a low profile.

title: Drone strike on market in disputed Sudan border region kills at least 153
description: Sudanese military officer acknowledges targeting fuel trucks bound for RSF paramilitaries as inferno engulfs civilian stalls in Abyei.
content: A drone strike on a market in Abyei, a border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan, hit a nearby fuel depot, killing at least 153 people, a local official said on Tuesday. Yohanna Akol Ngor, the Abyei administration’s caretaker information minister, blamed Sudan’s military for Monday’s attack on Amiet Market, north of Abyei town. Ngor told Associated Press by phone that the death toll was continuing to rise as the fire burned. A senior Sudanese military officer said the army carried out a drone strike Monday targeting fuel tankers arriving from South Sudan that he said were bound for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the press. The officer said those killed were RSF members and people involved in fuel smuggling. “We do not target civilians,” he said. AP could not independently verify his account of the targets or the identities of those killed. The officer said the strike took place outside the demilitarised zone along the border with South Sudan. In a statement on Tuesday, the UN secretary general condemned drone attacks near Amiet Market and Todach, saying dozens of civilians, including women and children, had been killed and many others injured. The statement did not identify who carried out the attacks. The UN said many people remained missing and the toll was expected to rise as the UN Interim Security Force for Abyei, known as UNISFA, continued verifying casualties. The peacekeeping force deployed medical personnel, firefighting capabilities and quick reaction forces to provide emergency treatment, help evacuate casualties and prevent the fire from spreading, the statement said. Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) said more than 20 wounded people were brought to Ameth Bek Hospital, where MSF teams were working alongside staff from South Sudan’s Health Ministry. “So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted,” said Dr Christian Lindauer, MSF’s medical activities manager at the hospital. South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry also blamed Sudan’s military, saying the attack hit multiple locations within the market, causing civilian casualties and extensive property damage. The ministry said it had summoned Sudan’s ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to “refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property”. It called for issues concerning Abyei to be addressed through diplomatic channels. Sudan’s military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have been fighting since April 2023, devastating large parts of the country and threatening stability along its borders. Ngor said the strike hit around 11am Monday. He said the fuel depot supplied local businesses. “It is a horrible and shocking situation,” he said. MSF called on all parties to stop attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, expressing concern about people’s ability to safely reach healthcare and other essential services. Amiet Market is a trading hub serving the Ngok Dinka and Misseriya communities. The oil-rich Abyei region’s status was left unresolved by a 2005 peace agreement that ended decades of civil war and remained unsettled when South Sudan became independent in 2011. A proposed referendum stalled over disagreements about who could vote. The region’s majority Ngok Dinka population favours joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favour Sudan. Abyei has also experienced deadly communal violence, including fighting over land between Ngok Dinka and neighbouring Twic Dinka communities.

title: Days before Brazil’s run-off, Lula and Bolsonaro seek to disqualify each other
description: Clash over alleged algorithmic bias and state messaging ratchets up tension ahead of Sunday’s knife-edge vote.
content: In the latest showdown from Brazil’s increasingly rancorous presidential race Tuesday, both candidates called for the disqualification of their rivals over allegations of social media malfeasance, according to court filings and campaign officials. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s campaign said they would request the disqualification of right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro on Wednesday over alleged election interference by tech giant Meta. Later Tuesday, Bolsonaro’s team struck back with its own court filing, seen by Agence France-Presse, accusing leftist Lula of “abuse of power” in the mass dissemination of government postings on WhatsApp during the campaign. Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term in office but is facing stiff competition from his challenger, the son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio Bolsonaro received 47 per cent of the vote over the incumbent’s 45 per cent in the first round earlier this month, and polls show a technical tie ahead of Sunday’s run-off. Lula’s petition was initially expected to be submitted Tuesday to Brazil’s top electoral court concerning alleged “algorithmic manipulation” by Meta aimed at harming Lula’s chances of winning, the campaign source said. But Lula’s campaign coordinator, Senator Camilo Santana, later told reporters the filing would occur Wednesday. The information was first revealed Monday by Brazilian newspaper Folha de S. Paulo. Meta and lawyers from both campaigns met at the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) on Tuesday, a court source said. The court on Monday gave Meta 24 hours to prove it was complying with an order to treat both campaigns equally, threatening a daily fine of around US$200,000 if it did not. The order came after Lula’s campaign alleged that Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, was suppressing his online content to boost Bolsonaro. “We have completed the implementation of the measures to comply with the Superior Electoral Court’s decision,” the company stated on Tuesday. Lula’s campaign also alleged inconsistencies in WhatsApp’s artificial intelligence tool, saying Lula-related election content was limited while Bolsonaro content was untouched. Meta had denied taking any actions to favour one side in the election, but previously said that some of Lula’s campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors. Among measures the tech giant adopted, Meta said that now only candidates and parties registered with the electoral court can place ads on its networks. The company also said it removed 720 posts containing AI-generated content that lacked proper labelling. Meta’s London-based oversight board also said it had identified recurring failures with content about Brazil’s presidential elections and the US congressional elections. Dozens of Lula supporters protested outside the company’s Sao Paulo offices on Monday, bearing placards and chanting slogans like “Meta out of Brazil”. Lula, 80, has also accused the American government of meddling in the elections in favour of Flavio Bolsonaro. US President Donald Trump has not yet explicitly endorsed Bolsonaro, 45, but called his surprise first-round finish a “very, very big victory”. The run-off victor will either preserve the vast country of 214 million people as a left-wing stronghold in Latin America, or usher it into the ranks of right-wing administrations loyal to Trump. The shock result of the first round appears to have invigorated the left, with Lula’s camp staging massive rallies ever since and seeking to up its social media game. Flavio’s father Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his electoral defeat to Lula in 2022. Flavio Bolsonaro has sworn to liberate his father if elected.

title: China sees surge in border crossings amid visa-free travel boom
description: China logged a 24.1 per cent surge in visa-free foreign entries in the third quarter, while overseas trips by Chinese nationals also rose.
content: China recorded a surge in border crossings by both mainland Chinese citizens and foreign nationals in the third quarter of this year, as Chinese companies expand overseas and Beijing steps up incentives to attract foreign tourists. The country logged a total of 192 million border crossings in the July-September period, up 7.9 per cent year on year, according to data released by the National Immigration Administration on Tuesday. China received 11.6 million foreign arrivals, up 15.6 per cent, with visa-free entries surging 24.1 per cent to account for 77.5 per cent of the total. The top three sources of foreign visitors were Russia, South Korea and Vietnam in that order, followed by Malaysia, the United States, Japan, Singapore, Thailand and Australia, according to the data. Lu Ning, a spokesperson for the immigration bureau, said China’s expanding “unilateral and autonomous opening-up policies” had fuelled the growth in cross-border travel, as well as a rise in countries granting visa-free access to Chinese citizens. Beijing has granted visa-free entry to tourists from dozens of countries over the past few years, as it looks to use inbound tourism as a driver to boost the Chinese economy. The State Council has set a target of attracting 190 million inbound tourist visits per year by 2030, and raising spending by inbound travellers to more than US$150 billion per year. The body aims to achieve this by further expanding China’s visa-free policies, improving tourists’ access to digital payment services – previously a major barrier for foreign visitors – and expanding tax refunds for international tourists. Mainland residents also made more trips abroad in the third quarter, according to the data, with outbound border crossings rising 7.5 per cent year on year to 48.5 million. Hong Kong and Macau ranked as the top two most popular destinations for mainland travellers, followed by South Korea, Vietnam, Thailand, Japan, Singapore, Malaysia, Russia and Indonesia, indicating the importance of regional travel. One week after the revamped Huanggang Port reopened in Shenzhen on October 12 – the first Hong Kong–mainland border checkpoint to adopt a joint clearance system – it handled 886,000 passenger trips and 74,000 vehicle crossings, according to the bureau. The new model had slashed passenger clearance times from 30 minutes to just five minutes, it added. Countries including South Korea and Thailand have become popular choices for Chinese tourists in the past year, while Chinese travel to Japan has faced severe disruptions in recent months amid a diplomatic row between Beijing and Tokyo. The increase in outbound travel also comes as Chinese companies deepen their international reach and exports continue to grow. China’s outbound direct investment increased 8.1 per cent year on year to US$86.5 billion in the first half of the year, professional services firm EY has calculated.

title: Nvidia CEO to deliver keynote speech in Berlin as his firm faces investor scrutiny over AI
description: The conference, focusing on sovereign AI, automation and infrastructure, comes days after Jensen Huang’s meeting with German Chancellor.
content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is set to take the stage in Berlin on Wednesday, as the world’s most valuable company faces heightened investor scrutiny over whether the massive artificial intelligence spending boom – the engine behind the chipmaker’s meteoric growth – can deliver long-term returns. The conference agenda focuses on sovereign AI, industrial automation and operational infrastructure – key sectors where Nvidia hopes to drive demand beyond the handful of US tech giants currently dominating the investment landscape. It follows Huang’s meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Monday, when Nvidia and partner Siemens showcased AI deployments in production planning and circuit-board inspection. Huang’s keynote at Nvidia’s GTC conference, scheduled for 11am local time or 5pm Hong Kong time, comes as its customers battle rising borrowing costs and mounting delays in building the data centres required to run its processors. Financing risks across the AI ecosystem have come into sharp focus following a sell-off in the shares and bonds of CoreWeave, an Nvidia-backed cloud provider and major graphics processing unit (GPU) buyer. Due to its reliance on debt, CoreWeave is widely considered a bellwether for whether specialised AI cloud operators can sustainably fund their expansion. Research firm Gartner warned last week that more than US$3.5 trillion in global AI infrastructure spending could face impairment by 2030 if investment continued on its current trajectory, noting that projected revenues would be insufficient to yield profitable returns on planned capital expenditure. For Nvidia, these financial dynamics carry immediate consequences: even if demand for computing power remained strong, financial stress among key customers could stall purchase timing. Wall Street remains divided. Goldman Sachs upgraded CoreWeave to “buy” on Monday, arguing that investors might be overestimating financing costs and underestimating contract returns. The bank noted that distressed yields on unsecured bonds offered a poor guide to the asset-backed financing that underpinned most of CoreWeave’s expansion. Physical bottlenecks pose an equally urgent challenge. At least 47 major US data centre projects had been delayed, cancelled or blocked this year amid local opposition, permitting delays and power grid constraints, according to a Financial Times report on Sunday. With delivery schedules now as important to growth as chip performance, purchase commitments are only as valuable as the physical space available to plug them in. Research firm SemiAnalysis offers a more optimistic outlook. In a report published this week, it forecast roughly 50 gigawatts of additional global data centre capacity by 2027. Pointing to more than 24GW already under advanced construction, SemiAnalysis argued that modular designs, on-site power generation and international expansion outside the US would help overcome bottlenecks. At the same time, intensifying competition threatens to chip away at Nvidia’s market share. Custom accelerators like Google’s tensor processing units and Amazon Web Service’s Trainium offer major hyperscalers viable alternatives for specific workloads. While Goldman Sachs this month raised its shipment forecasts for Nvidia-powered server racks, it also lifted projections for competing AI servers due to growing demand for custom AI chips, signalling a broader market shift towards diversified hardware. Despite the headwinds, Huang has set an ambitious bar. At the company’s GTC event in California in March, he projected at least US$1 trillion in revenue for Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin platforms between 2025 and 2027, pitching an integrated ecosystem combining GPUs, central processing units, networking and specialised inference processors – all designed to slash the cost of AI output. Nvidia said in August that production shipments of its Vera Rubin platform were under way, projecting around 70 per cent revenue growth for its 2028 financial year – a target it noted remained bound by supply constraints.

title: China eases uncertainty over offshore trust taxes before grace period ends
description: New guidance exempts some offshore stock incentive trusts after an executive ‘successfully’ appeals tax treatment.
content: China’s tax authorities are accepting reasonable explanations when enforcing new rules on offshore trust gains, according to an executive who says their appeal was successful, offering some reassurance as a 90-day grace period expires on Thursday. The approach appears to be translating into greater clarity from regulators. Earlier this week, the State Taxation Administration published a question-and-answer series that suggested Beijing was implementing the rules in line with international practice. “We successfully defended ourselves,” said a person familiar with the matter at a Hong Kong-listed mainland Chinese company, who asked not to be identified because the issue was sensitive. About a month before the latest clarification was issued, the company was asked to pay tax related to an offshore trust for a non-Chinese executive. It appealed on the grounds that the vehicle was a stock incentive trust set up in 2021 before the company’s initial public offering (IPO), said the source. The offshore trust was estimated to hold around US$50 million worth of equity when it was established, based on the company’s pre-IPO valuation. Stock options are commonly granted to executives at overseas companies as part of their compensation, particularly in the tech sector. Many mainland Chinese clients regarded the 20 per cent levy on offshore trusts as “unreasonable”, according to a tax adviser who said they had seen demand for solutions rise after Beijing’s tax announcement. On Monday, the State Taxation Administration reminded taxpayers to review their offshore trust arrangements before the grace period expired. “To avoid late payment penalties and other related risks, they must file taxes and make payments in accordance with the law within the transition period,” it said. It clarified on the same day that company-established offshore stock incentive trusts were essentially compensation arrangements and would not be subject to the 20 per cent tax. Instead, personal income tax would apply when employees exercised stock options or received gains from dividend distributions and share transfers, it added. The tax agency also addressed five other frequently asked questions, including the treatment of offshore trust losses, interest payments, trust management fees, and transfers involving related parties. There are, however, still many unanswered questions. The clarification by the State Taxation Administration was only “a partial victory”, the source at the Hong Kong-listed company said. “Next, we need to see whether the local tax authorities would adopt the adjustment.” This year, China has tightened oversight of cross-border gains earned by mainland Chinese residents and beneficiaries through offshore trusts and investments amid mounting fiscal pressure. Local tax authorities in Beijing and Hangzhou in eastern China’s Zhejiang province were reported in August to have levied taxes on dividends and interest income from overseas insurance policies.

title: DeepSeek seeks ‘total victory’ over closed-source AI with new open-source tool
description: Open-source DeepInfer framework designed to make AI models cheaper and more efficient to deploy, Chinese start-up says.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence start-up DeepSeek has fully open-sourced an internally developed framework designed to run AI models efficiently, as a senior researcher at the company described the growing divide between open-source and closed-source AI as a battle between “light and darkness”. The company on Tuesday released DeepInfer, an inference framework tailored to support its DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash model on both Nvidia’s SM100 Blackwell graphics processing units (GPUs) and Huawei Technologies’ Ascend 950 chips. Inference refers to the serving and running of AI models, and frameworks such as DeepInfer help optimise that process. Released in September, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash introduced a new architecture that reduced the memory required to run the model while outperforming the company’s earlier V1 Pro model. An update released on Saturday made it one of the world’s most powerful and cost-efficient open-weight models, according to third-party benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis. As DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is an open-weight model – allowing third-party cloud providers to serve it on their own infrastructure – open-sourcing DeepInfer would “help the community lower compute costs, reduce energy use and make AI more affordable”, the company said. In a technical article published on Chinese question-and-answer platform Zhihu on Tuesday, DeepSeek suggested that a single computing cluster running its V4.1-Flash model on DeepInfer could generate revenue equivalent to US$38 per GPU per hour, based on off-peak pricing rates. It added that the inference framework improved cost-efficiency by retaining previously processed information for more than 72 hours, reducing repeated computation. The company did not disclose its operating costs or profit margins. Open source vs closed source … A decisive battle between two futures, two destinies for humanity Chen Deli, DeepSeek DeepSeek’s latest open-source release coincided with unusually combative comments from senior researcher Chen Deli. In a social media post on Tuesday, Chen described open-source and closed-source AI as representing two fundamentally different futures for humanity – in some of the strongest language yet from a Chinese industry figure amid intensifying China-US competition in AI. “Open source vs closed source … A decisive battle between two futures, two destinies for humanity,” Chen wrote. “However long they want to fight, we’ll fight. Until total victory.” Other DeepSeek staff have also weighed in on the company’s open-source push. Cui Tianyi, who leads DeepSeek’s Harness team, said in a social media post that the company hoped more businesses and organisations worldwide would “deploy DeepSeek models and profit from doing so”. Chen’s remarks and DeepSeek’s announcement come as Chinese AI companies continue to roll out more open-weight model upgrades, challenging the dominance of leading American rivals such as Anthropic and OpenAI, which have championed closed-source AI. In contrast to open-source AI, in which core technologies are released to the public and other commercial entities to be used and customised for their own use cases, closed-source AI remains proprietary technology owned and controlled exclusively by its developers. Leading US industry figures, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have repeatedly argued that open-source AI posed risks to humanity, while also accusing Chinese companies of “stealing” American AI technology. Despite such criticism, Chinese companies, including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Z.ai, have continued to release open-weight AI models. That momentum has continued even as Beijing moves to tighten oversight of the sector. Last week, China proposed draft export controls covering 23 AI-related technologies. However, a government spokesperson said Beijing would continue to encourage open-source AI and promote its adoption worldwide, particularly across the Global South.

title: LeBron James remains realistic after Philadelphia 76ers beat New York Knicks in NBA opener
description: The 41-year-old is the highest-profile addition and plays in a team also bolstered by the arrival of Jaylen Brown from the Boston Celtics.
content: LeBron James said the Philadelphia 76ers still had plenty of room for improvement after launching their NBA season with an impressive opening night victory over the New York Knicks on Tuesday. James, 41, launched his quest for a fifth NBA championship with 14 points and seven assists in a 106-100 defeat of the reigning champions at Madison Square Garden. But despite an encouraging first win in a Philadelphia uniform, James was keeping his feet firmly on the ground. “It’s going to take some time,” James said of the Sixers’ new-look line-up. “It’s just one game, but obviously we can learn from the good things that we did.” James, though, was happy the Sixers showed signs of development during Tuesday’s opener. “We’re still new to each other,” he said. “We will have some bumps in the road at times. But I mean, I think tonight when we had those bumps in the road, we were able to use what happened previously and then make the adjustment.” James was the highest-profile addition to the Sixers roster in the close season, and joined a Philadelphia team also bolstered by the arrival of Jaylen Brown from the Boston Celtics. James said Brown, the NBA Finals MVP in 2024 during the Celtics’ championship season, would help foster a winning culture in Philly. “He’s just another guy that can hold guys accountable because they understand, they see a guy that has gotten to the finish line,” James said of Brown. “It’s definitely very helpful. These guys that have been here are trying to be able to get to that point, obviously this is a marathon, and we’re not going to do it in day one. “But the experience that we have, the experience that we bring to this ball club, hopefully we can translate it to wins and more.” James intends to lead by example in the Sixers locker room. “I’m there before everybody gets to the gym, and I’m one of the last ones to leave,” James said. “I don’t just be like telling guys to do it. “I hold myself accountable, and if I’m not doing something, I want the guys to hold me accountable. So I think that goes a long way.”

title: Surveyors say presales at Pak Shing Kok residential project could begin in 2028
description: Consortium member New World Development announces outcome of bond exchange programme, with US$189.3 million of new, longer-term bonds issued.
content: New World Development and China Merchants Land broke ground recently on a joint residential project in Pak Shing Kok, Tseung Kwan O, with presales expected to begin as early as 2028, when surveyors say pricing pressure may have eased. James KT Cheung, executive director of the valuation department at Centaline Surveyors, said property prices remain lower than they were in 2022, when the consortium won the project. “If property prices can recover to 2022 levels by the time the Pak Shing Kok project is launched for sale, the pressure on developers regarding new project pricing will be relatively eased,” he said, adding that a land premium of about HK$3,800 per square foot of gross floor area was not “particularly expensive” when viewed in the context of recent land acquisitions. Alex Leung, senior director at CHFT Advisory and Appraisal, estimated the total cost of the project at HK$4,734 per square foot after factoring in the land premium and the HK$50 million entrance fee. Cheung and Leung both said they expected the project would sell for HK$18,000 per square foot of saleable area. Surveyors said applications for the presale of residential projects could be submitted up to 30 months before the expected completion date, which meant the Pak Shing Kok project could potentially be launched for presale as early as the second half of 2028. The project’s tender terms include a minimum size restriction that requires each flat to have a usable floor area of at least 280 square feet. “For the smallest flat, with a saleable area of 280 square feet, assuming a low floor with a less desirable view and orientation, the lowest price is expected to be around HK$4.6 million (about HK$16,400 per square foot),” Leung said. New World Development said at the groundbreaking ceremony that it was committed to unlocking the value of its land bank and “turning premium land resources into highly competitive development projects”. It said it would continue to work closely with strategic partners to enhance overall development efficiency and create long-term returns for stakeholders. Meanwhile, the indebted developer also announced the official closing and final outcome of its bond exchange programme, which expired on Tuesday. Investors handed in US$199.28 million worth of older, short-term bonds that will be cancelled and exchanged for new, longer-term bonds. The total amount of new bonds being issued – US$189.3 million – is below the company’s maximum limit of US$600 million. Zhu Wen-kai, chairman of China Merchants Shekou and China Merchants Land, said the Pak Shing Kok project, next to Hang Hau MTR station, was expected to provide about 600 small and medium-sized homes and would include a clubhouse, parking and other facilities. MTR Corporation awarded the Pak Shing Kok project in April 2022 to a consortium formed by New World Development and China Merchants Land. Market sources said the land premium for the project was HK$1.1 billion. Based on a total gross floor area of about 27,000 square metres (about 290,700 square feet), that equates to a land premium of about HK$3,789 per square foot – a record high for Tseung Kwan O district at the time. It exceeded the previous record of about HK$3,600 per square foot – set in September 2020 for Phase 13 of Lohas Park – by about 5.3 per cent. The consortium was also required to pay an upfront fixed bid of at least HK$50 million and agree to a profit-sharing arrangement based on future property sales. MTR Corp has said the Pak Shing Kok project is expected to be completed in 2031. Additional reporting by Cheryl Arcibal

title: Letters | Are we chasing the right kind of happiness in Hong Kong?
description: Readers discuss ideas such as self-compassion and time wealth, redevelopment of Victoria Park tennis courts, and eye care costs.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. I refer to “Hong Kong’s Generation Y unhappiest amid housing and economic pressures, poll finds” (October 6). As a 40-ish millennial, I found myself nodding in agreement that my happiness level is medium at best, given the mounting economic pressure and self-perceived midlife crisis. Growing up, I was heavily influenced by my (Gen X) parents’ views on education, employment, housing and wealth accumulation, which they said would constitute the basis of happiness. Unquestioningly, I followed this so-called formula for success, laboriously studying and working, being careful in terms of life decisions, trying to avert crises and jump at opportunities that would give me a relative advantage in the pursuit of success and happiness. In retrospect, the way I spent my formative years might have paid some dividends, ensuring I was able to land a relatively stable job, and with it, a chance to get on the housing ladder and a shot at financial freedom. Yet, would I consider myself happy? To be brutally honest, I’ve had makes and misses. I have had my fleeting ups but also my fair share of downs.
