A health crisis knocked on my door and although I recovered, minor maladies seem to be constant reminders of the stress my body is subjected to. In the traditional sense, success at work could mean a pay rise or a promotion. If these are the yardsticks of success, however, it appears elusive for me. Luckily, my understanding of happiness has been fundamentally altered by Dr Laurie Santos, a professor of psychology at Yale University who hosts the podcast The Happiness Lab. Her tips – acknowledge and use negative emotions wisely, embrace self-compassion, prioritise time wealth over monetary wealth – are life-changing words of wisdom. All too often, we are too caught up in the belief that fame and fortune can bring us eternal gratification, yet the reality is that material possessions and titles are only badges of honour that give temporary pleasure, similar to rushes of dopamine. As portrayed in the animated film Inside Out, our emotions are complex and multifaceted. The emotional roller coaster we go on daily is a fact we need to embrace and accept, and each emotion has a role to play in terms of keeping us grounded. Balanced doses of anxiety, anger, sadness, joy, ennui, fear and disgust are perhaps the best medicine. Understanding how emotions work may help us achieve happier lives. Jason Tang, Tin Shui Wai Upgraded Victoria Park must preserve our tennis memories I refer to “Hong Kong hopes to begin Victoria Park Tennis Centre redevelopment by 2030” (September 19). I am eagerly anticipating the Hong Kong Tennis Open. Bringing together world-class players, the event will undoubtedly draw numerous fans to Hong Kong, making it a stellar showcase for our mega-events economy and a powerful boost to our image as a vibrant city. Victoria Park is not only a landmark in Hong Kong tennis but also the starting point of many home-grown tennis careers. As the authorities study how to upgrade the venue to host higher-tier competitions, modernisation should not erase its community roots. While better infrastructure is welcome, we must protect its unique character. The new design could incorporate classic elements of the existing structure and include a corner showing its history. Equally important, courts should remain open for public bookings during normal times. By balancing elite sport with local community memories, Victoria Park can become a modern arena that still stays true to the people. Beck Wu, Tseung Kwan O Eye-popping eye care costs I refer to the letter, “Don’t overlook eye health as Hong Kong ages” (October 8). The assertion that eye health is a smart investment is insightful, especially given the substantial medical fees it can entail. A friend of mine was advised to undergo cataract surgery, but the cost – around HK$30,000 per eye – was astronomical. Before that, she underwent a less expensive treatment involving thermal pulsation to melt the hardened oils blocking her eyelid glands. The procedure took about 15 minutes and cost more than HK$10,000. The amounts alone are enough to make my eyes pop. Ho Kam-tong, Yuen Long

title: Shark kills woman swimming off South Africa’s Eastern Cape
description: Two beaches closed after 65-year-old retired radiographer is fatally injured during a morning swim at Orient Beach.
content: A 65-year-old woman was killed on Tuesday in a shark attack off South Africa’s southeastern coast, police and municipal authorities said, prompting the closure of two beaches. Officers were called to Orient Beach in KuGompo city, formerly East London, at about 7am, where they found the woman’s body, Eastern Cape police spokesperson Col. Siphokazi Mawisa told Associated Press. An inquest has been opened into the death. “The Buffalo City Metropolitan Municipality is deeply saddened to confirm that a fatal shark attack occurred at the Orient Beach this morning, resulting in the tragic loss of a swimmer,” municipal spokesman Luzuko Buku said in a statement. Fellow swimmer Mike Loewe told state broadcaster SABC that members of an open-water swimming group responded to the woman’s distress signal and brought her ashore. A medic in the group tried to save her, but she was declared dead at the scene, he said. “She liked to swim solo,” Loewe said. “She was courageous.” He described the victim as a recently retired nuclear radiographer and a musician, and said her death had devastated the swimming community. The municipality has closed Orient Beach and nearby Eastern Beach until further notice. They will reopen only after safety assessments and expert advice. It also urged beachgoers to swim only in designated areas while lifeguards are on duty, from 8.30am to 5pm. South Africa is known for its great white sharks and shark tourism, but shark attacks are rare. According to municipal records, the city’s last fatal shark attack was in 1997, and its most recent reported attack occurred in 2023. The Florida Museum of Natural History’s International Shark Attack File recorded 29 unprovoked bites in the country between 2012 and 2021, an average of about three a year. Six were fatal.

title: Russian satellite’s close approach to European spacecraft highlights orbital risks
description: Cosmos-2612 deliberately adjusted its orbit to shadow a Finnish-operated satellite that provides imagery to Ukraine.
content: A Russian satellite moved within just 100 metres of a European commercial spacecraft that supports Ukraine’s military at the weekend, orbital tracking data showed, raising concerns about Moscow’s activities in space. Russia launched the Cosmos-2612 military satellite into low Earth orbit in April. It began changing course late September and eventually moved into the same orbit as ICEYE-X36, a satellite operated by Finland’s ICEYE under contract with the United States. The two spacecraft came within 100 metres of each other on October 18, according to orbital tracking data analysed by Agence France-Presse. “There is no reason it would have needed to manoeuvre the way it did... and into such close proximity to the ICEYE satellite for a benign reason,” Clayton Swope, a space security specialist at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said. The incident has drawn attention from space experts, who say such close approaches can be used to inspect, monitor or interfere with other satellites. While Russian satellites have passed near foreign spacecraft before, experts said several factors of this case stood out. “It was a combination of factors that made this event so concerning”, Swope said. The Russian satellite not only approached the Finnish spacecraft but deliberately adjusted its orbit to closely match it, he explained. ICEYE’s satellite constellation also provides imagery and space-tracking data that supports Ukraine in its war with Russia. An ICEYE spokesperson said the company was aware of the incident and “tracking it closely”. The US Space Force accused Russia of unusually “fuel-intensive” manoeuvres in May to move four military satellites close to a Western commercial satellite used by Ukraine. ICEYE’s satellites use radar technology that can capture images of the Earth’s surface at night and through cloud cover, making them particularly valuable for military intelligence. The satellite approached by Cosmos-2612 uses the same tech as another ICEYE spacecraft involved in the May incident. The US Space Force says Russia has launched several satellites in recent years to test technologies that could be used to intercept or disrupt other spacecraft. Swope stressed, however, it was impossible to confirm whether Cosmos-2612 carried a weapon. In a published note, he said the incident should be viewed in the broader context of Russia’s efforts to challenge Western space capabilities. Since the start of its Ukraine invasion, Moscow has argued that Western commercial satellites supporting Kyiv are indirectly taking part in the conflict. A Russian foreign ministry official in 2022 warned at the UN that such “quasi-civilian infrastructure” could become a legitimate target for retaliation. By Monday morning, Cosmos-2612 was moving away from ICEYE-X36 and the two satellites were again separated by several kilometres. Analysts at the US-based ISR Institute last week predicted that another close approach involving Russian satellites and an ICEYE spacecraft could take place in the coming weeks.

title: Battery giant CATL posts surprise profit slowdown, mainland China shares tumble over 10%
description: CATL’s profits slowed sharply in the third quarter, as analysts warn the firm is vulnerable to headwinds in China’s electric car industry.
content: Chinese battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) extended its stock price rout after recording a surprise slowdown in third-quarter net profits, as analysts warned the company could be hit by slowing demand from China’s electric car industry next year. The world’s largest electric vehicle (EV) battery maker saw its shares continue to tumble by over 10 per cent in Shenzhen and 8.6 per cent in Hong Kong in the morning session on Wednesday. The Fujian province-based firm posted a net profit of 21.25 billion yuan (US$3.18 billion) for the July-September period, up 14.54 per cent from a year earlier, according to an exchange filing on Tuesday. The increase marked a sharp slowdown from the 36 per cent jump recorded in the second quarter of the year and a peak of 57 per cent in the final quarter of 2025. The company’s third-quarter revenue grew 58.58 per cent year on year, reaching 165.22 billion yuan. Both the earnings and revenue figures missed analysts’ consensus forecasts of 26.03 billion yuan and 175.05 billion yuan, respectively. CATL’s shares slumped 6.58 per cent to HK$411.80 in Hong Kong and 2.97 per cent to 259.08 yuan in Shenzhen on Tuesday, before the earnings results were announced. The company’s stock price has plunged since Chinese EV makers Xiaomi and Li Auto announced they were partnering with tier-two battery manufacturers in September, with CATL’s shares down over 20 per cent in Hong Kong and 31 per cent in Shenzhen since the start of the year. On Tuesday, JPMorgan lowered its rating of CATL’s Hong Kong-traded shares to neutral, as the bank is increasingly worried about a faster-than-expected deterioration of profitability in the Chinese EV industry, which could affect demand for CATL’s batteries. The bottom lines of Chinese EV makers were already under pressure due to China’s resumed battery consumption tax, export tax rebate pullback and heavier external trade barriers, according to the investment bank, though it added that CATL would emerge as a winner in the battery industry over the long term. Market concerns over weaker-than-expected demand for energy storage systems (ESS) have also fuelled the sell-off over the past few weeks. Citigroup said it expected global battery demand growth to slow to 26 per cent next year, citing smaller room for EV penetration in China and potential ESS growth on higher base effects, according to a note published earlier this month. CATL’s inventory surged 53 per cent to 144.77 billion yuan for the first nine months of the year, while projects under construction grew by 44.7 per cent to 43 billion yuan over the same period. The battery maker attributed the rises to its business expansion and capacity growth, respectively. CATL continued its share buy-back spree on Monday by repurchasing nearly 50 million yuan of Shenzhen-listed shares. In July, the firm announced its largest-ever buy-back scheme worth up to 40 billion yuan on the mainland stock markets. For the first three quarters of the year, CATL’s revenue grew 56 per cent year on year to 442 billion yuan and its net profit expanded 31.6 per cent to 64.5 billion yuan.

title: China university offers course pushing students to call strangers to build confidence, social skills
description: The unique course defies the traditional Chinese ethos of keeping a low profile and living by the mantra, ‘do more, speak less’.
content: An unconventional course at prestigious Nanjing University encourages students to call strangers to hone their social skills, challenging the traditional value of “do more, speak less”. At the top-tier institution in Jiangsu province, eastern China, former television producer and director Xu Kai launched a course called “Oral Expression” in 2015. Over the years, it has become one of the students’ favourite public courses. The course includes a legendary assignment: students must call a stranger at random and interview them over the phone. Several students have posted on social media about how difficult they found the task. Some asked their parents or friends to pose as strangers. Others tried to find strangers by posting on social media. A student who goes by the name Connie also posted online looking for strangers, but later changed her mind and began calling random numbers in Nanjing. Some people thought she was a scammer. After several attempts, she reached another student in Nanjing, who agreed to be interviewed. Another student, Hong Yiming, also dialled random numbers in Nanjing. Only five of the more than 30 calls he made were answered. Three people hung up immediately, one thought he was a scammer, and the last agreed to be interviewed. His interviewee, who works in the IT industry, shared advice on planning a career path, talked about how they spent their leisure time in Nanjing, and told him about their two cats. Connie admitted that the assignment had become increasingly difficult because people are now reluctant to answer calls from strangers, fearing harassment or scams. Some students dropped the course because of the assignment, while many who completed it asked Xu never to cancel it. Xu said he created the assignment to help students learn empathy. “It is never easy to express yourself, and students should learn to appreciate other people’s help,” he said. He said he designed the course to help students build confidence, improve their communication skills and become more mature. Xu reflected that the traditional value of “do more, speak less” has encouraged people to be low-profile and down-to-earth. While this benefits their research, he said, it can hinder their personal development and social skills. Furthermore, many young people in China describe themselves as introverts or say they have “social phobia”. But Xu said they simply lack opportunities to learn how to communicate. He also hopes the course will help new students adapt to their surroundings. Connie said she enjoyed expressing herself as a primary school student, but that was seen as “showing off” when she entered secondary school. As the pressure of the gaokao, or national college entrance examination, mounted, her classmates became increasingly withdrawn. Xu believes his class is making up for what students missed in their elementary education. Alongside teaching students how to speak, he also designs activities to help them understand the importance of body language in communication. The course has been named one of Nanjing University students’ favourite courses for many years. Xu has also won awards at the university, including “My Favourite Teacher” and “Teacher of Charisma”. “This course is more important than some major courses at a university,” one online observer commented. “What young people today lack may not be knowledge, but basic social skills like these,” said another.

title: Shipping giant Cosco launches new routes to ride out Iran war, climate risks
description: The Chinese shipping giant is focusing on resilience as it responds to rise in geopolitical conflicts and extreme weather.
content: China Cosco Shipping Holdings, the country’s largest ocean carrier, has prioritised resilience as it rolls out an emergency response system to cope with rising geopolitical conflicts, infrastructure bottlenecks and climate-related disruptions. The company is launching fresh capacity and new trade routes as part of the plan, as it looks to ensure its supply chains can withstand a mix of potential shocks, according to chairman Wan Min. “We believe that true resilience is not merely restricted to a single route,” he said at the North Bund Summit, a shipping industry ­conference, in Shanghai on Tuesday. “A fully resilient shipping system should comprise adequate backup to ensure a safe and stable operation through the entire supply chain.” Cosco had also added road transport into its routes as a way of dodging the impact of conflicts in the Middle East, the chairman added. The global container shipping industry has been racing to implement structural re-routing strategies since the US-Israel war on Iran erupted in late February. The tensions have not only disrupted shipping traffic in the Middle East, but have also raised energy costs for container lines, forcing firms to increase freight rates in response. Wan said massive investment in infrastructure and transport equipment would be needed to adapt to military conflicts and unexpected climate-related disruptions, with 80 per cent of global trade currently being conducted via ocean freight. Worries are mounting that a massive construction of new vessels will immensely add new capacity that may become redundant in future Zhang Jieshu, Shanghai International Shipping Institute Container ocean freight rates have jumped 130 per cent since February amid the prolonged Middle East conflicts, according to a report released by brokerage firm Jefferies earlier this month. Changes to shipping routes could increase freight costs and affect the movement of goods across major global trade corridors, it added. Hong Kong-listed Cosco reported a net profit of 13.4 billion yuan (US$2 billion) for the first half of 2026, down 23.6 per cent from the same period last year. Its revenue dropped 2.6 per cent to 111.9 billion yuan. The company invests in and operates 65 port terminals and runs more than 350 container lines around the world. Global container lines have also been ordering more vessels to raise their capacity as they implement their re-routing strategies. “Freight rates look set to grow since an end to the geopolitical conflict is not in sight yet,” said Zhang Jieshu, secretary general of the Shanghai International Shipping Institute, a government-backed research organisation. “But worries are mounting that a massive construction of new vessels will immensely add new capacity that may become redundant in future.” The two-day North Bund conference, starting on Tuesday, attracted hundreds of government officials including Minister of Transport Liu Wei and executives with major shipping and aviation companies to discuss promoting the resilient development of the global logistics industry. Shanghai has been the world’s biggest container port since 2010, when it overtook Singapore. Ports in Shanghai handled 55.1 million 20-foot-equivalent units (TEUs) of containers in 2025, 6.9 per cent more than a year earlier.

title: Style Edit: Cartier’s Into the Wild collection blends craftsmanship with rich fauna heritage
description: The line’s namesake exhibition comes to Hong Kong’s Villa Haw Par, where the maison’s panther motif meets the location’s historic tiger legacy.
content: At Cartier, the animal kingdom has long been a source of creative inspiration. What began with birds and insects in the early 20th century gradually expanded to include reptiles, big cats, zebras and elephants, establishing a distinctive menagerie in which nature is reimagined through precious materials and exceptional craftsmanship. Now, with Into the Wild, the maison revisits this rich heritage, bringing five striking creatures into focus: the tiger, parrot, carp, crocodile and rhinoceros. Presiding over this imaginative universe is the Panthère, whose three-dimensional sculptural form first emerged in 1948. More than an emblem, she embodies the spirit of Cartier’s animal creations: powerful, sensual and poised between naturalism and abstraction. Her influence resonates throughout the collection, where sculptural jewellery captures the distinctive anatomy and personality of each creature without sacrificing the maison’s unmistakable graphic sensibility. As Pierre Rainero, Cartier’s director of image, style and heritage, explains: “The Cartier fauna is distinguished by its character. First of all, in the choice of species – big cats, reptiles, savannah animals – and also in the creative treatment, between naturalism and extreme stylisation. “Through the interplay of design, materials and execution, Cartier questions the very perception of the animal and opens up extraordinary possibilities for exploring forms. Each creature, each creation reveals its own symbolic force, reflects an attitude, a personality trait or a state of mind. It becomes an opportunity to deliver a message about yourself.” The artistry lies in the details. Rings shaped around expressive animal heads bring together platinum, gold and an adventurous palette of precious and ornamental stones. Coral and tsavorite garnets lend the parrot its vivid plumage; spessartite garnets and smoky quartz evoke the rhinoceros’s warm, earthy tones; while sapphires, aquamarine and dumortierite quartz conjure the tiger’s striped coat. On the crocodile, diamonds, emeralds and onyx create a striking interplay of light and shadow. The crocodile bracelet and necklace exemplify this union of artistry and engineering. The sculpted head combines geometric diamond scales with black onyx spikes, while a concealed clasp sits within the creature’s mouth. Along the articulated body, inverted-set diamonds alternate with onyx, bordered by chrysoprase and rubellites. The result is a fluid, tactile composition that preserves the animal’s formidable character while moving effortlessly against the skin. Such creations demand a remarkable collaboration of specialist métiers. Jewellers sculpt and articulate the forms, lapidaries carve stones into precisely contoured details, and gem-setters employ techniques – including fur setting – to mimic the effect of an animal’s coat. They also use calibrated rail settings to suggest feathers, scales and stripes. Surfaces are polished or brushed by hand, lending the pieces a tactile, almost living presence. From October 29 to November 8, Cartier will present the “Into the Wild” exhibition at Villa Haw Par, a historic Hong Kong landmark known for its blend of Chinese and Western design. Visitors can discover the history behind the maison’s animal creations, including the work of creative visionary Jeanne Toussaint, and watch Cartier artisans demonstrate techniques such as gem-setting and engraving. Open to the public, the exhibition celebrates Cartier’s enduring relationship with nature, its artistic imagination and the craftsmanship passed down through generations.

title: BBC slashes 100 jobs, pulls channels amid ‘immediate cost pressures’
description: Cash-strapped UK public broadcaster will pull BBC Three and BBC Scotland from traditional airwaves as licence fee revenue falls.
content: The BBC announced more than 100 job cuts and the closure of two channels Tuesday as the cash-strapped UK broadcaster aims to save £500 million (US$668 million) over the next two years. BBC News announced the “net closure of just over 100 roles”, according to an internal note by director Rachel Jupp, part of some 2,000 job cuts the broader organisation is eyeing to achieve its planned savings. The job cuts represent £5.5 million in savings, said Jupp. She was appointed BBC News’ director this month, after her predecessor stepped down amid a row over a misleading edit of US President Donald Trump in a BBC documentary last year. The BBC also said it would end the broadcast of BBC Scotland and BBC Three – a youth-oriented channel – which will be available on its online iPlayer streaming platform instead. It also announced the closure of Radio 4 Extra, with its mainly archive-based programmes made available on BBC Sounds, an audio streaming platform. “We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. We all know that means tough choices,” BBC Director General Matt Brittin said in a note to staff. “Much of the great content they currently carry will still be found where audiences already enjoy it on iPlayer and Sounds,” the former Google executive, who took the helm of the BBC earlier this year, added. Scottish culture minister Mairi McAllan said moving BBC Scotland online was “wholly unacceptable”. The BBC in June announced plans to axe another 550 roles in its news, nations and content teams by the end of this financial year to deliver £160 million in savings. It comes amid severe cost pressures after income from a licence fee used to fund the corporation in large part fell by around a quarter in real terms since 2017. The broadcaster – which claims 94 per cent of UK adults use its services monthly – has also been plagued by a series of controversies and scandals in recent years that have rocked public confidence in it. “The way people consume news is changing rapidly, and too many audiences, particularly younger audiences, are not finding us,” Jupp said in her message. Jupp added the BBC’s news service could be required to save more than anticipated: “Given the BBC’s financial pressures, the savings requirement for News could increase”. The BBC revealed earlier this year it planned to save £500 million from its roughly £5 billion annual budget over the next three years by cutting up to 2,000 jobs, in its biggest round of redundancies since 2011.

title: Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis
description: Actor says she is ‘back at square one’ despite still experiencing severe mobility issues and symptoms that mimic the autoimmune condition.
content: Christina Applegate, who has candidly shared raw details about her journey with multiple sclerosis for years, revealed on Monday her doctor says she does not have the autoimmune disease and was misdiagnosed. “I’m back at square one where I don’t know what’s going on with me,” the actor said on the latest edition of her podcast “MeSsy”, along with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler, who has been public about her own battle with MS. Applegate first publicly announced in 2021 that she had been diagnosed with the disorder that causes the immune system to attack the cells in the central nervous system. On Monday’s podcast, Applegate revealed that despite the misdiagnosis, she still has “every symptom of someone with MS,” adding: “I still have to use wheelchairs when I go to the doctor’s office. I can’t walk from the car to the room”. There is no single test for MS, and a diagnosis usually involves ruling out other causes. It can take years and seeing multiple doctors before one puts the clues together. Dr Benjamin Greenberg, a neurologist who specialises in multiple sclerosis and autoimmune neurological disorders at the UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, said the most reputable studies put the MS misdiagnosis rate at 10 per cent. “We rely on the clinical symptoms, the history, the MRI, often spinal fluid, and then a series of tests to rule out potential mimics. And unfortunately, those tests are not universally codified,” he said. Greenberg said Applegate’s experience has lessons for both medical providers and patients. For doctors, it was a reminder to ensure a single diagnosis does not lead to a system-wide bias towards that conclusion. “If I put ‘multiple sclerosis’ as a diagnosis on an MRI, a radiologist is far less likely to say, ‘Well, this isn’t multiple sclerosis. You really should consider something else’. It can permeate the system,” he said. “For patients and families, my general recommendation is whenever receiving a significant serious or chronic diagnosis, if feasible, there is never a harm in getting second opinions.” Applegate said the news had put her in an odd place since she and Sigler have become prominent advocates for people with MS. “It’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down,” she said. “It’s very unnerving, and it’s really confusing for me.” Most autoimmune diseases, especially in adults, are not caused by a specific gene defect. Instead, a variety of genes that affect immune functions can make people susceptible. Scientists say it then takes an “environmental” trigger, such as an infection, smoking or pollutants, to set the disease in motion. On the podcast and earlier this year while promoting her memoir, You with the Sad Eyes, the Emmy-winning Applegate has been candid about unpredictable symptoms that have forced her to use diapers and scoot down stairs on her butt. “My life has in some ways shrunk to the size of my California king,” she writes in her book.

title: Can China unlock the Greater Bay Area’s tech potential through closer financial links?
description: New guidelines aim to ease cross-border financial barriers and strengthen links between investors, tech firms and research institutions across region.
content: China plans to expand venture capital and long-term funding for technology companies in the Greater Bay Area while strengthening financial links between Hong Kong and the mainland, as part of efforts to turn the region into a leading innovation hub alongside Beijing and Shanghai. In guidelines published on Monday, the People’s Bank of China and 10 other government departments set out plans for “an open technology finance system” across the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area. The proposals included closer coordination of financial rules and fewer barriers to the cross-border movement of capital and other resources, while the broader aim is to improve financial services for technological innovation in three major economic regions: the Greater Bay Area and the areas surrounding Beijing and Shanghai. Zhang Danhong, an adviser at the Centre of Geopolitics for the Global South, said the guidelines reflected the unique strengths of each region. For the Greater Bay Area, she added, openness and cross-border integration were at the heart of its strategy. The region, which includes Shenzhen, Hong Kong and Macau, was well positioned to attract global “patient capital” – funding that takes a longer-term view and tolerates higher investment risks – by drawing on its talent pool and the potential for deeper cross-border cooperation, Zhang said. The guidelines envisaged a greater role for the national venture capital fund in supporting emerging and future industries. They also called for better use of existing state-backed investment funds for tech companies and the development of funds focused on mergers and acquisitions. Liu Feng, chief economist at the International Institute of Green Finance at the Central University of Finance and Economics, said the measures aimed to address a deep-rooted weakness in China’s financial system: household savings remain high, yet technology companies in need of long-term capital can still struggle to secure financing. The Greater Bay Area, Liu said, was an ideal testing ground for tackling the problem because of its unusually complex institutional landscape spanning three currencies, customs regimes and legal systems. A system that better aligned financial rules, eased the movement of capital and other resources and improved coordination across the innovation ecosystem could eventually serve as a model for the regions around Beijing and Shanghai, he said. To strengthen the Greater Bay Area’s role as a national centre for scientific research, the guidelines also backed closer cooperation between universities, research institutes and businesses in strategic locations such as Guangming Science City in Shenzhen, Songshan Lake Science City in Dongguan and Nansha Science City in Guangzhou. Liu said the three areas had complementary strengths but also faced different weaknesses in their innovation ecosystems. Shenzhen led in research and development spending, much of it driven by companies, but had comparatively less basic research and fewer original technological breakthroughs, he said. Hong Kong had strong university research but faced challenges in commercialising it, while Guangzhou had a relatively large concentration of research institutes that were not always closely connected to industry, he added. Closer financial cooperation could help bridge these gaps by linking research, capital and commercial applications, Liu said. The guidelines also aim to deepen financial integration between Hong Kong and Shenzhen by aligning rules and improving the cross-border exchange of information. Over the past two decades, initiatives such as Stock Connect, Bond Connect and the Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect scheme have made it easier for capital to move between the mainland and Hong Kong. But the ability to transfer money across the border had not removed all the practical obstacles facing investors, Liu said. A Hong Kong venture capital fund investing in a Shenzhen technology company, for example, may struggle to obtain the information needed to assess the business, verify credit information, estimate the value of intellectual property and navigate the legal framework governing contracts. To address these barriers, the guidelines called on institutions in Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macau to improve the sharing of credit information across borders. They also proposed exploring arrangements to ease cross-border data flows and the commercial use of intellectual property across jurisdictions. The guidelines also called for implementing the mainland’s Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement with Hong Kong and Macau, while supporting more Hong Kong-listed companies in the Greater Bay Area to list on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange.

title: Hong Kong Open: Louis Oosthuizen admits it’s ‘time to move on’ from LIV Golf
description: Ex-Open champion and LIV team captain set to return from a two-month injury lay-off to play at ‘a course I love’ this week.
content: Louis Oosthuizen has joined the LIV Golf exodus, saying it was “time to move on” after four years on the breakaway tour. Twice a LIV tournament runner-up, and captain of the Southern Guards GC team, Oosthuizen is poised to return from a two-month injury lay-off in this week’s Link Hong Kong Open from Thursday. The bottom fell out of LIV this year when its Saudi Arabian backers turned off the money taps. Players have until Sunday to declare whether they would commit to a new iteration, after the rebel circuit secured a possible US$300 million from investment firm BC Partners Credit with a view to staging a 2027 season. Oosthuizen said the prospective stripped-back schedule would demand “a lot of international travel for single events”, and he has duly followed fellow major champions Jon Rahm, Brooks Koepka and Patrick Reed in quitting LIV. Abraham Ancer, the 2024 LIV Hong Kong winner, has also walked away. “I need to arrange my own schedule and look after my body,” Oosthuizen told the South China Morning Post. “I want to play near one spot for three weeks at a time, not have all the big travelling for one tournament. “I loved LIV and the team aspect, but it’s time to move on.” The 2010 Open champion, Oosthuizen missed this year’s edition in July because of a back problem. Sidelined again since he finished tied-43rd at LIV Indianapolis two months ago, the South African said the “time off not really doing much” had stoked his appetite to “play as much as I can”. “You see the guys playing on TV and you miss it,” he said. “I feel I can still play and compete.” Only eight players have had more major runner-up finishes than Oosthuizen’s six, but he believes he can still add to the championship he won at St Andrews 16 years ago. The Open is returning to the Scottish links next year. “I’ve had some success at majors, but you work and play to have a sniff of that again,” Oosthuizen, who turned 44 on Monday, said. “I’m at a different stage of my golfing life [from when he won his major] but it’s pretty sweet when you still get called the Open champion. “I hope to get my body and my game in a place next year [to compete for majors] … the Open is at a course I love and where I’ve won. The goal is to get my game as sharp as possible, to have myself ready, then see how it goes.” Tied third in the 2025 Hong Kong Open, 17 years after his debut appearance in the city, Oosthuizen was equally gushing about the event’s storied Fanling venue. “It’s a course I love, and not one you really overpower,” he said. “I’d have been a bit more nervous going back [after injury] to a course where I had to really hit big drives. I remembered last year how much I liked it here, and I’ll play every year if I can.” Feeling “relaxed and calm” ahead of his return to tournament play, Oosthuizen had “a few drinks up until midnight when it was my birthday” after arriving in Hong Kong late on Sunday. On Monday, he went with his wife and friends to the Michelin-starred Beefbar restaurant in Central. “There were nine of us and we had some good fun,” he said. Oosthuizen was talking on the sidelines of a press event staged on The Peak, where Taichi Kho and Travis Smyth were also guests. A winner on the Asian Tour for the second time when he claimed the International Series Morocco title in June, Hongkonger Kho said he had started the year “not in the best of places”, after 12 months spent trying to locate his form. “I felt like I was quite lost, and I’m really proud of how I was able to rediscover my own game and what makes me good,” Kho, 25, said. “Learning about that side of myself has made the year more special, because I’ve been able to get through some adversity, which is like an entry fee to professional golf.” In addition to a handsome pay cheque, the winner of the Hong Kong Open will again gain entry into next year’s Open Championship and US Masters. Smyth secured a DP World Tour card for 2027 after topping the Challenger PGA Tour of Australasia Order of Merit this year, while the Australian had tournament successes in the ISPS Handa-Japan Australasia Championship and International Series Japan, in March and April, respectively. “I’ve always said to people who go to watch the Masters that I’ll never go until I play,” Smyth said. “I really want to go, so I guess I’ll have to win this week.” Fresh from a tied-ninth finish at last week’s SJM Macau Open, where he managed four sub-70 rounds, the 31-year-old said “getting my self-belief where it needed to be” had been responsible for what he has called a “life-changing year”. “It’s one thing for everyone back home and my team to say ‘You’re a great player’, but until you believe that, and put yourself in positions to win tournaments, it tests a lot of you,” Smyth said. “I started working with a sports psychologist about a year ago, and that’s been a huge help. “Technically, I haven’t changed much; it’s more my overall attitude. Constantly being aware of that little voice inside your head, and trying to get it to where you need it to be to compete against world-class players.”

title: Why Anthropic has a major China problem ahead of its blockbuster IPO
description: Surging demand for low-cost Chinese AI models is sparking investor jitters, with some fearing ‘massive capital destruction’ in Silicon Valley.
content: The growing popularity of Chinese artificial intelligence models has emerged as a key risk factor for Anthropic ahead of its blockbuster initial public offering, according to US research firm Hedgeye Risk Management. “It’s all about Chinese competition when analysing Anthropic,” said Felix Wang, managing director and global tech sector head at Hedgeye. “Many of my clients are asking the same question.” The assessment comes as Anthropic faces renewed investor jitters over whether its massive AI investments will deliver commensurate returns, with the company’s latest reported financial figures sparking sell-offs of leading AI chipmakers, including Nvidia and Intel, in recent days. Anthropic told investors at a private briefing last week that third-quarter revenue rose nearly 50 per cent from the previous quarter to US$16.8 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter. Despite the quarter-on-quarter jump, the figure marked a slowdown from the company’s explosive growth in the first half of the year, when revenue more than doubled in the second quarter as companies raced to purchase subscriptions for its powerful Claude Code coding agent tool. Low-cost Chinese alternatives The deceleration has coincided with a sharp jump in the global popularity of Chinese open-weight models. According to AI research group Exponential View, open-weight models now serve around half of all AI “tokens” – the core unit of AI usage – globally. While Chinese AI start-ups still significantly lag their US counterparts in total revenue, they have seen explosive growth in the last year. Beijing-based Z.ai, for instance, has seen its annual revenue run rate jump more than sixfold since March on the back of soaring demand for its GLM models. Crucially, the Chinese industry has managed to grow sales while steadily raising prices. Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, has increased prices for its model services at least three times this year, while Hangzhou-based start-up DeepSeek more than doubled prices for its flagship V4 model in August. Even so, Chinese models remain among the cheapest on the market while trailing leading US models by only a few months in terms of capabilities, according to third-party benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis. Total demand for your tokens may be going up, but if the price is flat or falling, then you’re not making more money Felix Wang, Hedgeye Risk Management This dynamic meant Chinese open models were not only taking market share from Anthropic but were also setting the floor for AI pricing, Wang said, pointing to Chinese start-ups Moonshot AI and DeepSeek as popular, cost-effective alternatives to Anthropic’s Claude. Hedgeye’s internal models showed that Anthropic had experienced a third-quarter slowdown as growth in enterprise AI spending cooled, Wang said. Self-reported data from C-suite executives support this finding. Boston Consulting Group’s latest “Applied AI Index” found that nearly three-quarters of the world’s most sophisticated enterprise AI users had set usage limits or spending controls, even as they continued to promote internal adoption. For Anthropic, this implied that even as token demand continued to increase, downward pricing pressure prevented the company from generating as much revenue as it might have without Chinese competition, Wang said. “Total demand for your tokens may be going up, but if the price is flat or falling, then you’re not making more money,” he said. Adding to Anthropic’s challenges is the recent resurgence of domestic rival OpenAI, which has seen rising demand for its coding tool Codex and new flagship model GPT-6 Astra. Defence against distillation Anthropic’s IPO is expected next month, though some investors are now discussing a lower valuation of around US$1.5 trillion – a significant drop from the roughly US$2 trillion target the company previously sought, Reuters reported on Friday. Meanwhile, OpenAI has delayed its own IPO until next year. These headwinds have prompted some analysts to forecast a market meltdown for the US AI industry. Earlier this month, Jefferies’ global head of equity strategy Chris Wood cited cheaper Chinese models as a key driver for his prediction of “massive capital destruction” in the US, arguing that cheaper Chinese alternatives were poised to dominate. However, it remains unclear whether Chinese models can sustain their competitive edge against US rivals. Anthropic has repeatedly accused Chinese firms of illicitly improving their own models using Claude outputs – a practice known as “distillation” – but last week the company said it had made “substantial progress” in curbing the distillation of its models by as much as 99 per cent. The firm also told investors that its crackdown on distillation had partly caused its recent revenue slowdown, with the campaign representing a 5 to 7 per cent hit to top-line figures, the Financial Times reported. Many China AI industry analysts have underestimated how reliant the country’s AI progress has been on distillation, according to Wang. While Chinese companies would remain competitive, a successful clampdown by Anthropic could force the Chinese firms to invest more on research and development, hurting their margins, he added. “The China dynamic is very fast-moving when it comes to analysing Anthropic and OpenAI,” Wang said.

title: 6 easy steps for planning an essay
description: Use mind maps to brainstorm topics and make an outline to organise your ideas.
content:
Writing an essay can sometimes seem daunting, especially if you have numerous ideas swirling in your mind. Nonetheless, dedicating some time to outlining your essay before you begin writing can help streamline the process and make it more pleasant. Here’s a straightforward guide to help you plan your essay efficiently in just a few easy steps.
Make sure you thoroughly comprehend the task before you start the mapping process. It’s important to know what the assignment entails. What is the subject matter? What format should you adhere to? Are there particular instructions regarding length or citation styles? Clarify these details from the beginning to help maintain your focus.
After you identify your topic, take some time to brainstorm. Consider all the different ideas, viewpoints and examples you might incorporate. During this stage, don’t hold back; write down every thought that comes to you. You can utilise techniques such as mind mapping, list-making or free writing to help spark your creativity.
Once you’ve finished brainstorming, the next step is to organise your thoughts into a clear, logical structure. Begin by pinpointing the key points or claims you wish to present. Cluster similar ideas together and prioritise them based on their significance or relevance to your topic. This approach will help you establish a smooth and logical progression for your essay.
Now that you’ve organised your thoughts, it’s time to construct an outline. This will act as the framework for your essay, specifying each section and what it will include.
Once you’ve created your initial outline, take a step back and review it. Does it make sense? Does it cover all the important points? Is there anything that feels out of place or missing? Revising your outline at this stage can save you time later on.
With your comprehensive outline in hand, you can begin drafting your essay. Stick to your outline and let your thoughts progress smoothly. Don’t stress about making the first draft flawless; you can revise and refine it later.
Planning your essay before you begin writing can turn a challenging task into something much more approachable. By clarifying your assignment, organising your thoughts and outlining your main points, you can prepare yourself to write a clear and convincing essay. So take out a pen and paper and start charting out your next writing project! Enjoy the writing process.

title: Style according to … Anabela Chan, Hong Kong-born jewellery designer
description: The London-based designer shares her lifestyle, from sustainable jewellery and beauty staples to Mayfair haunts and a family-run Tahitian pearl farm.
content: Hong Kong-born jewellery designer Anabela Chan moved to Paris when she was 10 years old. Now based in London, where in her student days she trained as an architect and worked with the late designer Alexander McQueen, Chan is known for striking pieces made of materials such as recycled drink cans and fruit-derived dyes. Here, she shares her favourite finds from London and beyond. Beauty essentials My make-up staples are always Pat McGrath’s eye shadow palettes and liquid eyeliner, and Tom Ford’s red lipsticks in Cherry Lush and Ruby Rush. My go-to fragrance is Siamese Water from Panpuri. I never wear foundation but I’m religious with my SPF 50 daily rain or shine, and currently loving Korean brand Thank You Farmer. After cleansing, I use Medik8 Vitamin C Serum and The Ordinary’s Hyaluronic Acid, followed by Augustinus Bader’s The Rich Cream. Best souvenirs Anabela Chan x Rachel Vosper scented candles are hand-poured in Belgravia, London, and when in Hong Kong, I always buy friends a lucky jade charm for the year according to the auspicious Chinese zodiacs from Cat Street or Man Mo Temple on Hollywood Road. Insta-ration I love following @danielroseberry for a behind-the-scenes look at his creative journey, @magnuslundgrenphotography and @jacintashackleton for wildlife photography, @hkreminiscence for nostalgia and I’ve recently discovered the fun and frivolous fashion of @myfriendhannah__. London haunts Lilibet’s Mayfair serves the best seafood and French fries in town. It is a beautiful, treasure trove-like restaurant that was the first home and birthplace of the late Queen Elizabeth. After hours, Upstairs at Langan’s is my favourite spot for live music every Thursday. On weekends, you will find me in Holland Park or Hyde Park for tennis with the kids and walks with our French bulldog. My favourite stationery and art supplies store is L Cornelissen & Son in Bloomsbury. I used to live right behind it when I studied architecture at University College London, and I shop there to this day. Bucket list I’d go to French Polynesia to see our third-generation family-run Tahitian pearl farm, Kamoka Pearls, whose unique practice restores coral reefs and brings back near-extinct fish species in the process. Timepieces My late father gave me a Chopard Happy Sport Watch with diamonds for my 21st birthday, and I gifted myself a vintage yellow gold Piaget wristwatch with an opal dial from the 60s for my 30th. I treasure both as family heirlooms. Perfect stays We stayed at Villa Cortine Palace in Sirmione, Lake Garda and it was magical. We ski twice a season in Austria and have always returned to Naturhotel Forsthofgut in Leogang, an hour’s drive from Salzburg. For a girls’ weekend, I’d stay at Hotel Miramalfi on the Amalfi Coast or Faena Hotel in Miami Beach. For a romantic getaway, the Orient Express hotels in either Rome or Venice. Cultured tastes Chef’s Table is my favourite programme on Netflix – I watched all seven volumes and always learn something new. I find a lot of synergy between chefs and jewellers – the attention to detail, innovation and balance – we both rely on the skills of our hands and our craft. I just finished reading Emma Grede’s book Start With Yourself and loved it – it is written for those who dream big and are prepared to work for it. I watched Toy Story 5. I loved Toy Story as a child and still do now as an adult. Keeping our childlike wonder is perhaps our greatest superpower.

title: In pictures: curios on Hong Kong’s Cat Street market through the decades
description: Antiques, art and souvenirs attract collectors, tourists and bargain hunters to Upper Lascar Row, as they have done for decades, giving the Central thoroughfare its unique character.
content: Located below Man Mo Temple and running parallel to Hollywood Road, Upper Lascar Row, famously known as Cat Street, is one of Hong Kong’s most renowned destinations for antiques and curios. In the 1800s, the street was home to Indian seafarers (“lascar” being a term for a sailor or militiaman from the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia or the Arab world who was employed on a European ship). The alley grew into a notorious hub for gamblers and “cat burglars” trading in stolen goods. Other theories as to why the feline name was adopted include the fact that in Cantonese, thieves and petty criminals were referred to as “rats”, and stolen property, “rat goods”. Bargain hunters who “gobbled up” these stolen items were therefore thought of as “cats”. The hawkers’ pidgin English cry of “catchee”, meaning “to buy”, could also have played a part. By the 1970s, the drunken sailors, gamblers, prostitutes and opium addicts had largely been moved on and the street transformed into a vibrant antiques bazaar where hawkers laid out mats along the pavement on which to display their treasures. Collectors and bargain hunters flocked here to sift through old porcelain, vintage coins, books, propaganda posters and rare knick-knacks. Although further government clean-ups in the mid-90s removed unlicensed vendors and pared down the number of street stalls, overseas tourists and local collectors still gather to search out vintage vinyl, classic timepieces and unique souvenirs, keeping the treasure hunt along Cat Street going. Here’s a look back at how South China Morning Post photographers have captured the transformation of the street.

title: Trump administration says it has revoked over 300,000 visas
description: The numbers show an acceleration in the pace of revocations in recent weeks, as the government continues its sweeping immigration crackdown.
content: President Donald Trump’s administration has ⁠revoked over 300,000 ⁠US visas during his second ⁠term, the State Department said on Tuesday as the federal government continues its sweeping immigration crackdown. The number showed an acceleration in the pace of visa revocations in recent weeks. In an update ‌issued on August 10, the State Department had put the number of visa revocations since Trump’s current term began in January 2025 at over 175,000. Trump says his immigration crackdown and deportation drive aim to improve domestic security. Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due process ⁠and free speech rights and has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, ‌who have raised concerns about racial profiling. In announcing the latest number on social media, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said the ‌Trump administration “has revoked more visas at a faster pace than any ⁠administration in history”. Pigott ⁠said the administration had “zero tolerance for foreigners here on visas who break the law, commit ‌fraud, or undermine our national security”. Among visa revocations particularly condemned by rights advocates are those of pro-Palestinian foreign ‌protesters demonstrating ‌against US ally Israel’s attacks on Gaza and of foreigners over their ‌social media comments about conservative commentator Charlie Kirk’s assassination. In addition to attempts ⁠to deport foreign protesters, the Trump administration has enforced tightened social media screening of ⁠immigrants and visa applicants. Rights advocates say the government has deployed national security reasons to target critics and used isolated cases of fraud to ‌broadly target immigrant ‌communities such as the Somali American community in Minnesota. While Trump campaigned in 2024 on stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also made legal immigration more difficult – for example by imposing expensive fees for certain work visas.

title: Musk says SpaceX and Tesla are exploring blockbuster merger deal
description: His two companies have formed special committees to look into what would rank as the largest corporate tie-up of all time.
content: Elon Musk said SpaceX and Tesla Inc have formed special committees to explore a potential merger, a preliminary step towards what would rank as the largest corporate tie-up of all time. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies,” Musk, the chief executive officer of both companies, said on Tuesday on SpaceX’s earnings webcast. “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” Musk said he is not taking part in the committee discussions because he is a conflicted party, and that the committees have yet to agree on terms. A blockbuster deal would unite Tesla’s electric vehicle, energy and robotics businesses with SpaceX’s rocket launch and satellite internet operations. Underpinning it all are the companies’ shared ambitions in artificial intelligence – or what some in the industry are now calling superintelligence – fuelling investments in areas such as data centres and driverless cars. SpaceX shares rose 4.6 per cent in postmarket trading after reporting quarterly results, while Tesla climbed 1.2 per cent. The scope of a potential merger is staggering, with both SpaceX and Tesla among the largest companies in the world and holding dominant positions in their respective industries. SpaceX, formally known as Space Exploration Technologies Corp, has a market value of about US$2 trillion, while Tesla is worth nearly US$1.5 trillion. SpaceX and Tesla already have numerous business ties, overlapping investor bases and even some shared personnel. The rocket maker has bought more than US$100 million worth of Tesla Cybertrucks, while xAI is a major customer of Tesla’s utility-scale batteries. A combination has been widely expected since SpaceX rode a wave of investor enthusiasm to a record initial public offering this year, giving the company both currency and an implicit green light from shareholders to make a play for Tesla. Bloomberg News reported in January that SpaceX had weighed a Tesla merger before ultimately deciding to acquire xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence start-up. Musk cautioned that a merger is not certain and would require shareholder support. He said Tesla would need approval from 50 per cent of all shareholders, rather than simply a majority of those voting. “Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty,” Musk said. “I think that would be overstating it.”

title: Editorial | China’s stronger-than-expected GDP growth sends positive signal
description: The revival of factory-gate prices, if demand-driven, indicates that Beijing’s push to upgrade manufacturing is working, but consumption and the housing slump need attention.
content: China’s economy has delivered a welcome, if qualified, surprise. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 4.5 per cent in the third quarter, up from 4.3 per cent in the second. The figure beat the 4.4 per cent consensus of economists surveyed by Wind and lifted growth for the first nine months to 4.6 per cent, within Beijing’s full-year target range of 4.5 to 5 per cent. Besides the latest quarterly GDP figure, the revival of factory-gate prices is worth noting. The producer price index returned to positive territory in March and has gathered momentum since, reaching 5 per cent in September. For a manufacturing superpower, the PPI matters. Sustained gains suggest Beijing’s push to restructure industry is bearing fruit. The nature of the rebound is crucial. If it is driven mainly by spikes in imported raw materials, it is cost-push inflation that squeezes margins. If it is demand-driven, it could move the economy into a positive reinforcement loop. More detail is needed, but the evidence points to a combination of both, weighted towards demand. The global artificial intelligence buildout has supercharged China’s trade in semiconductors and related components. There are indications that the Middle East war’s energy shock has been withstood at the moment. Such strong external demand can accelerate Beijing’s core economic policy: upgrading manufacturing. Production is shifting towards high value-added segments, and together with the latest research and development spending figures, this suggests steady progress. Authorities have backed technology while discouraging investment in traditional manufacturing and sectors with excess capacity. Mao Shengyong of the National Bureau of Statistics spoke of “innovation-led and high-quality development despite mounting pressure”. On this evidence, the strategy is working. The home front, however, remains a weak spot. Retail sales growth picked up to 1.1 per cent in September from 0.4 per cent in August, its fastest pace in six months, helped by a 31.1 per cent surge in purchases of communications equipment. It’s still feeble. Fixed-asset investment shrank 7.2 per cent in the first nine months, and real estate investment plunged 20.6 per cent as the housing slump continues to sap consumer confidence. For now, Beijing has chosen to nibble at the policy edges: countercyclical adjustments, 550 billion yuan (US$82 billion) for infrastructure and emerging industries, local government bond purchases and new mortgage interest subsidies. That is a far cry from the “bazooka” of two years ago, with interest rate and bank reserve-ratio cuts, and a share-purchase swap facility which helped mainland and Hong Kong markets beat the S&P 500 last year. With two months left in the year and the Fifth Plenum to convene next week, more policy intervention may yet come. The economy may yet deliver a decent outcome: growth sufficient to meet Beijing’s target, but not so weak as to force major stimulus. External demand is keeping the economy afloat, making aggressive stimulus unlikely. Diplomacy has bought some breathing space with the United States; it remains to be seen with the European Union. Brussels talks big but may yet compromise in the end. Buying time and averting escalation are often the goal of trade talks. Intense negotiations with Washington lie ahead. As this newspaper exclusively reported, the two sides are working on a board of investment and an extension of their trade truce. Europe, facing a trade deficit with China exceeding €1 billion (US$1.1 billion) a day, is harder to placate; EU leaders last week threatened a “kill switch” to eject Chinese firms from priority sectors in extreme circumstances. Risks loom. A US-Iran flare-up could tip the PPI rebound towards the more harmful cost-push variety. A potential bust in the massive investment frenzy over artificial intelligence, as some veteran US investors have warned, would hit the exports on which this year’s target depends. Beijing should use this reprieve wisely. Industrial upgrading is succeeding; now the virtuous cycle must extend to households. That means stabilising housing and reviving consumption, to return to a well-rounded, healthy economic growth.

title: How microplastics react with water to damage our bodies and cause inflammation
description: A recent study found water reacting with six fossil-fuel-based plastics to create particles that damaged red blood cells and proteins.
content: Plain old water could be responsible for making plastics harmful to people, according to a new study that portends significant consequences for human health. The study, published in the journal Nature, found chemical reactions between water and six types of fossil fuel-based plastic-created particles that damaged red blood cells and proteins in laboratory tests. As plastic in the body breaks down into smaller and smaller bits – known as microplastics and nanoplastics – the potential danger increases, says study co-author Wei Min, a Peking University graduate who is now a professor of chemistry and biomedical engineering at Columbia University in New York. “Is this phenomenon 5 per cent responsible or 90 per cent responsible for the health effects we are seeing, I can’t answer,” Min says. “But I would be surprised if it doesn’t play any role.” The study comes amid increasing concerns about plastic pollution in the Great Lakes, the source of drinking water for 40 million people in the United States and Canada. Interactions between water and plastic could help explain why other studies have shown that microplastics trigger inflammation, which contributes to a variety of diseases that together account for more than half of all deaths globally. For now, it is impossible to prevent these reactions within the body. Human blood is about 50 per cent water and cells are up to 80 per cent water, Min says. “This challenges the reigning theory that plastic is inert (meaning it doesn’t prompt chemical or biological reactions),” says Sherri “Sam” Mason, a chemist at Gannon University in Erie, Pennsylvania, who studies plastic pollution in fresh water. “I think it highlights the need for truly biodegradable plastic, rather than what industry increasingly puts out into the marketplace,” says Mason, who was not involved in the new study but was one of the first researchers to find microplastics throughout the Great Lakes. Scientists are also finding microplastics in nearly every part of the human body – the brain, the heart, ovaries and testicles. The mostly invisible bits course through blood and pass from mother to child through the placenta and breast milk. Rapidly emerging research suggests the ingestion and inhalation of microplastics, nearly all of which are made from climate-changing fossil fuels, contribute to or outright trigger heart disease, dementia, Parkinson’s disease, impaired fertility and premature births, among other health problems. Min and 11 colleagues, including researchers from the University of California Berkeley and Rutgers University, found water molecules behave differently when coming into contact with microplastics. Water essentially acts as a catalyst that spontaneously creates particles known as hydroxyl radicals, unstable molecules linked to ageing and disease. Two common types of plastic – polythene and polypropylene, used widely to make food containers, packaging, milk jugs and bottle caps – produced the most hydroxyl radicals detected by the researchers. The finding suggests certain plastics could be reformulated or phased out of consumer products, Min says. “Our bodies have natural defence mechanisms,” says Phoebe Stapleton, a Rutgers professor of pharmacology and toxicology who co-wrote the study. “But depending on other exposures we’ve had, our genetics and lifestyle choices, all of these [hydroxyl radicals] could build up to a point where we can’t handle them any more.” More than 8 billion tons (7.25 billion tonnes) of plastic already pollute the Earth. Manufacturers, including the world’s largest oil companies, are planning to triple production by 2060. Craig Davis, senior director of plastics chemistry at the American Chemistry Council, the industry’s chief trade group, says that the study “offers a novel look at microplastics outside the body”. But, Davis says, “it does not establish whether the observed effects occur within the body’s complex biological systems or at actual human exposure levels to microplastics. Additionally, limited information about the particles tested in the version provided also makes the findings difficult to fully evaluate. Those gaps matter before drawing conclusions about human health.” Min acknowledged the study’s limitations. Still, he says, the findings should help direct future research. He noted that a group of Chinese researchers recently found that stirring plastic waste into hot water prompted similar chemical changes that broke down the polymers into building blocks of new plastics, raising the possibility of a less-toxic, more effective way to keep plastic litter out of the environment.

title: Commercial lenders shouldering heavier AI burden than central banks: ICBC president
description: Financial and legal liabilities when ‘something bad happens’ mean commercial bankers face a ‘more miserable’ transition, Liu Jun says.
content: As artificial intelligence reshapes the finance industry, commercial bankers are facing a “more miserable” transition than their central banking counterparts, the head of the world’s largest lender by assets said. Industrial and Commercial Bank of China president Liu Jun said that while central bankers focused on oversight and policy, commercial lenders bore direct financial and legal liability when deploying AI at scale. “If [ICBC] deploys AI tools … towards different business lines, and all the benefits contribute to the IT balance sheet and income statements, it means I take the responsibility of the AI deployment,” Liu said during a panel discussion at the Shanghai Bund Summit on Monday. “If something bad happens, I’m going to have to pay the victim and give the final answer to the market.” He said commercial banks, which served the public and industry every day, could only rely on well-established technology. Yet they were only just entering digital transformation, and the journey ahead was one where “we never know what’s going to happen”. Liu cited four mismatches between AI and conventional banking: disclosure, data storage, sovereignty and credibility. He said a major hurdle was assigning liability when developers, deployers and users each handled distinct parts of an opaque system. ICBC had deployed hundreds of AI models and given them more autonomy in data-heavy work,” Liu said, while keeping human teams in client-facing positions. To mitigate operational risks, he said ICBC had introduced a framework called the “proof of benefit” – an approach that directly tied accountability to those who reaped the financial returns and made independent decisions within the system. On the same panel, Arthur Yuen Kwok-hang, deputy chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, echoed Liu’s concern about accountability as banks adopt agentic AI – systems that can plan and carry out multi-step tasks. Institutions typically split one application across six to eight agents, he said, but if each agent and the human supervisor were responsible for only part of the task, “nobody is responsible for the whole thing”. To address such challenges, Hong Kong’s de facto central bank unveiled an updated AI governance framework focused on accountability, resilience and trust last week. Under the new framework, the HKMA will publish a discussion paper on supervising such a system, exploring accountability tied to intent, a registry of material AI agents and ways to intervene. Yuen said the Hong Kong government aimed to foster an environment in which financial institutions could safely “fail fast”. “We, as supervisors, become more facilitative rather than regulatory,” he said. “If you have an idea, go in, test it out.”

title: As I see it | Britain’s ban on pro-Palestinian author Sally Rooney makes it a laughing stock
description: When Western governments try to suppress protests against Israel’s alleged genocide, readers end up with the censorship of leading authors like Rooney.
content: “Actions have consequences,” British Minister of State for Skills and former home secretary Baroness Jacqui Smith said of Palestine Action, the protest group proscribed as a terrorist organisation across the United Kingdom. She was lecturing the group’s members and supporters, who are legion in Britain, on taking responsibility for their actions. From where everyone else is sitting, she might as well have been talking about her Labour Party colleagues, such as fellow former home secretary Yvette Cooper, who spearheaded the proscription under former prime minister Keir Starmer. They have made their country a global laughing stock, not just for the proscription itself but for all the consequences that have flowed from it. The latest development is that UK stores can no longer sell books by Sally Rooney, the Irish literary sensation sometimes credited with getting young people to read again. Why? Because Rooney supports Palestine Action and has pledged to use her earnings to help the group. Under UK terrorism law, that could amount to financing terrorism. That was certainly the legal view of Faber & Faber, Rooney’s prestigious publisher, whose list of authors includes T.S. Eliot, W.H. Auden, William Golding, Philip Larkin, Seamus Heaney and Sylvia Plath, among others. “Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work,” it said in a public statement, explaining why her books can no longer be supplied in Britain. Why is that a big deal? Rooney is the English-speaking equivalent of the late Eileen Chang, the go-to writer for every sensitive, lonely and misunderstood schoolgirl across the Chinese-speaking world. Imagine being unable to buy Chang’s books in Chinese territories today. The BBC turned Rooney’s bestselling novel, Normal People, into its biggest television hit of the year during the Covid-19 lockdown in the UK. If you haven’t been following British news, you might wonder what the pro-Palestine group did to land in the same league as Hamas, Hezbollah, al-Qaeda and Islamic State. Well, its activists broke into the Royal Air Force base at Brize Norton, spray-painted two refuelling planes red to symbolise the blood of those killed in the Gaza genocide and caused millions of pounds’ worth of damage with crowbars. The government banned the group in July last year, a move many legal and human rights experts – including UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk – consider overkill. The High Court ruled that the ban was unlawful in February, but the Court of Appeal overturned that and said in June that the proscription was lawful. Pro-Israel groups and political advisers, including Lord Walney, the government’s former independent adviser on political violence, had pressed the Starmer administration for a severe crackdown. The case now goes to the Supreme Court. According to the latest Home Office statistics, there were 3,867 terrorism-related arrests in the year to June, up from just 234 the year before. Most of those arrests were linked to support for the group. Among those arrested were the poet Alice Oswald and King Charles’s former environmental adviser Sir Jonathon Porritt. The Palestine Action activists might well be naive and idealistic. They might even be making fools of themselves, but they are clearly no terrorists. Even so, many people are missing the forest for a single tree. The crackdown on Palestine Action is not an isolated incident, in Britain or in other Western countries. Extensive documentation from human rights organisations, legal watchdogs and UN experts, including the International Federation for Human Rights and the European Legal Support Centre, confirms unprecedented crackdowns, legal prosecutions and threats against pro-Palestinian advocacy and rights groups across Western nations such as Germany, the United States and Britain. The mechanisms might differ by country, but the goal is the same. In Germany, authorities have imposed sweeping protest bans, heavily policed demonstrations and restricted Palestinian symbols, slogans and flags. UN human rights experts have criticised authorities for “criminalising, punishing and suppressing” legitimate, peaceful solidarity activism. In the US, campus encampments and nationwide advocacy have met immense institutional and legal pressure, resulting in thousands of suspensions, arrests and lost jobs. Furthermore, the threat of expulsion and deportation has been aimed at foreign students and resident aliens who engage in pro-Palestinian speech or protest. In Britain, as we have seen, the government has weaponised counterterrorism legislation to proscribe a direct-action group. That designation criminalises basic membership and support, needlessly causing thousands of arrests and prosecutions, not to mention raising the group’s profile. The UK might have made itself a laughing stock, but this assault on freedom is no laughing matter.

title: 19.2 million Afghans could soon face ‘acute food insecurity’: UN
description: The United Nations is also warning that over four million babies and children under six will need treatment for acute malnutrition next year.
content: The number of people facing acute food insecurity in Afghanistan is set to rise above 19 million this winter, the United Nations warned on Tuesday. The food crisis gripping Afghanistan is projected to affect millions of young children in 2027, the United Nations’ humanitarian agency OCHA said. More than four million babies and children under six will need treatment for acute malnutrition next year, it warned. Between September and October, 15.9 million people – or nearly one in three Afghans – were facing food insecurity at crisis levels or worse, including 3.4 million in emergency conditions, the agency said. The outlook is set to deteriorate further during the winter lean season from November to April. “The number facing acute food insecurity is projected to rise to 19.2 million, of which five million are expected to face emergency levels of hunger,” which is “one step away from famine”, said OCHA’s Afghanistan spokeswoman Olga Cherevko. “We must act before winter, not after families have exhausted all the options.” “That means getting food assistance to people in need, protecting livestock and productive assets, supporting farmers before critical planting windows close, and keeping essential health, nutrition and water services accessible.” The latest snapshot of the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification projects that more than four million children aged six months to five years old will need treatment for acute malnutrition next year. “Over one million of these children are expected to suffer severe acute malnutrition,” Cherevko told a press briefing in Geneva, speaking from Kabul. “These numbers represent children whose parents cannot afford nutritious food and families whose ability to cope has been worn down by years of conflict, economic hardship, drought and other shocks.” In the midst of this hunger crisis, around one third of nutrition sites across the country have closed or have suspended services, “largely due to funding cuts”. “Once these services disappear, the consequences could be irreversible, particularly for children,” Cherevko said Afghanistan has seen a sharp decline in international aid since 2021, when the Taliban authorities returned to power. They have imposed a severe version of Islamic law, including a series of rules limiting women’s access to education and public life. The Taliban government remains largely excluded from the international community, which criticises its repressive measures. International aid to Afghanistan has dropped sharply, with the United Nations saying it had received less than 30 per cent of the funding needed to provide life-saving assistance as of late August. The humanitarian crisis has been further worsened by several natural disasters and the forced return of millions of Afghans from Iran and Pakistan since 2023. Cherevko said humanitarian aid could save lives but it could not compensate indefinitely for the absence of economic opportunity and public services. The food crisis in Afghanistan was not simply about whether the food was available but also about whether people could access and afford it, she said. While better rainfall and agricultural production this year have helped, one good harvest “cannot undo the damage of several years of drought”.

title: UK rearrests duo on suspicion of aiding Iran in alleged plot at US-run airbase
description: The 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national were arrested under the National Security Act.
content: British police said on Tuesday that they had rearrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service in a suspected plot at a US-run airbase in England last month. Counter Terrorism Policing said the men, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, were arrested under the National Security Act. One of the suspects was first arrested on September 27, when the suspected plot against the US-run base at RAF Fairford took place. The airbase in western England has been used to bomb Iran during this year’s war. The second suspect was first arrested on October 1. Until Tuesday the men had been bailed pending more investigation. Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area.
