Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant – petrol – in three vans at the site, but no explosives. British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which led the US to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, or IRGC. Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. Five other men in their 20s were arrested earlier then released on bail pending further investigation. No one has yet been charged. Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK, said detectives are looking at “many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation”. “This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement,” he said in a statement. “Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it,” he added. Last week the head of Britain’s MI5 spy agency warned that both Iran and Russia were expanding their attacks against the UK and that the RAF base incident was not unique. Ken McCallum, who leads the UK’s domestic security service, said Tehran is seeking to intensify its attacks in Britain beyond the traditional targets of Iranians opposed to the country’s Islamic authorities. In all, more than 50 people have been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year, McCallum said.

title: What is Discovery Loop, Chinese teen AI prodigy Nathan Chen’s rumoured next destination?
description: Launched just two months ago, the start-up has quickly attracted industry attention due to its star-studded founding team.
content: Just days after announcing his departure from Moonshot AI, teen Chinese artificial intelligence prodigy Nathan Chen Guangyu seems to have found his next destination. On Tuesday, Arfur Grok, a widely-watched anonymous social media account that tracks AI talent movements in the US, posted that the former Moonshot AI researcher was joining Discovery Loop, an AI start-up founded by four former Google senior researchers including former chief scientist Jeff Dean. Launched just two months ago, the start-up has quickly attracted industry attention due to its star-studded founding team as well as its ambitious mission: to automate scientific research with AI. Discovery Loop has already recruited several star researchers from US big tech giants, including other former Google engineers. But at just 17 years old, Chen is likely to be one of its youngest members. Chen did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. Discovery Loop said it does not comment on personnel matters. One of China’s most promising young AI talents, Chen’s announcement last week that he was leaving China for the US sparked widespread speculation about his next destination. Despite a stint at Moonshot that lasted less than a year, Chen helped pioneer technical breakthroughs that delivered cost-efficiency gains for its flagship Kimi models, making them competitive with US heavyweights such as OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude. Moonshot has emerged as one of China’s strongest AI model labs, with its K3 model gaining global traction due to its powerful capabilities and open-weight nature. In a social media post after Chen’s announcement, Moonshot senior researcher Du Yulun wrote that he and Chen had “several long conversations about his decision” to leave, but it was ultimately “best for [Chen] to explore and follow his new curiosity as much as possible at his age”. Though Discovery Loop has yet to release any products, it is already seeking a valuation of around US$50 billion in another funding round, Business Insider reported last month. Its initial funding round was led by Radical Ventures and Khosla Ventures, with Google parent Alphabet also an investor. In one of his first public appearances after leaving Google, Dean said at the Agentic AI Summit at the University of California, Berkeley, in early August that his start-up’s work would be similar to efforts to achieve recursive self-improvement (RSI) – the stated goal of leading AI companies in both the US and China. Just as RSI looks to automate AI development through AI itself, Dean explained that AI could one day autonomously run thousands of scientific experiments in parallel and use the results to identify the best experiments to do next, thereby shortening the scientific process from years to hours or even minutes. “By building models that are really good at understanding many, many different domains of science and engineering, you can get PhD-level expertise in a model across many different domains,” he said.

title: EU unveils Arctic strategy to counter increasing Russia, China influence
description: The European bloc is stepping up some of its efforts in the resource-rich region, but says it still wants fossil fuels to stay in the ground.
content: The European Commission has presented an updated strategy for the Arctic as climate change and rapidly melting ice open up the remote but resource-rich region. “With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition,” said European Union foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday. With the new strategy, the commission aims for the EU to keep pace with rivals as new shipping routes and mining opportunities, including for critical raw materials, become available. “Access to Arctic sea lanes and natural resources is of strategic interest to the EU,” Kallas said. Geographically, the northern parts of EU countries Finland and Sweden lie within the Arctic region. The vast Arctic island of Greenland, which is not part of the EU but belongs to the Kingdom of Denmark, is also of major importance to the EU. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his desire to take control of the resource-rich island. A senior EU official told reporters in Brussels that there were also concerns Russia could shift more of its attention to the Arctic once the war in Ukraine ends. “To defend our interests, we are stepping up efforts in surveillance, infrastructure, military mobility and defence technologies that can withstand the harsh climate,” Kallas said. Planned measures include improving the protection of undersea cables and other critical infrastructure, strengthening the EU’s ability to operate in extreme Arctic conditions and expanding Europe’s icebreaker capacity. The ⁠Arctic is one place ‌where the tectonic plates of geopolitics ‌are colliding. ‌And it ‌is not someone else’s frontier. ⁠It is part of ⁠the EU European Commission President Ursula ‌von der Leyen Values that underpinned security ⁠can no longer be ‌taken for granted, European Commission President Ursula ‌von der Leyen said. “The ⁠Arctic is one place ‌where the tectonic plates of geopolitics ‌are colliding. ‌And it ‌is not someone else’s frontier. ⁠It is part of ⁠the European Union,” she said. “When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the rules that have underpinned stability in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act and change our strategic posture.” Kallas said the bloc ⁠remained committed to “ensuring ⁠that oil, coal ⁠and gas stay in the ground, including in Arctic regions”. “Due to its specific vulnerabilities, the Commission will work with partners to protect the Arctic environment and prevent all hydrocarbon reserve developments that pose a ⁠threat to the Arctic ecosystem,” the new strategy also says. However, it ‌does not repeat a pledge from the previous strategy, issued in 2021, to ‌work towards “a multilateral legal obligation not to allow ⁠any further ⁠hydrocarbon reserve development in the Arctic or contiguous regions” or buy ‌any products from those developments. Norway has called on the EU to drop its opposition to new drilling in ‌the Arctic. With ‌many ageing fields, Norwegian production is set to decline in the 2030s unless companies such as Equinor make new discoveries outside mature areas. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: China’s hybrid car exports to EU surge by more than 200% as import cap looms
description: Exports climbed to nearly 100,000 vehicles in September ahead of limits due to take effect at the end of the year.
content: China’s hybrid car exports to the European Union tripled in September from a year earlier, with shipments expected to remain elevated before an import cap agreed during recent trade talks takes effect. The country shipped nearly 100,000 hybrid cars to the bloc last month, up 18.9 per cent from August and 204.2 per cent from a year earlier, customs data showed on Tuesday. The surge outpaced a 142.7 per cent year-on-year rise in China’s total exports of passenger cars to the EU. Analysts said the rapid growth likely reflected carmakers front-loading vehicles ahead of high-level negotiations held in Beijing in early October. “Dealerships may have sought to get as many purchases in as possible before potential quotas or tariffs ahead of trade talks,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING. After months of rising tensions, Chinese and EU officials met for trade talks earlier this month in Beijing, where they agreed to cap hybrid car imports into the bloc for four years. The limit starts at 350,000 units a year and will rise 6 per cent annually from the second year. “With the import cap set to go into effect on December 1, we would likely see elevated imports in the next two months of data as well,” Song said. Chinese carmakers have increasingly pivoted to hybrid cars for the European market since Brussels imposed tariffs of up to 35.3 per cent on pure electric cars from the country in 2024. China exported about 670,000 hybrid cars to the EU’s 27 member states in the first three quarters of this year, nearly double the 356,000 recorded for the entirety of 2025, according to customs data. Xu Tianchen, a senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said Chinese carmakers had previously shown a pattern of shipping vehicles early to get ahead of potential restrictions, citing Brazil’s tariff increase on electric vehicles (EVs) last year and changes to Thailand’s EV subsidy programme at the end of 2023. He expected exports to remain elevated through October and November, noting that the China-EU trade understanding did not appear to place any restrictions on front-loading. “But it will not hurt trade ties because an agreement has already been made, and the EU should be quite happy with China’s concession,” Xu said. China’s total exports to the EU rose 25.3 per cent year on year by value in September, while the country’s total exports surged 36.3 per cent, far above market expectations. Strong exports have helped support economic growth amid persistent weakness in domestic demand, with China’s economy expanding 4.5 per cent in the third quarter. Song said the expected increase in car shipments ahead of the import cap, alongside continued strength in technology-related trade, should “help keep China’s exports strong to close out the year”. “I expect China will reach a new record high for its trade surplus in 2026,” Song added. China’s trade surplus reached a record US$1.2 trillion last year, drawing heightened scrutiny from Western trading partners. Despite the EU’s recent agreement with Beijing, European officials called for further trade measures to counter imbalances last week.

title: Chinese table tennis star Sun Yingsha warns fans against organising birthday events
description: The 25-year-old’s stance echoes her long-time mixed doubles partner, Wang Chuqin, who previously issued a similar appeal about celebrations.
content: Chinese table tennis star Sun Yingsha has warned fans against organising any birthday celebrations ahead of her turning 26 years old, calling on supporters to redirect their attention to the court. In recent years, supporters of prominent Chinese athletes have increasingly mirrored the entertainment industry’s so-called “fan circles” by organising lavish tributes, including commercial LED billboard campaigns in city centres, charity drives, offline promotional displays and drone light shows. Born on November 4, 2000, Sun took to social media on Monday to state she only wanted to concentrate on training on her birthday. “Hello everyone, my birthday is approaching. Every year at this time, I receive so many blessings,” Sun wrote, thanking fans for their continuous encouragement. “I hope more to focus my energy on training,” the 25-year-old said, adding she aimed to play every match well and repay supporters through her on-court performances. “Therefore, I will not host, participate in, authorise or encourage any birthday support activities. Please do not organise or promote any related support campaigns in my name,” she stated, adding: “See you on the court.” Sun’s stance echoes that of her long-time mixed doubles partner, Wang Chuqin, who issued a similar appeal ahead of his own 26th birthday in May. Wang posted a statement urging supporters to cancel any planned festivities: “I do not advocate for or participate in any form of birthday support activities; focusing more on the matches is the best support for me. Let’s cheer for Team China together!” While his younger compatriots were pushing back against lavish fan campaigns, veteran Ma Long offered a quieter, more personal alternative as he marked his 38th birthday on Tuesday with a candid open letter about his life, training and charity work. Despite stepping back from international events, Ma revealed he still trains once or twice a week. “I love the sport of table tennis,” Ma said. “No matter when, this love will not diminish with age. It is not for competition, but because table tennis has long become a habit in my life.”

title: China creates state-owned firm in Xiongan to develop nation’s AI data resources
description: The new firm – based in China’s ‘city of the future’, Xiongan – is tasked with developing a national data industry ecosystem.
content: China has set up a new state-owned enterprise dedicated to managing the country’s massive data resources, a significant move designed to turbocharge the nation’s artificial intelligence industry and bolster its digital economy. The National Data Group Co – based in China’s “city of the future”, Xiongan New Area in northern Hebei province – is tasked with “developing and utilising data resources, unlocking the value of data elements, serving AI development and fostering a data industry ecosystem”, according to a report by state news agency Xinhua. Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang attended the company’s launch ceremony on Tuesday. Ding described the creation of the state-owned company as a “major strategic decision” made by the party leadership, led by President Xi Jinping. The move was crucial for China to “seize the initiative in AI development, accelerate the construction of a ‘digital China’, and build new national competitive advantages”, Xinhua quoted Ding as saying. The creation of the new company came as Xiongan, known for housing state-owned institutions relocated from Beijing, moves to nurture its own industries and attract technology firms, according to reporting by the South China Morning Post. Officials were looking to attract tech companies that could reach valuations of 10 billion yuan (US$1.5 billion) and potentially list on major stock markets – including Hong Kong’s – over the next few years, according to sources. Key target sectors included AI, satellite internet and robotics, they added. Established in April 2017 under a plan championed by Xi, Xiongan spans three counties and surrounding areas in Hebei province, about 100km (60 miles) southwest of Beijing. State-owned enterprises have anchored the first wave of arrivals. China Satellite Network Group and China Huaneng, a major power generation company, have moved their headquarters to Xiongan. Since 2023, Xiongan has attracted 157 second- and third-tier subsidiaries of central state-owned enterprises.

title: UK to deploy fighter planes to help Saudi Arabia’s defence against Houthis
description: ‘These aircraft will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis,’ the British government said, referring to Yemen’s rebel group.
content: British fighter planes will be deployed to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against increasing attacks from Yemen’s Houthi rebels, the UK government announced on Tuesday. The defence ministry said the deployment formed part of “additional defensive military support” to Riyadh. “The UK will fly defensive counter air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure against aerial attack, using RAF Typhoon fighter jets,” the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement. “These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis.” The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable Defence minister Wes Streeting Britain will also deploy a military transport aircraft “to support the movement of defence material within Saudi Arabia alongside UK military advisers to support Saudi staff officers”, the statement added. “The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable,” said defence minister Wes Streeting. “The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to (to) escalate the situation in the region,” he added. The Saudi capital’s international airport has been targeted by strikes 20 times since the start of the month, with a recent attack killing 13 people and wounding more than 300. The Houthis have imposed a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, hitting its tankers, seizing swathes of Yemen’s Red Sea coast vital for oil exports and causing energy prices to jump, while also raining missiles on the kingdom. Yemen’s civil war, in which Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the government since 2015, reignited in September after the collapse of a years-long truce. Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government and the United States accuse Iran of backing the Houthis, an allegation Tehran denies.

title: China’s rare earth magnet exports to EU and US rebound in September
description: While shipments to Japan fell nearly 20 per cent amid diplomatic tensions between Beijing and Tokyo.
content: China’s exports of rare earth permanent magnets to the European Union rebounded last month to their highest level since February, ahead of trade talks between Beijing and Brussels that helped ease concerns about a potential trade war. Shipments to the EU rose 20.5 per cent month on month to 2,454 tonnes in September, following sluggish growth in July and a 4.9 per cent decline in August, according to data released by China’s General Administration of Customs on Tuesday. The rebound came as China and the EU held high-level talks in Beijing earlier this month amid mounting tensions over trade imbalances. Following those negotiations, Beijing pledged to “continue to facilitate” export licence approvals for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU through a “green channel”. The two sides also reached an understanding to cap Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc over the next four years. China dominates the processing of rare earths, making it the world’s leading supplier of rare earth permanent magnets, which are widely used in hi-tech products ranging from electric vehicles and smartphones to wind turbines. Exporters still need permission before shipping magnets overseas, after Beijing imposed export controls on seven rare earth elements and permanent magnets in April last year following US President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs on Chinese goods. China’s exports of rare earth permanent magnets to the United States rose 18 per cent month on month in September to 604 tonnes, rebounding from a 20.9 per cent decline in August. The increase coincided with a high-profile summit between President Xi Jinping and Trump in Washington in late September. The US was China’s third-largest buyer of rare earth permanent magnets last month, following South Korea and Germany. Meanwhile, shipments to Japan fell 19.1 per cent month on month to 172 tonnes amid a diplomatic impasse between Beijing and Tokyo. Overall, China exported 6,165 tonnes of rare earth permanent magnets in September, up 23.04 per cent from August.

title: Who is Yuki Chen, China’s ‘superstar’ hacker who just joined AI leader Z.ai?
description: Chen recently uncovered 23 cyber vulnerabilities in Microsoft’s Windows operating system using Z.ai’s flagship GLM models.
content: Yuki Chen, a prolific Chinese cybersecurity researcher, has joined leading Chinese artificial intelligence model company Z.ai as the country’s AI sector grapples with the technology’s growing impact on global cyberspace. Chen’s appointment comes amid growing concern over AI-assisted cyberattacks and autonomous agents acting beyond their instructions, including recent cases involving Chinese tech giant Tencent Holdings as well as US start-ups OpenAI and Anthropic. “New journey, new mission!” Chen wrote last week in a social media post announcing his move to Z.ai. “Thrilled and grateful for the opportunity to help build a safer cyberspace with the power of frontier AI.” In a statement, Z.ai said that Chen, who also goes by the moniker “Guhe”, had recently helped the company uncover 23 cyber vulnerabilities in Microsoft’s Windows operating system using Z.ai’s flagship GLM models, with the US tech giant acknowledging the discoveries. “[Chen’s] decades of vulnerability research have helped, and will keep helping, the community build a safer cyberspace with GLM,” the company said. The announcement did not detail how much human involvement there was in identifying the 23 vulnerabilities or the extent of the model’s contribution. One of China’s most legendary civilian “hackers”, Chen has more than 15 years experience in discovering cyber vulnerabilities in both software and hardware systems, according to his public profiles. He previously headed the vulnerability research institute at Qihoo 360, a major Chinese cybersecurity company known for its antivirus software, before becoming an independent researcher. Chen is part of the global “white-hat” community, whose hackers investigate software weaknesses and report them to vendors so they can be fixed. His work has earned him recognition from Microsoft and fellow security researchers, including a top ranking on Microsoft’s annual “Most Valuable Security Researcher” five times – in 2019 and each year from 2021 to 2024. In 2024, the Center for Security Studies at ETH Zurich identified him as one of China’s most prominent “superstar hackers” operating in the civilian sphere. He has twice been awarded with a “Pwnie Award”, a prestigious honour in the global hacking community sometimes called the “Oscars of hacking”. Z.ai’s recruitment of Chen comes as GLM, like other frontier AI models globally, is becoming increasingly competent at uncovering and exploiting cyber vulnerabilities. The Beijing-based company said in August that its latest flagship model, GLM-5.3, was one of the world’s best at vulnerability discovery and significantly better than its predecessor, GLM-5.2. Last month, US start-up Anthropic said in a report that GLM-5.3 had similar cyber offence capabilities as its controversial Claude Mythos model, including the ability to autonomously develop end-to-end cyber exploits. In late September, Chen wrote on X that he was switching to using GLM-5.3 to assist him in his work after reading Anthropic’s report. In a report last month, the US government ranked GLM-5.3 as the most capable publicly released open-weight model for cybersecurity, though it said the model was still around four months behind the US frontier on cyber capabilities. China’s AI industry is increasingly turning its attention to mitigating frontier AI risks, with TikTok owner ByteDance announcing last week that it was setting up a new department dedicated to AI safety. China and the US also agreed to launch a bilateral AI safety dialogue at last month’s leaders’ summit in Washington, with AI expected to be a major point of discussion in President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump’s two remaining meetings this year.

title: Asian Para Games: Hong Kong fencers win silver, gain valuable preparation for LA Paralympics
description: Women’s foil team go down in final to China for third straight Games, but learned lessons from format to be used for 2028 Paralympics.
content: Hong Kong’s fencers have set their sights on the Los Angeles Paralympics after winning silver in the women’s foil team event at the Asian Para Games on Tuesday. Lam Ka-man, Yu Chui-yee, Tong Nga-ting and Chung Yuen-ping lost 30-12 to China in the final at the Nagoya City Inae Sports Centre, having come from behind to beat Thailand 30-23 in the semi-final. Despite the presence of veteran Yu, who also took women’s foil category A bronze on Monday, Hong Kong were always chasing gold and trailed 15-4 after the first three bouts before losing by 18 points. The result marked a third straight Para Games final loss to China for the city’s women, although this was the first defeat under a new scoring system that moved from nine bouts of 45 points to six bouts of 30. It is the format organisers plan to use in the United States in 2028. “We knew it was going to be difficult facing China in the final, but honestly, knowing that we completed our mission in winning a medal, I wasn’t too nervous, and just wanted to perform my best level,” said Yu, 42, who over the course of five regional Games has amassed 18 medals: five gold, seven silver and six bronze. “This was the first time we used it at the Asian Games, and because of changes in tactics and formations, we spent some time readjusting. We will use this new scoring system at the Paralympic Games qualifiers in Los Angeles, so this is a good opportunity to prepare.” Hong Kong also reeled in two silver and five bronze medals in para table tennis at Sky Hall Toyota on Tuesday. Chiu Kan-shan narrowly lost 3-2 to China’s Wang Rui in the women’s singles (Class 7) final after fighting back from two games down, while Wong Ting-ting also tasted defeat at the hands of Miya Yamaguchi of Japan, losing 3-2 in the women’s singles (Class 11) final. Earlier, a pair of bronze medals came from Wong Chi-yin and Wong Hon-lam in the men’s singles (Class 9). Pang Wing-ka (Class 6), Wong Yue-ching (Class 7) and Lam Yan-yu (Class 10) also finished on the podium in their respective events. Coupled with a women’s 100m backstroke (S14) bronze medal by Chan Yui-lam in the swimming at the Nagoya City General Gymnasium today, and a silver medal from Lau Chiu-yee in the women’s 200m freestyle (S14), as well as another bronze medal by Wong Hon-yin in the men’s 200m freestyle (S14) on Monday, Hong Kong have now won 12 medals, including four silver and eight bronze medals, at the current Aichi-Nagoya Para Games. Hong Kong sent a delegation of 80 athletes to compete in 10 sports at the Japan Games, which run until this Saturday. The Jockey Club Athlete Incentive Award Scheme is awarding cash incentives ranging from HK$62,500 (US$7,963.69) to HK$250,000 for an individual medal, with the amount doubled for each medal in team events.

title: China calls on Apec to boost coordination in AI, supply chains at Hong Kong summit
description: The Apec event in Hong Kong is a precursor to the leaders’ summit scheduled for Shenzhen on November 18 and 19.
content: Beijing has underscored the need for members of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum to boost coordination on macroeconomic policies, accelerate transformation and cooperation on artificial intelligence, and enhance openness and supply chain resilience during the first day of the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting in Hong Kong. In his keynote address on Tuesday, Chinese Finance Minister Lan Foan said the Asia-Pacific region needed to shoulder greater responsibility “as the engine of global economic growth”. The minister said the need for better cooperation was made starker by the current international situation, which involved intertwined, multiple challenges to global growth, and as the new industrial transformation – exemplified by AI – gathered momentum. “Given the profound uncertainty in the current international environment, we should enhance the robustness of our own policies while strengthening communication and coordination to prevent negative spillovers resulting from policy adjustments,” said Lan. By doing so, the finance minister said, Apec members could prioritise development for shared prosperity and ensure the stability and smooth operation of industrial and supply chains. Beijing has set four key themes for the two-day event: fiscal policies supporting livelihoods, financing for digital infrastructure, inclusive finance tailored to local conditions and exchange and cooperation among young finance professionals. China’s finance ministry said earlier that the topics would address “both immediate priorities and longer-term considerations”. Through the joint efforts of all parties, Lan said the four themes have yielded preliminary results. The Apec event in Hong Kong is a precursor to the leaders’ summit scheduled for the southern Chinese megacity and tech hub of Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. More than 500 guests, including finance ministers from Apec’s 21 economies, have travelled to Hong Kong for the meeting. Beijing described the event as one of the most significant ministerial gatherings to offer “key deliverables” for the leaders’ summit next month, which will see the third meeting this year between Chinese president Xi Jinping and US president Donald Trump. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has skipped Hong Kong to focus on preparations for the upcoming Xi-Trump summit. As the host of this year’s Apec, China is expected to showcase its achievements and promote its vision for finance and economic governance. The Chinese economy, meanwhile, remains a focus as Apec delegates discuss a range of financial and economic issues. A joint statement is expected and would be seen as the most significant outcome of the meeting. In his speech, Lan said the Chinese economy has “for years” accounted for 30 per cent of global economic growth and that the keys to sustaining this would include new drivers of economic growth, consumption, a unified national market as well as continued opening up of the economy. At a separate press conference in Beijing on Tuesday, China’s top economic planning agency, the National Development and Reform Commission, also pledged that, when there was a need, it would introduce new “incremental policies” to sustain growth “within an appropriate range” and expand consumption. The Chinese economy picked up some steam in the third quarter, with GDP expanding 4.5 per cent year on year, up from the 4.3 per cent in the second quarter – the slowest quarterly clip seen since the end of 2022. China’s year-on-year growth for the first three quarters came in at 4.6 per cent, suggesting Beijing’s goal for 4.5 per cent to 5 per cent growth for 2026 may be within reach. Top policymakers, nonetheless, still face pressure to further strengthen support to revitalise domestic demand, which remains stubbornly weak. Beijing has announced a slew of incremental policy measures in recent months as momentum started to fizzle out despite a strong start to the year. These include accelerating bond issuance, construction of major infrastructure projects known as the Six New Networks, and rolling out new mortgage interest subsidies to support homebuyers. Additional reporting by Denise Tsang

title: HKMA to swap jobs of 2 deputy heads as part of succession planning: sources
description: Deputy chief executives Darryl Chan and Howard Lee will take over each other’s roles next month.
content: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) will reshuffle the roles of two deputy chief executives next month as part of the de facto central bank’s succession planning strategy, two sources with knowledge of the matter told the South China Morning Post. Darryl Chan Wai-man will take over as CEO of HKMA’s Exchange Fund Investment Office from November 9, where he will manage the HK$4.46 trillion (US$568 billion) Exchange Fund – the war chest used to defend Hong Kong’s local currency, according to one source. Chan would replace fellow HKMA deputy chief executive Howard Lee Tat-chi in the position, with Lee assuming Chan’s current role in monetary management on the same date, the source said. This type of reorganisation is normal practice within HKMA, with the institution using it as a way to help train its next generation of leaders, according to the source. “By reshuffling roles between the senior executives, it would help them to be exposed to more different areas of knowledge and to establish different contacts, which would be useful to train them up to take up more senior roles in future,” the source said. A spokeswoman for HKMA declined to comment on individual appointments, but said the authority reorganised roles from time to time. “The organisation and division of labour of the HKMA would be arranged according to the needs of the operations and development,” the spokeswoman said. “HKMA would review the organisation and human resources regularly to make proper adjustments and arrangements according to the development and operational needs of the authority.” The Exchange Fund, which dates back to 1935, is the reserve used to back banknote issuance in the city and defend the Hong Kong dollar against speculative attacks. The fund is managed by HKMA’s Exchange Fund Investment Office, which invests the capital in Hong Kong equities and overseas stocks, global bonds, global real estate and other long-term projects. The Hong Kong government is also keen to add in gold investment. Under Lee’s leadership, the reserve posted record full-year earnings of HK$337.4 billion in 2025, a 54 per cent jump year on year and the best annual gain recorded since the HKMA was set up in 1993. Chan, formerly a civil servant, joined HKMA in 2013 as an external executive director and was appointed deputy chief executive of the institution on November 1, 2022. Lee, who was also a civil servant, joined HKMA in 2009 as division head and was appointed as deputy chief executive in 2018. HKMA also reshuffled the roles of a number of middle managers in May and June, with Kenneth Hui moving from an external executive director to a role in banking conduct. He replaced Alan Au, who was reassigned to become executive director of risk and compliance and chief risk officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Au took the role of Grace Lau, who in turn moved to become executive director of corporate services. Her predecessor there, Archie Ng, shifted to a monetary management role. Another source said all these reshuffles were part of a succession planning strategy aimed at training up HKMA’s future leadership, as the current top team had reached the retirement age of 60. HKMA chief executive Eddie Yue Wai-man turned 62 in September, and his current term expires in 2029. Lee was appointed for a two-year term starting in October after reaching the normal retirement age, with his current term to expire next year. Another HKMA deputy chief executive, Arthur Yuen Kwok-hang, has been renewed twice for two-year terms beyond the retirement age, with his current term due to expire in 2028.

title: Behind the carton: the story of the classic US Chinese takeaway container
description: Patented in the US in 1894 to carry oysters, the one-piece cardboard box became a favourite of Chinese restaurants for packaging takeaway.
content: It is an icon, that small white receptacle made from a single piece of cardboard folded into a trapezoid-shaped box. Sometimes there is a wire handle, sometimes a bright red graphic of a Chinese-style pagoda on the side. And inside, deliciousness. The Chinese takeaway container – at least, as it is commonly seen in the United States – is actually about as American as it gets, with its mix of ingenuity, immigrant cultures becoming home-grown staples, and the desire for convenience (also known as sitting at home in your pyjamas). The idea of what is essentially a paper bucket dates back to 1894, when inventor Frederick Weeks Wilcox was granted a patent for what he called “a new and useful improvement” for pails used to carry oysters. A single piece of material would be folded in such a way that it would have structural stability and a lid, while limiting the ways it could leak. That is the container. What about the contents we assume are inside it? Chinese immigrants started heading to the US in the mid-1800s, taking part in the California gold rush and working to help build the railways. The communities they created, known as Chinatowns, rose up in places such as San Francisco. They included eating spots where the foundations of an Americanised style of Chinese food were laid. After World War II, there was a “real profusion of Chinese restaurants, diversifying away from just chop suey and chow mein … we see this explosion of interest and growth in Chinese food,” says Michelle King, professor of Chinese history at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Crucially, it was also the start of an association in the public mind of Chinese food with cheaper prices, availability and convenience, she says. And restaurant owners wanted to be considered accessible, in which takeaway played a part. “You need to take it home, you have a dinner party you want to cater for, we can do that for you, right?” King says. At some point in the 1970s, at a packaging company then known as Fold-Pak, the pagoda design was added, sometimes along with words printed in a Chinese-style font. “It kind of becomes claimed as a Chinese-American food eatery item, like the pizza box or something like that might be for Italian food,” King says. These days, takeaway cartons come in a variety of shapes, and the food landscape has expanded to include a range of cuisines that might show up in the former oyster pail. Even so, it is still an icon – quite literally. Check your emojis for “takeaway”.

title: China celebrities speak out on mental health diagnoses to seek authentic connections with fans
description: Conversely, sceptics argue that bringing mental illness so deeply into the digital spotlight risks trivialising severe diagnoses.
content: An increasing number of Chinese celebrities are voluntarily sharing their histories of mental illness, rather than following the previous practice of keeping them hidden, in what some see as an effort to win empathy and audience support. These conditions include depression, anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). In January last year, famous actress Zhao Lusi’s suspension of work due to severe depression put celebrities’ mental health struggles in the spotlight. Last December, online influencer and entrepreneur Luo Yonghao revealed in a public speech that he had lived with ADHD for more than a decade. Since the start of the year, more entertainers have publicly disclosed their mental health issues. Among them are top-tier stand-up comedians Xiao Qi and Lin Jianqi, who have ADHD. Actress Yu Na and singer Ye Yiqian said on variety shows that they had experienced or were experiencing anxiety. Actress Zhao Yingzi said during a live-stream that she was struggling with depression after experiencing repeated online abuse. Their disclosures were met with sympathy and support on social media. One internet user told Zhao Lusi: “I feel sorry for you. I am also ill. I totally understand how painful it is.” This stands in stark contrast to what another star, Ma Sichun, experienced years ago. Ma, a native of eastern Anhui province, is a Best Actress winner at Taiwan’s Golden Horse Awards. On a variety show in 2020, Ma said she was ill and regularly took medication to treat her condition. Although Ma did not explicitly disclose her illness, internet users soon concluded that she had depression. Many accused her of “sadfishing,” while some mocked her for gaining weight, a possible side effect of taking medication. Show business observers told the media outlet Vista Kan Tian Xia that many entertainers now regard their mental health struggles as a protective shield, thanks to growing public awareness of these issues. As a result, audiences take celebrities’ mental health into consideration when judging them. Luo, for example, sparked controversy by offending many influencers and celebrities online. After his ADHD diagnosis became public, some people might see his aggressive behaviour as related to his condition rather than his personality, experts said. As a result, internet users became less hostile towards Luo, since few people would want to be at odds with someone who is ill. According to the experts, audiences’ general mindset has also shifted: instead of expecting stars to have perfect personas, they now try to see themselves reflected in them. Since many people also experience pressure, anxiety, loneliness and psychological trauma, a star’s vulnerability or illness can bring them closer to audiences and resonate widely with the public. But critics warned that the growing visibility of mental health struggles risks turning these conditions into internet sensations, making it harder for ordinary patients to seek understanding. “Some internet users claim to have depression after taking a simple test online. But people with genuine conditions often dare not talk about their problems, or they may be misunderstood if their struggles do not appear serious enough,” a psychological consultant identified as Rain told the media.

title: Meet The View alum Debbie Matenopoulos, who wants to succeed Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece
description: The Greek-American television personality, cookbook author and skincare entrepreneur is boldly campaigning for the post.
content: Just last week, Kimberly Guilfoyle was ousted from her position as the US ambassador to Greece amid allegations of financial misconduct. Since then, The View alum Debbie Matenopoulos has offered herself as a strong candidate to succeed Guilfoyle. In an Instagram reel posted on October 15, Matenopoulos wore a white polo shirt with Greece’s flag and cited a number of reasons why she is the best fit for the role. “Number one, I speak the language. It’s my first language before I even spoke English. Number two, I have a Greek passport. I have a Greek and an American passport. My entire family lives in Greece with the exception of my immediate family. I was the first person in my family to be born in America. Everyone else was born in Greece and got their citizenship after living here,” Matenopoulos said. She continued to mention that she owns property in Greece, spends her summers there and has previously published two “very successful” Greek cookbooks. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Debbie Matenopoulos (@iamdebbiem) “You don’t need any qualifications, really, to be a US ambassador to any country,” Matenopoulos said. “You don’t even need a college degree. You don’t need a diplomatic background. You don’t need a life in politics. You just need to be an entrepreneur, a successful businesswoman or man, or a political donor. And you have to be appointed by the president and approved by the US Senate, or you could, obviously, be nominated.” The former The View panellist continued to list her qualifications in the caption, citing her journalism degree from New York University and her “30 years’ experience on live television and public-facing persona”. Here’s everything you need to know about Debbie Matenopoulos. What is Debbie Matenopoulos’ background? Debbie Matenopoulos was born in December 1974 in the US to Greek parents. She began her career in media as a 17-year-old when she interned for MTV News. While studying journalism at New York University, Matenopoulos had a chance meeting with journalist, television personality and co-creator of The View, Barbara Walters, which landed her the role of a lifetime as one of five original co-hosts on the hit daytime show. She became the youngest person in history to hold a permanent position on daytime television, staying in the role for two seasons until she was let go in 1999. Matenopoulos’ role in The View was parodied on Saturday Night Live, where she was portrayed as “clueless” by celebrity guests including Cameron Diaz and Sarah Michelle Gellar. Matenopoulos, now 51, even joined the cast of SNL in 1997, playing herself for a skit on the show in 1999. Following The View, Matenopoulos continued to build a career in media, hosting various shows including The Daily 10, Instant Beauty Pageant and Live from E!. Her work has earned her four Daytime Emmy Award nominations, per her IMDb profile. What else does Debbie Matenopoulos do? Aside from being a television personality, Matenopoulos is also an actress and has made appearances in television shows such as Half & Half and American Dreams. She also starred in the 2024 film The Image of You. In 2014, Matenopoulos published her first cookbook, It’s All Greek to Me. Her second cookbook, Greek.ish, followed in 2025. In 2020, the Greek-American launched her own skincare line named Ikaria. Per her bio, her products feature “natural, organic and indigenous ingredients from her native Greece, namely the island of Ikaria for which the skincare line is named”. Is Debbie Matenopoulos married? Matenopoulos eloped with Jon Falcone in Greece in 2013. Before that, she was married to music executive Jay Faires from 2003 to 2008. She welcomed her firstborn, daughter Alexandra Kalliope Falcone, with her husband in October 2020.

title: Ukraine receiving early missile warnings again after US talks, Zelensky says
description: Vital intelligence alerts restored following talks in Oslo and a call with Rubio, though Washington denies aid was ever withheld.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday that Kyiv was once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles following recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice, leaving civilians vulnerable. For at least a week, the Ukrainian leader has said that his country has not received early warnings about ballistic missiles aimed at the capital. Such intelligence, he said, saves lives by allowing the public to be alerted and giving military units time to try to intercept the missiles. Zelensky said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I’m speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming,” Zelensky said on a visit to Norway. “So we are thankful to American side now that it works.” Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio acknowledged mutual frustration between the US and Ukraine over intelligence sharing and weapons supplies but emphatically denied that the Trump administration has made any changes to previous policy on either issue. In other developments, Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said, as Zelensky sought more American and European help. Zelensky was joined in Norway by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine towards a settlement to end the war. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met with the Ukrainian president in Norway’s capital. Witkoff arrived in St Petersburg on Wednesday for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Russian news agencies reported. At the White House, President Donald Trump stepped up the pressure on Zelensky to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again. “We want Zelensky to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.” If that does not happen, “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing”. The conversation with Rubio came after Zelensky told a bipartisan group of US lawmakers Monday that he believes “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us”. Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air defence interceptors that it needs to stop Russian ballistic missiles, according to Zelensky, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine. The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country’s use of Starshield, the military-grade version of US company SpaceX’s satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations. Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia, a move that Zelensky slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow’s full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February. Zelensky said he had “a substantive conversation” with Rubio. “I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position,” Zelensky said on social media. Rubio, who arrived Tuesday in India on an official trip, denied that the US is withholding assistance from Ukraine. “Nothing has changed,” he told reporters. The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he said. European countries, worried about Russia’s plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow’s ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any fall-off in US supplies, but some key assets are American-made. European countries and European Union institutions have allocated €237 billion (US$266 billion) to support Ukraine, compared with €115 billion (US$129 billion) from the US, according to Germany’s Kiel Institute, which tracks assistance to Kyiv. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday questioned whether US negotiators have been honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace. “Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin’s terms “because Europe has been supporting Ukraine,” Kallas said. Four people were killed and 27 others wounded, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said. Three were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged, police said. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, while hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police. On Tuesday morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. The dead included the driver of a shuttle bus that was hit. The bus transports people from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery. Two more people were killed in a Russian attack Tuesday on warehouses on the outskirts of Dnipro in central Ukraine, authorities said. National grid operator Ukrenergo reported power outages in 12 regions of Ukraine following the Russian attacks. The Russian Defence Ministry said in a statement that its forces carried out drone strikes on logistics centres, port infrastructure and three cargo ships in the port of Reni in the Odesa region. It said that another bulk carrier was hit at sea on its way to Odesa. Meanwhile, air defences intercepted 136 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.

title: Meet Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans, who appears fully nude in documentary You Can See Everything
description: The A24 production, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim and shot before Holmes was sent to prison, has made a big box office debut.
content: Nearly five years after Theranos founder and CEO Elizabeth Holmes was convicted of fraud, the disgraced entrepreneur is back in the spotlight, thanks to Nathan Fielder’s acclaimed new documentary You Can See Everything. Directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the A24 production notched a US$15 million opening at the North American box office, despite only being screened at 855 theatres. It is the biggest debut for a documentary since Michael Moore’s 2004 hit Fahrenheit 9/11, which raked in US$23.9 million. You Can See Everything follows Holmes, now 42, and her 34-year-old partner, Billy Evans, during the 34 days before she began serving her prison sentence of 11 years and three months in Bryan, Texas. The directors were invited by the couple into their rented home in Del Mar, California, for the R-rated documentary. At one point, Evans appears fully nude on screen. “It seems like he really had something he wanted to show to us and to the world,” Oppenheim told Vulture. So, what do we know about Billy Evans? Read on to find out. What is Billy Evans’ background? William “Billy” Evans grew up in San Diego with parents Susan and William Evans. His grandparents, William and Anne Evans, founded the Evans Hotel Group, which owns three Southern California resorts and boasts a notable private collection of antique cars. Evans is the eldest of three siblings and attended Francis Parker School, a private institution, per Wired. According to the outlet, a contemporary described him as a “classic spoiled rich kid”. He later attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he earned a bachelor’s degree in economics. What does Billy Evans do? According to his LinkedIn, Billy Evans is the CEO of the biotechnology research company Haemanthus, which he founded in 2022. In a 2025 X post, Haemanthus insisted that it was not “Theranos 2.0” and denied Holmes’ involvement in the company. Evans previously worked as a special projects manager at Luminar Technologies, which filed for bankruptcy in December 2025, per Forbes. His work history also includes a stint at LinkedIn as a strategy and leadership programme analyst. How did he meet Elizabeth Holmes? According to Forbes, Evans met Holmes in 2017 through a mutual friend at San Francisco Fleet Week. The pair reportedly got engaged at a Taylor Swift concert in August the following year. They welcomed their son, William Holmes Evans, on July 10, 2021. In February 2023, the birth of their daughter, Invicta, was reported. Evans supported Holmes through her trial and regularly visits her at Federal Prison Camp Bryan. Holmes is set to be released on February 22, 2030, after her sentence was reduced by two years. People reported that she will move to a halfway house in Del Valle, Texas, in August 2027.

title: Indonesia holds off foreign aid despite ongoing forest fire crisis
description: Minister claims the country can manage as haze worsens and international offers arise.
content:
Indonesia has held off on seeking foreign aid from its neighbours to contain months-long forest fires fuelling a toxic transboundary haze, insisting it is “still capable” of handling the crisis.
Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs Dudung Abdurachman attributed the decision to Jakarta’s delay in declaring the fires a national disaster, despite Japan’s Self-Defence Forces conducting aerial firefighting operations in the country last month. The deployment follows a pact signed in May between Jakarta and Tokyo to expand defence cooperation, including disaster relief.
“This means that if a national disaster is declared, assistance from foreign countries would become available,” Dudung said on Monday, as quoted by local news outlet Kompas.
“It’s not about the assistance itself. There would also be many technical challenges on the ground.”
National disaster declarations are rare in Indonesia, which last assigned the label to the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020. Even cataclysmic events such as the 2018 Lombok earthquake and last year’s Sumatra floods – which left hundreds dead – were not designated national disasters.
Daniel Johan, a lawmaker heading a parliamentary panel on forestry, said the declaration could unlock more government funding and manpower for firefighting.
Environmental campaigners have slammed the government’s response. Greenpeace activist Belgis Habiba rebuked officials for failing to act quickly despite early warnings that the El Nino weather phenomenon would exacerbate dry conditions.
“This situation hasn’t been handled seriously, [as] evidenced by the failure to declare the [fires and haze] a national disaster,” The Jakarta Post quoted her as saying last week.
Indonesia’s apparent U-turn comes just days after Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said the regional aid mechanisms were “already in progress” and had received presidential approval, according to state news agency Antara.
Dudung said Indonesia had the resources to extinguish the blazes, which have blanketed parts of Southeast Asia in a thick smog, forcing school closures, disrupting flights and triggering a spike in respiratory illnesses and demand for medical oxygen and air purifiers.
“For now, we are still capable. Our country is still capable,” he told Malaysian state news agency Bernama on Monday. “As I said earlier, Malaysia has offered assistance, and if a national disaster is declared, that assistance will be extended.”
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Sunday that Kuala Lumpur had proposed an Association of Southeast Asian Nations-level mechanism to boost coordination and preparedness against the haze. Last month, Malaysia offered to deploy 52 personnel, three helicopters and an aircraft, but Reuters reported that no ⁠follow-up action had been taken.
Singapore has also renewed its offer of support. According to news channel CNA, Home Affairs Minister K. Shanmugam on Monday reiterated the city state’s readiness to help, while placing the blame for the fires on corporate greed.
A September report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air said that fire-related haze caused 1,700 deaths in Indonesia the previous month.
The fires also threaten endangered orangutans across six provinces where authorities have mobilised over 60,000 personnel and appointed a new disaster mitigation agency chief to quell the flames.
National police chief Suyudi Ario Seto on Monday said that authorities are investigating 98 firms linked to the fires, adding that their identities would be disclosed once evidence gathering was complete.
According to The Straits Times, the companies under investigation include firms from “neighbouring countries”.

title: Hong Kong Premier League coach urges local football chiefs to help grow game in city
description: Kitchee manager Inigo Calderon ‘trying to do my part’ to attract fans, while saying he is unsure about merits of David Silva playing one game.
content: Inigo Calderon has called on local football chiefs to join him in “trying to do my part” to grow the game in Hong Kong. The Spaniard’s easy-on-the-eye Kitchee team delivered “probably the most complete” performance of his 15-month reign to embarrass Lee Man 5-1 on Monday, leaving him to conclude that it was a good time to say his piece because “we won and I’m not making excuses”. Unhappy with kick-off times and routinely poor playing surfaces, head coach Calderon said a 6.30pm start had aided the top-of-the-table spectacle, favourably comparing it with a 0-0 draw against North District back in August when both sets of players cooked in sweltering afternoon temperatures. Reigning champions Kitchee’s victory over Lee Man drew a crowd of 3,393 to Mong Kok Stadium, while the local Premier League has averaged four-figure gates for matches this season. It is a decade since a full top-flight campaign recorded average attendances of more than 1,000 in 2015-16. “We can do things to make the show better, and when it’s better more people come,” Calderon said. “If you don’t look after the pitches, and you play at times when it’s not easy, it affects the show. “They gave us good conditions [against Lee Man], and I think the people who watched will come back. “The football culture in Hong Kong is massive. Every kid plays, and the pitches are always full, but you see the stadiums empty. I don’t like it. I try to do my part, to play in a way that is attractive for fans and, hopefully, we can keep growing, because I think everything is there for Hong Kong to grow its football.” In Asier Illarramendi, Kitchee boast a former Real Madrid and Spain midfielder. His teammate and compatriot Victor Camarasa has played in the Spanish and English top flights, and was an under-21 international. It is another Spaniard who has been generating noise around Hong Kong football, however, with 2010 World Cup winner and former Manchester City forward David Silva poised to play for Supreme Sha Tin against BC Rangers next month. Although he said it was a “good thing that more fans will come to that game”, Calderon was unsure about the merits of parachuting in a star name for one match. “I have to be careful what I say,” he said. “It’s good that big players are coming, and I respect what [Supreme] are doing. We have good players, and they stay here with the coaches: not just one day and that’s it. “But David Silva is a great player.” With the city representative team currently underwhelming, their Fifa Asean Challenge Cup success notwithstanding, it is on Kitchee to keep Hong Kong football on the map in their AFC Champions League Two campaign. They drew 1-1 against Kuching City last Thursday, after a complicated and tiring journey to Malaysia, following a stalemate with Gangwon FC in their opening match. They face group leaders Phnom Penh Crown in Cambodia next Thursday. Calderon said he had gasped when he saw the fixture computer had sent Kitchee to Lee Man four days after the Kuching fixture, but that his side were “embracing the challenge” of trying to compete on five fronts, with three domestic knockout trophies also up for grabs. “I was tired before the [Lee Man] game, so I can’t imagine how the players felt, but we knew this season would be more difficult because of these things,” he said. “We’re not going to make any excuses, we’re going to try to find solutions. We’re happy with the players because they’re working really hard.” Against Lee Man, Kitchee blended their characteristic possession football with a succession of passes launched beyond the hosts’ hopelessly vulnerable high defensive line. “It was probably the most complete game [of my time in charge],” Calderon said. “Even though we’re Kitchee, we can play long. There are times we have to play 25 passes, but, sometimes, one pass is enough to win a game.”

title: Night of violence lingers over Paris as one Chinese cafe owner counts the costs of protest
description: French government admits it was unprepared for the level of chaos unleashed by rioters, which forced civilians to protect their businesses.
content: Two days have passed since the scenes of chaos and looting on Saturday, but walking down Rue Beaurepaire in Paris on Monday, one can still smell smoke in the air, likely coming from the heaps of burned rubbish and charred bicycles left among the smashed shopfronts. Among the most damaged was La Barrique, a local bar-tabac – a French establishment combining a cafe, bar and tobacco shop – that was burned down by rioters. Its owner, Aline Li, a middle-aged Chinese immigrant from Zhejiang province, was overseeing workers boarding up the ruin. Her face still bore cuts and bruises from the attack on Saturday, but she also began to smile, greeting the residents who came by to check in on her. “I’m fine, what matters is that you guys are also OK,” she said. The image of Li in tears on Sunday, standing in front of her torched bar, was shown across French media and on prime-time news. She became the unfortunate face of the roughly 3,000 businesses hit by looting across France, capturing the real cost of the worst urban riot France has seen in years, and of what the French government has since admitted was an intelligence failure that left police unable to do their job. It all started at around 2.30pm on Saturday when Li saw the protest at nearby Place de la Republique was turning into something violent. She and her family took in the tables and put down the metal gates. Just as they thought they could safely wait out the turmoil from inside the cafe, the family heard shouts of, “Le tabac, le tabac, le tabac !” – referring to Li’s corner bar – before rioters lifted the metal gates and started to smash windows and doors. Rioters then attacked her. “We said to ourselves, there is nothing we can do, so we just let them loot,” she told journalists gathered outside the bar on Sunday. Li said she was shocked by the children she saw in the group of looters, recalling that the first face she saw was that of a child, who she guessed was roughly 12. The shop was eventually torched. She was one of many business owners who found themselves having to defend their own properties as police were overwhelmed by the situation. “When we called the police they told us they could not intervene,” said Audelia Sitbon, the owner of a looted pharmacy on the same street. “I have a patient who has a treatment worth of €13,000 (US$14,000) that was in my fridge, the one that they burned … he was waiting for his medicine … there are people who need their medication,” she told reporters in tears. French Commerce Minister Serge Papin said on Monday that at least 3,000 businesses had been directly affected by the riots. A day earlier, Alexandre Bompard, Carrefour CEO and president of the French retail federation FCD, estimated the damage at “several hundred million euros”. Facing the high level and cost of damages, the French government admitted that it had mismanaged the situation. While some 550,000 people took part in Saturday’s protests across France, the government was originally only expecting around 200,000 people to show up, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told France Inter radio on Monday. “It means that the police presence we have in place was in certain places in asymmetry to the volume of protesters … but also troublemakers, looters and ultra-left militants,” he said. Nunez said he presented his resignation to French President Emmanuel Macron but was rejected. Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin admitted on Monday that there was an intelligence failure. The government declared partial curfews for Paris and some other major cities on Monday. Macron’s televised speech on Sunday was criticised by most major political parties. With calls for further protests on each of the next three Saturdays, the situation in France is unlikely to calm down any time soon.

title: Suzhou Dongshan’s US$1.8b Hong Kong IPO trails expectations amid US trade risk concerns
description: With the overallotment, the circuit board maker could raise US$1.84 billion, compared with expectations of up to US$3 billion a week ago.
content: Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing raised less than expected in its Hong Kong initial public offering (IPO), as investors weighed potential US trade restrictions on its optical modules business amid the city’s cautious appetite for mega listings, analysts said. The company has started taking investor orders for a Hong Kong listing, offering 113.7 million shares at a maximum price of HK$93.80 per share, according to its prospectus on Tuesday. A total of 20 cornerstone investors have agreed to buy US$680 million worth of the shares. They include JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s asset management arm, Alibaba Group Holding, Jane Street Capital, Montage Technology, Yonglian Investment, LMR and Foresight Funds. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. The cornerstone tranche would account for up to 50 per cent of the total funds set to be raised, Dongshan Precision said. With the overallotment option, the Chinese printed circuit board maker could raise about HK$12.3 billion (US$1.84 billion), compared with market expectations of US$2 billion to US$3 billion a week ago. “Since H-share pricing must reference the A-share with a discount, the fall in the parent stock directly reduced the H-share fundraising size,” said Jasper Chan, manager at Phillip Securities (Hong Kong). He said a cautious market appetite for mega IPOs had led to reduced cornerstone commitments as well. The Hong Kong debut price reflects a discount of 35 per cent to the 122.15 yuan closing price of the firm’s Shenzhen-listed shares on Monday. Dongshan Precision entered the optical module business in September 2025 by acquiring Source Photonics, a key driver of its gross profit surge in the first half this year. However, the business was under threat because of market speculation about potential US restrictions. Morgan Stanley issued a report on October 1 that said the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) might include 3.2-terabit-per-second (3.2T) high-speed optical modules on its restricted list as early as October, requiring 65 per cent of the bill-of-materials value to originate from US firms for import eligibility. The FCC has not proposed or enacted formal rules restricting Chinese-made optical transceivers, according to Dongshan Precision’s prospectus. The company said its optical transceiver revenue reached 19.2 per cent of total revenue in the first half of 2026. Besides its plants in Chengdu and Changzhou, subsidiary Source Photonics has manufacturing capacity outside mainland China, offering supply flexibility for overseas deliveries, the prospectus said. Optical transceivers are critical components in AI data centres, converting electrical signals into optical signals to enable high-speed data transmission between servers and computing equipment. The Suzhou-based firm has seen its Shenzhen shares drop 26 per cent this month to a near six-month low, bringing its market capitalisation to 223 billion yuan (US$33.34 billion). Dongshan Precision expects to list its shares in Hong Kong on October 28. UBS, Guotai Haitong Securities, GF Securities and Citic Securities are joint sponsors for the Hong Kong listing, according to its prospectus.

title: Why are protests sweeping across Europe, from Spain to Portugal, France and Albania?
description: Political turmoil and clashes in France, Belgium, Italy, Albania, Spain and Portugal are fuelled by soaring rents, dilapidated schools, inflation and reported c
content:
Discontent with the state of schools, growing fuel costs, declining public services and a housing crisis have created perfectly stormy weather for an autumn of protests in Europe.
Crowds have taken to the streets for weeks in major cities, resulting in arrests, looting, injuries and violence across France, Italy and Albania. In Spain and Portugal, tent camps have sprung up in protests against unattainable rents and housing costs.
Young Europeans are experiencing “a strong sense of uncertainty and a lack of control,” said Maria Silvestre, professor of sociology at the University of Deusto in Spain. “And when specific situations come together, a spark suddenly ignites that is capable of channelling that discontent and driving people into the streets.”
Cities have turned into battlefields as top European Union economies, including France, Italy and Spain, approach pivotal elections, while far-right parties have made electoral gains in Germany and could do so elsewhere.
It also comes as Europe faces a critical moment in its support for Ukraine, with President Donald Trump making overtures to President Vladimir Putin even as Russia is blamed for increasingly frequent hybrid attacks in Nato countries.
Many of the protests have been fuelled by frustrated young people. Here’s a look at what’s driving the unrest.
In France, which has a centuries-old tradition of popular protest, high schoolers have staged blockades and demonstrations for more than three weeks, demanding more resources for schools they call understaffed and dilapidated, especially in lower-income neighbourhoods.
The protests then broadened as members of the General Confederation of Labour (CGT), one of France’s largest trade unions, and other activists joined in while students paused for a fall break.
The movement now includes demands over rising living costs and public services.
Despite hundreds of thousands of people marching peacefully, the weekend’s unrest led to 2,400 arrests and serious disturbances in parts of France, including looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux.
In Limoges, flames engulfed the 19th century City Hall and nearly destroyed the building. Some schools were set on fire. As students and rioters threw firebombs and law enforcement responded with tear gas, hundreds were injured.
French President Emmanuel Macron condemned Saturday’s violence, accusing far-left activists of trying to foment chaos by attacking buildings and police.
“Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” Macron said Sunday in a rare televised address.
In Spain, elementary and secondary school teachers in Madrid began an indefinite strike last week to demand better pay and working conditions. Discontented teachers staged similar walkouts elsewhere in Spain this year.
In Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol, tarpaulin tents have blanketed the square for weeks to protest rising housing costs, sparked by the eviction of Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman who later died while hospitalised. Smaller protest camps followed in other Spanish cities.
The public pressure led the ruling Socialist government to approve affordable housing measures, but they lacked support in Parliament, triggering a snap election announced by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez for November. A general strike also was called for November – the first in 14 years.
Similar housing protests have sprung up in Portugal’s largest cities, Lisbon and Porto, and in Barcelona, a focal point of Spain’s overtourism and housing challenges.
Spain’s minimum wage is €1,221 (US$1,370 or HK$10,760), while the average monthly rent for an 80-square-metre flat is around €1,130, according to an analysis by the business newspaper Expansion.
“Most of my pay cheque goes to the rent. My roommate struggles to make ends meet just like I do,” said Diana Manzanares, a 20-year-old waitress at the Madrid encampment. “This is my reality and the reality of most of us living in this city.”
“Italia in Piazza”, or Italy in the Streets, has galvanised thousands of demonstrators, voicing demands for better employment, healthcare, education and access to housing, as well as higher wages. Inflation in Italy rose to 4.2 per cent in September, surpassing the euro zone’s 3.8 per cent, according to government data.
The peaceful marches were followed by violent riots in Turin and Bologna, and in Italy’s finance and fashion capital of Milan, where masked rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire. Milan police said 271 people were arrested – most of them minors – and 14 security officers were injured during two days of unrest.
Now a newly formed group calling itself the “Oct. 17 Movement” has announced what it describes as a “permanent mobilisation” to demonstrate every Saturday at 3pm in cities across Italy.
Anti-government protests have stretched over a week in Albania’s capital of Tirana, with clashes escalating after high school and university students joined the broad anti-government “Flamingo” movement calling for Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
Rama has condemned the protesters as “ideologised and radicalised” by Antifa, an umbrella term for loosely organised far-left militants in the United States, where Trump has designated the movement a terrorist organisation.
Ending corruption is a major demand of the movement, which was named for the natural habitat of flamingos in an area where Rama’s government agreed to allow a major luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law. They also want protections for healthcare, education and public pensions, according to its website.
In Serbia, the university students leading mass anti-corruption protests for nearly two years are challenging an attempted return to power by the Balkan country’s former populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in parliamentary elections.
The former authoritarian president is aiming to be named prime minister after the October 25 vote. The youth-backed Students’ List party is believed to be running close to Vucic’s party, making the outcome uncertain and fuelling fears of possible violence.

title: Review | Bird of Paradise review: Catherine Chau takes up pole dancing in light-hearted family drama
description: The lighthearted film led by Catherine Chau has its fair share of funny and sweet moments, but its drama relies on remarkably low stakes.
content: 2.5/5 stars In Bird of Paradise, a dutiful middle-aged Hong Kong woman takes up pole dancing and shatters her thankless routine of cooking and cleaning for her family. Marking the feature debut of writer-director Joey Wu Chui-yi, this perfectly pleasant family drama offers an easy watch for viewers seeking light-hearted domestic quibbles. More sophisticated audiences, however, will find it slightly shallow and naive. Crucially, the film provides a rare leading role for Catherine Chau Ka-yee. She plays 46-year-old Yuen, a frustrated housewife who dedicates her life to her teenage son, Hang (Jayden Cheung Dik-man of Queerpanorama), and her square, unappreciative husband, Ming-lam (Peter Chan Charm-man). Yuen’s subjugation is total – she even executes Ming-lam’s meticulously dictated breakfast plans every morning. Her rigid domesticity fractures when she impulsively signs up for a pole-dancing course at a friend’s gym, discovering a vibrant life beyond her spotless flat. The film’s central plot hinges on a massive coincidence. Shan (Yeung Nga-man) is Hang’s lively classmate and not-so-secret crush, as well as a target of Ming-lam, a teacher at her school. As the school’s disciplinary head, he sees Shan as a problem student because of her penchant for earrings and marginally shortened hemlines. Conveniently, Shan is also Yuen’s best pal in pole-dancing class. This connection brings Yuen closer to her son as she offers romantic advice, while Shan serves as the narrative device guaranteeing Ming-lam’s discovery and disapproval of his wife’s new hobby. Although Bird of Paradise has its fair share of sweet and amusing moments, surprise is not on the agenda. Its drama relies on remarkably low stakes, and the few confrontations pass without lingering resentment; even an awkward early scene in which Yuen catches Hang masturbating is swiftly swept aside. Wu’s script champions the necessity of tending to one’s emotional needs. Yuen’s courage to finally put herself first is further inspired by her free-spirited mother (Elaine Jin Yan-ling), a 70-year-old matriarch who continues to casually date men young and old.
