While the film’s pole-dancing sequences are nicely captured, the broader narrative lacks a realistic exploration of mid-life crisis and ennui – a superficiality perhaps betraying the young director’s lack of first-hand exposure to the subject. In particular, Ming-lam is boringly conservative, so his eventual change of heart feels utterly unconvincing. After being reminded of the notion of “risking one’s life to do something”, he goes home to search for the concept’s meaning online. Despite its shortcomings, Bird of Paradise remains a wholesome watch thanks to Chau’s natural charisma. After years of stealing scenes in supporting parts, it is a distinct pleasure to see her break out in her own vehicle. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Chinese carmakers gear up European production to sidestep tariffs, import quota
description: Analysts say idle factories in Europe could be prime targets as Chinese carmakers look to localise production.
content: Chinese carmakers, facing a European Union import quota targeting their hybrid electric vehicles (EVs), are gearing up for more local production to reinforce their go-global drive. They plan to either splash out billions of yuan to set up their own factories or tap international marques’ idle plants to build their vehicles, looking to sustain a sales boom in one of the world’s major automotive markets. “Global growth shifts from exporting vehicles to Europe to producing them locally, from price-led market share gains to margin-led positioning, and from a single export channel to a multimarket footprint,” Morgan Stanley analysts said in a research note issued last week after Beijing and Brussels agreed on an import quota for Chinese-made hybrid vehicles. “Such a development would favour Chinese EV leaders with the scale, balance sheets and European manufacturing plans already in motion to pivot quickly.” On October 9, China and the EU reached an “understanding” on trade that would see Brussels impose a quota on imports of Chinese-made hybrid vehicles from next year. The European Commission was likely to grant an initial annual quota of 350,000 units, and would increase it by 6 per cent a year over the following four years, Bloomberg reported. Analysts said idle plants in Europe could be highly sought after by Chinese carmakers looking to localise production to sidestep the import quota on hybrid cars and high tariffs imposed on pure EVs. The EU currently subjects Chinese-made pure electric cars to tariffs ranging from 17.8 per cent to 45.3 per cent. Our plans for local production in Europe are largely set Zhao Fei, Changan Automobile On October 12, Zhao Fei, president of state-owned Changan Automobile, told a news conference during the Paris Motor Show that it would be able to produce 180,000 units in the EU in 2028 through a tie-up with a local partner, and would increase that annual production capacity to 300,000 cars in 2030. “Our plans for local production in Europe are largely set,” Zhao said. “We are in active discussions with our partner and expect to announce the details before the end of this year.” BYD, the world’s largest EV manufacturer, was considering building factories in France and Spain, executive vice-president Stella Li told Bloomberg on October 12. The Shenzhen-based company announced early this year that its plant in Hungary would begin operations in the fourth quarter of this year. “Chinese carmakers have been cautious on setting up their own factories in Europe because of concerns about costs and regulatory hurdles,” said Qian Kang, the owner of a vehicle circuit board factory in Zhejiang province. “They are now seeking to create joint-venture factories or enlist local contract manufacturers to make their cars in Europe, where demand for their products is rising quickly.” Two years ago, Chery Automobile said it would build cars with Spanish partner Ebro at a former Nissan factory in Barcelona, and expected to begin deliveries at the end of this year or in the first quarter of 2027. In early May, Dutch-based multinational Stellantis said it had deepened its strategic partnership with Chinese EV maker Leapmotor, aiming to add an EV production line at a Spanish factory previously ­earmarked for petrol-powered Opel vehicles. Stellantis owns a 21 per cent stake in Leapmotor. In July, Geely Auto, China’s second-largest carmaker, signed a deal with Ford Motor to use the American company’s redundant capacity in Spain to build its EVs. China shipped 452,000 hybrid cars to the EU in the first half of this year, according to data from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association. JPMorgan said in a report released last week that the quota could “deal a serious blow to Chinese carmakers” as it estimated that the country’s exports of hybrid vehicles to the EU could top 800,000 units this year. Chinese EV makers, buoyed by government subsidies and consumers’ willingness to embrace new technologies, have leapfrogged their European and American counterparts in developing smart pure electric and hybrid cars, sparking European fears about exports of excess production to the EU. The EV issue “is something that China needs to be aware of because it will create more and more restrictions and will create more and more friction between the two economies,” said Carlo Diego D’Andrea, vice-president of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China and chairman of its Shanghai chapter. “Some European car plants may be closed, and some of them may be restructured in order to optimise the workflow,” he said. D’Andrea added that negotiations on China’s EV exports were at a crucial stage as Beijing and Brussels attempted to find common ground to stabilise trade relations.

title: Indonesia backtracks on foreign aid to fight toxic haze choking Southeast Asia
description: Jakarta insists it can contain forest fires alone, holding back regional aid while refusing to declare a national disaster.
content: Indonesia has held off on seeking foreign aid from its neighbours to contain months-long forest fires fuelling a toxic transboundary haze, insisting it is “still capable” of handling the crisis. Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs Dudung Abdurachman attributed the decision to Jakarta’s delay in declaring the fires a national disaster, despite Japan’s Self-Defence Forces conducting aerial firefighting operations in the country last month. The deployment follows a pact signed in May between Jakarta and Tokyo to expand defence cooperation, including disaster relief. “This means that if a national disaster is declared, assistance from foreign countries would become available,” Dudung said on Monday, as quoted by local news outlet Kompas. “It’s not about the assistance itself. There would also be many technical challenges on the ground.” National disaster declarations are rare in Indonesia, which last assigned the label to the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020. Even cataclysmic events such as the 2018 Lombok earthquake and last year’s Sumatra floods – which left hundreds dead – were not designated national disasters. Daniel Johan, a lawmaker heading a parliamentary panel on forestry, said the declaration could unlock more government funding and manpower for firefighting. Environmental campaigners have slammed the government’s response. Greenpeace activist Belgis Habiba rebuked officials for failing to act quickly despite early warnings that the El Nino weather phenomenon would exacerbate dry conditions. “This situation hasn’t been handled seriously, [as] evidenced by the failure to declare the [fires and haze] a national disaster,” The Jakarta Post quoted her as saying last week. Indonesia’s apparent U-turn comes just days after Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said the regional aid mechanisms were “already in progress” and had received presidential approval, according to state news agency Antara. Dudung said Indonesia had the resources to extinguish the blazes, which have blanketed parts of Southeast Asia in a thick smog, forcing school closures, disrupting flights and triggering a spike in respiratory illnesses and demand for medical oxygen and air purifiers. “For now, we are still capable. Our country is still capable,” he told Malaysian state news agency Bernama on Monday. “As I said earlier, Malaysia has offered assistance, and if a national disaster is declared, that assistance will be extended.” Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Sunday that Kuala Lumpur had proposed an Association of Southeast Asian Nations-level mechanism to boost coordination and preparedness against the haze. Last month, Malaysia offered to deploy 52 personnel, three helicopters and an aircraft, but Reuters reported that no ⁠follow-up action had been taken. Singapore has also renewed its offer of support. According to news channel CNA, Home Affairs Minister K. Shanmugam on Monday reiterated the city state’s readiness to help, while placing the blame for the fires on corporate greed. A September report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air said that fire-related haze caused 1,700 deaths in Indonesia the previous month. The fires also threaten endangered orangutans across six provinces where authorities have mobilised over 60,000 personnel and appointed a new disaster mitigation agency chief to quell the flames. National police chief Suyudi Ario Seto on Monday said that authorities are investigating 98 firms linked to the fires, adding that their identities would be disclosed once evidence gathering was complete. According to The Straits Times, the companies under investigation include firms from “neighbouring countries”.

title: Beijing warns London of ‘firm countermeasures’ if it aligns with EU import curbs on EVs
description: Ministry of Commerce responds to British minister’s call for London and Brussels to ‘work together’ on measures targeting Chinese carmakers.
content: As London considers aligning with EU trade measures targeting imports of Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), Beijing has warned of “firm countermeasures” if the UK imposes restrictions. “We hope the UK will abide by World Trade Organization rules and think twice before acting, rather than blindly following the EU,” the Ministry of Commerce said on Monday. “China will closely monitor developments and take firm countermeasures if the UK insists on restricting Chinese electric vehicles.” The ministry’s statement was in response to remarks last week by Anas Sarwar, the United Kingdom’s trade minister, who said Britain and the European Union must “work together and act in lockstep” to address China’s dominance in the automotive sector. The British government was continuing discussions with the EU on potential tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, he said. The UK currently imposes a 10 per cent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles, with no additional country-specific duties, according to the Ministry of Commerce in Beijing. By contrast, the EU imposed additional duties of up to 35.3 per cent on pure electric cars from China in late 2024 after more than a year of anti-subsidy investigations. Lower tariffs have helped make the UK a relatively more accessible market for Chinese EV makers. Chinese brands accounted for 26.7 per cent of the UK’s new-energy vehicle market in the first eight months of the year, the second-highest share among European markets after Italy, according to data released by the China Passenger Car Association this month. The UK is weighing up the imposition of additional tariffs on Chinese EVs even though Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds – Sarwar’s boss – said last week that the British government would not change its trade rules to tax Chinese vehicles because of pressure from Brussels. On Friday, Downing Street said that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” – which aims to increase manufacturing’s contribution to the EU economy. Under a Franco-German proposal, British participation in the scheme would be conditional on aligning with the EU’s trade-defence measures. A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in the UK said early this month that Beijing “firmly opposed” any discriminatory tariffs or restrictions on Chinese products, warning that such measures would “only disrupt the normal order of trade and harm the interests of consumers”.

title: China’s tax authority issues final call for wealthy citizens to declare offshore trust gains
description: Tax bureaus have used a variety of channels, including circulars and text messages, to urge individuals to audit their global trust assets.
content: China’s tax authorities have issued a final call for high-net-worth individuals to disclose their overseas trust gains, a move analysts believe will further raise concerns in Hong Kong and other overseas tax havens used by wealthy Chinese. “We remind relevant taxpayers to promptly review their offshore trust arrangements,” the State Taxation Administration said on its website on Monday, three days ahead of the 90-day grace period set to expire on October 22. “To avoid late payment penalties and other related risks, they must file taxes and make payments in accordance with the law within the transition period.” Ravi Wong Wai-ho, a vice-president at Yan Yun Family Office (HK), said ultra-high-net-worth individuals were more likely to face audits but it was unlikely that everyone would immediately be pursued for back taxes. “Clients from the mainland are naturally somewhat concerned that investing in Hong Kong or acquiring Hong Kong-based assets could lead to large tax liabilities,” Wong said. “However, given the alternative – where their capital remains trapped and is unable to move offshore – they would rather pay the taxes, as doing so offers a legal and compliant way to resolve the issue.” Wong added that clients still preferred using trusts even if it meant having to pay taxes, since trusts offer more effective asset segregation than holding assets as an individual. “They believe that by placing assets into a trust – holding them in the name of the trust rather than as an individual – it becomes significantly more complex and difficult to trace them back to the ultimate beneficial owner,” Wong said. Beijing’s scrutiny of overseas gains was flagged in a joint circular by the Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration on July 24, in which the regulators ordered Chinese tax residents holding offshore trust arrangements to declare their gains and pay a 20 per cent income tax. Many wealthy mainland Chinese families have set up overseas trusts, primarily in Hong Kong, the Cayman Islands and other jurisdictions considered tax havens. “Tax authorities will provide taxpayers with detailed tax guidance and administrative services, helping them fulfil their tax obligations in accordance with the law and safeguard their own rights and interests,” the government notice said. In the past three months, tax bureaus across the country have used a variety of channels, including circulars and text messages, to urge relevant individuals to audit their global trust assets and submit disclosures. Reports that some wealthy families sold their shares or sought loans – as was the case for Zhang Yong, founder of Chinese hotpot chain Haidilao – have led to speculation that the tax rule will be implemented strictly. An insider in the asset management industry, who requested anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the matter, noted that although many clients from mainland China had recently inquired about the new tax regulations concerning offshore trusts, very few had actually proceeded with the filing process. “Actually, we do advise mainland clients to make a declaration, but they often prefer to wait and see, so they choose not to. Ultimately, whether or not to do so is a decision for the clients themselves,” the person said.

title: ‘Risks tilted to the downside’ amid geopolitical tensions, Paul Chan says
description: Hong Kong’s finance chief urges open trade and investment channels, closer regional cooperation as Apec finance ministers meet in the city for the first time.
content: Geopolitical tensions and uncertainty over trade policies pose downside risks to the global economy, Hong Kong’s finance chief has warned, calling for regional efforts to safeguard stability and keep trade and investment channels open rather than creating new barriers. Speaking at a gathering of Apec finance ministers in Hong Kong on Tuesday, Paul Chan Mo-po told fellow delegates that geopolitical disruption had pushed up energy prices, fuelled inflation, weighed on investment and constrained fiscal space. He said the global economy had shown resilience, but that “resilience is uneven and under strain”. “Geopolitical tensions and trade policy uncertainty cloud the outlook, with risks tilted to the downside,” he said. Hong Kong is hosting the Apec meeting for the first time on Tuesday and Wednesday, with Beijing’s support. It will be followed by the Apec leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen next month. Observers said the city had used the meeting to showcase its financial strengths to the world, helping to dispel misperceptions abroad about Hong Kong’s economy and development while drawing business leaders from around the world. Chan said Asia continued to outpace global growth, driven by technology-related trade and investment, but faced headwinds from prolonged geopolitical disruption and concentrated exposure to AI-related assets. He called for vigilant financial oversight and closer cooperation in information sharing, risk monitoring and emergency response. Predictable, investment-friendly government policies and modernised regulatory frameworks were needed to give businesses the confidence to innovate and invest, he said. “Regionally, we need open channels for trade and investment, not new barriers. Connected markets allow capital to reach productive uses and technologies to be adopted across borders,” he said. “Hong Kong, China stands ready to work with fellow economies to seize opportunities, manage risks and support more resilient, sustainable and inclusive growth across the Asia-Pacific.” At a dinner with delegates, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the meeting marked “a historic occasion for Hong Kong”. “For more than three decades, Apec has demonstrated the power of dialogue and cooperation, promoting economic growth and improving people’s lives across the region,” he said. “Together, we seek to build economies that are more resilient, innovative and inclusive, to create continuing opportunities for our businesses, communities and future generations.” Earlier in the day, at a summit on Greater Bay Area development, Lee expressed gratitude for Beijing’s trust and support in allowing Hong Kong to host the meeting for the first time, as well as its “high recognition” of the city’s status as an international financial centre. “Hong Kong will seize this high-level international platform to share its experience as an international financial centre, showcasing to attending Apec finance officials, representatives of international organisations and the global community our comprehensive development across the economic, financial and social sectors,” he said. Lee said Hong Kong would also highlight its dual advantages as a core city in the Greater Bay Area, connecting national and international opportunities. About 500 guests, including finance chiefs and senior officials from the 21 member economies, are expected to attend the meeting at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. On the sidelines of the meeting, some participating delegations boarded an official sightseeing bus on Monday evening to visit the Xiqu Centre and enjoy cultural performances, experiencing first-hand the essence of Chinese culture and the vitality of Hong Kong society, the authorities said. On Tuesday, delegates joined a series of study visits and tours to experience Hong Kong’s diverse appeal, the government said, adding that itineraries included The Peak, the Chinese Culinary Institute in Pok Fu Lam and Ocean Park in Southern district. Billy Mak Sui-choi, an associate professor in Baptist University’s department of accountancy, economics and finance, said hosting the meeting held significant importance because it would help clear up misperceptions abroad about the city’s economy and development. “This reflects member economies’ recognition of Hong Kong as a suitable host for this international event, a financial platform that allows different countries to pursue regional cooperation,” he said. “Also, after the city’s social unrest in 2019, the Covid-19 pandemic and Sino-US tensions, many countries hold misunderstandings about the city’s development. This event allows them to witness the true Hong Kong, helping dispel their misunderstandings and restore their confidence in the city.” Mak added that the meeting would reinforce Hong Kong’s role as a “superconnector”, deepen financial cooperation among countries and regions, and benefit the further development of the city’s offshore renminbi business. As the meeting will discuss topics including fiscal policies supporting livelihoods and the promotion of inclusive finance, Mak noted that it could enable different nations to use Hong Kong for financing, such as developing payment systems and establishing multilateral rules. Lawmaker Alan Chan Chung-yee, who is also chief operating officer of Miramar Group, said Hong Kong’s hosting of the high-level meeting had pushed high-end hotels in Wan Chai and Causeway Bay to full occupancy. “The occupancy rate of four-star and five-star hotels in Wan Chai and Causeway Bay is actually at 98 per cent, with average room rates exceeding HK$2,000 [US$255],” he said. “The event has attracted business visitors from around the world. Five-star hotels in Tsim Sha Tsui and on the Kowloon side have also benefited, with occupancy rates of 95 per cent.”

Smaller protest camps followed in other Spanish cities. The public pressure led the ruling Socialist government to approve affordable housing measures, but they lacked support in Parliament, triggering a snap election announced by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez for November. A general strike also was called for November – the first in 14 years. Similar housing protests have sprung up in Portugal’s largest cities, Lisbon and Porto, and in Barcelona, a focal point of Spain’s overtourism and housing challenges. Spain’s minimum wage is €1,221 (US$1,370), while the average monthly rent for an 80-square-metre flat is around €1,130, according to an analysis by the business newspaper Expansion. “Most of my pay cheque goes to the rent. My roommate struggles to make ends meet just like I do,” said Diana Manzanares, a 20-year-old waitress at the Madrid encampment. “This is my reality and the reality of most of us living in this city.” Untenable living costs as inflation rises in Italy “Italia in Piazza”, or Italy in the Streets, has galvanised thousands of demonstrators, voicing demands for better employment, healthcare, education, and access to housing, as well as higher wages. Inflation in Italy rose to 4.2 per cent in September, surpassing the euro zone’s 3.8 per cent, according to government data. The peaceful marches were followed by violent riots in Turin and Bologna, and in Italy’s finance and fashion capital of Milan, where masked rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire. Milan police said 271 people were arrested – most of them minors – and 14 security officers were injured during two days of unrest. Now a newly formed group calling itself the “Oct. 17 Movement” has announced what it describes as a “permanent mobilisation” to demonstrate every Saturday at 3pm in cities across Italy. Students in Albania join anti-corruption protests Anti-government protests have stretched over a week in Albania’s capital of Tirana, with clashes escalating after high school and university students joined the broad anti-government “Flamingo” movement calling for Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. Rama has condemned the protesters as “ideologised and radicalised” by Antifa, an umbrella term for loosely organised far-left militants in the United States, where Trump has designated the movement a terrorist organisation. Ending corruption is a major demand of the movement, which was named for the natural habitat of flamingos in an area where Rama’s government agreed to allow a major luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law. They also want protections for healthcare, education, and public pensions, according to its website. In Serbia, the university students leading mass anti-corruption protests for nearly two years are challenging an attempted return to power by the Balkan country’s former populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in parliamentary elections. The former authoritarian president is aiming to be named prime minister after the October 25 vote. The youth-backed Students’ List party is believed to be running close to Vucic’s party, making the outcome uncertain and fuelling fears of possible violence.

title: Fifa president hopes to woo Asian football federations ahead of re-election bid
description: Gianni Infantino meeting AFC chiefs, some of whom criticised proposed US$4.2 billion sell-off plan for the World Cup, in Japan on Wednesday.
content: Gianni Infantino’s campaign for re-election as Fifa president is set to move this week to Japan and a meeting scheduled for Wednesday with the Asian Football Confederation. This comes after Infantino apologised last week in Zurich, Switzerland, to Fifa’s 37-member ruling council – which he chairs – for “mistakes” he made in assembling a now-scrapped US$4.2 billion sell-off plan for the World Cup. The council is the main decision-making body at Fifa with a global spread of officials. The planned meeting with Asian football leaders will be held in a five-star hotel in Tokyo with the media largely excluded. Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, the president of the AFC, expressed early opposition to Infantino and his plan to create a subsidiary to run the World Cup, but may have moved closer to the Swiss, The Athletic has reported. Infantino has offered an open, independent review of how Fifa makes its decisions, in a bid to appease his critics. An Associated Press tally indicates Infantino is close to landing the simple majority of the 211 Fifa member federations he needs to win re-election in March for a fourth term. Some of the deciding votes could come from Asia. The AFC had joined the criticism of Infantino in the wake of the proposed World Cup sell-off, but its members appear far from united. Qatar, the 2022 World Cup host, have expressed support for the Fifa leader while Jordan have declared their opposition. The Fifa Council is scheduled to meet next on December 16 in Doha, Qatar. The Associated Press count shows 87 of the 211 Fifa member federations have indicated support for Infantino – either in individual comments or by endorsing statements of support by their regional confederations. The largest block of opposition comes from Europe. No sitting Fifa president has lost an election since 1974. The deadline for a candidate to compete against Infantino is November 18. Fifa rules state candidates must have “played an active role in association football for two of the last five years before being proposed”. They must also have “declarations of support” from at least five of the 211 members. “Fifa is a massive patronage network,” Jules Boykoff, a political scientist at Pacific University and a former professional football player, said. “It brings in billions from the men’s World Cup and distributes it to football associations around the world in exchange for loyalty.” “The funds that Fifa distributes to football bodies around the world are meant to develop soccer, but there’s scant oversight,” Boykoff added. “To say Fifa is in need of structural overhaul is to make an enormous understatement.”

title: Must-visit places in Uzbekistan, Central Asia’s ‘cultural crown jewel’ on the old Silk Road
description: A trip starting in the former Soviet state’s capital Tashkent reveals architecture, art and food shaped by centuries of cultural exchange.
content: Central Asia is becoming a travel hotspot thanks to its countries’ visa-free entry and improved transport connectivity, and a growing demand among travellers for crowd-free destinations. The region is surrounded by online buzz, but is it just another internet fad? We went to Uzbekistan – said to be Central Asia’s “cultural crown jewel” – to find out. From Hong Kong, we board a flight to Shanghai before connecting to Tashkent, the Uzbek capital. The journey takes 15 hours in total. Direct flights between Hong Kong and Almaty in Kazakhstan are slated to begin in January 2027, and Tashkent is likely to follow suit. The first thing we notice when we arrive in Tashkent is how sleek and clean the paved roads are. Cars have ample space to drive, and pedestrian roads are connected in a wide network. Yandex, a taxi-hailing app, comes in handy when travelling in Uzbekistan. Those who prefer public transport can also ride the city metro. Kosmonavtlar station, with its ceramic medallions honouring various Soviet astronauts, is part of the Tashkent Modernist Architecture Unesco World Heritage site. Positioned along the ancient Silk Road, Uzbekistan was shaped by centuries of conquest, trade and cross-cultural dialogue, with the country’s traditional crafts bearing influences from Turkic, Mongol, Persian and Arabic traditions. Uzbekistan was a Soviet state from 1924 to 1991, and Russian influences can be found in the art and architecture. The art coming out of the country reflects these historical changes, and one of the first stops we make in Tashkent – as part of a press tour organised by the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent (CCA) – is the arts studio of Kyrgyz-Uzbek artist Vyacheslav Akhunov. In the small but sunlit room filled with large canvases and a mess of sketching paper, he reveals his many pieces that subvert Soviet iconography. Flipping through satirical illustrations of Lenin, he explains that he had to hide many of his more critical pieces in inconspicuous folders to avoid persecution. Some of his work is currently on show at the 2026 Venice Biennale. We tour Soviet-era modernist buildings and complexes, including some of the 10 built between the 1960s and 90s that, alongside Kosmonavtlar station, were inscribed onto the Unesco World Heritage List in July 2026. The Chorsu Bazaar, in Tashkent’s old town, is also on this list. The turquoise dome houses an iconic market. I walk in, eyeing textiles and embroidered scarves, and find myself in a maze of vendors selling everything from slabs of horse meat to towering jars of pickles and sugared peanuts, a popular local treat that I end up buying a huge bag of. The young man who sells me loose tea leaves at the bazaar is from Tajikistan. Like many in the region whose families have immigrated and been displaced within Central Asia across decades, he can speak multiple languages. Tourists with Russian proficiency will have an easier time getting around since, after decades under Soviet rule, it remains the lingua franca of the region. Otherwise, Uzbek is a beautiful blend of Arabic, Persian and Russian that reflects Uzbekistan’s proximity to the Middle East. We don’t quite know what to expect of Uzbek cuisine, but are pleased to find kebabs – known as shashlik – and fresh salads packed with sweet mint leaves. There is also mastava, a thick tomato soup native to Uzbekistan and Tajikistan containing lamb and rice and served with the yogurt-like condiment qatiq. The soup is known as the liquid version of pilaf, a rice dish eaten in Central Asia, the Balkans, South Asia and East Africa. While in Uzbekistan, we find it is locally made with julienned carrots, cubes of lamb and a lot of garlic and onions. But we are most excited to try horse meat, a delicacy hard to find in Hong Kong. The meat comes in a salad called norin, in which fine strips of the cured meat are served with wheat noodles. Dressed in a delicious spicy sauce, the horse meat tastes like beef but gamier and sweeter. Soon enough, it is time to head around 300km (185 miles) southwest of Tashkent to Samarkand, a city famous for its Silk Road architecture. The journey takes two hours on the Afrosiyob high-speed train, which passes picturesque mountains and plains along the way. Our first stop in Samarkand is at Registan Square. The square, which features towering buildings adorned with blue and turquoise mosaics as well as colourful dome buildings and the vast mausoleum, was built between the 15th and 17th centuries as the centre of the Timurid Empire, a late-medieval Turkic-Mongol empire that stretched across Central Asia and encompassed parts of modern-day Iran, Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, India and Turkey. Tucked into the walls of the square are small shops where we pick up silk scarves with impossibly intricate stitch designs as mementoes. Another of Samarkand’s must-visit sites is the Shah-i-Zinda necropolis, where, legend has it, the cousin of the Prophet Mohammed was buried. We climb the stairs through the tall, blue-tiled buildings and feel as if we have been transported to a medieval town. Tourists speaking Cantonese, Japanese and English line up to gape at the buildings. We only spend one day in Samarkand before taking a one-hour flight back to Tashkent, from where we will fly back to Hong Kong. But before my night flight, we use our free time to visit the mahallas – neighbourhoods – further out of the city. We take a 15-minute Yandex ride out of the centre and walk into residential areas featuring old one-storEy houses with metal roofs and doors. The ground, made of raw soil or cracked pavement, reveals decades of footprints, and children are playing football outside their homes. These parts of Tashkent are in stark contrast to the modern roads in the city centre. We linger for a while, saying hello to curious youngsters, and return to central Tashkent. There is a lot that the videos online about “Central Asia-maxxing” don’t show – and certainly much more that we have yet to see. Trendy content tends to glamorise the gritty aesthetics of nomadic life and features snapshots of traditional nomadic culture. But Uzbekistan is not a small nomadic country stuck in the past; it is at the forefront of using the arts to preserve its history. It is now time to head back to Hong Kong, with a layover in Beijing. Visiting Uzbekistan was surreal and leaves us determined to return while also exploring Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.

title: Hong Kong ranks second in Asian pension systems, behind Singapore, as ageing tests retirement
description: Global retirement schemes under pressure as life expectancies rise, while experts call for more flexibility around retirees’ income access.
content: Hong Kong’s retirement system remains one of Asia’s stronger performers this year, ranking second and trailing only Singapore. The two remain clear regional leaders, ahead of Malaysia, mainland China, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea, according to a report. The city retained its B grade, with its score edging up from 70.6 to 71.2, ranking 16th globally out of 55 systems, according to the annual Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension report by Marsh, a New York-based global professional services firm, and CFA Institute, on Tuesday. In particular, Hong Kong continued to score strongly on integrity, receiving an A grade of 89.4 for governance, regulation, member protection and communication. Hong Kong’s Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF), its compulsory retirement savings scheme, covers 4.97 million members. The city has no statutory retirement age and most people retire between 60 and 65, with MPF benefits generally accessible from age 65. Mainland China also lifted its overall grade from C to C+, ranking fourth in Asia and narrowing the score gap with third-placed Malaysia. Mainland China, together with Australia, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Panama, has improved their index grades this year. As fertility rates fall and life expectancies rise, the world’s retirement income systems face mounting pressure. Traditional retirement ages of 60 or 65 are becoming increasingly misaligned with the realities of longer, healthier lives, the report said. As the boundary between work and retirement continues to blur – driven in part by the rise of gig and part-time work – pension systems must evolve to reflect the way people actually live and work in later life, it added. “The data makes [it] clear that even the best-performing systems need to keep evolving. No system can afford to stand still in the face of these demographic shifts,” said Tim Jenkins, lead author of the report and partner at Marsh Investments and Retirement. “Retirement design must become more flexible – in when people access income, in how products are structured and in how we think about the line between work and retirement. That flexibility is no longer optional,” Jenkins said. Globally, the retirement income systems of the Netherlands, Denmark, Iceland, Singapore and Israel retained their A grade this year, with index scores above 80. Most other Asian pension systems posted higher overall scores, but either held or fell in regional rankings, as peer economies improved faster. The common challenge is turning retirement savings into sustainable income for longer lifespans, alongside expanding coverage, improving minimum support for lower-income retirees and supporting older workers to remain in the workforce, the report found.

title: Letters | 3 small steps to strengthen minority integration into Hong Kong
description: Readers discuss how to better integrate minority groups, and the Chinese culture of saving.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Hong Kong’s ethnic minority youth are an integral part of our community. The Government’s recent measures on language training, employment support and community care teams are sincere and welcome. They reflect a genuine commitment to inclusion and social cohesion. Many were born and raised here, attend local schools and aspire to build their futures in the city. Their successful integration is therefore not only a matter of fairness, but also of social cohesion, economic participation and Hong Kong’s long-term competitiveness. Yet two basic realities remain. In education, many ethnic minority or non-Chinese-speaking (NCS) students still cluster in a small number of schools, limiting daily interaction with local peers and reducing opportunities to acquire Cantonese. In housing, barriers in parts of the private rental market and affordability pressures often channel many ethnic minority families into older, lower-rent districts and subdivided units, reinforcing patterns of residential concentration even without a formal policy. Against this backdrop, a persistent trilingual requirement (Cantonese, Mandarin and English) for many jobs, including parts of the civil service, can still limit opportunities for some jobseekers in practice, even as the government has in recent years lowered or flexibly adjusted Chinese language requirements for some civil service positions. While many individuals overcome these obstacles through determination and family support, the cumulative effect can still reduce opportunities for interaction, mobility and advancement. Without major reform, three modest steps could strengthen integration. First, the Education Bureau could introduce a small, flexible reserve of places for NCS students in publicly funded schools, with unused places going back into the general pool. This would encourage greater interaction among students and reduce concentrations of NCS students in a small number of schools, without imposing rigid quotas or displacing local students. Second, the Housing Authority could use allocation incentives and bilingual communications to help ethnic minority families live across a wider range of estates, while the Equal Opportunities Commission steps up efforts to address discriminatory practices in the private rental market. Third, in employment, more departments and public bodies could build on the flexibility already introduced by adopting job-oriented Chinese tests and bilingual job notices and publicising these options more clearly. These incremental measures would build on existing efforts, enhance social cohesion and ensure every resident can contribute fully to Hong Kong’s long-term development. They would also send a clear signal that inclusion remains a shared responsibility across schools, employers, public institutions and neighbourhoods. Ahmed Ashfaq, Tsim Sha Tsui Understand the Chinese culture of saving Reading “EU’s ‘moment of truth with trade and China’” (September 21) in your In Focus pages, I was not surprised by the viewpoint expressed by Mr Pascal Lamy. His viewpoint is not without good reason, but like most Westerners, he sees things from their perspective. It’s too big a subject to go into at length, but I would like to present two important facts that the West has to understand when engaging China in trade or war. First, given the Western hostility towards communist China, the country has really had no choice but to fight for its survival; failure might mean plunging the country back into the dark ages of foreign exploitation, internal political turmoil and deep suffering. China had to build up economic strength in as short a period as possible, and certainly before the West could wake up to the fact that it was losing its dominance over a nation of 1.4 billion people. Second, if one visits or lives in China today, one has no grounds to say the Chinese government is not doing its best to raise domestic consumption. Cities are lively and people are willing to spend on better, healthier living. But one has to understand the Chinese have a history and culture of putting aside more money in case of rainy days, compared to the North Americans. This culture has been passed down from generation to generation since the ancient dynasties, because of endless wars, corrupt governments, political turmoil and foreign exploitation. Only someone who does not understand Chinese culture would blame a healthy level of savings among the Chinese on the government not encouraging domestic spending. Edward Shen, Happy Valley

title: InfoSpark: Save these typhoon tips for a rainy day

title: Chinese AI idol’s ‘pregnancy’ stunt sparks backlash, debate over digital boundaries
description: An observer notes that the moment it goes live, it commodifies a sensitive topic that should never be exploited.
content: A Chinese AI girl group has sparked intense online backlash after announcing that one of its virtual members was “pregnant” to explain her departure. BABYQUEEN, a four-member, K-pop-style AI girl group managed in Liaoning province in northeastern China, formed in September and has around 1,100 followers. On October 13, the group posted an announcement written from member Mity’s perspective. Saying she was “pregnant” and would pause all public activities, Mity asked fans to respect her privacy and her new life, without identifying the “father.” The post went viral, attracting more than 78 million views on Weibo and igniting fierce debate over the boundaries of humanlike identities for digital personas. Netizens swiftly expressed outrage and disbelief. “Real idols wouldn’t dare mention pregnancy, yet she chose it from among countless excuses,” one user commented. Others questioned the logic: “Mity doesn’t have a physical body. If AI characters can get pregnant, should they claim maternity leave and childbearing subsidies?” A third quipped: “The team simply ran out of money for tokens and came up with a lame excuse to cut computing costs.” The group’s creators later admitted that managing several AI idols at once had become overwhelming, prompting them to scale back. In an apology, they acknowledged that using pregnancy as an excuse for Mity’s departure was inappropriate and clarified that the entire narrative was fictional. The creators also explained that BABYQUEEN was created by a few young female K-pop enthusiasts as a passion project for their own enjoyment, with no intention of making a profit. However, the apology failed to quell public anger. Critics accused the creators of using women’s bodily experiences as a narrative device and public sentiment as clickbait. “The moment it was posted, it commodified a sensitive topic that should not be exploited,” one observer noted. Another asked: “When humans create fake online personas, it breaches regulations. Does AI get a free pass?” Zhang Yong, a social work scholar from Hubei province in central China, told the SCMP that the incident highlights a structural issue with AI-generated content. “AI lowers the barrier to content creation, making sustained, high-quality storytelling scarce while shifting the burden of fact-checking onto the public,” Zhang said, questioning whether the stunt exploited the emotional and moral weight associated with women’s reproductive experiences. Other analysts pointed to a sharp disconnect in the AI era: “Despite securing vast development resources, AI seems to serve sensationalism and copyright controversies far more often than it delivers the high-value content the public actually expects.” On October 14, a day after the pregnancy announcement, the group released a cover music video of South Korean girl group Aespa’s hit song Next Level, prompting further accusations that the controversy was a cheap publicity stunt to drive traffic to a “poorly executed release.” A few voices, however, called for empathy, saying: “It’s just K-pop fans making content for fun. People don’t need to turn this into a major moral crusade.” Controversies involving virtual influencers are mounting across China. In July, AI actress Fang Taozi gained 400,000 followers through mini-dramas and reportedly charged more than 250,000 yuan (US$37,000) for a 60-second advertisement. However, after reviewing contact lenses in a video and claiming they “felt comfortable after wearing them all day,” her account saw a wave of unfollows and was flagged by market regulators for deceptive advertising.

title: Hong Kong mother spared trial over neglect of chronically underweight daughter
description: Mum placed on three-year bond order after girl lost 4kg in a month, with justice department citing public interest in such decisions.
content: A Hong Kong mother accused of neglecting her 12-year-old daughter who had been chronically underweight has been spared trial as the prosecution agreed to place her on a good behaviour bond, with the justice department saying public interest is generally a key factor in such decisions. The South China Morning Post has learned that prosecutors at West Kowloon Court dropped a child abuse charge against the 53-year-old housewife earlier this month in exchange for her agreeing to a three-year bind-over order. Her daughter dropped from 24.9kg to 20.9kg (55lbs to 46lbs) from March to April in 2023. The mother admitted she sometimes failed to follow doctor’s advice and feed her daughter three times a day. The girl’s weight at the time was about 8kg below the third percentile for her age. She had been underweight since age six, and at one point in 2021 was placed on a feeding tube in hospital. At the hearing on October 8, the mother, who was only identified by her initials FPYC, promised not to commit any child abuse in the next three years. If she violates the bind-over order, she will have to pay HK$3,000 (US$382) and face a more serious penalty. A summary of the facts of the case was not read out in court but was made available to the media. According to the court documents, the girl’s school sent one of its social workers to her home in April after she had been regularly absent for months. The social worker found the home was unsanitary and insisted on sending the girl to hospital, despite her mother’s objections. The girl stayed in hospital for more than a month. The mother was arrested two months after her daughter was released and she was formally charged in May 2025. The mother told police officers she “did not know how to take care of her daughter”. The court document revealed that the girl had been under the “custody of school” upon discharge from hospital, which suggested that a Child and Protection Order had been issued by the Juvenile Court. Such an order is pursued when law enforcement or social workers need the court’s intervention to protect a child. The prosecutors did not identify the type of school the daughter was placed in or the care plan. The court also did not hear an explanation from the prosecution as to why they withdrew the charge. Without commenting on a specific case, the Department of Justice told the SCMP that it must conduct an “objective and professional analysis based on the available evidence and relevant law” when deciding whether to prosecute a case, including child abuse offences. “Generally speaking, prosecutors will decide whether to agree to the bind-over procedure based on the actual facts of the case, the evidence and applicable law. It strictly follows the factors listed in Paragraph 10.7 of the Prosecution Code and ensures it is in the public interest,” it said. According to the code, a bind-over arrangement is considered appropriate for first-time suspects who admit wrongdoing and pledge to be on good behaviour. Other rationales for the order include the views of the victim and the attitude of the suspect towards their wrongdoing. Prosecutors will also consider whether the consequences of a harsher punishment for the offender would be out of proportion to the gravity of the alleged offence. Public interest in pursuing the prosecution, the likely penalty, the age, criminal record and mental state of the suspect can also be taken into consideration. Recently, a coach was spared from prosecution after she admitted to slapping an eight-year-old boy and ordered him to stand under the sun at a training camp in 2024. The 51-year-old woman was originally charged with a count of ill-treatment or neglect by those in charge of a child and another of assault by a person caring for a minor. She agreed to a three-year good behaviour bond in exchange for the charges being dropped.

title: Style Edit: King Fook Jewellery’s Radiant Arc and Pure Edge collections balance curves and geometry
description: The Hong Kong jeweller offers versatile creations that range from fluid, nestling rings to modern geometric statement pieces.
content: One of the many joys of fine jewellery is the dazzling number of ways it can complement the human form. It’s a quality that’s never been more vividly demonstrated than by two new collections introduced by King Fook Jewellery. They take radically different approaches to the business of bodily adornment: one of them, Radiant Arc, presents a sinuously curvilinear profile to the world, while the other, Pure Edge, combines a well-placed dash of sparkle with a bracingly modern, pleasingly geometric quality. The pieces in the Radiant Arc diamond ring collection flow over the fingers like water, in honour of the element that inspired them. An assemblage of sculptural shapes, the 12 rings in the collection, each with openwork detailing along its inner band, are equally at home worn individually or stacked so that their curves nestle against each other. Offered in a combination of white, rose and yellow gold, some of the rings come fully paved with diamonds, while others deploy the coveted rocks more sparsely. The pavé pieces are particularly eye-catching, with brilliant-cut and rose-cut diamonds arranged in an enchanting irregular pattern, one that features spaces between the stones that help to accentuate their radiance. Other stunners in the collection showcase rubies, emeralds and sapphires that have been ingeniously set using a clever reverse setting technique. It means that their pavilions – the pointed section of the stone that’s usually located at the bottom – are proudly on display, making for a unique play of light across their shimmering surfaces. For a bold, contemporary approach to jewellery that offers a subtle and restrained take on the glamour of gold and gemstones, look no further than King Fook Jewellery’s Pure Edge collection. This discreetly shimmering collection comprises necklaces, rings and earrings, all of which come in either rose gold or yellow gold. The stars of the show here are the rectangle cut gemstones that form the centrepieces of each design in the collection. Elongated links of gold are set with these geometrically shaped gemstones, which are complemented by diamonds arranged in straight lines that sometimes form rectangles or rounded lozenge shapes. Some of the rings, meanwhile, take a slightly more maximalist approach, spotlighting elegant pavé arrangements, while preserving the collection’s clean lines and understated elegance. Natural and unique by nature, each diamond and gemstone may reveal slight variations in its characteristics – a reflection of its individuality. title: Style Edit: Chanel reimagines its heritage for spring/summer 2027
description: Matthieu Blazy explores Gabrielle Chanel’s many selves through cloudlike silks, smocked tweed and playful bags for SS27.
content: A wardrobe can be about more than clothes. It can be a time capsule, preserving earlier versions of its wearer: the silhouettes, textures and other details that, over the years, are either abandoned or endure. For Chanel’s spring/summer 2027 collection, artistic director Matthieu Blazy turns that idea towards Gabrielle Chanel herself, tracing the many identities that shaped her approach to dressing. Titled La Conversation – Part Three – Different Faces of the Same Coin, the collection continues the artistic director’s dialogue with the house’s founder. But rather than presenting a chronological retrospective, it considers how Gabrielle Chanel’s changing tastes and experiences might coexist in today’s wardrobe. “Throughout their lives, women become multiple selves, different faces of the same coin,” Blazy explains. “It’s about the women within a woman. And here, it’s about one woman, Gabrielle, who then became Chanel.” The clothes move between the constraints Gabrielle Chanel encountered and the freedom she sought. Edwardian corsetry and tailoring leave their traces in shadow boning, curved bodices, peplums and ruffled collars. However, these details serve as reminders rather than full reproductions: fragments of an earlier fashion taxonomy carried into something lighter and less restrictive. Masculine tailoring provides another source of inspiration. Here, the shapes of formal men’s daywear and evening wear are cut into raw-edged gilets, paired with trousers or reshaped as pencil-skirt suits. The transition between masculine and feminine dress continues in gowns with a 1930s inflection: sequinned and bias-structured, or knitted and beaded, yet made to slip on with the ease of a T-shirt. Room is made for both decoration and practicality. The emphasis on ease is fully brought out in the collection’s softer, flowing pieces. Different weights of printed sheer silk are layered in billowing cuts to suggest cloud formations, moving through the colours and moods of morning, golden hour and nightfall. The effect introduces the passing of time as another layer of the story, expressed through fabric rather than historical pastiche. Meanwhile, birds, particularly swifts and swallows, offer a recurring image of freedom. They appear in buttons, jewellery and embroidery, but the idea extends beyond ornament. Woven and knitted fabrics place a strong emphasis on movement and lightness, making freedom something the wearer can feel as well as recognise. The most direct expression is the new “smocked tweed”. Closing the collection’s journey from jersey underwear to the suit, it gives a familiar house material stretch, suppleness and mobility. Suits worn against bare skin connect the intimacy of underwear with the public language of tailoring. Some might see this as a departure from Chanel’s traditions, but to others it is simply a means of pursuing them differently. Accessories make the same connection between continuity and change. Model Dyanira Hurbuscher begins and ends the collection carrying Gabrielle Chanel’s own 2.55 bag from the Patrimoine archives. Around that anchor sit flap bags old and new, a new classic with a watch-chain lock, cloud bags and a birdcage minaudière with escaped birds. “This is not a historical collection; it’s a collection about Gabrielle Chanel’s layered stories,” says Blazy. In other words, heritage need not dictate a fixed look. It can instead supply the inspiration of a thoroughly modern collection, with self-expression and the freedom to move remaining the constants.

title: Saudi Arabia postpones ‘Davos in the Desert’ summit to 2027 after deadly attacks
description: The flagship event was scheduled for October 26 to 29, but the kingdom has faced repeated missile and drone strikes from Yemen’s Houthis.
content: Saudi Arabia has decided to postpone its flagship investment conference until next year, organisers confirmed in a statement on Monday, following deadly attacks which rocked ‌the kingdom in recent weeks as the Middle East conflict widens, disrupting business. The Future Investment Initiative, or FII, was planned for October 26 to 29, but will now take place in 2027, with a new date to be announced “very soon,” the organisers said. Reuters reported earlier Monday that the in-person event had been scrapped and organisers were weighing postponing the event. The conference, set for its 10th edition, has become ⁠a must-attend event for some of the world’s top financiers. Informally dubbed “Davos in the Desert”, in a nod to ‌the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Switzerland, the state-backed annual event has showcased the kingdom’s ambitious investment plans in a bid to attract billions of dollars needed to fund ‌its economic transformation away from hydrocarbons towards tourism, sports and technology. Expected speakers for this year’s event ⁠included Goldman Sachs CEO and ⁠Chairman David Solomon, Standard Chartered CEO Bill Winters and Citi’s CEO Jane Fraser, according to a draft programme. The US-Israeli war with Iran this ‌year has disrupted the Gulf’s busy calendar of events, with several conferences cancelled, postponed or retooled in the UAE and Qatar in the first part ‌of the ‌year, when the countries bore the brunt of the attacks while Saudi Arabia suffered fewer hits. The kingdom ‌in recent weeks has faced an escalating war with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis, which have struck military, energy and civilian ⁠infrastructure across the country, including state oil company Aramco’s headquarters and Riyadh’s international airport, where strikes killed at least 18 ⁠people and hundreds were wounded this month. FII said it wanted to ensure the event delivered “the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact that our community has come to expect”. Reuters reported last week that ‌the FII organisers considered a ‌hybrid format, allowing executives to tune in remotely. Semafor reported Monday that big banks and private-equity firms have privately relayed safety concerns about attending the event to Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund Governor Yasir Al-Rumayyan, adding that CEOs feel pressure to attend the four-day event.

title: Succession? Survey finds 66% of ultra-rich’s young heirs not ready to take over
description: World’s wealthy worry more about handing over the family firm than political uncertainty, while China, UK step up plans to tax the affluent.
content: Global ultra-rich families worry more about wealth succession than political uncertainty, as most of their next generation are not yet well prepared for the trillions of dollars’ worth of transfer, a survey by Julius Baer showed. The findings came after the Swiss private bank and its partner EY analysed responses from more than 700 financial professionals worldwide who advise ultra-high-net-worth (UHNW) families with wealth of 50 million Swiss francs (US$60.7 million) or more in the latest edition of the Julius Baer Family Barometer. This year, the intergenerational wealth transfer climbed by one notch to the second most concerning societal factor among the polled ultra-rich families, surpassing political stability. Taxation remained the top concern globally, as major billionaire homes like China and the United Kingdom stepped up efforts to tax the affluent this year. However, wealth planning topped the families’ needs with 43 per cent of respondents, far higher than tax and legal issues’ 23.1 per cent in second place, according to the survey. It came as the survey found only 22.6 per cent of the next generation were ready and fully prepared to take over the family business, while nearly 66 per cent of young heirs were not ready for the succession and 11.6 per cent said they were not interested in it. Among families considering a transfer or sale, only 2.3 per cent said they were fully ready. “Families are confronting these questions in real time,” said Christos Anagnostopoulos, head of family office solutions and advisory Asia at Julius Baer. “Does the next generation want to take over? Are they prepared to do so? If not, what alternatives exist?” Julius Baer expected a total of US$15 trillion in wealth to be transferred from individuals with a net worth of US$5 billion by 2030, citing a report by research firm Wealth X. In the coming two decades, the world is projected to record a transition of more than US$83 trillion, according to a UBS report in 2025. With business founders ageing, the transition of family firms to their children has been happening across the world in recent years. In China alone, Hangzhou-based beverage giant Wahaha, Chengdu-headquartered miner Tianqi Lithium and chilli oil producer Lao Gan Ma have seen the next generation take the helm and are being closely watched by the market. Julius Baer found that the wealth transfer had not been fully discussed, with only about 18.5 per cent of the next generation described as “actively participating” in the communication. Among the regions surveyed, Asia reported the lowest level of active next-generation participation in post-sale planning at 8.4 per cent. “Education, gradual participation and guidance from earlier generations remain among the most valuable investments a family can make,” said Maria Eugenia Mosquera, head of wealth planning at the Swiss bank.

title: Alibaba’s RISC-V IP powers over 6 billion shipped chips as tech giant targets AI, autos
description: The milestone comes as Chinese chipmakers seek to reduce dependence on foreign tech amid US-led export restrictions.
content: Alibaba Group Holding’s research arm, Damo Academy, has seen more than 6 billion chips shipped based on its XuanTie RISC-V architecture, marking a milestone as the tech giant doubles down on the open standard in artificial intelligence and automotive systems. Meng Jianyi, chief scientist at Damo Academy, announced the figure on Monday at the annual RISC-V Summit China in Shenzhen. The achievement comes as Chinese companies seek to play a greater role in the global RISC-V ecosystem, an alternative to established chip architectures developed by the likes of Intel and Arm. Alibaba, based in Hangzhou, was an early mover in China’s RISC-V landscape and is expanding its AI infrastructure capabilities. Because the architecture is an open standard, developers can use it to design processors while potentially reducing reliance on foreign chip-design technologies amid US-led export restrictions. Highlighting the architecture’s rapid global adoption, Meng cited forecasts from research firm Omdia that global RISC-V processor shipments would grow by nearly 30 per cent annually and could account for about 25 per cent of the worldwide processor market by 2030. The shipment milestone follows the launch earlier this year of the XuanTie C950, a flagship RISC-V processor that Alibaba called the most powerful of its kind globally. The company said it was developed to support AI agents and other workloads in cloud and high-performance computing environments, and that it delivered more than three times the performance of its predecessor, the C920. The C950 is part of a broader push by Chinese tech companies to develop the computing infrastructure needed for AI. Alibaba, Tencent Holdings and ByteDance are also competing to develop AI agents – software that can autonomously perform tasks on behalf of users or other systems – and integrate them into their apps. RISC-V, short for fifth-generation reduced instruction set computer, is an open-standard instruction set architecture that allows developers to design central processing units (CPUs). It is managed by the non-profit RISC-V International. Free for anyone to use and modify, RISC-V is considered a potential route for China to achieve greater self-sufficiency in chip design. The architecture offers designers an alternative to Intel’s x86 and Arm’s namesake architecture, which power devices running Microsoft Windows and Google Android, respectively. Despite the progress, however, Meng highlighted the engineering challenges involved as Alibaba seeks to improve the performance of its RISC-V CPUs when running large language models. “The biggest challenge lies in co-design,” Meng said in an interview with RISC-V International, released by the Damo Academy last week. “Isolated raw computing power means little; the key is balancing computation, data movement and software optimisation.” For large AI models such as Qwen3.8-27B, he added, techniques such as quantisation, matrix instructions and memory bandwidth must be integrated as a unified system. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: What exactly is an ‘AI city brain’ and should Hong Kong follow Hangzhou’s lead?
description: While the government says it is drawing lessons from mainland cities, scholars caution that Hong Kong must not simply copy their formulas.
content: When Severe Typhoon Dolphin approached eastern China in August, more than 110,000 delivery riders across Hangzhou received automatic alerts and personalised safety guidance on their mobile phones every minute. With a few taps, Hangzhou’s “riders’ code” system navigated them to the nearest shelters, which authorities said had reduced their occupational risks under extreme weather. Behind the tailored and quick support was Hangzhou’s artificial intelligence (AI) urban management system, which had been in place and evolving for more than a decade. This is what the Hong Kong government aims to build: an AI-powered system that links databases on landslide monitoring, fallen trees, water pipes, weather and public complaints, among others. The handling of extreme weather will be the first scenario to put the ambitious initiative to the test. While the top official leading the project confirmed the government was drawing lessons from mainland Chinese counterparts such as Hangzhou and Shanghai, scholars cautioned against simply copying their formulas and said Hong Kong could build a globally recognised benchmark in AI city governance. They argued that Hong Kong should forge its own model anchored in robust data governance and a clear division between government-led AI interventions and civic engagement. Experts also agreed that developing a well-functioning “AI city brain” required reshaping civil servants’ attitudes towards technology adoption, alongside meaningful participation from the private sector. In his recent annual policy address, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the government would build the AI city brain system to enhance city management and strengthen emergency response capabilities, consolidating data held by multiple government bodies and creating a real-time data-sharing environment to support precise decision-making. Learning from the mainland A task force chaired by the city’s No 2 official, Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki, will be set up to steer the project. Chan recently told the South China Morning Post in an exclusive interview that the system could help draw a “full picture” of Hong Kong. Chan also said the government would learn from the experiences of multiple mainland cities, including Hangzhou, Shanghai and Shenzhen. “Based on experience in mainland China … it is proven to be very effective in city management,” he said. “I would say it is a fully integrated hub with most, if not all, of the government departments and city governance systems integrated into one single platform.” Chan said a pilot version of the system targeting extreme weather would be in place before the typhoon season next year. Authorities expected to officially launch the first phase of the AI city brain in the first quarter of 2028, and would connect the database of the 1823 complaint hotline to the system in the third quarter of that year, he added. But Chen Yun, an international relations and public affairs professor at Fudan University in Shanghai, said both Hangzhou and Shanghai had unique advantages in industrial ecosystems or the size of their application scenarios, and Hong Kong should not simply seek to replicate their success. “Hong Kong can, by leveraging its own characteristics, create the first AI-powered city governance benchmark aligning with international privacy standards, widely engaging community stakeholders, and connecting to the international market,” she said. Hangzhou first piloted the idea of an AI city brain in 2016 and launched the first version, focusing on traffic management, the following year, relying on the data infrastructure of locally headquartered tech giant Alibaba, the owner of SCMP. It is now evolving into its third generation, in which the authorities are exploring the use of AI agents, highly capable technology that can automate many tasks. Chen said Hangzhou’s success was largely market-driven, with the government designating many scenarios for the private sector to put its technology into real-world applications. Shanghai, in contrast, adopted a top-down approach, in which the government used its coordinating power to build large-scale infrastructure and open up massive, mega-city scenario environments, such as traffic management and autonomous driving testing involving a population of nearly 25 million, to nurture industry giants and drive regional AI integration, she added. Chen said Hong Kong should instead focus on its advantages in the vibrancy of community organisations, international connectivity that would facilitate the diffusion of Hong Kong’s model, data protection underpinned by the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance and its uniqueness in cross-border data exchange within the Greater Bay Area. She said that the robust privacy ordinance would enable Hong Kong to develop strict data-sharing rules based on the existing legal framework, reducing the costs of trial and error. A Hong Kong model? Professor Danny Lam Wai-fung, director of the School of Governance and Policy Science at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), agreed that Hong Kong should explore its own pathway to AI urban management solutions. “Hong Kong does not have to mirror the mainland because society here is more vibrant,” he said. “Hong Kong should think about whether it should go that far.” Many jurisdictions had similar AI-enabled urban management initiatives, yet none had built systems as intrusive or far-reaching as those on the mainland, Lam said. This restraint, he argued, stemmed from a deliberate calculation of costs that went far beyond fiscal budgets, as far-reaching AI systems could raise doubts over privacy and surveillance. “How much privacy do we wish to sacrifice? How much trust in government are we willing to erode? Mainland cities might marvel at traffic lights that instantly fine jaywalkers, but for other societies, that trade-off is just not worth it.” In Hangzhou, the AI city brain is also about crime-fighting. Officials take pride in police being able to identify suspicious circumstances within five minutes of an incident and apprehend suspects within 20 minutes with the help of multiple AI-powered monitoring systems. This contrasts with the practice in many jurisdictions, where AI solutions stop short of tracking individuals. Virtual Singapore, a 3D digital twin platform developed by the city state, simulates populations with spatial and environmental tools to test urban policy, transit changes and infrastructure projects. Instead of tracking its residents, the platform can test transport infrastructure with agents programmed to simulate commuter flows and even run extreme weather events to stress-test drainage and evacuation systems. In Europe, Spain is a pioneer in smart city governance and has hosted the annual Smart City Expo in Barcelona since 2011. Spanish smart city systems combine extensive fibre-optic infrastructure with Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, open-data platforms and citizen-focused urban design. Under European privacy laws, smart cities such as Berlin, Hamburg and Barcelona must prove their data-collection platforms serve a clear, limited public interest, maintain strict retention limits and conduct data protection impact assessments (DPIAs) before deploying new AI tools. Chan, Hong Kong’s No 2 official, told the SCMP that the AI city brain would not involve any personal data and the system would not be used for surveillance purposes. He also said the collection, storage and use of all data would be strictly governed by privacy laws. Despite having advantages in a number of areas, Hong Kong’s ambition to build an AI city brain also faces many challenges. For CUHK’s Lam, the bottleneck for Hong Kong in developing such a system does not lie in infrastructure or talent, but in the gap between high-level vision and bureau-level operational needs. City leader Lee announced in his policy address that the government would create the post of commissioner for AI under the Digital Policy Office to help bureaus with AI-related tasks. Lam said while centralised steering would be essential, knowledge of both AI and policy issues at bureau level would also be indispensable. “A centralised commissioner cannot think thoroughly, as he or she might know AI well, but the understanding of policies and issues under each bureau could be limited,” Lam said, calling for the cultivation of talent within the civil service with knowledge of both policy and technology. He also urged providing more incentives for bureau secretaries to implement AI-related solutions, while closer collaboration among different bureaus would also be important. Chan, the chief secretary, said Hong Kong’s AI city brain would be hosted on the government cloud and would not engage third-party service providers, to ensure data safety. But Lam identified the need to maintain a large group of in-house talent within the civil service as another challenge and a source of financial burden, calling on the government to engage the private sector in less-sensitive scenarios by procuring services from private companies. “The government is very inflexible like a bus that turns slowly. Private enterprises are like sports cars. Wherever you want to go, you are much better off borrowing a sports car,” he said. Breaking down silos Professor Chen said Hong Kong should work towards breaking the silos among stand-alone government data sets, as well as administrative hurdles between bureaus. While the post of AI commissioner would assist and advise bureaus on AI-related matters, Chen said it would be helpful to set up a dedicated government body to manage and coordinate data from different departments to facilitate interdisciplinary data sharing. She added that the government should also upgrade the Emergency Monitoring and Support Centre into a unified command hub connecting all safety-related departments, streamline workflows to automate emergency responses by removing multi-tier approval processes, and facilitate the cross-border flow of compliant data. “The government should establish a regular training mechanism on AI literacy and digital governance within the civil service to strengthen officials’ understanding of AI risks and opportunities, break reliance on traditional administrative mindsets, and provide sufficient talent support for the implementation and operation of the AI city brain,” she said. Innovation and technology sector lawmaker Duncan Chiu, a deputy leader of the government’s AI efficiency enhancement team, said another hurdle was the capacity of the government cloud. He said the government cloud was approaching its capacity limit, and the government might have to seek more funding from the Legislative Council to build more data centres. The government had earmarked HK$200 million (US$25.48 million) for the first phase of the system’s development. But Hong Kong also faces infrastructure constraints. Authorities previously noted the city’s overall supercomputing power was only five exa-floating-point operations per second (EFLOPS) as of June 2025. In simple terms, one EFLOP represents one quintillion – or a billion billion – calculations per second. Written out, that’s 1,000,000,000,000,000,000 operations every single second. Capacity is only expected to reach 180 EFLOPS after the Sandy Ridge data facility is completed in 2032. In contrast, the Hangzhou government is already planning to roll out 100 EFLOPS of computing power in 2027. “We must consider storage and cloud capacity – how much space is actually needed, where it will come from, and when it will be built. All of this needs to be mapped out in a clear road map,” Chiu said. “I believe the final investment will go beyond the initial funding announced so far, and the government will ultimately need to return to the Legislative Council to seek additional funds,” he added, while stopping short of estimating the amount. For Chiu, building an AI city brain aligns with the international trend, and Hong Kong has the capability to resolve all the obstacles ahead. “It all comes down to a matter of money and time, as well as determination,” he said.

title: Charity football tournament offers hope, ‘reduces stress’ for marginalised in Hong Kong
description: Featuring 16 teams and around 250 players, the seven-a-side contest expects to raise more than HK$1 million for good causes in the city.
content: A charity football tournament in Hong Kong on Monday allowed some players a temporary release from the “quagmire, anxiety and stress” of their daily lives. The event at Kings Park was staged to raise funds and awareness for Branches of Hope (BoH), the non-governmental organisation that serves refugees, asylum seekers and human trafficking survivors in Hong Kong. Featuring 16 teams and around 250 players, the seven-a-side Home and Away Charity Football Tournament was expected to raise more than HK$1 million (US$127,000) for good causes. “That’s around 10 per cent of our annual income,” Irving Choi, BoH’s partnerships manager, said. “This is our one opportunity every year to spread the message about what we do.” Competing alongside corporate teams, and others composed of groups of friends, was one from the Christian Action Centre for Refugees (CACR), and another representing BoH.
