One of Hope United’s players, a 39-year-old who asked not to be named for fear of prejudicing his asylum case, fled Uganda eight months ago. The manager of a band, a musician and aligned with the opposition party in his country, which since 1986 has been under the control of president Yoweri Museveni, the player came to Hong Kong to “escape persecution”. “I was quite well known, so I had to bribe the immigration officer at the airport to allow me to get out of the country,” he said. Given that context, playing football in the searing heat was a doddle. Not even a 1-0 defeat by CACR immediately before speaking to the South China Morning Post could soften the player’s gratitude for the opportunity to feel like he “fitted in with society”. “A lot of people look at asylum seekers as trash,” he said. “We’re seen as people who are useless, not knowing that we might have serious backgrounds, that we’re educated people. “I majored in marketing … but people judge you before listening to you. Here, we get to meet and mix with different people, and be part of the wider community.” Nathan de Lyster, the BoH executive director, said: “We’re raising the profile of refugees and asylum seekers here in the city … and creating opportunities where people can see shared humanity, regardless of our backgrounds, skills or languages.” There was a nod to the event’s fun side when it was won by a team called Chicken Water, christened in honour of an episode during the friends’ school lunch break many years back. Lunch here was filled with a set from local rock band Plan Victory, while magic and clown shows added to the entertainment, as 65 volunteers and 18 BoH staff bustled between the four playing fields. De Lyster said the charity existed to help “people navigate systems they’ve never had to deal with”. “We try to provide stability in the day, whether that’s financial, housing or medical support, education or connecting them with other organisations,” he said, adding that BoH’s work was also future focused. “We help with skills people might need on a resettlement pathway, we don’t want them leaving Hong Kong after five, 10 or 15 years having taken no steps forward.” Having had to leave four children behind in Uganda, the Hope United player said that “you’re never settled as an asylum seeker”. “You’re expecting a call every day,” he said. “I’m not allowed to work, so I’m in the house all day: 24 hours for me is a long time. We left behind professions, we didn’t leave because we wanted to come to Hong Kong. You leave because life is the most important thing. We fought hard to get out from young, but anybody who tries is shot. “Now, every day, there is lots of stress and anxiety. You don’t know when your case will be heard or finished, so you’re living in a quagmire. “BoH supports you psychologically. They take you to church to pray. Events like this reduce the stress a bit, they keep you busy, I wish there was one every month.” The player’s teammate, Lawrance Ssekimwanyi, is the chairman of Hong Kong’s Uganda community, having arrived from the African country 16 years ago. Unlike the anonymous player, whose situation became grave after he joined the National Unity Platform political party, whose leader Bobi Wine fled to the United States after losing an election to Museveni’s National Resistance Movement in January, Ssekimwanyi’s circumstances became pressing after the death of his opposition politician father. “The child is often targeted to be sacrificed,” Ssekimwanyi said. Like his younger colleague, he came to Hong Kong alone. He now has a partner and five children. “I came here because I trusted the judicial system, and the people embraced me,” he said. Also unable to work with his asylum case ongoing, Ssekimwanyi, who can speak Cantonese, has dedicated himself to fostering a community for refugees and asylum seekers. Hope United featured players from Pakistan, India, Tanzania, Kenya, Sri Lanka, Togo and Guinea. “My brothers,” Ssekimwanyi said. “This tournament is fantastic, it allows us to be together. Some people have talent, but very little chance to show it. We can’t play in some tournaments because of documentation, but here we can be involved. We’re a smaller community and it’s important people can see us and know we’re participating.” At King’s Park from 6.45am to dress the venue, Choi said planning for the event had begun immediately after last year’s edition, with preparations accelerating over the past six months. Teams could pay HK$15,000, HK$25,000 or HK$50,000 to enter, while each had online fundraising pages. Donations and fund matching swelled the charity pot. Brassed off with his team’s management, one Hope United player left before their final match. “Don’t give up, bro,” said his anonymous teammate. He looks younger than his 39 years. “I’d look better if I was relaxed,” he said. “I appreciate everybody at BoH, they keep you busy and away from crime. It goes back to what’s good about Hong Kong. You can sleep and wake up the next morning.”

title: Hong Kong to cement its role as a yuan bond hub by appealing to more sovereign borrowers
description: APEC meeting a golden opportunity to highlight the city’s financial markets and attract more Asia-Pacific sovereign debt issuers: analysts.
content: Hong Kong is opening its arms to more sovereign debt issuers, as this week’s Apec Finance Ministerial Meeting (FMM) provides a good opportunity to demonstrate the depth and advantages of the city’s financial markets. Its signature dim sum bond market could leverage low fundraising costs relative to that of developed markets and risk diversification considerations to make the city a magnet for sovereign borrowers, including many members of the Asia-Pacific organisation, according to analysts. “Elevated US interest rates have increased the cost of dollar borrowing, making issuance in alternative currencies – including offshore renminbi – more attractive for many issuers, such as sovereign governments,” said Marcus Yin, assistant vice-president of the sovereign risk group at Moody’s, a credit rating agency. The yield to maturity for dim sum bonds, yuan-denominated bonds issued outside the mainland, is 2.01 per cent as of late September, according to FTSE Russell, while the yield to maturity for US Treasury bonds is roughly 5.1 per cent as of mid-October, according to the US Treasury Department. The finance ministers of Apec’s 21 member economies, which account for 62 per cent of global GDP, are expected to address debt issues and the mounting pressures of rising sovereign borrowing costs in their talks this week. Hong Kong’s Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po, who highlighted the city’s unique role in debt financing for developing economies in his blog on Sunday, could step up lobbying during the ministerial talks. “As the world’s largest offshore renminbi centre, [Hong Kong] offers liquidity, settlement systems, market-making capacity and a specialised investor base that few competing financial centres can match,” Yin said. Mainland China and Indonesia have already turned to Hong Kong for dim sum bonds in the past. The Chinese Ministry of Finance issued a record 68 billion yuan (US$10.2 billion) in treasury bonds in Hong Kong in 2025 and is expected to reach 84 billion yuan this year. The Indonesian government issued its inaugural dim sum bonds in Hong Kong in 2025, totalling 6 billion yuan. Dim sum bond issuance is a key component mentioned in the Hong Kong government’s five-year plan. Yin said the city vowed to expand the supply of high-quality yuan-denominated assets and increase offshore yuan circulation. Hong Kong’s dim sum bond issuance reached 266.9 billion yuan as of late September, up 13.8 per cent year-on-year, according to HKEX data. The outstanding size is close to 1.9 trillion yuan, making it the world’s largest market. Agnes Tsang, partner at legal firm A&O Shearman, said the Southbound Bond Connect scheme, launched in 2021, allowed mainland institutional investors to invest in dim sum bonds, thereby “add[ing] access to a growing pool of mainland institutional investors alongside international demand”. Hong Kong also offers bonds in various currencies and digital green bonds that might attract Apec members’ interest. Malaysia, an Apec member, has listed Sukuk, also referred to as Islamic bonds, in Hong Kong in the past, most recently US$1.5 billion in July this year. Last month, Hong Kong broke global records by issuing digital green bonds worth around HK$20 billion (US$2.55 billion) in four currencies in September, the fourth in a series of issuances since 2023. Digital green bonds are digitally native debt securities used to finance environmentally sustainable projects. Tsang, who had advised the government since its first digital green bond issuance, highlighted “Hong Kong’s work on integrating different forms of digital money, including tokenised central bank money and tokenised deposits, in the primary issuance settlement process”. This “could position Hong Kong as a leading venue for sovereigns considering their first digital green bonds”, she added.

title: Six legendary libraries, where architecture and academia meet
description: Some of the world’s finest library buildings are worth discovering in their own right, never mind the cultural treasures they house.
content: Libraries are hard drives containing the memory of the world in an ancient form. Less pocketable than anything digital, but in many cases far prettier, these buildings are also sometimes works of art in their own right and cathedrals of humanism, whether erected four centuries ago or by a still-living architect of global acclaim. Their beauty is inessential to their function but celebrates the knowledge they contain, the power and wealth or taste and intellect of those who commissioned them, or plays a role in preserving the essence of cultural identity. You might visit one to see the masterful carpentry of ornate shelving, elaborate spiral staircases and walkways, stained glass, trompe l’oeil frescoes, carved marble and art, in addition to displays of rare and ancient books, maps, treaties, manuscripts and other historic documents. To the atmospheric silence and the smell of wax polish found in churches is added the warm aroma of ancient leather bindings. You might enter for some relief from the haste, heat and hustle of a big city, or because the libraries themselves have become popular meeting places, with cafes and places to sit. Here are six institutions whose collections or buildings should not be overlooked, whatever reason you have for being in town. The Real Biblioteca del Monasterio de San Lorenzo de El Escorial, Madrid, Spain Philip II of Spain (1527-98) ruled one of the greatest empires in human history and did so much of the time from El Escorial, creating here the national library of the Kingdom of Spain in a room intended to be one of the most magnificent in the palace, and a rival for the richest libraries elsewhere in Europe, particularly cultural competitor Italy. The main royal collections were transferred to the new building in 1566, even before the rest of the complex was ready for Philip to move in, although his advisers regretted that such magnificence was created in a remote spot, rather than in one of the university cities of the time. Today, its improbable out-of-town location is part of the attraction, just a short local-train journey northwest from Madrid, followed by a stroll through pretty countryside that’s a pleasant relief from the capital’s intensity. The palace is ever more imposing as approached, and the heavily frescoed ceiling of its library, by a Milanese master referencing Michelangelo’s Sistine Chapel, is worth the trip in itself, even without taking into account what’s beneath it. This includes ornate shelving and displays of ancient maps, coins, medals and scientific instruments. Philip’s giant armillary sphere, like a skeletal globe and representing the great circles of the heavens, has stood in the same spot here since 1593, when it was still thought that the sun and the rest of the heavens revolved around the Earth. And there’s still the great church and the labyrinth of palace chambers, with their tapestries, art and furniture to see, before a reflective journey back to Madrid. Veneranda Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Milan, Italy Italy’s fashion capital is home to at least five historic libraries, of which the 18th century Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense is perhaps the most beautiful. But in terms of its collection, the Ambrosiana is the greatest of all, with more than a million volumes, including thousands of incunabula: printed books from before 1501, which are now very rare. It was also one of the first in the world to open its doors to anyone who could read or write, and its users included mathematician, inventor and astronomer Galileo Galilei (1564-1642) – not your everyday influencer – who called it “heroic and immortal”. He may turn out to be right; opened in 1609, it has lasted for more than four centuries so far. The hush of its long red-carpeted main room, with an ornate arched ceiling and dark bookcases in two tiers, is home to the world’s greatest collection of drawings and writings by Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519), much of it on open display. Here, the polymath painter of The Last Supper (1495-98) and the Mona Lisa (1503), who was also an architect and engineer, can rather thrillingly be seen thinking out loud about geometry, anatomy, physics and assorted inventions, with many detailed illustrations in his own hand. The Ambrosiana complex also incorporates an art gallery with masterpieces by Caravaggio, Botticelli, Raphael and many others, spanning four centuries. You’ll need at least half a day here. The Real Gabinete Português de Leitura, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil While beautiful ancient libraries are most numerous in Europe, the 16th century voyagers to the New World took their ideas with them, and Rio’s Real Gabinete was founded in 1880 as a memorial to modern Brazil’s Portuguese roots, and to that country’s era of maritime dominance, by then already a fading memory. While the library’s calm and cool interior is a welcome break from the swimwear parades of Rio’s beaches, there’s vibrant colour and decorative detail enough almost to match the city’s famous carnival. The eye scarcely knows where to rest, and many visiting photographers seem unsure where to point their lenses first. Spiralling wooden pillars with gilded bosses support three galleried tiers of shelves. The heavily ornamented Manueline style of Portuguese cathedrals from 350 years earlier has been adapted to new purpose, but the interior is colourfully illuminated by a stained-glass dome in a cast-iron frame that was hi-tech for its day. This is certainly memory in built form, harking back to past cultural ascendancy. The facade is a copy of a Lisbon monastery – carved limestone panels were created in Portugal and shipped out – and the library’s most prized possession is a first edition of poet Luís de Camões’ epic Os Lusíadas of 1572, widely considered Portuguese literature’s greatest work. The library’s luxurious pseudo-antiquity is an almost shocking discovery in a humdrum Rio backstreet, although it’s far from merely a monument. The Real Gabinete still receives copies of every book published in Portugal, and so holds the largest overseas collection of Portuguese works. The Morgan Library and Museum, New York, United States Modern Madison Avenue may hardly seem the place for quiet contemplation, but here in 1906, the fabulously wealthy banker and industrialist J. Pierpont (JP) Morgan built himself a library that’s now part of a modern complex by “starchitect” Renzo Piano (he was behind the modern glass atrium and expansion completed in 2006), who also designed The New York Times Building (opened in 2007) and the Whitney Museum (current location opened in 2015). But entering the Morgan Library makes you feel as though you’ve stepped through a time portal, as the building is in a style that was popular in the early 20th century, called American Renaissance, which harks back to the Europe of three centuries earlier. There are triple tiers of walnut shelving beneath a coffered ceiling copied from a Roman villa, murals of literary figures and walls hung with tapestries, which, with an ornate fireplace, manage to give it an air of domesticity. The main draw, though, is Morgan’s acquisitions, which include the original manuscript of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol (1843), the original score of a Mozart symphony, the only surviving complete draft of a Jane Austen novel (the early Lady Susan of 1794) and original prints by English poet, painter and printmaker William Blake (1757-1827). It’s all highly restorative before a return to New York’s bedlam. The Qatar National Library, Doha, Qatar Although we’re now in the era of the e-reader and the on-demand download of just about anything, the age of great library-building is not over. Doha’s Rem Koolhaas-designed building of 2018, with its 45,000 square metres of floor space, is supposed to resemble two folded pieces of paper, emphasising the importance of the written word in Qatari heritage. But on first impressions, it looks like a UFO about to launch itself into the sky. The library’s vast and airy interior, well supplied with spaces in which to sit and read, is a haven against Doha’s often scorching heat. It’s more like a town square, and is a popular place to meet, with access to 3D printers and other tech as well as more than a million volumes in 16 languages available for loan. The interior is so vast that it looks ready to hold hundreds of millions more. Only the basement recalls ancient European libraries, its warren of smaller spaces containing a magnificent display of Arabic calligraphy and illuminated manuscripts, very early maps of Arabia and accounts of both European exploration and the French invasion of Egypt, in 1798. Yururi Yusuhara, Yusuhara, Japan Libraries can be great without being grand or intimidating, and even the biggest architectural stars sometimes involve themselves in small projects. Yusuhara, a sleepy community of 3,300, high up in the central mountains of the Japanese island of Shikoku, well away from the hordes tramping the famous 88-temple pilgrimage around the coastline, has almost become a second home to Kengo Kuma. The architect is known for his large-scale projects, such as the Japan National Stadium, in Tokyo, but at Yusuhara, he’s indulged himself with local materials and a desire to develop traditional Japanese styles and techniques to produce something fresh. Amid typical Japanese domesticity, he’s built six wooden buildings, including a corridor bridge, a hotel that faintly resembles a haystack and an extraordinary library. To enter from the wooded hills of the surrounding countryside is to seem to arrive at a forest rather than leave one. From a smooth cedar-wood floor (shoes must be removed, of course), pillars fork as they rise and end in a tangle of criss-crossing branch-like structures that descend again from the ceiling. At floor level, the building is constructed of shelving that doubles as seating and as stairs forming multiple levels that also seat audiences for public events. This isn’t a library in which to escape the pressures of the outside world, but a fully functional modern community service – complete with more than 70,000 volumes – unlike any other you may have visited.

title: Detained Suu Kyi receives royal package from UK’s King Charles: Myanmar government
description: The former Myanmar leader has not been allowed to meet any foreign leader or envoy since her detention in February 2021.
content: Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi received a package from Britain’s King Charles on Monday, authorities said, releasing the first pictures of the detained Nobel laureate in two months and describing her as a “special female prisoner”. It is the first time Myanmar authorities have used the term to describe Suu Kyi, who was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED. The coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April following an election that did not include Suu Kyi’s party, and she was moved to house arrest soon afterwards. Home ministry officials met her on Monday to deliver a package of two books about soil, “one sealed envelope, and a sealed diplomatic communication sent by King Charles of the United Kingdom to the special female detainee”, Myanmar’s presidential spokeswoman said on social media. Britain is Myanmar’s former colonial power and the monarch is known to have a keen interest in gardening and the environment. Accompanying the statement were two images of Suu Kyi meeting two men with their backs to the camera. The pictures appeared to be in a similar room to the last released images of her, when she met a Red Cross representative in August, her first publicised meeting with a foreign official since her ousting. Fact-checkers from Agence France-Presse examined the latest photos and found no evidence of manipulation using Meta Generative AI or OpenAI tools. Suu Kyi remains detained on charges rights groups say were concocted to return power to the military, which has historically ruled Myanmar since independence. “I have been extremely lenient towards her,” Min Aung Hlaing said in an interview with Time magazine published last month. The Foreign Office in London did not say whether British diplomats had sought to deliver the package in person, or been refused permission to do so. Britain condemns what it describes as Suu Kyi’s “arbitrary detention” and calls for her immediate and unconditional release.

title: Editorial | Ensure standards of Hong Kong’s civil engineering work remain sky high
description: Recent scandals involving shoddy construction and maintenance work have shaken public confidence in professional practice and institutional safeguards.
content: Hong Kong’s civil engineering work is reputedly among the world’s best, as evidenced by the awe-inspiring infrastructure marvels and skyscrapers that have been built with exceptional efficiency and high standards across the city. These hard-earned credentials are not accidental but rooted in generations of professional practice and robust institutional safeguards and monitoring. Yet public confidence has been shaken by a series of scandals involving shoddy construction and maintenance work. From steel-reinforcement shortfalls at a luxury property development in Stanley to the forced demolition of three substandard towers at a starter home project in Kwun Tong, the incidents paint a disturbing picture of slipping standards in a city that once set benchmarks for civil engineering excellence. The latest controversy involves alleged corner-cutting and false declarations related to fire-safety components in the replacement of 48 lifts at two public housing estates. According to the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department, Taizoom Elevator (Hong Kong) submitted fire-resistance test reports upon project completion, but it actually only installed fire-resisting doors for the lifts without the required frames. On Friday, the police arrested a director of the company and two registered lift engineers in connection with the case. Subsequent inspections found lifts in at least 338 blocks handled by the contractor were not installed with fire-resistant door frames. The department has ordered all lift contractors to review their work and declare within one month that the landing doors and associated frame components installed over the past 10 years are of “good design and construction” with valid documents certifying compliance. Given the urgency and the large number of lifts involved, the measure is understandable. Concerns have been raised about whether individual contractors will be honest with the self-inspection and declaration requirement. Arguably, the primary responsibility for compliance with safety and operational standards rests with contractors. But ultimate safety and regulations come under the department. Officials therefore cannot just rely on self-checks and declarations. A citywide random inspection is called for. In mid-August, 24 of the 28 lifts at a new 34-storey clinical block at Queen Mary Hospital malfunctioned because of “deviations in lift shafts” and installation defects. The problem has not only delayed full commissioning of the building but also raised questions about how the defects passed through layers of monitoring and approval. This was followed by allegations that a luxury house at One Stanley had been built with insufficient steel bars, prompting a full investigation amid questions about why the project had been issued occupation permits by the Buildings Department despite the alleged defects. Meanwhile, three of the six residential blocks at a “starter home” development in Kwun Tong by CK Asset will be demolished and rebuilt in the wake of substandard steel reinforcement work revealed two years ago. Separately, the Housing Authority ordered the contractor of a Tung Chung public housing project to submit rectification plans after discovering substandard concrete in the structural components of three blocks under construction. These are not minor defects. The fact that they slipped through layers of supervision and certification before being unearthed and followed up on has called into question the integrity and professionalism of stakeholders and the monitoring authorities. If a contractor can allegedly cut corners across dozens of lifts, and reinforcement can deviate materially from approved plans, the failures are unlikely to be just a moment of negligence involving a single individual or a particular layer of supervision. It points instead to deficiencies in the entire chain of responsibility. Integrity, safety and public trust are at stake. The government has responded with appropriate urgency, with the chief executive directing the Development Bureau to oversee the One Stanley investigation, pursue violations rigorously and strengthen penalties and legal deterrence. The public rightly expects the pledges will be followed by enhancements in standards and compliance, and consequences for those held accountable.

title: How to prevent osteoporosis, from strength training to eating calcium-rich food
description: With one in five postmenopausal Hong Kong women at high risk of a hip fracture, experts share how training and nutrition can safeguard bones.
content: Osteoporosis is a stealthy condition. The disease, which weakens bones by making them thinner, less dense and more likely to break, advances slowly and silently, says Dr Edith Lau, founding president of the Asian Pacific Osteoporosis Foundation (APOF), and for most people the first sign is a broken bone. That break can follow something that does not seem serious – a minor fall, lifting something heavy, even a bout of coughing or sneezing. Sufferers most commonly break their forearm, spine or hip, and a broken hip can have profound consequences: one in five patients will die within a year because of complications. The risk seems especially acute in Hong Kong. Working with the Hong Kong Centre for Clinical Research, the APOF found that more than one in five postmenopausal women in the city face a high risk of an osteoporosis-related hip fracture within the next decade. Calcium is the fundamental building block of strong bones, while vitamin D acts as the key that allows the body to absorb it. But for many in Hong Kong, getting enough of either is a challenge. Hong Kong-based orthopaedic surgeon Jason Brockwell says part of the problem lies in the traditional Cantonese diet, which tends to be low in calcium. “Many Hong Kong people are lactose intolerant, so they avoid dairy products, which are rich in calcium,” he says. Sun avoidance also plays a role, he says. Because sunlight on the skin triggers the body’s natural synthesis of vitamin D, city dwellers who stay indoors or use heavy sun protection often become vitamin D deficient – leaving their bodies unable to process the small amount of calcium they do consume. A third Hong Kong-specific factor, Brockwell says, is that most women in the city don’t use hormone replacement therapy (HRT) after menopause. “It has many benefits, one of which is helping to protect bones,” he says. World Osteoporosis Day on October 20 is a timely reminder to safeguard our bones so we can age well. We asked Hong Kong experts how best to protect our skeletons. Stay on your feet “Low bone density – osteoporosis – does not really matter until you break a bone,” Brockwell says. One way to avoid breaking bones is to avoid falling. Having strong muscles enables you to stay upright if you trip or stumble. Older people can lose muscle rapidly if they are bed-bound or otherwise incapacitated by illness, even for a week or two, so steering clear of common illnesses such as the flu and Covid-19 through vaccinations and good hygiene helps. Know your risk, load your bones At Total Health by Hong Kong Sports Clinic, physiotherapists Kelly Suen and Kevin Ho see many clients aged 45 to 65, “probably due to greater awareness of the importance and benefit of resistance training and fitness in general”, they say. To safely load bones without causing injury, physiotherapists use frameworks such as Exercise and Sports Science Australia (ESSA). By assessing bone density, fracture history and balance, they assign a risk level to tailor the intensity, combining heavy resistance work, impact training (such as jumping) and stability drills. Suen says high-intensity and high-impact exercises are effective in improving or maintaining bone density in the lower back and thigh bones of postmenopausal women. To improve bone density, bone tissue must be subjected to physical loads “above what is normally experienced during daily physical activities”, about two times their body weight. Impact exercises differ from resistance training, Suen says, because they introduce “sudden, fast-paced, vertical loading to the skeleton through ground reaction force”, which targets feet, shins, thigh bones, the hip and the spine. The importance of balance is often forgotten, but it is crucial to avoid falls. Suen says that balance deteriorates as we age, but it can be trained no matter how old we are. “Doing exercises that safely challenge our stability can improve our balance and reduce our chances of a fall,” she says. Balance relies on three primary systems: vision, body awareness (proprioception from our joints) and inner-ear feedback (the vestibular system). Simple exercises, such as standing on one leg, can help. Falls account for 95 per cent of broken hips, according to the United States’ Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Lift, but lift smart Kushal Gurung, manager at Raw Personal Training in Hong Kong, explains why strength training is so important. Muscles and tendons pull on bone, loading the skeleton. “By applying stress to the bones through lifting, we stimulate the bone remodelling process, which makes them denser and stronger,” he says. Lifting must be progressive and suited to the individual. Start light, train regularly – at least twice a week – and build up slowly over months. “A person should first learn good technique and then gradually increase the resistance,” Gurung says. Walking has benefits, he adds: “It supports cardiovascular health, mobility and general activity, and can help people who are currently inactive.” But research in postmenopausal women suggests walking alone has little or no significant effect on bone density. “More targeted loading is usually needed to provide a strong enough stimulus” for bone building, according to Gurung. Men get osteoporosis, too Panda Li, a former Hong Kong Olympic team physiotherapist and founder of Hong Kong physiotherapy clinic PhysioMotion, says that while women make up most osteoporosis cases, men also suffer from the disease. Osteopenia, the precursor to osteoporosis, is common in men, and one in five men over 50 has a lifetime risk of experiencing a fragility fracture, such as a broken hip, spine or wrist. The main causes are similar for both sexes: ageing, which lowers the bone-protective sex hormones testosterone and oestrogen; a rise in circulating inflammatory proteins known as cytokines (dubbed “inflammaging”); and falling vitamin D levels. Men face specific risks, though. Treatment for prostate cancer often involves depriving the body of testosterone, which can cause hypogonadism – a medical condition in which the body produces little or no sex hormones – and in turn compromise bone health. Steroid and alcohol use can also weaken bones. Li says many people assume that having osteopenia or osteoporosis means they should avoid heavy weights. In fact, with supervised technique, heavy lifting is exactly what builds bone. Her gold standard is strength training with a high load, low repetitions (about five) and high sets (about five). She also encourages men to play sports such as basketball and tennis. The constant stop-starts and changes of direction create tensile load on the muscles, and a game may be more appealing to many men than a session at the gym. Li urges men to consider having a bone density scan – also called a bone mineral scan, bone densitometry, Dexa or DXA – as many women do. The scans reveal muscle-to-fat ratio and, if done early enough, can provide a useful baseline for bone health. Without enough muscle to pull on bone, she says, we cannot properly support our skeleton. Feed your bones Healthy bones rest on three daily pillars: weight-bearing exercise, vitamin D and calcium. Hong Kong-based dietitian Kirti Tatiwala recommends those who are lactose intolerant or avoid dairy to consume plant- and seafood-based alternatives. “Finger millet [ragi], sesame seeds and tahini, moringa leaves, broccoli, kale, bok choy, collard greens, calcium-set tofu, calcium-fortified plant milks and dried figs can also contribute to calcium intake,” she says. “Sardines eaten with their bones are another good source.” What you avoid matters as well. According to dietitian Carmen Lo Ka-man, some foods can cause calcium loss, with hidden salt in ultra-processed foods being a primary culprit. Too much alcohol or coffee can interfere with calcium absorption, too. And, unsurprisingly, smoking is terrible for bones. For those who cannot meet their calcium needs through food, supplements are an option. Lo says the upper limit is 2,500mg a day. Taking too much for too long can raise the risk of kidney stones and even cardiovascular disease. Tatiwala notes that supplements cannot prevent osteoporosis. “They can help bridge dietary gaps when needed, but bone health depends on multiple nutritional, lifestyle and medical factors,” she says. Although the effects of osteoporosis may not show until later in life, bone health is a “lifelong investment”, says Tatiwala. “Strong bones are built early, supported throughout life and protected as we age.” Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Alberta voters choose Canada over independence in boost for Carney
description: Overwhelming referendum result rejects path to separation, cementing national unity amid an ongoing trade war with the US.
content: Voters in Canada’s oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with early referendum results Tuesday delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for national unity amid US President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats. With more than 1.4 million votes counted, 76 per cent supported remaining in Canada, while close to 24 per cent backed beginning a process towards separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta. The referendum was not a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path towards a future vote on separation from Canada. “Albertans made a clear choice,” Carney said. “They chose unity, to build together and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.” Carney said that the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its centre. Alberta’s separatists, however, saw a silver lining. “We don’t have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media. Smith, who called the referendum amid pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party, or UCP, despite opposing independence, said that she would address the province Tuesday evening about the results and Alberta’s future. “We are a solid country that’s united from coast to coast to coast,” Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters. Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday. Alberta, a province of 5 million people that holds the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment towards Ottawa runs deep, but has not traditionally translated into widespread support for independence. Alberta’s referendum follows two previous referendums on separation in the majority French-speaking province of Quebec, in 1980 and 1995. Quebecers voted to stay in Canada in both instances. First Nations groups have also objected to the ⁠idea of an independent Alberta, as their land treaties with Ottawa predate the province’s creation within Canada. Despite the Alberta proposal’s apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that would not disappear. Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity. “Vote like Canada’s future depends on it, because it does,” he told a rally on Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up. Smith has blamed Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau, for igniting the separatist fire, accusing him of trying to crush oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda. Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1 per cent or 2 per cent of the vote, former premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over Covid-19 restrictions helped mobilise activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said. Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st US state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular. At a separatist referendum night gathering at an Edmonton restaurant, the crowd fell quiet as results rolled in. “We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project. “We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.” Rath had said he would be thrilled if 30 per cent of Albertans voted to begin the separation process. He wants Smith ousted as UCP leader and said that the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party. Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said that Albertans have long been mistreated by Ottawa. “Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony,” he said after voting Monday. “They want to take and take and take from us, and not return anything.” Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticised spending money on a “referendum on a referendum” rather than healthcare. With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said: “It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united; instead we’re fighting among ourselves”. Additional reporting by Reuters and Agence France-Presse

title: Money manager eyes Asia-Pacific property for growth, but tells investors to keep bet on US
description: Principal Asset Management executive says appetite for commercial properties in fast-growing markets underpinned by higher interest rates.
content: US-based money manager Principal Asset Management says it is poised to become more active in Asia-Pacific property markets, believing investors have been “underweight” in the region’s office property segment. Richard Hill, its senior managing director and head of global real estate research and strategy, said the group was also seeing continued interest from institutional investors in the Asia-Pacific region looking to access opportunities in US commercial real estate as it was “too big to ignore”. “In my global travels, meeting with investors, whether it be in the US or in Europe or even the Middle East, investors are waking up to the reality that they are structurally underweight in the Asia-Pacific region relative to its share of total global commercial real estate valuations,” Hill said in an interview. Principal is part of the Principal Financial Group, headquartered in Des Moines, Iowa, which managed US$808 billion in assets in the second quarter of the year, according to its latest financial report. Hill said the appetite for Asia-Pacific commercial properties was underpinned by elevated interest rates in the United States and elsewhere, leading investors to look for fast-growing markets to drive growth. “We are in a higher interest rate environment today, really across the world, than we have been at any point in time over the past 15 years,” he said, noting that “the only way” to drive returns in such an environment was to find commercial real estate opportunities that were growing fast enough to offset higher financing costs. “You do that by picking the right property types in the right markets, and you do that by manufacturing net operating income growth through development and redevelopment opportunities,” Hill said. “So the reality is, I think investors are now expanding the universe of markets that they’re willing to look at to find those returns.” The US Federal Reserve embarked on a new monetary policy tightening course last month with a quarter-point increase in its benchmark interest rate, the first in three years, to rein in inflation. In August, the inflation rate in the world’s largest economy remained at 3.4 per cent, well above the Fed’s long-term target of 2 per cent. Investors are now coming to the reality that the only way you’re going to drive returns is through fundamentals Richard Hill, Principal Asset Management In the first half of the year, investment in Asia-Pacific commercial real estate rose by 29 per cent year on year to US$103.7 billion, according to financial data provider MSCI. The region’s share of global cross-border investment had been climbing since 2022 and hit a record 32 per cent late last year, it said. “For the better part of the past two to three years, many investors were hoping for a lower interest rate environment to drive returns,” Hill said. “That’s off the table now, and so investors are now coming to the reality that the only way you’re going to drive returns is through fundamentals.” Australia, Japan, Singapore and South Korea were likely to be the focus of investors’ interest in the region, he said, adding that no time frame had been set for Principal’s plan to be more active in the region, which only accounted for “percentage points” of the group’s portfolio. Meanwhile, Hill cautioned investors against pulling out of the US commercial real estate market amid heightened geopolitical uncertainties and rising interest rates. Foreign investment in US commercial real estate was estimated to have accounted for just under 5 per cent of total transaction volumes in the second quarter of this year, Hill said, down from a peak of 22 per cent in the fourth quarter of 2015. “The US market is too big to ignore, but we do recognise the bar for investing in US commercial real estate has risen,” he said. “The US is the largest commercial real estate market in the world, and if you are not investing in the United States, you are making a conscious decision to be structurally underweight in commercial real estate on a global basis.” US President Donald Trump signed an “America First Investment Policy” memorandum early last year that said the US would “use all necessary legal instruments”, including the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), to block China-affiliated investments in American “technology, critical infrastructure, healthcare, agriculture, energy, raw materials or other strategic sectors”. In the order, Trump said his administration would “protect” American farmland and real estate near “sensitive facilities”.

title: Woman tells UK court Russell Brand dragged her into bar toilet and raped her
description: Third complainant says actor told her ‘don’t be a spoilsport’ during alleged 2004 assault; defence insists incident ‘did not happen’.
content: A woman told police that British actor and comedian Russell Brand had grabbed her breasts before dragging her into a toilet at a bar and orally raping her, a London court heard on Monday. Brand, once one of Britain’s most high-profile broadcasters and the former husband of US singer Katy Perry, is on trial accused of three counts of rape, three of ‌sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women between 1999 and 2009. The 51-year-old denies the allegations, and told police after his arrest that he had never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity and the accusers might have reimagined events. The third of the six complainants to give evidence alleged Brand had assaulted her after she met him at a party in a London bar in 2004. In a tearful police interview played to jurors at Southwark Crown Court, the woman, who worked for MTV, said she ⁠had wanted to meet Brand because she had seen him on television and thought he was really funny. But less than a minute after talking ‌to him at the bar, she said, he assaulted her. “He literally just grabbed my boobs in the middle of the conversation,” she said, adding that he had a weird, maniacal grin on his face as he did it. Immediately afterwards ‌while she was in shock and disbelief, she said he grabbed her arm and pulled her to the toilets that were ⁠nearby. It was there that ⁠he allegedly orally raped her. “It happened so fast,” she told police. “He said ‘come on, come on, don’t be a spoilsport’,” she recounted, saying he was holding her forcibly by her head ‌and hair. “I just froze. I didn’t know what to do.” She said while his words were not threatening, the force of the encounter and the look in his eye had been. She rejected Brand’s lawyer ‌Ian ‌Winter’s suggestion that she had been very excited to meet him, saying she “wasn’t star struck … I wasn’t a giddy schoolgirl”. Winter put it to her ‌that had she been groped at the bar or dragged into the toilets, people would have seen. “Let’s be clear he did not do that to ⁠you,” he said of the alleged sexual assault. “You happily accompanied Mr Brand into the lavatory,” he added, a suggestion she rejected. He said the alleged incident ⁠in the toilet was “physically impossible and it did not happen”. Winter also queried why she had never said she was raped until after a 2023 documentary and press report about Brand, having told friends and her sister he had tried to force himself on her ‌but she had got away. “I didn’t ‌want people to judge me … I felt ashamed,” she said. Last week, the first complainant told the court that Brand had raped her after she met him at a fringe event at the 1999 Labour Party conference in southern England. The second of the complainants told London’s Southwark Crown Court that in 2001 a “wild-eyed” Brand had tried to pull her into the male toilets at MTV Europe, in London, where she was working. The trial, which is expected to last around six weeks, continues.

title: Zelensky accuses US of delaying missiles as Trump calls for new Ukraine negotiator
description: Public clash deepens after US president defends Russian diesel deal and says wartime leader ‘doesn’t know what he’s talking about’.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused the United States on Monday of deliberately delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles to his country, as tensions between Kyiv and Washington escalated over military aid and intelligence sharing. Kyiv said it had no early warning of powerful Russian missile strikes, echoing similar claims made last week. Speaking to US senators on Monday, Zelensky said “the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles” already paid for by European countries and that the shipment was waiting for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s signature. He also said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were still awaiting US approval. “The missiles are ready, and they could already be in Ukraine,” Zelensky said. “But unfortunately, there is still no approval.” The United States has denied making any changes to intelligence-sharing with Ukraine. Trump has also denied ordering a reduction in speeds on the US government-owned and -controlled Starshield network after Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX developed it, said the order could only have come from the White House. Relations have been strained between the two capitals since Trump partially lifted sanctions to strike a diesel-supply deal with Vladimir Putin and slammed Zelensky as a warmonger for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. On Monday, Trump defended the diesel deal while once more slamming Zelensky. “Zelensky doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” Trump said. “To be honest, I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.” Trump also said he was ready to meet with Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China next month to discuss denuclearisation, adding that the talks could also cover the Ukraine war – fuelling fears in Kyiv that it was being sidelined. Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said that such a meeting would “only encourage Putin to continue this war”. Against that backdrop of mounting diplomatic friction, news outlet Axios reported that White House envoy Steve Witkoff was travelling to Oslo on Tuesday to meet Zelensky and European leaders, before heading to Russia to meet Putin. The Norwegian government confirmed that Zelensky would be in Oslo on Tuesday to meet the prime minister of Norway and the president of Finland. “President Zelensky has asked Norway and Finland to organise a meeting as part of ongoing diplomatic efforts, at a critical moment for Ukraine,” it said. Meanwhile, Zelensky also spoke to Pope Leo on Monday, according to the Vatican, days after the Catholic leader held a similar call with Putin. The Vatican said the Pope had urged both sides to allow for the flow of aid into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky and civilians to leave. Russia’s latest strikes again hit Ukrainian energy facilities and infrastructure across the country, knocking out power to more than 500,000 people and forcing emergency repairs to the battered grid. “Once again, there was no early warning from our partners,” Zelensky said, as he catalogued the damage, deaths and injuries. Six people, including three children, were killed in a strike near the northeastern city of Kharkiv, the authorities said. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on a visit to Uzbekistan on Monday, denied that intelligence-sharing had been withdrawn with Ukraine, backing Trump’s call for Zelensky to focus on ending the conflict. Talks to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II are deadlocked, with Russia refusing to give up its claim to Ukrainian territory and Ukraine steadfastly refusing attempts to force it to do so. Trump had vowed a swift end to the war when he returned to office but since then has appeared to tilt towards Russia, including calling for Zelensky to be replaced.

title: Palestinian activist takes deportation fight to US Supreme Court
description: Mahmoud Khalil seeks to ensure non-citizens can challenge Trump administration attempts to punish protected speech.
content: Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil on Monday asked the US Supreme Court to overturn a ruling that opened the door for US President Donald Trump’s administration to rearrest and deport the Palestinian activist. Khalil’s lawyers asked the justices to take up his case after the Philadelphia-based 3rd US Circuit ‌Court of Appeals ruled that federal immigration law barred a lower-court judge from ordering his release from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody. Khalil was among the most prominent foreign students to be arrested last year as the Trump administration pursued a campaign to detain and deport non-citizens who engaged in pro-Palestinian activism on college campuses. His lawyers say the Supreme Court should make clear immigration law does not prevent non-citizens from pursuing cases arguing they have been detained to punish them for speech that is protected by the US Constitution’s First Amendment. “If the Trump administration can punish someone for their pro-Palestine speech, this ⁠or any future administration can punish anyone for any speech,” Khalil told reporters on Monday. If the 3rd Circuit’s decision is allowed to stand, Khalil faces the prospect ‌of arrest and deportation, after the Board of Immigration Appeals in April rejected his challenge to an immigration judge’s order that he be removed to Algeria or Syria. A lower court order barring him from being re-detained remains in place for now until the ‌Supreme Court rules. A separate appeal of the immigration judge’s order remains pending. A spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ⁠ICE, in a statement said the ⁠Trump administration acted within its authority in Khalil’s case and it encouraged him to self-deport. Khalil, a prominent figure in pro-Palestinian protests against Israel’s war in Gaza, is an Algerian citizen who ‌was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria. Immigration agents arrested him in March 2025 in the lobby of his university residence in Manhattan despite his being a lawful permanent resident, or green-card holder. His wife ‌and their ‌one-year-old son are both US citizens. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had invoked an obscure provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act to deem Khalil removable, citing ‌his involvement in “antisemitic protests and disruptive activities” at Columbia in 2024 that the government said fostered a hostile environment for Jewish students. He was released from a Louisiana ⁠detention centre in June 2025 after the New Jersey-based US District Judge Michael Farbiarz, an appointee of former president Joe Biden, ordered the Department of Homeland Security to ⁠release him. In January, a 2-1 panel of the 3rd Circuit overturned Farbiarz’s decision, saying that under the Immigration and Nationality Act, Khalil’s claims could not be addressed through a district court and instead could be raised in an appeal of a removal order from an immigration judge. After the ‌full appeal court declined to reconsider the case, ‌Khalil turned to the Supreme Court. Federal appeal courts are split on whether district judges may hear challenges like Khalil’s or whether such claims must proceed first through immigration courts, which are not part of the federal judiciary but are instead run by the US Department of Justice. The Trump administration last month asked the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling in a similar case favouring Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri, another pro-Palestinian advocate detained by ICE who was ordered released.

title: US charges 28 in California sweep targeting alleged non-citizen voting
description: Trump administration seeks emergency order over mail ballots, while state officials dismiss allegations as baseless political theatre.
content: US federal authorities charged more than two dozen foreign nationals Monday in California as part of a statewide sweep targeting people who officials say have illegally registered or voted in US elections. The arrests are part of a Trump administration effort to root out non-citizen voting ahead of next month’s midterm elections, even though data shows that the problem is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races. The charges escalated a simmering voter roll fight that came into focus last week when the Justice Department sued California and warned that local election workers who knowingly process or tabulate ballots submitted by non-citizen voters are at risk of investigation and potential prosecution. The Justice Department said the 28 people who were charged as part of a sweep dubbed Operation Protect the Vote are lawful permanent residents – but not US citizens who are permitted to legally vote. They are charged with crimes including making false statements on a naturalisation application and submitting fraudulent voter registrations. “This causes real damage to real elections and real damage to American citizens,” Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department, said during a news conference in Los Angeles. Rob Bonta, California’s Democratic attorney general, said Monday that there is no widespread voter fraud in California and that while “one-off” examples of voter fraud are possible, those instances are “a drop in the bucket” considering the state has 23 million registered voters. Bonta said he expects his state to prevail in the federal government’s lawsuit, saying the Republican administration “has provided us with no facts of any ineligible voters, just a conclusory statement with no evidence to back it”. Among the dozens of people arrested was a 72-year-old Belize-born man who is accused of voting illegally in four elections. Dozens of federal agents descended on Omar Alexander Munoz’s residential cul-de-sac in Commerce, a small city in Los Angeles County, to make the arrest. Munoz was put in handcuffs in his pyjamas and taken into federal custody downtown. Esmeralda Munoz, 70, said her family was furious that agents showed up to their home in full tactical gear with guns drawn to arrest her husband before dawn. “It’s a show for them,” she said, calling it a “shame” that government officials arrived with camera crews and news helicopters. She and her three children and 10 grandchildren are all US citizens, she said; Omar Munoz is a legal permanent resident, she said, and they did not realise that he was registered to vote. When they do talk about politics, Esmeralda said Omar has been a vociferous supporter of Trump. The arrests were the latest in a flurry of activity that has unfolded in heavily Democratic California, which is not typically regarded as a key battleground state but does have a handful of competitive congressional races that could help determine which party controls the US House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term. The administration last week sued California to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as “likely” non-citizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. The complaint was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely non-citizens who were sent ballots to participate in the November 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. Explaining why it was important to address voting by non-citizens even though it’s rare, McCotter noted that some races in California have been decided by just hundreds of votes. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, criticised the state’s election officials for not cooperating with the department’s demands. “Why is California refusing to show their voter rolls?” he asked. “What are they afraid of? What are they hiding?” As part of its lawsuit, the Justice Department filed paperwork Monday seeking a court order that would force California to set aside ballots from suspected non-citizens and to independently, or in conjunction with the federal government, verify their citizenship status before tabulating their mail-in ballots. The Justice Department asked for the order to be entered in time for the November 3 election. Absent that order, the government said: “there is a significant risk that American votes will be diluted”. Requests for comment sent Monday to the secretary of state and governor’s office were not immediately returned. Governor Gavin Newsom on Monday published a series of X posts seeking to undermine the Justice Department’s announcement. “WOW. First Assistant Bill just admitted in front of the press that not all of those arrested today may have voted,” he wrote in one post, referencing Essayli.

title: 4 fall checked shirts for everyday wear, from Ralph Lauren to Brad Pitt’s co-founded label
description: Elevate your layered look this season with these luxury checked or plaid shirts from Polo Ralph Lauren, The Attico, God’s True Cashmere and Aimé Leon Dore.
content: Checked and plaid shirts are quintessential fall layering pieces that pair well with almost anything, from formal trousers and blazers to everyday basics. Here are four of our favourite designer styles to flaunt this season. Polo Ralph Lauren Those leaning towards preppy styles should consider adding Polo Ralph Lauren’s plaid cotton twill shirt (HK$1,680) to their shopping cart. The top is designed for a boxy fit and carries the brand’s embroidered logo on the chest. Available at Mytheresa. The Attico It comes as no surprise that The Attico – the brand founded by Italian designers and street style stars Gilda Ambrosio and Giorgia Tordini – is behind this trendsetting checked cotton shirt (HK$5,500) featuring dropped shoulders and a signature scoop cut-out on one side. God’s True Cashmere Actor Brad Pitt and jewellery designer Sat Hari Khalsa are the twin creative forces behind God’s True Cashmere. The label’s collection of plaid shirts, like this one (HK$19,530), is crafted from buttery soft cashmere and studded with healing gemstones that double as buttons. Aimé Leon Dore Aimé Leon Dore’s plaid cotton workshirt (HK$1,690) is an ideal throw-on piece to layer over a simple white T-shirt. For an elevated touch, the buttons are decorated with the New York-based label’s signature crest. Available at Net-a-Porter.

title: Saudi Arabia executes 2 Bangladeshis over ‘indecent acts’ in a Mecca mosque
description: Dhaka says it was given no prior notice of executions as Saudis cite ‘gravity’ of violating sanctity of Islam’s holiest city.
content: Saudi Arabia has executed two Bangladeshi nationals, a man and a woman, after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” in a mosque in the Muslim holy city of Mecca. Bangladesh said it was not informed before the sentences were carried out and has sought information from Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Interior Ministry said the Bangladeshis were executed because of “the gravity and seriousness of their actions in violating the sanctity of both time and place”. It did not elaborate.

title: Rwandan government critic found beheaded in Uganda
description: Police probe murder of former soldier Robert Kabera after headless body was discovered outside Kampala.
content: A former Rwandan soldier living in Uganda, where he had become a vocal critic of his government back home, was found decapitated near Kampala, a police spokesperson said Monday. Rwandan authorities have been accused of assassinating opponents of President Paul Kagame, who has ruled the country with an iron fist since taking power in the aftermath of the 1994 genocide that claimed 800,000 lives, primarily among the Tutsi community. Robert Kabera, a former sergeant who fled Rwanda several years ago, was not outspoken during his time in the military but grew increasingly opposed to Kagame. His YouTube channel, “Major Robert TV”, which has 144,000 subscribers, included a song praising opposition figure Victoire Ingabire, a rare voice of dissent in Rwanda, who has been repeatedly imprisoned. Ugandan police said they were investigating the “murder of a male adult, (around 50), whose head was cut off, and up to now the head has not yet been recovered”, spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke told reporters on Monday, adding that the body had been identified by relatives as Robert Kabera. The body was found in Luwala, a village near Kampala, and the murder likely took place late on October 16 or early 17, he added. In Uganda, “Robert had no issues with anyone,” his brother, Victor Agaba, told Agence France-Presse. “Our problem comes from home... The army created a criminal case against him. It was a witch hunt,” he said. Kabera was declared a fugitive after leaving Rwanda, and he was accused of corrupting a minor, which he denied. He is not the first opposition figure in exile to be assassinated. In 2021, a former lieutenant in the Rwandan army, Revocant Karemangingo, was shot dead in Mozambique, where he was suspected of secretly supporting an opposition force. Outspoken opponent Seif Bamporiki was gunned down in South Africa the same year, while a former Rwandan intelligence-chief-turned-critic, Patrick Karegeya, was strangled in his South African hotel room in 2014. Another exile, former general Faustin Kayumba Nyamwasa, who co-founded the Rwanda National Congress (RNC) opposition party with Karegeya, has survived several assassination attempts.

title: Police probe wave of hoax bomb threats targeting schools across Europe
description: Classrooms evacuated in the UK, Hungary and Serbia as authorities treat flood of threatening emails as unfounded.
content: Hundreds of schools in Northern Ireland, Scotland, Hungary and Serbia were sent bomb threats on Monday, with some evacuated as authorities said the warnings appeared to be a hoax. It is not yet known whether the incidents were connected to each other. “Police investigating the circumstances of threatening emails sent to schools across Northern Ireland this morning … are treating the matter as a hoax,” authorities said. Northern Ireland police said up to 300 schools had received “the same emailed message which contained a generalised threat” which was also received by “some schools across the UK”. Earlier on Monday, Northern Ireland Education Minister Paul Givan said the emails appeared to be “from Islamists threatening that sharia law will be brought into our country and that there are viable devices within those school settings”. Givan said the email was signed off “Allahu akbar”, meaning “God is great”, and some schools had closed as a result. “I want to absolutely condemn the actions of those who sought to disrupt our education system today by issuing threatening emails to our schools,” Givan added. Meanwhile, Scottish police said “threatening messages” had also been sent to “a number of schools across Scotland”. “These are being treated as a hoax and officers are investigating,” Police Scotland said in a statement. In central Europe, Hungary saw emails sent to local media, claiming that bombs had been placed in more than 70 schools across the country, according to police. Many of the establishments were evacuated, but officials said no bombs were found. “Based on the investigations carried out so far, this morning’s threats have proved to be unfounded,” Hungary’s interior minister Gabor Posfai said on Facebook. In neighbouring Serbia, state broadcaster RTS reported that more than 100 schools had also received bomb threats. The nature of the messages outside Northern Ireland remained unclear, and the Northern Irish education authority said in a statement that “the majority of schools remained open”.

title: US Supreme Court rejects bid by accused 9/11 mastermind to revive plea deal
description: Ruling leaves Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two co-defendants facing death penalty as Guantanamo military trial remains set for 2028.
content: The US Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal by accused September 11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two alleged accomplices that sought to revive plea deals which were later revoked. Mohammed and two others charged with involvement in the 2001 September 11 attacks – Walid bin Attash and Mustafa al-Hawsawi – struck pre-trial agreements to avoid the death penalty in 2024, during the administration of president Joe Biden. After criticism by some victims’ families, Biden’s defence secretary Lloyd Austin ordered the plea deals to be thrown out, sparking a legal battle over whether such a move was permitted. An appellate court ruled last year that Austin had “acted within the bounds of his legal authority”. A brief, unsigned opinion by the Supreme Court on Monday said it would not take up the appeal. The trio are among the handful of detainees still held at the notorious Guantanamo Bay US military base in Cuba and are set to go on trial in June 2028. Mohammed, also known as “KSM”, was considered one of al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden’s top lieutenants before he was captured in March 2003 in Pakistan. Much of the legal jousting in the September 11 defendants’ cases has focused on whether they could be tried fairly after having undergone torture at the hands of the CIA (Central Intelligence Agency).

title: Trump to create new National Institutes of Health division, task force for women’s health
description: The new task force will not replace the agency’s Office of Research on Women’s Health but will have a broader mandate beyond research.
content: US President Donald ⁠Trump will sign an executive ⁠order alongside first lady Melania Trump on ⁠Monday creating a task force and a National Institutes of Health (NIH) division focused on women’s health, the White House said. The task force will be led by Trump’s White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently announced that she is cancer-free, and US ‌Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jnr, a White House official said. The new Women’s Health Division at NIH will not replace the agency’s Office of Research on Women’s Health but will have a broader mandate beyond research. “President Donald J. Trump & First Lady Melania Trump sign an executive order creating a Women’s Health Division at the NIH & a White House Women’s Health Task Force, aiming ⁠to close research gaps & modernise care for women,” a post on social media announcing the signing said. Representatives for the ‌Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the NIH, could not be immediately reached for comment. The order was first reported by USA Today. In planned remarks at ‌the event, Melania Trump is expected to address the need for using artificial intelligence to ⁠speed women’s health discoveries ⁠as well as access and affordability of care, the official said. Trump and his administration have pushed for healthcare cuts, including at NIH, ‌and last year moved to downsize the federal healthcare workforce. During Trump’s second term, his administration sought to cut NIH grants for research on ‌diversity-related topics ‌and reportedly is moving to allow political appointees to control health-research funding. It also launched a controversial safety ‌review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, that could pave the way for restrictions. Major medical groups have criticised ⁠the move as politically motivated while anti-abortion groups argue the review is moving too slowly. Earlier this month, ⁠US officials told a court the review would be completed by March. US health officials also removed a long-standing safety warning from many hormone replacement therapy products, tightening supplies and leading to shortages, ‌and have urged more manufacturers ‌to study testosterone therapies for women that could support future approvals of female-specific products. HHS has also targeted family planning funds, announcing earlier this year that for the first time it would require applicants for Title X funding to align their programmes with Trump’s political priorities, prompting legal action.

title: Kenyan cult leader convicted of murder over starvation of nearly 200 children
description: Paul Mackenzie and 28 sect members found guilty in the Shakahola Forest doomsday tragedy.
content: Starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and 28 others were found guilty of murder by a Kenyan court on Monday over the deaths of 190 children and an adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related tragedies in recent history. The preacher was arrested in 2023 after police received a tip-off, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola Forest near the coast in southeastern Kenya. Prosecutors say ‌Mackenzie and his Good News International Church organised a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended. The case has gripped Kenya since the discovery of the mass graves. It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola Forest, police said. Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument. He and the others convicted will be sentenced on November 6. Defence lawyer Lawrence Obonyo, who represents Mackenzie and almost all ⁠of the others convicted, said he had been instructed to appeal. In total, more than 400 bodies have ‌been recovered from the Shakahola Forest. Many of the children’s bodies were severely decomposed, with only 26 able to be identified, and investigations into the other deaths were ongoing. Justice Diana ⁠Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more ⁠than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched. The director of public prosecutions, Renson Ingonga, told reporters afterwards at the Mombasa High Court: “That is the best judgment we would ever get”. Mackenzie was in court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, one of the co-accused. When his name was read out by the judge, he was silent, staring into space. The case has led to calls for tougher oversight ‌of churches and ‌other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life. Kenyan President William Ruto said in 2023 that government agencies should have been able to prevent the deaths. ‌He said he took responsibility as president. People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities have told Reuters that Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and ⁠young men, and finally the remaining men. A former taxi driver, Mackenzie forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, branding such institutions as satanic, relatives of ⁠some of his victims told Reuters for a 2023 article. Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names like Jerusalem and Judea. The plight of his followers began to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told police that his brother and wife had starved their children to death in ‌the forest on Mackenzie’s orders. Mackenzie was arrested but released ‌on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police arrested him again in April 2023 and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves. Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied. Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, which lies about 30km (18 miles) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

title: Houthi attack kills 53 at Yemen government training camp
description: The camp is located in Shabwa, an energy-rich province that also houses Yemen’s largest industrial investment.
content: Fifty-three people ⁠were killed and 200 were ⁠injured in an attack ⁠on Monday by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen’s Shabwa province, according to the local authority, as fighting in the impoverished country intensifies. Video verified by Reuters from Shabwa province ‌showed injured people and bloodied bodies scattered across the ground. The Houthis and the internationally recognised government, which is backed by a Saudi-led coalition, have been trading attacks since the group advanced in September towards territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea. Local authority sources ⁠who spoke on condition of anonymity said the Houthis had launched three ballistic missiles at security ‌forces during a training exercise. Shabwa, an energy-rich province in south-central coastal Yemen overlooking the Gulf of Aden, is home to the ‌Balhaf liquefied natural gas facility, Yemen’s largest industrial investment. Government forces this month began ⁠a campaign aimed ⁠at recapturing areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the strait, while the group besieges Taiz, ‌the last major urban stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in the southern highland area of Yemen. The conflict in Yemen has ‌become another ‌front line in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran as the Houthis have ‌escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest crude exporter, targeting Riyadh’s international airport ⁠and the state oil company Saudi Aramco. War broke out in Yemen in 2014 when ⁠the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, driving the government south. A Saudi-led military intervention the following year led to a bloody stalemate until the sides agreed ‌a 2022 truce ‌that held until this year. Yemen is already one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with aid agencies warning of rapidly deteriorating conditions there.

title: China updates drone export rules: less red tape for some, tougher restrictions for others?
description: The changes simplify export procedures for some models while tightening scrutiny on sensitive components and hi-tech capabilities, analysts say.
content: China has updated its export rules on drones and industrial equipment, tightening restrictions on some parts and capabilities while easing requirements for less sensitive models. The changes could simplify overseas sales of consumer drones but increase compliance costs and delivery times for industrial models, analysts said. Announced on Monday by the Ministry of Commerce and other authorities, the changes added critical drone components, including high-performance brushless motors, and certain technologies such as autonomous navigation and obstacle avoidance, to the export-control list for military and civilian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). At the same time, the rules eased restrictions on less sensitive drones.
