The payload threshold for a licensing exemption was raised from 20 litres (5.3 gallons) to 80 litres, while licensing procedures were simplified for some models. Zhang Yi, founder and chief analyst at consultancy iiMedia, said most consumer drones were expected to face few barriers when sold overseas. Industrial UAV exporters, however, would have to complete compliance filings and verify end users, which would “inevitably extend order delivery timelines and increase compliance costs”, Zhang added. The new UAV export rules, jointly issued by the Ministry of Commerce, the General Administration of Customs and the Equipment Development Department of the Central Military Commission, will take effect on November 18. “The global drone industry and technologies have developed rapidly in recent years, and some products that were previously considered as advanced have now become consumer goods,” a commerce ministry spokesperson said on Monday. The changes “demonstrate China’s resolute stance against the unauthorised use of drones for non-peaceful purposes, while highlighting the firm commitment to supporting Chinese companies in conducting international trade and cooperation in the civilian drone field”, the spokesperson said. The updates were announced alongside updated export controls on other equipment with potential civilian and military uses, including tunnel boring machines and dredging vessels. Under the new rules for tunnel boring machines, exporters must obtain a licence before shipping to “sensitive countries and regions with disputes with China”. Exports to other destinations require only prior registration. Wu Guoxiong, director of the Customs Law Committee at Shenzhen-based Guanghe Law Firm, said one significant update concerned the length of time drones could remain airborne. Previously, drones capable of flying more than one hour required an export licence, Wu said. The updated rules extend that threshold to three hours, reflecting advances in battery technology. Certain drones with flight times between 30 minutes and three hours can register with the commerce ministry without needing an additional licence. “This reflects the regulators’ response to technological development of consumer and industrial drones,” Wu said. “It prevents the blanket overregulation of mid-to-long-endurance industrial drones and reflects a strategy of ‘targeted control’.” Wu said another rule change allowing exporters of qualifying drones to simply register before shipping goods would address industry concerns that licensing procedures had disrupted routine exports. Restrictions on the most advanced industrial drones had been tightened and those for consumer-grade models streamlined, Wu said. “The new rules mark a shift in regulatory focus from vehicle performance towards key components and combat-enabling technologies, while the authorities are leveraging streamlined licensing procedures to make the enforcement more targeted,” Wu added. Meanwhile, Zhang of iiMedia said the changes also underscored the growing importance of export compliance for drone makers and suppliers. “Smaller players with limited compliance resources may be forced out of high-performance markets overseas,” he said.

title: Elderly man dies after being pulled unconscious from flat during fire in Sai Ying Pun
description: Flames erupted in flat in Hang Fai Building on Pok Fu Lam Road, with about 60 residents evacuated.
content: An elderly man died in hospital on Monday night after he was pulled unconscious from a flat during a fire in a residential building in Hong Kong’s Western district. Police received a report at 8.57pm that flames had erupted in a flat in Hang Fai Building on Pok Fu Lam Road in Sai Ying Pun. Firefighters deployed two water jet and breathing apparatus teams to tackle the fire, which was extinguished at 9.54pm. A man in his 70s was found unconscious and was rushed to Queen Mary Hospital in Pok Fu Lam. He was declared dead at 10.40pm. About 60 residents evacuated the building of their own accord as emergency crews put out the flames. No other injuries were reported. Following an investigation, the Fire Services Department said it suspected the fire originated in the kitchen and was caused by cooking.

title: Hong Kong police arrest woman after dog allegedly thrown into sea
description: Force says 59-year-old woman’s two dogs showed no visible injuries and are trying to establish whether one was animal thrown into the water.
content: A woman has been arrested on suspicion of animal cruelty after allegedly throwing a dog into the sea in Hong Kong. The woman was reportedly seen throwing a dog from the waterfront near 29 Tai On Street in Sai Wan Ho into the water at around 1pm on Thursday. She then retrieved the animal and left the scene. A passer-by who witnessed the incident alerted police. Following an investigation, officers arrested a 59-year-old local woman on Saturday near the junction of Tai Hong Street and Lei King Road. She was detained on suspicion of cruelty to animals and later released on bail pending further inquiries. The case has been assigned to the Eastern district criminal investigation team for follow-up. Police said the woman owned two dogs – a male Jack Russell terrier and a female beagle – and that neither showed any visible injuries. The animals were handed to the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals for further examination and care. Investigators are trying to establish whether the dog allegedly thrown into the sea was one of the woman’s two pets.

title: China’s milestone in polar region satellite broadband narrows gap with Elon Musk’s Starlink
description: The breakthrough came when scientists in the Arctic established video links with China’s Qinling station in Antarctica using domestic satellites.
content: China’s recent milestone in extending its home-grown satellite internet coverage to polar regions has given the country “fully self-controlled polar communications”, ending its long-time reliance on foreign technology to achieve the same capability, according to state media and industry experts. The breakthrough came during trials conducted as part of China’s 16th Arctic expedition – launched in early July and expected to conclude this month – when scientists aboard vessels in the Arctic established video connections with the Qinling research station in Antarctica using domestic satellites, according to a Monday report by the state-backed People’s Daily. Li Taoyang, analyst at China Securities, said the accomplishment, made possible using the home-grown GW satellite constellation, “filled a critical gap in China’s ability to maintain independently controlled, end-to-end satellite communications in polar regions”. “In the short term, [China’s] polar communication is pivoting from reliance on foreign technologies towards a domestically controlled system,” Li wrote in a note to clients earlier this month. During the trial, the video communications had a transmission latency of less than 1 second, allowing researchers at opposite ends of the planet to communicate in near real time. Other tasks, from the exchange of scientific expedition data to real-time transmission of voyage logs, were also validated during the expedition, underscoring the growing capabilities of the GW constellation, developed by the state-backed China Satellite Network Group (China SatNet). The GW network supports peak upload and download speeds of more than 30 megabits per second, enough to handle multiple high-definition video links and parallel transmission of scientific expedition data. A total of 300 files containing over 100 gigabytes of data were transmitted and more than 40 video connections were made during expedition testing, according to the People’s Daily report. Beyond scientific explorations, the technology could also support maritime communications and emergency rescue operations. It was used for remote medical consultations, allowing doctors in the eastern Chinese city of Qingdao to assess expedition members who fell ill via video links, according to the People’s Daily report. The move comes as China accelerates deployment of its GW satellite constellation to challenge Western providers that already provide satellite broadband coverage to polar areas and other remote locations. China SatNet’s GW constellation plans to deploy nearly 13,000 satellites by 2035, with an interim target of around 1,300 by the end of 2029. Despite its ambitious plans, it remains far behind Elon Musk’s SpaceX, whose Starlink network already operates around 11,000 satellites and has provided connectivity in the Arctic since 2022, giving the US company a substantial head start in polar communications. China launched the expedition to survey Arctic sea ice and study ecological and atmospheric environmental changes as part of an investigation into global climate change and its impact, according to a separate report by the state broadcaster CCTV. An unmanned survey network was deployed in the central Arctic Ocean during the expedition. It consists of domestic equipment including buoys and was supported by the GW satellite constellations to collect year-round data on sea ice and ocean conditions, according to He Jianfeng, chief scientist of the 16th Arctic expedition. He added that less expensive Chinese equipment would allow researchers to economically build a large-scale survey network, allowing the country to make greater contributions in understanding and responding to climate change and push for sustainable Arctic development. The advances come as Beijing steps up efforts to turn home-grown tech breakthroughs into practical applications across industries, from exploration to retail and logistics. The Ministry of Commerce and eight other government agencies issued a draft policy last week, calling for greater use of domestic technologies from AI, cloud computing and embodied intelligence to improve industrial efficiency and create new drivers of economic growth. The guidelines pledged support for the commercialisation of frontier technologies, including embodied AI, while expanding access to computing resources and strengthening data security, underscoring Beijing’s push for technological self-reliance.

title: Busan 2026: 10 of the festival’s best movies, from Midday Meal to Satoko Always
description: From Long Long Night to Silver Express and Possible Love, here are 10 of the best films that were shown at the 2026 Busan Film Festival.
content: The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF), which closed on October 15, drew 277,027 visitors, roughly 40,000 more than last year and the highest since 2015. The 10-day event screened more than 300 films from 59 countries. Alongside 95 world premieres, the programme featured the Asian premieres of several prestigious award winners from Cannes and Venice, including Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner Fjord and May el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion recipient Woman Unknown. Other highlights included Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, starring John Malkovich as a jaded CIA agent, a role many are tipping for Oscar glory. Closer to home, first-time Hong Kong filmmaker Isabella Lam Lok-hin’s thriller Dead End, produced by Soi Cheang Pou-soi, also received its world premiere. While it is impossible to do more than scratch the surface of such a wide selection, here are 10 of the best films that screened at the festival. 1. Possible Love South Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong’s latest masterpiece may have already premiered at last month’s Venice International Film Festival, but the rare chance to experience this searing examination of class, betrayal, grief and anger in front of a local audience on the festival’s giant IMAX screen was an opportunity not to be missed. Netflix, which will release the film globally on November 6, also hosted a riveting masterclass with cinematographer Kim Ji-yong, who spoke about his process of shooting one of the year’s best films. 2. Jim Queen One of the most consistently hilarious films of the year, Marco Nguyen and Nicolas Athane’s outrageous animated romp follows Jim Parfait (voiced by Alex Ramires), gay influencer extraordinaire and head of the “Gym Queens”, after he contracts the mysterious Heterosis virus that turns him straight. Having lost his status and fashion sense – while inexplicably gaining an understanding of football – Jim teams up with shy twink Lucien (Jeremy Gillet) on an odyssey through Paris’ queer subculture to find a cure and save the liberated community that once hailed him as a god, before it is eradicated forever. 3. Midday Meal Winner of the best film award at this year’s festival, Majid Majidi’s compelling drama is now eligible for consideration for the coming best international feature film Oscar. Set in an arid, brutally inhospitable wasteland and featuring a cast of non-professional actors, the film sees 40-year-old part-time teacher Solan (Mohammad Rahimi) risk his freedom by engaging in illegal fuel smuggling to earn the extra cash needed to sustain the food programme at the tiny school where he works. While Solan’s actions are praised by his elderly mother and the desperate community, questions are raised over his true motivations. 4. Satoko Always Kasumi Arimura, Hikari Ishida and 16-year-old Kashun Himeno – in a breakout turn that rightly won her a best acting award – star as three women named Satoko, who are from three different generations and are all compelled to start writing by their everyday experiences. Deftly constructed by Japanese writer-director Shuichi Okita (The Story of Yonosuke), this playfully intricate tale has each of its protagonists’ stories mirror the others just enough that we repeatedly question whether these women are, in fact, the same character at different stages in her life. 5. The First Taste of Loneliness Another film focusing on three female characters at different stages of their lives is Gu You’s poetic and beautifully constructed family opus. The third instalment in the Chinese director’s “Landscape” series, which started with 2019’s Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains and continued in 2023’s Dwelling by the West Lake, explores how the death of a family patriarch affects his wife (Xi Meijuan), daughter (Zhou Xun) and granddaughter (Wang Shengdi). Gu’s style is reminiscent of his contemporary Bi Gan in its use of long takes and sequences that defy traditional boundaries of time and space. Actress and singer Zhou won the festival’s other gender-neutral acting prize for her performance. 6. The Scar-faced Cat: Way of Asura Writer-director Wang I-fan follows Get the Hell Out (2020), his frenetic zombie comedy set in the corridors of Taipei’s legislature, with this lushly constructed period martial arts thriller. Han Ning is transformed here from supporting ingenue into trailblazing action star as a vengeful geisha in Japanese-occupied Taiwan who tears through the countryside on a bloodthirsty revenge mission after she is raped and her husband is murdered by law enforcement officers. Visually ravishing and packed with breathless action and copious bloodletting, this film was the undeniable highlight of Busan’s Midnight Passion sidebar. 7. The White Snake Enchantress Released in 1958, Taiji Yabushita’s dazzling adaptation of the classic Chinese folktale, The Legend of the White Snake, was not only Japan’s first feature-length animated colour film but also reportedly inspired a young Hayao Miyazaki to forge a career in animation. Clearly influenced by early Disney classics such as Snow White and Bambi with its musical numbers and cute animal sidekicks, the story of a young man bewitched by a snake goddess was painstakingly crafted using tens of thousands of hand-painted cels. Nearly 70 years on, the film has lost none of its romantic power or visual majesty. 8. Long Long Night The best South Korean film in this year’s competition is an enchanting animation from first-time director Youm Kyu-bock that is guaranteed to leave viewers in tears. Norden (voiced by Park Ki-wook) is an orphaned white rhino who is raised by a family of elephants. Through a heart-wrenching series of traumatic encounters, Norden ultimately finds himself wandering the Earth with a baby penguin (Kim Gyu-na). Narrated by Bae Suzy, Long Long Night is an epic roller coaster of incident and emotion that exposes the best and worst of humanity’s interactions with the animal kingdom, while celebrating family in all its peculiar forms. 9. Ibuku When a desperate mother (Christine Hakim) learns that her daughter, Sri (Ayushita Nugraha), is facing execution in Saudi Arabia after murdering her abusive employer, she is faced with the impossible task of travelling from her remote rural home to a foreign land to reconcile with her estranged child before it is too late. An ambitious and experimental drama from Indonesian filmmaker Eddie Cahyono, Ibuku (also known as My Mother) unfolds in an elliptical, almost dreamlike fashion as it explores the ongoing plight of women in societies where they remain stripped of voice and agency, even in the 21st century. 10. Silver Express An unconventional romantic drama from first-time writer-director Miki Tanaka, Silver Express follows Chieri (Yui Okamoto), a self-proclaimed “Silver Lion” who rejects love and physical intimacy. A university student with little time for her friends’ endless obsession with romance, she nevertheless seeks out male companionship, only to be repeatedly let down when their advances overstep the mark. Okamoto’s performance is understated yet empathetic, but most interesting is how the film addresses her asexuality – refusing to label it as an ailment to be cured, but rather presenting it simply as a way of life to be respected. title: Chinese basketball player Barry Wang tipped as NBA prospect after US university match
description: Playing for the Massachusetts Minutemen, who compete in NCAA Division 1, the 21-year-old has important role in future of men’s national team.
content: Rising Chinese basketball star Barry Wang Junjie was tipped to be an NBA prospect after he flourished in only his second game with his new team, the Massachusetts Minutemen, on Sunday. Wang erupted for 31 points on eight-of-12 shooting, including knocking down a pair of three-pointers and converting 12 of his 13 free throws, to go with six rebounds as the University of Massachusetts beat Brown University 88-86 in a tight exhibition game. The Massachusetts Minutemen represent the university in NCAA Division 1 men’s basketball in the United States. “I think 31 points is my career high, so let’s just keep doing it,” Wang said in a post-match press conference. “I am back here for the third week, so I am doing better with the team. “Everybody was getting to know each other on and off the court, we know each other more, and play more smoothly. I think that helps me play more easily on the court.” Immediately after the game, a basketball scout under the name JPR on X (formerly Twitter) said he was “pretty confident” Wang was the best NBA prospect in the MAC (Mid-America Conference), where his new university play. “Legit 6ft 9in with a burner and moves his feet much better than he gets credit for,” he said. “Think we’ll see a lot more of his game at UMass this year than what he showed at San Francisco.” Feel pretty confident saying Junjie Wang is the best NBA prospect in the MAC. Legit 6’9” with a burner and moves his feet much better than he gets credit for. Think we’ll see a lot more of his game at UMass this year than what he showed at San Francisco. https://t.co/uSmmM6A1pv — JPR (@Scouting_Col) October 18, 2026 The comment drew positive and negative responses, with some agreeing Wang “shot very well from deep” on the day, but others did not have the same amount of faith, questioning if the team’s offence matched Wang’s abilities. Nevertheless, the 21-year-old was considered an important part of the next generation of players to be cultivated by the Chinese men’s basketball team, after he was a part of the NBA Academy in China when he was about 13 years old. Born in Xuzhou on April 3, 2005, Wang was one of the first few Chinese players to enrol at the NBA Global Academy in Canberra back in 2022. He committed to the University of San Francisco and played 53 games for the team in his junior and senior seasons. In July 2025, Wang made his senior national team debut at the Fiba Asia Cup, where China finished second to Australia in the 16-team tournament in Saudi Arabia. Averaging 13 points and 4.2 rebounds while shooting 56.1 per cent from the field – including a staggering 47.8 per cent from long range – Wang was named to the all-tournament team alongside compatriot Hu Jinqiu. In San Francisco for his junior season, Wang, however, was again deployed as a role player and averaged 8.5 points and 3 rebounds per game. At the end of last season, Wang was transferred to the University of Massachusetts. Speaking to local media earlier this month, the head of the Massachusetts men’s basketball team believed Wang, standing at 6ft 9in (2.06m) and playing as a forward, could create possible mismatches on the offensive end. “Barry is a special offensive talent. With his size and skill, he’s pretty good offensively. He can really score and pass,” Frank Martin, head coach of the Massachusetts Minutemen, said. While Wang came from another college, Martin was relying on those in his inner circle to determine if the Jiangsu native would be a good match with his system. “And when those people swore to me what he was about, I was willing to hit the fast-forward button. I knew I had two weeks to figure out if we could make it work or not,” the 60-year-old from Florida, who was heading into his fifth season with UMass, said. Contracted to three-time and reigning National Basketball League (NBL) champions Hong Kong Bulls, Wang was expected to remain playing overseas as he continued to pursue a potential career in the NBA. A potential opportunity to play in the city could, however, arise in the coming months if the Hong Kong-based team joined the Chinese Basketball Association (CBA) league – the top-tier basketball league in China – next summer.

title: US, China should learn from Cold War-era arms control to tackle AI risks: ex-US official
description: Robert Rubin also called on both sides to take action to address global economic imbalances.
content: Washington and Beijing should put aside their mutual distrust to address the risks posed by artificial intelligence, much as the United States and Soviet Union cooperated on nuclear arms control during the Cold War, a former US Treasury secretary has urged. Robert Rubin, who served as US Treasury secretary under former president Bill Clinton from 1995 to 1999, cited the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks (SALT) between Washington and Moscow decades ago as an example of two superpowers working together despite massive differences. “Unfortunately, the United States and China have this distrust and mutual antagonism,” Rubin said via video at the Bund Summit in Shanghai on Monday. “Just as happened with SALT and nuclear matters, we should put aside the distrust, put aside the antagonisms and work together on an issue that can so massively and powerfully and adversely, severely affect both our countries.” During a fireside chat with Huang Yiping, dean of Peking University’s National School of Development, Rubin warned of potentially severe AI safety risks, including cyberattacks. Those dangers, he added, were growing as open-source AI made the technology available to more people and progress towards artificial general intelligence (AGI) continued. “There’s no ready, permanent answer to that, but one thing I am absolutely convinced of ... is that our political systems in both our countries should be focused on this very carefully, very intensely, and we should be working together,” he said. “If one country focuses on it and the other doesn’t, that doesn’t work either.” China and the US held their first AI dialogue last month, led by Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, days before the summit between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Washington. Beyond AI safety, Rubin also discussed the widely debated issue of global economic imbalances, saying both countries needed to take action. Washington should rein in its fiscal deficits and Beijing should boost domestic consumption, he said. The strength of the US economy left it well placed to reduce its deficit, although doing so would require a willingness to take difficult steps, he added. “It does take a certain political will, and my guess is we’ll have to wait for the next administration for that to happen,” he said.

title: France imposes curfews in Paris and major cities after worst riots in years
description: Government struggles to restore order as half a million take to streets over soaring prices.
content: France announced partial curfews in Paris and other cities on Monday after weekend demonstrations over soaring prices degenerated into some of the worst street violence in recent years. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu did not rule out imposing a state of emergency after the interior minister said police had “lost control”. Tourists in Paris had a taste of the disruption on Monday when they found the Louvre closed because of a small group of student protesters, while the US embassy in Paris urged American citizens to avoid the demonstrations. Facing accusations that it failed to anticipate and respond to the violence, the government has vowed to re-establish order, while officials scrambled to contain public anger. The unrest, erupting just six months before France elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron, threatened to continue, with organisers calling for a new round of protests next Saturday. Authorities said partial curfews would be enforced from Monday evening to Tuesday morning in a number of cities including Paris, Lille and Lyon, to protect businesses. In the capital, a curfew was ordered from 11pm, while demonstrations were banned from 8pm. “I’m absolutely determined to restore public order,” Lecornu said. Other European countries have also seen demonstrations over rising prices, with smaller clashes breaking out in Milan and Belgium over the weekend and protests simmering in Spain and Portugal. Some half a million people turned out across France on Saturday to denounce the surging cost of living, a culmination of four weeks of protests that began with students demanding better conditions at high schools. What started as peaceful demonstrations descended into violence in many cities, as masked groups attacked law enforcement, broke into public buildings and set some ablaze, looted shops, and set fire to cars, bicycles and scooters. On Monday, France’s digital minister, Anne Le Henanff, urged online resale platforms to remove listings for “stolen items” following Saturday’s looting and summoned representatives of companies including Vinted and eBay. After the weekend scenes of chaos, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez offered his resignation, but Macron refused to accept it. More than 2,500 people were arrested and nearly 1,000 members of the security forces injured. Protesters were also hurt, with one demonstrator’s hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade. Macron acknowledged failures in the government response, which had seen 60,000 law enforcement personnel deployed on Saturday. Nationwide, more than 2,513 people have been taken into police custody since the weekend, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said. He added that 67 had been jailed and “dozens” of criminal cases opened. Darmanin also said authorities would use facial recognition on social media to identify perpetrators. At least 3,000 shops were damaged, with the cost running into hundreds of millions of euros. In an address to the nation Sunday, Macron slammed the “unbridled” violence. The European Union called the violence “unacceptable” but warned that the right to peaceful protest “must be protected” in France. Germany condemned the violence and updated its travel advice for France, saying “further outbreaks of violence in the coming days cannot be ruled out”. China has warned citizens travelling to France to be aware of risks and take safety precautions, state broadcaster CCTV reported. In Paris on Monday, a dozen demonstrators blocked the entrance to the Louvre, the most visited museum in the world, while bewildered tourists looked on. “We don’t want to get involved. We want to stand back and get away from them,” Pat Boland, a tourist from Australia, said of the protests. The pensioner, 73, spoke to Agence France-Presse outside barricades that had been erected at the Louvre, which was closed because a small group of protesters stood by its famed glass pyramid entrance. The unrest has flared before presidential elections in April and May that will elect a new French president after a decade of centrist Macron. Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate, is riding high in the polls. The government has accused ultra-left groups of stoking the violence to boost the chances of the far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon in the presidential polls. The interior minister and intelligence services were to meet late Monday to discuss the violence. During the weekend, clashes broke out on the sidelines of a cost-of-living demonstration in Milan. “I’m very worried because it’s a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself,” mayor Giuseppe Sala said. In Belgium, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in Brussels and Liege. In Spain protesters have set up tents in the heart of Madrid to denounce soaring housing costs, with similar encampments going up in neighbouring Portugal’s main cities of Lisbon and Porto.

title: China plans 18 active ETFs as regulator seeks to shore up stock market
description: Beijing’s securities regulator also vows tougher action against misconduct and outlines four measures to create a healthy market.
content: The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has approved 18 actively managed exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which could channel tens of billions of yuan into the A-share market, as it seeks to strengthen investor confidence and market resilience. Speaking on Monday in Beijing at the opening ceremony of the Financial Street Forum, one of China’s top national-level economic conferences, CSRC chairman Wu Qing also pledged to crack down on market irregularities as the regulator pushes to manage growing risks from global financial volatility while encouraging listed firms to buy back shares. The first batch of 18 actively managed ETFs from domestic public fund managers won approval after a three-month review. Fund managers could announce their offerings as early as Tuesday, with sales starting on Friday and each product potentially raising about 2 billion yuan (about US$300 million), according to domestic media reports. “The move marks a major step forward in fostering fund product innovation and will bring more incremental capital into the market,” Wu said, adding that the CSRC would broaden sources, channels and access routes for medium- and long-term capital and deepen reform of the public fund industry. The approval comes amid a deep market correction since July, following a sharp sell-off in technology shares driven by concerns over US sanctions. Wu vowed the regulator would work to strengthen market resilience and urged efforts to bolster investor confidence as risks increasingly spread across borders, markets and sectors. “Global markets are showing significantly stronger spillover effects. Greater volatility and correlation can be seen across equities, bonds and foreign exchange markets, deserving close vigilance over cross-border, cross-market and cross-sector risk transmission,” Wu said. “The CSRC will follow the principle of pursuing progress while maintaining stability. Focused on its core tasks, the commission will further refine the capital market’s balanced investment and financing functions, bolster market resilience and investor confidence,” he added. Wu said the CSRC would strengthen law-based and stringent regulation while fostering a well-regulated, healthy market ecosystem. He outlined four measures that the commission would soon introduce. The first would establish a fund-industry monitoring centre responsible for registering private fund shares, collecting data from public and private funds and monitoring risks, he said. The commission would also issue guidelines on the secure and compliant use of artificial intelligence across the securities and futures sectors, he added. Wu said it would refine penalty rules for illegal share reductions to crack down on such violations with greater precision. Lastly, the commission would release guidance on advance compensation in the securities market to better protect the legitimate rights and interests of retail investors, he added. Other senior financial regulators also addressed the four-day conference. Ding Xiangqun, head of the National Financial Regulatory Administration, said the regulator would step up efforts to upgrade China’s banking and insurance sectors. It would also welcome more foreign institutions and long-term capital to operate and expand their businesses in China, Ding said.

title: Opinion | Palestine Action, Sally Rooney’s books and the absurd fallout of a UK ban
description: Books withdrawn. Elderly supporters arrested. The issue concerns the extent laws purporting to protect national security curb free expression.
content: Irish writer Sally Rooney is a publishing sensation, often described as the “voice of a generation” and the first great millennial novelist. More than six million copies of her books have been sold globally since her debut novel in 2017. But now, these beautifully written literary bestsellers, with their youthful exploration of romance and relationships, class and technology, are being withdrawn from sale in the United Kingdom. The generation of royalties for Rooney from the book sales, the author and her British publisher fear, might breach UK anti-terrorism laws carrying a maximum 14-year jail term. Rooney, who lives in Ireland, feels unable to visit Britain, believing she could be arrested. Last week, publisher Faber revealed the drastic step to stop supplying her books to the UK. It is a crazy situation. The issue has arisen as a result of the author’s publicly stated support for activist group Palestine Action, proscribed as a terrorist organisation by the British government last year. Rooney declared she would use her royalties to support the group. This might constitute a serious offence under the Terrorism Act 2020. Faber said the legislation prevented it from passing Rooney’s UK earnings on to her and to continue to sell her books in such circumstances would be “unconscionable”. Her e-books were removed from sale. Bookshops will still sell existing copies of print editions. Demand for them has, of course, soared. But stocks will not be replenished, and unless the position changes, the next Rooney blockbuster will be absent from the shelves. The novels will still be available in other parts of the world, including Hong Kong. This ridiculous state of affairs raises fundamental issues about the impact of anti-terror laws, intended to safeguard national security, on artistic freedom. Such legislation can have far-reaching and, perhaps, unintended consequences. The question of whether outlawing Palestine Action itself is legal will be determined next month when the group’s challenge reaches the Supreme Court. In February, the High Court ruled the proscription unlawful, finding it to have breached the home secretary’s own policy and to amount to a disproportionate restriction on free expression and the right to protest. But that decision was overturned by the Court of Appeal in June. The judges said the ban was justified and proportionate, and the home secretary was best placed to assess terror threats. Palestine Action, founded in 2020, aims to end what it describes as “global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime”. It has targeted UK military support for Israel. Shortly before being banned, the group carried out a raid on a Royal Air Force base in Oxfordshire, spraying two aircraft with red paint and causing an estimated £7 million (US$9.28 million) in damage. The government justified the decision to blacklist the group by reference to its “escalating campaign involving intimidation and sustained criminal damage, including to Britain’s national security infrastructure”. The appeal court said Palestine Action was a group that had gone beyond civil disobedience and was engaged in causing “serious damage to property using weapons”, risking injury to members of the public. It was described as a covert organisation seeking to prevent the capture of those involved in perpetrating such violence. But the direct-action protest group has attracted much support and its proscription has been widely criticised. The withdrawal of Rooney’s books is not the only absurd consequence arising from the move. It has sparked numerous peaceful demonstrations, featuring many elderly demonstrators. Those expressing support for Palestine Action, such as by silently holding up a placard, face arrest and – potentially – jail for supporting terrorism. Around 3,700 have been apprehended and 2,500 charged. The court case attracted an “intervention” from the United Nations Special Rapporteur on human rights and counterterrorism who argued the proscription order breached the UK’s international human rights obligations. Rooney warned, in a statement to the High Court, it was unlikely she would be able to publish a new book in the UK if the ban on the group remained and her existing works may have to be withdrawn. “The disappearance of my work from bookshops would mark a truly extreme incursion by the state into the realm of artistic expression,” she added. The issue goes beyond whatever view is taken of Israel’s treatment of Palestinians. It concerns the extent to which laws purporting to protect national security curb free expression. Ultimately, the Supreme Court will decide on the legality of the UK’s ban. But Rooney deserves credit for her courage and spirited determination to stick to her principles. The sooner her novels return to British bookshelves, the better.

title: Apec in Hong Kong: what to know as 500 delegates descend on the city
description: Beijing is using Hong Kong to showcase its financial gateway role ahead of November’s Apec leaders’ summit in Shenzhen.
content: Global attention will turn to Hong Kong this week as about 500 senior officials and delegates from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation’s 21 members gather in the city for the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday. It is the first time Hong Kong has hosted the meeting, with Beijing’s support, as mainland China prepares to host the Apec leaders’ summit in Shenzhen next month. Hong Kong joined Apec in 1991 and has continued to take part in the economic forum’s affairs under the “one country, two systems” framework since the 1997 handover of sovereignty from Britain to China. The South China Morning Post lists the key things you need to know about the meeting. Why is Hong Kong hosting the meeting? Some analysts believe Beijing’s decision to hold the finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong is a calculated move to bolster the city’s standing as an offshore renminbi hub and present it as a safe harbour amid lingering geopolitical tensions. Hosting the international event can also raise the city’s global profile as a financial hub, particularly by highlighting its role as a gateway connecting China with the rest of the world. The meeting is one of Apec’s most important ministerial exchanges. Beijing also hopes to use the occasion to champion its vision of a multipolar world. China is Apec’s host for 2026, with meetings taking place in cities including Suzhou and Guangzhou. The finance ministers’ meeting is a precursor to the summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. What is on the agenda? The two-day meeting begins on Tuesday, with China’s finance minister, Lan Foan, due to deliver a keynote speech. Chen Xu, chair of the Apec Senior Officials’ Meeting, will brief delegates on this year’s priorities and latest developments. Delegates and guests are also being offered a packed social programme from Monday evening to Wednesday, giving them a taste of Hong Kong’s soft power and technological strengths. Highlights include giant pandas, open-top bus rides, a Chinese cooking class, traditional opera, a harbour cruise, the Big Buddha, The Peak, the Hong Kong Science Park and Cyberport. A heavy police presence is expected around the venue, the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai, with officers patrolling around the clock. What comes next? The Shenzhen summit is seen as especially high-stakes and historic, with Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin all expected to attend.

title: Philadelphia 76ers fans dare to dream of NBA title with LeBron James in star-studded team
description: City of Brotherly Love has seen icons, from Charles Barkley to Joel Embiid, with Allen Iverson in between, but has not won it all since 1983.
content: Long-suffering Philadelphia 76ers fans haven’t celebrated an NBA title in 43 years, but with newly arrived LeBron James headlining a star-studded team, they are daring to dream. “We never had a team like this,” enthuses Kairee Harvey, a 32-year-old police officer and diehard LeBron supporter. “I still can’t believe it,” the resident of neighbouring New Jersey said of the arrival of James in July. “I feel like I’m in a dream a little bit.” Suddenly, Harvey said, “I think that this will be our year to win a championship.” On paper, Philadelphia’s starting five looks like a daunting prospect, boasting two former MVPs and a former Finals MVP. But the City of Brotherly Love has learned the hard way that talent does not always translate into trophies. Philly has seen NBA icons, from Charles Barkley to Joel Embiid, with Allen Iverson in between, but has not won it all since 1983. “I think there’s always gonna be some caution with Philly fans,” said Rob Nero, a local artist who has created several works depicting Sixers players, displayed on walls all across the city. “We’re so used to getting our hopes up and having our hearts broken,” Nero said. “But that’s never gonna stop us from getting excited and believing in our teams.” The Sixers’ final pre-season game at the Xfinity Mobile Arena was sold out, fans sharing a few early moments of euphoria. “They let me down at times as a team, but I’m there to cheer them on no matter what,” said Laurie Ney, who was accompanied by her two Yorkshire terriers – both, like her, wearing Sixers jerseys. Philadelphia is an Eagles town and in the streets the NFL team’s green dominates the blue of the Sixers. Even last year, Matthew Merovitz would have put Major League Baseball’s Philadelphia Phillies in second place in the city’s popularity scale. “But if you’re looking into this season where the other teams stand, I would say the Sixers are easily at the top of the city,” the young professional clad in a Sixers jersey said. Philly sports fans could certainly do with a lift from the Sixers. The Phillies were knocked out of the first round of the MLB playoffs. The Eagles are on a four-game skid with star quarterback Jalen Hurts out indefinitely and the Flyers are languishing in last place in the NHL Eastern Conference. The question is whether the show on the court will live up to the names on the marquee and whether the collection of stars come together to function as a unit. “We’ve already seen some exciting things in the pre-season, especially from Jaylen Brown and VJ Edgecombe,” Nero said. With no clear hierarchy yet established, many fans expect Brown, acquired in a blockbuster trade from Boston, to take control. “This is a lot of good players together,” Brian Yoder, a septuagenarian who remembers the championship Sixers of Julius Erving and Moses Malone, said. “They’ve just got to become a team.” The 1983 squad, which swept Magic Johnson’s Lakers 4-0 in the Finals, had also been shaken up the previous off season with the arrival of reigning MVP Malone. “They just gelled together,” Yoder recalled. “That’s what made it fantastic. They were a team.” Clemon Johnson, one of the heroes of the 1983 triumph, thinks it can happen again. “I’m looking forward to watching them raise the banner next year,” he said. Nothing less will do if King James is to reign in Philadelphia sports fans’ hearts. For most, the throne still belongs to electrifying point guard Iverson, who carried the Sixers to the Finals in 2001. Elijah Davis, a salesman at vintage jersey store Mitchell & Ness, said the two-year deal signed by James defines the window for success. “If we don’t get anything now or like in the next year ... I wouldn’t say the organisation is cooked, but it’s definitely going to need some changes for sure.”

title: Calls grow for India to lure tech talent home as US tightens job curbs
description: Washington has suspended a programme allowing foreign professionals to work in the US and potentially obtain permanent residency.
content: After completing a master’s degree in data science at Pace University in New York in May last year, Tarun returned to India in October, saying frequent changes in US visa rules and employer sponsorship requirements had made it difficult for him to find a job in the world’s largest economy. Tarun, who is from the southern Indian city of Tirupati, felt returning home was a more prudent move than pursuing a job in the US indefinitely. “I got a job within one month here [Bengaluru] with an American engineering company,” he said, without giving further details about his job. “At the end of the day, my decision is about my happiness. I am close to my friends and family.” Tarun’s experience mirrors a debate over whether growing uncertainty surrounding US immigration rules could spur more Indian professionals to return home, with prominent figures in India’s tech industry weighing in on the issue. In a viral social media post, Sridhar Vembu, co-founder and chief scientist of Chennai-headquartered cloud software company Zoho Corporation, urged Indian professionals in the US to return, arguing that India could turn the increasingly hostile climate in Washington towards foreign talent into a valuable opportunity to grow its technological capabilities. “Indians have made a major contribution to America’s technological prowess. Yet, a big part of America no longer wants us. Indians who are on a visa in the US face the painful prospect of uprooting the life you have built with hard work,” Vembu wrote on October 9. “Let this be the birth pains of a bold new future. Come back, let’s build India,” he said. Indians have made a major contribution to America's technological prowess. Yet, a big part of America no longer wants us. Indians who are on a visa in the US face the painful prospect of uprooting the life you have built with hard work. Let this be the birth pains of a bold… — Sridhar Vembu (@svembu) October 9, 2026 The US is home to the world’s largest Indian diaspora, estimated at between 5.8 million and 6.1 million people as January, many of whom hold senior positions at global technology companies. Former Indian education minister Dharmendra Pradhan has backed Vembu’s call to contribute to India’s tech growth, emphasising the need to strengthen local capabilities and foster innovation. “With confidence in our talent and a commitment to building indigenous capabilities, we can help shape the future of technology,” he wrote on social media. The posts have raised expectations of Indian tech talent to accelerate innovation in India. “It would be great if the government took more initiative to support professionals because there are a lot of highly talented Indians who are in the US. Many of them are struggling with visa pressures,” said Tarun. On October 8, the US administration suspended the Permanent Labour Certification programme, a key step for foreign professionals to work in the US and potentially obtain permanent residency under an employer-sponsored process, affecting Indian companies such as Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro, as well as US giants including Microsoft and Adobe. Speaking on the move on the same day, US Vice-President J.D. Vance accused major companies of fraudulently bringing in lower-paid foreign workers whom he described as “indentured servants” instead of employing Americans. India’s Ministry of External Affairs slammed his remarks as “deeply offensive” the following day. “We believe that such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem,” it said in a statement. Vance later clarified that his remarks were criticism of American companies and the visa system rather than of workers. Indian professionals said that his remarks showed a lack of respect towards them. “A professional is not ‘cheaper’ because they were born in India, China, Brazil or anywhere else. Their salary may be different. Their immigration status may be different. But their education, experience, expertise, ambition and dignity are not cheaper,” Dhananjay Ramakrishnappa, a manager of operations at Bengaluru-based software firm Flexara, said in a social media post, which also mentioned that he had previously worked in the US for 13 years. “What worries me even more is the fear that many immigrants now feel about simply travelling home to see their families,” he said. He said that a US-based family friend did not travel to India to attend her mother’s last rites because she feared that she would not be able to come back. Washington’s curbs against foreign professionals could tighten further as it is reportedly examining a proposal to levy a US$70,000 fee on international students seeking post-graduation work authorisation. Ramakrishnappa, who returned to India in 2017 after working in senior US-based executive roles with Microsoft, told This Week in Asia that Indian-origin professionals who had spent a decade or two working in the US tech sector could become successful entrepreneurs in India. Subbu K., head of technology at New York-based start-up Trust Guard AI, however, said he was torn between whether to stay in the US or return to India. His daughter, who is studying in a US high school, might not be keen to head home, he added. “I would love to do that [return to India] because it gives me the best of both worlds,” said Subbu, who still holds an Indian passport after spending over two decades working in the US tech sector. Nonetheless, tech professionals and analysts say India has to take steps to lure more tech talent home. Subbu worried about red tape in India, citing how a friend of his spent around eight months to get clearance from Indian regulators to start a business, compared with as fast as within a day in the US. Vivek Mishra, deputy director of the strategic studies programme at the Observer Research Foundation, said the significant salary gap between what Indian tech professionals could earn in the US and India could be a deterrent. “There has to be a calculated outreach to these people. Otherwise it will be just a slogan,” he said. Uday Chandra, professor of political science at India’s Ashoka University, said appealing to Indian talent to return home based on “innate patriotism” alone would not work. “Ultimately, highly skilled professionals will go wherever their talents are valued and they can pursue their ambitions. India will need to compete for such talent,” he added.

title: Chinese ambassador denies threatening Philippines after saying a war may prove easy to win
description: Foreign ministry in Manila summoned ambassador Jing Quan after his comments further inflamed long-running tensions.
content: Beijing’s ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan has denied making threats after he was summoned over his recent comments that China could “easily win” a war between the two countries. Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro met Jing on Monday to express “serious concern and strong objections” over his “provocative and unacceptable” language. Lazaro added that he had aggravated an already sensitive situation and undermined efforts to build mutual understanding between the two countries, according to the Philippine foreign ministry, which said he had “conveyed a threat”. On Thursday, Jing told a forum in Quezon City that Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro’s description of China as a regional “troublemaker” was “nonsense”. He added: “If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force and we love peace.” On Monday, Jing denied that this was a threat, saying he had been advocating for peace between the two countries, which are at loggerheads over their competing South China Sea claims. “What is a threat? ‘If you don’t follow me, I will hurt you.’ This is a threat,” Jing said in a statement issued by the Chinese embassy after the meeting. “But my point is despite our capacity, we don’t have the intention to use force. Because we are friends and close neighbours. There is no need to resort to force.” He said the two countries “should enhance dialogue, manage differences and deepen cooperation” and “let the good aspects prevail over bad ones”. He also accused Teodoro and other officials of trying to “attack and smear China”. The embassy said “no one should expect [it] to keep silent” in the face of such attacks, and urged the Philippines to stop “anti-China politicians and ill-intentioned forces from dragging our bilateral relations into the dangerous situation of confrontation”. It also urged Manila to understand China’s position and avoid “selective quotation, over-interpretation and overreaction”. The message echoed earlier comments by Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning, who said Beijing firmly opposed “certain individuals in the Philippines” who were “maliciously hyping up” the situation and undermining relations between the two countries. She told a daily press conference that while better relations were in both sides’ interests, the Philippines should “restrain the irresponsible words and deeds of certain politicians” – an apparent reference to Teodoro, regarded as one of Beijing’s sharpest critics. The defence minister was hit by sanctions in June that barred him and his family from entering mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau over what Beijing described as repeated erroneous remarks about the country. Tensions have been running high over the two countries’ competing claims in the South China Sea, where there have been regular clashes between coastguard vessels in recent years. Beijing claims sovereignty over nearly all islands and rock features and rights to the adjacent resource-rich waters, while Manila says these disputed features lie within its exclusive economic zone. The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei all have their own separate claims. Jing’s comments provoked a fierce backlash among Philippine officials and legislators. Within hours, the Philippine foreign ministry hit out at his “poor choice of words”, saying they seemed to “convey a thinly veiled threat of the use of force, which is hardly helpful in the context of the complicated bilateral ties between the Philippines and China”. President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr said his comments sounded “very much to me like a threat” and were “not a very diplomatic statement”. Several lawmakers have called for Jing to be declared persona non grata – a formal declaration he was not welcome in the Philippines that could lead to his expulsion. They included Senator Risa Hontiveros, who demanded a formal apology and retraction from Jing. She also described his comments as “grey zone aggression in diplomatic form, meant to intimidate and coerce while stopping just short of war”.

title: PBOC plans bond liquidity backstop, pilots onshore yuan market trading for foreign banks
description: Authorities will expand the pilot allowing securities firms to conduct foreign exchange settlement and sales to facilitate firms going global.
content: China’s central bank plans to roll out a liquidity facility for non-bank financial institutions to tackle systemic stress triggered by mass redemptions, putting a firewall in place to backstop the bond market in case of crisis. Pan Gongsheng, governor of the People’s Bank of China (PBOC), also pledged to step up efforts to make yuan-denominated assets more attractive to overseas investors, while streamlining access for foreign financial institutions to conduct yuan transactions in the onshore foreign-exchange market. Pan announced a slew of measures when he delivered a speech during the opening ceremony of the Financial Street Forum – one of the country’s top national-level economic forums – in Beijing on Monday. “Going forward, the PBOC will further boost high-quality policy supply,” Pan said, according to a transcript of his speech released by the central bank. He said the bank would also provide onshore foreign-funded banks with broader access to its short-term, collateralised liquidity, while pushing forward with greater bond market connectivity. The new liquidity tool targeting non-bank financial institutions, jointly launched by the central bank, the National Financial Regulatory Administration and China Securities Regulatory Commission, will establish a stabilising mechanism for the bond market, Pan said. It comes against the backdrop of sharply diverging onshore equity and bond markets starting in the second half of this year. China’s tech-driven equity index has tumbled recently while bond markets posted a minor bull run. Analysts said contracting financing demand was the dominant factor behind the bond bull market, making positioning already very crowded. Pan said the backstop mechanism would be activated under specific scenarios, such as when the bond market was caught in a negative feedback loop of redemptions and fire sales. Eligible non-bank financial institutions include securities brokers and mutual funds. These institutions must comply with macroprudential requirements and pledge high-grade collateral, so as to prevent pricing distortions and avoid creating the illusion of an unconditional backstop, he added. To promote better integration of yuan’s onshore and offshore markets, the PBOC will launch a pilot that permits eight onshore and foreign offshore yuan clearing banks to carry out proprietary transactions in the onshore interbank foreign-exchange market. Authorities have not released the names of the eight participants. Meanwhile, China’s central bank continues its efforts to further refine monetary policy framework. Pan said China would push forward reforms on loan interest rate pricing benchmarks, shifting from heavy reliance on the Loan Prime Rate (LPR) towards a more diversified pricing system. As the framework matures, financially robust enterprises may negotiate with lenders to choose either the interbank overnight repo rate or the LPR as the benchmark for floating-rate loans. The LPR will remain the pricing reference for small business and household loans. The PBOC will issue policy guidance to steer financial institutions on implementation. The PBOC will also work with other authorities to ramp up financial support for international science and tech innovation hubs in the Beijing metropolitan area, the Yangtze River Delta and the Greater Bay Area in Guangdong. At the forum on Monday Zhu Hexin, deputy governor of China’s central bank and head of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE), said the authority planned to roll out a package of measures to help firms better engage in international cooperation and competition. Among the initiatives, authorities will advance the opening-up of the foreign exchange market and expand the pilot programme allowing securities firms to conduct foreign exchange settlement and sales.

title: Japan’s mega-quake that never was, and the danger of false alarms
description: A software error triggering a false magnitude 9.9 quake in Japan sparks fears that eroding public trust could cost lives in a real quake.
content: Kanako Hosomura was working in a clothing store in Yokohama when an alert on her phone warned of an imminent magnitude 9.9 earthquake. “We all rushed outside,” Hosomura said, recalling how people poured out of nearby shops and offices to watch tall buildings and power lines for signs of shaking. But no earthquake came. Eight minutes after issuing the warning on Friday, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) cancelled the alert, leaving residents to wonder what had gone wrong. “These alarms do not go off very often – only maybe a couple of times a year – so when they do sound, everyone is worried that the quake is going to be really big,” Hosomura said. “Usually it takes maybe 20 seconds between the alarm and the earthquake, so when nothing happened we all just looked at each other. I was just about to go back inside when the second alert went [off], but a friend told me that it was just to cancel the first warning.” The incident has raised concerns among experts that repeated false alarms could erode public confidence in Japan’s Emergency Earthquake Early Warning system, potentially making people hesitate when a genuine disaster strikes. Earthquake warnings are designed to give people precious seconds to take cover before strong shaking arrives. If people begin to doubt the system, experts warn, even a brief delay in taking action could cost lives. The initial alert was issued at 12.40pm on Friday via mobile phones, television, radio and public loudspeaker systems. It predicted a magnitude 9.9 earthquake in Hokkaido and the Tohoku region of northeastern Japan, with shaking also expected in Tokyo and parts of central Japan. The system warned of shaking at level seven – the maximum on Japan’s seismic intensity scale – indicating violent tremors capable of causing severe structural damage, collapsing buildings and throwing people to the ground. A magnitude 9.9 earthquake would be larger than any recorded in history, surpassing the magnitude 9.5 quake that devastated southern Chile in May 1960 and the magnitude 9.1 Tohoku earthquake in March 2011. The 2011 disaster triggered a huge tsunami along Japan’s northeastern coast, killing more than 20,000 people and causing the worst nuclear disaster since Chernobyl. Causing further confusion on Friday, the agency used the same alarm to issue the cancellation eight minutes later, leading some residents to fear the second alert was a new warning rather than a recall. The JMA publicly apologised for the error during a press conference on Friday and reiterated its apology in a statement sent to This Week in Asia, attributing the blunder to a software error. According to the statement, the system’s sensors initially estimated a magnitude 9.9 earthquake off the disputed Northern Territories near Hokkaido. But the actual quake measured magnitude 6.9 and struck off the Kamchatka Peninsula, about 680km (423 miles) further north. The agency said its nearest observation point was 1,200km from the epicentre, making it difficult to gauge the tremor’s true size. A similar false alarm was issued in July 2020 following an undersea tremor near the Izu island chain south of Tokyo. In response, the agency decided to stop using data from sensors located more than 700km from an estimated epicentre to improve accuracy, but that protocol was not followed on Friday. The JMA said the error was likely caused by a manual input mistake and that software changes had since been made that should prevent a recurrence. Ayataka Ebita, director of the agency’s Earthquake and Tsunami Observation Division, said at the press conference that the error was not the result of a cyberattack. “We apologise for the considerable inconvenience and distress caused to the public by the erroneous issuance of the Emergency Earthquake Early Warning on this occasion,” the agency said in its statement, adding that an investigation was ongoing. Public opinion has been split. Some social media users have criticised the agency for triggering widespread panic, while others said an unnecessary warning was better than no warning at all. In an editorial published on Sunday, the Yomiuri newspaper called for a “prompt investigation” and measures to prevent a recurrence. “False alerts have a significant impact on people’s lives,” the newspaper said, citing disruptions including the temporary suspension of the Tokaido Shinkansen bullet train service. Local governments also expressed concern that repeated false alerts could cause people to lose trust in the system and fail to evacuate in future emergencies. Akiyoshi Kikuchi, an associate professor of disaster sociology at Meisei University in Tokyo, said the early warning system was an important part of Japan’s disaster prevention infrastructure, but that the mistake risked weakening public confidence. “I am concerned that repeated errors like this could undermine public trust,” he said. “Earthquake warnings require the public to respond immediately, so hesitation – even briefly, such as wondering whether the alert is accurate – could delay protective action and put people at greater risk.”

title: 5 hikers fall ill as hot weather grips Hong Kong on public holiday
description: At least five hikers require emergency assistance amid hot weather in Hong Kong on final day of Chung Yeung Festival long weekend.
content: Five hikers fell ill in separate incidents across Hong Kong on Monday as hot weather gripped the city on the final day of the Chung Yeung Festival long weekend. In one incident at Po Pin Chau, a popular hiking destination in Sai Kung, a 62-year-old mainland Chinese woman was hiking with friends near the High Island Reservoir East Dam when she became dizzy and weak at about 10.30am. Suspected of suffering from heatstroke, she was rescued by the Government Flying Service and flown to hospital for treatment. At about 12.20pm, a family of three – a couple and their son – were hiking from Tai Tong Country Park along the MacLehose Trail when the mother, in her fifties, felt unwell and vomited near Tai Lam Chung Reservoir. Her husband called for assistance, and she was airlifted to Ruttonjee Hospital for suspected heatstroke treatment. In another case reported at about 12.40pm, a brother and sister hiking from Sam Mun Tsai to Ma Shi Chau in Tai Po sought assistance near Tong Kai Tseng after the 63-year-old woman complained of heart problems. She was flown by helicopter to Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital in Chai Wan for treatment. At around the same time, a woman in her forties fell ill while hiking on Ho Hok Shan in Yuen Long. She reported feeling unwell near a cemetery, also showing signs of heatstroke. Firefighters assisted her and her three companions down the hill. Later, at 2.09pm, an elderly man hiking at Luk Wu Tung in Plover Cove Country Park in Tai Po reported feeling physically weak and called for assistance. The Hong Kong Observatory said an anticyclone aloft was bringing generally fine weather to southern China, while an easterly airstream affecting the Guangdong coast was gradually moderating. Conditions across the city were hot and dry during the day, with the daily maximum temperature reaching 32 degrees Celsius (89.6 Fahrenheit) at the weather forecaster’s urban headquarters and several degrees higher in parts of the New Territories.

title: Review | Hong Kong Ballet’s visually stunning Dunhuang: In Search of Light fails to fully tell tale
description: Dunhuang: In Search of Light dazzles with visuals and music but struggles with narrative depth.
content: There is nothing more difficult than living up to expectations. Dunhuang: In Search of Light is the first new full-length production for Hong Kong Ballet by the husband-and-wife choreographic team of Ricky Hu Songwei and Mai Jingwen since the multi-award-winning The Butterfly Lovers in 2024. The exceptional success of its predecessor raised the bar, and while the new work offers plenty to enjoy, it does not reach the same level. On the plus side, the lush, atmospheric score by Tian Mi (composer of The Butterfly Lovers) cleverly incorporates traditional Chinese instruments. The visuals are stunning, with Jonathan Wong’s outstanding sets, including an awe-inspiring giant Buddha head, well-imagined costumes by Dieuweke Van Reij and video by Dan Fong making effective use of the auditorium and stage. The final image of Guanyin descending from heaven is a dazzling coup de theatre. Nonetheless, these elements are the icing on the cake, and the cake itself is less satisfying. The main problem is the subject matter. The original commission was to create a ballet inspired by Dunhuang’s famous Mogao caves, with their treasure trove of Buddhist art. Magnificent as the caves may be, they are not obvious material for a full-length ballet, so Hu and Mai used Hermann Hesse’s 1922 novel, Siddhartha, about a young man seeking enlightenment through Buddhism. The ballet portrays Siddhartha’s journey of self-discovery as he encounters worldly temptations, experiences love and loss and ultimately finds peace. The trouble is that dance is ill-equipped to handle themes like spiritual aspirations, doubts and dilemmas – concepts that need words to express them properly. The choreographers have chosen to avoid telling the story as a direct narrative, which might have worked better. As it is, the work presents a series of tableaux, with grand-scale group sequences featuring a variety of people and creatures, from flying apsaras (celestial nymphs) to traders on the Silk Road to Buddhist monks. The choreographers make good use of the stage and deploy the dancers effectively, but as one large ensemble follows another, the structure becomes repetitive and instead of focusing on the protagonist, he is often lost in the crowd. The need to bring in the Dunhuang theme is another issue. The references to the lively atmosphere on the Silk Road are fine, but the sequence in which various gods, whose images feature in the caves, appear and supposedly represent the hero’s “inner demons” makes little sense. While there is some exciting dancing, the lack of connection between Siddhartha’s inner being and the apparitions makes this look a lot like that old device from 19th century ballet, the divertissement. To fully engage the audience in Siddhartha’s journey, the production needs more moments where he interacts in-depth with individuals or expresses himself through solos. The strongest sections are by far those that show his relationship with his lover Mara and their son. The scene where he seeks to reconcile with his estranged, embittered child is the ballet’s high point. It has tremendous power and shows Hu’s consummate ability to generate deep emotion and depict complex human relationships. These scenes are sharply real and compelling, in contrast to the rest of the ballet, which, while well-crafted and entertaining, is closer in feel to big dance dramas from mainland China – technically spectacular and danced to a high standard, yet simplistic in content – than the kind of work Hu has produced in the past. It is frustrating that there have been no Hong Kong reruns of Hu’s The Butterfly Lovers, The Last Song (2022) or The Rite of Spring (2019), which he choreographed with Yuh Egami. These outstanding works – all three received the Hong Kong Dance Award for Outstanding Choreography – are part of Hong Kong Ballet’s legacy and deserve to keep their place in the repertoire. It is to be hoped that these fine ballets will be seen again in the future, especially since the company will perform more after moving into the “Dancehouse” at the WestK Performing Arts Centre in 2027. Gouta Seki, one of the company’s rising stars, brought innocence, poignancy and elegant dancing to Siddhartha, Ye Feifei was a moving Mara and Jeremy Chan gave a performance of searing intensity as the son. There was a fine rendition of the score from the Hong Kong Sinfonietta, with guest musicians from the Hong Kong Gaudeamus Dunhuang Ensemble, under the accomplished baton of Vivian Ip. “Hong Kong Ballet: Dunhuang: In Search of Light”, Hong Kong Cultural Centre Grand Theatre. Reviewed: October 16.

title: Elon Musk says he will give SpaceX share to ‘every kid in America’
description: There are around 73 million children under the age of 18 in the United States.
content: Tech billionaire Elon Musk said on Monday that he would give every child in the United States a share in his SpaceX rocket company. “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America,” Musk, the richest man in the world, said on X. “This will be the first of many,” he said, without providing details about how the scheme would work. There are around 73 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, according to 2024 data from the US Census Bureau. Musk owns 38 per cent of SpaceX, according to Forbes. His announcement comes after President Donald Trump promised last month to give every American adult US$5,000 if his Republican party retains control of Congress in November’s midterm elections. SpaceX set the record for the largest initial public offering in history, raising US$85.7 billion in June. The company’s Starship megarocket reached orbit for the first time in September, a milestone for the rocket central to Musk’s Mars ambitions.

title: Long March shows why the Communist Party needs strong leadership: state media
description: People’s Daily article draws parallel between the importance of Mao’s leadership during the 1930s and Xi’s role today.
content: A Monday article published by the ruling Communist Party’s mouthpiece argued that a key lesson from the Long March was the need for the party to have a strong core leadership and for its members to uphold that core’s authority. “History shows us that only with a core can the party unite as one, and only with authority can its orders be effectively carried out … The most important thing is to establish and resolutely uphold the party’s core,” wrote Xie Chuntao, vice-president of the Central Party School, in the People’s Daily article. The Central Party School is the country’s top training institution for officials and part of a nationwide system that President Xi Jinping regards as crucial to maintaining ideological purity. Xi was the school’s head between 2007 and 2012. Xie said the emergence of a strong leadership collective with Chairman Mao Zedong at its core during the Long March was crucial to the party’s eventual victory in the civil war, drawing parallels with the present-day leadership under Xi. The article was published a week before the fifth plenum, scheduled for October 26 to 29, when the Central Committee is set to discuss measures to strengthen party governance and discipline. The current party Central Committee has been rocked by corruption investigations, with 35 of its 205 full members either under investigation or stripped of their seats in the National People’s Congress, China’s top legislative body, according to SCMP calculations. Many of them have been accused of disloyalty to the Central Committee. The article also comes as the party prepares to mark the 90th anniversary of the Long March’s conclusion on Thursday, when Xi is expected to deliver a speech. The Long March was a strategic retreat by the Communist Red Army from 1934 to 1936 to evade Nationalist forces during the Chinese civil war. The event is frequently invoked by the party as a symbol of its endurance, discipline and political unity. The Red Army travelled about 10,000km (6,200 miles) while pursued by Nationalist troops. The campaign, which was marked by internal divides and major disagreements within the Red Army, saw Mao first gain military leadership before going on to establish his absolute authority within the party. Xie said the decision by most Red Army troops to follow Mao northwards at a critical moment rather than join another force heading south reflected the party’s ideological conviction and unity. Xie drew parallels between the importance of Mao’s leadership during the Long March and Xi’s role as the party’s core today. He placed particular emphasis on the “Two Safeguards” – the requirement for party members to uphold Xi’s position as the core of the Central Committee and the party as a whole, and to uphold the authority and leadership of the Central Committee. He also highlighted the closely related “Two Establishes” – which establish Xi’s position as the core of the Central Committee and establish Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the party’s guiding ideology. “The ‘Two Establishes’ are a major political achievement of our party in the new era, a decisive factor in bringing about the great transformations of the new era, and the greatest certainty, the strongest source of confidence and the greatest guarantee for the party in dealing with all uncertainties,” Xie wrote. Xie said the central leadership’s ability to make political judgments, take decisions and act was particularly important amid growing global turbulence and mounting challenges to China’s modernisation. “On the Long March of the new era, [we must] continuously improve our political judgment, understanding and execution, and always maintain a high degree of consistency in our thinking, political positions and actions with the Central Committee with Xi at its core,” he wrote.

title: Seeking men’s approval? Chinese tennis star criticised for glamorous photo shoot with trophy
description: Backlash sparks massive debate: most fans defend tennis star, with one viral comment declaring, ‘strength and beauty are not opposites’.
content: After Chinese tennis player Zheng Qinwen won the China Open in early October, a series of photos showing her in a white dress and studded high heels, holding the trophy on the Great Wall, unexpectedly drew criticism from female internet users who accused the athlete of trying to please men and of not looking like an independent woman. Chinese social media celebrated Zheng’s victory, which made her the first Chinese player to win the championship in the tournament’s 22-year history. The 24-year-old has been one of the country’s most popular athletes since reaching the French Open round of 16 four years ago. She also won the women’s singles gold medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics. On October 12, she posted several photos of herself in a long dress and high heels, holding the China Open trophy on the Great Wall outside Beijing. The caption read: “The long-awaited photo with the trophy.” Her post has been viewed 1.8 billion times on Weibo and received 1.3 million comments. On RedNote, another leading social media platform, the post received 345,000 likes. The outfit, however, raised eyebrows because Zheng is usually seen wearing sportswear. While many people praised her new look as “beautiful and valiant,” some comments – apparently from female internet users – attracted significant attention. “Sister, your dress and high heels… I initially thought you were someone who thought outside the box. Now I realise that was just my expectation of you, not your own way of thinking. That’s my problem, not yours,” one disappointed user wrote.
