Another commenter asked: “Is it appropriate to wear high heels so soon after playing seven gruelling matches at the China Open?” “This outfit makes you look unlike an athlete,” a third user remarked. The comments soon sparked heated discussion, with most internet users supporting Zheng. “An athlete’s identity is defined by her performance on the tennis court, not by what she wears. When male champions pose for fashion photos in suits, people admire them as elegant and dashing. But when women dress up, some say they no longer look like athletes. That’s a clear double standard: the idea that strong women shouldn’t be allowed to enjoy dressing up,” one user commented on Sina.com. Another user wrote: “Being an independent woman doesn’t mean conforming to a stereotype. It means having the freedom to choose what to wear and being responsible for your actions.” “Strength and beauty are not opposites,” a third person noted. Zheng has not yet responded to the heated online discussion. The dress and shoes are by Dior, which recently appointed Zheng as a global ambassador. Zheng is not the first Chinese female athlete to be criticised for embracing a soft, feminine appearance. The outspoken 100-metre hurdler Wu Yanni often defends her pursuit of beauty, as many people disapprove of her glittery make-up.

title: Is Philippines’ laws on underwater cables lagging behind its digital hub goal?
description: A leading telco executive says bureaucracy is slowing cable repairs carried out by specialised vessels in Philippine waters.
content: The Philippines’ telco industry wants the country to become a regional digital hub anchored by stable underwater cables, but a leading executive and analysts warn that slow approvals for repairs, limited monitoring and fragmented official oversight could undermine the ambition. At a forum on archipelagic governance for subsea cables, PLDT, the Philippines’ largest telecommunications company, called for greater cooperation among government agencies and further reforms to expand the vital digital nodes connecting the country to the world. While the Philippines’ strategic location in Asia-Pacific presented an opportunity for it to be a key connection point for submarine cables, it would need to invest in high-value assets and simplify approvals for cable deployment and repair work, Albert Villa-Real, president and CEO of PLDT Global, said at the forum on September 29, according to a report by the Philippine Star. “The Philippines should not think of itself simply as the end point of these international cables. Our ambition should be to become a major digital crossroad of Asia-Pacific,” he added. PLDT is connected to subsea cable networks, including the Apricot Cable System, which runs across the Asia-Pacific, and the Jupiter Cable System, which links to Japan and the United States. Villa-Real stressed the importance of undersea cables in an archipelagic country such as the Philippines, which has more than 7,600 islands, saying that fibre lines would have to run underwater to provide connectivity that businesses needed to invest in various systems. However, multiple permits are required before specialised vessels handling cable repairs can enter local waters, which impedes such works, according to Villa-Real. His comments came just days before an outage in submarine cable segments connecting the Philippines to Singapore and Hong Kong disrupted connectivity and services nationwide. The Philippines has also encountered maritime activities that pose a risk to its critical subsea cables. On October 1, the Philippine coastguard said it intercepted a Chinese research vessel sailing off the country’s Batanes Islands, which are near cable corridors connecting Manila to Northeast Asia. “Most documented damage has been accidental, from anchors and typhoons. I have found no public case of confirmed deliberate damage to a cable in Philippine waters,” said Mark Manantan, chief investigator of the Southeast Asia–Australia Resilient Cable Connectivity Initiative. “There are also reported underwater surveillance drones attributed to a state actor found in Philippine waters, obviously mapping the country’s seabed. Security agencies treat the threat as growing, partly because of the wider maritime context,” said Manantan, who is a research fellow at La Trobe University’s Centre for Global Security. Analysts said while Philippine officials had made progress in creating frameworks to govern subsea cables, their pace of implementation and the regulatory scope still fell short. Manila should further streamline rules to facilitate subsea cable repairs and enhance seabed surveillance, said Manantan, noting that responsibility was spread across more than a dozen government agencies, leading to delays in repair and official approval. “No single agency is responsible for collecting consolidated incident and route data, and the country has not yet designated cable protection zones. Recent incidents showed what this costs. Responses were improvised, and restoration took months rather than days,” he said. Nonetheless, the Philippines is taking steps to strengthen related legislation and make it easier for foreign firms to be involved in the country’s cable industry, according to analysts. Francis Domingo, an associate professor of international relations at the University of the Philippines Diliman, said the Philippines’ Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), which is responsible for the protection and governance of subsea cables, had published the National Digital Connectivity Plan (NDCP), under which a regulatory framework would be developed to safeguard submarine cables as critical digital infrastructure. “It is safe to say that some officials have a clear understanding of the significance of subsea cables based on the NDCP,” Domingo said. Then secretary of DICT Henry Aguda said in February that the NDCP aimed to boost “resilient connectivity” for Filipinos, especially in underserved areas such as submarine cable systems, supported by public–private partnerships. Manantan cited the entry of foreign cable repair ships in Philippine territorial waters this year as a sign of progress. The introduction of the Konektadong Pinoy (Connected Filipino) Act to liberalise the cable market, and a recent announcement on cooperation between DICT and Australia on a cable protection framework were also steps in the right direction, he added. Domingo said that the Philippines’ largest telecommunications and internet providers were discussing forming a consortium to strengthen the country’s connectivity, given the country’s lack of systems to monitor, detect and protect subsea cables from threats and damage. Angel Redoble, chairman of the Philippine Institute of Cybersecurity Professionals, however, called on the government to take the lead role due to national security concerns. “To make sure that our national security interest is prioritised and protected, then we have to have the government become part of the process in anything that is related to submarine cables,” Redoble said. Manatan said that investors would look to Manila to manage digital infrastructure and implement robust rules to position the country as a subsea or data centre hub during peacetime and crisis. Citing typhoons and increasing geopolitical tensions, he added: “Officials increasingly see a cable cut as a risk to national security and continuity of government, not just a telecoms outage.”

title: Can Malaysian reform party Bersama survive a founders’ scandal?
description: The reform party’s election campaign in Melaka has been dealt a blow after co-founder Nik Nazmi was hit by a religious morality scandal.
content: A Malaysian reform party led by two former cabinet ministers faces a new test ahead of a crucial state election after one of its founders was sidelined over an alleged religious morality offence, threatening its appeal to voters disillusioned with the country’s political establishment. The controversy surrounding former environment minister Nik Nazmi Nik Ahmad could undercut Bersama’s promise of delivering a different kind of politics in next month’s Melaka poll, analysts say – although some believe its core base will dismiss scrutiny into his personal life. Nik Nazmi and former economy minister Rafizi Ramli relaunched Bersama in May after breaking with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s People’s Justice Party (PKR). Taking over a little-known party registered in 2016, they introduced a multiracial platform focused on wage growth, affordable housing, social protection and institutional reform. But Bersama’s effort to build a movement beyond its high-profile founders now faces controversy over an alleged incident of khalwat – an Islamic offence concerning unmarried or non-related men and women being together in secluded spaces that could give rise to suspicion of immoral conduct. The offence does not require proof of adultery. Nik Nazmi confirmed on Saturday that he and a woman were detained by Selangor religious authorities at a residence in Petaling Jaya, near Kuala Lumpur, on Thursday. He said they had been discussing a project with friends at a studio in Brickfields before moving to Petaling Jaya to examine materials, adding that only the two of them were present when enforcement officers arrived. “We did not engage in any improper conduct that would give rise to suspicion,” Nik Nazmi said, apologising to his wife, family and party for a “lapse in judgment”. Bersama has suspended Nik Nazmi from all official activities from October 20 to January 19, keeping him off the campaign trail. Party president Syukri Razab said the suspension was necessary to “preserve the party’s integrity, credibility and public confidence”. A video circulating online also shows a document labelled “NIK NAZMI” containing photographs, dates, addresses and map coordinates purportedly recording his movements since May. Entries identify locations including Tamarind Square in Cyberjaya, south of Kuala Lumpur, as well as premises in Petaling Jaya. Photos show a woman entering a parked car purportedly linked to Nik Nazmi, walking near buildings, sitting at tables and passing through an airport terminal. This Week in Asia could not independently verify the authenticity of the images, dates, identities of those pictured or the document’s source. The compilation does not establish the nature or purpose of the purported meetings. Nik Nazmi did not respond to requests for comment regarding the material or the potential impact of the controversy on Bersama. A credibility test Bersama has announced 15 candidates for the November 14 Melaka election. Its electoral debut in Johor in July resulted in all 15 of its candidates losing their election deposits after failing to secure the minimum threshold of votes. Party co-leader Lee Chean Chung has maintained that the controversy would not disrupt the Melaka campaign, saying Bersama respects the investigation and remains focused on winning support. Amir Fareed Rahim, director of strategy at political risk consultancy KRA Group, said the main danger lay in alienating undecided or reform-minded voters. “The Nik Nazmi controversy risks undermining the very proposition that Bersama represents a different kind of politics,” Amir said. “For a new party campaigning on reform, the reputational stakes are particularly high.” Amir said the swift suspension showed Bersama took its integrity seriously, but the broader challenge was building an organisation capable of winning votes without relying solely on the personal reputations of its founders. “National recognition does not automatically produce grass roots machinery, local loyalty or electoral credibility,” he said, noting that Bersama candidates had been campaigning early in Melaka after opting out of the recent Negeri Sembilan state polls to concentrate resources. James Chin, a professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania, was less convinced that the incident would hurt Bersama among its primary base, which he described as largely former PKR supporters who favour separating religion from politics. Chin said the party acted prematurely by suspending Nik Nazmi before any legal determination had been made. “He has not actually been found guilty; he was just arrested,” Chin said. “Bersama overreacted. They should have waited until the court case.” Chin added that the party’s decision appeared to be a pre-emptive attempt to manage social media fallout rather than a reflection of its core voters’ concerns. “They’re trying to be ahead of the social media wave because if they had done nothing, they are afraid of the social media blowback.”

title: Art or box office? How Hong Kong plans to measure the value of a play, ballet or symphony
description: Newer groups could get more access to public funds under proposed changes, but established companies urge realistic targets and a long-term view.
content: Established performing arts groups in Hong Kong should rely less on public subsidies to make way for emerging companies, industry experts have said, after the city’s leader announced a revamp of the funding model in favour of a more flexible, non-permanent and merit-based system. But a few directors of the city’s nine designated major performing arts groups in music, dance and theatre said the economic downturn had made private funds harder to secure and urged the government to take a long-term view, noting that arts development goals could take years to achieve. The new funding model will require policymakers to lay down targets for companies, prompting questions about how to assess merit in an industry where artistic quality does not always translate to commercial success. The South China Morning Post spoke to performing arts groups, cultural critics and a lawmaker amid the debate over how to better spend public funds to develop Hong Kong’s performing arts sector and how to determine which groups are deserving of support. Falling audience numbers When Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu delivered his policy address last month, calling for Hong Kong to play a bigger role as a centre for international cultural exchange, his proposals included a new funding mechanism tied to artistic merit and performance that would encourage innovation among the major arts groups while allowing promising newer companies to join their ranks. Hong Kong has had the same nine designated major performing arts groups since 2008, namely the Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra, Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra, Hong Kong Sinfonietta, Hong Kong Ballet, Hong Kong Dance Company, City Contemporary Dance Company, Hong Kong Repertory Theatre, Chung Ying Theatre Company and Zuni Icosahedron. Total government subsidies for the nine groups hovered between HK$340 million and HK$500 million (US$43 million and US$63 million) from 2020 to 2025. But government sources said attendance at performances by these groups fell from 360,000 in 2007 to 300,000 in 2025, while seat occupancy dropped from 77 per cent to 69 per cent. The decline had prompted the government to consider whether the subsidies could be better spent. Lawmaker Chris Ip Ngo-tung said a funding mechanism based on merit and performance had been discussed for years, but its inclusion in the policy address for the first time signalled to smaller or emerging companies that they might gain better access to subsidies previously directed only to established groups. The new mechanism could entail subsidies of different amounts creating a “funding ladder” and the merit-based system would prompt arts groups to be more strategic when deciding what shows to produce, Ip said. Arts group leaders would set their development goals more clearly to secure continued support as their companies grew. The sources said the number of major performing arts groups was not capped at nine, so new companies could join – a possibility that Ip said would incentivise emerging groups and encourage more comprehensive and sustainable development across the sector. The government had asked the groups to propose key performance indicators (KPIs), which could cover ticket sales, school outreach activities and talks, overseas collaborations and performances, the sources said. The time frame for meeting the targets had yet to be discussed, but groups would not lose their status after missing targets for a single year, they added. Setting standardised KPIs is no easy task Culture critic Kuh Fei said it was impossible to apply standardised KPIs across different art forms, that attendance and box office receipts did not necessarily reflect artistic quality and that there was a reason the government had designated those groups for support in the first place. “It’s a form of investment that the government is subsidising these groups. If the subsidies are suddenly taken away … would that mean they made the wrong decision from day one and that they should not have nurtured those groups for 18 years?” he said. Kuh acknowledged that the existing system was too rigid and did not allow promising smaller and medium-sized companies to access public funds, but added that the major groups, too, remained chronically underfunded even after receiving government subsidies. “In addition to public subsidies, the existing major performing arts groups have worked very hard to secure their own funding,” he said. “In a healthy ecosystem, they should take less [public funds] so medium-sized groups can move up.” Benny Lim Kok-wai, an associate professor of practice in cultural management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, said the proposed mechanism was intended to spur innovation but could have the opposite effect, discouraging major groups from taking risks that could lead to a loss of funding. “Almost all nine [major groups] are carrying out their own innovations, but what are the requirements and who determines them?” Lim said. He added that the government should clearly define what it meant by innovation, as the new system could put the nine groups under pressure. Lim agreed with Kuh that government subsidies could be reduced gradually over many years as the major groups secured funding elsewhere, freeing up subsidies for smaller companies. But Ip was sceptical that this could be achieved if the groups continued to rely on substantial government funding, with the subsidies acting as a crutch that prevented them from seeking private financing. Celina Chin Man-wah, executive director of the Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra, said finding new sources of income had proved challenging despite the group’s best efforts amid the economic downturn. The drop in audiences should also take into account broader changes over nearly two decades, including the falling birth rate and shifting consumption patterns, she added. Chin supported the new mechanism but said KPIs needed to be clearly defined in consultation with arts practitioners and should include both qualitative and quantitative measures. “Because we are using government resources, we look at whether we’ve helped nurture talents or represent Hong Kong internationally, and whether established artists or festivals in your field would want to work with the group. These could also be indicators,” she said. Not only about box office numbers Marble Leung, executive director of the Hong Kong Repertory Theatre, said his company had produced strong box office performances, with an average attendance rate of 94 per cent for its shows in the past four years. It had also quadrupled its number of shows in the same period. Despite this, he opposed assessments based purely on numbers. “If we want to increase numbers every year, that would be unrealistic,” he said. Leung said relevant KPIs could include audience support, whether the company’s work became a subject of research, its contributions to society and its financial capacity to sustain its development. Local and overseas experts could also help to assess artistic standards. With his company now setting its sights on becoming a top player in the country, Leung said that the impact of artistic work might become apparent only after several years, and an understanding of this time frame should be built into any change to funding policy. Christy Lee, executive director of Chung Ying Theatre Company, said the proposed mechanism presented an opportunity for industry players to review how performance should be measured. “Are shows that are more traditional or experimental any less valuable than commercially successful ones? It would be unfair to the former,” she said, stressing that original shows needed a period of incubation, while audiences needed time to warm to certain productions. She cited Les Misérables, now a staple of the musical genre, saying it had been poorly received when it was first staged four decades ago. “If we’re short-sighted and think it didn’t achieve any targets, we would’ve killed off the room for development for the work to become a classic,” she said, warning against any approach that placed too much emphasis on speed and efficiency.

title: PLA hits out at Chinese student accused of wearing Japanese rising sun flag in classroom
description: The student, reportedly from Nanjing, was confronted by other Chinese students at Moscow State University following the incident.
content: The People’s Liberation Army has criticised a Chinese student who reportedly wore the Japanese rising sun flag in a classroom at a Russian university, accusing him of whitewashing Japanese militarism. The flag, which is still used by the Self-Defence Forces, is widely seen as a symbol of Japanese militarism and aggression in many countries, including China. “Regardless of which country or campus one is in, advocating for militarism is an explicit offence against human conscience and is held in contempt by all,” Jun Zhengping, a social media account run by the People’s Liberation Army, said late on Sunday. The account described the incident as “egregious” and “shocking”. The incident took place on Wednesday during a history class at Moscow State University, according to Global Times, which is owned by the party mouthpiece People’s Daily. It said sources had told the newspaper that the student was from Nanjing – scene of the most notorious Japanese wartime atrocity in China when it was still known as Nanking – and was named Chen. The report added that the sources said the student had brought a 1930s Japanese military cap into the classroom and had draped the flag over himself. Some Chinese students objected and asked him to stop, but he refused and allegedly resorted to physical violence and verbal abuse in Japanese, the report said. Chinese students from other departments later gathered at the classroom to confront him. The Chinese Students and Scholars Association at Moscow State University said it had raised the incident with the university and had also reported it to the Chinese embassy. The university has launched an internal investigation, with a decision expected soon, the association added. Two Chinese-language videos appearing to show the student apologising have gone viral on social media. One, which showed the student’s face, was apparently filmed by other Chinese students on the day of the incident. In it, he admitted that his actions were “wrong”, offered a “sincere apology” and said he would “reflect on his behaviour”. He also pledged to promote a deeper understanding of the Nanking massacre, saying: “I think this is what we, as historians, should do.” The second video, said to have been filmed a day later, appeared to show the student wearing sunglasses and a face mask and saying that it was “completely wrong” to display the flag and had shown a “lack of respect” for his motherland and its people. The South China Morning Post could not independently verify the content of the videos. Moscow State University has been asked for comment. Beijing has repeatedly called on Japan to reflect on its wartime record and relations have come under increasing strain after the country’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said last November that a Taiwan Strait crisis could be a “survival-threatening situation” that could trigger military intervention from Tokyo. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. Japan, in common with most countries, does not recognise Taiwan as independent. Further controversy flared over the weekend after Takaichi sent a ritual offering to Tokyo’s Yasukuni Shrine for its autumn festival, although she did not visit in person. The shrine honours Japan’s wartime dead, including convicted war criminals, and is regarded by Beijing as a symbol of Japanese militarism. Takaichi said on Friday that she planned to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen if parliament permits.

title: China’s Guizhou province targets Hong Kong travellers with extended-stay mountain getaways
description: A Guizhou official says the number of homestay lodgings in the province has risen by 30 per cent over the past year.
content: China’s southwestern Guizhou province is seeking to attract more visitors from major economic hubs like Hong Kong through extended-stay tourism, capitalising on its cool climate and mountain scenery as it looks to boost the sector and support economic growth. “Tourists are increasingly moving away from sightseeing-focused trips towards more leisurely holidays and immersive experiences, making longer-term stays an inevitable trend in tourism,” Lu Yongzheng, head of Guizhou’s provincial publicity department, said on Sunday. Speaking at a tourism promotion event in Hong Kong that was hosted by the provincial government, Lu said Guizhou was seeking to build itself into a premier, nationwide destination for “seasonal living”, while upgrading infrastructure and services to support visitors. In July, the province unveiled a five-year plan to develop its long-stay tourism sector, targeting visitors from major population and economic centres, including the Yangtze River Delta and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area. The plan also called for improvements to transport, dining and other services. The move followed the province’s pledge last year to make tourism one of its pillar industries, after Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Guizhou in early 2025 and called for faster economic transformation, an improved business environment and closer integration with other regional economies. Lu said the number of homestay lodgings in Guizhou had risen by 30 per cent over the past year, which he described as the fastest growth nationwide. Yang Kun, deputy general manager of Guizhou Tourism Industry Development Group, said the province had also recorded an increase in inbound tourism this year. Visitors from Hong Kong and Macau, in particular, are extending their trips from just a few days to 10 or 15 days. “Guizhou’s cool climate and diverse charm leave many travellers feeling that a short stay just isn’t enough,” Yang said at the tourism promotion event on Sunday. The group is working with operators of homestays in mountain regions and urban areas to offer packages for longer stays, Yang said, adding that the aim was to give visitors more time to experience the province’s landscapes and culture. Hotel bookings in Guizhou rose more than 70 per cent year on year this summer, according to the provincial government in September, citing data from travel platform Fliggy. Separate data from Trip.com showed that Hong Kong visitors accounted for the largest share of tourists during the summer, local media Guizhou Daily reported on Saturday.

title: Terrorism squad probes car attack that critically injured Australian lawmaker
description: A man has been arrested after Haines was deliberately hit by a car outside her office.
content: Australian lawmaker Helen Haines was in a critical condition on Monday after being deliberately struck by a car outside her office, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese saying a terrorism task force would be investigating an arrested suspect. Albanese told a news conference it was too early to determine the motive for the attack but later pointed to the changing face of social media having raised the temperature around politics in a country where such ‌violence is extremely rare. Victoria Police said a 43-year-old man had been arrested after the attack on independent MP Haines in Wangaratta, around three hours’ drive northeast ⁠of Melbourne. Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason told a press conference that Haines was struck by a white Toyota Land Cruiser as it drove along Murphy Street, where Haines’ office is. The driver was detained by bystanders who saw the incident, he said. Mason said a knife was found inside the vehicle. Haines, 65, was airlifted to hospital where she is in a critical condition, police and Albanese said. When ⁠asked by public broadcaster ABC whether the increased anger around politics had led to worries about attacks on politicians, the ‌prime minister pointed to the anonymity of online content. “The concern, if you look at anyone’s social media feeds and look at the comments, people will say things that they ‌would never say face-to-face. But the temperature has undoubtedly been increased. Not just here in ⁠Australia, of course. We’ve ⁠seen incidents internationally as well,” he said. “Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community ‌and engage with people. I don’t want to see a political system in which you can’t have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the ‌street, at street ‌meetings, public forums. That’s an important part of our democracy.” Victoria Police’s Mason told a press conference there was no further threat ‌to the public and that they were treating it as an isolated incident. While the Australian police gave no details of any specific social media links or threats in this case, politicians worldwide are facing a surge in violence, threats and harassment, according ‌to ‌a survey published in February by the global Inter-Parliamentary Union. The IPU, which groups 183 national parliaments, said 71 per cent of all respondents reported experiencing violence from the public, particularly online. Home Affairs Minister ‌Tony Burke told the news conference with Albanese that incidents of threatening or harassing behaviour towards lawmakers in Australia had risen to 1,067 in the past year, against 951 previously. In Britain, two ⁠serving members of parliament have been killed since 2016. This month the British interior minister announced an urgent review of the security arrangements for high-profile public figures in the wake of ⁠the killing of an ex-minister in July which prosecutors allege was ideologically motivated. The US has also seen assassination attempts against President Donald Trump, including a shot that hit his ear during his 2024 campaign for re-election. Haines worked in nursing ‌and midwifery and as an academic before being elected to parliament as an independent in 2019 in the seat of Indi. Her website says she has opposed proposals including making political donations to the major parties more secretive, banning mobile phones in immigration detention and spending billions on fossil fuel subsidies. Haines’ family posted on her Facebook page, saying: “We thank the swift help of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for ‌their response.”

title: Opinion | China’s export boom creates a difficult bargain for Southeast Asia
description: The issue is whether the region can become more capable through trade with China or if it is simply a larger outlet for China’s production.
content: China’s export machine is accelerating as its domestic economy remains under strain. This comes amid growing trade friction as China’s partners question whether persistent surpluses can coexist with balanced and resilient regional growth. Last month, China’s exports rose 36.3 per cent year on year, while shipments to Southeast Asia jumped 52.3 per cent. The trade surplus reached US$133.5 billion, taking the nine-month total to US$938.1 billion. In contrast, retail sales grew just 0.4 per cent in August, according to the latest official figures. For the first eight months, fixed-asset investment dropped 7.2 per cent while property investment plunged 19.9 per cent. Yet industrial production for August rose 5.2 per cent. These figures do not prove that exports alone explain China’s resilience or that every factory is overproducing. But they reveal how external demand sustains production while domestic demand remains uneven. For Asian neighbours, that creates a difficult bargain. Chinese machinery, electronics, batteries and solar panels can lower costs and improve competitiveness. But the same export surge can also intensify price pressures on regional producers, especially those yet to develop their own strong technology, supplier networks or brands. The issue is not whether the rest of Asia should trade with China. It is whether the region is becoming more capable through that trade or simply a larger outlet for China’s production. An export boom can benefit both sides, but not evenly. China’s export strength reflects genuine advantages: dense supplier networks, advanced manufacturing capacity, logistics at scale and increasingly sophisticated technology. Last month’s surge was driven partly by semiconductors, computing equipment and green technology. Chip exports rose 108.1 per cent year on year in value, while vehicle shipments increased more than half, reflecting real demand for products that Chinese firms are well placed to supply. This success cushions the economy against domestic weakness. When households spend cautiously and property investment shrinks, overseas sales can help keep production lines busy, preserve economies of scale and support corporate revenues. Where domestic absorption lags, exporters have stronger incentives to seek buyers abroad, even when the resulting competition complicates other countries’ industrial ambitions. That pressure crosses borders through prices, market share and investment decisions. Southeast Asian consumers and manufacturers might gain from cheaper inputs, while local companies competing in the same product categories face thinner margins. Governments can welcome Chinese factories and capital yet still worry that domestic suppliers will remain confined to lower-value activities. The region is deeply connected to this system. China-Southeast Asia trade surpassed US$1 trillion last year and continues to grow strongly. The region’s demand helps sustain Chinese sales, while its factories are woven into production networks that Chinese companies increasingly shape. The surge should not be read as a contest between the two. Some exports are intermediate goods used by factories, while others compete with finished products. The distinction matters as the first can raise productivity, whereas the second can weaken companies unable to match in scale or price. This dual role matters. The likes of Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand benefit from the boom in artificial intelligence (AI), while regional firms rely on Chinese components, machinery and intermediate goods. AI-related exports support these economies, but skills and digital connectivity gaps limit the gains. Integration offers a ladder to advanced production, but local companies must still climb it. The risk is not merely an influx of cheap goods but trade expanding faster than domestic capabilities. An economy may export electronics while importing the components, designs and know-how that make them valuable. Assembly plants alone do not create deep supplier networks, and gross exports can exaggerate local gains. That distinction should shape how governments judge their relationship with China. Measures should include domestic value added, productivity, local procurement, research and development, skilled jobs and whether companies move into more complex tasks. These reveal whether integration builds capability or merely expands throughput. None of this makes protectionism an adequate answer. Chinese inputs can cut costs, support cleaner technologies and connect companies to global supply chains. Blanket restrictions could raise prices while protecting inefficient producers. The better response is to make openness work harder: invest in technical education, reliable power and logistics, research partnerships, supplier development and access to finance for domestic firms. That means setting measurable targets, reviewing support regularly and withdrawing it when firms fail to upgrade. Competition policy and transparent procurement also matter, because subsidies without accountability can entrench incumbents rather than build capability. Priorities differ. Malaysia can deepen semiconductor design expertise; Vietnam can build electronics suppliers; Thailand can develop engineering and components for electric vehicles. Indonesia must ensure mineral processing and battery investment generate technology, skilled jobs and competitive downstream firms, not merely more projects. China’s export boom may help stabilise its growth, but Asia should not mistake being a reliable outlet for being an industrial winner. The objective is not to sever economic ties with China. It is to turn those ties into learning, productivity and higher-value production at home. Integration should be judged by how much more Asia can make, design and improve through trade with China.

title: What to know about Disney Believe, Disney’s newest cruise ship
description: The Disney Believe, which sails from Florida in December 2027, will be packed with themed shows, including the first Encanto musical.
content: Disney Cruise Line’s newest ship will sail out of Fort Lauderdale, Florida, by the end of 2027, the company recently announced. The Disney Believe, the cruise line’s fourth Wish-class ship, will make its maiden voyage on December 18, 2027, to sail four- and five-night itineraries to destinations in the Bahamas and Caribbean. General on-sale bookings start today. During the theatrical announcement live-streamed from another cruise ship – the Disney Wish – on October 7, the Believe’s on-board storytellers Beatrice and Hugo revealed a Frozen-themed dinner show, themed lounges and main stage shows based on Tangled (2010) and Encanto (2021). Disney Cruise Line also unveiled a tower suite inspired by the Magic Kingdom. At the Disney fans convention D23 in August, the company revealed that a bronze statue of Moana will be the focal point of the ship’s Grand Hall. Buzz Lightyear and Woody will appear on the vessel’s stern and Tinker Bell will decorate the bow. Beyond the statue of Moana, the Grand Hall will be an “architectural meeting of the sea and sky” inspired by the Pacific Islands. Ocean hues can be found on the carpet, while the ceiling is scattered with constellations. The railings are inspired by designs in Moana’s skirt and the chandelier is modelled after the “ocean’s fluid movement”. Tangled: The Musical was unveiled as one of the main stage shows aboard the Believe, featuring “all new special effects and set designs”. As part of the announcement, actor Susan Egan – the official “godmother” of cruise ship Disney Destiny who voiced Megara in Hercules (1997) – came on stage to sing “When Will My Life Begin?” Songwriter and actor Lin-Manuel Miranda appeared by video to share the news that the first stage adaptation of Encanto will debut exclusively on the Disney Believe in the Walt Disney Theatre. Adassa, the voice of Dolores Madrigal in the animated film, was joined on stage by Broadway performers Arielle Jacobs, Bradley Gibson and Jacob Dickey to perform a medley of songs from the film. On the Disney Believe, the tropical landscape and cultures of Colombia will shine through the production’s costumes, set design and dance styles. A new, “untold” chapter in the Frozen story takes place at Oaken’s Table: A Frozen Family Feast, a new theatrical dining experience coming to the Disney Believe. The setting transports diners to a Scandinavian courtyard with reimagined tunes from Frozen and special appearances. Disney Believe features a broad slate of new venues for dining, drinking and entertainment geared towards cruise passengers of all ages. The Wishing Well lounge is inspired by the 1937 animated film Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. The space has three distinct settings, including a gothic castle theme at the bar, an enchanting castle courtyard with white blossoms and red apples in the seating area and a performance area with hand-carved wood framing. Gazelle is a new multistory entertainment hub inspired by the Zootopia films. By day, the venue will host guests of all ages before switching to adults-only entertainment by night. Guests with a sweet tooth can visit Inside Out: Joyful Sweets, a speciality dessert and sweet shop, featuring sculptures from Inside Out 2 and treats including 20 flavours of gelato and ice cream. Coffee lovers can get their caffeine fix at Big Hero Sips and Cafe Kakamora, inspired by Big Hero 6 and Moana, respectively. Staterooms feature artwork invoking characters and stories Just off the Grand Hall, guests can enjoy a piano lounge called Sea Notes inspired by Ariel’s grotto from The Little Mermaid, with a “pearlescent piano” at the centre of the space. The menu will feature cocktails and non-alcoholic drinks. An observatory-themed pub called Skygazers will make its debut on the Disney Believe with astronomical instruments, celestial maps and nods to classic Disney stories. The space features craft beers, speciality cocktails and light bites. Staterooms aboard the Disney Believe feature artwork invoking characters and stories such as Moana, Coco and Inside Out. On the Concierge level, guests will find themes inspired by Peter Pan and several special rooms with the spirit of Toy Story. There are two royal suites: the Royal Reef Suite themed after The Little Mermaid and the Royal Rose Suite, inspired by Beauty and the Beast. There is also the two-storey Believe Tower Suite, which sleeps eight inside the forward funnel and draws inspiration from the Magic Kingdom. Each room is modelled after a different themed land and features elements from the park such as firework- and balloon-inspired light fixtures. Worlds of Marvel and 1923 both return to the Disney Believe as main dining venues after debuting on previous Wish-class ships. On the upper decks, guests will find Mickey and Friends Festival of Foods, an open-air food court with themed food stalls. Guests can try the new Pluto’s Pita Platters with a Mediterranean-inspired menu. The popular Haunted Mansion Parlor, a “fully immersive bar” inspired by the Disney Parks attraction, will return on the new vessel. Other adult-only venues include Palo Steakhouse, Enchante by Chef Arnaud Lallement and The Rose lounge. Quiet Cove also returns as a secluded area for adults only on the upper decks. Guests can visit Senses Spa and Senses Fitness, or book a personal pampering session at Untangled Salon or Hook’s Barbery. The 760-foot (231-metre) water ride AquaMouse seen on other Wish-class ships will appear on the Disney Believe. Guests can enjoy the live stage show Disney Seas the Adventure in the Walt Disney Theatre. There is also the Pirate’s Rockin’ Parlay Party deck show on the outside decks of the Disney Believe. Guests can experience the Hero Zone sports arena, the Disney Uncharted Adventure, an interactive mobile device experience, and the Wonderland and Never Land cinemas – which will feature complimentary showings of classic and first-run films from Disney, Pixar, Marvel, Lucasfilm and more. Disney Believe will make stops at one or both of the cruise line’s destinations, Disney Castaway Cay and Disney Lookout Cay at Lighthouse Point, in the Bahamas. Disney Cruise Line plans to expand to 13 ships by late 2030.

title: Contractor injured as brief fire breaks out at Hong Kong Cultural Centre
description: Woman, 29, received electric shock while removing stage installations and was taken to Queen Elizabeth Hospital.
content: A brief No 2 alarm fire broke out at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui on Monday, leaving a contractor injured after she received an electric shock. The Fire Services Department said it received an alarm at the venue at 11.23am. When firefighters arrived three minutes later, the fire had already been extinguished. “After investigation, a female staff member was found to have been injured in an electric shock accident,” a department spokesman said. The worker was taken to Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Kowloon for treatment. Police said they received a report at 11.42am that a 29-year-old contractor worker had suffered an electric shock. “A contractor staff member was removing stage installations when she received an electric shock,” a police spokesman said. The fire department dispatched two water jet and breathing apparatus teams, which stood by to handle the No 2 alarm. Fires reported at locations with heavy foot traffic or of strategic importance, such as hospitals and dangerous goods stores, are automatically classified as No 2 alarm fires. The Leisure and Cultural Services Department said on Monday evening that the contract worker was employed by a performing arts group and was dismantling stage installations backstage at the Grand Theatre at the time of the accident. “The operations of the Hong Kong Cultural Centre remain unaffected. The Leisure and Cultural Services Department, the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department and the Labour Department are currently following up on the incident,” it said.

title: Chinese discovery of doughnut-like topology at tipping points breaks physics convention
description: Study bridges critical phenomena and topology, opening new pathways for fundamental science research.
content: Chinese physicists have discovered that a tipping point – a threshold where a physical system rapidly shifts states – can possess a smooth mathematical structure resembling a doughnut’s hole, challenging a belief that the two phenomena must be studied separately. For decades, mainstream physicists have mostly treated critical phenomena, which describe how physical systems change at critical points, and topology, which studies the properties of geometry, as separate areas of research. A classic illustration of topology is the difference between a sphere and a doughnut. The two cannot be transformed into each other by stretching or bending alone because they have a different number of holes, unless the surface is cut or glued. The study by researchers at Singaporean and Chinese institutions was published in Nature on October 7, with Cheng Zheyu and Zhang Xiuhai, both affiliated with Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, as co-first authors. Cheng and his colleagues set out to investigate whether doughnut-like topological properties could exist at critical points – the thresholds at which physical systems change their behaviour. “Our research found that the critical point itself can have topology,” Cheng told the South China Morning Post. The findings could prompt researchers to revisit physical systems studied for centuries to investigate whether they have overlooked fundamental properties at critical points and, more broadly, in systems undergoing critical transitions. “The work was significant because it challenged a long-standing separation between two areas of physics, potentially opening a new direction for research into the mathematical properties of tipping points,” Cheng said. To illustrate how critical phenomena work, Cheng pointed to the cluster-Ising chain, a model representing a row of tiny magnets, each of which can point up or down, with interactions between them influencing their collective behaviour. As these interactions change, the system can shift from one state to another, with the critical point marking the transition and potentially possessing topological properties that researchers had previously overlooked. A separate study by researchers in mainland China and Hong Kong published in Nature on the same day reported related findings in one- and two-dimensional systems, using engineered phononic crystals to investigate critical topology and directly image distinctive topological modes along boundaries between different states. Together, the studies provide experimental evidence for a previously underexplored area of physics. “This is a very young field, and we are still exploring it,” Cheng said, adding that scientists were beginning to investigate whether other physical systems studied for their critical behaviour might also possess topological properties. The findings also raise a broader question: could topology help scientists understand tipping points in more complicated systems found in nature and society? In complex-systems research, scientists study warning signals that may indicate when a system is approaching a tipping point, such as the degradation of an ecosystem or a shift in climate behaviour. Cheng said critical phenomena could be connected to this broader field, but he could not confirm whether tipping points in complex systems also possessed topological properties. His team’s experiments have so far focused on relatively simple physical models rather than the more complicated systems found in nature or society. The researchers have also used entropy-based analysis – a technique for measuring randomness and disorder – to study critical points, linking their work to mathematical tools used in statistical physics. However, the findings cannot be directly applied to ecological, climatic or social systems. For now, the main contribution is to fundamental science rather than an immediate practical application. “It is too young to see any applications in the short term,” Cheng said. His team’s next step would be to investigate systems involving many-body interactions, allowing researchers to explore more complicated physical behaviour, he said.

title: From English courses to furniture, actor Daniel Wu expands his business interests in China
description: Wu, 52, has stepped back from acting in recent years and Arox, the name of his furniture brand, marks his latest business foray.
content: US-born Hong Kong actor and filmmaker Daniel Wu Yin-cho has launched a furniture brand as the latest endeavour to cash in on his long-built fame in the Chinese market. Wu, 52, has stepped back from acting in recent years and Arox, the name of his furniture brand, marks his latest business foray. The actor’s previous ventures include an English course launched last year to teach fans spoken English, a coffee brand named Whatever, and a cycling helmet design project. Raised in California, Wu majored in architecture at the University of Oregon for his undergraduate studies. In a video posted on Chinese social media platform RedNote last month, Wu said he had long wanted to design furniture but ended up becoming an actor after he graduated. Yan Yuejin, vice-president of the E‑house China Research and Development Institute, a Shanghai-based property consultancy, said furniture was a low-frequency purchase and interest from fans and market attention tended to surge at launch. A shift from “homebuying to better living” was helping drive sales in the sector, according to Yan. “Still, its long-term momentum depends on product quality and delivery, after-sales and related services,” Yan said. Wu personally designed the first product under Arox brand – a sofa – which he described as attractive, comfortable and affordable. Arox stands for “Architectural Resonance Original Experience”, and the manufacturing was outsourced to a factory in Foshan, Guangdong province, according to the video he posted. The post drew mixed reactions from fans. Some said the furniture industry was fiercely competitive and urged him to pull out, while others wondered whether he had taken on a heavy debt by pursuing different business ventures. Wu recently returned to Hong Kong cinema after a years-long hiatus, with a role in the crime thriller Cold War 1994. China’s home furnishing sector has bottomed out following the property market downturn since late 2020. The recovery in property sales and home renovation demand remained sluggish, a research report from Industrial Securities said in September. In the second quarter of this year, net profit for the home furnishing sector dropped 54 per cent year on year, the report said. Against this tough market backdrop, Swedish furniture brand Ikea shut seven stores in mainland China in February, as it grappled with a weak property market and sluggish consumer spending. Figures from the National Bureau of Statistics showed China’s furniture manufacturing industry recorded sales of 612.51 billion yuan (US$91.66 billion) last year, down 10.7 per cent year on year, while total profits declined 12.1 per cent to 32.81 billion yuan.

title: French protests over declining school standards amid China catch-up ambitions turn violent
description: Student rallies over ailing high schools are hijacked by looters who rampaged through major cities, angered by rising fuel and living costs.
content: France experienced a weekend of shocks as weeks-long high school student protests for better study environments were hijacked by violent looters across major cities, angered by rising fuel prices and an ongoing cost of living crisis. While the rallies saw hundreds of thousands protest peacefully, clashes over the weekend led to chaotic scenes: hundreds of shops were pillaged, the historic city hall of Limoges was burned down and multiple public buildings across cities like Paris, Marseilles and Bordeaux were attacked. In his televised speech to the French people on Sunday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron called for a clear distinction between those who destroyed properties and the peaceful protesters. “For several weeks, our youth have been expressing a deep anxiety in high schools and universities, worrying for their future, their living and study conditions … the idea that they will not have a desirable future,” Macron said, vowing that their voices “will be heard”. This grievance behind the protests points to issues with France’s education system that analysts say could threaten the country’s ambition to innovate and catch up with the US and China. In the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD) last Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) report published last month, France has only 9.8 per cent of top performers – those who reached level 5 or 6 – in science, reading or mathematics, compared to 55.5 per cent for mainland China, covering students from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang. “It shows that in terms of people that are top performers, that in theory will have the best jobs will have the capacity to innovate, the proportion is decreasing [for France] every PISA cycle … now action should be taken,” said Eric Charbonnier, an education analyst at the OECD. The report showed that 9.3 per cent of the Chinese students tested reached level 6 in science, compared to only 0.8 per cent in France. For maths, the gap was even bigger, 30 per cent for China and only 0.7 per cent for France. On paper, despite rising public debts and recent efforts to bring down government spending, France did not cut its budget for education. For the 2027 budget, the government is planning €64 billion (US$71.9 billion) for education, up by €1 billion year on year. But the problem for Charbonnier is not how much money was invested but how well it was spent. A lot of the investment is blocked in paying for social benefits: 32 per cent of the proposed education budget in 2027 will go to pensions, according to the French government. “It’s not an investment on the quality of education. It’s not an investment on teachers, on improving the working condition,” Charbonnier said. Meanwhile, the teacher shortage issue is worsening in the country. Some 65 per cent of French schools were missing at least one teacher this year when school started in September, up by 5 percentage points compared to 2025, according to the SNPDEN, France’s largest union of secondary school principals. In a centralised country where Paris dictates a lot of the rules, France has also seen a high level of policy uncertainty in education, according to Charbonnier, adding that France had 12 education ministers in the past 15 years and each one of them attempted to do their own reforms, creating confusion for schools. A lot of funding was also put into building maintenance, according to Sacha Courtial, co-president of Volt France, a pro-EU party active on the younger generation. Many French high schools were built many years ago, under the Third Republic, and need a huge amount of investment just for maintenance, he said. During the weeks of protests, many high school students complained about studying in extreme heat without air conditioners or during winter times in classrooms with inadequate heating. Moreover, compared to China, the US or northern European countries, France also lags in digitalisation efforts and the teaching materials are outdated with no mention of new technologies such as AI, according to Courtial. “Every politician will say that youth is the future but we have to admit that … the education policies have not been prioritised enough,” he said.

title: Flowers, roast pork and paper ingots: families keep Chung Yeung traditions alive
description: From elaborate rituals to simple bouquets, Hong Kong families observe festival, although shops selling offerings say times are tough.
content: Hong Kong families paid tribute to their ancestors on the final day of the Chung Yeung Festival break, expressing their respects through everything from elaborate traditional rituals to a simple bunch of flowers. More than a dozen people queued outside Chai Wan MTR station on Monday morning, a public holiday, for the special tomb-sweeping service to the cemeteries. Citybus staff said demand had been greater the previous day, when buses – running every 20 minutes – were full, carrying more than 80 seated passengers. A man surnamed Yeung, who had come from Lam Tin, was waiting at the bus stop with one of his parents and two bags of offerings. “We bought roast pork and chicken for grandpa, who used to enjoy eating those, and I also bought paper Coke cans to burn for my grandma, who loved drinking it a lot,” he said. The crowds on the escalators leading to the cemetery and nearby ones were thin in the morning, but picked up slightly towards noon, when up to 200 people were using them at the same time. On Sunday, up to 200 people queued for the escalators at a time, waiting up to 10 minutes to board. Many families carried flowers, food, joss paper, spirit money and other offerings for ancestor worship. Among them was a man who gave only his first name as Ming and said he had come with more than a dozen family members. “We sweep the tombs every year on Ching Ming and Chung Yeung together as a whole family to pay tribute to our past family members,” he said. “It’s never difficult for us to gather together to do this.” The family folded paper gold ingots and flowers together in front of the cemetery. “We spent more than HK$1,000 [US$127] on offerings this year. On top of that, we bought a whole roast suckling pig especially for the ritual, and it cost HK$888,” he said. Another man, who only gave his surname as Yeung, said he had come with his father, brother and nephew to pay tribute to their late grandmother and mother. “We bought nothing special, but everything needed as usual, including paper spirit clothes and paper money,” he said. “We go tomb sweeping at least once a year. We did it at Ching Ming and have come again today to avoid the heavy traffic [on Sunday],” Yeung said, adding that “this is a very important tradition that we always want to stick to”. Others came alone, carrying lighter gifts but with the same wishes. A retiree living in Chai Wan, who only gave her surname as Yuen, said she would sweep the tombs by herself and had spent less than HK$500 on simple offerings, including roast pork and char siu bao. She said the roast pork was a few dozen dollars more than last year, but she would still buy it as a necessity. “I used to buy a suckling pig too, but I’m older now and keep things simpler. The most important thing is the thought of coming to visit,” she said. Another woman, who only gave her surname as Cheung, carried a hiking bag with a bunch of flowers sticking out of it. “Though I bought these flowers for just HK$30 at a nearby street market, I still want to sweep the tomb myself and pay my respects,” she said. “It’s also a good chance to go hiking and enjoy the public holiday.” Shops near Chai Wan, however, said business had been tough. A manager, who only gave her surname as Lam, said she had been running a temporary shop selling ritual offerings near Chai Wan Park for more than five years, but there were fewer customers this holiday. “If I had to describe this year’s business in one word, it would be ‘bad’. People have gone to mainland China for fun, and fewer are willing to come to pay respects to their ancestors in person,” Lam said, noting that many now bought offerings online. “Not to mention that everything can be digitalised now. Even ancestor worship can be done on a phone.” Lam said although some shops had raised prices, she had refrained from doing so for years. “Our business has been getting worse anyway. Take these chrysanthemums, for example: a bunch cost HK$10 more than a decade ago, and we are still selling them at the same price,” she said. She added that most customers bought only the most traditional and simple items, such as a HK$8 set of incense and a HK$10 set of spirit clothes, while few bought the pricier HK$168 packages. Some special products, such as paper camper vans and designer handbags, had sat on the shelves for years, she said. A nearby roast meat shop reported the same struggle. “Business is very bad. We could say it gets worse every year,” said a staff member, shaking their head. The shop also sells a HK$980 roast suckling pig set for ancestor worship, but staff said it had not attracted much interest, without revealing how many had been sold. The festival’s name, which translates as “double yang”, comes from its occurrence on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month. That numerical alignment also gives the occasion its alternative title, the Double Ninth Festival. Like Ching Ming Festival, Chung Yeung is an important occasion for family reunions and ancestral reverence in modern Hong Kong.

title: Face Off: Should Hong Kong universities have a cap on non-DSE students?
description: Each week, two readers discuss a hot topic in a parliamentary-style debate that doesn’t necessarily reflect their personal viewpoints.
content:
If you are interested in joining future Face Off debates, fill out this form to submit your application.
In recent years, universities in Hong Kong have been increasing the quota for non-local students to attract global talent. However, these decisions have raised concerns about the city’s goals.
According to an analysis by the South China Morning Post, 75 per cent of first-year non-local undergraduates at Hong Kong public universities were mainland Chinese in the 2024-25 school year. Meanwhile, the percentage of non-local students from other countries decreased. This came after the government increased the cap on non-local admissions in 2023.
While Hong Kong is attractive to international students, if it is primarily drawing students from mainland China, it will not become more culturally diverse . Therefore, removing the caps serves no purpose if it does not contribute to establishing an “international education hub”.
Secondly, removing caps on non-local students means that many of them might seek private housing in the city.
A 2025 report from real estate agency Colliers projected a shortage of 120,000 student beds by 2028. During the 2024-25 academic year, Hong Kong had 92,000 non-local university students but only 48,100 hostel beds available for them. Consequently , many students turn to private rentals. This shift has increased the demand for private housing, which in turn can drive up rental prices for everyone else living in Hong Kong.
Lastly, a report on students who took the Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) exam shows that among the 2024 graduates pursuing full-time studies, 92.2 per cent stayed in Hong Kong. Meanwhile, only 7.8 per cent studied abroad.
In contrast, data collected by the English Schools Foundation (ESF), the largest international school organisation in Hong Kong, revealed that only 30.7 per cent of its 2024 graduates remained in Hong Kong.
This comparison highlights that DSE students are more reliant on the local university system. If the government further increases competition for DSE students, it may become challenging to retain local talent.
To conclude, Hong Kong should not stop students from applying outside the local exam system, but we should have a limit on these students so that economic risks are minimised and local talent is preserved.
While I believe it is important to protect opportunities for local students, having a cap on applicants who are outside the Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) system is unfair and harms Hong Kong’s global reputation .
The cap on non-DSE candidates is unfair, as they should not be at a disadvantage simply for choosing a different examination system.
The International Baccalaureate (IB), A-levels and Advanced Placement (AP) programmes are all internationally recognised qualifications that provide students with alternative routes to demonstrate their academic abilities. These international exam boards have far greater universal recognition than the DSE.
It is also important to note that the Hong Kong government has already established effective protections for DSE students. Currently, Hong Kong provides 15,000 government-funded first-year university places specifically for local students, and the government has stated that this number will not be reduced.
Therefore, this additional cap on non-DSE students is unnecessary and restricts students who have worked equally hard to gain admission through an alternative system.
Furthermore, not all students in Hong Kong take the DSE exam. This cap disproportionately affects students who have grown up in the city and wish to continue their education at one of Hong Kong’s universities.
The limit on students applying through pathways other than the DSE could be undermining Hong Kong’s growing global reputation as a university destination.
Recently, Hong Kong universities have achieved record results in the Quacquarelli Symonds (QS) World University Rankings. The Hong Kong government has been investing heavily in education and is striving to develop the city into an international hub for education and high-calibre talent.
International students can provide significant economic benefits. They spend money on accommodation, food, transport, telecommunications and retail, thereby stimulating the economy.
Ultimately, restricting the number of students who can enter Hong Kong’s universities with international qualifications would mean sacrificing the broader benefits that the city receives from their presence.

title: Safety checks on Taizoom lifts uncover 186 more affected buildings in Hong Kong
description: Number of buildings with lifts lacking critical fire-safety door components rises to 338 as authorities carry out citywide inspections.
content: An investigation into work carried out by a lift contractor in Hong Kong has found another 186 buildings lacking crucial components designed to prevent flames and smoke from entering the shaft in the event of a fire. The checks pushed the number of buildings with substandard lifts installed by Taizoom Elevator to 338 on Monday. According to the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department (EMSD), its latest inspections covered lifts installed by the company at 184 single-block buildings and two others at two housing estates. All the lifts lacked the required fire-resistant door frame components. The department has also asked other registered lift contractors to check the lifts they have installed over the past 10 years and submit reports by mid-November. The department will then conduct random checks. The compliance failures have also prompted calls for the department to look beyond reports signed off by registered engineers when assessing lift safety and review accreditation requirements to help prevent contractors from cutting corners. The citywide inspections of lifts serviced by Taizoom were launched on October 16 after fire-resistant door frames were found missing from 48 newly installed lifts at two public housing estates. Lawmaker Scott Leung Man-kwong called on the EMSD to review whether it was appropriate to rely so heavily on reports signed off by registered lift engineers, given a manpower shortage in the industry. “As to how to avoid determining whether a check passes standards by relying on one information source, I believe the EMSD would need to deploy more manpower on these checks after this incident,” Leung said. Police on Friday arrested a Taizoom director and two registered lift engineers on suspicion of deception over safety certificates allegedly stating that the work had been fully completed. Leung said the department currently relied on reports signed off by registered lift engineers to determine whether lifts had passed inspections or met professional standards after repairs. But he added that a shortage of registered lift engineers had left them with heavy workloads. “At the site of the check, can these engineers monitor every step to ensure there are no problems before signing off?” he said. “It really relies on workers on-site to provide relevant information for their judgment.” Leung said introducing a third party to verify lift safety checks would be ideal. But he acknowledged that finding a suitable party would be difficult because the work required specialist knowledge. He also suggested establishing an internal communication mechanism between relevant government departments and the Hong Kong Housing Authority, a statutory body that retains ownership rights in some public housing estates. Under his proposal, departments would privately notify the authority of ongoing investigations into contractors, allowing it to make better-informed decisions when exercising its voting rights as an owner on estate maintenance matters. “With this internal communication mechanism to give the Housing Authority more information when casting its vote, I think this could be a form of protection too,” he said. Electrical engineer Ho Wing-yip, an adjunct professor at the faculty of engineering at Polytechnic University, said it was too early to determine whether the deficiencies found in Taizoom’s lifts reflected a wider industry problem. But he added that the large number of defective lifts installed by the contractor suggested the company might have instructed workers to omit the required components, possibly to cut corners and boost profits. While the components only accounted for about 10 per cent of the cost of a fire-resistant door system, omitting them across a large quantity of lifts could result in significant savings, he said. “It could be possible that the firm thinks it could save a lot of money by cutting costs in every project,” he said. Ho said he had found that the reports required under the current system did not cover the missing door frame component, identifying this as an area for improvement. He added that authorities had little scope to operate the inspection system without relying on professionals. But the scandal could prompt a review of how engineers were accredited, including the emphasis placed on professional ethics. “This shows that we haven’t paid attention to professional ethics. This needs to be evaluated or even amended as [accreditation metrics] represent whether the most fundamental tenets of the industry are working properly,” he said.

title: Japanese deputy mayor crushed to death under giant festival float
description: Police probe whether three-tonne wooden structure fell or official lost footing during centuries-old autumn procession.
content: A deputy mayor in western Japan died after being crushed under a giant float during a local parade, officials said on Monday, a week after two others were reportedly killed at separate traditional festivals. Akihiro Nabae, deputy mayor of the city of Saijo in the Ehime region, was carrying a giant float with other participants on Saturday before becoming trapped beneath it, city and police officials said. He was taken to hospital and later pronounced dead, local media said. The exact circumstances that led to his death – including “whether the float fell down or he somehow lost his balance” – remain under investigation, Makoto Hagiyama, deputy director of a local police station, said. Local media said 11 floats were lined up, side by side, and as much as three tonnes may have come crushing down on Nabae. Organised by local shrines, the annual Saijo festival is a “gorgeous and flashy” affair, punctuated with a procession of floats sculpted to symbolise flowers, birds and warriors, the city explains on its website. The tradition dates back to Japan’s Edo period (1603 to 1868) and is meant to thank deities for an abundant harvest of grains. Two people reportedly died the previous Saturday during two separate festivals in western Osaka that saw floats topple over while participants attempted high-speed turns. Two people also reportedly died in February following a crush at Japan’s “Naked Man Festival”.

title: How a US$110 million fishing harbour in Tanzania serves China’s food and security goals
description: Kilwa Masoko port promises local jobs while feeding Beijing’s long-term strategy for maritime power and seafood supply chains.
content: About 300km (186 miles) south of Dar es Salaam and near the ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani, the fishing town of Kilwa Masoko has a new port designed to accommodate fishing vessels far larger than the boats that have long worked this stretch of Tanzania’s coast. The fishing port had passed its completion inspection, China’s ambassador to Tanzania Chen Mingjian said last week, while hailing it Tanzania’s first large-scale modern fishing harbour. Designed to land 60,000 tonnes of fish a year, it aims to boost Tanzanian fish markets, cut spoilage and create jobs – Tanzania’s labour minister Deus Sangu expects about 30,000 direct and indirect jobs. Some of the catch could reach Chinese buyers as China’s appetite for seafood grows. In recent years, Beijing has signed agreements allowing more African countries to export fish and other aquatic products to its market. China imports live lobster from Namibia and Comoros, and crab and dried anchovies from Kenya. It agreed to import requirements for Tanzanian wild aquatic products, while a separate protocol provides for Somali tuna, lobster and other wild seafood to enter the Chinese market. The 280 billion Tanzanian shilling (US$110 million) port was built by the state-owned China Harbour Engineering Company as part of Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative and incorporates fish-processing and ice-making plants, cold storage and a workshop for repairing fishing boats. Kilwa Masoko is part of a wider push to build fishing infrastructure across Africa with mutual benefits, with African governments offered more locally landed fish, less seafood wastage and more jobs in processing. Meanwhile, for China such ports can help secure seafood supplies and support fishing vessels operating far from home, according to Miren Gutierrez, a principal investigator in communication studies at Spain’s University of Deusto and a research associate at the London-based ODI Global think tank. “China’s backing and construction of overseas fishing ports in Africa is not a series of isolated commercial projects,” she said. “Rather, it represents the culmination of a decades-long strategic trajectory that integrates food security, industrial expansion, diplomatic leverage and geostrategic maritime presence.” China’s distant-water fishing industry began operating in West Africa in 1985 when the state-owned China National Fisheries Corporation sent its first fleet there, Gutierrez said. Beijing’s “Go Global” policy, which was introduced in 2000, encouraged companies to expand overseas, supported by subsidies for fuel, vessels and processing facilities. More recently, the Maritime Silk Road had placed fishing and overseas bases within a broader strategy to build maritime power and link China to global supply chains, Gutierrez said. Chinese vessels fish in Somali waters after an earlier agreement saw Somalia license 31 Chinese longline vessels to catch tuna and related species. And China is funding and building fishing ports across Africa. In Ghana, a Chinese-built port at Jamestown in Accra was commissioned in 2024 with a US$60 million grant. Similarly, in Guinea-Bissau, China provided about US$25 million for the second phase of Alto do Bandim port in Bissau, handed over in May 2023. In Mozambique, China Harbour Engineering Company rebuilt and expanded Beira’s fishing port with a US$120 million loan from China Eximbank, completed in 2019. Meanwhile, in Sierra Leone, a US$55 million grant is funding the construction of a port at Black Johnson village near Freetown, following years of delays and local opposition. China’s expanding fishing presence in Africa has drawn scrutiny. In parts of West Africa, Chinese fleets have faced accusations of depleting fish stocks and fishing illegally. For fleets operating thousands of miles from China, overseas bases or ports can provide places to refuel, resupply, repair vessels and offload catches. “Dedicated fishing ports provide the landing, cold storage and processing infrastructure needed to turn raw catch into stable supply chains for Chinese cities or re-export markets,” Gutierrez said. Where Chinese companies controlled both vessels and facilities ashore, they could reduce costs while gaining greater control over landings, she argued. “By controlling both the vessels and the shore facilities, Chinese companies reduce delays and shield offloaded catches from close oversight.”

title: Why mainland Chinese still drive Hong Kong’s housing market despite Beijing’s 20% tax
description: After a sharp drop, Hong Kong residential property transactions rebounded by 18.5% in September, with the total value rising by 29.3%.
content: Although the Chinese government imposed a 20 per cent tax on rental income and capital gains derived from overseas properties transferred into offshore trusts by mainland residents, agents said these investors remained a key driver of the Hong Kong property market. China’s Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration said in July that rental earnings – profits from the sale of properties and investment gains derived from assets including real estate, stocks or equity interests held by mainland Chinese residents through offshore trusts or overseas holding companies – were now subject to individual income tax at a rate of 20 per cent. The new rule provides taxpayers with a 90-day compliance window, allowing them to voluntarily declare and pay any outstanding taxes to mainland tax authorities – up until the October 22 deadline – in exchange for an exemption from penalties.
