Kit Lam, senior associate director at Ricacorp Properties, revealed that the new tax regulations announced by mainland China also hit the Hong Kong property market, but the market quickly absorbed the impact. “In recent months, mainland Chinese buyers have accounted for about 15 to 20 per cent of transactions for smaller, entry-level properties in the New Territories, such as those in Tuen Mun and Tin Shui Wai,” he said. “Most of these purchases are for personal use, for instance, to facilitate their children’s education in Hong Kong. This group of end users is the least affected, and there has recently been an uptick in inquiries from mainland buyers.” The primary reasons for mainlanders to purchase residential property in Hong Kong, such as the need for cross-border education for their children and asset allocation, remained in place, Lam explained. “Many mainland buyers are simply adjusting the proportion of their holdings, rather than abandoning the Hong Kong property market entirely,” he noted. Following the tax announcement, the total volume of residential property transactions in Hong Kong plummeted by 47.5 per cent, dropping from a year-to-date high of 7,650 units in June to a year-to-date low of 4,019 units in August. The total transaction value also fell by 52.1 per cent, declining from HK$75.6 billion (US$9.6 billion) in June to a low of HK$36.2 billion in August, according to data from Centaline Property. But the data showed that the overall volume of residential property transactions in September rebounded by 18.5 per cent month-on-month to 4,761 units, while the total transaction value also rose by 29.3 per cent to HK$46.81 billion. Several individuals from mainland China, who requested anonymity due to the sensitivity of the issue, revealed that the mainland Chinese government had never sought to collect a 20 per cent personal income tax although the Hong Kong residential properties they own for investment and rental purposes were held in their personal names. In reality, they said that they did not proactively declare the income, as it was very difficult to track transactions down due to the complexity of cross-border matters that involved numerous departments and lengthy, cumbersome audit processes. Henry Chung, senior managing director at Midland Realty, explained that under mainland China’s personal income tax regime, a 20 per cent tax was levied only on gains derived from assets, while the mere act of holding property did not trigger taxation. “Mainland China and Hong Kong have an agreement for the avoidance of double taxation (DTA),” he explained. “When a mainland resident rents out a property in Hong Kong, the owner must first pay a 15 per cent property tax to the Hong Kong Inland Revenue Department.” Upon declaring this income on the mainland, the owner is entitled to a tax credit for the amount already paid, he said, as they were only required to pay the difference to the mainland tax authorities, rather than paying an additional 20 per cent tax. King Lau, regional investment director for the Greater Bay Area at Yui Yin Property, said that mainland Chinese had planned to put their plans of buying property in Hong Kong on hold after the new regulations were announced. “Now most mainland buyers remain cautious regarding the new rules,” he added. “They are continuing to view properties while simultaneously taking a ‘wait-and-see’ approach to observe how strictly the regulations are actually enforced.” The property market continued to warm up this month. Last Saturday, two new residential projects – Phase 2C(2) of Sierra Sea on Sai Sha Road and Phase 1 of The Atlas in Yau Tong – launched 142 and 220 flats for public sale, respectively. Both projects sold out completely on the same day. Yuexiu Property, the developer of The Atlas, has stated that during the first round of sales for the project earlier this month, 30 per cent of the buyers were from mainland China and foreign countries.

title: Credit card fraud reports over iPhone Duo pre-orders jump to 130 cases, police say
description: Hong Kong police say complaints continue to rise, with total amount involved hitting HK$5 million after Apple failed to activate 3D Secure system.
content: Hong Kong police received nearly 20 more reports of unauthorised credit card transactions linked to iPhone Duo pre-orders over the weekend, bringing the total amount involved to HK$5 million (US$637,100). A police spokesman said the force had received 130 reports of unauthorised smartphone purchases as of 9am on Monday. The cases were provisionally classified as “obtaining property by deception” and were being investigated by the cybersecurity and technology crime bureau. Police said on Saturday that residents had begun reporting suspicious credit card transactions involving the foldable iPhone Duo after online pre-orders opened at 8pm on Friday. Apple had decided not to activate 3D Secure (3DS), which helps authenticate buyers’ identities during online transactions, despite being urged to do so by police. The force said it was gravely concerned about Apple’s failure to fulfil its corporate responsibilities, leaving the door open for criminals to prey on customers. An Apple spokesman said on Saturday that all current iPhone Duo orders were being reviewed before processing and that the company was working to identify and cancel fraudulent transactions quickly. Asked on Monday to respond to the police criticism and whether it would activate 3DS, Apple reiterated its earlier position and said it had nothing to add. The rise in reports over the weekend marked the second time in just over a month that an iPhone launch had been marred by reports of widespread fraud. Police said they were still investigating 1,572 reports of suspicious credit card transactions involving the iPhone 18 Pro series, which became available for pre-order on September 12. Those transactions totalled more than HK$31 million.

title: Hong Kong’s Huanggang crossing absorbs 366% surge as travellers stream back
description: Revamped land crossing handles 9,401 inbound travellers in two hours, a 366% jump over the same times in September as smooth flow replaces Sunday delays.
content: Inbound crossings at Hong Kong’s revamped Huanggang Port surged by 366 per cent on Monday afternoon over comparable periods in September, as the first long weekend since its reopening came to a close, with authorities expecting an even greater rush later in the evening. A steady stream of travellers returned to Hong Kong through the checkpoint on Monday, with crowds growing noticeably by 5pm, peaking at around 6.15pm, and tapering off by 7pm, as observed by the South China Morning Post. Unlike Sunday, when departing travellers complained on social media about long wait times during peak hours, Monday’s inbound flow remained orderly. “It’s a very nice port – the bathrooms are clean, it’s huge and spacious … what a great thing to see in our lifetime,” said 66-year-old retiree Adam Ko, who was with his wife, Mary. The couple said they were aware of the large crowds at the crossing over the weekend. “It’s still early in the night, so we decided to come here hoping to skip the peak hours. It was very smooth and we just breezed through,” said Ko. However, he noted minor traffic congestion while approaching the port by taxi in Shenzhen at around 4.30pm. “We were stuck on the roads for maybe 10 minutes. Acceptable, but I’d think twice if it was any later in the day.” A Shenzhen resident in her forties who works in the garment industry and gave only her surname, Tang, said she preferred the revamped port for its convenience. “This new arrangement saves me about 20 minutes crossing the border,” she said. According to the Security Bureau, 9,401 travellers entered Hong Kong via Huanggang Port between 2pm and 4pm on Monday, a 366 per cent surge from the average number of inbound crossings through the former Huanggang/Lok Ma Chau control point during the same hours across the four weekends in September. It expected the number of inbound travellers to rise further in the evening. With the expected surge in crossings, all immigration clearance channels were opened, while authorities prepared crowd-control measures and designated waiting areas for passengers using public transport. The holiday marked the first major test for the revamped crossing between Hong Kong and mainland China, which reopened on October 12 with a new joint immigration clearance system designed to cut processing times from about half an hour to as little as five minutes. Travellers can complete clearance by presenting a single identity document and passing through an automated channel with three gates. Yung Ka-wai, deputy commander of the Immigration Department’s Lok Ma Chau Division, said clearance at Huanggang had been smooth on Monday and expected the afternoon-to-evening period to be the busiest for foot traffic. “We will continue to monitor the situation at the control points in real time and flexibly deploy manpower according to passenger flows to speed up the clearing of crowds,” Yung said. “Travellers are advised to plan their journeys early, choose a suitable control point and avoid crossing the border during peak hours.” He also reminded eligible residents to register in advance if they wished to use the new clearance model. Commissioner for Transport Winnie Tse Wing-yee inspected Huanggang Port on Monday morning, instructing officers and public transport operators to closely monitor passenger and traffic flows and deploy resources flexibly. She also asked bus companies to run additional short-haul special services to clear travellers more quickly. The Transport Department said about 120 franchised buses, 40 minibuses and 130 cross-border buses had been deployed for service and standby on Monday. Headways for franchised buses would be shortened to two to three minutes during peak hours, and to three to four minutes for minibuses and cross-border buses. Huanggang handled more than 152,000 crossings on Sunday, with some travellers waiting up to two hours amid congestion that lawmakers attributed to unfamiliarity with new clearance procedures, a surge in traffic and computer system reboots. Immigration Department figures showed the port handled 152,068 crossings, the highest daily total since it opened on October 12. These comprised 77,166 outbound trips and 74,902 inbound journeys. Hongkongers accounted for 133,265 crossings, while mainland visitors made 16,832 trips. The facility is designed to handle up to 300,000 travellers and 15,000 vehicles a day, with daily passenger numbers initially expected to range from 100,000 to 200,000. As the Chung Yeung Festival break fuelled a surge in cross-border travel over the weekend, the Security Bureau issued a “busy” advisory for Huanggang on its “Easy Boundary” portal on Sunday afternoon, warning that clearance could take up to 45 minutes. Some mainland visitors, however, reported queuing for as long as two hours. Lawmaker Ben Chan Han-pan, chairman of the Legislative Council’s transport panel, said travellers’ unfamiliarity with the new “collaborative inspection and joint immigration clearance” model was the main cause of congestion on Sunday, with some attempting to use the automated channels without registering beforehand. He added that the sudden surge in passenger numbers had also overwhelmed the control point. Chan said computer systems at the immigration counters had slowed after running for extended periods and needed to be rebooted, further lengthening queues. Lawmaker Chong Ho-fung said the long queues at the newly reopened port over the weekend were inevitable given the large number of travellers crossing the border during the Chung Yeung Festival peak. He said that close to 40,000 people crossed at Huanggang between 10am and 2pm on Sunday, averaging nearly 10,000 an hour, and even with each passenger taking just a minute to complete clearance, queues could easily result in an hour-long wait. “The government’s projections and my own both forecast this would happen. It is a chaotic situation that was within expectations,” Chong told a radio programme. He urged authorities to step up publicity about registration procedures and eligibility requirements for the new “joint clearance” automated channels. Children under seven cannot use the automated channels and must be accompanied by their parents to staffed counters to complete clearance. Those aged seven to 17 can use the “joint clearance” channels once their parents have registered them. Chong said clearer information would help prevent families with young children from reaching the front of the queue only to discover they were ineligible and had to move to staffed counters, adding to their clearance time. “There were too many different reasons why a passenger could not complete clearance, and staff on the ground may not be able to identify the exact reason immediately, causing a chaotic situation,” he said. He also suggested designating more clearance lanes for use by both foreign travellers and Hong Kong residents to speed up the process. Chong said he had also observed system reboots on Sunday in the “joint one-stop” vehicle clearance lane because of mismatches between Hong Kong and Shenzhen data. But he said the congestion was unlikely to persist, as clearance should become smoother once more travellers had registered properly.

title: McLaren put five iconic F1 cars driven by champions and Brad Pitt up for sale
description: The cars are expected to raise tens of millions of dollars and will be prepared by the reigning constructors’ champions for ‌their new owners.
content: McLaren are selling five fully-functioning Formula One cars driven by champions, including Lewis Hamilton and the late Brazilian Ayrton Senna, with one also tested by Hollywood actor Brad Pitt. The cars, to be sold through high-end dealer Tom Hartley Jnr and expected to raise tens of millions of dollars, will be prepared by the reigning constructors’ champions for ‌their next owners. Hartley Jnr also sold the collection of former F1 supremo Bernie Ecclestone and 20 road cars belonging to the late McLaren co-owner Mansour Ojjeh. “We have decided to part with these iconic McLaren Formula One cars because we feel that having them simply sitting in storage is a disservice to what they represent,” McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown said in a statement on Sunday. “These cars were built to be driven and raced, and we want to see them being used and enjoyed. We believe that is ⁠the best way to keep our history alive and our heritage business active.” The five span 32 years of ‌McLaren history, starting with two MP4/6A cars (chassis numbers 04 and 07 with Honda V12 engines) raced by Austrian Gerhard Berger and tested by Senna during the 1991 title-winning campaign. Chassis 04 finished second in a one-two at ‌the San Marino Grand Prix with the McLarens lapping the entire field. Chassis 07 came second at McLaren’s home British ⁠Grand Prix. Both have been in ⁠McLaren’s possession ever since. A 2012 McLaren MP4/27A (chassis 01) raced by 2009 world champion Jenson Button and tested by seven-time world champion Hamilton is also for sale. Two cars raced exclusively ‌by reigning champion Lando Norris in 2021 and 2023 complete the group. The 2021 McLaren MCL35M took Norris to the podium in Imola, Monaco and Monza while the 2023 MCL37A-03 won successive ‌races in ‌Singapore and Japan and was tested post-season by a roster of drivers including Norris’s teammate Oscar Piastri and Mick Schumacher, son of ‌F1 great Michael. The 2023 McLaren was driven by Pitt in a private test at Austin’s Circuit of the Americas in June last year in ⁠connection with his starring role in F1 the Movie and is the most modern F1 car offered for sale to a private owner. Pitt reportedly ⁠took it up to a speed of 197mph (317km/h). “It is incredibly rare for a collector to have the opportunity to acquire race-driven grand prix cars directly from the manufacturer and team that built and campaigned them, and that makes this a very special ‌offering,” Hartley said. “These five cars will ‌be offered individually and there is no time pressure whatsoever. Our priority, and McLaren’s, is to find the right homes for them.” Although no prices were given, they are expected to range from £5 million (US$6.7 million) to as much as £10 million. A McLaren MP4-25A raced by Hamilton to victory in Turkey in 2010 sold for £4.8 million in 2021 while a winning 2001 Ferrari raced by Michael Schumacher fetched US$7.5 million in New York in 2017.

title: Exclusive | From pandas to Peak vistas, Hong Kong sets out to captivate Apec delegates
description: Packed social programme for 500 VIPs features Big Buddha, giant pandas and tech hubs in bid to showcase Hong Kong’s soft power.
content: Giant pandas, open-top bus tours, a Chinese cooking class, traditional opera, a harbour cruise, the Big Buddha and The Peak are among the highlights of a packed social programme for VIPs attending this week’s meeting of Apec finance ministers in Hong Kong, the South China Morning Post has learned. According to official itineraries obtained by the SCMP, about 500 delegates and guests from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum’s 21 members have been offered a range of activities running from Monday evening to Wednesday. In addition to the city’s landmarks and attractions, authorities will showcase Hong Kong’s technological strengths at its two innovation hubs: the Science Park in Pak Shek Kok and Cyberport in Pok Fu Lam. “The VIPs will be able to experience the natural beauty of the city via the Ngong Ping 360 cable car, take in the skyline from The Peak, and see the giant pandas – our national treasures – along with cultural heritage sites,” an insider said. “They will be fully immersed in Hong Kong’s soft power.” Some senior officials and delegates arrived as early as Friday for the meeting, to be held at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai on Tuesday and Wednesday. The social itinerary begins at dusk on Monday with open-top Big Bus tours through quieter-than-usual streets, as the city observes the Chung Yeung Festival public holiday. Visitors will also tour the Xiqu Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong’s largest dedicated venue for Chinese opera and part of the West Kowloon Cultural District. There are two full-day itineraries on Tuesday and Wednesday. One focuses on the city’s cultural heritage, beginning with a cable car ride to Ngong Ping Village and Po Lin Monastery, home to the Big Buddha. It will be followed by a tour of Tai O Village, a traditional fishing village on the western tip of Lantau Island famous for its stilt houses, canals and waterways, seafood and street snacks. The tour will end at the Tai O Heritage Hotel, converted from a former marine police station built in 1902. It is also an award-winning historic building preservation project. The other itinerary keeps visitors mainly in the city centre, starting at The Peak before moving to Ocean Park in Southern district. There, VIPs will get a close look at six giant pandas: mother Ying Ying, father Le Le, their twin cubs – ‘elder sister’ Jia Jia and ‘younger brother’ De De – and the other pair, An An and Ke Ke. The city tour will conclude with cooking classes at the Chinese Culinary Institute in Pok Fu Lam. “Tuesday’s tours are mainly for spouses and delegates as finance ministers and senior officials will be locked in the opening of the meeting and panel discussions,” the insider said. After the meeting ends at lunchtime on Wednesday, senior officials and delegates can take a sunset cruise on Victoria Harbour aboard Aqualuna, the city’s red-sailed junk boat. Other options include visits to the Hong Kong Palace Museum in the West Kowloon Cultural District, the Museum of Art in Tsim Sha Tsui, the Science Park and Cyberport. Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said in an exclusive interview with the SCMP on Thursday that the city had “a lot more to offer, including natural landscapes, heritage, and frontier developments in information technology and others.” He said exhibition booths would be set up at the venue to showcase these aspects of Hong Kong and he hoped that the curated tours would help delegates see “a broader side of Hong Kong that is relevant to both their work and lives, which will hopefully encourage them to return soon”.

title: How a new generation of Sri Lankans is reshaping Colombo’s restaurant and bar scene
description: Open Door Policy and Kampong reflect a growing dining scene rooted in Sri Lankan flavours, local history and a rising generation of talent.
content: For decades, Colombo has been treated less as a cultural destination and more as a quick stopover between the Sri Lankan capital’s airport and the country’s more popular southern coast, where tourists flock to five-star resorts, beachside bars and premier surfing spots. That is beginning to change. As Sri Lanka continues to recover from a 26-year civil war (1983-2009) and the fallout from a recent economic crisis (2019-2024), there is new life in Colombo’s culinary and hospitality scene. “Tourism in Colombo really started to pick up about two and a half years ago,” says British-Sri Lankan chef Dom Fernando. London-born Fernando is best known for Paradise, his acclaimed contemporary Sri Lankan restaurant in the British capital that operated from 2019 to mid-2026. At Paradise, he introduced the cuisine of Sri Lanka – his parents’ birthplace – to a wider Western audience, pairing its flavours with seasonal British produce. For more than six years, Fernando brought his UK team to Sri Lanka every two to three weeks to source ingredients, particularly traditional spices that were difficult to find in London. During one visit in early 2023, he came across a site in Colombo overlooking the Laccadive Sea, beside the city’s famed Marine Drive, and was drawn to the openness of the space. “The area wasn’t nearly as developed as it is now,” he says, “but I thought, ‘Maybe this is the next evolution for me: to open a chef’s table where we put hospitality at the forefront.’ “I wanted to spend more time sourcing from local farmers, learning about the roots of my culture and showing the next generation of talent that we can deliver world-class experiences in Sri Lanka and in Colombo, and that they don’t have to go to Dubai or Singapore to get a job.” Fernando says Sri Lanka has long faced a talent vacuum, as young people often move overseas in search of better opportunities. But the ongoing conflict in West Asia has prompted some hospitality workers to return – an unexpected benefit for Fernando and his new restaurant. In April 2026, he opened the 10-seat Open Door Policy (ODP). The name stems from his vision for an evening dining experience that is “open to the elements and the neighbourhood”. “It creates a juxtaposition – we’re close to the sea and the jungle, but surrounded by the urban landscape of Colombo,” he says. The nine-course tasting menu changes weekly depending on the harvest. In these early days, Fernando often treats guests to extra bites of dishes he is developing. Among the crowd-pleasers are the lacto-fermented watermelon rasam (a traditional tangy South Asian soup) and the elevated eggs and soldiers (British soft-boiled eggs with buttered toast), served with sweetcorn curry, chilli pol sambol and kade paan (traditional Sri Lankan shop bread). Despite the mix of culinary classics, Fernando avoids the overused word “fusion”. “It’s a different presentation where we have room to play and push boundaries without being stuck to one genre, as long as we’re respecting both cultures,” he says, “sort of bridging the two worlds that I’ve been living between. “There’s a genuine story behind this. It is my background.” Drinking to Colombo’s complex history The following night, I visit Kampong, a new cocktail speakeasy opened by the Dayawansa brothers: Shanil, 38; Nadishka, 36; and Nelaka, 32. If ODP draws on Fernando’s dual cultural background, and ultimately traces its roots to Britain’s colonisation of Sri Lanka, Kampong – opened in November 2025 behind a replica local gram store – offers a darker dive into that history. Meaning “village” or “community” in Malay, Kampong – spelled kampung in modern Malay – pays homage to the historic Malay community in Colombo’s Slave Island neighbourhood. The area’s grim name reflects its use as a place of confinement for enslaved people from Africa and South and Southeast Asia during the Portuguese, Dutch and British colonial eras. Although it was renamed Kompanna Vidiya (“company roads”) in 2023, most signs still read “Slave Island”. Over the centuries, the area’s ethnically diverse population significantly “influenced Sri Lankan food and beverage culture”, Shanil says. “We wanted to highlight what the neighbourhood was back in the day, before the current gentrification happened and all the big hotel brands came in. We wanted to give it due respect.” To the left of the entrance, a large painting depicts Slave Island as it might have looked around 450 years ago: a lake and lush greenery in the foreground, with a modern building in the background. Shanil says the artwork reflects Kampong’s aim to honour Colombo’s past while embracing the future through the bar’s storytelling. And it is just as well. Despite its proximity to construction projects and luxury hotel chains, Kompanna Vidiya has retained the feel of a low-income residential neighbourhood. “Slave Island is smack-bang in the middle of an extremely developed part of Colombo, but in a really weird position,” says Nelaka, Kampong’s lead mixologist. “It’s maybe two minutes away from the five-star hotels that people are staying in, but they won’t get down here or would be too scared to even ask or figure out what this area is.” Kampong aims to introduce locals and tourists alike to the often overlooked history beneath Slave Island’s gritty streets. The team has mapped 10 historic sites and buildings around the bar, some of which still stand today, and named its reinvented classic cocktails after them. Cocktail-making in Sri Lanka may sound simple, but it comes with its own challenges. Strict government regulations and frequent import shortages can make essential ingredients hard to find, forcing the team to adapt. “Situations like that push us against the wall and force us to create our own liqueurs and ingredients, which sometimes actually end up making better drinks,” Nelaka says. When the Italian liqueur Bitter Bianco was unavailable for the white negroni-inspired Rio Negroni, for instance, Nelaka and his team made their own in-house version. Other drinks include Beira Daiquiri, made with pandan-infused rum and coconut; Kiri Pani, a mix of local buffalo curd, palm treacle (a traditional Sri Lankan dessert), mescal and spiced rum; and the Kompanni Sour, featuring arrack, a South and Southeast Asian spirit distilled from the fermented sap of coconut flowers or sugar cane. A collaborative community Fernando and the Dayawansa brothers have a meaningful connection – the chef held the launch preview for ODP at Gini, the trio’s fine-dining restaurant, which opened in 2023, after two years as a supper club. “It’s not competition,” Fernando says. “We want to level up everybody’s game in Colombo. Whether you’re a small roti or hopper shop, we’re all trying to give more airtime to the provenance of Sri Lankan cuisine. “You’ve got all these new players coming in and really boosting the scene, and I just wanted to be a part of that. It was and still is very, very exciting.” The Dayawansa brothers agree with Fernando’s view that Colombo has seen a wave of new bars and restaurants over the past two to three years. They believe younger people like themselves are bringing a fresh perspective to the city’s hospitality scene. “I feel like there is a good momentum right now in Colombo, where people have seen the potential and growth in the city, and they are moving away from big international hotel chains, which is what Colombo is known for,” Nelaka says. “It’s pushing individual-owned businesses to do something outside the box, reinvent their thinking, and create products and spaces on an international level that is on par with a lot of countries abroad.” “There’s so much potential in the city,” Fernando says. “The energy in Colombo right now is phenomenal.”

title: Sydney opens US$4 billion second airport with few flights
description: Western Sydney International launches commercial operations with a sparse schedule as major airlines remain cautious.
content: After more than half a century of political procrastination, environmental protests and funding shortfalls, Sydney finally has a second airport. But the new A$5.6 billion (US$4 billion) site’s commercial prospects are already in question. Western Sydney International, 50km (31 miles) inland from the city centre, will handle its first passenger flight on Sunday – a Jetstar service to the Gold Coast. But the facility has attracted only a handful of airlines and has half a dozen or fewer scheduled flights a day for the next 12 months, according to aviation data company Cirium. Australia’s biggest aviation infrastructure development in decades is opening just as the global travel industry endures its toughest period since the pandemic. Around the world, airlines are sounding the alarm on rising fuel costs and fares as the Iran war drags on. Many, including dominant Australian carrier Qantas, are cutting back on domestic capacity rather than laying on more flights. Airlines are also struggling to get their hands on new jets, leaving few spare aircraft to send to start-ups like Western Sydney International where passenger demand is unproven. Compounding the government-owned airport’s challenges, a planned rail link would not open until 2027 at the earliest, while a shuttle bus to the centre of Sydney costs A$55 and takes about one hour. That means Sydney Kingsford Smith, 20 minutes by taxi or train from the central business district and Australia’s primary gateway, remains a more practical option for most people. “The main airport is much more convenient to almost all travellers,” said David Levinson, a professor of transport at the University of Sydney. Western Sydney International’s passenger forecasts look “a bit optimistic,” he said. Named for pioneering Australian aviator Nancy Bird Walton, the new airport expects to handle 8.4 million passengers a year by the end of the decade, and almost 20 million annually by 2045, according to its master plan. Both figures are fractions of the numbers handled by the city’s main airport. Western Sydney International is built on old farmland at Badgerys Creek. The government settled on the site in 2014, ending a debate about the need and location for a second airport that stretches back to 1946. Construction started in 2018 and the airport opened for cargo flights in July. The surrounding population is key to the facility’s commercial fate. By 2030, half of Sydney’s 6.1 million people will live in the city’s west, according to the airport’s master plan. Some 40 per cent of Greater Western Sydney’s population was born overseas, which should generate demand for flights to countries such as India, China and Vietnam, the document says. Yet Qantas plans to operate little more than one domestic flight a day, on average, from March next year, according to Cirium data through September 2027. Virgin Australia, the country’s second-largest carrier, has no flights scheduled. The new airport’s main customer is Jetstar, the leisure-focused, low-cost carrier owned by Qantas. “We are looking closely at the Western Sydney opportunity and assessing whether it would fit into a network and schedule that best serves the needs of our customers,” Virgin Australia said in a statement. Qantas referred to a speech by Chief Executive Officer Vanessa Hudson in June, when she described Western Sydney as “such an important market”, specifically highlighting its relevance to Jetstar. “We expect demand will grow, and when we see that, we’ll put more frequency in,” she said at the time. Other airlines that will use the new airport are Air New Zealand, VietJet, Fiji Airways and Singapore Airlines. In an interview, Western Sydney International Chief Executive Officer Simon Hickey said more airlines would use the airport in time, and talks were taking place with several other carriers. “Right now, I’m really happy with where we’re sitting,” he said. But Hickey also needs the local population to give the airport a chance, which would help him persuade other carriers that there’s demand to capture. “It’s use it or lose it,” he said. “That will mean that we continue to grow and other airlines will come and join the pack.” To be sure, long-term appetite for air travel is relentless. Worldwide passenger demand was expected to more than double by 2050, according to the International Air Transport Association. And while it may be off to a slow start, Western Sydney International has some advantages over Sydney’s main airport. Most importantly, it has no overnight curfew like at Kingsford Smith, allowing international airlines to schedule departures that connect with other flights at their own hubs. The new airport expects to handle 82 million passengers a year by 2063 and ultimately become Sydney’s primary air-travel hub. It takes time for a new airport to establish itself, said Stephen Beckett, CEO of Airlines for Australia & New Zealand, which represents Qantas, Jetstar, Air New Zealand and Virgin Australia. “Some airlines will sit back and make their own commercial assessments based on passenger demand,” he said. For now, Western Sydney International is already drawing unfavourable comparisons with airports elsewhere that ultimately failed to live up to expectations. Levinson, the transport professor at the University of Sydney, compared Western Sydney International to Mirabel Airport outside Montreal. Mirabel opened in 1975 in time for the Montreal Olympics but handled its last commercial passenger flight in 2004. The airport now operates chiefly as a freight hub. Right now, Western Sydney International is trying to serve a market that does not yet exist, Levinson said. The new airport’s opening is “early, given actual demand,” he said. There was a risk Sydney’s secondary airport would end up with a similar status as Avalon Airport, which is more than 50km outside Melbourne, according to Peter Forsyth, an aviation economics consultant who’s a former professor at Monash University. Avalon, where Jetstar has operated flights since 2004, has never broken through as a genuine alternative airport to Melbourne’s main airport, he said. Growth at Sydney’s new airport would be a slow burn, said Forsyth. “There is a market there,” he said. “But exactly how big it is, I don’t know.”

title: The human touch behind the virtual technology for preparing child cancer patients
description: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist Shara Lee created Herocare, a simulation programme that calms the nerves of young radiotherapy patients.
content: Hong Kong Polytechnic University professor Shara Lee Wee-yee has been using a mixed-reality programme to reduce the fear and uncertainty children face before radiotherapy, with personalised rehearsals that allow families to experience the treatment journey before entering hospital. The simulation programme, Herocare, also helped carers understand what to expect while enabling future radiotherapists to develop the empathy and communication skills for patient care, she noted. Lee is a finalist in the innovation category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Herocare recreates hospital radiotherapy environments within PolyU’s Hybrid Immersive Virtual Environment (HiVE) facility. It was launched during the Covid-19 pandemic, specifically when carers and social workers were restricted from hospital areas, and was later built around the HiVE facility, set up in 2022. The 600-square-foot (55.7-square-metre), six-sided facility is equipped with 360-degree projections to simulate treatment rooms, equipment and sounds without requiring children to wear headsets. Radiotherapy can require children to remain completely still for 15 to 30 minutes while machinery moves around them. Some also need close-fitting head casts. Lee said a radiotherapy course can entail up to 30 sessions over six weeks, with general anaesthesia traditionally used when young patients cannot remain still. Herocare prepares families before that stage. Each session lasts about 90 minutes and is tailored to the family. Each session begins with the team asking parents about their child’s interests. Radiation therapy students then create stories and activities around those interests before introducing the treatment process and guiding the child through a rehearsal. She recalled that a six-year-old boy with a brainstem tumour had been distressed in the early stages and was expected to require general anaesthesia for 30 sessions of palliative radiotherapy. After learning that he loved the video game Minecraft, students turned his rehearsal into a game-like mission centred on a favourite character. His mother demonstrated the procedure first before he tried lying still himself. He subsequently completed his radiotherapy sessions awake. Avoiding anaesthesia is only part of the purpose, she said. The programme is intended to help children understand what will happen so that unfamiliar equipment, sounds and routines become less frightening. Carers are also supported through the process. While students work with the child, Lee and other team members speak separately with parents, inviting them to ask questions and discuss worries that may be harder to raise during a busy hospital visit. The programme also gives students sustained contact with patients and families before clinical practice. Shara, who had years of clinical experience before she started teaching at the university, said students can become overly focused on clinical skills, equipment, positioning and other technical requirements. Herocare gives them time to understand the person receiving treatment. “You cannot teach this simply by telling them,” she said, referring to softer skills such as empathy and communication. “They need the experience of working with a child themselves.” By August 2026, Herocare had supported 85 families and involved more than 500 students. Since 2021, Herocare patients have completed 1,733 paediatric radiotherapy sessions without anaesthesia. In a separate patient-level measure, 71 or 94.7 per cent of 75 children assessed for treatment while awake completed their radiotherapy courses without general anaesthesia. Treatment time per session was also reduced by an estimated 77.8 per cent, from about 90 minutes to 20 minutes. “This also means hospitals can get more out of their radiotherapy capacity, with fewer staff and less machine time needed for each patient,” she explained. Lee thanked the Lee Hysan Foundation and the University Grants Committee for providing funding to support the programme. She said the model could eventually be adapted for adults who need special preparation for radiotherapy, including breast cancer patients required to practice breath-holding during treatment. “Innovation gives us the tools, but it’s the human touch that makes the difference,” she said. The Spirit of Hong Kong Awards were established in 2013 to recognise the city’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention.

title: Lula and Bolsonaro trade barbs in fiery Brazil run-off debate
description: First face-to-face clash descends into personal attacks one week before high-stakes presidential vote.
content: Brazil’s Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva traded barbs in ⁠their first face-to-face presidential debate on Sunday in a contentious back-and-forth just one week before the election’s run-off. Polls before the debate suggested Bolsonaro, the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, would enter the October 25 vote as the favourite after finishing nearly two points ahead of Lula in the election’s first round earlier this month. But surveys have also shown a narrowing race, and Lula has expressed confidence he can be the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s to finish second in the first round and go on to win ‌the election. The debate, which allowed the candidates to tensely move about the stage and interact with each other with limited moderation from the host, turned quickly into a heated exchange of corruption accusations and personal attacks. Lula pressed Bolsonaro on alleged links to jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro, and Bolsonaro questioned Lula about accusations involving his son and a pension fraud scandal. “Lying is the Bolsonaro family’s strong suit,” Lula said, while Bolsonaro said Lula has a “very clear problem in your DNA” and is “always tainted by corruption”. Sunday’s debate was the first between Lula and Senator Bolsonaro after the candidates both declined previous opportunities. A second debate is scheduled for October 23 just ahead of the run-off. Lula told reporters before the debate that he hoped to win over the 33 million voters who stayed home in the election’s first round, equal to about ⁠one in five eligible voters. The debate’s format at times fuelled tense exchanges and vocal frustration from the audience. A confident Bolsonaro gestured and paced several times behind Lula when it was the president’s turn to speak, ‌a move that moderators said was within the rules but that drew complaints from Lula’s team. “Bolsonaro had a slight advantage overall, more so based on posture than on content, because Lula was uncomfortable and nervous throughout the entire debate,” said Lucas de Aragao, a partner at Brasilia-based consultancy Arko Advice. At one point, Lula refused to stand near Bolsonaro, ‌calling him a “militiaman”, alluding to allegations of the senator’s ties to Rio de Janeiro paramilitary groups. Bolsonaro, in turn, quipped that it was good he had left his wallet behind, an apparent ⁠jab at Lula’s 2017 corruption conviction that was ⁠later annulled. The candidates largely repeated campaign promises on policy. Bolsonaro, for example, pledged to designate Brazil’s major gangs and militias as narco-terrorist organisations and build more than half a million prison spaces. Lula defended his economic record, arguing that growth comes from putting money “in the hands of many” ‌rather than a few, and pointed to above-inflation minimum wage increases during his presidency as a sign of his commitment. The candidates clashed over high food prices, which have weighed on Lula’s support even with inflation falling and unemployment hitting a record low. The candidates also accused each other of betraying national sovereignty. Lula accused the Bolsonaros of lobbying the US to impose tariffs on Brazil and of ‌hoping Brazil would suffer. “It’s notable to the Brazilian people that the Bolsonaro family is subordinate to American interests,” Lula said. Bolsonaro rejected Lula’s claims and said that under Lula, Brazil was “subordinate to globalists and terrorists”. Earlier on Sunday, ⁠Bolsonaro supporters filled Sao Paulo’s Paulista Avenue, while Lula supporters packed the plaza at the heart of Brasilia’s government district, and students in Rio de Janeiro marched against Bolsonaro. The demonstrations laid bare some of the grievances ⁠behind the polarisation that has gridlocked Brazilian politics for nearly a decade. Many Bolsonaro supporters believe Lula should be imprisoned over corruption scandals that engulfed his Workers’ Party. Many Lula supporters, meanwhile, say former president Bolsonaro’s conviction for a coup attempt was justified. Lula spent 580 days in prison in 2018 and 2019 on a corruption conviction that was later annulled over flaws in the investigation and legal proceedings. Former president Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years for plotting a coup after losing his 2022 re-election bid to Lula. He is serving the sentence under house arrest because of health problems. The younger Bolsonaro has called his father’s trial a “farce” and has pledged to seek amnesty for him if elected president.

title: Left paralysed after crash, Hong Kong Keeta rider caught in insurance limbo
description: Delivery worker’s world reduced to hospital bed as he waits for platform’s insurer to pay in absence of government law covering app-based couriers.
content: After a traffic accident on a delivery run for Keeta left courier Joe* paralysed, his world has shrunk to the view of the ceiling above his hospital bed in Hong Kong. The tragedy took place in May when the 54-year-old motorcyclist was momentarily distracted on the road by a notification from the Keeta app reminding him to accept an order, and he collided with a car in front. Despite undergoing major surgery, Joe sustained irreversible neck injuries that left his body and limbs paralysed, although he is able to speak. In his fifth month in hospital, Joe said there had been no progress in his insurance claims submitted to Keeta and not a single representative from the company had followed up on the case. He relies on full-time care at the public hospital, with a physiotherapist coming in for a daily check-up. He also has difficulty swallowing, which affects his speech. “My body feels numb, I can’t engage [my muscles] to move,” he said with a stutter. Joe’s case exemplifies a familiar plight faced by Hong Kong’s delivery platform workers. They are classified as self-employed, despite a ruling from the Labour Tribunal in 2023 establishing an employment relationship between couriers and platforms. Under Hong Kong labour law, in cases of permanent total incapacity, employees between the ages of 40 and 55 are entitled to compensation of at least 72 months’ earnings, or a minimum payout of HK$584,220 (US$74,440). The Employees’ Compensation Ordinance also stipulates that the employer is responsible for medical expenses, including covering inpatient treatment at up to HK$500 a day. The Labour and Welfare Bureau released a Legislative Council paper in July proposing that food and goods delivery workers be entitled to compensation for injuries or death sustained while doing work secured through platforms. Until such legislation is enacted, delivery workers remain entirely dependent on commercial group insurance policies arranged by platforms. Before switching to Keeta in 2023, Joe had worked full-time as a pizza delivery man. According to his wife, who asked to be identified only by her first name Yee, he earned up to HK$30,000 a month and worked almost every day. They have a daughter in her twenties who works overseas. Replying to questions from the South China Morning Post, Keeta said it had contacted Joe’s relatives and sent regards. “The claim has been submitted to the insurance company and is being processed,” the platform said. “Keeta’s operations team is maintaining close contact with the family to offer appropriate support.” It confirmed that Joe’s situation fell within the scope of work-related coverage and that the insurance plan covered the courier’s commute time an hour before going online and an hour after logging off. Under the plan, the maximum compensation for permanent disability is HK$1 million. The SCMP learned that the insurance company was still awaiting Joe’s complete medical report before processing his claims. Justine Lam, programme officer of the Hong Kong Christian Industrial Committee, which advocates for workers’ rights, said the insurer had failed to set a time frame for the handling of claims, and that victims had to wait a long time for reimbursements while paying their medical bills out of pocket. She added that the platform also did not monitor or follow up on the process. Joe’s wife said she visited him every day in hospital after work and spent one or two hours with him. Yee, who works in the procurement business, said her husband was worried that his condition would worsen. “Every day when I walk into the ward, I never know how he will react,” she said. “I vividly remember him being in constant, agonising pain in the earlier stage, and later on suffering from frequent spasms and severe confusion.” Yee said on good days, her husband showed her how he could move his fingertips and slowly turn his left ankle. But when things were rough, all she could do was massage him to ease his pain. During visits, she fed her husband soft meals such as congee, which she described as tasteless. To add some flavour to the blandness, she brought savoury snacks, and added pork floss and fish sausage to the congee. The most pressing issue was finding a care home for her husband, where he would be transferred after he was discharged. Yee said she avoided overthinking and lived each day with the attitude of “taking things as they come”. “Once he told me that he was scared that I would stop visiting him one day … or that the day would be our last,” she said. * Name changed at interviewee’s request

title: US prize-winning cancer scientist Wan Fengyi joins China’s Zhejiang University
description: The former Bloomberg School of Public Health professor pioneered groundbreaking research into links between a stomach bug and colon cancer.
content: A Johns Hopkins University scientist whose award-winning work suggests that a brief stomach bug could raise the risk of colon cancer has moved to China full time. Wan Fengyi, a professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, has joined Zhejiang University in Hangzhou, according to his new profile on the Chinese university’s website. Wan returned to China this month and now holds a chair professorship at Zhejiang University. He is based at a national laboratory at its Second Affiliated Hospital, which develops devices placed inside blood vessels. He is one of at least five senior scientists from leading US institutions to take up full-time positions at Zhejiang University this year, according to the university. They include Qian Jiang, a Johns Hopkins eye expert whose arrival was announced this month, and Lin Fanghua, a New York University mathematician and a member of the US National Academy of Sciences, who joined in September. Mei Jianguo, a former head of chemistry at Purdue University, also joined in September. In May, Ge Kai, a senior scientist at the US National Institutes of Health, took up a post at one of the university’s hospitals. The South China Morning Post has contacted Wan for comment. At Johns Hopkins, Wan studied how germs, the immune system and the trillions of microbes in the gut interact – and how that interplay can keep the gut healthy or lead to inflammation and cancer. In 2022, his team reported in the journal Cancer Discovery that even a short-lived gut infection made mice more likely to develop colon cancer. The bacteria released a toxin that damaged the DNA of cells lining the gut. It is not yet clear whether the same happens in people, but the work won him the Bloomberg School’s Shikani/El-Hibri Prize for Discovery and Innovation the following year. In 2024, Wan’s team reported in the journal Cell that proteins in breast milk help shape the bacteria that settle in a newborn’s gut, protecting baby mice from a dangerous infection. In lab tests, the team found the same proteins in human breast milk. “This represents an important expansion of our understanding of breast milk’s protective mechanisms,” Wan said in a university statement at the time. Wan graduated from Wuhan University in 1999 and earned his PhD in biophysics at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 2003, according to his LinkedIn profile. He then spent six years as a researcher at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases before setting up his own lab at Johns Hopkins, where he rose from assistant professor to full professor. His lab at the Bloomberg School won more than US$4.7 million in National Institutes of Health grants between 2011 and 2025, according to the agency’s grant database. The most recent, from the US National Cancer Institute, aimed to find drugs that could treat cancer with fewer side effects.

title: Letters | Hong Kong must ensure independent artists have control over their voice
description: Readers discuss voice rights in the age of AI-generated songs, why AI giants cannot be left to self-regulate, and Elon Musk’s Starlink row in India.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Search for almost any K-pop, C-pop or J-pop star on a video platform and, sooner or later, you will hear them sing a song they never recorded. The voice sounds like theirs. It was built by an artificial intelligence model trained on their recordings and posted by someone who never asked. I run a global music conference and publish a music magazine in the United States, and my view is simple: a voice belongs to the artist. Not the record label, not the app, not the person with a laptop. I have seen too many cases where the people holding the contracts end up with more control over a voice than the person it came from. Asia has seen where this leads. In 2023, AI covers in the voice of Singaporean singer Stefanie Sun drew millions of likes on Chinese platforms when she was years into a break. A year later, the Beijing Internet Court ruled that using AI to mimic a voice-over artist’s voice without her permission infringed her personal rights. The company that handed over her recordings was the company that held them. Having her recordings did not give it the right to her voice. Since September 2025, China has required AI-generated content, including audio, to be labelled. That helps. But a label tells listeners a voice is fake, not whether the singer consented to the use of her voice or was paid. To fans: an AI cover of your favourite idol comes from a good place. But love is not payment. If the artist earns nothing from that song, even the fan is taking from them. I am asking for a system where the artist is asked first and paid when the answer is yes. Hong Kong, Seoul and Tokyo are among the world’s great music hubs. They should lead with protection, starting with independent artists. The biggest stars have agencies and lawyers. An independent singer in a small studio has her voice and not much else. Hong Kong has paused its AI copyright amendment to draft guidelines first. That is a chance to put the artist’s consent at the centre. Music is food for the soul. The artists who make it deserve to be fed by it too. Michael T. Neely, CEO, Global Music Conference Waiting to regulate AI is a mistake I refer to “Trump relies on AI giants to self-police after ruling out China deal” (September 30). It appears that history is repeating itself. When social media platforms such as Facebook and Instagram first emerged, they expanded largely unchecked. Championed as tools for networking and information sharing, they benefited from a laissez-faire regulatory approach. Governments operated under the assumption that commercial firms would self-regulate and prioritise user well-being. Decades later, their systemic impacts are becoming clear. These include a youth mental health crisis, cyberbullying, algorithmic echo chambers, and addictive engagement loops. To mitigate these harms, governments worldwide are now scrambling to implement restrictions. For instance, Australia enacted legislation blocking minors from major platforms. Nations across Europe have introduced measures such as age-gating. A similar paradigm is unfolding with artificial intelligence. Currently, AI development remains concentrated in commercial hands, propelled by a high-stakes race under the premise that self-regulation is sufficient. However, because AI acts as foundational, general-purpose infrastructure that can reshape economics, labour and information integrity, its potential risks – ranging from cognitive offloading and displacement of white-collar jobs to realistic deepfakes and autonomous decision-making – are broader and deeper than those of social media. If regulators wait until catastrophe strikes, history suggests they will be too late. Pre-emptive, binding legal guardrails and independent audits are essential now to avoid repeating past mistakes. Rosemary Chiu, North Point Security risks are a bitter pill to swallow As we enter the age of satellite telecommunications for household users, it opens the door to national security risks should a country allow a foreign company to provide services. Recently, Elon Musk took on Mukesh Ambani amid his struggle to launch Starlink in India. Before accusing India or an Indian, Musk should ask whether the United States government would allow an Indian company to run satellite services there. Rishi Teckchandani, Mid-Levels

title: Your Voice: Harmful ‘nonchalant’ trend and battling tiger parents (long letters)
description: This week, one reader explains how ‘nonchalance’ hurts ambition, relationships and mental health while another urges parents to let children make their own choi
content:
Have something to say? Send us a letter using this form.
Tiffany Taw, German Swiss International School
The “nonchalant” trend has become ubiquitous on social media feeds. The not-so-new trend, which has skyrocketed in popularity, is characterised by effortlessness, indifference and performative apathy. It applauds seemingly natural talent and deems any degree of effort and care as “cringe”.
The trend initially garnered massive amounts of participants – and views. But ordinary internet users and critics are starting to question it, suggesting it may have significant negative impacts on its viewers, particularly younger ones.
First, some argue that the “nonchalant” trend erodes authentic ambition, particularly in young people. If showing interest or enthusiasm becomes tantamount to social suicide, experts observe a phenomenon called “quiet quitting”: when students feel compelled to put in only the bare minimum and stop trying anything difficult, especially at school.
In contrast, a “growth mindset” sets students up for success. It embraces setbacks and mistakes, allowing them to build up grit and self-confidence. This trend teaches them the opposite – that effort is embarrassing, and failures should be hidden.
Not only does this thinking lead to academic underperformance, but also increasing avoidance of challenges and even dulled aspirations and passions for hobbies. I have seen the negative effect of this trend with my very own eyes, with classmates reluctant to join clubs or activities due to a fear of being deemed cringe and too “chalant”.
More severe than diminished motivation, perhaps, is the worsening of young people’s mental health. The apathy, which suggests a deeper emotional disconnect than indifference, created by this trend masks vulnerable feelings such as fear, anger and anxiety. It can worsen depression, as emotions go unprocessed and unvalidated.
More significantly, perhaps, is the emotional isolation. Being “nonchalant” takes a toll on relationships, be it familial, platonic or romantic. Genuine connections require the display of honest feelings, vulnerability and care.
The trend results in repressing emotions, which not only stagnates the development of your relationships but can also prevent some from forming entirely. It can lead to misunderstandings and misinterpretations, outbursts, impulsive actions and eventually conflict.
Relationships are at the heart of interpersonal connection, and with Gen Z already being recognised as the “loneliest” generation, this trend is ironic and harmful. It is lethal to the very relationships that combat this loneliness.
In conclusion, the “nonchalant” trend is more than just a fleeting social media fad – it is a cultural phenomenon. While it may garner popularity both in real life and online, it is imperative to recognise the tangible, negative consequences.
Stigmatising effort and vulnerability stifles ambition and exacerbates emotional isolation, jeopardising the development and well-being of an entire generation. Fortunately, content creators and students are starting to flag these dangers and push back, once again popularising authenticity, effort and emotional honesty over the hollow appeal of performative coolness.
Chloe Chan, Kiangsu-Chekiang College (Shatin)
Tiger parenting, an authoritarian style or stereotype associated with Chinese and other East Asian parents, is favoured by many parents in Hong Kong. The parenting style is characterised by a high level of investment in ensuring children’s success, especially in academic and extracurricular achievements.
I believe children should be allowed to choose how to spend their spare time. First, forcing children to participate in extracurricular activities adds unnecessary pressure on them. The high depression rates in Hong Kong are already alarming.
Packed schedules and high expectations are key contributors. Cutthroat competition in school leads to exceptionally high stress levels among children today. Hong Kong parents relentlessly compare their children with others, leading to insecurities and self-doubt.
Students then have to attend after-school tutorial classes practically on a daily basis. Along with endless piles of schoolwork and unrealistic expectations from parents, the pressure is absolutely unbearable. Extracurricular activities simply cannot fit into students' tight schedules.
Second, forcing children to participate in activities they lack interest in and passion for is a waste of their time and their parents’ money. Parents believe extracurricular activities are a good use of children’s free time. They foolishly believe their children can rest or relax as they learn new skills. But for students, this forced “fun” is just more hard labour.
Children who are not motivated to actively take part in classes will neither discover new interests nor develop creativity. They will solely focus on when the lesson will end. However, if children are given the opportunity to manage their free time independently, they might learn a few useful skills.
Third, allowing children to manage their own free time strengthens family relationships. When parents dictate every hour of the day, children become bitter and see their parents as controllers rather than allies. This simmering resentment erodes the parent-child bond and breeds a tense, hostile atmosphere at home, placing yet another burden on a child’s already fragile mental health.
When children are trusted to make their own choices about how they spend their spare time, they feel respected and valued. This paves the way for open communication and greatly diminishes daily conflict. Children who are free to explore their genuine interests are more likely to develop a secure sense of self and long-term emotional resilience.
A child’s lack of maturity should not be an excuse for stopping them from making long-term decisions. If youngsters are never given the chance to manage their own time, they will never learn discipline because they will never face the consequences of not making good use of it.
In conclusion, children should have the right to manage their free time. They will experience less pressure, actively discover interests and learn time-management skills.

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: medical student draws from experience of volunteer work
description: Alfred Lam says helping elderly people and disadvantaged communities allows him to look beyond symptoms and understand those he may one day treat.
content: Years of volunteering to serve elderly people and disadvantaged communities have informed medical student Alfred Lam’s approach to medicine, teaching the University of Hong Kong undergraduate to look beyond symptoms and understand the people he may one day treat. Lam is a finalist in the youth category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, which recognise the city’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention. The awards are co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post, and Lam was nominated by the NGO HandsOn Hong Kong. He became more active in volunteering when he was in secondary school through HandsOn programmes that included bread collection, meal distribution and activities for elderly people. Much of his time was spent with older people living alone or experiencing dementia. Lam and other young volunteers devised board games and other activities to encourage interaction, and also organised outings. He later stayed on to help guide a new group of student volunteers. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Lam saw how reduced social contact affected some elderly people. Starting a conversation could itself be difficult, he recalled, so activities such as board games created an easier way for them to interact with volunteers and one another. Those experiences have remained relevant since he entered medical school. Lam joined Medical Outreachers, a student-led medical volunteer group, and has taken part in its health education and outreach programmes, both in Hong Kong and overseas. During a recent trip to Cambodia, students visited communities with limited healthcare resources, assisted local doctors and provided basic health education. One encounter there left a particular impression. During a clinical session, a patient disclosed that he had tuberculosis. Some students instinctively stepped back and put on masks. Lam noticed that the local doctor responded differently. While taking the necessary precautions, the doctor remained composed and continued speaking to the patient without displaying alarm. The encounter reminded Lam that a doctor’s response can affect a patient as much as the clinical interaction itself. His earlier work with elderly people has given him a similar perspective. Lam said volunteering allowed him to spend time with people he might otherwise rarely have encountered in his daily life. “These elderly people may become patients in the future,” he said. Lam noted that such interactions were especially valuable for medical students, who often come from comfortable backgrounds with strong educational opportunities, whereas their future patients might come from vastly different circumstances. Since starting medical school, he has also joined outreach activities in Sham Shui Po, where he has met homeless people with conditions such as poorly managed diabetes. He hopes that as he gains more medical knowledge and qualifications, he will eventually be able to offer more expertise as a professional than he does as a student. Volunteering has shaped his thinking as an altruistic young person. While bread runs and activities with elderly people first exposed him to communities beyond his usual circle, medical outreach now allows him to consider treatments as a future doctor. Lam knows finding time may become harder once he starts working in medicine, but he hopes volunteering will remain a key part of his life.

title: Update | No danger found after bomb threat diverts Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv
description: Bulgarian MiG-29 fighter jets escort Airbus A320 into Sofia before all 57 people aboard are safely evacuated.
content: A bomb threat forced an Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna to divert to Sofia late on Sunday, but searches found no danger and the aircraft was cleared to resume its journey overnight, the airline and Bulgaria’s BTA news agency said. BTA reported that the crew declared an emergency as the aircraft approached the Romanian border, prompting the Bulgarian Air Force to scramble MiG-29 fighter jets. Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that the threat was called in by an Austrian national who was not on board the aircraft, without identifying the source of the information. The airline confirmed that flight OS82 made an unscheduled landing in the Bulgarian capital following a threat, but said comprehensive security checks of the aircraft, its 51 passengers and six crew members uncovered no hazard. The flight continued on to Vienna with all passengers aboard following the sweep. Flight-tracking service Flightradar24 identified the plane as an Airbus A320-200, an aircraft that typically seats up to 180 passengers, indicating the flight was flying at less than a third of its capacity. The scare came less than three weeks after an off-duty co-pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai jet allegedly attacked the captain with an axe in an attempt to crash the plane. Prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said last week that the Omani co-pilot had planned a suicide attack intended to slam the aircraft into a terminal at Ben Gurion Airport before he was overpowered. Last week, Croatia and Germany also scrambled fighter jets after a commercial flight from the Greek island of Corfu to Nuremberg accidentally transmitted a hijacking transponder code. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: China’s economy grows 4.5% in third quarter, staying on track for annual target
description: GDP growth picked up pace from the second quarter’s 4.3 per cent expansion, beating expectations and putting year’s goal in sight.
content: China’s economy expanded by 4.5 per cent in the third quarter, keeping it broadly on track to meet this year’s growth target but also maintaining pressure on Beijing to deploy further support to address weak domestic demand. China’s year-on-year economic growth for the first three quarters of the year came in at 4.6 per cent, the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) said on Monday. Beijing is targeting gross domestic product growth between 4.5 and 5 per cent this year, down from the “around 5 per cent” goal in previous years. The third-quarter growth was above the 4.41 per cent consensus forecast of economists surveyed by Chinese financial data provider Wind. It picked up pace from the 4.3 per cent expansion recorded during the second quarter, which was the lowest quarterly growth rate reported since the end of 2022. “The steady economic performance from the first three quarters has laid a good foundation for the achievement of the annual target,” said Mao Shengyong, deputy director of the NBS, at a press conference in Beijing on Monday. Most indicators in September had shown an improvement from the two months prior, Mao noted, adding that some of the drag on industries under pressure in the second quarter, such as oil and coal, had eased in the third quarter. But the international environment was volatile and domestic demand remained insufficient, he said. Growth has been driven by strong exports, but domestic consumption and investment remain sluggish amid a prolonged downturn in the property market and weak employment prospects. The key macroeconomic message is that China’s economy is still supply- and production-side driven Zhang Yuhan, The Conference Board Industrial output grew by 5.5 per cent year on year last month, compared with an increase of 5.2 per cent in August. Meanwhile, retail sales, a major gauge of consumption, rose by 1.1 per cent year on year in September, beating the 0.7 per cent forecast from the Wind poll and higher than August’s 0.4 per cent. Retail sales of communication equipment surged 31.1 per cent year on year in September, driven by the launch of new mobile phone models from several brands, according to the NBS. Tobacco and alcohol also recorded strong growth while sales of automobiles and gold and silver jewellery fell by 21.2 and 9.6 per cent, respectively. Overall fixed-asset investment – covering major items such as infrastructure, manufacturing and property construction – decreased by 7.2 per cent year on year in the first nine months of 2026, identical to the decline recorded from January to August. Exports surged 36.3 per cent year on year in September, far above market expectations, driven by global demand for artificial intelligence and hi-tech products. “The key macroeconomic message is that China’s economy is still supply and production-side driven,” said Zhang Yuhan, principal economist at The Conference Board’s China Centre. “This supports near-term growth and industrial upgrading, while continued efforts to strengthen household consumption, services demand and consumer confidence would make the recovery more balanced and sustainable,” he said. Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said the economic momentum remained subdued in September, but growth in the first three quarters was still above the lower end of the growth target zone. “I wonder if this means that the government doesn’t need to make significant changes to its policy stance in the fourth quarter to achieve the growth target for the full year,” he said. Marcella Chow, global market strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, said growth was stabilising but remained uneven across the economy. “External demand and parts of the industrial and technology sectors remain resilient, while domestic demand continued to recover at a more moderate pace,” she said. Analysts from ANZ Bank wrote in a research note on Monday that the coming fifth plenum of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee later this month could offer a clue into policymakers’ willingness to deploy stronger fiscal support. “In our view, fiscal policy is the most effective instrument for boosting demand in the current scenario,” the analysts said, noting that stronger public-sector demand might be necessary to offset weak private-sector spending. Technology-led growth in sectors such as semiconductors, AI-related hardware and advanced manufacturing had boosted exports and industrial output, but had not automatically translated into significant improvements in household earnings and consumption or a broad-based recovery, they added. Chinese stocks closed mixed on Monday, with the Shanghai Composite rising 0.39 per cent while the ChiNext narrowed losses of more than 2 per cent to close 0.94 per cent lower. Defence and home appliance stocks gained, while agriculture and real estate led the declines. Beijing has rolled out a series of incremental policy measures in recent months to bolster the economy, including accelerating bond issuance, announcing plans for the construction of major infrastructure projects and releasing new mortgage interest subsidies for homebuyers. Property investment, an entrenched drag on economic growth, fell 20.6 per cent in the first three quarters of the year, compared with a fall of 19.9 per cent in the first eight months, the bureau said. Among 70 major Chinese cities, the selling prices of commercial residential properties in first-tier cities continued to rise month on month in September – by 0.1 per cent for new homes and 0.2 per cent for second-hand homes – while the month-on-month declines in second- and third-tier cities generally narrowed, the NBS said. In year-on-year terms, declines in housing prices in all 70 cities narrowed. This pointed to a “broader, gradual stabilisation” in China’s property market, said Zhang of The Conference Board. “The increases remain modest, though, so the evidence supports a measured recovery rather than a rapid upswing,” he said, adding that continued improvement in transaction activity, inventory absorption and land-market confidence would further consolidate the positive trend. China’s overall urban unemployment rate stood at 5.2 per cent in September, compared with 5.3 per cent in August.

title: No fuss, just dinner: China couple trade wedding extravagance for US$11,000 feast, cash gifts
description: The couple’s ‘four no’s’ wedding eliminates traditional mainstays: no bride pickup, no car fleet, no MC, and no videographer.
content: A young couple in eastern China have gone viral on social media for skipping elaborate wedding traditions and instead holding simple nuptials, spending money only on banquets and cash gifts for their guests. The bride, surnamed Zhu, is from Ningbo in Zhejiang province, while the groom, Wang, is from Taizhou, also in Zhejiang. The couple, both in their early 30s, held wedding celebrations in their respective hometowns in September, according to the Ningbo Evening News. Rather than follow extravagant wedding traditions, the couple held what they called a “four no’s” wedding. The four no’s were: no picking up the bride from her home, no fleet of luxury wedding cars, no hired master of ceremonies for the banquet, and no videographer to record the proceedings. They also had no groomsmen or bridesmaids. As a result, there was no wedding hazing – a custom in which groomsmen play pranks on the newlyweds and bridal party. But Zhu and Wang did not skimp on their wedding banquets. In Zhu’s hometown of Ningbo, they invited hundreds of guests to a banquet with 45 tables. They spent 70,000 yuan (US$11,000) on expensive seafood and other lavish dishes. In China, it is common to give guests cigarettes as wedding favours. Zhu opted to give them red envelopes containing 200 to 300 yuan each, saying she thought few of her guests smoked. Usually, the newlyweds’ parents give speeches to offer their blessings. But Zhu’s father kept his speech to just 41 seconds, thanking the guests for attending and saying he hoped they enjoyed the meal. Zhu said she and her husband were both introverted and disliked bustling scenes. They also did not want to trouble their relatives or friends. “I have attended some large weddings before. I found that the newlyweds, their parents and their guests were all tired. So I hoped to simplify my wedding,” she was quoted as saying. “If our parents became ill from the stress of organising our wedding, it would not be worthwhile,” Zhu added. Their parents initially did not accept the idea but later came around, Zhu said. She said there was no need to film the wedding because “no one would watch the video after the wedding”. However, she did value having wedding photos taken. The couple travelled to Yulong Snow Mountain, a popular tourist destination in Yunnan province, southwestern China, for the photos. “It is meaningful to me because the photos were taken at a place I like,” Zhu said. Lu, Zhu’s aunt, said after the banquet that she was surprised by the absence of traditional wedding rituals but was nevertheless pleased with the celebration. “But the banquet was wonderful. The food was the most delicious I have ever had,” Lu told the media cheerfully. The couple’s simplified wedding went viral after being shared by major domestic media outlets. Many people supported them, with one commenting: “It is a good idea. After all, at many weddings, the newlyweds seem to be acting in front of their guests.” Others disapproved. “The wedding lacked the proper celebrations. They will regret not taking their big day seriously,” one person commented.

title: After Tai Po fire, children make slow but steady recovery through play therapy
description: NGO and researchers from Hong Kong Shue Yan University provide trauma-informed interventions to 153 children across seven schools and a housing project.
