content: Almost a year after a catastrophic fire tore through Hong Kong’s Wang Fuk Court, 11-year-old Jackey* still remembers the home he lost. “I sometimes think of Wang Fuk Court and the things I left behind there,” the Primary Six pupil said. “I wanted to go back and get them, including the gifts my mum gave me.” Now living with his parents in a transitional housing flat, Jackey turns to the two calm-down bottles he made himself: transparent containers filled with water, glue and glitter. When distress builds, he shakes them and watches the glitter swirl and slowly settle. “I shake them and watch them, which makes me calm down,” he said. The psychological toll of the blaze still lingers. The psychological toll of the blaze still lingers. The fire, which broke out at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on November 26 last year, raged for 43 hours. It killed 168 people, including a firefighter, and displaced nearly 5,000 residents. Yet affected residents, including children, are finding ways to cope and rebuild their lives. Siu Ting, principal of Tai Po Baptist Public School, said pupils and their parents had made progress in their recovery, with affected families taking part in school activities. “They are actively trying to pull themselves together,” she said. Jackey, who attends the school, made the bottles during trauma intervention therapies organised by Save the Children Hong Kong for those affected by the fire. The NGO, together with a research team from Hong Kong Shue Yan University, has provided trauma-informed interventions to 153 affected children across seven Tai Po schools and Trackside Villas, a transitional housing project. These include play therapy, comprising six weekly 90-minute sessions in which staff guide pupils through games and role play to express their feelings, relieve anxiety and rebuild a sense of security. The expressive arts therapy, comprising eight weekly sessions, uses media such as drawing and percussion to help pupils identify and express emotions and improve mental resilience. Wong Shek-hung, director of the Hong Kong programme at the NGO, said some children were still recovering from the fire. They reacted to sounds of alarms or sudden noises, and struggled with painful memories. Parents, meanwhile, faced pressures from rebuilding their homes and uncertainty over their economic and housing prospects, she said. “We see that children still need time to recover,” she said. “We are not talking about three months or a single term. Some children might take five or six years.” But Wong said proper mental health support could help speed up the recovery, reduce their levels of anxiety and improve their psychological resilience. A study of 51 children who took part in play therapy and 23 who joined expressive arts therapy found that their anxiety levels fell by 85.7 per cent from a score of seven to one after play therapy. Distress caused by relocation, loss of familiar surroundings and life changes fell by 65.4 per cent from a score of 13 to 4.5. The study also found that post-traumatic stress symptoms fell by 31.1 per cent among children who underwent play therapy and by 61.2 per cent among those who underwent expressive arts therapy. Researchers said the findings showed that timely, professional mental health support could mitigate the impacts of trauma on children. “There was a significant reduction in trauma, whether through the play therapy or the expressive arts therapy – this was the area we most wanted to improve,” said Bess Lam Yin-hung, an associate professor at Hong Kong Shue Yan University’s department of counselling and psychology, who was involved in the study. To extend support to affected children, the NGO said it would continue providing the therapies while making a series of policy recommendations. These included incorporating children’s mental health recovery into the disaster response mechanism, and establishing preventive and early mental health intervention systems in schools. It also urged the government to promote a family-centred mental health support policy, increasing interventions, enhancing parent training and emotional support, developing family mental health educational tools and incorporating parent support into regular funding scopes. It further called for long-term community recovery support systems and diverse, child-friendly mental health intervention models. “What we need is the support of society as a whole, so that children can keep moving forward,” Wong said. *Name changed at interviewee’s request.

title: Zheng Qinwen’s withdrawal not a reflection on Hong Kong event, says city’s tennis boss
description: Not for the first time, one of the Prudential Hong Kong Open’s star attractions has pulled out at the last minute.
content: Zheng Qinwen’s status as a Prudential Hong Kong Open participant lasted just six days, but the city’s top tennis official does not believe her withdrawal on Sunday has damaged the tournament’s credibility. The Olympic champion had previously pulled out of the Wuhan Open, citing injury and fatigue, but said last week she was excited about the prospect of making her Hong Kong debut next month. Now, however, she has opted to end her season altogether, just weeks after making history as the first home player to win the China Open. “After these last couple of long weeks, I need to listen to my body and make sure I take the proper precautions,” Zheng said in a press release. “I had been looking forward to playing in Hong Kong for the first time, having heard so many great things about the tournament. I wish everyone a successful event this year and that I can return in 2027.” It is not the first time Hong Kong has lost big names at the last minute, with Naomi Osaka and Emma Raducanu both dropping out in recent years, but Michael Cheng Ming-git did not believe that reflected poorly on the WTA 250 event. “Shaping an event destination takes time, and Hong Kong has built a tennis brand over the last 10 years attracting top players, the depth of field for our two ATP and WTA events were arguably the strongest among all the 250s,’ said the president of the Hong Kong, China Tennis Association. “You have to look at the tennis season, and the make-up of the tennis season as a complete package, and not just focus on individual withdrawals. Zheng’s shutting down her entire season, that tells you it was a genuine medical issue.” Rather than a pattern, Cheng preferred to look at the loss of Osaka and Zheng as “isolated incidents”, and pointed to the well-known players who return year after year. In the case of the women’s tournament, Tokyo Olympic gold medallist Belinda Bencic and 2023 Hong Kong winner Leylah Fernandez are both expected to be back at Victoria Park Tennis Stadium in a fortnight. “These players keep coming back to Hong Kong, and this is how you build credibility and integrity, because they trust the tournament organisers and they trust Hong Kong,” Cheng said. Alongside Bencic and Fernandez, 2024 champion Diana Shnaider, rising Philippines star Alexandra Eala and 23-time grand slam winner Venus Williams are in a field Cheng called “one of the strongest” in the tournament’s history. Others expected to take part include China’s teen sensation Sun Xinran, who presently sits at the top of the girls’ World Tennis Junior Rankings, and won her first junior grand slam title at the US Open this summer. “There is an outstanding mix of international stars, established champions and exciting local and regional talent,” Cheng said. “Our ticketing numbers had also been improving over the years, that means our spectators are buying into the overall brand of Hong Kong tennis season, and not looking at individual players’ appearance or disappearance. “We’re not attaching the entire Hong Kong tennis season to a player or two, the return of multiple players tells you about the sustainability of the event. Getting one star player to come was a quick fix but here we are building a long-term identity, and ‘a soul’ to the Hong Kong tennis season. It’s entirely different things.”

title: Opinion | Tai Po fire: public accountability needed to honour those who died
description: If the government suppresses the independent committee’s findings on the fire over privacy concerns, it will convince no one of its commitment to accountability.
content: While celebrating the Chung Yeung Festival, we are reminded of the harvest, family reunions and the need to pay our respects to those who have departed. Spooky season is upon us, too, and Halloween is about more than just trick-or-treating. It also reminds us of the autumn harvests and those who have recently passed. The victims of the Tai Po fire – the city’s worst disaster in recent memory – are very much on our minds. The 168 lives lost and the homes ravaged as buildings burned for more than 44 hours last November shook Hong Kong to its core. The city showed a sense of community we haven’t seen in a long time. We also learned just how far our systems have fallen short in protecting Hongkongers’ lives and property. Even in the early days after the blaze, questions were raised over how the overlapping systems designed to avert disasters like the Wang Fuk Court inferno had failed. Much has been said about what role the use of non-fire-retardant materials in the renovation of the buildings played in this tragedy. The regulatory systems meant to ensure that renovation works of this scale meet safety standards failed the residents of Wang Fuk Court and the people of Hong Kong. In addition, it has emerged that the fire alarm system did not function as it should have. While arrests have been made in the disaster’s aftermath, there is much more to uncover after widespread systemic failures that span construction, property management and government oversight came to light. Beyond the substandard materials used and the disabled fire alarms, there are the regulatory loopholes and the long-standing issues of bid-rigging and industry corruption. These problems have long been known, but they keep returning to haunt us after being swept under the carpet. Smoking is now banned at construction sites, extinguishing one factor behind the fire. That was the easy part, though. Inspections and enforcing regulations are the challenge, not just setting rules. Blaming a burning cigarette butt distracts from the reality that it shouldn’t have burned the netting put up around the building, that residents should have had a greater chance to escape, and so much more. The only way to honour those who lost their lives and the families affected by this man-made disaster is to make sure the truth is laid bare and that lessons – however unpleasant – are learned. As we anticipate the independent committee’s report, the government must bear in mind that the people of Hong Kong have not forgotten. We have not forgotten Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s pledge to get to the bottom of the fire and hold people accountable for failures that were paid for by a massive loss of life. The government has already established a task force under the Public Service Commission – an independent statutory body that advises on civil service appointments and promotions – to conduct an internal investigation into the fire and pursue accountability. Once the report is received, it will get to work – at least in theory. Meanwhile, the submission of the independent committee’s report was delayed by a month, given the sheer amount of documents it had to review. It was always going to take time for the origins of problems to be identified, and responding to the committee’s findings would be a lot to ask of a government hosting a high-profile event such as this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation finance ministers’ meeting. Bad news doesn’t arrive at convenient times, however. The closer we get to the anniversary of the Tai Po blaze, the harder the government must work to regain public trust. It was distressing to hear Secretary for the Civil Service Ingrid Yeung Ho Poi-yan say recently that the government might not make the commission’s investigation report fully public over privacy and confidentiality concerns. Surely redactions, if done properly, could address those concerns. The public has a right to know what went wrong. If the government insists on using privacy concerns to hide the findings under layers of bureaucratic procedures, its commitment to accountability will be called into question. It is already clear the Tai Po disaster stemmed primarily from human factors. The inquiry’s lead counsel Victor Dawes pointed to a “litany of failures” that included an unclear division of responsibility among government departments. Layers of overlapping red tape and bureaucratic procedures contributed to the tragedy. Responding with more impenetrable processes will not inspire confidence in the government. We must honour those who died with the solemn promise to ensure a tragedy of this kind never happens again.

title: China’s investors flock to dividend stocks as returns double those of state bonds
description: Investors are pivoting from volatile tech trades to high-yield equities as low bond yields, uneven economic growth persist.
content: Chinese investors have been flocking to dividend stocks, taking shelter from market turmoil spurred by sell-offs in technology companies and K-shaped economic growth in the Asian nation. Two key gauges of the mainland-listed companies with the highest dividend yield ratios outpaced the benchmark heading into October, when fears of financial tightening in the US and China’s flagging domestic demand weighed on investors’ risk appetite. The Shanghai Stock Exchange Dividend Index of the 50 selected stocks has risen 2 per cent this month, while the CSI Dividend Index, which tracks a broader pool of 100 such stocks on the Shanghai and Shenzhen bourses, has gained 1.6 per cent. In comparison, the CSI 300 Index has fallen 4.3 per cent and the chip-centric Star Market 50 gauge has tumbled 11 per cent. The two dividend indexes offer at least a 4 per cent dividend yield, trouncing the 1.65 per cent yield on China’s 10-year government bond. The set-up has highlighted a major shift in investor sentiment, with the frantic artificial intelligence trade dominating the market for most of the year until recently. A hotter-than-estimated US inflation print has fanned speculation about interest rate increases either this month or in December, while the latest readings on China’s economic data reinforced the assessment that uneven growth may persist. “Value may outrun growth in the following one or two years,” said Chen Gang, an analyst at Soochow Securities. “Liquidity and the industry trend may have both reached the turning points. Global central banks’ easing cycles are basically over and the resilience of AI hardware is probably waning. While we reckon that the AI revolution isn’t over yet, the next leg of investments will be more difficult.” Within the universe of dividend stocks, Chen said that he preferred resource companies, which have benefited from rising energy and commodity prices, to consumer names that were grappling with a weakened labour market. Shanghai’s SSE Dividend Index was dominated by the energy and financial industries, which had a 34 per cent and 31 per cent weighting, respectively, at the end of September, according to a fact sheet. The most heavily weighted constituent was Cosco Shipping Holdings with a 5.3 per cent representation, followed by Guanghui Energy with 3.9 per cent and Shanghai Zhonggu Logistics with 3.6 per cent. The CSI dividend gauge had financial stocks as its biggest industry component, carrying a 26 per cent weighting, while energy and industrial companies ranked second and third. Its top three constituents were the same as the SSE Dividend Index. The 50 dividend stocks on the Shanghai bourse had an average dividend yield of 4 per cent, and those on the CSI gauge returned an average yield of 4.2 per cent, the fact sheets showed. The recent decline in Chinese government bond yields has also made dividend stocks more appealing, with investors chasing fixed-income products in anticipation of weak economic growth. The yield on the 10-year bond is approaching its record low of 1.6 per cent. Dividend stocks may continue to stand out, as China’s patchy economic growth leaves investors with fewer broad opportunities in the stock market. “We maintain our more cautious stance on China equities,” Morgan Stanley said in a report last week. “Stronger exports and targeted policy fine-tuning should help defend the growth floor, but subdued domestic demand and ongoing household deleveraging remain constraints on a broader earnings recovery.”

title: Hong Kong’s Apec meetings give Beijing a venue to pitch the virtues of its system
description: Analysts say interest in China’s approach bolstered by perceived ‘inadequacies’ in ability of Western doctrines to address challenges.
content: As Hong Kong hosts the Apec finance ministers’ meeting on Tuesday, this two-part series examines the summit’s significance and its implications for Beijing on the global stage. In part two, Frank Chen explores how the event could help Beijing pitch its philosophies and urge cooperation in digital infrastructure financing. China’s hosting of this year’s Apec meetings, including a finance ministers’ gathering in Hong Kong, will see a more confident Beijing seek to pitch its economic and financial governance philosophies to other countries, analysts say. That desire – and ambition – to showcase the feats and experience of the world’s second-largest economy to member nations of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum was bolstered by perceived “inadequacies” in the ability of Western doctrines to address challenges, they added. “China has evolved from a participant in global governance to a real architect … Beijing knows the delegates will spend three days in Hong Kong, and a month later leaders will be in Shenzhen. The message is in the setting: come see how this works, come see what we’ve built,” said Zak Dychtwald, founder and CEO of Young China Group, a Shanghai-founded market advisory consultancy. About 500 guests, including some finance ministers from Apec’s 21 economies, are set to congregate in Hong Kong from Monday to Wednesday. Finance Minister Lan Foan will deliver a keynote address and China will also present a policy statement on enhancing cooperation in digital infrastructure financing across the Asia-Pacific region. “When some Western governance principles are unravelling and becoming inadequate to resolve economic and financial challenges and as America retreats from its leadership role, China is proposing its visions as a solution to the complexities,” said Wang Yong, a professor at Peking University’s school of international studies. “The hope is that Chinese initiatives can become Apec consensus.” Dychtwald said China would be deft in peddling its vision. “Beijing will look to create economic dependencies and continue positioning itself as a reliable partner, which has been a successful policy amid continued unpredictability from America and Europe,” he said. One indication of China’s effort to lead this year’s discussion and how well Chinese proposals are heeded and adopted will be the finance ministers’ joint statement, the most significant outcome of the gathering. “Governments in this region are pragmatic. They’ll take the parts of China’s offer that help them and, within the constraints of maintaining a positive relationship, ignore the parts that don’t,” Dychtwald said. Beijing has set four key themes for talks between financial officials: fiscal policies supporting livelihoods, financing for digital infrastructure, inclusive finance tailored to local conditions and exchange and cooperation among young finance professionals. China’s finance ministry last week said these topics would address “both immediate priorities and longer-term considerations”. “Economies across the region now face common tasks of stabilising growth, fighting risks and safeguarding livelihoods,” said a ministry spokesperson, referring to the changes brought about by artificial intelligence. “There is an urgent need to strengthen communication and coordination on macroeconomic policies and to adopt appropriate measures to support innovation.” The spokesperson called the finance ministers’ meeting one of the most important ministerial exchanges in the Apec grouping – demonstrating the significance Beijing attaches to the Hong Kong event – as it will help “build financial-sector deliverables” for the leaders’ summit next month. Beijing also aimed to continue to champion values of a multipolar world. “China stands ready to work with all Apec economies to uphold multilateralism [and] safeguard stability and industrial supply chains for the region’s long-term, sustainable growth,” said the spokesperson. The conversation that matters most this fall is the one between Washington and Beijing Zak Dychtwald, Young China Group In a sign of Beijing’s efforts to back multilateralism and the role of international agencies, representatives from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and Asian Development Bank would present their global and regional economic and financial outlooks to Apec financial policymakers, according to the meeting agendas. On Saturday, China’s central bank governor Pan Gongsheng also said in Bangkok that Beijing supported the IMF in boosting the surveillance of fiscal risks in “major advanced economies” and their spillover effects. Meanwhile, the likely absence of the US’ top finance official might make discussions smoother and give Beijing more room to boost its influence, according to Peking University’s Wang. The South China Morning Post has reported that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent may skip Hong Kong to focus on preparations for US President Donald Trump’s visit to Shenzhen and his talk with President Xi Jinping at next month’s Apec leaders’ summit. The two countries aim to secure a more durable trade truce, which is due to expire in January. Dychtwald said the outlook for a third Trump-Xi summit this year might dominate discussions in Hong Kong. “Everyone at the finance ministers’ meeting understands that the conversation that matters most this fall is the one between Washington and Beijing, and that one is happening just across the border,” he said. Dychtwald added that Bessent’s absence could be a reminder that only one superpower was a regional partner. That said, China’s recent slowdown in gross domestic product growth, with a 4.3 per cent year-on-year rate reported in the second quarter – lower than Beijing’s full-year target of 4.5 to 5 per cent – may draw attention to some issues afflicting the Chinese economy even as Beijing touts the outlook and applicability of its approach. “China as the host may still face different voices from other countries on certain issues concerning China, like market access, subsidies, transparency, industrial policy, exports and debt, as well as insufficient consumption,” Wang said. He said the country’s bulging trade surplus, with outbound shipments rising 36.3 per cent year on year to US$447.18 billion last month, might also spark debate at the gathering. Dychtwald said other countries might seek to use Apec to gain some leverage over China. “The idea that Beijing wants continued access to export markets, and will work to protect that access, isn’t novel,” he said. “Everyone at Apec knows it. What’s interesting is whether it becomes a bargaining chip for other participants. “China’s export reliance isn’t going away due to the softness in domestic consumption. I’d expect the smart governments at Apec to use that leverage in the way they work with Beijing.”

title: Why AI can’t replace vet visits for your pet
description: Dr Angel Ngo explains why you shouldn’t rely on chatbots for animal medical advice and when the technology can be useful.
content:
Just a few years ago, pet owners would ask vets about information they found online for their pet’s symptoms. Now, “Dr Google” has turned into “Dr AI”. But can artificial intelligence (AI) replace a visit to a real vet?
While online tools are tempting, the short answer is no, though AI can be a great sidekick if used correctly.
Relying solely on AI carries real risks, such as delaying emergency care. If AI suggests that something is just a minor issue, owners might wait too long to get help, only for the pet’s condition to deteriorate.
AI also lacks a vet’s ethical judgment and ability to weigh complex decisions about an animal’s quality of life.
AI relies on the accuracy of the user’s description of an animal’s symptoms, but if you misinterpret what you see, a chatbot’s diagnosis will be completely off track.
AI also tends to agree with what users say. If an owner asks, “Could my dog’s limping just be a pulled muscle?”, the chatbot will often agree rather than warn of a bigger problem. AI can also give advice that sounds true but is factually wrong.
Even when vets try to answer an owner’s questions over the phone, it is often different from examining the animal in person. Because owners see their pets daily, it is hard for them to detect tiny changes that accumulate over time.
Animals cannot tell us whether their belly feels bloated or whether their drooling is from a sore tongue or from something bitter they licked.
Vets use hands-on examinations to assess patients, such as performing a skin tent test, checking the gums for dehydration and listening to the heart.
AI cannot feel a stomach mass that seems like a mild stomach bug. Also, a chatbot might suggest waiting out a bloated, restless dog’s pain, but a vet instantly notices the signs of a life-threatening twisted stomach that needs surgery.
Still, this does not mean you must avoid AI altogether. After a vet visit, you can use a chatbot to help explain complex medical terms to better understand your pet’s condition.
Tell the AI to find information only from reputable , vet-verified platforms, such as vet university pages or animal hospital websites. Always consult your vet before taking any action based on AI advice.

title: This elderly ‘Uncle’ spends his retirement making tiny toilet models
description: Uncle Richard used to work in home renovation. Now, the 75-year-old Singaporean has won the internet’s heart with his miniature bathrooms.
content:
In the still hours of the late night, an elderly man removes a miniature basin from its tiny mould . He sands its rough edges to perfection before spraying on a coat of paint.
Known affectionately as Uncle Richard*, this 75-year-old Singaporean has won the internet’s heart with his detailed miniature bathroom models.
Richard used to work in home renovation. But after retiring three years ago, his love for home design did not fade. The idea for the next chapter of his life came one day while he was washing his face.
“I looked at my bathroom sink and wondered how I could apply my skills to shrink it down into a tiny model,” he said.
Over the last year and a half, Richard has sold nearly 500 miniature toilet models, each for 22 Singapore dollars (HK$135).
“One is never too old to learn,” he said. “Keeping myself open-minded and staying adaptable allows me to stay connected to a changing world, even if this is just a hobby.”
Most of the people who buy from Richard are teenagers who like to decorate their spaces with the miniature bathroom models.
Each model takes about six days to build. After discarding ones that do not meet his standards, Richard produces about 30 models every month.
The sink basin takes the most time. Richard mixes plaster powder with water and presses the mixture into a mould before leaving it to dry for a day.
“There are times when a piece breaks and must be discarded, but nine out of 10 attempts are successful,” Richard said. In the meantime, he assembles the mirror, toothpaste and soap dispenser.
“If I can buy a part online, I buy it. If not, I make it by hand,” Richard explained.
Once dried, the plaster requires about an hour of processing. After assembling the final model, it is ready for pickup.
A few customers have requested miniature toilet bowls. One even asked for a replica of Singapore’s half-lion, half-fish Merlion mascot. But Richard remains focused on standard models for now while he looks for the right materials for custom builds .
“Maybe in the future, I will make a … dai pai dong model,” he said.
Developing a meaningful hobby is more important than ever today, Richard said.
“People are glued to their phones,” he said. “If you cut back on screen time, you free up space to invest in yourself and your future. You can learn so much more by observing and studying the world and people around you.”
He added, “Spending all your time staring at a screen is a waste of your youth.”
*Full name withheld at interviewee’s request.

title: Emily Xu’s top pick: ‘Keeper of the Lost Cities’ by Shannon Messenger
description: The nine-year-old from Kowloon Junior School shares what she enjoyed about the book.
content:
Do you have a book, film or television show you love? Send us your recommendations using this form .
Emily Xu An-zhi (aged 9), Kowloon Junior School
A book I would recommend is Keeper of the Lost Cities by Shannon Messenger. It is an interesting story, full of unexpected twists and the adventures of Sophie Foster.
In the book, Sophie is raised by human parents and lives a normal, happy life. Then, on a school field trip to a museum, an elf named Fitz comes in and tells Sophie that she is an elf, too. The next day, Sophie, very unwillingly, leaves her family to live with the elves, where she thinks she belongs.
But can she ever belong, having been raised in the human world? And to make matters even more special, Sophie’s real mum is not her human one. Later, she learns about a group of rebels called “The Black Swan” who have somehow tweaked her DNA, giving her special abilities.
Meanwhile, an unnamed rebel group in the first book is determined to kill Sophie. Sophie’s abilities can only protect her so much, and she is determined to learn more about her birth parents and kill the rebels who want to hurt her.

title: Letters from readers about favourite subjects, hobbies and love for music
description: This week, readers write about the animals that give them happiness, teachers that influence them and the instruments they enjoy playing.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
My favourite subject is Physical Education because there are many fun sports to play.
My hobby is drawing because it helps me relax and be creative. Since I like geography, I always draw maps and flags.
My favourite animals are cats because they are energetic and cuddly. They are mischievous pets that push stuff off shelves. Don’t feed them chocolate because theobromine and caffeine are toxic for them.
I have an elder brother, mum, dad and grandmother. My grandmother is kind because she always buys food for my brother and me.
My brother is generous; he always buys me gifts.
I love going to school, and my favourite subjects are PE, computer, maths, music and art.
I am an only child. Some of my hobbies are dancing, drawing, singing and learning to play new instruments.
My favourite teacher at school is Ms Jennifer Chan. She is very kind and helpful, and she always says positive things.
Some of my favourite things to do are spending time with my family, playing board games and watching films.
I love my family and myself the most in the whole wide world. My dad is the best at mental maths, and my mom is the best at English, spelling and grammar. I am good at both because of my parents.
Magnus Tsang (aged 14), Tuen Mun Catholic Secondary School
I love playing instruments; they bring me a sense of comfort and allow me to immerse myself completely in the music.
My love for music actually started in my childhood. Back then, I was a super energetic kid, often described as a bit of a “handful”. However, my parents noticed something remarkable: whenever music was playing, I would settle down and listen.
Learning music was a game-changer. Over the years, playing the violin has brought me great joy and achievements, and I have recently taken up the piano as well.

title: Feature of the Week: Chun Chan’s short story titled ‘Key to serenity’
description: The nine-year-old from Po Leung Kuk Camoes Tan Siu Lin Primary School writes a tale about a secret sanctuary.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
Clara tightened her grip on the old, weathered brass key. It was a secret she had protected for over two decades. The antique shop she ran in the historic heart of Sheung Wan sat quietly in the sweltering Hong Kong humidity, far from the neon buzz of the city.
For 20 years, she had meticulously catalogued rare maps and fading manuscripts on Google Books. Yet, this single key, handed to her by a mysterious traveller, unlocked nothing in her own world.
It was a physical remnant of a forgotten dimension – a place where time did not march relentlessly forward, but pooled in quiet, reflective eddies.
When the sun finally dipped below the skyline of Victoria Harbour, painting the sky in deep indigo and gold, the moment arrived.
She walked to the far corner of her shop, pressed the key into the ornate keyhole of a lacquered wardrobe, and turned it. It yielded with a deep, resonant click.
Instead of dusty linens and mothballs, a rush of crisp, pine-scented mountain air spilled into the cramped room.
Clara stepped through the door, leaving the chaotic hum of the metropolis behind. She emerged in an alpine meadow blanketed in starlight.
There, time stood completely still. She inhaled deeply, listening to the absolute silence of a world untouched by human history.
Here, she was neither ageing nor tired. She could finally sit by the tranquil, glasslike lake and read the original manuscripts she loved on Project Gutenberg without rushing back to the morning’s shipping invoices.
It was her sanctuary – a fragile, secret haven between the pages of reality, accessible only when the bustling world went to sleep.

title: Advice: My divorced parents have remarried other people and I don’t know where I fit in
description: On this page, you’ll find advice from our team of psychologists to help you through all the ups and downs of life.
content:
Seeing your parents split up and find new families can be stressful, especially if it feels like you are stuck in the middle. It is natural to feel sad, angry and worried.
Your parents’ relationships have changed. But their new marriages do not erase their roles as your parents. You still share your past experiences – and the chance to make more memories in the future.
Talk to your parents about your feelings. Then, find new ways to spend time together.
What do you enjoy doing with your parents? You might not do them with both parents, and you might see them less often. Still, make plans with them to continue these activities.
You can also try spending time with their new partners and families. You do not have to pretend that everything is perfect. But being polite and asking them questions can make things easier. Everyone can get to know each other over time.
If you feel worried, talk to your parents about how to make these meetings more comfortable for you. You can do an activity that you all enjoy. Or keep the meetings short until you feel better.
Your parents’ divorce might affect your self-esteem. It can feel like you are alone. But other people have experienced something similar, even if the details are different.
Family counsellors are trained to handle situations like this. Support is there, whether you confide in a friend, parent or school counsellor.
This question was answered by clinical psychologists from Shall We Talk, a mental health initiative under the Department of Health launched with the Advisory Committee on Mental Health

title: Kai Tak chiefs should target NFL, monster trucks, says stadium designer
description: Company responsible for designing city’s newest sports park also takes charge of staging American football events around the world.
content: Kai Tak Sports Park would provide an “amazing venue” for a regular-season NFL game, according to one of the masterminds behind the HK$30 billion sporting complex. What began as a novelty initiative when the NFL first staged a game outside the United States, in Mexico 21 years ago, has grown into a global phenomenon. Ten international fixtures are planned for next season, up from nine this year. Roger Goodell, the NFL commissioner, recently raised the prospect of Japan becoming the league’s debut Asian hosts, after Australia welcomed a match for the first time last month. Populous, the company responsible for Kai Tak’s design, oversees all of the NFL’s foreign games. They have been in charge of managing the Super Bowl’s stadium facilities and operations for the past 41 years. The NFL did not want to comment on whether the 50,000-capacity Kai Tak Stadium would be a good fit for its product, but James Pearce, Populous’ senior principal and senior architect, said: “We’ve squeezed NFL into a fair few different places, and I’m sure Kai Tak would be an amazing venue. “The NFL has its plan, and it’ll do what’s needed to find the right places for it in the future, but I’m confident that Kai Tak’s scale, and the way we’ve created the venue, offers some pretty exciting opportunities.” An American Express study estimated that London would receive a £90 million (US$120 million) economic boost from the three NFL games the English capital is staging this month. One of the biggest challenges for hosts, according to Pearce, is the need to provide adequate room for the “60 to 90 people” who comprise each franchise’s player and support staff. Crafted with a heavy focus on hosting elite rugby sevens, Kai Tak’s 20 changing rooms go some way to addressing that problem, while ample clear ground around the arena would allow organisers to hurdle security obstacles. “[NFL] have a full airport level of screening, and magnetometers, about 100 meters from the venue,” Pearce said, adding that Populous “made that work” at Melbourne Cricket Ground, where San Francisco 49ers beat Los Angeles Rams 27-7 in front of 100,021 fans five weeks ago, despite the stadium’s perimeter not being set up for it. “Kai Tak has the ability to fit all of that around the precinct,” Pearce said. “All of those challenges were accounted for in its design.” The usually isolated nature of games in distant territories has also required “some of the biggest temporary merchandise areas [Populous has] constructed”. “Everybody wants to get something, so that provides different challenges, but that’s the excitement of having one-off moments,” Pearce said. Described by Liverpool’s chief commercial officer, Ben Latty, as the “game changer” that convinced his club to visit Hong Kong in 2025 following an eight-year absence, Kai Tak has attracted 10 elite European football clubs, staged sold-out city team matches, and two editions of the Cathay/HSBC Hong Kong Sevens since its March 2025 opening. Global fencing and snooker tournaments have visited Kai Tak Arena, while its Youth Sports Ground has lured international rugby. Pearce has equally drawn satisfaction from seeing the complex quickly evolve into an every day hub where “community sport is happening, people are rock climbing, playing basketball or taking their kids to the playground”. “Seeing people using it is very cool,” he said, but the Australian believes the venue has the potential to host lots of different events. Thinking laterally, Pearce believes there is scope for Kai Tak to lay on the types of competitions “when stadiums manage something you would never expect”. “I’ve seen fields filled with water, so they can stage boat shows,” he said. “You could put on monster trucks. “I’m interested in the events that catch us off guard, like when drone racing potentially becomes massive, and people are in the stands with things flying around them. There are always occasions that you didn’t know venues would be capable of staging until you see them in the flesh.” Still, Pearce, whose firm specialises in supplying the overlay for major occasions, said Kai Tak Stadium would allow Hong Kong to chase more conventional, big-ticket spectacles. “There’s talk of Asian, Olympic or Paralympic Games,” he said, acknowledging that Hong Kong would have to co-host any multi-sports events with its neighbours in Guangdong and Macau, as it did with last year’s National Games. “Kai Tak [Stadium] was designed around a rectangular field of play, so it’s not conducive to athletics or cricket,” he said. “But that was a conscious decision, because it creates an intense environment. It’s also how you generate an awesome live music atmosphere.” Citing the example of another Populous project, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, accommodating marquee boxing bouts, Pearce said Hong Kong had the ability to follow suit. “Being able to quickly take out the turf gives you so much flexibility,” he added. “Once you have that concrete pad, it opens up a whole world of possibilities. “Tottenham has no roof, but still it gets huge crowds for boxing. We have an acoustically sealed, closing roof, and an air-conditioned arena. What you can do with it is phenomenal.” Locally, Pearce said allowing the Standard Chartered Hong Kong Marathon to finish in the area had been among the “very robust brief” provided by Kai Tak chiefs. “I lived in Hong Kong for four years [during the Kai Tak build], and I’ve had more people want to visit since I left than I had when I was there,” Pearce said. “Because of Kai Tak, the city’s constantly on the world stage. We’ve got something pretty special here, and it stands out.”

title: India needs more fighter jets. It cannot build them fast enough
description: Delayed engines and assembly bottlenecks leave India’s domestic output falling behind the pace of fleet retirements.
content: India has a soaring ambition to modernise its air force, built around a fleet of domestically developed fighter jets. Yet production of these aircraft has been hampered by engine delays and other bottlenecks that defence analysts say could limit its ability to fight future air wars. On October 11 at an airbase in Jodhpur, Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh strapped into a Tejas jet for the last time. It was his final fighter sortie before retiring later this month and he flew it in an Indian-built jet to show support for the country’s domestic defence industry. A week earlier, he had warned that the Indian Air Force (IAF) faced a critical shortage of fighter squadrons. “We need to induct two fighter squadrons every year,” Singh said on October 3, noting that “between 36 and 40 aircraft” would need to be produced annually to meet India’s target of having 42 fighter squadrons in service. “Actually, we need even more than that,” he said. The Tejas programme, which dates back to the 1980s, has become emblematic of India’s drive to build up its domestic defence industry. A Mark 1A variant of the light combat aircraft was unveiled last year and a Mark 2 is still under development. Induction of the Mark 1A is only now about to begin, 2½ years late, after the F404 engines needed from US manufacturer GE Aerospace arrived late and the various radar, weapons and software systems took longer to integrate than planned. Vice-Chief of the Air Staff Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit said in late September that induction was expected to begin within one or two months, following a protracted development cycle and exhaustive operational evaluations of the aircraft’s avionics suite. GE Aerospace, the Tejas programme’s only engine supplier, recently stepped up deliveries to principal manufacturer Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), shipping three F404-IN20 engines in August and another four engines in September. That makes 14 engines delivered so far, against the 20 that are due to arrive by the end of this year. State-run HAL aims to produce 24 Tejas fighters annually. The IAF has already ordered 83 Mark 1As, wants to add 97 more and is also actively considering the Mark 2 variant. Projections indicate at least 350 – and potentially more than 400 – Tejas will eventually be built, with the aircraft expected to form the backbone of India’s air force in future. However, “repeated delays in certification, weapons/radar integration and engine supply show that indigenisation still needs execution, not just policy”, said Gurcharan Singh Bedi, a retired IAF air marshal. “Having acquired the capability to produce the aircraft, we are then just talking of scale, which can be boosted. But it will take a very strong focus by the government and a very hard commitment by HAL or whosoever produces these aircraft.” Fleet depletion India’s air force badly needs replacements for the ageing aircraft that are leaving active service. The IAF officially retired the last of its Cold War-era Soviet-designed MiG-21 jets in September last year – 36 in total – with another six squadrons of Anglo-French Sepecat Jaguar ground-attack fighters due to be phased out between 2028 and 2031. To keep the remainder of its Jaguar fleet flying, India is buying nine of the aircraft that Britain’s Royal Air Force retired in 2007 to use for spare parts. Three MiG-29 squadrons and three squadrons of the French-designed Mirage 2000 are set to also be retired through the mid-to-late 2030s. Each IAF squadron contains about 18 active aircraft, plus three or four in reserve. Bedi agreed with outgoing air force chief Singh’s assessment that roughly two new squadrons per year would be needed simply to maintain the number of aircraft India had in service. HAL’s target of 24 Tejas fighters a year would fall short of that goal, but a second programme could help close the gap, he said. In February, India cleared the purchase of 114 Rafales from France, under a government-to-government deal as part of its Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft programme. Taken together, Bedi said this would bring annual deliveries close to the 32 or 36 aircraft required. Final talks on price and production arrangements for the Rafales are still pending, though local media reports indicate manufacturer Dassault Aviation has agreed to 50-60 per cent “Make in India” content for the aircraft, as well as technology transfers and the integration of Indian weapons and systems. Bedi said a “genuine acceleration” of India’s fighter jet production would depend on HAL meeting or beating its target of 24 combat aircraft per year, the timely delivery of multi-role fighters from France and retirements not outpacing inductions. “The chief has spelled out the requirement, but it’s difficult to meet in the near future,” he said of Singh’s assessment. “At the same time, I believe anything is possible.” ‘The real constraint’ Several new aircraft are on the way. The first flight of the Tejas Mark 2 is expected between June and September 2027, with initial induction planned for 2030-31 if development stays on track. India also wants to have a prototype of its fifth-generation stealth fighter, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), airborne for a test flight by September 2028. Bids to develop and produce the AMCA prototype have come in from India’s Tata Advanced Systems and domestic consortiums led by Larsen & Toubro and Bharat Forge, while France’s Safran is competing with a partnership formed by India’s Reliance and Britain’s Rolls-Royce to supply AMCA’s engine. Sanjay Iyer, a retired Indian Army brigadier, said these overlapping programmes were likely to hit another bottleneck: the fact that they had to draw from the same pool of test pilots, certification staff and integration engineers. “That is the real constraint, not shop-floor space,” he said. “And even if every Tejas [production] line ran flat out, you would still fall short of 36 to 40 a year.” Iyer argued that India’s aircraft production problems could best be tackled through increased domestic engine manufacturing, design discipline and boosting private industry’s role. Much time was lost on the Mark 1A’s development because of design changes, he said, adding that private companies – some of which already made fuselages and wings for HAL – should also be allowed to assemble aircraft. “As long as one American supplier decides when your fighters fly, your output figures are really their output figures,” Iyer said regarding the Tejas’ GE engine. “And geopolitical considerations matter too. The US is not beyond twisting India’s arm if its other interests are affected.” Holding buffer stocks of engines could serve as a costly stopgap solution, he added, further calling the opening of AMCA development and manufacturing to domestic private industry a “good sign”.

title: Swarms of Bogong moths in Australia show hope for the endangered species
description: These insects are harmless to humans, but they are key to Australia’s ecosystem.
content:
Swarms of moths blanketing homes in Australia’s southeast earlier this month show that the endangered species is recovering, authorities said.
Bogong moths, with a wingspan of up to 5cm, have experienced years of steep population decline. But they have had a comeback this year.
“The Bogongs are terrific for our ecosystem, ‌supporting our treasured native wildlife like the pygmy-possum and pollinating our eucalyptus trees,” said Steve Whan, ‌who represents the Monaro region in the New South Wales parliament.
According to authorities, the population of the moths, which are harmless to humans and legally protected, have fallen due to drought, ‌agricultural intensification and habitat ‌loss.
One theory for the rebound is that more rainfall makes extra food for the insects’ larvae.

title: TV showman Robert Chua spells out his vision for his vast collection of Chinese antiquities
description: One of Hong Kong’s most influential television broadcasters is also one of the city’s most enthusiastic collectors. PostMag goes on a tour of Robert Chua’s ‘home museum’ to find out how he plans to turn a lifetime of accumulated objects into his next production.
content: Robert Chua Wah-peng does not have the air of a stereotypical collector. He does not demand of you the donning of cotton gloves or scrubbing of fingernails before touching his Chinese antiquities; he excitedly invites you to pick up vases and vessels with your bare hands; he encourages you to engage with his acquisitions up close. Most of them are not sequestered away behind glass or acrylic. He also does not have an exact number for how large his collection is. “Could be hundreds of thousands of pieces,” he muses when asked. Originally from Singapore, Chua began collecting in 1967 – the year he arrived in Hong Kong – but it was not until his first visit to mainland China, in 1979, that he got serious about his hobby. He became a regular presence at the antiques dealers’ shops on Hong Kong’s Hollywood Road, sweeping through new shipments twice a week for decades, like clockwork, buying entire lots – everything from late-Qing ceramics bearing illustrated foo dogs in bright orange and terracotta “stickmen” from the Han period to wooden mooncake moulds and snuff bottles. In his home in Kowloon, he has a room dedicated to blue-and-white porcelain from the Ming and Qing dynasties to the Republic era, rows of Chinese wedding cabinets heaving with tableware, wardrobes bursting with vibrant stoneware and jars, a corridor with more than 180 horse sculptures, shelves groaning beneath fossilised dinosaur eggs and Neolithic pottery, and drawers holding delicate jade accessories and brass buttons. Neolithic, Warring States, Han, Sui, Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming, Qing – Chua’s collection reads like a chronicle. Inching along narrow pathways cleared between stacks for necessity’s sake, he is talking a mile a minute, propelled by obvious fervour, sharing historical facts, stories about how he obtained an artefact, the technique used to make it. Chua is an oddity among his peers in the collecting community in that his incentive to collect really isn’t that deep. “Honestly, I don’t know,” he shrugs. “I just love beautiful things. Never do I buy anything and at any moment say, ‘I bought this for HK$1,000. One day, maybe it will fetch me HK$5,000.’ Never. I buy for the beauty. And if I see something that is lovely, I’ll buy 30 of them, to share with people.” Among Chua’s extensive accumulation, one theme stands out, not only in quantity but also in peculiarity: his collection of ancient Chinese mingqi – “spirit objects”, traditionally placed in tombs as funerary items to comfort the deceased in the afterlife. As far as the eye can see, there are small-scale models of dwellings, animals, furniture and carriages, as well as figures of guardians and attendants. For visitors familiar with Chinese customs, it might come as a shock to see Chua living among mingqi. Despite their exquisite craftsmanship and three-colour sancai glaze, keeping burial goods intended for the dead in one’s home is thought to invite misfortune and disruptive yin energy into the household. Chua is aware of the taboo, but it doesn’t faze him. “I am a bit Western in that sense,” he says. “Western collectors don’t mind antiques like these, but Chinese collectors are too superstitious to want them, so that made it easier for me to acquire them; the demand was lower and they were not difficult to source. I have thousands of happy spirits at home. I’m not worried about anything – there’s so much company. It’s always a party Robert Chua “But I’m happy. I have thousands of happy spirits at home. I’m not worried about anything – there’s so much company. It’s always a party,” he laughs. Indeed, Chua has a penchant for entertaining and hosting. His calendar is ordinarily filled with visits, events, meetings, lunches and dinners, both personal and professional. He likes to receive guests in the sunroom. He has a talent for driving conversations, and his candour and quick wit work in tandem to put people at ease. To understand and appreciate Chua’s gravitational pull towards people and telling stories, taking a gander at his own history pulls back the curtains. Chua, 80, made his name in television broadcasting. His first job, as a property assistant at ADS Channel 7 in Adelaide, Australia, in 1964, sparked an enduring fascination with the industry. After rotating through several positions at the Australian network, he returned to Singapore two years later, to produce for Radio Television Singapore, gaining experience in light entertainment. It wouldn’t be long before another door opened for Chua: he was offered the role of senior production executive at Hong Kong’s TVB in 1967, to help set up its first colour-television station. At just 21 years old, he created Enjoy Yourself Tonight, which became the city’s longest-running live variety programme, airing more than 6,610 episodes between 1967 and 1994 on the TVB Jade channel. Colin Bednall, the then-general manager of TVB, “trusted me to do the job. Had I failed, he would have lost his job for sure. But luckily, everything went so well. I am grateful to him”, Chua says of the opportunity extended to him despite his age. As someone who avowedly attributes his life’s trajectory to an improbable series of events and a chain of people betting on him against all odds, Chua has held up his end of the bargain to deliver on those instincts and that faith in his potential. Enjoy Yourself Tonight garnered him acclaim, promotions and opportunities. Chua rose through the ranks to serve as the special assistant to the managing director and also brought the Miss Hong Kong Pageant to the local network in 1973, before leaving TVB to start his own production house. Back then, freelance television facilities were few and far between, due to the high upfront costs of launching one. Coupled with its founder’s established reputation, Robert Chua Production House (RCP) readily landed work with broadcasters, agencies and corporate clients to do commercials, shows, documentaries and the like. Chua expanded his business to the mainland in 1979, brokering deals on behalf of foreign advertisers looking to gain a foothold in the market. Over a decades-long career in television, Chua put his mark on numerous other ventures, but his success and tenacious pursuit of achieving “firsts” did not come without challenges. In March 1995, after more than three months of experimental screenings, his Chinese-language China Entertainment Television Broadcast (CETV) channel began airing around Asia, showing original productions, films, soap operas, children’s series and more through 24 hours of daily programming. CETV reached millions of households across the region over the 21 years it was in operation, but it also proved to be one of the most difficult periods of Chua’s life. Already burdened by the stress of keeping the station financially afloat, in January 1999, he suffered from a build-up of excess blood fluid in his brain, which required urgent surgery. While recuperating at home – his first time off since his marriage, in 1974, to his former assistant at TVB, Peggy Jen Ping-ping – and spending more time among his collection, by then already formidable, Chua began to view his antiques in a different light. Damaged and incomplete pieces caught his attention in particular, planting a seed for a new artistic vision: to flip the script on the notion that, in their marred condition, these objects were useless or to be discarded, and revive them through novel methods. The resulting “Antique Arts” is part of Chua’s mission to find new meaning for his pieces. “An antique does not lose its soul because it is broken,” he explains, and neither should they be valued only for what they once were. A shattered vessel or a shard of porcelain is not just “a remnant of the past. It is a survivor. It carries memory, human touch, craftsmanship, cultural identity and the passage of time”. Rather than restoring them to their original state, Chua believes that transforming them into new artworks allows them to keep existing through a modern narrative. Combining periods, dynasties, shapes, textures, mediums and contexts, his “Antique Arts” tell a fresh story, simultaneously embodying a metaphor for Chua’s own journey of recovery. (He would go on to have a second brain surgery, in 2008, informing his decision to take a step back from his company.) Where collectors, dealers and auction houses see broken antiquities as defective, Chua thinks of them as a continuation. “Antique Arts” is his attempt to symbolically collaborate with the “many hands” of bygone makers, resulting in a creative dialogue across time. A Song dynasty pot fragment is paired with Neolithic earthenware to depict the pouring of tea, bridging thousands of years; the remaining handle of an ancient jug is juxtaposed with a modern ink painting to “complete the gaps” of the one-time vessel, leading to an abstract installation. Chua’s personal relationship with the material feeds into his creation process, too. Anonymous objects they are not. He has lived with them, studied them and cared for them across decades, forming an intimate connection with the pieces. From a slim case, he pulls out slender sticks of ivory, their tips wrapped in thread, ending in thin brushes of fine hair. Qiancao – cricket ticklers – are tools used in cricket combat, to goad the insects into fighting each other for sport. “When I have an antique, like this one, I wonder who it belonged to. I imagine what their lives were like. Everything I look at, everything I touch, I feel someone in my mind – the people who used these objects, these pieces that lived in their homes. Frankly, that’s better to me than something that’s brand-new.” He continues, “How much is the value of a piece? It’s not so much about the actual monetary value, but how much it really means to you. ‘Expensive’ is in the mind of the person. “For most collectors, when something breaks, it’s gone forever. But for me, if something breaks somehow, my consolation is that I can give it a new life. What I have, what’s broken, I try to put them together anyway. I never break anything on purpose. Sometimes, it just happens. But I wait for the right moment. I find the right pieces that will come together, and if they don’t, I won’t rush it.” As he left broadcasting behind, the “right pieces” ended up falling into place, anyway. Chua’s affinity for entertainment, connecting with an audience and shaping narratives continued to find ways to manifest through different avenues. In 2013, Chua followed his entrepreneurial nose and snapped up the Asia-Pacific franchising rights to Tim Ho Wan, often hailed as the cheapest Michelin-star restaurant in the world, launching it in Singapore with his brother, Harry Chua Wah-eng. He credits “luck and fate” as the reason for their winning bid – at the time, neither sibling had any experience in the food and beverage industry to speak of – but it was, once again, trust that paved the way to the next chapter. “At TVB, [Bednall] shouldn’t have given me Enjoy Yourself Tonight, and likewise with Tim Ho Wan, they shouldn’t have given it to me with all the food and beverage professionals out there, but they did,” he told the South China Morning Post in 2024. Tim Ho Wan co-founder Mak Kwai-pui was a fan of Enjoy Yourself Tonight, and Chua’s unconventional thinking – unhampered by orthodox restaurant strategies – allowed him to be bold and brave. When Tim Ho Wan arrived in Singapore, Chua positioned the brand as an elevated dining experience, growing its footprint to more than 40 outposts. Kam’s Roast (known in Hong Kong as Kam’s Roast Goose) followed in 2016. “Entertainment and food are the same to me,” he explains. “It’s a people’s business. I look at food as my programmes and I look at my chef as my director.” Four years later, he founded Joy Luck Teahouse, a chain of food kiosks specialising in Hong Kong-style cha chaan teng snacks, and in 2021, he launched Sinstant, a gourmet line of ready-to-eat and -cook Asian meals designed for home consumption. At 80, most people would slow down. But Chua, being the “ideas guy”, has not stopped thinking about the future. As he considers his collection, and the richness it holds, there is but one thing left to do with it: share it with the world. He has laid out the blueprint for his vision, combining his passion for food and Chinese antiques: an all-day restaurant-cum-museum, where the cuisine echoes a rotating curation of pieces from his personal Aladdin’s cave. Imagined as a “cultural-dining landmark”, Treasure of China is designed as an immersive destination to close the distance between heritage, gastronomy and storytelling. Guests will indulge in refined dishes, surrounded by centuries-old artefacts, with restaurant staff providing the backgrounds behind each object to engage visitors. “Many restaurants, hotels and clubs have their own collection, but the art is just part of the furniture. It’s not interactive. It’s not engaging. It doesn’t change,” says Chua. “Here, the artwork is part of the meal. Whatever you see and touch has a story.” Chinese history and culture shape each pillar of the museum-restaurant, down to the beverage programme, which will exclusively feature Chinese wines, baijiu, huangjiu and teas. Chua’s “Antique Arts” creations are also planned to be part of the display, and select works – both ancient and “new” – will be made available for purchase, with a percentage of the proceeds donated to charities. Regional Chinese flavours, ranging from Cantonese and Sichuan to Jiangsu, Fujian and more, will make up the concept’s culinary foundations. But something that is, perhaps, unexpected is that Chua intends to place the experience in the “affordable premium” bracket, offering Michelin-level dining at accessible prices, making good on his ambition to embrace and give back to the wider community. “Bringing art to a greater audience and developing a concept that not only preserves history, but presents it as a new experience that people can engage with, breaks down barriers,” says Chua. “Antiques are precious because they are records of history, but that doesn’t mean you can’t engage with them on an interpersonal level, because that’s what really creates a connection for people to appreciate them.” With more than 200 seats envisioned in the estimated 7,000 sq ft floor plan, interactive elements – such as hands-on “touchable history” encounters to hold fossilised dinosaur eggs – and aesthetic spatial design engineered for the social-media generation, Chua plans to appeal to residents and tourists alike. Treasure of China feels like a natural next step for Chua, whose joy in amassing antiques is matched only by the unadulterated delight he expresses when sharing their stories. On our tour of his “home museum”, through rows of gleaming porcelain and stoic figurines, it is his enthusiasm that leaves the biggest impression. But this project is not Chua’s alone to bring to fruition. Adviser Jacco Klip, a Dutch F&B professional with nearly 40 years of experience in opening and managing restaurants, provides guidance on the charitable arm of the business. Meanwhile, Choi Biu, a veteran of Hong Kong’s dining scene and long-time member of the Shun Tak Fraternal Association and local Shunde community, and Lawrence Chong, a property-development consultant who has held positions at Sino Land and Galaxy Entertainment Group, serve as co-founder and special adviser to Chua, respectively. Chua’s concept is still in its early stages, and there’s a lot of work ahead. His collection needs to be catalogued, the search for a suitable venue is ongoing and most of the items he owns hold taboo connotations within Chinese cultural norms, raising questions about how guests will perceive the curated works and whether superstitions around their provenance will win out against curiosity. Not to mention, there are like-minded backers to find and convince. None of these hurdles seem to be stopping the lifelong pioneer from forging ahead to secure interest and investors in Treasure of China. He has already mapped out a multi-stream revenue model, which includes brand collaborations, merchandising and licensing – a “gastro-tainment” approach, so to speak. “We’re looking for people with passion,” Chua says. “When I do any business, profit is not my No 1 priority. You must make sure you do a good job. If you think profit comes first, you’ll never be successful, because you’re trying to compromise. I want the partners to feel proud of how they are contributing to society.” Whether the museum-restaurant sets its roots down in Hong Kong or Macau is still to be determined, but Chua believes that the objective of his cultural destination – to entertain, educate and connect – aligns with either city’s broader tourism goals. “Over the years, I have always believed in creating ‘firsts’ that change how people think and experience things” Robert Chua Whatever shape his new project takes, Chua’s mission has not changed. From “Antique Arts” to Treasure of China, giving the pieces in his collection a new voice remains central to his pursuits, as a poignant reminder that history can be palpably felt, reimagined and revived. “Over the years, I have always believed in creating ‘firsts’ that change how people think and experience things,” he says. “With art, if it’s something you like, you enjoy, you appreciate, it doesn’t have to be that profound, right? I look at these objects, and some of them look so rough. But to me, they are beautiful because they hold so many stories and years of life.”

title: Cry for help as French-Swiss lake dries up after record-breaking heatwaves
description: Drought, as well as geological fissures, have caused the Lac des Brenets to dry up, with weeds growing on the exposed lake bed.
content:
The Lac des Brenets between France and Switzerland has dried up after a record-breaking hot summer. Locals are asking for help to save the lake.
They have scratched the words “HELP” and “SOS” in the weeds on the exposed lake bed.
The drought has ruined boat tourism, and some question whether the lake will ever return to enduring full health.
“It’s utter despair: no more lake,” said 76-year-old David Favre, who lives in the Swiss village of Les Brenets.
The lake has dried up due to a mix of factors, including geological fissures that drain water underground, below-average rainfall and repeated heatwaves. The months of June, July and August were each the hottest ever recorded in Switzerland since measurements began in 1864.
A task force was set up by French and Swiss authorities in 2022 to explore ways of limiting the water draining into the fissures, but it has not resulted in decisive action.

title: CXMT shares fall 7.8% despite blockbuster earnings figures
description: The firm also forecasts a 742 per cent revenue surge year on year.
content: Chinese memory chip giant ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) saw its shares fall more than 8 per cent in early Monday trading, despite forecasts of strong profits and plans for a share buy-back amid a global sector-wide market rout. CXMT shares dropped 7.8 per cent on Monday to close at 41.52 yuan. The company’s stock surged to a peak of 61.8 yuan in August – up as much as 614 per cent from its initial public offering price of 8.66 yuan in July – before paring back gains. The market reaction came after the company forecast a record net income of up to US$19.8 billion for the first nine months of 2026, as the domestic chip champion cashed in on artificial intelligence-driven demand and mounted an aggressive challenge to global rivals including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. “The crowded trade in technology stocks is unwinding, and declines in overseas memory stocks are adding to the pressure,” said a technology-focused fund manager who requested anonymity. “Lower quarterly profit margins are also a factor, but the main issue is how investors are positioned.” He said he had moved money from the tech sector into listed banks such as the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China. Meanwhile, Zhu Yiming, chairman of the Hefei-based memory giant, proposed to buy back 1 billion yuan (US$149.56 million) to 2 billion yuan in shares over 12 months, pending board or shareholder approval, to fund employee incentive plans or reduce registered capital. CXMT projected the preliminary net income to range between 131 billion yuan and 132.5 billion yuan from January to September, compared with a net loss of 5.3 billion yuan in the same period last year, according to a stock exchange disclosure on Friday. Its revenue in the period was expected to reach 265 billion to 270 billion yuan, marking a 742 per cent surge compared with the 32 billion yuan at the same time last year. Significant correction in the memory players’ share prices could imply that the market may have underestimated both the capacity ramp-up and potential for technology breakthrough from China Goldman Sachs That implies a third-quarter net income of 53.4 billion to 54.9 billion yuan, following its 77.6 billion yuan net income recorded in the first half of 2026. Sales in the third quarter could come in at between 114.7 billion and 119.7 billion yuan, posting a surge of up to 620 per cent compared to the same period last year. The massive surge in preliminary sales and profit was fuelled by surging demand for AI computing power since the second half of 2025 which resulted in a supply shortage and sharp price increases in the global dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) industry, CXMT said in the document filed with the Shanghai Stock Exchange. “The company has been steadily advancing its capacity expansion, product research and development, and process technology improvement, which further boosted per-wafer output and capacity utilisation,” CXMT said. “The company’s economies of scale have continued to materialise.” CXMT’s blockbuster earnings come as the Chinese chip giant is under the global spotlight after revealing key progress on a new type of cell architecture to boost memory density. The company announced last week a plan to roll out a new server-memory product based on the “4F square” design, which enabled higher storage density by fitting more cells onto a single chip. The plan posed new challenges to global competitors, including Samsung and SK Hynix, which are all pursuing similar technology. CXMT said it expected to release a new generation of DDR5 enterprise-grade server memory incorporating the advanced technology by the end of the year. Amid intensifying competition from China and broader market headwinds, a sector-wide market rout has hit global memory suppliers including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, Micron Technology, SanDisk, Kioxia and CXMT in the past week, erasing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value from the industry leaders in total. “The recent significant correction in the memory players’ share prices could imply that the market may have underestimated both the capacity ramp-up and potential for technology breakthrough from China,” Goldman Sachs analysts led by Giuni Lee wrote in a research note on Friday. However, Lee noted that the market may have overestimated China’s memory advancements, given “the considerable time it would take to complete customer qualifications and then achieve mass production at high yield levels, as well as narrow the gap in advanced DRAM technology such as high bandwidth memory”.

title: Beijing park’s holiday caterpillar hunt targets an invasive ‘monster’
description: Native to North America, fall webworm larvae can damage more than 300 plant species.
content:
For most families, China’s “Golden Week” holiday is a time to relax, eat well and visit the country’s tourist hotspots.
But at the Beijing Wildlife Park, some people spent their holiday hunting for fall webworm larvae. This is an invasive species ‌of caterpillar. The park has called it “the forest food monster”.
The park asked visitors to catch as many of the caterpillars as possible. Those with the heaviest haul were rewarded with prizes, including as many as 10 park tickets.
The caterpillar, native to North America, can damage more than 300 plant species, including crops and fruit trees.
After a crash ‌course on how to spot the larvae, participants spread out across the nearly 550-acre (223-hectare) park with disposable gloves, plastic containers ‌and chopsticks.
“Call for warriors! Battle the ‘forest food monster’ and win grand prizes!” read a poster behind a table stacked with containers of caterpillars.
As of October 5, more than 310,000 caterpillars ‌with a combined weight of 47.65kg were caught by some 2,077 people since the ‌competition ‌began on September 28.

title: Editorial | As Ocean Park weathers stormy seas, nostalgia can’t be its lifeline
description: Hongkongers hold the park, which marks its 50th anniversary, in great affection, but it needs to have a distinctive offering to survive the challenging new environment.
content: Ocean Park has a special place in Hongkongers’ hearts. For half a century, the beloved theme park has been as much a leading conservation and education institution as an old friend. Yet it is struggling like an endangered species amid the mantra of survival of the fittest. As it marks its 50th anniversary with new facilities and celebrations, opportunities and challenges abound. In store for the golden jubilee are a revamped panda pavilion and a new marine mammal conservation centre featuring the complete skeleton of a Bryde’s whale found stranded in Sai Kung in 2023. In support of local creative industries, the park will bring together more than 50 original intellectual properties, including McDull, B.Duck and its own Panda Friends to meet visitors. The public can also submit old photos, video clips and written stories of park visits, which may be used for anniversary promotions. For generations of Hongkongers, Ocean Park is not merely a place to ride a roller coaster or watch dolphins. From school outings, family weekends and first dates to birthday celebrations and childhood encounters with animals, visits to the park have become part of the city’s collective memory. The park’s conservation and education work, albeit not as popularised as its shows and attractions, has also cemented the institution’s reputation as one of the best in the world. Through its anniversary celebrations, with the theme “growing with nature”, the park is seeking to capitalise on its emotional standing in local life and success in conservation for future development. Yet in the increasingly competitive world of entertainment and tourism, nostalgia is not an asset that readily translates into revenue and fiscal sustainability. The decades-old park secured a lifeline after the legislature approved scaled-down government funding earlier. Long-term survival remains uncertain. There are grounds for cautious optimism. In 2024-25, combined attendance at Ocean Park and Water World rose 10 per cent year on year to 3.46 million, the fourth consecutive year of visitor growth. Local visitors increased 9 per cent to 2.21 million, while non-local visitors rose 12 per cent to 1.25 million. Revenue climbed 9 per cent to HK$1.29 billion, with in-park spending up 35 per cent and merchandising income up 20 per cent. Aided by government conservation funding, the park recorded an operating surplus of HK$42.4 million (US$5.4 million). The arrival of four giant pandas – two born in Hong Kong and two gifted by the mainland – has helped. The bears have given families, tourists and panda enthusiasts a fresh reason to visit the park while also reinforcing its identity as a conservation and education institution. The new panda pavilion, expected to open in 2027, should build on that momentum by offering better habitats and closer public engagement with animal care. But the financial picture remains troubling. Despite higher attendance and revenue, Ocean Park’s deficit widened to HK$274.7 million in the year to June 30, 2025, from HK$71.6 million previously. This reflects higher depreciation and other expenses, as well as continuing losses at Water World, which recorded an operating deficit of HK$148.3 million. The park is far from a self-sustaining venture; some have even called it a failed business unworthy of further taxpayers’ money. Like many revenue-dependent operating facilities struggling to adapt to a changing market, Ocean Park is still weathering stormy seas after gaining some breathing space with the government’s bailout. The resources have helped stabilise operations, renew facilities and test new ideas. But with tourist arrivals to the city still falling short of pre-Covid levels, more new cultural, entertainment and sports offerings competing for visitors and the trend for locals heading north for leisure intensifying, the theme park obviously cannot just rely on nostalgia to survive. It must offer something distinctive: a combination of nature, conservation, education, local identity and memorable experiences so that visitors from near and far will keep returning. Having shown it can attract more visitors and generate revenue with enhanced offerings in recent years, the park must prove that it can turn the recovery into a durable future. As a home-grown brand that attracts strong public support and affection, Ocean Park deserves every chance to reinvent itself.

title: What dementia care around the world teaches us about dignity, community, avoiding burnout
