description: Anthea Rowan examines what dementia taught her about the nature of care, how it varies globally, from healthy habits to living environment.
content: This is the 100th instalment in a series on dementia, including the research into its causes and treatment, advice for carers and stories of hope. When this series launched, my mother was still by my side. My first column explored what looking after her taught me about dementia. Now, as I write this 100th piece, I reflect on what dementia taught me about the nature of care itself. Before she was diagnosed with dementia – but likely as her memory began to fray – my mother was admitted to hospital. As she forgot things, she failed to ring the bell she was meant to sound whenever she needed help – for example, when she needed to get up to go to the toilet. Instead, she just got up and made her way to the bathroom on her own. The nurses grew increasingly frustrated with her failure to listen to their instructions. “Ring the bell and one of us will take you,” they insisted. Mum kept forgetting, so eventually they attached an alarm to her seat. Every time she stood up from her chair after that, a shrill ring sounded through the ward. Mum was startled every time it happened – because, of course, she forgot what would happen when she stood up. She became increasingly distressed, near hysterical. Late that night, the hospital called to tell me how upset she was. I could hear her in the background. “Disconnect the alarm,” I said. It felt obvious to me, but the nurses resisted, asking who would take responsibility if she fell. “I’ll take the risk,” I insisted. They turned off the alarm. Mum did not fall, and her distress evaporated. I have thought of that night often as I read about how we care for people with dementia, because it seems to contain much about the care problem in miniature: a system built around safety and control, applied to everyone irrespective of their individual needs, at the cost of the very person it was meant to care for. Who are the carers and how many are there? The scale of the problem of dementia care is growing. A recent University of Hong Kong report estimates that about 100,000 people in Hong Kong are living with dementia, a number expected to triple by 2040. That will put far greater strain on informal carers, usually family members. According to the World Health Organization, unpaid care by family and close friends makes up more than 50 per cent of the total cost of dementia care globally – tens of billions of hours every year. As Amanda Pang, co-founder and COO of Hong Kong home-care agency Evercare, points out, families rarely anticipate how quickly home care escalates into a 24/7 burden. “Providing elder care at home presents a triple challenge: medical complexity, physical safety risks and emotional isolation,” Pang explains. “Most family members step into caregiving roles unexpectedly without clinical training, turning the home into a high-stress environment.” It is not surprising that carers suffer burnout, which is not a sign of personal weakness, but “a major public health concern”, she says. Preventing it requires shifting from a “sole-carer” mindset to a community-based approach built on scheduled relief, skill training and shared caregiving responsibilities. Lessons from a nursing home Dutchman Teun Toebes, 27, embraces this community approach. He is on a global mission to change the way we care for older people. As a 21-year-old nursing student, Toebes moved into the closed ward of a nursing home to “experience up close how we can change the system for the better by listening to my housemates living with dementia”. He lived in care homes for more than three years and wrote a book about it, The Housemates: Everything One Young Student Learnt about Love, Care and Dementia from Living in a Nursing Home (2023). After that, he set out with his friend, Dutch filmmaker Jonathan de Jong of Super7even Productions, to see how the world cares for its elderly. They spent three years filming in 11 countries across four continents, producing the documentary Human Forever (2023) and a follow-up book. How the world cares The pair discovered the emphasis on elderly care differs from place to place. Though the Dutch system that Toebes is well acquainted with is widely regarded as a model of elder care, he worries that it excludes people with dementia rather than including them. He describes having “the key to freedom” because he knew and remembered the code to unlock the door to the care home unit he lived in. His “housemates” did not, so they remained locked up, excluded. South Korea leans towards prevention through healthy lifestyle habits; South Africa focuses on family care. In Denmark, Toebes says, the living environment is central to care, with residents granted an element of autonomy and allowed to lie on the floor to enjoy the underfloor heating, for example. One Danish care home dispensed with technology and modelled itself on a regular home, with cats and dogs and lots of plants. In nursing homes where Toebes spent time in the Netherlands, there were only plastic plants, “because someone decided that people with dementia eat plants. If even one person has taken a bite out of a leaf, it is immediately turned into a collective problem.” Quality of care is not just about money, he says. According to health data from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, the Netherlands spends around 4.1 per cent of its GDP on overall long-term care – the highest proportion in the world. Figures cited by Toebes show that more than €18 billion (US$20.2 billion) a year of that national care budget goes directly towards elderly institutional and nursing care. This, he adds, is paid for by citizens professing to never wanting to live in the type of care homes their taxes help fund. The biggest surprise Toebes encountered on the filming journey was Moldova, among the poorest nations in Europe. It lacks dedicated nursing homes. Instead, individuals displaying “misunderstood behaviour” are placed in psychiatric hospitals. Yet when Toebes and de Jong visited one, Toebes was struck by something unexpected: a deep sense of shared humanity. Rather than viewing support as an institutional duty, residents and staff simply helped one another. To Toebes, it was care as a community habit rather than a medical system – and it felt “inclusive”. Risk and identity Because risk dictates how every person in a care home is managed, Toebes worries people are no longer regarded as individuals. A person might forget names and change their behaviour, but they will not forget how we make them feel. Locking them up or forgetting they have an identity is unlikely to make them feel good. “We focus on keeping people safe, but a care system which focuses on zero risks will result in zero life,” he says. “So good care includes taking risks. Not because safety is not important, but because it’s about weighing different values to facilitate someone’s wish.” Not every person with dementia carries the same risk, so why do we treat them all as if they do? Dementia, Toebes says, is a societal issue, not a care problem. The answer is not more nursing homes but more supportive communities and more social forms of living, where good care is available but does not necessitate being excluded from the people and places you are rooted in. Dignity over risk When I began to care for my mother at home, I often recalled that night in hospital that caused her such distress, how upsetting she had found that single incident of curtailing her liberty. I let her handle an electric kettle to make tea for us both. I did not mince or mash her food until near the end. As long as she could walk, I let her walk on her own – keeping a watchful eye as she strolled in the garden. I worked quietly nearby while she pottered among the plants, untouched by unnecessary restrictions, anchored in her home. Three top tips to safeguard carers’ health Evercare co-founder Amanda Pang suggests these ways to keep carers from experiencing burnout. 1. Schedule regular, non-negotiable relief Treat time off as a health necessity, not a luxury. Using hourly healthcare workers or temporary coverage keeps the patient safe while the primary carer rests, recovers and avoids physical collapse. 2. Upskill and delegate caregiving duties Share the caregiving workload. Train helpers or family members in mobility and hygiene support so the entire routine does not depend on one person. 3. Watch for early burnout warning signs Watch for signs of burnout, including fatigue, irritability and insomnia. Seek counselling or join a carer support group before stress becomes overwhelming. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Hongkonger Coleman Wong’s historic tennis gold at the Asian Games
description: The 22-year-old has also won a place at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
content:
Anyone watching tennis player Coleman Wong Chak-lam win his historic men’s singles title at the Asian Games earlier this month might have wondered if he even knows what pressure is.
The 22-year-old Hongkonger was facing China’s Wu Yibing, ranked No 111 in the world. Winning would also come with a place at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
Wong’s 6-2, 6-4 triumph at Higashiyama Park Tennis Centre would suggest it is the 99 players ranked above him who should worry.
Wong’s gold was the eighth the city’s athletes had won in Japan. Within the city’s overall medal count of 54 is a record 11 golds, three more than in 2023.
“Before the Games started, I was just hoping to win a medal, regardless of the colour,” Wong said. “But honestly, now reaching this point, winning this medal, you can call it unlocking an achievement.”
Wong also explained the role his family played in getting him to this stage of his tennis career.
“Since I was young, my family always had the mindset of, ‘OK, if you want to do it, just go for it’,” Wong said. “I went abroad ... to try at a very young age.”
He hopes his success can convince other families in the city to take a leap of faith in sports.

title: Albanian PM rejects resignation calls as violent protests enter sixth day
description: More than 270 injured in Tirana clashes as demonstrators attack police stations and ministries over tuition fees, living costs and corruption.
content: Albanian police fired water cannon and tear gas Sunday as violent anti-government protests entered a sixth day and Prime Minister Edi Rama rejected demonstrators’ demands that he resign. Violent demonstrations have rocked Tirana since Tuesday with protesters calling for action over poor university conditions, high tuition fees and corruption. Hundreds of protesters gathered again at noon in front of the education ministry chanting “Rama, resign” amid a tense stand-off with police. After police bid to disperse the crowds the protests scattered across the city centre, escalating in hours-long violent clashes. Protesters set ablaze litter bins in the streets, smashed windows, including at the headquarters of the governing Socialist party, and set fire to a police station and the entrance of the interior ministry. Chaotic clashes extended to the main boulevard and square with demonstrators throwing rocks, Molotov cocktails and firing pyrotechnic devices, as the police responded with rubber bullets and tear gas. Ambulances were seen rushing in and out of the scenes of clashes to pick up the injured. The Ministry of Health said that 16 police officers were injured – 14 of them when protesters attacked the police station. Albert Nushi, from the police public security department said on Sunday evening that a police station in Tirana was attacked with Molotov cocktails and pyrotechnic devices that endangered both officers and people held in custody. “An attack on a police station is not a protest. Violence against police officers, attacks on institutions, and actions that endanger human lives cannot be tolerated,” he said. He urged protesters to stay away from masked individuals behind the violence and “assemble in a peaceful manner”. According to the Ministry of health, 28 people were injured on Sunday – 19 police officers, four protesters, four passers-by and a journalist. Before the protest, shops and offices in the city centre secured their doors and windows with metal shutters, while city workers removed paving stones to prevent them being thrown by protesters. In a video broadcast lasting more than an hour, Rama ruled out resigning, stating that the protests are the “work of an outside hand”. According to Austrian federal press service Rama’s official visit to Federal Chancellor Christian Stocker scheduled for Monday, has been cancelled by the Albanian side. Writer and activist Lura Elezi, 38, said that she is protesting for “a better life, rule of law and against crime and corruption”. “I love my country, but my government does not respect us – it defies us. Every citizen must take responsibility for their country, taking on the duty to lead, to love, and not to destroy one’s own nation,” she said. Tirana saw its harshest violence on Saturday when protesters threw rocks, Molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins to use as barricades against advancing police. Buildings including a court, banks and a post office were set on fire or severely damaged. According to a health ministry report issued Sunday, 65 people were injured, including 37 police, with 12 people hospitalised during Saturday’s protests. Since Tuesday, 272 people have been injured in the clashes, including 169 police, the ministry said. Albania’s close ally the United States reacted late Saturday. Its embassy in Tirana urged “restraint and calm on all sides”. The European Commission in a written statement “condemned the use of violence in Tirana and other cities”, adding that the response to it “must remain proportionate”. “In a candidate country firmly committed to the EU accession process … grievances should be handled through constructive dialogue and in a peaceful manner,” the statement said. The unrest follows months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to US President Donald Trump’s family.

title: Bitcoin is making a comeback, but the risk of more ‘sharp pullbacks’ is real
description: The cryptocurrency is unlikely to climb back above US$100,000 this year as risks remain from interest rate rises to an escalation in Iran.
content: Bitcoin may extend its rebound but is unlikely to break above US$100,000 before the end of the year, as rising interest rates and the Iran conflict continue to weigh on crypto assets, according to analysts. The crypto asset class is likely to end the year higher than it is today, but below the peak reached last October, according to Alice Liu, head of research at crypto data platform CoinMarketCap. “The worst of this year’s downturn is behind us, but the recovery will be uneven and led almost entirely by bitcoin,” Liu said, describing her outlook for crypto assets in the fourth quarter of this year as “cautiously positive”. Bitcoin, the world’s largest cryptocurrency token, has been mired in a prolonged slump this year. After hitting a historic high of US$126,000 last October, a market rout wiped a record US$19 billion off its value, and for months afterwards the coin largely traded below US$70,000 – just over half its peak price. A surge in August that took bitcoin back above US$80,000 renewed hopes for the return of a crypto bull market, but the token has since lingered near US$85,000 without gaining further momentum. The original crypto token traded at US$81,404 on Saturday, after falling about 0.4 per cent over the previous five days. Macroeconomic headwinds are likely to dampen investors’ appetite for crypto assets in the coming months, as the 10-year US Treasury yield earlier this week surged to a 24-year high of 5.36 per cent. “The biggest constraint right now is the cost of capital,” said Angela Ang, APAC managing director at digital asset infrastructure firm BitGo. “Investors can earn attractive yields on lower-risk instruments such as Treasuries, so crypto is competing for capital on harder terms this quarter.” Another important driver for the crypto market going forward will be the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision at its coming meeting from October 27 to 28. A pause in interest rate rises with a softer guidance could trigger a bull market, but a second increase would likely send bitcoin back to around US$75,000, according to Liu. The odds of another rate increase are rising. The US Consumer Price Index rose 0.6 per cent in September, representing stronger-than-expected inflation that has “raised the stakes” for the Fed’s late October meeting, according to Ang. “The risk of further tightening could weigh on sentiment,” she said. CoinMarketCap expected bitcoin to fluctuate between US$75,000 and US$95,000 for the rest of the year, and finish between US$85,000 and US$92,000 following “a grind higher punctuated by sharp pullbacks”, Liu said. Digital asset trading firm QCP Capital expected bitcoin to trade between US$80,000 and US$90,000 as its base case for the fourth quarter, the company said in a report earlier this month. The token might drop below US$70,000, however, if further escalation in the Middle East lifts oil prices, among other factors, the firm noted. “Bitcoin has started to move inversely to oil,” CoinMarketCap’s Liu said. “Every de-escalation headline has lifted crypto, and every escalation has sold it off.” “Tensions with Iran, not any event within crypto, are the single biggest swing factor for bitcoin this quarter,” she added. Still, some analysts see reasons to be optimistic. Bitcoin has already climbed about 40 per cent from its low point in June, despite the challenge of high interest rates, said Brendan Ma, head of investment strategy at Arbitrum Foundation. “If there is no material hawkish surprise and flows continue to rise, there is room for bitcoin to breach US$100,000 by year-end,” Ma said.

title: Students create fire alarm system targeting elderly Hongkongers
description: Pupils at Islamic Kasim Tuet Memorial College combined science and social care for their award-winning idea.
content:
A terrible fire tore through a residential complex in Hong Kong last November. After the tragedy, teens Zarina Insar and Asmaul Husna Lazu – who goes by Asma – felt it was important to help their community.
The duo formed a team with six other schoolmates at Islamic Kasim Tuet Memorial College. They designed a prototype fire alarm system called Eldsafe 360.
The deadly blaze at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po killed 168 people. Investigations found that the fire safety systems had been turned off. Many elderly residents failed to escape in time. This motivated Zarina and Asma’s team to design a system built for their needs.
“Many of these elderly ... were living alone, with limited resources, disabilities and visual impairments,” said Zarina, 15. “So, we decided to make that our target.”
The prototype has not been turned into an actual product. Still, the school’s STEAM coordinator, Lawrence Lam Man-fai, praised the idea. He said it merged science education and social care.
The prototype combines a temperature detector and a speaker. It also has an elderly-friendly mobile application.
Users can place multiple Eldsafe 360 detectors throughout the home. This allows them to monitor fast temperature changes in different rooms.
If a detector senses unusually high temperatures, the app’s display will turn bright red. It will also sound an alarm through the speaker.
If temperatures continue rising and users don’t act quickly, the app automatically alerts emergency services and pre-saved emergency contacts.
The team spoke to their elderly family members during the design process. This helped them learn what accessibility features to include. The app features high-contrast colours and large font sizes. It also has large touchpoints and text-to-speech tools.
“I think this is related to STEAM and technology. And I think this was a [good] chance for ... experiential learning ,” said Asma, 16.
The prototype helped the team earn third place at the Schools Challenge Hong Kong 2026. It is a social innovation competition for junior secondary school students organised by Junior Achievement Hong Kong and JPMorgan Chase.
Joining this project changed how the students view safety and emergency readiness.
Zarina said she realised that emergencies are unpredictable. “In emergencies, the fact is that nobody can anticipate them,” she explained.
“The best thing to do is prepare for them. When [they] actually arrive, then you have things to protect [yourself] or others.”
In July, the Education Bureau announced new recommendations for the Health Management and Social Care (HMSC) curriculum.
HMSC is an elective subject in Hong Kong’s Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) system.
The course will soon include topics on disaster management and emergency preparedness.
The new curriculum will launch in phases. It will begin with Form Four courses in the 2028-29 school year.
Zarina is a current HMSC student. She supported the updates, calling disaster awareness “essential”.
“It’s really important not only for HMSC students, but for everyone. In case of fire, you need to know where the emergency kit is, what [evacuation] location you need to have ... in your mind,” she said.
Lam suggested that the government expand the curriculum. He thinks these lessons should reach more students.
“If [the Education Bureau] believes this is important, they should also include parts of it in the junior curriculum. HMSC is only taken by a specific group of students. Some schools might not even offer the HMSC elective,” he said.
“More importantly, I think we need to help students understand how to prevent disasters from happening in the first place.”

title: Hong Kong teens prioritise elder accessibility with fire alarm design
description: Students at Islamic Kasim Tuet Memorial College merged science and social care through their prototype, developed to alert the elderly to emergencies.
content:
After a devastating fire tore through a residential complex in Hong Kong last November, teens Zarina Insar and Asmaul Husna Lazu – who goes by Asma – felt a sense of obligation to help their community.
That feeling of duty grew into something bigger in February of this year when the duo led six other schoolmates at Islamic Kasim Tuet Memorial College in designing Eldsafe 360, a prototype fire alarm system tailored to assist the public, especially the elderly, during emergencies.
Zarina, 15, and Asma, 16, explained that they were motivated to focus on Hong Kong’s older population after learning about the troubles the elderly residents of Wang Fuk Court had escaping the blaze.
“Many of these elderly ... were living alone, with limited resources, disabilities and visual impairments,” Zarina said. “So, we decided to make that our target.”
The team built a physical model of their prototype – which combines a temperature detector, speaker and an elderly-friendly mobile application interface – using cardboard, pins, thermal wiring, speakers and batteries.
Given the team’s lack of coding experience, their mentor suggested leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) tools to bring their digital interface to life.
The prototype eventually helped the team earn third place at the Schools Challenge Hong Kong 2026 – a social innovation competition for junior secondary students organised by Junior Achievement Hong Kong and JPMorgan Chase.
While the prototype has not been turned into an actual product, the school’s STEAM coordinator, Lawrence Lam Man-fai, said the initiative served as a vital bridge between science education and social care.
“Eldsafe might not be a practical tool in the real world, as there are many restrictions and limitations,” Lam said.
“[But] the thinking process and awareness are much more important than the prototype itself ... These imperfections provide key opportunities for students to explore and develop better, more innovative products that will truly work in the future.”
The fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po broke out on November 26, 2025, and burned for more than 40 hours, killing 168 people.
More than a third of the complex’s 4,643 residents were aged 65 and older, according to Hong Kong’s 2021 population census.
Investigations found that the fire alarms in all eight residential buildings had been negligently turned off a week before the tragedy struck.
Still, Asma and Zarina said they believed reliable alarms could have alerted people earlier and provided a crucial window for escape, especially for older residents with mobility issues.
To ensure their product met the actual needs of the older population, the team consulted their elderly family members during the design process.
“We asked [our grandparents]: what would help you the most from technology alone if there was to be a fire?” Zarina explained.
Their advice helped the team build accessibility features designed for the elderly: the app features high-contrast colours, large font sizes, enlarged touchpoints and text-to-speech tools.
Users can place multiple Eldsafe 360 detectors throughout the home to monitor rapid temperature fluctuations . Different temperature settings can be used for each space – for example, a kitchen could have a higher temperature than other rooms.
If a detector senses unusually high temperatures, the connected app’s display will turn bright red and sound an alarm through the speaker.
If temperatures continue spiking and users fail to intervene quickly, the app automatically alerts emergency services and pre-saved emergency contacts.
Although actual technical limitations remain, Lam emphasised that the human-centred design thinking and heightened safety awareness the students gained were more valuable than the physical prototype itself.
Asma said she appreciated the opportunity to build her STEAM skills.
“I think this was a [good] chance for ... experimental learning,” she said.
Joining this project also transformed how the students view safety and emergency readiness.
Zarina said she realised that emergencies are unpredictable, making preparation the ultimate line of defence.
“In emergencies, the fact is that nobody can anticipate them,” she said. “The best thing to do is prepare for them so that when [they] actually arrive, then you have things to protect [yourself] or others.”
She added that she now finds herself instinctively looking for emergency exits whenever she enters shopping malls or high-rise buildings.
In July, the Education Bureau announced new recommendations for the Health Management and Social Care (HMSC) curriculum – an elective subject in Hong Kong’s Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) system – incorporating topics on disaster management and mitigation , as well as emergency preparedness.
The current plan is to begin implementing the curriculum progressively starting in the 2028-29 school year, beginning with Form Four.
As a current HMSC student, Zarina supported the updates, saying she believes disaster awareness is “essential”.
“It’s really important not only for HMSC students, but for everyone. In case of fire, you need to know where the emergency kit is, what [evacuation] location you need to have ingrained in your mind,” she said.
Asma echoed Zarina’s views, emphasising that basic safety skills should be taught across all age groups.
“Outside of classroom academic knowledge, I think if we ... students also look into practical, real-life world situation[s], I think this is a good thing,” Asma said.
Lam suggested that the government expand the curriculum to reach a wider range of students.
“If [the Education Bureau] believes this is important, they should also include parts of it in the junior curriculum, as HMSC is only taken by a specific group of students. Some schools might not even offer the HMSC elective,” Lam said.
“More importantly, I think we need to help students understand how to prevent disasters from happening in the first place.”

Hong Kong authorities are warning teenagers about covert triad recruitment tactics. Local gang syndicates are increasingly using messaging apps and online gaming chat rooms to promote illicit part-time jobs as easy ways to make quick cash.

Experts say Hong Kong triad groups have evolved over the past decade, simplifying traditional rituals and adapting to changes in the law.
The Prisons Ordinance was amended last year to tighten restrictions on inmate visits, including a prohibition on receiving outside food. The changes were made after the enactment of the national security law.
Gregory Lau Tat-keung, a former superintendent who retired from the police force in 2013, has written a book about triads.
Lau said he believed the amendment was effective in deterring minor offenders from taking the fall for syndicate bosses because they were subject to stricter prison rules while in prison waiting for trial.
“Before, it was relatively easy [for bosses] to convince them to break the law for the mastermind, because they mistakenly believed that as long as they could receive outside food, their boss still controlled everything,” he said.

The stricter rules also made it more difficult for visitors to bring inmates cigarettes, which served as a kind of “underground currency” in prisons, Lau said.

He added that some triads held ceremonies in the mountains, on barges or in mainland China to avoid attention from law enforcement.
Lau said: “A lot of people have been misled into thinking that the triads are all about loyalty and brotherhood.”
Lau recalled that many of the gangsters he had arrested had lined up to be prosecution witnesses.

title: Listen Up: Robotic elephants in Indian temples draw crowds and controversy
description: Practise your English with our short listening exercises: play the audio and answer the questions in our quiz.
content:
Listen to the podcast and answer the questions in the quiz. If you’re still unsure about a question, read the script provided to help you.
This week’s podcast is voiced by Young Post production editor Sakina Abidi and Cathy Hilborn Feng, SCMP’s health and wellness editor.
Voice 1: The life-size robotic elephants in Prasanth Prakashan’s backyard workshop have ears that flap, tails that swish and trunks that squirt water. But that’s about all they have in common with their real-life counterparts, which are revered across India as representations of the divine. The animatrons, crafted from fibreglass, iron and rubber, are intended to replace live elephants in Hindu temples.
Voice 2: The proposed change pleases animal-welfare activists but upsets those who passionately believe that real elephants are inextricable from temple rituals and festivals. Elephants are granted superstar status at these rites and events.
Voice 1: The People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, or Peta for short, and other non-profit organisations have donated about 40 robotic elephants, costing about US$6,000 each – which is around HK$47,000 – to Indian temples to replace live elephants. A robotic elephant is much lighter but lacks the grace of the majestic pachyderm. Still, electric motors move its head and eyeballs. Body parts are pliable and can bend easily, making them appear lifelike.
Voice 2: Prakashan, who holds a degree in mechanical engineering, knows his elephant is far from the real thing. You can’t create an original elephant, just as you cannot duplicate a human, he said. But he tries to capture the animal’s essence as much as he can. One thing Prakashan’s elephants can’t yet do is walk, but he is working on it.
Voice 1: Elephants are seen as symbols of divinity in many cultures in the region. This love and respect for elephants is not unique to Hinduism or to India. Buddhists believe elephants are Buddha-like, symbolising patience, wisdom and enlightenment. In Kandy, Sri Lanka, 100 decorated elephants parade the streets in a sacred procession every July or August, with the largest carrying the Buddha’s tooth relic in a golden casket.
Voice 2: In Kerala, a state in southern India, festivals with live elephants are crowd-pullers. One temple’s annual parade for the festival of Pooram features about 100 elephants adorned in golden headgear and colourful silks. The elephants are escorted by handlers who fan them with peacock feathers and yak-hair whisks.
Voice 1: About 65km away, another temple houses nearly 50 elephants. It also hosts an annual elephant race and a feeding ritual in which the animals are given rice, butter, sugar, fruits and vegetables. Elsewhere in Kerala, St George Orthodox Syrian Church and the Pattambi Mosque routinely feature elephant parades during their festivals.
Voice 2: Khushboo Gupta, vice-president of policy at Peta India, said the beauty of live elephants doesn’t justify shackling, beating and separating them from their families. Stressed elephants can also be deadly. For example, nine people died in 2024 from elephant rampages at Kerala temple festivals. Gupta said these elephants would often be forced to stand for hours in the heat amid large crowds, drums and fireworks. Any trigger could cause them to go on a rampage.
Voice 1: Prakashan’s first robotic elephant, Raman, came to the Irinjadapilly Sree Krishna Temple in 2023. On a recent afternoon outside the temple, Raman stood motionless as two children played, giggling and hugging its trunk. The temple’s head priest said that the children would never be able to approach a live elephant so freely.
Voice 2: The priest added that religious texts spell out the rules for daily rituals in Kerala temples and don’t require the use of live elephants. He believes the practice began when elephants were part of kings’ armies and palaces a few centuries ago. The animals were also chosen as vehicles for the gods during processions because of their height.

title: Spark Study Buddy (Challenger): Drivers shouldn’t swerve to avoid deer on roads, experts say
description: The story on this page has some tougher vocabulary words and questions to improve your reading and grammar.
content:
Read the following text and answer the quiz below.
[1] The peak season for deer-vehicle collisions is approaching. Drivers are being warned to take extra care. GEM Motoring Assist is a road safety organisation in Britain. It said October to December is traditionally the most common time for deer strikes in much of the northern hemisphere. This is because the deer’s mating season coincides with darker evenings and busy commuting periods.
[2] The motoring safety organisation said the chance of a strike is not restricted to rural roads. Deer can appear on major roads and dual carriageways as they move through fields and gardens. Estimates from conservationists at the British Deer Society show that more than 40,000 deer are killed in vehicle collisions on UK roads each year. The resulting damage to cars is estimated to cost at least £17 million per year (HK$176.3 million), according to the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA).
[3] Researchers in the United States have documented an even larger problem. Around 1.5 to 2.1 million deer-vehicle collisions occur annually across North America, according to the Federal Highway Administration. These collisions result in 200 to 440 human fatalities and up to 59,000 injuries each year. They also result in more than US$10 billion (HK$78.5 billion) in annual economic losses.
[4] While the seasonal risks are “predictable”, they can “catch drivers out on even familiar roads”, James Luckhurst said. He is head of road safety at GEM. “Deer can emerge from cover with very little warning, and darker evening journeys reduce the time available to react,” he said. “We want drivers to recognise the risk, reduce speed where deer may be present and keep scanning the road and verges ahead.”
[5] “If a deer runs into your path, your priority must be to remain in control. Brake firmly if it is safe to do so, but avoid a sudden swerve. A sharp change of direction can put you into the path of an oncoming vehicle, take you off the road or lead to a much more serious collision,” he said.
[6] Drivers are advised to slow down and stay alert, particularly where deer warning signs are posted. Expect deer to be crossing roads at dawn and dusk. If a collision looks unavoidable, motorists should not swerve. This could push them into oncoming traffic, a ditch or other obstacles.
[7] German road safety experts have issued similar warnings. Auto Club Europa has advised drivers to reduce speed and observe road edges carefully. They should remain brake-ready on routes through forests or along field edges.

title: Study Buddy (Challenger): Dutch farmers test new crop to save sinking peatlands
description: This page is for students who want to take their reading comprehension to the next level with difficult vocabulary and questions to test their inference skills.
content:
[1] In a soggy field between Amsterdam and The Hague, farmer Sander Roeleveld ploughs a small white combine harvester into his crops, gathering a grain never before harvested in the Netherlands: rice. The surroundings could scarcely be more Dutch. Canals criss-cross land lying two metres below sea level. Windmills grace the horizon as cows – for centuries the country’s agricultural staple – graze in the nearby grassland.
[2] But the warming climate is allowing Dutch farmers to produce wine and even experiment with rice, previously unthinkable in such a wet, temperate country. Researchers behind the scheme hope rice cultivation could help address one of the country’s most pressing environmental challenges: peat soils – made from decomposed organic materials – that are sinking as they dry out, pushing parts of the low-lying Netherlands ever lower.
[3] “It’s extraordinary,” said Philippe Terheggen, chairman of the Land van Ons association that has provided the fields for the rice harvest. “We would never have thought ... that we would be able to grow rice in the Netherlands,” the 68-year-old told Agence France-Presse. “But it’s also scary because it tells you what is possible ... now [that] the climate has changed.”
[4] For now, the project is a pilot scheme, consisting of just 1.5 acres, with organisers hoping to produce around three tonnes of short-grain rice suitable for sushi or risotto. The team is working with 30 different rice cultivars from as far as Russia and Japan to see which grows best in the Dutch climate.
[5] The project is about more than crop diversification. Researchers believe it could help tackle one of the Netherlands’ most persistent environmental problems. Roughly one-tenth of the country is peatland, which farmers drain for grass to feed their cattle. As the peat dries out, it releases millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide while causing the land to subside by up to several centimetres a year in the worst-affected areas.
[6] According to Wageningen University, greenhouse gas emissions from Dutch peat soils account for around two to three per cent of the country’s total emissions. The only way to resolve this vicious cycle is to keep the fields wet, but then farmers would have nothing to grow there – until now.
[7] “Rice is an opportunity for this part of the world to adapt to climate change, to grow something that previously wasn’t possible,” said Julian Helfenstein, a researcher from Wageningen University and Research, who is piloting the project along with colleagues from nearby Leiden University. “But also to mitigate climate change because it stops this peat from degrading and emitting all the CO2 because you can keep it wet.”
[8] The peat issue affects not just the Netherlands, but much of northern Europe, including Germany, Belgium, even the Baltic states, he said. Helfenstein and his team are closely monitoring CO2 and methane emissions from rice cultivation compared with maintaining grassland to ensure the cure is not worse than the illness.

title: Meet Will Smith’s brother Harry, who’s behind new YouTube series The Creative Executive
description: The younger sibling of the Bad Boys star teams up with former Netflix executive Siddhi Sundar for a nine-episode series featuring celebrity guests.
content: Will Smith’s younger brother, Harry Smith, has partnered with former Netflix executive Siddhi Sundar to launch a new YouTube series that also doubles as a business platform, The Creative Executive. “Most of what creatives need to know about business, technology, and media isn’t taught in one place – and the people who’ve succeeded at the highest levels are often the hardest to access,” Harry Smith and Sundar said in a joint statement. “We created this platform to close that gap, turning real-world conversations and hard-won experience into practical education that helps emerging creatives navigate the future without losing their voice.” The first season of The Creative Executive will feature nine episodes with guests including Will Smith, Jada Pinkett Smith’s brother Caleeb Pinkett and Hollywood producer Todd Black, among others. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Creative Executive (@the_creative_executive) Aside from the celebrity interviews, Harry describes the series on his LinkedIn profile as an education platform where “we help creatives master the business side of their art. We work directly with organisations and leaders as a consulting and experience-design practice: building custom educational curriculum across business, leadership, creativity, and technology and AI topics, designing community platforms, advising on creative, community, and tech strategy, and shaping hospitality and live experiences at the highest levels.” Here’s everything you need to know about Will Smith’s younger brother, Harry Smith. What is Harry Smith’s background? Harry Smith was born in West Philadelphia to parents Willard Sr and Caroline Smith on May 5, 1971. Aside from his famous older brother Will, Harry has two other siblings: his older sister Pamela, the eldest of the Smith bunch, and his twin sister Ellen. Born into a middle-class family, Will has previously opened up about his complicated relationship with his father, whom he described in his 2021 memoir as “violent” but also a present parent. “My father was violent, but he was also at every game, play and recital. He was an alcoholic, but he was sober at every premiere of every one of my movies,” the actor wrote. “He listened to every record. He visited every studio. The same intense perfectionism that terrorised his family put food on the table every night of my life.” Willard Sr and Caroline Smith eventually divorced in 2000 and he went on to later welcome another daughter named Ashley Marie Pettway, according to People. Harry is the former CEO of Smith Global Media and founder of Treyball Development. Harry and Will have worked together for several years The Smith siblings often appear in each other’s Instagram posts and seemingly share a close bond. Harry and Will have worked together throughout the Fresh Prince of Bel Air star’s Hollywood career. After initially managing Will’s finances, Harry went on to work for Will and Jada’s entertainment company, Overbrook Entertainment. Before starting The Creative Executive, Harry served as the CEO of Smith Global Media, a film distribution company that he founded in 2016. Harry Smith is a father Harry became a father for the first time when he welcomed daughter Sydney with his ex, Melissa Montoya, in August 1999. In 2011, Harry welcomed his second child, son Langston, with Ananda Lewis. While Harry and Lewis kept their relationship out of the limelight, the two were together for 10 years before going their separate ways. Lewis tragically passed away in 2025 after being diagnosed with breast cancer. She was 52 years old.

title: Open Questions | Robin Xing on how China’s ‘two-speed’ economy can solve contrasting problems
description: Morgan Stanley’s chief China economist on how a new industrial revolution and demand-centric reflation can sustain China’s growth.
content: Robin Xing is chief China economist at Morgan Stanley. A famed economist and Peking University graduate, Xing has a PhD in economics from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and previously worked at Goldman Sachs and China International Capital Corp. In his second Open Questions interview, Xing dissects China’s K-shaped economic divergence and why he remains convinced that the “top half of the K” can offset challenges such as deflation and weak consumption. He also discusses Beijing’s real priorities, the “fallacy of composition” and why helping consumers will sustain and accelerate China’s tech advance. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump have met twice and are expected to meet two more times this year. Will the meetings deliver stability in trade, investment and broader economic ties? Can businesses now proceed with their trade and investment plans with greater clarity and confidence? Is the two-month extension of the tariff truce a disappointment? The successful meetings this year could help steer the US-China relationship towards managed competition: modestly expanding cooperation in non-sensitive areas such as trade, agriculture and other commercially practical sectors, while important strategic differences – particularly around technology and national security – are likely to persist. Deep economic interdependence gives both sides an incentive to maintain a floor under the relationship and reduces the potential for broader escalation. That should make bilateral ties more predictable, even as de-risking, localisation and restrictions in sensitive areas continue. We expect the improvement in clarity and confidence to be concentrated in non-sensitive sectors. Recent progress around the Board of Trade, including reciprocal tariff reductions on around US$30 billion of non-sensitive goods, suggests that both sides are willing to offer incremental stability where national-security concerns are less prominent. However, in technology, critical minerals and other strategically sensitive areas, we believe the broader direction remains towards localisation and tighter controls. Amid the slowdown, Beijing has rolled out new measures recently, including mortgage loan subsidies and rate reductions. Are they enough? Has Beijing become more tolerant of the slowdown while remaining convinced of long-term prospects? China is undergoing a challenging economic transformation, as old growth drivers face diminishing returns. Deflation pressures have persisted, and domestic demand remains weak. But in the meantime, there is a structural transformation taking place in the country towards what we call the Industrial Revolution 5.0. This transition will require a lot of spending and capital expenditure. We estimate around US$6 trillion factory upgrade investment in areas like robotics, smart machinery, industrial software, power grids and related infrastructure. In addition, we see another US$6 trillion investment being directed towards strategic new capacity. In total, this represents about US$12 trillion in incremental capex over the next 10 years. China is now in a two-speed, K-shaped economy. The top half of the K is showing some bright spots The hope is that this decade-long capex supercycle in advanced manufacturing can help offset the drag from deflation and gradually replace old growth drivers like housing and infrastructure investment. China is now in a two-speed, K-shaped economy. The top half of the K is showing some bright spots in manufacturing, artificial intelligence and in different emerging sectors. But you also have a huge bottom half of the K: an “old economy” like housing, consumption, a job-intensive services sector and so on. They are now under a cyclical, very painful adjustment. Beijing has stepped up targeted easing to cushion the downside. This signals a greater willingness to deploy central fiscal resources directly to support housing demand. Yet, the overall package remains modest, unlikely to reverse confidence-driven household deleveraging due to a weak job market outlook while the existing mortgage rate is still at 3 per cent. There is still the risk of continued pro-cyclical policy tightening amid structurally lower land sales and elevated local government debt. We thus expect full-year real GDP growth to remain near the lower end of the 4.5 to 5 per cent target range. So, what is your take on this two-speed, K-shaped economy? My view is that the top half of the K will be stronger in the future, leading to the next industrial revolution, contributing to US$12 trillion in new capex, and that’s going to be very powerful in offsetting the drag from old sectors. Housing investment as a share of GDP will decline to only 3 per cent, and the share for traditional infrastructure will also decline to 4 per cent. Industrial capex right now is 17 per cent of GDP. We think it will increase to close to 20 per cent in 10 years. That being said, 10 years is a very long horizon. For now, we are seeing deflationary pressure lasting longer than expected. At the end of last year, some observers assessed that China was gradually reflating, with housing prices stabilising and [consumer price index] and [producer price index] showing signs of improvement. They argued that maybe China was ‘out of the woods’. We disagree. China’s deflationary pressure remains quite prolonged. Another key issue is the ongoing household deleveraging cycle, which began around 2021, when the housing market peaked. Nearly five years on, households are still deleveraging. Household debt growth has now turned negative, marking the first absolute contraction on record. This suggests that precautionary savings remain very high, with households prioritising debt repayment while the housing sector continues to adjust. Even though households have not borrowed much in the past five years, the issue is that asset prices have also been falling. In other words, the denominator is shrinking as well. This creates a typical deflation trap: asset prices decline, sometimes faster than households can pay down debt. Thus, household leverage remains relatively high. People still feel the need, the urgency, to continue to deleverage. Deleveraging, in turn, is bad for consumption. In this environment, I think a typical approach should be much more aggressive countercyclical central government borrowing: the central government widens the deficit to support consumers and corporates. But I think policymakers appear to remain cautious about a much larger demand-side stimulus. They likely view a broad consumption transfer as unsustainable, which will not contribute to long-lasting productivity growth. Instead, the strategic priority remains firmly anchored on the supply side: self-sufficiency, manufacturing resilience, national energy security and related objectives. These remain the real priorities. That’s why, in my view, the bottom line for near-term policy is that it will likely defend the growth floor, rather than deliver a meaningful consumption or housing-led reflation package. Deflationary pressure may persist until the housing market finds a structural bottom and until the productivity benefits from AI are more fully unleashed as part of the transition towards a new industrial revolution. Over time, that could contribute to stronger potential GDP growth – but that will take time. Various government departments have recently made regulatory moves, including controls on cross-border capital flows and taxing offshore products, that have been seen by some as a signal of tightening. What is your view? How do they compare with the curbs seen in 2021? There are currently two contrasting narratives. The first is that there is growing discussion and hope for another pivot like September 2024: a larger demand-side stimulus package or a “bazooka,” aimed at reflating consumption and stabilising housing prices. Many argue that such support is needed because the economy is still in deflation, second-quarter GDP fell short of the target and high-frequency data is tracking at a subdued level. But on the other side, a lot of corporate leaders and foreign investors are asking a very different question: do recent policy moves signal a return to the 2021 playbook – that is, another round of broad-based regulatory tightening? My answer is “neither”. The 2021 tightening cycle was unique. It was a proactive, top-down regulatory reset across multiple sectors, including internet and tech, after-school tutoring, property, gaming, healthcare and others. It also took place against a different macro backdrop: China had been first into the initial Covid-19 shock, and among the first to recover from it. China’s growth was more robust back then. Against that backdrop, policymakers proactively initiated this broad regulatory reset. Today, however, I do not think what we are seeing is another policy reset. It looks more like stricter enforcement of existing regulations, because the overarching regulatory framework has already been in place for some time. In a deflationary environment, the housing market remains under adjustment, which means new project launches and land sales are likely to remain weak. At the same time, subdued nominal GDP growth weighs on corporate revenue growth. The result is growing pressure on government revenues from land and corporate value-added tax. The macro challenge is the “fallacy of composition”. Each micro-level action may be rational on its own – controlling risk, collecting revenue, closing fiscal gaps or maintaining stability. But if many agencies tighten enforcement at the same time, the aggregate effect can become macro tightening. That is essentially pro-cyclical tightening. This means when the economy is already under deflationary pressure, policy should arguably be moving in the opposite direction: widening the deficit, supporting households and easing pressure on corporates. Instead, we are now seeing pro-cyclical tightening due to micro-level enforcements. Pro-cyclical tightening can occur when governments enforce contradictory policies during an economic turndown, which can worsen the slump. What types of enforcement policies are currently in place that may contribute to this effect? There are three areas of recent enforcement. First, in housing, the shift from presales towards completed-home sales will slow developers’ asset turnover. Second, social pension contributions are being tightened. In the past, many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) contributed based on the minimum salary; but starting this year, they need to contribute based on a higher real wage. The third is taxation. Tax authorities are now paying closer attention to higher-income individuals. And lastly, some companies that previously benefited from local tax rebates or preferential treatment are also facing tax clawbacks. Based on our estimate, the tax and social security contribution measures could create a fiscal and cash-flow drag equivalent to around 1 to 2 per cent of GDP. This may not sound large, but in a deflationary environment, the last thing corporates and households need is an additional burden. In fact, there has been a de facto fiscal consolidation in the last 12 months, with the augmented fiscal deficit narrowing by 2.5 percentage points of GDP. The bigger issue is confidence. While this could further weaken private-sector sentiment and capex, more broadly, this kind of micro-level tightening runs counter to the need for more proactive reflationary policy. In September, Beijing unveiled a capital injection of 360 billion yuan (US$53.7 billion) into state-owned banks and insurers. What is your take? That was already part of the 2024 plan, which widened the deficit for a few purposes: partly to support consumers through trade-in programmes and partly to stabilise the financial system. So this is not new. The key issue is the trade-off between state-owned financial sector stability and household balance sheet stability. If we look at other countries, policy has often supported household deleveraging more directly, for example through aggressive rate cuts. In China, however, policymakers appear to have placed greater emphasis on financial-sector stability. As a result, while rates have been lowered, the reduction in household debt-servicing burdens has been more modest than in many other economies. The trade-off is that household deleveraging may take longer. Households are trying to pay down debt, but their mortgage burdens have not fallen meaningfully, especially as income growth has also slowed. So the risk is that the harder households try to deleverage, the more demand weakens – reinforcing a classic deflationary trap. Over the longer run, China needs to address unbalanced growth and weak consumption, which means shifting from a supply-led growth model to a more consumption-driven one. We believe more aggressive central government fiscal policy is needed – with a larger deficit aimed at supporting demand and consumption This can be realised by building a stronger social safety net. Better access to public housing, education, healthcare, pensions and unemployment protection would reduce precautionary savings and help unlock household spending. If China’s priorities remain as technology self-sufficiency, supply chain resilience, energy security and geopolitics, then fiscal and financial resources available to support consumers will be limited. That said, there is still a great deal China can do to gradually rebalance the economy, but this will take time and the risks of a deflationary trap may need to become more fully recognised. We believe more aggressive central government fiscal policy is needed – with a larger deficit aimed at supporting demand and consumption. US government debt continues to breach successive ceilings, triggering significant sell-offs that have driven up borrowing costs. What are the implications? What lessons should China, as a major holder of US Treasuries, draw from these developments? If we look at how the US uses government borrowing, the majority is on welfare-related spending, including healthcare. By contrast in China, it’s more on capital formation, capex and investment. These are two very different approaches. In my view, both economies need some form of rebalancing. For the US, the priority should probably be gradual fiscal consolidation, reducing the deficit over time while redirecting spending towards reinvestment. For China, given its large manufacturing base and extensive infrastructure, fiscal policy may be more effective if it is directed towards consumption, household welfare and social support. For investors, the near-term uncertainties are clear. There is still debate over the path of US monetary policy, including where the Fed’s terminal rate will settle, as well as how the US government may respond to pressure on Treasury yields. But my sense is that most global investors still view corporate America as profitable and innovative. While concerns about US government debt exposure may lead to some hedging, confidence in US assets remains broadly intact. A key reason is fundamentals: US companies continue to be seen as strong, profitable and innovation-driven, which helps support the broader appeal of American assets. In this part of the world, many still argue that US government debt is too high and without fiscal consolidation, sovereign credit risks could eventually emerge. When you speak with global investors, the picture is more nuanced. Many may adjust their exposure to US government debt or demand a higher long-term risk premium on Treasuries. Yet they remain broadly confident in corporate America. Thus, there are almost “two Americas”. China faces a different challenge. Global investors generally view the central government’s fiscal position and the state-owned financial system as quite robust, largely because China has prioritised financial sector resilience, especially the profitability and stability of state-owned financial institutions. Few investors are seriously concerned about Chinese sovereign risks, systemic financial risk or China’s long-term national competitiveness. If anything, China’s industrial strength and supply-chain advantages remain clear. The bigger concern is corporate profitability. Foreign investors are less certain whether Chinese companies can deliver sustainable earnings growth. This is also a challenge for China to attract more foreign capital and FDI. Yes, China’s supply chain advantages and geopolitical competitiveness are all well recognised, but the key question is whether these strengths can be translated into visible, predictable and sustainable improvements in corporate profitability. The yuan has been on a steady path upwards, despite Beijing reiterating it has neither the need nor the intention for competitive trade advantages through currency depreciation. What is your take? There are market voices talking up the possibility of further yuan appreciation, with some even predicting significant strengthening in the next few years. Their argument is largely based on China’s trade surplus. Given the sheer scale of that surplus, they argue that the yuan is likely undervalued. I am not fully convinced. If we look at other East Asian economies, such as Japan and South Korea, large trade surpluses have not automatically translated into sustained currency appreciation. A trade surplus is just one side of the story. The other side is the capital account. The key question is what happens to the surplus – is it reinvested domestically or deployed offshore in search of better returns? In the cases of South Korea and Japan, a sizeable portion of their trade surplus has been reinvested overseas – usually in US assets, like bonds or the stock market because their domestic yields are lower than offshore ones. China is facing a similar challenge. Yes, China does run a large trade surplus, but persistent deflationary pressure means domestic yields and assets remain relatively unattractive. Government bond yields have been hovering below 2 per cent, while the stock market has recovered from two years ago but is largely muddling through. Against this backdrop, it’s natural that many exporters, after receiving their export proceeds, may prefer to park their funds offshore and invest in overseas assets instead. If we look at the broader balance-of-payments picture, it does not clearly support the view that the yuan is undervalued. What would support a much stronger, sustainable yuan appreciation would be a genuine rebalancing of China’s economy, driven by faster and more effective domestic reflation. When nominal GDP growth recovers, corporate revenue and profit growth should also improve. In turn, bond yield and equity earnings will likely be higher too, making Chinese assets more attractive, which will provide a more durable foundation for yuan strength. This year, the yuan may even break 6.7 against the US dollar, but we don’t believe China is actively seeking a significantly stronger currency at this stage. In our previous interview in March 2025, you highlighted “green shoots” in the tech sector. With China’s AI boom and the rise of new players, from robotics to chipmaking, can green shoots evolve into a new growth driver? Can technology alone sustain – or even accelerate – growth? I think what we’re seeing now is more than just “green shoots”. In a K-shaped economy, the upper arm of the K is becoming stronger, supported by a profound structural transformation taking place underneath the surface of deflation, something we call the Industrial Revolution 5.0. Historically, there have been four major industrial revolutions: mechanisation; then electrification; then automation; and fourth, digitalisation, which broadly unfolded from the 1970s through the early 2000s. Now, China may be among the first economies to move meaningfully into a fifth industrial revolution, one enabled by industrial intelligence and the large-scale deployment of physical AI. This is not limited to humanoid robots. It is about the broader integration of AI-native operating systems into the physical economy – drones, EVs and robotics in different forms. Right now, China has 8 million such systems deployed across factories, transport and logistics. That number could rise tenfold to roughly 80 million by 2035. This large-scale deployment of next-generation AI in the real economy could help address China’s labour constraints. China’s population is ageing and shrinking, but the deployment of physical AI may be sufficient to offset much of the resulting labour shortage. That’s the first key enabler; we call it intelligence. The second enabler is resilience. Under the 15th five-year plan, China is trying to address all key chokepoints across its domestic technology stack, including areas such as semiconductor equipment, industrial design software and very high-end computer numerical control machines. China is entering this next industrial revolution from an unmatched starting point China has historically relied on foreign technology in several of these critical areas, and it is now trying to reduce that dependence with localisation. Finally, there is leadership. China is moving beyond just exporting finished goods assembled domestically to exporting a full-stack industrial ecosystem, including global standards. Taken together, intelligence, resilience and leadership suggest that China is entering this next industrial revolution from an unmatched starting point. China already accounts for 28 per cent of global manufacturing value added and the country covers all of the 666 industrial categories and subcategories defined by the United Nations. That breadth gives China extraordinary scale, depth and flexibility across the industrial system. China also has a large and expanding base of smart manufacturing capacity, including tens of thousands of smart factories supported by 5G and Internet of Things infrastructure. That’s why it can move away from just a factory country to something broader – an industrial operating system for the world. In conversations with international investors, China’s industrial story is often too quickly dismissed simply as a narrative of overcapacity, low margins or even trade war-induced decline. These narratives do not fully capture what is happening. We believe a more important story lies in what’s coming next: China transitioning from being the world’s factory to the world’s industrial operating system. This could help China address key chokepoints across supply chains. This is also a story about leadership. A lot of sectors could benefit, such as industrial automation, semiconductor equipment, robotics components, industrial ecosystem software and so on. If China can accelerate this technology revolution while adopting a more effective approach to economic rebalancing, for example, by using government financial resources to support consumption and welfare, its growth model could become much more sustainable. Importantly, the capex cycle associated with embodied AI does not have to be value-destructive. It could drive fundamental improvements in productivity, margins and potential GDP growth, creating a more durable foundation for long-term economic expansion. Through deeper reform and rebalancing, China could also break the deflation trap, which in turn will reinforce its technological progress. Stronger domestic demand is essential because firms need the ability to sell products and services at healthy prices in the home market. Ultimately, China would benefit from a demand-driven ecosystem, one that gives companies the confidence to invest, hire and spend more on research and development. If policymakers continue to deepen their understanding of this dynamic and deliver the reforms required, China’s Industrial Revolution 5.0 could become not only a technological transformation, but also a more sustainable growth model.

title: Spark Study Buddy (Explorer): Teen cyclists booked for breaking bike rules in Tseung Kwan O
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
Read the following text and answer the quiz below.
[1] Hong Kong police have clamped down on bicycle-related offences in Tseung Kwan O. Seven teenagers face prosecution. They allegedly failed to display bike lights at night and cycled on pavements.
[2] Police in Tseung Kwan O made a social media post last month. In it, they said officers had sent summonses to seven boys, aged 14 to 17. It was part of an enforcement operation. The force said the seven teens were facing prosecution for allegedly failing to display a front white light and a rear red light in the dark or in low visibility. The teens also cycled on a pavement “without obvious need”, police said.
[3] The social media post said Tseung Kwan O police would continue enforcement. They want to “combat illegal behaviour and ensure road safety”. The post urged residents to abide by traffic rules.
[4] The number of fatal cycling accidents in Hong Kong more than doubled in the first half of 2026 compared with a year earlier. There were nine deaths recorded. Police believe the rise in accidents is due to cyclists ignoring traffic signals and road signs. In early September, police in the New Territories North issued nine warnings and 159 summonses in two days. The orders were for breaking cycling-related rules. The clampdown came after a safety education campaign in August.
[5] Anyone legally found to have failed to display front white and rear red lights faces a fine under road traffic control regulations. It will cost up to HK$2,000. Anyone caught cycling on the pavement without an obvious need will face a fine of HK$500, or up to three months in jail.
[6] Police also warned against unregistered and unlicensed “electric mobility devices”. The term covers electric scooters, electric skateboards, electric unicycles and electric hoverboards. It also includes power-assisted pedal cycles. Using these on roads, pavements or cycle tracks is illegal. It can lead to imprisonment.
Source: South China Morning Post, September 27

title: Study Buddy (Explorer): From ‘Star Wars’ to rare comics, highlights from the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
[1] George Lucas, creator of the Star Wars and Indiana Jones franchises, and his wife Mellody Hobson want their massive spaceship of a museum to be an experience. The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opened last month in Los Angeles, California, in the United States. There is a lot to take in across 27,000 square metres and 4.5 hectares of park space. Instead of trying to conquer everything, here are some highlights.
[2] Tracey Bates, the museum’s chief executive, said Star Wars comprises only seven per cent of the museum’s inaugural exhibitions. But there is still plenty for fans to sink their teeth into. In the Slavko Vorkapich Theatre on the first floor, you can watch parts of an unreleased animated comedy series called Star Wars Detours . It was created by Lucas as a parody of the franchise in the early 2010s but never aired.
[3] In the “ Star Wars in Motion” exhibition on the fourth floor, you can stand before Luke’s landspeeder from the 1977 original film. The unassuming vehicle stands ready to conjure reverence in anyone who holds childhood memories of that film dear. For sheer spectacle, behold the first physical build of General Grievous’ Wheel Bike, an invention previously only realised in CGI but built specifically for the museum at Lucas’ request.
[4] Lucas is an unabashed comic fan. His love shows in his extensive collection, highlighted in the comics and graphic stories galleries. The crowning glory of the collection is arguably the first Flash Gordon comic strip. There is also an original splash page from Black Panther , as well as Peanuts strips from the 1950s and 60s.
[5] But fans of vintage comics of all kinds will be happy to see panels from Alley-Oop , Garfield , Tarzan and Prince Valiant . Here, as in all the other galleries, looking closely is key to finding hidden treasures. There is a stacked manga gallery for fans of that genre too.
[6] The museum’s library is open to visitors without a ticket and is all dressed up in dark wood, with cosy lighting and plenty of comfortable chairs and tables. A wall of windows looks out onto the lush main lawn, providing both a quiet place to read and a perfect perch for people-watching. It is not a lending library, but you can enjoy the more than 3,000 art books on site.
[7] As an added treat, the third and top floors of shelving contain a variety of art books donated by actor and avid art collector Steve Martin (the public can only access the first floor). On your way out, be sure to leave books on the bright orange carts featuring signs of Yoda imploring guests to follow the golden rule: “Reshelve, do not. Leave books here, you must!”
Source: Tribune News Service, September 22

title: Opinion | How China made climate resilience part of its economic growth strategy
description: What matters is whether climate goals, industrial policy and financial incentives support the same investments, and if responsibility for implementation is clear.
content: The war in the Middle East has disrupted oil and gas supplies, leaving governments to confront energy pressures as they prepare for next month’s Cop31 UN climate conference in Antalya, Turkey. The crisis raises an enduring question: how can climate action strengthen the resilience of an economy? China offers a useful case. Its factories supply technologically advanced products essential to the green transition at competitive prices. China has production cost advantages in electric cars, batteries and equipment for wind and solar power. Behind those products lies a development strategy. China has increasingly brought climate objectives into industrial policy and development planning. That gives the transition a purpose beyond compliance with international agreements: to protect people’s living environment, modernise production and create sources of growth. Understanding this matters for countries seeking to combine lower emissions with industrial development. A study last year by the UN Environment Programme Finance Initiative of China’s green banking system helps explain the connection. National priorities reach businesses through policy directives, investment standards and financial incentives. The lesson is practical: companies need to see where to invest and banks need reasons to finance those investments. The philosophical foundation is “ecological civilisation”, which places a harmonious relationship between economic activity and the natural environment at the centre of China’s vision of development. It expresses an ambition to change how growth is achieved, shifting from resource-intensive production towards innovation, advanced technology and higher productivity. China’s 2021 working guidance on carbon dioxide peaking and carbon neutrality translates that ambition into policy requirements. It calls for climate goals to be incorporated into development plans across sectors and regions. This makes their implementation a responsibility extending well beyond the environmental authorities to officials who shape investment, infrastructure and industrial production. The 2025 white paper “Carbon Peaking and Carbon Neutrality: China’s Plans and Solutions” further connects climate action with technological progress and economic upgrading. New energy industries can create business opportunities; cleaner production can improve competitiveness. These domestic benefits give firms and local authorities reasons to support the transition alongside China’s international commitments. A company considering cleaner production needs confidence in demand for its products and access to affordable financing. Industrial and financial policies can help create these conditions, making climate objectives part of business development decisions. Through these policies, China helped create an environment for companies to compete, innovate and improve manufacturing efficiency. China’s accumulated advantages in production and supply chains, reinforced by policy and financial support, are well documented by the International Energy Agency. China’s 2024 guidelines on accelerating the comprehensive green transition of economic and social development bring together changes in industry and energy with fiscal measures, investment support and greener consumption. As the UNEP study explains, supervisory measures encourage banks to consider environmental risks while project catalogues identify activities eligible for green finance and guide lending decisions. The central bank’s Carbon Emission Reduction Facility, launched in 2021, illustrates the link. It provides qualified lenders with low-cost funding equal to 60 per cent of the principal. Its supported fields include clean energy and emissions reduction technology. This gives banks a financing incentive to support projects consistent with national climate goals. Green finance promotion and environmental risk management reinforce each other. Financing cleaner technologies can help companies reduce their exposure to tighter environmental requirements, while assessing those risks helps banks judge which investments are viable. Implementation also needs to reflect local economic conditions. China combines national direction with local pilot projects, while paying attention to the pace and sequence of change. Beijing’s official principle of “establishing the new before discarding the old” recognises that replacement capacity must be developed before existing capacity is retired. Reliable energy and continuity of production help make the transition workable for businesses and households. Steel, cement and chemicals remain essential to economies still industrialising. Their transformation requires investment in different production processes, cleaner energy and more efficient equipment. Restricting finance to activities labelled as green would leave much of that work undone. Financing the transition of these industries must also be tied to measurable progress in reducing emissions. For a steelmaker, the question is whether financing will help replace an emissions-intensive process with a cleaner one, and how the lender will verify that improvement over time. China has not completed its journey towards a green economy. The 2024 guidelines acknowledge the weight of coal and traditional industries. Success in manufacturing clean technologies must be accompanied by sustained emissions reductions and support for workers and communities affected by industrial change. Countries wishing to learn from China’s experience will need to make their own institutional choices. A financing mechanism suited to China’s banking system may need a different form elsewhere, reflecting differences in political systems and administrative capacity. What matters is whether climate goals, industrial policy and financial incentives support the same investments, and responsibility for implementation is clear. Adopting a subsidy or a green label in isolation cannot provide that coherence.
