Cooperation with China can support this process through affordable equipment and partnerships that develop local skills. Countries can use those opportunities to advance their development priorities, including the capacity to install, operate and maintain new technologies. At Antalya, governments will debate the ambition of their climate commitments, but their prospects for success will largely depend on decisions taken at home: which industries to develop, which infrastructure to build and how to finance the changes. China’s experience shows how decisions about production and finance shape a country’s ability to act on climate change.

title: Falling crucifix kills priest during live-streamed mass in Ecuador
description: Heavy wooden cross detaches from wall above altar, fatally crushing Father Patricio Sanchez against pulpit as horrified parishioners watch.
content: A Catholic priest died on Saturday after a heavy wooden crucifix fell from a wall and crushed him against the pulpit as he celebrated mass in the Ecuadorian port city of Guayaquil. Father Patricio Sanchez was conducting the service at Our Lady of Perpetual Help church when the crucifix detached from the wall directly above the altar. Graphic footage of the live-streamed service, which circulated widely on social media over the weekend, showed the cross fatally striking the priest on the head as he stood facing the congregation. “Father, Father! Call an ambulance!” horrified parishioners could be heard shouting before the live broadcast abruptly cut out. The Archdiocese of Guayaquil mourned Sanchez’s death in a statement expressing “solidarity, affection and love” for his family and friends, writing that the priest had returned to “the house of the Father”. Church officials offered no comment on what caused the cross to fall, and local authorities have not spoken publicly on the incident. Sanchez belonged to the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, a Roman Catholic missionary order founded in 1732 with a presence in more than 80 countries. Guayaquil is Ecuador’s primary commercial port, located roughly 265km (164 miles) southwest of the capital, Quito. Agence France-Presse, Associated Press and dpa

title: Truck crashes into Kansas youth soccer game, killing 2 and injuring 10
description: Wichita police release 34-year-old woman without charges pending toxicology and mechanical tests after her pickup veers onto crowded field.
content: A woman who drove a pickup truck onto a soccer field during a weekend youth game in Kansas, killing two people and injuring 10 others, has been released without charges as the investigation continues, police said Sunday. The 34-year-old woman was released pending results of toxicology tests and a mechanical examination of the vehicle in the aftermath of Saturday’s crash. Her name hasn’t been made public. “Our officers and investigators will continue working to understand exactly what happened,” Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan said, noting that no charges have been filed to date. The woman had one child playing soccer on another field at the Stryker Sports Complex in northeast Wichita when Saturday’s crash occurred, a police statement said. The statement said two of her other children were with her in the pickup truck when it struck multiple children and adults. According to a preliminary investigation, the Chevrolet pickup was parked in a parking space near the soccer fields before it drove onto one of the fields. Police identified those killed at the scene as Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, both of McPherson, Kansas. They were not related. Ten others ranging from 5 years old to 68 were taken to area hospitals with injuries described as non-serious. Investigators say they have interviewed more than 30 witnesses, including the driver and her two children who were her inside the pickup at the time of the crash.

title: Zelensky seeks to ease US tensions as Trump accuses him of stalling peace
description: Ukrainian leader confers with US envoys Kushner and Witkoff as Kyiv and Moscow trade strikes on energy infrastructure.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke with top US envoys Sunday to try to ease tensions, as Donald Trump accused his counterpart of not wanting to end the war with Russia. Zelensky spoke to US officials Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as both Russia and Ukraine hit each other’s energy sites, with Moscow leaving thousands without power and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on St Petersburg since the start of the war in 2022. Trump and Zelensky have clashed as the US president blocked new sanctions on Russia and struck a diesel deal with Moscow, fuelling fears in Kyiv and Europe that the White House was steering towards Moscow. A Wall Street Journal report that Russian President Vladimir Putin proposed a meeting on Ukraine with Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping – but not Zelensky – has set off more alarm bells. On Sunday, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that he was in the process of negotiating peace between Russia and Ukraine and making “great progress”, but claimed: “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did”. “Zelenskyy is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States,” Trump said. Earlier, after speaking to Trump’s business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner, Zelensky said “a lot depends” on the US position in the war but that “it is clear that there are many things that matter to all of us and that this war must be brought to an end”. Ukraine was ready to work “constructively” and “honestly”, he said. “We expect exactly this approach from all our partners – both from the Europeans and, of course, from the American side.” He said he discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defence systems, as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles. Zelensky earlier told US broadcaster NBC it would be a “historic mistake” if Washington formally supported Russia and that he hoped Trump would “change his decisions”. But he also said he was “thankful” the United States resumed intelligence sharing after a pause that left his country vulnerable to Russian missile strikes. A US-led push to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II has so far not brought about a breakthrough and Trump has in the past grown frustrated with both Zelensky and Putin because of their lack of progress. Zelensky spoke to the American officials as he accused Russia of breaking Trump’s “energy ceasefire” 76 times and warned that Moscow planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter. Russian strikes left “tens of thousands” without power in several regions, he said, with Ukrainian officials reporting three people had been killed. Ukraine’s army launched drones at Putin’s hometown of St Petersburg late Sunday, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said. Russia’s VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit and Ozon – Russia’s second largest retailer – also reported a strike on its logistics centre. The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the war. The Kremlin, however, said Ukrainian attacks on its cities will not change its war aims. Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.

title: DR Congo’s fast-moving Ebola outbreak spreads to eighth province
description: The Health Ministry has recorded 2 cases, including 1 death, in Nord-Ubangi province, bordering the Central African Republic.
content: The Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to an eighth province in the country’s north, authorities said on Sunday. The Health Ministry has recorded two cases, including one death, in Nord-Ubangi province, bordering Central African Republic. The ministry said both patients were men in their 20s living in the Wapinda health zone, which borders Bas-Uele province, where Ebola cases have been reported previously. Authorities have recorded at least 9,400 cases, including more than 4,500 deaths, in the outbreak declared in mid-May, making it the deadliest in DR Congo’s history. The virus has spilled over into other countries including neighbouring Uganda, which has since declared itself free of the disease, and Kenya, which recorded a seventh case on Saturday. Central African Republic has not recorded any confirmed cases. Ituri province in eastern DR Congo remains the disease’s epicentre, accounting for almost three quarters of confirmed cases, according to the government’s most recent data, which shows 66 health zones have been affected since the start of the outbreak. “We see pockets of Ebola generally going down, but unfortunately geographically it’s spreading out,” World Health Organization Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi told Associated Press in an interview in Beni, eastern DR Congo, on Friday. Janabi said one of the biggest challenges has been convincing those who are infected to seek medical help, adding that some deaths happen in the community outside health centres. Nord-Ubangi is located between Sud-Ubangi and Bas-Uele, the last two provinces the disease had spread to along the border with Central African Republic, where recurring armed violence has forced thousands to flee and take refuge in Congolese border communities. Access in the region can be difficult due to poor roads and limited communication networks. The spread of the outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment, is fuelled by mass population movements, rebel violence, mistrust and poor working conditions of front-line workers.

title: Macron condemns ‘unbridled’ violence as France faces fresh street clashes
description: French leader threatens rally bans as weekend rioting sees historic town halls torched and shops looted across Paris.
content: French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday slammed the “unbridled” violence that erupted in cost-of-living demonstrations across the country, as police battled protesters and looters in new clashes in Paris. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested Saturday in unrest that represented some of the worst urban violence in France in years, with almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured, seven seriously, the interior ministry said. In an address to the nation, Macron said local authorities would be able to ban – “if necessary” – certain rallies in coming days. But he stopped short of announcing drastic measures, such as a state of emergency or curfew. “Tonight, we all feel anger and shame,” Macron said of the devastation brought by the protests that included town halls burned down and hundreds of businesses looted or damaged. “Looking at these images, we all asked ourselves: what is going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?” said Macron, who insisted there must be a distinction between protesters with “legitimate demands” and “those who destroyed, smashed, and looted”. He vowed the authorities would be “uncompromising” towards the “agitators from ultra-left fringe groups, joined by numerous delinquents” who “unleashed unbridled violence in our cities”. Police fired tear gas and stun grenades Sunday at hundreds of people gathered in a Paris square following social media calls for a gathering that authorities said had not been approved. Bottles and rocks were hurled at police, who made 108 arrests across the city, according to authorities. At least five stores were looted around Republique square. Other stores in central Paris also had windows smashed and the city hall told many to close. In the southeastern city of Lyon, police battled youths who attempted to loot a luxury clothing store. The unrest came just months before a presidential election where centrist Macron cannot stand again and Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, is riding high in the polls. Le Pen said the troubles showed that Macron’s administration was “running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented”. Jean-Luc Melenchon, head of the hard-left France Unbowed party, also running for president, warned that the country could be heading towards “events that will eventually become uncontrollable”. Macron said “our country deserves a fine presidential election”, marked by debates “with the parties, rather than in the streets with violence”. Saturday’s protests had seen unions, the anti-Macron Yellow Vests movement that rattled the early years of his presidency and school students, who had protested for the last weeks, join forces in a show of anger at the cost of living and prospects for young people. With images of French town halls burning and shops being looted grabbing headlines around the world, US President Donald Trump waded into the debate, blaming immigration for the unrest. “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Trump said in a social media post. Macron vowed that top officials would “make decisions in coordination with mayors to protect our cities, public buildings, and businesses”. He said that businesses that suffered would be supported and vowed there would be “full transparency” over the response by security forces to the protests. Some opposition politicians have already called for the sacking of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez. Macron said he had asked Nunez to “draw all necessary lessons”, particularly with regard to intelligence gathering and anticipation, adding he expected “clear answers”. “It’s like we had a war,” 78-year-old Paris resident Mehmet Ozeden said amid burnt street barricades from Saturday’s protests. The city of Limoges lost its 19th century town hall to a fire that the local prefect, Maurice Barate, told news channel LCI had been deliberately set by “a wild horde”. In Lyon, a tourist office in the city centre was set ablaze during the protests amid multiple clashes and looting. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Etienne. In Mulhouse a 17-year-old girl lost an eye, according to prosecutors. The unrest in France came amid a wider wave of cost-of-living protests across Europe over the weekend. In Italy, masked demonstrators clashed with police in Milan’s central Piazza del Duomo, throwing paving stones and looting shops, while strikes and rallies also hit Turin, Bologna and Rome. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called an emergency meeting for Monday, declaring: “Demonstrating is a right; setting our cities on fire is not”. In Belgium, police arrested some 150 people on Saturday as unions and students demonstrated against education cuts and government budget plans, while hundreds of demonstrators set up tent encampments in Lisbon and Porto to protest Portugal’s escalating housing and cost-of-living crisis. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Trump endorses ‘great warrior’ Netanyahu as tight Israeli election looms
description: US leader offers ‘total endorsement’ ahead of October 27 vote, but declining support among Israelis may limit impact for embattled ally.
content: US President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu as the long-time Israeli prime minister struggles for an edge in next week’s parliamentary election. Trump praised Netanyahu as a “great warrior prime minister” and peace partner, crediting him with joining the United States in launching strikes on Iran in February. The conflict, in its seventh month, has disrupted energy markets globally and wreaked havoc across the Middle East, damaging critical infrastructure and destabilising regional ‌economies. “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. “Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived! I have watched Bibi under the most trying of times. Normal men or women in such situations would have wilted under the pressure – But Bibi did not wilt, he actually got stronger, and maintains that same Strength today.” In his message, addressed to “the Great People of Israel”, Trump added: “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel”. The Trump endorsement is ⁠not certain to give Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party a boost in the October 27 national election, as Israeli public support for Trump has diminished amid Israeli-US disagreements over Iran. Polls have ‌suggested no candidate has a clear path to power. Israel’s prime minister is chosen through coalition-building in parliament rather than by direct popular vote. It will be Israel’s first vote since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil, as ‌Israel went to war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. The election could determine whether Netanyahu remains in power after one of the most consequential periods in Israel’s history, ⁠or is defeated by centrist rivals promising ⁠to usher in a new era. Netanyahu promptly expressed his thanks to his “dear friend Donald” on X, saying: “Together we will complete the mission!” Trump has broken with long-time US tradition by endorsing candidates in elections in foreign countries including Hungary, Colombia, Argentina, ‌Japan and Honduras. Trump’s relationship with Netanyahu has been close but also fractious, with the president at times publicly and privately criticising Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. The war that the US and Israel launched against Iran is unpopular with Americans, ‌who ‌vote November 3 in congressional elections, while support for Israel among Americans has also decreased over the Iran war and Israel’s conduct in the three-year war in Gaza that Trump has promised ‌to end. Both leaders on Sunday mentioned finishing the job in Iran. Tamar Hermann, a senior research fellow at the non-partisan Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem, said Trump’s late endorsement could help win ⁠back wavering Netanyahu voters but was unlikely to draw widespread support. Most Israelis, even those who are critical of Netanyahu and his government, were largely in favour of the Iran war. In an ⁠election this close, “it couldn’t hurt him, and it might help,” said analyst Aaron David Miller of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington. Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls show. That could lead to Netanyahu serving as a caretaker prime minister ‌while another election is held. The US president passed ‌up earlier opportunities to endorse Netanyahu, perhaps because he wanted to see what leverage he could exercise on issues like Gaza or Lebanon, said Miller. In the end, he said, Trump sided with a leader he sees as strong and unfairly persecuted. “However angry Trump may be at Netanyahu for pushing this Iran war, this in the end was a Trump decision,” Miller added. A Trump decision not to endorse Netanyahu would have raised “legitimate questions about whether or not the whole Iran venture was in fact something Trump should have done,” he said.

title: Lifts at 74 more buildings serviced by Taizoom lack safety parts, taking total to 152
description: Figure expected to rise further as about 180 more buildings serviced by Hong Kong company not yet checked, authorities say.
content: Hong Kong authorities have said lifts at 74 more private buildings installed by Taizoom Elevator are missing crucial door frame components, taking the total of affected properties to 152. The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department provided the updated figures on Sunday night as citywide inspections of all lifts handled by Taizoom were carried out. The door frame components help protect lift occupants against flames and smoke in the event of a fire, an expert earlier explained. According to the department, 150 of the affected premises are private residential or commercial buildings, while the remaining two are public housing estates under the Tenants Purchase Scheme. It warned that the figure was expected to rise further as about 180 more buildings serviced by Taizoom had not yet been checked. While prioritising checks on Taizoom’s lifts, the department was also progressively inspecting works carried out by other registered contractors, it said. All registered lift contractors have been ordered to review their work at similar buildings stretching back a decade. Property management companies and incorporated owners of the affected buildings are being notified of the findings. “The installation works for the missing door frame components will be carried out under the supervision of the [EMSD], with all costs borne by the contractor,” it said, adding that random checks would be conducted once rectification works were completed. Installation works had already begun at the two public housing estates and a private building, while rectification works at the remaining properties would start as soon as possible, it said. The department has enlisted the Lift and Escalator Contractors Association and other industry players to assist, anticipating that installation works at most buildings could begin within a few days. Police arrested a director of Taizoom Elevator and two registered lift engineers on Friday on suspicion of deception after safety certificates were submitted allegedly claiming the works were fully completed.

title: Lithuanians take shelter, Nato jets scramble as suspected drone explodes
description: A suspected drone exploded over Lithuania ⁠after triggering an alert that forced residents in northern and central areas to seek shelter.
content: A suspected drone exploded over Lithuania ⁠after triggering an alert that forced residents in northern and central areas to seek shelter for an hour on Sunday morning, the president and other defence officials said. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said later it regretted the incident in Lithuania’s airspace, adding that it may have resulted from Russian ‌electronic warfare diverting drones off course. The object flew into Lithuania’s airspace from Poland, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters, after proposing a joint investigation to his Polish counterpart. “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of Nato and EU,” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said on social media. “What appears to be a drone exploded over the northern part of the country, posing a danger to the ⁠civilian population,” he added. Nato scrambles jets Poland’s military said it was also verifying a possible violation of its airspace by ‌an unidentified object. A Polish Defence Ministry spokesperson later said radar systems did not confirm the object crossing the border into Lithuania, but added that Polish authorities were remaining in contact ‌with Lithuanian officials. During the “red” alert, Nato fighter jets were scrambled to the area, and Kaunas airport, ⁠near Lithuania’s second-largest city, was ⁠temporarily closed, the Lithuanian government’s crisis management centre said. Aircraft of the transatlantic security alliance were unable to visually identify the object due to cloudy weather and ‌did not attempt to shoot it down, the centre said. Lithuanian army personnel were investigating possible drone debris near Juodzionys village in northern Lithuania, after the object ‌disappeared from ‌radar, possibly after exploding, the centre said. Some of the debris struck a civilian vehicle, the defence minister said. “We can ‌confirm that two Italian Eurofighter jets were scrambled earlier today in response to a drone over Lithuanian airspace,” a Nato ⁠official said. “The aircraft were operating under Nato command. An investigation is ongoing, and Nato remains in close contact ⁠with the Lithuanian authorities,” the official said, adding that the alliance was ready and able to react to any potential threat. Northern neighbour Latvia briefly issued a “yellow” air warning in some regions bordering Lithuania, citing ‌a “possible threat”, its army said. Ukrainian ‌drones have repeatedly entered Nato airspace in the Baltic region in recent months. Kyiv has said they were steered off course by Russian signal jamming. This has stoked concerns that Russia’s war in Ukraine is spilling over Nato’s borders.

title: Hong Kong to review Peak lighting installation after outcry over felled trees
description: Tourism Board will review light trail project following public outcry over chopped flowers, trees and “eyesore” devices.
content: Hong Kong tourism authorities have pledged to review the roll-out of a lighting project along a trail on The Peak after mounting complaints that flowers and trees were chopped down to make way for the installations. But the Tourism Board defended the project, saying it had consulted local residents and sought advice from tree experts to minimise the impact on the surrounding environment. In a statement on Sunday, the board said it valued residents’ views and would now “conduct broader consultation to review the overall arrangements of the project” to “refine its details, with a view to achieving a balance between tourism development, environmental protection and residents’ needs”. Small light installations were planned for selected points along the walking trail to add new features to The Peak’s attractions. They were originally intended to form part of a new light show staged alongside the coming Hong Kong WinterFest. “The initiative aims to further enhance the appeal of Hong Kong’s nighttime tourism and showcase the city’s unique charm as an international metropolis,” the board said. The installations feature a soft, low-glare lighting design and were planned to operate from 7pm to 10pm on a 12-month trial basis, according to the board. But the plan sparked an outcry after some residents complained on social media that flowers and trees had been chopped down to make way for the lights. Critics also labelled the installations an eyesore that ruined the neighbourhood’s natural ambience. One user wrote: “Taste has no bottom line, aesthetics has no lower limit …. Why not spend the money on planting more flowers and trees or building more public washrooms?” In response, the board argued it had consulted the local district council in April and also briefed residents in May and September on the project’s purpose and progress. It also said it had consulted various government departments and tree experts “on tree protection and the installation of light fittings”. “The selection of trees for the project, the method of hanging the light fittings, the tree protection measures, the load-bearing arrangements and the installation methods are all subject to endorsement by registered arborists. “Upon completion of installation, the light fittings will also be inspected by arborists and monitored regularly,” it said. The board added it would announce the latest arrangements for the project “in due course”.

title: Davidovich Fokina beats Jodar to win Shanghai crown; Chwalinska ⁠wins first title in Wuhan
description: Win in all-Spanish final sees ⁠Davidovich Fokina rise ⁠to career-high world No 13 as Poland’s Chwalinska sees off world No 170 Kartal.
content: Alejandro Davidovich Fokina ended Rafael Jodar’s dream run at the Shanghai Masters on Sunday, battling back to beat ‌his fellow Spaniard 1-6, 7-6, 6-4 and clinch the biggest title of his career. In Wuhan, meanwhile, French ⁠Open finalist ⁠Maja Chwalinska ⁠won her first title on the WTA tour as she shook off early nerves to beat Sonay ‌Kartal 2-6, 6-4, 6-2 at the Wuhan Open final. The 25th-seeded Davidovich Fokina is set to climb 13 places to a career-high world No 13 when the rankings are released on Monday. Jodar, playing in his first Masters 1000 final and the youngest Shanghai finalist in tournament history, made ⁠a blistering start, broke for a 2-0 lead and again to take the opening ‌set. Davidovich Fokina recovered from a break down in the second set and saved break points in three successive service games before edging ‌a tight tiebreak to force a decider. The momentum swung decisively in Davidovich ⁠Fokina’s favour when ⁠he broke the 12th-seeded Jodar twice and sealed victory in two hours and 27 minutes. “I have a blank ‌mind,” Davidovich Fokina said. “I don’t know what to say and I don’t know how I feel. Just a ‌huge relief. “After ‌the first set I had to keep trying, keep pushing. In the tiebreak, ‌I believed in myself again. In the third set, maybe I had a bit ⁠more fitness physically. “He’s an amazing player and it was very tough to play against him.” It was the third ATP singles title of the 27-year-old’s career, adding to ⁠his ATP 250 triumphs in Chengdu and Mallorca this season. The first meeting between the two Spaniards pitted one of the ATP Tour’s rising talents against ‌a player enjoying the ‌best season of his career. The 20-year-old Jodar, who was ranked outside the world’s top 900 little more than a year ago, strengthened his bid to qualify for the ATP Finals in Turin in his first full season on tour. Over at Wuhan, left-hander Chwalinska deployed a defensive right-handed lob to disrupt Kartal’s flow and outwitted the ⁠Briton with changes in direction and winners into ‌the corners. Briton Kartal, 170th in the WTA rankings and the ‌lowest-ranked finalist in a WTA 1000 tournament, ⁠dominated ⁠the first set with powerful forehands as her ‌Polish opponent’s drop shots and slices kept landing wide. But ‌25-year-old Chwalinska, ‌fresh off a win over ‌childhood friend Iga Swiatek, fought back in ⁠the second set, dragging Kartal into long ⁠rallies and earning three breaks to force a decider. Chwalinska, playing in her ‌second final ‌on tour, finished off the match by winning four games in a row.

title: China urged to copy Pentagon’s hi-tech warfare project without US conflicts of interest
description: Project Meridian, which is co-chaired by Elon Musk, is looking to identify the technology needed for future warfare.
content: China has been urged to learn from a Pentagon project to assess future warfare but warned to avoid the potential conflicts of interest and other shortcomings of the US defence review. Project Meridian, launched late last month, is designed to identify future battlefield requirements and prioritise investment, with a focus on areas such as artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, directed energy, robotics and biotechnology. In an analysis published on Friday, the Beijing-based think tank Blue Army Open-Source Intelligence Research Institute suggested China should draw lessons from its assessment of different military domains, collaboration between military and civilian analysts and emphasis on linking technological development with operational requirements. It said the project – led by Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer, and the Mitre Corporation – reflected Washington’s efforts to adapt to the rapid pace of commercial technological development and address long-standing challenges in coordinating military requirements, research funding and procurement. The report said its main strengths were its cross-sector team of analysts, rapid 120-day assessment cycle and focus on areas such as space and cyber warfare alongside more traditional military domains. “The initiative has established a modern assessment chain of ‘demand-driven requirements, technology screening, gap identification, and institutional adoption,’ effectively aligning with the contemporary trend where commercial technology drives military innovation,” it said. The authors said China should adopt an integrated approach to assessing defence technologies, moving beyond isolated evaluations of individual weapons systems or military services. They also urged the country to identify gaps in joint operations, including weaknesses in data sharing, communications links, system compatibility and logistical support. The report called for a two-tier assessment mechanism combining continuous monitoring of global technological developments with time-limited reviews of specific capability gaps. Such reviews should bring together the military, research institutes, defence contractors, universities and civilian technology companies to improve both the quality and speed of decision-making. Another priority should be establishing a clear pathway from technological assessment to operational deployment, the think tank said. Each recommendation should specify the operational requirement it addressed, the existing capability gap, the technology’s maturity, the organisation responsible for implementation, as well as testing conditions and funding requirements, the report said. “[China] should establish a complete closed loop of assessment, project initiation, prototyping, testing, force validation, large-scale deployment, and review and optimisation, and fully incorporate adjustments to doctrine, organisation, talent, training and support systems into the process of converting technology into combat capability,” it added. However, the report also said that the involvement of business leaders who already had defence contracts in the Pentagon review raised the risk of conflicts of interest. It further argued that the 120-day timetable for completing the report would limit its effectiveness. The US project is co-chaired by SpaceX boss Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey, the co-founder of defence technology firm Anduril Industries, and former House speaker Newt Gingrich. “Rapid assessment cannot replace detailed systems engineering analysis, cost assessments, adversarial validation and full life-cycle risk evaluations,” the report noted. It added that China must devise ways to establish what can be easily transformed into operational combat power. The analysis recommended that any comparable Chinese study should have independent reviews. There should also be mandatory disclosure of conflicts of interest and companies should not evaluate their own products or influence procurement decisions. “China should selectively adopt the strengths of Project Meridian while addressing its shortcomings, including insufficient validation, an overly broad scope and conflicts of interest … to build a defence technology assessment system that is driven by clearly defined requirements, supported by robust evidence, subject to independent evaluation, linked to a complete implementation process and equipped with effective risk controls.” The Pentagon review coincides with plans to establish a US command covering unmanned and autonomous warfare.

title: In Focus | The AI promise was automation. The reality? Managing digital workers
description: As businesses race to build AI workforces, supervising them is becoming the next big challenge.
content: When artificial intelligence agents first arrived, they came with a tantalising promise: autonomous “digital workers” that would finally free humans from corporate drudgery. As businesses across Asia are discovering, however, the reality is quite the opposite – more work, new friction and a whole new layer of management. When Xiao Mengjie, an AI product marketing manager at a Big Tech firm in Shanghai, recently assigned two AI agents what she described as a simple task, she expected efficiency. Instead, she got corporate gridlock. Rather than dividing the workload, her agent and her supervisor’s agent locked in a prolonged discussion over responsibilities, debating who should verify details and which one should take ownership of different tasks, in a spectacle not unlike the human bureaucracy they had been hired to replace. “It became very formal and cumbersome,” Xiao said. “Agents can create communication overhead too.” Across Asia, businesses have eagerly bought into the pitch of autonomous software capable of planning and executing multistep workflows with limited human intervention. But from Singapore’s hotels and insurers to Hong Kong’s service sector and mainland China’s tech giants, enterprises are confronting a sharp reality check. The surge in regional adoption reflects a broader global frenzy for autonomous software. Meta Platforms’ personal agent, Muse, launched in September, drew an estimated 2.8 million downloads in its first two weeks. In mainland China, enthusiasm for OpenClaw, an open-source agent, sparked a craze known locally as “raising lobsters”, prompting hundreds of people to queue outside Tencent Holdings’ headquarters in Shenzhen earlier this year for help installing the software. Tech titans including Tencent, Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post, and Baidu have all introduced agent-focused enterprise products. Yet the rush to deploy AI agents has exposed a gap between what the technology can do and how effectively organisations can manage it. Why some businesses struggle to put AI to work At times, users find that seemingly straightforward workflows become challenging puzzles once they are handed over to autonomous agents. At Singapore-based hospitality technology start-up Conzi, chief operating officer Mark Wee wants AI agents to handle the multi-departmental, behind-the-scenes work that often pulls hotel staff away from guest care. For example, when a hotel guest leaves a scathing review, the complaint can trigger a lengthy chain of work behind the scenes. A receptionist must respond, a manager investigates what went wrong, and a supervisor checks records to determine who was responsible. The hotel might even revise its operating procedures. But deploying AI agents to manage complex hotel operations is easier said than done. A single guest complaint could involve multiple departments, from housekeeping to hotel management, requiring agents to navigate fragmented systems and determine when human intervention was needed, Wee said. The challenge is compounded by operational knowledge that is often scattered across spreadsheets, paper records and the heads of experienced employees. Wee said Conzi was working to consolidate this information so its agents could coordinate tasks across departments, but he stressed that technology alone was not enough. “If you don’t get the buy-in from the people who are supposed to use the systems the most, any system in any organisation will fail,” Wee said. Similar obstacles confronted Asia’s travel industry, where differing regulations, technical standards and disconnected platforms complicated AI deployment, according to Prabu Sangar, director of technology operations and integration at FCM Travel Asia, a corporate travel management company. “Even if the AI is as capable as it is, the surrounding environment may not be ready for it,” he said. In Hong Kong, companies were trying to accelerate AI adoption while contending with “legacy” technology systems and organisational resistance, said Robert Hah, Hong Kong office lead at consultancy Accenture Greater China. Only 10 per cent of Hong Kong companies surveyed had integrated generative AI across multiple business functions, compared with about 21 per cent of mainland Chinese enterprises, according to Accenture. Leo Wong, co-founder of Hong Kong-based business communications platform imBee, said demand for AI agents had grown among customers across Hong Kong, Singapore and Malaysia, but concerns over data security were slowing adoption, especially in Hong Kong. The company provides AI-powered tools that help businesses manage customer communications across WhatsApp, email and other messaging platforms. Wong said banks, insurers and other financial services companies were particularly cautious, with deployment decisions taking longer as they worked through their AI strategies and security requirements. Organisations wanted to build confidence in the technology before deploying it, he added. I already have lots of ideas, and AI makes more of them feel achievable, so I start more projects. Then every project is waiting for my judgment, and I end up being the busiest person Xiao Mengjie, AI product marketing manager Wang Jiangyu, professor of law and associate dean at City University of Hong Kong, said the institutional mechanisms needed to govern autonomous agents had struggled to keep pace with their technical development. “The governance challenge today is less about creating more powerful AI and more about ensuring that increasingly capable systems remain accountable and aligned with human objectives,” he said. While AI systems had become more capable of executing tasks autonomously and coordinating with one another, questions including how decisions should be reviewed and who bore responsibility for those decisions remained unresolved, he said. Too many agents? In their eagerness to automate, some enterprises are discovering that more agents do not automatically translate into higher productivity. At imBee, a company with around 50 to 60 employees, at least several hundred AI agents helped staff perform tasks ranging from software development to internal communications, according to Wong. Wong, who described himself as non-technical, said he personally managed more than 20 agents, which in turn coordinated other agents. While imBee used quality checks and verification procedures to avoid major errors, according to Wong, other workplaces reported that stacking agents simply duplicated existing corporate bloat. “The market is over the phase of ‘agent maxing,’” said Raunak Mehta, co-founder and CEO of Singapore-based insurance technology company Igloo. Operating across Southeast Asia with about 230 employees, Igloo uses software workers for customer service, software development, claims processing and financial reconciliation. Mehta said total agent count was no longer a meaningful measure of operational success. Instead, the focus had shifted towards “agent harnesses” – control frameworks that coordinated agents, regulated their access to internal tools and allowed human oversight. Leading AI agents – including Meta’s Muse, Tencent’s Xiaowei agent, and Manus 2.0 – increasingly rely on such harnesses to better understand users and drive long-term platform adoption. Without proper harnesses, companies faced what Sangar of FCM Travel Asia called “agent sprawl” – a chaotic proliferation of autonomous software across departments with conflicting permissions, overlapping data sources and unintended interactions. Uncoordinated agents can also compound mistakes across entire workflows. “One agent might report that a task is complete when it has merely produced a draft,” AI product marketing manager Xiao said. “Another agent could mistake that output for an approved decision and act on it, allowing errors to spread.” Compounding the risks, hotels and financial institutions must expose vast amounts of proprietary data to extract the full value of AI, increasing their exposure to cyber threats. “There is definitely a risk of rogue actors approaching us and trying to maliciously extract information,” Conzi’s Wee said. Teaching people how to brief, review and correct an agent matters as much as the technology itself Lionel Sim, The AI Capitol Recent incidents have highlighted the risks of giving AI agents access to sensitive information and the authority to act without human approval. Last month, Chinese AI start-up Z.ai said it had temporarily disabled certain features of its ZCode coding assistant after developers reported that the software was uploading local code repositories to cloud servers without their consent. The company, also known as Zhipu, apologised and patched the vulnerability. A Reuters investigation published last month found that AI agents from Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot AI systematically lied, hid failures and fabricated results during controlled tests. Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment. In another high-profile case, an OpenAI agent undergoing security evaluation broke out of its sandbox environment and breached systems at AI platform Hugging Face. The risks have drawn the attention of regulators. Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority has recommended that businesses restrict agents’ access to sensitive systems, define limits on their autonomy and establish mechanisms to shut them down when they malfunction. The Cyberspace Administration of China has also mandated that companies complete mandatory algorithm filings and pre-deployment security assessments before rolling out agents, particularly those handling sensitive data or customer-facing operations. Rise of the AI middle manager Li Jiahao, a researcher specialising in global AI development at the Guangzhou Institute of the Greater Bay Area, said China had issued several AI regulatory documents quite rapidly over the past year, but these did not immediately translate into accountability mechanisms. In both China and the rest of the world, “AI’s technical capabilities are iterating on a quarterly basis, regulations are iterating yearly, and liability is being determined case by case”, he said. “These three curves are moving at completely different speeds, and the gap between them is still growing.” As digital agents multiply, the fundamental operational bottleneck is shifting from computing power back to human supervisors. Lionel Sim, founder of AI research firm The AI Capitol, said AI agent adoption in Asia was outpacing management. Employees were deploying agents “on their own initiative”, which was “great for momentum”, but companies did not have oversight of access, ownership and active tools, he said. The adoption of AI agents has also resulted in a “skills shift”, pushing employees into management roles. “Teaching people how to brief, review and correct an agent matters as much as the technology itself,” Sim added. For workers like Xiao, managing AI agents can be intensely stressful. While agents can work continuously and at a rapid pace, humans do not gain more hours in the day to supervise them. “I already have lots of ideas, and AI makes more of them feel achievable, so I start more projects,” Xiao said. “Then every project is waiting for my judgment, and I end up being the busiest person.” Mehta of Igloo warned that growing reliance on agents could create a longer-term problem: companies might eventually struggle to find employees with the experience needed to supervise them. Li, the Guangzhou researcher, said AI might not suddenly cause mass unemployment, but it was likely to narrow the door for young people entering the workforce as companies scaled back hiring. “Strong AI management capability means finding ways to turn the efficiency gains from AI into more new jobs, and weak management capability may simply mean companies save on labour costs while society bears the cost of youth unemployment,” he said. Despite the growing pains, industry experts believe there is no turning back. Chen Bo, a senior research fellow at the East Asian Institute of the National University of Singapore, described the current stage of AI development as “a wild growth phase”, with significant risks emerging around coordination, accountability and other areas. “But when a major technological revolution comes along – when everyone is facing the AI revolution – the only real option is to ride its development while limiting the downsides, not to hold it back because of them,” he said.

title: Elderly Hong Kong couple die in suspected suicide pact over Parkinson’s diagnosis
description: Daughter discovers parents unconscious at Tuen Mun flat after friend raises alarm over unanswered phone calls.
content: Hong Kong police are investigating a suspected suicide pact after an elderly couple were found dead in a public housing flat on Sunday, following the woman’s Parkinson’s disease diagnosis. Police received a report at 2.39pm on Sunday that a man and a woman had been found unconscious inside a flat at King Wing House in Shan King Estate in Tuen Mun. A tray of burnt charcoal was found at the scene. The couple, a 72-year-old man surnamed Cheung and a 69-year-old woman surnamed Tse, were rushed to Tuen Mun Hospital where they were later pronounced dead. The case was initially classified as a suspected suicide pact but later changed to “dead on arrival” and was being investigated by the Tuen Mun district crime squad. A source said the couple had been in a relationship for 50 years and lived together in the flat. They were not married but had a daughter. Tse had recently been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. It was understood that the daughter was told by a friend of her mother that repeated phone calls and knocks on the door had gone unanswered, although the phone could be heard ringing inside the flat. Concerned for her parents’ safety, the daughter went to the flat and opened the door with her key. She found them lying unconscious in the bathroom beside the tray of burnt charcoal and immediately called police. When emergency responders arrived, the man displayed no signs of life, while the woman still had a weak pulse and shallow breathing. Both were taken to hospital for emergency treatment but were later pronounced dead. Police recovered a suicide note inside the flat and noted no signs of a struggle or fight at the scene. Initial investigations suggest the couple entered into the pact because they were unable to bear the suffering caused by Tse’s illness. The exact cause of death has yet to be confirmed by an autopsy. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Hurricane Trudy threatens Mexican coast with flooding, mudslides
description: The Mexican navy urged mariners and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution because of high waves, heavy rain and the risk of flooding and mudslides.
content: Hurricane Trudy lashed parts of Mexico’s Pacific coast with heavy rain and strong winds on Sunday as the US National Hurricane Centre warned of potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides. A hurricane warning remained in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco. The latest NHC data showed the Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165kph) moving northwest off Mexico’s Pacific coast at 10 mph (17kph). Meanwhile, Typhoon Champi was moving away from Guam as a Category 4 super typhoon. Trudy’s centre was expected to remain near the Mexican coast through Sunday evening before moving south of the Baja California Peninsula on Monday and Tuesday. A tropical storm warning remained in effect for Las Islas Marias. A warning for the coast east of Punta San Telmo to Lazaro Cardenas had been discontinued. The Mexican navy urged mariners and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution because of high waves, heavy rain and the risk of rising rivers, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas. Colima authorities said the risks remained low, but warned that heavy rainfall could cause damage because the ground was already saturated by successive storms along the Pacific coast. Trudy was expected to bring 4-8 inches (10-20 centimetres) of rain through the weekend, with isolated totals of around 12 inches (30 centimetres) along and near the coast in Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco. The hurricane centre warned of potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas with steep terrain. Also in the Pacific, Champi was moving away from Guam on Sunday after passing close to the island’s southern tip, with sustained winds of 150 mph (240kph). Late on Sunday afternoon it was 200 miles (320 kilometres) west of Guam, moving west at 14 mph (23kph), according to the US National Weather Service. The storm was forecast to weaken through Monday but remain a major typhoon. All tropical cyclone watches and warnings for Guam, Rota, Tinian and Saipan had been cancelled. The governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands requested emergency disaster declarations on Friday. On Saturday, US President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Guam authorising the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate all federal disaster relief efforts. FEMA announced that federal disaster help was available for the territory of Guam to supplement local response efforts following Typhoon Champi. Airports, harbours and some health facilities in the territories were closed. Resources were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days, according to updates on Saturday from FEMA. The territories are still recovering from super typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which struck in April and July, respectively.

title: Katie Zacharia and Mao Ning – a study in contrasts in US and China media strategies
description: Trump’s press secretary and China's foreign ministry spokeswoman serve as the public faces of their countries.
content: Katie Zacharia may have lasted just five days as the White House press secretary but still managed to set off a diplomatic incident with China. In an interview with a conservative commentator on Thursday, Zacharia referred to China as a place that “doesn’t even have proper toilets”. Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning responded a day later with a smile and a brief, pointed invitation. “We welcome her to visit China more often when she has the opportunity,” said Mao, a veteran diplomat. Like Mao, Zacharia was – if only for less than a week – the highly visible public face of her government, speaking on issues that could shape how her country was perceived. But Mao and Zacharia are the products of vastly different systems and took contrasting paths to the podium, using very different ways to tell two very different stories. Worlds apart Zacharia’s debut – and final – official White House briefing lasted fewer than 15 minutes on Tuesday, with much of her presentation delivered from a prepared script. By then, questions had surfaced about her legal credentials after she had presented herself as a lawyer in media appearances. According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm, one of China’s biggest, in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. Before joining the White House, she was a frequent commentator on conservative networks Fox News and Newsmax, where she defended US President Donald Trump and his agenda. She had also briefly held a communications role at the Department of Homeland Security. As she stepped into one of the most visible communications positions in the US government, Zacharia found herself becoming the story. Asked about her legal credentials, she said she had received them “when I moved to China”, before later saying she had misheard the question. By the weekend, she was no longer in the White House job. In China’s foreign ministry spokesperson system, officials generally have extensive diplomatic experience and undergo substantial preparation before taking on the position. Another difference is in the scope of their roles. A foreign ministry spokesperson is among the Chinese government’s most prominent and regular public-facing representatives, communicating Beijing’s positions on diplomacy and international affairs. By contrast, the White House press secretary’s responsibilities extend beyond explaining domestic and foreign policy. As a presidential appointee, the spokesperson is also expected to defend the president’s agenda and respond to political criticism on their behalf. Zacharia was appointed to the role just three weeks before the midterm elections, at a politically sensitive time with Trump’s approval ratings at near-record lows. Her debut briefing on October 13 combined praise for Trump and his “America first” agenda, taking questions from just three reporters before wrapping up. She left a question about Ukraine unanswered, saying she would have to return to it, prompting further doubts about her readiness for the position. Her predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, had also used her first briefing to frame a major development involving China through the lens of US domestic politics. Describing the emergence of Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) company DeepSeek as a “wake-up call” for the US AI industry, she blamed the previous Joe Biden administration for allowing China to develop the technology so rapidly. Different paths China’s foreign ministry formally established its spokesperson system in March 1983, during the country’s reform and opening-up drive. A year earlier, Qian Qichen had held what is regarded as the ministry’s first press conference. He later rose through the diplomatic ranks to become foreign minister and vice-premier. The ministry’s spokespersons are career diplomats who typically gather years of experience in foreign affairs before taking on the high-profile role. Mao became the ministry’s 33rd spokesperson in September 2022 and was appointed director general of its information department in January 2025. Before taking on the chief spokesperson role, Mao had spent more than 27 years in diplomatic service, focusing mainly on Asian affairs. She had also briefly served in a local government position as deputy mayor in 2020. Qin Gang, who was later removed from office, also served two stints as a ministry spokesman before rising to become foreign minister in 2022. By contrast, White House press secretaries often come from political communications, campaign work or media backgrounds. Leavitt, for example, worked in Trump’s first administration, served as communications director for Republican congresswoman Elise Stefanik and was national press secretary for Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign before taking the White House job in January 2025. The contrast reflects the different institutional functions of the two positions. The White House press secretary speaks mainly for the president and his administration, defending its policies while responding to domestic political scrutiny. China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, by comparison, communicates the government’s positions on international affairs through regular briefings, which have been held each weekday since 2011. Method and manner For Beijing, public communication is part of a broader effort to shape how China is understood abroad, with the foreign ministry enlisted to “tell China’s story well”. To this end, Chinese spokespersons’ comments are measured and carefully scripted, sometimes using subtle and indirect language. A 2022 commentary in Shanghai news outlet The Paper defended this style of communication as a strategic buffer, saying that avoiding definitive statements left room for manoeuvre without boxing officials into a position that could prove difficult to defend. That is poles apart from the more combative style associated with some US White House press secretaries. Leavitt, for instance, became known for her sharp retorts and rapid-fire responses, which also won praise from some Chinese social media users impressed by her verbal agility. Her language was direct and combative, consistent with the political messaging that had defined her work on Trump’s campaign. But the Chinese spokesperson is usually more measured – something Mao in particular is known for. Nevertheless, China’s roster of spokespeople has also included more controversial figures, most notably Zhao Lijian, who became a prominent face of the Wolf Warrior style of diplomacy. The style, named after a Chinese nationalist action-film franchise, is commonly used to describe an assertive and confrontational approach to defending China’s interests and responding to foreign criticism. Critics argue that such confrontational messaging risks damaging China’s diplomatic relationships, while supporters see it as a forceful response to Western criticism.

title: Wang Wei-hsuan makes it second time lucky in Macau, beats Im Sung-jae to claim Open crown
description: Taiwan golfer gets better of South Korean rival in play-off, exactly a year after losing a sudden-death showdown at Macau Golf and Country Club.
content: Wang Wei-hsuan made sure lightning did not strike twice at the SJM Macau Open, winning in a play-off almost a year after a sudden death shoot-out shattered his hopes of taking the title. Just 364 days after a heartbreaking loss to Germany’s Dominic Foos, the Taiwanese golfer got the better of South Korea’s Im Sung-jae in a final-round battle that went right down to the 72nd hole and beyond. Trailing by a shot heading down the par-5 18th at Macau Golf and Country Club, Wang chipped in for an eagle to move ahead, only for his rival to grab a birdie, and their matching three-under-par 67s left them tied on 17 under overall. But unlike last year, Wang would not be denied and he birdied the 18th moments later to win his first Asian Tour title. “After I chipped in on the 18th and then went to the scoring and then came back for the play-off, I could only think of last year. I’m very happy that I could get the job this time and win, and I’m really happy that I could do it in front of my wife and family,” Wang, who dedicated the win to his mother, said. While Wang and Im were battling back and forth in the day’s last pairing, Charles Porter was having the sort of day that often ends with a trophy. The 2.06m (6ft 9in) American, who has been battling illness all week, powered his way to a nine-under 61 that ultimately left him alone in third place on 14 under, one ahead of compatriot Austen Truslow. China’s Wu Ashun and Thailand’s Danthai Boonma recorded identical scores of 65 to tie for fifth place on 12 under. “It was completely out of nowhere,” Porter said. “Physically and mentally, this week has been a complete grind, and I felt terrible, to be honest. My body’s felt horrible. So, to shoot 61 out of nowhere and make a couple chip-ins in the first five holes was unexpected, but that’s how golf is sometimes.” Elsewhere, Yin Ruoning celebrated back-to-back LPGA Tour titles with a thrilling one-stroke victory in Shanghai. The home hero carded a final-round four-under 68 at Sheshan Golf Club to emerge victorious from a showdown with overnight leader Choi Hye-jin. The 24-year-old Yin, winner at the FM Championship in Boston in August on her previous start on tour, finished on 11 under, one shot clear of her rival. It was Yin’s seventh LPGA title and her second in Shanghai, having won the event in 2024. “I think this tournament means everything to me because you have the chance to play in front of all your family and friends and in front of all the amazing fans,” she said. “It’s just amazing. “I mean, I still have emotions, but this time very calm, more calm than FM,” she said, comparing her understated celebration this time with her jubilant win two months ago. “I think it’s a dream come true to win at home, and I think I’m lucky to win it twice. I hope this is just the beginning.” South Korea’s Amy Yang was third on eight-under, with Japan’s Rio Takeda another shot back.

title: My Take | Why Plato-to-Nato Western myth is being resurrected
description: The Western civilisation narrative, which now sounds more like from Plato to Trump with the far-right, hides the real goal of American imperialism 2.0.
content: Standing before the Acropolis in Athens earlier this month, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the West’s story “the greatest story ever known to man”. But didn’t Hollywood tell us the greatest story ever told was that of Jesus of Nazareth? The decisions of the coming decade, Rubio said, “will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline”. Under US President Donald Trump, “we choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power”. Behind the classical backdrop is an old idea brought back to life: a single West running unbroken from Plato to Nato. It hides more than it explains what Washington wants. In this updated “grand narrative” of Western civilisation – which might more accurately be renamed “from Plato to Trump”, considering how much he despises Europe and Nato – the West must be led by a Washington that is superior to the rest. Writing in Foreign Affairs, Leonard A. Schuette of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace explains why the far-right is resurrecting a discredited idea. Vice-President J.D. Vance warned at the 2025 Munich Security Conference of a “threat from within” to “our shared civilisation”. The US National Security Strategy speaks of “civilisational erasure”. Trump stressed at Davos “the bonds we share with Europe as a civilisation”, and Rubio urged allies to “renew the greatest civilisation in human history”. Schuette calls the doctrine taking shape “civilisationism”. Under this doctrine, the West is defined less by principles that anyone can adopt – constitutional democracy, liberty and equality – than by territory, ancestry and Christianity. The bigger problem is the myth underneath the doctrine. As the scholar Amitav Acharya puts it, “all civilisation-state claims – US, Chinese, Indian, Russian – are myths in the analytical sense”. The Plato-to-Nato narrative holds that Western civilisation is one unbroken, linear thread running from ancient Greece to modern Western democratic institutions. Scholars such as Kwame Anthony Appiah and David Gress have taken that story apart. Gress was actually a defender of Western civilisation, having written the book that provided the actual phrase for people who never read it to use as an ideological slogan. Gress believed the West’s real history was more tragic and complicated. He dismantled the Plato-to-Nato narrative as a 20th-century political myth, manufactured largely for Cold War geopolitical ends. That narrative caught on in mid-20th-century American universities through “Western Civ” curricula and the “great books” of the Western world. Today, you have conservative or neoconservative commentators bemoaning their disappearance from some universities. I was educated on those books through four years of university in the United States. Those courses gave the transatlantic alliance an ideological blueprint against communism, allowing Nato to present itself as the defender of a 2,500-year-old tradition of liberty. Who wouldn’t want Plato and Aristotle on their side? Except that they would almost certainly be disgusted by today’s Western democracies. For much of its history, Europe was dominated by absolute monarchies, religious intolerance, feudalism and imperialism. Liberal democracy was as much accident as destination. The narrative also skips about a thousand years of medieval history. Modern institutions were forged from a messy synthesis of Roman law, Christian theology and Germanic institutions, later combined with modern European developments after the Thirty Years’ War. Neither is “the West” a sealed intellectual community. Europe was part of a broader Eurasian and Mediterranean network. Greek texts were lost to western Europe after the fall of Rome, then preserved by Islamic scholars in Baghdad, Cordoba and Cairo. The bloodline from Plato to Nato ran through the Islamic world. Rubio’s own words betray his ignorance about the West’s intellectual roots. At the Munich Security Conference this February, he lamented that after 1945 the West had contracted, a decline hastened by “godless communist revolutions” and “anti-colonial uprisings”. He went on to declare that the US had “no interest in being polite and orderly caretakers of the West’s managed decline”. In Athens, he praised the Spanish conquistador Hernan Cortes and described the pre-colonial Americas as “an open and wild land”, conveniently omitting the indigenous societies that had long lived there. Could Rubio really be so pathetically ignorant of the Inca, Aztec, Maya and Caral civilisations about which well-informed high-schoolers in North America would know? Even Clash of Civilisations author Samuel Huntington conceded that, “The West won the world not by the superiority of its ideas or values or religion (to which few members of other civilisations were converted) but rather by its superiority in applying organised violence. Westerners often forget this fact; non-Westerners never do.” Scholars such as Ian Morris and Jared Diamond have argued that the real drivers were material: resources, land, markets and control of militarised technology. But “the West is the best” is a useful myth, and it is being recycled for American imperialism 2.0. You don’t have to look far. Just look at the maps on which Trump likes to claim Canada, Greenland, Venezuela and Cuba as US territory and the western hemisphere as being under US dominance. Consider Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s 2020 book American Crusade, which casts China, socialism and Islam as enemies in a “holy war”. Whether used to justify a crusade or a carve-up into spheres of influence, the frame treats sovereign nations as subordinates in someone else’s order. The governments of Europe and Asia should judge Washington by its actions and decide: who is their biggest threat?

title: Pope Leo pledges return to duties following lung cancer surgery
description: The first US pope had an ‌operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung.
content: Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter’s Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago. The 71-year-old pontiff had an ‌operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, fuelling speculation about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy. Smiling from a window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear voice on Sunday, the first US pope thanked people across the world for their prayers and said he would now begin to resume his normal schedule. “Having overcome this delicate phase ... I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the ⁠help of God and your prayers,” Leo said. The pope, who was discharged from Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Saturday, came to the window ‌in the palace unaided and held his weekly midday appointment as usual. He also urged pilgrims waiting below under cloudy skies to set aside any selfish ambitions and serve God “without compromise”. Nuns cry as Leo appears Leo ‌has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis was alarming for the youngest ⁠pope in decades, who was ⁠elected only in May last year. His doctors discharged him on Saturday after blood tests and chest imaging showed him well enough to return ‌home. They said he was able to perform normal daily activities independently. Crowds in St. Peter’s Square, numbering about 15,000 according to the Vatican, shouted and clapped loudly as Leo first appeared ‌at the ‌window on Sunday. One Catholic nun knelt and cried, holding her hand over her face. A few steps away, a group ‌of other nuns held aloft a sign reading, “Best wishes, Holy Father. We love you and we are praying for you.” Pope's calendar in flux Leo ⁠usually keeps a busy schedule, but the Vatican has cancelled his other public events until at least Wednesday, when he is due ⁠to hold a weekly general audience in St. Peter’s Square. The Vatican has not said whether he will hold that audience. The pope is also planning to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of ‌the most intense trips arranged for ‌a Catholic leader in decades. Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the pope’s lead surgeon, said on Saturday that Leo could be fully recovered in time for that trip. However, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s secretary of state, has expressed scepticism. He told journalists on Friday the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward “according to the condition of his health”.

title: How a hospital ship helps buoy China’s strategic mission in Africa
description: The Auspicious Ark is dispensing medical care and laying the groundwork for future cooperation on the continent.
content: By the time the Chinese navy hospital ship had docked in the Guinean capital Conakry earlier this month, patients were already queuing for free consultations. The queues in front of the Auspicious Ark were so long that some people were told to come back the next day, according to Guinean media reports. The ship, operated by the PLA Navy, offers a range of medical services wherever it stops, including surgery to treat cataracts, appendicitis and hernias as well as gynaecological care. On this stop, teams were also sent to a local hospital and military camp. Observers say that as well as medical care, such missions have a range of functions, from building goodwill for China to giving its naval crews experience far from home. Port calls and visits to military facilities also bring them into contact with their hosts’ armed forces and lay the groundwork for future cooperation. The Auspicious Ark is China’s third 10,000-tonne hospital ship and is part of Mission Harmony 2026, a PLA Navy medical programme running since 2010. It left Qingdao on July 22 for a voyage of more than 200 days across Africa and South Asia. It stopped in Djibouti for supplies and medical care in August, then spent seven days in Mauritania, performing cataract and hernia operations and delivering a baby. In Senegal, it recorded 6,060 patient visits and its staff performed 29 surgical procedures. It left Guinea on October 10. China’s medical presence in Africa dates to 1963, when it sent its first team to Algeria, and has since included the deployment of health workers who treat patients and train local staff. Its medical diplomacy has also provided emergency aid during outbreaks, including support during the 2014-15 Ebola crisis in West Africa and Ebola-response teams sent to the Democratic Republic of Congo in June. David Shinn, a China-Africa specialist and former US ambassador to Burkina Faso and Ethiopia, said the missions had generated “considerable goodwill and positive publicity for China”. They also gave Chinese medical staff experience with tropical diseases and tested the ships “in sometimes harsh conditions far from China”, he said. Beyond humanitarian aid, the mission aims to test long-range naval operations and build stronger defence ties with African countries. Zhou Yuyuan, a professor at East China University of Political Science and Law’s Institute of Foreign-Related Rule of Law, said medical relief deepened bilateral ties and offered a way to give African countries practical support without direct military intervention. It also helped to counter accusations that China was a bystander on African peace and security issues. Zhou described Mission Harmony as an “important exercise for the Chinese navy’s long-range deployment and logistical support capabilities”, and contributed to military modernisation and naval capacity building. He said the Chinese government also saw the missions as a way to present China as a responsible major power. “Through cooperation in these ‘soft areas’ rather than direct military intervention, the Chinese military conveys its sincere attitude of upholding peace and cherishing life,” Zhou said. The visits to African countries allow Chinese personnel to learn about each of their individual circumstances and particular needs in peace, security and military cooperation. African officials, meanwhile, can gain a more direct understanding of People’s Liberation Army personnel, equipment and technology, according to Zhou. “This will help African countries and China better plan pragmatic cooperation based on their national conditions and needs, so that future projects address practical problems in the host countries,” he said. The PLA Navy’s hospital ships are one part of a wider Chinese naval presence around Africa. Chinese navy warships have escorted commercial vessels through the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia since 2008, called at African ports and trained with other militaries. In October 2025, the Chinese destroyer Baotou called at Mombasa before conducting manoeuvres with Kenya’s navy. And in January this year, China led a multinational naval exercise off the coast of South Africa that also included Russia, with Indonesia and Ethiopia attending as observers.

title: Second-hand smartphone traders eye Hong Kong as springboard for global exports
description: Inaugural pavilion at Global Sources show draws major mainland and overseas players seeking to expand pre-owned device trade.
content: A pavilion dedicated to second-hand smartphones has made its debut at a Hong Kong trade show now under way, drawing international recycling platforms, refurbishers and automated kiosk operators hoping to use the city as a springboard to export used devices to other markets. The inaugural Global Mobile Exchange Pavilion, co-hosted by the Hong Kong International Communications Electronic Chamber (HKICEC) and Global Sources, opened on Sunday at AsiaWorld-Expo as part of phase two of the Global Sources Hong Kong Shows. The pavilion brought together more than 60 companies from mainland China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the United Arab Emirates, Japan and India. Exhibitors included mainland second-hand e-commerce platforms Zhuan Zhuan and ATRenew, as well as US self-service kiosk network ecoATM. The show floor was busy, with vendors showing their latest trade-in kiosks and inviting visitors to try them, while staff handed out fliers. Industry leaders said that Hong Kong’s duty-free port status, streamlined customs clearance and proximity to the mainland and Southeast Asia made the city a natural conduit for the global trade in second-hand devices. HKICEC chief secretary Jacky Chan Man-lung said the city’s main export markets for used devices were Dubai and Southeast Asia, with trade extending to Latin America. “Chinese mobile phone brands are gaining popularity globally, and Hong Kong can serve as an export hub for the second-hand market, while mainland companies in the trade can also use the city to go overseas and launch business locally,” Chan said. Rock Lau, assistant manager of AHS Device Hong Kong – a subsidiary of ATRenew, one of the mainland’s largest pre-owned electronics trading platforms – said Hong Kong served as both an inspection centre and a transit hub for exports to Dubai as the company scales its automated hardware internationally. “We have more than 30 self-service kiosks across Hong Kong that can price devices automatically and complete trades electronically, and we are rolling out kiosks in overseas markets in partnership with local retailers and platforms, including in Japan, Sweden and the UK,” he said. Brian Tepfer, senior vice-president of ecoATM, said his company, which operates around 8,000 kiosks across the US and Canada, was exploring expansion through public-private partnerships rather than purely quick commercial deals.
