He said ecoATM was looking at entering the mainland market, and that Hong Kong was one of its most valued strategic partners. “With the right government sponsorship and the right strategic partnership, it would be very easy to deploy this at scale,” he said. “The mainland already has half the ecosystem built. We would bring the kiosks and the technology, and local partners would handle the rest. In other countries, we have to build [the ecosystem] 100 per cent [from scratch].” Phase two of the Global Sources Hong Kong Shows, which runs until October 21, spans four product tracks from mobile electronics to smart home appliances. It features more than 2,100 suppliers across over 4,000 booths showcasing some 160,000 new products, with artificial intelligence a major focus through a dedicated AI zone and Tencent’s exhibition debut, alongside Vietnam sourcing and security technology sections.

title: 5 dogs found dead near San Tin fish ponds in suspected poisoning case
description: Police received a report of four dog carcasses at a San Tin fish pond before finding a fifth nearby.
content: Hong Kong police have launched an animal cruelty investigation after five dogs were found dead near fish ponds in the northern New Territories, with sources saying the animals may have been poisoned. The force received a report on Sunday morning from a passer-by who spotted four dog carcasses at a fish pond in San Tin, near Mai Po, and suspected the animals had been mistreated. When officers arrived, they found the four carcasses and discovered a fifth at a nearby fish pond. A source told the South China Morning Post that all five dogs, found at fish ponds in Hop Shing Wai, were mongrels. The force later handed the animals to the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, the insider added. No arrests had been made, police said, adding that the investigation was ongoing. Under Hong Kong’s Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance, anyone convicted of cruelty to an animal faces a maximum fine of HK$200,000 (US$25,482) and three years’ imprisonment.

title: Fake Hyrox Macau group admits to not being part of brand, but says race will go ahead
description: Association issues statement clarifying status, but insist it is ‘legally registered’ and plans to hold fitness challenge in February.
content: An organisation registered as the Hyrox Association of Macau has admitted to having no affiliation with the global fitness brand, days after claiming it planned to stage an event in the city. The group, which held a dinner last week to launch its plans, issued a statement on Saturday clarifying its position following the company’s move to halt the unauthorised use of its name and trademark. As part of its launch, the group said it intended to hold a fitness challenge in February, with the format bearing a striking resemblance to the global phenomenon that attracts thousands of competitors to each its events worldwide. In a statement issued on Saturday, the group, whose Chinese name translates literally as Macau Fitness Run Association, insisted it was “legally registered and established in accordance with Macau law”. While its comments were issued under its Chinese title, public records show the organisation was officially registered with the casino hub’s government under the English name, Hyrox Association of Macau. Still, it admitted that it had “no affiliation with any authorised or recognised organisations of Hyrox”. It added that the inaugural Macau Fitness Run Challenge, scheduled to take place at the Galaxy International Convention Centre on February 20 and 21 next year, was an “independently hosted physical fitness running event”. “This event is not an official Hyrox event, nor has it been organised, authorised, or sponsored by Hyrox in any form,” the statement said. The group insisted it would “strictly respect intellectual property rights and provide accurate and reliable information to the public”, while continuing its commitment to promoting local running and functional fitness sports. It also noted that prize money would be offered to winners in elite and team divisions to encourage participation. When contacted regarding the clarification, Hyrox said it had “no further comments at this moment”. The Macau government did not respond to request for comment. Last week, Gary Wan, the Hyrox Asia-Pacific managing director, told the South China Morning Post his organisation had already approached the group in Macau and told them “to stop using the Hyrox name and branding.” At the inaugural dinner, the group’s president Jofe Tam had said the unveiled plans for February’s race that included eight functional workout stations and an 8km run, almost identical to the signature format made famous by Hyrox. While public records from the Macau SAR Government Gazette show the association formally filed its charter in August with the explicit aim to “promote and popularise the development of Hyrox sports in the Macau region”, the venture triggered immediate scepticism online, with local fitness enthusiasts questioning whether the race was an unauthorised “knock-off”. Macau has never hosted an official Hyrox event, and the company has not confirmed whether it plans to expand into the territory.

title: Saudi closes Riyadh skyscraper as chopper pilots killed near Yemen
description: The Saudi coalition’s war with the Iran-backed Houthis has reignited during the US-Iran war, with regular attacks reported by both sides.
content: Riyadh’s Kingdom Centre skyscraper ordered remote working for office tenants on Sunday following repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, as the Saudi-led coalition said two pilots were killed in a crash near the Yemen border. The imposing, 99-storey landmark announced “mandatory” remote working until further notice. No reason was given for the order, but it comes a week after 13 people were killed in a major Houthi attack on Riyadh’s international airport. The Saudi coalition’s decade-plus war with the Iran-backed Houthis has reignited during the US-Iran war, with regular attacks reported by both sides. Tenants of the Kingdom Centre, which towers over central Riyadh, include financial services giant Merril Lynch, management consultancy McKinsey and the International Monetary Fund. “Please be advised that remote working arrangements are mandatory for all office employees at Kingdom Centre, effective immediately and until further notice,” the building’s management said in an email seen by journalists. “Kindly refrain from attending the offices during this period,” it added. The mall at the foot of the building remains open. It comes as schools recently extended remote learning measures and Riyadh’s airport remains closed after last week’s attack. The order came after the coalition announced the death of two helicopter pilots in Najran near the border with Yemen, blaming a “technical malfunction”, after the Houthis said they shot down an Apache helicopter in the area. “An AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter belonging to the Ministry of National Guard crashed inside Saudi territory in Najran Region due to a technical malfunction,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said, according to the official Saudi Press Agency. “The accident resulted in the martyrdom of its aircrew, consisting of two officers.” Late on Saturday, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had “downed an Apache helicopter belonging to the Saudi enemy” in the same area. Egypt mulls support After an uneasy four-year truce, Yemen’s conflict has surged back to life and intensified when the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. The Houthis have hit Saudi targets including tankers in the Red Sea, oil facilities and Riyadh’s King Khalid International airport. The Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government has launched repeated air raids on Houthi territory. The coalition said overnight it intercepted two drones in the Riyadh area and a third over the oil-rich Eastern Province. Saudi authorities had earlier issued a threat alert in the capital. The coalition also said two ballistic missiles were intercepted in the kingdom’s south. On Saturday, the Houthis reported that Saudi strikes killed 12 people in Yemen, including three children. The Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and captured territory around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the Red Sea chokepoint and vital export route for Saudi oil since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz. The Red Sea is a key shipping route, connecting Asia with Europe via Egypt’s Suez Canal. On Sunday, Egypt’s parliament will hold an emergency session after President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi asked lawmakers to authorise support to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. Sisi said he was willing to “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia if its leaders requested it. “I’m not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone,” he said on Saturday. “We are speaking only about defence.”

title: Sri Lankan writer Nifraz Rifaz’s debut novel confronts Islamophobia after Easter bombings
description: Hong Kong-based Sri Lankan Nifraz Rifaz’s novel Paper Plane explores the trauma faced by Muslims in the aftermath of the 2019 attacks.
content: On September 22, after a five-year trial, 15 men from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community were convicted and sentenced to 200 to 260 years in prison each for their involvement in the 2019 Easter bombings. The coordinated suicide attacks on luxury hotels and Christian places of worship on April 21, 2019, remain one of the deadliest terror incidents in the island nation’s history, claiming more than 250 lives. While the devastation and subsequent investigations were covered widely in the global media, the impact on Sri Lankan Muslims has not been as well reported; as a consequence of the bombings, they have endured discrimination, harassment, arrests, detention and physical abuse. In his debut novel Paper Plane, published by The Jam Fruit Tree Publications and which won this year’s Best Original Novel in English at Sri Lanka’s State Literary Awards, Hong Kong-based writer Nifraz Rifaz sheds light on the pervasive Islamophobia that emerged in the wake of the tragedy. He explores this through a protagonist named Zed, who returns to Sri Lanka from London shortly after the bombings. The novel charts the devastating personal toll on Zed’s family and friends, retelling real-life traumas such as women wearing the hijab suffering harassment, supermarkets removing halal-labelled food from shelves and the Muslim community effectively being forced into hiding. Everything looks peaceful on the surface, but you can still feel the fear Nifraz Rifaz For Rifaz, it became intensely personal in 2020, when his aunt and nieces told him how their home was raided by a mob of around 40 men. The women, simply by virtue of being Muslim, were found to be “suspicious” by their neighbours, he recalls. “They were so scared, they couldn’t complain to the police,” Rifaz says. Horrified by their ordeal, he promised his family he would use his writing to amplify their silenced story. Suffering xenophobia and the birth of Paper Plane At the time of the 2019 attacks, Rifaz, who works in corporate communications, was living in London. He had just flown into Colombo to visit his wife and children on Easter Sunday, and was travelling to the city in a taxi driven by a Catholic driver with a statue of Mary fixed to his dashboard. He still remembers the moment their phones started to vibrate with calls and public warnings and how they both fell silent. When he returned to Sri Lanka the following year, the idea for a novel started to take shape. The xenophobia suffered by his family and friends was an unprecedented experience for Rifaz, who was born in the coastal city of Galle. Growing up, he attended government schools where most of his friends were Sinhalese, the largest ethnic group in Sri Lanka, and he learned to speak Sinhala. Despite being part of the country’s less than 10 per cent Muslim population, he “never felt like a minority”. Long before the Easter bombings, Rifaz had started writing creatively alongside his day job. The first version of Paper Plane was based on a story he wrote as part of the “Write to Reconcile” project, led by Sri Lankan novelist Shyam Selvadurai. In 2013, four years after Sri Lanka’s devastating civil war had ended, the cohort travelled to the northern city of Jaffna, a frequent battleground between the majority Sinhalese government and the Tamil minority. When Rifaz visited for the first time, he says he felt as though he was in a different country. Their workshop was held at the Jaffna Public Library, which had been burned down in 1981 by a mob reportedly including government security forces. During the project, participants wrote a story about the war. “All 20 people wrote the same story about the Tamils and the Sinhalese,” Rifaz says. “But one community had gone missing. What about the Muslims?” Moving to Hong Kong and finding common ground with a singer Rifaz’s urge to share the Muslim Sri Lankan experience grew stronger. After moving to Hong Kong with HSBC in 2016 – he worked for the bank from 2005 to 2019 – colleagues and friends admitted they knew little about the country he grew up in. He also came across blatant discrimination. “Sri Lanka was the centre of my world,” Rifaz says. “But when I first moved to Hong Kong, people thought I was Indian, and they wouldn’t rent me serviced apartments. When I told them I was from Sri Lanka, they had no idea where it was.” Despite the ignorance and prejudice, he has also found Hong Kong transformative for his writing practice. “Hong Kong has a very nurturing environment for creative people,” he says. He has now lived in the city for almost a decade. While he visits his wife and children in Colombo regularly, Hong Kong has also become his home. Stylistically, each chapter of Paper Plane is named after a song by British-Sri Lankan singer Mathangi Arulpragasam, also known as M.I.A. The singer was born in London but mostly lived in Sri Lanka and India until she was 11, a period when her family was often in hiding from the Sri Lanka Army because of her father’s activism in advocating for an independent Tamil state. The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, widely known as the Tamil Tigers, were a militant group that became notorious for its specialised suicide attack unit. Although Arulpragasam’s father, Arul Pragasam, did not join the group, the singer’s career has been marked by accusations of supporting them. Rifaz notes that he and Mathangi Arulpragasam come from different minorities in Sri Lanka, and both have tried to find unique ways to share their communities’ stories with a global audience. He is channelling Arulpragasam’s “Tamil pain” to talk about “Muslim pain”, he says. “After the Easter attack, I felt her pain,” Rifaz says. “Before, Tamils were seen as suicide bombers; then after the 2019 attacks, a Muslim woman could be seen as a suicide bomber. M.I.A inspired me to use art as a way to have a voice.” ‘Sri Lanka is a traumatised country’ Rifaz has experienced some pushback since the publication of his novel, with some Muslim readers questioning his inclusion of music in his writing. “Islam doesn’t encourage music, and my Muslim readers were concerned about me using music as a device, but I used music deliberately as part of the storytelling,” he says. “M.I.A told her story using music, and I told mine using her music. This helped soften the gravity of what was a horrific incident.” While the Easter bombing court case has come to a close and the alleged perpetrators have been imprisoned for life, its ripple effects continue to be felt by the communities it impacted. “Everything looks peaceful on the surface, but you can still feel the fear,” Rifaz says. “Sri Lanka is a traumatised country.” Rifaz is now working on a second novel set in Hong Kong, where he says support from the literary community has “helped me to become a better writer”. In the meantime, his biggest hope is to meet Arulpragasam one day and share their stories in person.

title: Hong Kong excels at medical research. So what is holding it back?
description: Hong Kong’s biomedical ambitions face hurdles beyond research funding, experts say, pointing to limited industry investment, production capacity and specialist talent.
content: In the first of a four-part Health Matters wellness series on frontier medicine in Hong Kong, Elizabeth Cheung looks into how the city can turn world-class research into real-world treatments and what it needs to become a global biomedical innovation hub. Raymond Tong Kai-yu spent a decade overcoming challenges in cost and production to develop a device that could change lives: a robotic hand that helps stroke patients regain mobility and relearn everyday movements. The Hong Kong biomedical engineer is best known for “Hand of Hope”, which he developed 15 years ago at the age of 39. The device is now used in hospitals across 15 countries, but getting there was far from smooth. “It is challenging to turn scientific research products into real-life applications for others to use … breakthroughs in research and market access cannot happen at the same time,” said Tong, a professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s department of biomedical engineering. Before a product can reach a wider population, it must clear hurdles including cost, manufacturing, regulatory approval and market acceptance. Tong is one of a small number of Hong Kong pioneers in frontier medicine who have managed to turn cutting-edge healthcare technologies and world-class medical research into practical applications that improve patient care and treat previously untreatable diseases. Some of the examples range from genomic drug development and advanced diagnostic tools to surgical robots. Many others, however groundbreaking their findings or inventions, are still struggling to make that leap – despite the city’s ambition to become an international biomedical innovation hub. Experts told the South China Morning Post that Hong Kong had strong basic and clinical research, but a lack of industry support for funding and production had made that goal harder to achieve. To raise its game, they said, the city had to invest more boldly in early-stage research projects, expand research capacity and broaden its talent pool by attracting partially done overseas projects. In Tong’s case, moving manufacturing to mainland China cut the cost of each device from HK$100,000 to about HK$30,000. He also redesigned the hand, replacing the metal and motor components of the first generation with lighter, soft elastic materials. A smaller version was later developed so that physically disabled children could benefit as well. But to win approval for use as a medical device in hospitals, Tong had to spend years collecting clinical data and seeking certification from regulators. So far, the device has been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration and certified in the European Union. It is now being assessed by China’s National Medical Products Administration. “The difficulty is that if you want to enter a certain market, you need to do everything yourself – from manufacturing and sales to certification,” Tong said, adding that all of this required funding support, including from the private sector. About 60 per cent of Hong Kong’s special schools now use his device to train hand movements in physically disabled children, in addition to its use in some hospitals. Bright scientists, little industrial support Professor Joshua Ho Wing-kei, an assistant dean at the University of Hong Kong’s faculty of medicine who oversees innovation and technology transfer, said the city was well placed globally in frontier medicine research. “We have very good fundamental research in biomedical sciences as well as artificial intelligence, digital health,” said Ho, an expert in digital health innovation and technology. “What we do not have is an industry, private sector industry that can support rapid translation yet.” Using the invention of an AI system as an example, Ho said strong information technology expertise was needed to turn an idea into a market-ready product. “You need hardware support, computer servers, network support, cybersecurity support – these are things that are beyond normal academic research work,” he said. Pharmaceutical development, one of Hong Kong’s strategic priorities, also demands a very different set of skills. “From drug candidates to making a drug, they are completely different things,” Ho said. “You need a lot more optimisation, you need a lot more data, you need a lot more testing before it becomes an actual drug.” Such expertise was usually found in large pharmaceutical companies, he said. Ho, who founded a spin-off company in 2023 focusing on AI-driven health monitoring software, was able to identify an industry partner that helped him navigate the market. The Hong Kong government has been trying to attract more firms through initiatives including the Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises, set up in 2022. Through the office, major companies in strategic industries, including health technology, have pledged to invest and create research and development jobs in Hong Kong. Some are also expected to set up offices in the Hong Kong park of the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone, located in the 87-hectare Lok Ma Chau Loop. The area is expected to become an innovation and technology powerhouse through cross-border collaboration. Ho said those enterprises could work with local researchers and support promising research ideas. He envisaged an ecosystem in which Hong Kong’s researchers and start-ups received stronger industry backing. “Hong Kong will be so attractive that all the investors would just come and support our own start-ups and government’s public funding can take a step back a little bit,” he said. Time for industry to invest more Last month, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu pledged in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan to increase spending on innovation activities – including R&D and enterprises’ application development – to 3 per cent of gross domestic product by around 2030, up from 1.63 per cent in 2024. Lo Yuk-lam, president of the Hong Kong Bio-Med Innotech Association, said greater industry involvement would be essential to meet that target. Data from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development shows that in innovation-driven economies such as the United States, Germany, Japan and South Korea, industry contributes about 70 to 80 per cent of R&D spending, with government funding accounting for 10 per cent. In Hong Kong, however, the government contributed nearly 60 per cent of R&D spending in 2024, while local businesses accounted for about 40 per cent, according to Census and Statistics Department data. “The industry needs to invest more money in R&D; this cannot rely solely on the government,” Lo said, adding that greater industry involvement could also help drive economic development. Nevertheless, Lo urged the government to devote more resources to basic research, where Hong Kong already ranks among the world’s top 1 to 2 per cent. Further efforts, he said, should focus on raising the quality of that work into the top 0.01 per cent, enabling the city to conduct more sophisticated, cutting-edge studies. Dennis Lam Shun-chiu, founder of oncology pharmaceutical company Health Hope Pharma, said research needed to be combined with capital to take off. He said Hong Kong had a favourable environment for attracting both local and international investment. The government-owned Hong Kong Investment Corporation (HKIC), established in 2022 to manage investments from designated funds, has identified biotechnology and health technology as investment pillars. Some of the research projects funded by HKIC investment include Insilico Medicine, one of the world’s leading artificial intelligence-driven biotech companies, and Phase Scientific, a Hong Kong-based biotech firm focused on diagnostics for cancer and infectious diseases. Projects supported by the corporation after due diligence could encourage both local and international investors to follow suit, he said. Attracting talent through projects Lam, a prominent ophthalmologist and entrepreneur, said Hong Kong lacked sufficient talent in areas such as drug development. To address this, he said, the city needed to launch more research projects to attract talent. “You need to have a critical mass and enough research projects. Without projects, talent will not come,” Lam said. One way to expand the city’s research pipeline is to bring in partially completed research from elsewhere. Lam’s company has so far acquired two drug candidates – an oral chemotherapy treatment and another for age-related macular degeneration – that had encountered regulatory setbacks in the United States or financial difficulties. It brought the research to Hong Kong and the mainland, where phase three clinical trials will be conducted. He described acquiring such half-finished projects as “catching a falling knife”, because much of the early-stage research had already been completed. Should the government place a bigger bet? Experts said the government remained crucial to developing frontier medicine, even though industry support was increasingly important. The government launched the Research, Academic and Industry Sectors One-plus (RAISe+) scheme in 2023 to support the commercialisation of university R&D outcomes. It allocated HK$10 billion to the scheme, which has supported 73 projects across various technology areas, including cancer immunotherapy and clinical-grade blood-pressure monitoring on smartphones. Tong, of CUHK, said the government tended to fund projects that appeared more likely to succeed and had more mature technology and business plans. But he said more support should also go to pioneering projects with the potential for breakthroughs, even if they had not yet succeeded. “If Hong Kong is just a follower, or we only do what is trending right now … that is not too bad,” he said. “But if we want to be an innovation hub and drive research, we should give more chances to research with the potential for breakthroughs.” As Hong Kong pushes to develop life and health technology as one of its strategic pillar industries, with more research laboratories and firms expected to move into the flagship Hetao project, experts said the city was on the right track by bringing together universities and industry. “If we execute this properly, Hong Kong really has the potential to become the Silicon Valley of the East,” HKU’s Ho said. “We have all the right ingredients. We are not quite scaling up yet, but probably in the next five years or so, I think we will see some really good outcomes.” He highlighted that public support would be vital, even as frontier medicine might seem remote from most people’s daily lives. “If you want the community to continue to support you, you need to make sure they see concrete products,” he said. “When the people of Hong Kong feel the benefits, that is when it makes a substantial difference.”

title: Japan readies Martian moon mission to uncover origins of life
description: The uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.
content: Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars’ moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the Solar System and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region. The uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe, a collaboration with US and European space agencies as well as numerous universities and tech companies, could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration. The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX is set to blast-off from the Tanegashima Space Center Tuesday at 4.41am, according to the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “Being able to be involved in such a grand mission is incredibly exciting,” Makoto Arita, project manager of JAXA’s H3 rocket team, told reporters two days before the launch. The spacecraft will arrive near Mars around August next year, where it will orbit one of its moons, Phobos, before landing and collecting at least 10 grams of material from the surface during three years of operating within the Martian sphere. A rover dubbed IDEFIX – the French name for the comic hero Asterix’s dog – will first conduct surface observations aimed at ensuring a safe landing. “The sampling [from] Phobos is of course the world’s first, but it means … this is the first round trip to the Martian system,” MMX’s project manager Yasuhiro Kawakatsu said. JAXA said the mission will also explore the possibility of using Phobos as a “natural space station” by establishing the requirements for a round trip to Mars – something “essential for crewed Mars exploration”. It will also observe the Red Planet’s moon Deimos, although it will not land on it, before returning to Earth. Impact or capture JAXA hopes the mission will reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, a key piece of knowledge in working out how the Solar System was born. One theory for the origin of the Martian moons – the “giant impact” hypothesis – is that they formed after a celestial body collided with Mars. The “capture” hypothesis, meanwhile, postulates that the moons are asteroids captured by Mars’s gravity. Determining which theory is correct will help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets”, JAXA said, referring to the four rocky worlds closest to the sun – Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. “MMX will shed light on the transport mechanisms that delivered water, volatiles, and organic compounds from the outer Solar System to the inner rocky planet region – processes that may have played a key role in making these worlds habitable,” said Patrick Michel, a French astrophysicist working on IDEFIX. “If Phobos and Deimos are indeed remnants of these early delivery systems, they may hold clues to the origins of life itself, or, to be more correct, to the transport of the materials that were key to the emergence of life on rocky planets,” he said. Deep in the ‘gravity well’ MMX is a collaboration with France’s National Centre for Space Studies (CNES), the German Aerospace Centre (DLR), Nasa, the European Space Agency (ESA), and about 20 universities and tech companies. The development of the spacecraft’s landing legs was particularly difficult, as gravity on Phobos is extremely weak, JAXA scientists say. Japan’s uncrewed Smart Lander for Investigating Moon (SLIM) – the “Moon Sniper” – tipped over after touching down on Earth’s moon in 2024, but still transmitted data and survived several two-week lunar nights. Japan also has experience in bringing back samples from space, including JAXA’s uncrewed Hayabusa-2, which returned 5.4 grams of rock and dust collected from an asteroid several hundred million kilometres from Earth in 2020. On the coming mission “we have to travel very close to Mars and return”, which means escaping the planet’s heavy gravity, Kawakatsu told reporters. Phobos orbits about 6,000km above the Martian surface. “Going deep into what we call the ‘gravity well’ is difficult,” Kawakatsu said. China’s mission US and Chinese space agencies have been racing to be the first to return rock samples from Mars’ surface back to Earth. Nasa’s Perseverance rover, which has been roaming the Red Planet since 2021, has already collected samples. The mission, however, was effectively cancelled by the administration of President Donald Trump following a vote by the US Congress in January. China, meanwhile, has announced its Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled for launch around 2028 and hopes to return Mars samples to Earth as early as 2031 – potentially before the MMX’s return. JAXA scientists say sand and rocks from Phobos may offer a wider variety of samples than those on the planet itself, especially if it was formed by a collision between a celestial body and Mars.

title: 20 restaurants prosecuted for allowing dogs without permits since scheme launched
description: Seven diners were also prosecuted, with authorities urging owners to check restaurant permits before dining out with their dogs ahead of Halloween.
content: Hong Kong authorities have prosecuted 20 restaurants for unlawfully allowing dogs onto their premises since the city’s dog-friendly dining scheme launched in July. The Food and Environmental Hygiene Department said on Sunday that seven people had also been prosecuted for bringing dogs into eateries without permission, while four others were prosecuted for failing to keep their pets securely leashed in permitted restaurants. A department spokesman said it had adopted a “pragmatic and flexible” enforcement approach following the initial one-month adaptation period, balancing pet inclusivity with food safety and public hygiene. “The department will take decisive enforcement action against any violations,” the spokesman said, adding that both restaurant operators and dog owners were responsible for complying with the rules. More than 990 restaurants currently hold permits allowing canine visitors. With Halloween approaching at the end of the month, the spokesman urged residents planning to dine out with their dogs to check in advance whether an establishment was permitted to admit them. Permitted restaurants must not use open-flame cooking at dining tables, must keep dogs out of food rooms, and must refuse entry to fighting dogs or “known dangerous dogs”. “At all times while in a restaurant, a dog must be securely held by an adult on a leash not exceeding 1.5 metres in length, or securely tethered to a fixture,” the spokesman said. Since the scheme began on July 9, 940 restaurants and eateries have started allowing customers to dine with their dogs, ending a 30-year ban introduced to prevent rabies. But some restaurants later withdrew from the scheme, citing limited manpower, space constraints and cautious diners. The scheme drew about 20 complaints in its first week. Under the Food Business Regulation, operators who knowingly allow dogs onto food premises without approval face a maximum fine of HK$10,000 (US$1,275), three months’ imprisonment and a daily fine of HK$300 for continuing offences. Under the Dangerous Dogs Regulation, “fighting dogs” include pit bull terriers, Japanese Tosas, Dogo Argentinos and Fila Brasileiros, as well as crossbreeds of those four types.

title: Hong Kong’s primary residential market sees wave of launches, successful sales
description: Swire Properties, Chinachem Group also announced plans to redevelop three buildings into a premium grade-A office tower in Taikoo Place.
content: Hong Kong homebuyers are poised to see new residential launches in the coming days and weeks following a sell-out weekend of more than 360 flats in two major projects in the city. Sun Hung Kai Properties (SHKP), one of Hong Kong’s major developers and landlords, was set to hold a second round of sales for Sierra Sea Phase 2C(2) in Shap Sze Heung, which is between Sai Kung and Ma On Shan, with 152 flats on offer on Wednesday, it said in a statement. Among them, 128 flats would be sold via a regular price list and the remaining 24 flats would be offered for sale via tender. The new batch would include flats with layouts of two bedrooms and three bedrooms and saleable areas of 418 square feet (38.83 square metres) to 679 square feet. The flats to be offered via a price list would be sold at discounted rates starting from HK$12,714 (US$1,620) per square foot or a per-flat price of about HK$5.47 million (US$696,978) to about HK$9.87 million. The latest round of sales comes after SHKP sold all 142 flats on offer in the same project on Saturday. These flats also had sizes ranging from 418 to 679 square feet with discounted prices from HK$5.38 million. Yuexiu Property also sold out on the same day all the 220 flats it put on offer via a price list at The Atlas Phase 1 project in Yau Tong. The flats comprised layouts with one to two bedrooms measuring 285 to 510 square feet. Yuexiu on Sunday announced that 132 flats would be on offer via regular sale on Saturday. The flats would range in sizes of between 278 and 497 square feet. The discounted price per square foot would start at HK$13,038 to HK$16,769. “Primary launches continue to clearly outperform the secondary market,” said Derek Chan Hoi-chiu, head of research at Ricacorp Properties. “Developers maintain the upper hand by offering aggressive price cuts, flexible payment schemes and attractive rebates to drive swift inventory turnover.” CK Asset Holdings, the flagship property developer of billionaire Li Ka-shing and family, is also set to commence the soft marketing for its Montage residential development in Kam Tin North. The development provides 327 homes, including multi-storey layouts with one to two bedrooms as well as houses with two to four bedrooms. The anticipated flurry of sales comes after the US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate in September while major Hong Kong banks have so far held rates steady. The market generally expected the Fed to hold rates in October but another increase is possible by the end of the year. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority moves in lockstep with the Fed to keep the local currency’s peg to the US dollar. Higher interest rates could lead to higher mortgage payments by those seeking loans to buy property. “Given the expectation of an interest rate hike, developers are likely to adopt a distinctly ‘volume-led, price-capped’ pricing strategy to maintain a healthy leverage position,” said Norry Lee, senior director of projects strategy and consultancy at JLL in Hong Kong. Beyond the residential segment, Hong Kong’s office property received a boost with Swire Properties and Chinachem Group announcing plans to redevelop Sea View Building and Hoi Wan Building, together with the adjoining Chinachem Exchange Square, into a premium grade-A harbourfront office tower in Taikoo Place. The combined site spans around 35,000 square feet (3,252 square metres), enabling a larger, integrated commercial development. The project is expected to deliver about 500,000 square feet of gross floor area, comprising a 27-storey office tower, a retail podium and basement car parking facilities. The new development is expected to break ground in 2027. The planned office tower forms part of Swire Properties’ ongoing expansion of Taikoo Place under its HK$100 billion investment plan, while also advancing Chinachem Group’s commitment to enhance and optimise its portfolio over the long term. The redevelopment is taking place amid a gradual recovery in the city’s office property sector. Hong Kong’s overall prime office market saw its vacancy rate drop to 12.5 per cent in August from 13.5 per cent a year earlier, according to Morgan Stanley. Central led the recovery, with rents rising 7.3 per cent as vacancy declined to 7.8 per cent from 11.2 per cent.

title: Why stealing pumpkins for newlyweds is a blessing in ancient Chinese tradition
description: Some northern communities traditionally place a pumpkin under the wedding quilt as a blessing for future generations.
content: In ancient China, welcoming autumn could involve stealing pumpkins, sitting on giant hanging scales and eating extra meat – rituals reflecting how people connected seasonal change with fertility, health and good fortune. Historical records show that during the Qing dynasty (1644–1912), groups of young people would gather on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival to sneak into fields and take pumpkins. Far from being considered wrongdoing, the practice was often tolerated – and even welcomed – by farmers. By the Republican era (1912–1949), it had become particularly prevalent in rural communities. The pumpkins were traditionally given to newlyweds, with the bride eating the stem end. The custom drew on Chinese wordplay: the word for pumpkin sounds similar to the word for “son”, symbolising hopes for fertility and family prosperity. In some northern regions, placing a pumpkin beneath the wedding quilt was also considered a sign of good fortune for future generations. Agricultural historian Li Xinsheng has suggested that the custom may have involved melons before the Qing dynasty. After pumpkins were introduced to China, their vigorous growth and abundant seeds led them to become associated with fertility and the hope for “many children and many blessings”. Another traditional custom, known as “sticking autumn fat”, reflected ancient ideas about adapting the body to seasonal changes. On Liqiu, or “The Start of Autumn” – one of China’s 24 solar terms – people would weigh themselves on large hanging scales to see how their bodies had changed after the summer heat. Sitting in a basket suspended from the scale’s hook, they would be lifted by two people as the person conducting the ritual recited auspicious phrases. Those who had lost weight would begin “sticking autumn fat” by eating richer foods, especially meat, to restore their energy before winter. Rooted in traditional Chinese medicine, the practice focused on replenishing the body rather than simply gaining weight. Today, however, the tradition has taken on a new meaning. On Chinese social media, “sticking autumn fat” has become a popular way to welcome the season, with users sharing their “first autumn milk tea” or indulgent meals as rewards for hard work. Some even extend the custom to their pets by giving them extra treats. Health experts warn, however, that the traditional approach may not suit modern lifestyles. At a health forum in September, doctor Xia Zhiping noted that modern lifestyles have reversed the challenges of the agricultural era, with many people now facing sedentary work and physical inactivity. “Modern people are more likely to experience overnutrition, overweight and obesity. ‘sticking autumn fat’ is not suitable for everyone,” she said. Xia also warned that excessive consumption of high-fat foods could increase the risk of fatty liver disease, high blood lipid levels and unstable blood sugar.

title: Qian Jiang, former Johns Hopkins’ eye institute expert, joins hospital in China
description: Chinese specialist leaves US for Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital to research eye transplants and work on virtual cells to test drug responses.
content: Professor Qian Jiang, a senior eye expert at Johns Hopkins University in the United States, has moved back to China full time to pursue research on eye transplants. For more than two decades, Qian built and ran the genetic data hub at Johns Hopkins’ renowned Wilmer Eye Institute. He was welcomed at a ceremony on October 5 at Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital in Hangzhou, part of Zhejiang University, the hospital said. At the ceremony, Qian said he would also work on “virtual cells” – computer models that mimic real cells so scientists can test how they might respond to drugs or disease without lab experiments. He said he would draw on the doctors and specialists at Zhejiang University and its hospital to turn lab research into earlier diagnosis and new drugs for patients. He also hopes to bring computer-driven biology and eye medicine closer together. The South China Morning Post has contacted Qian for comment. At Johns Hopkins, Qian’s team wrote computer programmes to study how genes are switched on and off in the retina, the light-sensing tissue at the back of the eye. Knowing which genes control each type of cell and what goes wrong in disease could lead to better ways to prevent, diagnose and treat blindness. Qian held one of the institute’s endowed professorships, which Johns Hopkins calls its highest form of recognition for a professor. His lab had won more than US$8 million in grants from the US National Institutes of Health since 2004, according to the agency’s grant database. He has published more than 200 papers, including in leading journals Science and Cell, and other scientists have cited his work more than 19,000 times, according to the hospital. Qian studied at Shanghai Jiao Tong University between 1987 and 1991, according to his LinkedIn page, and he earned a master’s degree at the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Biochemistry in Shanghai. He then obtained his PhD at the Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research in Germany and did postdoctoral research at Yale University from 2000 to 2002, before joining Johns Hopkins. His new home has American roots of its own. Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital was built with money from Hong Kong film and television mogul Run Run Shaw and the Zhejiang provincial government. It opened in 1994 with help from Loma Linda University in California, which brought American-style medicine and management to Hangzhou. At Qian’s welcome ceremony, the hospital’s president, Cai Xiujun, hung a staff badge around his neck. “Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital is an open and inclusive hospital,” Cai, a surgeon who was elected to the Chinese Academy of Sciences last year, told Zhejiang outlet Tide News last year. “As long as people are good enough, we should recruit talent without sticking to convention.” According to the hospital, it has ranked in the top 1 per cent of China’s major public hospitals six times in a government review.

title: Rokid launches ‘no man’s land’ retail experience with Hong Kong flagship store opening
description: The unstaffed venue opened on Thursday in Harbour City.
content: When shoppers step into Rokid’s brand new flagship store in Hong Kong, they are greeted not by eager sales associates, but by glowing monitor screens and a robotic system waiting at the exit. In what the Chinese augmented reality (AR) gadget pioneer called an experiment in “no man’s land” retail, customers navigate the entire journey independently: testing artificial intelligence smart glasses, making payments on a screen and receiving their new devices directly from an automated system on their way out. No human salesperson was involved at any point. The unstaffed venue, which opened on Thursday in the Harbour City shopping centre, was the first of its kind in the global smart-glasses sector, according to Zoro Shao, vice-president and head of international business at Rokid. The company hoped the automated model would help it stand out from competitors as the company expanded internationally. During a trial period, the store sold five to six pairs of HK$4,688 (around US$599) wearables daily, far exceeding internal expectations, Shao said. The sales volume suggested there was genuine demand for premium AI wearables, even without a salesperson on hand to explain the product, Shao said, noting that Rokid had set no specific sales or conversion targets for the location. Instead, the main goal was to try new retail formats and set an example for the industry. Hong Kong was chosen as the testing ground due to its high consumer spending power and cultural affinity with mainland China, making it an ideal, low-risk springboard for experimental retail concepts before a broader global roll-out, Shao added. The store is also meant to look and feel different from those of rivals such as Meta Platforms. “I’ve been to Meta’s store in Los Angeles; [it is] very big, but they only have two spots for customers to try on the product,” Shao said, adding he believed Meta’s Ray-Ban stores prioritised brand display over hands-on engagement. In contrast, Rokid’s Hong Kong outlet features nearly 10 interactive demonstrations, designed to show how the glasses function in everyday life. Rokid said it currently commanded a 41 per cent share of the global market for AR glasses with displays. However, it faced an uphill battle in the broader smart-glasses arena. Meta maintained a dominant global lead in smart-glasses shipments in the second quarter with a nearly 69 per cent market share, according to research firm IDC, while Chinese competitors RayNeo, Alibaba Group Holding, Xreal and Xiaomi each held between 2.3 per cent and 3.6 per cent. Shao said Rokid’s glasses were 20 to 30 per cent lighter than competing products and offered longer battery life. Unlike Meta’s closed ecosystem, Rokid operated an open AI framework. Users in mainland China could pair their devices with local models like ByteDance’s Doubao and Alibaba’s Qwen, while international consumers could connect to OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Shao was open about the resource gap with technology giants. The company’s biggest hurdle remained brand awareness and global distribution compared with Meta’s, making product experience and customer services critical differentiators. Rokid has already built momentum across Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan, according to Shao. In Japan, its recent crowdfunding campaign on the Makuake platform raised a record-breaking 60 million yen (US$379,682). The brand is now targeting expansions into Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Australia and New Zealand, with a major push into the US – expected to become its largest single market – planned for next year. Looking ahead, the company has planned a full commercial launch of its full-colour AR glasses in mainland China on October 27, with deliveries scheduled for the first half of next year. A distinct version featured entirely separate hardware and software architectures that would be rolled out in stages on January 5 and April 10, Rokid representatives said. The domestic and international editions were engineered to satisfy regulatory compliance in both China and the US, according to the company. User accounts and data across the two regions would remain completely isolated. Addressing growing consumer privacy concerns, Rokid underscored its “local-only” approach: all photos and videos were stored strictly on the device and would not be uploaded to the cloud for training or review. The glasses can also detect when they are being worn, which is intended to prevent people from secretly taking photos.

title: Huanggang Port swarmed by holiday rush with reports of 2-hour waits
description: More than 30,000 departures recorded between 10am and 2pm, with security chief calling on travellers to use other checkpoints.
content: Massive holiday crowds swamped the revamped Huanggang Port on Sunday during its first real test over the festival long weekend, with some travellers reporting two-hour waits. Outbound passenger traffic was “exceptionally heavy” between 10am and 2pm, with more than 30,000 departures, according to the Immigration Department. The surge prompted officers to open all inspection counters and implement a tidal flow system to control crowds and ease congestion. The Hong Kong Security Bureau issued the “busy” advisory for Huanggang on its “Easy Boundary” portal at about 1.45pm, telling departing travellers to expect wait times of up to 45 minutes for clearance. The status was back to “normal” by 3.30pm. In contrast, the status of operations of the seven other land crossings, including Lo Wu, Lok Ma Chau Spur Line and Shenzhen Bay, remained “normal” throughout the morning and early afternoon, with clearance times as short as five minutes. The Chung Yeung Festival was celebrated on Sunday, with Monday observed as a public holiday, driving a surge in cross-border travel. By noon, social media platforms were flooded with posts warning others not to use the new port, with photos of long queues and huge crowds swamping the departure hall. Some mainland visitors claimed they had to queue for two hours to clear immigration. Posts on the mainland’s RedNote platform suggested the delays were primarily caused by large crowds flocking to traditional staffed immigration booths. One user complained: “Huanggang Port should not be opened if it is not ready yet. It took me 1.5 hours to get from Hong Kong to Shenzhen.” Another wrote: “The queues were chaotic, unmanaged. The staff seemed clueless. The officers did not seem to know what was going on. Despite good facilities, poor management makes for a terrible experience.” But the crowds had thinned by evening. At 8pm, it took a South China Morning Post reporter just 15 minutes to cross the border and reach the public transport terminal on the Hong Kong side. Among the travellers were Hong Kong residents Eva Lee and her friend Joe Chan, both in their 30s. They praised the crossing as fast and user-friendly, highlighting the efficiency of its biometric recognition system. Chan said he drove to the border and parked near the San Tin public transport interchange before crossing. He hoped more parking facilities would be added for drivers. “We had to wait for a space [at a privately run parking site] – we couldn’t get one until the returning drivers came back at about 5pm,” Lee said. Another cross-border commuter, a North district resident in her forties who identified herself only as Sung, entered the checkpoint in the evening to return to the city, noting that the clearance process was swift. “It took only about a minute at the gates … around 15 minutes for the entire journey,” she said, praising the hassle-free clearance. However, Sung said public transport connections could be improved. “[There are direct bus options,] but no direct connections towards Fanling and Sheung Shui [at that hour] – it is not as convenient as the Lo Wu port,” she said, adding that authorities should address the transport gap. In a Facebook post on Sunday afternoon, Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said on-site management had been strengthened to cope with the crowds and urged travellers to avoid using the checkpoint during peak hours. “Citizens and travellers are requested to follow the instructions of on-site staff and use the traditional manual counters or self-service gates in an orderly manner,” he wrote. “To avoid long waiting times, please plan your journey in advance and try to avoid crossing the border during peak hours.” According to Immigration Department figures, Huanggang Port recorded more than 92,000 crossings on Friday and the figure further grew to over 130,000 on Saturday. The facility is designed to handle up to 300,000 travellers and 15,000 vehicles daily, with initial daily expectations set at about 100,000 during early operations. Hong Kong officials have touted the adoption of the new “collaborative inspection and joint immigration clearance model” at the port. Unlike traditional clearance, where departure and entry procedures are handled at separate counters, the new arrangement allows travellers to complete clearance by presenting a single ID document while passing through an automated channel with three gates. Officials previously estimated that border clearance times could be cut from half an hour down to five minutes. Hong Kong residents who hold a valid mainland travel permit can use their ID cards interchangeably at the joint clearance channel for both outbound and inbound trips. For manual counters, travellers queue up once and present travel documents to officers from both sides. Officials earlier said the festival long weekend would be its first real test and contingency plans were in place. The original facility began 24-hour clearance in 2003, becoming the first round-the-clock land crossing connecting Hong Kong and Shenzhen for both travellers and cargo. It handled an ­average of 40,000 visitors a day and a peak flow of 65,000 people. On average, 9,000 vehicles used the crossing. Additional reporting by Vivian Au

title: Former China table tennis teammates Zhang Jike, Liu Dingshuo engage in public online spat
description: The pair, who once shared the same provincial training ground, trade accusations of ‘stirring up drama’, undercutting training fee prices.
content: Former Chinese table tennis teammates Zhang Jike and Liu Dingshuo have become embroiled in a public feud online, trading accusations of clout-chasing across their respective live-streams, despite having once shared the same provincial training ground. The dispute erupted when 28-year-old Liu took aim at Zhang during a recent broadcast without naming him directly, accusing the decorated Olympian of spending recent years “riding on the national team’s coattails, pulling seniority and stirring up drama”. Zhang, 38, whose retirement was officially confirmed by the Chinese Table Tennis Association in April 2023, has remained active in the sport by shifting his focus to youth development, tournament promotion and online coaching, alongside regular live streaming commentary and e-commerce sales. During and after the recent Asian Games, the grand slam champion frequently shared his personal assessments of matches and key players. Taking issue with the commentary, Liu claimed Zhang stepped away from competitive play not because of chronic injuries, but because he “could no longer beat anyone”. “It’s one thing to make petty moves and chase traffic, but you can’t go on endlessly … Look, does anyone else still hang out with him?” Liu said, openly questioning Zhang’s conduct and character. Both players hail from Qingdao in Shandong province and rose through the ranks of the same provincial squad. Liu captured mixed doubles and men’s team golds, as well as a men’s doubles bronze, at the 31st World University Games in Chengdu in August 2023 before announcing his departure from the national team a year later. Having transitioned into a digital sports creator and match commentator while preparing his own training academy, Liu also accused Zhang of disrupting the coaching market with unsustainably low fees. Zhang reportedly offered a 90-minute trial session for 25 yuan (US$3.74), well below the prevailing market rate of roughly 200 yuan per hour, a move Liu argued undercut industry peers. Zhang dismissed the remarks during his own broadcast, stating that his former teammate was not on his level and unworthy of engagement. “People of their level aren’t on an equal footing with me, friends, so I won’t even bother acknowledging them. They are people who can’t take the stage,” Zhang said, adding that despite making no secret of his whereabouts in Hangzhou, Liu would never dare show up at his doorstep to confront him. Zhang previously revealed on a stream that his academy employed a performance-based tiered pricing model, where training fees decrease as an athlete’s competitive results improve. “Regular trainees without results from the Talent Scouting Project pay 6,800 yuan a month, top-eight finishers in provincial championships pay 4,400 yuan, top three pay 3,400 yuan and those who finish in the top six at national championships pay 980 yuan,” Zhang explained. Rather than cooling down, the conflict escalated further during Liu’s broadcast on Friday, when he revealed he had deleted Zhang from WeChat and criticised his commercial sales tactics. “You can’t just shout ‘3, 2, 1, the link is up’ the moment you get a bit of traffic, right?” Liu said. “People harvesting their followers seem quite proud of it, but their lives aren’t really better than ours.” Liu maintained that he used his platform only to chat casually with fans without selling products, while accusing Zhang of “harvesting fans like chives”. He added that Zhang had “lost his light” and knew only how to belittle and undermine others. Online observers traced the friction to wider factional divisions among followers of current national team stars Wang Chuqin and Fan Zhendong. During the men’s singles quarter-finals at the Paris 2024 Olympics, cameras captured Liu smirking in the stands after Fan dropped the opening game against Japan’s Tomokazu Harimoto, sparking fierce criticism. Liu’s past role as Wang’s hitting partner, combined with Zhang’s repeated public praise of Fan’s technical prowess, prompted netizens to view the spat through the lens of rival fan factions. Addressing the controversy during his Sunday live streaming, Zhang said any player winning honours for China was “extraordinary” and beyond reproach, urging fans to offer quiet support instead of unsolicited critiques. “I have self-awareness, unlike some people who have none,” Zhang said in a thinly veiled parting shot. “If I can’t beat someone, then I can’t beat them. In my live streaming room, what you hear is the truth, nothing fake.”

title: Risky business? Chinese firm agrees to build rail tunnels in Qatar amid Iran war
description: The railway tunnel deal will help China deepen ties in the Middle East – but could also run into problems as regional conflicts rage.
content: A Chinese construction company has reached an agreement to work on tunnel projects in the tiny Middle Eastern nation of Qatar, as China’s global infrastructure push continues to gain momentum after recent railway deals in Southeast Asia and Latin America. The state-owned China Railway Tunnel Group has signed a memorandum of understanding with a subsidiary of the Qatari conglomerate Aamal Co, according to a statement released by the Doha-based company on Tuesday. The two firms had forged a “strategic collaboration” to work together on tunnel projects and associated supply chains in Qatar and the wider region, the statement said. The Chinese company specialises in building tunnels through mountains, under waterways and for mass urban transit networks. The Aamal subsidiary, Advanced Pipes and Casts Co, makes pipe systems and precast concrete products for infrastructure projects in Qatar and nearby countries. Qatar and neighbouring Saudi Arabia are building a 785km (488-mile) high-speed railway linking Doha with the Saudi capital Riyadh along with the two cities’ international airports. The line, which is due to be completed in six years, is designed to boost tourism and cross-border business between the two energy-rich countries. Qatar is also contributing to the Gulf Railway – 2,177km (1,353-mile) project involving six Middle Eastern countries that is scheduled to begin operations by 2030. “It’s part of an attempt by these Middle Eastern nations to secure a future that’s not only dependent on oil,” said Naubahar Sharif, head of the Education University of Hong Kong’s Department of Social Sciences and Policy Studies. However, some analysts cautioned that the project could face disruptions due to the ongoing conflicts in the region. Chinese contractors will probably pause any projects in the Middle East due to the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran and the October attacks on Riyadh’s airport by Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to Jayant Menon, a visiting senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. A project involving the Riyadh airport would definitely go on hold, he said. “The chaos in the Middle East will affect the pace of progress with these infrastructure projects,” Menon said, while noting that contractors would evaluate the Middle East’s stability over years or decades rather than just 2026. Chinese railway companies have won projects this year in Mongolia and Singapore. In Brazil, a Chinese consortium is building a cable-stayed bridge, and in Kenya a construction and engineering firm from China is building an 880-metre bridge over a rugged valley. Those projects, plus others, align with Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative, a vast global development scheme that focuses on building infrastructure connections across Asia, Europe and Africa. China Railway Tunnel Group’s agreement with the Aamal subsidiary should also “build goodwill” and long-term cooperation between the Chinese and Qatari governments, according to Sharif. “If it’s state owned, it’s not just commercial,” he said.

title: With Michelin’s Green Star gone, Hong Kong seeks to redefine sustainable dining
description: The city’s Beam Plus F&B and the UK’s Sustainable Restaurant Association offer new certification models that are rigorous, inclusive and commercially savvy.
content: David Toutain witnessed the birth of the Michelin Green Star in 2020. His eponymous restaurant in Paris was among the first to be awarded while Feuille, his Hong Kong outpost, secured one within a year of its 2023 opening. But even when Michelin quietly retired the award this year, he still never understood exactly how it was assessed. “I have no idea,” he says. “I don’t know the rules. I don’t know anything about it, to be very honest.” His confusion points to a larger problem. The Green Star was meant to recognise restaurants that, in Michelin’s own words, “hold themselves accountable for both their ethical and environmental standards”. It was a noble ambition, but an opaque one – Michelin never made public what its inspectors had in their notebooks. With the award now gone, an unanswered question lingers: what does it mean for a restaurant to be “sustainable”? True to form, Michelin offered no debrief to chefs when it announced it was phasing out the Green Star and replacing it with an editorial platform called Mindful Voices. It only said the award was “limited to gastronomy” and referenced an unspecified strategic pivot. But before blaming Michelin for retreating, consider what it was up against. Amid a broader cooling of ESG enthusiasm, the EU’s new anti-greenwashing rules took effect on September 27. The Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive requires that sustainability labels be independently verified and open to all companies, a standard the Green Star’s self-reported process could never meet. In this climate, an unverifiable green badge would no longer be an asset. It would be a liability. Certifying sustainability in dining is not like awarding stars for what’s on the table; it requires examining energy use, waste systems, labour practices and supply chains extending miles beyond the kitchen. Its inspectors were restaurant critics, not environmental assessors. Even a credible certification faces a more basic obstacle: economics. Alvin Leung, chef-owner of the farm-to-table Cafe Bau in Hong Kong, knows this first-hand. Certification, he says, would require staff to keep logs of every purchase and every bit of waste, plus regular inspections – none of which comes cheap. Even a 10 to 20 per cent increase in operational costs would force him to raise prices, which, in Hong Kong’s current market, would drive customers away. “You’d also need an inspector to come on a regular basis,” he says, “and I don’t think anybody can really do that.” For Leung, sustainability takes on two meanings – environmental and financial – and one can undermine the other. Use organic ingredients, let costs run too high and “your restaurant becomes not sustainable”. Cost, though, may be the easier problem to deal with since there is not yet a consensus on what the rules surrounding sustainability in F&B should even be, or whether the same rules should be applied everywhere. “No, the standard is not universal,” says Toutain, whose operations span locations as different as Paris, Hong Kong, Bangkok and Marrakech. “I think it [must be] case by case.” Certification bodies are now attempting to answer the question Michelin could not – with transparency and operational rigour. Sustainability programmes need support from the government because doing it alone is just not viable Alvin Leung, Cafe Bau The UK’s Sustainable Restaurant Association is blunt about what Michelin lacked: auditors trained in sustainability. Proper assessment, it argues, requires systematic evidence review. Its Food Made Good Standard begins with a questionnaire of 200 to 250 indicators – a “robust matrix of questions” – before moving to verification: corroborating documents and photographic evidence that no blind visit could capture. None of this is cheap, whether for certification bodies or for restaurants. In Hong Kong, at least one body is betting it can make the model work. Beam Society Limited (BSL) and the Hong Kong Green Building Council (HKGBC) jointly launched Beam Plus F&B Version 1.0 in July 2026. The scheme is voluntary, and its pitch to restaurants is commercial as much as ethical: “brand recognition, market credibility and distinct competitive edge,” says Harry Lai, executive director of HKGBC. Its framework is meticulous about operations, measuring areas such as energy, water, waste and staff well-being, and it assesses the menu from sourcing to whole-ingredient utilisation. Unlike the Michelin Green Star, which judged fine dining, its scope is deliberately broad: “all establishments regardless of size or age”, from restaurants and cafes to bars, fast-food outlets, ghost kitchens and catering services – a reach that extends far beyond fine dining. The scheme does not, however, assess whether the food tastes good. That is not its job – it is a building and operations certification, not a gourmet guide. BSL acknowledges the strain restaurants are operating under. Dr Calvin Lee Kwan, convenor of the steering committee for Beam Plus F&B v1.0, says restaurants “run on tight margins and high-turnover models” and that his organisation has tried to ease points of friction like cost, the administrative burden and “perceived interference with service quality”. Leung hopes governments can step in with both funding and policy to make the sort of sustainable practices Beam is examining more affordable. “We cannot do this alone,” he says. “All these sustainability programmes need support from the government because doing it alone is just not viable in terms of economics.” The Green Star may have fallen, but sustainable dining has a way forward – as long as diners choose to engage, governments are willing to support and certification bodies can earn the trust they are asking for.

title: Opinion | Economic realities threaten Asia’s green aviation ambitions
description: Even as pressure grows on airlines to adopt sustainable fuel, higher prices driven by the Middle East conflict are squeezing an industry operating on thin margins.
content: Asia-based airlines are battling stubbornly high fuel costs even as pressure mounts to accelerate their transition to more expensive sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). Singapore Airlines Group reported a 78.5 per cent surge in net fuel costs in the quarter to June, contributing to a S$76 million (US$59.3 million) net loss despite record revenue. Cathay Pacific has repeatedly adjusted passenger fuel surcharges as jet fuel prices fluctuated, while India’s low-cost carrier IndiGo introduced another round of fuel-related increases this month. With conventional fuel costs already squeezing margins, the industry’s green ambitions face an uncomfortable commercial reality: Asia’s airlines cannot afford to burn money simply to burn the greener fuel. Despite this, the pressure to decarbonise is only going to intensify as global passenger growth continues. That expansion means SAF production must not only replace a growing proportion of conventional jet fuel but also keep pace with one of the world’s fastest-growing aviation markets. Produced from materials including used cooking oil and agricultural waste, SAF is proven and offers a practical route towards lower aviation emissions. It can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in existing aircraft, but the twin headwinds of cost and availability remain barriers to widespread usage. International Air Transport Association (IATA) expects global SAF production to reach about 2.4 million tonnes this year, representing just 0.8 per cent of aviation fuel consumption. It estimates that the price premium could also add US$4.3 billion to airline fuel bills this year. For an industry operating on thin margins, the economics are difficult to ignore. Across the Asia-Pacific, however, SAF production and supply are gathering momentum. Singapore is already a major manufacturing hub, with Finnish energy group Neste’s Tuas refinery capable of producing up to a million tonnes of SAF annually. Hong Kong is strengthening its position as a regional distribution hub, targeting SAF to account for 1 to 3 per cent of fuel used by departing flights by 2030. Cathay Pacific is using SAF supplied by mainland Chinese producer Sinopec at Hong Kong International Airport, while Hong Kong-based EcoCeres is advancing plans for a major production facility in neighbouring Guangdong province. Malaysia is expanding its own production capacity, and Indonesia is developing domestic SAF feedstocks and supply chains. Thailand’s energy conglomerate Bangchak recently reached a milestone of operating SAF production at full capacity, with Thai Airways operating a flight using locally produced SAF. Like other countries in the region, Japan is exploring household cooking oil as a feedstock, while Vietnam is developing its SAF regulatory framework and the Philippines is backing regional cooperation. India is positioning itself as a major global producer, while Australia’s Jet Zero has secured funding to advance its own sugar cane feedstock SAF project. These developments demonstrate growing ambition, but announcements and production capacity are not the same as commercially viable supply. SAF producers need confidence that airlines will buy their fuel, while airlines need prices they can afford. Neither side can easily make long-term commitments without greater certainty from the other. We all want to make flying sustainable and have cleaner skies, and Singapore is working on a possible solution. Its SAF levy, which took effect on October 1 and applies to flights leaving from January 1, 2027, will add S$1 to S$10 (77 US cents to US$7.80) to economy-class tickets, with business and first-class passengers paying four times more. A similar levy on air cargo shipments was delayed for a year following industry feedback. The fixed charges are intended to spread the cost of greener fuel across travellers, while centralised SAF procurement pools secure better purchasing terms and give producers greater confidence. Should SAF prices rise, Singapore can calibrate the amount of SAF purchased and give passengers cost certainty. Singapore postponed the original levy by six months as Middle East tensions drove up conventional fuel costs, proving that even a government committed to decarbonisation recognised that timing and affordability matter. Asia does not necessarily need identical SAF mandates across every market. Its economies differ widely in resources, aviation demand and financial heft. That said, greater coordination on standards, investment and procurement would reduce uncertainty and prevent fragmented national approaches from unnecessarily raising costs. A broader regional approach to adopting SAF could help. Regional governments should support investment in refining capacity, feedstock collection and SAF certification. In turn, Asia’s airlines could negotiate joint purchasing arrangements and lock in longer-term supply agreements. Airports, frequent corporate travellers and financial institutions also have roles to play in creating dependable demand and sharing the cost. Asia has rapidly expanding aviation markets, substantial potential SAF feedstocks and growing industrial expertise. What it still lacks is a convincing commercial framework capable of turning those advantages into affordable, reliable SAF supplies. Asia’s greener aviation future therefore will depend not simply on producing more sustainable fuel but on finding a way to pay for it without undermining the airlines expected to use it.

title: More drug, semiconductor firms to set up or expand in Hong Kong, OASES head says
description: Head of Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises gives preview of government’s announcement of next batch of firms setting up in city.
content: Ten to 20 more companies are set to establish or expand operations in Hong Kong, including leading drug makers and a semiconductor business, with a roughly equal number of mainland Chinese and overseas firms, the head of a government investment office has said. Peter Yan King-shun, director general of the Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises (OASES), a government body under the Financial Secretary’s Office, offered a preview of the developments on Sunday ahead of the announcement of details on Thursday. Yan said the companies included several industry leaders with substantial market valuations. He expected the roughly equal split between mainland and overseas firms to continue, although maintaining the ratio was not an explicit recruitment target. Five of the world’s 10 top pharmaceutical companies have already established a presence in Hong Kong. Yan said the next batch of firms would include more drug makers from that group and they would conduct clinical trials and develop new medicines. “We are not in a rush, because we now have the conditions to give ourselves time to work out clearly what substantive activities they will carry out after establishing themselves in Hong Kong,” he told a radio programme. The office wanted pharmaceutical companies to contribute to the city’s industrial development, rather than simply sell drugs, he added. Successful projects had encouraged competitors to explore opportunities in Hong Kong, with some concerned about falling behind, Yan explained. “When the first, second and third successful cases emerge, others worried about missing out and became more proactive in approaching us,” he said. The office would also step up efforts to attract semiconductor and advanced manufacturing businesses, he added. Yan said a leading global company among the incoming batch had brought suppliers and other related businesses to cities where it had previously invested, and Hong Kong hoped to reap similar benefits. But he also stressed that company size, investment amounts and job creation were not the only considerations in evaluating businesses. He said the office had been in talks with more than 100 companies and would become increasingly selective, as a key consideration was whether a business could help the development of the city’s strategic industries. “More importantly, it is about aligning with our industrial policies, helping develop our industrial ecosystem and accelerating the implementation of those policies,” he said. Strategic enterprises were required to submit five-year plans detailing their proposed investments and job creation numbers, with more specific information required for the first year and the first three years overall. The office also wanted companies to provide concrete details of their first major project in Hong Kong. Asked whether firms should face penalties for failing to deliver results, Yan said there was little need for a separate penalty mechanism, as government funding schemes already required recipients to meet targets or commit their own funds before receiving matching support. “For most strategic enterprises establishing themselves in Hong Kong, government subsidies are not their main incentive,” he said, adding that access to talent, financing and international markets was also a key attraction. Yan said that more than 40 per cent of the over 120 strategic enterprises already established in Hong Kong had premises in traditional commercial districts. The coming Northern Metropolis development, including sites in Hung Shui Kiu and the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park at the Lok Ma Chau Loop, would give them more options, he noted. Yan said he expected strategic enterprises to take part in future tenders as more sites became available. OASES has attracted 124 companies in six batches so far, with the firms expected to invest HK$73 billion and create about 25,000 jobs over the coming years. Thursday’s announcement will mark the seventh batch.
