The previous group, unveiled in April, comprised 22 companies, including American pharmaceutical giant Pfizer, biotech firm Amgen and mainland ride-hailing platform Didi.

title: How AI is reshaping microdramas as the vertical video format takes a ‘generational jump’
description: Microdrama industry insiders share effects of recent AI advances, from aiding editing to replacing actors. Is it a useful tool or a curse?
content: Paddy Ma Wendi, a director of vertical dramas since 2023, has had a front-row seat to how fast and hard artificial intelligence has affected the mobile-first entertainment genre in 2026. Digital content farms have started churning out short productions – serialised stories made for smartphones and usually watched in portrait mode – using the latest AI technology. “When I was in the US [for a live-action vertical drama], I usually hired about 20 to 30 people, including the actors,” says Ma, who graduated from New York’s School of Visual Arts in 2015 and founded one of the first production companies specialising in English-language microdramas on the United States’ East Coast. He is currently based in Zhengzhou, in China’s Henan province, to take advantage of the relatively low labour costs there. “In China, I went up to 100 crew members once,” he says, “but now, for one AI drama, there are only a few, say two to five people doing this for a week.” However, AI filmmaking remains labour-intensive, he says, as generative AI tools yield highly randomised results; getting what you actually want right away is rare. A gruelling production loop Directors struggle to maintain visual consistency and narrative continuity across scenes, which is a critical flaw when trying to piece together a coherent microdrama storyline. Most of the time, the machine misses the mark completely. To make it work, teams must endure exhausting hours chained to screens, inputting prompts, reviewing the output and handling rough edits. Human labour is still essential for constantly revising commands and judging whether the footage is good enough. It’s a race to the bottom. Only very few projects [are] paid [enough] to make a better product. Paddy Ma Wendi, microdrama director But instead of hiring people in the film industry, such as cameramen and make-up artists, the technology traps the remaining workers who would previously have been editors or second directors in a gruelling, repetitive loop of trial and error to get usable clips. “If you want to get all the details right, you have to keep generating 20 [or] 30 times to get [the] right footage,” Ma says. “But this costs a lot of money.” He estimates 720p generation – using AI models that synthesise video content at a 1280×720 progressive high-definition resolution – costs about 10 to 20 US cents per second, depending on the platform, and that one prompt generates a clip of roughly four to 15 seconds of footage. Prompts cost anywhere from 40 cents to US$3. Therefore, getting 15 seconds of footage right can cost between US$8 and US$90. Right now there is an immense price war in China due to the extremely low barrier to entry. “It’s a race to the bottom,” Ma says. “Only very few projects [are] paid [enough] to make a better product. Most of the vendors [say]: ‘I just want 10 shows. Give me 10 shows.’ They don’t even need to speak English; they just prompt for the dialogue to be in English. “There are Chinese labourers in Zhengzhou who are paid 3,000 [to] 4,000 yuan [US$450 to US$600] monthly to make English vertical dramas. How are you going to compete with that? “To be honest, I’m trying to get out of this AI vertical drama business because the [profit] margin is too low now,” Ma says. “It’s getting into a labour-heavy business. It’s not like filmmaking any more.” Actors face a sudden drought Stevan Miladinovic, an actor from Serbia who starred in microdrama The Billionaire CEO’s Runaway Wife (2024), is among the first casualties in this shift. The 28-year-old was ready to jump back into the microdrama game in the first quarter of 2026. “Around January and February, my agent was contacting me, asking when I would come back to Thailand because there were a lot of casting calls,” he says. Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam and China were major microdrama production hubs because of the low labour costs. Producers would often fly in actors from around the region to star in the shows. According to Miladinovic, actors can earn up to US$8,000 for 10 days’ work as the lead in a microdrama. “I invested a lot of money coming back to Asia,” he says. “I was like, ‘One drama, I’m going to earn everything again and more, and I’m going to do at least four or five of them.’” However, when he wrapped up his project in Europe and returned in May 2026, all he heard were crickets: “I got in touch with some other actors … They were like, ‘It’s dead. Nothing is happening,’” he says. Miladinovic found out that he had been almost completely replaced by AI. “I started seeing those AI dramas and was like, ‘Come on, this can’t be real,’” he says. “But then I really started figuring that people are interacting. People would leave likes, comment, people would watch it.” Miladinovic also worries about the ability of production companies to “take our likeness and data on our faces, then use our partial or entire image for their film forever”. He is not alone in his concern. Jen Cooper, founder of microdrama industry news platform Vertical Drama Love, says: “From what [people in the industry] tell me in Los Angeles, work dropped by about 90 per cent in six weeks … by looking at the amount of jobs on things like [online casting platform] Actors Access, which is where the vertical dramas are mainly advertised for work. “It was only February or March [when] there were a few [AI dramas] beginning to pop up on platforms … and then it seemed to move very fast from just a few here and there to suddenly the main thing you were being shown on the apps was AI,” she says. “That was a very quick switch.” Quality concerns and the future Ma pinpoints the moment of change to February 12, 2026 – when Seedance 2.0, an advanced animation AI model, was released in China: “Seedance 2.0 became the only AI video generation model,” Ma says. “Nothing else comes even close. AI videos went from not good to very acceptable in one generational jump.” But not everyone agrees regarding the quality of AI microdramas. “A lot of it, I think, is fairly poor quality,” Cooper says. “The look and the voice tend to be the same. You know Henry Cavill’s look and voice in The Witcher? He’s been a busy boy this summer; he was the dragon king in a lot of dramas.” The flood of AI content has caused so much concern that China’s broadcasting regulator, the National Radio and Television Administration, is getting involved. It announced on September 17, 2026, that it will step up its initiative to promote and distribute high-quality microdramas, guiding platforms to create dedicated sections for live-action dramas while providing financial support so quality productions can find audiences and generate returns. But it is not all bad news for the bite-sized entertainment genre, which is now widely available on platforms such as YouTube, Bilibili and iQiyi. Timothy Oh, chief marketing officer at COL Group, the parent company of microdrama apps such as Flareflow, says AI shows, including Falling for My Bully, The Wicked Lycan Prince, are among its top performers. AI also opens up worlds creators previously could not explore within microdrama budgets, particularly in fantasy, sci-fi, animation and supernatural stories. “That creates opportunities to reach audiences we haven’t traditionally served,” he says. Cooper, for one, is looking forward to more content in that genre: “[AI] has enabled the fantasy and science-fiction realm a lot,” she says. “I am looking forward to special effects being done by it.” Ma is now exploring a hybrid feature film using AI. “I want to use human acting to drive AI, because it is actually very good at editing footage,” he says. “Let’s say if you input footage from the film Titanic, and you ask it to change Jack and Rose into Spider-Man and Mary Jane, it can do it absolutely perfectly. “I want to bring human actors [to] act in a studio, in a soundstage, and bring all the footage into AI to re-render it into a space station or a magic land,” he says.

title: Cherish peace and stability, John Lee urges Hongkongers during Chung Yeung Festival
description: City leader and senior officials attend annual tribute to city’s wartime defenders and those who died in service at City Hall Memorial Garden.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has urged residents to cherish peace and stability as senior officials marked the Chung Yeung Festival with tributes to the city’s wartime defenders and public servants who died in the line of duty. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu attended the annual ceremony at the Hong Kong City Hall Memorial Garden in Central on Sunday, laying a wreath to honour those who died defending the city between 1941 and 1945. “As we remember the heroes who sacrificed their lives in war and our compatriots who perished, we should learn lessons from history, jointly cherish and safeguard this hard-won peace and stability, and continue working for Hong Kong’s future,” he wrote on social media earlier in the day. The memorial service featured a flag-raising ceremony, a moment of silence with heads bowed and the laying of wreaths by official representatives. Legislative Council president Starry Lee Wai-king, who also attended the ceremony, said the sacrifices of those who died defending Hong Kong should remind residents to value the present and shoulder their responsibilities. She stressed the importance of helping younger generations understand the history of the city’s struggle and appreciate peace, so the fallen defenders’ spirit could be passed on and unite people in protecting their home and building Hong Kong’s future. Separately, Secretary for the Civil Service Ingrid Yeung Ho Poi-yan visited Gallant Garden on the government’s behalf, offering flowers for colleagues who died while performing their duties. She said those buried came from different government departments and ranks, and their dedication and selfless service would remain in colleagues’ hearts. “They are role models for us to learn from, and also remind us to stay true to our original aspirations and mission, and do our utmost to serve the public,” she wrote. She also laid flowers for the eight Hong Kong residents killed in the 2010 Manila hostage crisis.

title: Looters smash Paris shops as ‘unacceptable’ violence rocks France
description: Crowds of masked men clear shelves of sunglasses, clothes, jewellery and food as anger over cost of living deepens.
content: Smashing shop windows and snatching boxes of goods, looters in Paris poured into stores across the capital on Saturday, facing no resistance from authorities as nationwide protests degenerated into violence. Crowds of masked men wearing black hoodies yanked at metal store shutters until they gave way, clearing shelves of cigarettes, sunglasses, clothes, jewellery and food. The violence erupted as hundreds of thousands of demonstrators gathered across the country to denounce the cost of living, following weeks of student protests and stoking political uncertainty six months before France’s presidential election. Looters emerged from a supermarket carrying bags stuffed with cakes, fruit juice and alcohol. From a small jewellery shop across the street, they took antique clocks. On a street corner, entire display racks of sunglasses vanished. Inside the shops, they searched for the cash register, smashing it onto the floor, sometimes only to discover it was empty. Perched on a pavement terrace with a colleague, a 38-year-old art teacher who gave her name as Alma said she had “never seen anything like it”. The pair, who had joined an unsuccessful march earlier in the day to reach the French president’s residence, the Elysee Palace, said nonetheless that they “understand” the revolt. The violence began on the sidelines of marches in the capital and other cities that the interior ministry said were attended by 550,000 people. The CGT union, which took part, said 800,000 people attended. Police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who slammed the “violence of extreme intensity”, said late on Saturday that 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers hurt. Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said whole streets “have been devastated” in the capital, making a distinction between the “fundamental” right to protest and “unacceptable” violence. “I understand why people might be upset, but I think damaging property is fine, as long as we don’t physically harm anyone,” Alma said. Restaurants, hotels and residential buildings have mostly been spared, prompting surreal scenes of Parisians enjoying their usual Saturday lunch with friends while crowds wreaked havoc outside. Locals watched the scenes unfold from the safety of their flats. “What a sight,” said Jules, a 29-year-old civil servant. “They must have some pretty deep anger. They’re a part of society who doesn’t feel integrated.” While he agreed with the right to protest, he said the looters were “undermining their own goals”. “Just look at the state of the street,” he said. Near the famous Place de la Republique in central Paris, broken glass and debris littered the roads, as a pile of burning bicycles belched out thick smoke. Law enforcement was absent from the area, having clashed with protesters there earlier in the day.

title: Letters | Hidden crisis faces caregivers of neurodiverse children in Hong Kong
description: Readers discuss the well-being of caregivers of children with special needs, volcanic eruptions, and West Kowloon station.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. In many families, parents can breathe a little easier once their child turns 18. But for caregivers of children with special educational needs (SEN), parental challenges only increase and often multiply as the years go on. Love 21 Foundation recently surveyed 210 families caring for neurodiverse loved ones, and the findings are alarming. Sixty-three per cent reported at least one family member struggling with mental or emotional distress. The survey also revealed that many are facing financial strain, with 33 per cent having to reduce their meals due to lack of finances. The challenges are plentiful and complex. Our family support team regularly encounters caregivers on the brink of collapse: mothers deprived of sleep while tending to sleepless children; elderly parents struggling with depression while supporting their adult children who are going through the same battle. Many caregivers appear cheerful on the outside, but confided during our therapy sessions their feelings of hopelessness and even suicidal thoughts. However, these resilient and dedicated parents consistently do everything they can to prioritise their child’s health and happiness. At Love 21 Foundation we strive to improve our members’ well-being and self-care abilities, helping them to build healthy lives and integrate into the community through a wider range of activities. Our caring community model provides a safe space for members to feel connected and loved. We support caregivers by teaching practical parenting skills and building peer support networks for them to have fun and get some rest with fellow caregivers who face similar challenges. You too can play a part. This Mental Health Month, let’s commit beyond awareness by contributing towards fostering a community where every family feels seen, supported and valued. Jeff Rotmeyer, founder and CEO, Love 21 Foundation Don’t underestimate volcanic eruptions’ impact on weather Climate change with long-term global impacts differs from weather with short-term local or regional impacts. Due to this reason, extreme weather events such as floods and droughts reported by the media in different parts of the world cannot easily be regarded as evidence for climate change. The study of observation records in Hong Kong and elsewhere has shown the following: 1963, the driest year on record since 1844 in Hong Kong, was influenced by the Agung volcanic eruption on Bali, Indonesia; 1982, the second wettest year on record in Hong Kong, was influenced by the El Chichon volcanic eruption in Mexico; 1991, the 11th driest year in Hong Kong, was influenced by the Pinatubo volcanic eruption in the Philippines. Satellite tracking shows that the severe rainstorm on June 7, 2008 that resulted in 2,400 landslides on Lantau Island and elsewhere in Hong Kong coincided with the arrival of an eruption cloud penetrating the stratosphere. This cloud originating from the Chaitén volcanic eruption in Chile on May 2, 2008 circled the globe one-and-a-half times before reaching Lantau. The wettest year on record in Hurbanovo, Slovakia – 2010 – was influenced by the Eyjafjallajoküll volcanic eruption in Iceland. The 2011-2012 El Hierro submarine volcanic eruption in the Canary Islands apparently caused hot sea-surface water to develop in the North Atlantic; notable extreme weather events in 2012 included record low Arctic sea ice, accelerated Greenland ice sheet melting and Hurricane Sandy, which devastated New York. The long-lasting and strong 2014-2016 El Niño–Southern Oscillation was apparently caused by a combination of sub-aerial and submarine volcanic eruptions in the Pacific Ocean. Important contributors identified include Nishino-shima, Hunga and Wolf volcanoes. The record rainfall in eastern Australia and New Zealand in February 2022 was apparently a result of the 2021-2022 Tongan volcanic eruption cloud interfering with regional jet streams. The above findings have been contributed to the Volcanic Impacts on Climate and Society working group of the Past Global Changes project. Volcanic eruptions are an underestimated cause of regional weather variability. Wyss Yim, Pok Fu Lam Help high-speed rail passengers grab a bite I was disappointed to find that there are still no food outlets, beverage shops or vending machines inside the departure hall of West Kowloon high-speed rail station. Is there a reason for this? Some passengers may not have enough time to grab a bite before their train journey. Laychoo Wong, Admiralty

title: Dino-mite treasures: inside Singapore’s ‘Fort Knox’ storing playthings of ultra-rich
description: The triceratops fossil was on display during the lead-up to last weekend’s Singapore Grand Prix attended by ultra-high-net-worth individuals.
content: Stored in a climate-controlled environment within what is commonly known as the “Fort Knox of Singapore” rests the skull of a triceratops which once roamed the Earth 66 million years ago. The jagged edges of its frill and horns are largely intact, and according to its owner, Chaw Wei Yang, 26, it is one of the most complete triceratops skull fossils ever found. Chaw, who runs Fine Art Storage Services (FASS) located inside Le Freeport, formerly known as Singapore Freeport, along with his partners, acquired the option to the fossil while it was still in the ground in Montana, United States. It was dug up just a few months ago. “I love dinosaurs, and I’m not the only one. It’s a very universal thing – we grew up with dinosaurs, and that kind of segues to why I got into collecting them because for dinosaurs, the appeal is universal. For art, it can be very subjective,” Chaw said. He did not disclose how much he paid for the option and excavation. In July, a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton called Gus from South Dakota became the world’s most expensive fossil sold at auction, after fetching a record US$50.13 million. At 11.6 metres (38 feet) in length with a skull measuring 137cm (54 inches), Gus is one of the largest T. rexes ever found, according to Sotheby’s. Natural history artefacts such as fossils and meteorites are becoming increasingly popular among the latest generation of fine art collectors as the lines between the art world and palaeontology blur, according to Art News in May. The childhood fascination with dinosaurs appeared to be colliding with a new generation of wealth, the outlet reported, quoting experts as saying that the buyers are younger collectors who grew up during the explosion of dinosaur culture in the 1980s and 1990s, when Jurassic Park and natural history museums made it into popular culture. Chaw’s own fascination began as a child when his mother bought him a mosasaurus tooth from the Singapore Science Centre. “Something unique about this generation is that we grew up with a lot of pop culture and media, and the world has become so connected so people start to find different communities that resonate with them,” he said. “Dinosaurs just speak to the inner child in all of us.” He is aware of the naysayers who point out that these fossils should be left to be studied by scientists and displayed in museums but argue that there is a symbiotic relationship between private collectors who fund excavations and lovers of palaeontology. “It’s in the best interest of both parties. For the individuals who dig it up, if they find something unique, special or scientifically significant, they will work with museums and universities to get it studied,” Chaw said. “Obviously, there may be people who are a little bit more money centric, but most of the people that I’ve met and work with, they are all passionate people first.” Chaw has contacted museums to loan them his fossil but most major institutions already house triceratops fossils in their permanent collections. Quiet luxury The triceratops fossil was on display at the FASS space over the course of Formula One week in Singapore alongside meteorites, megalodon teeth and fluorides that are millions of years old. In the lead-up to last Sunday’s race, high net worth individuals flocked to the city state to attend meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions such as the Milken Institute Asia Summit and Token2049. It was the perfect time for FASS to show off its one stop service of storing, shipping, insuring and installing fine art and collectibles tax-free. Chaw was unwilling to disclose the exact value of the pieces that FASS handles, but said that it extended into the billions of dollars. Because of the high value of items in storage, its rooms are humidity- and temperature-controlled and fitted with gas suspension systems instead of water sprinklers in the event of a fire. Singapore’s appeal as a politically stable safe haven was another draw, he said. “When you’re storing such important or meaningful things, to a collector, you just want to have the best. You want it to be safe, and you want everything to be stored in the best conditions. It’s basically for peace of mind.” Following a S$3 billion (US$2.3 billion) money-laundering case involving 10 foreign nationals in 2023, Singapore tightened its asset recovery strategy. This included introducing laws that allowed authorities to petition courts to sell seized assets even before conviction, such as fine art, antiques, investment-grade wine, vessels, exotic livestock like fish and reptiles, and racehorses. Some of the confiscated items from the 2023 case – including jewellery, designer bags and watches – were stored inside a bulletproof, maximum-security vault at Le Freeport before their auction this year. FASS also connects collectors wanting to acquire pieces from each other. But the laws had little impact on sales since strict know-your-client checks were already performed before the unravelling of the case in 2023, Chaw said. “There’s very high-profile people that we’ve turned down before, just because they don’t pass the … checks,” he said. “We’re in Singapore and what people appreciate about us is that we are by the law.” For a select few, FASS puts on private exhibitions, displaying their best pieces, some of which are on sale. Saying that discretion was a priority for his clients, Chaw was unable to disclose the identities of the ultra-high-net-worth individuals and celebrities he hosted this year or how much was transacted during the week. “We bring out the best in class. This year was more natural history focused, last year was maybe more art focused, maybe next year we could do wine and watches. We try to bring in something unique and significant every year,” Chaw said. This year, his triceratops was a highlight of the exhibition. And while he admitted there was interest in the fossil over the week, he has no intention of parting with the object of his inner child’s desires just yet.

title: Opinion | China’s ‘golden week’ holidays come at a cost
description: A week of uninterrupted leave might look generous on paper, but it can conceal the working days shifted elsewhere to make it possible.
content: For iPhone users in China, the calendar has long presented a small but recurring problem. On a Sunday designated as a make-up workday, an alarm might remain silent. On a regular Friday converted into a day off, it might ring anyway. Nearly 17 years after entering the Chinese market, Apple quietly updated its operating system in September to automatically recognise China’s official schedule of adjusted holidays and workdays. The fix is modest, but it points to a larger question: what happens when a society’s working week no longer matches the natural cadence of the days? The issue transcends a foreign tech giant adapting to local rules. China’s holiday calendar is not a static record of dates but a dynamic mechanism for redistributing public time. By moving weekend leave to around national holidays, policymakers engineer longer continuous breaks at the expense of a predictable working week, effectively using time as an administrative lever. China’s practice of swapping workdays for extended leave is not an ancient cultural tradition but an instrument of modern macroeconomic management. Conceived in the wake of the Asian financial crisis in the late 1990s, the system was designed to jump-start domestic spending through multi-day “golden weeks”. By grafting adjacent weekends onto national holidays, the state converted leisure into fiscal stimulus, funnelling consumer capital into concentrated travel surges. However, that blueprint relies on borrowing time from the working week. While preserving traditional observances such as the Chinese New Year and Mid-Autumn Festival, the official calendar creates extended breaks without expanding overall statutory leave. To compensate, employees are required to forfeit standard weekends, enduring gruelling six-day working weeks. What functions on paper as an encouragement for tourism ends up disrupting the basic cadence of private enterprise and daily life. However, predictability determines the real value of leisure. Unbroken weekends provide the foundational certainty required to schedule medical appointments, organise childcare or maintain household routines. When an overnight administrative directive can convert a Sunday into a Tuesday, that microeconomic stability vanishes, extending state intervention into the domestic sphere. The United States offers a useful, though imperfect, contrast. In 1968, Congress passed the Uniform Monday Holiday Act, which took effect in 1971 and moved several federal holiday observances to Mondays. George Washington’s birthday, for example, is now observed on the third Monday in February rather than on its historical date of February 22. The reform made several federal holidays more predictable by placing their observance on Mondays, creating regular three-day weekends rather than allowing those holidays to interrupt the working week. The American approach accepts that a holiday need not be observed on the exact date of the event it commemorates. In contrast, China generally retains traditional festival dates while rearranging the surrounding work schedule to create longer breaks. The American system shifts the observance; the Chinese system shifts working days. Neither arrangement is free of compromise. The difference lies in how each system distributes the burden of coordination. Moving a holiday to Monday makes time off easier to anticipate. Rearranging the working week requires individuals and employers to adjust their routines, sometimes at the expense of the predictable weekends that ordinarily anchor working life. The economic rationale for China’s approach is to stimulate domestic consumption by concentrating travel and spending into extended holiday periods. However, higher spending in those windows might not be a bonus: some purchases are simply brought forward or compressed from other weeks. Concentration also carries a price that spending figures do not record. Crowded transport, rising accommodation costs and congested tourist sites reduce the quality of the leisure that the spending is meant to buy. A week of uninterrupted leave might look generous on paper, but it can conceal the working days shifted elsewhere to make it possible. When extended holidays are bracketed by unusually long working stretches, the fatigue they create can undermine the recovery that time off is meant to provide. A calendar can count days of leave with precision, but it cannot tell us whether people have had enough time to recover, maintain their routines or spend unhurried time with their families. Apple’s update addresses one small consequence of this system. The alarm can now follow an official schedule that a conventional weekly calendar cannot reliably convey. For users, this means one less source of uncertainty in a working week already made less predictable by official rescheduling. Technology has adapted to the administrative calendar, translating government decisions into a more dependable signal for daily life. Even so, the convenience of a better-timed alarm should not obscure the larger questions raised by the system itself: how working days are arranged, how much disruption economic efficiency can justify and who ultimately bears the cost of public time being reorganised. A policy designed to create longer holidays could generate economic benefits in the aggregate while imposing less visible costs on individual lives. Technology can make such a schedule easier to navigate, but it cannot determine whether its costs and benefits are fairly distributed. A holiday calendar is never merely an accounting of days off. It reflects a society’s priorities: which dates deserve protection, which economic objectives take precedence and how much flexibility people are expected to surrender. The question is not whether governments should organise public time but how far that authority should extend into private life. As China seeks to shift towards consumption-led growth, the ability to plan and enjoy free time might matter as much as the number of holidays on offer. A more effective calendar would not simply count days of leave. It would return control of time to the microeconomic actors who drive sustainable expansion.

title: US-Russia deal, Trump-Zelensky clash could leave Ukraine out in the cold
description: Analysts say Trump’s action, including lifting sanctions and tariffs on Moscow, would prompt Putin to continue the war.
content: From US threats to cut off intelligence support for Ukraine to a waiver of tariffs on Russian ⁠exports and a diesel deal that could help Russia fund its war, it has been a damaging week for ties between Kyiv and its most important ally, Washington. US President Donald Trump, frustrated by high energy costs he blames partly on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, has repeatedly criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. A disruption of US-provided satellite internet services raised fears that Ukraine could be vulnerable as it prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure. Zelensky responded to Trump’s barbs with an unusually sharp series of public criticisms of Trump, suggesting the US was now favouring Russia. He said Ukraine would defy Trump’s demand to stop striking Russian energy targets, citing Russia’s continued attacks. Intensifying the discord, Trump waived key US ‌Russia-related sanctions and tariffs on Friday, shortly before they were scheduled to take effect. That prompted Zelensky to say in social media posts that Trump’s action would encourage Russia to continue attacks on Ukraine. The widening rift has sparked concerns that Trump and Zelensky’s tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Trump could yet restrict the supply of weapons to Ukraine, follow through on threats to stop sharing battlefield intelligence, or strike more economic deals with Moscow. Despite Zelensky’s remarks, Kyiv wants to continue dialogue with Trump’s envoys, his friend Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Denys Sienik, charge d’affaires at Ukraine’s embassy in Washington, told Newsmax on Friday that Ukraine was grateful to Trump and his team for their efforts to end the war and said Ukraine was willing to engage in talks with Russia. Trump told reporters on Friday he would continue to deal with both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I want that war to end,” he said. Daniel Fried, the senior State Department official ⁠on Europe from 2005-09, said it was unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine, but the fallout was damaging prospects for an end to the war that began with Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. “It’s not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in ‌Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it’s not cost-free,” said Fried, now at the Washington-based Atlantic Council think tank. Trump’s relationship with Zelensky has long been uneasy. Trump and US Vice-President J.D. Vance publicly upbraided Zelensky during an Oval Office meeting in February 2025. Washington has paused or slowed military help to Ukraine under Trump, while allowing European allies to purchase US weapons for Kyiv. The relationship had steadied until Ukraine’s strikes this year on energy ‌sites in Russia began contributing to rising fuel prices. High petrol and diesel prices are a political headache for Trump ahead of November’s midterm election, in which his Republican Party could lose its majorities in the US Congress, according to analysts. Experts ⁠say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of ⁠the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz. Frustrated by Zelensky, however, Trump turned to Russia to increase fuel supply and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal debate, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Trump said on October 9 that he had reached a deal with ‌Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel. In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump also waived major Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs shortly before they were supposed to take effect under the Graham Act, which Trump signed last month. Although the law, named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, called for new penalties on Russia starting ‌next week, it ‌also allows the president to waive them if it is in the US national interest to do so. Zelensky said Trump’s latest action undercuts the Graham Act’s main goal and will fuel Russia’s “desire to keep killing people”. The US diesel deal with Russia and the waiver are the latest steps ‌in what Zelensky said he expects to be continued sanctions relief on Moscow. The prospect of the US continuing to pressure Russia to end the war has dimmed since Graham’s death in July, Zelensky said. Graham, a South Carolina Republican and a confidant of Trump, strongly supported Ukraine. “It’s difficult without him, ⁠I’ll be honest,” the Ukrainian president said. For Kyiv, the stakes are high and immediate. Zelensky said on Tuesday that Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a deadly Russian attack on the capital. Without US intelligence, Ukraine could face greater difficulty detecting and countering ⁠Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly against energy infrastructure that Moscow has repeatedly targeted during previous winters. Trump has said the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. But Zelensky told NPR that US officials had warned Ukrainian commanders intelligence could be reduced or cut off. Ukraine’s Starshield system, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink service, was disrupted after what two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said was an order originating from the White House. The service has been partially restored, ‌but the episode highlighted the vulnerability created by Ukraine’s dependence on technology controlled by ‌US companies and subject to decisions by the Trump administration. Trump may face resistance if congressional Republicans see his approach as weakening Ukraine while benefiting Russia. Ukraine retains support among Trump’s fellow Republicans, some of whom argue that Washington should not pressure Kyiv into accepting a settlement on terms favourable to Moscow. Zelensky’s tough responses to Trump were risky, but he may be counting on a power shift on Capitol Hill after the midterm election to make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia and further reduce military help to Kyiv, said Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and head of the Global Situation Room consultancy. “Zelensky knows who he’s dealing with,” he said. “Trump’s threats don’t have the same kind of effect as they did when J.D. Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office.”

title: How land power could help US forces counter China in the Indo-Pacific
description: US commanders say the army’s long-range missiles, air defences and ground operations are vital to deterring China and protecting its forces.
content: Senior US commanders have highlighted the importance of land-based troops and equipment stationed in the Asia-Pacific in any conflict with China, countering assumptions that such a war would be fought mainly at sea and in the air. General Ron Clark, commander of US Army Pacific, said the “tyranny of distance” made it difficult to rely on air and naval forces during a panel discussion at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting this week. The comments reflect mounting concerns among US commanders that China’s increasingly sophisticated air and naval forces could stop American forces operating freely in the region, leaving them in greater need of land-based support. Clark commands more than 107,000 soldiers deployed in US Pacific territories and in allies such as South Korea and Japan, with rotational deployments in the Philippines. He said the command covered “17 time zones, 52 per cent of the Earth’s surface, 60 per cent of the Earth’s population, four billion people, 25 per cent of the world’s land mass”. Deterrence had been “successful” because of the US Army’s combat-ready posture, “set forward” at scale in the first and second island chains, he added. Clark said the army now had the “true capability to operate across all domains” within the first and second island chains – strategically vital groups of islands that stand between China and the open waters of the Pacific – adding that this had “changed the outcome” in a series of war games. He said that without the army “holding terrain and providing the sustainment”, the air force and navy could not employ their “exquisite capabilities”. “Our ability to provide integrated air missile defence across the entirety of the region is an army capability that is leveraged by the joint force,” he added. Without naming China directly, Clark said “our adversary” had devised a strategy tied to “anti-access area denial” – a term American planners use for the People’s Liberation Army’s plans to keep adversaries such as the US out of strategically vital areas. Countering it required the US Army to provide assistance for air and sea “operations that can pulse into an access-denied environment”, he added. China has been steadily modernising its armed forces and has set a series of goals to be reached by politically symbolic dates such as 2027, 2035 and 2049. US intelligence and military officials have frequently cited these as a possible timeline for the PLA’s readiness to take Taiwan by force. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to bring it under its control. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise the self-ruled island as independent, but Washington opposes any use of force and is legally committed to providing Taipei with arms. China’s military reforms have focused on air and sea power, and in recent years it has unveiled a series of advanced weapons such as the Fujian aircraft carrier, the J-35 fifth-generation fighter jet and various unmanned and autonomous systems. Clark’s remarks reflect the US Army’s shift towards multi-domain operations, integrating cyber, space and electronic warfare. In June, the US Army set up the Multi-Domain Command-Pacific at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state to support joint and allied operations across the Indo-Pacific region. Joshua Arostegui, chair of China studies and research director of the China Landpower Studies Centre at the US Army War College, said there had been a “broader structural shift” in America’s defence strategy. “In an era where long-range precision fires and unmanned aerial systems are proliferating, the traditional model of massing large, static land forces is largely recognised as obsolete,” said Arostegui. “Instead, the Army is adapting to serve as a foundational ‘inside force’, designed to selectively fracture adversary networks so the broader joint force can operate effectively.” Shaun McDougall, a lead analyst covering the US defence market at Forecast International, said drone and missile threats were becoming “more ubiquitous”. “[Multi-domain task forces] are intended to serve as a deterrent to countries like China or to respond accordingly should a conflict arise,” said McDougall. “The army has also been prioritising its own development of unmanned systems, long-range strike platforms and air and missile defence capabilities.” Liselotte Odgaard, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, said long-range missiles such as the Typhon and High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems were one of the army’s “most significant contributions to deterrence against China”. “By creating multiple axes of threat, they raise the costs and risks of any Chinese attempt to project power beyond the first island chain or conduct operations against Taiwan,” she said. Meanwhile, Beijing’s latest five-year plan prioritised the transition towards “intelligentised” warfare, emphasising the importance of artificial intelligence, unmanned and autonomous systems, networked information infrastructure and emerging technologies. Clark said the wars in Iran and Ukraine offered lessons on how land-based forces could have an impact on aerial and naval warfare, particularly through long-range precision strikes and integrated air and missile defence. “In those two theatres [Iran and Ukraine], it’s not a near-peer adversary that we would be working against. Whereas in our theatre, it absolutely is,” said Clark. He said this raised the question of how the Army would tackle drones and ballistic missiles in an archipelagic environment. Speaking alongside Clark, General Xavier Brunson, commander of United States Forces Korea, said alliances offered the US “distributed locations” that offered a “position of advantage”, helping to protect critical assets from sensors and drones. He added that US adversaries were trying to imitate the network of alliances that the US had built, saying: “So if you look at Russia and [North Korea] and China, you see them continuing to collude … Well, they’ve learned that from us.” Odgaard said air defence and counter-drone capabilities had “significantly” increased the army’s importance given the possible threat from missiles and drones in the Indo-Pacific. Arostegui said integrated air and missile defence was “perhaps the US Army’s most essential strategic contribution” in the region. “Given the rapid advancement and proliferation of ballistic, cruise and hypersonic technologies, these fixed locations face acute vulnerabilities that only layered, ground-based defence systems … can mitigate,” he said. “Consequently, robust air and missile defence transforms the Army into a foundational prerequisite for any sustained military operation or crisis response in the region.”

title: Why is Hong Kong hosting the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting? There is another agenda
description: Decision for Hong Kong to host this week’s meeting is part of a broader strategy to bolster the city’s standing as an offshore renminbi hub, experts say.
content: As Hong Kong hosts the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday, this two-part series examines the summit’s significance and its implications for Beijing on the global stage. In part one, Simpson Cheung and Alfred Lam explore how the event could elevate the city’s status as an international financial centre at a pivotal moment. Beijing’s decision to have Hong Kong host the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting this week is a deliberate move to galvanise the city’s standing as an offshore renminbi hub and showcase it as a safe harbour amid continuing geopolitical tensions, analysts have said. About 500 guests, including finance chiefs and senior officials from the 21 member economies, are expected to attend the annual meeting on October 20 and 21, which Hong Kong will host for the first time. It will take place at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said Beijing’s choice of venue showed it deliberately intended to promote Hong Kong’s international status, especially as a financial centre. The event would bolster its standing as an offshore renminbi hub and a wealth management capital, support the city’s economic development and underscore its importance to China’s development, he said. “The Apec meeting … will allow Hong Kong to present itself to the world in grand style and refute false, negative portrayals by hostile external forces,” he added. Data from Swift – the Belgium-based cooperative formally known as the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication – showed the city handled about 76 per cent of the world’s renminbi payments as of August. Offshore yuan lending reached a record 935 billion yuan (US$140 billion) last year. Lau said hosting more international events such as Apec would strengthen the city’s global profile and status, particularly as a gateway to China’s vast economy. He added that the city’s international image and reputation had suffered considerably since the 2019 anti-government protests, the enactment of the national security law and the negative narratives about Hong Kong purveyed by the West. Lau said the meeting would bring many key officials, media representatives and businesspeople to China, giving them a chance to see Hong Kong’s robust, growing economy and investment opportunities, particularly in financial services and wealth management. The theme for Apec this year is “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together”, with openness, innovation and cooperation identified as the three priorities. China is hosting the Apec leaders’ meeting for the third time. The summit to be held in Shenzhen in November comes after earlier meetings hosted in Beijing in 2014 and Shanghai in 2001. Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu told the South China Morning Post in an exclusive interview on Thursday that the finance ministers’ gathering was timely as regional cooperation was increasingly vital given the state of geopolitical tensions around the world. He said Hong Kong was in the right position to organise the event, a rare occasion that would allow major representatives and finance ministers of the 21 member economies to see first-hand the city’s latest developments such as financial services, information technology and fintech, as well as to enjoy its natural landscape and heritage. Hui said the 2026 Apec year underlined China’s contribution to regional stability. China’s Ministry of Finance said on Wednesday that Beijing was willing to work with all Apec economies to stay committed to multilateralism, deepen macroeconomic policy communication and coordination, maintain stable and smooth regional industrial and supply chains, jointly promote the long-term sustainable growth of the Asia-Pacific economy and contribute to building a regional community. Lee Shu-kam, director of Hong Kong Shue Yan University’s business, economic and public policy research centre, said the city’s role as host would solidify its position as an irreplaceable offshore financing hub for Chinese companies and a buffer against geopolitical tensions as a separate customs territory. Lee noted that the expiration of the US trade truce with China on January 10 next year and the future direction of tariffs would have a significant impact, creating a period of uncertainty and sensitivity amid the ongoing geopolitical and technological rivalry between the two superpowers. “If Hong Kong can use this Apec meeting to gather finance ministers from the Asia-Pacific region to reach practical consensus on digital finance, it will prove to the world that even with many changes or potential crises in US-China relations, Hong Kong still has independent political mediation capabilities and can reach consensus with various countries,” he said. Institutions, including the International Monetary Fund, will give presentations during the meeting. Lee said the continuous and deep engagement of international multilateral institutions, which are extremely strict on compliance and legal risks, could effectively dispel doubts in the West about the rule of law in Hong Kong. “If major multinational institutions participate in the meeting, give speeches and conduct high-level substantive dialogues in Hong Kong, to a certain extent, it already reflects that Hong Kong’s rule of law and compliance environment are validated,” he said. “[They] send a very strong signal that Hong Kong’s common law system, contract enforcement capability and commercial arbitration mechanisms still possess complete legal validity and international credibility in multilateral financial cooperation.” The Apec leaders’ summit will be held in Shenzhen next month. Lee said Hong Kong and Shenzhen would play complementary roles, with Shenzhen positioned as a competitive innovation and technology hub amid the ongoing technological rivalry with the United States, while Hong Kong would handle global capital markets to support mainland China’s continued opening up. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po told a programme on Saturday that the Hong Kong meeting would serve as an opportunity for regional decision-makers and enterprise representatives to understand the city on the ground and build mutual trust, rather than just being an international conference. Chan added that closer cooperation among regional economies was extremely important under the shadow of geopolitics and trade protectionism. He said the city encouraged enterprises looking to develop their mainland businesses to list and raise capital in Hong Kong. “Hong Kong’s professional services have a great advantage in this regard, and we can also act as their consultants to open up the mainland market hand in hand with them,” Chan said. Jeffrey Lam Kin-fung, a member of the key decision-making Executive Council, said he believed the Hong Kong meeting would help attract more foreign investment to the city. He said he had hosted many foreign businesspeople over the past two years from the West and emerging markets such as the Middle East, and they had shown interest in investing in Hong Kong, as the city’s low taxes, common law system and recent development as an international arbitration centre were attractive to them. “After visiting Hong Kong, every one of them said they found the city different from what they heard in their hometown,” he said. “They find Hong Kong a stable city, politically, economically and socially. They discovered so many opportunities for future development.” Lam said he had passed on information to them about the Greater Bay Area, Northern Metropolis and Hung Shui Kiu Industrial Park Company. Lam is the chairman of the company’s board of directors. Latest government figures showed a record 11,070 companies from the mainland and overseas were operating in Hong Kong last year, an 11 per cent rise year on year. A drafting session for the finance ministers’ joint statement will take place on Monday, followed by two days of meetings. Chinese Finance Minister Lan Foan will deliver an opening speech on Tuesday afternoon. Ambassador Chen Xu, who chairs the Apec Senior Officials’ Meeting, will speak about Apec’s priorities for the year. There will be eight sessions during the two days of meeting. On the first day, there will be three sessions covering the global and regional macroeconomic and financial outlook, fiscal policies supporting households and digital infrastructure financing. On the second day, another three sessions will cover financial access and opportunities for all, a young financial talents dialogue and the Apec finance ministers’ 2027 process priorities. These will be followed by the signing of the joint statement drafted on Monday. The meeting will end with closing remarks by Lan, followed by a press conference. China’s Ministry of Finance said on Wednesday that various visits would be arranged for the delegates after the meeting. “Hong Kong … will fully demonstrate its recent development achievements and urban charm, inviting everyone to jointly experience the diverse vibrancy and growth opportunities of Asia’s World City,” it said. Additional reporting by Denise Tsang

title: SailGP has the look of a runaway train, but co-founder Russell Coutts ‘far from satisfied’
description: Sailing circuit, which starts its next season in Hong Kong, has large revenue, millions of TV viewers, but CEO wants ‘whole lot of new fans’.
content: On the face of it, Grand Slam Track should have worked. The brainchild of Michael Johnson, the four-time Olympic gold medal sprinter, the initiative was designed to give track and field a regular season narrative; to position track and field in the global spotlight and reward the world’s best athletes with the cash rewards and superstar profiles that their talents merited. Still, poor crowds for Grand Slam Track’s (GTS) April 2025 debut in Jamaica raised the first red flag. Attendances over the following two meetings were moderate, and the whole thing went pop after financial issues resulted in the scrubbing of a proposed fourth leg in Los Angeles. In January this year, GTS filed for bankruptcy with debts of more than US$40 million, and last month it was reported that a number of athletes were still waiting for monies owed. It is a sorry story, but one that casts an even more favourable light on SailGP, the sports disruptor that only seven years after its establishment has the look of a runaway train that is still gathering pace. In 2025, SailGP generated more than US$200 million in revenue and attracted an average 18 million television viewers per race. “To be straight, we weren’t sure that we could commercially ticket this product from day one,” Russell Coutts, SailGP’s co-founder and CEO, told the South China Morning Post, ahead of the circuit’s first Hong Kong stop next January. Chief among the priorities for Coutts and his fellow co-founder, tech billionaire Larry Ellison, as they plotted to catapult sailing into the mainstream, was to make their sport accessible for a largely uninformed public. While most of the world’s population have run and jumped, so can relate in some form to track and field, very few have piloted a boat or slavishly followed the quadrennial America’s Cup. “I love that this new form of the sport is bringing a whole lot of new fans,” Coutts said. “At some of the venues, 85 per cent of the people packing the grandstands have never been in a sailboat. “Some kids watch and say, ‘I like the look of this, I want to try it’. “I love the challenge of building up a new sports property from the start. We’ve had considerable growth, but we’re far from satisfied. We want to build this into one of the world’s top-25 sports properties.” A 1984 Olympic champion and three-time America’s Cup-winning skipper, Coutts did not launch SailGP entirely on a whim. Cautionary tales abound: the likes of NFL Europe and the North American Soccer League eventually died off after entering markets as fish out of water. Initial studies that gauged the enthusiasm for SailGP of individuals whose interests differed between sailing, racing, general sports and lifestyles, discovered “big spikes in engagement” from all four groups. “That gave us a lot of confidence, and it’s proved well founded when we’ve gone into markets like Germany and attracted 2 million TV viewers,” Coutts said. SailGP’s maiden 2019 season featured six teams and five race weekends. In 2027, 14 boats will compete over 13 grands prix. “From there, we intend to add six more teams,” Coutts, 64, said, adding that prospective investors were jostling for ownership of a new Chinese franchise, after the previous iteration disappeared following SailGP’s debut campaign. All 13 existing teams have entered private ownership, with New Zealand’s Black Foils the last to be sold back in June when MSP Sports Capital paid more than US$60 million for a majority stake. That was more than three times the US$20 million that it cost Ben Ainslie, the four-time Olympic champion sailor, and business partner Chris Bake for a majority slice of the TeamGB boat five years ago. Nonetheless, Coutts believes his fast-growing product remains “somewhat underdeveloped”, noting that individual teams’ licensing programmes amounted to only “a fraction of our total revenue”. “For lots of sports properties, licensing makes a significant contribution to revenue,” he said. “There’s lots of untapped potential.” After “thinking about venturing into Asia for some time”, the idea crystallised this year after Hong Kong-based investment management firm Blue Pool Capital bought into the Germany SailGP franchise. “We spoke to Ollie Weisberg and Chris Wu [Blue Pool CEO and managing director, respectively], then talked to the Hong Kong Tourism Board,” Coutts said. SailGP has initially signed up for one year in the city, “with a view to a lot more”. “We had a three-year term in Perth, but at our first event last year, their regional officials said they wanted to agree a long-term deal,” Coutts said. “We like to get in front of people, so they recognise what this is, then build from there.” Also a two-time America’s Cup-champion CEO for the Oracle boat owned by fellow SailGP mastermind Ellison, Coutts said that Hong Kong had been given a January date because “it fits well in our sequence of events, and the wind conditions there are best at that time of year”. Equally, Coutts wants race weekends to acquire “appointment-to-view” status. “Staging an event at the same time every year is a big part of retaining and growing fandom,” he added, pointing to sports such as Formula 1 and tennis that have “had years of development … and everyone knows when their grands prix or tournaments will be staged”. “We want to expand to 20 events, and have a regular calendar,” Coutts added. The New Zealander is also keen that teams become established over long periods, allowing fans to develop allegiances and the athletes to “grow into household names”. Still, he acknowledged that the modern sports follower demands more than action on race days. Formula 1’s popularity and revenue have increased exponentially since the 2019 debut season of Drive to Survive, its Netflix fly-on-the wall docuseries. SailGP produces its own excellent behind-the-scenes documentary, Racing on the Edge, with a new eight-part docuseries, produced by Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman, set to air on Disney Plus next year. Coutts acknowledged that “all sports were trying to emulate Drive to Survive”, but said actors Reynolds and Jackman, part-owners of Australia’s Bonds Flying Roos team, would “bring a certain style to the entertainment product”. “The question is always, how do you differentiate yourself?” he added. Reynolds is an executive producer of the wildly popular Welcome to Wrexham series, which charts his co-ownership of the English Championship football club. “Their ability to tell stories around previously unseen content in an authentic way is incredible,” Coutts said. “We expect it to be a multi-year project: it’s a bonus we weren’t planning on.” If Coutts was taking a bit of a flier in his belief that a substantial new audience could be wooed by SailGP, the initiative at least had the buy-in of the wider sport – unlike, for example, the breakaway LIV Golf circuit whose future is shrouded in uncertainty four years after its brash introduction. The sight of soaring F50 catamarans whistling around tight race circuits at speeds of more than 100km/h has captured imaginations to the point that SailGP has seen around 40 per cent of first-time attendees return, and others scrambling overseas for race weekends. “We’re seeing more and more instances of groups of friends getting together and travelling to races,” Coutts said. “Around 68 per cent of our fandom at European events was from outside the host city.” Coutts is anticipating premium hospitality for the American Express Hong Kong Sail Grand Prix, which will be staged on January 23 and 24, “selling out very quickly”. “In future, we’ll add more scale, but the fact we’ll sell out with what’s in play gives us confidence to build,” he said. “All the marketing dollars and promotions aren’t for just one year.” Knighted 17 years ago, Coutts said he would “have loved” an opportunity to compete in SailGP. “I love sailing and love that we’re able to reimagine people’s perception of what it can be as a sport,” he said. “I love the traditional elements of the sport, but I also love that this new form is bringing a whole load of new fans.”

title: Trump’s second Asean summit presence comes at a price for region
description: On the president’s list are supply-chain security, critical minerals, technology cooperation, AI and investment in the US, experts say.
content: US President Donald Trump is expected to drive hard bargains on tariffs and critical minerals in his return to the Asean summit in Manila next month, with Washington seeking greater economic and strategic concessions while remaining hawkish on China. The Philippines confirmed on Wednesday that Trump would fly in for the summit from November 16 to 18, before attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen that same week. Trump’s second consecutive appearance at the forum signals continued US engagement despite his preference for one-on-one deals, analysts say. The timing of the trip ahead of an expected meeting with counterpart Xi Jinping in Shenzhen is also seen as a chance for the US to reassure regional partners of its commitment. But they warn that renewed US tariff pressure and demands for closer alignment could push the Association of Southeast Asian Nations members into competing bilateral deals that would undermine economic ties with both superpowers. “His attendance at two consecutive Asean summits is significant, given his preference for bilateral engagement and transactional diplomacy over multilateral institutions. The fact that the Philippines is a close treaty ally of the US also makes a difference, particularly given their strong defence cooperation and shared security interests in the South China Sea,” said Joanne Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. Lin added that Trump’s visit was a positive sign that Southeast Asia remained important to Washington. “As an ally, President Trump is here to strengthen the Philippines’ position on many issues that confront both countries in Southeast Asia and the wider Indo-Pacific,” said Julio Amador, CEO of Amador Research Services and visiting fellow at Perry World House. “While it is tempting to look at the Apec summit as the main goal, I believe that the East Asia summit, which figures a lot in security issues, is more vital to the visit.” Security concerns Analysts said that a large part of Trump’s agenda in attending the Asean summit would deal with trade and economic security. “A big part of it is to show that the US is still vital to the security of the region, and shoring up its alliances and partnerships and putting forward a case for economic security,” Amador said. He added that as US foreign policy primarily focused on alliance and security, the visit was also likely to affirm the economic aspect, particularly the Luzon Economic Corridor – a connectivity project that could inject as much as US$100 billion into the Philippine economy – as a crucial part of bilateral ties. “The administration has made it clear that economic security is now closely linked to national security,” Lin said. “Beyond securing better market access for American products, Washington will likely be looking for concrete commitments on supply-chain security, critical minerals, technology cooperation, AI and greater investment in the US.” The order of Trump’s stops is “telling”, according to Asean observer Vu Lam. “As chair and treaty ally, Manila has pledged to conclude a legally binding code of conduct in the South China Sea by the end of its chairmanship. Visiting an ally just before Beijing offers reassurance and some leverage,” Lam said. Collins Chong, a foreign affairs and security analyst at Universiti Malaya, said that Trump’s visit was a calculated move to sustain the momentum of his diplomatic engagement with the region after his trip to Malaysia last year. “Trump recognises that personal diplomacy and direct engagement with regional leaders remain indispensable tools in preserving American influence, especially at a time when China continues to expand its … presence across Southeast Asia,” Chong said. Total US-Asean trade in goods and services reached US$686 billion in 2025, reflecting the region’s growing importance. “Asean is now an increasingly important geopolitical and geoeconomic battleground, encompassing critical minerals, semiconductors, energy security, advanced manufacturing, maritime connectivity and diversified supply chains,” he said. As such, Washington cannot allow Beijing to become the “overwhelmingly dominant economic and strategic reference point” for Asean. “The challenge is not simply to contain China’s military rise, but to prevent Beijing from accumulating structural influence over the industries, infrastructure, technologies and maritime routes, eventually gaining strength to challenge the US in key areas,” Chong said. “Trump is seeking to translate American market access, security commitments and technological advantages into greater strategic returns, while ensuring that China cannot turn Southeast Asia into an uncontested platform for its expanding regional power.” Tariff talks Following a new wave of US tariffs under alleged forced labour practices in its Section 301 investigations in July, levies will continue to be the focus, according to the experts. “The main difference is that we are moving from the initial tariff shock to a more established pattern of bilateral bargaining,” Lin said. “The pressure on Southeast Asian economies remains, but it is becoming more targeted and tied to specific regulatory and economic-security commitments.” This could push members into making separate bilateral deals, she added. “Ultimately, Asean cannot prevent its members from pursuing bilateral deals, but it should ensure that these arrangements do not undermine regional economic integration or weaken Asean’s collective position.” Lam said such agreements were likely, pointing to developments last year, when Thailand agreed to remove tariffs on nearly all US goods and Vietnam gave preferential access to almost all US exports. “Expect commitments on intellectual property, purchases of US goods and tighter rules on Chinese transshipment too. In return, they hope for lower tariffs and fewer future US trade actions, but nothing is guaranteed. Their concessions are long term, while US tariff relief can be withdrawn at any time,” Lam said. Trump’s hard bargains in matters such as export controls, supply-chain security, technology governance and trade practices involving third countries could increasingly involve geopolitical considerations, Lin said. “We saw how similar provisions in the earlier agreements with Malaysia and Cambodia became politically sensitive because of China’s concerns about ‘poison pill’ clauses.” Asean countries faced a difficult balancing act as “they want more predictable access to the US market, but they also need to preserve their economic relationships with China and avoid commitments that could constrain their strategic autonomy”.

title: Silvia Furmanovich on her Asprey collaboration and redefining jadeite – interview
description: Her collaboration with the British luxury house sees the Brazilian designer blend jadeite with bamboo, wood and horsehair for nature-inspired creations.
content: British luxury house Asprey gave Brazilian designer Silvia Furmanovich access to its jadeite, from stones in the usual vibrant green to rarer shades such as pink, lavender, red, white and orange. The pieces Furmanovich created pair jadeite with unexpected materials such as Japanese bamboo, wood and woven horsehair. Here, the designer tells us more. What makes jadeite so special? Unlike stones that announce themselves through brilliance or sparkle, jadeite draws you in through its depth and luminosity. I did not know much about jadeite until Asprey introduced me to it, and I have grown to admire the reverence for jadeite across many Asian cultures. As someone approaching the material from my own perspective, for the very first time, I felt a great sense of responsibility. Rather than trying to reinterpret its history, I wanted to celebrate its individuality and allow its natural beauty to lead every design. What I love most is that jadeite carries emotion. It feels alive in your hand, almost as if it has absorbed time itself. As a designer, I never feel that I am imposing something onto the stone. Instead, I try to listen to what each piece wants to become. Jade jewellery can look a bit old school in Asia. How do you make it modern and cool? Rather than treating the stone as something formal or ceremonial, I surrounded it with unexpected materials, sculptural forms inspired by nature and artisanal techniques that create texture and dimension, while always allowing the jadeite to remain the protagonist. I think today’s collectors appreciate authenticity. They don’t want tradition to disappear; they want to experience it in a fresh way. Where did the idea of incorporating materials such as horsehair and wood come from? I never think about jewellery simply as gemstones set in gold. I think about creating small worlds where different materials, each with their own history and character, coexist. Wood has memory. Every grain tells the story of a tree that has lived for decades, sometimes centuries. Horsehair introduces an extraordinary texture and movement that cannot be replicated in metal alone. How to pick what to pair with the jade? Every stone has its own colour, personality and energy, so the surrounding materials and gemstones were selected individually rather than following a formula. Diamonds were a natural choice because they bring light without overpowering the jadeite. Organic materials – such as wood, bamboo, horsehair and marquetry – soften the composition and allow the stone to feel even more alive. What did you discover about jadeite? Working with Asprey introduced me to an exceptional palette – vibrant greens, delicate lavenders, soft pinks, luminous whites and warm oranges. Each colour suggested a completely different emotional landscape. Some immediately reminded me of orchids or tropical flowers, while others evoked leaves, forests or birds. Rather than designing one collection and applying different stones, I allowed each jadeite to guide its own artistic composition. Every stone has its own character, and the role of the designer is not to dominate it, but to reveal its individuality.

title: Across US, ‘No Kings’ events seek to boost early voting and thwart Trump
description: The protests come amid fears that the Republican president will seek to undermine the results of the coming midterms if his party loses.
content: Carrying an umbrella painted with the words “vote, power, people”, retired teacher Sabine Carlson said the lesson plan for Saturday’s “No King” marches was clear. “It’s great to voice your anger, and we have long lists of complaints, but the most important thing of all is to go and vote,” the 66-year-old Democrat from Washington’s suburbs said. At the demonstration near the country’s Capitol, Carlson joined one of the estimated 3,000 events organised by the prominent anti-Trump movement across the US on Saturday. Rather than holding massive marches, the latest “No Kings” events varied across the country – with honking convoys, concerts and neighbourhood gatherings. It was the fourth iteration of the demonstrations since US President Donald Trump returned to office. The stated goal of the event was to fire up voters just as Americans begin casting ballots in the midterm election, where majority Republicans face fierce opposition. Democrats are seeking to take control of Congress by campaigning on cost of living issues and an unpopular war in the Middle East. Focused on early voting ahead of election day on November 3, the events ranged from New York to Los Angeles and other blue stronghold cities to small towns across the nation. “I think it’s one of the most important votes that is coming up, and it’s really important to make people aware, and also make sure they know where to look up the procedures and make sure they’re registered correctly,” Carlson said. “Don’t go to the wrong polling station.” Most areas of the United States allow voters to cast their ballots ahead of time, sometimes weeks in advance. Alma Couverthie, who oversees grass-roots organising efforts for democracy watchdog Common Cause, said the point of the “No Kings” rallies was “reclaiming voting for what it truly is: an act of power, an act of service and an act of joy”. Trump has openly criticised the practice of mail-in voting, and opponents have expressed concern that the administration will attempt to undermine the results – especially if Republicans end up losing, as opinion polls show is likely. By advocating for voting early, “No Kings” organisers hope to cut off the potential for any wrongdoing. “The best way to prevent any funny business from this administration after election day is to make sure that our turnout is massive, so clear and so overwhelming that our victory for democracy is impossible to question,” Couverthie said. One 52-year-old military veteran who joined Saturday’s protest did so seeking catharsis from the current state of American politics. “I am so disillusioned by what I thought I was serving versus what this country has become,” the Virginia resident said, declining to give his name. “Over the last 18 months – I finally came to this conclusion about six months ago – I’ve been mourning my country.” Carrying an umbrella with the message “Vote for humanity. End this circus now. We want our country back”, he said he hoped to see “a robust response come November 3 from the American people”. Beyond Washington, like-minded Americans echoed his hopes and fears. Outside a church in Gastonia, North Carolina, women carried signs that read “Honk for Democracy” and “Make a plan to vote!” In Portland, Maine, demonstrators bundled up against the autumn chill waved the American flag and carried signs reading “Your Vote is Your Voice” and “No Kings, No Cowards Collins”, referring to Republican incumbent Senator Susan Collins, who faces a tough re-election race. In Wilton Manors, Florida, demonstrators spent the sunny day sporting shorts and sunglasses, carrying signs reading: “Enough is enough.”

title: 19 dead, 25 hurt in stampede at India religious festival
description: A seven-year-old girl was among those killed after sudden rain prompted the fatal crush at a Hindu gathering in Kolkata.
content: At least 19 people were killed and two dozen more injured on Saturday in eastern India after a stampede that occurred during sudden rainfall at a Hindu religious gathering, officials and Indian media said. West Bengal’s Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari told reporters the fatalities included a seven-year-old girl, adding that 25 other people were injured outside a pavilion “in a stampede” at the Hindu festival of Durga Puja in the city of Kolkata. “Six bodies have so far been identified,” Adhikari said. A senior police official at the scene said an announcement caused “commotion” after it started raining at night and the “crowd waiting outside the pandal (pavilion) was pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.” Afterwards medical workers were seen moving injured people on stretchers, including a police officer, into a local hospital. Several relatives of victims cried and held one another as they mourned the loss of loved ones. Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the tragedy in a short statement on social media. “The stampede in Kolkata is saddening. Condolences to the bereaved families. Wishing the injured a speedy recovery,” he wrote. “The West Bengal Government is providing all possible help to the affected families.” Adhikari originally announced 17 fatalities. The Press Trust of India (PTI) reported the death toll rose by two to 19, quoting Adhikari in a later statement. Nine dead bodies have been released to their families, the PTI reported. It also said police had taken the closed circuit footage of the festival and authorities would initiate action against those seen on CCTV who appeared to fail in their responsibility for crowd control. Videos shot before the stampede appeared to show large crowds of people waiting to enter the pavilion, in an area with narrow lanes that allow only a few people to walk in at a time, according to Indian Express. Deadly crowd incidents are a frequent occurrence at Indian mass events, such as religious festivals, due to poor management and safety lapses. A speeding truck reportedly lost control in the early hours of Sunday and hit devotees gathered at a temple in Gwalior, in the central state of Madhya Pradesh, killing 13 people. Last year, a stampede at India’s Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others, and 11 fans were crushed to death in Bengaluru during celebrations for the local cricket team’s first Indian Premier League title.
