The same year, 40 people were killed after a stampede broke out at a campaign rally of a popular actor-turned-politician in southern Tamil Nadu state. In 2024, 121 people were killed in northern Uttar Pradesh state during a Hindu religious gathering.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong cannot afford to neglect youth mental health
description: Sobering figures should prompt a fundamental rethinking of what better support can be rendered to young people.
content: World Mental Health Month, observed each October, may not command the same public attention in Hong Kong as it does elsewhere. Yet the latest revelations about suicides among local school children should serve as a sobering call for more urgent action. With those aged 15 or below accounting for 60 per cent or more of suspected student suicide deaths over the past three academic years, and the under-15 suicide rate climbing to 2.9 per 100,000 – the highest since 2016 – the city cannot afford to treat youth mental health as a peripheral concern. It is worrying that the respective numbers of suspected student suicide cases reported to the Education Bureau by primary and secondary schools hovered between 23 and 33 in the three school years between 2023 and 2026. The proportions of cases involving students aged 15 or below were 60 per cent, 67 per cent and 65 per cent, respectively, according to figures submitted to the Legislative Council. The Hong Kong Jockey Club Centre for Suicide Research and Prevention at the University of Hong Kong earlier estimated that there were 976 suicide cases, or 13 per 100,000 residents, last year – a slight decline from 2024, based on data provided by the Coroner’s Court. While rates declined across nearly all age groups, the figure rose among those aged under 15 to 2.9 per 100,000, the highest level since 2016. These are not just cold numbers. Behind them are individual sad stories that add up to a disturbing social ill. Sorrow and sympathy aside, the disturbing trend should prompt a fundamental rethinking of what better support can be rendered to young people, with regard to classroom and exam pressures, digital environments and family relations. The government, to its credit, introduced a three-tier mechanism in 2023 to identify and help students in distress. Now covering Primary Four to Form Six students, the scheme focuses on early identification and immediate assistance by prioritising the students using school resources, and in more severe situations, activating an off-campus network for outside help. It was revealed that 855 cases had been referred to the off-campus support network teams, while 547 cases were referred to psychiatric services between December 1, 2023, and July 31 this year. With an average of 17 high-risk referrals every month since 2023, the official mechanism is arguably serving its purpose. But it also reflects that the general mental wellness of local students leaves a lot to be desired. The suicide trend among youngsters sits within a broader pattern of distress among different age groups. A happiness index of Hong Kong adults only scored 5.87 out of 10; down from 5.95 last year. More than 40 per cent of the respondents reported moderate to severe depressive symptoms, according to a study by HK.WeCare, an initiative under non-profit organisation Wofoo Social Enterprises. There is no shortage of studies on the factors contributing to suicide. From study pressure to peer influence and family problems, youngsters can be victimised easily if they lack support and guidance through difficulties. It remains unclear whether those who took their lives had received professional help under the three-tier mechanism. But the suicide tallies over the past few years show prevention must be further strengthened. Suicide is complex, shaped by interpersonal, social and personal factors that no single measure can fully address. But the prevailing trend among youngsters points to systemic issues that society must seriously address lest more tragedies happen. The measures outlined in the chief executive’s policy address to enhance mental health are positive steps. These include extending the school-based mechanism, expanding the Healthy Mind Pilot Project to all District Health Centres, strengthening education and support for parents and teachers on mental health and broadening participation in the Mental Health Workplace Charter. A genuinely effective preventive mechanism against suicide starts with a culture rooted in positive values and a healthy environment for personal growth and development. With wider public discussion and more proactive policy support, the city can hopefully mark future mental health months with more good news.

title: ‘It’s never hurt less’: Chinese ultrarunner’s knee pain fades on 20,000km Silk Road trek
description: 7,000km into her Silk Road endurance run from Vladivostok to Lisbon, Ria Xi shares the toll on her body and mind, from foot pain to migraines.
content: When Ria Xi set off on her 20,000km (12,400-mile) endurance challenge, she had no idea what the impact on her body would be. But she was curious to find out. The Beijing-born former tech executive who used AI to develop running training plans has now developed a daily test to track her biometric data alongside memory, motivation and energy levels as she runs across Eurasia. The extraordinary journey, which began on May 1, 2026, from Vladivostok, Russia, will see Xi run the ancient Silk Road across 17 countries to reach Lisbon, Portugal, in summer 2027. Should she succeed, she will be the first person to achieve this feat. Xi has already set a fastest known time (FKT) covering China on foot, from the east coast to the western border with Kazakhstan. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Almaty Marathon (@almatymarathon) Running at least 50km a day – an ultra-marathon, often for nine to 10 hours, with occasional rest days – Xi is discovering how sustained endurance exercise can affect her physical and mental health. This includes undergoing brain scans along the route to investigate possible changes in grey matter volume. One of her biggest concerns to date has been weight loss, having lost 7kg (15lbs) in five months. Despite consuming an estimated 3,000 to 4,000 calories daily, she believes she needs considerably more to meet the demands of running. “It’s really important to keep eating enough,” she says on a video call from Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. “The weight loss is slowing down, but if I lose more, it’s pretty concerning in terms of having a bone stress fracture.” To keep herself fuelled while she runs, Xi consumes up to two litres (0.5 gallons) of fruit juice daily alongside energy gels and high-carbohydrate snacks such as honey-glazed sweet potato. The constant sugar intake has also raised concerns about her dental health, prompting a check-up before leaving China to ensure her fillings were intact and she had no cavities. And while the weight loss was predicted, Xi’s body has changed in other ways she had not anticipated. Xi began the challenge with long-standing knee problems following ligament and meniscus tears nearly a decade ago. Initially painful, her knee gradually improved. “It’s never hurt less,” she says. “It’s really amazing just how much the body adapts.” Other problems have been less forgiving. Xi has suffered hip pain, persistent soreness in the soles of her feet, migraines, diarrhoea and two bouts of food poisoning. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Ria X | The 20,000km Experiment (@whereisriax) But the greatest difficulties have been psychological. “I definitely noticed a significant impact on my memory,” says Xi, who has devised daily tests to monitor her cognitive performance. Her results suggest her memory performance has declined since beginning the journey. Sleep deprivation has compounded the problem; Xi is managing her own social media accounts each evening after running an ultra-marathon, meaning she only has time for six to seven hours of sleep. During the Gobi Desert crossing, where temperatures reached 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit), Xi switched to running at night. Despite sleeping during daylight hours, she struggled with exhaustion and began hallucinating. “I would be so tired, and I would see these silvery patterns,” she says. “In some places they have these police statues on the side of the road, and it looks like a human, but it’s not moving, and it really, really messes with my mind.” Finding motivation trekking along the Silk Road Another mental challenge has been finding a way to cope with the monotony of running every day. Keeping her mind occupied has become essential. She calls the experience her “running university”, listening to audiobooks about local cultures, including works by Kyrgyz author Chinghiz Aitmatov, alongside science fiction. When motivation disappears, she turns to a shared Spotify playlist featuring songs chosen by her followers. “Having low motivation is harder than having a painful body,” she says. Despite the toll, Xi remains determined to finish, motivated by supporters who say her journey has inspired them to tackle their own challenges. “That’s the whole reason I wanted to do this,” she says, “to bring hope to people and to bring this possibility that we can rewrite our narratives.” She still has about 13,000km to go. To stay abreast of Xi’s progress, visit her Instagram page. To donate to help defray her costs, click here. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. title: Write to Win: If you could only keep one thing from your home, what would it be? (Round 6)
description: In our writing contest, students are eliminated one at a time based on your votes and YP editors’ picks.
content:
We have prepared some exciting prizes for our top three contestants:
Winner: Kindle, City’super voucher and a YP certificate
First runner-up: Instax camera and a YP certificate
Second runner-up: City’super voucher and a YP certificate
Bonus prize: Every winner will also walk away with 2 tickets to Hong Kong Disneyland !
Read the responses to this week’s Write to Win prompt and vote for the answer you like most using this form . The deadline for voting is 12pm on Tuesday, October 20.
Venus: If I could only keep one thing from my home, I wouldn’t grab my phone or my book. Instead, I would rescue my childhood stuffed toy – a tragically ragged, one-eyed rabbit that has been my partner in crime since infancy. Whenever I see it, I feel safe and comfortable, as if I’m back at home. To anyone else, it may not look attractive. The fur is matted, the left ear is hanging by a thread and the cotton stuffing is definitely deflating. But to me, it is irreplaceable. This toy has been my silent therapist through every challenge I faced, from terrifying primary school maths exams to late-night deadline struggles and even the night before my stage performances. While other objects can be replaced with money, the comfort I find in its faded fabric cannot be bought anywhere else. It holds all of my childhood secrets and fears. Growing up can be stressful, but holding and hugging this rabbit serves as an instant reset button, bringing back a sense of total safety and happiness. We can always buy new furniture anywhere, but the rabbit represents a lifetime of loyalty that nothing else can replace. It is my ultimate source of comfort, my favourite and truly the best.
Jupiter: If I could keep only one thing from my home, it would be my Instax Mini camera. When I was nine years old, I won my school’s annual creative writing contest and received an HKTV mall voucher. After scrolling through hundreds of products, I chose the Instax Mini camera. At the time, it felt like just a new toy, but I never realised how important it would become in creating lasting memories. Since then, my camera has been with me through some of my favourite moments. It accompanied me when I visited my cousins in India to celebrate my grandfather’s 70th birthday, and it captured memories from my first trip to the United States. Each photo it prints is more than just an image; it reminds me of the love and laughter that made those moments special. Even today, I continue to use that camera. More than just a device, it has turned into a collection of my friendships and family memories. If I could keep only one thing from my home, it would undoubtedly be this camera. Even if I cannot hold on to old moments, I can always create new cherished memories filled with warmth and love.
Mars: If I could only save one item from my home, I would immediately grab my digital camera. While most people rely on smartphones for quick snapshots, I use my camera as a more intentional way to capture the world around me. This camera is incredibly special because my dad bought it when he was young, and passing it down to me inspired my favourite hobby: photography. This hobby allows me to explore the world as a passionate photographer. Practising photography has taught me patience and observation as I use my lens to freeze raw emotions and uncover hidden stories in everyday life in Hong Kong. My camera holds a visual archive of my life, including precious photos I have taken since I was small – candid smiles of my family and beautiful landscapes from our holidays. It captures high-quality photographs that hold irreplaceable emotional value, which must not be lost. By holding on to my camera, I ensure that my favourite memories are preserved. It serves as a bridge to my past, allowing me to look back at happy times. With this precious gift from my dad, I will continue to take beautiful pictures to capture wonderful memories of my own future journey.
Neptune: People often say that home is not just a place; it’s where your favourite people and memories are. I agree with that sentiment. If I had to choose just one item to keep if everything else in my home were to be discarded, I would choose either my favourite stuffed animal, Cow Cow, who has been with me for as long as I can remember, or my family picture wall, which holds some of my fondest memories. The picture wall showcases special occasions like birthdays and treasured childhood moments. It serves as a reminder that, despite the hustle and bustle of life, I can always find tranquillity with my family. On the other hand, Cow Cow is an inseparable part of me. I still recall the little secrets I would share with her at night and how her scent feels just right. I brought her along on every trip, even school outings. Much like Andy’s love for Woody in Toy Story , I have a deep affection for Cow Cow, and I could never bring myself to donate her. Our stories and adventures aren’t over yet. I believe that to live a full life, it’s essential to look forward. Even though the picture wall is irreplaceable, it wouldn’t accompany my family and me on new journeys. Without the wall, I would learn to cherish the time I spend with my family. Ultimately, I’ve decided that I want to experience all of this with Cow Cow, so the one thing I would choose to keep is her.

title: In Focus | Beyond EVs and perception, how China is gaining ground in Central Asia
description: Footprint can be seen across Kazakhstan’s futuristic capital Astana, as Beijing vies with Washington and others for influence in the region.
content: In Kazakhstan’s futuristic capital Astana, car dealer Auyez Kabdygali is planning a big change to his business as he switches from importing European cars to Chinese electric vehicles. Kabdygali says there is increasing demand for Chinese EVs both from locals and Russian customers due to their competitive price and quality. His grandfather is among the converts – he has an order in for a BYD Han, the carmaker’s flagship model, and plans to collect it from a terminal on the border with China and drive it hundreds of kilometres home. The 33-year-old car dealer is among a growing number of Kazakhs who hold positive views of China. It is a sentiment driven not just by its EVs, but the economic pay-offs from China’s expanding footprint in Kazakhstan and its posture as a cooperative, non-interfering partner. Strolling through Astana – a city of more than 1.3 million people – feels much like walking through the most developed major cities in northern China. Its modern architectural landmarks loom over Soviet-era blocks, while a newly opened Chinese-built light rail train runs along the city’s central axis. China’s footprint can be seen across the city, from the high-rise Beijing Tower to the Chinese consumer goods and cosmetics lining the shelves in stores. This shift is taking place as the broader Central Asian region has become a more crowded arena for diplomacy, with Beijing and Washington – along with Tokyo and Seoul – all competing for strategic influence. But observers note that while Beijing has made economic inroads, there is still scepticism towards China in the region and unease over its rivalry with the United States, and Astana is among the capitals trying to balance relations with the two powers. ‘Friendly market’ Astana car dealer Kabdygali welcomes investment from China, a country he views as a friendly neighbour with more cultural similarities to Kazakhstan than the US. China for him represents economic support – and enormous market potential. “[Nearly] all the products we’re buying are Chinese products … so you can say that they are really helping everyday life here,” he said. “China is helping us to maintain the economy.” Kabdygali’s positive views have also been shaped by visits to the country and Chinese friends he made while studying English in Malaysia. His brother went to Shanghai for a university course in 2007, and Kabdygali regularly visited him during the two years he was there. The whole family later travelled to China’s southern tropical island Hainan for a holiday, and in 2012 they went to Beijing to consult a traditional Chinese medicine practitioner about some health issues. Today, the young businessman drives a BYD, pays with Alipay at his local coffee shop, and regularly tunes in to a Chinese gaming streamer on YouTube. Kabdygali is not worried about the country becoming overreliant on China. He said trade with China was “necessary” and the whole world was buying from the country. But he added that he hoped Kazakhstan could export more food and manufactured goods to China to balance the trade deficit. He also shrugged off concerns over the intensifying US-China competition in Kazakhstan and the region. “China is more of a friendly market. They focus on their own economy and just want to make good products, whereas the US manipulates things. They invade countries and make things worse,” he said. “If there are no competitors, if there was no US, China would become the US.” Central Asian view After Beijing launched its global infrastructure scheme – the Belt and Road Initiative – in Kazakhstan in 2013 there was a dip in favourable attitudes towards China in both Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, according to a study in the journal Post-Soviet Affairs in August. But public sentiment in the two countries has turned more positive since 2021, driven largely by the tangible economic benefits of Chinese investment. More than 49,000 people were surveyed for the study across Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan between 2017 and 2023. Jessica Neafie, the paper’s co-author and assistant professor at Kazakhstan’s Nazarbayev University, said that in the early years of the belt and road strategy, the unprecedented exposure to China and a large influx of visible investments in Central Asia triggered a backlash. She said it fuelled a “mix of concern for foreign investment and its effect on local identity and nationalism”. The study pointed to the heightened anti-Beijing sentiment that led to a Chinese firm in 2020 scrapping a US$280 million logistics centre project in Kyrgyzstan after hundreds of residents took to the streets in protest. Neafie said public sentiment had improved since then as tangible economic results were seen and China’s regional image improved. “A lot of people saw their concerns not come to fruition, but rather see again more jobs, infrastructure and benefits,” she said. “So the ways that they’re exposed to China don’t end up in all cases harming them.” Neafie said respondents to the survey cited Beijing’s policy of non-interference as the top reason they viewed China favourably. But while there was some improvement, the study found that concerns over Chinese debt and land acquisition had persisted and that continued to have an impact on perceptions of China. Geopolitical anxieties – particularly fears that closer economic ties with China might jeopardise relations with Russia – remain one of the main drivers of negative sentiment. “Confidence in the economic benefits of Chinese engagement can coexist with – and in many cases outweigh – anxieties about debt, land and geopolitical realignment, but it does not erase them,” according to the paper. But Neafie noted that younger people – with more access to social media and more exchanges with Chinese – tended to view China more objectively. She said anxiety over geopolitics was largely found among the older generations who lived through the Sino-Soviet tensions of the 1970s, when Central Asia was part of the Soviet Union. China in Astana In Astana, the light rail is now the fastest route from the airport to downtown. At the brand new airport station there are turnstiles that support facial recognition technology. The train runs along an elevated track every five minutes, as it whizzes past the city’s gleaming skyscrapers, monuments and landmark buildings. Corruption allegations had stalled the project but it eventually began operations in May, more than a decade after it was first proposed. Built with Chinese technology, standards and equipment it is Central Asia’s first urban light rail and the region’s first fully driverless train system. A second phase of the project to expand the network is now under way, with Chinese-run construction sites visible across Astana. Back in 2013, Astana was the first to sign up to Beijing’s belt and road programme. China has since then ramped up investment across Kazakhstan and wider Central Asia, targeting small and medium-sized projects as a strategy to expand its influence in the region. Infrastructure is not the only sign of the growing Chinese presence in Astana. In the city’s shopping malls, Chinese powerhouses draw steady crowds – from drinks chain Mixue to variety chain store Miniso, consumer tech giant Xiaomi and sportswear brand Li-Ning – while Chinese beauty brands such as Shanghai Song have been embraced by local cosmetics stores. Yichang beer is a bestseller in liquor stores but it is actually brewed in Kazakhstan with rice to mimic the crisp Chinese-style beers. Its producer started exporting the beer to China in 2024, creating a buzz on social media. On the roads of the capital there are more Chinese EVs, alongside established brands such as Kia and Hyundai from South Korea and Toyota from Japan. In the first four months of 2026, car dealers in Kazakhstan sold some 2,122 electric and hybrid vehicles, according to official data. Of those, more than 2,000 – or over 97 per cent – came from Chinese carmakers, including BYD, Li Auto, Geely Galaxy, Zeekr and Rox. A taxi driver in Astana who gave only his first name, Abylai, was driving a BYD and planned to upgrade to the new Han sedan. “It’s a good car for the price,” he said. “Almost all my friends drive Chinese cars such as BYD and Changan.” Kabdygali, the car dealer, said his customers were drawn to the cost-efficiency of Chinese EVs and modern features such as infotainment systems, while concerns about quality had eased over time – mainly due to word of mouth. Geopolitical ambitions Several major powers – including Japan, South Korea and Turkey – have been vying for more influence in Central Asia in recent years, competing for critical mineral resources, trade routes and infrastructure contracts. Beijing has opted for a different path as it seeks smaller projects to quickly establish ties and build enduring influence, according to Neafie from Nazarbayev University. She said China had the capacity and risk tolerance to finance smaller, high-risk projects, which competitors like Japan or South Korea could not easily afford if they failed or underdelivered. “It’s not just altruism. These things lead to better economic outcomes … [and] have a long-term effect on relationships and public diplomacy,” she said, adding that in the long run these middle-level projects could “make a huge amount of difference”. Accelerated by the fallout from the war in Ukraine, cooperation between China and Central Asian countries has evolved into an institutionalised partnership, expanding beyond energy to include public health and digital technology. Zhu Yongbiao, director of the Centre for Afghanistan Studies at Lanzhou University, said that compared to the US approach, China’s investment in the region was more practical and comprehensive. “Whether it’s cutting-edge tech and flagship products – like electric vehicles, solar power, the digital economy, AI and TikTok – or everyday goods like socks and screws, China has it all,” he said. “Crucially, it can deliver tailored products and solutions suited to the diverse needs of different Central Asian countries, an advantage the US simply lacks.” Central Asia has shifted from being a security partner to a cornerstone of US regional strategy as Western economies seek to de-risk supply chains from China and Russia, with the Donald Trump administration focusing its attention on Kazakhstan – drawn by its critical mineral reserves. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio began a five-day trip to India and Uzbekistan on Saturday. In Samarkand, the top US diplomat will lead a delegation of more than 200 business leaders and take part in a series of bilateral engagements with senior officials from all five Central Asian nations – Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan. But intensifying US-China rivalry in the region may not be a bad thing, according to observers. Zhu said Beijing and Washington actually had opportunities to cooperate in Central Asia on environmental protection, energy market access and regional security surrounding Afghanistan. And in Kazakhstan the geopolitical pressure is minimal, according to Neafie. She said China and the US were both focused on economic engagement rather than military or security influence, and in a country that is developing fast that economic competition might even be welcomed.

title: Opinion | In Singapore, does unhappiness go hand in hand with fewer births?
description: A former minister said unhappiness could be a precondition for achievement. But some are opting out of a system optimised for progress.
content: At a recent Bloomberg forum, Singapore’s former foreign minister George Yeo was asked about the city state making the lists of the richest and unhappiest countries. He let slip what may be founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew’s coldest legacy quote: “We can promise economic development, infrastructure, education, whatever. But never promise happiness.” Yeo added that unhappiness may even be a precondition for achievement. In the national pledge, citizens of Singapore promise to achieve “happiness, prosperity and progress for our nation”. Sixty years on, we have nailed prosperity and progress. We have the hospitals, the schools, the trains that run (mostly) on time. Shouldn’t we be happy we pulled off the feat of rising “from third world to first”, as the title of Lee’s memoirs goes? Apparently, happiness is an aspiration but not the promised land. Speaking as a Singaporean, none of this shocks me. We’ve long known our national default setting is “achieve”, not “enjoy”. But it raises an awkward question: if happiness was never on the to-do list, what exactly have we been grinding away for? In the first place, how did we end up here? Historian Wang Gungwu, on a recent podcast, may have offered an explanation. He set out the old Confucian “mandate of heaven” concept whereby capable, caring rulers govern well and good subjects know their place and don’t complain – a political operating system that struck me as remarkably similar to the one in Singapore. Which brings me to my theory, submitted with the usual disclaimers about my own confusion and audacity: Singapore’s version of applied Confucianism got us from third world to first. Personal happiness was never in the road map. At its core, Confucianism was never a philosophy about how to be happy. It was a philosophy about how to be governable. Read it as a management manual rather than a moral one and the picture clicks into place: everyone gets a role and your job is to perform your role well under a hierarchy that is drummed into you from birth. Singapore even tried adding Confucian studies to the national curriculum in the 1980s. I was back in Singapore recently, and by day three I was reminded of the national sport: competing for a seat. On the MRT at 8am, at the hawker centre at noon and again on the ride home at 6pm. Three times a day, the city reminds us there isn’t quite enough to go around, so we all have to be quicker or better than the next person. As I sipped my warm soy drink, however, it struck me this was never really about seats. It’s a daily rehearsal for the multi-stop race Singaporeans are conditioned to take part in: study hard, graduate, work, apply for a BTO (Build-To-Order flat), get married, have kids, get them into a good school, keep their grades up, get them into university, then watch them retrace your steps. A society where everyone knows their lane is easy to manage – and that, not individual well-being, has always been the point. Nowhere is this clearer than in our national exams, where teenagers compete to validate their self-worth, in a tradition going back 1,400 years to the Sui dynasty. Singapore’s version of applied Confucianism got us from third world to first. … At its core, Confucianism was never a philosophy about how to be happy. It was a philosophy about how to be governable Scholars back then didn’t compete to differentiate themselves in a marketplace of ideas. They competed to align as closely as possible with whatever the emperor wanted so as to be granted the privilege of serving as a loyal extension of imperial authority. It was essentially selection masked as competition. This is still very much alive today, except that the emperor has been rebranded as a government scholarship. However, the cast meant to perpetuate this order may be quietly walking off the set. Singapore’s total fertility rate hit a record low of 0.87 last year, down from 0.97 the year before. If there was never a promise of happiness, perhaps some Singaporeans have decided they cannot, in good conscience, promise it to anyone else either – least of all their own child. Wang’s explanation offers a clue here: the mandate of heaven depends on people being satisfied with good governance and people have always had a way to deliver their verdict. Previously, that meant rebelling and toppling a dynasty. Today it’s quieter: it could be a friend taking a job overseas, a couple moving to Thailand, a woman deciding not to have a second child, or a first. Nobody storms the palace. People just stop showing up for the roles assigned them. Lee never promised us happiness, and to be fair, he never pretended otherwise. But without it, life in Singapore starts to look like a very long, very efficient commute to nowhere in particular.

title: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats, beat up French mayor in West Bank
description: Bernard Baudoux says masked assailants kicked him and hit him with iron bars as he joined Palestinian olive farmers.
content: Israeli settlers attacked a convoy of European diplomats in the West Bank and beat up a visiting French mayor on Saturday, witnesses said, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned against a brewing “crisis” in the territory a day after an American photojournalist was injured in a brutal attack. The 78-year-old mayor said masked settlers yelled defamatory comments about France, kicked him and hit him with iron bars as he joined Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank alongside the top French and Belgian representatives in Jerusalem and Polish diplomats. “I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government,” Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, said after he was attacked. “The whole world needs to know what’s happening,” he said. “For me, I’ll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here.” Baudoux, who was wearing a sash with the French tricolour, was seen collapsed on the side of the car after the attack, but he did not need hospital care. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in a statement that Israel must “urgently halt criminal violence” and arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux, while his Belgian counterpart issued a similar call. The attack came just one day after settlers beat an American photographer for The Washington Post, who was in moderate condition with broken vertebrae on Saturday. “We’re very disturbed by those images and what we’re seeing,” Rubio told reporters on Saturday, adding that US President Donald Trump “does not want to see friction or anything – a crisis going on in the West Bank.” Trump “doesn’t want to see a new spark”, Rubio added. Israel’s foreign ministry condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation. But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, days away from an election in which he is seeking to shore up support from the far-right, instead alleged a “smear” campaign against settlers. Netanyahu said the diplomats should have coordinated their movements with the Israeli military and pointed out that Baudoux is a communist known for supporting the Palestinian cause. “We urge caution before drawing conclusions” about the attacks, Netanyahu’s office said in a statement. His main rival in October 27 elections, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, strongly criticised Netanyahu over the violence, saying it was “burning away the little legitimacy the State of Israel still possesses”. The attacks are “Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government”, Eisenkot said. Belgium called for an end to “impunity for violent settlers” after the latest attack. Baudoux, the mayor, said he had come to the town of Taybeh, a Christian stronghold, along with his local pastor from France to sign a goodwill agreement. He was attacked just as he joined the harvest as a symbolic gesture with the Palestinians, for whom olives are an important cultural symbol. Extremist Israelis have issued calls to stop the Palestinians’ harvest after months of growing attacks in which settlers have stolen land and property. There has also been violence against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting dead a settler last month. Bashar Fawadleh, a priest in Taybeh, said settlers had already attacked the harvest and snatched olives before beating the mayor. “One person was hit in the head and needed stitches. They also beat up an older lady in her 70s after insulting her with very bad words,” the pastor said. The West Bank violence has shocked much of the world, with Britain leading economic sanctions that in turn caused Netanyahu to voice outrage. Netanyahu had also sought to throw doubt on the circumstances behind the beating Friday of the photographer, Heidi Levine, suggesting that Palestinians and “far-left” activists caused trouble. But President Isaac Herzog, who holds a mostly symbolic role, took the initiative on Saturday to call Levine in hospital, calling the attack “outrageous and shocking” and saying it weighed on his conscience. Israel Gantz, head of an umbrella settler group, blamed the recent incidents on “groups of provocateurs and terrorists” and implicitly acknowledged some Israelis’ responsibility, saying that they caused harm to the settlers’ cause. Settlers earlier this month also beat up Agence France-Presse photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he covered the olive harvest tensions, fracturing several of his ribs. Netanyahu’s government has ramped up approval of West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law. Some 500,000 Israelis live in the West Bank, which Israel seized in 1967, alongside three million Palestinians.

title: ‘Cockroach’ party founder released by Indian police
description: Abhijeet Dipke had been arrested amid a crackdown on protests against the country’s election authority.
content: India’s youth-led Cockroach Janata Party founder Abhijeet Dipke was released from detention on Saturday, a day after his arrest during a police crackdown on protests against the election authority. Dipke, 31, was detained Friday in New Delhi as he headed to join a rally that the CJP protest movement had called in the capital’s central Connaught Place district. He walked out of a police station on Saturday afternoon waving to the media and giving a thumbs up as he was driven away. “Abhijeet Dipke released,” CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media. Opposition parties and CJP activists have defied a security crackdown, rallying to demand the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner after accusing the poll body of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party. The commission, which oversees voting in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing. Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on October 14 after entering Jantar Mantar, a decades-old protest site that police have declared off-limits for demonstrations. They remain in custody. “Now just waiting for my brothers to be free,” Dipke said in a social media post that included a photo of Ranka and Das. In a separate post on Instagram, Dipke said he “knew going to jail was inevitable” and that he was ready to face “whatever comes my way”. “Because the day I decided to come back to India, I placed my fate in the hands of the people of India and the Constitution of this country.” Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls. Rights groups and critics, however, say the Modi government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents – allegations the government rejects.

title: Albanian police fire rubber bullets as student protesters call for PM to quit
description: The protests have been fuelled by ‌anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
content: Police in Albania fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters on Saturday, the fifth day of mass student protests demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama step down. Reuters video footage showed police firing a shotgun towards crowds outside the education ministry during clashes with protesters. Reuters reporters found rubber pellets on the ground and pellets hit two Reuters journalists ‌and several protesters, leaving round marks. The incident marks an escalation in a confrontation between police and protesters that has engulfed central Tirana in recent days. Protesters have burned government buildings and banks and hurled rocks at police, who have responded with tear gas and water cannon. Albania’s police chief Skender Hita did not deny the use of rubber bullets when asked about it at a news conference on Saturday. “All means that were used were employed in a limited manner, including the most recent ones,” he said. Hita said seven police officers have been suspended and were facing disciplinary investigations for “exceeding their authority” ⁠and “failure to respect the principle of proportionality” in dealing with protesters. He did not specify the incidents that led to the suspensions. The protests have been fuelled by ‌anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. They have also drawn support from people who felt ignored during a summer of largely peaceful protest against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared ‌Kushner. The unrest poses the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who last year won a fourth term in office. “It’s been 13 years ⁠of corruption and 13 years of ⁠doing nothing and empty promises. So the jar is filled and we are here for our rights,” said medical student Juri Taullahu, 22. Police and the government condemned the unrest and ‌called for calm. Hita said that 1,067 people had been arrested and 388 criminally prosecuted. Scores of police officers and protesters have been injured. Rama’s administration has been dogged by corruption scandals, while analysts say ‌Albania ‌has become a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drug and weapons trafficking, complicating the country’s efforts to join the European Union. Villagers said ‌in July that their land had been wrongfully sold for the Kushner-backed development on a pristine stretch of coast in southern Albania. Reuters later reported that the man ⁠who sold the land was wanted by prosecutors on suspicion of drug trafficking, accusations his lawyer denied. Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who ⁠is not directly involved in the villagers’ dispute. Rama, who denies wrongdoing and told Reuters this week that he would not step down, said on Saturday that his government respected the students and their right to protest. “My responsibility is even clearer during these difficult times ... to protect our ‌citizens, guarantee justice, and move Albania forward – together ‌with this governing majority, which holds a very clear mandate: to see Albania in the European Union by 2030,” he said on Facebook. Along with Montenegro, Albania is leading the EU accession process among Balkan countries. Albania’s unrest coincides with growing street protests elsewhere in Europe. In France, student protests demanding more teachers and better facilities have spread into a broader wave of unrest. Spain has seen protests against high rents and a lack of housing, prompting the government to call a snap election.

title: Hong Kong orders lift contractors to review doors installed over past 10 years
description: Government investigation finds missing fire-safety components in lifts in at least 78 private buildings and two public estates.
content: Hong Kong authorities have ordered all lift contractors to review the design and construction of landing doors installed over the past 10 years, after a government investigation found missing fire-safety components in lifts in at least 78 private buildings and two public estates. The director of the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department issued the order in a letter after inspections into lift contractor Taizoom Elevator revealed “serious deficiencies”. The company is under intense scrutiny after it was found to have installed fire-resistant doors without the required door frame components at numerous estates across Hong Kong. A source previously said that police had arrested the company’s director and two lift engineers. “[The] Electrical and Mechanical Services Department’s recent inspections reveal serious deficiencies in the major alteration of lifts undertaken by a registered lift contractor,” said chief engineer Kwan Kar-mun, who issued the letter for the director. “Although a fire-resisting rating certificate was submitted, it was found that only the fire-resisting doors were installed as required, but the corresponding door frame components were missing, and the lift works were claimed to be complete.” With a “view to ensure better assurance” of the installation and operation of lift systems, the department said it was requiring all registered lift contractors in Hong Kong to take a series of “step-up measures”. The four requirements include registered lift contractors having to review any landing door replacements or additions they carried out over the past 10 years starting from October 17, 2017. The letter said the contractors would have to review and declare that the landing doors and associated frame components installed were of “good design and construction” with valid documents certifying the doors complied with the required fire-resistant ratings. Contractors are also required to review any other landing doors and associated framing components to ensure they are in safe working condition. It urged all lift contractors to submit the relevant declaration forms by November 15. The department also said in a social media post that it would conduct random inspections to verify the submissions. A webpage has also been set up to disclose the inspection results to the public. According to the webpage, as of Saturday, lifts in 78 private blocks handled by Taizoom were not installed with fire-resistant door frames. Owners will be notified and the contractor must fix the problem at its own cost under the department’s supervision. The saga unfolded on Thursday, when the department revealed that an inspection, triggered by a complaint, found that Taizoom had installed fire-resistant doors without the required door frame components at the two estates, involving at least 48 lifts. The department said the contractor had submitted a fire-resistance rating certificate and claimed it had completed the works. The department later expanded its inspection to cover other lifts installed by the same contractor. Separately, a source earlier said three personnel from Taizoom Elevator had been arrested on suspicion of deception. The company had replaced 48 lifts at public housing estates: nine at Tsui Ping (North) Estate in Kwun Tong and 39 at Pok Hong Estate in Sha Tin. One of the suspects was a 79-year-old director and shareholder of Taizoom. The other two were registered lift engineers, aged 63 and 82, who examined the installations and signed safety certificates. The insider said officers raided the company’s office in Chai Wan, and the investigation had found that the missing components were “critical smoke control devices”. According to the department’s quarterly performance ratings for lift contractors, Taizoom scored three out of five in service quality and had the same score in safety performance as other companies. The arrests came two months after 24 of the 28 lifts in Queen Mary Hospital’s new 34-storey clinical block were deemed unfit for use.

title: How Taiwan’s new AI satellite system aims to speed up early warning against PLA moves
description: Technology is intended to rapidly search for and identify enemy forces and activity at military bases and elsewhere near the island.
content: Taiwan will acquire an AI-powered satellite imagery system capable of rapidly identifying People’s Liberation Army ships, aircraft and missile launchers, as it seeks to boost early-warning capabilities in the face of growing military pressure from Beijing. The NT$46.55 million (US$1.45 million) system will use artificial intelligence (AI) to analyse satellite images covering 100 sq km (38.6 square miles) within minutes, potentially cutting the time and manpower needed to track changes in PLA deployments, according to the island’s defence ministry. In a public procurement notice this week, the ministry’s Communication Development Office (CDO), a primary military intelligence unit, awarded the contract to ThinkTron, a Taiwan-Japan joint venture specialising in AI, geospatial information systems and monitoring technology. The contract took effect on September 25, and the system is expected to be completed by the end of April. Taiwan’s defence minister, Wellington Koo Li-hsiung, confirmed earlier this year that the island’s military planned to develop a prototype AI satellite imagery recognition system. Ministry officials said the technology was intended to rapidly search for and identify enemy forces and activity at military bases and elsewhere near Taiwan, automatically compare new imagery with historical data and flag changes for intelligence analysts. Sources familiar with the project said the aim was to improve strategic early warning and support combat-readiness decisions. The system could analyse several 10km by 10km areas within minutes, identifying ships more than 10 metres (about 33 feet) long as well as smaller targets such as aircraft, missile launchers and radar vehicles, they said. According to Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies in Taipei, the project should not be confused with the acquisition of new reconnaissance satellites. “The system’s main function is to use AI to help the CDO rapidly analyse imagery and information received from satellites,” he said. The CDO did not itself operate the military-grade imagery satellites providing the data, Wang added. Rather, the AI would serve as an analytical layer processing imagery obtained from other sources. That distinction also helps to explain the project’s relatively modest cost. Wang said building an entire satellite reconnaissance architecture – from operating satellites to receiving their imagery – would require far greater investment. The new system instead sits at the end of the intelligence pipeline, automatically screening large quantities of imagery that would otherwise require labour-intensive analysis. Max Lo, executive director of the Taipei-based Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, said the underlying technology was already mature and used by advanced militaries and remote-sensing organisations. He explained that the significance for Taiwan lay in operationalising the technology and integrating it with the island’s existing intelligence capabilities. “The PLA is already capable of installing AI systems directly on satellites to conduct preliminary analysis of imagery before the data is transmitted to the ground, allowing it to respond more quickly,” Lo said. But the Taiwan project is different, he added, noting the analyses would be done on the ground at the CDO. Lo said there would be no difficulty for the island to set up such an AI-powered system, noting that ThinkTron was jointly established by Taiwan’s Sinotech Engineering Consultants and Japanese geospatial specialist Kokusai Kogyo. According to ThinkTron’s website, its existing “Tron Eyes” technology uses convolutional neural networks to analyse imagery for applications ranging from disaster prevention and infrastructure inspection to agriculture and transport. Lo argued that AI could help address a growing intelligence challenge for Taiwan’s military: the sheer volume of information generated by frequent PLA operations around the island. “Instead of requiring analysts to manually search large satellite images for ships, aircraft or mobile missile launchers, the system could automatically flag potential targets or changes for closer examination,” he said. This would be particularly useful when monitoring large areas of sea, he added, with synthetic aperture radar, or SAR, detecting vessels at night and through cloud cover, while optical imagery could provide greater detail in clear daylight conditions. By comparing successive images, AI could also help analysts track changes in the location and movement of military assets, Lo said. “Potentially more important is the ability to combine what Taiwan’s intelligence apparatus ‘sees’ with what it ‘hears’.” The Linkou-based CDO in northern Taiwan specialises in signals intelligence, intercepting and analysing electronic emissions and communications associated with the PLA. Lo said AI-assisted imagery analysis could be cross-checked against such signals intelligence. An unidentified vessel detected in satellite imagery, for example, could be compared with radar or radio emissions collected from the same area to help analysts determine whether it was associated with the PLA. Such intelligence fusion could be particularly useful when military vessels operate among civilian shipping or switch off their Automatic Identification System transponders, making conventional tracking more difficult, according to analysts. Wang said the system could help Taiwan more quickly assess PLA exercises, changes in tactics and force deployments. “Most importantly, it could help Taiwan monitor PLA force movements and its broader strategic deployments, allowing the military to identify developments earlier and prepare appropriate responses,” he added. The CDO is one of Taiwan’s most sensitive military intelligence organisations and has long specialised in collecting signals from mainland China. Lo said the office’s strength in signals intelligence meant the new imagery system would complement rather than replace existing collection methods. Intelligence generated by the system could also be compared with information obtained through cooperation with the United States and other partners, he noted, although details of such arrangements are rarely made public. Wang said the project could lay the groundwork for wider use of AI within Taiwan’s military intelligence apparatus. “I believe this system represents part of the technological foundation for further innovation by the Communication Development Office,” he added. “In the future, we are likely to see additional and more comprehensive systems developed to analyse intelligence on the PLA.” Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Alexander Zverev stunned by Alejandro Davidovich Fokina in Shanghai semi-finals
description: The 25th seed will play fellow Spaniard Rafael Jodar, who beat Daniil Medvedev, while world number 170 Briton reaches Wuhan Open final.
content: Top seed Alexander Zverev fell to a relentless Alejandro Davidovich Fokina in the Shanghai Masters semi-finals on Saturday over three tense sets. Davidovich Fokina, ranked world No 26, fought back to win 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 and will play fellow Spaniard Rafael Jodar in the final on Sunday. The 20-year-old Jodar beat fifth-seed Daniil Medvedev, a decade his senior, 6-3, 6-4 to deny the Russian former world No 1 a chance to return to the championship match he won in 2019. Jodar, ranked 13th, started the season ranked 168th. It is his first time in a final at the prestigious 1000 level. Davidovich Fokina fired 36 winners in the two-hour, two-minute contest to secure only his second victory over Zverev in eight meetings. ‌His previous win against the German came in the round of 32 at the Canadian Open in 2023. The 25th seed earned his first break of the match to take the second set, forcing a decider with a stunning backhand passing shot on the run that capped a bruising baseline exchange and brought the crowd to their feet. Carrying that momentum into the final set, ⁠Davidovich Fokina broke Zverev for a 2-0 lead and never relinquished control, booking a place in the second ‌ATP Masters 1000 final of his career after finishing runner-up in Monte Carlo in 2022. Landing 82 per cent of his first serves and repeatedly exposing Zverev on the ‌forehand side, he secured one of the biggest victories of his career. “I knew that if ⁠I stayed there ⁠all match, I could get at least one chance and I took it there in the second set,” Davidovich Fokina said. “Then ‌in the third set, I think I was better physically. The early break in the third set gave me a lot of power. “I ‌focused ‌on just playing, not mattering about the result but enjoying.” Davidovich Fokina, who missed the North American hard-court ‌swing in August because of injury, has now won nine consecutive matches in China after lifting his ⁠second tour-level title at the ATP 250 event in Chengdu last month. It was a disappointing end to ⁠the week for Zverev, a seven-time ATP Masters 1000 champion whose best result in Shanghai remains his runner-up finish to Medvedev in 2019. The 29-year-old has otherwise enjoyed a fine season, ‌ending his grand slam drought ‌at the French Open before claiming a second major title at the US Open and securing the ATP year-end world No 1 ranking after Jannik Sinner was sidelined for the remainder of the season with a knee injury. Fifth-seeded Russian Medvedev was playing 12th-seeded Jodar, 20, in the second semi-final. At the Wuhan Open, world number 170 Sonay Kartal became the lowest-ranked player to reach a WTA 1000 final when she knocked out Jelena Ostapenko with a gritty 7-6, 7-6 win on Saturday. The 24-year-old Briton is playing just her second tour event since returning from a six-month injury lay-off, having suffered a spinal stress fracture that sidelined her from March to September. Kartal, who was ranked a career-high 44 in the world 15 months ago, is the lowest-ranked WTA 1000 finalist since the format’s introduction in 2009. In a close affair with 2017 French Open champion Ostapenko, Kartal showed tremendous composure and dug herself out of multiple holes to become the first British finalist in Wuhan Open history. “Wow, that was probably one of the toughest matches I’ve ever played,” said Kartal, who survived 50 winners coming off Ostapenko’s racquet to reach the biggest final of her career. “I knew exactly how she was going to play. At times she’s unplayable and sometimes you just have to ride that wave. “Mentally I think this is one of the best performances I’ve had in my career. I’m very proud of that one.” After dismissing three consecutive seeds in her previous rounds, including No 6 Elina Svitolina and No 9 Belinda Bencic, Kartal made the 35th-ranked Ostapenko her latest victim to reach her second career tour-level final, and first at the WTA 1000 level. Kartal will face Poland’s Maja Chwalinska after a ⁠left-leg injury ⁠derailed Iga Swiatek as she went down fighting to her compatriot ‌and childhood friend 7-5, 6-1 in the other semi-final on Saturday. Six-time grand slam winner ⁠Swiatek had to take a ‌medical timeout while trailing 6-5 in the ‌first set and continued the ⁠match ⁠with a bandaged left thigh, ‌but found it difficult to put pressure ‌on ‌her leg and struggled ‌to chase returns across ⁠the court.

title: China’s embassy issues fresh Thailand travel alert over kidnappings, job scams
description: Latest advisory alerts citizens to risks after Chinese nationals targeted in kidnappings and trafficking schemes involving fake job offers.
content: China’s embassy in Thailand has warned citizens to carefully plan their trips and pay extra attention to transport security following a string of high-profile kidnappings targeting Chinese nationals. Online influencers and artists were also advised to remain vigilant against high-paying job scams operating in Thailand in the latest such warning issued on Friday. There have been a number of high-profile incidents in recent months in which online celebrities and travellers were kidnapped in Thailand and trafficked to scam syndicates in Myanmar. The Bangkok embassy urged travellers to “pay attention to transport arranged by others” and “plan their itinerary and choose licensed transport and legal operators”, while being “careful not to take any free rides from acquaintances or strangers” alike. Individuals should also refuse sudden changes to venues or travel routes and keep their families informed of their whereabouts, Friday’s notice posted to the embassy website said. While the embassy issued a similar warning in April, its latest advisory highlighted particular concern over the growing number of entertainers and online influencers being lured to Thailand and trafficked. The latest statement also gave detailed warnings about the use of transport in Thailand. According to Thai media reports, a 30-year-old Thai man arrested on October 10 in Tak province along the Myanmar border is suspected of being part of a trafficking ring that lured three Chinese nationals to Thailand with fake job offers before transporting them to the border area. Transnational criminal networks are known to operate multibillion-dollar scam compounds along the Thailand–Myanmar border, using false high-paying job advertisements to entice foreign victims into forced labour, human trafficking and online fraud operations. Several scams targeting live-streamers and performance artists have used fake invites to shoots and auditions to trap victims, including a high-profile case last year where a Chinese actor named Wang Xing was lured under the guise of a filming project and subsequently trafficked. Earlier this month, a 34-year-old Chinese photographer went missing after travelling to Bangkok for a shooting job. His family, after receiving a ransom demand while searching for him in Thailand, reported the abduction to Chinese and Thai authorities. In another case, an urgent social media post on October 1 alerted the public to the disappearance of a Shanghai music teacher, who went missing in Thailand on September 25. In August, The Beijing News reported that a Chinese tourist was abducted in Thailand after getting into a vehicle she mistook for that of her tour guide. She was freed only after shouting for help at a police checkpoint. All of these individuals have reportedly returned to China with the help of the embassy in Bangkok. Thanapol Cheewarattanaporn, president of the Association of Thai Travel Agents, said in June that the forecast for Chinese tourist arrivals this year had been revised down to around 7 million, from an initial estimate of 9 million. Safety concerns had become Thailand’s primary challenge in the Chinese market, as they directly affected travel decisions, he said, adding: “Such stories have spread quickly across Chinese social media and short-video platforms, further hurting Thailand’s image as a safe destination.” Wang Xing’s story remains one of the most prominent cases of a Chinese national being lured to Thailand and trapped in a human trafficking pipeline. A telecoms fraud syndicate lured the actor to Thailand in January with the offer of a fake filming project, then forcibly moved him to a scam compound in Myanmar. According to a documentary broadcast earlier this year by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, Wang was resold across three different scam operations within just four days before Chinese embassy officials successfully mediated his release. Though safely back in China, he is still saddled with massive online loans he was forced to take out while captive in Thailand and Myanmar. The high-profile case dealt a severe blow to Chinese tourism to Thailand throughout 2025, with visitor demand only beginning to recover this year.

title: AI glasses as travel guides? Cheaper in China, but technical hitches slow adoption
description: Affordable AI glasses can translate languages, identify landmarks and provide travel tips, but limitations remain, analysts say.
content: Artificial intelligence-powered glasses can act as tour guides, snap photos hands-free and translate foreign languages. The devices also sell at relatively affordable prices in China. But are they the perfect travel companion? Not yet. AI glasses were slowly catching on with travellers as the technology improved and more devices entered the market, analysts said, but technical hitches were slowing mass adoption of the smartphone-linked gear that could be worn like ordinary spectacles. “They can be particularly useful when walking, sightseeing or interacting in unfamiliar environments, making them especially helpful when travelling in foreign countries,” said Flora Tang, principal analyst at market research firm Counterpoint. “We believe both Chinese outbound travellers and international travellers visiting China are potentially among the more receptive user groups,” she said. “The availability of lower-priced products is also helping lower the entry barrier and raise consumer awareness.” Technology companies and tourist sites have already begun exploring the potential of the devices. Meta Platforms’ Ray-Ban AI glasses, released in 2023, were designed to identify landmarks, translate signs and provide live interpretation, according to the company website. In China, Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen Glasses was working with the Hangzhou Culture, Radio, TV and Tourism Bureau to “pioneer” AI-enhanced travel experiences, according to a statement in May. It had also joined a China-Italy association to explore how AI glasses could interpret and share culture. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. “Our goal is to seamlessly integrate AI into everyday life, using popular cultural and tourism experiences as our launching pad,” a Qwen Glasses spokesperson said. “This creates exciting new ways for people to explore local art, culture and travel.” When comparing leading Chinese and foreign brands, AI glasses are definitely cheaper in China Mark Natkin, Marbridge Consulting Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies and Xiaomi-backed start-up Superhexa have also released AI glasses. Shanghai’s Yuyuan Garden tourist attraction said it was separately testing AI glasses for tours and multilingual translation. The global average selling price for AI glasses was US$360 per unit in late 2025, according to Counterpoint. By comparison, Xiaomi AI glasses with clear lenses retailed for about 2,000 yuan (US$298), while a pair of Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3 glasses could sell for US$450, said Mark Natkin, managing director at Hong Kong-based market research firm Marbridge Consulting. Alibaba launched its latest smart glasses series on Tuesday, including the Qwen Glasses N1, which is priced at 2,218 yuan for a standard version. A more advanced version with an eye-tracking function for visual interaction starts at 2,600 yuan. “When comparing leading Chinese and foreign brands, AI glasses are definitely cheaper in China,” Natkin said. Global shipments of smart eyewear were expected to reach 18.66 million units this year, including both AI-capable and non-AI models, according to forecasts from tech market research firm IDC. Some 909,000 smart glasses were sold in China in the first half of 2026, according to market research firm Luo Tu Technology. During the year, travellers worldwide were expected to shift from “passive response to proactive service” when using smart eyewear, said Julia Sonnemann, public relations manager for business-to-business travel trade show ITB China. That meant glasses would increasingly anticipate user context and provide relevant information or suggestions without requiring explicit prompts. “For tourism, I see the greatest potential in hands-free, contextual information – asking about a landmark while looking at it, translating a sign, receiving spoken information during a tour or accessing personalised recommendations without constantly taking out a smartphone,” Sonnemann said. However, battery life, AI service accessibility and response accuracy remained issues, said Layla Ye, a research analyst with IDC China. As a result, smartphones remained better suited for complex interactions and visual tasks, she added. According to Meta, its Ray‑Ban (Gen 2) and Oakley HSTN glasses could operate for up to eight hours on a single charge, while their charging cases provided up to 48 additional hours of use. Chinese brands often featured “superior raw hardware specs” compared with foreign rivals, but users could encounter software and ecosystem hitches overseas, Natkin said. They were typically integrated with Chinese apps such as Baidu Maps and Alipay, which offered less support outside China, he added. Meta’s glasses were not officially sold in China and Chinese users had reportedly faced difficulties accessing the company’s AI services. “Smart eyewear as a travel tool is still in the early adoption phase globally, but the growth rate is accelerating,” Ye said.

title: All Blacks coach vows to stick to running game at World Cup after humbling Wallabies again
description: Dave Rennie, coach of Hong Kong’s RWC opponents, says tactics that favour ball speed, width more likely to work against holders South Africa.
content: New Zealand coach Dave Rennie said his team would be ⁠sticking to their expansive ⁠style at next year’s World Cup after ⁠the All Blacks thrashed the Wallabies for a second successive week with some sensational attacking rugby on Saturday. Two convincing wins over Australia have got the New Zealanders back to winning ways after they lost a four-match series against South Africa 3-1. Hong Kong will face both sides when they make their Rugby World Cup debut next year, playing hosts Australia in the tournament’s opening match on October 1 and then facing the three-time world champion Kiwis two weeks later. The city side face Chile in their other Pool A match in between. Rennie said that although the Springboks had ridden ‌a physical, conservative playing style to back-to-back World Cup triumphs, he remained convinced the tactics that put a premium on ball speed and width would be effective against it. “There’s no point playing this way and then going to a World Cup and trying to play risk-free footy,” he told reporters after the 42-21 victory at Stadium Australia. “We’re well aware you can put yourself ⁠under pressure the way that we’re trying to play, but we’ll also back ourselves that we’ll profit more than ‌we’ll suffer in those situations. “I don’t think you want all the teams in the world playing the same game. I think if you look at the Wallabies, they’re ‌pretty similar to us. I think they’ll want to play, and it’s a point of ⁠difference, part of the ⁠DNA of both sides. “If you want to just get into arm wrestles with a couple of the big sides in the world, it’ll ‌be a struggle,” he said. Despite his team scoring six tries with some breathtaking rugby in the first half on Saturday, Rennie said there ‌were still ‌improvements to be made. “We’re trying to grow our game, and we’ve got a long way to go,” ‌he said. “We just want to be able to play at a tempo that will test other sides.” Australia coach Les ⁠Kiss called Australia’s performance “unacceptable” but said there was time to improve before the World Cup. After a 50-19 thrashing in Auckland last week, Kiss was hoping his young side would bounce back in Sydney, but they were routed in a devastating first-half. They conceded three tries in the opening 20 minutes and six in the first 40. “Look, it’s unacceptable, 22 points like that, and you put yourself on the back foot, and the boys know that,” he said. “It’s just not on. You can’t do that. We’ve had two bad halves now in the past two weeks, and it hurts you.” The All Blacks tore the Wallabies defence to pieces, undoing a lot of the improvements seen since Kiss took over in July. He had enjoyed five wins and a draw from his first six tests before coming face-to-face with the All Blacks juggernaut. Australia were missing some key players including fly-halves Carter Gordon and Ben Donaldson, and centre Len Ikitau, but it was nevertheless a sobering lesson a year out from the World Cup. “You know a lot of young guys, single test numbers, learned a lot tonight for sure,” said Kiss. “But as a team I think there’s got to be a little bit more thinking about what it really means to actually turn up in that first-half and make sure we don’t make those errors that we did. “We could have scored three times but we just didn’t work hard enough to get around the corner to score those tries. So there’s little things there that are just hurting us.”

title: China’s proposed AI tech export bans may create short-term costs, long-term gains: analysts
description: A key uncertainty is how open-weight AI technologies would be affected by the proposed controls.
content: China’s proposed export bans and controls of artificial intelligence technologies aim to tighten Beijing’s grip in the strategically vital sector, casting a cloud over the commercial prospects of domestic model developers in the global AI race, analysts say. The new measures come as concerns mount globally over the risks of advanced AI systems, following a string of recent cyberattacks, while also underscoring AI’s growing national security importance for both Beijing and Washington. Zhang Yi, founder and chief analyst at consultancy iiMedia, said the new measures would inevitably introduce short-term adaptation costs for Chinese companies, at a time when they were targeting international markets. Under the draft plan, jointly issued by China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and the Ministry of Science and Technology on Friday, export prohibitions and restrictions would be imposed on 23 AI-related technologies, including models, agents and chip designs. Export bans and restrictions on critical technologies relating to the biotechnology and photovoltaic sectors were also proposed. For foundational AI models, the core drivers of advancements in the sector, the authorities outlined several thresholds for restrictions to be imposed. These include models “trained on China’s important data”, developed with computing power reaching 10²⁶ FLOPs – a widely used threshold denoting frontier AI models – sized at 2 trillion parameters or more, or ranking in a global top 10 leaderboard. AI has grown increasingly central to China-US relations as the two countries seek to work out ways to jointly address growing AI risks in the midst of fierce commercial and geopolitical competition. Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump agreed to set up a bilateral dialogue to manage AI risks during last month’s summit in Washington, with AI expected to be a major agenda item at the two remaining meetings between the pair this year – at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen next month and the G20 summit in Miami in December. Still, Beijing’s growing scrutiny of the industry should not be interpreted as an effort to prevent Chinese companies from deploying their AI services globally, according to Zhang. “The key lies in keeping core engineering technologies controlled, while keeping commercial services open,” he said. The assessment was echoed by a MOFCOM spokesperson, who said on Friday that “the scope of AI technologies covered by the regulation this time is targeted and limited”. The spokesperson sought to clarify that some ways in which Chinese technology companies are providing AI services overseas, including through official application programming interfaces (APIs) and mobile apps, would not be covered by the new export restrictions. “Once the measures take formal effect, the vast majority of AI technologies will still be freely exportable,” the spokesperson said. A key uncertainty is how open-weight AI technologies, an area in which China leads globally, would be treated under the finalised export regime. Growing numbers of Chinese open-weight AI developers such as Kimi model maker Moonshot AI and GLM maker Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, are entering into revenue-sharing agreements with major US hyperscalers such as Amazon Web Services to deploy their open-weight models on their cloud infrastructure, representing a new major source of revenue. Under the current wording of the new measures, several Chinese AI models, which are some of the world’s leading open-weight systems, would meet the technical thresholds. However, the MOFCOM spokesperson said on Friday that China was continuing to encourage open-source AI, with new licensing requirements to be expedited as “immediate clearance upon filing”. The addition of various AI technologies to the export control list was intended to “ensure the security and controllability” of AI technologies amid growing risks, the spokesperson said, such as the misuse of powerful AI systems by “non-state actors and malicious entities”. Still, the new compliance requirements might delay or prevent Chinese AI companies from partnering with global cloud providers to deploy their most powerful open-weight models, as this would involve exporting the “weights” of the models outside China, said Alex Colville, an analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute specialising in Chinese AI. “There’s still a lot of things we don’t know,” he said, noting that much depends on how key provisions are worded in the finalised version of the plan, such as what “automatic approval” for open-sourcing AI technologies would mean in practice. “The Chinese side has prided themselves on being as flexible as possible in AI regulation so far. If the field dramatically changes within the next six months, they can just change the export control requirements to reflect that,” he said. A month-long public consultation period for the draft plan would last until November 15, the authorities said on Friday. You Yunting, senior partner at Shanghai DeBund Law Offices, noted that the new measures seemed to be a targeted reaction by the authorities to US tech giant Meta Platforms’ aborted acquisition of Chinese AI agent developer Manus earlier this year. One of the new proposed measures would require prior registration with MOFCOM before restricted Chinese technologies could change hands to an overseas owner or controller. Originally founded in mainland China in 2022, Manus’ parent company Butterfly Effect relocated to Singapore last year, allowing the firm to sidestep US technology export and investment controls, which paved the way for its $2 billion acquisition by the US tech giant. However, Beijing called a halt to the transaction soon after, citing national security grounds. Manus announced last month that it had formally resumed independent operations. You noted that compliance costs for domestic AI companies venturing abroad would rise in the short term, but the export controls could yield long-term competitive advantages for the country. “Given the substantial domestic investments in the sector, implementing reasonable controls is necessary [to protect those investments],” You said.

title: Coming up roses? How Trump planted a new seed for Chinese gift diplomacy
description: US president was so taken with the ‘beautiful’ flowers at the leadership compound in Beijing that he requested some for the White House.
content: Donald Trump was apparently captivated by the “beautiful” roses in the garden of the Communist Party’s leadership compound when he visited Beijing in May. It was a relaxed moment between the US and Chinese leaders – otherwise locked in disputes ranging from trade to technology and Taiwan – that led to a new opportunity for gift diplomacy between the rival powers. Strolling around the former imperial garden at Zhongnanhai with Xi Jinping, Trump was so taken with a China rose variety in bloom that he asked his host for some to be sent to Washington. “These are the most beautiful roses anyone’s ever seen,” Trump told reporters at the time. “I asked the president, ‘Could you get me some for the Rose Garden?’ And he said ‘yes’. I’ve never seen roses so big!” Xi responded through his interpreter that some rose seeds would be sent. Soon Trump will be able to admire them in the Rose Garden at the White House, after the Chinese leader came good on his promise. The flowers were sent to the White House when Xi visited in late September. More than 20 types of China rose – or Rosa chinensis – in seven colours were sent and it was the first time those varieties had entered the United States, according to a Beijing TV report on Tuesday.
