They were selected for their suitability to Washington’s climate, their resilience, the size of their blooms and their colour, The Beijing News reported. Most of the varieties were bred in Beijing, where the China rose is the official flower and a big part of urban greening efforts. More than 3,000 cultivated varieties of the rose have been planted across 20 sq km (7.7 sq miles) in the capital city. Reflecting on last month’s Washington summit, Foreign Minister Wang Yi said the China roses sent by Beijing were a symbol of the goodwill and friendship of the Chinese people, according to a ministry statement. They were not the only gifts sent by China. Photos from Xi’s visit released by the White House included one of the Chinese leader presenting a golden model of the Hall of Supreme Harmony to Trump in the Blue Room. The hall is the largest in Beijing’s Forbidden City and was a ceremonial venue where Chinese emperors hosted enthronement and wedding ceremonies. In return, Trump presented Xi with a silver plate bearing his signature. At a state dinner that evening, Trump also gave Xi a sculpture of a bald eagle, a bird native to North America and his country’s national symbol. While the roses, models and statues had symbolic weight, it was the gifts that arrived on four legs that captured the most attention in the United States. Giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang arrived at Zoo Atlanta on September 27 under a 10-year loan agreement. The pandas will spend a month in quarantine before they make their public debut on November 6 at a facility that has just been renovated at a cost of US$6 million. Zoo Atlanta is one of only three in the US that has giant pandas. The animals are native to central and southwestern China and are seen as a national treasure. As such, Beijing retains ownership of every giant panda sent abroad under international agreements. They are seen as living emissaries of goodwill in a tradition known as “panda diplomacy” that dates back to 1972, when Beijing presented Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing to a zoo in Washington following then-US president Richard Nixon’s landmark visit to China. The pandas were a hit and served as a gentle bridge between the two nations after decades of diplomatic ice. The US government sent China a pair of musk oxen in return. China has stopped giving giant pandas as gifts, instead moving to the loan arrangements as it tries to protect the endangered species.

title: AI used for first time to analyse lawmakers’ 5-year plan, policy address debate
description: Legco president says AI was used to produce an overview of the three-day debate, with talent and Northern Metropolis as the top themes.
content: Hong Kong’s legislature has for the first time used artificial intelligence (AI) to analyse lawmakers’ remarks during a three-day debate on the city’s first five-year plan and the latest annual policy address, with talent and the Northern Metropolis emerging as the most-discussed topics. Legislative Council president Starry Lee Wai-king said on Saturday that an overview of the six-session debate had been produced using AI. The session on improving livelihood protections drew the largest number of speaking lawmakers and accounted for nearly 30 per cent of the total debate coverage, she said. “The overview will be provided to lawmakers for reference and submitted to the government, with the aim of helping authorities accurately grasp the key focus areas of the motion debate,” she said on social media. Lee said the overview identified the top 10 most frequently mentioned themes in the lawmakers’ remarks: talent; the Northern Metropolis; innovation and technology; education; data and computing power; the Greater Bay Area and Shenzhen-Hong Kong cooperation; AI; finance and international financial centre; youth; and employment. According to the overview, 77 lawmakers touched on talent, followed by the Northern Metropolis, which was mentioned by 71 legislators. “The lawmakers’ suggestions reflected a holistic perspective, focusing on key issues vital to Hong Kong’s long-term development such as talent, technology and urban governance while remaining deeply attentive to public livelihoods,” she said. Lee said the Legco secretariat was exploring ways to more effectively leverage AI to analyse the key themes and characteristics of lawmakers’ debates on motions. Earlier this month, the legislature passed motions supporting the city’s first five-year plan and thanking Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu for his latest policy address following the three-day debate. The city leader unveiled the annual policy address last month alongside the five-year plan, which aims to align Hong Kong’s development with the national development strategy. The two documents set out initiatives to accelerate the Northern Metropolis megaproject and strengthen the city’s position in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology.

title: Bangladesh tourist resort fire kills 10
description: The fire chief said the resort lacked fire safety and that no government agency approval was given for the resort’s construction.
content: At least 10 tourists have been killed in a fire at a seaside resort in the southeastern Bangladeshi district of Cox’s Bazar, the country’s largest travel destination, officials said on Saturday. Dolon Acharya, an officer at the Fire Service and Civil Defence department, said the fire broke out in the morning at Tuptup Resto and Resort at Patuartek beach. The flames gutted the entire facility. The scene is located more than 320km (199 miles) southeast of the capital Dhaka. Acharya said firefighters pulled the charred bodies from inside the resort. Six other wounded people were rescued and rushed to a hospital, he said, adding three fire engines took nearly two hours to douse the blaze. Talha Bin Jasim, spokesman for the Fire Service and Civil Defence department, said the dead included five women and a 5-year-old boy. Most of them had travelled from the capital Dhaka. He later said that the identity of four more bodies found in the debris could not be determined. The resort, housed in a two-storey wooden-framed building, was operated as a beachfront retreat located directly along the scenic Marine Drive. It offered eco-style accommodation with panoramic views of both the sea and the hills, according to the resort’s website. The reason behind the fire was not known immediately. Sultanul Afreen Junaid, chief of the Fire Service and Civil Defence department, said at a news conference at the department’s Dhaka headquarters that the resort lacked fire safety. He said no approval was given by any government agency for the construction of the resort. M A Mannan, the chief administrator of the district, said an investigation was launched to determine the cause of the fire and the damage it caused. Famous for the largest unbroken sandy sea beach on the bank of the Bay of Bengal, Cox’s Bazar is Bangladesh’s main tourist destination, frequented by more than 3 million travellers annually. Most of them are domestic tourists, according to Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics.

title: What Christopher Nolan’s The Prestige reveals about his cinematic obsession 20 years on
description: Christopher Nolan’s 2006 film The Prestige is a complex story of obsession and ambition, played out with a stellar cast.
content: Before The Dark Knight made him a household name in 2008, Christopher Nolan crafted intricate thrillers such as Following (1998), Memento (2000) and Insomnia (2002). But 2006’s The Prestige, which turns 20 this month, is the most labyrinthine by far. Made just after Batman Begins (2005), but a far stranger and more personal proposition, it is set in 1890s London. Here, we are introduced to stage magicians Robert Angier (Hugh Jackman) and Alfred Borden (Christian Bale), who risk their lives, and more, trying to outdo each other. Both men want to perfect a teleportation illusion – originally known as The Transported Man – and neither is above using underhand tactics. “The film has been written according to the principles of how a magic trick works,” Nolan told Empire magazine in 2006. “Our narrative plays tricks with the audience. It has stories within stories and misdirection and so forth.” “Are you watching closely?” Borden asks at the beginning. Chances are the answer is no. Based on a 1995 book by Christopher Priest and adapted by Nolan and his younger brother Jonathan (the showrunner of the equally thorny Westworld), the film boasts a fantastic script, full of fiendish foreshadowing and devilish twists, if a little too complex to synopsise. Suffice it to say, the film follows Angier and Borden’s seesawing fortunes as they lie, scheme and backstab each other in pursuit of perfection, even if that means losing themselves and those they love in the process. What seemed at the time like an impressive cast has only grown in stature since. Bale brings his usual surly charisma to Borden, never once trying to make him likeable. Jackman, perhaps too clean-cut for the darker aspects of the role, captures Angier’s showmanship with panache. As their mentor John Cutter, Michael Caine is all rueful charm, while future luminaries such as Scarlett Johansson, Rebecca Hall and Andy Serkis have small but pivotal roles. There is even a cameo from an endearingly awkward David Bowie as the inventor Nikola Tesla. “I wanted someone who, while not a movie star per se, was charismatic and had a star quality in a different way – and Bowie was perfect for that,” Nolan told Empire. The filmmaker reportedly flew out to New York to ask the musical maestro personally, telling him no one else could possibly play the part. Bowie’s star power was such that Bale’s mother considered the casting proof that her son had finally made it. Certainly, nobody could have recreated Bowie’s odd Serbian-American cadences – one of many misjudged accents in the film. The science of wizardry For the most part, however, the film is wonderful. The Nolan brothers and their team evoke the 1890s as an age of boundless invention, when science occupied a similar space to wizardry. As he would prove in film after film, Nolan excels at showing just how far obsessed men will go to reach their goals. These are not just exceptional men, but divided ones; ruinous in life and love, and dangerous to those around them. There is some clever doubling. Angier and Borden are equals and opposites; Borden has a secret twin (Fallon, also played by Bale), and Angier has learned how (through Tesla) to make copies of himself, which he uses to create the ultimate Transported Man trick. Likewise, Tesla is in competition with Thomas Edison – a rivalry with a real historical basis. Nolan’s rocky track record with female characters is well documented, and the film’s various wives, girlfriends and daughters are largely there to advance the plot, get fought over or killed. As Cutter remarks, “A pretty assistant is the most effective form of misdirection.” Ironically, though, the Borden/Fallon misdirection does not quite work. Because we never really see Fallon’s face, his make-up is not quite up to scratch and everyone else in the film is famous, we are left wondering who this character might be, undermining one of the main twists. There is also a plot hole large enough to step through. Borden sends Angier to Tesla to get him out of the way. What are the chances, then, that Tesla could create a machine capable of the very magic Angier seeks? A cinematic rehearsal None of this detracts too much from a fascinating film, which combines narrative invention with a sense of ambition that would ultimately lead to the likes of Inception (2010), Oppenheimer (2023) and The Odyssey (2026). Incidentally, the film also contains the first ever IMAX 70mm shot used in a narrative feature – a trial run for the coming The Dark Knight. And that is perhaps how history will remember The Prestige: as a rehearsal for the flawed superheroes Nolan would become famous for. But it also has a deeper intent, offering a profound reflection on why directors like Nolan – and Angier and Borden – give their all to their art: not just to trick us, but to delight us. “The audience knows the truth: the world is simple. It’s miserable, solid all the way through,” Angier says. “But if you could fool them, even for a second, then you can make them wonder, and then you … then you get to see something really special. You really don’t know? It was … it was the look on their faces.” It might as well be Nolan talking. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: UK deports Romanian convicted of arson at ex-PM Starmer’s homes
description: The court found that the men had acted on the orders of a Russian-speaking contact on Telegram.
content: Britain has deported a Romanian man jailed for two years in June for arson attacks on two properties linked to then British prime minister Keir Starmer, the interior ministry said Saturday. Ukraine-born Stanislav Carpiuc was found guilty of the attacks alongside Ukrainian citizen Roman Lavrynovych, who was jailed for seven years over the May 2025 attacks on two London houses and a vehicle. “This individual has now been deported from the UK,” a Home Office spokesperson said, without indicating the country to which Carpiuc was being expelled. “This was an abhorrent attack and the conviction and imprisonment of these men should send a clear message to anyone blinded by the promise of money from strangers. You will be caught and face severe consequences,” the spokesperson added. Several British media have linked the attacks to Russian online sabotage. The judge in the case did not indicate a direct Russian link in his summing up, but the court found that Carpiuc and Lavrynovych had acted on the orders of a Russian-speaking contact on Telegram, identified as “EL” and saved in their phones under the name “El Money”. The court found Carpiuc was tasked with attempting to collect money offered for carrying out the attacks. A BBC investigation named “EL” as a young Russian diplomat, Evgeny Lyukshin. The attacks’ organiser posted messages on Telegram groups aimed at Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking people seeking work in London, according to the Financial Times.

title: Corrupt officials have nowhere to hide, China’s anti-graft watchdog warns
description: Senior figures told there is ‘no way out’ after the start of a probe into Huang Qifan, who had survived a string of previous scandals.
content: There is “no way out” for corrupt officials no matter how senior they are, China’s top anti-corruption watchdog has warned following the downfall of a former big-city mayor who survived numerous previous scandals. This week, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) announced both the probe into Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing, and the expulsion of a senior figure in Sichuan province. On Saturday, the commission said these developments showed the party’s “unwavering resolve” in fighting corruption and sent a “strong signal there are no restricted zones”. It added that the anti-corruption campaign would adopt a “zero-tolerance” approach and cover all areas. “It is also a warning to all the party members and cadres that no matter how senior they are, how big their contributions were or whether they are retired, if they have engaged in corruption, there is no way out or safe landing,” the CCDI said. Officials must therefore always remain loyal to the party, and maintain their honesty and integrity, it added. On Friday, Qiushi, the party’s flagship magazine, published a January speech by President Xi Jinping, in which he said: “The fight against corruption is a major battle that we cannot afford to lose and must never lose. “We cannot stop for a moment or retreat even half a step … [We must] uproot or cut down ‘sick trees’ wherever necessary.” It is a common practice to publish old speeches by Xi with the aim of sending a political message at a particular time. The latest was released less than two weeks before the fifth plenary session of the party’s 20th Central Committee in Beijing, when senior officials are expected to discuss and adopt a major document aimed at “deepening party self-governance”. On Wednesday, the CCDI announced that Bao Hui, former head of the standing committee of the Chengdu people’s congress in Sichuan, had been expelled from the party for serious violations of discipline and law, a standard euphemism for corruption. The previous day, it said that Huang, 74, who was mayor of Chongqing between 2010 and 2016, was under investigation. During his tenure, he helped oversee an economic boom in the southwestern megacity while navigating the scandals that brought down two of his former superiors, Bo Xilai and Sun Zhengcai, who are both serving life sentences. Huang had been seen as a capable economic technocrat and was nicknamed the “financial mayor”. His reputation as a great survivor also prompted media comparisons to a round-bottomed roly poly doll that wobbles but never falls over. He was last seen in public on September 8 at a forum to discuss the maritime silk road in Fujian province. He was taken away from his home along with his son Huang Ranfei, who is currently the chairman of investment firm Hongqiao Holdings, Caixin magazine reported. It added that two senior executives from Yufu, a major financial platform established during the older Huang’s time in Chongqing, had already been placed under investigation.

title: Pope Leo leaves hospital 4 days after lung cancer surgery
description: He will lead prayers at the Vatican for pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square on Sunday, his first ⁠public engagement since he went into hospital.
content: Pope Leo left hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican four days after surgery for lung cancer, an illness that has prompted speculation about how it might affect his 17-month papacy. The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital. He was pictured smiling broadly and waving through an open window when his black SUV left the hospital. He waved again to crowds as he was driven back into the Vatican but did not speak to anyone there before re-entering the world’s smallest country. His doctors had said earlier on Saturday that he was well enough to return home after they carried out the latest blood tests and chest ⁠imaging, and that he was able to perform normal daily activities independently. The pope, who had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe ‌of his right lung, will hold his first ⁠public engagement since ⁠surgery on Sunday when he leads weekly prayers with pilgrims in St. ‌Peter’s Square at noon. Leo has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the ‌most common form ‌of lung cancer. The diagnosis for a pope ‌known to be relatively young and energetic and who was ⁠elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about ⁠the future shape of his papacy as he deals with the illness. The pope’s doctors have said his ‌surgery was completed successfully, ‌without complications. They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.

title: Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
description: The demonstrations began at high schools, where anger over teacher absences and shabby facilities morphed into a nationwide movement.
content: Rioting erupted in cities across France on ⁠Saturday as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades. While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers. In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze, in Marseille black-clad protesters broke into City Hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti and in Lyon protesters torched the city’s tourist office. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be “intimidated” by violence and blamed the unrest on the “far-left” and criminals just months before a presidential election next year. “To ‌those who clearly want to use this violence as a ‘warm-up’ before the presidential election, I say clearly: we will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence,” he said on social media. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters that about 400 people had been arrested after violent incidents, most of whom were adults. Around 550,000 people took part in the demonstrations across the country, he said. The CGT union said it estimated protesters at 800,000 people. President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prosecute and punish people who had performed such attacks. “We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who only seek to undermine our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so,” he said on social media. Belgium, Portugal and Italy also faced smaller-scale protests on Saturday as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. Protesters said most people ⁠had marched peacefully and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. Many held signs bearing slogans against the police, the president and the wealthy. “We are fighting because the cost of living ‌is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions,” said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris. Most protests kicked off around midday, with some beginning before the official start of the demonstrations. In some parts of Paris, police ‌fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas. Rioters tried to break into the ⁠Galeries Lafayette department store, smashed up banks, ransacked a Lacoste store ⁠as well as other boutiques and looted an SFR mobile phone shop. Protesters had been setting objects ablaze all day, including numerous cars. In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms ‌they fear will make higher education less accessible. In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down. In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing ‌prices in ‌Portugal have doubled since 2017, fuelling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe. In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into disorder, with police clearing the central cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannons to try ‌to disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported. The protests in France began last month at high schools in Paris’ working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into ⁠a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards. In Paris on Saturday, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked President Emmanuel Macron’s previous term in office. Saturday’s protests eclipsed the size of the crowds at the peak ⁠of the Yellow Vest movement, though they were far lower than the levels seen at the protests in 2023 against Macron’s pension overhaul. Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy. France’s efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in over two decades. Police tactics have drawn criticism following injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking ‌up a stun grenade. The police watchdog is investigating at least two ‌dozen allegations of police violence. Lecornu said more than 900 police officers had also been injured in previous protests. Nunez said one person lost his hand in clashes with police on Saturday. French media reported he tried to pick up a stun grenade. The UNSA police union posted a video on social media showing crowds attacking police vans with clubs and bricks in multiple locations. The union warned the government police forces were at breaking point. “Today again, in every corner of France, our colleagues are being used as punching bags. Pelted with stones, injured, trapped in real ambushes,” the union said. “Let everyone take responsibility: this cannot go on indefinitely. The rope is stretched to its maximum.”

title: Strangers and railway staff help Chinese couple bring quintuplets home by train
description: Despite a previous diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome, a condition that can make pregnancy challenging, the 24-year-old mother conceived naturally.
content: When a couple from Xinjiang took their quintuplets home on a 36-hour train journey, the babies became favourites of both the train crew and fellow passengers, who took turns caring for them. The five babies were born on February 26 at a major hospital in Wuhan, in central China’s Hubei province. Their father, known as Abu, and their mother, Dili, are both from Hotan in northwestern China’s Xinjiang region. The 24-year-old mother conceived naturally despite having previously been diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome, a condition that can make pregnancy difficult, Hubei Daily reported. After their birth, the quintuplets – one boy and four girls – were cared for in Wuhan by their parents and their aunt. On the evening of October 9, the family boarded a train to begin their journey home to Xinjiang and visit the babies’ grandparents. Railway staff helped them carry their many belongings onto the train, including five strollers, bottles of formula, diapers and clothes. A staff member helped the family switch from a middle berth to a lower one, making it easier to arrange their belongings and care for the babies. Train crew members and nearby passengers took turns feeding the babies, holding them and soothing them to sleep. Their help gave Abu, his wife and his sister a chance to rest. News of the quintuplets soon spread through the train, drawing passengers to their carriage. Videos that went viral showed curious passengers lining up to see the babies, take pictures and even feed them. An excited young woman held one of the sleeping babies and told her friend: “I can’t move. I’m nervous that I’ll wake her up.” “I saw them in a news report. I’m so lucky to meet them on the same train. I have to seize this chance to see the five babies, who all look exactly alike,” a male passenger said in a video. A passenger surnamed Zhao, who was in the upper berth above the family, barely slept that night and offered to help care for the babies. Whenever she heard them cry, she climbed down from her berth to assist them. When Abu and Dili repeatedly thanked Zhao, she replied: “When we’re away from home, helping each other is what we should do.” Abu said he was mainly responsible for caring for the babies through the night, while his wife and sister took over during the day. “I feed the babies every four hours and check on them. I catch up on sleep after dawn,” he told the media. On the morning of October 11, the family got off the train at a station in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang. The 3,500-kilometre journey had taken 36 hours. Abu said the family would soon take another train to Hotan, in southwestern Xinjiang, where they would hold a 100-day banquet for the quintuplets. The banquet is a traditional celebration held 100 days after a baby’s birth to wish the newborn health and longevity. Abu had to postpone the event because of the arduous journey from Wuhan to Hotan. The family planned to return to Wuhan a month later for treatment of the baby boy’s eye condition, details of which were not disclosed in the report.

title: Is China’s Shenzhen ready to host Xi, Trump and Putin during Apec summit?
description: This is not the first international event hosted by the southern Chinese city but the authorities are taking preparations to new heights.
content: In Shenzhen, drones are banned, shiny new hotels have opened their doors and taxi drivers are carrying devices that can translate nearly 150 languages. Since President Xi Jinping announced last year that China’s southern tech hub would host Apec meetings in November, the city has done all it can to get ready under the watchful eyes of the local, provincial and national authorities. While every Apec summit draws the world’s attention, this year’s edition is considered to be especially high-stakes as Xi, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are all expected to attend. Last year, Putin did not join the summit in South Korea. In the past few weeks alone, Guangdong’s provincial Communist Party chief Huang Kunming has inspected Shenzhen twice to make sure preparations are going as planned. “Shenzhen must, on one hand, maintain focus on details to comprehensively plug any gaps, optimise and refine service guarantees, and go all out to ensure the conference is held safely, smoothly and successfully. On the other hand, it must take the hosting of the Apec meeting as a new starting point to accelerate the expansion of high-level opening up,” he said last week. Compared with Shanghai and Beijing, which hosted Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summits in 2001 and 2014, respectively, Shenzhen is less internationally known. However, analysts say the city could benefit from the event in the long term. When Xi made the announcement, he noted that Shenzhen had “transformed from a backward fishing village into a modern international metropolis in just a few decades”. “Together with surrounding areas, it forms the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area, which can be considered a growth pole of the world economy,” he added. This narrative emphasised Shenzhen’s alignment with the meeting’s agenda, said Zhang Jingjia, an economist at the Apec Study Centre at Nankai University. China has made “openness, innovation and cooperation” priorities for the summit, and Shenzhen was a living example of that, she said. When Beijing and Shanghai held the meetings, they focused on diplomacy and international finance, said Han Yonghui, executive dean of the Guangdong Institute for International Strategies. But Shenzhen’s tech companies, manufacturing system, ports and border crossings could show how the digital economy can function in real-world scenarios, he added. Hosting an inter-governmental meeting would test a city’s organisational abilities, Han said. It required proper venues, hotels, ports, railways, telecommunication networks and security, as well as diplomatic coordination, multilingual services, volunteers and community support, he added. The city has made security its top priority. Since July, local police have imposed a strict no-fly zone covering the city centre and stepped up random checks of subway passengers. A statement from the provincial public security bureau said at the time that hidden conflicts and risks should be detected, while street crimes – including thefts and robberies – needed to be “completely eradicated”. “Ensuring Apec safety is a major political responsibility for police around the province,” the statement said. “We need to plan early … and act with a heavy fist.” Special teams have also been equipped to patrol the region. Shenzhen police have formed a low-altitude drone unit to patrol more than 600 routes and reach any point in the city centre within three minutes, authorities said. This week, the government also called for residents to take leave or work from home to reduce traffic during the summit. The venue for the summit – the Shenzhen International Exchange Centre in Futian district – was built especially for the event. In July, it hosted the Apec Forestry Ministerial Meeting, which Zhang described as a “test run” for the leaders’ meetings. Shenzhen previously hosted major exhibitions, including the China Hi-Tech Fair, the International Cultural Industry Fair and the China International Optoelectronic Exposition, which showed that the city had the capacity to host large-scale meetings, said Peng Peng, executive chairman of the Guangdong Society of Reform, a prominent think tank affiliated with the provincial government. According to the Shenzhen authorities, the city has focused on upgrading its airport, crossings and railway, including this week’s opening of the revamped Huanggang Port that connects the city to Hong Kong. Language is also a concern. More bilingual signs have been erected in the airport and bus stops, while taxi drivers have been issued with translation devices able to handle 146 languages. Downtown Shenzhen’s Huaqiangbei – the world’s largest electronics marketplace – was offering language training sessions to vendors, and multilingual volunteers were stationed in community service centres across the city, a report on the local government website said in August. According to media reports, parks, gyms and commercial centres have also been renovated. More than 1,500 training sessions were organised for officials, business owners, delivery riders, residents and volunteers on languages, diplomatic etiquette, business English and public service. “In addition, Shenzhen’s tech enterprises and industrial achievements are themselves content that can be showcased to all parties during the meeting, which is a feature other cities are unlikely to have,” Zhang said. Shenzhen could benefit from hosting this meeting, just like Beijing and Shanghai did, analysts said. After hosting Apec, Beijing’s suburban Huairou district developed a whole industry around international exhibitions and hosted several more global summits, Zhang added, while Shanghai saw greater development in tourism and commerce. Shenzhen’s residents are mostly happy to see parks revamped and other infrastructure improved, but are also looking forward to the return of normality. A local doctor said she and her colleagues were placed on call for the duration of the summit to handle potential emergencies, and all leave was prohibited. But she said she “welcomes and supports” the city hosting a meeting of such importance for the first time. “For ordinary people, what’s most useful isn’t the buzz during the meetings, but the public services and environment that stay,” Zhang said. She added that the new exhibition centre could host public events, while the summit would raise the city’s international profile and foster global cooperation – ultimately driving investment and job growth.

title: Meet Geoffrey Ogunlesi, who just married Tobey Maguire’s ex-wife, Jennifer Meyer
description: The Spider-Man star officiated Meyer’s wedding to the music mogul, with A-listers like Courteney Cox, Leonardo DiCaprio, and Jeff and Lauren Sánchez Bezos in attendance.
content: Tobey Maguire’s ex-wife Jennifer Meyer married Geoffrey Ogunlesi on October 10, less than a month after she finalised her divorce from the Spider-Man star, from whom she separated a decade ago. Meyer and Ogunlesi held their wedding at the Four Seasons Resort Lanai in Hawaii and exchanged vows in front of A-list guests including Courteney Cox, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos. Tobey Maguire officiates the wedding of his ex-wife and her new husband, a billionaire heir. ( 📸 Backgrid) https://t.co/kXAbaLn4up — FearBuck (@FearedBuck) October 11, 2026 The ceremony was officiated by Maguire, who has maintained a close relationship with his ex-wife. Maguire and Meyer also co-parent their two children, Ruby Sweetheart, 19, and son Otis Tobias, 17. Here’s what we know about Meyer’s new husband, Geoffrey Ogunlesi. What is Geoffrey Ogunlesi’s background? Geoffrey Ogunlesi hails from an extremely rich family. He is reportedly the son of 70-year-old Nigerian lawyer and investment banker Adebayo Ogunlesi, who had a net worth of US$1.7 billion in 2024, according to Forbes. Adebayo is the co-founder of private equity firm Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP), which co-owns London Gatwick Airport, earning him the nickname “the man who bought Gatwick Airport”. GIP was acquired by BlackRock for US$12.5 billion in January, notes US media. Adebayo’s father, Theophilus Oladipo Ogunlesi, was reportedly the first professor of medicine in Nigeria, per Forbes. Meanwhile, Adebayo’s wife, Dr Amelia Ogunlesi, is a retired optometrist who lives with her husband in New York, according to The White House Historical Association. Meyer, who is a jewellery designer and has a namesake label, also comes from a privileged background, being the daughter of Ronald Meyer, co-founder of Creative Artists Agency, and former president and chief operating officer of Universal Studios. According to US media, Geoffrey obtained his undergraduate degree from Amherst College in Massachusetts, where he studied from 2008 to 2012. Before that, he went to an expensive boarding school in Connecticut called Hotchkiss, adds the source. What does Geoffrey Ogunlesi do? While his father made a name for himself in the banking world, Geoffrey has gone in a musical direction. After working for 300 Entertainment and Warner Music Group, he founded his own music management company, The Ogunlesi Group, in 2021, per LinkedIn. The Hollywood-based agency represents musicians like Young Thug, Charlieonnafriday and Myles Frost, notes the group’s LinkedIn page. His relationship with Jennifer Meyer According to US media, the duo have been romantically linked since the summer of 2023 and made their red carpet debut just months later in November. The couple confirmed their engagement in 2024 via an Instagram post. Many of Meyer’s famous friends congratulated her in the comments section of the post, including Paris Hilton, Kate Hudson, Jennifer Garner, Olivia Munn and Bianca Gates. Meyer replied to Gates’ message, saying the proposal was a “total surprise”. He shares a child with Jennifer Meyer In June this year, Meyer confirmed that she had welcomed her third child and her first with Ogunlesi when she paid tribute to her now-husband on Father’s Day. “A perfect month with our perfect baby girl. We love you the most,” she wrote. Meyer’s children with Maguire are reportedly close to his long-time friend, Leonardo DiCaprio. The Titanic star – who is Ruby’s godfather, according to The Things – often joins the family for outings like beach trips and brunch. Who else has Jennifer Meyer dated? Meyer – who is fairly private about her love life – has dated a handful of A-listers. After splitting up with Maguire, she was linked to Rich Paul – who’s now engaged to Adele – in 2019.

title: Knicks chase back-to-back titles in NBA built to stop dynasties, face LeBron James first up
description: New York hope for repeat in league that has had eight different winners in eight ⁠seasons; will face LeBron James and his new club in opener.
content: New York have barely stopped celebrating their first NBA title in 53 years, and the Knicks are already chasing a repeat in a league that is built to stop one. The NBA has crowned a record eight different champions in the past eight seasons. Rules that make it tougher to ‌stack a roster with superstars have turned the league into a free-for-all. The Knicks, however, have a big edge: the band is back together. New York return their five best players – Jalen Brunson, Josh Hart, Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby and Karl-Anthony Towns – along with the chemistry that carried them to the title. The LeBron plot twist The offseason’s biggest story was where the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, LeBron James, would land after splitting with the Los Angeles Lakers. The surprise winner of ⁠the sweepstakes was the Philadelphia 76ers. James admitted he would have liked to play for the Knicks, but said that door ‌closed once they won the title. So the 41-year-old will take his talents to Philadelphia instead of the Big Apple, although he will reportedly be living part-time in New York and commuting by helicopter. “I’ve done it before,” James said on Friday. “Just another way of transportation – that’s all.” At the 76ers, he joins Jaylen Brown, who was stunningly traded by the Celtics in the off-season, along with Joel Embiid, ⁠Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe. The ⁠question is whether the pieces fit, since all five players are accustomed to having the ball in their hands. “They are like a room that has five ‌beautiful couches in it,” ESPN’s Brian Windhorst said. “But you don’t need five couches in a room. You need a couch and a chair, a table, a ‌TV and ‌a mirror, and that’s going to be a challenge. Can they all fit, or do you have to put one ‌couch up along the wall?” Welcome to the Garden James could hardly have a more dramatic debut. The four-time champion opens his Philadelphia ⁠career at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday, just after the Knicks raise their championship banner. His teams have often started slowly in his ⁠first season with them. If that happens again, Philadelphia’s famously impatient fans may not wait long to let everyone know how they feel. The payoff could be historic. A title in his record-extending 24th season would make James ‌the first player to win championships ‌with four different teams. On Friday, he was introduced to a roaring ovation in his first pre-season game for the 76ers in Philadelphia, and gave a sneak peek of the fun that could be ahead. James scored eight points and had eight rebounds against the Boston Celtics, but it was the dunk off a pass from Maxey – a close friend whom James has credited with swaying his decision to sign with the Sixers – that made him a crowd favourite in Philadelphia. “This is a connection that we have,” James said. “Some of the best things for us offensively are going to be to get up the floor.” Everyone else wants in The rest of the league has its own plans when the 2026-27 season tips off on Tuesday: Victor Wembanyama and the San Antonio Spurs want revenge after a bitter Finals loss to the Knicks last season. In the 25th annual survey of NBA team general managers released on Thursday, the French superstar and his team were predicted to win the 2027 title with him taking the MVP honours. The Spurs were ranked the top choice as champion for the coming campaign by 50 per cent of the 30 executives with Oklahoma City second on 43 per cent and New York and Philadelphia, James’ new club, also receiving votes. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and the Oklahoma City Thunder are going for a second title in three years. Over the summer, Gilgeous-Alexander devoted his time to increasing his versatility on both ends of the floor and taking his conditioning up yet an additional notch. The Thunder had their NBA title defence come to an end against Wembanyama and the Spurs in Game 7 of the Western Conference finals last season. Stephen Curry, meanwhile, leads a Golden State Warriors team trying to revive their title hopes.

title: Man arrested for alleged HK$450,000 theft of wife’s Chanel and Hermes bags, Rolex
description: Woman, 34, reported her husband to police after suspecting he stole HK$450,000 worth of goods from their home.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested the husband of a 34-year-old woman for allegedly stealing luxury goods worth HK$450,000 (US$57,700) from her at home. The woman, surnamed Chan, reported the case to police at around 8.30am on Saturday morning at their home in the Ocean One residential development in Yau Tong. According to police, Chan suspected that her 40-year-old husband, surnamed Lam, had stolen goods worth HK$450,000 in total. The items involved were Chanel and Hermes bags worth HK$300,000 and a HK$150,000 Rolex watch. Police later arrived at the scene and arrested Lam on suspicion of theft after a preliminary investigation. He is currently being detained for further investigation.

title: Shisha smoking will cause 1 million new lung cancer cases globally by 2050: WHO study
description: Western Pacific region will bear the brunt of such cases, says Dr Mahdi Sheikh of International Agency for Research on Cancer.
content: Water pipe smoking will contribute to about 1 million new lung cancer cases globally by 2050, with the Western Pacific region bearing the brunt, according to a study led by a World Health Organization (WHO) research agency that was recently presented in Hong Kong. The study, which is yet to be published, was headed by Dr Mahdi Sheikh, a scientist of the early detection, prevention and infections branch at the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). It estimated that there would be 82 million new lung cancer cases around the world between 2025 and 2050, with 944,700 or 1.1 per cent of them caused by water pipe smoking. “One per cent does not seem a lot, but when you translate it into numbers, it’s 1 million cases – when we want to save lives, every life matters,” Sheikh told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the World Cancer Congress, which was held in Hong Kong for the first time in late September. “Most of these countries have a low or medium human development index … it means that the burden is going to cluster in the countries with the least resources, which could bear the least burden of cancer.” Traditional cigarettes remained the primary cause of lung cancer, accounting for 60 to 70 per cent of cases, alongside other risk factors such as air pollution and occupational exposure, he said. Combining data on water pipe prevalence, cancer risk and WHO projections across 78 countries, the research team estimated that the Western Pacific region would see 350,400 new cases of water pipe-related lung cancer over the 25-year period. This was followed by 265,700 cases in the European region. In terms of proportion of cases relative to population, the Eastern Mediterranean region, largely covering countries such as the Middle East, topped the chart with 5.1 per cent, followed by the African region with 2.6 per cent. Notably, countries which were among the least developed, as indicated by their low Human Development Index, would suffer the heaviest proportional toll, with water pipes causing 3.3 per cent of their lung cancer cases, followed by countries of the medium index at 1.8 per cent. Sheikh said the Western Pacific region topped the total case count because it contained countries with either high exposure to water pipe smoking or massive populations. The Eastern Mediterranean region, meanwhile, held the highest water pipe smoking rates globally due to deep historical roots and rising popularity among younger generations. “The tobacco industry is coming up with strategies to increase the use of these products among the youth [there],” Sheikh said. “If young people use these products today, the impact will be obvious two decades from now. We need to raise awareness before this happens.” Sheikh noted that manufacturers added flavours and framed water pipe use as a social activity to entice youth while spreading disinformation that water filtered out toxic substances. However, unlike traditional cigarettes, water pipe smoking received far less regulatory scrutiny despite the WHO issuing its first guidelines more than two decades ago, he added. According to the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, 79 per cent of parties to the treaty reported water pipe tobacco on their national markets in 2023, but only 57 per cent had implemented specific regulations. “The guideline is there. Some countries have worked; a lot of countries still lag behind and are way behind [on regulations for] combustible tobacco products,” Sheikh said. A major shortcoming was the lack of monitoring, as the research team could only obtain data from 78 countries, with severe data gaps in Africa and the Western Pacific. “The burden is much, much bigger than what we think … I believe there is a lot of underestimation,” he said. “One of the basic policies that we require at WHO is monitoring.” While further studies are under way, Sheikh urged countries to implement the guidelines of the global health watchdog and guard against tobacco industry interference. In this process, he believed Hong Kong could serve as a successful example, pointing to its single-digit smoking prevalence rate. Hong Kong’s smoking rate is 8.5 per cent, while the rate of water pipe smoking is less than 1 per cent. “The guidelines are there, the policies are there, and we see some countries are extremely successful with that,” he said. “We have to work together to prevent the interference [of the tobacco industry]. They should not have a seat at the table. They are the ones that cause this problem, and they should be accountable for that.”

title: Opinion | Language matters in Hong Kong’s birth rate debate, not just money
description: Hong Kong’s fertility woes are not just about affordability. They might also involve language use and how it shapes our views of the future.
content: When Hong Kong debates how to raise its birth rate, the conversation usually revolves around money: bigger baby bonuses, tax concessions, housing support, cheaper childcare and so on. These economic measures are necessary. Lowering the cost of raising a child removes some real and immediate barriers. However, there is another, lesser-known factor that works more subtly and implicitly. It comes not from economics but from the structure of the language or languages we speak each day. Consider a simple contrast. In English, one says, “Yesterday it rained. Now it is raining. Tomorrow it will rain.” In Chinese, the same three sentences need no such grammatical marking. The verb does not change. The future is not grammatically separated from the present. This is the distinction around which behavioural economist Keith Chen built his research. He classified languages by whether they oblige speakers to mark the future grammatically. English does. Chinese does not. Chen found that speakers of languages with weak or no future-time marking tend to save more, plan more and invest more in long-term health than speakers of languages with strong future-time marking. The logic is simple. If the future is not grammatically distant, it feels present. If it feels present, its burdens feel present, too. That is why speakers of weak future-time languages tend to save more and plan more – they are already living with the future. However, the same closeness that drives saving can also drive anxiety and hesitation. A young couple who feel the future as present might also feel the weight of a child’s future as present and hesitate to take on a commitment that stretches decades ahead. English works differently. “Tomorrow it will rain” places the future at a distance. The burden might be real, but it belongs to a time that has not yet arrived. A couple speaking English might feel the same obligations but feel them less immediately, therefore finding it easier to take the first step. Chen was not writing about fertility directly, but his finding allows a logical projection. If weak future-time marking brings the future closer in the mind, then future obligations could also feel more imminent. The long commitment of raising a child can feel heavier and more immediate for precisely that reason. Chen’s data even touches on contraceptive use, though he classifies it as a health behaviour rather than a fertility decision. Read differently, it could point in a similar direction: using condoms more often can mean fewer children. This is not to claim that language determines or causes fertility directly. It only says that the way we speak might shape how vividly we imagine the future and how much weight that imagined future carries in making significant life decisions. Hong Kong is well placed to examine this projection. According to the most recent census, Cantonese remains the usual language of about 88 per cent of the population while English is the usual language of about 4.6 per cent. The complication is that many residents are not monolingual. Among higher-skilled workers, about 85 to 91 per cent can read and write both Chinese and English. Roughly 57 to 60 per cent possess “biliterate and trilingual” abilities covering Cantonese, English and Mandarin. This means many Hong Kong couples do not simply speak one type of language. They move between them, often within the same conversation. If Chen’s findings hold, the grammatical structure of the language they are using at any given moment can subtly shape how close or distant the future feels and how much weight it carries. This is not an argument against economic measures. Baby bonuses, housing support and childcare subsidies address real barriers, and they should remain central to fertility policy. My argument is for adding another dimension that might have been overlooked. If language structure shapes how people perceive the future, then policies that affect language use can have effects that current policy evaluation does not yet capture. Economic measures alone will not solve this issue completely. There is value in pursuing alternatives. One way to explore this would be to examine whether the language in which couples discuss family planning makes a difference to how they describe their plans, hopes and hesitations. A simple exercise like a future family portrait can help couples map the future generations they can imagine and the languages, places and hopes associated with each. This would not solve the fertility problem instantly, but it might help couples articulate what they want and help policymakers see how they imagine the future. In short, Hong Kong’s fertility challenge might not be only an affordability problem. It might also partly be a problem of which language we speak and how that shapes the way the future is perceived. No policy can make someone want a child. Policy can shape the conditions in which that desire is formed, though, and language can be one of those conditions. The question is not only “Can families afford a child these days?” but also “Can they see the future their children will live in?”. How they see it might depend on the language in which they see it.

title: A missionary’s stories of the Kowloon Walled City live on at a new exhibition in Hong Kong
description: Jackie Pullinger’s journey to the Kowloon Walled City, as well as art by those helped by St Stephen’s Society, can be seen at Central Market.
content: St Stephen’s Society looks more like a contemporary art gallery than a rehabilitation facility. At the non-profit Christian charity’s compound in Hong Kong’s New Territories, there are corridors lined with sketches, canvases and photography and a wall of art supplies. Founder Jacqueline “Jackie” Pullinger, a British missionary now in her eighties, proudly looks at the artwork created by its residents. A selection will be showcased at the upcoming exhibition “285 and Counting”, named for the number of spaces across Hong Kong the charity has used to provide shelter, at Central Market from October 18 to 21. “Everybody else considers them failures,” Pullinger says, “but I believe they are the future of Hong Kong.” Some of the featured artists are former school dropouts, while most are in recovery from substance addiction. “They possess immense talent in dance, filmmaking, music and drama. If you look around, they have produced remarkable art,” Pullinger says with a smile. “They are simply bright enough to fail the traditional examination system.” In 1997, the Hong Kong government made land in the city available to the society, which it used to create multi-purpose rehabilitation homes that currently serve around 30 members overcoming drug dependency, as well as those who live alongside and support them. A few units also accommodate elderly residents. The facility provides vocational training and emotional expression through fine art and photography classes. Pullinger remains convinced that the key to transforming young lives lies in uncovering their inherent talents rather than judging them by academic metrics, which Hong Kong society stereotypically views as a primary measure of success. How she found purpose through charitable service For more than four decades, Pullinger has championed a non-medical, holistic approach to helping individuals overcome addiction through music, art and spiritual care. In the 1960s, Pullinger, a graduate of the Royal College of Music in London and a Protestant Christian determined to find purpose through charitable service, boarded a ship to Hong Kong carrying little more than £10. “Poverty was very obvious,” she recalls. “On every street, people were living on the pavements, including young children and teenagers. Elderly people were begging along Ladder Street. There were unattended children, and infants carried by sisters who were only five or six while their parents worked. There was no free education. I prayed, ‘Dear God, if I spend my life here, perhaps I can help care for these children.’” Her charitable work did not begin immediately, as her resources were scarce and local missionary organisations initially viewed her intentions with scepticism. She took teaching positions at Diocesan Preparatory School and later St Stephen’s Girls’ College to support herself. Entering the Kowloon Walled City Eventually earning the trust of local religious leaders, Pullinger was introduced to the Kowloon Walled City, once deemed the most densely populated place on Earth. Every evening after work and throughout the weekends, she ventured into the infamous enclave. “Schooling cost HK$4 a month, but most children in the walled city could not afford that,” she says. Local children guided her through the labyrinthine settlement. “It felt like navigating underground tunnels, completely deprived of natural light in many sections. Soon, I encountered drug addicts, elderly sex workers and young girls [trapped in exploitation].” Pullinger recalls a 14-year-old boy – whose name she pronounces with a perfect Cantonese accent – who was expelled from a Christian school for academic failure. “I found him selling tickets at what they call in English a ‘blue film’ [adult film] theatre,” she says. She appealed to the school to reinstate him, but administrators declined, noting they were pleased to be rid of a student who damaged their reputation. “I was very upset because I believed faith calls us to welcome the most [vulnerable], yet they did the opposite,” she reflects. “The boy’s father suffered from addiction, and his mother worked in prostitution. His life was written off before it had even begun.” In response, Pullinger established a youth club, opening its doors to any young person unable to afford school. Members played table tennis, while Pullinger taught music and nursery rhymes. She also organised mountain hikes and summer camps. “Every time I started telling them about Jesus, they went out of the room to smoke and whistle. When I finished the Christian bit, they would return,” she says with a laugh. “Yet over time, they began to listen. They knew I loved them, and then we had a couple of miracles where two people prayed, and the power of the Holy Spirit came upon them. They spoke in a language they hadn’t learned, and they came off drugs without pain.” At the time, Pullinger says that the only way doctors got patients off drugs was to put them on other drugs. Seeing how faith and music worked wonders, she said to herself, “Well, I might as well go on doing that.” Opening up her home The journey was not without hardship, and situations turned perilous at times. On one occasion, gangsters who were involved in drug distribution ransacked her youth club after a boy she welcomed was coerced into informing on her activities. That same youth, struggling with opium dependency, later returned seeking help. “An opium den is a cramped space with low platforms where users recline,” Pullinger says. “The platform is covered with slime that comes out of every opening in a man’s body.” When offered free opium on one occasion, the youth refused and began singing hymns he had learned at the club. “I told him, ‘You cannot walk into a drug den and pray for strength to resist,’ and he replied, ‘That is where I live.’” Struggling to find suitable shelter for him to start anew, Pullinger welcomed him into her home just outside the walled city. One guest soon grew into a dozen. Eventually, she resigned from teaching to devote herself entirely to St Stephen’s Society, which she established in the 1980s to serve the impoverished, marginalised and individuals struggling with addiction or crime beyond the walled city. “Our board members include former addicts,” she notes. “There’s nobody important. We’re just simple people.” The challenges young people face today The Kowloon Walled City was demolished in 1994. Today, Pullinger observes a shift in the challenges facing youth. Rather than overt material poverty, she identifies widespread identity crises and a lack of belonging. “What happens here [in our society] with the young people is they want to be part of a family more than anything, and that’s what they’ve missed,” she explains, noting that intense academic pressure often leads youth astray. “They’ve been told to get good grades and enter good schools, but not ‘You’re loved as you are, and it doesn’t matter if you excel in anything at all.’” In addition to student artworks and archival photographs documenting the society’s work in the now-gone walled city, the Central Market exhibition programme includes a documentary screening featuring former residents, live musical performances at Kowloon Walled City Park and worship sessions. “When we stage a concert or dance performance, everyone participates – not merely those with refined talent,” Pullinger says. “We dedicate our energy to ensuring every individual feels valued, loved and included.” “285 and Counting”, Central Market, 93 Queen’s Road Central, Central, October 18-21, 2026.

title: Reporter’s notebook: Kimi’s AI credit card turns spending into computing quotas – with limits
description: The Kimi card promises to turn everyday spending into access to AI services, including agent usage quotas and coding tools.
content: China’s artificial intelligence companies have spent years persuading consumers to pay for their technology. Now, Moonshot AI, the start-up behind Kimi, is taking a different approach: offering AI computing benefits through a credit card. The company has teamed up with the Agricultural Bank of China (ABC) and American Express for what it calls “the world’s first AI native credit card”. After getting one for myself, the experience offered an intriguing way to bring AI services into everyday finance, but with limits to the promise. The card comes in two versions. The premium platinum offers cardholders two months of Kimi’s second most expensive Allegretto membership, now rebranded as Pro, priced at 199 yuan (US$30) per month, after they spend at least 5,888 yuan (US$830) within one month. The standard version offers eligible new ABC customers three months of the entry-level Andante membership, now known as Go, priced at 49 yuan per month, after making three purchases of at least 18 yuan each. My initial attempt to obtain the higher-end card was denied at an ABC branch in Beijing, where I was told that my annual income did not meet the requirement. In my case, the requirements focused on traditional banking eligibility rather than anything related to AI use. I then applied online for the standard card, and eventually received it within a week. The Kimi co-branded card, launched in July, followed a wave of AI-themed bank cards introduced by Chinese lenders since June. China Merchants Bank’s engineer card, for example, mainly gives new users a one-off token gift pack. But the Kimi card promises to turn everyday spending into access to AI services, including agent usage quotas, coding tools and premium subscriptions. The Andante membership that came with my card provides additional access to Kimi’s AI agent functions, including document processing, website deployment and coding capabilities. For a frequent AI user, the rewards are more attractive than shopping vouchers or airport lounge access provided by traditional credit cards. With the benefits, I tried vibe coding, asking Kimi to refine the visual design and interactive features of a project. The experience was initially promising. But after roughly six rounds of adjustments, Kimi informed me that my usage quota had been exhausted. It was a frustrating reminder that access to premium AI services does not necessarily mean having unlimited usage quotas to complete a task. There are also limits to how long you have access. For example, the memberships that came with the card were just for a few months, not permanent subscriptions. Neither Moonshot, ABC nor Amex responded to requests for comment. Moonshot and its partners previously said they would explore additional services, such as agent-based payments, linking tokens to credit quotas, and establishing two-way integration between reward points and computing power. The push into AI-focused financial services comes as China’s credit card market contracts. The country had 677 million credit cards and debit-credit combo cards at the end of June, down from 807 million in the third quarter of 2022, according to the People’s Bank of China. Wang Zebin, an investment manager at Shenzhen-based private equity firm JG Investment who focuses on AI investments, said the shift towards computing-based rewards reflected banks’ efforts to attract and retain high-net-worth customers through more targeted offerings. Whether such products can generate meaningful long-term growth for banks’ credit card business would depend on how lenders integrated AI into their operations, improved credit approvals and risk management, and sustained investment in the AI computing ecosystem, Wang said.

title: Landmark China trial gets 84% efficacy in treating cancer with cue from waste water tech
description: Nano-carbon iron injection halts tumour growth in 16 patients, induces shrinkage in two, with Phase II trial now under way with 52 others.
content: For patients with advanced, metastatic cancer that has progressed despite systemic therapy, options remain critically limited. Now, Chinese scientists are pointing to an unconventional therapeutic agent – the element iron. This idea originated in industrial waste water treatment: iron can react with hydrogen peroxide to generate hydroxyl radicals, which degrade various organic and toxic molecules in waste water. Chinese scientists wanted to treat malignant tumours the way they treat waste water – by combining iron with a nano-carbon injection to form a nano-carbon iron injection called CNSI-Fe, where Fe stands for iron – more specifically ferrous iron. In a first-of-its-kind trial in hospitals across China, physicians injected this solution directly into the tumour sites of 19 patients with advanced tumours. Clinical follow-up showed that tumour growth stopped in 16 patients with advanced cancer (84.2 per cent), with tumour shrinkage observed in two of them. This study was published on October 1 in the peer-reviewed journal Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. “Overall, CNSI-Fe demonstrated a favourable safety profile and promising antitumour activity,” wrote Professor Wang Yongsheng, executive deputy director of the Cancer Centre at West China Hospital and the Department of Oncology at West China School of Medicine. Wang completed the Phase I clinical trial, where he served as the lead principal investigator, at three hospitals in Sichuan, Hubei and Shandong provinces. A Phase II clinical trial is now under way across 10 top Chinese hospitals to evaluate the therapy’s safety and efficacy in 52 patients. For the first phase, scientists used a clinically approved nanocrystalline carbon injection and combined it with ferrous sulphate to prepare the CNSI-Fe. The injection remained stable for six hours after preparation and reached peak serum iron levels within half an hour of administration. Iron specifically eliminates tumour cells in the body while causing relatively little damage to normal cells. This is because normal cells possess antioxidant systems such as glutathione, which can repair damage to their cell membranes. However, within tumours, the free radicals produced by iron will “rust” through their cell membranes. In previous animal experiments, this CNSI-Fe injection was shown to inhibit tumour growth in six tumour models, including colorectal cancer, breast cancer and pancreatic cancer. The 19 patients who took part in the Phase I trial had various tumours, including sarcoma, head and neck cancer, pancreatic cancer, non-small-cell lung cancer, ovarian cancer, breast cancer and vulval cancer. Among them, 16 subjects had stage IV metastatic tumours, also known as end-stage advanced tumours. All of these tumour patients had previously received at least two lines of systemic therapy, including chemotherapy, radiotherapy and immunotherapy. They received injections of different doses of CNSI-Fe directly into the tumour site and observed responses in the tumours and their distant lesions. The trial results showed that across all patients, the overall objective response rate or tumour shrinkage was 10.5 per cent and the disease control rate – where tumours stopped growing – was 84.2 per cent. The therapeutic effect on the injected target lesions was superior to that on all systemic lesions. In this clinical trial, the most common adverse reactions were injection pain (89.5 per cent) and hypertension (52.6 per cent), while one patient withdrew from the trial due to a hypersensitivity reaction. No severe haematological toxicity, hepato-renal toxicity or other adverse effects commonly seen with other tumour therapies occurred. “In this study, we present a first-in-class Phase I trial to evaluate the potential of CNSI-Fe, which is a ferroptosis-inducing agent, for treating patients with refractory solid tumours. While more than 20 classes have been explored preclinically, CNSI-Fe is the first to achieve clinical translation,” Wang concluded in the paper. “CNSI-Fe administered by intratumoral injection is effective for treating ferroptosis-sensitive solid tumours, but this single-arm study has limitations and requires further evaluation through randomised Phase II/III trials,” he added.

title: European delegates walk out on Russian finance minister at IMF summit
description: Nearly a dozen delegates left the room when Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov began ⁠speaking at the steering ⁠committee meeting.
content: Many delegates to ⁠the International Monetary Fund’s steering ⁠committee walked out of a meeting on ⁠Saturday when Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov addressed the group in Russian, three sources familiar with the matter said. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 has roiled the International Monetary and Financial Committee, preventing it from reaching consensus statements in the years ‌since. There were deep divisions again at this week’s annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok, as new tensions flared between the US and Ukraine. “Many delegations walked out, including members of the European Union,” one of the sources said. A second official in the room said nearly a dozen delegates left the room when the Russian official began ⁠speaking. Delegates from Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia were among those who left, the ‌official said. “The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe,” one European diplomat said. “We cannot normalise relations with Russia.” Germany on Thursday warned against efforts to bring ‌Russia back on to the international stage after Siluanov attended a meeting of G20 finance ⁠ministers and central bankers, ⁠just over a month after the US had hosted his first in-person G20 appearance since Russia invaded Ukraine, at a meeting ‌in Asheville, North Carolina. US Treasury Undersecretary Erin Browne said the same day that Washington, the current leader of the G20 nations, supported ‌Russia’s ‌presence despite European concerns. “We think it’s really important if you’re going to solve a crisis, you ‌need to have open dialogue and open conversation,” she said. “And you can’t have … dialogue, and ⁠you can’t have resolution to conflict if no one’s talking to one another.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, speaking at ⁠a European Union summit on Friday, blasted US President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and welcomed the prospect of European allies stepping up their role in peace talks. EU ‌leaders rallied around Zelensky after ‌Trump again criticised Ukraine, calling its strikes on Russian refineries a “disgrace”. The EU was hosting Zelensky at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, with missiles and drones raining down on Ukrainian cities and fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.

title: Police urge Apple to fix security after 110 reports of fraud over iPhone Duo
description: Force says company ignored suggestions on strengthening cybersecurity following similar reports last month, with one case involving HK$229,788.
content: Hong Kong police have raised concerns over Apple’s refusal to activate an additional security protocol to prevent fraud despite repeated calls, as the force received more than 110 reports of unauthorised credit card transactions following the pre-order launch of the company’s latest model. The force said on Saturday that residents began reporting suspicious credit card purchases of the foldable iPhone Duo after online pre-orders started on Friday at 8pm. The largest transaction involved HK$229,788 (US$29,280), equivalent to the price of about 12 iPhone Duos. The force said the more than 110 reports involving HK$4.6 million in total concerned transactions made using credit cards issued by different banks. The reports were being listed as suspected cases of obtaining property by deception. It is the second time in just over a month that an iPhone launch has been marred by reports of fraud. Police said they were still investigating the 1,572 reports of suspicious credit card transactions involving the iPhone 18 Pro series that became available for pre-order on September 12. Those transactions exceeded HK$31 million. Senior Inspector Lo Chun-kong, of the technology crime division’s cybersecurity and technology crime bureau, said the force had not made any arrests. The force had kept in contact with Apple to explore improving preventive measures since September, and the company had adopted some initiatives, including reviewing and modifying its internal fraud risk model and strengthening transaction monitoring. However, Lo said Apple had decided not to activate 3D Secure (3DS), which helps authenticate a buyer’s identity during online transactions, despite multiple calls from police. “Unfortunately, Apple still did not activate 3DS during the iPhone pre-order last night, failing to effectively prevent similar fraud cases from occurring,” he said. “The police express grave concern over Apple’s failure to proactively assume its corporate responsibilities, which has left the door open for criminals. Pointing to the reports the force received in September, he added: “It is deeply regrettable that the same situation has happened yet again.” Lo also called on consumers who noticed suspicious credit card transactions to report them to the relevant bank, Apple and police. In response to media inquiries on Saturday, Apple said all current iPhone Duo orders were being reviewed before they were processed. “[We] are working to quickly identify and cancel any fraudulent transactions that may have been placed,” the company said. A spokesman for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority said on Saturday that four banks had notified it of related unauthorised fraudulent transactions. The affected customers had told their banks and reported the cases to police. He said individual merchants might choose not to use, or temporarily suspend, additional authentication arrangements such as in-app authentication for operational reasons. In such cases, the merchant had to bear the liability and financial loss for unauthorised transactions, he added. Regarding the earlier incident, he said the authority had urged Apple to adopt 3D Secure more widely to enhance the security of online credit card transactions, adding that it would continue to follow up on the arrangements. “The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is highly concerned about the incident and has been maintaining communication with relevant stakeholders, including the merchant concerned, urging them to implement a series of appropriate credit card security measures,” the spokesman said. HSBC said it was aware of online discussions about repeated and unauthorised credit card transactions for the pre-orders. “Customers will not be responsible for repeated transactions, which we will identify and void,” the bank said. HSBC added that customers could suspend their credit cards via its mobile app or by calling the bank. The lender said it would investigate and guide consumers through the refund process, while noting they had a responsibility to use their cards responsibly and report suspicious transactions promptly. It also said 3D Secure could add protection, but the merchant determined whether it applied. HSBC reportedly apologised to affected consumers, noting that some transactions were duplicated on Friday night and the system would automatically arrange cancellation, which was expected to take one to two days. Hang Seng Bank said it would fully support affected customers who had used its credit cards responsibly. Francis Fong Po-kiu, honorary president of the Hong Kong Information Technology Federation, said network congestion and system response delays during a product launch could lead to a merchant website resubmitting transaction requests. Banks generally would cancel duplicate transactions after verification, he said. Fraudsters used stolen credit card information to make a huge number of unauthorised transactions, which 3DS could help prevent, he said. “Apple should fully enable 3DS as soon as possible to intercept fraudulent transactions at the source and to optimise its back-end anti-duplicate charge mechanisms,” he said. Fong noted that some individuals had not bought any phones but received an unauthorised transaction message, pointing to a “severe security vulnerability”. Victims took to social media platform Threads on Friday night, with one user claiming to have ordered an iPhone Duo using an HSBC credit card after 8pm and being charged again at around 10pm. Another user who reported a similar problem called the card centre, which said Apple sought HSBC’s authorisation a second time to complete the transaction and the first one was pending cancellation.
