A separate user who said they had not ordered the new iPhone posted two SMS records from HSBC, which indicated their credit card had been charged twice by Apple. The price of the Duo begins at HK$17,499, and the model will be available from October 23.

title: Modi under pressure as India’s youth protests rise to highest level in a decade
description: Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014.
content: Despite ⁠tens of thousands of security personnel deployed to stop them, youth protesters in India scaled barricades last ⁠week, chanted anti-government slogans and scuffled with police officers trying to drag them away. “Long live the revolution,” shouted one young man before police bundled him into a bus. Street protests in India this year are likely to be higher than at any time in the past decade, the independent Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project has said, as dissent mounts against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and Gen Z activists pour on to the streets. Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014, with people under 30 making up nearly one quarter of the country’s 1 billion voters. But his government remains stable and the ‌next general election is not due until 2029. The nation has suddenly found its voice Yogendra Yadav, an anti-government activist “The nation has suddenly found its voice,” said Yogendra Yadav, an anti-government activist who has played a leading part in the demonstrations. “I would not say this is the beginning of the end of the Modi regime, but this definitely is the beginning of a downward spiral.” The government and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) declined comment. Anti-establishment mood The recent protests in the capital New Delhi and elsewhere were focused on demands that Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar resign over a voter roll revision that activists and opposition parties say favours the BJP and has helped it win several recent state elections. The ruling BJP, the government and the Election Commission deny the accusations. The BJP says the party’s wins have come from Modi’s popularity and strong economic growth. But the demonstrations are also reflecting something larger: growing anger at Modi for failing to deliver jobs to millions of unemployed youth in his 12 years in power despite the surge in headline economic growth. Other issues have also fed into the anti-establishment mood, including leaks of ⁠question papers in key examinations for jobs and education, the high number of crimes against women and the rise of billionaire businessmen alleged to have close links to Modi. Modi has a strongman image and his government has previously cracked down on pockets of dissent harshly, but that ‌has not fazed the youngsters on the streets. “The fear in us is gone,” said Ananya Raturi, a 21-year-old Delhi University student who was part of massive protests in the capital last week. Speaking after she clung to the windscreen wipers of a bus that police were using to detain protesters, Raturi said: “We don’t fear being detained or beaten up by the police. This generation enjoys it.” Police have denied allegations that they beat up people at the ‌demonstrations, saying protesters were handled according to prescribed procedures. The protests have been energised by the emergence of the first nationally resonant youth-led movement of the Modi era, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which grew from online ⁠satire into a nationwide campaign this June after India’s chief justice likened ⁠the unemployed to “cockroaches”. India’s mainstream media is mostly pro-government, critics say, and has covered the protests sparingly. But thousands of protesters armed with mobile phones as well as independent news channels on YouTube have amplified the unrest and made internet stars of leaders like CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and firebrand left-wing activist Neha Bora. Opposition parties that were subdued under Modi’s grip ‌on power have been re-energised, with Congress Party leader Rahul Gandhi and tens of thousands of followers also on the streets. The unrest has drawn comparisons with neighbouring Bangladesh and Nepal, where youth-led protest movements brought down governments in recent years, although analysts caution that India’s political landscape and Modi’s popularity make such parallels imperfect. Lack of jobs Many of the youth protesters grew up during Modi’s rise ‌to power, ‌buoyed by promises of jobs, opportunity and cleaner governance. A decade later, many say those aspirations remain unfulfilled and they say the Hindu nationalist government appears more focused on religious issues and divisive politics against minorities, especially Muslims. The government has previously said the economy generated 168.3 million new ‌jobs in the six years through 2024. Modi has repeatedly rejected allegations of any bias, saying his government works for all Indians. Gauri Seth, a medical student based in Kolkata, became a voter in 2014, the same year the Modi government came to power. When anyone speaks against them, it is labelled as treason or sedition. Gauri Seth, a medical student The 30-year-old said the Modi government promised “a ⁠lot, but has failed to deliver”. “Instead they focus on things like religious infrastructure. There are cases of violence against minorities. When anyone speaks against them, it is labelled as treason or sedition.” When Modi came to power, he promised the creation of millions of jobs ⁠each year. Yet, despite India’s strong economic growth since then, unemployment remains at slightly above 5 per cent, according to government data. A Reuters poll last year said that data masks the severity of joblessness, especially among the youth. Unemployment among the 367 million people in the country aged 15-29 stood at 9.9 per cent in 2025, according to the data. Research by Azim Premji University’s State of Working India 2026 report found unemployment among graduates aged 15-25 was nearly 40 per cent, while about one in five graduates aged 25-29 remained ‌jobless. In May, unrest erupted across the country when the government invalidated examinations for ‌national medical colleges, a pathway to jobs for the poor and the middle class, after test papers were leaked. Rubby Singh, a 30-year-old social activist in Delhi, said repeated examination paper leaks had deepened a sense among young Indians that the system was denying them opportunities even after years of study. “This generation has been facing the brunt of not having proper education, which leads to not being able to get good opportunities,” she said. While national elections are not due for almost three years, the country’s biggest state, Uttar Pradesh, goes to the polls early next year, which could provide a test of Modi’s popularity. Analysts however remain cautious about the outcome. The BJP may not be as strong as it was a few months ago, said Rahul Verma, a fellow at the Centre for Policy Research in Delhi. “But whether there are going to be electoral implications, it is too early to say.”

title: Security fears in Norway as Chinese smart cars record sensitive military data
description: Videos recorded by the rentals’ on-board cameras show the personnel using the cars, routes taken and gate codes to military facilities.
content: Chinese-made cars filmed sensitive information during a Norwegian military exercise, including access codes at secure sites and officials’ comings and goings, raising concerns about the risks posed by connected vehicles. During a security exercise at Oslo airport on September 14 to 18, waiting soldiers tapping on their vehicle’s screen discovered videos recorded by the on-board cameras, the Dagens Naeringsliv newspaper revealed. The recordings showed who was getting in and out of the cars, the routes taken and even the codes used to open gates or doors to military facilities. In its report three weeks after the exercise, the newspaper said the recordings came from rental vehicles – at least two of them Deepal brand cars, made by Chinese state-controlled carmaker Changan. They were supplied to the army by Hertz Norge, which is indirectly owned by the Chinese auto group Geely. “Yes, soldiers from the Home Guard found videos from the vehicles’ sensors stored in their systems,” Norwegian Home Guard spokesman Lieutenant Colonel Per Gunnar Grosberghaugen confirmed. It was not known if the recordings were shared with a third party, notably in China, but the officer could not rule out the possibility. ‘Rolling computers’ The case highlights a paradox: while Europe’s armies are bolstering their protection against espionage and hybrid threats, the vehicles they use can collect sensitive information. Even after discovering the leaks, the military continued to use the vehicles until the end of the exercise due to a lack of alternatives and the soldiers deleted the videos. Judging that the impact of a general ban on Chinese-made vehicles would be disproportionate to the potential security gain, the military said it preferred security procedures tailored to each site, with possible local bans on vehicles equipped with cameras and sensors regardless of their origin. Hertz Norge stresses that it complies with Norwegian and European regulations. “Our customers’ data is safe with us,” said Hallvard Nerbovik, its marketing and communications director. “No personal data related to our rentals is shared with car manufacturers, our owners or other third parties without explicit legal grounds,” he added, without specifying whether the on board videos may have been transferred. Changan Group did not respond to questions. Last year, tests carried out for Oslo’s Ruter public transport authority revealed that Chinese manufacturer Yutong could theoretically remotely immobilise its electric buses with their “over-the-air” update system. Norway could use the buses one day to evacuate the population in the event of an emergency. Ruter said it had since introduced mechanisms enabling it to monitor and delay incoming signals to control updates. Modern vehicles are not the only potential Trojan horses. Smartwatches and fitness apps such as Strava, popular with joggers, can also expose sensitive military information. In 2018, data published by Strava made it possible to identify military sites and soldiers’ routes, notably in Afghanistan and Syria. In March, French newspaper Le Monde was able to locate the French aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle in almost real time in the eastern Mediterranean, thanks to a sailor on board using the app. The Norwegian National Security Authority said modern vehicles were “rolling computers that collect information”. “We don’t know for sure where the information is sent or what it’s used for,” authority official Andreas Skjold-Lorange said. The organisation, which is responsible for minimising strategic risks including digital, said that beyond the data collected, Norway should be wary of excessive dependence on a single country – especially if that country did not cooperate with Norway on security matters. “If we become too dependent on services or products from a given country, that makes us vulnerable, whatever that country may be,” Skjold-Lorange warned.

title: Abby Choi’s partner tells murder trial she hid ex-in-laws’ financial reliance on her
description: Chris Tam tells court slain Hong Kong socialite revealed she was supporting her former in-laws after a bitter family row and urged him to cut ties.
content: Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s partner told a court this week she initially misled him about her former in-laws’ wealth before describing them as horrible and ungrateful after a bitter family dispute. Chris Tam Fong-chun’s testimony also shed light on his complex relationship with Choi and his former classmate Alex Kwong Kong-chi. The three remained connected through their four children, as Choi had two with each man. During the third week of the murder trial, Tam told the High Court that the 28-year-old model had initially portrayed her former in-laws as financially independent and comfortable. She feared her two children from her first marriage would be looked down on in their new home because of their background, the court heard. After an acrimonious row over parenting in mid-2022, Choi allegedly told Tam for the first time that she had been supporting the Kwong family financially and urged him and his father to cut ties with them. But Tam said he and Choi had kept up a friendly facade in front of her former in-laws while seeking to sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) home registered in Kwong’s father’s name. He acknowledged he had been “a bit sneaky”, but said this was unavoidable as the couple tried to recover what belonged to them gradually and through diplomatic means. Asked whether he still viewed his former classmate in the same way after the dispute, Tam said: “I would say the friendship was no more.” Kwong, 31, is standing trial on a joint count of murder alongside his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35. The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial began last month. Prosecutors argued that the murder stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of the luxury flat at the upmarket Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin. They said Choi had registered her former father-in-law as the owner to avoid paying HK$9 million in double stamp duty but had never intended to give the property to her former in-laws. The court heard that Choi had a heated argument with her former mother-in-law, Jenny Li Sui-heung, at the Kadooria flat in June or July 2022, when the influencer’s elder daughter had a fever. Li allegedly told her son Alex to stay away from the child because she could infect him, prompting Choi to accuse her of favouring sons over daughters. Kwong Kau allegedly joined the row, twice attempted to attack Choi, swore at her and called her a “birthing machine”. The elder Kwong was subsequently barred from visiting the flat and seeing his two grandchildren, the court heard. But the children were allegedly taken to see him and his girlfriend while Choi was attending a fashion event in France during the Chinese New Year holiday in 2023, much to her dismay. Tam became friends with Alex Kwong in 2008, when they were studying at Concordia International School in Kowloon Tong, the court heard. Tam later continued his studies in Australia, while Kwong moved to Sear Rogers International School, where he met Choi, the court was told. Tam appeared surprised when Kwong’s counsel, Andrew Raffell, suggested he had wanted a “romantic and sexual relationship” with his client when they were schoolmates. “Definitely disagree,” the witness said. Tam said he first met Choi in late 2013 or early 2014, during a brief holiday visit to Hong Kong to see Kwong, who was then married to her. He said his relationship with Choi changed after Kwong “totally disappeared” one day in 2015. That year, Kwong began divorce proceedings and absconded from a trial over his alleged involvement in a HK$6.3 million theft case. Tam and Choi began dating in December 2015 and held a wedding banquet a year later, although they never registered their marriage, the court heard. Their daughter was born in September 2016 and their son three years later. “After Abby and I were together, I knew through Abby that Kwong Kong-chi was fine with our relationship and sent us his blessing. I also know his relationship with Abby was something in the past,” Tam said. He added that he and Choi would meet Kwong during leisure trips to mainland China. The three saw one another more often at family gatherings after Kwong returned to Hong Kong in 2022. Asked whether they had remained close until Choi’s disappearance, Tam said it was reasonable for them to do so because of their children. He said the Kwong brothers and their mother appeared calm and unconcerned after Choi disappeared on February 21, 2023. Li allegedly suggested that her former daughter-in-law had been abducted and that they should delay reporting her disappearance to police until the supposed kidnappers made their demands. Anthony Kwong, who was working as Choi’s stand-in driver at the time, allegedly evaded questions about her whereabouts and pretended to help by driving Tam around to look for her. Parts of Choi’s dismembered remains were found at a rental flat in Lung Mei village, Tai Po, on February 24. The trial also shed light on the Tam family’s wealth and financial dealings with Choi and her former in-laws. Tam’s father, Tam Chak-kwan, founded the popular restaurant chain TamJai Yunnan Mixian and received a share of the proceeds from its HK$1 billion sale to a Japanese company. In 2019, the family moved into their current 4,000 square foot home on Begonia Road in Kowloon Tong, which the elder Tam bought for HK$168 million. He said he had given his previous home, a 1,800 square foot flat valued at HK$41 million at the Manhattan Hill private estate in Lai Chi Kok, to Choi in 2018. But he had not expected his de facto daughter-in-law to live there, as he wanted to share a home with his grandchildren. The court heard that the elder Tam gave Choi at least HK$200,000 a month to cover living expenses for her and his son. He also gave her more than HK$80 million in total to invest. Chris Tam said Choi had made money investing in luxury watches, although he was unsure whether she had done so through her ex-husband. Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, accused Alex Kwong of failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million her daughter had given him to invest. She also called him a “brute” and dismissed his claim that he had supported her financially as “a pack of lies”. Choi also allegedly put money into the Kadooria flat and an egg waffle shop run by Anthony Kwong, but Chris Tam said both had proved poor investments. The court also heard how Kwong Kau had helped settle a dispute over a HK$5 million gambling debt Chris Tam incurred in Macau in August 2021. The younger Tam said he had refused to repay the loan because he knew the casino, run by SunCity Group, was about to close following the arrest of its founder and CEO, Alvin Chau Cheok-wa. Tam’s father said he had approached Kwong Kau for help because he wanted to resolve the dispute. He said he had transferred HK$5 million to Kwong Kau’s personal bank account in March 2022 and paid him a further HK$450,000 in gratuities for people with triad affiliations who had stopped debt collectors from harassing his family. The elder Tam said Kwong Kau later asked him for a HK$400,000 loan, saying police had frozen his account. Tam agreed to lend him HK$250,000, which had yet to be repaid, the court heard. He added that he had ignored Kwong’s request for help with legal fees after the former officer was remanded in custody in connection with the case. The trial continues on Tuesday before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: Over 3,000 bears culled in Russia after wave of deadly attacks: ‘we’ve never had this’
description: While the number of bear attacks across Russia has remained constant at around 20 to 30 a year, a series of recent maulings has caused alarm.
content: Seeing what looked like a brown blob in a tree while driving through Siberia’s Irkutsk region, 36-year-old Daria Tyurneva pulled over, curious to get a better look. She was not expecting to find a bear cub, perched on a branch, several metres up. “We stopped, without turning off the engine or taking off the gear, because we knew the mother could be somewhere nearby,” Tyurneva said, showing a phone video she recorded of the bear. Her sighting was one of several to spook Russians in recent weeks, as the country grapples with a spate of deadly bear attacks. Russia is home to the world’s largest population of brown bears. Experts say interactions with bears are becoming more common, as habitat loss and climate change force the animals to find food where humans live. Their numbers have more than doubled since 1990, from around 130,000 to almost 308,000 in 2026, according to an estimate from Russia’s natural resources ministry. While the number of bear attacks across Russia has remained constant at around 20 to 30 a year, according to the ministry, a series of recent maulings has caused alarm. At least 26 people have been killed in bear attacks this year, seven of which were in Siberia’s vast Krasnodar region, according to Russian state media. In September, a bear was reported to have killed a 66-year-old woman after dragging her from her window, while a week later, a 39-year-old logger was killed guarding machinery in a forest. A Siberian town reported last month that it was “under siege” from the furry animals. Bears flee in the vast majority of encounters with humans, according to the Russian government. The number of deadly attacks this year has not yet reached the record of around 80 deaths, last seen in 1996, according to the state-owned TASS news agency. Scary sightings This year has seen abnormally large bear sightings, said Mikhail Strelkov, a ranger in the Lake Baikal national park. “We’ve never had this,” he said of the recent incursions of bears into urban areas. “There is no pine nut in the forest, the main food source that the bear eats and uses to fatten before hibernation,” he added. He showed videos his team had recorded of bears frolicking at the edge of Lake Baikal, one of which scampered away upon hearing their boat approach. Vladimir Odulo, an angler from Russia’s far east, told the Komsomolskaya Pravda newspaper in October how a female bear rushed at him on the banks of a river. “Believe it or not, I didn’t even have time to get scared. I started fighting it off with my fishing rod,” he said. He said he escaped after a fight that left him with injuries across his body. Authorities have introduced curfews in some municipalities and formed bands of hunters but some environmental activists say the government may be overestimating the bear population. So far, in 2026, officials have culled more than “3,400 dangerous bears”, TASS reported earlier in October. Russian tourist Alla said she turned back at the entrance to a hiking trail near Lake Baikal after seeing a sign warning of bears. “Maybe I will come again to see. Maybe in summer, maybe in winter, when they’re hibernating,” she said. Other tourists were unfazed. “I’m not afraid of bears,” said 39-year-old Chinese tourist Nick, who also only gave one name. Brown bears eat a mixed diet that can include up to 90 per cent fruit and vegetation. Russia’s emergencies ministry says the best way to avoid bear encounters is to make loud noises and that in the rare event a bear starts to attack, “to give up”. “It’s common for a bear to stop attacking when it feels the threat has been eliminated. Remain motionless for as long as possible,” it said. “If you move and the bear sees or hears you, it may return and resume the attack. In rare cases, an attacking bear may mistake a person for food.”

title: China cuts US Treasury holdings to 18-year low in August as American debt fears mount
description: Japan also offloaded US bonds in that month, although increases in holdings by Britain and Canada partly offset sales from the two Asian countries.
content: China has further reduced its holdings of US Treasuries to an 18-year low in August, as it continued to diversify its foreign exchange reserves amid rising geopolitical tensions and concerns over Washington’s fiscal outlook. China’s holdings fell to US$590.7 billion in August, down US$27.3 billion from US$618 billion in July, data released by the US Treasury Department showed on Friday. That marked the lowest total recorded since August 2008, when its holdings tumbled to US$573.7 billion, according to Chinese financial data provider Wind. China joined Japan, the largest foreign holder of US debt, in offloading the bonds that month. Japan cut its holdings to US$1.07 trillion in August by selling US$35.6 billion from US$1.1 trillion in July. Overall foreign holdings of US Treasuries climbed to US$9.33 trillion in August from US$9.25 trillion in July, the data showed, as increases from Britain and Canada partly offset sales from Japan and China. Britain, the second-largest holder of US debt, saw its portfolio rise to US$1.01 trillion from US$998.3 billion, official data showed. Canada’s holdings increased by US$38.3 billion to US$464.6 billion. Worries over Washington’s fiscal sustainability deepened in August as total US debt topped a staggering US$40 trillion, while the 30-year Treasury yield remained above the 5 per cent mark. To support liquidity in the bond market, the US Treasury announced in mid-August that it would “at least double” buy-backs of 10- to 30-year securities. The US also worked jointly with Japan to prop up the yen that month, with Tokyo spending 15.4 trillion yen (US$97.2 billion) on the intervention between July 30 and August 26, according to data from the country’s Ministry of Finance. Long-term Treasury yields continued to climb in recent weeks, with investors reacting to the US Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates by a 0.25 percentage point – its first rate increase in over three years – due to inflation concerns. On Friday afternoon, the 30-year US Treasury yield fell to 5.43 per cent after trading around a 24-year high recently. The 10-year yield stood at 5.08 per cent. China slipped to third place among foreign holders of US Treasuries in March last year – behind Japan and the UK – continuing a gradual but uneven retreat that began during US President Donald Trump’s first term amid rising tensions and concerns over the weaponisation of the US dollar. In contrast to its broader sell-off of US debt, China has steadily added to its gold reserves, widely viewed as a hedge against geopolitical and financial risks. Official data showed the People’s Bank of China increased its bullion holdings for the 23rd consecutive month in September, bringing the total to 77.47 million troy ounces (2,400 tonnes).

title: Hong Kong’s skiers flock to mainland as indoor slopes mushroom nationwide
description: Indoor ski resorts are springing up across mainland China amid a winter sports boom – and Hongkongers are keen to take advantage.
content: A rising number of travellers from Hong Kong and Macau are flocking to indoor ski centres in Guangdong province, as new venues mushroom across the mainland amid a winter sports boom. Chinese indoor ski resort operator Bonski said 20 to 30 per cent of visitors to its facility in Guangzhou were now coming from Hong Kong and Macau, as the company’s venues continue to attract a growing customer base. “Most visitors to indoor ski venues are local residents, and we have seen steady inflows of customers from Hong Kong and Macau,” said Liu Wensheng, president of Bonski. “Skiing enjoys relatively high penetration rates there and many residents already have solid skills, but they don’t have indoor ski facilities in their home cities.” Liu added that the trend was in line with a broader increase in Hongkongers travelling to the mainland for leisure and shopping trips. Bonski already operates 11 indoor ski venues in China and is building four new sites to meet growing demand, as the company sees massive potential in the country’s winter sports market. China’s ice and snow industry has boomed in the wake of the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics, with the market topping 1 trillion yuan (US$149 billion) in value last year, according to a report released by research firm Asia Digital Group on Thursday. Chinese consumers made 67.3 million ski trips during the 2025-2026 ski season, up 22.8 per cent from the 2023-2024 season, the report found. The growing demand has also lifted confidence among ski equipment suppliers. Italian snow-making systems maker TechnoAlpin – which supplies 90 per cent of large-scale ski resorts in China – said it was optimistic about the coming winter ski season. The company accounts for over 50 per cent of the Chinese market and has established three subsidiaries in the northern province of Hebei and northeastern Liaoning. “While Europe remains our main market with a more mature sector there, China boasts fast growth and stands as a key market we aim to further develop,” said Sunny Shen, China marketing director at TechnoAlpin. “We see substantial growth potential here, given that the number of Chinese people taking part in skiing and ice skating across the country still remains very low.”

title: Endangered bogong moths make a comeback in Australia
description: These insects are harmless to humans, and they are important for local ecosystems.
content:
Moths covered homes in Australia’s southeast earlier this month. This shows that the endangered species is recovering.
Bogong moths have a wingspan of up to 5cm. They are harmless to humans and protected by the law.
For years, their population has been declining. But this year, they have had a comeback.
“The bogongs are terrific for our ecosystem, ‌supporting our treasured native wildlife like the pygmy-possum and pollinating our eucalyptus trees,” Steve Whan said. He ‌represents the Monaro region in the New South Wales parliament.
The moth’s population fell due to drought, ‌farming and habitat ‌loss.
One theory for the rebound is that more rainfall makes extra food for the insects’ larvae.

title: Hong Kong Pet Club’s emergency ambulances bring critical vet care to animals
description: The service has three vehicles across Hong Kong Island, Kowloon and the New Territories, with paramedics who help with illness and accidents.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises based on the story we’ve written.
Snakes can be great at hiding signs of illness. But one pet owner in Hong Kong noticed that something was wrong with their python, which had stopped moving. The owner immediately called for a pet ambulance from the Hong Kong Pet Club.
The python was diagnosed with a respiratory infection. It later made a full recovery.
“It was a reminder that the bond between humans and their pets is … strong, and our role is to help whenever we can,” Zoie Cheng Kam-shan said.
Cheng is the ambulance service’s business development director. Founded in 2019, Hong Kong Pet Club helps dogs and cats access vet care in critical moments.
“When a pet suddenly collapses or has an accident at home, owners often have no choice but to carry them to a clinic themselves, which can cost precious rescue time,” Cheng said.
The pet ambulance service receives calls from pet owners every day. There are about six cases every night.
Medical calls often involve heart or breathing problems in older dogs. Paramedics also handle emergencies. These can include traffic accidents, falls from a height, choking and accidental food poisoning.
The three pet ambulances cover Hong Kong Island, Kowloon and the New Territories. Members pay a monthly fee to access their services, while non-members can pay a one-time fee. These fees help the service run.
They also receive support from partner organisations, including banks and insurance companies. These partners refer members and sponsor projects.
Each ambulance has a 140cm animal stretcher. They have adjustable side rails and restraint straps. These stretchers can safely secure animals of all sizes. Other essentials include first aid kits and splints for treating cuts and broken bones.
To keep pets calm and safe during the drive to the animal clinic or hospital, the ambulance provides soft blankets, warm pads and safety nets. There are also special oxygen masks for cats and dogs.
“Our oxygen masks are made of soft medical-grade plastic or silicone, with flexible edges that conform to different animals’ facial contours ,” Cheng explained.
Cheng oversees emergency pet transfer procedures. She also provides training in first aid care. She has been in this field for more than 15 years.
An overlooked part of a pet paramedic’s job is also keeping pet owners calm.
“Owners naturally feel guilty or overwhelmed, so my first step is to comfort them and assure them that their pet is in capable hands,” Cheng shared. “I always make sure to explain our immediate medical actions and estimated arrival time. Knowing what to expect reduces fear.”
She added: “Because animals easily sense human stress and become even more upset, I always ask the owner to speak to their companion to calm them both down.”
Students interested in working with animals might focus on traditional jobs such as becoming a veterinarian. But Cheng urged them to consider becoming a pet paramedic.
While Hong Kong does not have an official government licence for pet first aid, there are animal first aid courses available in the city.
“When every second counts, having the skills to help an animal can mean the difference between a tragic loss and a second chance at life,” Cheng said.

title: Hong Kong’s revamped Huanggang Port quiet ahead of expected holiday rush
description: Security chief Chris Tang expects daily trips to exceed 100,000 over Chung Yeung Festival break, with extra staff deployed to handle travellers.
content: Hong Kong’s revamped Huanggang Port is expected to handle more than 100,000 passenger trips a day over the Chung Yeung Festival long weekend, although its departure hall remained quiet on Saturday morning. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said the border crossing had operated smoothly since opening on Monday, handling about 80,000 passenger trips a day, with the figure exceeding 92,000 on Friday. That represented a 1.5-fold to almost twofold increase from the 30,000 to 40,000 trips recorded before reconstruction, he said. Meanwhile, passenger trips at the Lo Wu and Lok Ma Chau control points fell by between 3 and 7 per cent. “As we already saw over 90,000 trips on Friday, I believe we will inevitably have over 100,000 trips during the peak [of the festival holiday],” he said. “We have the capacity to handle it, as the maximum capacity of the new port is at least 200,000 [trips].” The festival falls on Sunday, with Monday designated a public holiday in substitution. Tang said authorities would deploy additional staff so that all automated and manual clearance channels could open whenever needed. Staffing would also be increased at public transport pickup and drop-off points to prevent congestion. He said waiting times were generally under five minutes and no longer than 15 minutes, with passengers often able to pass through the control point with almost no wait. “While the duration is roughly the same as before, we need to consider that the passenger volume has more than doubled … and you only need to undergo one inspection to enter the mainland, without queuing again for a second check,” he said. “If you look at it this way, the overall efficiency has effectively increased by at least fourfold, meaning it is four times as fast.” The crossing, which opened after six years of redevelopment, is the first border checkpoint between Hong Kong and mainland China to use a “joint clearance” system for immigration. Tang said 300,000 residents had registered for joint clearance through a dedicated mobile app. The arrangement allows passengers to complete both departure and entry procedures by presenting the identity document required at their destination and passing through a three-gate automated channel. A South China Morning Post reporter at Huanggang Port on Saturday morning saw travellers arriving by bus from across Hong Kong move swiftly into the departure hall, with almost no queues at the automated border control gates. Hong Kong resident Yan Li said she usually visited Shenzhen about twice a month, and she had chosen Huanggang Port to cross this time because the bus journey from Tai Wo Hau, with a change at Tai Lam Tunnel, was faster and cheaper than travelling via Lo Wu. “My trip today cost HK$12.50 [US$1.60] and took me 45 minutes, compared with me using the Lo Wu crossing, which would be HK$48 and would take up to 80 minutes,” the trading professional in her thirties said, adding that the journey had been smooth overall. Medical professional Michael Leung, a Hong Kong resident in his thirties, said he visited the mainland about once a month with his girlfriend or friends, usually staying in Shenzhen for food and massages. “When borders first reopened after the pandemic, we were drawn by good value for money on the mainland compared with Hong Kong, but that is not as pronounced any more because of the strengthened exchange rate,” he said, adding that he typically spent about HK$1,000 on a day trip to Shenzhen and usually tried restaurants or massage parlours he had not visited before. “We go because it feels like a small getaway now.” Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said on Saturday that rising fuel prices had posed a challenge to Hong Kong’s tourism sector this year by affecting short-haul visitor numbers. She added that arrivals from Southeast Asia had declined. “But visitor numbers from the mainland and long-haul markets remain favourable as they are attracted by the many mega-events in Hong Kong,” she said. “Since we have many coming mega-events, which will bring in a large number of visitors towards the end of the year, I am confident that the total number of visitors for the full year will reach [the target of] 53.8 million as expected.” Law said the opening of the new Huanggang crossing on Monday was a positive development, giving tourists another crossing option and greater convenience. “As the new Huanggang Port operates 24 hours a day, visitors will no longer feel rushed to return to the mainland; they can stay longer to eat or dine after concerts,” she said.

title: Asean climate monitor issues highest alert level over toxic haze
description: The months-long spell of haze has been disrupting life in large parts of Southeast Asia, closing schools and spiking respiratory complaints.
content: Ongoing fires in Indonesia that have blanketed parts of Southeast Asia with toxic haze have triggered the highest-level alert by the regional bloc’s climate and fire monitor. “Activation of Alert Level 3 for the Southern Asean region,” the Singapore Asean Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) said on its website, seen on Saturday. Based near Singapore’s Changi Airport, the ASMC uses a four-tiered alert level system, from zero to three, with the highest triggered if there is a “high risk of severe transboundary haze in the region”. This included significant and persistent hotspot activities with widespread moderate to dense smoke haze, observed over two or more consecutive days, dry weather persisting and wind continuing to blow haze towards Association of Southeast Asian Nations neighbours. The ASMC alert was issued on Friday, but similar alerts have already been handed out twice this year – on August 26 and March 27. The months-long spell of haze has been disrupting life in large parts of Southeast Asia, closing schools and spiking respiratory complaints. On Friday, Singapore said it would issue warnings to seven companies in Indonesia it identified as responsible for fires but warned the worst may yet to come. Singapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions in Indonesia are reportedly based in the city state. Four people died in East Java’s Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park fighting the blazes on Thursday, authorities said. Two others suffered serious burns and were receiving further medical treatment. “This incident serves as a reminder that forest and land fire extinguishing is a high-risk operation,” the forestry department said on Friday, adding that personnel safety remained a primary concern. The department in the same statement said there was a significant jump in hotspots in several areas in six “priority provinces” where 615 hotspots were detected. A hotspot is a location where a satellite detects an unusually high temperature, indicating a potential fire or other strong heat source.

title: Asian Angle | Why Asean’s Myanmar peace push needs Japan’s ‘silent diplomacy’
description: Tokyo knows how to back an Asean-led process without taking ownership of it, as decades of regional mediation show.
content: Japan has long established itself as a pioneer of mediation in Southeast Asia. In 1990, for example, its officials helped broker talks between Cambodia’s warring factions, supplementing international efforts to end conflict in the country. Now, Tokyo is seeking to upgrade its diplomatic toolkit. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ International Peace Mediation Unit was set up in March, followed by the launch of the Parliamentary Association for Peace Mediation in May. Around the same time, the Tokyo-based Sasakawa Peace Foundation separately opened a Centre for Mediation Support, providing another channel for Japanese actors to engage in peacemaking efforts. For Myanmar, these developments are relevant because Japan has stayed quietly engaged since the coup. Yohei Sasakawa, the well-connected Japanese philanthropist, calls this Japan’s “silent diplomacy”. Tokyo took part in the Oslo Forum’s round table on Myanmar in June, Sasakawa himself visited Naypyidaw in August and two Japanese parliamentarians followed a month later. Japan has engaged in dialogue and offered to mediate peace in Myanmar for years. When Western nations condemned the violent crackdown on the Rohingya in 2017, for instance, Tokyo worked through private actors to promote human rights in Rakhine state. In November 2020, Sasakawa mediated an informal humanitarian ceasefire between the military and the Arakan Army (AA), despite the civilian government designating the group a terrorist organisation that same year. He kept mediating after the 2021 coup and successfully brokered another informal ceasefire in November 2022. That second truce lasted for about a year; thereafter, the AA launched a new offensive in 2023 and took part in Operation 1027 as part of the Three Brotherhood Alliance, alongside the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) and Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA). By late 2023, the AA had begun capturing townships in Chin and Rakhine states, contributing to heavy territorial losses for the military. For Myanmar’s military, the collapse of the 2022 ceasefire left a lasting impact on how it views international mediation. The junta had hoped the truce would improve its international reputation and rehabilitate its image in Rakhine, especially after its 2017 crackdown on the Rohingya. Instead, the AA used the pause in fighting to consolidate local support and mobilise its forces. It then reneged on the agreement and resumed its offensive following Naypyidaw’s abysmal performance against the Three Brotherhood Alliance in northern Shan state. The resumption of hostilities not only undermined Sasakawa’s mediation efforts but also appears to have convinced the regime that ceasefires are increasingly ineffective at serving its interests. Moreover, the AA’s distrust of external mediators grew too. China’s subsequent mediation led to the transfer of Lashio, northern Shan state’s economic hub, from the MNDAA to the junta in 2025. The handover of this city may have further reinforced the AA’s scepticism towards externally brokered arrangements and made it less willing to return to the negotiating table. Despite the military’s reservations about another internationally brokered ceasefire, Sasakawa’s recent visit to Naypyidaw suggests it has not ruled out externally facilitated deals entirely. Japan also has the advantage of being viewed as more trusted and less coercive than other major powers. This lends it greater credibility as a mediator both sides in a civil war might accept. As Japan steps up its peace diplomacy, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations could find in it an effective partner on Myanmar. Tokyo’s long experience of engaging with the country through its kakehashi (bridging) approach, including its previous ceasefire efforts, could help inform the benchmarks for measuring progress in Myanmar that Asean foreign ministers agreed to develop on July 12. Possible entry points for this encompass the agreement struck in May between Japan and the Philippines to strengthen cooperation on peace mediation expertise and capacity, as well as the attendance of representatives from the Singapore embassy in Tokyo at the inaugural meeting of the Parliamentary Association for Peace Mediation that same month. According to the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute’s latest State of Southeast Asia Survey, Asean members place a relatively high level of trust in Japan to “do the right thing” for peace, security and prosperity, which will help it to remain a consistent and reliable partner regardless of which member state holds the Asean chair. Tokyo remains attentive to Beijing’s growing influence in the Myanmar peace process. China has been expanding its peace mediation role in Southeast Asia, as its shuttle diplomacy during the 2025 Thailand-Cambodia conflict showed. It has also played the most prominent external role in Myanmar’s ceasefires, though largely by favouring bilateral engagement over supporting Asean-led efforts. Japan’s approach to peacebuilding, meanwhile, has a strong Official Development Aid component, stressing the importance of human security as the basis of long-term conflict prevention and delivering material benefits to regional partners. About 300 Japanese companies also continue to operate in Myanmar, giving Tokyo potential economic leverage. Japan’s decades of engagement in the Mindanao peace process demonstrate its ability to sustain long-term peacebuilding efforts. It also has deep institutional experience working with Asean mechanisms for humanitarian and emergency response assistance. Through its Official Security Assistance scheme, for example, it supplied material support to Asean observer teams during the recent Thailand–Cambodia dispute. Tokyo thus knows how to support an Asean-led process without taking ownership of it. A similar model could make Japan a quiet partner in Asean’s Myanmar engagement, providing mediation experience and resources while supporting the bloc to steer the dialogue process. Hirokazu Omatsu is an independent researcher focusing on peacebuilding and civil conflict. Kyi Sin is a Research Officer in the Myanmar and Thailand Studies Programmes at ISEAS - Yusof Ishak Institute. This article was first published by the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg

title: As more young couples say yes to lab-grown, are natural diamonds losing their sparkle?
description: Lab-grown diamonds are becoming a popular choice for engagement rings, as younger couples weigh style, price and sustainability.
content: At the end of the day, it all comes down to price. That is why Pat Chung prefers lab-grown diamonds. The 36-year-old Hongkonger says they are much cheaper than a natural diamond for the same quality and size and they are easier to source. “I searched for the exact colour, size and shape that I wanted and sent it to my jeweller,” Chung says, adding that more people are opting for lab-grown diamonds compared to a decade ago. The global trend shows how dramatically the diamond business has changed in recent years. They want a big stone for a small price. That’s the new thing Tim Juzwick, jeweller The popularity of lab-grown diamonds has disrupted the economics of the natural diamond industry by hurting the demand for natural diamonds, reducing prices and forcing jewellers to adapt to lab-grown stones to survive. Unlike imitation stones such as cubic zirconia, lab-grown diamonds have the same chemical and physical properties as natural diamonds. However, they are produced in hi-tech laboratories instead of being mined. And nobody wants lab-grown diamonds more than young couples shopping for engagement rings, sellers say. For a generation of brides and grooms who want the biggest possible stones without spending a fortune, lab-grown diamonds offer an irresistible proposition – they are virtually indistinguishable from natural stones and are sold at a fraction of the price. While a one-carat natural diamond can cost anywhere from US$4,000 to US$7,000, depending on its quality, a comparable lab-grown diamond can cost roughly US$400. And even that US$400 price is a fraction of what lab-grown diamonds cost just five years ago when they typically sold for about half the price of a natural diamond. The plunge in price has made lab-grown diamonds even more of a no-brainer for consumers who care about appearance and price. According to Statista, these diamonds accounted for 21 per cent of the world’s diamond market share in 2025. Lab‑grown diamonds are becoming more affordable thanks to surging supply, challenging the natural diamond market. Some couples deliberately choose lab-grown diamonds because they don’t want to support the unethical and environmental concerns that have been associated with some natural diamond-mining operations, including a history of conflict and violence and exploitation of mine workers, dangerous working conditions and environmental damage. For those couples, buying a lab-grown diamond is a deliberate choice that reflects their values. Paul Bieker, owner of GeekJewelry.com, estimates that lab-grown jewellery now accounts for about half of his business. “The working-class consumer, like the Target and Walmart shoppers, they just want the sparkle,” Bieker says. “They just want the rock – whether it’s natural or lab-grown.” And once shoppers understand how little they have to spend to get that bling, Bieker says the maths becomes difficult to argue with – especially when the more expensive product doesn’t look any different to the naked eye. Bieker’s argument for lab-grown gets even more pointed when he talks about what happens after a diamond leaves the jewellery store. “Imagine spending US$5,000 on a natural diamond,” he says. “You’re very proud of yourself. But things don’t work out. You’re sad. You decide to sell the ring. They’re going to offer you US$2,000, if you’re lucky.” That is a US$3,000 loss. “In the same scenario, if you spent US$1,500 on a lab-grown, you can sell it on eBay or wherever, for US$400 and at least get a couple of bucks back,” Bieker says. “Or, you can throw it in the freaking river – you’re still up.” And then there is De Beers. The 138-year-old diamond giant built one of the world’s most powerful luxury brands around the idea that a diamond is rare, precious and worth paying a premium to own. But in 2018, De Beers got into the lab-grown business. The company launched Lightbox, with the idea of differentiating lab-grown diamonds as affordable fashion accessories that were inexpensive, fun and disposable rather than investment-grade heirlooms. The idea was to drive down the price of lab-grown diamonds. But the move backfired. The De Beers name, technology and marketing muscle actually helped cement lab-grown diamonds as a legitimate part of the diamond market. Nonetheless, the price collapse for lab-grown diamonds has been extraordinary in recent years, and now De Beers is walking away from the experiment. The company announced in May 2025 that it would close Lightbox and refocus its synthetic diamond business on industrial and hi-tech applications rather than jewellery. For all the damage human-made diamonds have done to the natural diamond market, many customers who can afford to buy the real thing still want natural diamonds. Tim Juzwick has spent 35 years watching those customers who love natural diamonds walk through his doors at Liberty Avenue Jewelry Exchange in the Clark Building, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. However, five years ago, Juzwick also got into the lab-grown diamond business. Today, his sales are roughly 75 per cent natural diamonds and 25 per cent lab-grown. “That’s what the new generation wants,” Juzwick says. “They want a big stone for a small price. That’s the new thing.” But many of the customers Juzwick has served for decades don’t see diamonds that way. Customers in their forties and fifties and older mostly prefer natural stones. They want something that holds at least some value if life changes and they ever decide to sell it. “Something that you create in a 48-hour period doesn’t compare to a natural diamond that takes thousands of years to develop in the earth and be extracted and cut,” he says. For 26-year-old Hongkonger Janice, she says she will reserve natural diamonds “for major milestones where that traditional rarity and deeper sentimental meaning matter more to me”. Additional reporting by Charmaine Yu

title: Ex-Malaysian minister Nik Nazmi admits lapse in judgment after ‘khalwat’ arrest
description: The Parti Bersama Malaysia co-leader said he was discussing a project with the woman at a residence in Petaling Jaya.
content: Former Malaysian minister Nik Nazmi Nik Ahmad has confirmed that he was one of two individuals detained by the Selangor Islamic Religious Department (Jais) over an alleged khalwat case. Nik Nazmi, who helms Parti Bersama Malaysia, said he was at a residence in Petaling Jaya on Thursday with a woman after they decided to continue a discussion about a project there. “We had initially started the discussion with friends at a studio in Brickfields, Kuala Lumpur, before moving to Petaling Jaya to view some materials related to the project,” he said in a statement on Saturday. “When Jais officials arrived, only the woman and I were there. I admit that this was an offence. Like what I told the officials, we did not engage in any improper conduct that could raise suspicion,” he added. Khalwat is an Islamic moral offence under Malaysia’s state sharia laws for Muslims that prohibits unrelated men and women from being alone together in private or secluded places where sexual misconduct might be suspected. Nik Nazmi also apologised to his wife, both their families and others affected by what he described as “a lapse in judgment”. He also apologised to Bersama, saying he had disappointed the party’s members and supporters, and that he would accept whatever decision the party made. The former Setiawangsa MP added that he would cooperate in all legal proceedings and urged all parties to respect the legal process and refrain from prolonging the matter through the media. It was reported that a 44-year-old politician was detained at about 6pm on Thursday. A source reportedly said a five-member Jais enforcement team entered the residence and found the politician and the woman, believed to be the founder of a non-governmental organisation, inside. Both were taken to the Jais office in Shah Alam for documentation purposes. Jais director Mohd Shahzihan Ahmad said on Friday the two have been detained under Section 29 of the Syariah Criminal Offences (Selangor) Enactment 1995. Those convicted under the provision face a fine of up to 3,000 ringgit (US$730), imprisonment of up to two years, or both. This article was first published by The Star Additional reporting by SCMP’s Asia desk

title: The butterfly effect: one man’s mission to help nature and communities coexist
description: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist Yau Wing-kwong unites people through butterfly gardens, with a vision for greener urban development in the city.
content: Hong Kong’s next phase of development should make room for both butterflies and buildings, conservationist Dr Yau Wing-kwong has said, arguing that biodiversity can be incorporated into parks, schools and neighbourhoods without holding back the city’s growth. Yau, founder of Environmental Association Limited, has spent nearly three decades promoting community-based conservation. He is a finalist for the Spirit of Community Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. His best-known project, the Fung Yuen Butterfly Reserve in Tai Po, began as an effort to protect butterfly habitats from collectors and other disturbances. It soon became an early example of a different approach to managing ecologically valuable private land. Hong Kong announced its New Nature Conservation Policy in 2004, and Fung Yuen was among the first sites selected for a pilot management agreement scheme the following year. The arrangement allowed a non-profit organisation to work with private landowners, with government funding, to manage land for conservation. “We did it almost like volunteers, with many volunteers and friends helping. We really made a model,” Yau said. The pilot scheme later became part of Hong Kong’s conservation system, with similar management agreements introduced at other ecologically important sites. Fung Yuen has long relied on community participation, with volunteers working alongside a small team of staff to maintain the reserve and support its conservation and education work. Yau said volunteers help with planting, weeding and path maintenance, while university students joined as interns. Retired teachers, civil servants and others also took on various roles. “Volunteers sometimes receive an unexpected reward. When they are working, a butterfly may fly past or land on their shoulder,” he said. “They feel as if the butterfly has come to thank them.” The reserve also conducts monthly surveys to monitor its ecology. Yau said about 90 per cent of Hong Kong’s butterfly species had been recorded at Fung Yuen. He added that the discovery, within a single year, of seven species not previously recorded in the city, some associated with warmer areas further south. Such sightings could offer clues about climate change, he said, although longer-term data were needed before firm conclusions could be drawn. Conservation can also begin with everyday household habits. For more than a decade, the association has collected potted citrus trees discarded after Lunar New Year, as their leaves provide food for butterflies. Surplus trees are given to farmers, keeping them out of landfill and giving them a second life. Yau believes the same approach can be applied as Hong Kong develops. Citing the Northern Metropolis, he said new parks and open spaces should provide wildlife habitats rather than focus mainly on ornamental greenery. He said different planting choices could allow butterflies and other species to live in newly developed districts. Hong Kong’s Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2035, updated in 2025, similarly calls for biodiversity conservation and sustainable development to advance together, with “harmony between humans and nature” among its stated goals. Yau now wants to connect habitats beyond Fung Yuen. His interest in butterfly migration routes grew after a butterfly marked in Japan was found in Hong Kong following a journey of about 2,500km. His concept is “point, line and surface”, in which individual butterfly gardens serve as points, flight routes connect them into lines, and enough connections eventually form a citywide network. Schools across Hong Kong have joined Fung Yuen’s Butterfly Garden Certification Programme, and certified gardens have also been established in Shenzhen and Macau. The initiative has involved cooperation with organisations in Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and Malaysia. After nearly three decades, Yau said the work had also changed his understanding of conservation. Visitors could find calm in nature, while some students with special educational needs had become more communicative after helping to care for butterfly gardens. “Protecting butterflies is also, in a way, protecting ourselves,” he said. The Spirit of Hong Kong Awards were established in 2013 to recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention. Yau has joined the race for Hong Kong’s Election Committee poll in November, standing in the Heung Yee Kuk subsector. The elected members will join 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies, and select Hong Kong’s next chief executive in March next year.

title: Chinese kindergarten owner given life sentence over lead paint poisoning scandal
description: Five others are also jailed after more than 200 children in Gansu were poisoned by paint used to improve the appearance of canteen food.
content: The owner of a Chinese kindergarten has been jailed for life after more than 200 children were poisoned by lead in the country’s worst food safety scandal for almost two decades. A total of six people were jailed by the Lanzhou Intermediate People’s Court in Gansu province on Friday for making or selling harmful foodstuffs. Li Huifang, owner of the Peixin Kindergarten in Tianshui, was handed a life sentence and fined 500,000 yuan (US$75,000), while Zhu Jinglin, the principal, was jailed for 15 years and fined 300,000 yuan. Four canteen staff – Niu Aiyuan, Wen Yafang, He Xuxia and An Chunling – were jailed for between six and eight years and given fines. The scandal emerged in July last year, when more than 200 children were found to be suffering from lead poisoning. Police said at that time that canteen staff bought decorative paint online with the consent of Zhu and Li, diluted it and added it to food. Laboratory tests confirmed that the paint – which had been clearly marked as not safe for consumption – contained lead. Of the 251 children at Peixin Kindergarten, 233 were found to have abnormal blood lead levels while 18 returned tests within the normal range. Food samples from the kindergarten were found to contain more than 2,000 times the national safe limit for contaminants. The case, one of the worst food safety scandals involving children for several years, sparked nationwide fury. Some drew comparisons with the 2008 case, when some 300,000 children were poisoned after suppliers added melamine, a chemical used to make plastic, to powdered milk to artificially boost protein levels. People’s Daily, the Communist Party mouthpiece, said on Saturday that the latest scandal had “dealt a severe blow to food safety standards”, but there would be “zero tolerance” for any act that harmed public health. It said the authorities should not overlook any cases of this kind and “deal a heavy blow” to all those responsible for safety breaches. “Only by making the cost of crime prohibitively high can we deter misconduct and compel businesses to respect the rules and hold the bottom line,” the article said. Earlier this week, the Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission, the top Communist Party body overseeing national security and intelligence, said illegal acts that endangered food safety should be “severely punished”. It also called for a focus on areas of public concern such as the food served in schools as well as fruit and vegetables.

title: Exclusive | Hong Kong touts key advantages over London in bid to become global gold hub
description: Financial services minister Christopher Hui says government backing, integrated settlement and Shanghai ties will distinguish city’s gold trading ecosystem.
content: Distinctive features will set Hong Kong apart from London, a major bullion hub, as the city accelerates efforts to develop an international gold and precious metals trading ecosystem covering the entire value chain, a minister has told the South China Morning Post. In an exclusive interview on Thursday, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said the city would officially launch a central gold clearing platform in the first quarter of next year. It would handle both physical delivery and payments, with the latter linked to the real-time gross settlement system. Hui said the ultimate aim was to connect regional liquidity with international market standards, giving participants a venue in the Asian time zone for trading, storage, clearing, refining and risk management. “We are confident [of] achieving [this] because in the Asia time zone, we see Hong Kong as uniquely positioned to do that,” he said. In the wide-ranging interview, Hui also discussed the city’s efforts to promote the international use of the yuan, the development of China’s digital currency, the e-CNY, and next week’s Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting in Hong Kong. Asked about the Saudi Central Bank’s departure from mBridge – a China-led multilateral central bank digital currency platform seen as an alternative to the traditional US dollar-dominated payments system – Hui said the project would still press ahead. The Saudi Central Bank, a key participant, confirmed last month that it had left the project after completing what it described as a limited proof-of-concept trial in May last year. “Fundamentally, what we try to do is, through Hong Kong, at the same time through these measures, to engage different players across the industry in such a way that they can work on some live cases or new cases to test out this technology,” Hui said. “So technology as it is, people still see the benefit. At the same time, what Hong Kong should do is continue contributing our expertise and also our relevance here.” Hong Kong is a founding member and co-developer of mBridge. The city is also accelerating the development of its gold trading ecosystem as a key part of its first five-year plan, which runs to 2030. The initiative is intended to support the development of mainland China’s gold economy, which boasts the world’s largest domestic production and consumption of the precious metal. Hui said that government ownership and backing, integrated delivery-versus-payment settlement and cooperation with Shanghai would distinguish Hong Kong’s offering. The cross-border cooperation would allow eligible gold stored in the city to be used to settle trades in both markets. Asked about competition with Singapore as a regional gold trading hub, Hui said Hong Kong was focused on improving its own performance. “What Hong Kong tries to do is always to compete against ourselves, because fundamentally we have to focus on areas that are within our control,” he said. The minister expressed confidence in Hong Kong’s competitive advantages. “What sets a global commodities market [apart] from the other markets is that it is really a market that is not just about financials but also close to the real economy,” he said. “It has to be about also storage, about logistics, and also, at the same time, about trading, of course. And also when it comes to disputes, there could also be some legal issues. “So actually, it’s a whole value chain in terms of the potential composition of this industry association to be set up before the end of this year.” Hui added that following a trial in July, the system with integrated delivery-versus-payment settlement service was due to launch officially in the first quarter of next year. “The clearing system now in the UK is run by the London Bullion Market Association, which is an industry association,” he said. “But the clearing house in Hong Kong is owned and run by the government. So I think this government backing sets us apart in terms of credibility. “Another thing that is different between Hong Kong and London in that context is the fact that our current system will not just do physical delivery but also money settlement.” Hui said 11 banks were already taking part in the payment settlement arrangements and others had expressed strong interest in joining, adding that the city would discuss cooperation on delivery standards with the London association. Hui, who chairs the board overseeing the clearing facility, said a representative of the Shanghai bourse served as deputy chair. Under the cross-border delivery connect arrangement, physical gold stored in certified Hong Kong vaults can be used to settle contracts traded in the local market and on Shanghai’s international board. “If there is gold that is going to satisfy both the settlement in the Hong Kong contract and the Shanghai contract, they can use the vaults in Hong Kong, catering for both the Hong Kong market and the Shanghai market to do that,” he said. “It is an area that is uniquely Hong Kong.” He added that the government was aiming to increase Hong Kong’s gold storage capacity to more than 2,000 tonnes within three years, with half at the airport and the remainder expected to come from the private sector. Some gold refineries have also been established in the city. Asked how Hong Kong could help the mainland gain greater influence over gold pricing, Hui said this would come once the city had attracted enough market participants and built sufficient liquidity. “I see pricing more as an outcome, in the sense that once we build up a sufficient liquidity, [and] at the same time a quantum of gold here ... it will eventually come,” he said, stressing the importance of creating a critical mass of market participants. On products, Hui highlighted the relaunch of a US dollar-denominated gold futures contract and said details of a yuan-denominated contract would be announced before the end of this year. With this work under way, Hui hoped to share the latest developments in Hong Kong’s gold trading ecosystem when the city hosted the London Bullion Market Association Asia Forum in April next year. Reflecting on this month’s conference in Sorrento, Italy, which he attended, he said industry stakeholders had responded positively to Hong Kong’s plans. “First of all, they are quite impressed in terms of the timeliness of this project, in a sense that in this world of changing geopolitics,” he said, adding that they were also impressed with the city’s ecosystem approach, its “concrete” plans and “Hong Kong speed”. Hui said the initiative had progressed rapidly since its announcement in the October 2024 policy address.

title: Shunned in the West, Ye hands Indonesia a rare mega-tour coup
description: The controversial US rapper, formerly known as Kanye West, is expected to attract 15,000 foreign fans to Jakarta this month.
content: Taylor Swift and Lady Gaga each chose Singapore as their only Southeast Asian stop on recent world tours. Fellow American singer Olivia Rodrigo played Thailand and the Philippines, but likewise skipped Indonesia. Next weekend, however, Jakarta is finally getting the big international headline act it has been craving – in the form of Ye. The controversial American rapper, formerly known as Kanye West, is set to play Indonesia’s capital next Saturday, marking the only Southeast Asian appearance on his current tour. The promoter, Raw Vision Collective, expects 15,000 international visitors to attend. In the first 24 hours of ticket sales going live, foreign buyers from 73 countries made up 52.8 per cent of purchases, according to marketing and communications lead Karen Tjahja. “For the first time in Indonesia’s concert history, international attendees are expected to exceed more than 5 to 9 per cent of concertgoers,” Tjahja told This Week in Asia. But the choice of Ye, who has faced travel restrictions and had concerts cancelled over his controversial remarks, has prompted questions about whether he is the right act to put Indonesia back on the international music map. Capital gains Raw Vision Collective says it invited Ye “less as competition” with neighbouring countries and “more as an opportunity to strengthen Southeast Asia’s live-entertainment ecosystem”. It points to a large domestic audience, a vibrant creative scene and Jakarta’s Gelora Bung Karno Stadium, which can hold about 77,000 concertgoers. Officials have thrown their weight behind the performance. At a press conference held by Raw Vision Collective last month, Indonesia’s Tourism Minister Widiyanti Putri Wardhana noted the potential for concerts by major overseas acts to generate benefits across various economic sectors, from accommodation and transport to food. Jakarta Governor Pramono Anung also pledged the city’s full support for the concert, calling it an opportunity to showcase Indonesia’s capital to the world. “We believe Jakarta can build on its own strengths,” Tjahja said, adding that successful productions elsewhere in the region had helped “establish Southeast Asia as a stronger destination for global tours”. “We hope that with the success of this concert, this will just be the beginning of Indonesia positively being back on the global stage.” Singapore serves as an example. The city state “has shown how major concerts can attract regional visitors and drive tourism”, Tjahja said. Yet Singapore’s success has often come at the expense of its neighbours. Swift played six nights in the city state and nowhere else in the region in 2024. A year later, Lady Gaga also played four exclusive nights. Permits and piety Musicians who know the scene well say paperwork is part of Indonesia’s problem. Herry Sutresna, also known by his stage name Morgue Vanguard and the founder of Indonesian hip-hop group Homicide, told This Week in Asia that Indonesia could attract foreign talent but was a harder sell than Singapore or Australia, partly because of its famously unwieldy bureaucracy. “It’s not really about convincing the artists themselves, but rather the difficulty of organising concerts locally regarding permits, costs and all the other red tape involved,” he said. Still, plenty of foreign performers have played Indonesia in the past. Hikmawan “Indra” Saefullah, who played guitar in the Indonesian indie band Alone at Last from 2002 to 2013, listed Deep Purple, Mick Jagger, Sepultura, Metallica and Green Day, as well as multi-day live music events such as the Java Jazz Festival and Hammersonic. Lady Gaga was meant to play Jakarta in 2012, with all 52,000 tickets already sold for a concert when several organisations, including the Islamic Defenders Front, objected to the singer’s dance moves and outfits, calling her “a devil worshipper”. Police subsequently refused to issue an event permit, saying they could not guarantee safety, and the show was ultimately scrapped. Sutresna said such mass protest campaigns were relatively rare, however, pointing instead to routine logistical and bureaucratic issues as the cause of most event disruptions in Indonesia. Purely business? Ye is “a special case” because of his past controversies, according to Saefullah. The rapper has been widely condemned in recent years for making antisemitic remarks that cost him major sponsorships and performance opportunities. Last year, he released a song titled “Heil Hitler”, which several streaming platforms banned, after previously expressing admiration for the Nazi dictator in interviews, publicly denying the existence of the Holocaust and saying he identified as a Nazi himself. Planned Ye concerts in Poland, France, Switzerland and India have been cancelled this year, with venues variously citing security and legal concerns. He was also slated to headline a festival in Britain this summer before the entire event was aborted after he was barred from entering the country. In January, he took out a full-page advertisement in The Wall Street Journal, explicitly apologising to black and Jewish people, opening up about a previously undiagnosed brain injury and detailing his treatment for bipolar disorder. Saefullah said Ye had a strong fan base in Indonesia, where rap had long been popular in “inspiring the growth of the hip-hop subculture within the local music scene” – but he still saw opportunism in Ye’s Jakarta booking. “Regarding him performing only in Jakarta, I see it as a purely business-driven decision,” he said. “Raw Vision Collective capitalised on the situation Ye and his team were facing, with tour dates being cancelled elsewhere.” Tjahja said the promoter understood “the concerns surrounding Ye’s past public statements” but was “not in a position to comment on an artist’s personal views or ideology”. This Week in Asia has asked Ye’s management for comment. Yohanes Sulaiman, a lecturer in international relations at Jenderal Achmad Yani University, said Ye’s past remarks were unlikely to be much of an issue in Indonesia, given its tense relationship with Israel, with which it has no formal diplomatic ties. A number of Indonesian public figures had made antisemitic remarks over the years without consequence, he added. “In Indonesia, he will probably have a lot of cheerleaders,” Sutresna said. “Unless he suddenly swings in another direction, like supporting [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu … That would be a different story.”

title: 3 Mexican men jailed for over 158 years for Australian, US surfer murders
description: The bodies of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson and their American friend, Carter Redd Rhoad, were found on a Mexican beach in 2024.
content: A judge has sentenced three Mexican men to more than 158 years in prison each for the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, a case that tarnished Mexico’s image by exposing the risks foreigners face when visiting the tourism-dependent country. Friday’s sentencing, which came a week after the men were found guilty, marked the end of a lengthy legal process over the killings of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson, and American Carter Redd Rhoad. Their bodies were found in May 2024, and at least four people were arrested for their alleged involvement in the crime. A judge in the coastal city of Ensenada, in Baja California state, ruled that Jesus Gerardo Garcia, known as “El Kekas”, Irineo Francisco “N” and Angel Jesus “N” would each serve 158 years and nine months in prison for murder, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence. Antonio Otanez, president of the Baja California surfers’ association, welcomed the outcome, saying: “Justice has been served.” But he acknowledged that the killings had caused a “major drop” in tourist visits, particularly by surfers, to the region known for its beautiful beaches. The Robinson brothers – Callum and Jake – and their American friend travelled to Mexico in late April 2024 to pursue one of their passions, surfing, at a beach in Punta San Jose, about 80km (50 miles) from Ensenada. Unaware of the risks they faced, the three friends camped on the beach on the night of April 27, 2024. Their attackers confronted them there, shot them dead in the early morning hours and then dumped their bodies into a well more than 15 metres (50 feet) deep. The bodies were found on May 3 after several days of searching. The Baja California prosecutor’s office announced on May 5, 2024, that it had arrested Garcia, identifying him as the suspected gunman in the killings of the three foreigners. State authorities said Garcia had a criminal history in Ensenada involving alleged drug dealing, unlawful entry into a home, domestic violence and vehicle theft. Garcia’s former partner, Ary Gisell Silva Raya, and two of his alleged accomplices, whose surnames were just given as “N”, were also arrested in the case. Silva Raya, whom authorities found in possession of a mobile phone belonging to one of the victims, agreed to an abbreviated trial and in November was sentenced to 20 years in prison for aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence. State prosecutor Maria Elena Andrade alleged that the attackers wanted to steal the tyres from the foreigners’ pickup truck and that the victims resisted. “The attackers pull out a gun they were carrying and kill the person who initially resisted the robbery, then turn on the other two,” she added.

title: Letters | For Hong Kong, climate change is no longer a distant headline
