description: Readers discuss the necessity of proactive climate risk management, and ‘lighting enhancement’ along Lugard Road.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The deadly floods along the Nepal-Tibet border in August marked the second major deluge in little more than a year. The recurrence highlights a fundamental challenge for climate adaptation in mountain regions, that disasters in these environments unfold through complex physical processes whose timing and progression remain difficult to anticipate. Recent evidence further indicates that strong El Nino events are becoming more frequent as global temperatures rise, reinforcing concerns about future climate extremes. Yet, these mountain disasters are not far-off tragedies to be observed with passive sympathy. They offer a stark preview of climate volatility that is directly relevant to urban areas like Hong Kong. Hong Kong has been experiencing its own acute surge in extreme weather. As global temperatures rise, the city faces increasingly intense typhoons, prolonged heatwaves and unprecedented cloudbursts that test its dense urban layout. To its credit, the Hong Kong government recognises the challenge. The city’s Climate Action Plan 2050 outlines foundational decarbonisation strategies while its first five-year plan acknowledges the importance of environmental risk prevention and control. However, while the current policy framework emphasises carbon neutrality targets, achieving true climate adaptation requires moving beyond long-term mitigation to immediate, proactive risk management, especially in Hong Kong’s hyper-dense built environment. The city must translate a high-level resilience strategy into aggressive action. First, urban planning must embed multi-hazard resilience into the city’s physical foundation. Hong Kong must establish a comprehensive defence system that integrates shoreline management, slope stabilisation, advanced drainage networks and climate-resilient building codes. Crucially, local research capabilities must be bridged with industrial application. Collaboration between universities, tech firms and government agencies should be incentivised on a local and regional scale within the Greater Bay Area. Second, climate adaptation must transition from reactive firefighting to anticipatory governance. By harnessing artificial intelligence, big data and real-time sensor networks across the Greater Bay Area, city authorities can build predictive digital twins of urban systems. These platforms can forecast compound risks – such as simultaneous storm surges and grid overloads – allowing decision-makers to implement dynamic load management and deploy emergency services before critical thresholds are breached. Finally, building a resilient city requires an alignment of public policy and private initiative. Community-level emergency preparedness, transparent risk disclosures and localised adaptation initiatives should be actively fostered to ensure that top-down directives meet bottom-up civic engagement. From retreating Himalayan glaciers to unprecedented local typhoons, climate change is no longer a distant headline. Possessing financial capital, technological sophistication and strong governance, Hong Kong must act swiftly and decisively to adapt its systems to this daily urban reality. Zhang Weishi, associate professor, Faculty of Geography, Tianjin Normal University, and Xu Ying, assistant professor, School of Government, Central University of Finance and Economics Hong Kong Trail doesn’t need a light show The recent “lighting enhancement” unfolding along Lugard Road on Victoria Peak is a tragic example of treating an irreplaceable natural heritage trail like a commercial shopping district. Lugard Road is celebrated globally as a tranquil green lung. It is home to native wild orchids, climbing wax flowers and vulnerable nocturnal wildlife, including civet cats, porcupines and the globally protected short-legged horned toad. Yet, the Tourism Board has chosen to develop, apparently without public consultation, this fragile corridor. Mature tree trunks have been tightly wrapped in heavy black synthetic sheets and metal brackets to support commercial spotlights. High-voltage circuit breakers are bolted continuously along the historic iron railings, while thick electrical cords snake loosely through the roadside bushes. To add insult to injury, contractors are now deploying heavy-duty pallet jacks to install artificial, fibre-optic “reed” lights in bulky planters that obstruct an already narrow path. And shockingly, workers have been caught dumping construction debris and wooden pallets straight into the brush. While dynamic, multicoloured light festivals have their place in urban concrete plazas like Tsim Sha Tsui, flashing lights into a native woodland destroys its historic character, causes severe light pollution and disrupts fragile wildlife habitats. The government must halt this invasive commercialisation immediately. Our remaining natural sanctuaries deserve strict ecological preservation, not the tacky, ecologically destructive aesthetics of a commercial theme park. Janchai Delecate, Wan Chai

title: Your Voice: Thrifting, ‘Niu Lai’, fencing in Hong Kong and the timeless yo-yo (short letters)
description: This week, students discuss why shopping second-hand clothes has become cool, how a low-budget Chinese animated film went viral and the timeless yo-yo.
content:
Have something to say? Send us a letter using this form.
Second-hand clothes are not only sustainable but are more affordable than new clothes. Stigma and hygiene concerns once shrouded the sustainable fashion industry; pre-worn clothing was thought of as unclean, cheap alternatives to fast fashion.
Today, Hong Kong youth are embracing thrifting. Local chains like Mee and Gee are luring in shoppers and tourists with racks of HK$10 blouses and blazers.
Second-hand pop-ups like Old But Gold and TOP Swop are beginning to emerge around the city. And independent Instagram shops are gaining traction as users race to claim one-of-a-kind listings.
But why has thrifting suddenly become the definition of cool?
One reason is its destigmatisation, following “hauls” and “challenges” on social media, where favourite influencers flaunt finds and make thrifting feel aspirational. Fashion trends from the 2000s help second-hand clothing branded as “vintage” or “Y2K” sell. Social media also gamifies thrifting with quests for hidden gems and deals.
Increasing awareness of the environmental damage caused by fast fashion has also contributed to this. Consumers are recognising the repercussions of profit-chasing brands churning out cheap clothing.
Hillie Ip Hoi-yin, St Catharine’s School for Girls
A low-budget animated film has become a burning topic on Chinese social media. Directed by Xin Yumeng and written by his mother Sun Lifang, Niu Lai was made on a reportedly tiny budget of just 20,000 to 30,000 yuan (HK$23,430 to HK$35,150).
The film took over five years to make and was finally released in August.
It follows Niu Lai, a newborn calf who struggles to stand up. He passes out and has a dream about courage, friendship and sacrifice. As he wakes up, he brings his new-found strength and bravery back into the real world.
But this charming plot has little to do with the film’s virality.
Initial box office sales struggled until the film suddenly became a talking point online for its low-quality animation. Its notoriously bad graphics and animation, and some stand-out dialogue, paved the way for the film’s surprising success.
The film features stiff movement, rough rendering and horrible visuals. It accidentally made for perfect meme fuel. Its budget was so low that it did not have marketing allowance, resulting in some cinema staff hand-drawing the posters themselves.
The film has shockingly become one of the most profitable films ever in terms of a gross-to-budget ratio.
Eve Constance Chung, St Mary’s Canossian College
What is fencing? It is a vigorous physical and mental game that builds muscle, hand-eye coordination, patience and concentration.
As a foil and épée fencer in Hong Kong, competing has helped me build confidence, emotional control and a great sense of achievement.
In fencing, you score by touching your opponent with your sword, which can be a foil, épée or sabre. Although it might seem scary, I highly encourage trying the sport out!
Hong Kong has incredible fencers to look up to. In foil, Cheung Ka-long won back-to-back Olympic gold medals through sheer perseverance. In épée, Vivian Kong overcame multiple injuries to achieve her Olympic gold dream.
Their journeys prove that hard work and self-belief lead to success. Don’t be afraid to chase your dreams or step out of your comfort zone to try something like fencing!
Abigail Cheung Sin-yin, Christian Alliance S.C. Chan Memorial College
Considered one of the oldest toys in history, archaeological records trace yo-yo-like items back to ancient China and Greece, around 440BC.
Ancient Greek vases depict children playing with terracotta, wood or metal discs on strings. When these children grew up, tradition dictated they place their childhood yo-yos on the family altar to pay homage to the gods.
So, how do you play with it? When you hold a wound-up yo-yo, it has potential energy. Dropping it lets gravity convert that into kinetic energy. The rapid spin creates angular momentum, acting like a gyroscope to keep the yo-yo perfectly upright.
To make it return, give the string a slight upward tug. This slack causes the string to catch against the spinning axle, forcing the yo-yo to wind itself back up to your hand.
Why is it so popular? First, it is highly portable. You can play anywhere without needing a partner or large space. Second, controlling a fast-spinning, chaotic object with a single finger provides a strong sense of personal achievement.
The yo-yo is a world-famous toy and features in childhood memories for many. While they can be hard to find in modern toy shops, if you spot one, I highly recommend picking it up and giving it a try!

title: ‘Thai people already poor’: developing nations protest IMF’s austerity call
description: The IMF should focus on climate financing and tax reforms rather than demand governments cut subsidies and social spending, critics say.
content: Coconut farmer Sombat Chuekrod travelled more than 200km (120 miles) to join hundreds on the streets of Bangkok on Friday demanding that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank change how they deal with the developing world. Finance ministers, central bank governors and other top policymakers gathered this week in the Thai capital for the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, as decision makers tackle an inflation crisis fuelled by the Iran war and other economic shocks. The message from the IMF has been clear: after years of economic crises starting with the pandemic and continuing through the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, worldwide debt is too high and governments need to cut spending. For the hundreds at the protest in Bangkok, as well as for rights groups and analysts, that message is the wrong one. “We want the IMF and World Bank to rethink their role,” said 51-year-old Sombat, as he walked alongside banners demanding reform of the institutions. “Thai people are already poor. Please don’t make them any poorer.” Protest organisers called on institutions like the IMF to focus on climate financing and tax reforms that aid poorer citizens rather than demand governments cut subsidies and social spending. “Governments across the Global South are being forced to squeeze vital spending on public health, education and social protection just to service illegitimate debts to wealthy nations and private creditors,” Lidy Nacpil, one of the protest organisers, said in a statement. Speaking on the sidelines of the meetings, Oxfam executive director Amitabh Behar said the world was facing an “inequality emergency”, and that the IMF’s calls for fiscal consolidation were code for cutting spending on essential social support during the war-fuelled inflation crisis. “It will lead to [more] price rises. It might lead to hunger,” he said. “You will see cuts further happening in terms of health, in terms of education, in terms of basic social security. So all that is going to suffer in a time when you actually need it more.” The IMF this week upgraded its world economic outlook, citing unexpected “resilience” in economic growth. But it warned that prosperity was fragmented, with vulnerable countries falling even further behind. It highlighted oil-importing low-income countries not exposed to the boom in artificial intelligence investment as being the most vulnerable. ‘No other choice’ Yet the fund’s advice to all countries at a time of rising global debt levels has been to cut spending and rebuild fiscal buffers after years of spending on crises. Asked what vulnerable countries should do, IMF deputy chief of research Petya Koeva Brooks said that while their situation was indeed “more difficult”, they had “no other choice” but to address their fiscal balances by either cutting spending or increasing revenues. The IMF has proposed making energy and food subsidies offered in the wake of the Iran war more targeted, even as the UN Development Programme warned this week that if such subsidies were cut entirely, it could plunge 130 million people into poverty. Protest organiser Nacpil questioned in an interview how one could draw a line between who deserves a subsidy and who does not. “How poor do you have to be for them to think that you will need some support?” she asked. Reza Baqir of Alvarez & Marsal’s Sovereign Advisory Services said he had experience with the difficult trade-offs policymakers in low-income countries face in such crises. “During my time as Pakistan’s central bank governor, I saw first hand how difficult it can be for countries to balance the needs of the countries’ citizens with the needs of the IMF programme,” he said. “At the same time, it also reinforced the importance of addressing domestic governance challenges, so countries can build their own resources and fiscal buffers, reduce their reliance on the IMF and support their citizens in a targeted and prudent manner.” Christina Segal-Knowles of the Rockefeller Foundation said developing countries were “effectively being given two bad options” – either take on debt at currently sky-high interest rates, or make extraordinary spending cuts and potentially give up on development goals. She proposed a “growth and investment reset” that ramps up funding to countries in need as part of a set of measures designed to provide sustained support at concessional rates. On the streets of Bangkok on Friday, protesters prepared to spend the night under a flyover. “We are raising our voices because we believe that the network of citizens present here are key stakeholders in the negotiations,” said activist Supaporn Malailoy. “This is not merely a matter of borrowing money; it is about shaping the very structure and direction of the nation’s development.”

title: Trump pauses Russian sanctions package after striking diesel deal with Putin
description: Named after late senator Lindsey Graham, the measure had sought to clamp down on the flow of financial resources fuelling the Ukraine war.
content: US President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest. Named after late South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, the measure had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling the war against Ukraine. The move comes a week after Trump stunningly said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in the war, now into its fifth year. Tump’s decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress. The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest. Trump invoked a waiver clause under the law, which also codified and expanded sanctions targeting Moscow. While suspending the implementation of tariffs, the directive does formally impose the levies, meaning that Trump could apply them at another time if he chooses. The measure gave Trump 30 days to impose 100 per cent tariffs on all goods from the top five buyers of Russian crude. It would also slap sanctions on numerous Russian entities and impose 500 per cent tariffs on all US imports of Russian energy products. That one month deadline was set to expire on Sunday. The Trump administration has remained mostly quiet since the recent passage of the bill with large bipartisan majorities in the House and Senate after Graham’s sudden death in July – with lawmakers urged ahead by Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky. Trump has increasingly lashed out at Zelensky, blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting. Putin deal Trump’s latest action followed the president announcing on social media last week that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in the country. Instead, Trump announced that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tonnes “within a short period of time” after that. The measure also had become a campaign centrepiece for Senator Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term, who is also running to replace him in the Senate more permanently. In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham – who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week – said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed but acknowledged it was the president’s purview as to how he implemented it. “It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.” Waiving the tariffs risks fresh pushback from members of Congress, including many Republicans who were outraged by his decision on Russian diesel. A bipartisan group of senators signed a letter this week demanding that Trump rescind the deal with Putin and enforce the provisions of the Graham law. Waiving the law also avoids a potential clash with the top purchasers of Russian energy products, China, India and Turkey. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: A companion between appointments: Hong Kong student’s AI tool for cancer patients
description: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist Claudia Chan draws on cancer survivors’ experiences to build an AI tool designed to offer emotional support.
content: For cancer patients in Hong Kong, emotional distress can persist beyond the clinic, with a large combined analysis of multiple studies linking depression and anxiety to lower chances of survival. Claudia Chan Shu-ying, a medical student at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), is developing CancerCompanion, a digital companion designed to offer emotional support between appointments, including late at night when professional help may not be immediately available. The system uses AI-powered conversations to offer structured support while directing medical questions to healthcare teams and flagging potential cases of self-harm for human review. Chan is a finalist in the youth category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. She is taking a year out from her medical degree to complete a master’s degree in research medicine. The project grew out of conversations she had during community health screening programmes in her first two years of medical school. Cancer patients and survivors described the emotional burden of the disease, including times between appointments when they had no one to talk to or did not want to burden their families. Chan said the team had built safeguards into the AI to prevent it from giving medical advice and direct clinical questions to healthcare teams instead. The team is also mindful of the risk that vulnerable patients could become too dependent on an AI chatbot. “I don’t see it as replacing human connection. It’s something that can provide support in between,” she said. The system is intended primarily for people experiencing relatively mild emotional difficulties. Those with moderate or severe mental health needs would still require professional help, and users would be encouraged to maintain real-life connections. Another safeguard is designed to detect language suggesting self-harm or suicidal thoughts. These cases would be reviewed by a person and, where necessary, referred to social workers or other professionals. CancerCompanion remains in development and is not yet available as a general patient service. A clinical study to assess the companion’s effects on patients’ mental health and quality of life received ethics approval in August. The system draws on principles of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). The team has also filed a US provisional patent application for its AI-powered conversational system. Chan said testing would proceed gradually. Researchers initially plan to observe participants using the system and gather immediate feedback. In a later phase, patients would use it for four weeks before researchers assessed measures including depression and anxiety scores. Patient input has guided the project from the outset. The team conducted in-depth interviews with cancer survivors before development began. Survivors, NGO staff and CUHK professors in psychiatry and oncology have since reviewed versions of the system. Chan said the guiding principle was to develop the technology with patients rather than assume what they needed. CancerCompanion won the undergraduate group category at the Professor Charles K. Kao Student Creativity Awards in 2025 and was first runner-up in CUHK’s Vice-Chancellor’s Cup of Student Entrepreneurship that year. Chan’s other work includes a deep-learning project to assess joint conditions at CUHK Rheumatology, which won the Vice-Chancellor’s Cup in 2026. She has also worked on software engineering and embedded programming with the CUHK Robotics Team. She credited her CancerCompanion teammates and advisers, including CUHK professors in psychiatry and oncology, patient advocates and NGO staff. She also acknowledged the rheumatology researchers advising her master’s research. Chan plans to return to medical school next year for hospital placements. In the longer term, she hopes to pursue academic medicine, combining research with clinical work. The Spirit of Hong Kong Awards were established in 2013 to recognise the city’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention.

title: Chinese man celebrates wedding to one woman, baby with ex-lover at same venue on same day
description: According to a legal expert, although Wu’s case does not legally constitute bigamy, he could still face civil liability.
content: A man in southwestern China has sparked widespread criticism after holding a wedding with one woman and a celebration for his baby with another at the same venue on the same day. According to The Beijing News, Wu Linfeng, from Liupanshui, Guizhou province, held a wedding ceremony with Kong Sihan on the first floor of a restaurant while hosting a 100-day celebration for his son with his former girlfriend, Lin Si, on the second floor. One poster at the venue showed Wu and Kong in wedding attire alongside the words: “We met, came to know each other, and fell in love.” Another poster nearby showed Wu, Lin and their son celebrating the child’s 100th day, marking “1,314 days since Dad and Mum began their journey together.” In Chinese, 1,314 is pronounced similarly to “a lifetime.” Guests at the two events reportedly argued, prompting restaurant staff to call the police. The restaurant manager said the two families had signed separate contracts for the banquets. Both events went ahead as planned, and all payments were settled. At the time of writing, it remained unclear whether the two women knew each other or whether Wu had deliberately scheduled the events for the same day. A source familiar with the matter also claimed that Wu allegedly owed Lin 100,000 yuan (US$15,000), though the allegation has not been verified. Videos filmed by guests went viral on social media, prompting many online users to question whether Wu could face bigamy charges. In China, bigamy is punishable by up to two years in prison. A local government investigation found that Wu had legally registered his marriage only with Kong, making her his legal spouse. Although Wu and Lin have a son together, they had previously lived together only as an unmarried couple. Therefore, the child’s birth did not constitute bigamy. Authorities also confirmed that Wu and Lin were involved in a financial dispute. Fu Jian, a lawyer at Henan Zejin Law Firm, said Wu’s case did not meet the legal definition of bigamy but could still involve civil liabilities, including obligations to support his child born outside marriage. Fu added that Wu’s conduct ran counter to social norms and public morality. At the time of writing, Wu had not publicly responded to the incident. One online observer commented: “Wu mishandled his relationships, leaving both women in a deeply embarrassing and painful situation. He deserves strong condemnation.” “This episode is so outrageous that even a mini-drama creator would struggle to invent such a storyline. It challenges basic expectations of marriage, loyalty and respect,” said another.

title: Air rage incidents in Japan surge, led by late check-in ‘flashpoint’
description: More cabin crew are experiencing verbal abuse, physical attacks and sexual harassment from Japanese and international passengers.
content: Airline employees in Japan are experiencing a surge in abuse incidents from customers linked to delays or cancellations of flights or from being refused boarding due to late check-in, according to a survey. Some 30 per cent of ground staff or cabin crew reported bearing the brunt of passengers’ anger over such matters in the past year, according to the survey by the Japan Federation of Aviation Industry Unions released last month, rising from 7 per cent in its previous survey in 2023. In September, Japan’s aviation authorities and airlines tightened check-in deadlines, including requiring passengers on domestic flights to complete travel procedures 30 minutes before their scheduled departure time, up from 20 minutes previously, which observers say may lead to more confrontations between airline staff and passengers in the future. “The most commonly cited cause for passengers’ complaints was a delay or a flight being cancelled,” said Tomomi Kikuchi, spokeswoman for the federation. “Some airlines have been requesting more firmly that customers board on time in the last few years and enforcing their rules strictly by refusing those who show up to boarding gates less than 10 minutes before departure time,” she said. In 2024, Japan Airlines (JAL) and All Nippon Airways (ANA) introduced new guidelines on behaviour by passengers in an effort to eradicate customer harassment. The guidelines identify a range of actions that will not be tolerated by staff on board aircraft, at check-in or during interactions over the phone. These include the use of language that is abusive, aggressive, insulting or discriminatory, using threatening words or actions, physical assault of a member of staff, unreasonable demands and sexual harassment. The ANA policy also identifies voyeurism and stalking as breaches under its new code of passenger conduct. JAL and ANA cited incidents in 2024 that had affected their staff, including a passenger throwing a cup at a flight attendant after being given the wrong drink and another who wanted to use the toilet while the aircraft was preparing to take off. When asked to sit down, the passenger scolded the crew, saying they should obey a customer demand. In another incident, a traveller who was furious over a flight delay demanded that a senior manager come to the airport terminal where he was to apologise in person. He later demanded instead that an airline representative visit his home to apologise and threatened to confront ground staff. In a statement released to This Week in Asia on Friday, ANA said it had been leading the industry campaign against harassment of staff “by promoting various initiatives both internally and externally”. “Our goal is not only to reduce the psychological burden on our employees, but also to ensure a comfortable environment and fair access to services for other customers,” the airline said. “We have established internal guidelines specifying criteria for identifying customer harassment and procedures for handling incidents, alongside conducting training for all officers and employees as well as seminars for managerial staff,” it added. ANA said it was also boosting interdepartmental collaboration to ensure its staff could deal with customer interactions with a “firm and resolute stance”. This Week in Asia has also contacted JAL for comment. While the new survey did not specify the nationalities of people who were abusive to staff, Kikuchi said Japanese passengers were also at fault and becoming more demanding. “Japanese have been used to receiving high-quality service, which sometimes causes an expectation of higher levels of service,” she said. “This has been changing and can be seen in the disrespect shown towards staff. So I assume these incidents involve, in most cases, Japanese travellers.” Ashley Harvey, a travel marketing analyst who has worked in Japan’s travel sector for more than 15 years, said such problem behaviour had always existed but was being called out more frequently since the end of the pandemic. “There is greater awareness and less tolerance for misbehaviour in every sector of Japan’s business world, so incidents that were not previously recorded and totalled up every year are now being more closely watched,” he said. At the same time, however, the airline experience at times is becoming increasingly unpleasant for customers, according to Harvey. “There are too many people and never enough space, while in the past you would go to the counter to speak to someone to check in, but now airlines require us to do it all by ourselves with automated check-in,” he said. Harvey played down suggestions that foreign travellers were causing the most problems, referring to the example cited by the domestic industry of a Japanese passenger who demanded an apology from an airline official. “It’s easy for the press to blame foreigners but domestic flights are just as busy as international flights and I have been on plenty that have been delayed, which is the obvious flashpoint,” he said. One Japanese stewardess, who declined to be named, said, however, that there was a perception in her industry that crew members who flew on domestic routes found it easier to serve Japanese passengers than customers on board international flights. “I think most Japanese passengers are more respectful of airline employees and ground staff than many other nationalities, which is why many cabin crew request to fly these routes,” she said. Nonetheless, cabin crew need to be “constantly alert” to the behaviour of passengers in general, the stewardess said. She said she had witnessed incidents of staff being touched inappropriately, shouted at and threatened. Some passengers would even proposition flight crew, including a male passenger who “demanded my phone number”, she added.

title: Foreign banks trim China branch networks as low returns test strategy
description: Foreign lenders are closing branches and shifting to wealth management as weak returns put pressure on their China operations.
content: Almost two decades after gaining permission to conduct yuan business for local clients, foreign-funded banks are still refining their strategy in China, where the financial sector is dominated by state-owned lenders. While Citi exited its China retail banking business, other foreign banks have continued to close branches and sub-branches, focusing instead on digitalisation, wealth management and core clients to strengthen their foothold in the market. Deutsche Bank (China) announced the closure of its Chongqing branch last month after closing its Qingdao branch earlier this year, leaving the German lender with only four branches outside its Beijing headquarters. HSBC Bank (China) and Standard Chartered (China) have each closed a Chongqing sub-branch over the past 12 months. HSBC also shut down a Beijing sub-branch this year. “The problem for foreign banks is an inability to generate any real profitability,” said Jason Bedford, visiting senior research fellow at National University of Singapore. Among 27 locally incorporated foreign banks, the median return on equity was 1.61 per cent last year, Bedford said, citing data from the annual financial statements of banks. That made them “by far the most unprofitable subset of the banking system in China”, he added. A return on equity of 10 per cent or higher was generally considered healthy, a threshold met only by two of the 27 banks, Bedford said. Compared to the growth of investment banking and other financial services, which could receive a further boost at next week’s Financial Street Forum – where China’s top financial regulatory bodies gather to announce new financial reform and development policies – the expansion of foreign banks in the country has long been subdued. The 41 foreign-funded banking entities in China reported combined assets of 4.87 trillion yuan (US$727 billion) by the end of 2025, accounting for 1.3 per cent of the country’s banking industry assets, according to government data. Foreign banks “simply cannot compete with Chinese banks in conventional lending and deposit-taking, given local players’ enormous advantages in scale, distribution networks and customer relationships”, Bedford said. Grace Wu, senior director for financial institutions at Fitch Ratings, said she viewed the closure of sub-branches as “selective network optimisation, rather than a retreat”. “Digitalisation has reduced reliance on physical outlets, particularly in lower-scale locations,” said Wu, highlighting yuan internationalisation and digital payments as strategic priorities for foreign banks in China. She added that the closures differed from consolidation in China’s domestic banking sector, which Wu said was “policy-led and aimed at strengthening financial stability, supervision and resilience among weak local lenders”. China has been consolidating small and rural banks as part of its financial de-risking campaign in recent years, with 670 entities closed in 2025, according to the National Financial Regulatory Administration. Major Chinese commercial banks have also been closing outlets and reducing their use of ATMs amid the rapid rise of online banking. Wu said she expected foreign banks to remain focused on higher-value wealth management and cross-border business. Assets under management per private banking client at foreign banks averaged 2.1 times those of domestic peers, according to Chinese media reports. Bedford added that profitability did not fully capture the economic value of foreign banks’ presence in China. “Onshore operations can generate substantial business for offshore offices,” so foreign banks in China could still be “strategically valuable to its parent group”, he said. Asked about the recent bank closures, an HSBC spokesperson said that “since 2024, HSBC has opened 15 wealth centres across 11 cities in mainland China.” A Standard Chartered spokesperson said the bank had “a sub-branch strategy” and adjusted locations “from time to time”. A Deutsche Bank spokesperson said the lender’s “long-term commitment to China remains unchanged”.

title: Opinion | Philippines’ ‘China-free’ manufacturing strategy is a high-risk bet
description: Despite support and progress on the Luzon Economic Corridor and Pax Silica initiatives, Manila faces many challenges and much competition.
content: China and the Philippines recently traded accusations over the medical evacuation of a Philippine serviceman from a grounded naval vessel in the hotly disputed Second Thomas Shoal in the South China Sea. The incident has sparked renewed worries about potential armed skirmishes in a global artery of trade. But Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr was also quick to emphasise the economic dimensions of a major conflict. After a decade of rapid economic growth, the Philippines is facing potential “stagflation” due to multiple headwinds. Both the ill-conceived US war on Iran and the domestic flood-control corruption scandal, which has hobbled infrastructure projects across the Philippines, have hammered the nation’s economy. Reeling from record low approval ratings, Marcos is doubling down on attracting multibillion-dollar investments from traditional partners. In particular, he is betting on the newly launched Luzon Economic Corridor, which has Japanese and European support, and the US-led Pax Silica initiative. US President Donald Trump is expected to sign a framework agreement for Pax Silica during a visit to Manila next month. By positioning itself as a “China-free” critical minerals producer, and leveraging its burgeoning security ties with Western powers, the Philippines hopes to become a new manufacturing investment hub in the Indo-Pacific. The administration wants to transform the country into a centre for consolidating what experts call “allied scale”, namely the combined technological and industrial capacity of the United States and its allies in a brewing cold war with China. It’s a high-risk strategic bet. It’s hard to overstate the Philippines’ brewing economic crisis. Growth slowed to 2.3 per cent in the second quarter, according to the latest official data, while inflation has risen to 7.2 per cent. With growth rates halving year on year and core inflation nearly doubling, economists are warning of a “stagflation lite” nightmare. In stark contrast, regional peers such as Vietnam, while also hit hard by the Iran war’s energy disruption, has managed to post a third-quarter growth of just under 10 per cent on the back of increasingly high-value-added manufacturing exports. Even industrialised neighbours such as Taiwan and South Korea, also heavily reliant on energy imports from the Persian Gulf, are experiencing a boom year amid a global demand spike for advanced chips. Once one of Asia’s fastest-growing economies, the Philippines is again facing being the “Sick Man of Asia”. No wonder the Marcos administration is scrambling for massive investments from allied nations. After all, rising geopolitical tensions with Beijing have torpedoed prospects for large-scale Chinese investments in recent years, with the Philippines effectively pulling out of the Belt and Road Initiative. On one hand, there is the Luzon Economic Corridor, an initiative to consolidate the Philippines’ industrialised northern regions into a global manufacturing hub. Eager to tap the Southeast Asian nation’s massive economic potential, hundreds of Japanese companies are exploring investments, especially in the manufacturing sector. Europeans have also expressed interest, making the Luzon Economic Corridor a global investment initiative. “The US is not the alternative, it’s everybody else,” said Greg Poling of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. “All of us are working in concert to provide attractive alternatives to China’s.” Top Philippine officials remain bullish. Jose Manuel Romualdez, Philippine ambassador to Washington, has said that the Luzon Economic Corridor is “going to be the example again of what can be done and duplicated all over the country”. Then there is the more controversial Pax Silica, which has drawn heavy criticism from civil society groups in the Philippines over environmental and community displacement concerns. Philippine officials have insisted no data centres would be part of the initiative, but the final contours of the deal remain murky. Foxconn has reportedly shown interest in joining the initiative as an “anchor locator” for the planned 1,619-hectare (4,000-acre) manufacturing hub in New Clark City. Meanwhile, top security officials have emphasised the importance of attracting investments and enhancing the country’s economic foundations as a matter of national security. Defence Secretary Gilbert Teodro has said the country needs to build up a “resilient defence industry” anchored in domestic heavy industries such as steel, which has faced massive competition from China in recent years. The Philippine dream of becoming a new regional manufacturing hub faces multiple challenges. To begin with, Marcos is in his twilight years of office, raising serious concerns over the country’s long-term geoeconomic strategy. Surveys show Beijing-friendly political figures such as Vice-President Sara Duterte and senator Christopher Go as favourites for president and vice-president in next year’s election. Allegations have surfaced that the Duterte family received massive financial support from Beijing-affiliated elements. A major foreign policy U-turn soon is not improbable. Moreover, the Philippines lacks a robust industrial strategy to harness new investment opportunities. Manila’s policymakers are generally “free market” advocates and have overseen a steady erosion of the manufacturing base in favour of an economy driven by labour exports and low-end services. To attract large-scale manufacturing investments, however, the Philippines needs to harness a proactive bureaucracy and implement a long-term support strategy to create conducive conditions for high-value-added manufacturing. Faced with a fiscal crunch and corruption scandals, it’s unclear how the Philippine government plans to address the infrastructure bottlenecks and high energy costs that have been a bane of manufacturing investments. Ultimately, the Philippines faces stiff competition from neighbours such as Malaysia, Vietnam and Thailand, which have far more robust manufacturing supply chains and have local conglomerates integrated into high-value-added production. For all its big ambitions, it remains unclear how the Philippines can credibly attract big-ticket Western investments to upgrade its flailing economy.

title: Being Chinese | I grew up eating bowls of Chinese migration history. You?
description: I once dismissed British Chinese food like salt-and-pepper chips, though it was shaped by the same cultural process as what my family ate.
content: The dining table disappeared beneath a lavish procession of dishes. Our family took food seriously. It was sacred, even. Dinner was never merely about eating. It was the one time each day when everyone was expected to gather, regardless of schedules, moods or whatever else the world demanded outside that room. At the centre sat the pièce de résistance: a whole steamed fish, usually sea bass, topped with ribbons of ginger and spring onion in a fragrant pool of oil and soy sauce. Alongside it were slices of char siu, slightly charred at the edges; Hakka pork belly with preserved mustard greens, and steamed Vietnamese rice noodle rolls, bánh cuốn, whose resemblance to Cantonese cheung fun never struck me as remarkable until much later. As a child, I thought I was simply sharing a family meal. Only as an adult did I realise the dishes on our table carried invisible threads of migration and geopolitical history, woven so seamlessly into everyday life that I couldn’t yet recognise them. If the fish was quintessentially Cantonese, the Hakka pork told a different story. The heavy terracotta clay pot of braised pork belly was perhaps the least photogenic dish on the table. Dark and unassuming after hours of simmering until the meat yielded at the prod of a chopstick, it lacked the visual drama of Cantonese steamed fish or the colours of fresh Vietnamese herbs. It was comfort food rarely celebrated beyond the dining table at home. The dishes on our table were not simply family favourites, but the accumulated record of ancestors who moved from the northern Chinese plains into Guangdong, then to northern Vietnam, left for Britain and eventually returned to China through me The dish connected me to my Hakka ancestry, shaped by successive waves of migration over centuries of war, upheaval and dynastic change. Its appearance was humble, but its history was anything but. Some dishes were harder to place. The noodle soups I grew up eating rarely fit neatly into a single category. Sometimes the flavours felt unmistakably Vietnamese, resembling herb-laden pho. Other versions felt closer to the clear, delicate broths of southern Chinese cooking, where the emphasis lay on purity rather than an abundance of garnishes. I never thought to distinguish between them. They were simply different versions of the same soup, ingredients, noodle-making techniques and broth bases having travelled alongside those who crossed borders. Between mouthfuls of broth, fragments of family history surfaced as my grandfather reminisced. Stories of land ownership and loss hinted at the political upheavals that accompanied revolution and communist land reform in northern Vietnam in the 20th century. Each bowl carried traces of my grandfather’s bitterness. His stories were never just about food or family, but a Vietnam shaped by French colonialism, Cold War politics and escalating Sino-Vietnamese tensions that complicated life for mixed-heritage families like ours. Family lore traces our roots to ancestors who left Guangdong for northern Vietnam during the waning centuries of imperial China, as trade routes flourished across the region. They settled there generations before French colonial rule, the rise of British Hong Kong and, eventually, migration to Britain in the 1970s reshaped our family’s trajectory. Growing up, I regarded British Chinese food with fascination and bewilderment. Plates of salt-and-pepper chips smothered in curry sauce, deep-fried sweet-and-sour chicken balls and an endless spectrum of beige bore little resemblance to the food on our table. I remember wondering what exactly made these dishes Chinese at all. Beginning in the post-war decades, waves of immigrants from Hong Kong adapted their cooking to British ingredients and tastes. The result was a cuisine unfamiliar to Guangzhou or Hong Kong, yet deeply familiar to generations of Britons. What I once dismissed as a culinary anomaly was, in fact, the product of the same process of migration and cultural negotiation that had shaped the food on my own family’s table. For much of my childhood, Chinese food in Britain existed in two worlds: the British-Chinese takeaway and the Cantonese cuisine served in Hong Kong-style dim sum restaurants. Beyond my family’s kitchen, I had little exposure to China’s culinary diversity. The problem wasn’t that I had misunderstood Chinese food, but that I had mistaken one regional tradition for the whole. It was only after moving to China that the scale of my ignorance became clear. Chengdu, my first stop on the mainland a decade ago, introduced me to mala – the fiery, tongue-numbing combination of chilli and Sichuan peppercorn. Later came hearty Dongbei stews, Xinjiang cumin-infused lamb and other regional cuisines that challenged my assumptions about what Chinese food could be. Retracing the origins of the meals I grew up taking for granted led me through migration, colonial history and displacement. The dishes on our table were not simply family favourites, but the accumulated record of ancestors who moved from the northern Chinese plains into Guangdong, then to northern Vietnam, left for Britain and eventually returned to China through me. Long before I understood any of this, I had already been eating it.

title: Growing number of ex-officials enter race for Hong Kong Election Committee seats
description: Influx of former senior officials into Election Committee race will broaden representation and boost body’s legitimacy, observers say.
content: A growing number of former senior government officials have joined the race for seats on Hong Kong’s Election Committee, a trend observers say will enhance the prestige and legitimacy of the body tasked with choosing the city’s next leader. As the two-week nomination period draws to a close next Tuesday, the Registration and Electoral Office had received 1,115 nominations for 982 elected seats on the Election Committee as of Friday. The poll will be held on November 22 and the elected members will join 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies, to select Hong Kong’s next chief executive in March next year. A notable feature of this year’s nominations is the number of former senior officials returning to politics. Former justice minister Rimsky Yuen Kwok-keung is standing in the legal subsector, while former health minister Sophia Chan Siu-chee and former undersecretary for health Libby Lee Ha-yun, now the Hospital Authority’s chief executive, are running in the medical and health services subsector. Former innovation and technology secretary Alfred Sit Wing-hang, former development secretary Eric Ma Siu-cheung, and Wai Chi-sing, former managing director of the Urban Renewal Authority and former permanent secretary for development, are contesting seats in the engineering subsector. Former financial services and treasury secretary Ceajer Chan Ka-keung, now chairman of WeLab Bank, is seeking re-election in the finance subsector. Simon Li Tin-chui, former head of the Civil Aviation Department and now president of the Hong Kong International Aviation Academy, is running in the transport subsector, while Annie Tam Kam-lan, former permanent secretary for labour and welfare, is standing in the social welfare subsector. Veteran political commentator Sonny Lo Shiu-hing said the participation of more former officials would improve the committee’s diversity and legitimacy. “In the past, not many former officials took part in the election committee. Now, not only people from that particular sector are taking part, but also former officials … Their ministerial and government portfolios are broad, which will expand the breadth of election committee members,” he said. “This also enhances the competitiveness of the poll, which is beneficial to its legitimacy.” Lo added that former officials had an advantage because they enjoyed Beijing’s trust, which helped ensure political reliability while making the body more pluralistic. Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said including more former ministers with extensive political experience would enhance the prestige of the committee. He added that the trend reflected a broadening of officials’ career paths and would help attract new talent into public service. Although the ex-officials still have to compete in the election, Lau believed their networks, reputations and political experience accumulated during their tenure would give them an edge in their campaigns. As in previous polls, major developers have also entered the race, including billionaire Pacific Century Group chairman Richard Li Tzar-kai, Henderson Land Development chairman Martin Lee Ka-shing and Sino Land chairman Daryl Ng Win-kong, who are seeking re-election. Other prominent candidates standing include Jardine Matheson executive chairman Benjamin Keswick, Hysan Development executive chairman Irene Lee Yun-lien, Sun Hung Kai Properties executive director Christopher Kwok Kai-wang and CK Asset executive director Justin Chiu Kwok-hung. Hopefuls also include New World Development executive director Sonia Cheng Chi-man and Shangri-La Group chairman and CEO Kuok Hui Kwong. Several leading bankers have also submitted nominations. They include HSBC’s vice-chairman for Hong Kong, Diana Cesar; HSBC co-CEO for Asia and the Middle East David Liao Yi-chien; Citi Hong Kong CEO and head of banking Aveline San Pau-len; Standard Chartered Bank’s CEO for Hong Kong, Greater China and North Asia, Mary Huen Wai-yi; and Bank of East Asia co-chief executive Adrian David Li Man-kiu. Other high-profile candidates include table tennis player and Olympic medallist Doo Hoi-kem and blind singer Michelle Siu Hoi-yan. The 1,500 members of the committee will be responsible for nominating and selecting the city leader next March and electing 40 of the Legislative Council’s 90 members in 2029. The committee comprises five sectors representing 40 subsectors, ranging from commercial, financial and professional groups to labour unions, district representatives and Hong Kong representatives on national bodies. The full list of nominations can be seen here.

title: ‘Hot economics, cold politics’: why China gave nod for expanded Japanese trade trip
description: Allowing more executives to visit Beijing shows that China aims to use economic leverage to pressure Tokyo, experts say.
content: Beijing’s decision to allow a bigger Japanese business delegation to go to China next month may be cause for some optimism but “hot economics and cold politics” will continue to dominate the strained relationship between the two countries, observers say. Kyodo news agency reported this week that Beijing had agreed to allow the Japanese Business Federation – the country’s most influential business lobby, also known as Keidanren – to expand its delegation coming to China next month. The group will increase from five people to around 20 for a trip that could coincide with this year’s Apec summit in Shenzhen in mid-November. The notice from Beijing came soon after former foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya’s trip to the Chinese capital with a 50-member Japanese trade delegation. Iwaya met with China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and Vice-Premier He Lifeng. The talks were the first publicly disclosed meeting between senior Chinese leaders and a Japanese politician since bilateral ties were rocked in November last year by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s suggestion that an attack on Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan. In the aftermath of Takaichi’s comments, all intergovernmental exchanges between Beijing and Tokyo were suspended. Several legislative and business groups have visited China since then to try to break the diplomatic impasse. But analysts warned that Beijing’s green light for the expanded Keidanren visit may be less about rapprochement and more about applying pressure, suggesting that Beijing was leveraging economic channels to force Tokyo into concessions. Rintaro Nishimura, a Tokyo-based senior associate at The Asia Group, said Beijing’s selective engagement with business delegations was designed to apply pressure through business interests. “Engaging in dialogue with business delegations while keeping government dialogue at a minimum is a clear signal that Beijing wants businesses to influence Tokyo’s decision-making on China policy,” Nishimura said. “It’s clear that Japanese businesses would prefer a stable business environment with Japan’s largest trading partner, and the political situation is not ideal for that.” Japanese media have reported that the planned Keidanren trip is aimed at building momentum for an even bigger visit to China in March, which could involve three of Japan’s main business groups – Keidanren, the Japan-China Economic Association and the Japan Chamber of Commerce and Industry. It’s clear that Japanese businesses would prefer a stable business environment with Japan’s largest trading partner Rintaro Nishimura, The Asia Group Senior executive figures from Nippon Steel, Nippon Life Insurance and Mitsubishi could join the trip in March, Japanese media reported. Since 1975, business delegations led by the Japan-China Economic Association have visited China annually, pausing only during the Covid-19 pandemic. Even when bilateral ties nosedived in 2012 after Tokyo nationalised the disputed Diaoyu Islands, which Japan calls the Senkakus, a scheduled visit was only postponed by a few months. The association planned a visit at the start of this year, but it was shelved due to challenges in securing enough meetings with Chinese government agencies and leaders. The parallel tracks of economic pragmatism and political antagonism would continue to underscore the countries’ relationship, with businesses navigating a relationship of increasingly overlapping commercial opportunities and national security concerns, experts added. “Economic activity has long remained subordinate to political considerations [for Beijing],” Hotaka Machida, a visiting senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics in Tokyo, said. He added that economic exchanges could help to improve the atmosphere, but changes in political leaders’ “messages or behaviours” and communication at the political level were necessary to spur a sea change in bilateral ties. This year, Chinese customs authorities extended processing and inspection windows for Japanese imports – particularly Japanese sake, foodstuffs and general goods – making it more difficult for the products to enter the country. Beijing also introduced export controls on several rare earth elements earlier this year, resulting in a drop in exports to Japan. Furthermore, it banned the export of dual-use goods, software and technologies to Japan’s military and related entities, while discouraging its citizens from travelling to Japan. Yet the persistence of business-led outreach reflects economic realities that neither Beijing nor Tokyo can easily ignore. “Japan and China have developed mutually intertwined economic relations over the previous decades,” Machida said. “More Chinese companies are getting aware of the importance of cooperation with Japanese companies in the context of going abroad and global, and they are not willing to be affected by the bilateral relationship. “Without development in the political sphere, it is difficult to foresee substantial results through economic exchange alone.” Nishimura added that a flurry of visits made by Japanese businesses showed that China remained a vital economic partner, and such visits were meaningful in shaping Tokyo’s thinking about China. “But the diplomatic relationship has shifted to one about managing issues and pursuing mutually beneficial outcomes – something that is becoming increasingly challenging as each side’s concerns overlap with core national security interests.” Machida said Iwaya’s high-level reception in Beijing was seen by the Chinese counterparts of Keidanren as an indication that Beijing was willing for economic exchanges with Japan to go ahead. “But this change cannot be regarded as a big change in the Chinese stance on Japan.” When meeting Iwaya, Wang Yi called for a “correction” rather than a “withdrawal” of Takaichi’s remarks, which has been interpreted by some in Japan as representing a subtle diplomatic opening by Beijing. Nishimura said Wang’s message could be a “nudge to signal Tokyo” that the ball was in its court to change bilateral relations for the better. “Given how uncertain geopolitical dynamics are today, it would be better [for Beijing and Tokyo] to have managed peace than a relationship of animosity and tension.”

title: Trump mocks popularity of Mohammad as Muslim name during campaign speech
description: Rights advocates have repeatedly criticised Trump for rhetoric that they say demonises Muslims, immigrants and ethnic minorities.
content: US ⁠President Donald Trump made a ⁠joke about the popularity of ⁠the name Mohammad in the Muslim world as he mocked Iran’s presidency during a campaign speech on Friday. “You know, if you’re in doubt about somebody’s name from the Middle East, just say ‘Mohammad’,” Trump told a ‌crowd in Dalton, Georgia. “You have about a 65 per cent chance. ‘Hello, Mohammad.’ I’ve done it for years now. I’ve never been wrong.” Mohammad is one of the most common male names among Muslims, who often name their sons after the Prophet Mohammad, the founder of Islam. Trump made the comment as he was discussing Iran during ⁠a rally in a hangar at Dalton Municipal Airport in Georgia, where he campaigned for Republican ‌political candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. “Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president,” Trump said, then ‌pretended to ask several people named Mohammad whether they wanted the job. ⁠Masoud Pezeshkian has been ⁠president of Iran since 2024. The Georgia crowd gave the joke a muted response. Rights advocates and Muslim ‌advocacy groups have repeatedly criticised Trump for rhetoric that they say demonises and mocks Muslims, immigrants and ethnic minorities. He has ‌escalated ‌such rhetoric during the midterm campaign season, particularly against Somali and Muslim Americans including ‌Muslim Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat ⁠who came to the US as a Somali refugee. Trump repeated his vow that Iran would ⁠never get a nuclear weapon, seven months after the United States and Israel launched a war on Tehran aimed in part at crippling its nuclear ‌programme. A critical swing state, Georgia is unlike many of the solidly Republican places that Trump has recently visited, including Alabama, Montana and Tennessee. That means gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman, and Senate candidate Mike Collins, a two-term congressman, are likely to need more than Trump stalwarts to defeat their respective Democratic opponents, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and Senator Jon Ossoff. When protesters decrying the Trump administration’s immigration policies interrupted his speech, the president suggested that “left-wing loser” Ossoff had paid the demonstrators to cause a scene. An annual report by ‌the Council on American Islamic Relations released earlier this year attributed rising Islamophobia in the US in part to Trump’s crackdown on immigration and pro-Palestinian protests during his second term. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Japan’s Takaichi sends offering to controversial Yasukuni war shrine
description: Takaichi, who routinely visited the Shinto shrine before becoming prime minister, has refrained from doing so since taking over the helm.
content: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Saturday sent a ritual offering to Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo, regarded by Japan’s neighbours as a symbol of the country’s past militarism, at the start of its three-day autumn festival. Takaichi, known as a conservative who routinely visited the Shinto shrine before becoming prime minister a year ago, was unlikely to visit the shrine during the festival, a source close to her said, amid strained relations with China and relatively stable ties with South Korea. The shrine honours Japanese leaders convicted as war criminals by a post-World War II international tribunal, along with millions of war dead, and has long been a source of diplomatic friction with China and South Korea. Takaichi sent a “masakaki” offering of evergreen twigs to the shrine for the biannual event in her capacity as prime minister, following the practice of her predecessors. Meanwhile, economic and fiscal policy minister Minoru Kiuchi paid a visit to the shrine on Saturday. Kiuchi made a similar offering, as did House of Representatives Speaker Eisuke Mori and Senate President Masakazu Sekiguchi. “I offered my heartfelt condolences and paid homage to the spirits of heroes who gave their precious lives for the nation and renewed my pledge to renounce war,” Kiuchi told reporters after the visit. A cross-party group of Japanese lawmakers plans to visit the shrine on Monday. While serving as a minister, Takaichi had visited the shrine during its spring and autumn festivals and on August 15, the anniversary of Japan’s 1945 surrender in the war, but she has refrained from doing so since becoming prime minister on October 21 last year. During this year’s war-end anniversary, Takaichi bowed twice, clapped twice and bowed once again towards Yasukuni Shrine, in an apparent act of Shinto worship from a distance, after arriving at the venue for the government-sponsored memorial ceremony across the road. The last Yasukuni visit by a sitting Japanese prime minister was in December 2013 by Shinzo Abe, Takaichi’s political mentor. Yasukuni enshrined 14 Class-A war criminals, including wartime prime minister General Hideki Tojo, who was executed in 1948 for crimes against peace, in 1978. Past visits to the shrine by Japanese politicians have sparked harsh criticism from neighbouring Asian countries. Japan invaded large parts of China before World War II and colonised the Korean peninsula from 1910 to 1945. Tensions between Tokyo and Beijing continue after Takaichi said in November last year that an attack on Taiwan could prompt Japan’s Self-Defence Forces to act in support of the United States. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Japan and South Korea have improved their ties in recent years following progress on the issue of alleged wartime forced labour, resuming the practice of reciprocal visits between their leaders in 2023.

title: Reflections | How China’s macabre practice of human sacrifice in burials came to an end
description: In China, elites were buried with human companions as far back as the Neolithic period. Over time, symbolic figures replaced real people.
content: Archaeologists have long found a disturbing pattern in the graves of ancient rulers: the dead were sometimes accompanied by other dead. Around royal tombs, the remains of people – who appear to have been killed specifically to follow their masters into the afterlife – lie alongside precious objects and weapons. A new study from Egypt has brought this practice back into the news. At the ancient royal cemetery of Abydos, archaeologists re-examined the skulls of people buried around the tombs of early rulers. They found signs of serious injuries on many of the skulls, including fractures consistent with powerful blows inflicted around the time of death. The pattern suggests that at least some of these people did not simply die naturally and happen to be buried near their rulers. They may have been deliberately killed to accompany them into the next world. Human sacrifice was part of funerary rites of the powerful across the ancient world, from Egypt and Mesopotamia to Europe and the Americas. The practice was also a feature of elite society in ancient China, where it rested on the belief that the dead continued to exist in another world and would need servants, attendants and companions. Archaeological evidence suggests it appeared as early as the Neolithic Liangzhu civilisation (3300BC-2300BC) in the Yangtze River Delta, but it reached its most extensive and systematic form during the Shang dynasty (1600-1046BC). The royal cemetery at Yin, the last capital of the Shang, provides some of the clearest evidence. Excavated tombs contain the remains of large numbers of people who appear to have been deliberately killed and buried alongside their masters. The victims included prisoners of war, servants and members of the ruler’s household. In some royal burials, the scale was extraordinary. The tomb of King Wu Ding, who died in 1192BC, contains the remains of 164 human victims, while other Shang royal tombs have yielded dozens or even hundreds. The Zhou dynasty (1046-256BC) inherited the practice, but its scale was greatly diminished. By the Spring and Autumn (770-476BC) and Warring States (475-221BC) periods, intellectual and moral attitudes were changing. The killing of people for the benefit of the dead increasingly attracted criticism, and clay and wooden figures began to serve as symbolic substitutes for living attendants. In 384BC, the state of Qin formally abolished human sacrifice. The enormous mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang (259-210BC), the first emperor who unified China, with its famous Terracotta Army, is perhaps the most spectacular illustration of the new solution: instead of sending a real army to the afterlife, the emperor could take an army made of clay. Later dynasties saw rare instances, mainly in royal and aristocratic circles, when people killed themselves, or were killed, to follow their masters or husbands to the grave. Even as late as the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), palace women could still be compelled to follow an emperor in death. Emperor Yingzong of the Ming dynasty formally abolished the practice of sacrificing palace women in 1464, but isolated cases persisted into the early Qing period (1644-1911). Finally, in 1673, the Kangxi Emperor prohibited servants from dying with their masters. Archaeological and written records reveal a dramatic reduction in the scale of human sacrifice after the Shang dynasty, even as isolated cases persisted for centuries before the practice finally disappeared. A practice once capable of claiming hundreds of lives in a single royal burial gradually gave way to symbolic substitutes: first wood and clay figures, and eventually the paper effigies burned for the dead today.

title: Malaysia’s shoppers love Chinese e-commerce. But is the bargain worth it?
description: Pinduoduo’s arrival has thrilled bargain hunters, even as direct e-commerce shipments price out local firms and waste chokes landfills.
content: In hindsight, it was only a matter of time before Esha Yusof joined the growing ranks of Malaysian shoppers being drawn to Chinese e-commerce giant Pinduoduo. Esha is a relative newcomer. She signed up in July, more than half a year after the platform launched in Malaysia – and has been smitten with it ever since. Rock-bottom prices, a vast range of products and seamless payments through a popular local e-wallet make it easy for the 32-year-old to spend an average of 500 ringgit (US$122) a month on everything from home decor and kitchen supplies to fashion and stationery. “Most items are much cheaper than in the Malaysian market. It’s hard to compare because they come directly from factories or warehouses in China,” said Esha, who works for a competing e-commerce site. Delivery takes at least two weeks, far longer than many of the app’s local rivals. But that delay has had the opposite effect to the one you might expect. “With the long wait, it makes more sense to buy almost every week, so the wait feels shorter when parcels keep arriving every week,” Esha said, adding that she still used local platforms for urgent orders. Many Malaysians are now doing the same. Since the app’s launch in the country last December, social media has been awash with delighted shoppers showing off their hauls, from smartphones to sofas, rolls of toilet paper and even bags of cement. But surging demand for goods shipped direct from China through the likes of Pinduoduo often comes at the expense of local retailers and manufacturers that struggle to match their Chinese rivals’ deep discounts. Meanwhile, the millions of parcels flooding into Malaysia and the waste they create are testing the limits of the country’s ability to collect and dispose of it all. Disappearing margins Pinduoduo is far from the only e-commerce platform active in Malaysia. Small local businesses, especially in physical retail and manufacturing, have already seen their margins shrink amid intense competition from earlier entrants like Lazada and Shopee. Still, the app’s arrival has prompted an outcry from local businesses, who complain that direct shipments from far larger competitors in China have unfairly priced them out of their own market. Shipping direct from China is the strategy that has powered Pinduoduo’s growth since its founding in 2015, giving more established e-commerce players such as Taobao and JD.com a run for their money. Lazada and Taobao are subsidiaries of Alibaba Group, which also owns the South China Morning Post. Pinduoduo built its empire on a simple premise: allow consumers to pool their purchases into bulk orders directly with factories and wholesalers to get better deals. “The influx of low-priced products from foreign e-commerce platforms is putting tremendous pressure on Malaysian retailers, wholesalers and manufacturers, particularly micro and small businesses,” said Chin Chee Seong, president of the SME Association of Malaysia, an umbrella body for the country’s small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Chin said operational costs had shot up by 80 per cent or more this year, citing an SME Association survey in April that found 76 per cent of respondents reported being hit hard by rising fuel and energy costs, with 45 per cent bracing themselves for a cash-flow crunch over the next six months. “Malaysian SMEs are being squeezed from both sides – rising operating costs and increasingly aggressive price competition. Many simply cannot afford to keep reducing their prices,” he said. A widespread slump in SME activity would be disastrous for the economy. Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises account for nearly 97 per cent of all registered businesses in Malaysia and employ around 8 million people, roughly half the entire workforce. “As local shops and businesses lose sales or cease operations, they will reduce hiring and reduce demand for supporting services such as banking, advertising, accounting and other business services,” said Lee Heng Guie, executive director of the Socio-Economic Research Centre, a Malaysian think tank. “Closed shops result in commercial and retail outlet vacancies, and the landlords may be forced to reduce rents to attract fewer available tenants, reducing property income.” Retailers of imported consumer goods, from fashion to general merchandise, are likely to be the most immediate and visible casualties. Yet economists warn that the greater danger is that posed to Malaysia’s all-important manufacturing sector. The rapid shift to buying electronics, apparel, footwear, cosmetics and furniture from overseas sellers could cause local factories to permanently lose their share of the domestic market, said economist Yeah Kim Leng of Sunway University. “The distinction matters because retail displacement can be transitional as traders pivot to services or niche products, whereas manufacturing capacity, once lost, is far harder to rebuild,” he said. Trashy dilemma E-commerce began taking root in Malaysia in the mid-2010s, but demand truly exploded during the Covid-19 pandemic, when strict movement restrictions forced millions of people to do their shopping online between 2020 and 2022. That habit has become even more deeply ingrained in the years since. An estimated 900 million parcels were delivered across Malaysia in 2025, according to the latest available government data, a multifold increase from the 52 million a decade earlier. The appeal for e-commerce players is clear. A February note from equity and market analysts at Kenanga Research forecast that the value of e-commerce merchandise in Malaysia would reach 1.5 trillion ringgit in 2027, up from 1.2 trillion ringgit in 2024 (US$268.9 billion). But this penchant for hyper-consumption could overwhelm the country’s capacity to deal with the vast amounts of rubbish generated. Malaysia’s 135 landfills are already close to capacity, handling an average of 39,000 tonnes of solid waste daily, according to government figures from last year. Any increase in e-commerce shipments will almost certainly add to the growing trash pile. The government has also pointed to a low recycling rate of 37.9 per cent of recoverable materials and poor waste separation practices at household and local council levels. “The growth of online shopping, driven partly by competitive prices and convenience, has increased the volume of packaging waste,” said Randolph Jeremiah, vice-president of the non-profit Environmental Protection Society Malaysia. “Although some online platforms, retailers and manufacturers have begun reducing packaging and switching to more recyclable materials, such as paper filling instead of polystyrene, these efforts may not be sufficient to keep pace with rising consumption.” A raft of government policies has been introduced in an attempt to modernise solid waste management, broaden the use of sustainable plastics and materials, encourage recycling and reduce waste generation. But grand plans meant little if the problem was not addressed at the source, said Jeremiah, adding that efforts to reduce unnecessary packaging by a handful of platforms, retailers and manufacturers needed to be extended across the entire supply chain. “At the same time, consumers should make more informed purchasing decisions and practice proper waste separation and recycling,” he added. Fair play The overseas e-commerce blitz is not all bad news for Malaysia, however. For some, losing business in one area opens up opportunities in another. “We had a 40 per cent drop in demand over the past few months for small parcel deliveries because a lot of people can just get their items delivered straight to their homes,” said a local courier operator who asked not to be named. “But demand has gone up for shipments of bigger items like furniture and kitchenware and even machinery for factories and construction.” An early investment in warehouse space in Guangzhou, China’s outbound shipping hub, made all the difference for them in securing a steady stream of clients, the operator said, adding: “A lot of our customers nowadays buy direct from factories in China, so having our own warehouse there makes it easy to arrange shipments for them.” Even entrepreneurs worried about the fallout from direct-to-consumer sales from overseas enjoy the savings as shoppers. “You must also look at the other side [of the coin]. The consumer is very happy. I’m very happy that I can buy my socks for just 12 ringgit,” said the SME Association’s Chin. What local businesses wanted was not to stop Pinduoduo and other foreign e-commerce giants selling in Malaysia, he said, but a level playing field. Under Malaysian law, a 10 per cent sales tax on low-value goods took effect in 2024 to cover imported items worth 500 ringgit or less. But trade groups say many direct overseas shipments slip through untaxed, giving foreign sellers an edge.
