Local industries have also warned that directly shipped items such as electronics and toys are not subject to Malaysian safety regulations and may endanger consumers. “Malaysian businesses should not be disadvantaged simply because they pay local taxes, employ Malaysian workers and comply with our laws and regulations,” Chin said. “We must protect consumer interests without sacrificing Malaysian businesses, jobs and our domestic manufacturing ecosystem.” When unveiling next year’s budget on October 9, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the government would introduce an e-commerce bill at the next parliamentary sitting to close legislative and enforcement loopholes and protect local businesses from unfair competition. But the government must do more than just draft a new law, said Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman. “Malaysian entrepreneurs are not asking for government handouts. They are not asking for competition to be shut down entirely. They only want fairness, so that competition is fair,” he told parliament during the budget debate. “[Foreign e-commerce sites] need to establish a local presence. Work with local businesses, open offices and hire workers in this country … I am proposing a middle ground, not shutting them down entirely.”

title: Olympian-turned-singer Fong hoping to inspire Hong Kong by swimming from city to Macau
description: Alex Fong will tackle the 35km from Lantau Island to Hac Sa Beach next month, with the aim of raising HK$10 million for underprivileged.
content: Alex Fong Lik-sun will have to battle jellyfish, unpredictable weather, and some unknowns of the deep when he dives into the sea next month for his latest charity challenge. The Olympian-turned-pop star has set his sights on a 35-kilometre cruise from one of Hong Kong’s outlying islands to Macau, in the hope of raising HK$10 million (US$1.3 million) on behalf of InspiringHK Sports Foundation. Fong will start his attempt to cross the Zhujiang River Estuary from Peaked Hill on Lantau Island at 5am on November 19, with Hac Sa Beach in the neighbouring special administrative region his ultimate destination. He hopes that around nine hours later he will have completed his mission, one designed to benefit children from disadvantaged backgrounds and those with special educational needs. A former national team swimmer, Fong once owned 11 Hong Kong records. At his only Olympics appearance in Sydney in 2000, he smashed the city’s records in the 200m backstroke and the 400m individual medley, times that stood for 21 years, until they were broken by Hayden Kwan and Peter Whittington, respectively. Records are not the driving force behind next month’s ‘Legacy in the Waves’ swim, which was the idea of Fong’s younger brother William Fong Yuen-ming, who leads the foundation’s board of directors. Rather, his younger sibling had appealed to Fong’s new status as a father, reminding him that the charity was “all for the next generation. You are a father now; you should really do this”. The singer and actor said he saw a similarity in the murky waters separating the points on land at which he would arrive and depart, and the challenges sometimes faced by those he was trying to raise money for. “Yes, it’s almost a straight line, but I can hardly see what’s ahead of me when I am swimming in the sea,” said the 46-year-old, who has run his Hong Kong Swimming Academy since 2018. “I rely on the kayakers guiding me from the sides. Grass roots and SEN children probably don’t have the brightest futures when they are born either. “But they have loving families around them, and with the help of charitable organisations, they can have a better future. This is what makes it more meaningful for me, like some extra motivation.” An ambassador for the foundation since 2015, Fong said he still remembered an incident from years ago, when a pupil attending a running event had arrived wearing a pair of leather shoes because his family “could only afford one pair of shoes. These are my only shoes; I don’t have any sports equipment”. Contrast that, Fong said, with those from better backgrounds with more resources who consider sport to be a hobby and “something that they can stop doing at any time”. “But for some underprivileged children, being given a sport to train in can build their confidence and give them a platform to prove themselves,” he added. “They will cherish it very much, which is why they will be very focused and dedicated and give it their all. So this charity swim is a perfect fit with my identity as a new father. “Sports have changed so much about my personality and confidence, and I firmly believe in their power to change a person in so many ways.” Little was needed to convince the foundation that Fong was the right man to take on the swim, with CEO Iris Wong describing the actor and singer as “a true role model”. “Our lives, our very existence, are like an ocean, full of unpredictable changes,” Wong added. “Whether the weather is good or the current is strong, there are always various difficulties. The message that our charity swim conveys to young people is about overcoming difficulties and doing things well, no matter what.” This will not be the first charity swim that Fong has undertaken, although there was a gap of 15 years after he ended his professional career when he avoided anything to do with a pool. Then, eight years ago, he was “trying to find something to do”, and eventually ended up swimming around Hong Kong Island for the first time in 2019, albeit after 18 months of training. The 45km solo swim helped raise more than HK$10 million for a programme that aimed to provide clean water for over 1 million people in Southeast Asia. His time of 10 hours, 43 minutes and six seconds was a record, surpassing the previous best set by Simon Holliday two years earlier. It opened a new door in the sport, and he took part in two further relay swims around the city, for former school, St Joseph’s College, in 2021 and 2025. It was not only the open sea that Fong was diving into, as he returned home from the World Masters Championships in Singapore with three gold medals last year. Fong also revealed he hoped to smash Holliday’s record next month, after the Hong Kong-based Briton finished the same course 12 years ago, finally exiting the water in 10 hours, 20 minutes and 30 seconds. “I want to break that record, of course, but it’s a real leap into the unknown, swimming for more than 30km,” Fong said. “Firstly, you won’t be able to train for such a distance, and the course won’t necessarily be available. “There are also many unknowns in the ocean, be it jellyfish, rough seas, and the physical discomforts your body will experience. You might get heatstroke or sunburn, bump into something, or fail to replenish your fluids properly.” Fong added that he expected to swim more than 100km this month to prepare, and that he would begin to cut down his training load in the two weeks before the event, focusing more on massaging his body and managing his diet. And it won’t just be him and the kayaks in the water, there will be support swimmers too, although unlike Fong they will be able to wear wetsuits. “I won’t think about getting out of the water at the finish line when I start my swim next month. Without a watch, I’ll have a mental clock and just stick to my pace,” he said. “Unlike my first around-the-island swim, there are no buildings on the land to gauge my progress this time. “I’ll probably be looking forward to my refreshments every hour. For the first three hours it’ll probably be energy drinks and snacks, and then normal food afterwards. “Maybe congee with minced meat or pancake balls with syrup – just some high-carbohydrate foods along with things I crave that are easily absorbed.”

title: North Korea says it tested new torpedo with AI tech
description: Artificial intelligence was used for target detection and guidance in the new high-speed precision-guided weapon, state media says.
content: ⁠North Korea conducted an underwater ⁠test of a new torpedo weapon system on Thursday to verify technological upgrades, state news agency KCNA reported on Saturday, describing the test as a success and a significant step in ‌the country’s naval development. The test verified propulsion technology developed through more than 180 tests over the past five years, KCNA said, adding that artificial intelligence was used for target detection and guidance in the new high-speed precision-guided torpedo. The test is the latest ⁠in a run of North Korean weapons launches. It comes amid heightened tensions ‌on the Korean peninsula, as both Koreas race to develop weapons capable of evading missile defences. The test was part ‌of routine defence research activities aimed at advancing the country’s ⁠weapons systems, ⁠KCNA said, adding that it showed improvements in propulsion efficiency and the performance of the torpedo’s ‌rocket propulsion system. The latest test came after North Korea said it had tested two types of submarine-launched strategic ‌cruise missiles on Wednesday to verify its navy’s mission capabilities and ‌the reliability of its war deterrent. Pyongyang has been seeking to develop modern ⁠missile submarines alongside ballistic and cruise missiles, test-launching them from various platforms, including ⁠an ageing submarine. Meanwhile, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test-firing of a domestically developed hypersonic missile last week. Seoul’s ‌test of a hypersonic ‌glide vehicle, a manoeuvrable weapon that can change course during flight, came days after North Korea said its leader, Kim Jong-un, had also overseen a test of an intermediate-range hypersonic missile.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong’s media regulations must allow room for innovation
description: As the government seeks to strengthen the Hong Kong media’s global reach, it could consider adopting a lighter, smarter regulatory approach.
content: Hong Kong’s media stands at a crossroads, and how the city chooses to regulate it will shape not only the health of the industry but the vitality of “one country, two systems”. A robust, commercially viable media sector strengthens the city’s international standing. Licensing laws and regulations must therefore be treated as an integral part of efforts to build an ecosystem in which local media can grow, not just domestically but overseas. Technological disruption has upended the economics of news and entertainment. The advertising-based model that sustained legacy outlets for decades has lost ground. It’s not all bad news. The proportion of Hong Kong respondents paying for online news increased by nearly five percentage points to 22.2 per cent, and the most common way to pay remains a direct, ongoing digital subscription or membership to a news service rather than through an aggregator. But for local Chinese-language media especially, subscription income remains stubbornly thin. Against this backdrop, recent government moves are welcome. Hong Kong’s first five-year plan pledges to “strengthen the global reach of the mainstream media”. The government has also promised to help local media expand their networks overseas. This week, the Executive Council renewed the free-to-air licences of TVB, HK Television Entertainment and i-Cable Hoy for 12 years. The broadcasters have committed to investing a combined HK$9.45 billion over the first six years. In return, they gain greater flexibility to air programmes in non-designated languages, reduced airtime for designated programmes, and streamlined administrative and complaint-handling procedures intended to lower compliance costs. The Communications Authority will consult the public on amendments to the industry’s code of practice before the end of the year, with implementation targeted for mid-2027. It says the review will adopt a principle-based model and remove outdated and prescriptive requirements, including, it is hoped, rigid controls on advertising placement. These are sensible steps, but they should not be the last. The Broadcasting Ordinance dates back to 2000. Today, free-to-air broadcasters compete with internet platforms that face few equivalent obligations. Loosening some regulations can ensure fairer competition. Lee has vowed to ensure regulations keep pace with the times. The promised review of the ordinance should be comprehensive, extending from radio and television to online media. There is a balance to strike. Licensing conditions exist to protect the public interest, and the new subtitling and local production requirements have merit. Lee’s mandate to tell “good stories of Hong Kong” may not always sit comfortably with commercial imperatives. Content that travels abroad succeeds only if it is credible to audiences spoilt for choice. Professional editorial judgment, not prescription, is what earns attention overseas. To enhance public support for overseas expansion, alongside funds for the development of various sectors such as the movie industry, officials should consider an arm’s-length fund, to be independently administered. Such a media fund could facilitate outlets’ upgrades and technology adoption – especially the development and application of artificial intelligence, which requires substantial investment amid tech-driven competition – and extend partnerships and host meaningful events to connect Hong Kong and the world, without compromising their integrity and independence. Besides a foreign audience with growing interest in information about China, including Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area, there are millions of ethnic Chinese living overseas. Many have a lasting affinity for the city and are a natural audience for our media, which provide Chinese- and English-language services and events. The markets of Southeast Asia and Belt and Road Initiative countries offer room for expansion. Bilingual and well versed in both Chinese and international norms, our media are well placed to serve them. A lighter, smarter regulatory hand can remove obstacles for businesses to innovate. The government should press ahead with an overhaul, so that Hong Kong’s media can thrive at home and compete abroad. But local media must also do their part to stay competitive besides asking for regulatory relaxation.

title: Hong Kong rugby player and cancer survivor on why screening is key even for young and fit
description: Being athletic didn’t stop Tsang Sin-yan from getting lymphoma. Now she raises awareness with the charity Phenomenally Group.
content: When Sonia Chandiramani lost her mum to ovarian cancer in 2017, she found solace in an unexpected place: the rugby pitch. “I was spending five nights a week with my team, plus weekends,” says the 33-year-old Chandiramani, who had been playing since she was 14. “It was my second family. “At her funeral, people showed up, and it meant a lot,” she says. “It’s just a reminder that there are more families than just your family.” Two years later, Chandiramani and some fellow players established Phenomenally Group, a Hong Kong-based charity dedicated to cancer awareness, proactive healthcare and providing accessible early screening services. Today, Phenomenally Group runs two main programmes: Phenomenally Pink, focused on breast cancer awareness, and Phenomenally Mo, targeting men’s health. It offers six types of screenings – breast, thyroid, upper abdomen, lower abdomen, testicular and prostate – covering cancers that rank among Hong Kong’s 10 most common. While October is the official breast cancer awareness month, Chandiramani says every month should be cancer awareness month, and for all types of cancer. “It is an all-year topic,” she says. “It’s not like it matters more this month, this month or this month.” Bringing screenings to the sports field Phenomenally Group is on track to deliver close to 5,000 screenings in 2026 alone, and its pop-up clinics have appeared at tournaments, corporate offices, shopping malls and even the Rugby Sevens at Kai Tak Stadium. “A full-time sevens rugby player, who was barely 31, came by,” Chandiramani says of the Rugby Sevens screening. “He came to our check-up, and he didn’t know he was going to be picking up on something – and he picked up an early diagnosis of testicular cancer.” Two months later, the player reached out again for a second scan and then attended its Men’s Health Month event to thank them personally. “People think you’re still healthy because you’re doing sports,” Chandiramani says. “Athletes are the lowest-hanging fruit – they’re conscious about fitness and performance, but their actual health check-ups are something sports institutions don’t necessarily take care of.” The next screening will take place at The Mills in Hong Kong’s Tsuen Wan neighbourhood over the weekend of October 24, 2026, and will be accompanied by a community run. Phenomenally Group has gradually expanded beyond rugby to work with lacrosse, cricket and netball communities, all the while regularly hosting events with She Runs Collective – a Hong Kong women’s running community – as well as a coffee club initiative called Fill Your Cup. Its rugby team, Valley Pink, is supported by Societe Generale Valley Rugby Football Club, Phenomenally Pink and Rugby For Good. For Chandiramani, the work is deeply personal; it is a continuation of the support her rugby community provided during her mother’s illness. “This is obviously a love letter,” she says. “It’s something that continues.” Taking warning signs seriously The diagnostic blind spot surrounding young, active individuals is something Phenomenally Group member Tsang Sin-yan knows all too well. Tsang, 34, is a Hong Kong international rugby union player who represented the city during its first-ever Women’s Rugby World Cup appearance in 2017. In early 2024, she began experiencing severe chest pain and gasping for air, but put the symptoms down to exhaustion as a result of her demanding schedule as an athlete and physical education teacher. “I would be teaching and feel like I couldn’t get enough air,” she says. “I’d finish a sentence and be gasping. But I didn’t suspect anything – I just thought I was too tired or the weather was too humid.” When the pain became unbearable in April, she took a taxi to accident and emergency, only to be told her X-ray showed nothing serious. “They said I was young and played rugby, so it was probably just a muscle strain,” Tsang says. “They didn’t even want to give me Panadol.” She returned home empty-handed, and for the next two months, could not sleep lying flat. “I would get up in the middle of the night to do foam rolling, just to make the pain manageable,” she says. She travelled to Japan with the Hong Kong squad for training, where a physiotherapist tried acupuncture, still believing it was a soft tissue injury. Nothing worked. I thought, I’m young, I play sports, I eat well – what could go wrong? Tsang Sin-yan, rugby player One summer night in June, she got up in the early hours to stretch again and immediately collapsed. “I stood up and fainted,” she says. “I had no awareness of it at all.” Her roommate called an ambulance. When paramedics arrived, they saw her rugby kit and her age. “They said, ‘You’re young, you play sports, you’ll be fine,’” Tsang says. “They kept asking if I actually wanted to go to get checked, and it seemed like they were trying to convince me not to.” At the hospital, a doctor told her that there was a shadow on her chest. She was admitted that night, marking the beginning of a month-long stay filled with tests and inspections before a definitive diagnosis emerged. In early July 2024, doctors confirmed she had Stage 1B primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBCL), a rare and aggressive subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) that accounts for just 2 to 4 per cent of all NHL cases and predominantly affects young women. Tsang’s tumour was located dangerously close to her heart and major vessels, making the biopsy difficult. Her treatment plan involved six rounds of intensive chemotherapy, each requiring a six-to-seven-day hospital stay with continuous infusion. Between rounds, she had roughly three weeks at home to recover. What kept Tsang going, she says, was her identity as an athlete. “I didn’t cry when I was diagnosed,” she says. “I think it’s because I’m so goal-oriented. Every day I was working towards something. I told myself: I have six rounds to do, I’m going to complete them, and then I’ll get better.” After the first round, her hair fell out in clumps; she temporarily lost her voice after a catheter was inserted near her vocal cords; and eating became a daily battle, to the point where all bland foods like white rice and tomatoes made her vomit. Tsang broke the treatment down into manageable milestones, continuously telling herself that “small successes make a difference”. “Before each hospital admission, I’d have a nice meal,” she says. “When I was discharged, I’d celebrate with another good meal. I focused on my routine, on making each round as smooth as possible.” The long road back to the pitch Tsang’s Hong Kong teammates and coaches rallied around her, gifting her a rugby ball signed by her loved ones, as well as letters and a cookbook with healthy recipes, full of bookmarked pages that they thought she would like. She finished her final chemotherapy round in early November 2024. But the road back to rugby was far from straightforward. When she was cleared to return to training mid-2025, she started with gym work, then cycling, then running. “My heart rate had changed completely,” she says. “Before cancer, my resting heart rate was 59. After chemo, it was hitting 80, 90, even 100 with the slightest exertion.” While she has made incredible progress – she played and won her first competitive rugby match for Kowloon RFC in January 2026, 18 months after her diagnosis – she is not yet satisfied with her recovery. She recently completed a Bronco fitness test – a running-based fitness test with a total distance of about 1.5km (0.9 miles) designed to assess aerobic capacity and speed endurance – in seven minutes and 30 seconds. That was two minutes slower than her personal best. “Compared to how I trained before, it’s really far off,” she says. “These things sometimes, during this period, are actually quite frustrating. I know I need to be kinder to myself.” Tsang has become an advocate for regular health checks, sharing her story at community events and on social media. Her message is simple: take your symptoms seriously. “I never had a full body check before,” she says. “I thought, I’m young, I play sports, I eat well – what could go wrong?” For more information on Phenomenally Group’s Pink Run on Lantau Island on October 24, its Tackle Cancer Walk/Run to raise funds for cancer on the final weekend of October 2026 and on getting free or subsidised ultrasound cancer screenings, visit phenomenallygroup.com. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: China warns EU not to ‘fantasise’ on trade approach as Brussels confirms new ‘kill switch’
description: Latest flare-up suggests danger of trade war between two of the world’s three biggest economies has far from de-escalated.
content: Beijing warned Brussels not to “fantasise” that taking a hard line will force it into concessions, as the bloc confirmed plans for a gung-ho new kill switch that will allow Brussels to “immediately” kick China out of the single market. Exactly a week after the two sides struck a surprise deal to restrict the volume of hybrid cars China ships to Europe, the flare-up suggests the threat of a trade war between two of the world’s three biggest economies has far from subsided. “The EU should not fantasise about gaining benefits through pressure, nor should it underestimate China’s determination and ability to safeguard its own interests,” read a Ministry of Commerce statement on Friday. The statement was in response to reports from the South China Morning Post and other media that Brussels believed that tough talk from Europe had forced Beijing to make a deal. This came after the two biggest EU members – France and Germany – jointly proposed a new weapon aimed at hitting back at Chinese coercion and economic distortions. In the run-up to this week’s European Council summit, it was often said that the “two-track” approach to China – dialogue and the threat of action – had worked. “The claim that ‘pressure from the EU side proved effective’ is entirely groundless,” the ministry said, in a stern rebuke. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen confirmed plans to develop the new weapon on Friday during a press conference after the European Council summit in the Belgian capital. This will come alongside intensified dialogue with Beijing. “Building on this [French-German] paper, we’ll develop a new instrument for decisive action by limiting access to the single market where it is in the union’s interest – fast and immediately,” said von der Leyen. She had pitched the idea to the bloc’s 27 leaders a day earlier, where it gained unanimous support. Among the strongest critics of China’s policies at a lunchtime debate was German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, a remarkable turnaround for a leader who, barely half a year ago, called for a free-trade agreement with Beijing. Now, EU officials say Berlin wants to be “driving the train” on the EU’s China policy. German officials on the margins of the summit confirmed there would be no going back now, speaking with an air of ebullience that all other member states had rallied round the so-called “kill switch” idea. Von der Leyen confirmed that more trade safeguards are coming, allowing quotas and tariffs to be implemented on broad groups of products. While she did not say which sectors would be chosen, von der Leyen told the leaders chemicals and machinery were the priorities, the SCMP reported on Thursday. French President Emmanuel Macron said in his post-summit press conference that the bloc should target chemicals, plastics and ferroalloys. Official sources said they want to propose the new instrument in December as part of a package that also includes a diversification instrument, which would force companies to reduce their reliance on Chinese supplies, and a solidarity mechanism to compensate those hit by Beijing’s retaliation. They said it would be used if Beijing coerced Europe, for example by cutting it off from rare earth mineral exports in response to the ramping up of EU trade probes. The instrument would need the support of 13 of 27 member states to be triggered. However, it is acknowledged that making it compliant with World Trade Organization rules will be challenging. Von der Leyen described “remarkable unity” in the room – a sea change from previous summits, where leaders were often so unlikely to agree on China policy that the topic was frequently kicked off the agenda. Other EU national leaders lent their support to the “two-track” approach towards China during Thursday and Friday’s summit. “There’s a complete consensus around the table that we need to work on that problem, problems of currency depreciation, subsidising overcapacity and organising critical dependencies and weaponising these dependencies are problematic,” said Belgian Prime Minister Bart de Wever, at a press conference. “The advantage of all being in the negative [trade balance] is we finally all agree that this cannot go on like this,” said the Belgian premier, adding that the “very good debate” was a “step in the right direction”. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda told reporters on the summit’s margins that the so-called “kill switch” would be used to “restrict the entry of Chinese products into the European market, including a complete closure of our market”, should “China engage in certain unfair trade practices”. “That would be an extreme measure, a drastic instrument,” Nauseda added.

title: Oregon teen gunman was tackled by ‘heroic’ teacher then shot by students’ father
description: Attacker Griffin J. John II, an ex-student at the school, killed four people and had 44 rounds remaining when he died.
content: A teacher threw her phone at the teenage gunman who killed four people at an Oregon junior school, then tackled and fought with him – probably saving lives before he was shot by a father who followed him into the building, police said Friday. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called the teacher’s actions “heroic” during a news conference and said she was not injured. He identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II and said all of the victims were shot in the same classroom. Authorities said John had been a special needs student at the school and had attacked a classroom with special needs students. He fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed, Krantz said. “Everyone wants to know why, including us,” he said. “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.” The police chief added that police are also still trying to determine how the shooter obtained the gun. The attacker’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, told reporters outside her apartment near the school that if she could have done something to prevent the shooting, she would have. “I miss my boy,” Nickerson said, sobbing and crying, according to The New York Times and CNN. “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.” She declined to say how the 16-year-old obtained the pump-action shotgun and did not comment further when other outlets knocked on her apartment door later. In a 2020 interview with the local news station KTVZ, Nickerson identified the boy, then 10, as a participant in a special needs programme run by the school district. It was called Nest, for Nurturing Empathy, Safety and Trust, and aimed at helping students experiencing intensive behavioural and social skill challenges. Nickerson said he struggled trying to learn from home during the pandemic. In a statement read to reporters Friday, Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, shot the gunman in Thursday’s attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend. She said he is the father of two girls at the school. “He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said, noting that her son is a lifelong resident of Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 in central Oregon. She said her family was asking for privacy “during this difficult time”. The youngest victim, just five years old, was a fast runner and fearless climber who loved reading and his stuffed animals, his aunt said on Friday. “He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” said his aunt, Swan Sheridan, who described him as “a little ball of energy from the moment he was born”. US President Donald Trump on Friday praised the actions of a “great hero” who he said “took care of business”. “It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump told reporters at the White House, adding the tragedy would probably have been much worse. At a news conference hours after Thursday’s attack, Governor Tina Kotek – without naming Giamanco – said he had followed the gunman into the school and helped end the rampage as police began arriving. “Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” Kotek said. Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighbourhood filled with newly built homes. Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartener at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that someone pursued the shooter. “I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. “I’m feeling very grateful.” The shooter was found dead in the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Krantz said. He shot through locked doors to get inside, police said. The children who were killed were ages five, eight and 11, Krantz said. Another seven-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, he said Thursday. The wounded teacher was identified by family as Becky Drury. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on social media that she had injuries to her left arm and right hand and was recovering from surgery. The attacker used a pump-action shotgun bought by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to publicly discuss the investigation. Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent. The first emergency call came early in the afternoon from someone outside the school who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, the police chief said. More emergency calls came from inside the school, police spokeswoman Sheila Miller said. The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said. The school has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education. Classes and all other activities were cancelled on Friday for schools across Bend, a tourism and outdoor recreation hub that has ballooned in population and sits about 200km (125 miles) southeast of Portland. The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the US this year, according to a database maintained by Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.

title: New details emerge in US investigations of Chinese-American scientists over China links
description: House committee on China releases results of investigations into some 30 scientists as chairman pushes for stricter research security rules.
content: A US congressional committee has released details of investigations into dozens of researchers, many of them Chinese-American, revealing the scale of government scrutiny sweeping academia over alleged links to China. The documents – running to hundreds of pages – were released alongside a separate report by the House Select Committee on China. Titled “How to Stop China’s Theft of Taxpayer-Funded Research”, the report pushes back against arguments by universities and academic groups that tighter research security rules threaten academic freedom. According to the committee, the records derive from investigations by the National Science Foundation’s Office of Inspector General (NSF OIG), including details of previously unreported cases. The NSF, which funds much of America’s basic research, declined to comment. The files detail investigations into about 30 researchers over undisclosed Chinese payments, talent programme contracts and grants. It is unclear whether all the cases were pursued under the China Initiative – launched during US President Donald Trump’s 2017-2021 first term – though many date to the programme’s active years around that time. American universities routinely receive foreign grants and corporate sponsorships to support research and development. Department of Education data shows US universities have reported nearly US$70 billion in foreign gifts and contracts since 1986, including more than US$5.2 billion in 2025 alone. Critics argue that those investigations, with the China Initiative being the most high-profile among them, selectively and unfairly targeted scholars of Chinese descent by criminalising these standard international academic partnerships. The July 2024 suicide of Jane Wu, a Chinese-American neuroscientist, highlighted the most chilling impact of investigations against researchers suspected of having undisclosed ties to Beijing. Wu, who worked at Northwestern University, came under scrutiny in a National Institutes of Health crackdown on undisclosed foreign ties that ran alongside the China Initiative. Her case is not among those in the NSF files. “The records document cases involving undisclosed foreign appointments, compensation from [Chinese] institutions, participation in Chinese talent recruitment programmes, conflicts of commitment, and repeated failures to disclose information required by federal research funding agencies,” the House Select Committee on China said in a statement this week. The cases had varying outcomes. Most ended without criminal charges, though some were referred for criminal investigation. A few resulted in prosecutions and convictions, some of which were later overturned. Some researchers left their university posts or left the United States altogether. In many cases, the NSF’s inspector general recommended suspending grants or barring future federal funding to the researchers involved. The stated aim of the China Initiative, launched by the Department of Justice in 2018, is to counter alleged Chinese economic espionage and theft of US intellectual property and research. Hundreds of researchers – many of them of Chinese descent – are believed to have been investigated under the programme before it was closed in 2022 by then president Joe Biden, after critics said it had failed to uncover espionage while subjecting Chinese-American researchers to heightened scrutiny. One of the cases not previously detailed publicly is that of Chu Xiang-qiang, a former Wayne State University physicist who is now an associate professor at City University of Hong Kong. NSF accused her of spending long stretches in China and holding additional employment there that she had not disclosed. A since-withdrawn American Physical Society abstract listed her as affiliated with the graduate school of the Sichuan-headquartered China Academy of Engineering Physics, which conducts Chinese nuclear weapons research. Chu rejected the NSF allegations in an emailed response to the South China Morning Post, saying she had always disclosed employment held in China. She also insisted that her move to Hong Kong “was a personal decision and had nothing to do with [the investigation]”. “I joined the Graduate School of China Academy of Engineering Physics [in Beijing] as a full-time professor, which was fully disclosed during the years I worked there,” she wrote. “I resigned from the US university and returned the unused portion of the funding to NSF before any action was taken to suspend it. I have no knowledge of whether NSF barred me from serving as a reviewer or panellist for three years.” The NSF’s inspector general recommended in April 2019 that Chu be barred from serving as a reviewer or panellist for three years. The publication of the investigation comes as House committee chairman John Moolenaar pushes for tighter research security rules and the passage of the Securing Innovation and Research from Adversaries Act. The proposed legislation would bar federally funded researchers from collaborating with entities on US government restricted lists, permitting exceptions only under rare, case-by-case waivers. A 2021 survey by Chinese-American advocacy group the Committee of 100 and the University of Arizona found that 42.2 per cent of scientists of Chinese descent felt racially profiled by the US government. Haipei Shue, president of the non-profit organisation United Chinese Americans and an outspoken civil rights activist, said the newly released documents immediately brought back “troubled memories” of the early days of the China Initiative. “Though the initiative was shut down, the fallout has been immense,” he said. “It eroded trust by causing Chinese-Americans to feel their patriotism was questioned, chilled global scientific collaboration, and triggered academic ‘decoupling’ between the US and China.” If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Martial arts action franchise Street Fighter is back … but who is its star Callina Liang?
description: The Canadian actress features alongside Andrew Koji, Noah Centineo and Jason Momoa in the latest outing for the video game adaptation.
content: Despite two much-maligned live-action film adaptations inspired by the popular fighting video game Street Fighter in the past several decades – its namesake 1994 film and Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li (2009) – it seems Hollywood has yet to give up on the franchise. Paramount Pictures just premiered its live-action reboot film Street Fighter starring Andrew Koji, Noah Centineo, Jason Momoa and Callina Liang. The film’s plot follows the game’s fighter avatars Ryu (Koji) and his estranged adopted brother Ken Masters (Centineo), who are reunited when Chun-Li (Liang) enlists their help for the World Warrior tournament. Chun-Li is perhaps one of the most recognisable video game avatars. Introduced by Street Fighter in 1991 as its first playable female character, Chun-Li has become a pop culture symbol, and even inspired Nicki Minaj’s hit 2018 track “Chun-Li”. Here’s everything you need to know about actress Callina Liang, who portrays the fan-favourite character. What is Callina Liang’s background? Liang was born in Vancouver, Canada, and spent her early years living in Beijing, China. In 2010, Liang relocated to Sydney with her father for his work. During her time there, Liang attended the Australian International School and earned the “Top in the World” Outstanding Cambridge Learner Awards for her IGCSEs in Drama. After living in Australia for four years, Liang moved to Singapore where she continued to pursue acting at LASALLE College of the Arts and took part in a number of stage productions. How did Callina Liang get into acting? In 2019, Liang moved to New York and landed her first television series role in the 2022 British teen drama show Tell Me Everything. In 2024, Liang appeared in the psychological horror film Presence starring Lucy Liu and Julia Fox. That same year, Liang landed her first starring role in the film Bad Genius, where she portrays a student who runs a school-wide cheating scheme to help her schoolmates pass their exams. Who is Callina Liang dating? Liang has sparked dating rumours with her Street Fighter co-star Noah Centineo. They were seen holding hands at the Street Fighter premiere after-party at The Bird Streets Club in Hollywood on October 12. Neither has confirmed their relationship status. Centineo, known for his performance in To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before, was last rumoured to be dating Zoe Kravitz in 2025. Kravitz got engaged to Harry Styles in April this year.

title: 8 top grooming tips, featuring Romeo Beckham’s hair, Dior and Chanel
description: Diptyque, Tom Ford, Salt & Stone and Orb Oils all bring their own sensory magic to this season’s round-up.
content: Here are ways to keep yourself looking good and feeling fresh as we move into the cooler months. Our latest round-up of product releases from the world of beauty covers all the bases, from skincare and hair, to fragrances. Plus there’s a look at the undeniable cool of David Beckham’s second son, Romeo. Chanel Fans of Bleu de Chanel – the cooling scent remains a highly coveted men’s fragrance – can spray on the matching deodorant (HK$320) to ensure a harmonious olfactory profile throughout the day. Dior Dior Sauvage Extrait, perhaps the most highly concentrated scent in the entire Sauvage catalogue, isn’t a fragrance for the understated or those looking to play it safe – it offers unparalleled staying power and extreme longevity on the skin. Industry veteran Francis Kurkdjian, Dior’s perfume creation director, has enriched this nocturnal, woody formulation with new signature ingredients including Vietnamese oud essence, Indonesian patchouli, Madagascan vetiver and Virginia cedarwood. Diptyque Products from Diptyque’s Les Rituels de Soin body care collection will elevate your dawn and dusk routines – establishing a grounding ritual we could all benefit from. Modelled after ancient bathing traditions, the line features morning and evening sets that bring nourishing body cleansers, made in collaboration with French perfumer Natalie Gracia-Cetto, together with beauty tools and even decorative accessories. Combine the Dry Body Brush and Natural Soft Body Sponge, for example, to gently exfoliate and lift away surface impurities. Hermès Hermès’ H24 refreshing deodorant spray (HK$440) is also available in an alcohol-free stick format for those with sensitive skin. It carries a crisp, aromatic scent of clary sage, narcissus and rosewood. Orb Oils Melbourne-based perfumer Orb Oils has teamed up with Evan Mock’s co-founded lifestyle label Wahine on a scent that evokes a day spent on O’ahu’s North Shore – highlighting notes such as bergamot, grapefruit, cedarwood, patchouli and pink pepper. The 29-year-old skateboarder, who is half Filipino and was raised in Hawaii, has also branched out into acting and modelling for various luxury brands. This limited edition fragrance is nestled next to a flipbook and a keychain in a lidded tray inspired by the lunch plates ubiquitous in O’ahu. Romeo Beckham There is a genuine coolness to Romeo Beckham’s deliberately mismatched hair. The British model sported bleach-blonde locks along with his natural goatee and moustache for the Willy Chavarria men’s spring/summer 2027 show in Paris this summer. The look frames your face and signals a casually rebellious, “couldn’t care less” attitude. Salt & Stone Those wanting a fresh addition to their bathroom shelves should turn their attention to Salt & Stone, available at Lane Crawford. The California-based brand was founded by former professional snowboarder Nima Jalali and specialises in bath and bodycare products infused with invigorating, nature-inspired scents. Check out their refreshing body washes, which rinse off easily and are free from parabens or other potential irritants. Tom Ford Fragrance minimalists will be particularly drawn to Tom Ford’s Oud Wood all-over body spray (HK$715), which features an exotic woody blend of cardamom, pink pepper, patchouli, amber, oud and tonka bean.

title: Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs moved to new prison after reports of luxury lifestyle behind bars
description: Combs was allegedly having fellow inmates cook, clean and give him massages, and using a contraband phone to view an ex-girlfriend’s nudes.
content: Sean “Diddy” Combs has been moved to a federal prison in Pennsylvania after reports that the hip-hop mogul was living the high life and was injured in a fight at his New Jersey lock-up, a person familiar with the matter said on Friday. The federal Bureau of Prisons is transferring Combs, 56, from FCI Fort Dix to FCI Allenwood Low, a low-security facility south of Williamsport and about 250km (155 miles) west of New York, the person said. The person was not authorised to speak publicly and did so on condition of anonymity. The Bureau of Prisons confirmed the move but provided no further details. The agency said it does not discuss conditions of confinement for anyone in its custody, including reasons for transfer, for privacy, safety and security reasons. “Decisions about inmate placement are made by the BOP, and we are not in a position to speak to the circumstances surrounding this transfer,” said Combs’ spokesman, Juda Engelmayer. “Sean remains focused on moving forward, and we hope that his time at the new facility will be productive and without unnecessary disruption.” Combs is serving a four-year, two-month sentence for his conviction last year on prostitution-related charges for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters. The case featured harrowing testimony about violence and sex parties he called “freak-offs”. It was a forceful reckoning for one of music and entertainment’s most influential figures. Last month, NBC News reported that Combs was continuing to enjoy aspects of his millionaire lifestyle at FCI Fort Dix, smuggling in Hennessy, having fellow inmates cook, clean, make his bed and give him massages, and using a contraband cellphone to view social media and an ex-girlfriend’s nude selfies. On Wednesday, TMZ reported that Combs was injured in a fight with another inmate at Fort Dix and had to be taken out of the prison for treatment. In a rare rebuttal, the Bureau of Prisons refuted TMZ’s report, telling Associated Press: “The story you are referring to is false and did not happen.” In the wake of the NBC report, Combs was placed in the prison’s special housing unit, a heavily secured part of the facility away from the general population, for inmates with disciplinary issues or security concerns. He has also been docked 41 days of good-conduct credit, pushing his release date back to March 2, 2028, according to the person familiar with the matter. In April, the 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments in Combs’ bid to overturn his conviction and sentence, which his lawyers argued was too harsh. The court has yet to rule.

title: Paraguay’s tech minister defies Beijing sanctions, says Taiwan ties ‘not up for negotiation’
description: Gustavo Villate, blacklisted alongside Belize’s foreign minister, suggests the move was retaliation for excluding Huawei and ZTE from 5G.
content: Paraguay’s technology minister said on Thursday that sanctions imposed on him by Beijing over his country’s ties with Taiwan would only accelerate joint projects with the island. Gustavo Villate, who heads the Ministry of Information and Communication Technologies, wrote in a lengthy social media post that the relationship with Taipei would “never be on the negotiating table”. He also suggested that Beijing had acted to protect Chinese telecoms suppliers kept out of Paraguay’s networks. “This sanction is, at its core, a certification that what we have been doing since 2023 is the right path,” he wrote. Beijing has been steadily peeling away Taiwan’s diplomatic allies, persuading Honduras to switch recognition in March 2023 and Nauru in January 2024. Paraguay is the only country in South America that still recognises Taipei, and its farm lobbies have long argued that ties with Beijing would open the Chinese market to Paraguayan soybeans and beef. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with the mainland, by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise it as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to change the status quo by force and is committed to supplying the island with defensive weapons. China’s foreign ministry announced on Monday that it would freeze any property Villate holds in China, bar people and organisations there from dealing with him and deny him entry to the mainland, Hong Kong and Macau. It imposed the same measures on Francis Fonseca, the foreign minister of Belize, another of the 12 countries that still recognise Taipei. Taiwanese media described it as the first time Beijing had sanctioned officials of Taiwan’s allies. The measures are largely symbolic, since officials from those countries rarely travel to China, and Villate said he held no assets there. They were issued under the Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law, a 2021 statute Beijing has mostly used against Western politicians and defence firms. The orders called the two men “anti-China politicians” acting out of personal interest, but made no reference to 5G or artificial intelligence. The announcement came two days after Taiwan’s national day, and a day after Villate posted a greeting on social media to the “Government of the Republic of China (Taiwan)”, the island’s official name. Foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said the two ministers had acted as “pawns” of Taiwan’s attempt to seek independence by relying on outside forces. She accused them of visiting the island, hosting Taiwanese officials, whom Beijing regards as separatists, and spreading “false information” about Chinese cyberattacks. That charge goes back to July, when Villate’s ministry and the US embassy in the Paraguayan capital, Asuncion, said a joint review had found several threat actors linked to the Chinese government inside state networks. A similar review in November 2024 had pointed to the China-based group Flax Typhoon. Beijing called the July accusations groundless in a statement issued by its consulate general in Sao Paulo, Brazil. US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said Washington opposed “coercion and aggression by China against countries in our hemisphere”. China had not responded publicly to Villate’s post as of Friday morning. Huawei and ZTE kept out of 5G In his post, Villate said the pressure on Paraguay was rooted in “technical decisions, not political ones”. He cited a 5G auction in which the state demanded guarantees that no foreign government held undue influence over network builders. He said the same test now applied to a data centre financed by the Inter-American Development Bank and to AI, because “supply chain security is national security”. Run by telecoms regulator Conatel last year, the auction required bidders to present a report from a Paraguayan diplomatic mission in the country where their radio equipment was made. In practice, the rule excluded Huawei Technologies and ZTE, since Paraguay has no diplomatic relations with Beijing. Tigo and Personal, the country’s two largest mobile operators and both heavy users of Chinese equipment, stayed out of the bidding, and licences went to Claro and Nubicom. Villate returned to that process when he asked why Beijing would react at all. “If the suppliers left out by our technical, transparent and impartial standards were truly independent private actors, why would a foreign government respond by sanctioning a Paraguayan official?” he wrote. AI venture with Taiwan Much of the rest of the post was devoted to Yguazu Digital, an AI data centre to be run jointly by the two governments, agreed in Taipei in May in the presence of Paraguay’s President Santiago Pena and Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te. Villate said it could become “bigger than Itaipu was in its time”, a reference to the hydroelectric dam Paraguay shares with Brazil. The first phase is far more modest, a 10-megawatt facility that his ministry has estimated will cost more than US$300 million. Villate told Bloomberg Linea in June that Taiwan would supply Nvidia chips while Paraguay would provide state land and cheap hydropower, with the centre due to open by late 2027. He said he would also accelerate other joint projects, including a national health information system that he said already runs in 1,000 public facilities. Paraguay and Taiwan will mark 70 years of diplomatic ties next year. “Freedom is not negotiated, frozen or sanctioned,” he wrote. “Paraguay is a democracy that decides for itself.”

title: Americans see China more positively than Russia, but both near bottom of G20: Pew report
description: New study finds Americans have ‘very cold view’ of Russia, while their opinion of China remains more negative than positive.
content: As the US prepares to host the G20 summit in Miami in December, Americans’ views of participating countries vary, with China viewed more favourably than Russia, although both rank near the bottom, according to the latest Pew Research Centre report. Americans gave China an average rating of 37 out of 100, compared with 27 for Russia, Pew found in a report released on Friday. Canada, Australia, Japan and Italy received the warmest ratings, with average scores in the mid-to-high 60s. “Russia stands out for its especially icy ratings: 51 per cent of Americans have a very cold view of the country, significantly more than the third or so who have very cold views of China,” Pew researchers wrote. The G20 brings together major advanced and emerging economies to discuss global economic cooperation and policy challenges. Beyond China, Russia and Saudi Arabia, which received an average rating of 36, the countries surveyed included the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Mexico, South Korea and Brazil, all of which received more positive average ratings. Indonesia, Argentina, South Africa, India and Turkey received cooler average ratings, generally ranging from 45 to 48. Americans’ views of China remain more negative than positive, although they have warmed significantly since 2021. In an earlier analysis published ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s September visit to Washington, Pew found that China’s average rating had risen to 37 from 28 in 2021. Xi is also expected to attend the G20 summit in Miami, where he could meet Trump for a fourth time this year, following their expected meeting during the Apec summit in Shenzhen in November. Pew uses a “feeling thermometer” to measure attitudes towards countries, asking respondents to rate their feelings on a scale from zero, meaning as cold and negative as possible, to 100, meaning as warm and positive as possible. A score of 50 represents a neutral view. Pew’s broader polling has found that views of China have improved in many countries. In several countries surveyed, particularly middle-income nations, China is also more trusted than the US and the European Union to regulate artificial intelligence. Although Australia had one of the highest average ratings, Canada received the largest share of “very warm” ratings in the latest survey, with 48 per cent of Americans expressing very warm feelings towards their northern neighbour. This comes despite trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa. However, Americans’ views of Canada have cooled slightly since 2018, with its average rating falling from 71 to 67. The shift has been driven largely by Republicans, particularly those aged 50 and older. Democrats’ ratings have remained broadly unchanged since 2018, according to the report. Political affiliation and age also shape views of other countries. Democrats generally rate countries more warmly than Republicans, while younger adults tend to give warmer ratings than older Americans, including for China and Russia. The report draws on four US surveys conducted between January and September 2026, involving more than 10,000 Americans.

title: China pushes back as US lawmaker seeks blacklist of universities and tech labs
description: Beijing condemns targeting of institutions including Tsinghua University, as critics warn restrictions may undermine scientific cooperation.
content: A Republican lawmaker is requesting the Pentagon blacklist 58 Chinese universities and 62 technology labs as national security threats, a move Beijing calls Cold War-style overreach and critics warn could freeze US-China scientific collaboration and ultimately undermine American innovation itself. In a letter to US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth, House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar urged the Pentagon to add several prestigious Chinese institutions – some linked to Nvidia, Apple and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) – to the Section 1286 list. “The Select Committee has identified PRC [People’s Republic of China] research institutions with documented affiliations, formal agreements, oversight relationships, or other significant ties to China’s defence research and industrial base,” the select committee wrote in an October 14 press release, accompanying the letter. The letter was dated October 1, but was made public this week. In response to the letter, Chinese embassy spokesperson Liu Chang said that China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security and the politicisation or instrumentalisation of what he called normal scientific, educational and academic exchanges. “Scientific innovation and academic development require open cooperation; restricting normal research exchanges will ultimately harm the interests of all parties, including US researchers and institutions,” he said. “The US side should abandon the Cold War mentality and foster an open, fair and non-discriminatory environment for educational, scientific and people-to-people exchanges between China and the United States.” Tsinghua University among elite institutions proposed for blacklist Among the institutions listed by Moolenaar is Tsinghua University in Beijing, an elite organisation whose alumni cover top political and business leaders. The university’s board executives include those from major US tech giants, including chipmaker Nvidia, technology giant Apple and semiconductor company Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). Nvidia, Apple and AMD did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A large number of the targeted institutions focus on critical technology sectors, including artificial intelligence, semiconductors and quantum computing, according to the letter. The letter also urged the department to add 14 Chinese Academy of Sciences Institutes “identified as core CCP [Chinese Communist Party] defence partners” as well as “22 foreign malign talent programmes, and the China Scholarship Council and affiliated scholars” to the Section 1286 List. Many of the institutions have recruited numerous scholars serving in the United States in recent years to strengthen their basic research. For example, Omar M. Yaghi, the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry laureate, joined Tsinghua University in July this year to lead a new AI-driven research centre. It remains unclear whether similar appointments will still be possible if Moolenaar’s list is adopted. The letter also requests that the China Scholarship Council (CSC) be included on the list because “it requires sponsored students to report to PRC embassies or consulates every three months, detailing their academic progress” and subjects students to mandatory political/ideological guidance sessions abroad. The South China Morning Post has contacted Tsinghua University, Peking University and several CAS institutes on the list; none has officially replied so far. Created under the 2019 National Defence Authorisation Act, the list identifies foreign institutions and talent recruitment programmes that “present national security risks to the US research enterprise”. Moolenaar’s push follows the expansion to 88 mainland Chinese organisations, including civilian universities Fudan University and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, when the US Department of Defence last updated its research watch list in July. Historically, the list has focused on People’s Liberation Army academies and institutions tied directly to the defence industry, but Washington has increasingly broadened its push against unwanted Chinese influence. This reflects the committee’s view that the talent and research systems associated with military-civil fusion are no longer confined to institutions traditionally designated as national defence academies. Geoff Wade, senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said Tsinghua is one of the educational institutions “most tightly linked with China’s military aspirations”, calling the inclusion on the Section 1286 List “clearly warranted”. “Tsinghua University is assessed by ASPI’s China Defence Universities Tracker as very high risk due to its extensive defence research activities, focus on armaments science research, secret-level security credentials, ties to the military – industrial complex, and IT infrastructure allegedly linked to cyberattacks,” he said. US targeting of Chinese universities may impact future scientific collaborations Meanwhile, some critics and researchers worry that widening the blacklist to include prominent civilian universities could significantly affect broader scientific collaborations between the US and China. Zhou Mi, a scholar at Tsinghua University’s Centre for Strategic and Security Studies, told Hong Kong-based newspaper Wen Wei Po that such blockade measures have obvious limitations. According to Zhou, US blockades ignore the realities of modern technology, which requires international labour sharing and large-scale market adoption to succeed. Rather than cutting China off from global scientific networks, Zhou contends “the restrictions will, on the contrary, drive other nations to partner with Beijing while locking American tech firms out of critical foreign opportunities”. Zhu Ying, director of the Centre for American Studies at Southwest University of Political Science & Law, shared a similar idea in an interview with Global Times in August. “In addition to expanding [the 1286 List], the US side’s controls on scientific research cooperation with China are also continually expanding, which has already created a chilling effect in US academic circles,” Zhu said. “Such moves will weaken the United States’ own ability to attract talent and undermine the open research ecosystem on which it relies to maintain its advantages.”

title: China bar exam row sinks Trump press secretary Katie Zacharia after just 5 days
description: The US president says he told his embattled spokeswoman, who has been on the job for a mere week: ‘I think you’re better off being happy’.
content: Katie Zacharia was “let go” as White House press secretary on Friday, a White House official said, five days into a tenure dominated by questions over her claimed legal career in China, where she said she had passed a bar exam. Her exit came on the same day Beijing invited her to visit China more often, responding to her remark that the country “doesn’t even have proper toilets”. US President Donald Trump said he had urged her to reconsider the job but denied firing her. “I told her: ‘I think you’re better off being happy, and I’m not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.’ There’s nothing easy about this stuff,” Trump told reporters outside the White House before flying to Georgia for a campaign rally. He added: “I said to her honestly, ‘If I were you, I’d reconsider … think about it. But I would reconsider.’ Maybe it’s not for her.” Asked whether he had fired her, Trump said: “No, no. I want her to have a good life.” He added: “She’s been brutalised by the media.” When Trump unveiled her appointment on Truth Social on October 9, he called her an attorney. On Friday, he said she had been hired to speak for the White House, not to practise law. A senior White House official told Fox News that Zacharia was “transitioning out” of the role. Her comment about toilets came in a conversation with conservative commentator Jack Posobiec on Thursday, as she recalled a sense around 2016 that the US was in decline and China was on the rise. “I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking, ‘How is China the next country on the horizon? They don’t even have proper toilets’,” she said. Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning responded on Friday with an invitation: “[We] welcome her to visit China more often when she has the opportunity.” Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile lists her as an associate in the Beijing office of Zhong Lun Law Firm, among China’s largest practices, between 2011 and 2013. She had moved to the country after law school for her husband’s job at an American private equity firm, a White House official told Military.com. Questions about that period intensified on Tuesday, when reporters asked where she had passed the bar and she answered: “When I moved to China.” She did not say which jurisdiction she meant. Foreigners may work at Chinese law firms but cannot qualify as lawyers in China. Speaking separately to Posobiec and to Fox News host Sean Hannity on Thursday, she conceded that she did not pass the California bar exam, which she sat in 2011 after completing her law degree at Pepperdine University, and that she holds no licence to practise in the US. “I knew I would be living in China and the result of the bar would be inconsequential,” she told Hannity. She told Posobiec there had been “a lot of misinformation” about the fact that she “labelled myself ‘lawyer’”. In a statement, Zacharia said she had “practised international transactional law, with all the appropriate credentials”. CNN reported it was unclear which credential she meant. A partner at Zhong Lun told The New York Times that the firm employs foreigners to help it navigate language and cultural differences and that “they are not practising Chinese law at any time”. He said her role would likely have resembled a paid internship. The White House had stood by her as recently as Wednesday, when communications director Steven Cheung told Fox News she was “uniquely qualified and whip-smart”. The jibe sat awkwardly with Trump’s deferential treatment of Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump made a state visit to China in May and welcomed Xi to Washington last month. The two leaders are expected to cross paths again at the Apec summit in Shenzhen next month and at the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December. Zacharia, who succeeded Karoline Leavitt, gave just one briefing. On Tuesday, she fielded questions from only three reporters before wrapping up after about 14 minutes. Leavitt’s debut ran close to 47 minutes. Zacharia told Hannity she had done her “very best” with little preparation, having been in the job for “less than maybe eight hours”. She had previously advised Trump Media & Technology Group on communications and, earlier this year, spent six weeks as a Department of Homeland Security spokeswoman. An unnamed White House official told MS NOW earlier this week that she needed to improve quickly or she would “break Scaramucci’s record”. Anthony Scaramucci lasted 10 days as White House communications director in Trump’s first term before being pushed out in July 2017.

title: From hospital, Pope Leo pushes Putin for ceasefire in contested Ukraine city
description: The call suggests the pontiff, who is recovering from a lung cancer operation, is still hard at work.
content: Pope Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin by phone on Friday, calling for a ceasefire in a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine, as he recovers in hospital from a lung cancer operation. The Vatican said that Pope Leo “expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance, and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population”. The surprise notice from the Vatican on Friday evening suggested that the recovering pope is still hard at work, despite Tuesday’s operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung. Residents of Oleshky in southern Ukraine are facing a worsening humanitarian crisis with shortages of food and medication as they are caught in the crossfire between Russian and Ukrainian troops. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk denounced on Friday a “desperate” situation in the city, calling on Russia to enable civilians to evacuate. In a note, the Kremlin said the two had talked and “a detailed explanation was provided regarding the Kyiv regime’s responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation” in Oleshky. The Kremlin said Putin also wished the pope a speedy recovery and stressed the “importance of Russian-Vatican cooperation in promoting unifying spiritual and moral values”. Earlier on Friday, Leo celebrated mass on the top floor of Rome’s Gemelli hospital, as seen in the first images of him released by the Vatican since the procedure. The images showed the 71-year-old Chicago-born pope in front of a makeshift altar in a room on the 10th floor, dressed in a green vestment. He appeared relaxed and in good form in the two photos released, standing with his private secretary, Peruvian priest Edgard Rimaycuna, at his side. “He celebrated with the medical and nursing staff of Gemelli, some people who were present there, who were clearly off duty at that moment,” the Vatican press office said, adding that members of the police also joined in. “He thanked all the staff, doctors, nurses, orderlies, for their service and their closeness to people, for their care of people’s fragility, and in particular, evidently, for the care, attention and treatment given to him in these days,” the press office said. The pope is expected to lead the traditional Angelus prayer on Sunday, but a Vatican source would not say whether it would be from the hospital or from the Vatican. The Angelus prayer is traditionally recited by the pope every Sunday from the window of the Apostolic Palace overlooking St Peter’s Square, to crowds of faithful gathered below. Doctors have said that the pope’s recovery after surgery is progressing normally, but ongoing tests will determine the future course of his treatment. His doctors said on Thursday that a chest X-ray indicated “good recovery of the operated lung”. On Friday, they said tests had shown “a steady improvement in his general condition”. The pope was now carrying out “his normal daily activities completely independently”, they said. Test results to determine whether the cancer has spread are still pending. The press office has not given an update on the possible timing of the pope’s discharge from hospital, repeating a doctor’s original statement that his recovery would take about a week. Were Leo to recite the Angelus from the window of the Gemelli hospital, it would not be a first for a pope. On February 6, 2005, 84-year-old John Paul II appeared at the hospital window while recovering from flu-related respiratory issues, as an aide beside him read out the Angelus prayer. Pope Francis on July 11, 2021, then 84, also gave the prayer from the hospital window after surgery on his colon, telling the assembled crowd: “I am glad to be able to keep the Sunday Angelus appointment, even here.” Also on Friday, the Vatican released a selection of letters and drawings sent by children at the hospital, including a picture of a tree “For Pope Leo”, complete with grass, sun and clouds, and a letter from an 18-year-old girl who wrote to Leo: “Better days will come for the both of us.” A seven-year-old boy named Angelo wrote that he, too, had been on the 10th floor of the Gemelli hospital for the past 36 days for a head operation. “My mother and I pray for you every night,” he wrote. “I hope you get well soon.”

title: Elon Musk unveils Tesla’s ‘flying’ car
description: The new Roadster has 10 nozzles and ‘ultra high-pressure air tanks’ to propel itself into the air and accelerate quickly on the ground.
content: Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a “flying” car, equipped with thrusters, during a live-streamed event at his SpaceX rocket company’s facility on Thursday. Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground. Musk revealed his new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas. During the demo, which was live-streamed on Tesla’s X account, the car launched from a steep steel ramp and performed a full barrel roll in mid-air before landing on its wheels. “Flying cars are real,” Musk said during the event. Musk said that while the vehicle’s “success is not guaranteed … it will probably work”. The two-seater sports car did not have a driver for the demo “to make sure we don’t kill anyone”, he added. Musk said the car was equipped with 10 nozzles and “ultra high-pressure air tanks” to propel itself into the air and accelerate quickly on the ground. The car can go from 0 to 100km/h (60mph) in under one second and reach a top speed of 370km/h (230mph). The tech billionaire described the development as “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company”, referring to Tesla and SpaceX. “It can basically fly like a rocket,” he said. Musk said the Roadster was “not necessarily a safety-optimised car” but it would “be an actual car that’s on the roads”. “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions, but there will be such a car that someone can own,” he added. Musk said the vehicle would go into production in 2028, though he is known for announcing release dates for his Tesla or SpaceX products that end up being pushed back by several years. The unveiling of the Roadster was postponed many times and had been expected for at least nine years. On Tesla’s website, interested customers can reserve a “Performance” Roadster model or a “Thrust” model, with boosted thrusters. The final sale price has not been disclosed. American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuted the first flying car prototype in 1917. But successful designs have become more seriously contemplated only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.

title: Zelensky asks EU for extra $79 billion to sustain Ukraine’s war effort
description: Kyiv warns annual wartime costs will hit US$174 billion as European leaders debate tapping frozen Russian assets to bridge funding shortfall.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Friday asked European Union leaders to provide Kyiv an extra 70 billion euros (US$79 billion) in funding next year to help it keep fighting Russia. “The war will cost 155 billion euros next year. And we need at least 70 billion euros more from you – for defence, for weapons and for our resilience,” Zelensky said in a speech at an EU summit in Brussels. “This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.” The EU - Ukraine’s biggest intentional backer – is currently paying out instalments of a 90-billion-euro loan for Kyiv that was set to help cover funding to the end of 2027. But the Ukrainian authorities have warned they will still face a major budget black hole as Russian strikes have battered the country’s economy. Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday the European Union would have to find more money to finance Ukraine. “We must do everything we can to help Ukraine through the winter and also to help next year,” Merz said at the start of a two-day summit of EU leaders in Brussels for crunch budget talks. “We will have to increase the funds again here in order to really assist Ukraine on a lasting basis.” The European Commission has said it is working with Kyiv to get a definitive figure for what is needed next year. Diplomats said EU foreign ministers could hold discussions on the issue in December. The talks around the new funding have reignited calls for the European Union to tap around 200 billion euros in frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine. But there seems little momentum on that front as Belgium, where most of the funds are held, remains opposed. The EU is meanwhile pushing other international backers of Ukraine – such as Britain, Canada and Japan – to come up with more money to help plug the gap.

title: In Focus | A US scholar’s take on how shifts in US-China relations are felt in a Tsinghua classroom
description: Denis Simon says this year’s Trump-Xi summits are helping to shape conversations at the Beijing university’s Schwarzman College.
content: China and America are talking again. There are leaders’ meetings, phone calls and a new channel for discussing artificial intelligence. Officials are cautiously trying to keep the relationship from veering into crisis. And yet some of the hardest questions remain untouched. Neither side is giving much ground on advanced chips, export controls remain a battlefield and neither Washington nor Beijing appears ready to slow its race to develop increasingly powerful AI.
