So what, exactly, does it mean to “talk” when the two countries are still competing over the technologies that will shape the next decade? It is a question Denis Simon is confronting in the classroom. A veteran US-China technology and higher-education strategist and former executive vice-chancellor of Duke Kunshan University, Simon is now teaching at Schwarzman College at Tsinghua University. The residential college and its Schwarzman Scholars programme were founded by Blackstone chief executive Stephen Schwarzman with the aim of bringing together future leaders from around the world. The programme, which celebrated its 10th anniversary last year, is described by some observers as one of the crown jewels in the bilateral relationship. Simon’s course focuses on China’s science and technology policy and innovation strategy, but the country’s relationship with the US will not stay in the background. He was teaching the second seminar of the course in Beijing when US President Donald Trump went to China in May, and the third when Trump’s Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, went to Washington last month. “That’s a kind of very interesting coincidence of time that gives the course a booster shot,” he said in an interview from Beijing. “The students are aware of both meetings. They’re much more informed about what’s going on.” His students are studying a relationship that has become deeply contradictory: Washington and Beijing are rebuilding channels of communication even as they narrow the space for technological and scientific links. The summits have not resolved that, but they have changed the atmosphere in the classroom. “These leadership meetings really created a much more positive environment,” Simon said. Before May, when the two sides were not talking, things were “topsy-turvy”, he said, adding that neither the Beijing visit nor the Washington trip was “a resounding big deal”. But what registered was simpler: the fact that the two leaders were talking and had met twice within six months. However, Simon said the “biggest change” was that some students “have become seemingly somewhat more cautious about revealing where they actually stand”. For example, an argument about export controls can sound like an argument about America, while a criticism of Chinese technology policy can become a political declaration. Even defending academic exchanges may raise questions about political loyalties. “They have become much better at distinguishing what they think from what they believe they ought to say in terms of political correctness,” he said. “That distinction matters enormously in a classroom. A good seminar depends upon intellectual risk-taking.” Over the past three years, the discussions have, in several respects, become more sophisticated even as students have become a bit more restrained. That is partly because while 40 per cent of students are American and 20 per cent Chinese, the others come from all over the world and are asking why they should have to choose between the two superpowers. “They are not merely referees,” Simon said. “They have their own interests.” He said they wanted American technology and capital, and they wanted Chinese markets, manufacturing capacity, infrastructure and technology. But they did not necessarily see technological alignment with either Washington or Beijing as inevitable, or desirable. In some ways, the students who are not American or Chinese are the ones who make the classroom genuinely international Denis Simon, Schwarzman College “In some ways, the students who are not American or Chinese are the ones who make the classroom genuinely international,” Simon said. Their presence has also pushed Simon to modify the course, including replacing older readings with newer ones that reflect what has happened since the leaders’ meetings. He no longer sees the technology relationship as a straightforward story of engagement followed by competition. Technology, economics, national security, industrial policy, scientific research and geopolitics have become too deeply entangled. The old idea of separating economic and security issues has largely disappeared. But Simon is equally wary of the opposite assumption: that everything involving China and technology should now be treated as a security issue. His students study semiconductors, export controls, AI, data governance, supply-chain resilience and industrial subsidies and are also asked some fundamental questions: where should the two countries compete, where should they put guardrails in place and where should they deliberately remain connected? Simon uses a red-yellow-green framework to assess the security situation, with red – covering areas where national security is at stake – being relatively straightforward. The same applies to low-risk green areas, including basic science and ordinary educational exchanges, but Simon added that yellow was the “really difficult category”, which meant proceeding with “conditions, transparency, safeguards or limits”. His concern is that Washington increasingly has a tendency to turn yellow into red. “Once that happens, the burden of proof shifts,” Simon said. “Instead of asking, ‘Why should this be restricted?’ we begin asking, ‘Can anyone prove that it is completely safe?’” That, he added, was not a sustainable basis for technology policy. The same tension is visible in the emerging AI channel between Washington and Beijing. Simon argued there was value in the new mechanisms for communication, but warned “communication” and “governance” were not the same thing. A hotline can provide a way to communicate after an accident or during a crisis, while dialogue can make contact habitual, but neither of these things settles questions such as who gets access to advanced chips, how frontier AI should be developed or what happens when the two sides disagree about the rules. He added: “Great-power relationships often advance in very small increments. The existence of a channel may look insignificant until the day you desperately need the channel.” The question is whether those channels become durable institutions or remain dependent on the political mood of the moment. Simon said that concern extended to the academic sphere, with universities are being increasingly being forced to “price geopolitical risk” into their calculations given the cost of being caught up in a political controversy. His recent experience at Duke University in the US sharpened these concerns where a China science and technology graduate seminar he had taught for several years was dropped even though funding was available. “What it told me is that the issue is no longer simply whether there is money to teach a course,” Simon said. “The institution is also asking: what is the reputational and political risk of teaching it? “If American universities stop teaching about China’s innovation system because the China issue has become politically difficult, we will create an extraordinary paradox: we will become less capable of competing with a country precisely because we have become less willing to study it.” Inside Schwarzman College, that question takes on another dimension. Students are watching China’s transformation from the “factory of the world” into an innovation power in electric vehicles, batteries, robotics, clean energy and AI. To many observers, this change appears sudden, but Simon, who has followed China’s development for 40 years, sees something different. “It really is part of a gestation period over time over the last 30-plus years in which China has steadily moved to make itself into an innovation-driven nation. So when people seem to be shocked, it’s that they haven’t been following this for 40 years, like I have.” For Chinese students, he said, this was not simply a story of national technological achievement but the economy where they had to find jobs. Many had assumed the factory era was behind them and that innovation was the next place to stand, but robotics and AI have complicated that assumption. They may be headed back into the factory, but not the one their parents left. Meanwhile, international students are confronting a different reality: China’s technological rise will shape the competitive environment in which they build their own careers. The question, Simon said, was no longer simply whether China could innovate, but “how China’s innovation trajectory will alter international S&T [science and technology] affairs, including the once dominant role of the US”. He said that ultimately that was what he wanted his students to understand, saying they should not expect a return to the US-China relationship of the 1990s or 2000s, while technological competition could not be wished away. The objective, instead, was to build enough “connective tissue” around the new relationship that competition remained competition without becoming continuous conflict. That is the wager behind institutions like Schwarzman College, NYU Shanghai and Duke Kunshan: not that they can eliminate strategic competition, but that they can continue putting people who might disagree in the same room, and teach them how to keep talking when agreement is no longer possible. “Cooperation does not have to mean agreement, technological sharing, or slowing down,” he said. “Cooperation can mean simply agreeing on what happens when we disagree.”

title: Hong Kong police arrest 2 men over HK$1.7 million Kowloon break-in spree
description: Suspects targeted unlocked residential homes in Kowloon at night, stealing cash and goods before using stolen credit cards online.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested two men over their alleged involvement in at least six break-ins across Kowloon over the past three months, with total losses amounting to HK$1.7 million (US$216,629). The pair – a 54-year-old mainland Chinese man and a 34-year-old Hong Kong resident – were arrested separately on Thursday in Sham Shui Po and Tsim Sha Tsui, respectively. Police identified and located them following a break-in targeting four flats in a private residential building on Farm Road in Kowloon City, where more than HK$100,000 in cash and watches, as well as some credit cards, were stolen. At a press briefing on Friday, Tsang Ka-chun, a senior inspector with the Kowloon City district crime squad, said police attached great importance to the case and were able to identify and locate the two suspects after reviewing surveillance camera footage. Initial investigations showed that the pair generally targeted private residential homes with unlocked windows or doors, while the flats were unoccupied at night. “The mainland man would break into the flats and steal valuables. He would subsequently hand over the stolen credit cards to the Hong Kong man, who used them to make online purchases totalling around HK$30,000,” Tsang said. “After subsequent investigations, detectives also believe the duo are connected with at least five burglary cases that took place in Kowloon City and Cheung Sha Wan between July and October,” he added. In those cases, about HK$1.6 million in cash, handbags and jewellery were stolen. The mainlander was arrested for attempted burglary and illegal immigration, while the local man was arrested for handling stolen goods and obtaining property by deception. During Thursday’s operation, officers seized cash, credit cards and valuables, as well as clothes and shoes believed to belong to the suspects. The two men remained in police custody for questioning on Friday evening. Tsang urged flat owners to remain vigilant and take simple precautions, such as locking windows and doors before leaving home, and to install surveillance cameras. Under the Theft Ordinance, the maximum penalty upon conviction for burglary or handling stolen goods is 14 years’ imprisonment, while obtaining property by deception carries a maximum sentence of 10 years. Hong Kong logged 344 burglary cases in the first half of 2026, down 22.7 per cent from 445 in the same period last year, according to police statistics. Burglaries fell to a record low of 818 cases, a 33.1 per cent year-on-year drop, in 2025.

title: Japan drop table tennis star Mima Ito, could axe Sora Matsushima-Miwa Harimoto partnership
description: Ex-Olympic champion replaced by breakthrough star Hitomi Sato in national team, but speculation surrounds high-profile mixed-doubles pairing.
content: Former Olympic champion Mima Ito has been dropped from Japan’s latest national table tennis squad, replaced by 28-year-old breakthrough player Hitomi Sato, who finished runner-up at the recent WTT China Smash. Across the border, meanwhile, followers of rival powerhouses China have focused their attention on widely circulated Chinese media reports that the Japan Table Tennis Association plans to dismantle the high-profile mixed-doubles pairing of Sora Matsushima and Miwa Harimoto. Under the reported plan, Matsushima would step back from multi-event duties to focus exclusively on men’s singles, clearing the way for Miwa to join forces with her older brother Tomokazu to create a potentially formidable combination. World No 3 Miwa Harimoto was named in the Japan Table Tennis Association (JTTA)’s national team roster for the second half of the 2026 season named on Thursday, with the seven-player women’s squad headlined by the 18-year-old. The notable omission was 25-year-old Ito, who missed out on both the primary roster and the reserve list. The remaining spots on the primary roster went to Hina Hayata, Satsuki Odo, Hitomi Sato, Honoka Hashimoto, Miyu Nagasaki and Rin Mende. A core member of Japan’s elite set-up since the 2016 Rio Olympics, Ito famously partnered Jun Mizutani to defeat China and secure Japan’s first Olympic table tennis gold medal in mixed doubles at the Tokyo Games four years later. Ito captured the full set of medals in 2020, adding a women’s team silver and a singles bronze. Taking her place on the primary roster is Sato, who earned promotion after reaching the women’s singles final at last week’s China Smash in Beijing. During her run, Sato ousted Chinese contenders Zhu Sibing and Chen Xingtong in succession to become the first defensive chopper in history to reach a WTT Grand Smash singles final, where she lost to world No 2 Wang Manyu. Meanwhile, Japan’s men’s primary roster remained unchanged from the first half of the season. The five-player line-up is led by new world No 1 Matsushima, alongside Tomokazu Harimoto, Shunsuke Togami, Hiroto Shinozuka and Yukiya Uda. While the Sora Matsushima-Miwa Harimoto split has not been officially confirmed, fans believe the move carries substance, stoking debate and concern among Chinese table tennis followers. Having previously teamed up at youth level, Matsushima and Harimoto captured the WTT Star Contender Doha title on their senior debut as a pair early last year. However, while solid, their partnership had yet to establish itself at the very summit of the discipline. Tensions flared after their semi-final loss to South Korea’s Lim Jong-hoon and Shin Yu-bin at the China Smash, where Matsushima visibly vented his frustration on court. In a post-match interview, Miwa conceded: “Neither of us can understand each other’s playing style in mixed doubles; we’re just playing freely.” By contrast, Matsushima produced a dominant run in men’s singles, defeating Chinese Taipei’s Lin Yun-ju in the final to claim his second WTT Grand Smash crown of the year. Speaking at the post-match press conference in Beijing, Matsushima was unequivocal about his priorities, acknowledging that doubles was not his natural forte. “First of all, among the three events I play, singles is the most important to me, and my feelings towards singles are different from any other event,” Matsushima said. “However, as long as I am playing doubles and mixed doubles, I understand that as Team Japan, we have to win, of course. But I am not very good at doubles and mixed doubles. Having won the title in singles this time, I have a stronger desire to produce more results in singles.” Matsushima has repeatedly stated that he aimed to win the men’s singles gold at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The prospect of a Harimoto sibling partnership and Matsushima’s singles specialisation prompted immediate reaction across Chinese social media. Some highlighted the pressure of family dynamics, with one user writing: “The chemistry and pressure of a brother-sister pairing: anyone who has fought side-by-side understands how complicated that is.” Others remained optimistic about the duo’s potential. “Looking forward to their upcoming matches,” a commenter posted. “They’ve trained together since childhood, and as a duo, they certainly have real strength.” A tactical observer pointed to the logistical challenge of two right-handed players. “The only drawback is that both are right-handed,” the fan noted. “If the siblings join forces to attack aggressively in the first three shots, they can largely cover up the footwork issues of having two right-handers.” Meanwhile, many endorsed Matsushima’s singular focus. “Matsushima himself said he isn’t good at doubles,” one widely shared post read. “Specialising in singles makes far more sense than forcing him to juggle multiple events – it’s reasonable.”

title: Japan taps foreign tech to plug defence gaps as China’s power grows. Will it pay off?
description: From Ukrainian drones to multinational fighters, Tokyo is seeking expertise and capacity to supplement its domestic industry.
content: Japan is increasingly turning to foreign companies to accelerate its military modernisation, drawing on overseas technology, expertise and production capacity to plug defence gaps that could prove critical in a potential regional conflict involving China. The push has gathered momentum over the past week, with Tokyo confirming a contract for Ukrainian interceptor drones and a multinational fighter consortium preparing to expand its design operations in Japan. French defence giant Thales is also reportedly planning what could become Japan’s first foreign-run military maintenance facility, initially serving the Maritime Self-Defence Force. Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi confirmed last Friday that Japan had signed a contract to acquire interceptor drones from Ukrainian start-up SkyFall. The company’s combat-tested P1-SUN family is designed to intercept unmanned aerial systems, including reconnaissance and attack drones, but Tokyo has not disclosed which model it ordered. The acquisition follows Japan’s fast-track mass-procurement contract for the Terra B1 interceptor from Japanese company Terra Drone, which has also invested in two Ukrainian drone manufacturers to tap into their military technology and combat experience. Hirohito Ogi, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics and a former Japanese defence ministry official, described Tokyo’s approach as a “two-phase” strategy of acquiring foreign systems to address urgent capability gaps while simultaneously developing domestic alternatives over the longer term. Some overlap between the two was acceptable to avoid capability gaps during the transition. He identified weaknesses in one-way attack drones and AI-enabled operational support systems, saying Japanese manufacturers had technical expertise but lacked know-how gained from “real-world battlefield experience”. Beyond drones, Edgewing, a joint venture of Japanese, British and Italian defence companies, plans to open a design and development centre in Japan next year for a next-generation fighter programme. According to Japanese news service Nikkei, the Aichi prefecture facility could eventually employ around 1,000 people. Taken together, these developments point to a broader shift in Japan’s approach to military modernisation. Tokyo has long acquired foreign-made weapon systems, mainly from the United States, but in recent years it has also sought partners elsewhere for advanced technology, joint development, production and maintenance. Tokyo has acknowledged the limits of domestic industry. Its 2026 defence white paper highlights pressures on the country’s defence-industrial base, including limited production volumes and companies withdrawing from the sector. It advocates international research and development, licensed production and advanced foreign technology, while Japan’s Defence Buildup Programme calls for shorter development timelines to field urgently needed equipment faster. Underpinning this shift is Tokyo’s stark assessment of regional security, with the white paper labelling Beijing’s growing military power and activities as Tokyo’s “greatest strategic challenge”. Experts say closer cooperation with foreign defence companies could help Japan gain combat-tested technologies more quickly, share the costs and expertise required to develop advanced weapons, and expand its production and maintenance capabilities – potentially strengthening its ability to counter the People’s Liberation Army. In a study released in July, Celine Pajon, head of Japan and Indo-Pacific research at the French Institute of International Relations, argued that foreign partnerships could ease Japan’s rising development costs, production constraints and dependence on US technology. Her study linked a stronger domestic defence industry to Japan’s “strategic autonomy” and identified European countries as promising partners for joint development and technology-sharing. Defence expert Yoshihiro Inaba, the Japan correspondent for the Naval News website, highlighted gaps in uncrewed weapons, low-cost missiles and AI capable of “processing vast amounts of information”. Companies such as Anduril, Palantir and General Atomics were among those supporting Japan’s efforts to address those shortfalls. In its fiscal 2027 defence budget request, Tokyo proposed developing and acquiring low-cost stand-off missiles. Inaba argued that importing such weapons could help Japan fast-track its long-range strike capabilities while developing domestic alternatives, without requiring major changes to Self-Defence Forces equipment. He pointed to China’s growing “quantitative advantage” over Japan, including its fleet of “highly capable but expensive surface combatants”. Japan could therefore improve its ability to counter these vessels by combining its existing domestically produced missiles with “a larger inventory of lower-cost cruise missiles”, supported by the surveillance and command-and-control systems needed to identify and target them, he said. Still, even if larger stocks of inexpensive weapons helped Japan to counter Chinese warships, sustaining their use throughout a prolonged conflict would pose a separate challenge. Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, cautioned that the bigger test was whether Tokyo could “produce, maintain and replace” military equipment on the scale needed during a prolonged conflict. She noted that China’s much larger defence-industrial base gave it a capacity for expansion that Japan “cannot readily match”. While foreign partnerships could help address specific shortcomings, they would not eliminate the fundamental imbalance between the two countries. Matsuoka also warned that Japan’s military preparations could reinforce Beijing’s perception that Tokyo and its partners were “preparing for confrontation”, deepening mutual mistrust. Beyond these geopolitical risks, Japan would still face major industrial challenges. Foreign partnerships could accelerate technology transfers, Matsuoka said, but producing weapons “reliably at scale” required skilled workers, qualified suppliers and secure access to components and materials. Reliance on foreign export approvals, software support and critical components could leave Japan vulnerable during a conflict with China, Matsuoka warned. Japan could also struggle to sustain operations if it acquired systems it “cannot repair, modify or replenish independently”. Ogi also cautioned that foreign defence companies’ growing presence in Japan did not necessarily reflect Tokyo’s military requirements. Such moves were “primarily motivated by the commercial interests of foreign companies”, he argued, as they anticipated further increases in Japanese defence spending. For Japan, the challenge will be turning foreign technology and expertise into military capabilities quickly enough to address some of China’s advantages, while ensuring those systems can be maintained, produced and replenished if a longer conflict disrupts overseas supply chains. “Foreign cooperation does not eliminate dependence; it redistributes it,” Matsuoka said.

title: Alibaba to embed AI throughout Taobao, Tmall merchant operations in 2027: executive
description: The plans include Qwen Work-powered tools for merchants and AI-driven product discovery for consumers.
content: Alibaba Group Holding’s two major domestic online marketplaces, Taobao and Tmall, plan to greatly expand the use of artificial intelligence across merchants’ operations next year, a senior executive said, as the e-commerce giant doubles down on the technology to drive growth amid a challenging consumer landscape. “Starting next year, AI will comprehensively enter the internal enterprise workflows of merchants,” Liu Bo, president of Tmall, said at the company’s Singles’ Day media briefing on Thursday. An important product driving the push would be Qwen Work, Alibaba’s enterprise AI assistant, Liu added. The e-commerce version of the assistant began testing earlier this week and is designed for merchants selling across multiple platforms. The move comes after the roll-out of AI on Taobao and Tmall over the past year “exceeded expectations”, Liu said, adding that merchants were already using platform-level AI tools for product launches, advertising and customer service. The remarks came ahead of Alibaba’s annual Singles’ Day shopping festival, with official sales set to begin next Tuesday and a record 1 million global brands expected to take part. The company, which launched the event in 2009, is using this year’s festival as a testing ground for AI-driven growth. Alibaba has aggressively rolled out AI-powered tools to consumers and merchants as it grapples with intense competition from rivals including JD.com and PDD Holdings. The company said this year’s festival would feature deeper integration of its flagship Qwen AI model across its e-commerce ecosystem. For consumers, a Qwen-powered shopping assistant launched in May is designed to help users compare products, virtually try on clothes and select promotional discounts. According to Liu, young, active Taobao and Tmall users currently buy goods from an average of 15 product categories annually. He said the platforms aimed to expand that figure to between 25 and 30 categories by using AI to better connect shoppers with a wider range of products. “AI allows us to open up a larger vision,” Liu said. “It can match the rich supply of goods with the diverse demands of the crowd in ways traditional algorithms simply could not achieve.” Alibaba is also introducing “AI tokens” as a new product category on its platforms. The company is partnering with major Chinese AI model developers, including Z.ai and MiniMax, to sell computing power directly to end users. The tokens would be packaged into customised bundles tailored for different groups of users such as students, researchers and small teams, Liu said. Tmall is also partnering with hardware giants such as Intel and Advanced Micro Devices to sell personal computers with Qwen models pre-installed. Alibaba’s first large-scale deployment of generative AI across Taobao and Tmall came during the same event in 2025, when it integrated large language models into its core search and recommendation engines. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: AI-powered drones to help detect hill fires during Chung Yeung Festival
description: With the Chung Yeung Festival approaching, authorities will also strengthen manpower to monitor high-risk locations for fires.
content: Hong Kong’s Fire Services Department will launch three new AI-assisted drone technologies to strengthen fire detection and its response to heightened risks during tomb-sweeping activities ahead of the Chung Yeung Festival on Sunday. Wong Tak-fai, acting divisional officer for information and communications technology, said on Friday that the technology would improve the speed and accuracy of fire detection to help the department operate more efficiently. “Artificial intelligence [AI] not only speeds up the processing of drone images but, more importantly, helps our staff continuously analyse large amounts of images from different drones across various locations to identify situations needing priority attention,” Wong said. With the Chung Yeung Festival approaching, the department will strengthen manpower to monitor high-risk locations for fires and step up district patrols and public education efforts with the Civil Aid Service and other district organisations. The department will also deploy 159 firefighters on Saturday across 12 locations in New Territories North, 10 spots in Kowloon and another six locations in New Territories South. On Sunday, an additional 166 firefighters will be deployed. Hong Kong recorded 693 hill fires in 2025. The department will also mobilise a newly bought remotely operated aerial surveillance system consisting of an off-road vehicle from mainland Chinese manufacturer Geely retrofitted with two drone docking systems and a generator. The HK$1.2 million system will allow officers to survey hard-to-reach fire hazard areas. Its drones can conduct automated patrols within a 3km radius and be controlled remotely. A real-time artificial intelligence video analysis platform will also be used to speed up the analysis of drone footage and images to generate timely alerts for fire hazards or drownings. The system uses AI to accurately identify signs of smoke and people who may be drowning, reducing the need for staff to review drone surveillance footage. “The new platform will be able to receive the footage in real time during a drone flight and then simultaneously run an artificial intelligence analysis,” Wong said. Currently, footage analysis takes place after a flight ends, with officers manually transferring the files from an SD card in the drone to a computer. The department will also have two high-payload drones equipped with water-bomb systems ready for deployment against remote hill fires. Each drone costs HK$500,000, including batteries. These drones can carry weights up to 150kg and are equipped with an 80-litre water tank, allowing them to release water bombs where needed. Wong said that in departmental tests, while it took firefighters one hour to carry rescue equipment 5km uphill, the large drone could do it in 10 minutes. “The Fire Services Department is exploring the use of large drones in frontline operations, hoping to move from surveillance and observation to delivering firefighting equipment,” Wong said. However, the acting divisional officer said artificial intelligence would in no way replace firefighters, as he stressed that all operational decisions would still be made by humans.

title: China’s R&D spending keeps up steady rise as No 1 US seeks further funding cuts
description: China’s research and experimental development spending crossed 3.9 trillion yuan in 2025, National Bureau of Statistics data shows.
content: China’s R&D investment grew by 8.2 per cent last year – fuelled by double-digit growth in fundamental science and university funding – in sharp contrast with deep budget cuts across the US research sector. Total investment in research and experimental development crossed 3.9 trillion yuan (US$583 billion) in 2025, “maintaining a trajectory of steady growth”, the National Bureau of Statistics said when releasing the data on Friday. State news agency Xinhua noted on Friday that in the five years to 2025, China’s R&D spending grew at an average annual rate of 10 per cent, placing it at the forefront of the world’s major economies. Friday’s data puts China behind only the United States in total research and development expenditure, outspending Germany by 3.4 times and Japan by 3.5 times. Notably, China has seen substantial increases in funding for basic research and higher education at a time when the US is significantly scaling back government support. Basic research grew the fastest among the three R&D categories – outpacing both applied research and experimental development with a 13.3 per cent year-on-year increase. However, at 283.46 billion yuan, the total allocated amount accounted for just over 7 per cent of the overall national figure. R&D spending by higher education institutions reached 340.7 billion yuan, rising by 11 per cent from 2024. Meanwhile, sweeping cuts to scientific research funding initiated under President Donald Trump continue in the US. A Harvard Business School article earlier this month said the Trump administration had frozen or terminated some US$3 billion in National Institutes of Health (NIH) grants in early 2025, affecting about 3,800 projects. The administration’s proposed 2026 budget calls for reducing NIH spending by 39 per cent and cutting National Science Foundation funding by 55 per cent. In response, multiple universities have announced cuts to doctoral programmes, and some have laid off staff. Over in China, Science and Technology Minister Yin Hejun last month outlined plans to strengthen basic scientific research, describing this as essential for achieving technological breakthroughs, boosting national security and addressing other strategic priorities. Beijing will further intensify efforts to resolve bottlenecks in critical sectors such as semiconductors, industrial machinery and high-end instruments, according to Yin. Research into frontier technologies – including artificial intelligence, quantum technology, biotechnology and brain-computer interfaces – will also receive greater support as China seeks a competitive edge in emerging fields. In terms of investment intensity, China’s R&D expenditure reached 2.8 per cent of gross domestic product in 2025, continuing a rapid upward trend. Ranking 12th globally, it surpassed the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development or OECD average for the first time. The corporate sector drove the bulk of China’s R&D investment last year, with enterprise spending crossing 3 trillion yuan for the first time to make up over 77 per cent of the total. Government-affiliated research institutions, universities and other entities accounted for the rest. The spending was heavily concentrated in China’s developed coastal provinces and tier one cities. The provinces of Guangdong, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Shandong, alongside Shanghai and Beijing, each recorded R&D investments exceeding 200 billion yuan. During the annual legislative sessions in March, the central government boosted science funding by 10 per cent year on year. It marked the largest percentage increase among the government’s major spending areas, outpacing defence, diplomacy, public security and education.

title: Anti-China protectionism backfiring on American carmakers’ EV plans: analyst
description: Trivium China’s David Zhang says industry concerned that US ‘has failed to come up with a coherent long-term EV strategy and stick to it’.
content: While Washington’s efforts to block Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) were originally intended to protect its domestic automotive industry, they have sparked concerns the strategy is hurting America’s carmaking competitiveness. With a lack of a coherent industrial policy discouraging long-term investment, the protectionist approach was backfiring on Detroit’s EV transition, said David Zhang, a macroeconomics and policy analyst at Trivium China, who added that EVs could be a “perfect concession” in US-China trade talks, and that China had “ample reason” to push for market access. Chinese EV makers face tariffs of more than 100 per cent in the United States, while Washington has also imposed restrictions on China-linked software and hardware to address data security concerns. US lawmakers have also introduced bipartisan bills seeking to further restrict American sales of EVs linked to China. While the protectionist measures were intended to give US legacy carmakers time to adjust to challenges from Chinese EV competition, Zhang said such a strategy could only work alongside long-term industrial planning and execution. “There’s actually growing concern that the US has not only fallen behind in the [EV] race but has failed to come up with a coherent long-term EV strategy and stick to it,” said Zhang, who is based in Washington. During his second term as US president, Donald Trump has been retreating from government EV incentives, including rescinding incentives for EV production and watering down fuel economy standards. “We’ve seen quite dramatic reversals when the political leadership changed,” Zhang said. “That makes it very difficult for not only Chinese but also US carmakers to plan investments that might take five or 10 years to pay off.” He added that policy inconsistency was prompting US carmakers to scale back EV expansion plans, including cutting production targets and delaying or cancelling the introduction of new EV platforms. The US market has long been seen as a sort of holy grail in terms of global-scale high margin sales David Zhang, Trivium China Such uncertainty has also discouraged some Chinese carmakers from entering the US market. At this month’s Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore, BYD vice-president Stella Li said the company was not planning to sell passenger cars in the US due to the market’s lack of “clarity, visibility and stability”, Reuters reported. Despite the restrictions, Zhang said the US market remained attractive because it was “significantly underserved” when it came to affordable EVs – an area where Chinese companies could leverage their advantages in battery technology and low-cost manufacturing. That made EVs a potential bargaining chip in future US-China trade negotiations. “On paper, the market is actually a perfect concession for US-China trade talks,” Zhang said. “The US market has long been seen as a sort of holy grail in terms of global-scale high margin sales. “And there’s tremendous interest [from Chinese carmakers] … as they’re trying to escape the price wars at home and chasing higher profit margins elsewhere.” Signs of potential flexibility have emerged, with Trump indicating early last month that he would allow Chinese car manufacturers to produce cars in the US if they built factories that would create jobs. Those remarks sparked a backlash from the American automotive industry, with a letter from six major automotive trade groups urging Trump to “maintain policies that keep the door firmly shut to Chinese automakers”. However, some US carmakers are pursuing selective cooperation with Chinese companies, attracted by their technological advantages and cost competitiveness in key areas such as batteries and EV supply chains. Ford Motor, for example, is working with Chinese battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) on a battery factory in Michigan, with CATL serving as technology and service provider for the project. The Chinese company said in May that US carmakers needed “the best lithium iron phosphate technology to compete globally”. “The US is not likely to dismantle its restrictions wholesale any time soon,” Zhang said, citing the broad bipartisan support for restricting Chinese carmakers’ access to the US market. “But there may be more room for selective firm-level cooperation on technology and manufacturing in places where American companies themselves see a commercial benefit to cooperation.”

title: ASML eyes hybrid bonding, report finds, as Chinese firms adopt chip packaging technique
description: The company has reportedly filed dozens of patent families related to the technology, which can improve chip performance.
content: Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML is expanding into next-generation hybrid bonding, a technique that creates dense electrical connections by directly joining chips or silicon wafers, according to a new report. Major Chinese companies are also adopting the technology to improve chip performance. ASML submitted 27 patent families related to hybrid bonding tools between December 2022 and November 2024, according to a report published by semiconductor and AI supply chain research firm SemiAnalysis on Thursday. The number could be higher because of publication delays affecting recent filings, it said. The filings suggest ASML is moving beyond lithography, a market it dominates, into back-end processes as demand for high-performance chips surges amid the global artificial intelligence boom. The company had also begun developing the architecture for a hybrid bonder with Dutch technology firms Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG, according to SemiAnalysis, citing industry media reports. “We believe ASML could gain an edge in alignment accuracy and particle control for hybrid bonding,” SemiAnalysis said. “These are the two factors that set bonding yield. And ASML has expertise in solving the same problems in lithography.” The company has not officially announced the extent of its progress on advanced packaging. But CEO Christophe Fouquet said during an April earnings call that the company was “continuing to look for opportunities to support our customers” in hybrid bonding. ASML told the South China Morning Post by email on Friday that it would “continue to look in which directions [the] 3D integration industry will evolve and to see how this relates to ASML’s roadmap, and where ASML’s expertise can be of added value”. Hybrid bonding allows ultra-high-density electrical connections and is widely viewed as one of the next major trends in chipmaking. Recent breakthroughs by China’s Huawei Technologies and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) involved using the technique to improve performance as United States-led export restrictions limit access to some advanced semiconductor equipment. Under those restrictions, Huawei and CXMT cannot import ASML’s most advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. Hybrid bonding can reduce the thermal resistance in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks by about 30 per cent, according to a September report by Guotai Haitong Securities, which cited Samsung data. Lower thermal resistance can help heat escape more easily, potentially reducing cooling requirements and the need for related investments. Huawei disclosed new details this week about its flagship Kirin 9050 series, the first mass-produced chip to use its proprietary LogicFolding architecture developed under a framework it calls the Tau Scaling Law. The company said the design integrated more than 50 million hybrid bonds and increased overall transistor density by 53.5 per cent. CXMT, meanwhile, announced last week that its latest “4F square” dynamic random-access memory architecture used hybrid bonding, which could allow it to increase wafer bit density without relying on advanced EUV lithography. Despite the potential benefits of the technique, China remained heavily dependent on imported hybrid bonding equipment, particularly advanced machines, according to a separate report by Huaan Securities. The report noted that domestic equipment manufacturers were stepping up research and development to narrow the gap, with Piotech and Xinhui Lianxin among the leading players. Piotech’s hybrid bonding equipment generated 136 million yuan (US$20.3 million) in revenue in 2025, up 41.9 per cent from a year earlier, according to its annual report. Nomura analysts said in a report last week that Huawei’s LogicFolding architecture could drive demand for bonding equipment, as well as Piotech’s mainstay thin-film deposition tools.

title: Opinion | Nobel Peace Prize: the message behind Navi Pillay’s win
description: With global institutions under attack and Trump’s power politics on the rise, the award is a firm rejection of the ‘might is right’ doctrine.
content: The awarding of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay matters for reasons that go well beyond the laureate herself. The award does three things at once. First, it restores credibility to the prize. Second, it rejects in unambiguous terms the Thrasymachian doctrine that might is right, which has become the operating philosophy of major powers. Third, it highlights a warning of what happens when a hegemon decides it is above the law. The correction was overdue. Last year, the Norwegian Nobel Committee gave the Peace Prize to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, in what was widely read as a political signal. Machado, however, then gave her prize to US President Donald Trump. Whatever one’s view of Venezuelan politics, that act made a mockery of an institution founded on Alfred Nobel’s will: that the prize go to the person who has done the most for fraternity between nations, for the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and for the promotion of peace congresses. A Nobel Prize cannot be re-gifted like a souvenir. As the organisers made clear, “a medal can change owners, but the title of a Nobel Peace Prize laureate cannot”. In choosing Pillay this year, the Nobel Committee cited “her efforts to promote peace and international law” and her work showing that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide can and must be prosecuted. It said: “The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack. We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence.” 2026 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion. A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time. This year’s laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law. She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, until recently, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Today Navi Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide. In historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence. Navi Pillay has also contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law. Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time. Learn more about the 2026 #NobelPeacePrize: https://t.co/JMjpp1jPKc #NobelPeacePrize #NobelPrize — The Nobel Prize (@NobelPrize) October 9, 2026 Honouring Pillay is therefore not only about her biography; it is about upholding a principle. In the West, it is the refutation of Thrasymachus’ contention in Plato’s Republic. In response to Thrasymachus’ declaration that “justice is nothing other than the advantage of the stronger”, Socrates answers that this cannot be justice at all. As Socrates puts it: “No physician, in so far as he is a physician, considers his own good in what he prescribes, but the good of his patient.” In the East, the same contest is wangdao vs badao: the kingly way vs the hegemonic way. According to Mencius, he who uses force under the pretence of humaneness is a hegemon while he who uses his virtue to practice humaneness is a true king. The message is clear: a king dispenses benevolence with virtue; a hegemon appropriates benevolence by force. Confucius also rejected rule by force: a ruler must govern by virtue and humaneness, holding the mandate of heaven by moral rectitude, not coercion. His great antagonist, Han Feizi, China’s Machiavelli, argued the opposite: man is selfish, order comes only from shi (positional power), fa (the law as an instrument of the state) and shu (techniques of reward and fear). For Han, the first principle of political theory was the reality of human nature. This was the legalist doctrine favoured by China’s first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, who unified the country in 221BC. I place Pillay firmly in the Socratic-Confucian lineage – might may prevail but that does not make it right, and even the strongest state is bound by law. The third reason is more immediate, and it concerns Trump. His petulance at not receiving the Nobel Peace Prize – last year and, again, this year – would be comical if it were not consequential. Earlier this month, he argued that he should win the Nobel Peace Prize for having settled “eight wars”. What is consequential is how American power has been deployed against the very institutions that Pillay, a former judge of the International Criminal Court (ICC), helped to build. In February last year, Trump issued an executive order announcing sanctions on 13 ICC officials. On October 9 this year – hours after Pillay’s prize was awarded – the US Treasury added the ICC itself to its sanctions list, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying: “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.” For China, this moment carries a particular lesson. As a major power, China will be judged not only by its growth but by its rectitude. Pillay’s career suggests what that choice requires. Her most controversial work was as the chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on ‌the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded last year that Israel was failing to prevent and actively committing genocide. The commission found that four of five acts defined under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention had been committed, and that Israel’s President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant had incited genocide. Israel dismissed the report as a “libellous rant” and “scandalous”. Pillay, who in 1967 became the first woman to establish a law practice in South Africa’s then Natal province, who in 1973 won a case for Robben Island prisoners including Nelson Mandela to have access to lawyers, and who served as a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda that investigated the 1994 genocide, in which about 800,000 people were killed, knows that the law is fragile. The world needed to understand that the alternative is the situation Thrasymachus and Han described. The 2026 prize is a reminder that we can still choose the normative path.

title: Indian police detain ‘cockroach’ movement leader ahead of New Delhi protest
description: Authorities have moved against Abhijeet Dipke, who is calling for the resignation of the election commissioner over voter roll changes.
content: Police detained India’s ‘cockroach’ movement founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday, student leaders and supporters on Friday as hundreds poured into central Delhi, waving the national flag and demanding the resignation of India’s election chief. The youth-led ‘Cockroach Janta Party’ (CJP), opposition groups and student organisations have held almost daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over a revision of voter lists that critics ⁠say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party. More than 130 million voters were deleted ‌during the revision, but the Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of ‌trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes. Dipke called Friday’s protest ⁠in support of ⁠two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site ‌in violation of a ban. The group and left-wing student organisations had urged supporters to gather at the Central Park ‌in Delhi’s busy Connaught Place shopping and food district on Friday evening to wave and hoist ‌the national flag. Dipke was detained as ⁠he stepped out of a house in central Delhi, with police hauling him into a police car and driving away after a brief argument. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Cockroach Janta Party (@cockroachjantaparty) Student activist Neha Bora, a prominent face of the protests, was also detained as she tried to reach Connaught Place with dozens of supporters. Senior police officer Sachin Sharma told Reuters that Dipke and Bora had been taken into preventive detention. “Abhijeet is detained by Delhi Police,” CJP posted on social media. “This government is so scared of ‌the youth waving national flag.” Earlier on Friday, police met Dipke and warned him ‌against going ahead with the protest. Security was stepped up and the park itself shut by civic authorities. Nevertheless, nearly 500 protesters managed to reach Connaught Place in groups and protested in about half a dozen places around the Central Park, waving flags and shouting slogans. A few ‌were detained and taken away in a police vehicle. “If waving the tricolour in the country has become a crime then I am happy to go to jail,” said Saurav Kumar, a data analyst, before he was detained. “The government ‌not giving ‌us the space to protest, not accepting faults in the system is not a healthy sign for a democracy.” Small protests ‌were also held in financial capital Mumbai and tech hub Bengaluru, while student organisations held a demonstration in the eastern city of Patna, with people waving flags of their organisations and pushing against ⁠police barricades. The cockroach movement has emerged as one of the biggest political challenges faced by Modi and his BJP in his 12 years in power. A weeks-long ⁠sit-in by its supporters earlier this year forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation over exam paper leaks. The latest demonstrations erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar’s two deputies raised concerns internally about voter list changes, registration procedures and digital systems. The 130 million names that were removed from voter lists starting last year – equivalent to more ‌than the population of Japan – included 28 million people ‌who had died, 63 million who relocated and 30 million who could not be traced, according to the Election Commission. Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslims and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, allegations the commission and the BJP reject. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said the demonstrations were the main opposition Congress party’s attempt to “seize power”. “Instead of channelling the energy of the youth towards nation-building, they are being used as pawns in the politics of anarchy,” he said at a media briefing on Friday.

title: Asian Cup football remains on track but golf, cycling events affected after Saudi attack
description: Football sticking to January–February plan as Asian Tour postpones Saudi International, UCI axes Urban Cycling World Championships.
content: Golf’s Asian Tour has postponed the Saudi International indefinitely and cycling’s Urban World Championships have been cancelled following a deadly attack on Riyadh, although local organisers said next year’s Asian Cup football tournament remained on track. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement claimed ‌responsibility for Saturday’s strike on Riyadh’s international airport that killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300. The Urban Cycling World Championships had been scheduled for November 3-7 in Riyadh, while the US$5 million Saudi International, the flagship event on the Asian Tour, was due to take place at Riyadh Golf Club from November 18 to 21. Other events have also been disrupted. The Six Kings Slam exhibition tennis tournament in Riyadh has already been moved from October to December, while Fifa on Thursday postponed the Fifa-e Finals 2026 video game competition in the Saudi capital until ⁠an unspecified future date. The disruption had raised questions over whether the ⁠24-team Asian Cup could still go ahead in Saudi Arabia from January 7 to February 5 next year. Asian football chief Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said earlier this week that a postponement of the continental championships until 2028 was possible if necessary, but ‌the local organising committee said on Friday it was sticking to the original schedule. “Preparations across all organisational and ⁠operational areas are progressing according ⁠to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services,” it said in a statement. “[The LOC] will continue to monitor developments relevant to the tournament and ‌ensure the appropriate conditions are in place for its successful delivery.” Attacks disrupt sports calendar The Asian Tour said the Saudi International had been postponed following an ‌assessment of the challenges involved in staging the tournament. “The decision to postpone was ‌taken following an assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament and ensuring the event is delivered to ⁠a standard befitting its international stature,” an Asian Tour statement said. The Urban Cycling World Championships, which would have featured some of the world’s ‌best riders in trials and BMX freestyle, were cancelled soon after Australia withdrew its team citing safety concerns over travelling to Riyadh. In last year’s event, China captured the top three spots in the women’s BMX freestyle park event, with Sun Sibei winning gold with 95.86 and Sun Jiaqi finishing second with Fan Xiaotong third. Two male and two female athletes in BMX freestyle park were set to earn a place in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics line-up. “The decision follows ⁠a joint assessment of recent developments in the region and their impact on the logistical organisation of the Championships,” the UCI said. “The UCI will communicate ⁠shortly on the sporting consequences of this announcement.” AusCycling said its decision to withdraw the Australian team from the urban ⁠World Championships was made “with the safety and well-being of our athletes and staff our highest priority”. The Australian government is advising travellers to “reconsider” trips to Saudi Arabia. The Saudi government has invested heavily ‌in sport through its Public Investment Fund (PIF) in recent years and the Asian Cup was pitched as an early rehearsal for hosting the Fifa World Cup in 2034. According to a report on US news website Semafor earlier this week, PIF is preparing to tell the world football governing body that it would scale back stadium plans for the 2034 tournament as part of a broader review of domestic spending.

title: As tariff threats ease, US in fashion again among Chinese exporters
description: But exhibitors at Canton Fair say European market outlook clouded by regulatory and financial hurdles.
content: With the US set to lower tariffs on US$30 billion worth of shipments from China, Chinese exporters said this week they expected a new wave of orders from American buyers and planned to reactivate idle factory capacity. Many among the 32,000-plus Chinese exhibitors and 210,000 preregistered foreign buyers at the twice-yearly Canton Fair, China’s oldest and biggest trade exhibition, shared that upbeat outlook this week – though it was tempered by stiffer headwinds from the European market. Chinese manufacturers at the fair, which runs for nearly three weeks and is widely seen as a bellwether for the health of China’s vast export machine, expressed growing optimism that tariff cuts would boost their full-year orders from the American market by roughly double-digit orders of growth compared with last year. A steady stream of buyers from the United States on Thursday, the fair’s opening day, bolstered that outlook. Following President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US last month, Beijing and Washington announced details of a bilateral Board of Trade that will oversee tariff cuts on goods worth US$30 billion on each side. Chinese products on the list are mostly everyday consumer items, such as toys and household goods, and over 90 per cent of them would return to most-favoured-nation tariff treatment when entering the US, with all additional duties waived, according to the Ministry of Commerce. Xu Zhiman, general manager of Hangzhou Zheben Technology, a family-owned manufacturer of weighing scales, said there were already signs US order volumes would be up at least 15 per cent on last year. She said she was optimistic for even further growth if the tariff cuts came into effect. US clients are sharp negotiators who always squeeze margins, so everything hinges on product differentiation Chen Haibo, Crossbow Brand Electric “If the tariff cuts actually go through, we’re expecting this momentum to carry right into next year,” Xu said. “We’ll definitely ramp up production, since we’ve got over 30,000 square metres (322,917 square feet) of factory space, and a chunk of it is just sitting idle right now.” Zhou Nana, sales manager at Chongqing Huifan Technology, said several American clients were among the dozens of buyers who visited its booth on Thursday. The firm supplies biometric identity solutions and palm vein recognition technology. Chen Haibo, general manager of home appliance maker Crossbow Brand Electric, said the pending US tariff cuts on some consumer goods had “clearly” brought back buyer interest. “US buyers in home appliances have a much stronger drive to attend the fair and place orders,” he said. “Previously, several American clients kept pushing us to build factories overseas to bypass tariffs, but now they seem to have dropped that push.” Chen said that instead of offering discounts, his firm had kept its baseline wholesale prices for US-bound products like air coolers and air purifiers unchanged from those quoted at the previous fair in April. “US clients are sharp negotiators who always squeeze margins, so everything hinges on product differentiation,” Chen said. “Factories must balance local market needs with client profitability through steady innovation.” China registered a 36.3 per cent year-on-year jump in worldwide exports last month, and a record US$133.5 billion trade surplus. Shipments to US rose against a low base last year, growing 39.56 per cent in September. But exporters at the fair anticipated smaller order sizes, stricter price demands from clients and longer payment cycles in the massive EU market. Fitch Ratings says European demand is being hampered by weak consumer spending and regulatory hurdles. Liang Xiong, a lighting exporter focused on Europe, said France was a barometer and was in a “slow-moving recession.” “Order volumes in Europe will shrink, and prices will come under pressure, yet customers still demand the same quality while pushing for longer payment terms,” Liang said. New European Union environmental rules, from carbon footprint requirements to product packaging, were also influencing buyers’ cost calculations, said Liu Kaiming, founder of the Shenzhen-based Institute of Contemporary Observation and a long-time supply chain researcher. “Even if they reach an agreement at the fair, orders may fall through later if they cannot provide required compliance documents,” Liu said. Regulatory and financial hurdles could weigh on exporters’ bottom lines well into next year, vendors and analysts said, adding that if European buyers pushed for longer payment terms and placed smaller orders, Chinese firms would face higher upfront costs. Exporters at the fair said diversifying into emerging markets, particularly South America and the Middle East, remained an indispensable workaround for volatility in Western markets. Zheng Donghua, a sales manager for agricultural drones at TopXgun, said strong demand for agricultural spraying had tripled the company’s market share in South America. And at Shadow Technology – which provides interactive touch projection systems that turn surfaces into interactive touch screen displays – sales manager Billy Gong said South America accounted for 70 to 80 per cent of overseas sales, even though it only began selling there this year.

title: Sorry, Darwin: Chinese fossil shows that not all early birds evolved to fly
description: Discovery suggests that adaptation branched out into more diverse, terrestrial non-flying niches much earlier than previously thought.
content: Chinese scientists have unearthed a fossil of the earliest known flightless bird, offering compelling evidence that not all early birds evolved to take to the skies. The discovery could also challenge long-held assumptions – including ideas dating back to evolutionary theorist Charles Darwin – that flightlessness in birds arose only as a secondary adaptation after earlier species had mastered flight. The 150 million-year-old fossil of the Late Jurassic avialan Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis found in China’s southeastern Fujian province suggests that early bird adaptation branched out into more diverse, terrestrial non-flying niches much earlier than previously thought. “Selection for powered flight has been viewed as the main driver of early avialan skeletal modifications,” the researchers said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature on October 14. Wang Min, an author of the study and professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Paleoanthropology, said the team was “struck” by the mix of features found in Yuezhuornis. “It possesses birdlike pelvic and hindlimb structures yet retains the specialised predatory foot and teeth of a small meat-eating dinosaur,” said Wang, according to a CAS statement. “The mosaic features present in Yuezhuornis demonstrate that acquisition of the bird body plan was not a systematic progression towards flight optimisation but a complex process involving the rapid exploration of different niches,” the team wrote in their paper. In his seminal 1859 book On the Origin of Species, Darwin proposed that the flightless nature of some birds resulted from wing “disuse” owing to an absence of predators. The English naturalist proposed that natural selection increased the ostrich’s body size over generations and that “its legs were used more, and its wings less, until they became incapable of flight”. English biologist Richard Owen, whom Darwin cited in the book, once said: “There is no greater anomaly in nature than a bird that cannot fly.” While the origin of flightless birds has long been subject to debate, modern genetic studies show that groups like the ratites – which include ostriches, emus and kiwis – evolved from flying ancestors. The transition from non-avian dinosaurs to their only living descendants – birds – was long assumed to be driven mainly by adaptations for powered flight, which triggered the development of elongated wings and flight feathers. Understanding the origin and early diversification of birds has been hindered by a scarcity of fossils from the Jurassic period. The new fossil comes from the Zhenghe Fauna in Fujian, a major site that has yielded several important Jurassic species, including early birds and birdlike dinosaurs. With an estimated body mass of 821 grams (1.81lbs), the Yuezhuornis specimen is believed to be an adult or subadult. Its unique mosaic of features, including limb proportions similar to modern ground-dwelling birds, provides “strong evidence for a terrestrial, flightless lifestyle”, according to the team. The researchers said the traits suggested the species “was a small-sized carnivore well adapted for running, occupying an ecological niche rarely accessed by other early avialans”. Using phylogenetic analyses, the researchers placed the species among the earliest diverging birds. Notably, it lived alongside Archaeopteryx – a famous Jurassic feathered dinosaur seen as an evolutionary bridge between non-avian dinosaurs and modern birds. Together with other discoveries in this region, Yuezhuornis highlighted the “extraordinary breadth” of ecological and physical diversity present at the dawn of bird evolution, the team said.

title: Lifts in another 39 buildings found to be lacking proper components
description: Three arrested over missing fire-safety parts in 48 Hong Kong lifts, source says.
content: Hong Kong authorities have found that lifts in another 39 buildings are lacking proper door-frame components following an investigation into faulty replacement works carried out by a contractor involving missing fire-safety parts. The South China Morning Post also learned on Friday that police had arrested a director and two registered lift engineers from the lift contractor, Taizoom Elevator, on suspicion of deception over work at 48 lifts at two housing estates. The latest incidents come just months after a fiasco involving lifts at a new hospital block, with experts saying on Friday that a thorough review of the regulatory process could be needed. The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department said it had launched inspections of lifts installed by Taizoom across Hong Kong. As of 2pm on Friday, it said it had inspected 39 buildings including one in a housing estate. The other 38 were stand-alone buildings. “Random inspections revealed that lifts in all these buildings lacked door-frame components,” it said. The department said it would not disclose the names of the affected buildings as they were privately owned but would contact the relevant property management companies and notify owners. It added that it had also begun inspecting lift works by other contractors. Investigations into 25 other buildings found that all lift frame components had been installed correctly, it said. Separately, a source said three personnel from Taizoom Elevator had been arrested on suspicion of deception. The company had replaced nine lifts at Tsui Ping (North) Estate in Kwun Tong and 39 lifts at Pok Hong Estate in Sha Tin. One of the suspects was a 79-year-old director and shareholder of Taizoom. The other two were registered lift engineers who examined the installations and signed safety certificates, aged 63 and 82, respectively. The arrests came a day after the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department said its inspection, triggered by a complaint, found that Taizoom had installed fire-resistant doors without the required door frame components at the two estates. The department said the contractor had submitted a fire-resisting rating certificate and claimed it had completed the works. Suspecting fraud and false statements, the department reported the case to police. The insider said officers raided the company’s office in Chai Wan, and the investigation had found that the outstanding components were “critical smoke control devices”. “The registered contractor and the registered engineer responsible for inspecting the lifts allegedly concealed the construction defects intentionally and falsely reported to the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department and the owners’ corporation that the works were completed in accordance with the contract,” the source said. The case has been referred to the regional crime unit of New Territories South. According to the department’s quarterly performance rating for lift contractors, Taizoom scored three out of five in service quality and had the same score in safety performance as other companies. The arrests came two months after 24 of the 28 lifts in Queen Mary Hospital’s new 34-storey clinical block were deemed unfit for use. Law Wing-chai, a registered lift engineer involved in the hospital project, was sentenced to 160 hours of community service last month after being convicted of submitting misleading documents and improperly issuing safety certificates. Professor Ho Wing-ip, an adjunct professor at Polytechnic University’s department of electrical and electronic engineering, said both incidents might have been the result of lapses in supervision and a thorough review could be needed. “After the two incidents, the public’s trust in registered lift engineers seems to have been shaken a bit … We still do not know if they are just the tip of an iceberg or extremely rare cases. The department has to look thoroughly into the sector and report to the public,” he said. “If they are the tip of an iceberg, then it requires a review of the existing system and mechanism.” A lift can only go into service after the director of electrical and mechanical services issues or renews the required permit. Only registered lift contractors can undertake works, which should be examined by a registered lift engineer. Ho said the door frame components were intended to prevent flames and smoke from seeping through gaps if a fire broke out. Typically, door frame components were only visible from the top of the lift car, he explained, adding that the department might have to request registered lift engineers to inspect them and include photos as records in the examination report. Ho noted that lifts underwent monthly maintenance and annual inspections, but given the number in the city, checking every concealed part each time was unrealistic. According to official information from February, Hong Kong had 73,393 lifts. Louis Szeto Ka-sing, past chairman of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers’ mechanical, marine, naval architecture and chemical division, said authorities should first check whether similar problems existed in other lifts. He pointed out that the problem might not only involve the contractor, registered lift professionals and the department, but also the supplier of the lift components, logistics parties, workers and work supervisors. Szeto said it was possible the stakeholders had failed to communicate properly and could not identify the risks in advance. “We have to look into the incident,” he said. “Only training and communication can help resolve potential risks.” The department said on Thursday that it had started a comprehensive review of the installation of new equipment and lift modernisation, inspection and maintenance works, site supervision system and systems under the Lifts and Escalators Ordinance.

title: Singapore targets 7 companies over wildfires in Indonesia as toxic haze worsens
description: The environmental agency has ordered the firms to stop burning and submit prevention plans as air quality worsens to unhealthy levels.
content: Singapore has identified seven companies it says were involved in wildfires in Indonesia that are choking the city state with haze, and plans to issue notices requiring them to take preventive measures, the Business Times reported. The companies will receive notices under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act requiring them to stop or refrain from burning and submit plans to prevent a recurrence, the newspaper reported, citing Sustainability and the Environment Minister Grace Fu at a Friday press conference. Fu did not specify whether they were Singaporean or Indonesian companies, and the government will make the list public on a later date. Singapore and Malaysia have been blanketed for weeks by toxic smog from a severe wildfire season in Indonesia that has been exacerbated by a powerful El Nino weather pattern, bringing dry weather to the region. Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong vowed on Thursday to investigate firms responsible for fires and warned those found culpable could face legal action. Blazes stemming from the use of slash-and-burn techniques to clear farmland have long been a feature of Indonesia’s dry months, and the situation has been exacerbated by a particularly intense dry season this year, with a blockbuster El Nino weather pattern threatening to break records. The companies were identified by analysing satellite imagery and meteorological data on hotspots and smoke plumes from the fires, according to the Business Times report. Singapore enacted the transboundary haze law in 2014, allowing it to fine companies as much as S$100,000 (US$78,000) per day of pollution. The city state tried to enforce it in 2015, but the environment ministry conceded at the time it was having difficulty getting information from its Indonesian counterpart on firms suspected of illegal burning. A decade on, four companies continue to be under investigation. The law targets those responsible for causing or condoning fires when resulting smog keeps the pollutant standards index at unhealthy levels for at least 24 hours. The 24-hour PSI ranged from 160 to 227 across the island as of 5pm local time on Friday. Air quality is considered “very unhealthy” when levels are 201 and above. A reading higher than 300 is considered “hazardous” and can trigger school closures.

title: China urges Israel to end West Bank settlement expansion and ease Gaza crisis
description: Top diplomat Wang Yi calls attention to ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ in Beijing’s highest-level engagement with Israel since the war erupted in 2023.
content: In talks with Israel’s president on Thursday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi called for an immediate easing of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and for Israel to reverse its West Bank settlement expansion. “The imperative priority is to fully open access routes into Gaza. Two million civilians must not be left to struggle on the brink of survival, nor can this humanitarian catastrophe be allowed to spread,” Wang said, according to a Chinese foreign ministry statement on Friday. The meeting with Israeli President Isaac Herzog took place at Israel’s request on the sidelines of a summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia in Baku, Azerbaijan. It marked Beijing’s highest-level engagement with Israel since October 2023, when the latest Israel-Gaza war broke out. According to figures cited by United Nations agencies relying on Gaza health authorities, more than 70,000 people in Gaza have been killed, including 20,000 children, and over 100,000 have been injured since October 2023. Nearly all of Gaza’s 2.1 million residents remain displaced, with vast swathes of the enclave reduced to rubble and the region recording the highest proportion of child amputees globally. A ceasefire reached in October last year eased conditions somewhat but, the UN reported, Israeli aid restrictions and near-daily deadly attacks persisted. On Thursday, Wang urged Israel to halt and reverse its forced settlement expansion in the West Bank – referring to Israeli communities built in territory occupied since 1967. Deemed illegal under international law, rapidly expanding Israeli settlements continue to fuel territorial disputes over land designated for a future Palestinian state. Calling the Palestinian issue “the greatest historical injustice of this century”, Wang stressed that a two-state solution remained the only viable path forward. The framework envisages an independent state of Palestine existing peacefully alongside the state of Israel, based on pre-1967 borders, with Jerusalem as the capital of both states. Sino-Israeli relations have been strained since the war.
