While Beijing has consistently advocated for a two-state solution, Israel has voiced disappointment that China did not explicitly condemn Hamas, a Palestinian militant group and former de facto governing authority of the Gaza Strip. During Thursday’s meeting, Wang invoked the memory of Herzog’s late father, Chaim Herzog, who was Israel’s sixth president and played a pivotal role in establishing formal diplomatic ties between the two countries, becoming the first Israeli head of state to visit China in 1992. A separate statement released by the Israeli government said Herzog on Thursday highlighted the strategic threats facing Israel across the region, particularly from “Iran and its terror proxies”. The Israeli president underscored the importance of Sino-Israeli relations, particularly in trade, economics and culture, it added. According to the Chinese statement, Herzog referred to China as an important constructive force in global and regional peace, praising Beijing’s efforts to foster regional stability and conveying a readiness to maintain close communication. Separately on the summit’s sidelines, Wang held talks with Palestinian Foreign Minister Varsen Aghabekian Shahin, pledging China’s continued support for the Palestinian cause and urging international backing for a two-state solution. Beijing’s top diplomat said the Gaza crisis should not be marginalised amid wider regional escalation. Shahin said the Palestinian people hoped to keep deepening relations with China, expecting Beijing to continue upholding justice on the Palestinian issue and play a more prominent role in realising the two-state solution.

title: Meet Dan and Dave Buck, co-owners of Art of Play, the store feuding with Kelly Clarkson
description: The singer recently complained on social media about an unpleasant encounter at the Brooklyn shop run by the Buck twins, who are known as the ‘godfathers’ of cardistry.
content: A New York store named Art of Play has become the centre of a feud with Kelly Clarkson after the singer went on X and alleged she was treated as if she couldn’t afford the shop’s items. “Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me. Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale,” Clarkson wrote on October 10. “But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts’ character in Pretty Woman. For sure, check it out,” she continued. In response, Art of Play posted a statement on Instagram on October 11, explaining that Clarkson had inquired about a singing bird automaton named “Molly”, which, according to the store, was not for sale. “Yesterday, Kelly Clarkson visited us in Brooklyn and inquired about buying ‘Molly’, a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton who plays an important role in the magic shows we host here. Molly is permanently attached to the wall and isn’t for sale. However, the negative experience Kelly described on twitter would resonate with anyone who has ever felt judged in a shop.” The response only seemed to upset Clarkson further, and she called them “liars” on her Instagram Stories, adding that Molly had a price tag hanging on the wall. She said she’d been told the piece was for sale, “but it costs US$15,000, so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can.” “That all never happened and now it’s not for sale,” Clarkson wrote. In another Instagram post, Art of Play said they tried to explain to Clarkson that the piece in question wasn’t for sale, but that “a nearly identical automaton” was available for the same price in Seattle. They added that they’ve tried to reach out to Clarkson to clear the air privately. Twin brothers Dan and Dave Buck, along with Adam Rubin, co-own Art of Play, and Rubin told New York Magazine that, because of Molly’s popularity after the feud, the piece now costs US$15 million. But who are Dan and Dave Buck, the now-famous Brooklyn store owners? Read on to find out. What is Dan and Dave Buck’s background? Dan and David Buck, who go professionally as Dan and Dave, were born in 1984 in Sonora, California. The twin brothers were 12 when they first saw American magician and illusionist David Copperfield on television, which inspired them to become illusionists. When they were 13, the brothers found a VHS instructional tape on card tricks and became obsessed. “We discovered card tricks and thought that was more of our style, more of our thing, since we were into the extreme sports that fit our personality a little better so I guess we just picked it up from there,” Dan said in a 2008 interview. How did their cardistry career take off? Within a year of becoming obsessed with cardistry, a performance art of card flourishing, the Buck brothers had invented several of their own moves and recorded them on VHS tape, which they sold at magic conventions. This would come in handy later when the brothers moved to Las Vegas, where they learned filmmaking and produced instructional DVDs on cardistry. Dan and Dave are widely credited with popularising cardistry through their videos, and have been dubbed the “godfathers” of the performance art. When did they open Art of Play? Dan and Dave founded Art of Play in 2013 and have described it as a “wonder emporium of sorts offering a collection of playing cards, puzzles, games, toys and home goods”. They co-own the store with Rubin, a children’s book author. Little information is available online about Dan and Dave’s personal lives.

title: Malaysia’s Negeri Sembilan ruler orders chief minister out of sight in rare public rebuke
description: In a video, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir is seen giving Chief Minister Ismail Lasim a public dressing-down over efforts to unseat him.
content: A Malaysian ruler known for being reserved has publicly berated his chief minister over efforts to unseat him, telling the politician to “go away” and withdraw his claim that the monarch no longer holds the throne. Negeri Sembilan, south of Kuala Lumpur, has been caught in a dispute since April over who is its rightful ruler, bringing down one state government aligned with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition and leaving its newly appointed chief minister without a state executive council. In a video circulating online on Friday, Negeri Sembilan ruler Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir confronts Chief Minister Ismail Lasim over a letter he says endorsed his removal and was sent to the official overseeing Malaysia’s royal council. He told Ismail not to come and see him again unless he retracted the letter. “Ismail Lasim wrote to the Keeper of the Rulers’ Seal saying that the decision he made with the executive council was valid and that I am no longer the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan,” Muhriz says, using his royal title. “So why come and see me? Until he retracts what he said, don’t come and see me. Go away. Don’t see me. I don’t want to see you. Understand?” the ruler said. The rebuke is a striking departure for a monarch known for his reserved manner and preference for keeping a low profile. Dressed in pink traditional Malay attire, Muhriz addresses Ismail as attendants and onlookers stand nearby. The chief minister, in blue, is seen raising his joined palms towards the ruler in a gesture of respect. The feud centres on an attempt to replace Muhriz with another royal, Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar. Four territorial chiefs issued a proclamation in April seeking to remove him over allegations that he had breached his royal duties, but federal legal authorities said there was no evidence that he met the constitutional grounds for removal. Unlike the other monarchies in Malaysia that decide succession by birthright, Negeri Sembilan’s ruler is elected by four chieftains, known as undangs. Ismail, an Umno politician sworn into office before Muhriz in August, has given conflicting accounts of his role. On September 9, he said he had signed the proclamation under duress, lodged a police report and maintained that the document was invalid. Eight days later, he confirmed that his executive council had unanimously backed it and instructed the state secretary to proceed with its formal publication. Local media, citing the state opposition PH, reported that Ismail also wrote to the Keeper of the Rulers’ Seal on September 17 asking that Malaysia’s rulers be informed of Muhriz’s removal and Nadzaruddin’s selection as his replacement. The Attorney General’s Chambers said on September 17 that the chief minister and his council had no unilateral power to remove the ruler and that the proclamation failed to meet constitutional requirements. Muhriz dismissed all 10 executive councillors on September 20, leaving Ismail in office. The crisis prompted the Conference of Rulers – which comprises the heads of Malaysia’s nine royal households, including from Negeri Sembilan – on Wednesday to call for restraint and for the competing sides to find a “dignified solution” that would not undermine the state monarchy. Online, some viewers said they had never seen Muhriz so angry, while others mocked the chief minister’s public dressing-down. “If I were Tok Mail, where would I hide my face?” one commenter wrote, using a familiar name for Ismail. Another joked that the chief minister had “turned into a meowing cat”.

title: China invites Trump press secretary Katie Zacharia to visit after ‘proper toilets’ slur
description: China extends open invitation to Zacharia ahead of US president’s expected visit to Shenzhen for Apec summit.
content: Beijing has invited White House press secretary Katie Zacharia to visit the country more often after she said in an interview that China “doesn’t even have proper toilets”. The newly appointed spokeswoman for the Trump administration made the controversial remarks in an interview on Thursday with conservative commentator Jack Posobiec, when talking about the perception around 2016 that “the gold days, the glory days of the US were over and China was on the horizon”. “I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking, ‘How is China the next country on the horizon? They don’t even have proper toilets’,” she said. Asked to comment on Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said: “[We] welcome her to visit China more often when she has the opportunity.” Zacharia previously lived in China with her husband. On her LinkedIn profile, she said she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm, one of China’s biggest, in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. She faced scrutiny over her legal credentials after she told reporters on Tuesday that she had passed a bar exam “when I moved to China”, without specifying the jurisdiction. Chinese law firms can hire foreign nationals, but they cannot be licensed as lawyers in China. She acknowledged in the same interview that she had sat the California bar exam after graduating from Pepperdine University’s law school in 2011 but did not pass. Zacharia told Posobiec there had been “a lot of misinformation” about the fact that she “labelled myself ‘lawyer’”. The White House has defended her, with communications director Steven Cheung saying “she is uniquely qualified and whip-smart”. She could be returning to China as early as next month when President Donald Trump is expected to take part in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern city of Shenzhen. Zacharia’s toilet comments are at odds with Trump’s warm approach towards Chinese President Xi Jinping, whom Trump hosted in Washington last month, following the United States president’s state visit to China in May. Trump pulled out all the stops to make Xi’s visit a grand affair and the two leaders met several times during the visit, including at a ceremonial airport welcome, a White House reception and for talks on a wide range of topics, including trade, tariffs and Taiwan. The two presidents are also expected to meet in Miami in December for the Group of 20 summit. After Trump and Xi’s meeting in Washington, the two sides pledged to build a “constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity”.

title: Inspections ordered at 8 more houses in Hong Kong’s One Stanley after rebar scandal
description: After structural lapses found at one house, authorities order developer to conduct wider checks, including on home bought by Mongolian mining family.
content: Hong Kong authorities have ordered the developer of One Stanley to inspect eight more homes, including one acquired by a Mongolian mining tycoon’s family, as concerns over substandard work at the seaside luxury estate mount. The details of the inspection were contained in a sales brochure updated by developer K&K Property on Friday and follow an announcement by the Buildings Department last month that it would conduct random checks on buildings at the estate. Online property news platform WuChatProp earlier reported that insufficient steel bars had been used in parts of detached house No 35. According to the updated brochure, the department had spotted irregularities in the house, including the absence of wire mesh on the concrete cover of a ground-floor beam, as required by the approved plan, and deviations in the steel reinforcement of some slabs. The department told the developer to inspect houses No 5, 8, 16, 17, 19, 32, 33 and 36, as well as the common area of a flat, Block 9. According to a source, buyers had signed provisional purchase agreements for three of the houses – No 5, 16 and 17 – but none had requested to terminate the contracts so far. The development comprises 32 detached houses and 11 low-rise blocks containing 50 flats in total. The department told the South China Morning Post that commenting further on the case was inappropriate as investigations were under way. The SCMP earlier reported that Tisara Holdings, whose director is Tselmuun Nyamtaishir, signed a provisional agreement in January to buy No 5. Nyamtaishir is the president and CEO of Mongolyn Alt, a mineral conglomerate founded in 1993 by her father in Mongolia and the largest coal exporter in the country. She earlier told the SCMP the block was intended to be used as a retirement residence by the group’s founders. Land Registry records show house No 16 was sold to Supreme Harmony for HK$116.8 million (US$14.9 million). The company, whose sole owner is mainland Chinese, signed the purchase agreement in June. House No 17 was sold for HK$118 million to an individual, who signed the document in August. Speaking to the press on Thursday, Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho declined to provide more details about the case, saying the investigation into No 35 was ongoing. Asked why the department deemed it appropriate to issue an occupation permit, Linn said some problems might remain hidden to authorities. “Sometimes, when an occupation permit is issued, there may be hidden areas that were not visible at the time,” she said. “We will definitely make the investigation results public, act in accordance with the law and punish offenders according to law.” News outlet WuChatProp reported on October 2 that an on-site inspection of No 35 found insufficient steel bars in parts of the building, and the amount in certain areas fell short of the approved structural plan by as much as 75 per cent. The owner, who submitted a complaint to the department in January, was unhappy about the government’s inaction, according to the report. The property is a four-bedroom, 3,000 square foot (278 square metre) detached house, which the owner reportedly bought in 2024. The price was HK$115.8 million, according to a transaction list obtained by the SCMP. Hong Kong has been hit by a string of construction scandals, including issues with concrete samples from three public housing blocks under construction in Tung Chung, prompting further review and testing in September. Earlier in August, 24 of the 28 lifts in Queen Mary Hospital’s new clinical block were deemed unfit for use. The widespread installation defects delayed the full commissioning of the Pok Fu Lam hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block by up to a year. City leader John Lee Ka-chiu has declined to comment on individual cases but said he was concerned as to whether the professionals involved in the projects had discharged their duties properly. Such matters concerned professional standards and the quality and safety of the city’s construction works, he said. In response to the scandal at One Stanley, K Wise, a subsidiary of K&K Property, earlier said it would offer a six-year structural warranty to homeowners and arrange free independent inspections. It also said the owner and the developer had agreed to jointly hire an independent surveyor to determine the circumstances.

title: Ex-father-in-law failed to repay HK$250,000 loan, Abby Choi murder trial hears
description: TamJai founder Tam Chak-kwan details series of requests for money by Kwong Kau, including help in paying for legal representation after his arrest.
content: The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung failed to repay a HK$250,000 loan from her partner’s father and asked for help in hiring lawyers after he was remanded in custody for allegedly killing the model three years ago, a court has heard. Tam Chak-kwan, founder of the popular restaurant chain TamJai Yunnan Mixian, testified in the High Court on Friday about his interactions with Kwong Kau in the year leading to the latter’s arrest for his suspected role in Choi’s murder in February 2023. Kwong, 68, allegedly enlisted his two sons to help kill the 28-year-old influencer after she tried to sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the upmarket Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin that was registered in his name. He is standing trial alongside his sons Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, and Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, Choi’s ex-husband. The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, is also contesting a charge of preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body, an offence to which his two sons pleaded guilty before the trial began last month. The court heard Tam’s family wealth increased significantly after he received part of the profits from selling his business to a Japanese company for HK$1 billion. He told the court it was “a little bit of an achievement”, but Deputy Judge Brian Keith said he did not have to be unduly modest. The former restaurant owner said his son, Chris Tam Fong-chun, had a very happy relationship with Choi even though they never registered their marriage. He and his wife, Yau Mei-fung, never took issue with the model being a divorcee with two children from her first marriage to Alex Kwong, the court heard. He said he gave Choi a HK$41 million flat at the Manhattan Hill private estate in Lai Chi Kok, where he used to live, and more than HK$80 million for investments. The court was told that he and his wife also bought her luxury gifts including handbags and jewellery. Asked why he allowed his de facto daughter-in-law to handle finances, the elder Tam said Choi was more mature and organised than his son, whom he said was not serious about work when he was young. He added that the socialite was able to handle money well and make good investment decisions. Wrapping up his testimony on Friday, Chris Tam said his father spent about HK$6 million to help him settle a HK$5 million gambling debt he incurred when he visited Macau with Choi and Anthony Kwong in August 2021. The younger Tam said he believed the additional payments were gratuities, colloquially known as “tea money”, given to people with triad affiliations for stopping debt collectors from continuing to harass his family. The elder Tam said he was approached by five “fierce” men on a day in early 2022, telling him Choi owed HK$5 million because of his son. The elder Tam said he was shocked to later confirm with his son that he had borrowed money to gamble in Macau. He then approached Kwong Kau, who advised him to report the matter to police, the court heard. The witness said that as he was frustrated by the progress of the police investigation, he asked Kwong Kau for help again. Kwong Kau allegedly said he could resolve the matter through “people in the underworld”, but Tam insisted the matter should be settled using a law firm. The elder Tam said he transferred HK$5 million into Kwong Kau’s personal bank account and gave him HK$450,000 as “tea money”. He also paid about HK$60,000 to the law firm handling the paperwork for the repayment, the court heard. According to the elder Tam, Kwong Kau sought a HK$400,000 loan from him in December 2022, saying his bank account had been frozen by the commercial crime bureau because officers deemed the HK$5 million transfer suspicious. Tam said he only gave his counterpart HK$250,000. “Abby told me this person was not trustworthy, but because he had helped me settle this matter, I decided to help him,” the witness said, referring to the harassment by debt collectors. The elder Tam said Kwong Kau never repaid him, but he had no intention of chasing the money because he did not think the retiree would pay it back. Kwong Kau’s legal counsel, Oliver Davies, suggested that the elder Tam offered to lend his client money after the ex-sergeant said he was concerned that authorities would freeze his bank account. “Ridiculous,” the witness replied. The elder Tam said that after Choi’s killing came to light in February 2023, a law firm clerk sent him a photo of what appeared to be a handwritten letter from Kwong Kau, who asked him to hire lawyers on his behalf because he had been denied bail. The defendant allegedly called himself a man with integrity, while describing the elder Tam as a “very good friend”, as he explained he was in a difficult situation because he had no money to hire legal representation. “At that time I had a friend who was a lawyer and I consulted that person. I was advised to ignore him and that’s what I did,” the witness said. The trial continues.

title: China’s 400km/h trains getting closer to debut, numbering-system change hints
description: Overhaul of designation system creates new class for passenger service operating above 350km/h.
content: China’s national rail operator has added a new service category for high-speed trains running above 350km/h to accommodate faster routes in the future, signalling the impending commercial debut of its newest and fastest train model and potentially marking another milestone for the world’s fastest train fleet. China State Railway Group’s overhaul of its train numbering system would introduce the prefix “X” – short for xin, the Chinese word for “new” – for Fuxing trains with a maximum speed higher than 350km/h, according to a statement on Friday. “This is primarily intended for use on trains operating at higher speeds in the future,” the statement said. Fuxing refers to China’s flagship CR series of high-speed trains, designed and manufactured domestically. China has been testing its new CR450 trains, designed to operate commercially at 400km/h, some 50km/h faster than the fastest CR400 models currently in service. The new train model achieved test speeds of up to 453km/h in October last year, thanks to a 22 per cent reduction in wind resistance and a 10 per cent paring of weight, compared with its predecessor. The CR450 was also included in the National Railway Administration’s latest five-year plan for the sector released on Monday, with authorities pledging to further develop the series. Under China Railway’s new numbering system, the “G” prefix will be used for high-speed trains operating at a maximum speed of 350km/h, while “T” will indicate high-speed services up to 300km/h, significantly faster than the conventional express trains it used to denote. Between 2014, when the current train codes were introduced, and 2025, operational railway mileage rose 47.6 per cent to 165,000km, according to China Railway. In the same span, the number of high-speed trains operating at speeds of 300 to 350km/h more than tripled to 3,149, while the average daily number of passenger trains in operation more than doubled to 11,796. The new numbering system increases the number of designations available for high-speed trains by 40 per cent, the railway group added.

title: HKEX pushes back T+1 trade settlement to 2028 after brokers request more prep time
description: Despite the delay, the exchange said the market response had shown strong support for shortening the settlement time.
content: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing said it had delayed a plan to shorten the settlement time for share transactions to the second half of 2028, so it could address widespread industry requests for more preparation time. Confirming a report by the South China Morning Post on Wednesday, the exchange said in a statement on Friday that it would not proceed with the timeline it proposed in a consultation paper in April, aiming to implement a so-called T+1 system in the fourth quarter of 2027, replacing the existing T+2 cycle. A T+1 system means that trades are settled one day after the transaction. The delay came after respondents “highlighted several implementation considerations”, the exchange said, adding it had received 109 responses from brokers, investment managers and others. “Taking into account stakeholder feedback, HKEX now targets T+1 implementation in [September] 2028, subject to market readiness and regulatory approval,” the exchange said in a statement. Despite the delay, the exchange said the market response had shown strong support for shortening the settlement time. Consultation feedback identified several key focus areas for the transition to T+1, such as managing the increased operational demands from a compressed settlement cycle, the exchange said. There remain major concerns over areas including foreign exchange settlement and stock borrowing settlement, with many participants arguing the new settlement times may not be sufficient after counting the time zone differences. The market response also indicated that HKEX would need to ensure securities availability and settlement preparation in a timely manner for a shorter settlement cycle, the exchange said. “We at HKEX are pleased to be moving ahead with this significant market infrastructure enhancement, with the broad support from participants reflecting a shared recognition of the strategic importance to move Hong Kong’s securities market to T+1,” said HKEX CEO Bonnie Chan Yiting on Friday. “By reducing settlement risk, improving capital efficiency and strengthening market resilience, T+1 will reinforce the attractiveness and connectivity of Hong Kong’s markets, whilst keeping our infrastructure aligned with the continued evolution of major international markets.” The US and Canada shifted to T+1 in May 2024, while the UK and Europe were exploring the same option, Chan said earlier. Mainland China has long operated under a T+1 cycle. The exchange said on Friday it would adopt three layers of preparation for the introduction of T+1 – refine its market infrastructure, develop workflow tools for the new settlement time, and set up working groups with industry players to undertake the necessary preparations. Hong Kong’s market regulator, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), also supports the new HKEX timeline. “The transition to T+1 represents an important step in maintaining Hong Kong’s competitiveness as an international financial centre and ensuring alignment with developments in global markets,” said Rico Leung, executive director of the SFC’s supervision of markets division, in a statement on Friday. “We welcome HKEX’s consultation conclusions and its readiness-based approach to implementation. Industry participants are urged to begin their preparations early, assess the implications for their systems, processes and operating arrangements, and work closely with their counterparts and service providers to ensure a smooth and orderly transition.”

title: Exclusive | ‘I’m so excited’: Kim Jones on choosing Hong Kong as the home of his revived fashion label
description: The British fashion designer, who is reviving his eponymous brand after nearly two decades, tells SCMP why he loves Hong Kong.
content: One might not expect British fashion designer Kim Jones, a figure synonymous with modern luxury, to highlight reptiles as one of his earliest memories of Hong Kong. “I love Hong Kong, the weird side of it and the fact that there are king cobras that live here, and different snakes and the sort of things which most people probably get terrified of,” the 53-year-old says. Jones first visited Hong Kong after joining Dunhill as its creative director in 2008, visiting regularly in the late 2000s to study Asian tailoring traditions. He frequently logged more than 20,000 steps a day exploring the local markets, modern precincts and historic neighbourhoods. “I see everything and what people are wearing and what different types of people are on the street,” he says. His observations proved useful for his work at Dunhill, helping him develop fabrics and designs that allowed consumers to feel impeccably tailored yet comfortable in Hong Kong’s climate. “I was just looking at everything in the world that’s changing very fast: menswear, womenswear, petswear, everything,” he says. There’s no point making something beautiful if nobody wants to wear it Kim Jones In the nearly two decades since then, Jones has become a fashion heavyweight, designing for the likes of Louis Vuitton, Dior Men, Fendi and Bosideng – and his curiosity and discernment remain his greatest strengths. He returned to Hong Kong in October 2026 to announce the relaunch of his eponymous brand at the Central Yards complex in 2027. Fluid silhouettes and functional luxury Slated to debut for the autumn/winter 2027 season, Jones’ new label centres on menswear characterised by fluid, genderless silhouettes unrestricted by traditional sartorial categories. The apparel will be predominantly made in Japan, with leather goods produced in Italy. “We are creating reversible pieces, interesting fabrications and clothes that can be worn in different ways,” Jones says. “Luxury should be about quality and how something works for you. There’s no point making something beautiful if nobody wants to wear it. I’ve always loved functional clothing. I travel constantly, so I think about what people actually need.” Over time, the brand will expand into furniture, interior objects, art and design. “I want [my brand] to become a complete lifestyle world,” he says. Born in London, Jones spent his childhood moving between Ecuador, the Caribbean, Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania and Botswana due to his father’s career as a hydrologist, a scientist who studies the distribution and management of water. Interdisciplinary art is familiar territory for Jones, who studied graphics and photography at London’s Camberwell College of Arts before earning a master of arts in fashion from Central Saint Martins. “I’ve collected art and books for as long as I can remember,” he says. “It’s something I genuinely love, and it’s a huge part of my life. I’m constantly looking at things, whether it’s a photograph, a piece of furniture, an exhibition or something I’ve seen while travelling. It all feeds into the way I think.” In 2003, a year after graduating, Jones launched his original eponymous brand, but paused the project in 2008 when he started at Dunhill. Throughout his career at major European luxury houses, fine art and street culture remained core elements to his work. Jones frequently collaborated with contemporary artists – including Kaws, Hajime Sorayama, Daniel Arsham and Raymond Pettibon – to design runway sets and collections. He also drew inspiration from fine art movements, incorporating the surrealist palette of Rene Magritte into his collections for Dior. Long before luxury houses embraced urban sportswear, Jones pioneered the fusion of high-end design and street culture, most notably orchestrating the seminal Louis Vuitton and Supreme collaboration in 2017. This followed a partnership with British sportswear label Umbro in the 2000s. His work seamlessly merged youth subcultures, London punk aesthetics and athleticwear with classic European tailoring legacies. “I’ve been incredibly lucky to work at some amazing houses and with extraordinary people, and I’ve learned so much along the way,” Jones says. “But I got to a point where I thought, why not do something for myself again? I didn’t really want to go and look at another archive. I wanted to do something new, and it felt like the right time.” A flagship built on community When asked what creative territories he feels eager to explore next, Jones answers immediately. “Everything, genuinely,” he says. “That is the freedom of working under my own name. After decades operating within heritage house structures, I now have the autonomy to experiment and see where ideas lead.” Jones’ affinity for Hong Kong ultimately guided his decision to anchor his brand’s global retail presence in the city. He has long maintained close ties with Asia; his original label enjoyed a strong following in Japan, and in late 2025 he assumed artistic direction of Areal, a hi-tech luxury outerwear line launched with China’s performance apparel giant Bosideng. “This century is very much looking east,” Jones says. “What’s exciting now is how much confidence there is in Asian creativity. People have a very strong sense of their own style and a real understanding of fashion, art and design. It’s one of the reasons I’m so excited to be opening our first store here. “Hong Kong is where we’re bringing everything together for the customer. What’s exciting about Central Yards is the opportunity to create a physical space where people can experience the brand properly, from the clothes to the art, furniture and everything else I’m interested in.” He adds that the flagship layout will mirror the intimate aesthetic of his London home. Addressing concerns about luxury fashion becoming financially inaccessible for younger generations, Jones offers a candid perspective. “I stopped working in luxury nearly a year and a half ago,” he says. “One of the problems was the price points. When I started, [designer pieces were] actually quite affordable for young people to buy, but now it’s not.” At his Central Yards flagship, Jones plans to introduce other lifestyle categories alongside tailored apparel, including fragrances, toys and even cars. “I love the idea of how different types of people can go in the store and buy different things,” he says. “I want them to enjoy it, spend time in it and feel like they can make it their home, take something home, buy a present or buy something for themselves. “I want people to come in and feel like they’re part of a community. That’s the most important thing. The world is pulling people apart. We want to put people together.”

title: EU rallies around Zelensky as rift widens with Trump over Russia energy strikes
description: A Brussels summit pledges fresh backing for Kyiv amid mounting fears over US satellite limits and Washington’s stance towards Moscow.
content: European leaders on Friday rallied around Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky as Kyiv’s ties with US President Donald Trump have nosedived and worries grow that US leader is increasingly siding with Russia. Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since last week, when Trump eased sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel onto global markets. Zelensky infuriated Trump further by ordering Ukraine’s forces to restart strikes on Russian oil refineries in defiance of Washington’s demands. Meanwhile, anger in Ukraine has been heightened by disruptions to a critical US-provided satellite system that have hampered its military’s ability to counter Russia’s intense bombardments ahead of the harsh winter months. “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” European Council chief Antonio Costa said, standing alongside Zelensky at an EU summit in Brussels. “Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.” The Ukrainian president welcomed the backing of “real leaders” in Europe and said there were no signals that Moscow is ready “to end this war”. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that “the situation in Ukraine is currently truly dire, with numerous Russian attacks and a tense relationship between Ukraine and the US.” “It is crucial that we, as Europe, demonstrate our unconditional support for them today – and explore what additional steps we can take,” he said. Zelensky has had to endure a roller coaster relationship with Trump since the mercurial US leader returned to office last year vowing to cut Washington’s support for Kyiv. Trump on Thursday called renewed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure a “disgrace” and said Kyiv was driving up global energy prices. “I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” the US leader said in an interview with Newsmax. The Kremlin has sought to capitalise on the latest breakdown between Kyiv and Washington, blaming Ukraine for derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries. Ukraine meanwhile has accused the Trump administration of essentially helping Moscow during the latest falling out as the bad blood appears to have hit Ukraine’s ability to defend itself. Despite the tensions, European leaders are hoping that Ukraine can weather the storm and patch up ties as there is little substitute for key US satellite capabilities. “Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in [the] short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas said. Ukraine uses the Starshield system from Elon Musk’s SpaceX for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones. It is separate from SpaceX’s parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also uses but not for offensive operations. Tech billionaire Musk, who has also called for Zelensky to be replaced as leader, said his company was not behind any disruption to the system. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he added, referring to Trump. While the main focus for European leaders will be on overcoming the latest crisis with Washington, they will also focus on how to bolster Ukraine’s air defences and cover Ukraine’s dire budgetary situation. “We have to prepare for the winter. It’s not only energy, it’s also air defence and funding,” Zelensky said. EU leaders are set to open discussions about how to keep Ukraine afloat next year in the face of a growing realisation that funds will run dry. The EU has in place a 90-billion-euro (US$101-billion) loan for Kyiv that was set to help cover funding to the end of 2027. But the Ukrainian authorities have warned they will need tens of billions more as Russia’s strikes have battered the country’s economy. The talks around the new funding have reignited calls for the European Union to tap around 200 billion euros in frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine. “The frozen assets are there. That’s what should be used for supporting Ukraine,” said Latvian premier Andris Kulbergs. But there seems little momentum on that front as Belgium, where most of the funds are held, remains opposed.

title: Financial Street Forum forecast calls for more opening up by Chinese regulators
description: Visa’s long-awaited nod for a local card-clearing business raises hopes for more measures allowing deeper participation.
content: International investors will keep an eye on a forum next week for clues from China’s regulators on how they plan to further open its financial markets, after Visa’s long-awaited approval fuelled hopes for deeper participation in the world’s second-largest economy. Regulators could announce more measures at the Financial Street Forum to deepen the internationalisation of the yuan and optimise the Connect series of cross-border investment links between investors in mainland China and the rest of the world, analysts said. “As China’s economy develops and Chinese companies expand further overseas, we need a yuan-based financial system to serve the real economies of other regions around the world, just as the United States does with the dollar,” said Liu Jing, director of the investment research department at the Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business in Beijing. The Financial Street Forum, a four-day event starting on Monday, will feature keynote speeches from Pan Gongsheng, governor of the People’s Bank of China (PBOC), Ding Xiangqun, head of the National Financial Regulatory Administration, and Wu Qing, chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC). Over 400 financial heavyweights from more than 40 countries and regions are set to gather in Beijing for discussions themed on openness, cooperation and inclusiveness. PBOC’s nod to Visa on Tuesday, after a years-long wait, raised expectations for more opening-up measures. The US payment card company won regulatory approval to work towards setting up a wholly foreign-owned domestic bank card clearing business in China, after 40 years of handling cross-border and foreign currency transactions in the country. With a local clearing organisation, Visa would be able to settle domestic yuan transactions directly with its own network. On Thursday, an executive of the China Financial Futures Exchange said at an event that it was steadily advancing preparations for a pilot programme for yuan-denominated foreign exchange futures, pressing forward with the opening up of derivative products. Liu of the Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business said global card issuers like Visa stood to benefit from an outbound tourism rebound, despite digital payment tools from Tencent Holdings and Alibaba Group Holding dominating the domestic market. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. But international financial institutions still faced challenges in the market, he added. The PBOC and CSRC have undertaken a range of measures to promote international use of the yuan, from issuing offshore yuan treasury bonds and expanding the bilateral currency swap facility to extending the Connect Schemes and easing overseas listings by Chinese companies. The yuan accounted for 3.3 per cent of global payments by value in August, jumping from 1.9 per cent 10 years ago, data from the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication showed. The US dollar stayed on top with a share of 52.1 per cent. Hong Kong aims to include a yuan trading counter in the Stock Connect schemes by July 1. Tools like the Connect Schemes would play a key role as China encouraged funds to “go global” legally, by presenting opportunities for banking institutions, asset management firms and professional service providers, said Xu Tianchen, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit. In the future, Xu said, there would be potential to engage more sophisticated international financial institutions to supply more diverse products to meet growing demand for asset and wealth management.

title: India’s proposed social media ban for under-18s wins parents’ backing
description: Lawyers, however, advise against a sweeping ban, saying children could benefit from access to online educational content.
content: Digangana Mukherjee, a mother of a six-year-old girl and a 10-year-old boy, has banned television at her home in the Indian city of Mysore because she does not want her children to become addicted to watching content on screen. A year ago, when her son’s school started using a smart classroom board that streamed online content, she and her husband decided to enrol him in a school where teachers used chalk on a slate board, and the pace of lessons was slower. Now, she is happy that the Indian government is reportedly planning to prevent children below 18 years from opening social media accounts under a new law, in line with a Supreme Court ruling that such accounts signed up by minors should be considered void. “I approve of it as a parent. My son is 10 and knows how to browse YouTube. It is already becoming scary for me. I don’t know what content is visible to him,” Mukherjee said. While parents may welcome India’s proposed safeguards, enforcement could prove complicated in one of the world’s largest online markets. Legal experts warn that policing underage accounts and preventing users from getting around restrictions and privacy rights would be the main stumbling blocks, while a blanket ban would deprive young people of valuable educational resources. Other countries in the Asia-Pacific region have enacted such laws, with Australia setting the ball rolling last December when it banned social media access for children under 16 under its Online Safety Amendment Act. Mukherjee, who runs a library at her home filled with old books and conducts storytelling sessions for children, said she could distinguish between those who have unrestricted access to online screens and those with limited exposure. “I see a lot of children come in and out of my space. There is a stark difference between these children. The attention span is much less for those who have abundant access to screens. They are restless and are not able to sit still for long,” she said. Children with unlimited screen access have many entertainment options, and they are not keen on books, according to Mukherjee. “If there were fewer screens, people would read more books. Growing up, we had Sunday afternoons only to watch TV. The rest of the time, when I was really bored, I had to pick up a book,” she said. Many social media users younger than 18 in India do not face online curbs. Last month, India’s solicitor general Tushar Mehta concurred with the position of the Supreme Court, in response to a petition by the “Just Rights For Children Alliance” NGO, that social media accounts opened by minors should be voided. He said the federal government should step in to make such a ban mandatory. Australia deactivated 4.7 million social media accounts opened by those below 16 in the first month of its ban. India’s Goa state has been considering an Australia-like social media ban for children, amid growing concerns over the impact of excessive use on their mental health. Lawyers, however, warn that the proposed regulation to curb access for children in India is bound to face legal challenges. “I understand the Supreme Court’s request to bring in safeguards and the government’s stance to bring in stronger regulation to combat the risks posed. What remains to be seen is the extent and severity of restrictions that ultimately take form,” said Ashima Chalia, founder and senior partner at Bengaluru-based Ayaam Legal. The mother of a two-year-old baby said that she wished for such a legal curb to protect children from online risks such as sexual exploitation, cyberbullying and harmful content. “As a parent, I would also wish to baby-proof the whole world against anything that may harm my kid,” Chalia said. “No doubt there is a need for stricter legislation or rules, but the Indian government has a herculean task of balancing children’s access to education and beneficial digital resources,” she said. These rules would have to address a user’s rights regarding personal information collection and storage as well as age-verification processes, she added. While Chalia conceded that Indian regulators would face challenges from children in India lying about their age when opening social media accounts, she added: “An uphill battle surely, but absolutely attainable.” Striking a balance Ambareen Ali Shah, a New Delhi-based mother of a 14½-year-old boy, said she worried about how easy access to social media would affect children’s time management as they had to do online and offline school assignments. “Once you have access to – say Instagram – the content is so interesting that it causes distraction,” she said. Shah recalled that when she was a young girl, the only screen she had access to was the television, restricted to a few hours of viewing. “We need to curb the time a child spends navigating the internet. On the other hand, social media is making kids smarter because they get access to a lot of information,” she said. Amitraj Kaushal, a lawyer at the Supreme Court of India, said that there was a strong case for a statutory framework protecting children from risks associated with social media use. Citing the need to limit their exposure to age-inappropriate material, Kaushal said: “Legislation can provide clarity by placing the primary compliance responsibility on platforms rather than criminalising children or their parents.” Australia’s experience could be useful for India as its law requires social media platforms to take “reasonable steps” to prevent those below 16 years old from opening accounts, while children and parents are not penalised for non-compliance, according to Kaushal. Debasree Basu, an adviser at G.M. International School in Mumbai, said, however, that a sweeping social media ban would be counter-productive. “Restrictions do not work. We have already exposed today’s generation to so many things that to ban them now will only make them more rebellious,” she said. “The message should be that we want to protect you, so please help us to do that. Then their whole attitude will change.”

title: China tech city dog-walking limits criticised; some question ‘how dogs can get some sunshine’
description: “Do you think this is civilised? You still believe this world is only inhabited by human beings?” one member of public questions.
content: The eastern city of Hangzhou has sparked widespread controversy by banning residents in its downtown area from walking their dogs during the day. Under the city’s Restraining Dog Raising Rules, owners of small ornamental dogs in designated “key restraining” areas may walk their pets only between 7pm and 7am. Large dogs cannot be taken outdoors at any time. The rules stipulate that dog owners must keep their pets on a leash and clean up their excrement immediately. Violators face fines of 200 to 1,000 yuan (US$30-US$150), and serious cases may result in the revocation of a dog registration licence. In mainland China, people who want to keep dogs in cities must first register them with the authorities and pay an annual renewal fee. Otherwise, the government may treat the dogs as strays and confiscate them. According to Dahe News, Hangzhou introduced the rule in 1996 and amended it in 2004. There have been no subsequent policy changes regarding dog ownership. However, many local residents have complained on social media that officials from the urban management department have stepped up enforcement of the rule in recent months. Some people have speculated that the authorities’ actions are related to an incident that went viral in June. The case involved a woman surnamed Wang, who took her dog to visit a friend in Binjiang District. The dog urinated on a parcel left outside the door of a male neighbour. A few days later, when Wang visited her friend again, she encountered the man and argued with him. In a video Wang later shared online, the man appeared to behave indecently towards her in a lift. Wang was detained after police found that the video had been fabricated. The incident brought dog management under the spotlight. An official from the municipal urban management authority told the media that, when they receive a complaint about a pet dog for the first time, they usually warn and try to persuade the owner. They take action against owners who repeatedly violate the rules. The rules state that owners who need to take their dogs to a veterinarian during the day should bring the animal’s registration licence and immunisation certificate to explain the situation to officials. There have been calls for years to extend the permitted dog-walking hours. In 2023, an internet user’s suggestion on the local government’s website attracted significant attention. The user urged authorities to take a more humane approach and adjust the permitted hours so dogs could bask in the sun. The Hangzhou municipal urban management authority replied that it was researching the issue and aimed to revise the rule soon. Reactions to Hangzhou’s dog-control rule on Chinese social media have been mixed. “Thumbs up to Hangzhou. This is what a civilised city should be like,” an internet user with the handle @lenggebuleng said, garnering 163,000 likes. Another person agreed, saying: “These measures, helping prevent dogs from annoying residents and harming old people and children and reducing faeces pollution, should be promoted nationwide.” But many people oppose the restrictions on dog-walking hours. “Do you think this is civilised? You still believe this world is only inhabited by human beings? Why do you ban dogs from going outside? I feel sad that the country’s animal protection awareness has not been improved at all,” one internet user commented. “My favourability for Hangzhou is lowered because of its dog management rule,” another user remarked.

title: Lily Mo Sheen’s rising career: What to know about Michael Sheen and Kate Beckinsale’s actress daughter
description: The 27-year-old turned heads at the Los Angeles premiere of Sense and Sensibility – and she was in a film with Nicolas Cage.
content: Lily Mo Sheen, daughter of Michael Sheen and Kate Beckinsale, knows how to steal the spotlight. The 27-year-old actress turned heads at the Los Angeles premiere of Sense and Sensibility on October 7, effortlessly channelling Jane Austen in a white silk slip dress that she paired with black Tabi footwear. In March, Lily attended the Elton John Aids Foundation’s 34th Annual Academy Awards Viewing Party in West Hollywood, California, wearing a semi-sheer strapless beaded gown. Last December, she was spotted in a more casual look when she sat courtside with her famous mother at a basketball game between the Los Angeles Clippers and the Los Angeles Lakers at Intuit Dome in Inglewood, California. While her red carpet appearances have been few and far between – in 2025, Lily attended the New York premiere of Bugonia and a New York screening of Honey Don’t! – we may be seeing more of her soon, thanks to her slate of upcoming projects. Here’s everything you need to know about Lily Mo Sheen. Her parents split in 2003 Kate Beckinsale Hilariously Re-Creates Her Daughter’s Birth Photo pic.twitter.com/01FIcmFREY — History Defined (@historydefined) June 21, 2025 Sheen was born on January 31, 1999, in London, England. Her parents met in 1995 while working on a touring production of The Seagull and split in 2003 after filming Underworld together, per People. However, the pair remained friends and have co-parented Lily, who is close to both of them. According to her profile on IMDb, Lily grew up in Los Angeles, attended Harvard-Westlake School and later went to New York University (NYU). “My parents were very adamant about me having an education, which I really respect, and having some semblance of normalcy through my life,” Sheen told entertainment news platform Collider. How did Lily Mo Sheen get into acting? Lily was initially hesitant about following her parents into the entertainment industry. Her mother hoped she would become a doctor, and she focused on writing until she was 15, per W Magazine. Sheen ultimately caught the acting bug after performing Shakespeare at school and later learned the Meisner technique of acting at NYU before venturing into auditions. While her parents are supportive of their daughter’s career, Beckinsale told Entertainment Tonight in 2021 that it’s “really important to [Lily] to have her own thing and blaze her own trail and do her own stuff”. What roles has Lily Mo Sheen played? Lily is best known for playing Nicolas Cage’s on-screen daughter Addy in The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent (2022). She has played younger versions of her mother’s characters, Selene and Amy, in Underworld: Evolution (2006) and Everybody’s Fine (2009), respectively. Next, Lily is set to appear in Oliver Kienle’s horror feature Don’t Kill Loretta (2027) and Jackson May’s tragicomedy film Degrees. She will also star alongside her mother in Sean McEwen’s action dramedy film Turnbuckle.

title: China leans in to hi-tech systems to counter emerging AI-fuelled terror threats
description: Exhibition at global forum in Beijing showcases Chinese hardware spanning the entire chain of counterterrorism operations.
content: China revealed AI-powered drone interceptors and other uncrewed systems at an international counterterrorism forum in Beijing this week, as security experts warned that new technologies could enable new forms of terrorism. The equipment was on display at the Great Wall-2026 International Forum on Counterterrorism, which ran from Tuesday to Thursday and was attended by more than 320 defence experts and military delegates from 62 countries. Discussions focused on how advances in artificial intelligence and unmanned systems were enhancing counterterrorism capabilities while creating new and unconventional security risks. The hardware showcased included low-cost, high-speed interception drones equipped with artificial intelligence guidance systems designed to neutralise “low, slow and small” unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) with high precision and rapid response times. Humanoid robots, robotic dogs, unmanned ground vehicles, drone detection systems and laser-based defence systems were also featured in the exhibition, covering capabilities from reconnaissance to swarm defence and control, as well as precision response. According to state broadcaster CCTV, the exhibition showed that AI technology now spans the entire chain of counterterrorism operations, from situational awareness and incident response to post-action assessment. The event was organised by the People’s Armed Police, China’s paramilitary force responsible for internal security, riot control and counterterrorism, underscoring Beijing’s push to harness emerging technologies to address evolving security threats. Experts at the forum cautioned that terrorist organisations were increasingly exploiting emerging technologies – including autonomous drones, drone swarms, encrypted communications and AI – for radicalisation, recruitment, funding and conducting complex multi-domain attacks. Science and Technology Daily reported that the proliferation of AI and unmanned technologies was reshaping the threat landscape, with terrorist groups using them to expand strike ranges and methods, while continuously shifting the geographical focus of their attacks. Terror groups were increasingly fielding UAVs with greater autonomy, as well as upgrading their cyberattack capabilities, increasing the use of drone swarms and improving their resilience to electronic warfare, it said. The key challenge will be regulating autonomous intelligence systems – from who uses them and who sells them, to how they are bought, deployed and disposed of. Coordinated international regulation will be needed to prevent misuse and strengthen counterterrorism efforts. “Terrorists might exploit AI models for learning and training, for which the developers must configure their large language models to prevent misuse,” Wu Mingxi, an expert in military intelligence and systems, told CCTV. “Terrorists can also employ AI to research and engineer new attack equipment.” Malicious actors might use generative AI to produce deepfake videos and misinformation, which presents more challenges, he added. “If we do not pay attention to the application of AI technology and fail to prevent its misuse by terrorist organisations and violent extremists, the consequences will be disastrous,” said Peng Jijun, secretary general of the forum’s organising committee.

title: China’s AI boom, self-sufficiency push fuel earnings surge for local chip firms
description: GPU designer MetaX, listed in Shanghai and may soon list in Hong Kong, says it turned a profit in the first nine months thanks to more orders.
content: Chinese chip and tech firms have flagged as much as six-fold growth in unaudited third-quarter profits, as huge demand for home-grown processors and artificial intelligence infrastructure filters through links in the supply chain amid the country’s push for self-reliance. Shanghai-listed Yuanjie Semiconductor Technology expected its quarterly net profit to land between 403 million yuan and 453 million yuan, up 579 per cent to 660 per cent from a year earlier. The maker of laser chips for optical communications said data-centre demand was driving shipments and helping maintain high margins. Some public firms offered a glimpse of their financial performance in the first nine months of the year, ahead of final third-quarter results announcements. Graphics processing unit (GPU) designer MetaX, listed in Shanghai but also pursuing a Hong Kong listing, turned a profit in the period thanks to increasing orders. It estimated a net profit of between 587 million yuan (US$88 million) and 717 million yuan, reversing a year-earlier loss, even excluding non-recurring gains. Hygon Information, whose processors serve both general computing and AI workloads, projected revenue growth of 50 per cent to 64 per cent in the first nine months. It cited rising demand for high-end chips as customers increasingly choose domestic alternatives over foreign suppliers. Storage giant Shenzhen Longsys Electronics said its net profit during the period could reach 14 billion to 14.9 billion yuan, roughly 20 times the figure for the previous year. It noted that price increases for DRAM and NAND flash storage had slowed in the third quarter, giving profits a smaller boost. Memory prices could remain firm through 2027, according to a Morgan Stanley report on Sunday, which also warned that supply catching up or customers slowing their purchases could cool the boom even without weaker AI demand. Optical module supplier Accelink Technologies forecast a nine-month net profit growth of 65 per cent to 82 per cent, citing both global AI capital spending and Chinese cloud providers’ continued investment in data centres as profit drivers. Silicon wafer supplier Xian Eswin Material Technology said its production lines ran at full capacity in the first nine months, with sales volumes up about 43 per cent to 8.3 million wafers. Although its net profit of about 151 million yuan during the period was boosted by gains from investments in initial public offerings by its customers, it still expected a loss after excluding non-recurring items. China’s AI buildout and efforts to replace imported processors are bringing more business to local chip designers. Research firm TrendForce projected in August that Chinese-designed chips would account for almost 90 per cent of the country’s high-end AI processor market this year. The growth in chip production is also lifting materials suppliers. Hubei Feilihua Quartz Glass forecast nine-month net profit growth of 35 per cent to 56 per cent, citing stronger semiconductor demand and opportunities to replace imported products. The research firm Bernstein said in a Tuesday report that quartz components used in chipmaking equipment were already well localised in China, with further growth increasingly tied to orders for domestic chipmaking equipment.

title: World Fencing League bringing sport’s best and brightest to Hong Kong in April
description: Sources tell the SCMP that the new competition has targeted the city for its second event, with Kai Tak Arena the favoured location.
content: Hong Kong will host a World Fencing League event next year, bringing the sport’s best and brightest to the city for one day in April, sources have told the South China Morning Post. The brainchild of 2016 US Olympic team foil bronze medallist Miles Chamley-Watson, WFL staged its inaugural event in Los Angeles earlier this year, and featured the likes of Hong Kong’s Ryan Choi Chun-yin, who captained Team Shield. Sources said the league was being pencilled in for the penultimate week of April, a fortnight before the Hong Kong Grand Prix, which will be for senior men’s and women’s foil. The new event has not been sanctioned by the sport’s world governing body, the FIE, and while a venue is yet to be confirmed, Kai Tak Arena is understood to be the preferred choice. Antonio Lam Hin-chung, general secretary of the Fencing Association of Hong Kong, China, said while his organisation had no official role in the event, they had no objections to it taking place. “From our perspective, this kind of event is going to help promote the sport of fencing, so we welcome it, as long as it is nicely and neatly organised,” Lam said. View this post on Instagram A post shared by World Fencing League (WFL) (@worldfencingleague) In the first WFL, Choi led his team to a 5-1 victory over Team Blade, with seven-time Formula 1 champion Lewis Hamilton among the 6,000 spectators at the Shrine Auditorium and Exhibition Hall. The first WFL event featured two mixed-gender teams with a total of 12 elite athletes, from across all three fencing disciplines - épée, foil and sabre - competing in timed bouts. Tracking and visualisation technology was also employed to enhance the viewer experience. The debut of the US$100,000 (HK780,000) event was said to have generated 700,000 views during live streams, and 500 million social views. While the line-ups for next year’s edition will not be confirmed for a while, several Hongkongers are expected to be involved. Apart from former world No 1 Choi, two-time Olympic champion Cheung Ka-long, and Kaylin Hsieh Sin-yan, could also be shortlisted for the glittering event. In its debut in April, the likes of three-time Olympic gold medallist Lee Kiefer of the United States, five-time world champion Oh Sang-uk from South Korea, and Chamley-Watson were among those taking part.

title: Indonesia’s central bank insists it is independent. Investors want proof
description: Huge bond purchases, the president’s nephew on board and a shifting legal role leave investors asking who really controls Bank Indonesia.
content: Indonesia has spent months trying to persuade investors that its economy is on the right course. A weakening rupiah, mounting budgetary pressures and a series of contentious policy decisions have made that task harder. Doubts about the management of Southeast Asia’s largest economy have now coalesced around its central bank, whose independence has come under intense scrutiny recently as President Prabowo Subianto seeks to steer economic policy. The appointment of Destry Damayanti – initially as acting governor of Bank Indonesia (BI) in late July before her formal appointment last month – was meant to reassure markets. But analysts say that confidence will only return if economic policymaking becomes more credible and decisions affecting the country’s financial health become more transparent. In an interview with Reuters on Monday, Destry insisted the central bank had “full autonomy” to set interest rates while maintaining “synergy” with the government. “When we’re about to make a policy decision – whether to raise or lower interest rates or to ⁠use other incentives – we have full authority to make that decision,” she said. Her assurances follow a turbulent few months for Indonesia’s economy. The rupiah hit record lows this year, with major credit rating agencies Moody’s and Fitch cutting their outlooks on the country’s sovereign rating from stable to negative. Conflict in the Middle East has only compounded the challenges. Despite the soaring cost of oil globally, Jakarta has held subsidised fuel prices steady. State institutions have since had their budgets cut to pay for energy imports and Prabowo’s flagship welfare programmes. On Friday, fears of foreign capital flight were further stoked after index compiler MSCI said in a statement that Indonesia no longer merited emerging-market status, citing “significant concerns” about market dysfunction, “including continued suspected coordinated trading behaviour and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement”. The US firm said it was now proposing a downgrade to “standalone” status – worse than previously flagged – which would exclude Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracked by passive investment funds managing billions of US dollars. Indonesian stocks, already the world’s worst performers this year, plunged 11 per cent to multi-year lows on Friday in response – the steepest one-day drop since 1998. Other developments that have unsettled markets in recent months include a new policy to centralise commodity exports, the abrupt dismissal of former finance minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa and his replacement by Suahasil Nazara, and the appointment of Prabowo’s nephew, Thomas Djiwandono, as a deputy governor of the central bank. In June, parliament passed a revision to the financial sector law that now requires Bank Indonesia to support economic growth and job creation, in addition to its duties managing money supply, keeping inflation under control, issuing and circulating legal tender, regulating national payment systems and acting as a lender of last resort. Asked how much the government was involved in monetary policy, Destry said officials had been invited to attend part of the bank’s monthly policy review, adding that she herself had attended meetings with Prabowo. “In Indonesia, the president is the head of government and the head of state. BI is under the state of Indonesia, so automatically, if the president wants to know about developments, I think it’s normal,” she told Reuters. The central bank held its benchmark rate at 5.75 per cent at its latest policy meeting in September, after raising it by a cumulative 100 basis points between May and June to stabilise and support the rupiah, which was trading at a near-record low of 18,070 per US dollar as of Friday afternoon. Proof over promises Economists who spoke to This Week in Asia agreed that the new governor’s message was welcome, but said investors would need to see Bank Indonesia demonstrate its independence. “The governor’s reassurance is a constructive and necessary signal, but it is unlikely to restore investor confidence on its own,” said Josua Pardede, chief economist at Permata Bank. “Restoring confidence requires a broader and sustained improvement in Indonesia’s economic policy credibility, not merely reassurance from the central bank.” While Bank Indonesia “remains legally independent”, Pardede said the unexpected resignation of its previous governor and changes to its responsibilities had stoked speculation that its “institutional independence has weakened”. Destry’s predecessor, Perry Warjiyo, resigned in July citing personal reasons. Yusuf Rendy Manilet, an economist at the Centre of Reform on Economics Indonesia, called for government-central bank synergy to rest on “clear data”, saying that the bank should, for example, consult the government’s employment figures before setting the benchmark interest rate. “When that happens, I think BI can be interpreted as still being relatively independent in implementing its policies,” he said. Yusuf also wanted the bank to explain its purchases of government bonds. According to Reuters, Bank Indonesia bought nearly 300 trillion rupiah (US$16.7 billion) of them between January and September 30 to support economic growth. “BI must convince investors that its bond purchasing policy has strong justification as a monetary policy and not because it is an extension of the government,” he said. Deniey Purwanto, a senior researcher at the Institute for Development of Economics and Finance in Jakarta, said the central bank would be fully autonomous only when it could set rates “without considering its impact on government debt costs”. Downgrade danger Indonesia ran a deficit of 1.24 per cent of gross domestic product in the first nine months of this year, with the full-year target of 2.85 per cent coming in just under the statutory ceiling of 3 per cent. Analysts like Pardede say government spending is outpacing tax revenue, citing investor concerns that include the expansion of state spending commitments despite a “relatively narrow tax base”, rising energy subsidies, repeated changes among senior economic officials and “uncertainty surrounding the roles of state-controlled investment and commodity institutions”. MSCI’s Friday announcement about Indonesia’s market downgrade surprised officials, coming a month ahead of a scheduled review. In January, the index provider had warned about “ongoing opacity in shareholding structures” as well as co-ordinated trading behaviour that affected price information. It suggested a possible downgrade to frontier-market status at the time. Standalone status is reserved for markets that do not meet even this criteria. Argentina, Lebanon and Palestine are among the markets with the designation, with none in Asia, according to Bloomberg. Uncertainty surrounding the roles of state-controlled investment and commodity institutions Josua Pardede, Permata Bank economist Meanwhile, higher oil prices could weigh further on both the rupiah and Indonesia’s finances. International benchmark Brent crude has been stubbornly trading above US$100 in recent days following fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, threatening oil supplies and raising fears of a widening Middle East conflict. Yusuf expects little relief for Indonesia’s currency in the near term, forecasting that the rupiah will remain “quite volatile” against the US dollar through to the end of the year. Pardede’s prescription for Indonesia’s US$1.3 trillion economy was directed at the government rather than the central bank. “The government should prioritise disciplined budget execution, transparent public investment governance, regulatory certainty and policies that attract private capital rather than relying excessively on the state to drive growth,” he said.

title: China mulls new tech export bans covering AI, biotechnology and solar power
description: The proposed restrictions would cover 14 technologies in industries ranging from artificial intelligence to photovoltaic solar power.
content: China on Friday unveiled a draft plan to impose new export bans affecting 14 technologies in sectors ranging from artificial intelligence to biotechnology and photovoltaic solar power. The notice – jointly issued by China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology – proposes export bans for a string of AI-related technologies; certain cell and gene therapy technology platforms; and technology for producing certain kinds of solar cell modules. It also lists a further 26 technologies from the three sectors that would face fresh export restrictions. The AI measures cover 23 areas including advanced AI models, agents and computing clusters, but the notice specifies that the restrictions will not apply to technologies already in the public domain – such as open-source systems or those that have been published in academic papers. The government will begin a one-month public consultation for the draft plan starting on Friday. The new restrictions are designed to ensure that AI technology remains safe and controllable, the commerce ministry said in a statement. The technologies listed – such as AI models used for malicious coding – could be exploited to attack sensitive systems, including critical national computing infrastructure, defence and military installations, and core government functions, or used to bypass national security defence architectures, it added. “If acquired by non-state actors or malicious entities, these technologies could pose a grave threat to national security and common global security,” the statement said. “The Chinese government is implementing necessary management over such technologies to build a firm baseline for security, prevent misuse and malicious exploitation, ensure that AI remains strictly under human control, and advance international AI governance.” The ministry stressed that “the vast majority” of AI-related technologies would remain free to be exported. Entities would need to register with authorities before exporting a technology in four scenarios, according to the notice. These would be: transferring ownership of a technology to parties outside China; licensing technology for use outside the country; handing control of a company that owns a technology to an overseas entity; and other situations where the ministry requires registration. The ministry cited different concerns when explaining the need for export restrictions affecting biotechnology and photovoltaic (PV) solar power. In biotechnology, the measures are designed to build biosecurity barriers and ensure orderly international cooperation for China’s biomedical technologies, according to the notice. The government will give special authorisation or support to enable important international cooperation projects. For PV solar technologies, the concerns are mainly related to national security, given their growing use in strategic areas such as aerospace, defence and unmanned equipment. The measures also aim to improve the sector’s regulations on core technology exports, which can also cover related areas such as production and maintenance technology, according to the notice. The commerce ministry stressed that the restrictions would not affect the continued sharing of green technologies. The draft plan will only cover PV technologies that meet certain thresholds. “In principle, other PV equipment not listed is not subject to the announcement’s requirements,” the ministry said. The potential tightening of export controls comes amid an intensifying tech rivalry between China and the United States, with both sides wary of exchanges related to AI and other strategic sectors. Last week, Washington revealed it had fined the parent company of Plug and Play Tech Centre for failing to report an investment in a Chinese robotics company – its first penalty issued under rules governing American outbound investment in sensitive technologies. Beijing and Washington agreed to set up a bilateral channel to deal with AI-related incidents and launch an AI dialogue following a summit between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump last month, though Trump later said he did not want to work with China on AI safety. Technical teams from the two countries aim to make AI cooperation a potential deliverable for the next face-to-face meeting between the two leaders, at next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, the South China Morning Post reported earlier this week. Both Xi and Premier Li Qiang made comments on the AI industry on Friday, with Xi highlighting the importance of the national computing power network during a visit to northern China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region and Li calling for broader applications of AI at a State Council meeting. Hong Jiayang, managing partner of US law firm Joint-Win Partners, who focuses on trade compliance, said that the draft regulation could “impose a relatively onerous compliance review obligation” on Chinese companies looking to expand overseas. AI models that have at least 2 trillion parameters, show world-leading performance, or feature computation of at least 100 million exaflops may be subject to export control measures, according to the document.
