Very few companies met those criteria given current market conditions, Hong said, but he cautioned that regulators tended to apply a broad interpretation of what constitutes a “technology export”. That means that any overseas access could count as a technology export, which would have a substantial impact on Chinese companies going overseas, according to Hong. Additional reporting by Coco Feng and Vincent Chow

title: Thai raid foils cross-border cable ruse powering Myanmar scam centre
description: Authorities found a 48-core fibre optic cable, reaching 350 metres across the border, supplying an illegal casino and suspected scam centre.
content: Authorities in Thailand have uncovered an audacious scheme involving hundreds of metres of internet cable sent over the Thai border to keep a suspected Myanmar scam compound online, after finding two ramshackle village homes using enough daily bandwidth to power an entire village. Officers raided the homes in Nong Lu, a Thai border village in Kanchanaburi province, which is the gateway to the Three Pagodas Pass in Myanmar – now a notorious hub for cyber scammers. Many scam centre leaders have relocated after crackdowns further north inside Myanmar or in Cambodia. Thai authorities said they had acted after finding a surge in data use well beyond the needs of a small home on the Thai border. At one of the suspect properties police found a 48-core fibre optic cable – covered for use in robust environments – strung along pylons and reaching 350 metres (1,100 feet) across the border, supplying an illegal border casino and suspected scam centre. “They were using about 6 terabytes a day, which should be enough to serve around 300 to 400 people,” Trairat Viriyasirikul, deputy secretary general and acting secretary general of the National Broadcasting and Telecommunications Commission, told reporters after the raid on Thursday. “When we came in to inspect and we found the equipment … the suspect claimed it was for repair work.” In video footage the male suspect said he was paid 700 baht (US$20) a day to allow the cable to run through his premises into Myanmar, a tiny sum for the deep-pocketed scam gangs. Myanmar has become the epicentre of the global scam trade – inheriting the ignominious title from Cambodia which has been forced into a clean-up by the US and China. The mainly Chinese scam bosses have either abandoned large factory-style scam compounds for small hotels or begun running breakaway units of scammers in condo rooms and villas. Some have also upped sticks entirely to Myanmar and further afield. The Three Pagodas Pass area is protected by ethnic armed militias who shelter the criminals for a fee, leaving fugitive scammers busting borders from Cambodia, through Thailand and into Myanmar. NGOs say hundreds, possibly thousands, of people – some trafficked and forced into scamming – remain trapped in the scam centres just over Thailand’s western border. The scam centres extend deep into territory disputed by multiple ethnic armed groups, complicating rescues or missions to close them down. Logistics to Myanmar’s scam centres have theoretically been cut, as they mainly relied on Thailand’s strong infrastructure and supply routes, including for petrol and internet access. But with bottomless amounts of illicit cash, the scam gangs have proved resilient to crackdowns, bribing officials and securing new supplies of everything from diesel and Starlink satellite boxes to fibre optic cables plugging into neighbouring countries. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime in July estimated that scam-related losses across the Asia-Pacific reached between US$88 billion and US$114 billion in 2025 alone, a sum it said “even at the low end, outstrips the GDP of several countries in the region”.

title: As I see it | US tech bros are coming for Asia and Latin America’s power grids
description: While China builds its AI data centres at home, America’s hyperscalers are increasingly turning to the Global South for expansion – with Washington’s blessings.
content: Americans are souring on artificial intelligence, so Washington is trying to convince them the old-fashioned way: by citing, ad nauseam, the China threat. US President Donald Trump, flanked by tech executives at the White House late last month, warned voters that if they rejected data centres, companies would “be forced to go overseas”. He added that “whoever wins superintelligence wins” and that “you’re probably not gonna have a second place”. The implication was that detractors would be handing China the AI race. He did not define winning, or say whether it would merely enrich the already very rich tech bros or also benefit ordinary Americans, many of whom fear losing their jobs to AI. More of them now reject the data centres of the so-called hyperscalers, which suck up electricity and water from their neighbourhoods while pushing up costs. So more such projects are leaving American soil, but the profits stay American. Shareholders hope to get the best of both worlds: no data-centre controversy, more profits. The machines stand on someone else’s land, guzzle someone else’s water and strain someone else’s grid. As a recent Financial Times commentary pointed out, income at home from land and energy exploitation abroad has an old name: imperialism. The political architecture is already going up. Pax Silica, the State Department’s AI supply-chain club, aims to lock members into America’s computing empire and out of China’s. The Pentagon’s new Economic Defence Unit has reportedly invoked the East India Company as its model. Pax Silica’s first outpost is a 4,000-acre (1619-hectare) “economic security zone” in the Philippines. Washington reportedly sought US jurisdiction and immunity for its personnel there. Manila said no and insists the zone stays under Philippine law, though the project is proceeding. Others are less accommodating. Southeast Asia is asking, “At what cost?” Thailand has paused projects and Malaysia faces grid pressure. In Kenya, a US$1 billion data centre stalled after Microsoft and its Emirati partner asked the government to guarantee purchases of its computing capacity. Mexico’s president said her country need not become the world’s data centre. The Philippines, ever the dutiful vassal under President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, rolls out the red carpet. Latin America’s rightward drift is producing similar hospitality. A letter to the Financial Times argued that the region is increasingly attracting data centres from the US, citing land, energy and nearshoring opportunities. It said more than 20 projects are on track for 2026. Brazil has introduced tax incentives, while Chile is exploring government land for sites. Investment or invasion? Meanwhile, China is doing something less glamorous but far less offensive: building at home. The Open Data Centre Committee, whose members include Alibaba, Baidu, Tencent, China Telecom and China Mobile, met in Beijing to discuss unifying scattered data centres into one national computing network. According to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, China had built 10.85 million standard AI stacks by the end of June, up 30.7 per cent in a year. Denied advanced US chips, builders are working around the limits. The committee’s He Zekun cited breakthroughs in inter-chip communication across clusters mixing foreign and domestic semiconductors, and predicted AI computing power would be ubiquitous in China. Beijing keeps its machines within its own borders. American sanctions are forcing China’s leading developers to pool resources and become self-reliant, just as the earlier chip curbs did. The “superintelligence” race also has a financial sting. AI is spreading faster than any previous technology; many policymakers and investors treat it as a miracle cure, propelling tech stocks and exports from the US to Asia. Critics see a familiar bubble: circular funding loops, start-ups that make no profit, and retail and institutional investors heavily overexposed and buying every dip. Ruchir Sharma, chairman of Rockefeller International, warns in Foreign Affairs that such reliance and speculative mania invite a severe correction. AI spending has so far shielded the global economy from recent geopolitical shocks, which is precisely why its unwinding would be so painful. History suggests innovations inflate bubbles before settling into a durable economic ecosystem. But first the bubble bursts, and the world economy will be badly hit. Smaller economies, hosting the data centres, will suffer most without having enjoyed the boom years. Washington’s “winner takes all” rhetoric looks less like strategy or a sales pitch than a threat. For now, expansion abroad is on a freelance basis, with companies cutting deals that host nations can still refuse. But Washington increasingly clears the ground, and a refusing government can expect to face its wrath eventually. Like the capitalism of old, American AI breeds oligarchy at home and imperialism abroad.

title: LVMH touts ‘special bond’ with China as ‘subdued’ backdrop weighs on sales
description: Antoine Arnault praises firm’s ‘dialogue with Chinese culture’ during global event after lawsuit backlash and sluggish spending mar results.
content: French luxury giant LVMH Group kicked off a global open-house event showcasing its craftsmanship in Shanghai on Thursday, as the event’s founder Antoine Arnault hailed a “special bond” with Chinese customers at a launch event in Paris. It came as the group faced pressure from sluggish demand in China and a backlash over a lawsuit against a local tea company. At the launch event at the Samaritaine department store in central Paris for this year’s Les Journées Particulières, first initiated by Arnault in 2011, he mentioned the Shanghai event, which was the first among 71 venues across 13 countries to open to the public for the three-day event. “For the first time since the event was created, several LVMH houses have come together in a single venue to share our savoir faire and its dialogue with Chinese culture,” said Arnault, who holds multiple roles within LVMH and is the son of its chairman and CEO Bernard Arnault. “Because we share a special bond with China and our Chinese customers.” The exhibition in Shanghai will gather 15 brands from the group, including Louis Vuitton, Dior, Celine, Tiffany and Bulgari. Visitors will get a behind-the-scenes look at how some of the group’s iconic products are made, such as Louis Vuitton’s Speedy P9 bag. LVMH held an opening ceremony in Zhangyuan, a historic neighbourhood near Nanjing Xilu, on Thursday, featuring a Chinese calligraphy ceremony. Four venues in China will participate in this year’s event: two in Shanghai and one each in Hong Kong and Ningxia. The event came as the group announced disappointing numbers from China earlier this week in its third-quarter results: sales declined 5 per cent in Asia excluding Japan, caused mainly by a sharp macro-led deterioration in Chinese consumer sentiment, according to the group. Louis Vuitton’s lawsuit against local brand Molly Tea further complicated the situation for the French luxury giant in the world’s second biggest luxury market. The local tea chain was ordered by a Chinese court to pay 10.3 million yuan (US$1.5 million) in restitution in July over its use of a logo similar to the French brand’s four-petaled flower. The initial ruling, despite the appeal, sparked heated online debate and drew public sympathy for the Chinese company. “[It’s] very difficult to size a precise impact, but it’s probably fair to say that it had a negative impact, at least at the beginning of the quarter,” said Cecile Cabanis, LVMH’s chief financial officer, during an earnings call on Monday. “The news flow has not been particularly good in China in the summer, so this has really weighed on the feel-good factor and created a short-term subdued Chinese backdrop. We hope it will subside. We need to do more, but we have not stopped investing in China.” Like in previous years, LVMH will participate in this year’s China International Import Expo, set for Shanghai early next month.

title: Gritty Jakarta Biennale, polished Art Jakarta – both tell Indonesia’s story, haze and all
description: The city saw two events open on the same weekend, both highlighting its art scene and drawing attention to socio- and geopolitical anxieties.
content: At the 2026 Jakarta Biennale, visitors can plant cassava in moist soil. An evocative soundscape, including the calls of threatened birds-of-paradise, fills the air. Paintings made with natural pigments on tree bark hang on the walls. The installation by Papua-based artist collective Alyakha Kolektif draws attention to illegal gold mining and excessive logging that are damaging the environment in Indonesia’s Sentani region. The cassava planting, which continues until late October, is intended as a gesture of hope. That gesture feels particularly timely as thick grey haze, fuelled by forest fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, continues to blanket Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, with air quality hitting hazardous levels. “The biennale is themed ‘Kebal’, which is like when you feel so much pain that soon you don’t feel it any more,” says programme director Ayu Maulani, who explains that the Bahasa word roughly translates as “immune” or “resistant”. “It’s about how the people of Indonesia are trying to survive amid state policies that do not serve their interests.” Organised by Majelis Jakarta, a coalition of art collectives, the event opened on October 4 and runs until November 24 at venues across the Indonesian capital, including the Taman Ismail Marzuki arts complex. Across town, a very different art event concluded the same weekend the biennale opened. In contrast to the biennale’s gritty, DIY vibe, the contemporary art fair Art Jakarta offered a polished, commercial presentation of works by artists from Southeast Asia and elsewhere. Together, the two events showcase the diversity and dynamism of the contemporary art scene in the world’s largest city. Resilience and resistance Dating back to 1974, the Jakarta Biennale features more than 30 contemporary artists this year. Many of the works confront environmental and sociopolitical issues affecting communities across Indonesia. Yogyakarta-based artist Fitri DK’s installation of clay pots, straw hats and black batik fabric, for instance, depicts female indigenous Javanese farmers from Kendeng, who protested plans for a cement factory by encasing their feet in cement outside Jakarta’s Presidential Palace in 2016. Upstairs, Arifa Safura’s installation of shrouded mannequins pays tribute to women in Aceh, Sumatra, who live under strict sharia law. Among the most powerful works is Yadgari (2026), a fabric installation featuring poignant portraits of refugees printed on draped sheets. Video footage and poetic text written by refugees are projected across the cloth. The work was created by The Archipelago, a collective that includes Hassan Ati and Shams Najafi, Hazara refugees from Afghanistan now based in Indonesia. Ati, who took the portraits, likens being a refugee to a bird trapped in a room: able to see freedom through the glass but unable to escape. The thin fabric, which creates a barrier of sorts, echoes this idea. Najafi recorded the video footage, which includes scenes of protesters camping outside the Jakarta headquarters of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. A member of the persecuted Hazara minority, Najafi fled Afghanistan as a teenager. He flew to India, then in 2014 travelled by boat from Malaysia to Indonesia, where he spent three and a half years in a detention centre. In 2025, he founded a Montessori school for refugee children while continuing his art practice. “We tried to show the resilience of refugees,” Ati says. “We made this artwork so the audience can see there are people from other nations living in Jakarta who are struggling.” A dynamic art fair Just as the biennale captures the urgent sociopolitical anxieties of contemporary Indonesia, Art Jakarta’s commercial activity has also been affected by major geopolitical events. “The whole world is on tenterhooks with what’s happening in the Middle East,” says Jasdeep Sandhu, founder of Gajah Gallery, which has spaces in Singapore, Jakarta and Yogyakarta. “We’re just happy to be doing as well as we did last year.” At the gallery’s booth, where works were priced up to US$50,000, early sales included pieces by Indonesian artists Erizal As, Mangu Putra and Tantin Udiantara. This year’s fair, held from October 2 to 4 at Jakarta International Expo, drew nearly 42,000 visitors – about 4 per cent more than last year. It featured more accessible price points and a strong showing of emerging artists. “The fair’s definitely very dynamic,” says Singapore-based collector Rafiq Mohamad. “I appreciate the intimacy of scale and friendly price point [of the works].” More than half of the fair’s 75 galleries were local. The 33 international exhibitors included several first-time participants, such as PhD Group from Hong Kong, Tokyo-based Misako & Rosen and SNA Arts Management from Phnom Penh. SNA Arts Management’s booth featured Das Pralung (Rousing Spirits) (2024), a striking video performance by Cambodian artist Khvay Samnang in which he sits shirtless, pounding brass plates in the baking sun for three days in landscapes across Cambodia. Indonesian stalwarts Roh Projects and Ara Contemporary had some of the largest booths. Ara sold about 70 per cent of the works on display, including a woven print by Netherlands-based artist Nazif Lopulissa for US$18,000. Indonesian collector Abigail Hakim also bought a delicate work by Thai artist Alisa Chunchue from the gallery priced at US$2,500. Part of the series I Remember How It Felt (2026), the small work features red glass drops resembling blood affixed to stainless steel. Hakim plans to display the work in the private viewing space of her South Jakarta office. It houses more than 50 works from her East meets West-themed collection. The space includes works ranging from a playful, digitally manipulated photograph of Indonesian statesman and former president Sukarno with Marilyn Monroe, by Indonesian artist Agan Harahap, to sculptures made from human hair, by Thai artist Imhathai Suwatthanasilp. The rise of young art collectors According to Art Jakarta fair director Tom Tandio, Hakim is part of a wider trend of Indonesian collectors building exhibition spaces in their homes or offices, where they often host fellow art enthusiasts. Hakim has also noticed younger collectors becoming more engaged. She credits initiatives such as the One Piece Club (OPC), which she wishes had existed when she began collecting. OPC Indonesia, co-founded by veteran art patron Melani W. Setiawan and fellow collector Tandio, organises trips to art fairs and visits to private collections. “I’m seeing younger collectors becoming more serious now,” Hakim says. “Maybe in a few years, we will be visiting their collections.”

title: Private healthcare providers back proposed rules to make fees more transparent
description: New rules could apply from August next year, requiring bilingual price lists, budget estimates and explanations for bills at least 20 per cent higher.
content: Private hospitals and clinics have thrown their support behind proposed Hong Kong government measures that will make their pricing more transparent, such as publishing annual billing statistics, despite potentially higher operating costs. Healthcare providers said on Friday that the latest proposed measures, which could start with private hospitals from August next year at the earliest, were “feasible” and “reasonable”. Details were set out in a document submitted by the Health Bureau to the Legislative Council on Thursday evening, after the proposal was first floated in May last year. The measures will cover price information, budget estimates and billing statistics. “The government will introduce the regulation into Legco by the end of the year and draw up the codes of practice, with a view to implementing the regulatory measures in phases starting from the second half of next year in an orderly manner,” the bureau said. According to the timeline, the measures will start with private hospitals, followed by day procedure centres from November 2027 and clinics in mid-2028. Under the proposals, all 14 private hospitals in the city, along with day procedure centres and clinics, will have to provide fee schedules in Chinese and English in a specified format. The schedules must describe all chargeable items and services and give either a fixed price or a price range for each. Each facility must also clearly state whether additional charges apply for wards, operating theatres, medical procedure rooms or doctors’ services. If a price cannot be provided in advance, for example, because it depends on a patient’s condition, the facility must state that the information will be provided separately. All facilities must make their fee schedules available in printed or electronic form at all reception and cashier counters. Private hospitals must also make them available at admission offices and nursing stations, and on their websites. All private hospitals will also have to provide patients with budget estimates in a specified format before admission, unless booking confirmation is issued no more than 12 hours beforehand. In such cases, hospitals will have to explain to patients why they cannot provide an estimate. The estimates must cover both hospital and doctors’ fees. If the final bill exceeds the estimate by 20 per cent or more, the hospital must provide the patient with a written explanation, a requirement the government had previously outlined. “The purpose of setting the 20 per cent threshold is to ensure that patients are provided with an explanation when the final bill is significantly higher than the budget estimate, while avoiding the need for hospitals to provide explanations for ordinary charge variations,” the bureau said. Private hospitals must also publish annual statistics on their fees and charges on their websites and submit them to the government. Statistics on patients in standard beds who undergo a single treatment or procedure must be submitted to the government platform and published on hospital websites by March 31 each year. The figures must cover the previous calendar year. “This requirement aims to ensure consistency in the data concerned in terms of the scope of treatments and procedures and ward class, thereby enhancing the comparability of statistics across different hospitals,” the bureau said. Data submitted by private hospitals must be audited by a certified public accountant. If the audit cannot be completed by March 31, hospitals may submit and publish unaudited statistics first before completing the procedure. Dr Anthony Lee Kai-yiu, chief hospital manager and medical director of Union Hospital, said his facility had already been making its pricing transparent by publishing details of fees and charges on its website. He also said it would not be an issue to disclose billing statistics, which had been digitalised in its computer system. But he expected extra costs, as high as HK$100,000, could be incurred annually for his hospital, as the government required statistics to be audited. “We may need to spend a bit more in each financial year, but all the data is available,” he said. Dr Chung Kin-lai, CEO of CUHK Medical Centre, a non-profit private teaching hospital, backed the measures, describing them as “relatively reasonable”. “The measures have balanced the needs of the public … and the challenges of implementation faced by hospitals,” Chung said. He said his hospital had been positioned to provide transparent pricing so it was less affected by the proposed measures. While he said presenting audited statistics to the government could require extra manpower and costs, the data handling would be relatively simple due to digitalisation. Dr Luk Che-chung, chief of medical services at clinic chain Virtus Medical Group, also expressed confidence and described the proposed measures as “feasible”. But he said private hospitals would have to provide clearer pricing information to visiting private doctors, who would need to offer budget estimates of hospital procedures to patients.

title: Hong Kong housewife gets 3 months in psychiatric institution over seditious posters
description: Court sentences woman, 62, to 3 months in Siu Lam Psychiatric Centre for displaying colonial flag and seditious slogans outside flat.
content: An elderly woman who pasted materials containing pro-independence slogans and Hong Kong’s colonial-era flag outside her flat has been sentenced to three months in a maximum-security psychiatric institution for displaying seditious publications. West Kowloon Court ordered housewife Yang Chau-ki, 62, to undergo mandatory psychiatric treatment at the Siu Lam Psychiatric Centre on Friday. She was charged with knowingly displaying publications with seditious intent under Hong Kong’s Article 23 national security law, to which she pleaded not guilty. Principal Magistrate Don So Man-lung heard that Yang, who was not represented by a lawyer, put up materials with seditious intent outside her flat at Tin Chung Court in Tin Shui Wai between March and November 2024. The materials included a printout of Hong Kong’s colonial-era flag and prints with slogans from the 2019 anti-government protests, calling for the liberation of Hong Kong and her building. She also displayed a fai chun, a traditional Chinese New Year decoration featuring poetic couplets, that referenced a revolutionary slogan. So said that from the combined meaning of the slogans, it was “very clear” that Yang was dissatisfied with the current administration. “The defendant intended to incite like-minded people to persist in their demands, carry out a revolution, overthrow the national government and restore British rule to Hong Kong,” he ruled. “This interpretation must be the only factual interpretation; there is no other.” While So said he was satisfied with the defendant’s explanation that she was displeased with the security guard of her estate, he noted that pasting the publications “went way beyond that.” “She had intentionally displayed the items and was well aware of the meaning of the slogans.” So said that the slogans also did not display any suggestions for improvement for the current administration. “Her intention was not to improve but to encourage the overthrow of the entire system and its replacement by the colonial-era system,” he said. So ruled that Yang deliberately put up the items – which he described as “large and colourful” – on her door and in the public corridor for neighbours and other residents to see. The posters included the words “Look but do not touch” and “Tear this down and your whole family will die,” which So said were warnings intended for her neighbours and the building management, as she knew they would attract attention. He concluded that the defendant, knowing that the items and words were seditious, still posted them on the exterior of the flat with the intent of displaying them to neighbours and management staff. “She wanted to incite their dissatisfaction with the current system, sow discord and prompt them to overthrow the government and restore British rule,” he said. A psychiatric report previously obtained by the court indicated that Yang showed potential symptoms of schizophrenia and delusional disorder, though she was deemed fit to stand trial.

title: Japan’s Okinawa drops opposition to hosting crash-prone US Osprey aircraft
description: Governor Genta Koja, who took office last month, reversed the prefecture’s long-standing opposition to the deployment.
content: Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said on Friday he accepts the deployment of US military MV-22 Osprey transport aircraft at the Futenma air station, reversing the southern Japan prefecture’s long-standing opposition to their presence. Previous prefectural governments, under governors critical of US bases, had opposed the deployment of the tilt-rotor aircraft since before they were first stationed at the base in 2012, citing safety concerns. Koja assumed the post of Okinawa governor late last month. “More than 10 years have passed since the deployment. Considering that the Self-Defence Forces operate the aircraft, it is not realistic to call for a reversal of their deployment or use,” Koja told reporters at the prefectural government office. In a break from his predecessors, Koja, who won the gubernatorial election backed by Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party, supports the plan to relocate US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in densely populated Ginowan to the coastal Henoko area in Nago within Okinawa. Koja said his acceptance of the Osprey deployment is in line with his support for the relocation plan, which will see the aircraft transferred to Henoko. Ospreys, capable of taking off and landing like a helicopter but also cruising like a fixed-wing plane, have a track record of accidents both in Japan and abroad. Koja, meanwhile, said that concerns about the Osprey’s safety have not been dispelled. “I want the safety of the aircraft to be thoroughly confirmed,” he said. In November 2023, a US Air Force CV-22 crashed into the sea near Yakushima Island in Kagoshima prefecture in southwestern Japan, killing all eight crew members. In December 2016, an MV-22 belonging to the Futenma base crash-landed off Nago.

title: Pioneering heart stem cell expert Li Renke dies at 65 during a Chinese conference
description: A memorial service will be held for the Chinese cardiovascular scientist who used engineering principles to treat heart conditions.
content: Li Renke, a visionary cardiovascular scientist who applied engineering principles to the human heart and developed conductive biomaterials to repair tissue damaged by heart attacks, died while attending an academic conference in the Chinese city of Xian earlier this month. He was 65. His death on October 10 was announced by The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen (CUHK-Shenzhen), where he was presidential chair professor and associate dean of research and translation at the school of medicine, which he joined in March last year. The university did not specify the cause of death. Li was born in Harbin, Heilongjiang province, in 1961. He completed his medical and scientific education at Harbin Medical University, Shanxi Medical University and the University of Toronto in Canada. In 1993, he joined the medicine faculty at the University of Toronto as an assistant professor, rising to the rank of tenured professor in 2002. Over a prolific career in Canada, Li’s research earned him election to three of the country’s most prestigious academic bodies: the Canadian Academy of Health Sciences, the Royal Society of Canada and the Canadian Academy of Engineering. For decades, one of the most formidable challenges in cardiology has been finding a way to regenerate infarcted heart muscle. Li tackled this challenge at the intersection of tissue engineering and cell therapy, pioneering functional, conductive biomaterials designed to restore the heart’s electrical conduction network and treat post-infarction arrhythmia. He was included in the 2025 Global Top 0.05 per cent Leading Scientists Lifetime Achievement List released by ScholarGPS, ranking first in the world in cardiac physiology. An advocate for international collaboration, Li was the founding chair of the Toronto Chinese Professors Association. Throughout his career, he worked to advance medical science and technology exchanges between China and Canada, building enduring academic bridges between the two research communities. Alongside his laboratory advances, Li placed deep emphasis on nurturing the next generation of researchers. Over the course of his career, he mentored more than 120 postdoctoral fellows, doctoral candidates and graduate students, over 30 of whom have gone on to become professors or clinical scientists at leading universities across China and abroad. A farewell ceremony was held for Li at the Xian Funeral Home on Thursday. A memorial service will take place on Saturday at CUHK-Shenzhen campus.

title: IPO fraud, China’s export boom, US inflation: 5 figures investors are watching
description: A continuing cross-border stock buying spree and Hong Kong’s role in philanthropy also produce notable numbers.
content: Hong Kong’s market regulators cracked down on fraud with a multibillion-dollar asset freeze, while mainland trade momentum surged on robust tech demand. Meanwhile, mainland Chinese traders ramped up their exposure to local equities, and the city cemented its status as a top global destination for wealth philanthropy. Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week. Hong Kong watchdogs freeze US$590 million Hong Kong’s securities watchdog moved against two groups suspected of being involved in three alleged initial public offering fraud schemes involving assets worth HK$4.6 billion (US$590 million), according to a statement released on Tuesday. The Securities and Futures Commission also announced on the same day that it had suspended 65 listing applications in the first nine months of this year due to the poor quality of their listing sponsors’ work, in what analysts viewed as an effort to strengthen the city’s market quality. China’s merchandise shipments jump 36.3% Mainland China’s goods exports shot up 36.3 per cent year on year to US$447.18 billion last month, customs data showed on Wednesday, driven by solid global tech demand and a holiday export rush. The strong momentum kept the world’s second-largest economy on track for another substantial trade surplus this year, defying persistent global growth headwinds and supply chain fragmentation pressures. US inflation hits 3.7%, jolts Asian markets The United States reported a September inflation rate of 3.7 per cent, exceeding market expectations and fuelling worries of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. It coincided with a sell-off in AI stocks, which led Asian markets to plunge on Thursday, including a 7.57 per cent drop in South Korea’s Kospi index. China’s CSI 300 index fell 1.23 per cent on the day, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index lost 1.03 per cent. Cross-border traders buy net US$7.7 billion in stocks Mainland Chinese investors increased their net buying of Hong Kong-listed equities through the Stock Connect programme for a fourth consecutive month in September. They channelled a net HK$60.8 billion (US$7.7 billion) into local stocks in the month, bringing third-quarter net purchases to HK$134.1 billion as capital crowded into artificial intelligence and technology shares. Hong Kong ranked third-best city for philanthropy Hong Kong emerged as the third best city in the world for members of the wealthy set to exercise their philanthropic muscles in the medium term, following New York and Seoul, according to a study by Altrata. The ranking highlights the city’s expanding role as a premier wealth management and family office hub, where surging private fortunes are increasingly channelled into structured philanthropic initiatives.

title: Hong Kong aims for share of HK$350 billion yacht industry as travel scheme launches
description: Senior official signals more measures to boost share of global yacht industry as first mainland Chinese vessel enters Hong Kong under southbound scheme.
content: Hong Kong can capture a share of the global yacht industry, which is expected to reach HK$350 billion (US$44.6 billion) in six years, a senior official has said as the city launched a scheme to welcome leisure vessels from mainland China. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also announced fresh measures to attract overseas captains and draw superyachts to the city on Friday. The new Southbound Travel for Yachts from Guangdong scheme is part of the government’s broader plan to develop Hong Kong’s yacht economy, as outlined in the city’s first five-year plan and the latest annual policy address. Under the scheme, mainland vessels can register through the Marine Department’s Electronic Business System to sail in Hong Kong waters. Speaking at the launch ceremony, Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun said the global yacht market was expected to reach HK$350 billion by 2032 and that Hong Kong could capture a slice of the market. He noted that there were about 6,000 superyachts in the world exceeding 30 metres (98.4 feet). More than 90 of them were in Hong Kong and the government planned to roll out more measures to boost the yacht economy. “The outline of the national 15th five-year plan clearly calls for developing leisure consumption such as cruises and yachts, and Hong Kong’s first five-year plan also stated that we will actively develop it,” he said. “Our vision for the yacht economy also reflects the global trend.” Wong said they are also pushing to build four new yacht clubs at the airport, Lamma Island, Aberdeen and Hung Hom, which would provide more than 1,100 berths. The new yacht clubs would also have four “very attractive” clubhouses to improve and complete the infrastructure and ecosystem of the city’s yacht economy, he added. Wong also revealed that three of the five registered vessels were from Shenzhen, one was from Zhuhai and one from Guangzhou’s Nansha. The five vessels all moored at facilities in Discovery Bay provided by Lantau Yacht Club, which organised the launch ceremony. Transport minister Chan also said the Marine Department would coordinate with local training institutions to offer online courses for overseas captains, with the aim of turning the city into a hub for superyachts. Chan said the five yachts had varied itineraries, including sea tours and visits to urban areas, and that many of their passengers had booked hotels for stays of three to four days, reflecting “a new model of high-end tourism consumption”. Director of Marine Wong Sai-fat said on Thursday that 23 individuals or groups had registered under the new travel scheme as of this week. Max Teng, secretary general of the Shenzhen Boating Industry Association, was one of the five mainland yacht owners arriving on the first day. He said he came to Hong Kong specifically for an “ice-breaking journey to witness the historic moment”, and would stay only one night in the city. Teng was cautious, however, about his willingness to return. “Just the cost this time, not counting fuel, we already spent up to HK$40,000,” he said. Entry and exit clearance fees were 14,500 yuan, he said, which included a processing fee of 2,000 yuan per trip, port berthing fee of 2,000 yuan per hour and customs declaration fee of 1,000 yuan per vessel. He praised the smooth application through the official system, although he said some technical details still needed work. “There are some things that don’t quite match, for example, the shore power interfaces,” he said. “Freedom of navigation is the most important thing for mainland yacht owners. “Many mainland businessmen buy boats and register companies in Hong Kong for its international endorsement and tax incentives.” Teng said that he saw the scheme boosting Hong Kong’s yacht trading and benefiting nearby cities such as Shenzhen. Another Shenzhen yacht owner, surnamed Sheng, said he had come to Hong Kong with several friends for a three-day free and easy trip, and planned to shop in Central and Tsim Sha Tsui. “Shenzhen is very close to Hong Kong. Now that the government has made the process more automated and standardised, the more convenient it becomes, the more willing we are to come,” he said. “If this scheme had come into effect before National Day, we might have stayed a couple more days – during holidays the roads are congested, but the sea is not.” Sheng added that he would be more interested in sailing his yacht to Victoria Harbour to watch the fireworks during holidays. Franklin Mak, executive vice-president of hospitality at HKR International, the developer behind the Lantau Yacht Club, welcomed the “long-anticipated” scheme, saying the club had prepared for more mainland yachts coming to Hong Kong since 2019. “We have special rates for our berths, and we purposely reserve space for people who come in on a transient basis, so we can accommodate yachts, unlike other yacht clubs that usually sell all that space to long-term owners,” he said. Apart from berthing, the club also offers both long- and short-term service package discounts, including hotel accommodation and golf sessions, which are more cost-effective than a long-term membership. Mak also noted that 10 mainland yachts had registered for the Lantau Yacht Club Boat Show early next month and would start arriving from next week. They represented the largest number in years, up from just two or three previously. David Norton, commodore of the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club, said one boat from Zhuhai was set to spend the night at its Causeway Bay headquarters on Friday. Acknowledging that the club was quite full and could only offer berthing and hospitality on a case-by-case basis, Norton stressed the demand was real. “There is a big demand in mainland China for participation in water sports, 60 per cent of entries in Hong Kong Race Week at the beginning of the year came from the mainland,” he said, adding he was excited to see if the scheme could bring more mainland entries to water sports events in Hong Kong. Five designated berthing areas at Tai O, Repulse Bay, Tai Tam Bay, Stanley Bay and Three Fathoms Cove in Sai Kung will provide 115 berths, in addition to those at private yacht clubs. There are also seven kiosks supplying water to vessels and eight designated bunkering areas, according to the Water Supplies Department and the Marine Department. While saying the five anchorage areas were well located, Norton noted “there is a lack of facilities” around the areas. “It’s very hard to get water and find someone to dump some trash or empty the tanks from the toilet,” he said. He also added that tourists needed an easy way ashore: “They need a landing station, or maybe a water taxi service that will get them on and off the boat. So that’s what’s missing.” Lawmaker Roy Chu Lap-wai described the registration of five yachts on the first day as “encouraging”. “In the initial stage, I believe the five yachts that come here will go back and spread the word about how convenient and good Hong Kong is, if everything goes smoothly,” he told a radio programme. Chu said Hong Kong had many distinctive islands for visiting yachts to explore. He hoped tourists would go island-hopping during the day, then dine and shop in urban areas at night. “The government also held many successful big events regularly, and they could get more involved in different aspects, so these relatively high-end, big-spending yacht tourists can really spend more money in Hong Kong and contribute to our economy,” he said. Chu said the city could also develop a “one-day tour” and other services, such as chauffeur-driven cars with professional guides, adding that the Tourism Board could do more to promote these offerings and increase the economic benefits.

title: Why has a lake between France and Switzerland dried up?
description: Locals have written the words “HELP” and “SOS” in the weeds on the dry bed of Lac des Brenets.
content:
A lake between France and Switzerland, called Lac des Brenets, has dried up after a record-breaking hot summer. Locals are asking for help to save the lake.
They have scratched the words “HELP” and “SOS” in the weeds on the dry lake bed.
The drought has ruined boat tourism, and some question whether the lake will ever return to full health.
“It’s utter despair: no more lake,” said 76-year-old David Favre, who lives in the Swiss village of Les Brenets.
The lake has dried up due to a mix of factors. These include cracks in the ground that drain water underground, below-average rainfall and repeated heatwaves. The months of June, July and August were each the hottest ever recorded in Switzerland since measurements began in 1864.
A task force was set up by French and Swiss authorities in 2022 to explore ways of limiting the water draining into the cracks. But it has not resulted in a decision on what to do.

title: Envoy says China could ‘easily win’ conflict as Manila claims it is ‘thinly veiled threat’
description: Philippine President Marcos Jnr says comments by ambassador Jing Quan run counter to efforts to ease South China Sea stand-offs.
content: Manila has called for diplomatic restraint in response to suggestions from the Chinese ambassador to the Philippines that Beijing could “easily win” a military showdown in the region but had instead chosen peace. The war of words comes amid rising tension over the Scarborough Shoal in the South China Sea. Beijing has repeatedly driven away Philippine aircraft over the shoal in recent months, while accusing Manila of violating Chinese airspace. Ambassador Jing Quan made his comment on Thursday as he pushed back against China being labelled a “troublemaker”. On the sidelines of a South China Sea conference in Quezon City in the Philippines, Jing said: “That’s nonsense. Troublemaker? Who’s the troublemaker? Look at who go after Chinese teachers – they’re innocent.” Jing appeared to be referring to the departure of Chinese language teachers from the country after security allegations by Manila. “Those groundless accusations against China try to hype up the false narrative theory, try to incite that kind of hatred between the two countries. Who every day [tries] to always create some new problems, incidents that lead two sides to confrontation? Who’s the troublemaker?” he said. He said others should “feel fortunate enough that you have a neighbour like China in this region”. “If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we’ll not use force. We love peace,” Jing said. Within hours, Manila criticised the Chinese diplomat’s “poor choice of words”, saying it conveyed a “thinly veiled threat of the use of force” that was “hardly helpful in the context of the complicated bilateral ties” between the two countries. On Thursday evening, Manila’s foreign ministry also cautioned “all diplomats accredited to the Philippines” to choose their public words carefully, warning against eroding mutual trust and derailing bilateral dialogue. The Chinese embassy, in turn, criticised Manila’s “selective quotation and overinterpretation”. It said on Friday that Manila’s response showed there was “still a long way to go” towards effective bilateral communication and urged the Philippines to play a more responsible role. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr said the Chinese ambassador’s remark sounded “very much to me like a threat”, and that it was “not a very diplomatic statement”. Marcos added that he sought to clarify the exact meaning of the statement. The Chinese foreign ministry followed up, saying that Beijing’s position on improving bilateral relations was “clear”, and it hoped the Philippine side would “understand it accurately and comprehensively”. Ties between Beijing and Manila have been tense in recent years, fuelled by frequent South China Sea clashes that have escalated from maritime stand-offs to confrontations in the air. Scarborough Shoal – a coral atoll known as Huangyan Dao in China and Panatag Shoal in the Philippines – has been a particular source of friction. It has been under Beijing’s effective control since 2012, but Manila says it falls within its exclusive economic zone. Earlier this month, the two sides also traded accusations over a medical evacuation near Second Thomas Shoal, another major flashpoint where a Philippine naval vessel was grounded on the maritime feature decades ago. In his speech at the conference on Thursday, Jing said China-Philippines relations were at an “extremely sensitive and critical juncture” and could not simply be defined as good or bad. “One could say the atmosphere of relations is strained due to maritime disputes, yet the momentum of bilateral trade and people-to-people exchanges remains strong.” Managing bilateral ties required tailored strategies suited to specific fields and issues, the ambassador noted, warning that relations could otherwise slip into a “vicious cycle of mutual targeting and retaliation” – disarray that would play right into the hands of anti-China forces. Jing also called for greater cross-sector dialogue to share positive stories and good news that could help break the current “impasse” in bilateral relations.

title: Who is Nathan Chen, the Chinese teen AI prodigy being courted by Silicon Valley?
description: Chen’s move to the US comes after a short stint at Moonshot, where he played an instrumental role in several core innovations.
content: A 17-year-old artificial intelligence researcher formerly with Moonshot AI has announced his departure for the United States, sparking intense speculation about his next move amid heated competition for elite talent between Silicon Valley and China’s tech hubs. Nathan Chen Guangyu wrote on social media on Thursday that he had left the Beijing-based start-up after less than a year, describing his time there as “the best [year] of my life so far”. The announcement caught many industry observers by surprise, given Chen’s brief tenure and the timing – coming just months ahead of Moonshot’s anticipated initial public offering in Hong Kong. It also follows a string of successful releases by the start-up, including its latest flagship K3 model in July. The release sparked concern in Washington that the capability gap between US and Chinese frontier AI models had narrowed to its closest point yet. Despite his short stint, Chen played an instrumental role in several of Moonshot’s core technical innovations in the past year, which helped make its Kimi models some of the world’s leading open-weight systems. Among his contributions was a breakthrough technique known as “attention residuals”, which improves cost-efficiency and memory in Moonshot’s large language models. The method drew praise from high-profile industry figures, including OpenAI co-founders Andrej Karpathy and Elon Musk. Speculation regarding Chen’s next job mounted after prominent figures from US start-ups, including Anthropic and Prime Intellect, commented on his post, congratulating him and inviting him to visit the San Francisco Bay Area. One comment by Anthropic researcher Sholto Douglas suggested the two had recently met in person, sparking online rumours that Chen might join the Claude model developer. However, in a follow-up post on X on Friday, Chen denied he was joining the US company, responding to a user’s question with a simple “No”. As AI grows in geopolitical and commercial importance, young talent has become a hot commodity in China. Several key figures driving AI development at Chinese tech giants are Gen Z or millennials, including Tencent Holdings’ Vinces Yao Shunyu and Moonshot AI co-founder Yang Zhilin. Chen is not the first teenage AI prodigy from China to make headlines. Former DeepSeek researcher Tu Jinhao gained prominence last year after co-authoring the Hangzhou-based start-up’s breakthrough R1 model paper while still a high school student in Shanghai. Tu left DeepSeek to begin undergraduate studies at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before joining Moonshot, Chen interned at a Silicon Valley start-up and was named a Rhodes Trust Rise Fellow – a global talent programme for young people aged 15 to 17 funded by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and his wife, Wendy Schmidt. Chen’s departure comes at a sensitive time. Last month, Beijing codified new restrictions barring top tech talent from leaving the country if their move would violate export controls or technology transfer regulations.
