title: Beyond legal advice: Hong Kong charity helps bridge the gap in access to justice
description: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist Pro Bono HK links people in need with lawyers, social workers and community groups, while promoting legal education.
content: Pro Bono HK is known for helping people in need access justice in Hong Kong, but its work extends beyond legal advice to connecting clients with social workers and community groups for further support and promoting legal education. Founded in 2014, the organisation helps people who may not qualify for legal aid or cannot afford private representation. Its work ranges from tenancy and family disputes to inheritance matters and emergency legal support. Pro Bono HK and its volunteers are finalists for the Spirit of Teamwork Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. CEO Vincent Yeung said founder Davyd Wong established the organisation to improve access to justice for people unable to obtain help through either private legal services or Hong Kong’s legal aid system. “There are many people who require legal support but may not qualify for legal aid,” Yeung said. “That is the gap we are trying to address.” Much of the organisation’s community work focuses on everyday problems facing lower-income households, including tenancy issues affecting subdivided-flat residents. It also works with NGOs to help frontline workers and residents understand legal rights. Cases are screened before they reach a lawyer. Law students and interns handle initial inquiries, collect basic information and direct people to existing resources when legal advice is not needed. “Sometimes all that the client needs is to be pointed in the right direction or given access to the right information,” Yeung said. “If more support is needed, we pair the client with a volunteer who has the right expertise and availability.” Legal problems rarely arise in isolation, according to Victoria Wong Yin, a consultant supporting Pro Bono HK. Clients may also face housing, family or welfare difficulties, so the organisation works closely with registered social workers to identify those who need further support. “There are two sides to it,” she said. “Clients need legal support, while social workers also need some basic legal knowledge to identify when professional legal advice is needed.” The human side of legal advice is equally important, Yeung said. People seeking help may already be frightened or overwhelmed, particularly after a traumatic event. “It is like a doctor’s bedside manner. How you explain the case matters,” she said. After the deadly blaze at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po last November, Pro Bono HK and its volunteers produced bilingual legal information within 48 hours. They also mobilised hundreds of legal professionals to support affected residents through clinics, seminars and community outreach. Yeung said some legal questions emerged only after the immediate emergency had passed. “After a month or two, some affected residents began thinking about the legal issues,” he said, citing questions around property ownership, insurance and longer-term housing arrangements. Pro Bono HK also wants to expand legal education to help people before problems develop into disputes. Wong said such education should begin with young people, helping them understand the basics of contracts and scams, as well as the consequences of signing documents or allowing others to use their bank accounts. “Education is very important because many people do not know what rights they have or what options are available to them,” she said. Since January 2026, the organisation’s volunteers have contributed more than 1,500 hours of pro bono legal work, with about 70 lawyers and 30 students taking part, according to Yeung. The organisation is considering expanding its work with schools. It also aims to make pro bono service a more regular part of legal practice through continued collaboration with social workers and community groups. Launched in 2013, the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention.

title: China says only joint action, not exchange rates alone, can address global imbalances
description: Beijing calls for cooperation to tackle economic challenges, from protectionism and financial market volatility to risks linked to AI valuations.
content: China’s central bank chief has said exchange-rate adjustments alone cannot resolve global economic imbalances, urging surplus and deficit economies to share responsibility for addressing them. He also pledged to promote yuan-denominated bonds as “eligible collateral widely recognised and accepted globally”. Speaking at the third G20 finance ministers and central bank governors’ meeting in Bangkok on Thursday, Pan Gongsheng, governor of the People’s Bank of China, called for a “more comprehensive analytical perspective” to address global imbalances. “We should look beyond the current account to financial channels, paying greater attention to how financial factors such as capital flows affect imbalances, particularly as global financial integration deepens,” he said, according to a PBOC readout. “Deficit and surplus economies should work together to achieve a dynamic balance in the global economy.” Pan noted that exchange rates were influenced by a range of factors including economic growth, monetary policy, financial markets, geopolitics and unexpected events, and did not have a simple, linear relationship with a country’s current-account balance. His remarks came after the PBOC published a position paper on the yuan exchange rate last week, which argued China did not need to devalue its currency to gain a competitive edge and had never deliberately done so. China operates a managed floating exchange-rate system and has long faced accusations, particularly from the United States and the European Union, of keeping the yuan artificially weak to boost exports – a charge Beijing has repeatedly rejected. At Thursday’s meeting, Pan also warned that sharp swings in some countries’ sovereign bond markets and growing risks of a correction in AI-related asset valuations had increased financial vulnerabilities. Escalating geopolitical conflicts remained the biggest source of uncertainty for the global economy, he added. Pan also stressed that modernising financial regulation should not be equated with deregulation or come at the expense of financial stability and resilience. At the same meeting, Finance Minister Lan Foan said the “immediate priority” was to address geopolitical conflicts, rising protectionism and deepening fragmentation to create a favourable environment for global growth, according to a readout by the Ministry of Finance. Lan also urged the G20 to ensure that discussions of major global economic and financial issues remained “comprehensive, objective and balanced”. China would pursue a more proactive fiscal policy to sustain growth and “inject confidence and certainty into the global economy,” he added. At a separate seminar on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings on the same day, Pan pledged further support for global investors and issuers seeking access to China’s financial markets while pledging to expand the international use of yuan-denominated bonds, part of Beijing’s efforts to internationalise the currency. At a Friday media briefing, Erin Browne, the US Treasury undersecretary for international affairs, said Washington’s G20 presidency had drawn greater attention to the role of “non-market policies and practices” in driving global imbalances, particularly those associated with China and other economies. “For too long, non-market practices have distorted international trade and capital flows, undermined fair competition and created negative spillovers for the global economy,” Browne said, calling on the IMF to take a more assertive role in identifying these distortions and addressing “beggar-thy-neighbour” policies that contribute to them. Earlier this month, the US rallied most G20 members – excluding China, Brazil, Indonesia, Russia, Saudi Arabia and South Africa – to pressure Beijing on overcapacity, signing a joint statement calling for actions to address structural excess capacity. Separately, PBOC deputy governor Tao Ling said at a forum in Shanghai on Friday that Beijing would take further steps to meet offshore demand for yuan liquidity. The measures would include supporting cross-border yuan lending and trade financing, encouraging more overseas institutions to issue and trade panda bonds and supporting Hong Kong’s dim sum bond market, where yuan-denominated bonds are issued offshore. The central bank would also promote innovation in offshore yuan repurchase agreements and derivatives markets, support clearing banks in providing offshore yuan liquidity and expand regular currency-swap arrangements with more eligible countries and regions, Tao said. Additional reporting by Xinyi Wu

title: Haze-hit Singapore parents call for Hong Kong-style school air con
description: An opposition MP who has pushed for air-conditioned classrooms due to hot weather says his proposal is more urgent now because of the haze.
content: Salon manager Alice Pang says her 10-year-old daughter has likened the visibility inside her classroom in Singapore to Malaysia’s Genting Highlands, but while the mountain resort is often shrouded in fog caused by water particles, her child’s active imagination may have been triggered by worsening haze plaguing the city state. Pang told This Week in Asia that her daughter, whose classroom did not have air conditioning, was already suffering from bad sinus, and the haze had made her eyes water. While Pang would prefer her Primary 4 daughter to stay home as the pollutant standards index (PSI) climbs beyond 200 in some parts of the city state, the child is in the middle of exams. Pang is among several parents who are increasingly worried about the open-air classroom environments in Singapore amid the transboundary haze fuelled by fires across Indonesia, particularly in Sumatra and Kalimantan. “They have an air purifier in the classroom, but she says it isn’t working. It’s also too hot for the students. I think the government needs to step up and take action,” Pang said. She argued that schools should roll out air-conditioning in classrooms to complement the air purifiers. Currently, her daughter’s school has air-conditioning only in certain facilities such as the music room. On Wednesday afternoon, the PSI one-hour reading hit a high of 288 in the west of Singapore. The same day, Singapore began distributing N95 masks to vulnerable Singaporeans, including children aged between seven and 16, and providing air-conditioned rooms in shelters in community clubs and some residents’ committee centres. On Saturday, Education Minister Desmond Lee said in a social media post that lessons and national examinations had continued in enclosed venues with air purifiers, and that his ministry might consider school closures if the next-day forecasts entered the hazardous range with a 24-hour PSI exceeding 300. Across the 1km causeway in Malaysia, schools in several states have been shut until at least Friday. Under federal guidelines, educational institutions must close when the Air Pollutant Index (API) exceeds 180, or remains above 150 for three consecutive days. Both levels fall within the “unhealthy” range. General practitioner Lawrence Ng said that common conditions triggered by haze included ⁠upper respiratory infections, bronchitis, ⁠conjunctivitis, allergic rhinitis, known as hay fever, and⁠ asthma. “Children have smaller airways which are more susceptible to airway narrowing from pollutants,” Ng said. Asked if implementing air-conditioning in classrooms was being considered to tackle the haze, Singapore’s Ministry of Education directed This Week in Asia to its haze management measures. These include avoiding physical activities if the PSI is between 200 and 300, placing students in an enclosed indoor space with air purifiers and having those who are unwell temporarily placed in an air-conditioned room with an air purifier before they are brought to get medical attention. Opposition MP Kenneth Tiong, who reiterated his call to provide air-conditioning in classrooms this week, told This Week in Asia he was not advocating for the air-conditioning to be on at all times but to have the option when needed. In March, he advocated in parliament for air-conditioning in classrooms to help students and teachers handle the heat. “The recent haze makes it more urgent. It has been very difficult for the kids: many are coughing, and I can see the toll it is taking on their health,” said Tiong, who is a Workers’ Party MP for the Aljunied constituency. He noted that the National Environment Agency’s guideline said a purifier might not work as intended unless the doors and windows were closed, and that a closed, crowded room could build up heat. “MOE’s haze plan says students who are unwell ‘will be temporarily accommodated in an air-conditioned room with an air purifier’. I believe a child should not have to fall ill first,” Tiong argued. In March, then senior minister of state David Neo said Singapore had been careful not to rush into air conditioning, as the technology was not as energy efficient and instead relied on passive cooling solutions, such as cool paint, more breathable uniforms and school buildings designed for maximum natural ventilation. Neo stressed there was a need to balance other considerations, such as long-term heat resilience, acclimatisation, energy consumption and impact on the environment. Tiong told This Week in Asia that while sustainability was very important, air-conditioning in every classroom could be an insurance. “It has to be in place before the haze or the next heatwave arrives. Switched on only when needed, it uses far less power than air-conditioning left on all day,” he said. He noted that in Hong Kong, the government had moved to air-conditioned classrooms for all public sector schools since 2017 for a more comfortable teaching and learning environment in hot weather. A recurrent air-conditioning grant was provided from 2018 for Hong Kong schools to cover related daily expenses, including electricity charges and maintenance. A mother of a six-year-old who previously lived in Hong Kong said she was shocked to learn that her child’s Primary 1 classroom in Singapore would not be air-conditioned. Currently, her child’s kindergarten class is air-conditioned and has an air purifier, but she expressed concern about whether it had been serviced. “I’m not asking them to have the air conditioning turned on every day,” she said, speaking on condition of anonymity. She questioned if some people underestimated the haze, given “this haze situation has been there for 20 years”. Flynn Lee, a 50-year-old stay-at-home Singaporean mother of three children aged 11 to 16, however, said she trusted the government’s current measures. Only her daughter in Secondary 1 has air conditioning in her classroom. “Air con is good to have, but I guess not all schools can afford it. It’s also not cheap to maintain, and this situation is not forever, so I guess we just have to get through this period,” Lee said, noting that her children’s schools had stopped all outdoor recess playing, moved co-curricular activities and physical education lessons indoors and reminded children to drink more water. “It’s not really a fair statement to request for air con just because of the haze situation, which probably will last like weeks to a month and to have schools suddenly have to request to put up air conditioning.”

title: Beijing enlists multiple regulators to probe EV safety issue that raised quality alarms
description: Three ministry-level authorities to verify facts in viral video of snapping Maextro EV brake pedals.
content: Beijing has enlisted the support of its top internet watchdog to deepen the investigation into a car safety issue that put Chinese-made intelligent vehicles under the spotlight. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) said on Thursday that a joint investigation team including officials from the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) and the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) would verify facts regarding reports about brake pedal failures in tests of an electric vehicle (EV) made by the Huawei Technologies-backed Maextro luxury brand. The three ministry-level authorities “have paid close attention to the issue”, the MIIT said. “Relevant information will be released in a timely manner.” The statement showed that Chinese authorities would be resolute in addressing concerns about Chinese EV quality and reliability amid a falling domestic market, analysts said. On October 8, ByteDance-owned car-information platform Dongchedi released a video showing that brake-pedal brackets snapped on all three Maextro V800 multipurpose vehicles used in a test of emergency braking from 100km/h. The video went viral, while Communist Party mouthpiece People’s Daily said in a commentary on Sunday that the incident underscored the importance of strengthened oversight over the country’s “rapidly developed” EVs. “The internet regulator will be responsible for sifting out misinformation [about the matter] online that could taint the reputation of Chinese carmakers,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “Consumers will be eager to see the truth amid regulators’ heightened investigation efforts.” Maextro, jointly developed by Huawei and JAC and based in eastern China’s Anhui province, said in a statement on Thursday that it would fully cooperate with the investigation team to safeguard the interests of consumers and support the development of China’s EV industry. On Sunday, the brand said that it would address the brake pedal issue by the end of this month. JAC assembles Maextro vehicles. Tech giant Huawei, through its Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance, supplies technology for smart driving and digital cockpits to the EVs. The Maextro V800 is one of the most expensive EV models in mainland China, with a base price of 766,000 yuan (US$113,582). On Saturday, the MIIT, along with three other ministry-level departments, published draft rules stipulating that sufficient vetting measures including 30,000km (18,641 miles) of road testing should be completed before any new model was offered to consumers. Car sales in China slumped 21.7 per cent year on year to 13.3 million units in the first nine months of 2026 due to narrowing government support such as smaller EV purchase subsidies and a resumption of consumption tax. In August, MIIT vice-minister Xin Guobin said at a press briefing in Beijing that new auto products and technologies would be barred from entering the market unless they passed stricter approval procedures. Beijing is also carrying out a nationwide inspection campaign assessing the quality of Chinese-made cars.

title: Sharks use sound to identify humans in ocean encounters
description: Recent studies show that sharks detect human activity through unique sounds rather than just blood scent.
content:
Do you think sharks attack humans because they smell our blood? Turns out, the first thing a shark might notice about humans is the unique sounds we make in the ocean.
And great white sharks have really good hearing. Even a juvenile can detect you from as far as 100 feet (30.48 metres) away (see graphic). A new study has found that sharks often can tell from just our splashing that we’re not worth the nibble.
“There are dozens – if not potentially hundreds – of encounters daily at a beach with a lot of sharks and people. Why aren’t people being bitten? How do we explain this?” Chris Lowe said. He is the director of the Shark Lab at California State University Long Beach in the US. The research lab studies marine animals.
For years, Lowe and his lab have documented white sharks getting very close to people in
the water. The shark’s approach is never rushed or aggressive. Usually, something makes the shark curious, and as it creeps closer to investigate, it loses interest and swims on. In a first-of-its-kind study, the lab designed a hearing test for sharks.
Using a special machine that can capture not only sounds but also their three-dimensional movement, scientists recorded themselves doing three common ocean activities: freestyle swimming, kayaking and paddling on a surfboard.
They played the “sound bites” at different distances under water and observed whether a shark would move towards the speaker.
This study is ongoing, but the preliminary findings
are striking. Sharks could tell the difference between the three water activities. The louder, more chaotic sound of freestyle swimming can make a shark more likely to approach from a distance. This swim style is in the same frequency range as the sounds of a struggling fish.
With paddling on a surfboard, the sharks could recognise the sound, but they often tuned it out.
They did not react much to the gentle, continuous sounds of kayaking, said Whitney Jones, who led and designed the study.
“This is the first study to empirically show that they seem to be using sound to cue in to people at these greater distances,” Jones said.
Jaida Elcock is a shark biologist with the Marine Predators Group at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. It is a leading independent NGO in the US dedicated to the ocean. Elcock said more data would
make it easier for us to understand how important sharks are for their ecosystems.
“Sharks can be found in every type of ocean ecosystem – they’re deep-sea, they’re in shallow reefs, there’s even an Arctic shark,” Elcock said.
“If we don’t even fully understand how they function in the world the way it is now, it is going to be even harder for us to understand how those vital parts of our ecosystems will function as the ocean continues to change.”

title: Indonesian governor’s Singapore trip adds fury to forest fire, haze crisis
description: East Kalimantan’s Rudy Mas’ud said visit was for medical reasons, not leisure, as Indonesia accepts foreign aid to tackle the disaster.
content: The governor of an Indonesian province bearing the brunt of weeks of raging forest fires has sought to douse anger over his trip to Singapore, as Jakarta “welcomed” help from its neighbours choked by transboundary haze to contain the crisis. East Kalimantan Governor Rudy Mas’ud, who was spotted having breakfast with his wife at the famous integrated resort Marina Bay Sands in a photo posted online on Sunday, said he travelled to the city state for a medical check-up. Rudy’s clarification came after social media users accused him of going on a jaunt while ignoring the plight of residents gasping for clean air, calling the politician “Indonesia’s Marie Antoinette” and his actions “tone deaf”. “His constituents are struggling to breathe, fighting for their lives while he living it up, completely unbothered,” a user said. Others urged a ban on officials from Indonesia’s haze-emitting provinces. “Why are you guys letting the Kalimantan governor come to Singapore while Kalimantan is literally burning? Singaporeans and Malaysians are choking on the haze, yet you’re still welcoming them?” a commenter said. Another post also questioned Rudy: “Why are you in Singapore when your city is burning?” The toxic haze from Indonesia’s forest fires has also triggered school closures in Malaysia and severely degraded Singapore’s air quality, prompting the two sides to offer aid to the neighbouring nation. Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said on Thursday the mechanism for the assistance “has already been discussed and it is currently in progress”, state-run Antara news agency reported. “The president has also expressed his approval.” Calling the fires “an environmental issue that affects many parties”, President Prabowo Subianto said, as quoted by Tempo news magazine: “Although the fires are in Indonesia, their impact is felt by our neighbours. So, they want to help us, and we welcome that.” Last month, Malaysia offered to deploy three helicopters, an aircraft and 52 personnel to help contain the blazes, but there has been no ⁠follow-up since, Reuters said. Indonesia appointed a new disaster mitigation agency chief on Thursday as more than 60,000 personnel have been mobilised to extinguish the fires blazing across six provinces. The disaster also took a toll on firefighters and endangered orangutans in the country. Four men died while battling flames at the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java on Thursday, Agence France-Presse cited the forestry ministry as saying. Meanwhile, Deputy Minister of Home Affairs Bima Arya Sugiarto confirmed on Wednesday that Rudy’s permission to visit Singapore came with caveats. The itinerary had to be short and “he must coordinate disaster handling promptly”, Bima said. “When permission is granted, there are notes attached, since this was for health reasons,” Bima said, adding that Rudy could be subjected to further action amid speculation he was in Singapore to attend the Formula One race over the weekend. “We have not monitored that issue closely. But if there is evidence, then there will be further considerations. If it is true, yes. Because the permission was only for health purposes,” he said. Lawmaker Riyono, a member of the parliamentary commission overseeing ecological concerns, on Tuesday said officials “should be mindful of their comments and the feelings of the public who are struggling with the smoke every day”. “Certainly for local officials, governors, regents and police, they must work in synergy and collaboration to make every effort to extinguish the fires.” Indonesia has ramped up efforts to tackle the fires expected to continue until November and cracked down on companies linked to the disaster. According to the environment ministry’s data, 12 firms were sealed as of September 15. The government is also planning to seed the skies over South Sumatra with 1.5 tonnes of dry ice to clear the haze in its first trial of the technique. “The function of dry ice is to break down the smoke that was previously below so that it can rise upwards,” Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs Dudung Abdurachman said on Thursday, as quoted by CNA. “This way, there will be no more smoke accumulation in the city and its surrounding areas.” It will be used simultaneously with cloud seeding. “The dry ice seeding is specifically to disperse the smoke, while the [weather modification operations] continue to be implemented to stimulate artificial rain to extinguish the fires. So we are making all efforts from various angles,” Dudung said.

title: Anwar says Malaysia has done ‘everything we can’ against haze. Critics say it can do more
description: Smoke from Indonesian fires has blanketed large parts of Peninsular Malaysia, with Johor and Selangor among the worst affected states.
content: Malaysia has ruled out taking stronger measures against Indonesia over the worsening regional haze, even as widespread school closures and mounting public frustration fuel calls to punish those responsible for forest fires in the neighbouring country. “We need to safeguard the close relationship between the two countries. So, we are not going as far as sending a diplomatic note or taking legal action,” Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan told local media on Thursday. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the government had done its most to engage Indonesia to address the issue. “We have done everything we can,” he said on Thursday. Thick smog has blanketed large parts of southern and central Peninsular Malaysia, with Johor and Selangor among the worst affected states. The latest wave of school closures includes eight education districts in Selangor on Friday, keeping hundreds of thousands of students out of classrooms. As of 10am on Friday, Pasir Gudang in Johor recorded an Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of 209 while 30 other monitoring stations, including those in Kuala Lumpur and Selangor, registered readings of above 100. The API scale classifies anything above 300 as hazardous; readings of 201-300 are “very unhealthy”, 101-200 “unhealthy”, 51-100 “moderate” and 0-50 “good”. The mounting problem has sparked scrutiny of Indonesia’s efforts to contain forest and peatland fires, as well as raised questions over the effectiveness of regional cooperation in addressing the decades-old problem. In Singapore, where air quality has also hit unhealthy levels several days this week, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said authorities could pursue local companies linked to the Indonesian fires. “Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries,” he said in a social media post late on Thursday. The city state’s haze act came into force in September 2014, allowing authorities to take legal action against companies responsible for causing or contributing to haze pollution in Singapore, even if their activities take place overseas. Singapore had offered help to Indonesia and would continue working closely with the country and other Asean partners to address the issue, Wong said. Malaysian Member of Parliament Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman on Tuesday called for a coordinated diplomatic protest across Southeast Asia. In his parliamentary debate, Syed Saddiq proposed restrictions on financing for companies implicated in slash-and-burn practices that have caused prolonged air pollution across the region. He argued that major regional banks, including Malaysia’s Maybank, CIMB Bank and Singapore’s DBS, could exert their influence by cutting off financing for companies found to be involved. “We need to hit them where they hurt the most,” he said. He also called for the government to issue a clear diplomatic note with the support of other affected Association of Southeast Asian Nations members, particularly Singapore. ‘Louder than before’ Syed Saddiq’s remarks drew praise from Malaysian social media users. “We need to be louder than before for our children, please,” one user said. Another user thanked the lawmaker for his remarks, saying: “We need more politicians to voice out.” The government faced further criticism from former health minister Khairy Jamaluddin, who said Malaysia was being “too soft” in dealing with Indonesia. While acknowledging the need for diplomatic engagement to resolve the issue, he called for a firmer stance against Jakarta. Environmental group Greenpeace Malaysia on Thursday challenged Anwar’s claim, arguing that diplomatic engagement was insufficient to tackle a crisis that had persisted for more than three decades. “If Malaysia has truly done everything possible, why are communities across the region still suffering from the same crisis, year after year?” it said in a statement. The group urged Putrajaya to introduce a Clean Air Act with provisions to hold Malaysian-linked companies accountable for environmental damage abroad, investigate corporate links to fires in Indonesia, and strengthen regional enforcement cooperation. “The government does not lack recommendations. What remains missing is the political commitment to translate them into enforceable laws, stronger institutions and meaningful corporate accountability,” it said. Earlier this month, the group, along with its Indonesian counterpart and non-governmental organisation Pantau Gambut, identified Kuala Lumpur Kepong as one of 20 entities associated with fire-burning activities in Indonesia. The Malaysian plantation firm rejected the accusation, saying most fires originated outside its concession area, and reaffirmed its zero-burning policy. Indonesia is grappling with its worst fire season in more than a decade, with blazes across Sumatra and Kalimantan sending thick smoke across Southeast Asia. Greenpeace Indonesia identified 5,540 smoke source points between August and September, including hundreds within oil palm and forestry concessions. Fires continue to rage across the archipelago with satellite data from Nasa’s Fire Information for Resource Management System on Thursday showing dense clusters of active fire detections across Sumatra and parts of Kalimantan. President Prabowo Subianto had approved aid from other countries, the foreign ministry said on Thursday, and discussions were under way to determine how foreign resources could be used for firefighting. Last month, Malaysia offered three helicopters, an aircraft and 52 personnel to help contain the fires.

title: ‘Father of Lan Kwai Fong’ Allan Zeman pivots to Hong Kong’s luxury home market
description: The nightlife entrepreneur is bullish on the Northern Metropolis and says he would sell his Lan Kwai Fong assets if the price was right.
content: The wallpaper on Allan Zeman’s office desktop computer screen is an image of Chandara, the private estate in Phuket that he has owned for more than two decades. Now the “father of Lan Kwai Fong” is bringing the Thai resort-style concept to Hong Kong’s luxury housing market. Located in rural Sai Kung, 181 Clearwater is the first local residential project for Zeman’s Lan Kwai Fong Group. Developed with Far East Consortium and Hien Lee Engineering, the project – which has received presale approval and is slated for completion in mid-2027 – comprises 26 private garden villas ranging from 1,877 to 2,867 square feet. The villas are “like my house in Phuket,” the 77-year-old founder of Lan Kwai Fong Group said in an interview with South China Morning Post on Thursday. Zeman said he asked the architects to give the homes a “resort feel”, as Sai Kung’s greenery and coastal setting provided a different environment from the traditional luxury districts in Hong Kong. “You really get a feel that you’re in a tropical paradise.” The move marks a new direction for Zeman’s property business as he seeks opportunities in Hong Kong’s luxury housing market, even as the city’s commercial landlords contend with weak consumer spending and falling asset values. The veteran entrepreneur, who built his reputation transforming Lan Kwai Fong into a nightlife hub, is betting that demand for high-end homes will remain resilient as more people move to Hong Kong. Well-connected within the city’s business and political circles, Zeman’s longer-term optimism about Hong Kong also rests on the planned Northern Metropolis, a mega development zone near the border with Shenzhen that he sees as a potential new economic engine for the city. “[It’s] like a second Hong Kong along the border of Shenzhen,” Zeman said, describing the scale of the planned development, which includes proposed university towns that will focus on areas such as technology, liberal arts, commerce and biomedical research. “Education is key right now,” he said, arguing that universities, technology companies and the workers they attract would bring young people into the city, though it was a “little early right now” to commit to a project in the area. “Once it’s established around 2028 or 2030, you start to see a need for nightlife and entertainment,” he added, noting there will be room for that to develop with “more and more people”. The outlook reflects his broader view that population growth and the arrival of more professionals in the Northern Metropolis could support demand for housing and consumer services. Against this backdrop, the Lan Kwai Fong Group entered the residential market by betting on a different part of Hong Kong’s real estate market, one where mainland Chinese buyers were the primary interest group. Zeman’s company and its partners acquired the Sai Kung site in 2021 with a land premium of HK$369.86 million (US$47.1 million), equivalent to about HK$6,530 per square foot of permitted residential floor area. “Businesspeople are always thinking of how to make money,” he said. “We just saw the opportunity.” In the first half of the year, Hong Kong’s luxury market saw a rebound from a four-year slump but higher interest rates and mainland capital restrictions could dampen sales. For Zeman, the approach to market timing is simple: “If you build the right thing, it’s always good timing.” He also cited personal safety as a selling point for Hong Kong among overseas buyers. “For foreigners coming here, the beauty of Hong Kong is safety,” he said. “You can let your kids go out until five in the morning … in the rest of the world, if you’re wearing a chain or a bracelet or a watch, it’s gone.” Zeman’s optimism aside, Hong Kong’s commercial property market is under pressure, with landlords dealing with weak consumer spending and competition from Shenzhen. The pressure is reflected in recent property listings and sales on D’Aguilar Street, where Zeman opened California Restaurant in 1983 and began building a nightlife business. Shop A on the lower ground floor of Ho Lee Commercial Building, which housed the bar Insomnia, was recently sold through a receivership process for HK$58.68 million, down 65 per cent from HK$168 million in 2015. The transaction underscores the pressure on commercial property values in Lan Kwai Fong, although the extent to which the decline has affected Zeman’s own portfolio remains unclear. His group owns properties that include California Tower, 1LKF and The Plaza in Central. Asked whether he would consider selling assets, Zeman said he was open to it and bringing in partners. “For the right price, for sure,” he added. “I always have my eyes open. Opportunity knocks if there’s something coming along.” Zeman said the customer base in Lan Kwai Fong had changed dramatically since the pandemic, with expatriates leaving Hong Kong and more residents crossing the border for dining and entertainment. “Hong Kong itself has changed a lot. After Covid, [something] like 200,000 expats left Hong Kong,” he said. “We had the talent scheme to attract talent to Hong Kong, but we got a lot of mainlanders moving here.” The group has adjusted its tenant mix accordingly. California Tower now houses karaoke venues from Beijing and Guangzhou, alongside restaurants serving regional mainland Chinese cuisines. Looking ahead, Zeman said the group would consider other residential sites, including on The Peak or in Mid-Levels, where the design would be tailored to the location. “Residential is a very good market … especially now because people are moving to Hong Kong, so there’s going to be a need for housing,” he said.

title: Exclusive | Alo rakes in record HK$20 million in first-week sales at Hong Kong mall
description: US brand’s flagship records highest first-week sales among new stores at K11 Musea, excluding jewellery and watch retailers.
content: American athleisure brand Alo generated nearly HK$20 million (US$2.6 million) in sales during its first week in Hong Kong, breaking an opening-week record at a luxury waterfront shopping centre and highlighting growing appetite for premium wellness products amid an uneven retail recovery. The brand, which soft opened its first Greater China flagship at K11 Musea in Tsim Sha Tsui on September 25, recorded the highest first-week sales among new stores at the mall, excluding jewellery and watch retailers. The store is set to hold its official grand opening on Friday evening. The nearly HK$20 million haul came from its two-storey, 7,000 square foot flagship, which occupies the former premises of British luxury food retailer Fortnum & Mason. The British brand closed its Hong Kong outlet in January. Horace Lam, CEO of K11 Hong Kong, attributed the strong debut to the brand’s celebrity appeal, pent-up consumer demand and its ability to combine luxury fashion with wellness. “I think it has created the luxury wellness category,” Lam told the South China Morning Post, adding that traditional sportswear and luxury brands had rarely sought to combine the two concepts so deliberately. The brand’s strategy extended from product design and pricing to marketing and the in-store experience, setting it apart from more established competitors, he said. Lam said Alo’s opening was deliberately timed ahead of the National Day “golden week” holiday to capitalise on an influx of mainland Chinese tourists. Tourists accounted for about 60 per cent of the store’s sales, while local customers contributed the remaining 40 per cent, according to K11 Musea. The strong debut coincided with a rebound in inbound tourism. Hong Kong welcomed 4.03 million visitors in September, up 22 per cent year on year, according to figures released by the Tourism Board on Thursday. Mainland arrivals jumped 29 per cent to about 3.17 million, while total visitor numbers in the first nine months reached 40.7 million, an increase of 12 per cent. Lam said maintaining a healthy balance between local and tourist spending had become increasingly important for Hong Kong retailers, helping businesses avoid excessive reliance on peak holiday periods. He also credited Alo’s popularity to its community-focused marketing strategy, which included exclusive yoga, running and cycling activities ahead of the opening. The brand, endorsed by celebrities including Blackpink’s Jisoo and Kendall Jenner, had accumulated substantial demand in Greater China before establishing physical stores in the region, he said. Its celebrity appeal will be on display at Friday’s official opening, which Jisoo is expected to attend. Jackie Wong, director of occupier services at Colliers, said changing consumer preferences were driving demand for larger retail spaces among wellness and lifestyle brands. “Consumers are increasingly looking beyond the product itself and placing greater value on experiences, lifestyle, wellness and well-being,” she said. “For wellness and active-lifestyle brands in particular, a larger retail footprint makes strategic sense as the store is a part of the brand experience and brand positioning.” Wong said softer rents were also creating opportunities for retailers to secure prominent locations at more affordable costs, even as the leasing market showed signs of recovery. High-street rents rose 1.8 per cent in the first nine months of the year, according to Colliers, which forecast growth of about 3 per cent for 2026. “Brands are therefore becoming more selective rather than simply more aggressive,” she said, adding that retailers were prioritising prime locations offering strong visibility and footfall at viable occupancy costs. Growing demand from personal care, lifestyle and other experience-led operators also reflected the continuing evolution of Hong Kong’s retail mix, she added. Lam said the mall had been adjusting its tenant mix in response to changing shopping habits, with the arrival of Alo forming part of a broader strategy to introduce more lifestyle-oriented brands. K11 Musea, which also recently welcomed Prada, Miu Miu and Max Mara, said that in the past financial year it had recorded its highest annual sales since opening. Most of its current luxury-brand upgrades are expected to be completed by Christmas, with further changes planned for the upper and basement floors in 2027 and 2028. Alo, meanwhile, plans to open nine stores across Hong Kong, Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Chengdu and Macau as part of its Greater China expansion.

title: Trump rebukes Zelensky, calls Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries a ‘disgrace’
description: US president says the Ukrainian leader is ‘more difficult’ than Putin, portraying him as an obstacle to ending the conflict.
content: Ukraine’s resumption of strikes on Russian refineries is ⁠a “disgrace” that keeps ⁠global energy prices elevated, US President ⁠Donald Trump told the Newsmax news outlet in an interview aired on Thursday. Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after President Volodymyr Zelensky declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites that Trump had announced, ‌and criticised his willingness to strike deals with Moscow. “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump said in the interview, after Ukraine hit a Rosneft refinery southeast of Moscow which helps to supply the Russian capital. “There are a lot of targets you can ⁠hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, diesel oil, ‌and we need that, and the world needs that, then he’s not doing a good service for the world.” Russia rained down missile ‌and drone strikes, targeting energy facilities such as power stations, knocking out supply ⁠to hundreds of thousands, ⁠and Zelensky told the Financial Times that Ukraine’s patience had run out. Trump’s administration has been trying to ‌mediate a ceasefire deal to end the war that started with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. He repeated ‌to Newsmax ‌his belief that Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin hate each other, which ‌makes it hard to end the conflict. “I’m not a big fan of Zelensky,” Trump ⁠said. “I think they actually both would like to see it end, but I think I ⁠find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.” As Trump pressured Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, Ukraine faced reduced usage ‌of a satellite system ‌on which it relies for battlefield communications and drone operations. The order came from inside the White House, said two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter, without specifying who there made the decision or was responsible for implementing the order. Zelensky is set to join European Union leaders in Brussels on Friday for talks on further support for Ukraine. Additional reporting by dpa

title: Why the 1960 film The Wild, Wild Rose is the late Grace Chang’s greatest cinematic triumph
description: Mambo Girl made Grace Chang a star but, arguably, her finest role was Sijia, the sexually charged nightclub singer in The Wild, Wild Rose.
content: Grace Chang, also known by her stage name Ge Lan, died in August at the age of 93. She is widely remembered today for her lively performance in Mambo Girl, the 1957 Chinese-language musical that made her a star. Famed for pure roles expressing the aspirations of would-be middle-class Hong Kong girls, Chang initially played characters who were hip, popular, socially adept, conscientious and relatively well-off, possessing no hint of sexuality; her character in Mambo Girl is almost asexual. However, her best film is arguably 1960’s The Wild, Wild Rose, which fascinatingly blends story elements and songs from Georges Bizet’s 1875 opera Carmen with Mandopop and jazz, drawing heavily on American film noir. Demonstrating her finely tuned ability to take on different personas, Chang plays against type as a sexually charged nightclub singer who seduces a hapless pianist – a selfish act triggering his and her own downfall. She looks surprisingly comfortable as the sultry songbird Sijia, vamping it up with gusto on stage, geeing up her male admirers, and unleashing an unexpectedly vigorous sexuality. A bit of a bruiser, Sijia even has a violent brawl with a rival singer on the dance floor. “Mambo Girl was a real breakthrough for my career. A lot of fun to do, and a very big hit,” Chang told the South China Morning Post in a 1993 interview. “Another favourite is The Wild, Wild Rose, where I played a ‘bad girl’ role that was a total change from anything I had done before.” A complex femme fatale Produced by Motion Picture & General Investment (MP&GI; later Cathay Studios), one of Hong Kong’s two major studios in the 1950s and early 60s, The Wild, Wild Rose features a quality script by Nellie Chin Yu rivalling Hollywood films dominating the local box office. Its numerous plot strands all lock together well. A voracious woman, Sijia is proud that no man can resist her. When unassuming pianist Hanhua (Chang Yang) is hired as her accompanist, she initially dislikes him for replacing a musician in dire need of work to support his sick wife. That changes when Hanhua, in a rare narrative inconsistency, demonstrates kung fu skills while defending himself against his predecessor’s angry colleagues. Sijia, channelling Bizet’s Carmen, likes a man with red blood and vows to seduce him “or I am not alive!” Unfortunately for Sijia, the quiet Hanhua is happy with his pleasant, principled girlfriend. His polite reserve, however, proves no match for the wily songstress’ manipulations. Soon he becomes obsessed with her – and she unexpectedly falls in love with him. The relationship complicates further when Sijia’s gangster ex-husband (Tang Ti) is released from prison and wants her back. The twist is that, although Sijia lacks a stereotypical bad girl’s “heart of gold” – the character is more complex – she possesses the strong sense of justice permeating Cantonese-language dramas of the era. Realising her relationship with Hanhua is destroying him, she pretends to fall out of love. As in Carmen, Hanhua’s obsessive love makes him unable to take her rejection, with tragic consequences. Adapting Carmen The overall story thread – obsession leading to disaster – comes from Bizet’s opera, accompanied by numerous visual references to its Spanish setting. Sijia opens the film singing an adaptation of Bizet’s “Habanera”, teasing that men are “just for fun” while dressed in a flamenco-tinged outfit and holding a Spanish guitar. Later, she performs in full matador garb. But Sijia is very different from Carmen, who is usually portrayed as a strong force of nature. Not only is Sijia slight and sultry, she has a moral quotient absent in Carmen. The Spanish character leaves her lover out of boredom, preferring a glamorous matador. Sijia leaves Hanhua because she feels it is morally correct. The music is similarly adapted. Japanese jazz composer Ryoichi Hattori tailored Bizet’s songs to suit Chang’s style. The film also features Mandopop-style numbers – which later became hits with Cantonese translations – and a rendition of Giacomo Puccini’s “Con Onor Muore” (“To Die With Honour”), the finale of Madame Butterfly. The stand-out dance number, “Jajambo”, has nothing to do with Carmen. A jazzy cabaret song written by Hattori reflecting an exuberant, African-style chic, the number is performed by Chang, who undulates seductively while shaking maracas. Chinese musical fans have often wondered what “Jajambo” means; Chang addressed this in the SCMP interview: “I could never figure that out myself. Finally I went to the composer and asked him. He told me that it was a mixture of cha-cha and mambo.” Emulating Hollywood realism The film’s success partly stems from the believability of Chang’s Sijia, who appears to perform the musical scenes live rather than miming. Chang was actually singing on set. “Although the songs were pre-recorded, I always sang like I was recording them,” she told film historian Sam Ho. “Everyone on the set could hear me. I did that because the audience can tell if you’re not really singing. You have to use your lungs when you sing, and that makes the muscles in your face move. That’s one of the reasons the emotions in The Wild, Wild Rose seem so real.” Dialogue was similarly recorded with sync sound – live rather than dubbed, as became the norm later – adding further realism. This focus on quality extended elsewhere. The Wild, Wild Rose – directed by Wong Tin-lam, father of 1990s lowbrow film maestro Wong Jing – is beautifully photographed, featuring smooth camerawork reminiscent of American studio films of the era. It eschews the fast cuts and cheap-looking zoom shots that characterised Hong Kong films during the late 1960s and 70s. The nightclub scenes look wonderfully cool and modern, bathed in so much atmospheric cigarette smoke that one critic joked it should be considered an actual character. As Hong Kong transitioned to a modern society in the 50s, The Wild, Wild Rose’s stylish look was no anomaly. “Young people at this time hungered for Western music and Western movies,” Law Kar and Frank Bren wrote in their 2004 book Hong Kong Cinema: A Cross-Cultural View. “Foreign movies, especially American, dominated the [local] box office in the 1950s and 1960s.” Studios such as MP&GI sought to attract this emerging youth audience and compete with Hollywood imports. The company’s contract stars, such as Chang, were modelled on carefree American counterparts like Debbie Reynolds and Natalie Wood. Chang remembered the studio being well organised. MP&GI rivalled Shaw Brothers as Hong Kong’s major studio in the late 1950s and early 60s, making youth-oriented romances, comedies and musicals heavily influenced by the Hollywood look, though it declined after founder Loke Wan Tho died in a plane crash in 1964. Unlike the quick-fire Hong Kong films of the 90s, MP&GI provided fully finished scripts before shooting and held numerous pre-production meetings. This rigorous process paid off with The Wild, Wild Rose, which recently became the Hong Kong Film Archive’s second 4K digital restoration project. “It is an important film in Hong Kong film history,” Ho said. “A remarkable work of art. At a time when our society was still dominated by patriarchal values, a female character of such diversity and autonomy is extraordinary.” Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: China maps Israeli spoofing with flight data; new US press secretary: SCMP’s 7 highlights
description: From China approving Visa for local operations to Indonesia’s thick haze, here are top stories from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from this week’s news across Hong Kong, mainland China, the wider Asia region and beyond that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Chinese scientists say they spotted possible Israeli electronic warfare units Chinese military scientists claim they have developed an algorithm that could help identify electronic warfare units using civil aviation flight data. 2. New Trump press secretary says she passed bar exam in China, raising eyebrows Katie Zacharia, US President Donald Trump’s newly appointed White House press secretary, faces questions about her legal credentials after telling reporters on Tuesday that she passed a bar exam “when I moved to China”, without identifying the jurisdiction. 3. China gives green light to Visa for local clearing entity after 9-year wait The People’s Bank of China on Tuesday gave its approval to Visa to make preparations for a locally registered bank card clearing organisation, calling the move a major step in the country’s financial opening up in an online statement. 4. Slain model Abby Choi called ‘birthing machine’ by ex-father-in-law, court hears The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung called her a “birthing machine” and tried to assault her before he allegedly plotted with his two sons to kill her three years ago, a court has heard. 5. China keeps extending Shenzhen Apec deadline. Why are US execs so unenthused? Some senior American executives are lukewarm about attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and related business events in Shenzhen next month, according to people familiar with the matter. 6. ‘Forgive us’: Indonesians urge Singapore, Malaysia to sue Jakarta over haze Many Indonesians are urging foreign governments on social media, including those of neighbouring countries affected by the haze, to take action against Jakarta over its handling of the fires. 7.
