title: More than music: Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra strikes a chord across generations
description: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist takes Chinese music beyond the concert hall to strengthen family bonds and connect communities.
content: For nearly five decades, the Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra has worked to bring its music to a wider audience, including people who might never have considered entering a concert hall. Executive director Celina Chin Man-wah said the orchestra had long sought to ensure Chinese music was not seen as distant, formal or difficult to understand. That has meant commissioning new works, exploring different musical styles and developing programmes for younger audiences. “We cannot rely on the old repertoire alone,” Chin said. “New works are essential if Chinese music is to keep developing and speak to future audiences.” The orchestra has commissioned more than 2,400 works over the years, and its musicians have collaborated with composers and artists from Hong Kong, mainland China and around the world. Its international engagements have also helped bring Chinese orchestral music to wider audiences. Chin recalled an invitation to perform as part of the opening programme at Beijing’s National Centre for the Performing Arts, adding that overseas presenters had also requested programmes of contemporary Chinese music. She also said such invitations recognised not only the orchestra’s performances but also its role in creating and promoting new repertoire. Chin joined the orchestra in 1996 after holding arts management roles in theatre, film festivals and arts programming. Those roles gave her experience in production, logistics and programming that she would draw on at the orchestra. The orchestra is a finalist for the Spirit of Culture Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Its work extends beyond the concert hall. Chin sees Chinese music as a way to bring communities together, encouraging people of different ages and backgrounds to take part. The orchestra launched its Hong Kong Drum Festival in 2003 after the Sars – severe acute respiratory syndrome – outbreak, partly to help lift morale. Participants have since included children, parents, older people and members of rehabilitation organisations. The orchestra has also worked with young people in correctional institutions. Chin recalled programmes in which participants learned percussion and performed for their families, culminating in a piece they played together with their relatives. The aim, she said, went beyond music. “Sometimes a young person has an idea and the family may not understand it, or the family has expectations the young person cannot accept,” she said. “To complete the piece, they have to listen to each other and work together.” Chin advocates introducing children to music at an early age, whether or not they go on to become professional musicians. She also sees a growing range of career opportunities in the arts. Young performers may later move into teaching, composition, music therapy or other creative fields, while some independent artists develop their own projects and build careers outside traditional institutions. The orchestra also gives younger composers opportunities to have their new works performed by professional musicians, allowing them to hear how their compositions work in practice and exchange ideas directly with the players. Chin said such programmes could not always be judged by immediate audience numbers or ticket revenue. “Art cannot always be assessed by whether something is popular straight away,” she said. “Artistic development takes patience, and audiences need time to discover work with greater depth.” Launched in 2013, the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention.

title: Hong Kong schools urged to avoid grade repeats for students with SEN
description: Updated guidelines promote tailored support to address learning and mental health needs.
content:
Hong Kong schools should refrain from making students with special educational needs (SEN) or significant mental health issues repeat a grade, according to updated guidance from education authorities. This guidance cautions that such a practice may exacerbate their challenges in adapting.
The latest version of the Education Bureau’s School Administration Guide requires subsidised schools considering grade retention for pupils with special educational needs (SEN) to consult parents through a team of professionals, including an educational psychologist.
“Repeating a grade will only aggravate their social and emotional adjustment difficulties and increase mental health risks,” according to the guide, which was updated in August and came to the attention of the media on Tuesday.
The team should also include the school’s student support team and teachers, as well as psychiatrists when necessary, it said.
Schools should also provide support measures suited to the individual SEN student’s needs as an alternative to repeating a grade.
In its update, the bureau said schools should avoid repeated grade retention because it could reduce students’ interest in learning, damage their self-image, increase their risk of dropping out and heighten mental health risks.
When deciding whether a student should repeat a grade, schools should review the child’s overall circumstances, including academic performance, conduct, learning attitude, performance in extracurricular activities, other learning needs and the wishes of both the student and their parents.
“Schools should not regard grade repetition as the sole method to assist student learning, nor should it be used to punish students,” the guide said.
The bureau also urged schools not to arrange for a large number of students at a particular level to repeat a grade. Under the guide, a primary school’s overall repetition rate should not exceed 3 per cent of total enrolment, while the rate for secondary schools should not exceed 5 per cent.
Students may repeat a grade only once during their six years of primary school and may not repeat Primary Six.
Principals told the South China Morning Post on Tuesday that grade retention was a serious decision requiring a holistic assessment of each student’s circumstances and suitability, adding that the guidelines urged educators to think “more cautiously” about the matter.
Lee Yi-ying, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Subsidised Secondary Schools Council, said the learning needs of SEN students varied widely, and each potential case of grade retention should be assessed holistically according to the child’s needs and suitability.
“The guidelines are meant to ask us to be more cautious, especially for SEN students. Our concern is that more formulaic assessment [for retention] isn’t ideal,” Lee said.
The secondary school principal said she believed the guidelines did not impose a total ban on repeating a grade for SEN students, but required schools to take additional steps to assess their circumstances more holistically.
Lee said that even under existing practices, students with and without special needs required counselling when repeating a grade to ensure they did not see the measure as a sign of personal failure.
Schools would also evaluate whether a student needed to repeat a grade with a variety of factors besides performance, including the number of days in attendance.
Lee said that for some schools, a low rate of attendance suggested an incomplete immersion in campus life and could foster decisions for grade retention.
She added that repeating a grade could help some students who needed more time to master their learning, while others might benefit from dropping elective subjects or switching to another subject.
Langton Cheung Yung-pong, honorary chairman of the Hong Kong Aided Primary School Heads Association, said the updated guidelines were a step in the right direction.
Cheung said his school already consulted a multidisciplinary team of professionals when deciding whether a student should repeat a grade.
“The new guidelines are a response to actual needs,” Cheung said.
For students with intellectual disabilities, he added, additional time was not the key to improving their grades, making repeating a year an unsuitable measure for them.
Primary school repeater numbers in Hong Kong fell from 1,610 in 2015 to a 10-year low of 1,205 in 2025. The repeaters accounted for only 0.38 per cent of all primary students last year.
For secondary schools, while the number of repeaters decreased from 11,560 in 2015 to 9,273 in 2025, they still accounted for 2.67 per cent of the total secondary student body, according to the bureau’s statistics.
The bureau said the number of students with special education needs enrolled in public schools was 67,870 in the 2024-25 school year.

title: Xi’s pledge to ‘uproot sick trees’ aired weeks ahead of Communist Party conclave
description: Chinese leader’s speech to corruption watchdog contains a series of blunt warnings to the ruling party.
content: President Xi Jinping has pledged to “uproot sick trees” in the anti-corruption fight, according to a transcript of a speech published by the Communist Party’s flagship magazine ahead of a major party conclave later this month. The warning appeared on Thursday in the magazine Qiushi, which carried fresh details of a speech Xi delivered in January at the fifth plenary session of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), the party’s top anti-corruption watchdog. The speech contained a series of blunt warnings to the party. “The fight against corruption is a major battle that we cannot afford to lose and must never lose. We cannot stop for a moment or retreat even half a step … [We must] uproot or cut down ‘sick trees’ wherever necessary,” Xi said. The metaphor of “sick trees” comes from ancient Chinese poetry, suggesting that new life will flourish beyond decaying trees, with the new replacing the old. “Corruption is the greatest risk, threat and challenge facing our party. It is a roadblock and stumbling block to the development of the party and the country,” Xi said. He also emphasised that corruption remained widespread and prone to recurring within the party, and that the anti-corruption campaign continued to face a grim situation. The edited transcript was published less than two weeks before the fifth plenary session of the party’s 20th Central Committee, taking place in Beijing from October 26 to 29, when senior party officials are expected to discuss and adopt a major document aimed at “deepening party self-governance”. The plenum is expected to focus on tackling systemic corruption, strengthening political oversight within the party and closing institutional loopholes across the bureaucracy and government departments. The plenum also comes as work is under way on the power reshuffle that will be finalised during the party congress next autumn, when a new Central Committee will be formed and major leadership changes announced. The anti-corruption campaign has already taken a heavy toll on the Central Committee, with 34 of its 205 full members either under investigation or stripped of their seats in the National People’s Congress, China’s top legislature. On Tuesday, the CCDI announced a corruption investigation into former Chongqing mayor Huang Qifan – long regarded as a political survivor – eight years after his retirement. Thursday’s article also quoted Xi as calling for efforts to prevent officials from becoming idle before handing over power or rushing to deliver quick results after taking office, as local governments and party committees undergo leadership transitions this year. “[We must] step up investigations into corruption involving ‘principal leaders’, young cadres and others,” Xi said. Principal leaders in government departments and younger cadres are typically among the key candidates for personnel reshuffles and promotions during leadership transitions. Personnel changes at the regional level have picked up pace – since September, Beijing has appointed new top and second-ranking officials in six provinces. Xi also said that some of the party’s internal regulations were too broad and vague, while loopholes remained in how different rules and regulatory systems fitted together. He called for improvements to the party’s internal regulatory framework, saying “[we must] promptly establish regulations in areas where gaps exist, and revise and supplement those that are incomplete or outdated … to prevent using a cattle pen to confine a cat”. The Chinese phrase “using a cattle pen to confine a cat” describes safeguards with gaps so wide, or rules so lax, that they fail to impose effective restraints. Xi also said the party should place greater emphasis on harnessing big data and other technologies to improve the effectiveness of supervision, disciplinary enforcement and law enforcement. But he cautioned that the use of new technologies within the party must be accompanied by stronger ethical regulation and data security safeguards, and strictly comply with party disciplinary rules and the law.

title: Hong Kong Olympian wonders if AI is the answer to recapturing our humanity
description: In her memoir, high-achieving ex-swimmer Yvette Kong opens up on sporting goals and what it means to be human when we look beyond the scoreboard.
content: The 0.1 second that stood between Yvette Kong Man-yi and qualifying for the 2012 Olympics was “unbearable”, the Hong Kong swimmer writes in her newly published memoir, The Unmeasured Human. It was, the 33-year-old recalls years later, “too small to feel and too large to survive unchanged”. Fourteen years on, Kong is grateful for the heartbreaking experience, telling the South China Morning Post that “challenge is fundamental to human growth and spirit”. “I needed to find the courage to try again without a guarantee of succeeding,” she said. Kong ultimately swept away that crushing disappointment in the most apt fashion, qualifying for the 2016 Rio de Janeiro Olympics by the same vanishingly small 0.1-second margin. She was repeatedly told after competing in the 100m breaststroke and 4x100m medley relay in Brazil that she should document her story in print. “I thought my life had been mostly swimming, so I didn’t do it, but the seed was planted,” Kong said. “I have switched my identity since then … Now felt like a very good time, because I had enough to share.” Kong’s book draws direct parallels between her post-swimming quest to understand herself beyond the scoreboard, and the irresistible charge of artificial intelligence that is eroding the ability of people to “prove themselves through what they produce”. “We discuss what machines can do, or what the AI-human collaboration can do, but the human question is left behind,” she said. “This is a global conversation, and although this is a personal story … I feel a responsibility to have a voice out there, given all the angles I’ve seen from my lived experiences. “AI gives us an opportunity to relook at what it truly means to be human. Have we been trained to be too machine-like?” Kong writes unsparingly in her book about quitting swimming in March 2013, of how for one month she tried to kid herself she “had escaped”. Only, she writes, “now the pain had nowhere to hide”. In earlier pages, she had introduced the term “croggling”, used to describe swimmers so exhausted and racked with pain in training that they would cry into their goggles. Without swimming, the tears would visit unexpectedly: sometimes in her cognitive science classes at the University of California, Berkeley. After a diagnosis for complex post-traumatic stress disorder “made me feel found”, Kong steadily reimmersed herself in the pool, a place she had been happiest since the age of seven, when anyone who would listen heard about her Olympic dream. Hong Kong sent a 31-strong delegation to that year’s Sydney Games, but she was too young, too naive and too infatuated with her sport to pay any heed to the odds. Reaching Rio, she said, “gave that little girl her ending”, but this was an individual who at school would look askance at her contemporaries all “trying to become geniuses at something”. “Why were we not trying to become geniuses at life?” Kong wondered. Kong boasts a dizzying CV. She has lectured in transversal design at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), undertaken corporate roles for McKinsey & Co and Estée Lauder, established the art and innovation studio, Transversal Lab, and last year launched Arelyx, the start-up that aims to arm people with the “resilience, judgment, ethical clarity and agency to thrive in the AI age”, and which she called “the accumulation of a life’s work and lived experiences”. She was a founding board member of the mental health charity Mind HK. Since obtaining her degree, Kong has added postgraduate qualifications in business administration and management studies from Beijing’s Tsinghua University and MIT, respectively. A story that epitomises Kong’s high-achieving, go-getting character began with her casually mentioning in a previous conversation that she was considering putting pen to paper to chronicle her young life. Six months later, she messaged with “exciting news to share”. “Remember our conversation on writing a memoir? I spent the past few months getting it together,” Kong wrote. Little wonder that her response to the obvious, “what’s next” is to reveal plans to “take Arelyx beyond Hong Kong”. “I still have lots of ambition, but I have to think about what I want to do in life,” she added. “Is it just to keep achieving, or do I want to have a more whole life while doing that? The fullest of lives involve family and friends. “What we attain intellectually or achievement-wise is important, but I’m not sure how meaningful it is without those social spaces.” The title of Kong’s book refers to her no longer being judged on the all-seeing clock that delivered its definitive verdicts; that knew nothing of her early mornings, her hours in the pool or the pain in her shoulders and lungs. “The number appeared,” she wrote. “The world knew what to call me. Fast. Slow. Qualified. Almost.” “There are parts of us unmeasured by conventional standards,” Kong said. “I was measured by the scoreboard, and by grades, but these measurements should not define a human, because we’re way bigger than that.” That is one reason why “basing my worth on the number of books I sell wouldn’t be my thing”. “Writing my heart out and putting myself out there is enough,” Kong said. “The reward is in the process. Intensively writing for a few months, I gained a lot of insight and growth, because I had to go back, open different boxes in my life, and relook at them.” A blend of “prose and short sentences”, Kong wrote her book in two languages to accommodate for the translation from English to Chinese “not coming out right”. “The onomatopoeia’s different, the ticking of the clock and lapping of the pool didn’t translate, some words didn’t rhyme,” Kong said, adding that after wrestling with whether to hire an editor and publisher she decided to opt for “absolute freedom in how I wrote this”. “It’s a flow of my consciousness, I wanted it to feel like a cinematic, transformative and immersive experience for the reader.” At the outset, Kong reveals that her mother had questioned whether the Kawasaki disease her daughter suffered, aged three, had “affected my brain development”. Kong was first aware of feeling measured as she grappled with childhood demands: “Sit still, remember quickly, follow instructions, finish the page, pass the test, become the girl everyone seemed to understand.” Her youthful embarrassment leaps from the page when she recalls her family’s “almost comic” relief after her Primary Five mathematics score of 59.5 was rounded up to the 60 pass mark, sparing the expense of a repeated year. Kong’s parents’ shoe-trading business “faltered” early in her life. The family moved in with her grandparents and aunt. She writes evocatively about her ability to innocently find fun in the tiny living space. The seven short sentences she uses to describe her father leaving are tremendously moving; so jarring they demand rereading. “I definitely feel naked in some sense, because there are lots of private thoughts and feelings [in the book],” Kong said. “I’m used to writing intellectual or cognitive text. This is by far the most personal work I’ve done in my life.” At the book’s launch, timed to coincide with World Mental Health Day last weekend, Kong announced that a documentary inspired by her memoir was in production. Filming for Still Arriving is planned across Hong Kong, Switzerland, Bhutan and the United States. “If I’d qualified for the 2012 Olympics, life would have been very different,” Kong said. “I’d have followed a more regular path; had less of a detour. I keep putting myself outside the box, with the confidence and knowledge that I’ll be OK. It’s a rewarding journey.”

title: Is Philippines geared for El Nino? Critics say water-planning has run dry
description: An official’s call to use water buckets and water treatment kits has been criticised as proof again of Manila’s poor disaster planning.
content: As the Philippines braces for months of drought and shortages amid the deleterious effects of El Nino, questions are mounting over whether it could have been better prepared to deal with a crisis that had been predicted well in advance. The government’s haphazard response to the climate phenomenon reflects its persistent track record of failing to adequately plan, according to climate and risk specialists. El Nino is a weather phenomenon that triggers changes in winds and rainfall patterns, causing erratic weather around the world due to warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean. The 2026-2027 El Nino event was declared in June by the World Meteorological Organization and is expected to peak in November and December. On Thursday, Philippine Trade Secretary Cristina Roque told reporters that there was no need for residents to hoard bottled water and that supplies and prices of basic goods remained stable, following social media posts showing Filipinos buying water and other items in huge quantities at supermarkets. “There is no need to panic, there is no need to hoard. We have enough to supply,” Roque said. However, a demonstration on Wednesday by Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian, showing how government-issued kits could filter rainwater collected in buckets, did little to assuage public concern. One social media user complained: “Telling citizens, many of whom are already struggling with rising living costs, to rely on buckets is a temporary band-aid.” Analysts question Manila’s readiness to deal with a prolonged drought, amid reports that the government has cut Metro Manila’s water allocation in anticipation of El Nino peaking later this year. Ven Paolo Valenzuela, a research fellow at Singapore Management University’s College of Integrative Studies, said the Philippines experienced one of its strongest El Nino events in 1997 and disaster planning had not improved almost 30 years later. He said the problem was not the filtration technology, which he described as “very good” in helping communities hit by super typhoons and other natural disasters. Rather, it was the absence of a broader plan to address an event with potentially far-reaching effects. “Thirty years later, you still haven’t solved these problems, still haven’t put [the infrastructure] in place,” he said. Patrick Manuel, country director of Waves for Water, a non-governmental organisation supplying the filtration kits to the government, said that the devices could not address the challenges posed by El Nino on their own. His organisation first introduced the kits to remote communities whose access to clean drinking water was disrupted by the destruction caused by Typhoon Haiyan in 2013. Manuel said addressing the impact of El Nino required a whole-of-society approach involving federal agencies, local governments, the private sector, civil society organisations and communities to boost the country’s water infrastructure and promote responsible water use. “Through our work with communities from all across the country, we’ve seen that there’s much more work to be done to provide Filipinos with the right tools and infrastructure to be able to have reliable access to clean and safe water,” Manuel said. Pamela Cajilig, a Philippines-based disaster anthropologist and a fellow of the Atlantic Institute, said the government’s stopgap measures had fuelled distrust as they were seen as transferring responsibility for dealing with extreme weather to ordinary Filipinos. While Filipinos should do their part, the government’s overemphasis on household measures without implementing a systematic national disaster plan appeared to show its preference for “romanticising resilience”, Cajilig said. “There is also the practical question of how these filtration devices will work on a mass scale and for a prolonged period,” she said. “A quick demo for the press does little to help us imagine actual scenarios.” Keith Paolo Landicho, a research associate of the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’ humanitarian assistance and disaster relief programme, said Filipinos should be told how they would be protected by the state instead of being given another reminder on how to cope with the next disaster. “Filipinos are tired of their resilience being celebrated while the systems that leave them exposed remain unfixed,” Landicho said. “Being told to collect rainwater in buckets is not a sustainable solution; it is a stopgap dressed up as preparedness.” Compared with its neighbours, the Philippines appears to be lagging behind when it comes to disaster preparation, according to analysts. Valenzuela pointed to Vietnam, which invested in infrastructure projects such as irrigation systems and sluice gates to regulate water flows along the Mekong River following the 2015–16 El Nino event. Countries across the region have been preparing for this season’s El Nino, with Thailand reportedly enhancing its climate databases and Indonesia introducing drought emergency mechanisms in several districts. The Philippine government’s move to limit Metro Manila’s water supply was a clear sign that it had planned poorly to deal with El Nino’s effects, Valenzuela said. “We can’t even figure out how to put systems in place when it comes to decades of planning to prevent another major disaster that could happen in 10 or 20 years,” he added. Landicho said that Metro Manila’s water supply appeared to have improved compared to a few months ago, with water levels in the nearby provinces of Bulacan and Pampanga recovering from record lows in July. Still the country was ill-prepared for “one of the most forecastable hazards”, he said, with the Philippine state weather bureau Pagasa having issued El Nino forecasts as far back as March. Cajilig said an El Nino-related disaster could have a devastating impact on the Philippines in the long term. “Unlike rapid onset disasters in which we can immediately witness wide-scale loss of life, livelihood, and infrastructure, slow onset disasters like drought are less dramatic,” she said. “Yet studies show that their economic impact can be greater across time – mostly because their effects go unaddressed and therefore linger.” Athea Penaloza, executive director of the Asia-Pacific Alliance for Disaster Management-Philippines, expressed concern over a drop in food production and sustained price pressures for Filipinos, warning that the agricultural sector could be hardest hit if the dry conditions persist, particularly into the first half of next year. “This is where the government needs to prepare more proactively,” she said, calling on Manila to provide immediate support to agricultural communities. “It is important to put concrete measures in place now to support farmers, protect agricultural production and minimise the impact on food security and the cost of living.”

title: Editorial | A mega-events capital has little margin for error
description: Hong Kong has a largely successful record of hosting world-class events. That is precisely why the exceptions stand out.
content: Hong Kong has staked much of its tourism revival on an ambitious strategy of impressing visitors from near and far with world-class shows and events. The recent Hong Kong Cyclothon was meant to be one of those spectacles. Regrettably, a wrong turn by a lead vehicle and a congested finish turned the flagship sporting event into a cautionary tale. The setback is embarrassing and the lesson is telling. In the pursuit of the mega-events economy, success is built on good preparation and execution. The cycling festival sponsored by Sun Hung Kai Properties returned this year with an expanded “five tunnels, three bridges” route, drawing more than 6,000 participants from 21 countries and territories. Riders were promised a rare opportunity to cycle through the Central Kowloon Bypass and across landmark crossings including Tsing Ma, Ting Kau and Stonecutters Bridges. For a city seeking to market itself as “Asia’s capital for major events”, the festival was arguably the most symbolic display of the city’s vibrancy, infrastructure and organisational capability. The event remained a rewarding experience for some participants. The new arrangement to start and finish at the West Kowloon Cultural District, the extended course and the novelty of riding roads normally closed to bicycles drew positive feedback. In addition to the road race for competitive cyclists, a World University Trophy was introduced at this year’s event for cyclists from the top 100 global institutions, including Hong Kong and the mainland, joining the 56km non-race ride. The city is on the right track in promoting sports tourism and cycling and nurturing its global brand. Yet the mid-race route diversion and chaotic end unleashed a barrage of criticisms. It began with staff moving traffic cones to create an emergency access route for ambulances after two cyclists were injured, resulting in a lead vehicle missing the original route towards Ting Kau Bridge. A U-turn section near the finish line was also said to be too narrow, causing severe congestion and forcing many to dismount and finish by pushing their bikes across the line, according to social media posts. The Cycling Association of Hong Kong, China, which handled route guidance, set the right tone with an apology. But it did little to appease disgruntled cyclists who ridiculed the festival as a “push-a-thon” and the city as a “capital of embarrassing fails”. In an era where a single disgruntled social media post can spread like wildfire, the mocking labels are highly damaging to the city’s international reputation. Arguably, it is unfair to judge Hong Kong’s success by a single mishap. The city has a long and largely successful record of hosting events on a scale few places can match. The Hong Kong Marathon brings tens of thousands of runners through the streets each year. The Hong Kong Sevens remains one of the world’s most recognisable rugby festivals, combining elite sport with a distinctive carnival vibe. Similarly, Art Basel, the Wine and Dine Festival, large-scale firework displays and international concerts all justifiably reinforce the city’s credentials as a mega-events capital. Most of these occasions took place without serious incident. That is precisely why the exceptions stand out. When a city advertises excellence and unique experience, public expectations cannot be taken for granted. Two years ago, a government-subsidised exhibition football match involving Lionel Messi turned into a fiasco when the Argentinian player sat out the game due to alleged injury, prompting the organiser to withdraw its HK$16 million sponsorship application and offer refunds amid public pressure. The Cyclothon setback is another reminder of the importance of preparation and execution. For an international gathering involving highly challenging logistics, there is little margin for error. Some 1.75 million visitors were drawn to more than 130 events in the first half of this year, generating around HK$5.8 billion in spending and contributing HK$3.3 billion to the economy, according to the government. Another 100 events are scheduled for the second half of the year, including the Hong Kong Wine and Dine Festival later this month. The stakes are high and every effort must be made to ensure the events are well organised and participants leave with a positive experience.

title: Letters | It’s seriously time for Hong Kong to greenlight a transport museum
description: Readers discuss the need for a venue to celebrate the city’s transport history, and the rule requiring removal of bicycle wheels.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The retirement of the historic Yellow Bus, the shuttle which ferried passengers between San Tin and the old Huanggang Port for nearly three decades, drew crowds of nostalgic commuters and enthusiasts for its final run. This follows a familiar, bittersweet pattern. From the phased retirement of the East Rail line’s iconic “Fly Head” trains to the scrapping of the low-floor double-decker buses, vital artefacts of Hong Kong’s transit heritage are disappearing at an alarming pace. Whenever a beloved vehicle bows out, calls resurface for a comprehensive transport museum. Yet, for decades, these proposals have stalled due to a perceived shortage of space. Hong Kong now has an ideal, ready-made solution: the disused ground-level platforms at Hung Hom station, left vacant following the commissioning of the East Rail line cross-harbour extension. Converting this redundant infrastructure into a dynamic transport museum would preserve collective memories while delivering a high-impact tourism asset at modest public expense. Globally, the value of repurposing railway yards and historic stations into cultural landmarks is well proven. The National Railway Museum in York, the Kyoto Railway Museum and the London Transport Museum all show how authentic transit environments can anchor world-class educational and tourist attractions. By contrast, Hong Kong’s only railway museum in Tai Po Market is constrained by its heritage site boundaries, seemingly unable to accommodate full-length modern train sets. Meanwhile, franchised bus operators keep their vintage fleets tucked away in operational depots, out of public sight. The Hung Hom platforms offer unique spatial and logistical advantages. First, the existing heavy rail platforms, tracks and sheltered concourse already provide the load-bearing capacity needed to display real railway carriages. Portions of the tracks can easily be adapted to exhibit vintage road vehicles alongside trains. This would create an authentic, immersive setting without the heavy capital expenditure of greenfield building. Second, it would establish an international pilgrimage site for transit enthusiasts. Hong Kong’s public transport identity is globally renowned. Our streets gave rise to bespoke transit legends – such as the rugged Dennis Jubilant and Victory Mark 2 double-deckers engineered specifically for Hong Kong’s unforgiving gradients and heavy passenger loads. Together with our operational double-decker trams, these vehicles would attract global railway and bus enthusiasts. Housing them under one roof would create a compelling cultural landmark, diversifying the city’s tourism offerings. Third, located at the nexus of the East Rail and Tuen Ma lines and near the Cross-Harbour Tunnel toll plaza, Hung Hom boasts peerless connectivity. A museum here would naturally link with the Tsim Sha Tsui cultural belt, drawing consistent footfall. Realising this vision requires overcoming interdepartmental inertia. The Transport and the Culture Bureaus should collaborate with MTR Corporation and franchised bus operators under a public-private partnership. Incorporating driving simulators, themed dining and cultural merchandise would ensure operational sustainability. Our public transit network is the moving soul of Hong Kong, carrying the stories of generations. Rather than let the historic Hung Hom platforms languish, the government should act decisively to build a museum worthy of this city’s extraordinary transit legacy. Chan Wing-lun, Peng Chau Rethink rules regarding bikes on trains Bicycles shouldn’t need to have their front wheels removed on trains. It is a hazard for the cyclist carrying wheel and bike separately and for people who come into contact with them. The current enforcement of this rule creates severe, unnecessary practical barriers for cyclists, particularly those using mountain bikes or heavier utility bicycles. Forcing a commuter to detach a front wheel transforms a stable, controllable vehicle into multiple loose, awkward and heavy components. This process is difficult to manage safely in confined public transit environments, increases the physical risk of strain or dropped equipment on escalators and in lifts, and deters ordinary people from combining cycling with public transit. Many leading metropolitan rail systems globally – including London, Taipei, Melbourne and Berlin – accommodate fully intact bicycles during designated off-peak hours or within specific carriages without demanding mechanical disassembly. Given the Hong Kong government’s active promotion of green, low-carbon mobility and integrated multi-modal transport, the MTR’s strict legacy restrictions run counter to encouraging outdoor recreation and sustainable commuting. I urge the Transport Department to coordinate with the MTR Corporation to modernise these guidelines by introducing pragmatic alternatives, such as permitting fully intact bicycles during off-peak hours, designating specific carriages for larger sports equipment and bicycles, and aligning local practices with international smart-city transit standards to make cycling genuinely accessible to the public. Pau Yee-yu, Tai Wai

title: Review | Klara and the Sun review: Jenna Ortega is an android in upbeat but saccharine sci-fi fable
description: Jenna Ortega plays an android bought as a companion to a young girl, portrayed by Mia Tharia, in this optimistic tale of a dystopian future.
content: 3/5 stars Taika Waititi, the Oscar-winning filmmaker behind Jojo Rabbit (2019), brings his trademark quirk to Klara and the Sun, a sunny-side-up sci-fi fable that occasionally delivers flashes of darkness. Based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel of the same name, the film is set in a future where AI companions are the norm. The effervescent Klara (Jenna Ortega) is one such android, albeit a discontinued B1 model now being hawked from a city discount store. Klara’s escape comes when a young girl, Josie (Mia Tharia), petitions her mother, Chrissie (Amy Adams), to buy her. Whisked off to their countryside home, the synthetic companion must learn to be Josie’s friend. As it turns out, Josie has been “lifted”, a medical procedure that has finely tuned her academic and creative abilities. She can paint, write and speed-read with ease, but as the story reveals, this enhancement has come at a cost. Death looms over the family, especially Chrissie, a prim interior designer whose older daughter, Sal, died years earlier. Her husband left shortly afterwards; now Josie is all she has. Fearful of this robotic interloper, Chrissie threatens more than once to dispose of Klara. “You’re not the droid we’re looking for, honey,” she tells her – a wry reminder that Waititi has a Star Wars project stuck in development hell. Ishiguro has explored our futures before, notably in his dystopian clone drama Never Let Me Go (2005), moodily adapted for the screen by Mark Romanek in 2010. Waititi’s take on the Japanese-British author’s work favours a palette of primary colours, from yellow wheat fields to Klara’s burnt-orange top. As a sun-worshipper who believes the star holds true healing powers, Klara owes much of her charm to her profound naivety, ably realised by Ortega, who is best known for her title role in Tim Burton’s supernatural series Wednesday. The film’s finest moments come as Klara and Josie grow closer, with the former even impersonating the housekeeper’s voice so they can go for a joyride in the family’s self-driving car. However, with the arrival of Steve Buscemi’s mysterious character, the third act wobbles as Chrissie behaves increasingly erratically. “Grief messes you up,” she says, summarising a narrative that abruptly shifts focus towards the grieving mother and away from Josie, leaving Klara as a bemused bystander. The best of Waititi’s work consistently earns its emotional payoffs – notably 2016’s surrogate-son tale Hunt for the Wilderpeople – but here, the saccharine sentiment rarely stirs any tingles in your heart. Nevertheless, arriving just after Alejandro G. Inarritu’s Tom Cruise-led Digger offered a bleak look at a climate-altered world, this optimistic, fable-like portrait of the future at least provides a welcome ray of sunshine. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Crypto operator Solana abruptly cancels Shanghai event after office plan raises eyebrows
description: Company pulls plug after splashy marketing campaign that raised questions given Beijing’s ban on crypto activities.
content: Solana, which operates one of the world’s largest cryptocurrencies, has cancelled a high-profile event in Shanghai at the last minute as local police appeared on site, according to social media posts, just a day after the firm touted the opening of a fancy new office in the city. Solana was slated to host its Solana Accelerate China event in Shanghai on Friday morning, part of a week-long event across major cities in mainland China. Shortly before the event kicked off, however, the company said in an email update to attendees that the programme had to be “postponed” due to “last-minute logistical considerations”, according to screenshots circulating on social media. Social media posts also indicated that a few local police officers showed up at the event venue. Solana did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The abrupt suspension of the event followed a splashy marketing campaign in the city earlier this week, which raised questions about how the company was able to do so amid Beijing’s strict ban on crypto-related business activities. Solana had taken office space in Shanghai’s Pudong district, according to social media posts released by company executives on Wednesday. Vibhu Norby, Solana Foundation’s chief product officer, wrote in a post on X that the company had occupied “the highest commercially available office space in the world”, with an accompanying video showing an office with sweeping views of the Huangpu River and riverside skyscrapers including the Aurora Plaza. The video also showed an office reception area adorned with Solana logos and the Chinese characters for “grand opening”. Solana Foundation president Lily Liu, meanwhile, posted a photo on X of a massive digital ad for the firm covering the facade of Shanghai’s Citigroup Tower. Videos circulating online indicated that the crypto firm hosted an event aboard a riverboat in Shanghai on Wednesday night, with Solana co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko in attendance. Solana’s cryptocurrency was the world’s seventh largest token by market value on Thursday, according to CoinMarketCap. The splashy moves from Solana came as a surprise for some in the industry, given China’s strict ban on crypto-related businesses. “So high-profile, a bit unexpected,” wrote Liu Honglin, founder and director of the blockchain-focused Mankun Law Firm in Shanghai, in a social media post on Wednesday. While China was once the birthplace of many crypto businesses, an escalating crackdown from Beijing over the years has driven Chinese crypto firms and founders overseas. Binance founder Zhao Changpeng said on X on Thursday that it was “amazing to see that Solana was able to advertise and even get an office in China”. BNB Chain – the blockchain developed by Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange – “was not able to do this, so far”, Zhao said. Solana’s attention-grabbing moves in Shanghai preceded a series of events it is set to host across mainland China this month. The 2026 Solana Accelerate China tour will take place in Shanghai, Hangzhou, Shenzhen and Beijing from October 16 to 22, according to its website. “Excited to meet local builders and see what’s being built on Solana,” wrote Rachel Conlan, Solana’s chief strategy officer, in a post on X on Wednesday ahead of the Shanghai event. Solana Foundation, which focuses on the blockchain behind the Solana crypto token, had been “investing heavily” to support mainland China’s developer ecosystem, president Liu said at a blockchain industry summit in Shanghai last October. The foundation hoped to deepen collaboration with the mainland in areas such as decentralised payments and artificial intelligence, she added. Still, the firm’s foray into mainland China has faced challenges. Last October, Solana’s Accelerate APAC event in Shenzhen was cut short by a local police inquiry – though organisers attributed the disruption to overcapacity at the venue. Justin d’Anethan, head of research at private markets advisory firm Arctic Digital, saw Solana’s Shanghai ventures as more about “physical presence and engagement at the technological level” than “a full-blown advertising campaign for the token or an engagement to trade”. The company was likely aiming to gain a foothold in the region to engage companies and talents in areas such as AI, payments and security, he added. The broader US-China rivalry could be providing a window of opportunity for overseas crypto firms eyeing the Chinese market, according to d’Anethan. “With the US racing forward in AI, robotics, space exploration, biotech and more, and with China competing hard on all fronts, it’s not surprising that crypto projects would see an opportunity,” d’Anethan said. “One can see this both as a win for China and a positive expansion for an American project into Asia.”

title: Pork insecurity: China protein supply ‘exposed’ amid reliance on feed imports, study says
description: Producing nearly half the world’s pork and its largest farmed-fish harvest requires ‘more feed than China can grow’, study author says.
content: Heavy reliance on imported soy feed in China’s massive pork industry puts affordable protein supply for its 1.4 billion people at risk amid rising regional conflicts and climate change, a new study has warned. The nation, which relies largely on pork for its protein intake, was “exposed” to risks in access to this essential macronutrient, according to the Protein Sovereignty Index published by a Singapore-registered biotech firm on Friday. China faced a medium level of risk on a global scale, as it ranked 21st among 43 countries and regions assessed by Full Circle Biotechnology. Its challenges mainly involved import exposure and resource headroom, according to the study, released in advance of Friday’s World Food Day. In an era of growing focus on national security and resilience, the ability to secure affordable protein is being tested by Middle East conflicts that have disrupted fertiliser supplies and a strong El Nino weather pattern that has driven up fishmeal prices. The best-performing country against this backdrop was Canada, the only country the study ranked as “sovereign” due to its large food-producing base and world-leading potash industry, the study said. Ten countries or regions, including the United States and the European Union, were rated as “resilient”, while the rest were either “exposed”, “dependent” or “critically exposed”. China was rated as “exposed” because producing nearly half of the world’s pork and the world’s largest farmed-fish harvest required “more feed than China can grow”, said Felix Collins, founder of the firm and co-author of the study. While China grew almost all of its own rice and wheat, the top sources of calories, it imported about a third of its protein when counting animal feed – more than the US and EU imported combined, he said. China sources most of its soybeans from Brazil and the US for animal feed and edible oil, as it saves its limited resources for more critical food plants. “The North China Plain holds a quarter of the country’s cropland but less than 8 per cent of its water, so China cannot quickly grow more of its own feed,” Collins said. From January to September, the country’s cumulative grain imports totalled about 117 million tonnes, up 9.7 per cent year on year, according to latest Chinese customs data. Soybean imports accounted for 73 per cent of the total, or 86 million tonnes. A rapidly growing aquaculture sector, another source of protein, was also exposing China to risk because of increased demand for fishmeal imports, said Collins. Global fishmeal prices have hit all-time highs as the El Nino pattern warms the ocean near Peru, the world’s largest source of fishmeal, cutting its anchovy catch. Facing scarce water and arable land resources, Beijing has been calling on the public to move away from a traditional diet centred on staple grains and pork and towards a more varied diet with more poultry and fish. At a late-September press conference, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs said that China’s per capita meat availability in 2025 reached 72.5kg – about 1.5 times the world average – while per capita poultry and egg availability stood at 24.9kg, exceeding levels in developed countries. To ensure people “have enough to eat, eat well, and eat nutritiously and healthily, we must not only tap the potential of arable land but also build a more diversified food supply system”, said Chen Bangxun, ministry spokesperson, as it vowed to develop deep-sea aquaculture to secure more high-quality protein.

title: Chinese fugitive poses as dead twin brother for 2 decades exposed by sibling’s ex-lover
description: At his arrest, Chen was leading an ordinary life under a false name, confident his ruse would keep him hidden.
content: A Chinese fugitive who posed as his deceased twin brother for 19 years was recently arrested after his late brother’s ex-girlfriend identified him. In 2002, a robbery took place in Yuhuan, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province. Seven suspects abducted the victim and robbed him of cash and valuables. Local police quickly arrested six of the suspects, but the seventh, surnamed Chen, escaped. Police searched extensively for Chen but failed to find him, and the case eventually went cold. Five years later, Yuhuan police received a notice from central China’s Anhui province stating that Chen’s household registration had been cancelled because he had died in a traffic accident. The police therefore closed the case, seeing no reason to continue pursuing a suspect who was believed to be dead. However, 19 years later, Yuhuan police came across an unusual clue from Anhui during a routine review. It suggested that a man there had been living for years under the identity of his deceased twin brother. Criminal investigator Long Yuwen retrieved the 2002 robbery case file and compared the identities, places of origin and family ties involved. He found similarities between Chen and the man mentioned in the clue. Yuhuan police quickly formed a special task force and travelled to Anhui to investigate Chen’s status. There, Chen’s mother, sister and fellow villagers covered for him. They said it was the younger Chen who had died in the accident, when in fact he had taken the identity of his older twin brother, who was the one who died. Moreover, official records held by the local household registration office, traffic police and funeral home all confirmed Chen’s death. Police were also unable to obtain the original accident file, making it difficult to prove their suspicions. They then turned to their last resort: archived ID photos. Although the twin brothers looked strikingly alike, they had distinguishing features. While reviewing the records, police discovered that nine days after Chen was registered as dead in 2007, his “older” brother applied to change his name. At the same time, the “older” brother submitted a new ID photo, whose facial features, expression and other details differed completely from those in his previous photo. When Chen’s close relatives refused to cooperate, police tracked down his elder brother’s ex-girlfriend, Deng. She had been discussing marriage with him but abruptly ended the relationship after the traffic accident. After police explained the relevant laws and policies, Deng eventually confirmed that the person who died in the accident 19 years earlier was Chen’s older brother, not the fugitive. Police then arrested Chen in June – 24 years after he committed the crime. By then, he was living an ordinary, peaceful life under a new name, confident that his identity-switching plan would continue to work. He faces a prison sentence of three to 10 years under China’s Criminal Law. “The ex-girlfriend had it the worst in this case,” one online observer commented. “Haven’t Chen’s mother and sister also committed the crime of harbouring a fugitive?” another asked.

title: It’s your funeral: former academic gives Hongkongers more end-of-life choices
description: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist Dr Ng Kwai-lun provides transparent funeral care and end-of-life planning through his social enterprise.
content: After years of teaching Hongkongers about death and end-of-life arrangements, Dr Ng Kwai-lun realised there was a gap between what people were told they could do and the services actually available to them. Determined to bridge that gap, he left a stable university career to become an entrepreneur. Ng had worked at the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s medical school, where he managed embalming and helped run and promote its body donation initiative. But by 2020, the pandemic had exposed another problem. He encountered elderly people and families with little support when arranging funerals, while restrictions left them with fewer choices. Some, he said, also faced opaque pricing and rigid packages in a highly traditional industry. Ng subsequently left his university post and established funeral social enterprise Minimal Funeral, seeking to offer transparent prices, simpler arrangements and more choices. “I wanted to turn what I had been teaching about death and end-of-life planning into real choices that people could actually act on,” he said. The company was designed to be financially self-sustaining instead of depending indefinitely on grants. It began with Ng and his wife and has since grown to about 15 staff members. Ng is a finalist for the Spirit of Entrepreneurship Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Giving families more choices remains an important part of the business model. Families can see funeral venues, floral arrangements and other options on screen before deciding what they want, while simpler and greener arrangements are also offered. Ng said he did not want to discard traditional funeral customs, but to give families alternatives at a time when grief can make decisions particularly difficult. That social role was put into action after the deadly Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po last November, which killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000 residents. Ng said his team provided free funeral services, body restoration and grief counselling, as well as support for residents returning to their homes after the fire. Some work restoring personal belongings retrieved from the flats was still continuing at the time he was interviewed earlier this month. Ng said the response showed how resources across his different services could be directed towards a community emergency. The social mission also continues in the company’s regular work. Ng said about a third of the more than 300 funeral cases handled annually were for lower-income families or people with limited family support. His work has since expanded from funerals into earlier stages of ageing and end-of-life planning. A separate death education service offers advice to different age groups, while another of his social enterprises helps people make arrangements covering wills, advance medical planning and funeral wishes. The expansion responds partly to demographic change, he explained. Someone retiring at 60 and living to 90 could spend three decades in retirement, making advance planning increasingly relevant as more older people live alone or apart from their children. Ng describes the three social enterprises as an interconnected system dealing with different stages of later life, from education and planning to end-of-life care, funeral arrangements and grief support. A fourth venture focusing on trusts and care planning is currently in development. Ng said the service would particularly target middle-income older people living alone and families with disabled dependants, making forms of planning traditionally associated with wealthier families available to more people. His greatest satisfaction, he said, comes from seeing ideas discussed in lectures turned into services that people can benefit from. “Before, I could explain things such as advance medical planning, funeral wishes and end-of-life arrangements, but people might still struggle to act on them. “Now, we can help turn those choices into actual services and plans,” he said. Launched in 2013, the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might escape public attention.

title: South Korea-US alliance losing ‘trust’ amid widening cracks in ties
description: Growing frictions bleed into the security partnership, just as North Korea ramps up missile tests and Trump floats meeting with Kim Jong-un.
content: South Korea’s long-standing alliance with America is being tested by feuds spanning from investment deals to intelligence leaks, compromising Seoul’s ability to respond to North Korea. In a rare admission, Seoul’s top envoy to the US on Monday acknowledged an “issue” with Washington’s sharing of covert data. “There are limitations in our communication with the White House,” Kang Kyung-wha told lawmakers. “I find it somewhat frustrating.” That follows reports earlier this year that a South Korean official disclosed US intelligence about a secret North Korean nuclear facility. President Lee Jae Myung had rejected those allegations, calling them “absurd”. Underscoring the tensions, a prominent South Korean politician was forced to cancel a US trip this month after reports his visa was held up. US President Donald Trump has also scaled back military drills with South Korea, while in June local media reported the country’s spy agency was excluded from a trilateral meeting with the United States and Japan on North Korea at Washington’s request. Ties between Washington and Seoul have been rocky for months, marred by US accusations South Korea has slow-walked its investment deal and discriminated against American-listed e-commerce giant Coupang. Those frictions are bleeding into the security partnership, just as North Korea ramps up missile tests and Trump floats restarting talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. “The most damaging aspect of the friction over intelligence restrictions is it conveys the US does not have trust in Korea as an ally,” said Victor Cha, Korea Chair at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. “It’s serious because it hits at the heart of the military alliance.” While there is no sign the US will prematurely withdraw any of its 28,000 troops stationed on the Korean peninsula, reduced intelligence cooperation makes it harder for Seoul to respond to North Korea’s growing nuclear arsenal. The disagreements also add weight to Trump’s threat of new trade penalties. An official at South Korea’s presidential office said the government is working to strengthen trust with the US and stressed the alliance is the cornerstone of Seoul’s foreign and security policy. The National Intelligence Service did not respond to calls. A State Department spokesman said the US has been clear that it expects South Korea to uphold the standards of an alliance that, for over 70 years, has been a linchpin of security in the Indo-Pacific. “This is particularly true of intelligence and counter-intelligence matters,” the person added. “The United States has a strong relationship with South Korea,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said, adding that a meeting between Trump and Lee last month “enhanced” their relationship. At that meeting with Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Lee sought help restarting dialogue with North Korea. “President Trump kindly reminded me of our plan to play golf,” Lee said after the 30-minute sit-down. South Korea has set up a task force to prepare for a golf outing between the men ahead of the Group of 20 summit in December, Yonhap News Agency said. South Korea is not the only US ally struggling to maintain a stable relationship with Trump – but for Seoul, the stakes are especially high. Washington provides Seoul with direct military deterrence against North Korea, a country now capable of producing as many as 20 nuclear weapons a year and which has declared the South its “principal enemy”. Despite that reliance, Lee last month publicly questioned Washington’s characterisation of Seoul’s participation in a liquefied natural gas project in Alaska, saying cooperation was contingent on the deal being financially viable. That combined with Trump’s complaints South Korea has not done more to help with Iran and unrealised US promises to assist Seoul with nuclear-powered submarines has soured ties. South Korea’s problems are “more pronounced in scope and severity” than those of other allies, said Jenny Town, a senior fellow at the Stimson Centre. The issues “paint a picture of an alliance that’s highly strained and losing trust”, she added. In Trump’s first term, the US leader also demanded Seoul pay more for stationing American forces on the peninsula and scaled back drills as he courted North Korea’s Kim. Back then, however, South Korea’s national security adviser and the intelligence chief were key to arranging meetings between Trump and North Korea’s leader, said Kim Jung, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul. “This government’s ability to manage the situation is now being put to the test,” he added. Lee has, at times, struck a defiant tone. He told his cabinet this week that as a sovereign nation, South Korea should “avoid a submissive or overly deferential approach in relations with other countries”. That speaks to the South Korean leader’s style of “pragmatic diplomacy”, which has seen him warm ties with China while trying to keep the US close. His spy chief and unification minister are both seen as part of a faction that wants better relations with Beijing, which some analysts say has gone down badly among China hawks in Washington. “Domestic political pressures are intensifying the latest US-South Korea dispute,” said Bloomberg Economics’ Adam Farrar. “Trump is pushing the Alaska LNG project as he looks to bolster Republicans ahead of the midterms, while Lee has incentives to push back forcefully as he faces weak approval ratings.” Speaking in Seoul on Wednesday, former US vice-president Kamala Harris criticised Trump for undermining the strength of the alliance, referring to his decision to cut drills with South Korea and use tariffs to threaten partner nations. Changing circumstances “require a renewal of our commitment to South Korea”, she said. “America must be strategic in the use of our economic power, not reckless or spiteful.”

title: Sharks tune into human sounds, not blood, reveals groundbreaking study
description: New research reveals how aquatic noises influence shark behaviour and encounters.
content:
Forget about the smell of blood and the shark-related fears we’ve developed from films like Jaws and shows like Shark Week . Recent research suggests that the first thing a shark notices about humans may actually be the unique sounds we produce while in the water.
And great white sharks have really good hearing. Whether you are swimming, kayaking or paddling on your surfboard, even a juvenile can detect you from as far as 100 feet (30.48 metres) away (see graphic).
A new study revealed that while sharks respond to human noises, they can often tell from our splashing that we are not worth the nibble.
“There are dozens – if not potentially hundreds – of encounters daily at a beach with a lot of sharks and people. Why aren’t people being bitten?” said Chris Lowe, director of the Shark Lab in the US state of California. “We worked our way through all the different senses that a shark could use to go, ‘That’s a person,’ and we thought sound and vibration might be the most influential one.”
For years, Lowe and his laboratory have observed white sharks coming remarkably close to people in the water. The shark’s approach is never rushed or aggressive. As the shark gets closer to investigate, it often loses interest and simply swims away.
In a groundbreaking study, researchers developed a unique hearing test for sharks. They used a special multichannel hydrophone capable of capturing both sounds and their three-dimensional movements. The scientists systematically recorded themselves engaging in three common ocean activities: freestyle swimming, kayaking and paddling on a surfboard.
They then played back the “sound bites” at different distances underwater and observed whether a shark would change its angle and move towards the speaker.
This study is still ongoing, but the preliminary findings are striking. Sharks can clearly differentiate between three types of water activities.
Additionally, the louder, more erratic sound characteristics of freestyle swimming may increase the likelihood that a shark approaches from a distance.
While paddling on a surfboard, the sharks could clearly recognise the sound, but they more often tuned it out as background noise. And the gentle, more continuous sounds of kayaking elicited little reaction, said Whitney Jones, who led and designed the study.
“This is the first study to empirically show that they seem to be using sound to cue into people at these greater distances,” said Jones, who specialises in underwater acoustics and behavioural biology.
Jaida Elcock, a shark biologist with the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution’s Marine Predators Group, said the more data, the better when it comes to dispelling our misunderstanding of sharks.
“Sharks can be found in every type of ocean ecosystem – they’re deep sea, they’re in shallow reefs, there’s even an Arctic shark,” Elcock said. “If we don’t even fully understand how they function in the world the way it is now, it is going to be even harder for us to understand how those vital parts of our ecosystems will function as the ocean continues to change.
Most sharks feed on smaller fish and invertebrates. Some of the larger shark species prey on seals, sea lions and other marine mammals. Shark attacks are very rare. On average, there are about 60 to 65 unprovoked shark bites each year worldwide.
Out of these rare incidents, around six people die each year. In fact, numbers show that a person has a higher chance of getting hit by an asteroid than being killed by a shark.
Sharks sometimes attack humans when they are confused or curious. If a shark sees a person in the water, it may swim closer to see what is happening, which can lead to an accidental attack.

title: Exclusive | Hong Kong to carry out 24-hour patrols near Apec meeting venue and delegate hotels
description: Hundreds of officers to patrol Wan Chai around the clock as delegates begin arriving for finance ministers’ meeting.
content: Hong Kong police will conduct round-the-clock patrols in Wan Chai from Friday as part of enhanced security arrangements for the coming Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting, as delegates begin arriving in the city, the South China Morning Post has learned. Delegates from the 21 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation member economies will travel to Hong Kong as early as Friday for preparatory work, although most ministers are not expected to arrive until Sunday at the earliest. They will stay at several top Wan Chai hotels, including the Grand Hyatt and Renaissance Harbour View, sources told the SCMP. The meeting will take place at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai from October 19 to 21. A drafting session for the finance ministers’ joint statement will be held on Monday, followed by two days of meetings. About 500 guests, including finance ministers and senior officials, are expected to attend the annual meeting. A police source said hundreds of officers from the Police Tactical Unit would be deployed to patrol the area around the venue and nearby hotels 24 hours a day from Friday. “Not all the member economies will have their finance ministers coming,” he said. “Only a few economies will. Some will send deputy ministers or other representatives. So the security arrangement is not at the highest level.” According to the source, the VIP Protection Unit and Force Escort Group will accompany only serving finance ministers during their stay. The SCMP earlier reported that expected attendees included Chinese Finance Minister Lan Foan, Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers, South Korean Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il, Singaporean Transport Minister and Second Finance Minister Jeffrey Siow Chen Siang, and Taiwanese Finance Minister Chuang Tsui-yun. Each delegation will be welcomed at the airport by a designated group of administrative and executive officers from the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau, according to the source. Police’s Key Points and Search Division will search the venue and the hotels where guests are staying for explosives and suspicious items, the insider said. Security arrangements will also be adopted at Cloud 39, the city’s highest all-glass rooftop venue, atop The Henderson office tower in Central, where a dinner will be held next Tuesday. They will also be in place at attractions that guests and their spouses may visit, including The Peak, the Big Buddha on the Ngong Ping plateau and the Science Park technology hub in Pak Shek Kok. A command centre will be set up at police headquarters in Wan Chai, where Assistant Commissioner (Operations) David Jordan is expected to take charge. Designated demonstration areas would be set up near the venue, although no local or overseas activists were expected to stage protests in Hong Kong during the meetings, the source said. A separate source said the force was nevertheless ready to mobilise about 400 officers from the Regional Response Contingent at short notice should large-scale riots or attacks occur. The source added that a small team reporting directly to Jordan, led by Apec special duties Superintendent Ben Tsang Ting-pan, was coordinating police departments on logistics and security planning. “Since the number of dignitaries coming is not massive, and they are all concentrated in one area, it is not an operation that will be extremely demanding on manpower,” the source said. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said earlier that authorities would adopt arrangements, including contingencies for potential terrorist attacks and cyber patrols to safeguard national security, to ensure the Apec meeting was held safely and smoothly. The 2005 World Trade Organization Ministerial Conference in Hong Kong posed far greater security challenges, with police anticipating protests by more than 10,000 demonstrators around the venue, including about 7,000 activists mainly from South Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines. Demonstrations escalated dramatically on December 17 that year, prompting police to deploy 9,000 officers, about one-third of the entire force. About 2,000 frontline officers confronted more than 1,000 protesters, most of them South Korean farmers. Intense clashes broke out that evening, and anti-riot police used tear gas and beanbag rounds to disperse the crowds. The confrontation ended with the arrest of 1,146 people. All 14 defendants prosecuted either had their charges withdrawn or were acquitted in court. Hong Kong was originally designated by the central government to host the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting in September 2014. However, in February that year, Beijing announced that the summit would be moved to the capital, citing the need to “facilitate meeting arrangements”. The decision was widely attributed to growing political tension in the city surrounding the emerging Occupy Central movement, which broke out in late September. Annual Apec summits have often attracted large-scale demonstrations by civil society, labour and political groups. Last year, an anti-Apec coalition of 35 left-leaning political parties and civic groups staged rallies against American trade policies in Seoul and Gyeongju, while right-leaning groups also held anti-China and pro-Trump protests. South Korean authorities deployed 18,500 police officers and 1,800 military personnel, along with anti-drone systems, armoured vehicles and helicopters. In 2023, violent clashes broke out in San Francisco between supporters of Chinese President Xi Jinping and anti-China protesters during the Apec summit. Among the protesters were prominent dissidents including Wang Dan, a Tiananmen Square protest activist, and Hong Kong activist Anna Kwok Fung-yee, who is wanted by the city’s national security police. Activists advocating independence for Taiwan and Tibet were also present. The Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting will be held in Shenzhen in November.

title: Opinion | Pageantry matters for US-China summits, even with modest results
description: While Hong Kong was absent from discussions, this year’s summits show that Beijing and Washington can manage ceremony, dialogue and pragmatic compromise.
content: The most consequential outcome of President Xi Jinping’s Washington visit might be his US counterpart Donald Trump’s unusually lavish welcome. It told Beijing, US allies and global markets that, however fierce the strategic rivalry, China’s importance makes sustained diplomatic engagement essential. The airport greeting, lavish banquet at the White House and flyover by military aircraft restored the appearance of a workable relationship between two powers. Even so, Beijing has learned not to mistake presidential warmth for policy assurance. Trump visited Beijing only four months earlier. That May meeting produced plans for new trade and investment boards alongside Chinese commitments on aircraft and agricultural purchases. Yet in July, Trump’s administration imposed new tariffs on goods from 60 trading partners, including China, alleging they had failed to curb imports made with forced labour. That history gives the gentler symbols of the Washington visit their proper scale. The arrival of two giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, at Atlanta’s zoo was the visit’s softer punctuation mark and an enduring diplomatic symbol of friendship in a relationship that remains challenging. For Xi, the choreography mattered. A Chinese leader received with military honours and a White House banquet is plainly not being treated as the representative of a lesser power. The message to a domestic audience was that China must be dealt with on equal terms, even by a US administration that has made economic pressure and national advantage central to its foreign policy. The welcome also served a political purpose for Trump. He has a habit of treating personal diplomacy as proof of presidential authority. The hospitality also carried a political message: courtesy could be presented not as weakness but as confidence. The image was of a president confident enough to extend courtesy while claiming to have extracted trade concessions in return. Trump’s pat on Xi’s shoulder drew attention but should not be excessively analysed. More significant was his decision to avoid publicly provoking or embarrassing Xi. That restraint was diplomacy in itself. However, Beijing has reason to be cautious. During Trump’s first term, Xi welcomed Trump and his wife Melania to Beijing in November 2017 with similarly warm hospitality and carefully managed optics. The goodwill was short-lived as Trump’s administration began imposing tariffs and announcing further levies on Chinese imports in early 2018, setting off the US-China trade war. This time, the two sides’ trade truce lasts only until January 10. The harder questions have simply been deferred. The notable feature of the Washington visit was therefore its division between symbolism and substance. The symbolism was rich: pandas, gifts, ceremonial welcomes, cultural diplomacy and the presence of Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan alongside the president. For all the ceremony, the results were modest: the truce was extended to January, and both sides recommended US$30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction for more favourable tariff treatment. These are useful steps, but they do not amount to a wider settlement. That distinction matters particularly for Hong Kong. The city has every reason to welcome a less volatile US-China relationship. It benefits when commercial and financial decisions are not distorted by the prospect of sudden tariff shocks, restrictions or geopolitical tensions. A steadier atmosphere can support investor confidence, fundraising and cross-border trade. Hong Kong’s relationship with the United States is not the same as China’s, though. Improved US-China sentiment does not necessarily translate into a change in US policy towards Hong Kong. That is why this month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum finance ministers’ meeting matters. Hong Kong is hosting the gathering for the first time, bringing senior economic officials together at a difficult point in US-China relations. Such work can help companies, investors and households, but it does not alter the distinct US policy framework governing its relationship with Hong Kong. Executive Order 13936, signed in 2020, ended much of Hong Kong’s separate treatment under US law. Once the order expired in July, the Trump administration revised rather than dismantled parts of its sanctions regime. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu and other Hong Kong officials remain sanctioned, while property blocked before July 14 remains blocked. This produces an interesting contrast. At the highest level, the US and China can manage ceremony, conversation and limited compromise. Hong Kong, ranked third globally and first in Asia-Pacific in the latest Global Financial Centres Index, is largely absent from public accounts of those discussions. The pandas’ arrival in Atlanta is a small but welcome sign that the two sides still see value in maintaining contact. It settles nothing, but its significance shouldn’t be dismissed. For Hong Kong, a calmer relationship between Washington and Beijing is in the city’s best interests.

title: Hong Kong’s IPO fraud clampdown sends shock waves across financial sector
description: The tougher scrutiny is forcing the capital market to recalibrate, as sponsors become more cautious and some firms cancel listings.
