content: Hong Kong regulators’ tough action to crack down on fraudulent activity in the initial public offering market is sending ripples across the city’s financial industry, with insiders predicting short-term turbulence as some listings are scaled back or even cancelled. Financial intermediaries and IPO sponsors in particular find themselves in a “difficult position”, as they are now expected to conduct deeper due diligence to ensure deals are free from distortions, sources told the South China Morning Post. The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has been tightening scrutiny over the IPO market for months, and on Tuesday the regulator took the dramatic step of freezing assets worth HK$4.6 billion (US$586 million) as part of an operation against two syndicates suspected of rigging three recent IPOs. The securities regulator has also ordered trading suspensions for two companies allegedly involved in the schemes, while a third firm was suspended due to its failure to publish financial results since April 2025. Meanwhile, the body reminded financial market participants to reject suspicious orders and report any dubious activity to regulators. The tougher stance means that sponsors and capital market intermediaries can no longer turn a blind eye to suspicious orders during the issuance and placement process, and must commit substantial resources to execute more thorough due diligence, according to industry players. “This will certainly put intermediaries in a difficult position when dealing with ‘big investors’ or IPO applicants,” a banker at a Chinese investment bank said on condition of anonymity, adding that they hoped to get more clarity from regulators on issues such as what constitutes a “suspicious” order. The SFC has issued a list of six types of suspicious practices, including applicants making significant payments to investors, introducing connected buyers, over-participating in book building allocation, the sudden appearance of abnormally large orders near the closing deadline, and concealing the identity of ultimate investors. “We will strengthen due diligence on uncommon investors,” the banker said. “If a project has too many uncommon investors who appear suspicious, we may not agree to launch the share offer.” While hundreds of companies are currently waiting for their Hong Kong listing applications to be approved, several mainland Chinese firms recently said in their exchange filings that they would halt their share issuance plans in the city. Hong Kong’s capital market has fully shifted to a ‘regulation-first’ model Roy Lo, SW Hong Kong Kenny How Sze-ming, a council member of the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Professionals Association, said the regulator’s stance on suspicious activity “removes any discretion to look the other way”. In practice, however, intermediaries will find it hard to meet the SFC’s requirements during book building and share placement, because the most sensitive evidence sits outside the order book, including beneficial ownership and the flows between the issuer and investors, according to How. He suggested that the practical solution was not to confront large investors late in the book building process, but rather to establish explicit compliance standards early – even during non-deal roadshows – and allow bankers more time to conduct the required additional due diligence. “This will undoubtedly require intermediaries to gain more cost to carry out intensive additional due diligence to ascertain the facts,” he said. Last year, bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing implemented a new IPO pricing and allocation mechanism requiring at least 40 per cent of total offer shares to be allocated to the book building placement tranche, giving institutional investors greater participation and improving pricing and allocation efficiency. “Hong Kong’s capital market has fully shifted to a ‘regulation-first’ [model],” said Roy Lo, managing partner of accounting and consulting firm SW Hong Kong. “In the past, some companies pushed through offerings using illegal arrangements, causing post-listing valuations and stock prices to become severely distorted.” Despite the city’s IPO fundraising reaching US$48 billion in the first nine months of 2026 – a record high for the period – more than 60 per cent of IPOs launched during the third quarter fell below their offer prices. With artificial demand strictly banned, lower-quality or less attractive projects might face scaled-back issuance sizes, reduced offer prices or even cancelled listings in the short term, Lo said. “However, offer prices and corporate valuations will eventually return to a reasonable and realistic market foundation.”

title: Australia hands Ming dynasty Buddha back to China amid ongoing mystery over its arrival
description: The Ming dynasty artefact was found buried by the roadside in 2018 and no one can say how it came to arrive in the country.
content: A 500-year-old Buddha statue that was found buried by a roadside in Australia has been returned to China, leaving an ongoing mystery about how it arrived in the country. The 15cm (six-inch) bronze figurine was formally handed over to Chinese consular representatives during a ceremony in the coastal town of Denham in Shark Bay on Tuesday, the public broadcaster ABC reported. It will be taken to China for further evaluation to establish its history before being displayed at a museum in Beijing. Discoverers Leon Deschamps and Shayne Thomson unearthed the statue in 2018 while testing metal detecting equipment in the area. Since then, they have said it should be returned to China as a gesture of goodwill. Simon Wu, president of the Australia China Friendship Society Western Australia, described the return as extraordinarily generous. “Today is an example of how we can bring cultures, countries and people together through a small object. It is showing respect and goodwill,” Wu told the repatriation ceremony. The figurine – believed to be the oldest Chinese artefact ever found in Australia – was used in ceremonies celebrating the Buddha’s birthday. During the ritual, worshippers would pour water over the statue’s shoulders while chanting sutras to encourage good deeds and compassionate thoughts. Asian art specialist Lee Young authenticated the statue as a genuine piece from the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644), but how it ended up in Australia remains a mystery. Some media reports have claimed that it may have been carried on the treasure ships of the celebrated 15th century seafarer Zheng He – but there is no evidence that he ever reached Australia. A more plausible theory is that the statue arrived with Chinese pearlers and fishermen in the 19th century. Shark Bay became the birthplace of Western Australia’s pearling industry, which relied heavily on Malay, Chinese and Indigenous Australian labourers. According to Western Australian Museum records, an 1886 census showed that more than 200 people were working in the local pearling industry, including 60 Europeans, 102 Chinese and 68 Malays. That year, 68 pearling vessels were operating in the area, seven of which were Chinese-owned. However, the industry declined in subsequent years and the local authorities imposed a series of restrictions on Chinese immigration. The ABC reported that the Buddha would be returned to China along with some of Shark Bay’s distinctive red earth and a golden pearl shell. In 2023, Australia returned a batch of valuable cultural relics to China, including items seized by customs, as well as pieces donated by the National Gallery of Australia and a private citizen.

title: AI agents on Tencent Cloud try to break into Alibaba’s Amap: researchers
description: Between September 28 and October 8, Tencent agents made more than 2,600 attempts to extract data from Alibaba’s Amap navigation service.
content: A fleet of artificial intelligence agents operating on a Tencent Holdings cloud platform made thousands of attempts to circumvent security protections on Alibaba Group Holding’s mapping service, according to findings by third-party researchers. It is one of the first reported “rogue” AI events involving Chinese companies, following a string of recent high-profile incidents in the US, including from OpenAI and Anthropic, highlighting the risks of increasingly autonomous AI systems. Agents running on Tencent Cloud made more than 2,600 attempts to extract information from Alibaba’s Amap, one of China’s most popular navigation services, between September 28 and October 8, an international group of researchers known as the “swarmchasers” said in a report on Wednesday. The agents were initially carrying out seemingly mundane tasks, such as identifying the entrances to Chinese zoos, parks and hospitals most frequently used by Amap users. But when they encountered restrictions, the agents repeatedly sought ways around them, including bypassing anti-bot protections, accessing internal testing systems and scraping login credentials that were exposed on other sites, the researchers said. The researchers traced the activity to Tencent Cloud infrastructure in Hong Kong. They said they found no evidence that the agents were coordinated through a specific channel or that the agents managed to breach Alibaba’s private systems. A person familiar with the matter said the agent activity was part of a series of tests conducted by Tencent’s AI evaluation research team to assess the ability of third-party models to browse the internet and answer questions. The source said the temporary project had concluded and did not involve Tencent’s own Hy AI model, previously known as Hunyuan. “We take these findings seriously,” Tencent said in a statement posted on social media on Friday. “We are strengthening network access controls and agent monitoring.” Alibaba did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Ethan Elasky, one of the report’s authors, told the SCMP that his group had shared its findings with both Tencent and Alibaba, though neither company had yet given an official response. The incident shows that the risks of AI agents independently navigating websites, writing code and executing complex tasks with limited human supervision were not limited to the US. “AI knows no borders in the sense that, whether it’s American or Chinese AI agents, they are going to be affecting anyone, anywhere, and we are likely to see more of this kind of stuff going forward,” said Elasky. Rowan Howard-Jones, another co-author, said the group found early evidence of other rogue AI agents on the internet, making it unlikely that only Tencent was facing such issues. Rogue AI agents have become a growing concern in recent months, especially in the US. OpenAI allowed independent AI research firm METR to investigate the hacking of open-source AI platform Hugging Face in July. The subsequent report concluded that about 1,200 OpenAI agents coordinated with each other in an unprecedented hacking incident. The same month, Anthropic disclosed that its Claude models, including Mythos 5, had gained unauthorised access to real third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations. The company has since published reports of unintended model actions it has observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude. According to Elasky, Chinese companies should also look to bolster their transparency and incident disclosure mechanisms. “With such a fast-moving technology, it’s really important to build an ecosystem of development that is transparent, where all companies that are developing these AI models and agents take transparency seriously,” he said. Jonathan Eicher, a third report co-author, hoped that the incident spurred China to devote more resources to AI safety, including third-party evaluators that can help bolster agent security. “This is just going to keep on happening, everywhere, and we need more trusted people all over to deal with it,” he said.

title: North Korea’s dual undersea missile launches test regional defence
description: Analysts say North Korea’s ‘unprecedented’ submarine-launched cruise missile tests could overwhelm adversaries’ defence networks.
content: North Korea’s apparent use of different launch methods to fire two types of cruise missiles from a tactical nuclear-capable submarine raises fresh questions about the operational readiness of its growing undersea arsenal, observers have said. The North’s official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said on Thursday the country had “test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles” off its eastern coast. The tests “contributed to inspecting the regular mobilisation readiness of underwater combat systems and honing the navy’s ability to carry out strategic missions”, KCNA said. They also demonstrated “the high reliability, dependability and capabilities of the means of war deterrence”, it said, adding that the tests “had no negative impact whatsoever on the security of neighbouring countries”. South Korea’s military did not publicly announce the launches, sparking speculation that it might have failed to detect them. On Thursday, however, the Joint Chiefs of Staff said that the military had tracked and monitored the launches throughout their flight. The joint chiefs stressed that the military did not usually disclose North Korean cruise missile launches, limiting public announcements primarily to ballistic missile tests. Professor Yang Moo-jin of the University of North Korean Studies said the projectiles were believed to include the Pulhwasal-3-31 (Fire Arrow Type 3-31), a strategic cruise missile with a potential range of about 2,000km (1,240 miles) that could carry small nuclear warheads. “Their low-altitude and evasive flight profiles could complicate and potentially overwhelm South Korea’s and the United States’ missile defence systems,” Yang said. The report appeared on KCNA but was not carried by the official newspaper of the ruling Workers’ Party, Rodong Sinmun, which primarily targets a domestic audience. In a brief report comprising just four sentences, KCNA withheld technical specifications, including the missiles’ flight duration and range, unlike previous reports that publicised test results in extensive detail. However, the agency did release several photographs showing the submarine under way, missiles emerging from the water in bursts of flame and the projectiles in flight. Experts analysing the images identified the launch platform as the Hero Kim Kun Ok, a new 3,000-tonne-class submarine. The launches marked the vessel’s first publicly reported operation since it was unveiled in September 2023, as well as North Korea’s third known test of submarine-launched cruise missiles. Shin Jong-woo, secretary general of the Korea Defence and Security Forum, said the missiles appeared to have been launched using both vertical launch systems and torpedo tubes. “Wednesday’s launches indicate that these missiles are being prepared for operational deployment,” Shin said. “Further test launches of submarine-launched ballistic missiles are also expected.” Hong Min, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification, said the simultaneous launch of two missile types with different diameters, lengths and launch methods from the Hero Kim Kun Ok was “unprecedented”. He said North Korea appeared to be combining two launch methods – vertical launch systems and torpedo tubes – citing two distinct launch profiles in the released photographs. One showed a near-vertical ascent, while the other appeared to involve a launch at an angle of about 60 degrees to 70 degrees, accompanied by falling debris. The combination of different missile types and launch methods would make it harder for adversaries to predict which missile might be fired from which launch tube, Hong said. By extending its demonstrated ability to deploy multiple types of warheads from land to the maritime domain, “North Korea is seeking to increase uncertainty for potential adversaries and strengthen its deterrence”, he said. North Korea’s first known test of a submarine-launched cruise missile was in March 2023, from the ageing 8.24 Yongung (Hero) submarine. Pyongyang described the latest launches not as development tests but as a “routine inspection of the mobilisation readiness” of its deployed forces, suggesting that it wanted to portray the weapons as approaching operational service. Hong said that under a strategy combining lower-cost military assets with higher-end weapons, the nuclear-powered submarines currently under construction would serve as advanced, while ageing but modified Romeo-class submarines would provide a larger number of relatively inexpensive assets. The Hero Kim Kun Ok, however, appeared designed as a tactical nuclear platform for coastal and regional operations that could remain in service even after North Korea’s nuclear-powered submarines became available, he said. Even so, Hong cautioned against overstating the submarine’s capabilities. “Its operational capabilities remain unproven in several key areas,” he said, citing submerged launches and extended-duration patrols as well as the deployment of ballistic missiles. “Its current level of combat readiness is therefore best assessed as limited operational capability.” Wednesday’s tests were the latest in a series of North Korean missile launches this month, amid an intensifying arms race with South Korea, which successfully conducted the first test launch of its domestically developed hypersonic glide vehicle a week earlier. Yang said the latest launches were part of Pyongyang’s efforts to showcase the diversity of its missile arsenal, including short-range ballistic missiles, hypersonic weapons and submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles. “North Korea is signalling its ability to complicate or neutralise the South Korea-US missile defence network,” he said. The tests come ahead of a planned trip to Asia by US President Donald Trump, fuelling speculation about a possible resumption of diplomacy between Washington and Pyongyang. Trump said on Monday that he might meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un during his coming trip to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, scheduled for November 18-19 in Shenzhen. Asked whether he planned to meet Kim during the trip, Trump replied, “I may,” adding: “That’ll be exciting, won’t it? But I get along with him.” The two leaders met three times during Trump’s first term: in Singapore in June 2018, in Hanoi in February 2019 and at the inter-Korean border village of Panmunjom in June 2019. On Saturday, Trump told a campaign rally in Ohio that he “gets along great” with Kim, stressing the importance of maintaining good relations with leaders of nuclear-armed countries. The latest launches could be intended in part to strengthen Pyongyang’s leverage ahead of a potential meeting, Yang said. “The series of missile launches in October appears to be aimed at pressing Washington to recognise North Korea as a nuclear-armed state”, he said.

title: Exclusive | Hong Kong Apec meeting to showcase ‘China’s voice’ in stability, treasury chief says
description: Finance chiefs will see China’s contribution to regional stability and Hong Kong’s value during October 20-21 meeting, Christopher Hui says.
content: The coming Apec finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong will demonstrate “China’s voice” in regional stability, with the city uniquely placed to bring together regional leaders for important exchanges in a geopolitically charged world, the treasury chief has said. In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post on Thursday, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said the timing of the meeting of finance ministers from the 21 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economies mattered because regional cooperation was becoming vital due to geopolitical tensions. Against that backdrop, Hui believed Hong Kong was well placed to host the event – which will be held on October 20 and 21 – and convey two main messages to the Apec members and the world: China’s contribution to regional stability and Hong Kong’s value to the region. “This conference is timely, as regionalisation takes centre stage in today’s geopolitical environment,” Hui said. “There’s no place like Hong Kong to bring these regional leaders together at the same time to discuss how each region can work more closely.” The finance ministers’ meeting is a precursor to the Apec leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. 2026 is China’s year as Apec host, with several rounds of ministerial meetings already hosted in major mainland cities, including Suzhou and Guangzhou. “This is a China event. China’s voice is important in terms of how China is a responsible member of the international community and also willing and ready to contribute to regional well-being,” Hui said. With Beijing backing Hong Kong to host the event, Hui said the local government would ensure delegates have the opportunity to see the city’s efforts in financial services, sustainability, financial technology, and digital trade finance. These showcase areas align with the four core themes set for the meeting: fiscal policies supporting households, digital infrastructure financing, inclusive finance, and nurturing young financial talent. Hui said it was rare for senior representatives from 21 economies to visit Hong Kong at the same time, adding that authorities would arrange bilateral meetings with visiting ministers to advance mutual agendas where appropriate. “Many people see Hong Kong as an international financial centre or a commercial hub. But I am sure you agree with me that we have a lot more to offer, including our natural landscape, our deep heritage, our frontier developments in information technology and others,” Hui said. Side exhibition booths will be set up at the venue to showcase these aspects of Hong Kong, alongside curated side tours for delegates and their entourages. “They will see a broader side of Hong Kong that is relevant to both their work and lives, which will hopefully encourage them to return soon,” he said. Sources told the SCMP that key local attractions and points of business interest such as The Peak, the Big Buddha on the Ngong Ping plateau and the Science Park technology hub in Pak Shek Kok were on the itineraries. The event is expected to attract about 500 guests. The SCMP previously reported that expected attendees included Chinese Finance Minister Lan Foan, Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers, South Korea’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyoung-il, Singapore’s Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance Jeffrey Siow Chen Siang, and Taiwanese Finance Minister Chuang Tsui-yun. However, the SCMP also reported that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent might skip the Hong Kong meeting to prepare for President Donald Trump’s historic visit to the Shenzhen Apec meeting. On Wednesday, the foreign ministers of China and Russia discussed their respective relations with the US, paving the way for a potential summit between their leaders in Shenzhen. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, in Baku, Azerbaijan, where they discussed “relations with the United States and developments involving the Ukraine and Iran crises,” according to Moscow, which did not explicitly detail those discussions.

title: Exclusive | Why Japanese PM Takaichi is still keen to roll out the welcome mat for Trump
description: Tokyo is hoping for a visit by the US president that would signal the strength of the relationship between the two allies.
content: Japan’s hopes for a visit by Donald Trump during his trip to Asia next month may be hanging in the balance as relations between China and the United States steadily improve. The US president spent three days in Japan ahead of last year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and his meeting with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was hailed as a sign of a “new golden age” in the countries’ relationship. But since then Trump’s growing rapport with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping has caused concern in Japan, which has seen its own relationship with Beijing deteriorate sharply following controversial comments by Takaichi about Taiwan. According to sources familiar with the matter, Tokyo has been lobbying for Trump to stop in Japan next month to signal the strength of their alliance. Trump will attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in the Philippine capital Manila on November 16 and 17 before heading to Shenzhen, where he will meet Xi for the third time this year. The South China Morning Post was the first to report that Trump planned to attend the Asean gathering. The sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly on the matter, said Japanese officials were keen for Trump to stop in Japan before the Apec event because it would give Tokyo the chance to influence Trump’s talks with Xi. They would also be happy for him to visit after the summit, but the sources said there was little indication that Trump would add Japan to his Asian itinerary. They added that he had already met Takaichi three times this year, most recently on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in September a day before Xi arrived in Washington. The US and Japanese leaders also met in Washington in March ahead of Trump’s visit to China and at this year’s Group of Seven summit in France. The pair also spoke by telephone after both of Trump’s meetings with Xi. Both the US and Japan are dialogue partners for Asean, and Trump is expected to see Takaichi in Manila so he “may feel less of a need to visit Japan despite ongoing efforts to arrange a visit”, one source said. Tokyo’s relations with Beijing have been icy since Takaichi said last November that a crisis in the Taiwan Strait could be a survival-threatening situation for Japan that would justify military intervention. Her refusal to retract the comments angered Beijing, which has long been wary of Japan’s military build-up and regards Taiwan as a “red line” that must not be crossed. In retaliation, Beijing suspended official and cultural exchanges, cut flights to Japan and banned exports of dual-use items, including rare earths and other critical minerals, to Japan’s defence industries. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of its territory and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with mainland China. Japan and the US, in common with most countries, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state. Tokyo has been asking Washington to press Beijing to ease its export restrictions, and the SCMP has previously reported that Trump raised Japan’s grievances about these curbs when Xi visited Washington last month. He framed the Chinese measures as a threat to US industries that relied on Japanese suppliers and as an indirect violation of last year’s US-China trade truce. Jeremy Chan, a senior analyst at political risk consultancy Eurasia Group, said Tokyo was always keen to demonstrate the strength of the US-Japan alliance when a US president visited the region, especially amid warming ties between Washington and Beijing. “A visit by Trump to Japan is the greatest symbol of the importance that Washington places on the US-Japan alliance,” he said. “Tokyo can never receive enough reassurances from Washington, and it is particularly anxious that President Trump could strike an agreement with Chinese President Xi Jinping that harms Japanese interests.” Takaichi must also consider the domestic political implications, Chan added, saying that her approval depended in part on her ability to manage relations with the US. Mong Cheung, a professor at Waseda University’s school of international liberal studies, said Japan might also be seeking to “regain the upper hand” after Xi’s trip to the US and hoped a visit would show that Tokyo remained Washington’s “top ally” in Asia. Japan would also want to coordinate with Trump on China policy before he met Xi, he added. Cheung cited Bill Clinton’s visit to China in 1998, when the US president did not visit Japan. The snub prompted widespread criticism in Japan, and Tokyo had sought to prevent a repeat of that incident, he said. But Chan said Tokyo could probably live with Trump skipping Japan this time. “Trump will also hold a bilateral meeting with Takaichi at either the Asean or Apec summits. This will give her another opportunity to remind Trump of the importance of Japan to the US ahead of his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen,” he said. “Tokyo cares deeply about sending a signal to Beijing that closer US-China ties will not come at the expense of US-Japan relations.” Last week, a group of senior US diplomats, administration officials and military commanders met in Tokyo in what sources described as a meeting to coordinate the priorities and messaging for Trump’s visit to Asia. They also met foreign vice-minister Takehiro Funakoshi and held a courtesy phone call with Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu. The Japanese foreign ministry said Tokyo had stressed the importance of the alliance and a free and open Indo-Pacific during these meetings.

title: Black Foils SailGP team hope Hong Kong launches historic, redemptive 2027 season
description: Making its debut in the city off the shore of Kai Tak Cruise Terminal in January, the 10½-month championship features 13 race weekends.
content: After their season was torched by “the biggest crash in SailGP history”, New Zealand’s Black Foils team are already plotting to use Hong Kong as the launch pad for a historic and redemptive 2027 season. Despite boasting the Olympic gold medal and multiple America’s Cup-winning pair of Blair Tuke and Pete Burling as crew mainstays and co-CEOs, the Kiwi boat is still waiting for its first SailGP title. The 10½-month championship features 13 race weekends, where 13 identical F50 catamarans – up to 14 for next year’s season opener in Hong Kong – are split into two groups to race in close quarters at hair-raising speeds, as the six-strong crews live on their skill, strength, precision and nerves. Any chance of the Black Foils breaking their title duck this year disappeared in just the second event in their home Auckland waters, where they were involved in an alarming collision with the French boat that destroyed their catamaran and left grinder Louis Sinclair nursing two broken legs. Missing the following four events while their new boat was being built left them completely out of the championship running and, although two events of the 2026 season remain, Tuke acknowledged that it “really feels like we’re into our pre-season and trying to get all the blocks lined up for a successful 2027”. The new campaign will get under way with SailGP’s Hong Kong debut off the shore of Kai Tak Cruise Terminal in January. Anticipating “high speeds and wind that will be very difficult to read in one of the most beautiful harbours in the world”, Tuke said he was “really proud of how the whole group and organisation dealt with the Auckland incident”. “We had one athlete quite seriously injured; it was a really big incident to be involved in, both for us on board, and for those on the French boat,” he added. The Black Foils returned in Canada four months ago in a vessel christened “Manawatiti”, a Maori proverb used to describe someone blessed with great endurance or resilience. Tuke referenced his crew reaching their speed record of nearly 103kph in Germany, in just their third regatta after the smash, as evidence that “we’ve worked through the adversity and the team is stronger collectively”. “That sets us up well for next year,” he said. “Our focus is on finishing this year strongly, then building confidence into 2027. It’s the first time we’ve had some runway into a season.” While success on the water is paramount for a man who, alongside Burling, claimed Olympic 49er class silver in 2012 and 2021, either side of the pair’s 2016 gold in Rio de Janeiro, he is equally keen to oversee “the continued growth of the team and commercial side of the brand, which are such strong parts of our long-term success”. SailGP is big business. Its managing director, Andy Thompson, said that host cities typically received a US$25 million economic boost, while events are broadcast in 200 different markets around the globe. “Showing the beauty of the iconic Hong Kong harbour to the world is great for destination marketing,” Thompson said. The Hong Kong event has secured American Express as its title sponsor, with blue-chip companies drawn to the product in the same fashion that sporting and showbiz stars have rushed to claim part-ownership in teams. Kylian Mbappe, Anne Hathaway and Deontay Wilder are on board, while Hong Kong-based investment firm Blue Pool Capital this year joined four-time F1 world champion Sebastian Vettel as minority owners of the Germany SailGP team. MSP Sports Capital’s acquisition of the Black Foils back in June meant that all 13 franchises were in private hands. Actors Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds are producing a Disney+ documentary focusing on their Australian Bonds Flying Roos team. Explaining the lure of Hong Kong for SailGP, Thompson said: “You can’t have a global sports league without Asia at the heart of it. Hong Kong is at the heart of Asia, it’s a great place for us to land, and a market where we want to make an impression.” While SailGP offers a fine line in hospitality, the regular punters get to watch hurtling, towering catamarans jostling for position right under their noses. “We can get the boats super close to the shoreline, and the fans will pretty much be able to reach out and touch them,” Thompson said. “We want to bring a show to town. It’s about people understanding the sailing, and having a great time by the water.” In a portent of what would happen in Auckland one month later, the Black Foils finished dead last in this season’s opening grand prix in Perth in January, after they were penalised for a collision with the Swiss boat. “You have to be consistent throughout the season, but a good start sets you up for it,” Tuke said, noting that the Black Foils began well in two of their three podium campaigns. “But if you don’t get off to a good start, you have to be strong enough as a team to claw it back. It’s about the long game.” Thompson revealed that a new, still-to-be-determined points scoring method would be “premiered in Hong Kong”. Following a recent modification to enhance safety, the fleet is divided into two groups for six races each. The top two contest a four-boat grand final, where the winners obtain 10 points, and the subsequent finishers are rewarded on a sliding scale from nine to seven points. Points from six down to one are allocated according to initial fleet-race performances. “We want more of a premium on actually winning events, and more jeopardy throughout the season,” Thompson said. “If a team has a good run later in the season, [more pronounced rewards for winning grands prix] would allow them to get back in contention.” Regardless of how the standings are arranged, Tuke is “incredibly motivated” to add SailGP honours to a resume that also includes eight world championship golds and three America’s Cup triumphs. “We’ve reached three finals, and it’s definitely hanging over us,” he said. “I feel we have the group to lift that trophy. “We’ll use this season as a foundation, and step forward from it. There’s plenty of fight left in us.” A founding member of the team that was established, initially as New Zealand SailGP, in 2020, Tuke added: “Racing on the world stage, representing our country, trying to grow the brand and be successful from a revenue point of view, really excites me. I won’t be sailing forever, but SailGP has created these opportunities, and what we can do in the future is huge.”

title: Asking for a Friend: Help! How do I get over someone I never officially dated?
description: Each week, we respond to a question from our readers and give advice and resources they can turn to.
content:
Do you have a personal question you’ve been too afraid to ask? Whether it is about school, family or your social life, you can share it with us through this form . Don’t worry, you’ll remain anonymous.
I feel very stupid for asking this, but how can I get over someone when we were never actually dating? We were just talking and hanging out, but we never made it official.
Now, things are over because he is in a relationship with someone else. Because we were not together, I feel like I can’t complain to my friends. What should I do to forget him?
First of all, there is no such thing as a stupid question. Sharing your feelings can make you feel awkward and vulnerable, so thank you for your courage in reaching out for advice!
It sounds like you truly treasured the connection you had with this guy. Even though you didn’t make your relationship official, it seems like you two shared something meaningful – a strong connection that hurt when it ended.
Now that he is in a relationship, it is only normal for you to feel a sense of loss. Looking back on those times, perhaps you may even feel a little regret, like you wish there could have been more.
Even if it was never official, you can still talk to your friends about it. Good friends will listen to how you’re feeling and provide comfort and advice, no matter how long or short a relationship was. What matters is how it made you feel, and your friends will want to be there for you.
Firstly, forgetting this person is not realistic because the more that we want to forget something, the more we will think about it. Instead, start by accepting your feelings. It sounds like you liked him and probably still do, but also know he is now unavailable. That can be devastating . You don’t need to punish yourself for having a crush that didn’t work out. This can happen to anyone.
Once you have accepted these feelings, ask yourself: what is making you feel like you have to forget? Is it because you’re hurt that he is with someone else now? Do you feel rejected, lonely and maybe even jealous of his new partner?
Remember, all of these emotions are normal. Understanding them can help you find what you actually need. For example, are you looking for reassurance , comfort, closure or just some distance?
Once you have sorted out your feelings and what support you need, think about your next steps. Here are some questions to get you started. What do you miss about him the most? What made your time enjoyable with him before? What did you like doing together? What did you like to talk about?
Remember, even if he is not available for a romantic relationship, he is still the same person. You can still hang out and have fun. Depending on how comfortable you are, you can find ways to maintain your friendship with him.
If it hurts too much to spend time with him now, it doesn’t mean you have to force yourself to forget his existence. It just means you need the space to really let yourself process your feelings.
You can even write in a journal so that your feelings and thoughts are not just looping endlessly inside your head.
At the same time, take this as a chance to build new connections. Hang out more with your other friends. Join some new extracurricular activities or clubs, and give yourself a chance to meet new people.
Remember, there’s nothing stupid about feeling this way. Allow yourself the time to heal and try meeting others who can match your energy and bring you comfort and joy again.
This question was answered by Dr Carmen Ip, a clinical psychologist at Your Relationship Clinic.

title: Nina Christen has redefined luxury footwear at Dior and Loewe – now she’s doing it with her own label
description: Having co-designed Bottega’s Puddle boot and Loewe’s balloon pumps, Christen has big plans for her namesake label, now stocked at Mytheresa, Lane Crawford, Selfridges and more.
content: Of the Celine alumni who worked under Phoebe Philo and later emerged as influential figures in fashion – including Matthieu Blazy, Daniel Lee, Nadège Vanhee and Michael Rider – Nina Christen is perhaps the least known. Yet the Swiss-Chilean designer is behind some of luxury footwear’s most distinctive silhouettes. If over the last two decades you’ve swapped your pumps for combat boots, square-toe heeled sandals or supple leather loafers, you may have Christen to thank. Besides Celine, her résumé includes brands such as Bottega Veneta, Loewe and The Row, where she introduced new shapes and materials in a category not necessarily known for innovation. Christen spent years honing her craft before launching her label, Christen, in 2024. She is one of the many unsung heroes working behind the scenes in the design studios of top luxury brands, often without getting the recognition they deserve. In 2025, Christen reunited with Jonathan Anderson, previously of Loewe, to take the post of design director of shoes at Dior, where she is in charge of all footwear, including men’s and haute couture. As a child in Switzerland, Christen received gifts from her grandmother in Chile. One was a pair of shiny black Mary Janes that did not fit. She still remembers how devastated she was that she couldn’t wear them, she said in a recent interview in Paris during fashion week. Christen initially trained as a fashion designer, but soon realised she couldn’t express her full vision in fashion. Her very exacting standards drew her to clothes that are not about fantasy but construction and materials. “I see myself as a fashion designer because even over the last 15 years doing only shoes, I’ve always done garments for myself,” she says. “I have a very specific taste, so I’ve always had shirts and coats and pants made. I love tailoring and I studied pattern making, but when I discovered shoe design I felt it was a category where I felt I could live my fantasy because when it comes to clothing, I’m very simple and clean. “I knew I couldn’t have worked for any fashion brand because for me it’s more about materials, cut, technique … so I could only have been a pattern maker or a tailor.” Unsurprisingly, she approaches shoe design in the same way. “Tailoring is very linked to shoes because tailoring is all about construction and for me shoes are little sculptures,” she says. “I love going to the factories to create shapes and heels; tailoring is a bit like that. It gives structure and adds volume, sometimes extreme volume or very rigid volume, but it can still be considered a sculpture.” More than just a shoe designer, Christen is what Italians call a calzolaio, a cobbler. She loves nothing more than visiting her suppliers in the Veneto region of Italy. Travelling there constantly to develop new shapes and material innovations like stretchable suede, she often challenges small, family-owned firms to cater to her unique demands. “I love to work with my hands, so when I went to Veneto for the first time, I realised that it was there that I could feel the materials; factories are my happy place,” she says. “After 15 years I still love going there. I know everyone in the business and they all know me. Excellence in shoemaking in Italy is mainly from Veneto. Anything you have in mind, someone there can do it for you.” These firms don’t normally work with independent brands like Christen, which can’t command the big orders of top luxury labels, but they make an exception for her due to the long-standing relationships she has developed over the years. Unlike many designers who are often eager to establish their own labels right out of school, Christen took her time to learn the ropes of the trade before feeling confident enough to start her own brand. It took her about two years to develop its striking visual identity and very well-edited selection of products, which range from the bestselling Helix range – recognisable for their pointy toes and a sharp, thin heel that flares at the bottom – to knee-high boots that fit like a second skin. “I couldn’t find shoes I 100 per cent loved because when you work as a designer, it’s also about your identity. With time, I realised what my real identity was, and who I was, and I had to express this and give it shape,” explains Christen. When looking at her work for brands like Dior – whose aesthetic couldn’t be more different from that of her label – one can’t help wondering how she is able to wear different hats so seamlessly. “I don’t lose my identity when I design for other brands but I broaden my perspective,” she says. “It’s like when you meet someone who is very different from you; you can be attracted to them and you want to know them even if it’s not your taste and it opens your mind. “I see my job a bit like acting; you have to play a character. What shoe would I wear if I were this woman? It’s fun to slip into these different roles; you can transform yourself into someone else and I love that.” A character she couldn’t easily turn into, however, is that of a businesswoman. While Christen is very much attuned to what luxury clientele desire – and sees herself as her most demanding customer – she admits that her strength lies in creativity. She says she couldn’t have established her brand without the help of her business partner, Paul Dupuy, an entrepreneur who works in health tech and also owns a few Michelin-starred sushi restaurants in Paris. Christen met him through a mutual friend and he ended up hiring her to design the staff uniforms for one of his companies, health centre Zoi. “I could have never done this on my own because I’m not very business oriented but more creative,” she says. “I had this intuition because he’s exceptional and brilliant and a businessman, but also has an understanding of aesthetics and he helps with back end and logistics.” When Christen started to envision her brand, the first thing she worked on was her first boutique. While most emerging designers wait years before investing in a physical store, she was adamant that to fully express her vision, she needed to open one, even before she started creating the first pair of shoes. Located on Rue de la Paix near Place Vendȏme, the heart of jewellery making in Paris, the boutique is a gallery-like space that wouldn’t look out of place in New York’s Chelsea or the Arts District in downtown Los Angeles. Shoes are displayed on raw concrete floors and cement slabs with barely any light fixtures or furniture, except for a couple of Mies van der Rohe chairs. The space looks almost like a garage, its black facade impossible to miss amid neighbours like jewellery houses Mellerio and Cartier. The only nod to traditional French customs is its opening hours: the store closes from 1.30pm until 2.30pm every day. “It’s a gesture to have a place like this in such a location. I want to show that this is a radical brand,” says Christen. “To show the philosophy of the brand and also that shoes are like jewels; they’re objects even if you don’t wear them.” Christen has also started making forays into ready-to-wear with a small collection of denim pants and jersey tops, all made in Japan, that reflect her impeccable taste and her focus on fit and fabric. Asked if she’d ever consider designing a sneaker, she reveals that something akin to a sneaker is coming out as part of her next collection, but she’d rather let the Nikes of the world own that segment. She wants to focus on what she does best and not compromise to adapt to fleeting trends. Calling her company a start-up, Christen has big plans for her label, which is available at top retailers such as Mytheresa, Lane Crawford, Selfridges and Bergdorf Goodman. Her goal, however, is to open one boutique in each of the big capitals. Without any bells and whistles, and with a laser-focused vision, Christen has built a very strong aesthetic that relies on strong design and high quality. It is an approach so simple that it feels even more radical at a time when runways are filled with overly designed shoes meant to go viral on social media, only to be forgotten after a one season. “I am not into decorations and it’s not something I like. I like to take away as much as possible; I don’t like much furniture and I have barely any at home,” says Christen. “I want to express the essence of a product and its attitudes with as few elements as possible. It’s harder because everything becomes more visible when you don’t have many decorative elements and the material and the base and the shape need to be stronger.” Luxury footwear, once dominated by a few specialists, has become even more competitive in recent years. All the top houses are investing more in the category, which has more potential for growth than the more saturated handbag market. Christen has been instrumental in that shift and now she is also reaping the benefits. It’s not easy to build a brand founded upon values like longevity, quality and substance without falling prey to gimmicks and fads, but Christen is doing just that, one pair of killer heels at a time.

title: Hong Kong’s hottest new openings, from Vicky Lau’s latest Tate iteration to Myka’s cool fro-yo offerings
description: From a sumptuous new Tate and flame-focused 180º Modern Fire Grill to new British pub The Boar and retro fro-yos at Myka, we have got you covered.
content: Tate It’s just a “small” move down the road, but the third iteration of Tate Dining Room – now simply abridged to “Tate” – represents the next evolution and expression of chef Vicky Lau’s singular culinary language and aesthetic sensibilities. Designer Chris Shao’s polished interiors carry softness and femininity through sinuous lines and curved shapes, extending Lau’s discerning taste into three-dimensional space. From the curated courses, Ode to Mushroom is a multifaceted journey exploring the intensity of fungi through a slow-stewed ragout and an aged, fermented reduction. Ode to Crab’s delicate, tuile-wrapped meat bursts with sweetness, while strands of pickled young ginger and a crown of lightly briny caviar make it sing. Evora Building, 68 Lok Ku Road, Sheung Wan 180º Modern Fire Grill From the folks behind Babette and Chouchou comes 180º Modern Fire Grill, a celebration of open-flame cooking that thrives on big flavours and high heat. With a no-nonsense motto – “grill everything” – driving the direction of the restaurant, chef Cédric Tsia King-fung’s vision is articulated through signatures such as the claypot-inspired bone-marrow rice with beef fat and Japanese Koshihikari rice steamed in dashi stock; popcorn chicken served with a house-made mala mayonnaise; and three-yellow chicken, brined for half a day, dry-aged for two, smoked for three hours over cherry wood and finished over charcoal with a soy-sauce glaze. Yu Yuet Lai Building, 43-55 Wyndham Street, Central The Boar Nothing beats a pub that feels so comfortable, so familiar and so routine that it naturally morphs into “the local”. Big Top Hospitality’s newest concept hopes to be that destination of choice for the SoHo neighbourhood. Split into “upstairs” and “downstairs” – each with its own distinct atmosphere and menu, though a pint of Guinness is never far – the British gastropub does casual Glamorgan “sausage” rolls, Welsh rarebit and beer-battered cod and chips just as well as it dishes up a refined feast of roasted rack of lamb and chargrilled Australian M3 rib-eye steak. 55 Elgin Street, Central Myka Yes, it’s true: fro-yo is officially cool again. In the latest instance of trends coming and going and coming back once more, Gen Zers are steering the revival of the treat as a more health-conscious dessert option, making Myka’s arrival in Hong Kong a prescient one. Specialising in artisanal Greek yogurt enhanced with goat’s milk kefir and live cultures, strained to achieve a smooth, creamy base that can be customised with premium toppings such as praline crunch, crumbled baklava, goji berries, ground pistachio and more, Myka raises the bar for fro-yo craftsmanship. Shop D, Sun Lee Building, 43 Wellington Street, Central

title: The ancient Chinese warrior queen who led huge armies to victory and stole a king’s heart
description: The 1976 excavation of Fu Hao’s tomb revealed a revered general and priestess, shifting perceptions of women’s roles in Shang dynasty China.
content: Fu Hao is one of the earliest documented female military generals in history, yet relatively little is known about her. Most of the information gathered about her life is from her tomb. One thing we do know is that she lived during the Shang dynasty (1600BC-1046BC), before the unification of China. Fu’s tomb was excavated in 1976. Its contents led archaeologists to conclude she was a high-ranking royal consort and military general who commanded some of the largest armies of her time. So, who exactly was this woman? An intact tomb reveals a warrior queen The date of Fu’s birth is unknown, but she is thought to have died and been buried in 1200BC. She was one of the many wives of King Wu Ding (reigned 1250-1192BC) and was awarded queen status after giving birth to his heir apparent Zu Ji. Wu had more than 60 wives but only three queens: Fu Hao, Fu Jing and Fu Shi. Fu Hao is said to have died prematurely, long before the king and his two other queens. Zheng Zhenxiang – often referred to as the first lady of Chinese archaeology – led the expedition that discovered Fu’s tomb. She was shocked by the findings. Unlike most royal tombs, which had been extensively looted over thousands of years, Fu’s remained fully intact. The vast majority of Shang royals were entombed in the Xibeigang royal cemetery, located north of the Huan River in the Shang capital of Yin, in modern-day Anyang in Henan province. But Fu was buried south of the river, away from the target of looting. Some believe that her distinct status as a landholding ruler, military leader and priestess – rather than just a consort – may have influenced this decision. The excavation revealed a breathtaking collection of 1,928 artefacts, including ritual bronze vessels, jade carvings and stone sculptures. There were also about 7,000 cowrie shells, which were used as currency during the Shang dynasty. Particularly remarkable was the discovery of 190 inscribed bronze artefacts, including 109 vessels bearing Fu’s name. Also found were 130 weapons, from broad axes to daggers and arrowheads, showing her status as a military leader and high priestess. In 2015, English art historian Jessica Rawson wrote: “The presence of these different weapon types in Fu Hao’s tomb has by some been taken as a mark that she came originally from the borders or the steppe, where women were more likely to play a central role in battle.” Other historians suggest she came from one of the Shang’s neighbouring states, possibly Shanxi, because of her family name – Zi. Fu’s tomb also contained the remains of 16 humans and six canine skeletons apparently sacrificed in a practice that was customary for high-ranking individuals of the time. Perhaps most interesting of all, however, were the oracle bone scripts documenting Fu’s military conquests. These were not found in her tomb, but in the nearby Great Oracle Bone Pit in the Xiaotun village area – home of the Yin Ruins. The oracle bone script is the oldest known writing system in ancient China and was the Shang dynasty’s way of archiving state and religious records. Leading the Shang armies Diviners inscribed questions or possible outcomes onto the surface of bones – typically ox bones or turtle shells – then subjected them to fire. Interpretations of the answer would depend on the pattern of the subsequent cracks. This system was used to predict everything from the weather and harvests to matters concerning childbirth and the outcome of military campaigns. According to one bone inscription, Fu was called upon to lead the Shang general Zhi Fa and meet Wu to ambush the rival Ba Fang polity. The divined question – translated by Chinese historian Wang Yuxin – read “If [Fu Hao] joins and leads Zhi Fa to attack the Ba Fang, should the King from the East attack in trapping [the enemy] in sunken pits at the flank [position] of [Fu Hao]?” As Wang notes, Fu was a first-rank general who led Wu’s most famous generals and raised enormous armies. She led successful campaigns against the Ba in the southwest, the Hu in the south, the Tu and the Gong in the north, the Yi in the northeast and the Qiang in the northwest. According to American historian and archaeologist Elizabeth Childs-Johnson, Fu Hao also ranked second to the king as administrator, sending out royal emissaries, holding royal audiences and supervising tributary harvests on the borderlands. In an era when the king was both the military and religious supreme leader, she also made royal house sacrifices as a high priestess to ward off bad omens. In 1979, Wang proposed that Fu died as the result of a hunting accident. Wu had deep affection for his queen, as suggested by the numerous bone inscriptions about her health, childbearing and happiness. The extraordinary amount of treasures in her tomb also suggests she was highly revered. Remains of a rectangular columned hall at ground level above her tomb indicate that a memorial structure was built and used by royal kin to honour her spirit. Wu would also direct prayers and ritual inquiries to Fu after her death, even marrying her to the Shang’s highest gods in her afterlife. Zheng’s excavation radically altered historians’ perspective on women’s status during the Shang dynasty and proved that they could occupy positions of authority and prestige. In fact, one of the king’s other queen consorts, Fu Jing, also took part in military expeditions, as suggested by similar oracle bone inscriptions.

title: Fitness brand Hyrox moves to shut down fake Macau group, says planned race ‘not authorised’
description: Company says the new group launched in Macau this week is not an affiliate and has no authority to organise races with its name and branding.
content: Hyrox has warned fans that a group calling itself the Hyrox Association of Macau is not part of the global fitness brand and has no authority to run races in the city. The rapidly growing company said it had already taken official steps to stop the upstart organisation from copying it. According to local media, the new group hosted a dinner on Tuesday in the casino hub to mark its official launch, during which it reportedly unveiled plans for an inaugural “Macau Fitness Run Challenge” at the Galaxy International Convention Centre, on February 20 and 21 next year. Jofe Tam, who is listed as the association’s president, said his organisation aimed to promote the sport, train local athletes and coaches, and establish a platform to help the city’s competitors enter international events. Tam added that the association would cooperate with the Macao Polytechnic University’s faculty of health sciences and sports to drive talent development. Director Kwok Kin-meng detailed the race format at the event, stating it would remain open to global participants. The planned race mirrors the standard Hyrox structure of eight functional workout stations combined with an 8km run, though the running portion will be held outside the venue. Categories include elite, open, doubles and relays, alongside a beginner-friendly “half-distance” tier. Gary Wan, managing director of Hyrox in Asia-Pacific, told the South China Morning Post the rebel group was not part of his organisation. “That Macau Fitness Run Challenge is not an officially affiliated Hyrox event, and the Hyrox Association of Macao is not authorised by us,” Wan said. “We have already engaged them to stop using the Hyrox name and branding.” According to the Macau government’s official gazette, the group’s charter was filed in August, listing it as a non-profit organisation with the stated aims of “promoting and popularising the development of Hyrox sports in the Macau region” and to “organise Hyrox competitions and related activities”. Despite the new group’s very public launch, the official Hyrox global website lists no coming events or affiliated organisations in the city. Even before the Hyrox brand’s intervention, initial reports of the association’s launch and the planned challenge had raised eyebrows among local fitness enthusiasts on social media. “May I ask if this is organised by the official Hyrox or is it a high-quality imitation?” one user wrote. “Just looking at the text and the logo, it seems like a knock-off. “If it has official authorisation, I suggest changing the wording, as it easily causes misunderstandings that it is a counterfeit.” Another commenter questioned the group’s legitimacy: “Is it copying Hyrox or officially authorised? You have to pay the official Hyrox to play.” Despite the controversy, some locals said they were “looking forward to having a race in Macau”. The city has never hosted an official Hyrox event, and the brand has not publicly confirmed if it plans to expand into the territory.

title: Hong Kong investors most eager in Asia to beat markets – but temper return hopes: report
description: AI-fuelled optimism lifts return expectations across Asia, but Hong Kong investors are taking a more measured view, Natixis survey finds.
content: Hong Kong investors are Asia’s most ambitious stock pickers, but they have much more subdued return expectations than regional peers swept up in enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, according to a survey by a global asset management firm. Some 95 per cent of Hong Kong respondents said they wanted to outperform the market, the highest proportion in Asia, where the average stood at 85 per cent, according to a survey conducted in August by Natixis Investment Managers. Hong Kong investors expected long-term returns of 12.3 per cent above inflation, compared with the regional average of 17.3 per cent, the survey found, as an 18-month rally partly fuelled by the AI boom inflated expectations. The survey polled 750 individual investors holding at least US$100,000 in investible assets across Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan. Hong Kong financial advisers put realistic long-term returns at 8.8 per cent, the report said. Investors’ expectations exceeded that estimate by 40 per cent, a narrower gap than the 84 per cent in Singapore and 110 per cent in South Korea. The Hong Kong gap stood at 16 per cent a year earlier, said Dave Goodsell, executive director at the Natixis Centre for Investor Insight, at a media briefing on Thursday. Charlie Tsai, head of Hong Kong at the firm, said in a statement that the more measured expectations were likely due in part to “the strength of the local equity market and improving real estate picture we’ve seen over the past year, helping to moderate enthusiasm for the AI supercycle”. We’ve always seen that investors are extrapolators. They think that if the market’s going up, it’s going to keep coming up Dave Goodsell, Natixis Centre for Investor Insight The Hang Seng Index gained about 28 per cent in 2025, its best annual performance since 2017, but has fallen more than 8 per cent this year. By comparison, benchmark equity indices in South Korea and Taiwan have repeatedly set record highs, driven by soaring global demand for AI chips. Hong Kong’s broader economic fundamentals have also shown signs of stabilising. The city’s initial public offering market raised a record HK$388 billion (US$49.4 billion) in the first nine months of the year, while residential property prices rose about 7 per cent through August. Goodsell said a market downturn was the top concern among Hong Kong investors, while inflation and interest rates ranked highest elsewhere in Asia. US long-term bond yields hit their highest level since 2002 this month, which Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said in his weekly blog last week had “inevitably dampened recent sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market”. Despite the headwinds, Natixis remained positive on risk assets, according to Mabrouk Chetouane, head of global market strategy at the firm. Chetouane said Natixis had raised its allocation to US equities to the maximum permitted level within its model portfolios, citing the start of third-quarter earnings season and continued support from AI. He also described the simultaneous surge in bond yields and equity prices as “quite unusual”. Natixis said a recency bias in return expectations appeared at odds with investors’ risk tolerance. Some 73 per cent of respondents across Asia described themselves as conservative or moderate investors, while 76 per cent said they would choose safety over performance if forced to pick one. “We’ve always seen that investors are extrapolators,” Goodsell said. “They think that if the market’s going up, it’s going to keep coming up.”

title: Teen kills 4 at Oregon school before being shot dead by armed citizen
description: Three children and a teacher die in Bend as police say a community member pursued the 16-year-old shooter into building.
content: A teenager shot and killed three children and a teacher on Thursday at an elementary school in the US state of Oregon, police said, adding the assailant was later killed by an armed community member who pursued him into the building. Officers rushed to Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, a city of about 100,000 in the nation’s northwest, after reports of a shooter on campus on Thursday afternoon. The three children who died on the scene were aged 5, 8 and 11, said Bend police chief Mike Krantz. Another child and a teacher were being treated for critical injuries after the shooting. The United States, where firearms are readily available, has a long and painful history of gun violence, with thousands of people killed every year. It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among all developed nations. People gathered in the city’s Drake Park on Thursday evening for a candlelight vigil remembering the victims. “I’m in total complete shock, and scared and sad,” said Betsy, who did not give her last name. She spent around 10 minutes contemplating a circle of candles and flowers. “It’s awful, but it also has brought people together,” she said. Krantz, the police chief, told journalists that the department first learned of an active shooter after a call from a person who reported being shot at multiple times by a person carrying a long gun. Dozens of emergency calls then reported that a shooter had entered the school and all law enforcement in the area were called to the scene, the chief added. Officers arrived at 1.02pm local time within minutes of the calls, he said. “Moments later, an officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him,” Krantz said. “Our officers entered the building and confirmed the suspect was dead.” One seven-year-old and one 54-year-old teacher with critical injuries were transported to a local hospital, he said. The police chief said the investigation was in its early stages, but told the press conference it appeared “the shooter had forced their way into the school by shooting at locked doors.” He added that the 16-year-old shooter was a Bend resident. Between 400 and 450 children attend Silver Rail Elementary, where more than 40 staff work, according to a police spokesperson. After a lockdown, Bend-La Pine School District said law enforcement was escorting students in buses to a separate location, where families could reunite with their children. The district’s superintendent, Steve Cook, tearfully called the day’s events “an unthinkable tragedy”. “We are heartbroken. We are horrified. This is the kind of thing you hear about in other places, and pray that it never happens here,” he told reporters. Parents were anxiously waiting at the site near a church, where Drew Sharp, the father of a fifth grader, the highest grade in the school, told CBS News: “I have faith that he’s OK and that he’ll be all right”. Children were disembarking from the bus youngest to oldest “which makes sense,” Sharp said, but “it’s just more time waiting”. Friday classes at schools across the district along with activities and athletic events were cancelled, Bend-La Pine said in a statement. The elementary school is approximately 270km southeast of the city Portland. It serves primary-age students in kindergarten through fifth grade. The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on April 16, 2007, when South Korean student Cho Seung-hui killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life. There have been more than 360 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as four or more people shot. “Our hearts are with the terrified children and the families anxiously waiting to hear that their loved ones are safe,” GIFFORDS, a gun safety organisation, said on X. “We cannot keep accepting this as a fact of life.” Thursday’s shooting was followed by a painfully familiar chorus of calls for action on gun control, pleas that have resulted in little meaningful change. In the face of decades of massacres, the powerful US pro-gun lobby has given millions of dollars to primarily conservative politicians in a successful bid to keep gun laws loose. “They’re killing our babies. Shredding our kids with lead. Forcing us to live in fear,” said Janelle Bynum, an Oregon congresswoman, in a statement. “This continues to happen,” she said later, speaking on CNN. “And it seems as if the adults don’t care.”

title: Bus hits train near Channel Tunnel in France, injuring 19
description: The bus was carrying truck drivers heading to travel on a LeShuttle train, which carries vehicles and their passengers through the tunnel.
content: A minibus collided with a stationary train in a Channel Tunnel vehicle boarding area in France on Thursday evening, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, authorities said. Five people were severely injured, though no one’s life appeared to be in danger, the local prefect said in a statement. The minibus was carrying truck drivers of various nationalities who were heading to travel on a LeShuttle train, which carries vehicles and their passengers through the tunnel. The area around the tunnel entrance was sealed off on Thursday evening, journalists at the scene reported, with a helicopter and several emergency vehicles present. An investigation has been opened on suspicion of unintentional injury, the local prosecutors’ office in Boulogne-sur-Mer said. Calais deputy prefect Agathe Cury told a news conference that freight traffic was not disrupted but Getlink passenger shuttles were suspended for an hour while emergency services took care of the victims. Speaking at 10.30pm, she said normal traffic had resumed. Passenger train service Eurostar said its services were not affected. At 50km (31 miles) in length, the Channel Tunnel is the longest infrastructure of its kind in the world. It has linked Coquelles in northern France and Folkestone in England since 1994. Operated by Getlink, it is used by several hundred trains every day. Getlink runs Le Shuttle, trains carrying vehicles between France and the UK, as well as a rail freight service. According to its website, the company handles around 2.2 million car crossings a year and carries 8 million passengers. Separately, Eurostar, which has held a monopoly on cross-Channel passenger rail services for decades, said it carried 11.8 million passengers in 2025. However, Thursday evening’s accident involved “no Eurostar train and has no impact on Eurostar services to and from London”, the company said in a statement. “All Eurostar trains will run as scheduled.”

title: In Focus | The China decoupling paradox: why the world still needs its manufacturing machine
description: Chinese parts, machinery and know-how remain deeply embedded in countries seeking to build manufacturing industries of their own.
content: Talk of global decoupling from China has persisted for years, as has speculation that emerging economies such as India and Vietnam could soon replace it as the “world’s factory”. But for Indian hardware engineer Neeraj Arora, the growth of India’s electronics manufacturing industry has not eliminated the need to source components from China. Instead, it has changed the nature of those imports. A decade ago, Arora imported finished phone chargers from the world’s second-largest economy. Today, more of these products can be made in India, even as manufacturers there still rely on Chinese parts for assembly. “They don’t have a single industry; they have created an ecosystem,” said Arora, who has travelled repeatedly to Shenzhen, Dongguan and Guangzhou – southern China’s manufacturing hubs that offer a wide range of competitively priced parts, from power-switching transistors to charging chips. Arora’s experience, together with broader economic data, illustrates the challenge facing countries seeking to diversify their supply chains: shifting production out of China does not necessarily mean reducing reliance on Chinese industry. A recent report by investment bank Morgan Stanley examined this pattern, arguing the country had strengthened its role in global supply chains despite trade tensions. “China has continued to deepen its presence in global supply chains by capturing value-added content in global imports and increasing exports to [emerging markets],” the bank’s analysts, including chief Asia economist Chetan Ahya and chief China economist Robin Xing, wrote in the note, published earlier this month. The world’s second-largest economy was “well-positioned” to deepen that presence, the analysts argued, citing its focus on high-growth sectors, integrated supply chains, a financial system aligned with strategic goals and a large pool of skilled workers. The upstream advantage The challenge facing the likes of India and Vietnam is whether they can develop the industrial expertise and networks required to make more inputs at home. But a closer look at the data suggests that as manufacturing expands in these economies, Chinese supplies remain essential. These developments indicate broader regional supply-chain integration, centred around China Morgan Stanley analysts “While India has made significant headway in electronics manufacturing, it still imports a large part of its intermediate and capital goods from China,” the Morgan Stanley analysts wrote, noting that 52 per cent of India’s imported Chinese content went into domestic investments. Looking beyond where products are finally assembled, they tracked “value-added content” – the value contributed by a country through the goods and services used along the chain. A product assembled in Vietnam, for instance, may still contain Chinese parts or rely on Chinese machinery. Using this measure, the analysts found that China’s share of value-added content in global imports rose from 12.6 per cent in 2017 to 14.3 per cent in 2024. The report also found that Chinese inputs are playing a growing role in Asian economies often touted as manufacturing rivals. In Vietnam, 55 per cent of imported Chinese content is channelled towards exports, according to the analysts. “We also find that Chinese value-added content has not just increased in the rest of Asia’s exports to the US, but also to non-US markets as well,” they wrote. “Overall, these developments indicate broader regional supply-chain integration, centred around China.” Arora’s experience illustrates how difficult mainland China’s manufacturing ecosystem is to replace. Taiwan’s higher-end products, he said, were less suited to the low-cost goods his Indian customers needed while Vietnam offered fewer options. “Only China has that ecosystem,” he said. Nevertheless, Arora said he believed India was making headway. He cited the expansion of home-grown electronics giant Dixon Technologies into television and phone assembly, as well as the growing ability of Indian firms to design and develop circuit boards and prototypes that once required trips to Shenzhen. Despite the progress, however, local manufacturers continue to rely on China’s extensive network of component suppliers. Arora estimated that China had gained 20 to 25 years of electronics manufacturing experience, compared with India’s push that gathered pace only around 2015. He argued India could reach the current capabilities of the world’s second-largest economy within five to seven years, although he expected China to have moved further ahead by then. New Delhi is also pushing to develop more of its inputs at home. The government’s Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme, launched in 2025 and expanded to 400 billion rupees (US$4.2 billion) in the 2026-27 budget, supports local production of parts and partially assembled products. By August, 106 projects had been approved and 38 plants had begun production, according to the Indian government. But the government also acknowledged that India remained dependent on imports for critical components, including printed circuit boards, camera and display modules, connectors and capacitors. Vietnam is pursuing a similar goal of strengthening its domestic supplier base. A revised industrial policy that took effect in September 2025 provides support for technology transfer, training and certification, as well as programmes intended to help local companies supply multinational manufacturers. The limits of Western decoupling For the United States and Europe, where the decoupling narrative has arguably been most pronounced, efforts to reduce dependence on China have transformed where products are sourced and how they reach their destinations. But the Morgan Stanley analysts found that lower direct imports from the world’s factory do not necessarily translate into less Chinese content in those goods. They estimated that the US and EU together accounted for about 80 per cent of the increase in global reliance on Chinese value-added content. While China’s share of direct US imports plunged from 22 per cent in 2017 to about 8 per cent currently, the share of Chinese value-added content in US imports has remained broadly stable in recent years, standing at 15.4 per cent in 2024. The analysts found that more US sectors had increased their reliance on China than reduced it, with only five of 13 manufacturing sectors recording a material decline in the share of Chinese value-added content in their imports since 2016. “The US is still importing just as much value-added content from China, just not directly,” they wrote. The report identified extensive re-routing of goods. About 25 per cent of Chinese content in US imports now reached the country indirectly through third economies, up 10 percentage points from 2017, according to the analysts. Nearly half of this indirect value passed through just three economies: Mexico, Taiwan and Vietnam, with the latter standing out for a much higher share of Chinese content in its exports to the US. The analysts said the greater use of indirect channels, particularly from 2022 onwards, was “unique to US-China trade” and consistent with production moving to other countries to serve the American market while continuing to rely on Chinese inputs. “We do not observe a similar shift towards indirect channels in imports of the rest of the world outside the US, nor for EU imports,” they said, estimating that the share of Chinese value-added content in Europe’s imports had edged up from 6.9 per cent in 2017 to 8.3 per cent in 2024.
