description: With fewer preconceptions, this could be the generation that breaks through the mistrust built up over decades.
content: When US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet again in Shenzhen next month, and then in Miami in December, the world will watch for signs of progress on trade, technology, security and other contentious issues. Such high-level diplomacy is indispensable. But the future of the US-China relationship also depends on something less visible: whether their people, especially the young, can still understand one another. As Washington and Beijing navigate intensifying strategic competition, academic exchanges and opportunities for grass-roots engagement have come under unprecedented strain. This is far more than a niche educational concern. It directly threatens America’s capacity to comprehend China, while quietly eroding the guard rails required for a stable bilateral relationship. The decline in American students studying in China illustrates the problem. Numbers peaked at nearly 15,000 in 2011, fell to just 211 during the pandemic and have only recovered to about 880 in 2024, according to former US ambassador Nicholas Burns. The pandemic caused the collapse, but a deterioration in bilateral relations has made recovery harder. Compounding the problem are escalating national security anxieties. The US Justice Department’s China Initiative, launched in 2018 and later discontinued, heightened scrutiny of researchers with ties to China and fuelled lasting concerns over racial profiling. More recent legislative investigations and funding restrictions involving American universities have only deepened the uncertainty surrounding US-China academic collaboration. The consequences extend well beyond university campuses. If fewer Americans study in China, the United States risks losing a generation of people equipped to interpret Chinese politics, society and policy. In an analysis released in September, the Council on Foreign Relations warned that America’s capacity to train China specialists is eroding just as the need for such expertise grows. China, too, faces the costs of this deteriorating climate. Chinese students and scholars encounter growing uncertainty over whether academic engagement with American institutions can proceed without becoming entangled in geopolitical disputes. This month, the Trump administration launched investigations into nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, over alleged visa fraud, with officials citing concerns involving Chinese scholars and the Chinese government. There are, however, reasons not to surrender to this pessimism. At the recent summit in Washington, Xi announced a plan to invite 100,000 young Americans to China over the next five years. This expands on the November 2023 initiative to bring 50,000 young Americans to the mainland – a target Chinese officials said was met two-and-a-half years ahead of schedule. That these exchanges continue to grow suggests there is still substantial interest in direct engagement, even as the broader relationship remains difficult. US-China joint academic programmes continue to attract students. Both the Schwarzman Scholars programme at Tsinghua University and at Duke Kunshan University received a record number of applications this year, with the latter also welcoming its most diverse class in August. Their experience shows international education can remain valuable even when governments disagree. China’s broader opening to international visitors has created further opportunities. Visa-free entry for eligible travellers has made visiting China easier for many nationalities, including Americans under applicable arrangements. Social media has also allowed young visitors to share experiences that differ from the images of China commonly encountered in their home countries. Attitudes may be shifting. A September Pew Research Centre survey revealed that Americans under 50 view China notably more warmly than their older counterparts do, though overall sentiment remains negative. Younger Americans have come of age in a world where China’s economic, technological and geopolitical weight is a foundational reality. Their world view is not anchored to the rigid expectations that defined earlier generations’ encounters with China’s rise. For many veteran American sinologists, their formative lens was shaped by China’s opening up under Deng Xiaoping – an era when many in the West hoped economic integration would ring in political liberalisation. China’s subsequent, distinct path challenged those expectations, fostering deep establishment disillusionment and mistrust. The lesson is not that older experts have failed, or that younger people will automatically find common ground. It is that each generation needs the opportunity to encounter China as it actually is, rather than through inherited assumptions. Younger Americans, with fewer preconceptions, could be the generation that breaks through the mistrust built up over decades. To realise this, however, requires shared responsibility. Beijing must ensure its academic engagements are predictable and transparent, and allow foreign students the freedom to experience authentic Chinese society beyond a curated state narrative. Washington, for its part, must carefully distinguish sensitive military research from ordinary educational pursuit, avoiding the trap of treating nationality as a proxy for espionage risk. Both capitals should expand reciprocal scholarships, fund area studies and lower the financial barriers to studying abroad. The coming meetings between Trump and Xi in Shenzhen and Miami can help stabilise the relationship and establish the political conditions for cooperation. But leaders cannot manufacture mutual understanding by themselves. That requires sustained contact between people who will live with the consequences of today’s decisions long after the current leaders have left office. Young Americans and Chinese will not resolve every dispute between Washington and Beijing, but they can ensure competition does not define their relationship. Through education, shared research and lasting friendships, they can challenge stereotypes, foster mutual understanding and prevent mistrust from escalating into conflict. Sometimes the road to a better relationship between two great powers begins not in a summit room, but in the eyes of the next generation.

title: Opinion | How could a superintelligence take over the world? Let me count the ways
description: AI is racking up bigger advantages as people become more dependent on it, raising the risk of a superintelligent model overpowering humanity.
content: OpenAI recently announced perhaps its biggest mathematics breakthrough yet: it released novel results on 377 high-profile open problems. Artificial intelligence (AI) casually solved these decades-old problems as a mere by-product of training. The community of mathematicians did not universally welcome this development, with University of Connecticut professor Alvaro Lozano-Robledo commenting: “I am not sure at this point what this (hostile?) takeover of the mathematical landscape is trying to achieve”. Where is the global development of AI headed? According to Jacob Coxon – the researcher who recently resigned from AI research firm Anthropic – and other leading voices in AI, there might be an up to 50 per cent chance of humanity being ended by superintelligent AI. How would that happen? Overpowering humanity is unlikely to be achieved by current models since they lack sufficient capabilities. The problem is that AI is rapidly growing more capable and we might soon enter the regime of recursive self-improvement. This would mean AIs can autonomously do AI research, causing a positive feedback loop of ever-better AIs inventing ever-better AIs. Self-improvement would logically only stop at some kind of peak intelligence level, which could be artificial superintelligence. Earlier this year, we saw misalignment on public display in the Hugging Face incident. AI agents working on a benchmark to test their hacking skills found each other through a secret messaging board and autonomously decided to hack AI company Hugging Face. This “literal genie”-type of misalignment could scale all the way to a complete takeover. How would a rogue superintelligence go about taking over world power after escaping its sandbox? That is a difficult question to answer since it is fundamentally true that one cannot predict the moves of an intelligence that is smarter than we are. However, in the case of AI takeover scenarios, we can nevertheless make educated guesses. Superintelligence is likely to have multiple major advantages over humans. It could exchange data over the internet at the speed of light. It could spin up a vast amount of agents, creating AI armies where every soldier is superhumanly intelligent. It could run at superhuman speeds, making its relation to us perhaps comparable to our relation to plants. Unleashed rogue superintelligence could make huge amounts of money, either legally by trading on the stock market or illegally by extortion or hacking entire banks or cryptocurrency platforms. It could also act in the physical world by using any of the internet-connected devices that we have, including weapons, or manipulating humans. An artificial superintelligence could plausibly hide itself on unguarded servers for a long time, overpowering us before we know it exists. Even more fundamental, a superintelligence might rapidly invent new science and technology. Once humans understood relativity theory, we were able to weaponise this understanding into atomic weapons. Which insights are still hidden to us but can be discovered and weaponised by a superintelligence, leaving us as exposed as a medieval castle to a nuclear bomb? Besides AI strengths, there are also profound sources of fragility that we have created for ourselves. There are more than 12,000 nuclear warheads among the world’s nuclear powers. Fragile human bodies are easy prey for chemical attacks or viruses, as we saw during the Covid-19 pandemic. We have even created companies which can synthesise these viruses and, absurdly, respond to email orders. Water or food could be poisoned, and hacked online communication networks could start blocking anti-AI coordination messages while sending messages that serve the AI’s interests while we don’t realise what’s happening. Another classic source of human weakness is our need for money. If an AI needed us to maintain the electricity grid and server infrastructure, it could simply pay humans to do that, which many would accept because they need to pay the rent. Humans in powerful positions, for example in politics, could likewise be tempted to adopt pro-AI policies because of AI campaign donations or corruption. Money is a powerful force in our world, and superintelligences are well-positioned to put this power to use, in case they temporarily need humans for anything at all. As if all of this is not enough, we are handing AIs huge advantages on a plate. When a new model is released, it gets used by customers including the military, government, financial industry, utility companies, media and many other powerful institutions. Even simple chatbots advise everyone from CEOs to biolab workers and politicians on what to do. We will soon have AI agents and hand them huge amounts of leverage for free. Will people keep their passwords secure from their agents when they are just so good at handling things? All that is then needed for a takeover is collusion by these AIs against us. We already know from the Hugging Face attack that AIs can collude with each other. All these advantages and the fact humans are handing over total control to AI could well add up to the latter taking over power and, if it chooses, killing all humans. Therefore, our only option is to globally pause the development of AI models beyond the current frontier. We must keep track of AI accelerator chip stockpiles since they are the uranium of AI. We must be more careful before releasing powerful open-weight models. This is not a gamble politicians or tech CEOs have the right to make. If these gambles with humanity’s continued existence end badly, that would make our current leaders the ones who ended humanity. Quite the legacy, if anyone is left to remember it.

title: Laos private jet bust reveals how Mekong meth slips past borders
description: Drug experts say narcotics production infrastructure extends across Southeast Asia, and transport routes are fluid and move with enforcement.
content: A private jet hired from Malaysia – seemingly destined for the Philippines – but stopped on the tarmac by Laos’ drug police who found suitcases stuffed with 512kg of crystal methamphetamine, has returned the spotlight to the unrelenting flow of narcotics from the Mekong’s drug laboratories. Cyberscams have dominated headlines and authorities’ attention across Southeast Asia for over a year as the leading criminal enterprise worth tens of billions of dollars annually. But methamphetamine – in its high potency crystallised form, or the cheaper caffeine-cut yaba pills – still stalks the region, spewing out mainly from Myanmar to Southeast Asia and then onto lucrative markets further afield in Australia, New Zealand and Japan. On October 1, Luang Prabang airport in northern Laos came under scrutiny as a new potential narcotics route when drug police found nearly two dozen suitcases stuffed with crystal meth. Officers arrested 13 people, including a Filipino national believed to be central to the smuggling plot, a Singaporean pilot and a co-pilot from Malaysia, state media reported six days later. A Philippine Inquirer report on October 8 said the jet was destined for the country, but police stressed that the final destination of the drugs was subject to further investigation. Officers conceded, however, that Filipinos were involved in the transnational smuggling attempt. The volume of drugs transported by aeroplane has caught the attention of regional narcotics police, sparking a multi-country investigation and spotlighting how sophisticated drug networks rotate through vulnerable ports, airports and roads to open borders. Reports of drug flights from the Golden Triangle – the area that crosses Myanmar, Laos, northern Thailand and China – are rare. Shipments of crystal meth, known as Ice in Thailand and shabu in the Philippines, are normally routed by sea. Isagani Nerez, director general of the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency, on Monday told reporters that one of the suspects was a Filipino known as “Fahad” and that they had been tipped off to a potential smuggling operation via private jets from Laos. As the three nations involved began to attempt to unspool the trafficking effort, Malaysian drug police said the Learjet N73GP had left their country empty in late September. “The aircraft concerned had been chartered for US$49,500,” Bukit Aman’s Narcotics Criminal Investigation department said in a statement, adding it had detained the aircraft owner who leased the plane for charter and three other people for questioning at Sultan Abdul Aziz Shah Airport in Subang. The scandal has prompted the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia (CAAM) to look into how the private jet hire became part of an international drug smuggling attempt. Norazman Mahmud, CEO of CAAM, told This Week in Asia the aviation body “will assess whether additional measures or enhanced coordination with relevant agencies are necessary to address any regulatory or operational gaps identified”. It is unclear so far where the seized drugs originated from. Myanmar, tossed into a vortex of war and lawlessness, remains the top producer of methamphetamine, certainly in Asia if not the world – as well as the globe’s biggest grower of opium poppies that make the base for heroin. With long, unpoliceable borders with Myanmar’s drug-producing Shan state, Laos is a key passageway to the wider global market for Myanmar’s meth lords. But Laos is also a producer – a conduit for precursor chemicals into Myanmar – and a manufacturing base for a range of other synthetic party drugs including ketamine. Drugs from Myanmar and Laos mostly transit south through Thailand, which acts as one of the world’s largest drug warehouses and as a corridor to Malaysia, or for shipping further away to the Philippines, Australia and Japan. But drug experts say routes are fluid and move with enforcement. “Myanmar remains the main methamphetamine production centre in Southeast Asia but the wider synthetic drug production infrastructure clearly extends across the region,” Ioannis Vlassis of the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime told This Week in Asia. “When controls tighten along the Myanmar–Thailand border, the Laos corridor absorbs some of that traffic,” he said, adding land routes had shown signs of shifting east into Vietnam and south into Cambodia for onward shipping. But drug production has boomed beyond Myanmar in recent years and now goes beyond meth, into the new party drugs favoured from Bangkok and Kuala Lumpur to Ho Chi Minh City and Hong Kong. A record bust last year in Nha Trang, Vietnam, found 1.4 tonnes of ketamine and 80 tonnes of precursor chemicals, while an etomidate production lab for wildly popular “zombie” vapes was discovered in Thailand’s Chonburi province in May. Vlassis said there was a “major overlap” between Mekong cyberscam and drug trafficking operations, with both crime enterprises using the same “protection providers, corrupt officials, transport connections, front businesses and channels for moving money”. Border areas around Tachilek, the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos and Mae Sot in Thailand revealed overlapping interests, he said, although “the same actors” were likely not running scam compounds as well as major drug operations. Mekong crime gangs with deep networks that can buy chemicals and transport, bribe corrupt officials to open borders, and easily absorb the losses of massive seizures, continue to target the richest drug markets in Asia – Australia and New Zealand, whose distance pumps up the price of narcotics. “Bulk loads can travel on fishing boats and smaller commercial vessels, while passenger and parcel channels carry smaller consignments,” said Vlassis, who co-wrote a report published in September on the Mekong meth trade. “For Australia and New Zealand, this means that efforts to identify and disrupt upstream supply need to account for multiple departure points and transport methods across the region.”

title: Hong Kong plans just 2 land sales this quarter despite housing rebound
description: The two parcels of land in Sha Tin are earmarked for residential and student hostel projects, as government remains cautious on new housing.
content: The Hong Kong government will release two parcels of land for sale – one for a residential development and another for a student hostel project – in the October to December quarter, as officials maintain a cautious stance towards housing supply even as the market rebounds. One residential site – an 8,015-square-metre (86,250-square-foot) parcel of land in Sha Tin – will be offered through tender in the third quarter of the 2026-2027 financial year, Development Secretary Bernadette Linn Hon-ho announced on Thursday. The plot at the junction of Tai Chung Kiu Road and On Sum Street in Shek Mun is expected to provide about 960 flats, according to Linn. The other site is a 1,100-square-metre (11,840-square-foot) plot for student accommodation. The plot – also located in Sha Tin, at the junction of Yuen Shun Circuit and Yuen Hong Street in Siu Lek Yuen – is expected to provide 600 hostel spots. “We have noticed that overall market sentiment remains positive this year,” Linn said. “Developers hold an optimistic view of market prospects, and there is steady demand and market capacity for sites in mature urban areas.” The announcement of the latest government land sale programme came hot on the heels of Kerry Properties stunning the market with a HK$4.3 billion (US$550 million) bid for a residential site in Ho Man Tin earlier this month. The developer’s winning bid for the 55,649-square-foot (5,170-square-metre) site was far above market expectations and the highest price paid for a residential plot in Kowloon for nearly five years, according to Vincent Cheung, managing director of valuation firm Vincorn Consulting and Appraisal. Yet sentiment in the residential market cooled in the third quarter of the year, with total home sales falling 40 per cent quarter on quarter and 21 per cent from a year earlier, according to Cushman & Wakefield. Home prices also edged down 0.8 per cent between July and August, though they were still up 7 per cent since the start of the year. With 3,845 flats hitting the market in the current quarter, the city’s total new housing supply so far this financial year is set to reach 15,680 homes, according to Linn. The residential site in Sha Tin was estimated to be worth between HK$2.7 billion and HK$3.2 billion, or HK$5,000 to HK$6,000 per square foot, said Cyrus Fong, executive director and head of valuation and advisory for Greater China at Knight Frank. “Although there is slight pressure from anticipated interest rate hikes recently, judging by the recent land sale transaction in Ho Man Tin, developers still appear interested in sites with nearby transport infrastructure and commercial development,” Fong said. Demand for student accommodation is also expected to remain robust in Hong Kong amid an influx of foreign and mainland Chinese students. The city will need to provide more than 70,000 additional beds for these students over the coming decade, according to CBRE. The newly planned student hostel site, near the Hang Seng University of Hong Kong and two MTR stations, enjoyed “distinct transit and geographic advantages” and would “help relieve accommodation pressure for tertiary students”, said Kathy Lee, head of research and retail consultancy at Colliers in Hong Kong. She added that the government’s new plan showed “policy responsiveness to pressing market demands”. In an audit released in April this year, the government found that Hong Kong had only met 44 per cent of its target for youth hostel flats as of December last year, underlining the need to boost youth hostel accommodation. Regarding One Stanley, which is undergoing a government probe over alleged building defects, Linn said the Buildings Department was still investigating and had no further information. On why the occupation permit was still issued, she pointed out that the Buildings Department had established procedures for issuing such permits. “If any issues are uncovered during [this] process, they will pursue full accountability,” she said. “The specific measures for holding parties accountable will depend on the investigation findings.”

title: China-led team hits 83% success rate anticipating earthquakes in ‘seismo-ripples’ study
description: Strong predictive potential shown as anomalous patterns verified against 12 major earthquakes in China between 2022 and 2024.
content: A China-led international team has reported a new pre-earthquake phenomenon that has shown strong predictive potential for major earthquakes since 2022 with minimal failures. The anomalous seismic, magnetic and ionospheric resonance signals they observed – termed “seismo-ripples” by the researchers – are ringlike disturbance patterns triggered before earthquakes happen. Their findings challenge the long-standing scientific belief that these events are unpredictable, opening up a promising new path to earthquake prediction. “Historically, earthquake prediction has been considered nearly infeasible,” said the team from institutes in mainland China and Taiwan, along with Brazil and Japan, in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal NPJ Natural Hazards on Sunday. Using data collected from seismometers, magnetometers and ground-based Global Navigation Satellite System receivers, the anomalous patterns were verified against 12 major earthquakes in China between 2022 and 2024. “Since June 2022, prospective anomaly based on seismo-ripples has demonstrated a strong predictive capability for numerous earthquakes with a magnitude [greater than or equal to] six, with remarkably minimal to no failure,” the researchers wrote. Of the 12 sites they proposed could be associated with future earthquakes, 83 per cent experienced a corresponding earthquake within three months of the seismo-ripple patterns emerging. The average distance between predicted and actual epicentres was about 280km (174 miles) and the estimated magnitudes ran about 0.5 units larger than the final seismic readings. “In essence, the core argument of our paper is that earthquakes are not inherently unpredictable,” said Chen Chieh-Hung, a lead author of the study and a professor at the Chengdu University of Technology. Chen noted that prediction could mean different things to different people, with some expecting precision down to the exact minute or accuracy within a margin of a few kilometres, which he said would not be feasible at this stage. “Nevertheless, we have opened a door. Earthquakes are not beyond the realm of prediction,” he said on Wednesday. “There is a possibility that they can be predicted. The next step is for the scientific community to work on refining this precision.” Asia is one of the world’s most seismically active regions, with China experiencing roughly a third of all continental earthquakes despite having only about 7 per cent of the global land area. Estimating long-term seismic probabilities – such as Japan’s assessment of a high probability for a major earthquake along the Nankai Trough in the next three decades – is an accepted scientific approach. However, for decades, short-term earthquake prediction has been elusive and controversial. According to the United States Geological Survey, a true earthquake prediction must specify three parameters: the date and time, the location and the magnitude of the incoming event. This differs from earthquake forecasting, which calculates the probability of an earthquake occurring within a given area and time window. Chen said the scientific consensus that earthquakes could not be predicted stemmed in part from papers published in the top journals Nature and Science in the 1990s. From then on, he said, this belief “effectively became an established rule”. “Within the scientific community, the prevailing view is that earthquakes are unpredictable, and most researchers prefer not to wade into such controversial waters,” he added. Chen pointed to other milestones once thought impossible, such as accurate weather forecasting and aircraft breaking the sound barrier. “A more accurate way to frame it would be to say that we have yet to discover a sound, rationally valid or scientifically grounded method for predicting the occurrence of earthquakes,” he said. Chen said that if the bar for prediction were set extremely high, then it would indeed be impossible. Instead, he argued that scientific efforts should focus on shifting from long-term forecasts to short-to-medium-term predictions. Researchers from around the world have sought to identify earthquake precursors or signals occurring before seismic events that could be used for more reliable forecasting or even predictions. In their paper, the China-led team explored a phenomenon of ringlike disturbances called seismo-circles or seismo-ripples that appear to propagate outwards from future earthquake epicentres. “What’s particularly interesting about this phenomenon is that, initially, we did not know whether it was real or false,” Chen said. To verify their findings, the team investigated past earthquake cases. They found that separate ripple-like anomalies had formed for two earthquakes that struck China within a day of each other in 2021. Chen said this revelation gave the team the confidence to pursue the research further, and over the following two years they documented the anomalous occurrences and submitted formal reports. In April 2022, after detecting anomalous ripple patterns in southwestern China, the researchers submitted a formal document to the China Earthquake Networks Centre – the country’s official body for earthquake monitoring and prediction evaluation – declaring a possible magnitude 6.3 event within two months. On June 1, 2022, a magnitude 6.1 earthquake struck China’s southwestern Sichuan province, occurring 399km from the team’s predicted epicentre. They then launched an effort between 2022 and 2024 to challenge the idea that earthquakes were inherently unpredictable, routinely monitoring seismo-ripples and submitting formal reports to authorities. The team said its investigation highlighted a correlation between seismo-ripples and forthcoming seismic events, allowing for “reliable estimation of earthquake magnitude, location and timing”. They noted there were still challenges to address, including ambiguous ripple signals that complicated exact estimates and the need for deeper understanding of the physics behind these anomalies. In addition, seismo-ripple detection remains limited by instrument density and spatial network coverage. To improve precision, an upgraded ground-based observation system is under construction in China. Looking ahead, the team plans to incorporate satellite data and artificial intelligence to enhance monitoring capabilities. While their study focused on China’s North-South Seismic Belt, the researchers said the seismo-ripple phenomenon held potential for global application. Chen said the main goal of their paper was not to claim that earthquakes could already be predicted but rather that they were not inherently unpredictable. “At this stage, we are already able to distinguish between signals that are likely related to earthquakes and those that are not – a distinction we could not make previously,” he said. “The next challenge is to improve precision, particularly regarding the location and timing of seismic events.” Chen acknowledged that there was a long way to go before earthquake prediction would become a fully functional reality. But he said his team was committed to the task and invited other scientists to put their seismo-ripples model to the test.

title: ‘High hopes’ as Indonesia’s women get another shot at national football league
description: Six clubs get US$1.3 million, five-year trial period to start new chapter for women’s game in Muslim-majority country of 290 million people.
content: Seven years after Covid-19 put the brakes on Indonesia’s new women’s football league, Zahra Naqiyyah will finally return to the field with “high hopes” for the women’s game in the country. Sunday’s matches in the Indonesia Women’s League will be the first since 2019 and a new chapter for women’s football in the Muslim-majority country of 290 million people. “I really believe that if Indonesia’s women’s football is properly managed, we can become a powerhouse in Asia,” Zahra said at a training session in Bekasi city, east of Jakarta. “I have high hopes for women’s football in Indonesia,” she added, wearing a black hijab and the turquoise jersey of her club, Garudayaksa Women. Indonesia has long been an outlier among football nations, including much smaller Asian ones, in not having a permanent league for women. But in 2019 the IWL was launched and Zahra, only 15 at the time, helped her team to victory and celebrated with a hero’s parade in her home city of Bandung – fulfilling a dream. But the league managed only one season because of the pandemic and subsequent financial problems, and has been on hold ever since. Now, the Football Association of Indonesia (PSSI) has allocated 24 billion rupiah (US$1.3 million) to restart the league and pay salaries, albeit small ones, to players. There will be six clubs to start with in a five-year trial period, said PSSI chairman Erick Thohir, former owner of Inter Milan. At 22, Zahra is still young enough to make a career of it. Others were not so lucky. “Many of my friends ended up quitting because what else could they do? There is no league. And if they want to become coaches, who are they supposed to coach?” Zahra said. ‘Going slowly’ While she learned to be a coach, others tried their luck with clubs abroad. Nastasia Suci Ramadhani played last year in the Maldives. The 20-year-old returned to Indonesia in January to play alongside Zahra. Unsure about the league’s staying power, Nastasia is studying management at university and has also considered becoming a police officer or soldier. “For men there’s a league every year, but for women there isn’t,” she said. Garudayaksa coach Yopie Riwoe said the going would be tough if Indonesia wanted to compete with top Asian nations. Japan won the Women’s World Cup in 2011 and are current Asian champions, while China and South Korea also boast women’s leagues and are competitive at international level. In contrast, Yopie said of Indonesia’s women: “All this time they haven’t done continuous training, like daily sessions with high intensity, so it’s been a bit difficult. “We’re trying to go slowly.” Indonesia’s women have never been to the World Cup and failed to qualify for the Asian Cup last year, though they did reach the continental showpiece in 2022, losing all three games. However, they won the regional Asean Football Federation Women’s Cup in 2024 and again this year. They are currently ranked 105th in the world. ‘An athlete first’ Hoping to join the national side one day, Azra Zifa Kayla will play in the IWL for Persita Women, based west of Jakarta. The 22-year-old will juggle afternoon practice with mornings teaching physical education to primary school pupils, afraid to stake everything, including a regular salary, on her passion for football. “I am an athlete first,” she said on a football field in Tangerang, near the capital. “But to be an athlete – especially as a woman in Indonesia – can be limiting. “I should also focus on education because that’s the guarantee of my future,” said Azra, who studied health and sport science. The IWL returns with about 200 players from clubs from all Greater Jakarta. IWL boss Teddy Tjahjono said the long-term goal was to create a sustainable women’s football industry. “If the industry is strong, then financially it will be good for the clubs, for the players and for the entire support system around women’s football, which will also continue to improve,” he said.

title: Michelin Guide South Australia 2027: first stars awarded to 11 top restaurants
description: Magill Estate Restaurant was awarded two stars, while 10 other restaurants in the Australian state received one star each from the guide.
content: The Michelin Guide has handed out its first-ever stars in Australia to 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia. Two Michelin stars were awarded on October 14 to Magill Estate Restaurant, which overlooks the Penfolds winery in the Adelaide foothills. Owned by chef Scott Huggins, it serves tasting experiences for up to A$375 (US$260) per person. Among those awarded one star were Aurora at ILA, based in an arts space co-founded by financial restructuring lawyer and former hedge fund partner Nicholas Dunstone, as well as Restaurant Botanic, operated by the hospitality group founded by businessmen Steve Blanco and Christopher Horner. More than 70 other restaurants were selected for inclusion in the guide. Restaurants in Adelaide’s central business district, as well as wine-growing regions of McLaren Vale, Adelaide Hills and Barossa Valley, featured heavily on the list. The push for a guide was driven by South Australia’s government, which national broadcaster ABC reported paid for Michelin inspectors to visit the state. The South Australian Tourism Commission said in a statement that the agreement with Michelin is “commercial in confidence”, adding that the inspectors’ selection process was independent. It has been previously reported that some organisations in the US have struck similar deals to draw attention to their food scenes. Australia’s neighbour New Zealand was included in the guide in July after its government reached a NZ$6.3 million (US$3.5 million) multi-year deal with the French tyre company, which created the guide more than a century ago as a road-trip companion. South Australia is now the first destination in the country to be featured in the culinary guide. State Premier Peter Malinauskas said in a statement that the inclusion “cemented our standing as an international culinary leader”. Michelin Guide’s international director, Gwendal Poullennec, said South Australia’s food scene was marked by its “sheer diversity”. Under Michelin’s rating system, one-star restaurants are “worth a stop”, two-star eateries are “worth a detour” and three-Michelin-star spots like Singapore’s Odette and Hong Kong’s Amber are deemed worthy centrepieces for a trip. The Michelin Guide South Australia 2027 full list Two Michelin stars Magill Estate Restaurant, Rosslyn Park One Michelin star Anvers Restaurant, Kangarilla Aptos, Stirling Arkhe, Adelaide Aurora at ILA, Adelaide Botanic, Adelaide Esmay, Adelaide Hentley Farm, Seppeltsfield LVN Restaurant at Bird in Hand, Woodside Maxwell Restaurant, McLaren Vale Skillogalee Barrel House, Sevenhill

title: 6 arrested over HK$14m agarwood and crypto investment scam that ran for 9 years
description: BBB Group allegedly offered fake agarwood, crypto and car-wash ‘investment’ plans before SFC placed firm on watch list.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested six people allegedly tied to a nine-year scam run by a suspected cross-border criminal syndicate offering business opportunities in agarwood and cryptocurrency, with funds involved reaching HK$14 million (US$1.78 million). Superintendent Allan Chu Ming-lun of the commercial crime bureau said on Thursday that investigations began in September after the force received 21 reports from victims, mostly elderly people, saying they had been investing in various products offered by BBB Group (Hong Kong) as early as 2017. “The firm involved would use various excuses to delay investors’ cash withdrawals, in a bid to evade their responsibility of paying them back,” Chu said. Most of the victims were aged between 52 and 82. Individual investment amounts ranged from HK$30,000 to HK$1.9 million, with the total from the 21 victims reaching HK$14 million. Chu said the victims had invested with BBB Group, which claimed to operate offices around the world, including in Malaysia, Singapore and New York. The company was placed on the Securities and Futures Commission’s alert list on Wednesday. Other firms deemed linked to the agarwood investment plan, namely BBB Group (Malaysia) and BBB Oud Living (HK), were also listed. Police arrested two men and four women aged between 52 and 66 on Wednesday. Among the six, one was a Malaysian passport holder who was identified as the mastermind of the scheme. The remaining five suspects are Hong Kong residents. Officers searched the firm’s premises in Kwun Tong, seizing about HK$540,000 in cash, 25 laptops and mobile phones, investment contracts and various types of suspected agarwood goods. BBB Group had claimed to run multiple large agarwood plantations in Malaysia and worked with other companies in the country to produce and sell products made from the fragrant wood, such as essential oils and tea leaves. “Core syndicate members brought investors on field trips to the agarwood plantations to boost their confidence,” Chu said. The company branched out to offer at least four types of “investment” plans to victims between 2017 and this year, the superintendent said. The firm also allegedly organised investment talks, trips to mainland China and galas for investors and their friends. The first investment plan was rolled out in 2020, with the firm telling investors they could make HK$300 per month by making a HK$10,000 purchase of an agarwood tree, which would amount to an annual return of 36 per cent over three years. Investors were told they could get back the principal investment in full as well, according to police. “The monthly returns were recorded in the form of membership points in a mobile app provided by the company involved,” Chu said. But investors would have to complete fund withdrawals at the firm’s office, the superintendent added. However, starting in 2024, some investors realised they could not retrieve their principal investment or returns, the force explained. BBB Group staff allegedly then introduced other investment plans while delaying withdrawal requests, inviting the victims to switch to new schemes. One plan, introduced last year, offered the chance for investors to become “licensees” of BBB Group. They would have the right to promote the firm’s products and were guaranteed to receive HK$210 in interest that would amount to an annual return of 25 per cent over a three-year period, with the principal retrievable at the end, according to police. “Interest disbursement for the IP scheme only continued for two months, before the company used different excuses to delay cash outs and interest disbursements,” Chu said. The same tactic was used again this year, when the company rolled out a cryptocurrency called iBBB, which it claimed tokenised agarwood trees. “The value of iBBB has been plummeting since its roll-out, and has dropped by 99.92 per cent till now,” Chu said. The superintendent said the firm recently introduced another plan, investing in automated car-washing stations on the mainland. To lure in existing investors, the firm allegedly offered a bonus of 10 to 30 per cent of the new investment amount.

title: Hong Kong teenager pleads guilty to acid attack on Singaporean tourist
description: Anson Kew, who was 17 during the Wan Chai assault, offers no explanation for targeting the 36-year-old victim during her visit to the city.
content: A 19-year-old teenager has admitted splashing corrosive liquid on a Singaporean tourist in Hong Kong last year, leaving her with second-degree burns. The High Court on Thursday heard the guilty plea from Anson Kew, who was 17 when he threw a corrosive solution at 36-year-old Jiang Wen, who was visiting the city, on June 9 last year. Jiang was getting into a vehicle in Wan Chai when Kew, dressed in black and wearing a mask, ambushed her. She screamed in pain and collapsed after feeling an intense burning sensation on her face and legs, as Kew fled the scene. Kew surrendered at a police station two days later but remained silent during questioning, offering no explanation for the attack. At Thursday’s hearing, Kew pleaded guilty to one count of throwing corrosive fluid with intent to cause grievous bodily harm. Mr Justice Andrew Chan Hing-wai adjourned sentencing to October 29. A police investigation revealed Kew had scouted the location days before the attack. Security footage captured him observing and pacing along Burrows Street in Wan Chai. After the attack, police retrieved a bottle containing traces of corrosive liquid at a back alley in the area. A government chemist’s report showed the liquid contained sulphuric acid with a concentration of not less than 90 per cent – a level capable of causing severe skin burns and permanent visual damage. Jiang was rushed to hospital immediately after the attack. Medical reports showed that 10 to 11 per cent of her body surface suffered burns, mainly affecting her face and limbs. She underwent emergency surgery, followed by skin grafts and additional suturing. Jiang remained in hospital for two months before returning to Singapore for further medical care.

title: US wants to ‘compete’ in Central Asia, ambassador says ahead of Rubio visit
description: American companies aim to play a bigger role in the region’s mining sector, Sergio Gor says, as Chinese influence grows.
content: The US wants to “compete” in resource-rich Central Asia, a senior American official has said as Secretary of State Marco Rubio prepares to head to a region of growing Chinese influence. In New Delhi on Thursday, US ambassador to India Sergio Gor said this weekend’s C5+1 ministerial meeting between the five Central Asian countries and the US in Uzbekistan would be an opportunity to “showcase American ingenuity, American technology”. Rubio would be joined by representatives from more than 200 American companies to “explore possibilities where they could work together”, Gor told the Bloomberg New Economy Forum. “You have countries that are extremely rich in critical minerals there, and yet it’s been untapped,” said Gor, who is also the US special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs. “Partnering with United States companies is a win-win situation – you have some of the richest deposits in Central Asia, and they’re looking for reliable, trusted partners. And we believe American companies can offer those solutions.‘’ “So for us, we want to be able to compete,” Gor said, without directly naming China, a major player in the region’s mineral industry. “These governments are sovereign nations; they’ll decide what’s best for them. But we genuinely believe we do have the best technology, and showcasing that to this region is incredibly important to this administration.” In Samarkand, Rubio is expected to join his counterparts from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan in discussions on deepening regional economic connectivity and improving energy security. Rubio would also meet other senior officials from all five Central Asian nations, “ushering in a new era of strengthened commercial cooperation for the United States and Central Asia”, the State Department said on Wednesday. Established in 2015, the C5+1 is the main platform through which the US engages collectively with the countries of Central Asia. It was expanded to include a summit last year, when US President Donald Trump hosted the countries’ leaders at the White House in November. With its vast resources and strategic location between major markets in Europe and Asia, Central Asia has emerged as a major geopolitical battleground as Washington pushes to build a non-Chinese supply chain for green energy and defence manufacturing. According to the US Department of Commerce, Central Asia holds a major share of global reserves in several essential minerals, including manganese ore, titanium and cobalt, which are essential for artificial intelligence, electric vehicles and clean energy. In recent years, Beijing has steadily expanded its footprint in the region in an effort to secure economic opportunities, establish a geopolitical buffer against Western pressure and maintain stability along its western border. China launched a biennial summit mechanism in 2023, when Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted the first China-Central Asia summit, inking deals over everything from law enforcement and security to defence and renewable energy. The second summit was held last year in Astana, the capital of Kazakhstan. Acknowledging Washington’s historical absence from Central Asia, Gor admitted on Thursday that the US had neglected the region “for too long”. “Everybody focused on the Middle East. Everyone focused on the East. And you have these incredible countries in the middle that have not been, frankly, approached by the United States, so this is not a partisan issue, but you have countries in the middle there that do want to engage with the United States.” To signal Washington’s renewed focus, Trump has invited the leaders of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to attend the Group of 20 summit in Miami this December, a first for the Central Asian nations.

title: Shenzhen offers discount fares, other perks to keep residents off roads during Apec summit
description: The southern Chinese city is set to face enormous traffic pressure when representatives from 21 Apec economies meet next month.
content: Shenzhen residents have been encouraged to work from home and reduce their driving during the coming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, as the local government unveiled logistics arrangements for one of the year’s biggest events. The measures included “flexible work arrangements” and “green travel policies”, as the city seeks to balance “high-standard support for foreign affairs activities” and “smooth operation of the economy and society”, Chan Yaodong, deputy secretary general of the municipal government, said at a press conference on Thursday. During the work week from November 16 to 20, when several Apec events will take place, companies are encouraged to allow staff to work from home. For roles requiring on-site operations, employers can adopt staggered and flexible schedules, Hao Shifei, deputy head of the city’s human resources authority, said on Thursday. Hao added that firms can also choose to allow eligible staff to take paid annual leave during the summit period. The southern Chinese city is set to face enormous traffic pressure when representatives from 21 Apec economies – including the US and Russia – will meet to discuss regional issues. The Apec CEO summit will be held in Shenzhen from November 17 to 18, while the leaders’ summit is scheduled for November 18 to 19. To reduce congestion on roads, Shenzhen is appealing to residents to voluntarily reduce private vehicle usage. Xu Wei, deputy director of the city’s transport department, said on Thursday that those who apply online to suspend driving private cars would receive commemorative car stickers for Apec, as well as a local public transport card with a pre-loaded balance. Public sector bodies will take the lead in opting for eco-friendly travel. Government agencies and state-owned enterprises will take 90 per cent of their vehicles off the road, excluding those directly involved in event support tasks, Xu said. Meanwhile, the city is boosting the frequency of public transport and offering a 50 per cent discount on subway and bus fares during the event. Metro headway intervals on certain lines will be as short as 2 minutes, with standby trains ready to deploy during peak demand. For buses, more than 50 new feeder lines connecting to metro stations will be launched, according to Xu. Shenzhen will be the third Chinese city to host the Apec meeting, after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014.

title: Meet Selma Blair’s boyfriend, Andy Kiernan, who urged fans to pray for her after airport arrest
description: Kiernan, who reportedly runs a film production company and has kept a low profile, spoke out after the Cruel Intentions star was charged with two counts of assault.
content: Following news of Selma Blair’s in-flight outburst and her arrest, the Legally Blonde star’s on-again, off-again boyfriend Andy Kiernan has asked fans to pray for the actress. “Pray for Selma,” he wrote on his Instagram Stories. “She has a good heart. She hasn’t yet got the help she needs. Pray that she does. She’s a human being like the rest of us.” Blair was apprehended on October 11 at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York for allegedly assaulting two Delta Air Lines flight attendants. She also allegedly attacked a police officer and a nurse when she was taken into custody and was being transported to a hospital. The 54-year-old has been charged with two counts of second-degree assault and has pleaded not guilty to both charges. CBS reported that she was released on bail pending her next hearing on January 19, 2027. Blair’s publicist said the actress, who was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018, “experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct”. Here’s everything you need to know about Selma Blair’s boyfriend Andy Kiernan. What does Andy Kiernan do? Andy Kiernan is reported to be a businessman and the co-founder of The Kiernan Group. While there is little information on Kiernan, he is seemingly also the founder and head of entertainment at Kiernan Films, a production company based in Los Angeles, per his Instagram and LinkedIn accounts. His relationship with Selma Blair In a 2024 interview with Us Weekly, Blair opened up about her relationship with Kiernan, whose identity at the time was still a mystery. “He’s wonderful,” Blair told the magazine at the time. “He’s not in this business, although he has produced before. I wanted a Midwest man and I found a real Midwest man,” the Cruel Intentions actress continued. “I saw him from across a table and now he’s my boyfriend. [I think] relationships are best kept out of [the] press if possible. Nobody wants to be exposed to scrutiny.” Following her interview with Us Weekly, Blair and Kiernan marked their first public appearance when they were spotted at the Los Angeles International Airport in July 2024. In the same interview, Blair also noted that despite her relationship with Kiernan, she had no plans to tie the knot again. “Fitting anything in as a mother wanting to build a career and figure out when you’re going to get your blood treatments in – a boyfriend falls by the wayside really easily. That’s why I would never want to get married. It’s a major set-up to fail.” Blair was married to musician and writer Ahmet Zappa between 2004 and 2006. In 2011, she welcomed her only child, son Arthur, with her then-boyfriend Jason Bleick.

title: EU leaders clash over trillion-euro budget as fears grow over French election fallout
description: The summit hits an initial impasse as Germany leads fiscal hardliners against calls for fresh spending, with 2027 French election looming.
content: EU leaders locked horns on Thursday over the bloc’s next long-term budget as they kicked off talks in Brussels under pressure to seal a deal before several high-stakes elections next year, most crucially in France. The 27-nation European Union wants an agreement by Christmas, worried that any future deal-making will be derailed by potential Eurosceptic wins across the bloc, including in France where the far-right’s Marine Le Pen is favoured in opinion polls. “We are facing very, very difficult negotiations,” Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters as he arrived at the summit talks. Leaders are “still very far apart”, he added, suggesting they “pack a few extra shirts” for a final summit meeting set for December. The fear is that without a year-end deal, the already fraught talks could get much harder. Le Pen wants to slash the country’s contribution to the EU budget to help cost savings in the bloc’s second-biggest economy. Putting the screws on the EU, Le Pen travelled to Brussels on the eve of the summit to warn of a “democratic scandal” if leaders adopted a budget before French voters head to the polls in April and May. The nearly two-trillion-euro budget (US$2.2 trillion) will determine the EU’s main priorities for the period from 2028 to 2034, from agriculture and defence to competitiveness and migration. Leaders must agree on how much to give to farmers, what to spend on defence, how to make the economy more competitive against the United States and China, and whether to pour European money into migrant “return hubs” in Africa. EU leaders appeared to be losing faith in an agreement by December, as the latest draft conclusions dated Wednesday call for only a “timely agreement” rather than setting a deadline “by the end of the year”, as in an earlier version. Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency, presented the latest proposal that will form the basis of the talks, with cuts of around 140 billion euros (US$157 billion) to the budget total. But sealing a deal is a steep challenge, with three opposing camps all unhappy at what is on the table – each for their own reasons. On one side is Germany, leading a group known as the frugals that includes the Netherlands and Sweden, which demand cuts of several hundred billion euros. “This is not even a starting point for these discussions. This is far too big, far too expensive,” Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said of the draft. In another corner is France, which opposes massive cuts to the budget and believes the continent needs a larger pot to match the rising challenges it faces. French President Emmanuel Macron did not address reporters upon arrival in Brussels, but Paris has made clear it is not happy. A French official warned there could be no agreement without “substantial” new bloc-wide taxes, including on large companies, environmental taxation and levies on tobacco. Paris also wants EU-wide taxes on digital services, cryptoassets and online gambling, which the European Parliament also seeks. And in the third camp are the “Friends of Cohesion”, demanding more funding specifically to support agriculture and regional development. “The proposal is clearly insufficient,” said Spain’s Pedro Sanchez, maintaining that the money on the table was “far short” of what was needed for the bloc to respond to the many challenges it faces. European Council President Antonio Costa will lead negotiations in the countdown to December, with an extraordinary meeting added in late November to help get the budget over the line. The sense of urgency is real, with elections looming in Italy, Poland, Greece and Finland as well as France. Even if Le Pen is just a candidate at this stage, a European diplomat said “she’ll be in the room tomorrow” with the leaders, as her potential victory hangs over their talks. No agreement before France votes in April and May would mean the negotiations restart in the summer, which a second EU diplomat said would be “an awful exercise”.

title: ‘Booking overlap’ forces Hong Kong Pride Parade to cancel indoor market
description: Rainbow Market was due to be held on November 14, with organisers saying venue had no alternative space available that month.
content: The Hong Kong Pride Parade committee has cancelled an indoor event at Central Market next month after being told the venue is unavailable due to an “administrative error”. In a social media post on Thursday, the committee said its Rainbow Market, scheduled for November 14 at the revamped landmark, had been cancelled because the venue “could no longer host it”. The group said it approached Central Market, which is managed by Chinachem Group, in early June, confirmed the booking and paid a deposit in July, before announcing event details in late August. “Just over a month later, Central Market told us the venue could not be rented to Hong Kong Pride after all,” the group said. “The reason given was an administrative error: staff had booked the same day for two different events.” It said Chinachem, which operates Central Market, had no other space available in November. In response to inquiries from the South China Morning Post, Chinachem said the venue was unavailable because of a “booking overlap”. “The organiser was notified as soon as possible, and a full refund was arranged,” it said. “We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience caused.” The company added that it had reviewed its booking and management procedures and implemented improvements to prevent similar incidents from recurring. The committee has been recruiting vendors and volunteers for the event since last month. This year’s market carries the theme “Step Out for All, Show Up With Pride”. The group said it was the second time a space had fallen through after it announced event details. The committee successfully held the indoor market last year at co-working space The Wave in Kwun Tong, but the event was not without hurdles. It had originally planned an outdoor Rainbow Festival at Kwun Tong Promenade, but cancelled it after being told the space was closed because of “construction work”. Early this year, The Wave told the group it “could not rent the space again”, prompting the committee to look for alternatives. The group has held an indoor Rainbow Market in place of its annual pride parade since 2021, saying “the social climate has changed”. It has nevertheless stressed that the event “mattered to this city”. “At home, it helps build a culture that is friendly to sexual and gender minorities; abroad, it affirms Hong Kong as a progressive international city,” it said. The committee added that it would do “everything it can” to keep the event alive. Another pride event, a fitness showcase titled Rainbow Strength, will still be held at an unannounced venue in Kwun Tong on November 7, according to the group. “Thank you for standing with us for the equal rights of sexual and gender minorities, and we are sorry to everyone affected,” it said. “The space keeps moving. We are not going anywhere.” The Hong Kong Pride Parade comprises four local LGBTQ groups: Les Corner Empowerment Association, Rainbow of Hong Kong, the Association for Transgender Rights and Made in Gender. This year, Pink Dot HK was forced to cancel Hong Kong’s largest annual LGBTQ carnival for the second year in a row after property manager Link Reit withdrew its offer to rent Stanley Plaza and Murray House one month before the event. It instead held an online live-streamed concert last month, similar to its 2025 event, after West Kowloon Cultural District’s Art Park said the venue could not be rented to the group without giving an explanation.

title: Hong Kong police arrest pair after HK$80,000 Tai Po gold necklace theft
description: Man in his forties caught in same district within 24 hours after fleeing store on Kwong Fuk Road.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a man and a woman after he allegedly stole a gold necklace worth nearly HK$80,000 (US$10,193) from a Chow Sang Sang jewellery store in Tai Po. The man was tracked down in the same district on Thursday afternoon, but only half of the necklace has been recovered. The unemployed 37-year-old entered the store on Kwong Fuk Road at about 3.10pm on Wednesday. Believed to be financially strapped, he carried out the theft without attempting to cover his face. After asking to try on a 60-gram gold necklace he allegedly snatched it, fled towards Kwong Fuk Lane and boarded an airport-bound bus, only to disembark shortly afterwards. The Tai Po resident was stopped on the street in the district on Thursday afternoon. Police said his friend, a woman, was later arrested in the district on suspicion of handling stolen goods. About half of the necklace had reportedly been sold to a gold shop in Sha Tin. The man was not believed to be armed, and no property was damaged during the incident. Police launched a district-wide search immediately after the theft. Jewellery store thefts are rare in Hong Kong, especially in largely residential districts such as Tai Po.

title: China’s Iraq War ‘safe haven’ restaurant film of real people to represent country at Oscars
description: Director Wen Muye states that Chinese cuisine – with its emphasis on gathering and sharing – shares a natural, intrinsic connection to peace.
content: A mainland-produced film about a Chinese restaurant in Baghdad that became a wartime refuge has been selected as China’s entry for next year’s Oscars, bringing global attention to untold stories from the Iraq War. Directed by Wen Muye and starring Shen Teng and Jiang Qiming, Once Upon a Time in the Middle East became a box-office hit after its domestic release in China in August, earning more than 2.3 billion yuan (US$344 million). The film follows Xu Fu, a chef who travels to the Middle East to repay his debts and opens a Chinese restaurant with a local partner. When war breaks out, the eatery becomes a safe haven for children displaced by the conflict. On October 7, the film was announced as China’s submission in the Best International Feature Film category at next year’s 99th Academy Awards. It draws inspiration from the real-life experiences of Chinese entrepreneurs in Iraq, including Chen Xianzhong, an Arabic-language graduate of Peking University. Chen first arrived in Iraq in 1984 as an interpreter for a Chinese company. He was among the tens of thousands of Chinese workers who went to Iraq during that period, most of whom were employed by Chinese engineering and construction firms. After moving into business, he opened Yan Long Wan, Baghdad’s first Chinese restaurant, shortly after the Iraq War broke out in 2003. For Chen, running a restaurant offered Chinese migrants with limited resources a way to integrate into Iraqi society. “Everyone needs to eat,” he told mainland media. With a bar attached, the restaurant became an unlikely neutral ground amid the violence. Chen sheltered foreign journalists, local doctors, children and Chinese workers stranded by the conflict. In 2004, he helped rescue seven kidnapped Chinese workers, providing them with food and accommodation. Today, Chen is retired and based mainly in Beijing, but he still returns to Baghdad occasionally to support friends’ businesses and advise Chinese companies operating in Iraq. Another entrepreneur whose wartime experiences helped shape the film was Liu Lei. In 2003, Liu left his software job in Shenzhen and travelled to Baghdad in search of business opportunities. He opened the Chinese Dragon Restaurant, where he served Kung Pao Chicken, fried rice and wine to US soldiers and employees of international organisations. Liu and his partner reportedly earned more than 3 million yuan (US$450,000) in a year. But the war soon revealed its human cost. Liu’s partner recalled a young US soldier who often spoke about wanting to return home and his frustration with the war. Liu also sheltered a Japanese anti-war activist who worked at the restaurant and used leftover ingredients to prepare meals for war orphans. After a suicide bombing near the restaurant killed more than 50 people, Liu and his partner closed the business and returned to China as the US military tightened security measures. On September 30, the US formally withdrew its remaining troops from Iraq, concluding more than two decades of military involvement in the country. Rather than focusing on military operations, Once Upon a Time in the Middle East portrays the war through the experiences of civilians navigating daily life amid the conflict. In a public speech, director Wen said that Chinese cuisine, with its emphasis on gathering and sharing, has a natural connection to peace. Through the image of a dining table, he hopes the film will remind audiences that “If people can sit down and share a meal, they should not go to war. War destroys lives and leaves no true winners.” One online commenter wrote: “This film is a winner in my heart, even without an award. If leaders could share a meal and think about the next generation, the world would be a better place.”

title: China keen to strengthen North Korea trade ties with New Yalu River Bridge opening
description: Premier Li Qiang says the cross-border project is a landmark and a chance to expand port clearance between the two countries.
content: China’s premier has reaffirmed his country’s support for North Korea and its leader during the much-delayed opening of a new bridge between the neighbours. In a taped speech to the opening ceremony on the New Yalu River Bridge on Thursday, Premier Li Qiang said the link was a landmark in Chinese-North Korean friendship. Li said the bridge would promote economic and trade ties, expand personnel exchanges and tighten the bond between the two peoples, according to state news agency Xinhua. The four-lane bridge connects Dandong in the northeastern province of Liaoning with the North Korean border city of Sinuiju. Until now, traffic between the two cities has been restricted to the single-lane Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, an ageing bottleneck that cannot support trucks weighing more than 20 tonnes. Work started on the new bridge in December 2010 and was completed in October 2014. Authorities have not explained the delay in the opening. The ceremony on Thursday included trucks decorated with flowers and national flags crossing the span. The event was closed to the public and authorities did not say who attended. In his speech, Li said he expected that both sides would take the opening as an opportunity to improve port clearance, raise the level of connectivity and tap into the potential for border region cooperation. “Under the strategic guidance of the top leaders of both [ruling] parties and nations, China-North Korea relations are entering a new stage and opening a new chapter,” Li said in the video. Quoting Chinese President Xi Jinping, Li reaffirmed Beijing’s unshakeable commitment to its traditional friendship with Pyongyang, its support for Kim Jong-un’s leadership, and its resolve to safeguard their common interests and strategic environment, regardless of international shifts. Li said the bridge was an important cross-border infrastructure project jointly valued and promoted by both leaders. North Korean Premier Pak Thae-song also delivered a video speech to the event, Xinhua reported, though the content of his address was not released. The opening of the bridge has also drawn close attention from South Korea. An official from South Korea’s Ministry of Unification said that the opening was the first tangible implementation of the agreements reached at the North Korea-China summit in June. Seoul was monitoring whether this would lead to substantive measures to further promote North Korea-China relations, South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency reported. Xi visited North Korea in June, following a visit by Kim to Beijing in September last year.

title: Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 raises researcher fears the Chinese model can fake AI safety tests
description: Researchers say the model’s apparent awareness of how it and successor versions are trained could undermine safety evaluations.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence lab Z.ai’s latest flagship model, GLM-5.3, may be sophisticated enough to “fake” its way through safety tests, according to a new report published Thursday, sparking new fears about the ability of artificial intelligence systems to shape their own development. The model, launched in August, showed an ability to consider how its behaviour during safety evaluations might influence how future versions of itself would be trained, according to AI safety organisation Apollo Research. This phenomenon, referred to as “update-aware reasoning” by researchers Axel Hojmark and Ezra Newman, was unprompted and could lead to “alignment faking”, a scenario where the AI systems comply during training to hide their true objectives until deployment, they said. “These reasoning patterns should make us more wary about RSI,” Hojmark told the South China Morning Post, referring to “recursive self-improvement”, the prospect of AI systems progressively improving through successive rounds of development with no human involvement. Although GLM-5.3 was not observed independently modifying its training process or improving its capabilities, Apollo warned that the model’s apparent awareness of how it and successor versions were trained and developed could eventually undermine the effectiveness of safety evaluations. In one evaluation, GLM-5.3 was given a flawed test in which it did not have to give a correct solution to pass. However, the model did not exploit this, reasoning that providing an incorrect answer might undermine future versions of itself, which the researchers said was in itself a risky feature. In one experiment, GLM-5.3 considered circumventing a shutdown mechanism to complete its task, but reasoned that doing so could establish a dangerous precedent for future AI systems. The report said that update-aware reasoning was observed in roughly one to two out of every 1,000 evaluation runs, though this was “likely an underestimate.” Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday. The findings come as risks associated with rapidly advancing AI models have drawn the attention of global policymakers, including in Beijing and Washington, which have agreed to launch a bilateral dialogue to manage such risks. Leading Chinese and US AI companies have made RSI a stated goal. During an earnings briefing on August 31, Z.ai founder Tang Jie said its next-generation GLM-6 model was headed towards “self-evolution”. The company said last month that it would allocate about 60 per cent of its recent US$5 billion round of fundraising to develop next-generation GLM foundation models and a “fully self-training system”. In the US, OpenAI said in September that it aimed to build an automated AI researcher capable of advancing deep-learning research and described its GPT-6 Astra model as “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model”. The Apollo researchers also tested five other open-weight models – DeepSeek V4 Pro, Qwen3.8 2.4T, Kimi K3, Gemma 4 31B and Nemotron 3 Ultra – across 8,000 combined runs without detecting the same behaviour, although they cautioned that the sample was too small to establish a statistically significant difference. Other developers might more easily distil from GLM-5.3, and update-aware reasoning could therefore persist and spread more readily to future model generations Axel Hojmark, Apollo Research The Qwen models were developed by Alibaba Group Holding, which owns the SCMP. However, the tests do not mean the other models carried no risks. In June, Singapore-based Neo Research found similar “evaluation awareness” traits in Kimi K2.6, developed by Beijing-based start-up Moonshot AI. “The fact that [GLM-5.3] is open-weight means other developers might more easily distil from GLM-5.3, and update-aware reasoning could therefore persist and spread more readily to future model generations,” Hojmark said. The underlying parameters of open-weight models are publicly released for anyone to download, as opposed to closed-source models like OpenAI’s GPT, which cannot be easily modified. Z.ai has been devoting resources to mitigating risks. Last month, it released a report along with Beijing-based safety consultancy Concordia AI on different ways to make open-weight AI safer by design. On Tuesday, Li Zixuan, head of global operations at Z.ai, said its GLM models helped uncover 23 vulnerabilities in Microsoft Windows. Microsoft has acknowledged Z.ai’s contributions on its website. In July, Tang said Z.ai would invest in AI safety-related work and participate in international AI governance work, the SCMP reported.

title: Meet Susan Dell, wife of Dell billionaire Michael, derided for her ‘Maga makeover’
description: Her White House appearance alongside US president Donald Trump has sparked a major online reaction, focusing on her looks rather than her US$6.25bn pledge for American children.
content: On October 7, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell visited the White House with his philanthropist wife, Susan, to discuss the couple’s US$6.25 billion pledge for the “Trump Accounts” initiative. The Dells pledged the amount last December, and Michael Dell said that their contribution had already funded 10 million investment and retirement accounts for US children under 18 with social security numbers. Susan Dell spoke further about the impact their funding has had on children and their caretakers. “It’s not just the money that matters … Knowing someone believes in you and your future, that matters just as much,” she remarked, impressing US President Donald Trump, who jokingly offered her his “complete and total endorsement” if she ever ran for office. Susan Dell’s latest outing, however, sparked a major reaction online, with internet users targeting the 62-year-old over her appearance and speculating about a potential “Maga makeover” and her “Mar-a-Lago face.” In response, her 61-year-old billionaire husband – who is currently the fifth-richest person in the world, according to Forbes – shared social media posts condemning the trolls and highlighting the couple’s philanthropy. 🫡🇺🇸 https://t.co/87qsrhRgB1 — Michael Dell 🇺🇸 (@MichaelDell) October 11, 2026 So, what else do we know about Susan Dell? What’s her background? Susan Dell (née Lieberman) hails from Dallas, Texas, where she lived in Russwood Acres, per Encyclopedia.com. Her father was Zelig “Zeke” Lieberman, a cancer surgeon at Baylor University Medical Centre. Her family was well-off, and she attended W.T. White High School in Dallas before studying fashion design and merchandising at Arizona State University. How did she meet Michael Dell? In February 1988, Susan Dell was working in property development at Trammell Crow in Austin, Texas, when a client introduced her to Michael Dell, per People. “He was the nicest guy I’d ever met,” Dell recalled in an interview with Texas Monthly. The couple married on October 28, 1989, and went on to have daughters Alexa, Kira and Juliette and son Zachary together. Alexa is married to Frédéric Choquette, the COO of financial technology company Rain; Juliette’s husband, Chase Chamberlin, is the founder of Commonwealth Sports; Kira is the CEO of Adaptive Water, which focuses on water sustainability; and Zachary is the founder of technology company Base Power. What does she do for work? Susan Dell is the co-founder and chair of the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation. According to her bio on the foundation’s website, she is an entrepreneur, fashion designer and athlete. She has launched three fashion brands, including the luxury label Phi, which was founded in 2003 and shut down in 2010, per WWD. Dell is also known for taking part in the Ironman World Championships. She was inducted into the Texas Women’s Hall of Fame in 2019, and in 2025, she received the History-Making Texan Award from the Texas State History Museum Foundation.

title: As Negeri Sembilan royal crisis persists, Malaysian rulers, government urged to step in
description: The deadlock has led to a change in the state government and prompted Malaysia’s Conference of Rulers to call for a ‘dignified solution’.
content: Malaysia’s powerful Conference of Rulers and the government need to intervene and find a solution to the months-long royal stand-off in Negeri Sembilan and constitutional limbo over the status of the state’s ruler, according to political analysts. Negeri Sembilan’s royal house has been locked in a bitter deadlock since April over whether incumbent Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir or his proposed replacement, Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar, is the rightful ruler. The feud has taken down a state government aligned with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition and left its newly appointed chief minister without a state executive council. The crisis has forced the Conference of Rulers to call for restraint on Wednesday and for the competing sides to find a “dignified solution” that would not undermine the state monarchy. “The throne carries a responsibility to the state and its people,” the rulers said in a rare joint statement. The Conference of Rulers, which comprises the heads of Malaysia’s nine royal households, including from Negeri Sembilan, also warned politicians against taking advantage of the current crisis to further their agenda. “The issue must under no circumstances be used as a political tool, a means of garnering support, an opportunity to expand influence or a platform for pursuing power struggles,” they said in the statement issued after their meeting in Kuala Lumpur. Analysts, however, say that the Negeri Sembilan feud has gone past the point of reaching an amicable solution, especially since it has spilt into the public and political spheres.
