Political parties had jumped on the bandwagon to push their own interests, as seen in the August 1 state election, which saw Malay nationalist party Umno wrest power from PH, said Azmi Hassan, a senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research. “I think the Conference of Rulers should take steps to decide whether to keep the status quo or resolve it once and for all,” Azmi said. Umno triggered the state election after its 14 elected representatives in June withdrew support for the PH-led state government, claiming that it did not respect an April proclamation by Negeri Sembilan’s four territorial chieftains to remove Muhriz from the throne on allegations of misconduct. Unlike the other monarchies in the country that decide succession by birthright, Negeri Sembilan’s ruler is elected by four chieftains, known as undangs. The palace and the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang – the state’s highest customary council – dismissed the proclamation, arguing there was no basis for the claims of misconduct and that two of the four undangs had already been removed before the decision was made. The four purported undangs have since filed an application for a judicial review with the Seremban High Court seeking to compel the chief minister to enforce the proclamation. Despite the fallout, Muhriz consented to the appointment of state Umno veteran Ismail Lasim as chief minister on August 2, and a few days later approved the appointment of 10 state executive councillors, mostly from Umno. Barely a month into office, the executive councillors issued a joint statement validating the April proclamation and instructing the state secretary to execute protocols to remove Muhriz. This forced the federal attorney general’s chambers to issue a statement warning that the move was unconstitutional. Muhriz later sacked the entire executive council for going against their oath of office. The extent of the constitutional quagmire in Negeri Sembilan makes it necessary for the government to step in to push for a legally enforceable solution, according to political analyst Syaza Farhana Mohamad Shukri. Syaza, an associate professor of political science with the International Islamic University of Malaysia, said the courts would be the best arbiter of how the state constitution should be interpreted – and by extension, who gets to sit on the throne. “I think further intervention is needed, and that is precisely the role of the judiciary,” she said.

title: CTF Media eyes events expansion as traditional TV and broadband growth stagnates
description: Company previously known as i-Cable Communications outlines strategy to capture new markets following renewal of free-to-air licence.
content: Revamped CTF Media and Entertainment, which holds one of Hong Kong’s three free-to-air television licences, plans to expand its focus beyond TV programmes and broadband to entertainment and the sports economy as its traditional businesses stagnate. Revealing the new logo of the company previously known as i-Cable Communications, CEO and executive director Ivy Wong Nga-fan listed its five core areas going forward: event organisation and investment; celebrity merchandising and e-commerce; integrated market solutions; broadband and television. “The five pillars will help us expand our revenue, and we are looking to develop new business models in every area,” she said on Thursday. CTF Media and Entertainment was renamed in August and is controlled by Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, the private investment venture of the family of tycoon Henry Cheng Kar-shun. The private company also controls New World Development and the operator of Hong Kong’s flagship Kai Tak Sports Park. On Tuesday, the government renewed the free-to-air television licence of i-Cable HOY, a subsidiary of CTF Media and Entertainment, for 12 years, alongside those of TVB and HK Television Entertainment Company, which operates ViuTV. The investment amount pledged by i-Cable HOY for the first six years of the renewed period was the lowest among the three, standing at HK$950 million (US$121 million), compared with HK$6.2 billion by TVB and HK$2.3 billion by HK Television Entertainment. Wong said on Thursday that the HK$950 million was the minimum amount and the actual investment would be higher. She added that the company’s focus had switched from cost-cutting to revenue expansion after she became CEO in January. “Objectively, we cannot expand our broadband business by much as the internet population of Hong Kong is stable, so this is a lukewarm sector. Television, likewise, will not offer much growth either,” she said. “So we will keep these two core sectors and grow them slowly, and seek big expansion in our new businesses.” Wong said she expected the event sector would become the company’s largest source of income, but it would also look at cultivating an ecosystem surrounding major events, including artist collaborations, merchandise retail and hosting post-event parties. The licence renewals also came with new requirements, with authorities doubling the weekly minimum time for national education content to one hour. Licensees must also air English-language shows to “tell the good stories of Hong Kong” for at least one hour per week. Asked how the company would fulfil these requirements, Wong said that while its free TV channels would continue to promote national education, the requirement for English-language shows aligned with its strategy. “Our chairman has always believed that telling good stories of Hong Kong should not be done in Cantonese, but in a way comfortable with foreigners,” she said referring to Cheng. “That is why we have been investing in English-language programme production.” Wong added that these programmes would feature Cantopop, local culture, tourism and cuisine. The company will also revamp its three free TV channels later this month, with its current English finance channel HOY76 to be transformed into a sports-focused channel, supplemented with news and finance programmes in English. Wong said the decision was made after seeing a huge demand for sports among local audiences, especially following the recent Asian Games in Japan, for which i-Cable HOY was the sole franchised broadcaster in Hong Kong. The other two channels, HOY77 and 78, will focus on entertainment and news, respectively.

title: Seoul to maintain Ukraine aid despite spat over North Korea prisoner transfer
description: Seoul reassures allies that aid will continue as efforts proceed to resolve the row over Zelensky’s disclosure of the POW repatriation.
content: South Korea will continue supporting Ukraine “as a responsible member of the international community” despite a diplomatic dispute over the disclosure of two North Korean prisoners of war being repatriated to the South, a foreign ministry official said on Thursday. The official said Seoul would treat its help to Ukraine separately from the dispute, while continuing bilateral consultations to resolve outstanding issues. The remarks came after South Korean Ambassador to Ukraine Park Ki-chang was recalled to Seoul on Saturday, following a spat over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s public disclosure of the transfer during his UN General Assembly speech on September 23. The ambassador’s recall was one of several options Seoul considered after the disclosure, which it says breached a confidentiality arrangement intended to protect the soldiers and their families in North Korea. President Lee Jae Myung has demanded that Kyiv acknowledge the agreement and publicly apologise, warning of “additional measures” if it refuses. Kyiv has denied such an understanding existed. Meanwhile, the foreign ministry official also said three European countries had expressed hope that South Korea would continue supporting Ukraine and offered to help ease tensions between Seoul and Kyiv. The countries were not identified. The exchanges took place during separate high-level contacts with each country, rather than through a coordinated approach by the European governments. While the official said the messages did not constitute expressions of concern, they could reflect unease that Seoul’s recall of its ambassador might weaken international cooperation in supporting Ukraine against Russia. The unusual disclosure of high-level diplomatic exchanges could also be seen as an effort by the ministry to reaffirm South Korea’s commitment to continued assistance. Read the full story at The Korea Times

title: Hong Kong’s Lingnan University scraps English exit test for graduation
description: Undergraduates will take internal courses instead of exit exams, as university dismisses concerns over standards.
content: Lingnan University in Hong Kong has scrapped its requirement for undergraduates to pass an English proficiency test before graduating, replacing it with internal language classes. The move has sparked concerns among some observers that the change was intended to accommodate students who struggle to meet international standards. Lau Chi-pang, special adviser to the president on publicity, confirmed on Thursday that the university no longer saw a need for an exit exam, noting that 99 per cent of undergraduates had passed the requirement since the test was introduced. An announcement issued by the university earlier this week said its senate had approved a revision to the English language graduation requirement introduced in 2017. “Under the revised policy, undergraduate students must meet this requirement by completing the required English Language Enhancement Curriculum rather than meeting external benchmarks such as International English Language Testing System [IELTS] or the Password Test, etc with immediate effect,” it said. The change means undergraduates no longer have to take an external English test to demonstrate their proficiency. Lau noted that some students had previously been forced to defer graduation because they were unable to fulfil the English requirement. He said the benchmark test was introduced in 2017 in response to criticism from the Quality Assurance Council, a semi-autonomous non-statutory body under the University Grants Committee, over students’ English proficiency. “Since the introduction of the mandatory tests, 99 per cent of our students have passed the requirements and only a handful of students failed,” he said. A social media user who posted the announcement suggested that the move may be related to non-local students from mainland China being unable to meet the tests’ English standards. Another user, Jeanz0385, expressed frustration that university students were struggling to meet Lingnan’s basic IELTS requirement. “An IELTS score of 6.5 is honestly way too high for them. Requiring mainland Chinese students to get an IELTS 6.5 is literally asking for the impossible … they call themselves university students but have had four full years to prepare and still failed to hit basic requirements,” Jeanz0385 said. “The university lowering the bar this much … how useless are these graduates going to be?” However, Lau dismissed such speculation, stating that non-local students admitted to Lingnan University achieved excellent results in the gaokao, China’s national college entrance examination, and that their English proficiency was sometimes higher than that of local students. The university previously said the exit test requirement was intended to “ensure graduates attain an appropriate level of competency in English before graduation”. Under the previous framework, an overall band score of 6.5 in IELTS (Academic) was set as the default English language graduation requirement. Students majoring in Chinese were required to score at least 6.0, while students majoring in contemporary English studies, translation, cross-cultural studies, and corporate communication had to attain at least 7.0. Alternatively, students could also take an exam known as the Password Test to fulfil the requirement. Other public universities in Hong Kong require students to take English language courses and pass the associated course requirements.

title: TSMC confirms talks with Elon Musk over Texas ‘Terafab’ but insists on operational control
description: The negotiations underscore TSMC’s push to expand production and satisfy insatiable demand for AI chips from key clients like Nvidia.
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) is in discussions regarding a potential role in Elon Musk’s proposed Terafab project in Texas, according to company chairman and CEO C.C. Wei, although he stressed that TSMC would retain operational control of any partner factory. The plant “has got to be run by TSMC”, Wei said during the third-quarter earnings call on Thursday. TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, has sent teams to Texas to assess expansion opportunities beyond its US hub in Arizona, Wei said. He noted that the company was discussing with a potential Terafab customer whether it would use manufacturing capacity at the Texas complex, amid surging demand from major US customers who are urging the Taiwan-based to expand its US footprint. However, discussions had yielded no firm conclusion so far, Wei said. The ownership structure and scope of TSMC’s potential involvement remained unclear. The Terafab project is designed to manufacture high-performance chips to power Musk’s expanding ecosystem in artificial intelligence and robotics. Musk acknowledged the initial talks in an October 3 post on X, writing: “Just discussions, but something may come of it”. On October 7, Musk said Tesla and SpaceX intended to “build and run” the Terafab complex themselves, while leaving the door open for TSMC to sublease a portion of the site. The negotiations underscore TSMC’s broader push to expand production and satisfy insatiable demand for advanced AI semiconductors from key clients like Nvidia. In July, TSMC pledged an additional US$100 billion to expand its Arizona operations, bringing its total planned investment there to US$265 billion. The spending will support more lines for chips at 2 nanometres and below, as well as advanced packaging facilities. North American customers accounted for 79 per cent of TSMC’s third-quarter revenue, up from 76 per cent a year earlier. The share contributed by customers in mainland China fell to 5 per cent from 8 per cent. TSMC reported a record quarterly net profit of NT$763.1 billion (US$23.9 billion), up 68.7 per cent from a year earlier, while revenue rose 50.9 per cent to NT$1.49 trillion, or US$46.72 billion. High-performance computing, which includes AI chips and data centre processors, accounted for 68 per cent of revenue, compared with 57 per cent a year earlier. “We did not see any sign of slowdown,” Wei said of AI demand, adding that customer requirements continued to exceed TSMC’s ability to supply chips. The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion, implying growth of about 14 per cent from the third-quarter midpoint. Chief financial officer Wendell Huang said on the call that capital spending from 2026 to 2028 would be significantly higher than in the preceding three years, though he declined to provide specific annual figures beyond this year. TSMC maintained its capital spending forecast for this year at US$60 billion to US$64 billion.

title: AI use fuels frustration as Hong Kong customer service complaints top 2025 total
description: Consumer Council logs 3,078 complaints in first nine months of 2026, exceeding last year’s total of 2,715, with many involving firms’ AI use.
content: The Hong Kong public’s dissatisfaction with customer service is growing, with complaints in the first nine months of the year already exceeding the total for 2025 and many involving companies’ overreliance on artificial intelligence (AI). The Consumer Council received 3,078 complaints about traders’ customer service between January and September, compared with 2,715 for the whole of last year and 2,173 in 2024. “Among the consumer complaints received by the Consumer Council each year, many involved dissatisfaction with traders’ customer service, with common issues including being unable to contact customer service staff, lack of courtesy and slow follow-up,” the watchdog said. “Such complaints [this year] have already exceeded the total for the whole of last year. This reflects a gap between the quality of customer service provided by traders and consumers’ expectations, resulting in ongoing disputes.” The council said AI-powered systems had failed to provide adequate help in many cases. “Traders should also provide consumers with clear guidance on how to use such services, enabling them to better enjoy the convenience that technology offers,” it said. One complaint involved a consumer unable to use a HK$400 (US$51) event ticket because of a No 8 typhoon signal. The consumer contacted the company the following day to request a change of date, but its AI customer service system could not process the request. Attempts to reach a human representative through the online chat service were unsuccessful, and calls to the hotline went unanswered. During mediation by the council, the company explained that the complaint had not been referred to a human representative because the consumer had neither specifically asked to “speak to a human agent” nor selected “specialist service” in the online chat. The case was later resolved. Another complaint involved a consumer who discovered that his new broadband contract was more expensive. He called the sales representative the next day but received no answer. He then contacted the company’s customer service hotline, where staff told him only the salesperson could amend the contract and promised to arrange a callback. The representative never called back. The case was resolved with a refund after the council intervened. The council advised consumers to ask to speak to a human customer service representative or contact the trader through other channels if an AI system could not provide appropriate help.

title: 5 of the best things to do in Hong Kong this long weekend, October 16-19
description: Get yourself inked up, watch a ballet performance, indulge in an immersive yoga programme, or catch a road movie this holiday weekend.
content: Mid-October is a tease for Halloween fans – spooky season feels tantalisingly near, yet still just out of reach. Luckily, Hong Kong offers plenty to keep you busy until then, and remember that Monday is a public holiday. Whether you are after a new piece of ink, a perfect pour-over, a night at the ballet or a deeper stretch, there is more than one way to fill the long weekend. 1. Hong Kong China International Tattoo Exhibition 2026 The Hong Kong China International Tattoo Exhibition 2026 will be hosted at Soho House in Sheung Wan from October 16 to 18, bringing together top tattooists from around the world for a three-day celebration of ink artistry. Visitors can browse more than 60 tattoo booths to get new designs inked on the spot, while enjoying food, drink and live entertainment. A highlight of the event is the tattoo competition, which showcases impressive work from participating artists. Beyond the public-facing activities, the convention serves as an industry hub where tattoo artists can connect with traders for supplies, accessories and merchandise. The convention is the brainchild of Malaysian-born Hong Kong tattoo artist Gabe Shum, who has run Freedom Tattoo since 2000 and has left his mark on celebrities such as David Beckham and LeBron James. For more information and ticketing, click here. Soho House, 33 Des Voeux Road West, Sheung Wan. 2. PMQ Coffee Agenda Coffee Agenda is back for its 2026 edition, and this year’s festival brings together more than 50 local and international coffee lifestyle brands across two floors from October 16 to 19. There will be four themed zones to explore. #Personality invites visitors on a flavour quest to uncover their coffee profile – whether that is the refinement of a pour-over, the bold creativity of a signature drink or the comforting warmth of a milk coffee. #Lifestyle explores coffee’s intersection with music, film, design and craftsmanship, while #Professional brings award-winning international baristas and Hong Kong’s emerging brewers together for brewing and latte art showdowns. #Journey traces coffee from seed to cup, with a Roaster Village showcasing global origins and local farming stories. Tickets are required, but tasting sets are also available, which include a day pass, a tasting cup and coupons. For more information and ticketing, click here. PMQ, 35 Aberdeen Street, Central 3. Dunhuang: In Search of Light The Hong Kong Ballet is set to unveil its production of Dunhuang: In Search of Light, a world-premiere original ballet running from October 16 to 18 at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre’s Grand Theatre, in Tsim Sha Tsui. Co-commissioned by the Greater Bay Area International Theatre Festival, the production marks Hong Kong Ballet’s first collaboration with the Dunhuang Academy, bringing the essence of the Mogao Caves – a Unesco World Heritage site – to the stage. The Hong Kong Sinfonietta will be performing live with musicians from the Hong Kong Gaudeamus Dunhuang Ensemble. Inspired by Hermann Hesse’s Nobel Prize-winning novel Siddhartha (1922), the ballet follows a seeker’s spiritual journey across the Silk Road, encountering temptation, loss and eventual enlightenment. For more information and ticketing, click here. Grand Theatre, Hong Kong Cultural Centre, 10 Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui 4. Yoga Wheel Immersion Pure Yoga is hosting a three-day yoga wheel immersion workshop with yoga instructor Vinod Kumar from October 17 to 19 in Kwun Tong. Designed for practitioners of all levels, the immersion teaches participants how to use the yoga wheel to improve posture, deepen their practice, and explore creative ways to integrate the prop into their personal routines. The immersion is structured around three themed sessions. Day one uses the wheel as a supportive and dynamic tool to safely open tight hips, lengthen hamstrings and release lower-body tension with targeted techniques for deep tissue release. Day two focuses on opening the chest and shoulders, decompressing the spine during backbends, while day three builds stability for arm balances and inversions or handstands. For more information and ticketing, click here. Pure Yoga apm, 25/F, Millennium City 5, 418 Kwun Tong Road, Kwun Tong 5. Good Trip In Good Trip, a father and daughter’s impromptu final excursion unfolds as a deceptively playful comedy road movie. It tackles one of the most agonising subjects a family can face – the impending death of a parent – with surprising, life-affirming levity. Co-directed by Norris Wong Yee-lam (The Lyricist Wannabe) – who also wrote the screenplay – and Wong Hoi (Let It Ghost), and produced by the acclaimed filmmaker Mabel Cheung Yuen-ting, the film avoids unbearable sentimentality; it is instead anchored by the relaxed, lived-in charm of its two leads, Nick Cheung Ka-fai and Chung Suet-ying. By blending naturalistic performances with heartwarming humour, Good Trip delivers a meditation on mortality that is almost too tender to be true. Read the full review here. Good Trip is in cinemas now.

title: Could Trump join Xi and Putin for 3-way meeting at next month’s Apec summit?
description: Foreign ministers Wang Yi and Sergey Lavrov say they discussed relations with the US during their latest meeting in Baku.
content: The foreign ministers of China and Russia have discussed their relations with the United States, paving the ground for a possible meeting between their respective leaders at next month’s Apec summit in Shenzhen. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, met in Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan, on Wednesday, where they discussed “relations with the United States and the developments involving the Ukraine and Iran crises as well”, according to Moscow. China did not explicitly mention those issues. The dynamics between the three powers are widely seen as pivotal to the global order, not least because of Russia’s war against Ukraine and the US conflict with Iran. US President Donald Trump wrote on social media on Wednesday that he did not believe China and Russia were helping Iran “at all”. Last week Trump spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin by telephone and announced that the Kremlin had agreed to “immediately supply” more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global markets, with further shipments to follow. The deal drew criticism from Trump’s domestic opponents and US allies, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky saying he felt betrayed. About two weeks earlier, Chinese President Xi Jinping met Trump in Washington, where the pair agreed to extend their trade truce and stabilise relations “on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity”. Beijing and Moscow are preparing for the next summit between the two presidents, expected to take place during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen next month, where Xi and Trump are also expected to meet. The gathering, which will bring together leaders from the Pacific Rim’s 21 member economies, has also been seen as a possible stage for a three-way summit between Trump, Xi and Putin. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that such a meeting would be highly beneficial, but it remained unclear whether their schedules would align and what its agenda might be, according to Russia’s Tass news agency. In his meeting with Wang, Lavrov said Putin looked forward to “another conversation with his counterpart and friend” Xi at the Apec summit. The Chinese foreign ministry also announced that Premier Li Qiang would visit Russia next week and would meet his Russian counterpart Mikhail Mishustin. Wang said in a video released by Moscow that the summit would give Xi and Putin an opportunity to exchange views, adding that Beijing welcomed dialogue with the Russian leader. “The two sides also coordinated their positions on the next steps in China-Russia high-level exchanges and on international and regional hotspot issues of common concern, reaching a new consensus,” the Chinese foreign ministry added. Wang and Lavrov met on the sidelines of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia, an intergovernmental forum dedicated to strengthening cooperation, peace, security and stability across the continent. Lavrov said Russia and China’s strategic partnership played “an important stabilising role” on the international stage. “Our positions on most regional, international and global issues either overlap or are very close,” he added. He also said economic ties between the two countries were “making good strides” and “there is no doubt that this year will set another record for bilateral trade”.

title: US-born Bollywood actor Imran Khan told to leave India over political protest: local media
description: The former film star faces expulsion after taking part in a demonstration in Mumbai against the country's election chief.
content: Indian authorities have asked Bollywood actor ⁠Imran Khan to ⁠leave the country by ⁠the end of the month, saying he breached immigration laws after joining a protest against the election commission chief, local media reported on Thursday. Khan, 43, is a US ‌citizen, the Indian Express newspaper reported. Under Indian law, foreigners’ participation in political protests may be treated as a violation of immigration and visa rules. Khan was given until October 28 to leave the country, the Times of India newspaper said. The ⁠actor took part in a rally in Mumbai on Saturday, demanding ‌the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over voter list revisions that critics and opposition parties say favour ‌Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s party. “Apparently I’m going for a ⁠drive,” the ⁠actor wrote on social media on the same day, with a picture of him ‌posing with a victory sign in the back of what looked like a police van. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Imran Khan (@imrankhan) A ‌complaint was filed against him at a police station in Mumbai, ‌saying Khan had breached the law, and the Foreigners Regional Registration ⁠Office, a federal government agency responsible for tracking and monitoring foreign nationals ⁠in India, sent him a notice to leave based on the complaint, the Indian Express said. Khan did not immediately ‌respond to a ‌request for comment. A nephew of actor Aamir Khan and hailing from an illustrious film family, Imran acted in several hit Bollywood films from 2008 to 2015, before suddenly retiring.

title: Hong Kong ranks third globally as philanthropy hub, behind New York and Seoul, study finds
description: Altrata report highlights Hong Kong’s wealth infrastructure and growing culture of structured giving.
content: Hong Kong has emerged as the third best city in the world for wealthy individuals seeking to make philanthropic contributions over the medium term, trailing New York and Seoul, according to a study by Altrata. The inaugural Giving Opportunity Index by the US-based group that tracks the world’s affluent population ranked 100 cities based on three criteria: wealth, donor affinity and philanthropic infrastructure. The study defined the “global wealthy” as individuals with a net worth of more than US$5 million, while “donors” were defined as wealthy individuals who made at least one donation of US$1,000 or more between 2015 and 2025. “Similar to New York, the global financial hub of Hong Kong has a very high concentration of private wealth and extensive family-office and wealth-management infrastructure,” according to the eighth edition of Altrata’s High Net Worth Philanthropy report, including the index, which was released on Thursday. “Recent real estate and finance reforms have bolstered fortunes amid a structural pivot towards facilitating capital linkages with mainland China,” it added. “An established culture of family philanthropy is evolving through more formal giving opportunities, with trusted introductions and local networks still prominent.” Hong Kong scored 47.2 out of 100 in the index, compared with 60 for New York and 49 for Seoul. New York stood out because of its position as the world’s largest wealth market and its large pool of potential major donors, among other factors, the report said. “The city’s extensive philanthropic infrastructure, civic institutions, alumni networks and family foundations make for a sophisticated donor market, and one that is also extremely competitive, underscoring the importance of relationship-building and distinctive gifting propositions,” Altrata said. South Korea’s capital was recognised for its “expanding pool of wealthy potential donors” that was “driving rapid growth of more structured giving channels”. Other Asian cities in the top 10 included Tokyo, which tied with San Francisco for fourth place, and Shenzhen, which ranked 10th. By region, North America’s ultra-wealthy donated US$115 billion to charitable causes in 2025, accounting for about 46 per cent of global giving by this cohort. US donors alone contributed US$107 billion. Europe’s ultra-wealthy extended US$84 billion in 2025, up 35 per cent from 2022. Their counterparts in Asia gave US$34 billion, an increase of 42 per cent from 2022 and the second-fastest rate among regions, as “philanthropic infrastructure continues to expand”, according to the study. The report also found that wealthy women were more actively involved in philanthropy than men despite making up a minority of the global wealthy population. This year, women accounted for about 12 per cent of individuals with a net worth of at least US$30 million and 19.6 per cent of those with a net worth of at least US$5 million, according to Altrata. “There is a clear pattern of more frequent giving activity and across a wider range of causes among wealthy women, irrespective of an individual’s source of wealth,” the report said. “For example, among the global wealthy with self-made fortunes, the median number of gifts in the past decade by female donors was nearly twice that of their male peers.” The ultra-wealthy gave a total of US$250 billion to philanthropic causes in 2025, almost a third more than in 2022. “With public funding in retreat in many countries, philanthropic activity by individuals and corporations is gaining ever greater importance as a source of fundraising income,” Altrata said.

title: Cross-border matchmaking can lead to financial ruin, Chinese police warn rural men
description: Police in Hunan province have warned that men who use illegal agencies to find foreign brides could be defrauded.
content: Authorities in the central Chinese province of Hunan have warned of the potential risks of cross-border arranged marriages, saying some relationships lack genuine emotional foundations and can lead to financial ruin or legal trouble. Marriages can be risky when they are organised by illegal matchmaking agencies that charge high fees, according to a post on the Xintian county police branch’s social media account on Tuesday. For-profit international matchmaking is illegal in China. The post highlighted several risks, including fraud, immigration law violations, cultural conflicts and disputes over the custody of any children that result from the marriage. Xintian police urged the public to pursue only marriages built on genuine affection and to strictly follow immigration rules. The post is part of a broader wave of warnings issued by Chinese embassies and regional authorities – particularly in Hunan and Henan provinces and Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region – urging citizens to exercise caution amid a rise in cross-border bridal scams. In recent years, many men – especially those from rural or low-income backgrounds – have found it difficult to find partners. A major driver of this problem is China’s gender imbalance, as the country has tens of millions more men than women. Xintian is a largely rural, isolated county, which was officially designated as impoverished until 2020. Some Chinese bachelors have turned to international matchmakers, which usually operate in Southeast Asia, Pakistan and former Soviet countries, with African countries such as Egypt and Ethiopia emerging as new destinations. China’s embassies in Malawi and Myanmar have released warnings about the practice. Foreign brides might provide false identity documents, conceal existing marriages or otherwise misrepresent their backgrounds, the Xintian police post said. Others may leave China and cut off contact soon after the grooms pay exorbitant bride prices or matchmaking fees. In China, a bride price is a customary sum of money given to the bride’s family by the groom to show his sincerity and secure the marriage. In other cases, spouses might repeatedly request large amounts of money for purported family expenses, medical treatment or investments, the post said. Immigration and employment violations pose another set of risks. Foreign spouses who overstay their visas or work without the required permits could face fines, detention or deportation, Xintian police said. The authorities also highlighted the difficulties of cross-cultural marriages generally, warning that language barriers and differences in religious beliefs and parenting styles could create tensions and even lead to domestic violence. The post said that if an international marriage broke down, resolving disputes over the custody of children, visitation rights and the children’s nationality could be complicated. Xintian police encouraged the public to report any suspected immigration violations.

title: Indonesians urge Singapore, Malaysia to sue Jakarta as haze blankets region
description: Indonesians have expressed anger over the toxic smoke, with some even calling on foreign governments to impose sanctions on Jakarta.
content: Every time Kristaen Albert returns home, he reaches for one of the dozen cans of oxygen on a table by the entrance of his house in Central Kalimantan. The air in his neighbourhood has turned dusty amber, with air quality far exceeding hazardous levels. “My breathing is noticeably heavier whenever I step outside. It’s hard to concentrate and stay focused, and it is really affecting my work,” Albert, a 31-year-old software engineer, told This Week in Asia. “Living in this haze is awful.” “The government’s response to these devastating wildfires has been incredibly slow,” he said. “To put it bluntly, we are angry.” Albert is among many Indonesians who are urging foreign governments on social media, including those of neighbouring countries affected by the haze, to take action against Jakarta over its handling of the fires. Indonesians were “bowing their heads in regret” over the haze crisis, he said. “Please forgive us. You can help us to sue our government; we will support you.” One social media user called on foreign states and international environmental organisations to “demand accountability” from Jakarta in accordance with the law. “Please don’t turn a blind eye to our suffering,” said the user. “Kalimantan needs your help.” This year’s haze has been fuelled by fires across Indonesia, particularly in Sumatra and Kalimantan, where dry conditions have allowed forest and peatland fires to spread. The toxic smoke has hit Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines, Brunei, Thailand and even as far as Vietnam, as millions of Southeast Asians grapple with one of the worst haze episodes in more than a decade, with many complaining about the adverse health impact. Air quality in Singapore entered the “very unhealthy” range for the first time this year on Wednesday, while the smog has forced schools in several Malaysian states to close. Risayogi Wicaksana, who lives in South Sumatra, told This Week in Asia he felt a sense of accountability and guilt towards other countries because the province was home to numerous haze hotspots. “During the recent Formula 1 races in Malaysia and Singapore, key figures commented on the smoke. I really hoped the issue would then gain greater international attention,” he said. Maxwell Lane, a visiting senior fellow at the Indonesia Studies Programme at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, said the online outcry reflected mounting frustration over what many perceived as an inadequate government response to recent disasters. “You often hear among civil society that they feel the government is cuek [indifferent] to these disasters,” he said. Lane noted that the government had stopped short of declaring recent natural disasters national emergencies, citing floods in Sumatra that killed more than 1,000 people last year and an earthquake in August that displaced tens of thousands in the Flores region. According to Indonesia’s environment ministry on Tuesday, forest fires in the country were expected to be extinguished within a month. President Prabowo Subianto had demanded that all available resources be deployed to accelerate fire prevention efforts, the government’s communications agency said on Monday. Wildfires have been especially intense this year amid El Nino conditions, which some have described as being at “Godzilla-level” intensity, bringing warmer and drier conditions that can exacerbate fires. A trial involving the release of dry ice over South Sumatra to tackle the haze was scheduled for Thursday, Coordinating Security Minister Dudung Abdurachman said. The minister had previously ruled out declaring the prolonged forest fires a national disaster. “Not yet, not yet. We are still capable of handling it,” Dudung said after a cabinet meeting on Monday, according to local media. Singapore and Malaysia have offered to help Indonesia tackle the fires, but Jakarta has reportedly yet to accept their help. Malaysia’s Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said on Sunday that his country had offered a firefighting aircraft, three helicopters and personnel but was still awaiting a response. Abi Victor, a 27-year-old Indonesian, said he was “disappointed” that his country had yet to accept help. “I’m deeply saddened because as ordinary citizens there is little we can do,” he said. An Indonesian official’s remark that Singapore and Malaysia received their oxygen from Jakarta also triggered an online backlash, drawing ridicule and renewed criticism of his government’s handling of forest and peatland fires. “We’re not just sending smoke. If there’s no smoke, we’re sending oxygen. Singapore and Malaysia’s oxygen comes from our forests,” said Syahganda Nainggolan, the newly appointed head of the Government Communication Agency, as quoted by local news outlet Kompas on Saturday. Last month, a coalition of Indonesian civil society groups filed a lawsuit against Prabowo and his officials over their handling of the fires, urging sanctions against those responsible for alleged environmental crimes. Previous similar attempts have met with limited success. Singapore’s Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu said on Wednesday the city state would “keep its options open” on taking legal action against errant companies. Companies found guilty of causing or condoning fires under the 2014 Transboundary Haze Pollution Act can be fined up to S$100,000 (US$77,951) a day, capped at S$2 million in total. When asked if investigations were being conducted, the National Environment Agency (NEA) in Singapore said it was closely monitoring the situation and gathering data on hotspots. Investigations were launched into six Indonesian companies under the act in 2015 following a severe bout of haze, and two cases were closed based on the information provided. Investigations into four companies remained ongoing, said NEA. Singapore’s issuance of summons to several Indonesian companies over the haze in 2015 drew criticism from the then Indonesian government. Risayogi is sceptical of his government’s ability to manage the fires and has also taken to social media to express his frustration, even calling on other countries to impose economic sanctions on Jakarta. “The world needs to know what is happening here,” he said. “Anything that is needed to compel the government to take optimal action in addressing these fires.”

title: HSBC to double Hong Kong AI team to 300, outpacing Singapore plan
description: Bank unveils expansion plan after scrutiny of its Singapore AI hiring strategy.
content: HSBC, Hong Kong’s biggest lender, said on Thursday it would double its artificial intelligence specialist team in the city to 300, a figure much larger than the workforce planned for its recently announced AI centre in Singapore. The announcement comes after Hong Kong’s regulators were reported to have raised concerns about the Singapore hub. The bank would double its AI specialist headcount in Hong Kong from 150 to 300 over the next two to three years, said David Liao Yi-chien, HSBC co-CEO for Asia and the Middle East, in a media briefing after attending an industry event hosted by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). HSBC would also launch the Hong Kong AI Institute next year, he said. “Hong Kong is our home market at HSBC. We are using Hong Kong as the hub to develop our digital finance and embrace new technologies to better serve customers and support Hong Kong’s digital ambitions and growth,” Liao said. Four members of the bank’s 13-member group operating committee were based in Hong Kong, underscoring the city’s importance to HSBC, he added. The remarks marked the lender’s first public comments since it announced plans in late July to set up a Singapore AI centre and hire 100 specialists. A source told the South China Morning Post last week that the HKMA had privately questioned HSBC about the decision. Liao did not confirm the conversation with the HKMA, but said: “HSBC always has positive dialogues with the regulator.” He said HSBC, as an international bank, “will always invest in AI in different markets, including mainland China, the UK and the Middle East, but Hong Kong will always be the core part of that investment”. Hong Kong’s five-year plan, with AI as a pillar of development, “will give us a lot of opportunities”, Liao said. “HSBC has spent over [US$14 billion] on a buyout of shares from subsidiary Hang Seng Bank in January, which represents an important investment in Hong Kong.” Liao spoke on the same day that the HKMA hosted an AI summit and highlighted use cases for the technology in Hong Kong’s finance sector. Hong Kong’s development plan, with AI investment and development identified as a priority, could intensify competition with Singapore, analysts said. The HKMA said on Thursday that 20 banks and 14 technology companies had completed sandbox testing of 27 AI use cases. HSBC alone contributed two use cases, including a language-to-sign-language translator for customers with hearing difficulties, and the use of AI to detect deepfakes during account opening. The de facto central bank also announced new principles for banks’ use of AI, built around what it called the ART framework, which stood for accountability, resilience and trust. Under the principles, which took effect on Thursday, banks must appoint a responsible person for each AI application and maintain records of AI use cases and the associated risk-management measures. In the coming weeks, the HKMA would also introduce a discussion paper on the governance of agentic AI and launch a platform for sharing AI training data, it said. HKMA deputy CEO Arthur Yuen Kwok-hang said the discussion paper would focus on ensuring agentic AI systems operated according to their intended purpose and did not become “rogue agents”. Banks would need a “kill switch” to stop agentic AI systems if they malfunctioned, while also maintaining fallback arrangements that allow human intervention to take over tasks when necessary, Yuen said, adding that the approach was aligned with international practices. “The progression from generative to agentic AI represents an important new stage of innovation for the banking sector,” Yuen said. Under Fintech 2030, the HKMA has encouraged banks to embrace AI, although such development must be supported by effective risk management and governance, he added. “By pairing innovation with clear accountability, resilient operating models and effective human oversight, banks can fully realise the benefits of AI while maintaining the trust and stability of Hong Kong’s financial system,” Yuen said.

title: Macroscope | Why the AI investment boom could spark the next financial crisis
description: The AI ‘everything trade’ looks increasingly shaky as hyperscalers search for external financing, risking debt spillover to other markets.
content: For a truly staggering figure, look no further than an estimate from Columbia Business School Professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh of the cumulative investment in artificial intelligence-related infrastructure by 2032. In a paper last month, Van Nieuwerburgh said the AI buildout could reach US$10.3 trillion, the equivalent of 3.6 per cent of annual US economic output for the next seven years. The average annual capital expenditure dwarfs previous infrastructure booms, including railways, highways and plumbing for the internet. This year alone, the big US “hyperscalers” – the leading technology companies and cloud service providers – will sink more than US$750 billion into capital investments in a race to dominate AI. Since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, the AI boom has evolved from a popular investment theme into a massive economic and financial bet. It has also been the main source of resilience in the global economy and markets. Despite a succession of severe shocks, equity markets stand at a record high, the global economy is growing at its fastest pace since May 2023 and corporate earnings have risen dramatically. In a report on September 25, George Saravelos of Deutsche Bank said the global capital expenditure cycle – which is also driven by the ramp-up in defence spending and investments in building resilient supply chains – is the “superglue holding the market together”. On October 13, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) admitted it had underestimated global growth three years in a row mainly because of the “positive demand shock” from AI. In Bank of America’s latest global fund manager survey on October 13, investors had the biggest overweight position in the technology sector since August 2020. The most talked-about risks to the AI boom pertain to the economics of the technology, specifically whether there will be enough demand from end users quickly enough to justify the enormous sums of money being spent. Another concern is the increasing constraints to the AI buildout, particularly given the fierce backlash against the construction of new data centres in some countries and mounting calls for regulation. However, it is the boom’s profound impact on markets that is the biggest risk in the short to medium term. As a report last month from asset management firm Alliance Bernstein noted, the AI boom has become “the everything trade”. Not only is it “all-consuming in terms of investors’ attention”, “its demand for capital is creating linkages across asset classes that make diversifying AI exposure significantly harder”. Until recently, worries about concentration risk were confined to stock markets. As the hyperscalers’ free cash flows dwindle and force the tech giants to rely on external sources of finance, though, the AI trade has broadened to bond and credit markets. Hyperscalers now account for nearly 10 per cent of total investment grade corporate bond issuance, up from 0.5 per cent in 2024, according to IMF data. Morgan Stanley estimates that credit and corporate debt markets will account for roughly half the global capital expenditure on data centres through 2028. The dramatic shift in the financing of the AI buildout exacerbates vulnerabilities in global markets. As investor portfolios become a one-way bet on AI and the infrastructure buildout increases cross-asset linkages in markets, the probability of the boom triggering the next financial crisis has risen sharply. A disorderly and sustained unravelling of the AI trade would be far more damaging today than just a year ago. The bigger the leverage in the AI ecosystem, the harder the landing in the event of a loss of confidence in the monetisation of the technology. Although the US hyperscalers have strong balance sheets and ample liquidity buffers, the surge in AI-related debt increases the risk of spillovers to broader markets, especially given the build-up of leverage in stock markets amid the rise in interest rates. South Korea is a cautionary tale. The country’s semiconductor-led stock market – the best-performing major market in the first half of this year – has succumbed to a brutal, leverage-driven sell-off, plunging around 34 per cent since June 22. It is now the worst performer among its peers in the second half. Also, the politics, economics and financing of AI are not conducive to a prolonged, multi-year boom. AI doom scenarios are proliferating while Chinese AI model usage overtook US platforms globally for the first time in June. As Van Nieuwerburgh notes, “Long-duration debt and contractual claims are being written against assets whose utilisation, technological relevance and residual value remain unusually uncertain.” At some point, something is bound to break somewhere. Tellingly, global fund managers believe hyperscalers’ capital expenditures are the most likely source of a “systemic credit event”. This does not mean a crisis is imminent. However, the fact that such a massive bet is based on such uncertain foundations is deeply concerning. The “everything trade” is an accident waiting to happen.

title: 33 dead, mostly pupils, in Pakistan after school roof collapse
description: Emergency crews in Peshawar scramble to locate survivors trapped under debris following a fatal structural failure during lessons.
content: The roof of a school collapsed in Pakistan’s northwestern city of Peshawar, killing a teacher and 32 students, mostly aged under 14, health officials said on Thursday, as residents and rescuers scrambled to pull children from the rubble. Twenty more students were taken to hospital after the collapse, which authorities blamed on “weak infrastructure”. Others in the densely populated neighbourhood described a close call. Resident Sohail said “everyone began screaming in panic” after his niece managed to find her way home after escaping the building to tell them of the collapse. “When I arrived at the scene, I saw around 10 to 15 children trapped beneath the rubble, with debris piled up to their necks. We quickly pulled them out,” he said. Asim Khan of Peshawar’s Lady Reading Hospital said the death toll had risen to 33 by Thursday evening, with most of the victims aged between four and 14. “A total of 20 injured children were brought to the hospital, most of whom have been discharged. Three severely injured children, who sustained head injuries, have been admitted to the hospital,” Khan said. The injured and deceased included 12 girls and a female teacher, Khan added. A spokesman for the emergency rescue service in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province said schoolchildren were crushed and trapped after the roof gave way. “When the Rescue 1122 emergency response teams arrived at the scene, they found that one roof had collapsed onto another, causing the classroom below to be crushed and trapping children inside,” spokesman Bilal Ahmad Faizi said. Images released by the emergency services showed rescuers in high-visibility vests scrambling to move debris, rubble and dirt. A senior Peshawar-based official said initial reports suggested the roof collapse was due to “weak infrastructure”. “The school owner has been detained,” the official said on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to talk to the media. Bodies wrapped in white cloth were seen being carried out of the hospital as volunteers arrived to help identify the victims. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed “deep sorrow and grief over the loss of precious lives”, according to a statement. “The Prime Minister extends his condolences to the bereaved families and prays for them to have the strength and patience to bear this irreparable loss,” the statement said. President Asif Ali Zardari described the roof collapse as a “heartbreaking tragedy”. Resident Sher Ahmed blamed “substandard construction materials” for the tragedy and called for an investigation. “With profound grief and sorrow, I urge the authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and take strict action against anyone found responsible so that such tragedies can be prevented in the future,” he said. Roof and building collapses are common in Pakistan, largely due to poor safety standards and substandard construction materials in the South Asian nation of more than 240 million people. In June, more than a dozen children were killed when a roof collapsed at a tutoring centre in the eastern city of Lahore. In 2025, 27 people were killed and 10 injured when a five-storey building collapsed in the impoverished Lyari area of the southern city of Karachi.

title: ‘We’re done’: Ukraine resumes Russian refinery strikes, defying Trump
description: Kyiv targets Ryazan refinery after the Ukrainian leader lashes out at US intelligence cuts and continued Russian strikes on the power grid.
content: Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery ⁠on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites announced by US President Donald Trump, and criticised Trump’s willingness to strike deals with Moscow. By effectively walking away from Trump’s demand that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries and openly criticising the US leader, Zelensky risks deepening the biggest rift between Kyiv and Washington since Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine’s latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, which is owned by state oil major Rosneft and accounts for nearly 5 per cent of Russia’s refinery throughput, helping supply the capital. Regional governor Pavel Malkov said on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack ‌had caused a fire at the refinery. Russian President Vladimir Putin played down the effect of Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russian refineries, saying they had caused “nothing particularly significant”. After Trump’s surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy sites, Kyiv suspended attacks on Russian refineries, which Trump blames for raising diesel prices on global markets. But in the days that followed, Russia rained down missile and drone strikes, including on energy targets such as power stations, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of people. Zelensky’s relations with Trump have been testy, particularly after a February 2025 Oval Office meeting descended into a shouting match. Zelensky has since praised Trump and US help for Ukraine, and in recent days said Ukraine fully backed the energy ceasefire despite waves of Russian attacks. In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelensky said Ukraine’s patience had run out. “The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We’re done,” he told the newspaper. Zelensky also criticised what he ⁠saw as Trump’s willingness to strike deals with Russia, apparent admiration for Putin and an affinity for those wielding power or considerable wealth. “He (Trump) speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people,” the FT quoted him as saying. “Because ‌for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong.” In his comments to the FT, Zelensky also said he believed that changes in the capability of the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink receptors this week, which curbed Ukraine’s ability to pilot its drones, were a policy decision. “It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” he told the ‌FT. British Defence Minister Wes Streeting said on Thursday that he and US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth welcomed the restoration of the Starlink service in Ukraine and called for both sides to “move forward in a collective spirit”. “We ⁠need President Trump engaged on Ukraine. He has been, and the ⁠diplomatic track is as important in ending the war as making sure Ukraine has the weapons it needs to see off Russian aggression,” he said on Fox News. Zelensky was due to attend a European Union summit on Friday and in a series of meetings ahead of the gathering stressed the need to strengthen air ‌defences. In a social media post overnight, SpaceX boss Elon Musk said usage of the military version of Starlink, known as Starshield, was ultimately up to Trump as president of the United States. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote. Although ‌Trump has ‌described the ceasefire as a requirement for both Moscow and Kyiv, his public comments have focused mainly on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, which he said over the weekend had “damn well better stop”. Ukrainians worry that the rift could have severe consequences on the battlefield, ‌where the Ukrainian military still depends on technology provided by Washington. Ukrainian officials say that for several days they have not received the usual warnings, which rely on US satellite detectors, from Western allies about incoming Russian missiles. Trump has denied withholding intelligence. At the same time, military-grade ⁠Starlink receptors have stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory. A source in Ukraine’s defence ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working ⁠when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 160km/h (100mph). Ukrainian officials say that is too slow for mid-range attack missions and interceptor drones that defend against Russian drones. Defence experts said, and a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, meanwhile, showed that Russia had in just six weeks nearly finished building a major base in southern Russia for launching jet-powered drones. Ukraine has been using its long-range drones to target Russian refineries and logistics in recent ‌months, which it says is its only answer to nearly five years ‌of relentless Russian bombardment. The attacks have caused fuel shortages in Russia. Trump is under pressure to lower fuel prices, with his Republicans facing midterm elections in less than three weeks. Prices for diesel have reached record highs since he launched a war against Iran in February, though Trump says the Ukrainian attacks are driving up global prices. In the Black Sea, rescuers searched for seven missing sailors after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze in the latest attack on shipping along a vital route used by Ukraine. The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine’s targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts. It said earlier this week that the scope of the energy ceasefire had never been determined and work was ongoing to do so.

title: Notable Chinese demographer calls for 18-fold increase to nation’s childcare subsidies
description: James Liang says boosting the subsidy is crucial to reversing China’s shrinking population.
content: One of China’s most outspoken demographers has called for raising childcare subsidies to at least 200,000 yuan (US$29,883) per child – more than 18 times the total offered under the current national scheme – to reverse the decline in births and strengthen the country’s long-term economic competitiveness. James Liang, co-founder of Chinese online travel giant Trip.com Group, who has been vocal about Chinese demographics for years, made the proposal in an article published on Wednesday. Experts said this proposal could be a longer-term goal, with funding potentially coming from the central government or through redirecting some special-purpose bond funds. Beijing introduced a nationwide childcare subsidy last year, offering households 3,600 yuan a year for each child born on or after January 1, 2025, until they turn three – a total of 10,800 yuan over three years. Some local governments have also introduced their own subsidies. China recorded 7.92 million births in 2025, down from 12 million in 2020. Liang estimated that 8 million births would correspond to a total fertility rate of about 1.0 children per woman, well below the replacement level of 2.1 required to maintain a stable population, and among the lowest rates in the world. Liang warned that without substantially stronger government support, annual births could fall well below 8 million in the coming years, further threatening domestic demand and the workforce over the long term. Under his proposal, a subsidy of at least 200,000 yuan per child could help raise the fertility rate significantly. By comparison, Norway, known for its generous family policies, offers a monthly child benefit that would total 434,592 kroner (US$45,758) per child over 18 years if the rate remained unchanged, according to the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration. Liang said providing such an amount to 10 million children born in a year would cost about 2 trillion yuan for that birth cohort, equivalent to roughly 1.4 per cent of China’s gross domestic product in 2025. He added the amount would be lower than the 2.13 trillion yuan the country spent on export tax rebates last year. Zhang Hua, the executive director of the Chinese Association for Improving Birth Outcome and Child Development’s inclusive childcare working committee, said he agreed with the need for greater support but considered 200,000 yuan too ambitious as an immediate target. “Looking at the data and cases from other countries and regions cited in his article … you will find it is an overly ambitious target,” Zhang said. “A 200,000 yuan subsidy equals roughly twice per capita GDP and is 3.4 times South Korea’s level of support. No economy in the world has ever reached that level of support.” He suggested treating the figure as a medium- to long-term target towards 2030, with support expanded gradually. Funding could come from the central government, a reallocation of education spending to support children under three, expanded maternity insurance and employer-provided childcare, he said. He cautioned against relying on new local government special bonds, arguing that borrowing over the short term to finance investments in human capital whose returns may take decades to materialise would create fiscal risks. Liang has advocated more generous subsidies for some time. In August, he called for a package worth 62,000 yuan per child, arguing that it could boost China’s fertility rate by 25 per cent over the next couple of years. At the time, he also proposed monthly payments of 1,500 to 2,000 yuan per child until the age of 18 to move the fertility rate closer to the replacement level of about 2.1. Xing Zhaopeng, a senior China strategist at ANZ Research, said the latest proposed amount of 200,000 yuan was manageable when spread over 18 years, equivalent to an average of about 1,000 yuan a month per child. Xing also suggested redirecting some existing government funding allocated to special-purpose bonds. He estimated that the subsidies could cost 2 trillion to 3 trillion yuan a year, roughly half the annual special-purpose bond quota. Liang’s call comes as Chinese policymakers struggle to reverse the country’s population decline, with expanding affordable childcare services becoming a key policy priority as Beijing seeks to ease the burden of raising children on households. More public hospitals are opening childcare centres to expand access to care for young children. Last month, a childcare centre operated by a public hospital in Ganzhou, Jiangxi province, opened with 125 places for children under three. Monthly fees range from 1,400 yuan to 2,000 yuan per child, depending on the age group. Another centre, which opened in Ganzhou’s Shicheng county in March, offers care for children aged six to 36 months, charging up to 750 yuan per month per child.

title: Inside Nepal’s unending cycle of avalanches, floods and landslides
description: Experts warn such events could become an ‘annual occurrence’ and urge the government to rethink its development model.
content: Nepal has weathered three disasters in six weeks, including the deadly August flash flood, making this year one of the deadliest in a country where monsoon rains already frequently wreak havoc. Experts warn that climate change is only making matters worse. The rock-ice avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border that opened the floodgates in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26 killed more than 1,450 people, with nearly 6,000 others still missing. It was followed by a massive landslide after parts of a mountain collapsed into a river in the Mustang region in late September. And on Sunday, another rock-ice avalanche flooded the Budhi Gandaki River – which joins the Trishuli downstream – in central Nepal’s Gorkha district, with concrete-like slush swallowing houses, bridges and trekking trails, though no casualties were reported. “To have two similar events, nearby and in one year, is unprecedented in Nepal,” said John Pomeroy, director of the Centre for Hydrology at Canada’s University of Saskatchewan, who has been following the events. “While climate change did not directly trigger these catastrophes, the thawing of frozen ground, melt of glaciers, increased lubrication of frozen materials from rapid snowmelt and rainfall all destabilised the high mountains and created the preconditions that permitted these events to form.” Nepal’s cycle of disasters – evoking scenes from Hollywood doomsday films – made global headlines this year, but the same places have experienced recurring floods and landslides over the years. Before the August floods, the border area in Rasuwa was washed away in July 2025 after a superglacial lake burst, killing at least nine people. Chame in the north-central district of Manang experienced similar floods and landslides last month and in 2021, and such events have become cyclical in Mustang and Humla districts, both near the Tibetan border. Sudan Bikash Maharjan, a geologist at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, said his team’s analysis showed that only 11 glacial lake flood outbursts (GLOFs) were recorded in the Koshi, Gandaki and Karnali river basins between 2010 and 2019. However, seven such incidents occurred in the 2020-2025 period, suggesting there will be more in the coming years. “The patterns are different, but the cascading effects are making these disasters bigger,” he said. “Such events are increasing compared to before, and this could be an annual occurrence.” Global warning What is happening in Nepal is a warning to the world, as mountain rainfall occurs more frequently and intensely, according to climate scientists. Pomeroy said disasters due to thawing frozen ground, rapid snowmelt and glacier melt were increasing in mountain regions worldwide. He added that countries such as the United States, Switzerland and Canada were seeing related problems, prompting them to develop advanced early warning and hydrological forecasting systems, while GLOFs were occurring more frequently in Nepal, India, China, Central Asia and the Andean nations. “It’s a problem that is spreading globally,” he said. “High mountain regions are often impoverished, poorly serviced by infrastructure, populated by indigenous peoples, bisected by international boundaries, sparsely gauged and monitored, and far away from decision-making centres. This makes them particularly vulnerable to disasters such as those that have befallen Nepal in recent months.” Global events from the past five years alone make the case clear. A massive flood in Chamoli in India’s Uttarakhand state, triggered by a rock-ice avalanche, killed more than 70 people in February 2021. Over 55 died two years later in “one of the most catastrophic GLOFs to hit the Himalayas” in India’s Sikkim state, while a glacier collapse flattened the Swiss village of Blatten in 2025. In Argentina’s El Chalten village, scientists and officials are also watching Nepal’s disasters closely, knowing their mountainous region could face a similar catastrophe. An El Chalten official told The Guardian they were “preparing for the worst-case scenario”. “The disasters we are experiencing in the Himalayas should be an important exercise in learning and warning,” Maharjan said. “We cannot exactly say when or where they might occur, but they will happen.” Environment vs economy Decades of fossil fuel use and human activities have driven greenhouse gas emissions, pushing global temperature to around 1.4 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. And countries like Nepal, with negligible emissions, are paying the price. Losses from the August disaster exceed 408.28 billion rupees (US$2.66 billion). While the new government formed after last year’s youth uprising promised 7 per cent economic growth in the next five years, the World Bank projects growth will slow to 3.7 per cent next year. Arpita Nepal, an economist and director of research and development at Kathmandu’s Samriddhi Foundation think tank, said disasters affected Nepal’s major growth sectors, including energy, tourism and agriculture, and could dent people’s confidence in reinvesting in disaster-prone areas in the long run, creating endemic poverty cycles in those places. “Nepal’s public debt is 45.1 per cent of its GDP, and the current fiscal deficit level is 1.7 per cent of GDP – this implies that we do have fiscal space at the moment to invest in recovery and reconstruction,” she said. “As the number of disasters climbs, our fiscal space to react will contract. However, post-2015 earthquake recovery shows that recovery from a natural disaster is possible and growth can pick up.” But for that, analysts say Nepal should prioritise an ecologically friendly growth model and uphold environmental impact assessments for infrastructure projects, which critics say are largely ignored. The recent disasters have also put a spotlight on the country’s hydropower building spree – a dozen were destroyed in the August flood – largely built on mountainsides to harness electricity from rapid river currents. Sanjaya Devkota, a geoscientist and civil engineer currently heading the Forum for Energy and Environment Development at the Institute of Himalayan Risk Reduction, said Nepal should rethink its development model. He said planning should protect floodplains and natural drainages, establish setbacks based on local hazard assessments, and consider how roads, bridges, embankments, settlements and hydropower projects interacted. “The policy contradiction is that we depend on rivers for energy, agriculture and livelihoods while sometimes allowing development that constricts their space or increases exposure along their banks,” Devkota said. “We should be honest about whether Nepal has fully applied its own lessons. Producing a report after a disaster is useful, but learning becomes meaningful when it changes a road alignment, a construction approval, a warning procedure or a budget before the next event.” While experts call for stronger mitigation measures and the government plans reconstruction, survivors in flood-ravaged Trishuli are left staring at the mounds of mud and debris where their homes once stood. The heartbreak of losing loved ones has given way to fears of displacement and loss of livelihoods. Some are already considering going abroad for employment, a trend that has seen an exodus of young Nepalis, while others have little idea of what comes next. “One really does not recover psychologically from natural disasters – it becomes a collective trauma that we carry,” Nepal said. “Recovery requires demonstrable actions from the state to protect its citizens’ lives and property. [But] if we do not recover economically, then we will be brewing another revolution where citizens will keep looking for political actors who can deliver on their promises. This will make us more politically unstable in the long run.”

title: Q&A | Sofia Coppola on Cartier, Marie Antoinette and her love for Japan
description: We spoke to the Oscar-winning director in Kyoto at Cartier’s launch of the second chapter of the Le Chœur des Pierres high jewellery collection.
content: Cartier unveiled the second chapter of its latest high jewellery collection, Le Chœur des Pierres, at the Kyoto National Museum on Tuesday. Among the new creations are the Panthère Tunya necklace, embellished with emeralds, yellow diamonds, white diamonds and onyx; and the Undara earrings, made of white gold, diamonds and blue spinels. Cartier ambassadors including Jisoo from Blackpink, director Sofia Coppola and Japanese actor Ryo Yoshizawa attended the glamorous event, which culminated in a spellbinding kabuki performance. Style caught up with Coppola before the glittering soirée – and ahead of a Kyoto screening of a restored print of her film Marie Antoinette, presented by the Cartier Cinema Club. How does it feel to be wearing a high jewellery set from Cartier? It feels incredible to wear this high jewellery set. I visited the ateliers so I know how much work goes into these pieces and I’ve never worn anything like this; it’s very special. Tell me about your long-standing relationship with Cartier. Cartier is the ultimate to me; it has so much history and heritage. Getting to visit their archives … It has so much mystique to me and it’s the ultimate in French jewellery and design. I always get excited when I see a red box. As a long-time visitor to Japan, how do you feel being here with Cartier? When they asked if I wanted to come, I was so happy to come here and it’s so special to come to Kyoto. I haven’t been here very much. I always love coming to Japan as it has such a great respect [for] and history with craftsmanship, and just being able to discover new places is just incredible. I’m just thrilled to be here. Can you share a memory of Cartier? I’ve always had a Tank watch and I’ve always loved photos of Yves Saint Laurent wearing a classic Tank, and I’ve always loved their designs. I was also excited when they were relaunching the Panthère watch as that’s a cool era in watches. I also have the Baignoire. I am a fan. Their designs are classics but they’re not too serious and there’s a playfulness to them. Tell me about this year’s 20th anniversary of Marie Antoinette and the Kyoto screening as part of Cartier Cinema Club. I love the Cartier Cinema Club because they support culture and we get to have these screenings. We did one in Paris and now here in Kyoto. I can’t believe it’s been 20 years and that we’re doing a screening here. It’s a restored print of Marie Antoinette and we redid the colours, and I think it looks really beautiful. It still has its look and it’s exciting for me to see it refreshed after all this time and the costumes.

title: Abby Choi’s partner says he never sought sexual relationship with her ex-husband
description: Chris Tam appears surprised when defence counsel suggests he and Alex Kwong were romantically linked while students at international school.
content: The partner of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has denied seeking a sexual relationship with her ex-husband when they were young, saying he only remained in contact because their children shared the same mother. Testifying on Thursday, Chris Tam Fong-chun appeared surprised when a defence lawyer suggested he wanted a “romantic and sexual relationship” with Alex Kwong Kong-chi when they were studying at the same international school. “Definitely disagree,” Tam said after seeking clarification on the question from Kwong’s legal counsel, Andrew Raffell. Kwong, 31, is standing trial in the High Court alongside his father Kwong Kau, 68, and his elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, for allegedly killing the influencer on February 21, 2023. The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the lawful burial of the 28-year-old’s body, an offence to which his two sons pleaded guilty before the trial began last month. Raffell suggested that Tam and Choi maintained a close relationship with Alex Kwong after 2015, the year when he and the influencer started divorce proceedings and when the defendant absconded to mainland China to evade criminal proceedings arising from a HK$6.3 million theft case. The lawyer further claimed that Choi begged her former partner to return to Hong Kong in June 2022 because she was jealous he had a girlfriend. Tam said he did not know if the influencer was jealous, adding that he did not recall ever discussing with Alex Kwong the girlfriend he met across the border. The witness said it was reasonable for the trio to remain close because of the children. Choi gave birth to two children during her first marriage to Kwong, and had two more with Tam after they started dating in late 2015. “However you want to put it, Kwong Kong-chi’s children and our children are siblings, so if you’re saying our relationship was good, that was because of the children, they were what we valued most,” Tam told the court.
