Prosecutors alleged that Kwong Kau resented Choi for trying to sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the upmarket Kadooria development in Ho Man Tin that was registered in his name. Tam said on Tuesday that the two families clashed at the flat in mid-2022, during which Kwong Kau twice tried to attack Choi while calling her a “birthing machine”, prompting her to bar him from visiting the home or seeing his grandchildren. During cross-examination on Thursday, Raffell questioned whether Tam and Choi were pretending to be on friendly terms with Alex Kwong after the row so he would help persuade his father to agree to the sale of the flat. Tam dismissed the allegation but acknowledged he was “a bit sneaky” by maintaining a friendly appearance in front of his former schoolmate. “This was something unavoidable. The flat is something that belongs to us. Instead of challenging him head-on, we tried to take it back amicably,” he said. Kwong Kau’s lawyer, Oliver Davies, argued that his client had contributed half of the Kadooria flat’s HK$60 million purchase price when it was bought in 2019 for Choi’s two children with Alex Kwong. He also contended that Choi and Tam were not as wealthy as the prosecution had portrayed them. Tam rejected Davies’ contention that neither he nor Choi could afford to repay a HK$5 million loan he took out while gambling in Macau in August 2021, but said his father had ultimately decided to settle it on his behalf after being harassed by debt collectors. He said his father had also sought help from Kwong Kau because of the former police officer’s connections. He confirmed that Kwong Kau received no reward for his help. Asked why he refused to repay the loan, Tam maintained he was not obliged to do so because he believed the casino, run by Suncity Group, was about to cease operations. “This is human nature. Let alone HK$5 million, you wouldn’t want to pay even HK$50,000 if you knew [the moneylender] was going to cease operations, would you?” he added. Davies also challenged Tam’s account of the family row, saying his client’s anger towards Choi was understandable because she had yelled at his wife. He also maintained that Kwong Kau had not come into physical contact with Choi during the altercation. Tam acknowledged that he had not included every detail of the row in his written statements to police, but insisted that his testimony about Kwong Kau’s behaviour was true. “What I saw was that he was completely overwhelmed by anger. He was completely out of control,” he said. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: 8 old wives’ tales about colds and how to avoid them, from vitamin C to sleep to warm beer
description: From drinking warm beer to sweating it out, experts break down which popular cold remedies actually work and which myths to abandon.
content: Colds may be spreading where you are as the end of the year nears, and they are usually followed by plenty of tips on staying well – but are any of them worth your while? We asked scientists whether we should drink warm beer, head to the sauna, take vitamin C supplements and more. 1. If you let yourself get cold, will you catch a cold? This is partly true. However, feeling cold does not automatically make you ill, which requires viruses. “It is true that your body’s defences are weakened to some extent if you get chilled or feel cold,” says Dr Eva Hummers of the Institute of General Medicine at the University Medical Centre Goettingen, in Germany, and president of the German Society of General Practice and Family Medicine. People also say not to go out into the cold with wet hair and that makes sense, too. “You lose a lot of heat quickly through your head,” Hummers says. However, again, no viruses, no cold. “Conversely, dressing extra warmly won’t prevent you from catching a cold either.” 2. Does taking vitamin C supplements regularly prevent colds? No. “We have known for a long time from research that vitamin C supplements cannot prevent colds,” says Sonja Siegert, deputy editor-in-chief of the Health Information Department at the Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care in Germany. However, taking vitamin C regularly can shorten cold symptoms by around 10 per cent, for example, from 10 days to nine. “If you only start taking vitamin C once the cold has set in, studies have shown that it has no effect,” Siegert says. As a general rule, it is easy to meet the recommended vitamin C intake through diet, according to the German Nutrition Society (DGE). Good sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits, peppers, cabbage and potatoes. DGE specialists say there is no reason to take vitamin C supplements as a matter of routine. 3. Are rest and sleep not the best medicine? That is partly true. If you don’t get enough sleep, you become more susceptible to infections. “When you’re ill, it definitely makes sense to listen to your body and get some rest,” Hummers says. This does not mean you have to stay in bed with a cold if you don’t feel like it. A brief relaxed walk is fine, though she says to avoid strenuous exercise at all costs. 4. Can ice soothe a sore throat? Yes. The coldness of ice has a mild pain-relieving effect and helps many patients with a sore throat and anyone with a fever, according to Hummers. Try frozen applesauce, ice cream or fruit yogurt as alternatives. However, if you eat so much that you start to feel cold, you have gone too far. 5. Is warm beer an effective home remedy for colds? No. Hummers is not aware that warm beer helps with a cold. Alcoholic drinks are generally not recommended when you have a cold. Alcohol dehydrates the body and, by increasing blood flow to the blood vessels, causes us to cool down more quickly – which is counterproductive. Hummers’ advice is if you want something warm, “you’re better off having a cup of tea”. 6. Can nasal sprays be addictive? This is partly true. With nasal sprays, check carefully exactly what you are spraying, as the ingredients vary widely. “Nasal sprays, which often help well with colds, cause the mucous membranes to constrict, clearing a blocked nose and allowing you to breathe more easily again,” Hummers says. This is achieved by active ingredients such as xylometazoline and oxymetazoline. However, over time, these active ingredients can damage your mucous membranes. “It actually swells up even more, and you end up needing the spray all the time,” Hummers says. “It’s a kind of addiction.” Don’t use decongestant nasal sprays for more than a week – this is usually the advice in the package leaflet. “One trick to wean yourself off them is to always spray into one nostril each time,” Hummers says. You can generally use nasal sprays containing saline solution, nasal rinses and similar products without any concerns. However, they have a slightly different effect – they loosen your mucus and moisturise your nasal mucous membrane, but they don’t reduce swelling. 7. Can you ‘sweat out’ colds? No. “If you’re already shivering because of the cold, however, a woollen blanket can help the body raise its temperature. The resulting rise is, after all, a defence mechanism,” Hummers says. Avoid going to a sauna when you have a cold, as it can tax the body. However, Hummers says healthy people who use the sauna regularly accustom their bodies to rapid temperature changes, which may make them less prone to illness overall. 8. Can you shorten a cold’s duration? No. Colds usually clear up on their own within one to two weeks, and there is no way to speed up the process. “You can only alleviate the symptoms, for example with painkillers or nasal sprays,” Siegert says. “A cough caused by a cold can last up to eight weeks without this being a cause for concern in otherwise healthy people,” Hummers says. If you have a cold that will not shift, she recommends drinking plenty of fluids, not smoking and ensuring the air is as clean as possible. Clean indoor air reduces the spread of cold viruses and lessens symptom severity by lowering airborne irritants that trigger inflammation, according to the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

title: 1,000 Hongkongers to ride Baidu’s autonomous vehicles in city-first public trial
description: Baidu’s Apollo Go platform will offer free rides to Tung Chung residents from October 21 to November 3, as company seeks public feedback.
content: More than 1,000 residents are expected to ride in autonomous vehicles (AVs) after Chinese technology giant Baidu launches Hong Kong’s first large-scale public trial next week. Baidu’s autonomous driving platform for consumers, Apollo Go, will run the trial in Tung Chung from October 21 to November 3, inviting more than 1,000 residents to take part. Iris Wong Man-hei, senior project and business development manager for Baidu’s intelligent driving group, described the trial as a “milestone” for the city’s autonomous driving sector. “Through the public test rides, we hope to show Tung Chung residents and the wider Hong Kong public the latest achievements of our autonomous driving technology and our high safety standards,” she said. “We also hope to gather real-world feedback to drive the adoption of the technology in Hong Kong, laying a solid foundation for our autonomous fleet to join the city’s public transport system and move towards regular operations.” Wong said the company would collect feedback through questionnaires to help improve the technology. The trial route is a 5.1km (3.2-mile) loop that takes about 15 minutes. It starts at Yat Tung Estate’s car park 1 and ends at the Sheraton Hong Kong Tung Chung Hotel, with no stops along the way. Each autonomous vehicle can carry up to two passengers, who must be taller than 1.35 metres (four feet, five inches), or aged eight or above, with the front passenger seat left empty. The vehicles do not have barrier-free features, so passengers with limited mobility have been asked to take extra care. Each vehicle will carry a backup operator with an average of 10 years’ driving experience and at least 100 hours of autonomous driving training to respond to emergencies, according to Wong. For example, operators could pull over to the roadside in an emergency and evacuate passengers once safe, she said, adding that the company monitored the vehicles remotely from its control centre. During a test ride with a South China Morning Post reporter on Thursday, the operator kept his hands off the steering wheel and took control only when a large rubbish bag blew towards the vehicle. A touch screen between the rear seats allows passengers to adjust the air conditioning, seats and windows, and lock the doors. The Transport Department issued Baidu a pilot licence for autonomous vehicles in 2024. The company’s testing districts have since been expanded from Airport Island to North Lantau, Kowloon East and Southern district. In July, the department also approved driverless tests on Airport Island, with no in-vehicle backup operators. Baidu collaborated with rail operator the MTR Corporation and the Airport Authority in August to conduct a road test of a transfer service between Hong Kong West Kowloon station and the Airport Express Kowloon station. The company’s autonomous vehicles have travelled more than 280,000km (174,000 miles) safely in Hong Kong so far. This story has been updated to correct the name of Baidu’s autonomous driving platform from Apollo to Apollo Go

title: Hong Kong firm, Qatar bank to launch Chinese equity fund to lure Middle East capital
description: China’s rising AI and biotech sectors are key draws for investors seeking diversification, leaders of ChinaAMC and Lesha Bank say.
content: China Asset Management (Hong Kong) and Qatar’s Lesha Bank agreed on Wednesday to launch Qatar’s first sharia-compliant China equity fund, highlighting growing efforts by Chinese financial institutions to lure Middle East capital as institutional investors and wealthy families seek safe havens amid geopolitical turmoil. Among the key selling points of the mainland China and Hong Kong stock markets for Middle East investors are the mainland’s rising artificial intelligence capabilities and biotech strength, which provide needed diversification from the “crowded” US market, according to top executives of the firms. Domiciled in the Cayman Islands, the fund – potentially as large as US$1 billion – would be structured to provide qualified high-net-worth investors in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries direct exposure to mainland-listed shares and Hong Kong equities, the companies said. The GCC comprises Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. The tie-up built on recent diplomatic and economic outreach, including Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po’s official visit to the Middle East last month, which helped cement the city’s role as a vital financial connector between mainland China and Gulf capital markets, according to ChinaAMC. With initial seeding of US$50 million, the fund could increase to as much as US$1 billion within the next two years, according to Mohammed Ismail Al Emadi, the bank’s group CEO. “Through the fund, we hope to give investors in Qatar and wider region a way to invest in China’s ‘new quality productive forces’, meaning the innovative, high-growth companies driving the transformation and upgrading of China’s economy,” said Tian Gan, Hong Kong CEO of the Hong Kong-based asset manager, known as ChinaAMC. Chinese President Xi Jinping first used the phrase “new quality productive forces” in 2023, calling for a new economic model based on innovation in advanced sectors. While the vast majority of Lesha Bank’s client assets remained concentrated in Western markets like the US and Europe, there was compelling diversification potential in Asia, according to Al Emadi. “Today the Asian market is large, and the main driver of that market is from China,” he said. “This is the main reason, and to diversify for our clients.” The fund would track the FTSE Shariah China Index as its core benchmark, selecting equities that adhered strictly to Islamic law while targeting high-conviction growth themes, according to Jubin Jose, a portfolio manager at Lesha Bank. These included AI, advanced manufacturing, technology localisation and high-dividend assets, he added. Elaborating on the macroeconomic thesis, Gan pointed to structural advantages in Chinese equities relative to crowded Western benchmarks. “Because the US market today performs very well, it’s a very crowded market,” he said. “If you want to diversify from US assets, which market are you going to put your money in? The hottest topic is AI … and after the US, China is very dominant.” Looking ahead, the partners planned to expand their product pipeline, with cross-border exchange-traded funds next in line, he added. Raymond Jing, director and equity portfolio manager at ChinaAMC, said that fundamental industry shifts were uncovering deep value in Chinese firms. “Besides AI, biotech is also a fast-growing sector in China,” he said, adding that Middle Eastern investors were particularly drawn to Chinese biotech pipelines as Western pharmaceutical giants faced a looming patent cliff.

title: Why are visitors to Beijing Wildlife Park hunting fall webworm larvae?
description: The invasive species of caterpillar can damage more than 300 plant species.
content:
At the Beijing Wildlife Park, people spent their “Golden Week” holiday hunting for fall webworm larvae.
This is an invasive species ‌of caterpillar that is originally from North America. It can damage more than 300 plant species, including crops and fruit trees. The park has called it “the forest food monster”.
The park asked visitors to catch as many of the caterpillars as possible. Those with the biggest hauls got prizes, including as many as 10 park tickets.
After a lesson on how to spot the larvae, participants spread out across the park with disposable gloves, plastic containers ‌and chopsticks.
“Call for warriors! Battle the ‘forest food monster’ and win grand prizes!” read a poster behind a table stacked with containers of caterpillars.
As of October 5, more than 310,000 caterpillars ‌were caught by some 2,077 people since the ‌competition ‌began on September 28. Their combined weight was 47.65kg.

title: Promising Chinese teen basketball player joins top US high school, sparking training debate
description: Zhang Yuchen, who has drawn similarities to Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry, was once deemed ‘too short’ to play for national team.
content: A top American high school snapping up a talented Chinese teen basketball player once deemed “too short” to represent the national team has sparked debate online about the country’s rigid training and selection criteria. Zhang Yuchen, who has drawn similarities to Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry, left Guangzhou for Phoenix on Wednesday to join the CIA Bella Vista’s men’s basketball team. Winning both the Chipotle High School Basketball Nationals and the EYBL Scholastic titles last season, CIA was named the best high school team in the US. The teenager first rose to prominence six years ago when he was 10 years old after a video of him knocking down 17 three-pointers in a minute and a half went viral. Two years later, he moved to Beijing alone to study at the high school attached to Tsinghua University, receiving systematic basketball training while also maintaining excellent academic performance. However, Zhang struggled to break into the national youth teams as he was deemed “too short” to be a point guard at a height of 1.86 metres (6 feet 1 inch). His potential was finally noticed when he played in two warm-up games in Serbia before the Fiba Under-17 World Cup in the summer. In seven matches at the tournament in Turkey, the Guangdong native averaged 7.9 points, 3.1 assists and 3.0 rebounds as China finished 10th out of 16 teams. In August, Zhang helped China finish second to Australia at the Fiba Under-18 Asia Cup. A month later, the Chinese under-18 team lost 74-69 to CIA Bella Vista in Beijing. Zhang started the match and finished as the only one on the team with a positive player efficiency. CIA’s head coach Matt Gordon reportedly singled Zhang out and praised his “extremely strong shooting ability and all-around skills”. Zheng moving to the US has stirred debate about the limits of China’s “one size fits all” criteria in youth training and grass-roots talent selection. The rigid Chinese methodology excessively pursues height while neglecting the importance of small, quick and agile guards, and of basic skills. This means players such as Stephen Curry might have been overlooked if born in China. The training enforced by the Chinese Basketball Association follows strict physical testing standards, including shuttle runs and two-minute high-intensity shooting drills, stipulating that anyone who failed would be disqualified. Additionally, the national team coaching staff are very keen on attendance during summer training camps and long-term closed training, thus leaving behind players who cannot attend all training sessions. Chinese social media users were not happy with the rigidity of the training and selection criteria. “This is a vivid example of the entrenched mindset of Chinese coaches and sports associations,” one commenter said. “They are adept at applying one-size-fits-all approaches, managing sports with bureaucratic habits, just like other sports.” There were also comments suggesting that a point guard at 1.86m “should not be considered short by any standard”. Japan’s Yuki Kawamura, who was recently axed by the Los Angeles Clippers and was expected to feature in the G League this season, is 1.70m. The 25-year-old from Yamaguchi made 40 appearances with the Memphis Grizzlies and the Chicago Bulls over the past two seasons. In China, though, height seems to be key. From Yao Ming, Yi Jianlian, Zhou Qi and current Trail Blazers player Yang Hansen in Portland to NCAA players Huan Sinan and Zhang Boyuan, towering basketballers were never a problem for the Chinese national team. One comment might have summed up the issue best, saying the biggest problem with Chinese basketball was “the constant attempts to define what constitutes talent”. “[In China] 1.86m is considered too short; 2.03m is considered too thin, and once a player enters the national team, the criticism shifts to a lack of physicality,” the comment read.

title: South Korean boss jailed for shooting industrial air gun into Thai worker’s anus
description: The factory owner, who received a three-year jail term, also showed no remorse and deducted medical expenses from the victim’s wages.
content: A South Korean manufacturing company owner accused of severely injuring a migrant worker by firing high-pressure air from an industrial air gun into his body has been sentenced to three years in prison. Judge Koo Na-young of the Suwon district court on Thursday sentenced the owner of a metal-cleaning company, a man in his 60s identified only as A, to three years in prison on charges of aggravated bodily injury and violations of the Labour Standards Act. The court dismissed the case against A’s wife, identified as B, who had been charged with intimidation. A was indicted on charges of placing the nozzle of an industrial air gun against the anal area of C, a Thai man in his 40s, and blasting high-pressure air for about seven seconds at his factory in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi province, on February 20. C suffered injuries including a traumatic rectal perforation measuring more than 10cm (three inches) and underwent surgery. A was also accused of threatening C, who needed emergency surgery, by saying, “illegal immigrant, police”, suggesting that he would report C to police for his undocumented immigration status unless he returned to his home country. A’s lawyers acknowledged that he had fired the air gun about three times as a prank but denied part of the charges, saying, “It is true that he sprayed air about three times as a joke, but he did not insert the nozzle into the victim’s anus and inject air for seven seconds.” The court rejected the argument. “Considering the victim’s consistent testimony and medical records, it is established that the defendant held the victim by the waist with one hand, inserted the nozzle into his anus and sprayed air for seven or eight seconds,” the court said. “The victim resisted, saying, ‘It hurts’, but the defendant did not stop.” The court also said A showed no remorse after the incident and was reluctant to provide treatment for C’s injuries. “Although the defendant was told by the hospital where the victim received treatment that he needed immediate surgery at a higher-level hospital, he urged the victim to leave the country that night in an attempt to conceal the incident,” Koo said. “The seriousness of the offence is compounded by the fact that A deducted medical expenses resulting from his own actions from C’s wages.” As for B, the court dismissed the case because the intimidation charge cannot be prosecuted against the victim’s wishes and C had said he did not want her to be punished. At the final hearing last month, prosecutors sought a seven-year prison sentence for A and a one-year prison sentence for B. This story was first published by The Korea Times

title: Rare Van Gogh painting in Hong Kong; Forbidden City’s workshops: 7 Lifestyle highlights
description: From a Singaporean grandma deadlifting 67.5kg to Cantopop pioneer Anthony Wong Yiu-ming, here are seven stories from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven Lifestyle stories from the past seven days that resonated with our readers. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Rarely seen Van Gogh landscape on show in Hong Kong ahead of New York auction A collection of Impressionist and post-Impressionist masterpieces – including a rarely seen landscape painting by Vincent van Gogh – which have been hidden from public view for more than half a century, will be going under the hammer this November. 2. Merry Berry Love: Ji Chang-wook goes to Japan in hollow romcom K-drama Cross-cultural media ties between Japan and South Korea continue to blossom with Merry Berry Love, a rural romance starring Ji Chang-wook (The Worst of Evil) and Mio Imada (Trillion Game). Co-produced by South Korea’s CJ ENM and Japan’s Nippon Television, the show airs locally on Nippon TV and streams globally on Disney+. 3. ‘I’m a huge gamer’: Callina Liang on playing Chun-Li in Street Fighter When Kitao Sakurai, the Japanese-American director of a new film adaptation of the Street Fighter video game franchise, called to say she had the role, Callina Liang reacted the way anyone might expect. “I was in a park screaming at the top of my lungs,” the 26-year-old actress reveals with a giggle over Zoom. 4. Inside a 60-year-old Hong Kong home where every object tells a story There is a lot going on inside this 1,700 sq ft (158 square metre) Pok Fu Lam flat, which rejects the pared-back minimalism typical of Hong Kong homes. 5. How Cantopop pioneer Anthony Wong Yiu-ming shaped Hong Kong culture For Hong Kong’s culture enthusiasts, sitting just a few seats away from Anthony Wong Yiu-ming at an art-house film screening or standing steps from him at an underground gig has long been a serendipitous staple of the city’s arts scene. He is legendary for his ubiquitous presence as an ordinary spectator. 6. Fit for an emperor: inside the imperial workshops that served the Forbidden City At first glance, the peach-shaped box with coral inlay appears to be carved from red lacquer. But the piece – made specifically to celebrate the birthday of the Yongzheng Emperor (1678-1735) – is, in fact, a gold-bodied box with a surface overlaid with red coral. Each fragment of the vivid gemstone is cut and set so precisely that the joins almost disappear, creating a shimmering mottled crimson skin. 7. Singaporean grandma, 73, couldn’t walk without pain. Now, she deadlifts 67.5kg When 73-year-old Rosemina Hamzah stepped up to the hex bar at Singapore’s Mbold Seniors Hex Bar Deadlift Challenge in August, she was not just attempting her first deadlift competition ­– she was rewriting what ageing looks like. Latching onto 67.5kg (149lbs), more than her own body weight of 64kg, the novice lifter pulled it with ease – a personal best to win her category.

title: China’s CXMT gets pledge of support as provincial party chief vows chip-industry expansion
description: Anhui province party secretary and former MIIT head Li Lecheng vows to foster IC ecosystem during visit to memory giant’s headquarters.
content: Three weeks into his tenure as the Communist Party secretary of Anhui province, Li Lecheng carried out an on-site inspection at China’s home-grown memory chip giant ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) on Wednesday, pledging to grow integrated circuits (ICs) as an emerging pillar industry. During the visit to the company’s headquarters in the central province’s capital of Hefei, Li urged CXMT to further refine its product portfolio and actively expand into domestic and overseas markets. He emphasised home-grown innovation, pressing the firm to accelerate launches of new technologies and products. According to a photo published by Anhui News on Thursday, CXMT chairman Zhu Yiming took part in the tour and briefed Li on the firm’s products. Over the weekend, CXMT reported key progress on a new memory-cell architecture designed to raise memory density – an innovation also pursued by rivals including South Korea’s Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Cao Kanyu, the firm’s president, said in a statement that a new server memory product based on the advance would roll out by the end of this year. Semiconductor manufacturing and artificial intelligence hardware have emerged as the focal points of China-US strategic rivalry, fuelling a persistent tug of war over supply chains, technological bottlenecks and market access. During a symposium held after the tour, Li – previously head of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology – pledged full support for CXMT to further scale up and strengthen its operations. In the first half of 2026, CXMT’s revenue soared 874 per cent from a year earlier to 150.3 billion yuan (US$22.5 billion), according to filings released in late August. Its net income attributable to parent shareholders saw an even sharper jump, rocketing 3,428 per cent year on year to 77.6 billion yuan for the six-month period. Li said that Anhui would leverage CXMT’s role as an industrial supply chain leader to attract more upstream and downstream partners and bolster its IC sector. The province would strive to foster world-class advanced manufacturing clusters, he added. Founded in 2016, CXMT has been a top priority for the province’s previous party secretaries. Li’s predecessor Liang Yanshun visited the firm in July 2024. The so-called “Hefei model” is now being replicated by many cities across China. Under the framework, Hefei began backing promising yet loss-making enterprises in 2008, pouring capital into strategic industries and rolling out incentives to attract hi-tech players. Besides CXMT, Hefei now hosts a raft of corporate stars including electric vehicle (EV) maker Nio. Official data showed the city produced roughly one out of every 12 EVs manufactured nationwide last year, with its annual production capacity standing at about 1.37 million units.

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: start-up turns to tech to tackle urban waste
description: Founded by Jorch Wong, The Loops uses door-to-door services and AI to streamline recycling for households and corporate clients.
content: Inconvenience is one of the biggest obstacles to recycling, a challenge that prompted a Hongkonger to establish a one-stop recycling service. Jorch Wong Ching-hei left advertising in 2019 and started The Loops Hong Kong after finding that recycling different materials often required travelling to different collection points. With no prior background in the industry, he contacted recycling operators, visited plants and learned how paper, plastics and metals were processed. Wong also taught himself coding, spending about a year learning online before creating an early version of the platform used to arrange collections. The Loops is a finalist for the Spirit of Sustainability Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Its original door-to-door service sought to remove one common barrier by allowing customers to place various recyclables together, leaving the sorting to Wong’s team. Today, the company accepts more than 40 categories of recyclable materials. “We try to solve a very real problem with every service we introduce. We do a lot of research and speak to customers first to make sure the need really exists,” said Wong. That approach led the company to tackle harder-to-handle waste. Hong Kong’s move towards waste-to-energy treatment has opened another area of business for The Loops. Wong said liquid-heavy waste can reduce the efficiency of incineration, creating demand for companies that can separate liquids from packaging before disposal. Instead of discarding the packaging, The Loops cleans them and routes the materials back into recycling channels, reducing overall incineration volume. Drinks, dairy products, cosmetics and other liquid-filled goods are among the products it processes. The company is also using technology to address another major challenge facing businesses. While many firms know they generate large amounts of rubbish, few have detailed information about what is being thrown away. Its newest service uses cameras and artificial intelligence (AI) to analyse clients’ waste streams. The system categorises rubbish, estimates recyclable proportions, and tracks when and where specific waste is generated. Wong said these insights help companies figure out where recycling points were needed most. Cathay Group, which nominated The Loops for the award, has worked with the company on specialised recycling and an AI-assisted waste audit of its airport lounge operations. Technology has also been used to make a traditionally labour-intensive industry more transparent. Corporate customers can access collection records and reports through the company’s system, while service packages and prices are set out in advance. Although the government shelved the twice-delayed waste-charging scheme in 2024 because of insufficient social support, Wong remained optimistic about its eventual roll-out. “Hong Kong remains behind several Asian cities in using charging to encourage waste reduction, while such a policy could also make recycling more attractive to households and businesses,” he said. “I think it will happen sooner or later. It’s really a matter of when.” Running the company has required the same willingness to learn that got him started, with machinery, software, repairs, sales and operations all demanding new skills. “The hardest part is that you have to keep learning,” he said. The Spirit of Hong Kong Awards were established in 2013 to recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might escape public attention.

title: Vehicle may have sparked Mongolia wildfire, putting China rescuers on high alert
description: 3,400 emergency personnel deployed to the Chinese side of the border to combat the latest environmental threat from its neighbour.
content: A grassland fire in Mongolia has raised fresh concerns in China, underscoring the recurring risk of cross-border environmental hazards. This is not the first time an environmental disaster originating in Mongolia has threatened to cross the 4,700km (2,920-mile) border into China, with the impacts sometimes also affecting the Korean peninsula and Japan. The blaze, which erupted on October 8 in the inland country’s easternmost Dornod province bordering Russia and China, advanced rapidly towards China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, driven by strong autumn winds and drought conditions. China’s consulate general in Zamyn-Uud expressed Beijing’s concern over the steppe fire in a meeting with the province on Tuesday, urging timely updates and intensified firefighting operations. China was ready to support the rescue efforts, he said. China has deployed 3,400 personnel, including professional firefighters and local emergency staff, along the border to respond to any possible incursion of the fire, state news agency Xinhua reported on Tuesday. Artificial precipitation also brought light rain to the fire’s front line, it said. Emergency crews patrolling key sections of the border have been equipped with heavy equipment and have taken measures including suppressing cross-border flames, widening firebreaks and clearing combustible vegetation to intercept the advancing blaze. Photos and videos released by the National Forestry and Grassland Administration show firefighters working at night to extinguish flames along a barbed-wire fence. Dry grassland can be seen burning on the Mongolian side. According to Xinhua, the fire appeared to be under control as of Tuesday, with no visible flames or smoke points along the Chinese side of the border line. No casualties had been reported and local authorities would continue monitoring, it said. Some local media reports have said the fire was caused by a vehicle belonging to Mobicom, Mongolia’s first mobile operator, whose representatives were in the area at the time. Mongolian news outlet Eguur News reported on Thursday that a five-vehicle convoy led by Mobicom directors entered the protected area on October 8, with official permission. However, one of the vehicles caught fire, ultimately sparking the wildfire, according to outlet Eguur News, citing a company statement. Mobicom was founded as a joint venture between Mongolia’s Newcom Group and Japan’s Sumitomo Corporation, before being acquired by the Japanese telecom giant KDDI in 2016. Mongolia’s National Emergency Management Agency said on Wednesday that the fire had been brought under control, with firefighters remaining on site to conduct mop-up operations and ensure full extinguishment. Wildfires from Mongolia have crossed the border before. In April 2021, a fire that burned about 1,800 sq km (695 square miles) of Mongolia’s Sukhbaatar province spilled over to the Chinese side where it was blocked by the border patrol road and an emergency firebreak. Unlike fires that can sometimes be contained through human intervention, dust storms cannot be stopped at any border. Once strong winds lift sand and dust from Mongolia’s Gobi Desert and degraded grasslands, the particles can travel hundreds or even thousands of kilometres, reaching much of China’s northern provinces and occasionally as far as the Korean peninsula and Japan. In March 2021, one of the most severe dust storms in a decade swept across Mongolia and northern China. In Beijing, PM10 concentrations – a measure of inhalable particles that can harm human health – surged to the highest level in 10 years, with some local readings exceeding 9,000 micrograms per cubic metre. In Mongolia, the disaster killed at least 10 people, while hundreds of livestock were lost. Another major dust storm struck Mongolia and northern China in March 2023, affecting more than 4 million sq km and reaching 20 Chinese provinces. Other significant cross-border events in recent years have included a mixed dust-and-snowstorm in the Gobi Desert in April 2019 and a relatively rare autumn dust storm in October 2020. Scientists attribute these recurring disasters to a combination of land degradation in Mongolia, driven by overgrazing and unsustainable development, and the intensifying warming, drought and extreme weather associated with global climate change. Beijing has sought to address the cross-border hazards with its landlocked neighbour. Early environmental discussions began in the 2000s. However, formal joint action was slow to materialise until recent years. In a joint statement issued during Mongolian President Ukhnaa Khurelsukh’s state visit to China in 2022, the two countries pledged to strengthen cooperation on ecological and environmental protection, as well as desertification prevention and control. The two sides signed a framework agreement in Ulaanbaatar in the following year to support Mongolia’s 1 billion trees initiative. They also launched the China-Mongolia Desertification Prevention and Control Cooperation Centre to coordinate joint anti-desertification initiatives.

title: Start-up unveils prototype ‘heart’ of EUV lithography amid China chipmaking push
description: Shanghai-based Langdao Silex displays self-developed EUV light-source system, marking crucial step in Beijing’s chip self-reliance drive.
content: A Chinese start-up has unveiled a prototype extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light-source machine – a component often described as the “heart” of advanced lithography systems – marking an early but critical step in Beijing’s drive for self-reliance in chipmaking equipment. At the China International Industry Fair in Shanghai, Langdao Silex displayed its self-developed EUV light-source system. Ninety per cent of the machine’s components were localised, with the vast majority of core parts developed in-house, a company representative said, according to a report by Chinese news outlet Jiefang Daily on Tuesday. On-site staff described the prototype as a crucial step in moving domestically produced EUV light sources from the laboratory to industrial applications, although mass production remained “three to five years away”, according to the report. An EUV light source is a key subsystem in advanced lithography equipment, generating the extreme ultraviolet light required to expose microscopic circuit patterns onto silicon wafers. The public display provides a rare glimpse into China’s progress in EUV technology as the country remains cut off from the global supply chain for the most advanced chipmaking equipment amid the US-China tech war. Under Washington-led export curbs, Dutch giant ASML, the world’s sole manufacturer of EUV lithography systems, is barred from selling the cutting-edge machinery to Chinese customers. As a result, domestic chipmakers have relied on older deep ultraviolet equipment and creative multi-patterning techniques, spurring local researchers to aggressively pursue indigenous EUV capabilities. Despite the start-up’s progress, some global industry leaders remain sceptical about the prospects for rapid Chinese breakthroughs. On Wednesday, ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet said during an investor call that Chinese customers had little incentive to develop domestic alternatives as long as they retained access to the company’s products, adding that the country still had “a very, very long way to go” to match ASML’s technology. Founded in 2024, Langdao Silex is backed by a research team from Tsinghua University’s Gas Discharge and Plasma Laboratory that specialises in laser-produced plasma EUV light sources, according to its website. The Shanghai-based start-up has already secured multiple funding rounds from state-backed and prominent industry investors, including China Fortune-Tech Capital, an investment arm tied to China’s top foundry, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation, or SMIC. Langdao Silex is among a handful of Chinese companies and research institutes that have reported progress in advanced lithography development, although none has yet reached the commercial stage. Meanwhile, domestic equipment suppliers are expanding across other stages of the chipmaking process. At the concurrent WeSemiBay semiconductor expo in Shenzhen, Hwatsing Technology introduced a medium-current ion implanter, Leadmicro showcased advanced thin-film deposition equipment, and Piotech announced a carbon-film deposition technology for memory and logic chips. Driven by Beijing’s localisation drive and tighter supplies of key components from Europe and Japan, Chinese equipment manufacturers were rapidly increasing their adoption of domestically produced components, according to a report published by Bernstein Research on Tuesday. Domestic suppliers were expected to capture 52 per cent of China’s wafer-fabrication equipment market by 2028, up from an estimated 28 per cent this year, the report said. Additional reporting by Sylvia Ma

title: AI job losses set to rein in office demand in developed Asia-Pacific economies: report
description: CBRE says 3.9 per cent of office jobs in developed parts of region are vulnerable to replacement by artificial intelligence.
content: A mild displacement of jobs across the Asia-Pacific region as companies expand their use of AI would trim five percentage points off growth in office space demand in the next few years, according to property consultancy CBRE. In a report released on Thursday it said 3.9 per cent of office jobs were vulnerable to artificial intelligence-driven displacement in developed markets in the region, including Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Australia and New Zealand. However, only 1.7 per cent were similarly vulnerable in developing markets, including mainland China, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. CBRE’s head of Asia-Pacific research, Ada Choi, said in an interview that occupied office space was still projected to grow under a moderate-displacement scenario, “but at a slower pace of 13 per cent” by 2030 – 5 percentage points less than under the consultancy’s base case, which assumed firms in the region would incorporate AI-related productivity gains without job displacement. She said the moderate displacement scenario was “a downside sensitivity analysis” as opposed to a prediction of contraction. “The model also excludes potential upside from new AI-related companies, occupations and business formation,” Choi said. Most Asia-Pacific markets were expected to fall under the moderate displacement assumption, the report said. But Japan was likely to fall under a slow displacement scenario, with AI adoption limited by organisational and cultural barriers to change despite technological availability, and workforce adjustment occurring progressively – “with displacement extending well into the 2040s”. AI is unlikely to be the primary driver of office market weakness in Hong Kong Ada Choi, CBRE Meanwhile, mainland China could fall under a rapid displacement scenario, “where all occupations identified as highly vulnerable to AI are automated over the shortest modelled time frame”. The report said office employment would continue to expand across the Asia-Pacific region under such a scenario, but only slowly – by a total of 2 per cent by the end of 2030. Such a scenario was “most plausible in markets that combine advanced digital ecosystems, strong AI readiness and supportive policy frameworks designed to accelerate economic transformation”, it added. “Mainland China, with its strategic focus on technology-led growth and industrial upgrading, exhibits many of the characteristics associated with this trajectory,” the report said. It did not offer a forecast for office space demand in a rapid displacement scenario. The report said the labour markets in Hong Kong and other developed economies in the region were characterised by a high concentration of office-based employment, relatively high labour costs and strong digital readiness, which made them more sensitive to AI-related displacement. Office workers accounted for more than 35 per cent of employment in Singapore, Hong Kong and Australia compared with less than 10 per cent in India and Vietnam, it said. One stabilising factor that could help the region’s office property market weather AI disruption was slowing supply, CBRE said. Forecast annual office completions in 2028 would be equivalent to just 3.2 per cent of the estimated stock in the region next year, and well down on the 5.3 per cent seen before the Covid-19 pandemic. However, the impact of AI could intensify the market polarisation in Hong Kong that saw top-tier locations such as Central attract more leasing demand, CBRE said. “AI is unlikely to be the primary driver of office market weakness in Hong Kong,” Choi said. “Rather it is likely to accelerate the divergence between prime and secondary assets that is already evident.”

title: ‘Unforgettable experience’: interns at OSC on working with Hong Kong charities
description: Four university students share what it was like to visit OSC’s charitable partners and witness the work they do and the people they help.
content:
Summer internships are a great chance to learn workplace skills, but for four Hong Kong university students who interned at Operation Santa Claus (OSC) – the city’s annual fundraising campaign for local charities – the experience was eye-opening and even life-changing.
Established by the South China Morning Post and public broadcaster RTHK in 1988, OSC has raised over HK$415 million and supported more than 382 charitable projects across Hong Kong, benefiting more than 100,000 people.
The interns were tasked with helping OSC operations, which included listening to 30 shortlisted charities pitch funding proposals for projects intended to tackle social issues in Hong Kong, on-site visits to learn about charitable partners’ work first-hand, and helping with activities for beneficiaries.
For 19-year-old Ella Wen Tsz-yee, it was especially meaningful to see the many charities operating in Hong Kong and the innovative ways they help people in need.
“Through this experience, I got to know more charities helping different social groups, such as domestic workers and people with SEN [special educational needs],” said Wen, who is double majoring in social sciences and law at the University of Hong Kong. “It provided me with new insight about my future career path.”
The internship helped Wen realise she did not want her future career to be “purely money‑driven”.
“That sense of purpose is something I definitely want in my future career,” Wen said, adding that one of her goals is to understand the community’s needs and help people learn what their legal rights are and how to protect them.
Kyle Ng Ka-ho, a 21-year-old studying finance at City University (CityU), said the OSC internship expanded his knowledge about NGOs’ work and their importance.
“After these two months, it lets me understand more clearly that so many people need help, but we Hong Kong people don’t see it,” he said.
Ng said two NGOs made an especially strong impression on him. One was Splash Foundation, which teaches foreign domestic helpers, families from low-income backgrounds and children with disabilities, including special educational needs, to swim.
The other was Rugby For Good, which helps students from ethnic minority groups learn life skills and integrate through the sport.
“There are so many different ethnicities in our society, but [Hong Kong doesn’t] know their needs and doesn’t necessarily provide help to them,” Ng said.
He noted that he attended schools with few or no students with ethnic minority backgrounds and the site visits helped him gain a better understanding of the challenges this part of the population faces.
Intern Hailey Ho Hei-lui is a 23-year-old majoring in social policy at Polytechnic University. She hopes to work for an NGO after she graduates, so the OSC internship was a perfect fit. Still, she learned that helping others did not look exactly as she had expected.
She helped MindHK, an OSC charity partner that provides mental health intervention services, at an event for residents of Wang Fuk Court, the housing complex in Tai Po where a large fire broke out in November. Seven of the eight blocks were consumed by the blaze and its residents are still facing the trauma of losing their loved ones, belongings and homes.
“It was an unforgettable experience,” Ho said of the event for residents. “When I chatted with them, I felt they had a lot of knots in their hearts, but they welcomed me warmly and were so brave and strong in dealing with their hurt and pain … Even though I was sent to help them, I felt I’ve learned from them.”
Ariel Lam Yee-ching is a 22-year-old business economics major at CityU. She hopes to become a financial adviser and wealth manager after graduating.
During her summer internship, Lam visited charities such as Home of Loving Faithfulness, a lifelong home for people with disabilities whose families cannot take care of them, and Hong Kong Paediatric Rheumatism Association, which provides medicine to children suffering from the rare disease.
She said the internship reshaped her future goals: “In the future, I want to get involved in NGOs because I think the funding really helps people in need.”

title: 2 Hong Kong MTR disruptions may be linked, expert says
description: Edward Lo says incidents could be linked by shared track circuit or failures to reverse procedures after first disruption.
content: Two rush-hour disruptions at Hong Kong’s Lam Tin MTR station within 15 hours could be connected if they involved the same power supply circuit or exposed procedural shortcomings, an engineering expert has said, with a lawmaker urging the rail operator to offer more targeted compensation to affected passengers. The first disruption occurred on Tuesday evening, when an insulating rubber component in a track turnout caught fire, halting services for about an hour. The second struck on Wednesday morning, when wires overheated in an electrical room on the station platform, forcing trains to skip the stop for another hour. The MTR Corporation vowed to conduct a thorough investigation into the cause of the incidents and was ordered to submit a report to the government within a month. Edward Lo Wai-chau, former chairman of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers’ electrical division, told a radio programme on Thursday that it was too early to determine whether the two incidents were connected. He noted that the MTR’s power supply system was divided into separate sections for the station and the track and said the incidents could be linked if the components involved belonged to the same track circuit. Lo added that even if there was no connection in the power supply circuit, procedural failures after the first incident might have contributed to the second and should be investigated. “For example, after the first incident, they took certain actions, such as switching something off or on, and then forgot to reverse those steps,” he said. “There is no linkage in the circuit, but they forgot to reverse some changes in the procedures.” “As a result, some component may have been operating for too long, causing it to overheat and smoke.” Lo said the first incident, in which an insulating rubber component in a track turnout caught fire, might have been caused by foreign objects falling onto the track. He called on the rail operator to step up inspections to once a month to ensure safety and suggested it make greater use of technology, such as Internet of Things sensors, to gather more data and enhance track monitoring. Lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu, speaking on the same programme, said that if the investigation found the two issues were connected, the MTR should treat them as one incident and count the disruption hours together. Under the MTR Corp’s service performance rebate arrangement, the rail operator sets aside between HK$1 million (US$127,415) and HK$40 million for each disruption lasting 31 minutes or more that is caused by factors within its control. The amount increases progressively with the length of the disruption. It rises by 20 per cent if the disruption occurs during peak hours, from 8am to 9am and 6pm to 7pm on weekdays. Tang, the lawmaker representing Kowloon East, also called for more targeted compensation for affected passengers, noting that both incidents occurred at the same station and affected a concentrated group of residents. Under the current mechanism, once the rebate fund reaches HK$25 million, the rail operator returns it to all passengers as discounted fares on a designated Saturday or Sunday. He also criticised the contingency arrangements, saying many passengers were left unsure about what was happening and where to board shuttle buses. Hundreds of commuters were stranded on packed platforms and concourses during the incident, with some complaining that they received little information from MTR staff. Tang urged the MTR Corp to improve communication with passengers and better coordinate with district councillors and care teams through regular drills.

title: ‘Witch hunt’ sweeps up Asian men misidentified in alleged Cornell gang rape
description: Men sharing a name with one of the seven accused face a torrent of threats and doxxing by social media sleuths.
content: One message told him to “go to hell”. Others said he deserved to be imprisoned. Death threats poured in. Asians who share a name with one of the men accused of raping a US university student have faced a torrent of online abuse. The alleged 2024 gang rape of a Cornell University student, detailed in a recent lawsuit, has sparked an outpouring of outrage against the seven accused perpetrators. The case has sent internet sleuths scouring digital footprints for clues to track them down. All seven men have denied the allegations, maintaining either that their interactions with the woman were consensual or that they were not involved. One of the accused is a Korean man identified by US media as Winston Lee. The problem is that the world is full of people named Winston Lee. The rage misdirected at people who share that name, some of whom live outside the United States and look nothing like the accused, lays bare the perils of a chaotic internet, where people distrustful of public institutions become digital detectives. One of those wrongly identified was a Chinese-American whose LinkedIn profile identifies him as a New York-based finance professional who graduated from Cornell University in 2020 – four years before the alleged rape. “You can’t hide. Your future is over,” said one message he received via LinkedIn. “You’ll get exactly what you deserve … which is prison!! You’ll be gang raped there.” Another said that a “black magic” spell had been cast upon him. In a video on TikTok – where his bio reads “Not part of Cornell7” – he said he had hired a lawyer to press charges against a woman who posted his phone number and his parents’ address online. After a deluge of hateful messages, another man misidentified as Winston Lee posted a personal appeal to TikTok detectives. “I am Indonesian and not the Winston Lee named in the recent Cornell University case,” he said. “Please verify the identity of the person you are looking for before contacting, tagging, or making accusations against someone.” After a similar flood of messages, a Chinese-American student named Winston Lee at the University of Pennsylvania added a disclaimer to his LinkedIn profile: “I do not go to Cornell”. Those appeals did not appear to slow what Reddit discussion boards described as an “online hunt” for the seven accused, drawing many users down internet rabbit holes. With few verified details about the man actually accused, internet users continued searching aggressively for his whereabouts. One Reddit post claimed Winston Lee was now serving in the South Korean army. Another user on X said she had received tips suggesting Lee had been spotted on Cornell University’s campus. People with names like the other six accused also complained about rage spamming and threats. “These social justice warriors are literally messaging and harassing the wrong” people, said podcast host Brad Polumbo. “These things should be litigated through the criminal process or through some sort of fair process, not through a social media mob or witch hunt.” The criminal process has since resumed. Prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the alleged gang rape, with New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointing state Attorney General Letitia James to lead the case. That decision came after local authorities said they declined to prosecute in 2024 because the complainant’s testimony did not establish a lack of consent. As authorities re-examine the case, the fallout from online vigilantes continues to widen. A group of former Cornell students, who belonged to the same Chi Phi fraternity as the seven accused but graduated before the alleged incident, have also complained of online smear campaigns. “They are being wrongfully accused on social media of having involvement, are consequently receiving death threats and related hate mail,” their lawyer Adam Ford wrote in a letter to the university that was obtained by Agence France-Presse. “Most of them have had their employers and higher education institutions take adverse actions against them, including being placed on leave.” Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: On the Menu | Wagamama’s fish and chip ramen stirs up a storm online – and it all started with fake news
description: A fake news honey trap laid by a London lifestyle platform accidentally inspired Wagamama’s viral British-Japanese fusion noodle dish.
content: As someone who lived in London in the late 2000s, when Asian food was not as popular, accessible or unburdened by tradition as it is now, Wagamama was one of the early options for a little taste of Japan. Founded in 1992 by Hong Kong-born British restaurateur Alan Yau Tak-wai, the Tokyo ramen bar-inspired restaurant quickly ballooned into a nationwide chain – despite the liberties it would take with flavour. I had forgotten about this brand until recently, when a little storm in a teacup began to brew, involving popular lifestyle platform London On the Inside (Loti). The publication had a niggling suspicion that a rival media title had long been pilfering off their independent research on new restaurant openings and set into motion a honey trap to catch the thieves red-handed. In their September 24 article on the imminent opening of new Chinese noodle bar Cai Lin Ji – a historic brand founded in Wuhan, China – on Oxford Street, in central London, the publication included a fabricated detail. At the end of the story, they added the line “rumour has it, we could see a fish and chips inspired noodle dish on its menu …” Lo and behold, this throwaway titbit was picked up and allegedly parroted in subsequent coverage on the rival platform five days later. Loti later clarified that “there are no fish and chip noodles on the menu … we added in a false claim because we knew it would be copied without verification”. In a mega plot twist, the publication inadvertently manifested that oddball creation. The Wagamama team saw an opportunity – or took the bait, rather – and jumped on it, releasing a fish and chip ramen on October 7, reworking the British classic into a noodle dish. The fish and chip ramen features noodles in a curry broth, topped with tempura-battered hake, crisp sweet potato “chips” and crushed edamame to mimic the original dish’s mushy peas. “It’s all the good stuff from the traditional seaside classic, lifted with an unexpected Asian-inspired twist,” the brand says. Of course, that has given the brand a temporary bit of virality – content creators have been frothing at the mouth to try this monstrosity, some even saying they thought it was a joke at first. To be fair, tempura seafood on ramen is nothing new, nor is curry broth ramen. It is also not the first time there has been a British-Japanese mash-up of the sort – Koya, a noodle bar with branches across London, was the first to introduce an English breakfast udon, where the thick wheat noodles are topped with smoked streaky bacon, a gently fried runny egg and shiitake mushrooms in a light dashi broth. In some ways, I respect the liberties these places have taken with the classics. After all, it can be a bit boring to keep seeing the usual tonkotsu ramen bars, and Hong Kong’s sky-high rents often place a limit on how creative one can be. What about a cottage pie ramen with minced beef and fresh peas, done in the style of Hokkaido’s buttery, potato foam ramen? Or roast lamb and mint sauce tsukemen? You heard it here first.

title: Chung Yeung Festival: traditions, history and how the Chinese holiday is celebrated
description: From hiking and grave-sweeping to sharing a meal, the Double Ninth Festival brings families together to honour their roots and wish for longevity.
content: Autumn is a popular season for hiking in Hong Kong, offering crisp air and sweeping vistas across the countryside. Yet beyond leisure, October brings a significant cultural occasion to climb the hills: the annual Chung Yeung Festival, which falls on October 18 this year. The name of the festival, which translates to “double yang” in Chinese, originates from its occurrence on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month. This numerical alignment also gives the occasion its alternative title, the Double Ninth Festival. The festival’s origins trace back to Xu Qi Xie Ji, commonly translated as Continuation of Qi Xie’s Records, a compilation of strange tales by Southern Liang dynasty scholar Wu Jun (469-520). Wu recorded that the alchemist Fei Changfang warned his disciple Huan Jing of an impending calamity threatening his household on the ninth day of the ninth month. He instructed Huan to prepare crimson fabric bags filled with cornelian cherries (dogwood), fasten them to his family members’ arms, ascend a high peak and consume chrysanthemum wine to avert disaster. Huan followed the alchemist’s instructions. Upon returning home that evening, the family discovered that their livestock had perished suddenly from a swift plague, having borne the fatal stroke intended for the household. Over time, this legendary escape evolved into a cultural tradition of ascending high places. The festival is not solely solemn. In modern Hong Kong, Chung Yeung is an essential occasion for family reunions and ancestral reverence. Furthermore, the pronunciation of “nine nine” – gau gau in Cantonese, jiu jiu in Mandarin – serves as a homophone for “longevity”, symbolising enduring health and prosperity. Observances during the Chung Yeung Festival typically include tomb sweeping, ancestral worship and savouring seasonal delicacies. Families visit columbaria and hillside cemeteries, carrying incense, candles, joss paper, roast pork, fresh fruit and their ancestors’ favourite foods as tribute. Relatives clean the gravesites and burn paper offerings in a gesture of filial devotion. After these sacred rituals, families traditionally gather at dim sum halls and restaurants for a celebratory feast, which occasionally features roast pork. In other regions across China, such as Huizhou in Guangdong province, flying kites is an integral Chung Yeung tradition – captured in a Huizhou folk song: “The ninth day of the ninth month brings Chung Yeung; fly your kite high and wish the string long.” Driven by autumn winds, this airborne ritual has endured for generations. The Chung Yeung Festival stands alongside the Ching Ming Festival, which occurs on the 15th day following the spring equinox, as one of the two principal occasions dedicated to ancestral veneration. Yet while Chung Yeung is tied to autumn, Ching Ming – meaning “clear and bright” – marks the arrival of spring and typically occurs in early April. The origins of the Ching Ming Festival stretch back more than 2,500 years to the Zhou dynasty (1046-256BC), when imperial courts offered sacrifices to ancestors to secure peace, prosperity and abundant harvests for the realm. Ching Ming also shares historical ties with another ancient observance, the Cold Food Festival, which dictated the consumption of unheated dishes. While rare in contemporary Hong Kong, some places still enjoy cold, green sweet rice dumplings known as qingtuan as a nod to custom. Whether scaling serene mountain trails or gathering for traditional dim sum feasts, the Double Ninth Festival continues to weave ancient folklore into the rhythm of modern city life. It stands as a timeless reminder that honouring one’s roots and seeking higher ground remain deeply connected values across generations.

title: Emboldened by hybrid car deal, Europe coalesces around tougher China stance
description: Brussels is revving the engines and ready to accelerate a crackdown on Chinese trade practices after Beijing responds to its threats.
content: The EU’s surprise deal with China on hybrid cars last week was supposed to ease the pressure on Beijing. Instead, Brussels is preparing to intensify its crackdown on Chinese trade practices, emboldened by the discovery that its threats are finally delivering results. Now, those driving trade policy for the bloc believe they have landed on a two-track formula. Intensive dialogue is seen to have yielded results and will continue. But so too will the European Union’s efforts to counter what they see as distortive policies in China. There is a clear sense that Beijing responded positively to a threat last week from the two biggest EU members, France and Germany, to quickly close the market to Chinese firms. It represented a dramatic pivot from Berlin – by far China’s biggest trade partner in Europe – which has previously opposed assertive measures. In meetings with businesses, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao was said to have been struck by the shift. He noted, sources said, the potential for a political backlash in Europe if Beijing did not check its exports in important sectors, which they believe helped pave the way for a deal. “Why is China agreeing to something they’ve never agreed to before? We put that question to [EU Trade Commissioner] Maros Sefcovic and he said: ‘They start to realise that they are killing their customers’,” said a senior EU diplomat who, like others interviewed for this story, spoke on condition of anonymity. Buoyed by convincing China to accept an agreement that will limit its hybrid car exports to the EU at 350,000 a year – less than half the forecast volume for 2026 – Brussels is now revving the engines and ready to accelerate on a raft of unilateral actions. “It goes hand in hand – in order to have a credible dialogue, we are seen to have instruments that allow us to take action when needed,” said a second diplomat. A spate of safeguard investigations is expected soon in sectors ranging from pharmaceuticals, chemicals and machinery. They are likely to use tariffs and quotas to restrict Chinese access to industries in which they are dominant, much like the hybrid car arrangement, but are seen as a stopgap while officials come up with new tools. Before Christmas, the union’s top brass want to present a series of new weapons that will help them reduce dependencies on China and compensate those hit by Beijing’s retaliation. The cherry on top for Brussels would be a tool to close the EU market to Chinese companies should the government there take coercive actions in response. There are questions about whether such a complicated instrument could be ready by December, but a varied range of member states are now lining up behind the concept, first proposed in the Franco-German paper last week. “We see on export moderation that China agrees to the fact that there is a problem, that something needs to be done in terms of rebalancing, and that is of course a conversation that we will continue,” said Tomas Baert, a trade adviser to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, at an event in Brussels on Wednesday. “But that alone will not solve the structural imbalances. I think one sectoral solution is probably not enough to deal with the structural issue that we have, and that is where leaders tomorrow will actually take stock and see what more we need to do,” said Baert, referring to Thursday’s European Council summit, where the China policy will be discussed. It would be a stretch to say that Europe is speaking with one voice on China, but in the run-up to Thursday’s meeting, there are notably fewer discordant notes in the choir. “The French-German paper is helpful that it has shown the Chinese that we are quite united. I mean, if you bring together Germany on the one hand and France on the other, and it kind of I think gave also a boost of credibility to the EU,” another diplomat said. Talks with China are continuing at working level, with the EU’s top trade enforcer Denis Redonnet travelling to China for talks on medical devices in the next weeks. Sefcovic will speak with counterpart Wang in January by videoconference before another meeting in March. But the commission’s trade bureaucrats will continue developing sharper tools in the background, despite warnings from Beijing that it will retaliate against any deviation from the cooperative agenda. “You always have to be ready for escalation, but we shouldn’t let ourselves be led by fear,” said a third senior diplomat, who added that capitals remained galvanised by the task of tackling what is described as the China Shock 2.0. “I don’t think there are many member states on the table who see this hybrid deal and now it’s done. We’re chipping away and it’s not something you can do in one go. So more should follow,” they said. At the heart of the energy is a fear that if Europe does not move yet to protect its industries from high quality yet cheaper Chinese competition, there will be nothing left to shield. In Berlin, too, the success of the far-right party Alternative for Germany in recent state elections sparked fears that if mainstream parties do not do something about it, then populists will. The urgency was made plain in China’s trade data for September, published on Wednesday, which showed that last month alone, China’s trade surplus with Germany rose by 201.7 per cent compared to September 2025. For France, the gap expanded by 251.8 per cent, while for the whole EU it was up 52.3 per cent. “If current trends continue or accelerate, large parts of Europe’s industrial base are at risk and China’s supply chain dominance will continue to increase. That could undermine Europe’s prosperity, its social model and its ability to act geopolitically,” wrote Etienne Hora, a specialist in geoeconomics at Bertelsmann Stiftung, a German think tank. In a sign that the EU’s 27 members are coalescing around a hardline China strategy, a draft statement for the European Council summit was updated on Wednesday to demand the commission “urgently enhance the EU toolbox with new instruments to better address these imbalances”. The change was subtle, but significant by the careful standards of the EU – which remains reluctant to directly name China as it seeks to maintain some diplomatic decorum. It reflected, almost verbatim, oral conclusions communicated after the last summit in June, which were not made public. The shift on China – also breakneck compared to the glacial pace at which Brussels ordinarily moves – even caught EU trading partners by surprise. Both parties to the deal insisted that the quotas on hybrid vehicles should apply to all other countries, otherwise they would breach World Trade Organization rules. “China’s quota will not be lower than that of any other import source for the EU,” read a Chinese commerce ministry statement. This appeared to be news, however, to Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bulat, who met Sefcovic in Brussels on Tuesday. Asked after the meeting by the South China Morning Post what sort of quota his country – a major automotive hub – has been allocated for hybrid car exports, Bulat claimed it would not apply because Ankara has a customs union with the EU. “Therefore, it has nothing to do with the EU’s new deal with another country,” he said. The European Commission did not immediately respond to a request to clarify whether Bulat was correct, but trade experts agreed that his remarks were likely wide of the mark – a sign, perhaps, that Brussels’ new trade policy is moving so quickly that even some of its closest partners are struggling to keep up.

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: veteran who keeps flame of Cantonese opera alive
description: Leung Sum-yee’s Kim Sum Cantonese Opera Troupe has trained young performers and kept the traditional art form going for over three decades.
content: Veteran Cantonese opera teacher Leung Sum-yee does not expect every child who enters her classroom to become a performer. If they leave knowing what good Cantonese opera sounds and looks like, she considers that worthwhile too. “My purpose was not to train stars or idols. I wanted more people to understand Cantonese opera and to have more audiences,” she said. That approach has guided Leung through more than three decades of teaching and cultural advocacy. She founded an opera organisation in 1994 that was renamed Kim Sum Cantonese Opera Troupe two years later. It runs classes for children, teenagers and adults and brings Cantonese opera into schools and the community. Leung was also among the first practitioners to introduce Cantonese opera teaching in schools, an area she has worked in for decades. Some of her former students have since gone on to professional careers in the art form. Leung is a finalist in the culture category of the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Her own introduction to the art form came through family members who enjoyed watching Cantonese opera. She began learning at about four and later trained under veteran playwrights, gaining experience both onstage and behind the scenes. Teaching eventually became a major part of her work. Leung said young students need to understand the fundamentals, from movement and vocal projection to diction and theatrical conventions, even if they have no intention of entering the profession. “If you want to try being a performer, you have to learn the skills properly and understand the rules,” she said. To make the art form more accessible to beginners, Leung has written simpler pieces for young students instead of relying solely on excerpts from famous classics. Some take on contemporary issues, including scams, to introduce moral ideas through Cantonese opera. She said modern subjects could be used without discarding the techniques and values that give the art form its identity. The same principle applies to audiences, as greater familiarity allows people to recognise stronger performances and expect more from professional performers. Leung’s chief disciple, Doris Kwan Hoi-shan, said she had grown up training at Kim Sum before becoming a professional Cantonese opera performer. She later became involved in helping with teaching, administration and school outreach. “The most important thing my teacher taught us, apart from Cantonese opera, was how to conduct ourselves,” Kwan said. This included greeting people properly, thanking others and recognising the work of backstage crew. Kwan said she now teaches those same manners to younger students. Among younger students of the troupe, some said they had been introduced to Cantonese opera by grandparents or other relatives, while others said training had improved their speech, vocal projection and confidence. One student who had yet to perform publicly said she had already learned backstage etiquette, including thanking others and recognising the efforts of those working behind the scenes. Leung also adopts a flexible approach when school work demands more attention. Students preparing for examinations are allowed to take a break from rehearsals and return afterwards. Her former student Lee Sze-wai nominated Leung for the award. Lee said her former teacher’s contribution was evident in the achievements of former pupils who had gone on to professional careers, while Leung herself had continued teaching without seeking recognition. Leung hopes to keep teaching and creating more opportunities for students to perform in front of new audiences. “If we have an opportunity, we should put our best work on stage,” she said. “If audiences remember us and word spreads, that may open the door to another opportunity.” The Spirit of Hong Kong Awards were established in 2013 to recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose contributions may be overlooked.

title: Filipino migrants torn between safety and survival risks amid Middle East dangers
description: Analysts point to economic difficulties and insufficient assistance initiatives, as large numbers continue to remain abroad for work.
content: Lorelai Jacinto had worked as a domestic helper in Riyadh for two and a half years before she flew home to the Philippines on September 19, increasingly worried that the conflict in the Middle East was making it unsafe to stay. “When the conflict with Iran happened, I started feeling like it wasn’t safe there any more because I was right there in Riyadh myself, so the bombing, the missiles, were closer to us,” Jacinto told This Week in Asia. “I got worried, I got scared that maybe I wouldn’t be able to come home any more,” added the 29-year-old, whose six-year-old son lives in the Philippines under her parents’ care. While Jacinto made it home, more than 2 million overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) remain across the Middle East, including at least 800,000 in Saudi Arabia, where the widening regional conflict has heightened concerns about their safety. Many face a difficult choice of whether to stay on or return home and lose the incomes their families depend on. Over the weekend, two Houthi strikes hit Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, killing at least 13 people and injuring more than 300.
