Saturday’s attack has been described as the deadliest on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade and the bloodiest on a Gulf Arab nation since the wider conflict began in February. Seven Filipinos were among the injured in those strikes, Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac confirmed on Tuesday, up from an initial report of four wounded. One of the seven was reportedly in a critical condition, two remained in intensive care and four had been discharged from the hospital with minor injuries, Cacdac said, telling Philippine outlet One News that the Department of Migrant Workers was coordinating with the injured Filipinos’ families. The department said in a statement that it continued to provide necessary assistance and support to the victims of the Riyadh attack and was monitoring their condition. Risks abroad For Jacinto, the danger she felt while working in Riyadh was amplified by the sound of explosions and the precautions she and those around her took when they heard them. “There’s an alarm that goes off once we hear the explosions. So once we hear the alarm, we’d run downstairs,” she said. “In the building where I worked, we were on the third floor, so we’d go down to the first floor. We’d all be there, including my employers. It sounded like bombs.” Stories of fellow Filipinos narrowly escaping danger continued to weigh on Jacinto’s mind despite her employer’s reassurances about worker safety. “I have a friend who works in Al-Kharj, where the projectiles landed close to where they were. Other Filipinos I know feel the same; they’re also worried about their situation and want to come home,” she said. More than 12,000 Filipinos were repatriated from the Middle East in the seven months to July – including migrant workers, expatriates and their dependants – while upwards of 140,000 workers received assistance. Yet the number who returned home to the Philippines remains a small proportion of those who continue to work in the region. Economic difficulties were a major factor in whether migrant workers chose to return home or risked staying abroad, said Chat Dimaano, spokesman for Migrante International, a global alliance of OFW advocacy organisations. “They know that if they go home, their family will go hungry. Many of them still have children in school – so what happens to their children’s education?” he said. “They know everything’s getting more expensive across the board … their family keeps pressuring them to send more. So what do the OFWs do? They hold on for dear life – even amid war, it’s ‘come what may’.” The Philippines has one of the world’s most comprehensive labour protection laws, covering pre-departure procedures, overseas assistance and repatriation, as well as training programmes for returning workers, according to Arnold de Vera, director of the University of the Philippines Law Centre’s workers and employees programme. However, de Vera said the country’s weakest area was providing assistance to workers abroad, “given the inherent difficulty of assisting OFWs in foreign countries, especially in areas affected by calamity or violence”. The effectiveness of such assistance efforts was also dependent on the host country’s actions, he said. Dimaano shared similar concerns. “From experience, the government’s narrative is always ‘it’s the host country’s responsibility’, and this goes for migrant workers’ situations beyond the Middle East,” he said. Existing assistance programmes such as the Aksyon Fund for distressed workers and training initiatives for returning migrants were insufficient under current conditions, Dimaano said. “We always ask the government – what is the plan? How can they ensure OFW safety? The government only reacts once there’s a bombing or once things intensify … it’s alarming that the conflict is escalating. Now, Filipinos [have been injured],” he said. “Immediate assistance is needed. If an OFW is in danger, how do you get them out of that situation right away? And of course, the real endpoint of all this should be jobs in the Philippines.” Dimaano said the presence of undocumented Filipino workers further complicated efforts to protect citizens overseas, as these workers “have more hope of supporting their family abroad than at home”. Now back home in the Philippines, Jacinto has found herself struggling to make ends meet and says she may have to seek work abroad again, despite the risks. “I’ll look for a job again, because it’s so hard here. Here, it’s still the same situation … it’s hard to raise a child. I’ll probably just look for another country to work in,” she said.

title: SOTY 2025/26: Community Contributor winner empowers disadvantaged kids with sports
description: Owen Ng from St Paul’s Co-Educational College is passionate about giving all children equal access to sports through his Game On initiative.
content:
Owen Ng Yat-sun lights up whenever he talks about basketball. It is a passion he shares with the young kids at Game On, an initiative he founded to promote equal access to sports in Hong Kong.
The 17-year-old from St Paul’s Co-Educational College became aware of inequalities in sport at a young age. He recalled a basketball competition in Form Two against students from disadvantaged backgrounds.
It sparked an idea that would eventually grow into a citywide movement.
“I noticed the lack of resources among the underprivileged kids. We easily beat them. My teammates were thrilled, but I wasn’t,” Owen said. “Our opponents wore low-cost white canvas shoes, had no coach nor proper gear, whereas my teammates wore expensive trainers. That contrast stuck with me.”
After doing some research, Owen started Game On in the summer of 2022. The award-winning programme gives underprivileged children access to sports and free gear while also mobilising teenage volunteers. It has grown to engage over 5,500 students, of which 500 are volunteers.
At its core, Game On wants to help underprivileged young people build self-esteem and resilience.
“I remember an underprivileged boy, tall for his age, who had never played basketball but displayed great talent during training. He couldn’t even afford a ball for after-school practice. Immediately, I gave him my basketball and coached him for two years,” Owen shared. “Recently, his mother told me he’d been selected for the school team.”
Owen’s dedication and creativity were recognised when he won the Community Contributor category at the 2025/26 Student of the Year Awards, organised by the South China Morning Post and solely sponsored by The Hong Kong Jockey Club.
At the awards ceremony in July, finalists praised Owen’s acceptance speech, which captured the transformative power of community sport.
“Game On is not a one-man team,” Owen said on stage, thanking the volunteers and parents whose support has been integral to the initiative’s success.
Owen described turning Game On from a small organisation into a platform with wider reach.
“With a team of four, we couldn’t scale [up] if we were always the coaches. So I pivoted to a platform model, leveraging teenagers’ enthusiasm to volunteer to meet the kids’ needs, so we could scale up our impact,” he explained.
“Game On is … a bridge linking underprivileged kids with teenage volunteers, satisfying two needs at once: the children who need support and students who need volunteer hours for university.”
Much of the organisation’s growth has been supported by strategic partnerships with established institutions and corporate sponsors.
Owen credits these collaborations with helping Game On overcome many of the logistical challenges associated with delivering sports programmes across the city.
“I work with the Decathlon Foundation, which sponsors our sports gear and rackets. YMCA and the Home Affairs Department provide free venues, essential in cramped, costly Hong Kong,” he recalled.
“Recently SC Storage gave us free space for equipment after I pitched [to] their CEO. Transport was tougher. At first my dad had to do most of the driving, so I spent six months persuading GoGoX [formerly GoGoVan] to handle rides from storage to venues, and they finally agreed.”
Owen has shared his message with more than 15,000 people, speaking at major forums both in Hong Kong and abroad. He said it is important to tailor his message to different audiences to inspire action on sports equity.
“I always research my audience before any presentation. For teenagers, I use vivid analogies and trendy slang and hooks to draw them in,” he said.
“At a Dubai conference several years ago, the consul general of India’s speech left people sleepy, but when I referenced the viral ‘67’ trend and tied it into our volunteer story, the crowd woke up, laughed and gave me their full attention.”
One particular encounter shaped Owen’s philosophy: a meeting with former NBA star Derrick Rose. After being turned away at a press event, Owen spotted Rose’s agent and seized the opportunity to pitch Game On.
He was astonished when Rose and his team granted him a 10-minute one-on-one interview. Owen believes Rose’s upbringing in a disadvantaged community gave him a deep appreciation of sports equity.
“Derrick’s decision to prioritise a small, focused conversation over broader exposure taught [me] a crucial lesson: impact matters more than scale,” Owen said.
The experience prompted Game On to move away from pursuing large participation numbers and instead concentrate on intensive, high-quality coaching. Rather than superficially reaching thousands of children, the organisation invests deeply in a smaller number.
As he prepares for university, Owen hopes to continue making an impact by studying politics, philosophy and economics (PPE).
“Politics, philosophy and economics all involve a great deal of decision-making, especially when it comes to issues like poverty and inequality … That connects closely to the research I was doing and the work I was involved in with Game On,” he said.

title: Costa Rica latest to adopt Bukele blueprint with new mega-prison
description: President vows Costa Rica will become a ‘global benchmark’ for prison security as 5,100-inmate facility opens to confront cartels.
content: Costa Rica, considered for decades a peaceful enclave in turbulent Central America, has now made fighting drug trafficking one of its main goals. And it is turning to one of its Central American neighbours for inspiration in its hardline crackdown. On Wednesday, President Laura Fernandez inaugurated a mega-prison that emulates the Terrorism Confinement Centre (CECOT) that has become a symbol of Salvadorean President Nayib Bukele’s security strategy. Bukele has managed to reduce murders to a historic low in El Salvador but faces accusations of abuses during the state of emergency that began in 2022 and has imprisoned more than 91,000 people. Costa Rica is not the first to turn its attention to the man who has proclaimed himself the “coolest dictator in the world”. Ecuador has done it. So have the new presidents of Peru and Colombia. From Honduras to the Southern Cone, these countries are joining the hardline security strategy also endorsed by US President Donald Trump. Now, Costa Rica says it will incarcerate its most dangerous criminals in the High-Containment Centre against Organised Crime, with a capacity for 5,100 inmates and a cost of US$35 million. “The CACCO will force criminals to face a new model – a tough-on-crime model. Costa Rica ‌will become a global benchmark for prison security,” Fernandez said during the ⁠inauguration ceremony. For decades, Costa Rica was a “passive” transit zone for drugs from South America, according to the organisation Insight Crime. But without an army, and with extensive jungle and ports on both coasts, it began to attract Mexican and Colombian cartels. At the end of the last decade, a new cargo terminal transformed the Caribbean port of Limon into a storage and transshipment point for cocaine destined for Europe, according to the US State Department, which, in a 2025 report, also detected fentanyl distribution in the Central American country. Now, the two major Mexican cartels, Sinaloa and Jalisco, are present in the country, as are the Colombian Clan del Golfo, the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua – all considered terrorist organisations by the United States – and Italian mafias, while local cartels proliferate, explained Vanda Felbab-Brown, an organised crime researcher at the Brookings Institution. The cartels’ interest in new routes and the rivalry between the two major Mexican cartels “pushed local proxies to fight with each other and then drove homicides up” in Costa Rica, Felbab-Brown noted. Payments to these gangs in drugs developed local markets that further increased the violence, and the authorities felt overwhelmed. The alarm was raised in 2023 when the country registered a record 907 homicides – a figure that has decreased, but only slightly – and the government acknowledged that they were mostly due to organised crime. Insecurity, although far from that of Ecuador or Mexico, became the biggest concern for Costa Ricans and was a key factor in Fernandez’s election. It was then that Fernandez’s predecessor, Rodrigo Chaves, sought out Bukele, whose success in cutting down killings has led his counterparts in the region to turn to him for inspiration on security policy. Chaves bestowed him with a diplomatic honour, and sent his security minister to visit the CECOT. The Salvadorean president, in turn, donated the design for the prison to the Costa Rican government. The CECOT has become a symbol of Bukele’s security policy and is increasingly being imitated. Ecuador’s Daniel Noboa opened a similar prison last year. Honduras planned something similar on an island, though it has not yet been built. And Peru’s Keiko Fujimori has just announced a trip to El Salvador in response to the rise in homicides and extortion. The measures tend to be popular, and a large portion of the Costa Rican population supports the new mega-prison. “Many people are afraid,” said Carlos Avila, a business administrator. “I think it’s good that they’re building a prison and isolating the criminals.” Chaves opted for another tool against crime: in 2025, he carried out a constitutional reform to allow Costa Ricans to be extradited for drug trafficking and terrorism offences. In March of this year, the first extraditions to the United States took place, including that of Celso Gamboa, former security minister and Supreme Court justice, accused of drug trafficking. In recent months there have been high-profile arrests, such as that of Alejandro Arias Monge, alias “Diablo”, the country’s most wanted drug trafficker, and the president announced investigations into 200 police officers. Meanwhile, Costa Rica remains a staunch ally of Trump, with agreements to receive deported migrants and participation in the Shield of the Americas, which involves maritime patrols. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: 5 Guangdong-registered yachts to sail into Hong Kong as southbound scheme launches
description: Marine chief Wong Sai-fat pledges to step up patrols while dismissing concerns over possible harm to marine ecology, as yachts set to arrive on Friday.
content: Five Guangdong-registered yachts will sail into Hong Kong waters on Friday when the Southbound Yacht Travel Scheme launches, the city’s marine chief has said, adding that officers will step up patrols. A ceremony marking the scheme’s maiden voyages will also take place. The launch is a key step in the government’s plan to develop Hong Kong’s yacht economy, as outlined in the city’s first five-year plan and the latest policy address. Under the scheme, mainland Chinese vessels can register through the Marine Department’s Electronic Business System to navigate Hong Kong waters. “We treat everyone equally, whether they are local yachts or visiting ones, and we will take enforcement action if we discover any breaches of law,” Director of Marine Wong Sai-fat told a radio programme on Thursday. “Our dynamic system will monitor the navigational safety of yachts and their activities. Therefore, [the scheme] will not negatively affect navigational safety, use of waters or marine ecology.” Wong said 23 individuals or groups had registered through the system as of this week, with five yachts scheduled to enter Hong Kong waters on Friday. About 300 mainland yacht masters had qualified to navigate local waters, he added. Authorities have introduced certification, training and examination arrangements for those seeking to do so. Besides berthing at yacht clubs, visiting vessels can use five designated berthing areas at Tai O, Repulse Bay, Tai Tam Bay, Stanley Bay and Three Fathoms Cove in Sai Kung. Wong said the five areas would offer 115 berths, enough to meet demand from mainland vessels, and authorities would therefore not impose a quota on southbound yachts. Authorities previously said they would monitor and manage traffic at the berthing areas through a dynamic, real-time system. Wong said officers would step up patrols and could impose fixed penalties for minor breaches such as littering, while prosecuting more serious offences. He added that if a yacht left Hong Kong after an offence was committed, the department would refer the case to mainland authorities for follow-up. Asked about the Tai O berthing area’s proximity to the Chinese white dolphin’s habitat, Wong dismissed green groups’ concerns that the scheme could harm marine ecology, saying the government had assessed vessel traffic before designating the areas. “Across the five berth areas, there were a total of 10,000 vessel activities during the first five months of this year, and more than 6,000 took place in Tai O,” he said. “That means there has already been plenty of vessel activity in the area.” Wong added that the five areas did not provide water or electricity, but mainland yachts could obtain supplies from designated water-selling kiosks, bunkering points and marine service providers under the same arrangements as local vessels. The initiative aims to use the city’s extensive coastline and islands to attract more high-spending maritime tourists by easing regulations and introducing new technology. Beijing also approved the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau individual travel scheme for yachts in June. It allows Hong Kong yacht owners to sail to designated ports as part of a broader strategy to develop the yacht economy in the Greater Bay Area.

title: North Korea tests submarine-launched cruise missiles, heightening tensions with Seoul
description: State media said the launches ‘aimed to examine the current mobilised posture of the underwater combat systems’.
content: Pyongyang test-fired two types of cruise missile from a submarine, its state news agency said on Thursday, after weeks of friction with Seoul over a landmine explosion along their border. The missiles were fired into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, on Wednesday without “any adverse impact on the security of neighbouring countries”, the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said. Relations between Pyongyang and Seoul have been further strained since the landmine blast on September 21 in the Seoul-controlled area of the demilitarised zone (DMZ), which injured three South Korean soldiers. Both countries tested upgraded missile technology in the aftermath. The latest test “aimed to examine the current mobilised posture of the underwater combat systems” and served as a navy training exercise, KCNA said. The launches showed the “high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK”, the agency reported, referring to North Korea by the abbreviation of the country’s official name. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff ‌said on Thursday it had monitored and tracked the launches using various assets from before launch through ⁠the cruise and terminal ⁠phases of flight. A JCS spokesperson said the military assessed that one type of cruise missile was launched from a vertical launch system ‌and another from a torpedo tube. North Korea has carried out several missile launches from submarines in recent years, although its sea-based launch capabilities remain unclear. Cruise missiles tend to be jet-propelled and fly at a lower altitude than more sophisticated ballistic missiles, making them harder to detect and intercept. Proven submarine-launched ballistic missile capability would take North Korea’s arsenal to a new level, allowing deployment far beyond the Korean peninsula and a second-strike capability in the event of an attack. Photos released by KCNA showed one missile blasting vertically out of the sea, trailed by a thick plume of smoke. Another photo appeared to show a projectile erupting from the water at a 45-degree angle. Other images showed a missile flying horizontally over the sea, as well as a submarine travelling on the water’s surface. North Korea’s ability to launch missiles from submarines at two different angles carries “tactical significance”, Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification said, as the two launch methods serve different purposes. “Vertical launches allow missiles to climb steeply before descending towards their targets, potentially extending their range,” he said. “Angled launches, on the other hand, allow missiles to fly at lower altitudes from the outset, making them harder for missile defence systems to detect and intercept.” North Korea has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests in October, most recently on Monday. The two Koreas have engaged in a tit-for-tat series of missile tests this month, with both sides test-firing hypersonic weapons. South Korea test-fired its first home-grown hypersonic glide vehicle last week, days after Pyongyang said it had launched an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile. Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.

title: Letters | How Hong Kong’s civil service can inspire excellence
description: Readers discuss ways to better motivate government employees, and how to teach children better mental health habits.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. As Hong Kong’s enhanced civil service appraisal system begins to take effect, the government has an opportunity to clarify not only the consequences of underperformance but also what sustained excellence can lead to. More rigorous appraisal is justified. The Civil Service Bureau reported that only 94 civil servants – out of roughly 170,000 – were denied increments because of unsatisfactory performance between 2021 and 2025. It cited overly generous ratings that failed to distinguish between outstanding, average and substandard performers. Accountability, however, cannot rely on penalties alone. A stick may discourage underperformance, but does not necessarily inspire excellence. If reform is intended to build a high-performing civil service, civil servants should understand not only what happens when they fall short, but also how consistently strong performance can enhance their career opportunities. Hong Kong does not lack ways to recognise capable civil servants. Promotion, commendation, leadership development, training and important assignments already form part of the system. The more important question is whether civil servants can clearly see how sustained excellence improves their prospects of accessing these opportunities. The government could consider making that connection more explicit. The Civil Service Bureau could publish the criteria for leadership programmes, strategic assignments and interdepartmental postings, including how sustained performance is considered alongside competencies and operational needs. Consistently strong performers could also receive structured career development discussions that help them understand what experience and capabilities are required for future advancement. The objective is to establish a clearer and more credible pathway from demonstrated contribution to professional growth. If appraisal reform is partly about identifying and developing future leaders, Hong Kong should also think about widening the talent pipeline in addition to the traditional administrative/executive officer pathways. While the government already engages professionals through contract and non-civil service appointments, there may be scope for creation of opportunities for experienced mid-career professionals to enter the civil service. Such individuals can bring specialist expertise, fresh perspectives and experience gained outside government. At the same time, they should be provided with structured training, mentoring and coaching to help them understand public service values and adapt successfully to the civil service environment. Ultimately, reform should strengthen the government’s capacity to deliver. Roy Ying, senior lecturer, Department of Marketing, Hang Seng University of Hong Kong Children learn to rest by watching adults I refer to the Legislative Council education panel meeting on October 2. In the first six days of this school year, at least eight students died by suicide or attempted it, according to a figure cited in Legco. Yet the two-hour meeting largely dwelled on the Northern Metropolis and artificial intelligence, with about four minutes going to student mental health. Education Secretary Christine Choi Yuk-lin rightly said that the key is teachers and parents showing children they care more about growth than grades. Last month, the city worried about falling Pisa (Programme for International Student Assessment) subject scores, not about the same report placing Hong Kong students below the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) average in areas such as curiosity, perseverance and sense of belonging at school. Choi also said the bureau would review whether school arrangements, such as rushed lunch breaks, add to students’ stress. As a partner organisation of the bureau’s 4Rs Mental Health Charter, we help teachers and parents tend their relationships with children. Our partner schools survey students on relationships and school life and we review the results with each school. At one school, Primary Five and Six students rated recess poorly. We wondered whether the playground was too far away, leaving little time to play. A nearer space was made available and recess ratings rose. But rushed lunches are not only a student problem. Nearly eight in 10 Hong Kong teachers work more than 51 hours a week, a union survey found. We cannot give children what we don’t have, or ask them to do what we can’t do ourselves. So the work begins with us learning to look after ourselves first. Children don’t learn to rest from a circular. They learn it by watching us. Raymond Yang Sze-ngai, co-founder and executive director, Just Feel

title: How a fuel crisis is threatening Bangladesh’s reform goals: ‘it hit our citizens hard’
description: Surging inflation and rising prices are straining government finances as the new leadership battles to reform the country.
content: Faced with a fuel crisis beyond its control, Bangladesh’s government is spending the equivalent of hundreds of millions of US dollars each month to insulate its people from surging prices. But as growth slows and inflation rises, the new government’s reform plans are being tested before it has had much time to clean up the country’s troubled financial institutions or retool its young, abundant – but underemployed – workforce for the AI era. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman took office on February 17, elected on promises of sweeping economic and social reforms to turn the country of 175 million people into a US$1 trillion economy within a decade. An interim government had steered the nation through the treacherous months following former leader Sheikh Hasina’s downfall in 2024. She was ousted by a student-led revolt after what they called 15 years of repression, corruption and bad governance. Her critics say those years saw cronies freely dip into state banks, stuffing them with bad loans and leaving the healthcare and education systems in tatters, all while filling the civil service with loyalists to her Awami League party rather than competent administrators. But just 11 days after Rahman – a scion of a rival political clan to Hasina – was sworn in, the US and Israel attacked Iran, sending the price of oil and gas skyrocketing upwards. In Bangladesh, which imported about 65 per cent of its energy needs last year, that has meant power cuts, long queues at petrol stations and rising costs for everything from transport to food. “Energy is not just buying oil, gas or fertiliser,” Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, an adviser to Rahman, told This Week in Asia on the sidelines of the IMF–World Bank summit in Bangkok. “It hit our citizens hard,” he said. “Our estimates are that from late February [to now] we have spent an estimated US$4.1 billion in additional costs.” Some of the impact should have been cushioned by solar power, especially in a nation increasingly scorched by global warming. But “the previous government didn’t build any sustainable energy security infrastructure”, Titumir said, part of a legacy of years of mismanagement and corruption. The World Bank and Asian Development Bank have both provided hundreds of millions of US dollars in loans to help lighten the government’s energy cost burden. The IMF, which has about US$1 trillion in loan capacity, has also dispersed nearly US$3.6 billion to Bangladesh since 2023 – a loan Rahman’s government is hoping to renegotiate this week in Bangkok. But as the outside pressures build, the International Monetary Fund on Tuesday trimmed Bangladesh’s growth projection for 2027 to 3.2 per cent from 3.6 per cent this year, placing it behind Cambodia and climate-battered Nepal among developing Asian nations. It also forecast inflation to nudge upwards to 10.9 per cent in 2027 from 8.7 per cent this year – although Bangladesh’s government said both projections had not fully taken into account the impact of its structural reforms of financial institutions, indebted businesses and a hollowed out welfare state. “Unfortunately the people are suffering for the misdeeds of the previous regime,” Titumir said. “We have already brought five banks to be owned by the government … after fears there will be a bank run, that has now calmed. We want to bring discipline into the system [and] then provide finance for investment, finance for expansion.” He said future growth would sprout from foreign investment into new manufacturing – including electronics and toys – infrastructure, solar power, deep-sea ports and new special economic zones, including the US$1.3 billion China-backed zone in Anwara, southern Bangladesh. Bangladesh also has a young population, deep experience in manufacturing – including in its key garment industry – and a rich seam of cheap workers available to be tapped by firms looking to relocate from Southeast Asia, where costs are rising. But questions remain over how Bangladesh will equip itself with the energy, skills and infrastructure needed to capitalise on the AI revolution that now undergirds much of global growth. The IMF’s message in Bangkok this week pointed to a two-speed world economy: one weighed down by sky-high energy prices and another propelled by the trillions of dollars invested into AI and its spin-off industries, from data centres to semiconductors and printed circuit boards. “Who is taking the biggest hit? Low-income countries. Especially those who are energy importers or left out from technology boom,” IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday. She hailed Asia as “the engine of global growth” but warned nations hit by the energy crisis to run a tight ship, despite the political temptations to roll out sweeping subsidies. “First protect your buffers, protect your fiscal space,” she said, advising governments to give out “temporary and targeted support to the most vulnerable”. Bangladesh, South Asia’s second-largest economy, is now at a turning point. Rahman’s Bangladesh National Party government swept to power with a two-thirds majority in February’s election on a platform of reform, but it now faces a populace anxious for immediate change after the toxic Hasina era. His family has traded power with Hasina’s clan for much of the South Asian nation’s short but turbulent history. The 57-year-old returned from years in self-exile in London to successfully contest this year’s election, following a transition period overseen by an interim government, led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, which navigated the chaotic and violent aftermath of Hasina’s ousting by student protesters. “We have delivered in the past,’’ added Titumir, the prime minister’s adviser on finance and planning, noting that Rahman’s “political approval” had handed his administration a clear mandate for reform. Rahman’s mother, Khaleda Zia, served three terms as prime minister between 1991 and 2006. She was detained several times for her political activism during a decades-long power struggle with Hasina – the daughter of independence icon Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. Zia died last year. Her husband, the former army commander and war hero Ziaur Rahman, was assassinated in 1981 after leading the country for five years.

title: HSBC launches discretionary portfolio management service for retail investors
description: HSBC aims to lure younger, tech-savvy customers with discretionary investment service once only available to private bank clients.
content: HSBC has launched a discretionary portfolio management service for retail investors with a minimum investment threshold as low as HK$1,000 (US$128) per month, as Hong Kong’s largest lender aims to attract younger, tech-savvy customers. The new service, “Portfolio+”, allows HSBC’s retail banking customers in Hong Kong to build a discretionary investment portfolio via the company’s mobile apps with a lump sum of at least HK$10,000 or regular contributions of HK$1,000 per month, according to Winnie Ng, head of wealth and Premier solutions at HSBC Hong Kong. Investors could choose to allocate their investments at different risk levels or under themes such as green concepts, with the bank then investing the funds and rebalancing the investment mix according to its house view, Ng told reporters ahead of the service’s launch on Thursday. “We would like to capture the young investors aged 35 or younger who are too busy to invest or who have little or no investment experience. Our investment experts can invest for them according to their risk appetite and investment goals,” she said. “With the help of technology to do analysis and documentation work, we can now introduce the discretionary investment services to the mass market of retail investors. Previously, we could only provide such a type of service to private bank clients as discretionary services involve a lot of manual work.” HSBC Hong Kong has 7 million customers – a figure almost equal to the city’s population – and the bank has focused on promoting its investment and wealth management business in the city in recent years. The discretionary investment service will charge a fee of 0.5 to 0.8 per cent per annum, based on the portfolio’s assets under management, charged monthly, according to the bank. Allen Chiu, head of discretionary and funds specialists at HSBC Hong Kong wealth and premier solutions, said Portfolio+ would adopt a globally diversified approach, investing in stocks and bonds in the United States, Europe, the Asia-Pacific region and emerging economies. The lower-risk portfolios were more heavily weighted towards global fixed income, while higher-risk portfolios had greater equity exposure, particularly to US markets, he said. “Diversification would be the key of success for investors to cope with the volatile markets and achieve growth of their investment for the long term,” Chiu said. Ng said the bank would invest these assets via exchange-traded funds listed in London, while it would consider investing in Hong Kong ETFs in the next stage. The portfolios also include selective alternative-asset-style exposure, such as listed property and infrastructure ETFs.

title: Ancient Chinese families gave babies humble nicknames – ‘Dog’, ‘Pig’ – to ward off bad luck
description: Some believe these humble nicknames carry parents’ heartfelt blessings and should be preserved.
content: Like people elsewhere in the world, Chinese people often have nicknames in addition to their official names. Some of these may surprise people from other cultures because they sound humble or even unflattering. Chinese parents have traditionally given their children humble, sometimes vulgar, nicknames – occasionally using animal names such as “Dog” or “Pig.” The practice dates back to ancient times. Parents believed that the humbler a nickname sounded, the better, as it might help ensure their child grew up healthy. This practice was a desperate measure in ancient times, when medical technology was limited and people’s average lifespans were short. As a result, many families – from ordinary households to the imperial family – gave their children animal-related names, hoping they would be as healthy and resilient as animals believed to have strong vitality. Ouyang Xiu, a literary giant of the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), wrote in his book Dao Shan Qing Hua that families who wanted their children to grow up easily often chose humble words for their names. Examples include gou sheng (food left over by dogs), gou dan (dog and egg), gou shi (dog faeces) and zhu wa (piglet). Some parents named their children after hard objects, such as stones, iron hammers, iron pillars or locks. These names expressed the hope that their children would be tough enough to withstand illness and other misfortunes. Other parents gave their children rustic names, believing that an inconspicuous name would attract less attention from evil spirits and help protect them from misfortune. Emperor Wu of the Western Han dynasty (202 BC–9) had the nickname zhi, meaning “pig” in ancient Chinese. Sima Xiangru, a celebrated writer and diplomat of the Western Han dynasty, had the nickname quan zi, meaning “dog’s child.” Fan Ye, a historian of the Southern dynasties (420–589), was nicknamed zhuan er, meaning “brick.” Xin Qiji, a renowned poet and general of the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279), gave his son the nickname tie zhu, meaning “iron pillar”, according to one of his poems. Zhu Yuanzhang, the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), was nicknamed chong ba, meaning “the eighth,” because he was the eighth child in his family. Today, thanks to advances in medicine, few Chinese families – apart from some in rural areas – continue this practice of giving children humble nicknames. Parents no longer feel the same need to use such names to protect their children from misfortune. A woman born in the 1980s in northwestern China’s Shaanxi province wrote on social media that her nickname was gou dan (dog and egg). When her mother once visited her at university and called her by the nickname in front of her roommates, they could not help laughing. “How embarrassed I was at the time! But my mother is used to calling me that. Afterwards, I asked her not to use the name outside the home,” said the woman, who was identified by her surname, Zhang. She said her parents insisted on using the nickname because she had nearly died from an illness when she was just a few months old. In 2024, the comic TV series Gou Sheng Running Quickly, which tells the story of an orphan named gou sheng (food left over by dogs) growing up, brought the tradition of humble nicknames into the spotlight and sparked heated discussion. “These humble nicknames carry parents’ heartfelt blessings. I think this tradition should be preserved,” one person commented. Another user remarked: “I have an uncle in his 70s whose nickname is ye hu (chamber pot). Everyone in my family calls him that, and I don’t even know his real name.”

title: Malaysian tycoon goes on Singapore property buying spree to ‘catch up with the rest’
description: Lee Yeow Seng, who is eyeing the Kempinski hotel, seeks to challenge the wealthy clans that dominate Singapore’s property market.
content: Malaysian property tycoon Lee Yeow Seng is making waves as one of the most aggressive buyers of commercial real estate in Singapore, and he is not done yet. His IOI Properties Group is in exclusive talks and due diligence to purchase two property assets – Chijmes, a retail venue inside a former Catholic convent in its civic district, and the nearby Capitol Kempinski hotel, CEO Lee said in an interview. He declined to disclose how much a final agreement will value the two assets at, citing ongoing negotiations. Singapore developer Perennial Holdings has been trying to sell the Kempinski hotel, which was being marketed for about S$600 million (US$468 million), according to people familiar with the matter. Chijmes was valued at S$379 million at the end of 2025. IOI’s debt-fuelled buying spree has spurred a record year for real estate deals in Singapore. The firm is now courting investors for a new fund to ease the burden and give room for further expansion, as Lee seeks to challenge the wealthy clans that dominate Singapore’s property market. “I’m a latecomer and I want to catch up with the rest,” the 47-year-old CEO said on the sidelines of a Forbes event in Singapore last week. “Most of them don’t share the vision of me.” Perennial controls about a third of Chijmes and about 80 per cent of Capitol Singapore, a broader complex that contains the hotel, as well as a retail plaza and residential units. A vehicle backed by an unnamed Southeast Asian sovereign wealth fund has a minority stake in both assets, corporate records show. Other Chijmes investors include local food chain Breadtalk Group and Ronald Ooi, the former chair and CEO of Kim Eng, a stock brokerage. Representatives for Perennial, which is backed by investors including palm oil tycoon Kuok Khoon Hong and Chinese private equity veteran Fang Fenglei, did not respond to requests for comment. IOI is in talks to bring high-end fashion brands into Chijmes to raise rents, which have been depressed by a predominance of food and drink outlets, Lee said. It also wants a global ultra-luxury hotel brand to replace the Kempinski, he said. Lee’s Malaysia-listed firm, which has a large presence in its home country including one of the world’s largest shopping centres, has splashed out on a range of Singapore properties in recent years. It gained full control of South Beach, an office complex that also houses his luxury penthouse and the JW Marriott hotel, after buying the majority stake from partner City Developments, which was looking to reduce debt. More recently, it bought office building Asia Square Tower 2, ballooning his commercial portfolio to S$10 billion. It is also looking to form a joint venture with CapitaLand Investment, a property manager backed by Temasek Holdings, to buy One Raffles Place, people familiar with the matter said in August. The famous office complex is majority-owned by OUE REIT, which confirmed last week that it is in exclusive discussions with the firms on a potential sale. IOI’s rapid acquisitions have fuelled a surge in its borrowings, with its net debt rising to 85 per cent of equity as of end-June. In 2024, its board rebuffed a proposal by Lee to acquire Shenton House in Singapore amid concerns about heavy capital commitments in Singapore and Malaysia. Lee, who is a scion of a wealthy palm oil family in Malaysia, made the purchase on his own. The firm eventually agreed to acquire the office building and its liabilities this month to redevelop it. Even with a planned Malaysia real estate investment trust listing, that is expected to raise the firm’s gearing further. Lee said he aims to reduce the net debt to 30-50 per cent of its equity in the next three to five years. His plans largely hinge on the success of a private fund, which Lee said will be set up in two months. He has tapped ex-Pimco Prime Real Estate executive Varun Singh to oversee the vehicle, which will initially include two assets totalling S$6 billion: the office portion of South Beach and the firm’s marquee office building IOI Central Boulevard Towers, whose tenants include Morgan Stanley and Jane Street Capital. Lee said the fund has courted investors including private equity firms, sovereign wealth funds and insurers, but declined to share names. It is targeting an internal rate of return of 10-11 per cent, with semi-annual distributions, he said. The firm is looking to pare down its stake in the assets to about half by marketing minimum holdings of about S$500 million with a five to seven-year lock-up. It will look to inject more of its Singapore assets into the fund during that period, and eventually list it as a Reit. Lee is more optimistic about real estate prospects in Singapore than rival financial hub Hong Kong, saying the former does not have the baggage of being fully absorbed back into China in 2047 and will continue to be favoured by the wealthy and global companies. Still, other bets in Singapore have stumbled, including IOI’s plans to build a city centre luxury residential project with 683 homes. The firm is liable to pay a higher tax, having sold only about 15 units there. Lee said he has secured a short-term reprieve from Singapore authorities until next April and will keep appealing against paying the charge. The firm is pivoting towards renting out its units to expats, he said, blaming a 60 per cent levy imposed on most foreigner purchases in 2023 for the poor sales. But he remains undeterred in investing in Singapore, saying lenders and the company’s board remain supportive. “If I can expand, why should I hold myself back?” he said. “No one has asked me to slow down.”

title: Asian Cup could be switched to 2028, tennis’ Six Kings Slam delayed over Saudi bomb fears
description: Asia football chiefs say decision over whether to move tournament does not need to be made yet, while other sports monitor security in region.
content: The Six Kings Slam tennis tournament originally scheduled for ⁠October has been pushed back to late December, Fifa’s esports finals have been postponed, and officials are considering whether to move the Asian Cup to 2028, after the recent ⁠attacks on Saudi Arabia. A strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement claiming responsibility for the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Thursday, organisers of the Fifae Finals, which were expected to start in Jeddah this week, had been postponed. Brazil and Japan had already withdrawn their teams over safety concerns. “The decision follows an ⁠assessment of recent developments in the region and their impact ‌on the logistical arrangements required to stage the tournament,” organisers of the global video game ‌tournament said. “Further announcements on the FIFAe Finals will ⁠be communicated ⁠in due course.” A day earlier, officials had said the decision to delay the four-day tennis event until December 27 reflected a “commitment to delivering sporting events to the highest standards”. An assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament had been made, and the “potential impact on the quality of the audience experience” taken into account. Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic, Alexander Zverev and Taylor Fritz were set to take part in the event. Defending champion Jannik Sinner had previously withdrawn because of injury. While the tournament is an exhibition event, the record prize money draws the world’s best, with Alcaraz acknowledging in 2024 that the financial aspect played a role as he earned US$1.5 million ‌over four days. The attacks have threatened to disrupt sport in the kingdom, with golf’s Asian Tour also saying it is monitoring the security situation ahead of the Saudi International in Riyadh next month. Saudi Arabia is also set to stage the Asian Cup for the first time ⁠in 2027, a key test ⁠ahead of the kingdom’s hosting of the 2034 World Cup. The 24-team tournament is scheduled to kick off on January 7 across eight venues in three cities – Riyadh, ‌Jeddah and Al-Khobar. Asian Football Confederation president Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said they were in “no hurry to make a decision” on whether to postpone the tournament or not. “We can wait until the ‌end ‌of November. Things can change very quickly for better or worse in the region and it is a question of seeing what happens,” ‌he told reporters in Zurich where the Fifa Council is meeting. “If we need to make a decision then we will, but we ⁠could move back a year to 2028 if we need to. But at the moment we are monitoring the situation and everything ⁠is on schedule.” The 2023 tournament was postponed from June 2023 to July 2024 after China withdrew as hosts because of Covid restrictions and Qatar stepped in to host the tournament in the winter.

title: Hong Kong teen makes cents of finance, taps AI to tackle economic inequality
description: Spirit of Youth Award finalist Agastya Rekhi runs three student initiatives breaking down financial and technological barriers.
content: At 17, Hong Kong secondary school student Agastya Rekhi has been teaching finance and economics to younger children for nearly three years. Meeting families struggling to understand how prices, investments and economic news impacted their daily lives during voluntary work convinced him that access to information was only part of the problem. How that information was communicated was just as important. Rekhi, a finalist for the Spirit of Youth Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, has since launched three student-led projects spanning financial education, simplified economic news and AI support for smaller organisations. He started Launchpad at 14, leveraging his interests in games and art to teach economics, business and financial literacy to children. Rekhi said the project has held about 105 sessions, reaching 215 students across Hong Kong, India and the United Kingdom. Instead of relying on textbooks, lessons turn economic concepts into activities. For example, the concept of the “tragedy of the commons”, coined by American ecologist Garrett Hardin to describe how overusing shared resources causes collective ruin, was taught through a game in which children shared a plate of marshmallows using chopsticks. Through this, students learned how taking too many out of self-interest left fewer shared resources for everyone else. Rekhi said the intention was to make concepts that can appear intimidating more familiar, particularly for children who may not grow up discussing money or investing at home. “Financial literacy is often thought of as something that maybe privileged people talk about with their parents. That leaves a lot of the public without support,” he said. He also encourages young people to understand investment fundamentals and risk before putting money into speculative assets, cautioning against excessive leverage and short-term trading. Two years ago, he launched his initiative, Illuminet, connecting students interested in artificial intelligence (AI) with charities and small and medium-sized businesses that lack the resources to adopt the technology on their own. Students help these firms set up tools such as automated drafting or simple chatbots, so they can use AI without hiring full-time technical staff. Rekhi noted that while larger companies have greater capacity to use new technology, smaller organisations risk being left behind. A third project, The Bottom Line, began about a year ago as a school newsletter explaining economic and financial news in plain English. Rekhi said it has grown to an 18-member team, with about 23 partner organisations distributing it to more than 6,500 monthly readers as of September. The publication also prompted him to reconsider who his target audience really was. During a visit to subdivided flats in To Kwa Wan, Rekhi met a woman who was saving for her daughter to attend university in the United States while coping with rising household costs. Because she mainly spoke Cantonese, friends had to step in to translate. Rekhi said the encounter made him realise that publishing only in English had unintentionally excluded people who might benefit most from accessible economic information. A Chinese edition was subsequently introduced and distributed through local schools and charities. Although the three projects operate differently, Rekhi sees them as responses to the same problem: economic inequality. Launchpad equips younger students with financial knowledge, The Bottom Line makes economic news easier to understand, and Illuminet helps smaller organisations use emerging technology. Looking ahead, Rekhi hopes to study economics at university and eventually help shape policies that allow economic growth to benefit people across all income brackets. “I want to ensure that people from all backgrounds have the knowledge and interest to participate in the financial system,” he said. The Spirit of Hong Kong Awards were established in 2013 to recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might escape public attention.

title: Mainland China, Hong Kong stocks fall as US inflation spurs Fed tightening concerns
description: Asian markets slump as recent US inflation numbers boost expectations of a rate hike and a plunge in South Korean market dents sentiment.
content: Stocks in mainland China and Hong Kong slumped on Thursday, with the benchmark of yuan-denominated equities sliding to a 14-month low, as a hot reading on US inflation boosted bets that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates and a plunge in the South Korean market further dented sentiment. The CSI 300 Index slid 1.2 per cent to 4,166.01 at the close, the lowest since August 12, 2025. The chip-heavy Star Market 50 gauge tumbled to a six-month low with a 1.5 per cent decline. The Hang Seng Index fell 1 per cent to 24,062.72, while the Hang Seng Tech Index sank 2.7 per cent. South Korea’s Kospi index, a proxy for the AI trade, plunged more than 7 per cent, dragged down by heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix on unease over increased supply in the memory chip industry. China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies said that it would roll out a new product with more storage density by the end of the year following a technological breakthrough, challenging the monopolistic positions of the two Korean giants. Sticky US inflation added to a slew of headwinds capping Chinese equities, which have experienced whiplash from the unravelling of leveraged positions, a purported unwinding of equity holdings by insurance firms and a lopsided economy. Investors are turning their eyes to top policymakers, as speculation about more state support is mounting before a scheduled speech by the chief of the China Securities Regulatory Commission on Monday. A symposium convened by the stock-market regulator over the weekend to restore confidence fell short of shoring up the market. Higher borrowing costs are compressing equity valuations and dampening the earnings outlook by eroding corporate margins, while also spurring outflows from Asian markets and rotation to high-yielding US assets. “Higher yields both discount future earnings and raise the cost of funding AI capital expenditure,” said Gary Dugan, CEO of The Global CIO Office, which advises high-net-worth investors and family offices. The probability that the Fed would boost the benchmark borrowing cost by a quarter-point in December has risen to 64 per cent now from 50 per cent a month ago, according to the CME Group. The odds for an increase at the Fed’s rate-decision meeting at the end of the month stand at 29 per cent. US consumer prices rose 3.7 per cent from a year ago in September, growing at a faster pace than the consensus estimate of a 3.6 per cent increase. The September price increase was broad-based, extending beyond the categories directly hit by rising energy costs, according to Citigroup, which predicted that the Fed would deliver one hike in December before beginning to cut rates in June. Bank of America expected an increase this month, citing that more parts of the economy were under inflationary pressure. “Once borrowing costs rise enough, the problem can become self-reinforcing,” said Stephen Innes, a managing partner at SPI Asset Management. “Wider spreads increase the cost of capital, higher financing costs pressure project economics, weaker economics hit equity valuations, falling equity prices undermine confidence, and suddenly the same capital markets that funded the boom become more reluctant to roll the next tranche,” he added. Earlier data releases show that China’s patchy economic growth continued into September, when exports held up strongly and domestic demand remained sluggish. Consumer inflation was also subdued, while an acceleration of producer prices was mainly driven by surging oil, and long-term loan growth softened, indicating weak demand for investment and home purchases. The National Bureau of Statistics was due to disclose other key third-quarter economic figures on Monday. Further downside in Chinese stocks was limited because the unwinding of crowded trading on technology stocks was close to its end, according to Meng Lei, a strategist at UBS Group. “However, a rapid return of sidelined capital appears unlikely in the near term, as investor risk appetite may take time to recover,” he said.

title: Style Edit: Chanel unveils 2027 J12 Boat Race trophies as women’s event turns 100
description: The historic Oxford-Cambridge race on the Thames will get a sleek upgrade next year with cups designed by Chanel’s watchmaking lead, Arnaud Chastaingt.
content: For a sporting event steeped in British tradition, the Boat Race has always been as much about ritual as competition. In 2027, that history will meet a distinctly Chanel interpretation, as the maison introduces new trophies for the winning Oxford and Cambridge crews, marking both a new chapter in its partnership with the race and the centenary of the first Women’s Boat Race. The 2027 edition will be the third year of the Chanel J12 Boat Race, with the maison serving as title sponsor and official timekeeping partner. It is also the first time Chanel has created sporting trophies, bringing the language of its watchmaking into one of Britain’s most enduring sporting spectacles. Designed by Arnaud Chastaingt, director of Chanel’s Watchmaking Creation Studio, the trophies translate the J12’s visual codes into a form traditionally associated with sporting victory. Rather than simply reproducing a cup’s familiar proportions, Chastaingt has pared back its curves and volume, setting the polished silver form within a strong rectangular frame. This outer frame is rendered in polished white for the women’s trophy and polished black for the men’s, both accented with matt black detailing. The palette recalls the black-and-white identity of the J12, while the geometry gives the trophies a more contemporary, architectural character. A gold-plated silver medallion, edged in black, sits at the centre, marking the meeting of Chanel and the Boat Race. The objects are designed not merely to be admired but to be held. Their frames have been engineered with the winners’ moment of celebration in mind, allowing the crew to lift them comfortably together. That emphasis on function reflects the ethos shared by Chanel and the Boat Race: precision is meaningful only when it works in concert with discipline, timing and collective effort. Bringing the designs into physical form was British trophy specialist Thomas Lyte, holder of a Royal Warrant as Goldsmiths and Silversmiths to His Majesty King Charles III. Nearly two years of development and more than 320 hours of craftsmanship went into their making. The timing is particularly significant. The Women’s Boat Race was established in 1927, though crews initially raced separately rather than directly against one another and were judged on both speed and style. The students who competed were pioneers at a time when women’s rowing had yet to reach the Olympic Games. A century later, their legacy will be celebrated on the same stretch of the Thames. For the centenary edition, the men’s race will run first on the Championship Course, followed an hour later by the women’s race. Both crews will have something new to lift at the finish. “Our ambition is to support and safeguard what makes this historic event so exceptional: its traditions, uncompromising standards and the remarkable collective endeavour it celebrates. The creation of these trophies embodies that commitment,” says Frédéric Grangié, Chanel’s president of watches and fine jewellery. “Conceived with humility and respect for the heritage of The Chanel J12 Boat Race, they unite Chanel’s creative vision in tribute to the athletes whose precision, discipline and teamwork define every edition. We hope they will become enduring symbols of achievement for the crews who raise them, today and for generations to come.”

title: South Korea’s offender tracking under scrutiny after stabbing spree exposes ‘serious gaps’
description: Justice ministry statistics show that repeat sexual offences by people wearing electronic monitoring ankle tags continue to occur.
content: A stabbing rampage by a repeat violent offender wearing an electronic ankle monitor has raised questions about whether South Korea’s criminal justice system can adequately supervise those deemed high-risk and prevent attacks before they happen. The 59-year-old suspect told investigators he had become frustrated over what he perceived as mistreatment at a hospital, police said on Wednesday. Three criminal profilers were helping investigators establish the motive for Tuesday’s attack at a shopping centre in Incheon, which left 10 people injured, including a woman in her twenties who remained in a coma. “I did not target any specific person and I chose people who looked weaker than me, but I had no intention to kill,” the suspect was quoted as saying during questioning at Namdong Police Station in Incheon. He wielded knives strapped to both his hands as he moved between floors of the shopping centre, attacking people at random until a group managed to subdue him by throwing chairs at him. “He swung the knives at everyone he saw. People fled in panic. Most people were stabbed in their backs,” said an employee who was working on the shopping centre’s first floor. Another witness said: “He went after anyone he encountered. He just kept swinging his knives without saying a word.” Police said the suspect was carrying what appeared to be prescription psychiatric medication in his backpack but tested negative in a preliminary drug screening. According to police, he had been receiving treatment for athlete’s foot at a local hospital but was dissatisfied that his symptoms had not improved. In August, he began staging a one-man protest outside the hospital while holding a knife, prompting the facility to report him to the police, who brought him in for questioning. “I was unhappy because I was investigated by police after the hospital reported me,” he was quoted as telling investigators. President Lee Jae Myung visited the Incheon Metropolitan Police Agency on Tuesday and called for effective measures to prevent similar incidents from recurring. The justice ministry has apologised and pledged a thorough investigation, as well as a review of the country’s electronic monitoring system after the suspect was identified as a repeat violent offender wearing an ankle tag. “We will conduct a comprehensive review of the electronic monitoring framework and the system for supervising and guiding offenders, and promptly prepare measures to address any gaps,” the ministry said in a statement. “We will focus all our capabilities on preventing similar incidents from recurring, placing the lives and safety of the public as our top priority.” Safety shortcomings Lee Dong-gyu, a professor in the department of disaster and emergency management at Dong-A University, said the attack had exposed serious shortcomings in the surveillance and management of dangerous offenders. “This incident has laid bare the serious gaps in monitoring and controlling high-risk offenders,” he said. In South Korea, certain high-risk offenders can be required to wear an electronic ankle tag under court orders. The device continuously transmits location data through cellular networks to monitoring centres, allowing authorities to track an offender’s movements around the clock. If the wearer enters a restricted area or leaves a designated zone, the system alerts monitoring authorities at the justice ministry. However, Lee Dong-gyu said the ministry lacked sufficient personnel to monitor offenders’ movements and coordinate with police officers on the ground to intervene when necessary. He also suggested that the government upgrade the electronic monitoring devices so they could detect changes in physiological signals, such as an elevated heart rate potentially associated with alcohol consumption, and alert authorities to possible risks. The system’s limitations have been highlighted in previous cases. Last year, police were unaware for six days that a convicted sex offender had tampered with electronic monitoring equipment installed at his residence. Cho Doo-soon, who served a 12-year sentence for raping an eight-year-old girl and inflicting injuries that required prolonged medical treatment, repeatedly violated restrictions on leaving his home despite being under close supervision following his release from prison in 2020. “The government should have learned from the Cho Doo-soon case and bolstered its manpower and equipment to prevent similar incidents,” Lee Dong-gyu said. Justice ministry statistics show that repeat sexual offences by people wearing electronic ankle tags continue to occur, averaging about two cases a month. According to data the ministry submitted on Wednesday to Park Jie-won, a lawmaker from the ruling Democratic Party of Korea, 106 repeat sexual offences were committed by individuals under electronic monitoring between January 2022 and August 2026, an average of 1.9 cases a month. During the same period, there were two repeat murder offences and two repeat robbery offences under electronic monitoring, the data showed. Violations of court-imposed restrictions have also increased. The number of breaches of restrictions on leaving home rose by 26 per cent, from 759 in 2024 to 956 in 2025. Between January 2022 and August 2026, authorities recorded 4,552 violations of restrictions on leaving offenders’ residences, equivalent to roughly two or three incidents a day. The same period also saw 41 violations of no-contact orders protecting victims and 31 cases of tampering with electronic monitoring devices. Analysts attribute the trend in part to a decline in field supervision personnel, despite an increase in the number of offenders subject to electronic monitoring. The number of people under electronic monitoring rose by 23 per cent to 5,301 in August this year, from 4,316 in 2022. By contrast, the number of staff directly responsible for supervising and managing these individuals in the field fell by 21 per cent, from 255 to 234. As a result, the average caseload per supervisor increased from 17.1 offenders to 20.3. Lee Do-sun, a professor of police science at Hannam University, said the government needed to urgently increase staffing to prevent repeat offending. “There are manpower shortages both at the ministry tasked with monitoring dangerous repeat offenders and among police officers on the ground who should act quickly to bring offenders under control,” he said. He called for an integrated system through which government agencies and police could share real-time information about high-risk offenders, citing Britain as a potential model. “Electronic tags only reveal where the wearers are, but through these devices, you never know how dangerous they are or what their propensity for violence is,” he said. South Korea also needed more specialists capable of assessing the risk of reoffending, he said, including factors such as alcohol dependence, impaired impulse control, obsessive behaviour and other psychological problems. “With the current manpower, these tasks are almost impossible to carry out,” he said.

title: Opinion | Young Chinese are choosing healthy relationships over toxic filial piety
description: The support for Olympic diver Zhang Jiaqi amid struggles with her mother shows young people today have a different view of the relationship with their parents.
content: As the Chinese saying goes, “Even an upright judge finds it hard to settle family matters.” Whenever Chinese TV channels air reality shows that centre on couples or parent-child relationships, controversy is guaranteed. Heated debates ensue over who is right and who is wrong. Viewers examine every facial expression in microscopic detail and overanalyse every word before arriving at their verdict. Yet, that wasn’t the case with Zhang Jiaqi after the Olympic diving medallist and her mother, Xiao Yingjie, recently appeared on the reality show My Little One, produced by Hunan TV. Zhang received overwhelming support from young viewers. Many were particularly annoyed by the way Zhang’s mother constantly belittled her daughter and could not find a single compliment. They also took aim at Xiao’s repeated nitpicking, telling Zhang to stop eating snacks and having cold drinks. Zhang’s room was too messy; her cat too troublesome. Zhang recounted that she won her first competition at the age of 10, taking home more than 4,000 yuan (US$600). Since then, her mother has managed her earnings, bonuses and commercial income. Zhang has three bank cards in her name, but she has never had possession of them and doesn’t know the passwords. One constant thread in the online posts I have read concerned a letter from Xiao to Zhang. She wrote a few lines complimenting Zhang’s high achievements and said she had made her proud, but then quickly lashed out. “You’ve got quite a few flaws, but I still choose to trust you and forgive you,” the letter said, adding that Zhang needed to eat fewer snacks, get slimmer and taller, and perform better. During the show, Xiao’s behaviour didn’t seem to irritate Zhang much, and she showed little emotion. Of the letter, she simply said, “This is nonsense to me”, remaining nonchalant and not getting into an argument. Even though viewers were analysing Xiao and Zhang’s relationship in their comments, it is clear that, for many people, it also struck a nerve in their own lives. Indeed, this reality TV case was not simply an anomaly but, rather, a manifestation of the collective trauma felt by an entire generation – East Asian children trapped in a loveless relationship with their parents. In this region, heavily influenced by Confucian ideals, filial piety is stressed throughout a child’s life. When parents do or say something, it is more often than not for the child’s own good – or so they believe. Many children find it difficult to say no. If they do, they face immense psychological pressure and are often labelled “ungrateful”, “unfilial” or “heartless”. This is why Zhang’s story struck such a deep chord with so many people. We have all lived it at one time or another. It’s also clear that public opinion has made a progressive shift. I imagine things would have been very different if the show had aired 10 years ago. Back then, many more people would have supported Xiao, saying things like “Your mother raised you after all” and “There’s no perfect mother”. Today, after years of struggles, with young people expressing the pain caused by their controlling families, people have become more reasonable and can recognise toxic relationships without being constrained by society. A few years ago, I used to browse a channel on the cultural forum Douban called “Anti-Parents”, where people gathered to talk about how much psychological – and at times physical – harm their parents had inflicted on them. The founders wrote, “We don’t oppose for the sake of opposing. We oppose because it’s a constructive way to move further into society and become fuller versions of ourselves. This isn’t a refusal to honour our parents – we just want to live better.” A 2024 report from Fudan University found that young people had changed their feelings towards their parents over the course of a decade. Nowadays, they view “filial piety” as feeling grateful towards their parents and being willing to give back. At the same time, they don’t want to succumb to their parents’ every wish but want to be able to express their own identity. It’s good to see young people’s progress, from gathering on forums to rant about their parents to trying to more reasonably analyse their parent-child relationship and live better lives. When Zhang cut off her mother and moved away to another city, she was praised for being “independent” and “clear-headed”. It’s good that young people recognise such healthy behaviour rather than accepting that a toxic relationship is the norm.

title: Singapore open to legal action against errant firms as haze crisis worsens
description: Environment Minister Grace Fu said action could be taken under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act after collecting data on the haze.
content: Singapore will “keep its options open” on taking legal action against errant companies as air quality in the city state significantly deteriorated this week due to choking haze stemming from Indonesian wildfires. The government is collecting data on the haze as it weighs possible action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, Sustainability and Environment Minister Grace Fu told local media on Wednesday evening. The law, enacted in 2014, targets those responsible for causing or condoning fires if the resulting haze causes the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI), a measure of air quality, to remain in the unhealthy range for 24 hours or more. The index ranged from 127 to 211 across the island as of 11am local time on Thursday, with the western region recording the highest reading. Air quality is considered “very unhealthy” when levels are 201 and above. A reading above 300 is considered “hazardous” and can trigger school closures. Several Southeast Asian countries have been blanketed for weeks by toxic haze from forest fires in Indonesia. Governments are under pressure to step up and coordinate a response to what is shaping up to be the worst such episode in more than a decade. “We hope that the Indonesian authorities are able to contain the fires. It’s a very difficult year because of El Nino,” Fu said. “The weather has been very dry and we know that the issues are very complex. We wish them well and we stand ready to assist them where we can.” While Fu flagged possible legal action, past efforts have proven challenging. Singapore tapped the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act after record-breaking smog in 2015, but the environment ministry conceded it was having difficulty getting information from its Indonesian counterpart on companies suspected of illegal burning. A decade on, four companies continue to be under investigation. Those found guilty under Singapore’s transboundary haze law face fines of up to S$100,000 (US$77,855) a day, capped at S$2 million in total. The haze crisis is also driving a surge in demand for air purifiers and face masks in Singapore. Several models of air purifiers from brands including Xiaomi and Dyson Group were sold out, according to their websites. At home appliance retailer Gain City, sales of air purifiers have jumped to around nine times the levels recorded since the start of the haze season in August, marketing director Candy Cao said. “Demand remained particularly strong over the weekend, with some popular models selling out and some customers opting to purchase display sets so they could bring their products home immediately,” Cao said, adding that the retailer will continue to replenish stocks to meet demand. Some lawmakers cancelled house visits in their constituencies as the pollution worsened, while the government is distributing N95 masks to eligible Singaporeans and opening haze shelters at some community spaces. The city state’s haze task force is working with retailers to replenish supplies of the masks and ensure they remain available to the public, the National Environment Agency said, adding that retailers and the government have sufficient stocks. The Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore and Changi Airport Group said they are prepared to increase spacing between take-offs and landings, and switch on airfield lights during the day if the haze worsens. They are coordinating with airlines and unions to maintain safe operations at Changi and Seletar airports. Sixteen flights were diverted from Seletar between October 5 and 11 and some airlines have adjusted or cancelled services based on conditions. Singapore Airlines said its operations were unaffected, adding that “safety is the top priority”. Aerial firefighting efforts in Indonesia have recently been hampered by poor visibility. However, the country is repurposing a weather-modification technique pioneered in the 1940s in its latest effort to fight the pollution. Aircraft will disperse pellets of dry ice above South Sumatra province in an experimental approach that authorities hope will reduce the hazardous smoke.

title: Exclusive | US and China race to shape AI agenda ahead of Xi-Trump talks in Shenzhen, sources say
description: Two sides are said to be in discussions to make cooperation on artificial intelligence a potential deliverable when leaders meet next month.
content: The United States and China are in regular talks to iron out details of a framework announced last month for handling AI-related incidents and institutionalising bilateral dialogue, multiple sources told the South China Morning Post. The technical teams of the two countries aim to make AI cooperation a potential deliverable when presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen next month – their third face-to-face talks this year. Three sources said the artificial intelligence issue had taken on a more prominent role in discussions between the two sides as they explored ways to formalise cooperation in the field. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the matter publicly. Beijing and Washington have conducted intensive working-level discussions following Xi’s state visit to the US in September, when they announced plans to establish a bilateral channel for AI-related incidents and launch a China-US AI dialogue. The White House fact sheet and the Chinese government’s account of the eight outcomes from last month said the leaders had agreed to set up the dialogue mechanism to exchange views on the “risks and benefits” of artificial intelligence and to open a “bilateral communication channel” for AI-related incidents, with the next meeting scheduled for November. However, the initiatives remain largely declarative for now.
