The Chinese embassy in Washington said on Thursday that Beijing “remains open to maintaining communication” with Washington through the AI dialogue mechanism. “China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI. We take seriously the inherent and secondary risks of AI,” it added. A source said Washington and Beijing aimed to have a basic framework for addressing AI-related crises in place by the time leaders gather in Shenzhen, with operational details to be worked out later. “Adding flesh will come at a later date,” the source added. Another possible outcome of the two leaders’ Shenzhen meeting could be “an announcement establishing a continuing institutional mechanism for AI cooperation, involving government officials, research institutions and industry representatives”, a second source said. The two countries agreed to begin formal talks on AI governance following the Trump-Xi summit in Beijing in May, but the meeting was repeatedly delayed due to differences over the scope of the discussions and scheduling issues. The first AI dialogue was eventually folded into the broader economic and trade talks between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng in New York, just days before the Xi-Trump summit in Washington. The SCMP was the first to report on the merger of the two tracks. The November Apec meetings in Shenzhen “will provide a good opportunity to give the AI dialogue a more substantial political and institutional dimension”, one person familiar with the issue said. AI “has emerged as one of the most politically important areas in which Washington and Beijing might demonstrate that strategic competition does not preclude reasonable cooperation”, the source added. The source distinguished between an AI safety and incident-management agreement, which is already under discussion, and a broader AI economic cooperation framework, which would be “considerably more ambitious”. However, another source said that while the two sides aimed to provide institutional cover to the AI dialogue framework, it would not be an “easy task” given differences in their domestic regulatory structures and the competitive nature of the US-China relationship. The prospect of bilateral cooperation has coexisted alongside an intensifying AI race between Washington and Beijing, underscoring anxieties in the US that China is quickly eroding America’s technological edge. Despite growing concerns over AI safety, the Trump administration has rejected calls to slow the development of its frontier AI models, pointing to competition with China. Trump has instead placed the onus on AI companies to police themselves, meeting leading industry executives at the White House last month and backing a voluntary pact for firms to monitor and audit their own systems. He called the agreement “morally binding”. As Chinese firms have narrowed the gap with their US counterparts in advanced AI models, American tech companies and government officials have stepped up accusations that Beijing is extracting capabilities from US models to speed up the development of its own systems. “The technical word for stealing and copying American AI models is distillation. So, the Chinese distil our models, and they can never get ahead of us,” Bessent said last month. Model distillation is a widely used AI training technique in which a smaller model learns from the output of larger ones. China has dismissed the US allegations, describing distillation as “a common practice in the AI sector”. The bilateral discussions are being held as Washington and Beijing compete to shape global AI governance, with the US seeking to build a network of trusted partners through its Pax Silica initiative, while China advances the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation.

title: Chinese scientists use open-source data to spot suspected Israeli electronic warfare units
description: PLA scientists publish algorithm used to estimate sources of GPS spoofing around Israel using flight data.
content: Chinese military scientists claim they have developed an algorithm that could help identify electronic warfare units using civil aviation flight data. The researchers said they had located two sources of interference that were spoofing their locations near Israel during the conflict with Iran. The team did not explain why they had focused on the Israeli military. The researchers estimated the locations of the two units as being near Haifa, with reported positioning errors between 10.9km and 18.9km (6.7-11.7 miles). The South China Morning Post could not independently verify the claims. The study, conducted by Du Lan and a team at the People’s Liberation Army’s Information Engineering University in Zhengzhou, was published online on October 7 in the peer-reviewed Journal of Geomatics Science and Technology. The researchers analysed 43 days of aircraft-tracking data from open-source civil aviation systems, covering the period from February 27, the day before the US and Israel launched their attack on Iran, to April 10. Electronic interference may result in aviation data that shows abrupt jumps to a distant location or movements inconsistent with a normal flight path. The team’s algorithm used abnormal flight paths to estimate the possible locations of the sources of this interference. “The method requires no additional monitoring equipment and is low-cost and timely,” the researchers wrote. “It provides key technical support for civil aviation safety and situational awareness of spoofing interference in overseas conflict zones.” The team identified two distinct areas in the Mediterranean. “Target area 1 was about 80km northwest of Haifa, a major city in northern Israel, while target area 2 was about 30km northwest of the Gaza Strip. Both target areas were in the Mediterranean Sea,” the authors wrote. The researchers suggested that the different patterns could reflect attempts to counter different types of drone threats, although the intended targets could not be directly verified. “The spoofing source corresponding to target area 1 is inferred to have mainly countered long-range suicide drones with some resistance to spoofing, such as Iran’s Shahed-136, requiring a more complex dynamic spoofing strategy,” Du and her team wrote. “Target area 2 is inferred to have mainly countered low-cost, short-range drones used by groups in Gaza and the Houthi movement [from Yemen], whose resistance to navigation spoofing is weaker and which can be countered with a static, single-point spoofing strategy.” Du and her team used publicly available aircraft position and speed data from the Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast system. The researchers initially screened abnormal tracks using speed thresholds that were possible indicators that flight data was being spoofed. They then applied additional time, location, altitude and operating-period constraints to filter out factors such as data errors, aircraft manoeuvres, low-altitude flights and sources of interference being switched on and off. The team said future work would incorporate navigation data from ships to extend the method beyond civil aviation.

title: Hong Kong’s lack of heat action plans puts city’s vulnerable at risk, experts warn
description: New research shows extreme heat may have contributed to as many as 3,238 excess deaths in Hong Kong over a decade.
content:
The omission of a heat-health action plan in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and latest policy address is causing environmentalists and academics concern, who warn “common sense” is not enough to protect vulnerable residents.
Their comments came as new research from the University of Hong Kong (HKU) found that extreme heat might have contributed to as many as 3,238 excess deaths in the city over the 10-year study period.
In response to queries about the lack of a cross-departmental heat action plan for vulnerable groups, a government spokesman said there were ongoing efforts.
But environmentalists noted that neither the five-year blueprint nor the annual policy address, both delivered by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu in September, included a comprehensive plan for a systemic, overarching heat-health action plan to address urban heat.
A new management system known as the “city brain”, which aims to improve interdepartmental collaboration during extreme weather, was proposed in the policy address.
The World Health Organization outlines eight core elements for heat-health action plans, including governance, early-warning systems, surveillance and outreach.
Greenpeace Hong Kong campaigner Prudence Yeung said: “Including a heat action plan in the policy address or the five-year plan … could ensure heat adaptation and resilience as a citywide priority, and provide a foundation for investment in heat resilience infrastructure, research and public awareness.”
A Greenpeace survey, released in August, found that nearly 80 per cent of low-income elderly people surveyed in Hong Kong reported physical or mental distress during periods of extreme heat. That month the city logged its hottest single day – August 9 – since records began in 1884.
In a study currently under peer review, Professor David Bishai, director of the school of public health at HKU, and other researchers revised figures from research in 2024, estimating that heatwaves in Hong Kong between 2014 and 2023 may have contributed between 1,455 and 3,238 excess deaths.
An earlier estimate was 1,677 excess deaths.
Bishai’s projection was based on demographic data from the Census and Statistics Department, temperature data from the Hong Kong Observatory and relative risks derived from local research.
A simulation was used to estimate heat-attributable deaths under different definitions of a heatwave. These preventable excess deaths had largely gone unrecognised as they were exacerbations of underlying illnesses, rather than heatstroke, which was rare, Bishai said.
“Enacting an action plan in the face of extreme heat can be helpful in reducing death rates … We know that just leaving it to common sense is not working, because we are still seeing these excess deaths during heatwaves,” he said.
“It’s like running a marathon. The heart rate goes up, the blood vessels dilate, blood is shunted away from the brain into the hands and feet so that you can sweat more. And it is a very bad stress test that people’s bodies fail at those ages with those pre-existing conditions.”
Bishai cited Paris, where a heat action plan featuring proactive welfare checks on the elderly was projected to have cut heat-related mortality by around 77 per cent following heatwaves in 2003.
Hong Kong’s heat measures are activated when the Observatory issues a “very hot weather” warning, triggering the opening of temporary shelters in community halls. According to government figures, the 19 shelters that operated overnight on very hot evenings served between 120 and 210 users a day in June and July.
The Labour Department issues heat-stress alerts for outdoor workers – recently revamped following criticism – while the Department of Health provides public health advisories.

title: Li Ka-shing empire expands oil interests, turning heads in market
description: Deal for Canadian oil producer runs counter to global pivot to clean energy but makes sense as a buffer, analysts say.
content: As global capital flows towards clean energy and artificial intelligence, Hong Kong billionaire Li Ka-shing’s business group has expanded its oil exposure in a move analysts see as a buffer against geopolitical risks and a play for steady cash flow. The first major investment move by the widely watched Hong Kong tycoon after a slew of asset sales across the world has stirred curiosity at a time when financial markets are more volatile amid rising fears of inflation, monetary tightening and geopolitical sparks. Canadian producer Cenovus Energy, in which conglomerate CK Hutchison Holdings and a trust founded by Li together hold a stake of roughly 29 per cent, agreed on October 5 to acquire fellow Canadian firm Athabasca Oil in a deal valued at C$5.7 billion (US$4 billion). The deal comes less than a year after Cenovus – the Li family empire’s primary exposure to the oil sector – closed its C$8.6 billion purchase of Canadian oil sands producer MEG Energy. “In the world of heightened geopolitical risk, it’s wiser to not put all your eggs in one basket,” said Tommy Ong, managing director of financial advisory firm T.O. & Associates Consultancy. He said Li’s group was trying to keep a balanced portfolio of new and old economy businesses. Kenny Tang Sing-hing, chairman of the Hong Kong Institute of Financial Analysts and Professional Commentators, said the Athabasca deal would “create synergies” in the Canadian oil industry, where the Li family had been active for decades. CK Hutchison and a family trust bought into Husky Energy in the late 1980s and held almost 70 per cent of the firm when it merged into Cenovus in 2021. Many of the group’s investments have always leaned towards traditional infrastructure projects with stable cash flow Kenny Tang Sing-hing, Hong Kong Institute of Financial Analysts and Professional Commentators CK Hutchison’s first-half profit, driven by asset sales, also benefited from its Cenovus stake, as the US-Israel war on iran disrupted global energy supply and boosted demand for oil from outside the Middle East, according to the group’s interim report. At the same time, major asset disposals have helped the group build a substantial cash cushion. Earlier this year, CK Infrastructure – a CK Hutchison subsidiary – and two other Li-linked listed companies, Power Assets and CK Asset, sold British electricity distributor UK Power Networks to French utility Engie for £10.5 billion (US$13.9 billion). Separately, CK Hutchison sold its 49 per cent stake in British mobile operator VodafoneThree to Vodafone for US$5.8 billion. CK Hutchison’s cash and equivalents rose 25 per cent from the end of last year to HK$179 billion (US$22.8 billion) as of the end of June – a figure that does not include the proceeds from the VodafoneThree sale. At its annual general meeting in May, CK Hutchison chairman Victor Li Tzar-kuoi, Li’s elder son, reiterated the group’s cautious stance. “Cash is king,” Li said, noting that quality, stability and return remained the core criteria for any new investments. Li Ka-shing’s investment moves are closely watched. Experts said that Li had a sense of when to sell, citing Hutchison Whampoa’s exit from UK mobile operator Orange near the height of the dot-com bubble and CK Asset’s sale of a trophy Hong Kong office tower more than a year before the local commercial property market peaked. The group’s continued investments in fossil fuels run against the grain of broader global market trends. The International Energy Agency projects US$2.2 trillion in clean-energy investments this year – nearly double the US$1.2 trillion slated for fossil fuels. Meanwhile, prominent global investors are boosting AI investments. For example, Berkshire Hathaway recently expanded its stake in Google parent Alphabet to roughly US$36 billion, citing Google’s position as a “significant player” in AI as a fundamental factor. However, Ong of T.O. & Associates pointed out that even in high-growth tech sectors like AI, energy remained “the main determinant” of success. The CK group is building a full range of energy businesses worldwide to capture different opportunities, he added, pointing to the 2017 purchase of German smart-meter and energy-management company Ista by CK Asset and CK Infrastructure for about €4.5 billion (US$5 billion). CK Infrastructure said in August that new regulatory terms for its Australian power networks allowed higher returns and more investment, supporting projected growth from electrification and data-centre demand. “Many of the group’s investments have always leaned towards traditional infrastructure projects with stable cash flow,” said Tang of the Hong Kong Institute of Financial Analysts and Professional Commentators. “Although the oil industry will gradually feel the impact of clean energy in the long run, it can still bring very stable income.”

title: ‘Not tailor-made for us’: Hongkong Post staff say transfer scheme too narrow
description: Affected postal workers say clerical-focused transfer scheme does not match their skills, age or career needs.
content: Hong Kong postal workers denied permanent contracts have criticised a special government transfer scheme as too narrow, calling for more pathways into roles that match their experience, such as workman and artisan positions. Several affected workers told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday that the concessions offered insufficient support and failed to reflect their skills or circumstances. One postal worker, who asked not to be named, said that while the government had offered priority hiring for other civil service jobs, suitable vacancies were limited. “I checked the government vacancies system; most of the openings are for doctors, nurses, aircraft engineers and marine officers, which are not suitable for postal staff,” he said. “We cannot get an offer.” That left most affected workers with only two clerical grades to apply for, he added. The Civil Service Bureau on Tuesday announced a one-off special scheme allowing postal staff affected by cost-cutting measures at Hongkong Post to apply for assistant clerical officer or clerical assistant posts with relaxed academic requirements and hiring priority. They will also be given priority over other candidates if they receive the same score in applications for other civil service jobs. The measures aim to support about 200 employees who were denied permanent civil service positions and offered only two-year contracts because of Hongkong Post’s financial difficulties. Although the minimum academic requirement for assistant clerical officer was relaxed from five subjects in the Diploma of Secondary Education exam or Hong Kong Certificate of Education Examination to three – Chinese, English and mathematics – many workers still found it difficult to meet. “I believe it is rare for someone to pass Chinese, English and mathematics but fail their electives,” the worker said, questioning how meaningful the relaxation was. He planned to apply for a clerical assistant post, but urged the government to include more roles better suited to postal workers’ skills, such as artisan and traffic warden positions. He said he would not mind a possible pay cut, but preferred a role that better matched his experience. According to the bureau’s website, 18 positions are currently open for recruitment, including roles with lower educational requirements, such as artisan posts at the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department and motor driver posts at the Government Logistics Department. Another worker expressed concern about intense competition for the two clerical grades, noting that more than 200 affected employees would have to compete with thousands of other applicants in an open recruitment process. “The government has been recruiting assistant clerical officers and clerical assistants all year round. It is an ongoing exercise, not tailor-made for us. How is this supposed to help us?” he said. He added that only one option was currently available and echoed calls for the government to offer more non-clerical roles, including workman and amenities assistant positions. A third worker said he was anxious about his competitiveness in interviews and skills tests, such as typing assessments. Under the scheme, candidates must still pass such tests and interviews. “It would be better if the government could find positions more suitable for us, such as artisan and workman roles,” he said. “Many of us are in our thirties or forties. If we switch now to clerical work involving typing, we will be less competitive than younger people.” He noted that recruitment for the two clerical grades could take up to a year and worried that he would have little time left in his two-year contract to plan his next move if he failed to secure an offer. Hong Kong Postal Workers Union chairman Cheung Wai-kuen acknowledged the government’s efforts to respond to frontline concerns, calling the concessions a good start. But he noted that some employees did not meet the academic requirements for the two grades, while others struggled to pass clerical skills tests such as typing. “Some colleagues do not have high educational qualifications and may only just meet the academic requirements … while some are already in their late forties or early fifties,” Cheung said. “It is not that they do not want to apply for these two grades, but they may be unable to meet the standards.” Cheung called for a further special scheme to cater to their needs, offering posts closer to the outdoor and physical nature of postal work, such as workman or hawker control officer positions. The union will hold a meeting with affected employees next week and submit suggestions to the bureau after gathering their feedback.

title: ACL 2: Tai Po braced to face ex-England junior player on roll as coach in Far East
description: Lion City Sailors’ Mark Jackson arrived at Singapore club laden with trophies, says leaving England was ‘one of the best things I’ve done’.
content: Mark Jackson was a good enough footballer to make 18 Premier League appearances for Leeds United; to play at Old Trafford, Goodison Park, Highbury and Anfield; and to keep the prolific Ian Wright off the scoresheet in an FA Cup victory over Arsenal. As a coach, he led Leeds’ under-18 and under-23 teams to league titles. None of that afforded Jackson a second crack at management in his native England, after his first chance with MK Dons lasted only 4½ months. Not for Jackson the mulligan that is the privilege of the glittery names: the likes of Frank Lampard, Wayne Rooney and Steven Gerrard. “That’s the world of management, I’m afraid, particularly in England,” said Jackson, recently appointed head coach of Lion City Sailors, Tai Po’s opponents for their Asian Champions League 2 fixture at Mong Kok Stadium on Thursday. “People talk a lot about building, and creating environments, cultures and ways of playing. “But sometimes talk is cheap, and they expect that within three or four games. That’s not the case at any level of football. “I had to make the jump to leave England, and it’s one of the best things I’ve done. It’s really opened my eyes to football on this side of the world.” Back in September 2023, months after MK Dons pulled the plug on his 26-game reign, Jackson turned his world upside down to join Central Coast Mariners in Australia. In his first season, Mariners won the AFC Cup, the precursor to ACL 2, and the domestic championship. He was appointed by Buriram United soon after leaving Mariners of his own volition in October last year, and duly led the Thai club to the league title, FA Cup and Asean Club Championship. “I’m in no rush to go back [to England],” Jackson, 49, said. “The passion and quality of football in the countries where I’ve worked has been very attractive for me as a coach. “I’m enjoying the success I’m having and I want it to continue with the Sailors.” In his three years away from home, Jackson’s reputation has swelled such that Lion City central defender Toni Datkovic said: “When we found out who was coming, we knew we’d have a winner as a coach. “With somebody like him, you believe everything he says.” Until he received a call from Luka Lalic, the Lion City director of football, Jackson had been planning to rest after quitting Buriram last month. Out of work for only 11 days, he said: “It was very quick, but I had no hesitation. “I saw the quality in the squad, and that it was a club used to winning. It felt the right fit, and the right club to help me grow.” A central defender as a player, Jackson represented England in the 1996 European Under-18 Championship and the following year’s World Youth Championship for under-20s. He variously counted Rio Ferdinand, Michael Owen and Jamie Carragher as teammates, while the Argentina side that eliminated his England from the global tournament featured Pablo Aimar, Esteban Cambiasso and Juan Roman Riquelme. Nonetheless, it was from two managers he worked with at Leeds that Jackson gleaned some of his most valuable insight. He was under-23 boss during the idiosyncratic Marcelo Bielsa’s tenure, and then assistant to Jesse Marsch, who is now in charge of Canada. “From both of them I have taken that if you’re not a head coach who looks and learns all the time, you won’t last long in the game,” Jackson said. “Marcelo’s attention to detail really stood out. That and his individual development of certain actions in the game stuck with me. “Jesse was a man-manager, and he had a style of football that fitted with mine. I like to be on the front foot and aggressive. “You have to put those ingredients together and make sense of them. I’ve shown that when we get a team that understands how I want to play, and can execute it consistently, then everything points to success.” Datkovic, who was part of the Lion City team beaten by Sharjah in last season’s ACL2 final, said: “We’re going in the right direction and, hopefully, this year [Jackson] will put four more trophies in his cabinet.” The mood in the Tai Po camp was noticeably more downbeat. In the hours before Wednesday night’s pre-match press conferences, the local Premier League club confirmed it had “mutually agreed to terminate” the contract of Gabriel Mesquita, after the 19-year-old midfielder sent a racist message on social media platform Threads. He had been suspended 48 hours earlier. Asked about Tai Po’s stance, Lee Chi-kin, the head coach, said: “Today, the focus is on winning the match. I think [the Mesquita episode] is closed already.” Since being unbeaten in their three home ACL 2 matches last season, Tai Po have slashed their budget and lost a slew of key performers. “This [ACL 2 campaign] is different from last season, but we’ll try our best to make it difficult for Lion City,” an unusually subdued Lee said. Talismanic midfielder Philip Chan Siu-kwan was more forthright. “We were very proud of ourselves last season, but that doesn’t mean anything to me this year,” he said. “Every year is different, especially in Hong Kong football. “It’s out of our control. I don’t see this as a problem; I see it as a challenge to overcome as a team.” A renewal of Hong Kong-Singapore hostilities stirred memories of the city representative team fatally losing an AFC Asian Cup qualifier to the city state last November. “Singapore football has been improving, and we’re trying to do the same,” Chan said. “We look at [Singapore] as a reference. “We’ve put the Asian Cup behind us, and we’re not looking for revenge [against Lion City]. “We want to do it for the team, and for Hong Kong and Tai Po fans. Hong Kong is a very special place. We give every team that comes here a hard time.” Hong Kong’s other ACL 2 representatives, Kitchee, will play Kuching City in Malaysia on Thursday night.

title: Meet Emma Maclean, the designer behind Manteigaria and Luah’s interiors
description: Having lived in Hong Kong for over three decades, Maclean says the city’s designers have learned to overcome spatial constraints with ‘beauty and soul’.
content: Growing up in Hong Kong in a family of architects and interior designers, Emma Maclean was practically destined for a career in the field. Today her Sheung Wan-based studio – first started in 2018 as EM Bespoke before relaunching under the name Emma Maclean & Co in 2024 – creates spaces that reflect the remarkable contrasts that make this city eternally exciting for designers, where old and new, East and West, glistening skyscrapers and natural waters all somehow coexist in harmony. “I feel Hong Kong’s energy every day,” writes Maclean, who has lived in the city for 32 years and witnessed first-hand the evolution of its design during that time, from a gradual shift away from “cold minimalism” in the early 2000s towards “warmer, more personal styles” with Tuscan and Mediterranean influences, and more recently, the embrace of “lighter woods, biophilic details, Japanese elements and more sustainable materials”. That greater desire for more precise, carefully considered details and materials is where Maclean’s practice truly thrives, something further bolstered by the demand for more adaptive spaces during the pandemic. Luckily, says Maclean, adaptability has always been Hong Kong’s strong suit. “Its extreme density forces creativity,” she writes. “In a city where an interior’s walls seem to press inward and towers stack in relentless vertical layers, every square foot must perform harder.” For Maclean, this is reflected in spaces that appear bigger and brighter than they actually are through the usage of arched ceilings, as with her studio’s design of the Manteigaria pastry shop flagship in Central, or the expansive sunken shelves at the headquarters of Hong Kong jewellery brand Luah, perched on the tightly packed stairwells of Shin Hing Street. The “cross-pollination” of different nationalities living in Hong Kong as well as the constant ebb and flow of emigration here makes the city’s design landscape forever dynamic, Maclean believes. She also credits the discerning eye of Hong Kong’s cosmopolitan clientele with influencing her practice. “The pace is relentless,” she says. “The challenges are real. Designing in Hong Kong means solving practical problems with beauty and soul.” The way designers here embrace those challenges rather than shy away from them is exactly what continues to inspire her, keeping the local scene “sharp, competitive and endlessly inventive”. Spaces designed by Maclean’s studio borrow a great many design cues from their surroundings, blending in with the city’s frenetic landscape while bearing their own distinct character. That’s precisely what makes her stand out as one of Hong Kong’s most exciting young designers. Take the bespoke marble flooring of Manteigaria, for example, which pays tribute to the azulejo tilework motifs so common to the architecture of the Iberian Peninsula, but which also recalls the iconic mosaic wall tiles of the Hong Kong MTR. Or, the open floor plan and modular elements of Luah’s Shin Hing showroom in Central, designed to fit in with the street’s charming character and fulfil the demand for “retail environments that match the city’s restless appetite”, says Maclean. “There is no such thing as a spare corner,” Maclean adds, noting that the next chapter of design in Hong Kong “will not be about making rooms larger”. The growing role of “invisible technology”, she says, from “smart lighting that fully embraces the circadian rhythm” to “AI that provides context-aware comfort by controlling lighting, security and climate” will sit seamlessly side by side with “a stronger return to craftsmanship”, creating spaces that are “even more resilient and deeply human”. “Density, transience and restless energy are not obstacles,” Maclean says of practising in Hong Kong. “They are the conditions that keep pushing design forward. As an interior designer, I wouldn’t want to be anywhere else.”

title: AI-armed hackers tear through corporate Japan’s neglected defences
description: For years, the Japanese language was a defence against hacking in and of itself, observers say. But no more.
content: Japanese companies have faced a growing wave of cyberattacks in recent weeks, exposing millions of customers’ records as analysts warn that artificial intelligence is helping hackers exploit long-standing security weaknesses and overcome language barriers that once offered some protection. More than 500 breaches of corporate systems were reported in the year to this month, surpassing the total for all of 2025, the Yomiuri newspaper reported last week. On October 7, a ransomware attack on IDC Frontier – a Japanese cloud hosting and data centre services provider – paralysed systems used by 495 companies and local authorities in the country. Those affected included railway operator JR East, which confirmed that more than 6 million customer accounts had been compromised. Used book retailer BookOff also reported that data belonging to 6.43 million members had leaked. They were far from alone. Online travel firm Skyticket also said this month that a cyberattack on its servers had resulted in 14.6 million users’ data being accessed, while in September, vehicle rental service Times Car reported that 6.6 million members’ accounts had been exposed – potentially compromising the sensitive personal information contained on driving licences, such as residential addresses. “This is the result of an accumulation of systems that lack adequate security measures,” said Yutaka Sejiyama, deputy director of the Yokohama-based cybersecurity firm Macnica’s Security Research Centre, noting that Japanese companies had long failed to take adequate steps to protect their systems and customers’ private data. Many had concentrated their efforts on vulnerabilities that could lead to ransomware attacks at the expense of issues deemed lower risk, he said. It appears that attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities that had gone unnoticed for years Yutaka Sejiyama, cybersecurity researcher “But security measures are an ongoing process with no definitive end point,” Sejiyama said. “Now, it appears that attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities that had gone unnoticed for years.” He believes recent advances in AI are partly to blame for the latest wave of attacks, though he concedes that “no definitive proof” of this exists as yet. Still, “the methods employed and the scale of the damage suggest a level of sophistication beyond human capability alone”, he said, further noting that “the malicious use of AI has become commonplace in other cyberattacks”. Successfully probing a company’s cyberdefences might once have taken a human hacker weeks or months, but observers suspect AI has now hyper-accelerated this process. Barrier down Foreign hackers had largely ignored Japan in the past because its language made many systems hard to access and navigate, said Martin Schulz, chief policy economist at Fujitsu’s Global Market Intelligence Unit who analyses AI integration and distributed digital ecosystems. “Japanese was effectively a barrier,” Schulz said, pointing to the fact that bad actors predominantly used English-language hacking tools. “But in the last year, AI has progressed brilliantly and they have got around that barrier and can target Japanese organisations now.” Once inside a system, hackers could take advantage of close integration between Japanese companies and their partners, both foreign and domestic, to unleash a “tsunami” of attacks, Schulz said. Many firms’ defences were unprepared for the onslaught. “Their firewalls have been no match for the AI agents that are now knocking them down at will,” he said. These breaches “did not come out of nowhere”, Schulz added, pointing to the cyberattack on Jaguar Land Rover that began in August last year, forcing the carmaker to shut down its IT and automated production networks across the UK for five weeks. Although there was no suggestion that AI agents were used in that attack, the effects were still devastating. Full production did not resume until early 2026. The breach cost the company some £196 million (US$259.5 million) and the wider hit to the UK economy was put at £1.9 billion. “Because Japanese companies have so much more integration, I believe there is a very real risk that we will see a major breakdown in networks here,” Schulz said. South Korean firms have faced similar AI-driven attacks recently, including one that hit nine major financial institutions, with cybercriminals successfully compromising customer-facing web services and leaking sensitive data such as names, email addresses and account numbers. Schulz said he expected other economies in the region to take note as the tools that had allowed hackers to overcome language barriers in Japan would also dismantle other defences that once kept them away. Ordinary consumers can do little to protect themselves, according to Sejiyama. “While carefully selecting the services and websites where you register personal information can be a form of precaution, there are limits to this approach given how deeply IT has permeated society,” he said. Individuals should watch out for fraud and phishing emails, he added, and concentrate their efforts on limiting the damage after a breach had occurred. Members of the public had reported an increasing number of suspicious calls from people posing as police officers, he said, as well as emails from contacts they did not recognise. “We recommend remaining vigilant against such scams,” Sejiyama said.

title: Gross encounters: the Disgusting Food Museum opens in Hong Kong
description: Peruvian frog juice, deep-fried bull testicles and the smelliest canned food in the world – come to the Disgusting Food Museum for the controversial delicacies, stay for the reflections on what’s considered edible, what’s not and why.
content: It is rare for an exhibition to be repellent and attractive, but the Disgusting Food Museum manages to be both – and does it remarkably well. Having drawn more than half a million visitors since 2018 to its home base in Malmö, Sweden, as well as pop-up exhibitions from the United States to Taiwan, the concept debuts in Hong Kong at Gate33 Gallery in Airside, Kai Tak, showcasing more than 80 polarising delicacies from 35 countries. Co-founded by Dr Samuel West – a clinical psychologist who also created the Museum of Failure – and Andreas Ahrens, the Disgusting Food Museum’s mission is to trigger reactions “from disgust to reflection”, prompting visitors to think about the biases underlying food cultures. After all, ingredients we take for granted may elicit revulsion elsewhere. For instance, chicken feet are dim sum mainstays but are considered unwanted by-products and discarded in most other cuisines, while century eggs never fail to shock non-Chinese diners. Spread across five themes – The Savage Soiree, The Alchemic Feast, The Stench Works, The Verdict Table and The Last Supper – the exhibition combines real food, models, scent installations, archives and interactive elements. In The Savage Soiree, visitors encounter the Greenlandic Inuit dish kiviak – comprising small seabirds stuffed inside a seal skin, sewn tight and buried in frozen earth to ferment – alongside Rocky Mountain oysters, a euphemistic moniker for deep-fried bull testicles, from western North America. Meanwhile, The Alchemic Feast dives into folk remedies, such as Southeast Asian street-food balut and Peruvian frog smoothie, believed to boost vitality and treat asthma. Next, The Stench Works unleashes an olfactory immersion in such intense aromas as that of the pungent Swedish surströmming – canned herring that’s infamous for being one of the smelliest foodstuffs in the world – as well as Icelandic hákarl (fermented shark) and Sardinia’s notorious casu marzu (a sheep-milk cheese fermented through the digestive action of cheese-fly larvae, which is banned for sale in the European Union). Elsewhere, The Verdict Table explores how flavours we deem ordinary can seem horrifying to others, placing global habits side by side, such as Australia’s pitch-black, umami-packed Vegemite spread alongside beloved Asian culinary staples that are often misunderstood beyond the region. Finally, The Last Supper explores sustainable, low-carbon food innovations such as insect protein and lab-grown meat, inviting visitors to participate in the urgent conversation of food security. Upon entry, each guest is handed a vomit bag before diving into taste tests of fermented shark, crunchy crickets and surströmming at the Final Bite tasting bar. Maybe hold off on that big lunch beforehand. Disgusting Food Museum Hong Kong. Until November 26. Gate33 Gallery, 3/F, Airside, Kai Tak. For tickets, click here

title: Australia navy probes hidden camera found in women’s showers on ship
description: Senator Jacqui Lambie says footage of female sailors may have been uploaded online before the devices were discovered.
content: Australia’s navy said on Thursday it would audit bathrooms across its fleet after a video recording device was found in the cabin of one of its ships. Navy chief Matt Buckley has vowed a full investigation into the incident aboard the HMAS Leeuwin, a survey ship docked in the northeastern city of Cairns in the state of Queensland. A member of the armed forces has been identified as a “person of interest” and was assisting military police with enquiries, Australia’s defence ministry said in an update on Thursday. Buckley called the act a “most despicable betrayal of trust” and said authorities are “undertaking a 100 per cent audit of all of our bathrooms across the fleet”. “My highest priority, as always, is the well-being of our people. All potentially impacted personnel are receiving our strongest support,” the vice-admiral said in a statement. “You have my assurance and commitment that we will tackle this act of sexual violence with all of our energy. Any perpetrator will be held to account.” The defence ministry said late on Wednesday that the issue was under investigation after a lawmaker said she had received a message from a former member of the navy claiming concealed cameras had been found in the women’s showers. “Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered,” said Senator Jacqui Lambie, a prominent advocate for the armed forces. “How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent?” A royal commission that concluded in 2024 found that sexual misconduct remained a “systemic issue” across the Australian armed forces.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong’s arts hub must anchor vibrancy in sustainability
description: The West Kowloon Cultural District’s ballooning operating deficit despite rising visitor numbers should invite caution given the project’s key role in the city’s five-year plan.
content: Hong Kong’s West Kowloon Cultural District (WKCD) has never looked more vibrant. Visitor numbers climbed to over 17 million in 2025, up more than 10 per cent from the previous year. Since this year, more than 1,300 exhibitions, performances, programmes and events have been held, including the much-acclaimed showcase of ancient Egyptian treasures at the Hong Kong Palace Museum. Revenue from tickets, sponsorships and cultural and creative products jumped 19 per cent to HK$768 million (US$98 million). By any cultural metric, the district is fulfilling its promise as a world class arts hub. But the latest figures presented to the Legislative Council lay bare an uncomfortable truth behind the authority’s lofty mission. Despite years of hard work, the cultural success has yet to translate into financial self-sufficiency. With the authority’s operating deficit hitting HK$998 million, up 30 per cent from HK$769 million a year before, sustainability remains a long-term concern. The authority has played down the nearly HK$1 billion gaping financial hole, saying it remains under control. The higher deficit was partly attributed to lower interest returns and operating costs spiralling 13 per cent to HK$1.85 billion, driven by preparations for the soon-to-open performing arts centre, higher visitor numbers and upgraded facilities and technology. The authority remains optimistic about its fiscal health as revenues from residential and other commercial developments are expected to increase in the future. The financial pressure is not unique to Hong Kong. Many top overseas institutions rely heavily on public subsidies, endowments and philanthropy to balance their books. The flagship Hong Kong Palace Museum and M+ contemporary art gallery are on par or better than some global peers in achieving a cost recovery rate of about 50 per cent in 2026-26. But as a fledgling mega arts hub operating on a self-financing model, the challenges must not be taken for granted. The authority has taken positive steps to stabilise its finances. A US$1 billion bond programme and a HK$3 billion 10-year loan facility from ICBC (Asia) have eased immediate cash flow pressures and averted cutbacks in programming. These moves signal market confidence that future land sales, rental income and cultural activities can support repayment. The completion of the Artist Square Towers next year is expected to bring steady rental revenue from office, retail and entertainment space, while the tender of the first residential package, expected in the first half of 2027, promises a larger return further down the road. But borrowed money and time are no long-term solution for a world-class arts hub. The cultural district’s original endowment of HK$21.6 billion by the government in 2008 was intended to be sustained by WKCD’s own income and commercial development. The authority contributed HK$10.8 billion to gross domestic product in 2025, creating 14,270 full-time equivalent jobs and generating tax contributions of HK$910 million for the government. Impressive as that seems, the economic benefits are fragile if they are not underpinned by financially sound operations in the long run. With the funding depleting and deficits persisting, the imperative to turn WKCD into a self-sustaining ecosystem has never been stronger. The stakes have been raised as WKCD’s mission has been further elevated by the city’s first five-year plan that aligns with national development goals, under which the city is to become an East-meets-West centre for international cultural exchange. Far from being just a local arts venue to enrich city life, the cultural district has been officially recognised as part of the city’s soft power, with a mandate to act as a bridge to the world and to tell good stories of Hong Kong and the motherland. The mission requires not only rich cultural offerings but also financially sustainable operations. WKCD has come a long way in making its mark on the world’s map of art and culture. Yet its full potential is far from maximised. The performing arts centre is to open next year, providing a 1,450-seat Grand Theatre, a 600-seat Medium Theatre, a 270-seat Studio Theatre, The Hall with 148 seats, and “Dancehouse”, the first dedicated venue for dance arts in the city. The authority must make good use of the new facilities and capitalise on the commercial development so that the arts hub can truly rise to the challenge as a sustainable East meets West centre for global cultural exchange.

title: Hong Kong flat reimagined with open layout and natural light for couple and their 2 dogs
description: A Pok Fu Lam flat’s dark, cramped interior – plus a private terrace – has been transformed with an open-plan design.
content: Would you trust your husband to fully renovate your home, without any design input from you? Rachel Tong did. She did not even visit the flat, which took 10 months to redo, until a few days before completion. Fortunately for her, designer Nicole Cromwell of Nicole Cromwell Interior Design was a major factor in the concept, guaranteeing that the 1,000 sq ft (93 square metre) flat, with an equally large private terrace, would be a stylish affair. Tong and her husband Paul had lived in their one-bedroom, one-bathroom flat in Pok Fu Lam for at least 10 years when they felt it was time for a change. They considered buying elsewhere, but with two large dogs to add to the equation, nothing matched it. The flat had good bones and plenty of potential but a poorly thought-out layout. A wall directly in front of the main entrance concealed the kitchen and made it feel cramped, while the route to the bedroom involved navigating between the living room’s two sofas, whose focal point was a television screen on the far end wall. The adjacent reading nook was starved of light. It can be disconcerting to have your home, as you know it, virtually demolished, but Cromwell advises clients to trust the process, no matter how chaotic it initially seems. Her approach was to open up the floor plan and rethink both the architecture and the furniture layout. By removing unnecessary divisions and reorienting the spaces, she improved the sense of flow and connection throughout the flat. Laminate flooring was replaced with wide timber boards, while a more considered material palette and carefully positioned furniture brought a greater sense of cohesion. Because the couple love cooking, the designer stripped it back and made the space more functional. A tall wine fridge was incorporated alongside generous storage and a sizeable island clad in fluted timber. High-end appliances and details were the order of the day, including a Quooker tap for instant still, sparkling and boiling water, an extra-large sink and drying area, and a Gaggenau oven and hob. Paul Tong initially envisaged a more traditional woody palette, but Cromwell persuaded him towards a deeper, more contemporary dark blue. The colour gives the kitchen a stronger architectural presence and was subsequently carried through into the reading room, visually linking the two spaces. “The kitchen palette is striking without being too much, making the area an immediate focal point as well as highly functional,” Cromwell says. “I’m also particularly happy with the way the colour and shape of the built-in banquette seating in the dining nook turned out. Previously, there had been a wooden dining table and chairs, so this rich rust colour took a leap of faith from Paul.” The same emphasis on spatial flow and light is evident in the study. A lack of natural light had made the space unwelcoming, and consequently it had been underused. Cromwell relocated the desk from the darkest corner, where it had faced the wall, to beneath the window. Borrowing an element of Japanese design, she introduced a slatted timber panel alongside it, creating a degree of privacy without compromising the passage of light. Customised shelving accommodates the couple’s extensive book collection, with their varying heights influencing the unit’s composition. Low, marble-topped cupboards were built beneath, while integrated backlighting adds depth after dark. A comfortable armchair, floor lamp and circular rug help define the study as a distinct zone within the larger room, giving an overlooked corner a renewed sense of purpose. “Lighting was all important – here and throughout the apartment,” she says. “Paul and Rachel don’t like bright lights so everything is dimmable, even outside.” Good design doesn’t only change how a space looks – it completely reshapes how you live in it Nicole Cromwell, designer Cromwell’s initial brief had been limited to the interior, but it soon became apparent that the contrast between the newly renovated flat and the neglected outdoor space would be too stark. “The terrace was looking very tired and would have needed a makeover sooner rather than later,” she says. “It made much more sense to get all the dust and noise from upgrading the old floor tiles, painting the walls and building planters out of the way while the interior was being gutted and Paul and Rachel weren’t in the flat.” This outside area was consequently treated as an extension of the interior rather than an afterthought. Cromwell reworked the entire space around the couple’s lifestyle, installing a customised built-in barbecue station while ensuring that the layout remained practical for the dogs. Her clients also wanted to retain their existing palms, so planters were rebuilt to house them, and Cromwell worked with a Sai Kung landscaper to introduce complementary, lower-level greenery. “The terrace now feels huge and is a sophisticated extension to the living space,” she says. “Good design doesn’t only change how a space looks – it completely reshapes how you live in it.” Perhaps the million-dollar question is Rachel’s reaction to her “new” home. Reader, she loved it. Living room Sofa and rug from JG Casa. Coffee table and side table by Thomas Bina from Timothy Oulton. Artwork by childhood friend Joseph Stanley. Picture lamp and table lamp by Ian K Fowler from Lumino Lighting (lumino.lighting). Circus pouffe from Normann Copenhagen. Oak flooring throughout from Joyful Sky. Walnut wood audiovisual unit and detailing designed and made by Nicole Cromwell Interior Design. Reading area Shelving designed by Nicole Cromwell Interior Design and made by JL Meta. Chair, footstool and rug from JG Casa. Floor lamp from Artemide. Ceiling light from AliExpress. Dining area Shelving and banquette designed by Nicole Cromwell Interior Design and made by JL Meta. Dining table and chairs from JG Casa. Pendant light from Universal Lighting Services. Kitchen Kitchen designed and made by Nicole Cromwell Interior Design with ZOOM Kitchen Design (Michael Lau, tel: 9831 6636). Walnut wood island surround designed by Nicole Cromwell Interior Design and made by JL Meta. Bedroom Bed and blanket box from Fuurn. Bedside tables designed by Nicole Cromwell Interior Design and made by JL Meta. Allen mini pendant lights from Ralph Lauren. Bathroom Green marble from JES Stone. Arnhold brass fittings and copper sink from Kallista. Sink unit designed and made by Nicole Cromwell Interior Design. Outdoor terrace Sofa, coffee table and side tables by Diphano from Everything Under The Sun. Parasol from Patio Mart. Barbecue station and planters designed and made by Nicole Cromwell Interior Design. Tried + Tested Along with his-and-hers walk-in wardrobes off the bedroom, Cromwell custom-made a couple of dedicated drawers for Rachel Tong’s brooch collection. The compartments vary in size to accommodate different pieces and are topped with glass so she can see where each piece is at a glance. Brooch drawer designed by Nicole Cromwell Interior Design and made by JL Meta.

title: How Jardine Matheson’s street-shop sale reflects Hong Kong retail property’s struggles
description: British conglomerate sells Causeway Bay asset at a discount – after holding the property for more than 50 years.
content: Amid Hong Kong’s commercial property downturn, British conglomerate Jardine Matheson has sold a street shop in Causeway Bay for HK$80 million (US$10.2 million) after holding it for more than 50 years, accepting a price HK$10 million below its earlier valuation. The property, a ground-floor shop in H&S Building at 36 Leighton Road, with a gross floor area of about 11,727 square feet, was acquired by Uni Investment Development, according to Land Registry records. Jardine Matheson appointed an agent to market the property in early April, when it was valued at HK$90 million. The eventual sale price – equivalent to HK$6,822 per square foot – was about 11 per cent lower. Uni Investment Development’s directors acquired a high-floor shop at Parkvale on King’s Road in Quarry Bay from McDonald’s for HK$110 million in June, according to Land Registry records. Edwin Lee, founder and CEO of Bridgeway Prime Shop Fund Management, said the deal represented a bargain, citing the shop’s large floor area and its former use as a car showroom, despite its location on a secondary street in Causeway Bay. Lee estimated that the shop’s rent could reach HK$350,000 a month, representing a yield of about 5 per cent based on the transaction price. Stanley Poon Chi-ming, managing director at Centaline Commercial, said the shadow of interest rate increases continued to loom over Hong Kong’s commercial property market, prompting some owners to adjust their asking prices to accelerate disposals. “Shop transactions in the third quarter recorded a 23 per cent year-on-year increase to 222 deals, with a total value of about HK$4.36 billion,” he added. Poon expected the momentum in the street-shop market to continue into the fourth quarter, with transaction volume projected to rise to 240 deals and total value to reach HK$5.5 billion. However, with some distressed properties still coming onto the market, he said he expected street-shop prices to decline by no more than 5 per cent in the fourth quarter. According to sales materials, the H&S Building shop featured a 25-metre-wide signboard frontage, and had previously served as a showroom for several well-known European and American car brands. The podium portion of the building, including the ground-floor shop and a six-storey car park, was originally owned by Zung Fu Co, a Mercedes-Benz dealership, according to local media reports. In 2021, mainland Chinese car dealer Zhongsheng Group Holdings acquired all the equity in Zung Fu (China) from Jardine Matheson, excluding the properties held by Zung Fu. The H&S Building podium was subsequently transferred to Credence Properties Investment, an affiliate of Jardine Matheson, for HK$574 million in October 2021. Separately, the building’s six-storey car park was sold for HK$130 million in March, involving 199 parking spaces at an average price of about HK$653,000 each.

title: ‘China shock 3.0’ to be driven by AI, biotech and robot exports, economist says
description: China is developing its own competitive AI hardware and software and plans to export them once domestic demand is met, expert claims.
content: The world is on the cusp of a “China shock 3.0” driven by exports of artificial intelligence (AI), biotechnology and robots, which could hit harder than the current wave, a leading economist on China has said. “We are already at the starting point of the China shock 3.0,” Alicia Garcia-Herrero, a senior fellow at Brussels-based think tank Bruegel and chief economist for Asia-Pacific at investment bank Natixis, told the South China Morning Post from Taipei after a virtual panel hosted by the Washington-based Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE) on Wednesday. The third wave would centre on artificial intelligence, covering both hardware and software, along with biotechnology and robotics, she said. China, while still a major importer of advanced chips, was developing its own AI hardware and software and planned to export them once domestic demand was met, Garcia-Herrero said in the interview. These exports could come alongside bundled data centre and cloud services, and humanoid and industrial robots could follow, creating a shock that would exceed the current one, she said. “If you think about embodied AI, humanoid robots or industrial robots, think about the humongous shock that this is going to be, beyond [the] existing shock,” she said. On the panel, Garcia-Herrero said China’s cheap energy would give it the world’s lowest computing costs, carrying its competitive strength beyond industrial goods and into services. A huge economy that is competitive across the board but largely closed to imports, she argued, must be “extremely reasonable”. The term “China shock” was popularised by US economists David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson, whose research linked the surge in Chinese imports after Beijing joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 to the loss of US manufacturing jobs and the decline of factory towns. The “2.0” wave began around 2018, though some date it to the 2020s, and has been driven by more advanced manufacturing, including cars and machinery. European and US officials have accused China of overcapacity, meaning it produces far more than domestic and foreign demand can absorb, and of exporting the surplus at low prices. China has rejected the claims. In a position paper titled “China’s Position on the So-called Excess Capacity Issue,” published on July 28, the Ministry of Commerce said Beijing had never deliberately pursued a trade surplus and that its exports were driven by innovation and reform, not subsidies or weak domestic demand. “There is no necessary connection between industrial subsidies and overcapacity,” the paper said. China’s trade surplus reached US$938.11 billion in the first nine months of the year, customs data showed on Wednesday, keeping it on track to beat last year’s record of US$1.189 trillion. September exports jumped 36.3 per cent from a year earlier, and the month’s surpluses with both the US and the European Union (EU) topped US$34 billion. On October 7 in Paris, the US and 14 other economies, including the EU, signed a statement pledging action on structural excess capacity in sectors including electric vehicles, batteries, chemicals, chips and solar power. China was not among the signatories. Analysts have described the move as an effort by Washington and Brussels to assemble a “multilateral coalition” to pressure Beijing. Panellists at the PIIE event differed on how to respond. Nicolas Lamp, an associate professor of law at Queen’s University in Canada, argued the West should invite Chinese investment rather than treat all trade as a threat. Garcia-Herrero was more sceptical about the benefits of Chinese investment and business engagement, saying Chinese carmakers’ European plants would likely be assembly operations reliant on imported parts, and that Beijing’s security rules limited technology transfer. “China is impressively careful with its tech transfer,” she said, adding that this is “rightly so.” “That’s why the solution is harder today than it was then.” Yeling Tan, a professor of public policy at the University of Oxford and a non-resident senior fellow at PIIE, said China needed reassurance that the West was not seeking to contain, suppress or encircle it. All sides needed to find a way forward together, she explained. “I think we need wise and courageous politicians to get us there,” Tan said. “It’s a narrow corridor. But I wouldn’t say it doesn’t exist.”

title: Open Questions | Susan Thornton on US-China ties, post-midterms and averting a new balloon crisis
description: AI dialogue and security issues are among the most difficult bilateral points amid ‘fragile stability’, former senior American diplomat says.
content: Susan Thornton is a former American diplomat who for decades worked on US policy in Eurasia in the State Department before becoming acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs during the first Trump presidency. She is the director of the Forum on Asia-Pacific Security at the National Committee on American Foreign Policy and a senior fellow at the Paul Tsai China Centre, Yale Law School. She spoke to Orange Wang about keeping the lines of China-US communication open. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. What do you think overall of the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping? The summit was necessary. Leader-level meetings are the only guardrail we really have in US-China relations right now. It is very important that these meetings happen. I’m probably more positive on this than other people because I do think that leader-level meetings in US-China relations are always difficult to put together. And the fact that Trump has done this twice with Xi – once in Beijing and once in Washington – may help regularise such high-level meetings, which we absolutely need to keep the relationship on track right now since we don’t have much else. I’m not surprised by the negative coverage. The US-China summits are always held to a higher bar when it comes to outcomes of the meeting. There have been expectations built up over many decades that US-China summits are always a big deal when they happen because they’re very hard to mount, and then they always have to have these long lists of outcomes. We need to try to normalise these meetings between the US and Chinese leaders if possible. If you have to have a long list of accomplishments all the time, it’s going to be very hard to hold these meetings. Some argue that the prospect of multiple face-to-face summits this year has put constraints on both sides, especially when it comes to sensitive issues. How could the two sides avoid a repeat of disruptions to bilateral relations, such as the balloon incident in 2023 and the fallout from then-House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in 2022? What you’re getting at here is exactly the issue of whether we can have constructive strategic stability. In the US, I believe that constructive strategic stability – to the extent that people who agreed to that were really understanding what the Chinese side was talking about – is really about avoiding these worst-case scenarios. Avoiding conflict, avoiding a crisis that leads potentially to a conflict, et cetera. The key is for both sides to understand what those issues are that could lead us there. And I do think we have been making progress in this administration on those issues. President Trump is not new to this. He did this before for four years, and it ended quite badly under Covid-19. But I think whenever I’ve heard him speak about that time, it seems to me that he has thought about it and understands what the dynamic was that led things to get so out of hand and doesn’t want to see that happen again. I think others in the administration also understand this. I think [Treasury Secretary] Scott Bessent and [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio definitely understand that this is what they’re trying to accomplish. You put that strategic stability on top of all of these areas of difference that we have, and it does make it quite difficult to manage. But I do think with those high-level cabinet officials understanding what the boundaries are, there are additional touch points. Marco Rubio and [Chinese Foreign Minister] Wang Yi have been speaking more than previously. Scott Bessent has a lot of things on his plate, so it may not be as easy for him to engage regularly with his counterpart, but he has been managing to meet [Chinese Vice-Premier] He Lifeng frequently. And you’ve got a number of economic and trade officials under him and under [US Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer who are plugged in together and talking. I don’t think the crisis will come in the economic sphere. We can work through those questions and not have a crisis. We’ve really been doing this for quite a long time now. The crises will come in the security area, most likely, and in a way those are harder because the security bureaucracies in both countries aren’t very connected to one another and don’t really have regular dialogue mechanisms. We’ve always been talking about having some kind of military-to-military mechanisms for communication hotlines. There’s been a little bit of that in this administration and it’s got a bit improved, but it seems always very unstable. So, I think that’s the potential area that has to be guarded against. President Trump does know where [Beijing’s] red lines are on Taiwan. That has been a learning curve probably for him. But he has a pretty firm view on that issue now, and I feel like Beijing has been reassured that he understands what the mainland’s position is. It seems to me that the tension over Taiwan has abated, but the one question that Beijing keeps bringing up concerns Taiwan arms sales. I’m hopeful that the US side can find a way to manage that effectively. We’ve managed it in the past and should be able to do it again. And I think Trump will focus on it and try to take care that it gets done in a way that doesn’t cause a crisis. How do you view the role of this summit in potentially helping address difficulties and challenges ahead in the US-China relationship? I see US-China bilateral ties as being in a state of fragile stability. During the summit in Beijing in May and since then, many Chinese colleagues have been excited about the notion that we’ve been able to put a name on the relationship, so we have a framework within which we can know what we’re working towards, which is a constructive relationship of strategic stability. Looking at this summit, it’s important that they could meet and normalise that, but it’s also important that we be able to see them meeting in the future. We don’t have those kinds of mechanisms set up yet. In addition to the leader-level meetings, what would be important to maintain this constructive stability is the institutionalisation of the relationship, which we’ve lost over the last 10 years. We need to start building that back to maintain stability. The summit in September was the start of an institutionalisation of things that were agreed upon in May in Beijing. For example, the Board of Trade, which was announced in May but really didn’t do much between May and now because of the summits, was actually pressured to meet, set up working groups and talk to one another. There are groups of people under Jamieson Greer and under [Greer’s Chinese counterpart] Li Chenggang who are meeting and talking through these things. You need a lot more connectivity among professionals if you’re going to have stabilisation of this relationship in any way. The other area maybe that will move forward is AI, which was also announced in May. Scott Bessent announced that there would be an AI dialogue, and maybe that will meet in Shenzhen. So, we can start to see the institutionalisation of these things. It’s still not nearly enough between the US and China. I hope we’ll remember how hard it is to get mechanisms restarted because institutionalisation is a big job and it doesn’t happen overnight. Trump gave Xi a very high-level reception, breaking some traditional protocols, and that triggered a lot of questioning and even criticism in the US. How do you view that? Trump wants to appear welcoming and hospitable but also strong, so there was a jet flyover during the military review. A lot of this is just Trump’s personal way of thinking about how he wants to stage events. It doesn’t have as much to do with diplomatic protocol. There were previous occasions when a president went to meet someone at Joint Base Andrews, so it does have some diplomatic precedent. But I would hesitate to attach a lot of significance to the protocol. Think of all of the things that they did that are highly unusual for a presidential visit. Walking out to look at the presidential helicopter, going over to see the construction of the White House ballroom. All these things are very much a signature of Trump’s way of handling the visit. I think a lot of people just don’t understand this. That’s the main criticism: it’s very, very long on symbolism, pageantry, pomp and circumstance, and short on outcomes. This may signal a change in US-China summitry. We used to try to, in diplomacy, trade diplomatic protocol issues and ceremonial issues, which were very high on the Chinese agenda for a visit, for concerns on the US side, for substantive outcomes. But it’s no longer the case that we can expect that the Chinese are going to make concessions for only protocolary and ceremonial kinds of considerations. I think that is a change in the relationship that we’re seeing. Both sides offer high levels of protocol and neither side really gets any trade for that. Maybe we can dispense with the ceremony of a state visit in the future and focus more on substantive issues at regular leader meetings. Do you think that this summit has laid a proper foundation for Trump and Xi to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in November and Group of 20 (G20) in December? The Chinese side has called 2026 a “big year” for bilateral relations, with the two countries’ leaders having the chance to meet face to face four times. But what about next year? How could the US and China keep up this head-of-state diplomacy? They will have to make a big effort. This is why I think it is positive that President Trump seems to really value his meetings with President Xi and really wants to continue to communicate with him directly either via face-to-face meetings or other ways. I hope we’ll take advantage of that because that hasn’t always been the case with US leaders in the past. That is an important advantage that Trump offers in this very difficult time in US-China relations. He’s open to talking to President Xi anytime, I think. I would like to see if they could connect more on the phone. Next year they are probably not going to travel as much as they did this year. And that’s another reason the relationship has to be institutionalised in the way that we’ve been talking about. There’s such a thin layer of professional expertise in the government that is plugged in to the other side, and that is probably not going to change too much over the next couple years. The other thing we have to worry about is that if we institutionalise the relationship under this administration, what’s going to happen in the next administration? I hope the next administration would keep whatever institutionalisation has been started and build on that, not just try to always do their own thing. That’s not going to be a good way for us to proceed with the relationship. There has been discussion that the Apec gathering in November could open scheduling windows for a US-Russia, China-US-Russia or Trump-Kim Jong-un summit. How do you view the likelihood of these potential bilateral or multilateral meetings taking place? It definitely raises possibilities for dramatic diplomacy that could certainly appeal to President Trump. President Trump has already invited [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to come to Miami for the G20 summit, and it’s likely that he’ll attend. It’s creating some ripple effects in Europe because they may or may not be too pleased that he’s coming, but I think that will all be worked out. President Trump still sees himself as a broker of peace, and so he wants to create these opportunities for dramatic things to happen and big changes in some of the problem areas that we see. Certainly the Russia-Ukraine war is one of them, but North Korea is another one. We know that he wants to meet again with [North Korean leader] Kim Jong-un, and that has not happened yet. If that could happen in Shenzhen during Apec – several people have mentioned this as a possibility, or that Trump could do it on his way to China – those would be dramatic opportunities. We were talking earlier about the calendar for next year, and then Trump is getting towards the end of his term. It seems like he might want to do something in this area. It might make it more attractive for Trump to actually go to Shenzhen and for Xi to come to Miami if there is an opportunity for progress on Ukraine or the North Korea nuclear issue. It’s very hard to see the preparation going far enough between now and November or December to make dramatic successes out of such a meeting, however. Usually, such things take a lot more preparation, so I would be sceptical on that score. But I have heard a lot of people talking about such possibilities, so perhaps they will materialise. You mentioned the AI dialogue. The US and China appear to be taking different approaches to developing this technology. There is also debate within the US over whether the development of advanced models should be slowed. Given these international and domestic differences, how do you view the prospects for the bilateral AI dialogue? I do think it’s going to be extremely difficult. I participated in US-China discussions on mechanisms to report cyber incidents. The AI dialogue is not exactly the same as that, but in the area that the US is concerned about, I think it’s quite similar and also just as difficult, if not more so. The US and China have different concerns, and it’s very hard for the two of them to talk to each other because they’re just coming from completely different vantage points. The Chinese government – and Chinese interlocutors that I’ve talked to reflect this – seems to be quite confident in its ability to control its AI operators and make sure that things that it doesn’t want to have happen in the AI sphere will not happen. Is it overconfident? I am concerned they are not really thinking about the possibilities of loss of control on the Chinese side with AI. They’re mostly worried about what’s happening on the US side and the possibilities of loss of control, the fact that the US government doesn’t control these private companies, that the companies themselves are reporting a lot of things that are somewhat hair-raising and fear-inducing. The US government seems to be thinking that China is going to have the same concerns it has, whereas it really doesn’t. And also, the two systems don’t match up in terms of reporting, transparency and other things that you would need to talk about if you were going to try to share best practices or discuss a strategy for keeping incidents from getting out of control. Trump said that the line for AI safety in the US is the Department of Justice, in other words, the legal system, and that is just not the way the Chinese are going to operate in terms of AI safety. It’s going to be very hard from an institutional and bureaucratic set-up perspective, this security-to-security bureaucracy mistrust. The Chinese system is just not given to being transparent about these things. Chinese media have focused on various US AI operators who are trying to do the right thing by self-reporting accidents that have happened. In the Chinese system, these things would not be publicly reported. China has been criticising the US AI labs and taking advantage of this moment to make itself look like a more responsible actor, when I’m not sure that is fully justified. It’s also very hard to understand how the US and Chinese governments would put together delegations that would look at all similar and have the same kind of expertise. So, I find it a little bit head-scratching as to how this is going to go ahead. It’s important to get some of these people in the room together and have regular discussions. Maybe they can build up a little bit of personal familiarity that will help us at some point in the future when we hit a real problem. I think that would be an advantage. Xi has invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China over the next five years. You travelled to China this year and last year to attend events on subnational cooperation between the two countries. What is your read on the state of bilateral local and people-to-people exchanges? Are they still constrained by factors such as visas and flights? There have been recurring calls to reopen the US consulate in Chengdu and the Chinese consulate in Houston. How possible do you think that would be? This area is still a source of difficulty, even though the two governments have pledged to make improvements. I noticed that they did mention the number of flights. Certainly, they talked about students. But the question is how to make this happen. There’s still extreme suspicion in local-level, people-to-people exchanges, mostly coming from, to be honest, local-level politicians. There are some organised groups that are also pushing against people-to-people exchange between the US and China. I don’t see much change in this. I don’t know, if the US midterm elections in November see a huge shift in the Congress, what might happen there. Most of the local anti-China legislation is coming from Republican states, so it depends a little bit on domestic politics. I don’t know if the Democrats will focus on this as an issue, but in general Democrats have been much more open about people-to-people travel back and forth. I don’t know if they can affect the atmosphere on this issue. It is something to watch. Certainly, the downturn in Chinese students is noticeable.
