I work at Yale University, and we’ve got a number of Chinese students who were unable to come for the start of the semester because they didn’t get their visas in time. Visas are still an issue on both sides. I know people who are having trouble getting visas to go to China, so it’s a two-way thing, and it’s very unfortunate. But it’s really hard to see where a push is going to come from in the US to fix this problem. We should keep pressuring both sides to make improvements here. And again, the devil’s in the details. These two security bureaucracies have a deep, deep level of mistrust. Treasury Secretary Bessent said China and the US had agreed to extend the trade truce for two months, until January 10 next year. Why only two months rather than a longer period? What could the two sides achieve during this time frame? To me, it is a bit surprising that the extension of the Busan trade truce was so minimal. I think two months is about the minimum that they could have agreed. What that says is they did not want the truce to end because neither side is prepared for what might happen or the consequences of ending that truce. But they couldn’t come up really with any agreement to extend it, so they’ve just basically rolled over the agreement from last year. Both sides were probably hoping that they would be able to extend the truce and improve it, but apparently that didn’t happen. It’s probable that they didn’t have enough time to do that, because these kinds of negotiations take quite a bit of time and preparation. And you can’t just have a meeting on a Sunday in New York between top officials and expect to hammer these things out in that kind of time frame. So, my suspicion is that they did not manage to agree on any of the improvements in the rollover that they wanted, and they didn’t want to roll over the current truce, which is kind of minimal, for too much of an extended period of time because they still hope to get something better. Probably the January time frame is not much time to do anything either. But at least if there is a meeting in November, then that gives another forcing function, and there’s also the G20 summit in Miami in December, that’s a lot of connectivity between now and January 10. So, there is a possibility of getting something done there, although it will be difficult. And then we’ll hit January 10, and the truce will probably roll over one way or another. They won’t want to lose this truce, I don’t think, in January either. The one factor that probably was pushing on the US side is the midterm elections coming up in early November. I think the US side wanted to get something that would get us past the midterm elections and give some comfortable margin after that to assess where things are going. Observers in both countries argue that China is becoming more confident and increasingly sees itself as Washington’s equal, while perceptions of continuing US decline are growing globally. The narrative of “the East is rising and the West is declining” continues to surface in public discussions. What do you think about this? Before the September summit, some argued that China was in a stronger position at the negotiating table because of the war on Iran. If that is the case, how long could that last? I do think China is more confident, reasonably so. And certainly, the US has been losing influence on the international stage for a period of time. In the wake of the war in Iran, that has accelerated, probably. The question, really, is whether China is making gains from the losses that the US is inflicting on itself. I think China has made some gains, but it is not a slam dunk yet that China has made equal gains to the US’ losses. In other words, I don’t see that China is somehow displacing the US. The interesting thing to watch is we’ve seen President Xi go to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan and the Brics summit in India, talking in many of his speeches about China being a responsible player, that China stands for a continuation of globalisation, openness and free trade, and I think what people see China doing in practice is somewhat different from that. Or at least they are sceptical that this is what China is standing for and what China is all about. In fact, a lot of countries, especially in China’s neighbourhood, continue to have concerns about China and are actually threatened by China. And China hasn’t really done much to reassure those countries that they shouldn’t be afraid of China. I think this is the dilemma China has. It wants to take advantage of this moment when the US is on the back foot, clearly, in Iran and elsewhere, and it has taken some advantage, but it has not managed to really convince people of what its ambitions and intentions are. I think that is going to continue to be a tough balancing act for China. I hope China will start to show in its actions more what it’s actually thinking about for the long term, and I think that will be important in terms of the narrative too out there in the world. The US is clearly in a transition period. Domestic politics are at a turning point, and we’re going to have to work through that. So, it’s going to be a period of time. Whether China can take advantage of our domestic transition is really a question for China’s own policy and diplomats to work out. US allies such as Japan and the Philippines are strengthening their security ties, while tensions with Beijing continue to simmer in the South China Sea, the East China Sea and the waters east of Taiwan. Would this make it more challenging for Beijing and Washington to manage their bilateral relationship? As for the South China Sea, some Chinese experts have said that Beijing’s goal is not to expel US influence from the region and that it could consider opening certain island infrastructure to US vessels to help ease tensions. Do you think this is realistic? I don’t know about that specific proposal, but certainly China can’t be happy about what it’s seeing in terms of its immediate neighbours linking up in tighter coalitions for their security. China hasn’t been doing much to reassure them that they shouldn’t be worried about China, and so that’s going to produce this natural kind of build-up of defence and military capability and trying to link with other countries in the region to strengthen their posture. It’s exactly what you would expect. And it can’t be something that China sees as a good development. I have to say that it’s really hard for these countries to see in the future how China is going to not behave in a very kind of domineering way towards them. This is how things have been playing out in the region, which is why they seem to be so eager to have US engagement stay in the region. I think that’s a big question mark right now, which is making people in the region even more worried about the future. How to assure these countries about their future security, their relationship with China? How is China going to treat these countries? That’s a huge question. And right now, it’s not going so well. Taiwan has, of course, always been at the centre of relations between Washington and Beijing. That issue is a bit special and separate from some of these other issues. But the same dynamic is really at play there, the fear of what the relationship with Beijing would be like in the future. I think Beijing hasn’t given very clear or positive signals about that to anybody yet. Confidence is one thing, but how you wield your confidence is very important.

title: Hegseth calls US$1.5 trillion defence budget ‘critical’ to counter China
description: Pentagon chief warns US risks falling behind China in drones, robotics and AI without major investment in military capabilities.
content: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has called a nearly US$1.5 trillion defence budget request “absolutely critical”, warning that whoever falls behind in autonomy, robotics and AI will fall “even further behind” as Washington eyes China’s rapid military modernisation. Speaking at a panel discussion during the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition on Wednesday, Hegseth said that Project Agincourt, the Pentagon’s initiative to accelerate drone and autonomous warfare capabilities, is the “end state” of what the administration has focused on since “day one”. Under the current US Department of Defence plan, announced by Hegseth on September 30 during his State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Project Agincourt includes the creation of a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command by October 1, 2027, building on the Replicator initiative from the Joe Biden administration and the Drone Dominance Programme initiated in 2025. Asked how significant the increase to nearly US$1.5 trillion in the defence budget is, Hegseth replied that it is “absolutely critical” and a “one-time generational investment” that gives Washington a chance to “fully rebuild” the military amid threats from adversaries. “We’re in a different moment. We’ve got a near-peer adversary who’s building a military, the most historic military build-up potentially in world history,” said Hegseth, in a tacit reference to China’s recent military modernisation drive. “That’s not hyperbole. That’s just objective truth. You add up the step changes in autonomy, in robotics, in space, AI, whoever’s ahead now is going to get much further ahead. “Whoever’s behind now is going to fall even further behind. And so investments now are going to matter, and they’re going to ripple not just for years but for decades across our joint force.” The rare panel discussion had Hegseth speaking alongside the civilian heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force – acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and Air Force Secretary Troy Meink – as well as Derrick Anderson, assistant secretary of defence for special operations and low-intensity conflict. The Pentagon has requested US$54.6 billion for the Defence Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG), established last year for coordinating, testing and integrating autonomous weapons across all military domains, for the financial year 2027 budget, an almost 24,000 per cent increase from US$225.9 million in the previous year. According to the Department of Defence Fiscal Year 2027 Mandatory Budget Overview published in April, which explains the fiscal allocation of the Trump administration’s record-breaking US$1.5 trillion defence budget request, DAWG was allocated US$53.6 billion under the US$350 billion reconciliation package, leaving US$1 billion under the base request. The budget included US$39.2 billion for a multi-year investment in autonomous systems procurement, domestic production capacity and advanced capabilities, and US$14.4 billion for counter-unmanned systems development and deployment. The Trump administration has repeatedly used budget reconciliation to secure increases in defence spending. The process allows legislation to pass the Senate by a simple majority, bypassing the usual 60-vote threshold and reducing the need for Democratic support. Hegseth defended the use of the process as a means to “supercharge” the architecture of Autonomous Warfare Command and “reestablish a deterrent to rebuild the military around the world” by acquiring “a million” drones. China’s drone build-up has been one of the major drivers for the Trump administration to ramp up its autonomous systems acquisition. During the panel discussion, Meink referred to China as having “the largest weapons build-up probably in the history of the world,” resulting in Beijing “leveraging” over Washington, such as using low Earth orbit satellites to target US weapons systems. “So the question is, what do we do about that? How do we degrade their systems? How do we make sure our systems are survivable no matter what domain we are in?” said Meink. “And that’s what we’re working with entire joint forces to do. And the autonomous systems are going to be part of that.” Under the 15th five-year plan released in March, covering the period from 2026 to 2030, China prioritised the People’s Liberation Army’s transition towards ‘intelligentised’ warfare, emphasising artificial intelligence, unmanned and autonomous systems, networked information infrastructure and emerging technologies. A satellite imagery analysis also suggests that the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has stationed over 200 obsolete 1960s-era J-6 supersonic fighter jets – converted into attack and cruise-missile-like drones – across six airbases near the Taiwan Strait. China is also known to be the world’s largest exporter of drones. According to a report by the Washington-based think tank Centre for Strategic and International Studies, Chinese companies accounted for more than 80 per cent of global drone supplies. Hegseth criticised the previous Biden administration for treating the world as “stagnant” and taking a “nap” on advanced military technologies such as hypersonics, space weaponisation and drones, even as adversaries like China were rapidly expanding their capabilities. He said the Trump administration was now working to regain its “competitive advantage”. “Now we’re changing the cost paradigm for our adversaries on the battlefield, and they’re the ones having to understand how to deal defensively with our capabilities,” said Hegseth. “The drones that this will require, all of those investments are part of reconciliation of that 350 [billion dollars] … The coming months will be critical, and it’s not hyperbolic to state whether or not we rebuild our military to meet the threats of the country will depend on funding the president’s vision for US$1.5 trillion, and our goal, come hell or high water.” On the question of how he came up with the decision to establish a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command despite Congress’ call to reduce the number of general officers in the past 15 years, Hegseth said that it “completely meets the intent” as it requires sufficient authorities to “ensure we can drive change quickly”. Hegseth said building up drone capabilities required more than training and cooperation with industry. It also meant getting the technology into the hands of frontline commanders, who could test it on the battlefield and learn how to “iterate it, change on it, innovate on it”.

title: Opinion | Can China’s coal industry ride to the rescue of a world in oil shock?
description: China’s quick and efficient coal-fired power plants are a stopgap solution even as its coal chemical sector offers oil product substitutes.
content: Be warned. The global economy is likely to experience a recession next year. War across the Middle East is set to escalate, wrecking energy supplies for many years, even as the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble is ripe to burst. This, however, would also create an energy leadership opportunity for China. High energy prices already fuel demand for Chinese renewable energy products and electric vehicles. But as a leader in building coal-fired power plants, China can also offer the global market a quick substitute for Middle Eastern oil and gas, attracting a boom in investment and export revenue. China could well become the new global energy epicentre, strengthening its geopolitical position. Since the United States launched its war on Iran over seven months ago, the global oil shortfall has run to 3 billion barrels. The release of strategic reserves by countries around the world has largely kept oil prices at around US$100 a barrel. But both national and commercial reserves are now running low. China, a major buyer, is estimated to have cut its oil imports by 5-7 million barrels a day since the war began. If we estimate conservatively that China has been releasing 3 million barrels a day, half of its reported 1.4 billion barrels of reserves are now gone. Its expected return to the market soon to top up reserves may yet put a ceiling on oil prices. But the global supply situation is worsening quickly, as the war spreads to infrastructure for oil and gas production, processing and transport. Saudi Arabia’s massive Abqaiq petroleum processing facilities have reportedly been hit by Houthi missiles. Its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, bypassing the logjam in the Strait of Hormuz, had to be shut down temporarily after an attack last month. The Red Sea route itself is looking uncertain as Houthi rebels in Yemen occupy the crucial Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi support for Yemen’s government makes its oil infrastructure targets in a widening war. Before the year is out, the destruction could disrupt most of the supply of hydrocarbons and related products from the Middle East for many years, possibly a decade. Saudi Arabia could cease to be a major petroleum supplier for years. US President Donald Trump has halted attacks on Iran ahead of the November midterm elections but the US is likely to strike again. To avoid a war of attrition, it could concentrate attacks on Iran’s oil infrastructure. Iran’s retaliation would be to visit the same on US allies in the Middle East. Tit-for-tat strikes could take out most of the region’s oil and gas production. The major theme for 2027 is therefore shaping up to be the destruction of oil demand through high prices and/or rationing. Unfortunately, the developing economies in the Global South would be priced out of the market first. Demand is set to be hit in the Global North too but not before inflation forces up bond yields. The full impact of the oil shock, delayed and mitigated by the release of strategic reserves, is coming home to roost. The AI bubble is not likely to survive surging bond yields. Under the fantastical stories of every major financial bubble that has burst was debt, a lot of it. The AI bubble won’t be an exception, even as the true scale of debt is hidden off balance sheet through special purpose vehicles. When the credit tide goes out, these vehicles will be exposed. The AI talking heads are trying to prolong the bubble by talking up the doomsday risk. They hope people will be too scared to pay attention to the slowdown in performance progress. The reality is, doomsday or not, they need trillions of dollars to keep going. There isn’t enough money out there. If the AI bubble bursts, it will have a major impact on China. Its exports are surging on a massive base, mainly due to rising demand for electronics, including data centre components as US hyperscalers build AI centres. The increase in China’s exports this year could be equivalent to Japan’s total exports. If the AI bubble bursts next year, the most important pillar in China’s export boom will be gone. The unfolding energy crisis also offers opportunities for China: solar energy, wind power and electric vehicles are the usual suspects. But a bigger opportunity, at least for the next five years, could be coal. Coal-fired power plants can be an effective interim solution to an oil and gas shortfall. China has a huge industry in building coal-fired power plants. Chinese coal-fired power plants are much more efficient than those of other countries. As the global leader by far, China can build these plants cheaper and faster than anyone else. More importantly, coal-rich China can expand its coal chemical industry to produce substitute oil products. China can and should produce enough fertiliser, diesel and aviation fuel to meet global demand. China can turn itself into the new energy centre of the global economy. The US may want to replace Middle East hydrocarbons with Venezuelan oil. It has the reserves and has them under control. Making Europe and East Asia dependent on energy from US-controlled sources will revive its economy and geopolitical power. But building up the Venezuela’s supply capacity will take a long time. China can build its coal-based alternatives faster and more cheaply. It is a great economic opportunity and also strengthens China’s geopolitical position. If China becomes a superpower in energy as in manufacturing, it basically wins the geopolitical competition in the 21st century.

title: ‘Time for Zelensky to go’: Musk escalates satellite slowdown row
description: SpaceX boss deflects blame to the Trump administration as Kyiv warns Starshield limits cripple drone defence and battlefield strikes.
content: Tech billionaire Elon Musk called on Wednesday for Volodymyr Zelensky to “go” as Ukraine’s leader, after insisting any disruption to the war-torn country’s use of his satellite communications system was the fault of the US government, not his company. The comments came as Kyiv raised doubts over US support for Ukraine in its war with Russia, accusing Washington this week of helping Moscow by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling Kyiv’s military response through changes to the SpaceX-designed system it uses for communications. “And so the slaughter continues,” Musk wrote on X. “Time for Zelensky to go.” Musk earlier said that “any limits on speed or usage” of his SpaceX company’s Starshield systems were “decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS”, referring to US President Donald Trump. He drew a distinction between Starshield, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications, and the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Kyiv also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations. Musk was responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said that “Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160km/h is being restored”, but that “removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defence”. Ukrainian defence officials have suggested Washington is behind slower speeds reported on some internet terminals that help the country’s military hit Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones. Kyiv has also accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes, with the city hit by ballistic missiles for two nights in a row before air raid sirens could sound to warn residents to take cover. A senior official in Kyiv also said that the United States had in recent days threatened to stop providing intelligence about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks – which Trump has denied. Trump, facing key midterm elections next month in which soaring fuel prices are a major issue, has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the squeeze on supplies and increase in prices at the pump. Opposition Democrats in the US Senate and House denounced Trump’s administration over the reported interrupted connections. “Trump’s making a choice – and it directly aids Putin’s slaughter of Ukrainian civilians,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats said in a post on X, describing restrictions as “unconscionable” while Ukraine faced an onslaught of Russian drones and missiles. In the Senate’s Foreign Relations Committee, top Democrat Jeanne Shaheen said the “restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starshield must stop immediately,” adding that “lives are at stake”. Shaheen also said that the defence department is required to notify “Congress if it pauses or downgrades intelligence sharing with Ukraine”, and called on Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth to immediately provide that notification if there are changes.

title: US stocks drop to their worst day since July as inflation worsens
description: Inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent, fuelling expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again.
content: US stocks dropped to their worst day since July on Wednesday, following the latest signal that inflation is getting worse. The S&P 500 sank 1.1 per cent for a fifth loss in the six days since setting its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 48 points, or 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slid 1.9 per cent as stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry led the way lower. Stocks felt pressure from rising yields in the bond market, where worries grew after a report said US consumers had to pay prices for fuel, food and other costs of living last month that were 3.7 per cent higher overall than a year earlier. That means inflation accelerated from its 3.4 per cent rate in August and was worse than the 3.6 per cent that economists expected. Inflation has remained more painful than anyone would like since the economy catapulted out of the crevasse created by the Covid-19 pandemic. It has accelerated recently in part because of jumps in fuel prices caused by the war with Iran, and the price for a barrel of Brent crude added 0.4 per cent Wednesday to US$106.06. That has added to the long-standing worries about fast-rising debt loads for governments, signals that the US economy is still growing and other factors that have sent bond yields to their highest levels in years. The centrepiece of the US bond market, the 10-year Treasury, saw its yield briefly jump above 5.32 per cent from less than 5.17 per cent just before the inflation report’s release. It eventually gave back much of the gain. Yields on shorter-term Treasurys had even bigger leaps as traders raised their expectations for coming hikes to interest rates by the Federal Reserve, though they also moderated as the day progressed. The Fed recently raised the interest rate that it controls, which affects very short-term loans, for the first time in three years in hopes of reining in inflation. Higher rates do that by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money and slowing the overall economy. Traders now see a nearly 35 per cent chance the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its next meeting in two weeks, up from the 22 per cent probability seen a day earlier, according to data from CME Group. Part of what is keeping inflation high is that Americans overall are continuing to spend, which encourages businesses to keep raising prices for their products and services. As Americans become more “price-sensitive” and the economy also benefits from greater productivity by workers, Vanguard Senior Economist Adam Schickling said inflation should slow, but “patience will be required”. Much of Wall Street’s pain on Wednesday was due to drops for companies riding the AI frenzy to huge profit growth and stellar stock gains. Higher bond yields making borrowing money more expensive could make it more difficult for companies to raise cash to build data centres and fill them with AI chips. Drops of 3.2 per cent for Nvidia, 3.1 per cent for Broadcom and 5.7 per cent for Advanced Micro Devices were among the day’s heaviest weights on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, tumbled 15.5 per cent for its worst day since February. GE Vernova, which is hoping to electrify power-hungry data centres, dropped 6.2 per cent, and Oracle sank 8.8 per cent. Smaller companies also feel the bite of higher interest rates because many need to borrow to grow. The Russell 2000 index of the smallest US stocks fell 1.9 per cent. Higher yields in the bond market push downward on prices for all kinds of stocks, and the main way companies can offset that is by delivering bigger profits. That is exactly what analysts are expecting, and it is how the S&P 500 has been able to set records despite the many challenges weighing on Wall Street. But the high expectations also mean companies are likely to get punished if they fall short of targets for growth. Bank of America dropped 4.8 per cent after reporting weaker profit and revenue for the summer than analysts expected. The profit would have failed to meet expectations even if the US Treasury Department had not announced US$1.2 billion in fines late on Tuesday for alleged violations of anti-money-laundering and sanctions laws by the bank. State Street sank 4.1 per cent after reporting weaker revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though its profit was slightly above their forecasts. All told, the S&P 500 fell 86.51 points to 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 48.62 to 51,621.48, and the Nasdaq composite sank 511.51 to 26,692.87. In stock markets abroad, indexes ticked higher in Europe following a weaker finish in Asia. They rose 0.7 per cent in London and fell 0.9 per cent in Shanghai for two of the world’s bigger moves.

title: Bank of America fined US$1.21 billion as US flags suspected Chinese money laundering
description: Second-largest US bank failed to report hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of transactions linked to Chinese money-laundering networks.
content: Bank of America, the second-largest US bank, failed to promptly report hundreds of millions of dollars in suspicious transactions bearing signs of Chinese money-laundering networks, US regulators said on Tuesday, announcing more than US$1.21 billion in penalties for broader anti-money-laundering and sanctions failures. The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, said the activity included large wire transfers to counterparties in China, repeated credit-card purchases at major retailers and shipping companies, and payments towards cards held by third parties without an apparent commercial purpose. Most of the suspected network activity involved a group of customers purporting to operate in logistics or electronics, according to a consent order. The agency said their transaction patterns were inconsistent with legitimate commercial activity for those businesses. The China-related findings form part of a wider enforcement action against the bank. FinCEN imposed a US$1.2 billion penalty, against which it will credit a US$750 million payment to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). Bank of America admitted the facts and violations set out in the FinCEN order to resolve the case, including wilful failures to comply with the Bank Secrecy Act. The order describes the underlying transactions as suspicious and does not establish that every payment involved criminal proceeds. “Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” a Bank of America spokesperson said in response to questions from the South China Morning Post. The bank said it had invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combating financial crime, adding that its team was “far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators”. The spokesperson did not directly address questions about the suspected Chinese money-laundering networks or whether the customer relationships involved remained open. FinCEN said the bank failed to report more than US$5 billion in suspicious activity on time. More than US$1 billion involved national security and other priority illicit-finance risks, a category that includes suspected Chinese laundering networks, fraud and potential trade-based money laundering connected to the US southwest border. The order did not provide an exact total for the suspected Chinese network activity or identify the customers and counterparties involved. In response to the SCMP’s questions, the US Treasury Department referred to the consent order. Warning signs included large transfers to China with generic descriptions such as “for goods”, without a discernible business rationale. FinCEN also identified repeated transfers to counterparties with no web presence operating from residential addresses. The bank’s credit-card monitoring had gaps, including shortcomings in triggering investigations when spending routinely exceeded a cardholder’s stated income, according to the order. In January 2024, Bank of America developed a feature to identify potential trade-based money laundering, including credit-card activity. But during the period covered by the order, it used that feature only for activity already under investigation, rather than to generate alerts or trigger new investigations, FinCEN said. Some suspicious transactions continued after the bank adjusted its monitoring thresholds, the agency added. The order’s China-related section does not identify a specific cartel or establish that the transactions involved fentanyl proceeds. It also does not allege Chinese government involvement. The Chinese embassy in Washington had not responded to a request for comment. In a separate action, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement of around US$11.7 million for 475 apparent sanctions violations involving about US$14.8 million in transactions between September 2021 and April 2025. Those findings concerned sanctions programmes targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Myanmar, Somalia, narcotics and global terrorism. OFAC’s release did not identify a connection to the suspected Chinese money-laundering networks described by FinCEN. The sanctions failures included payments through blocked banks and transactions by individuals whose names and dates of birth exactly matched sanctions records. Bank of America said its third-quarter results would include a non-tax-deductible charge of US$1.2 billion, reducing net income by around 17 US cents per share. OFAC classified the case as non-egregious but said the bank’s incomplete disclosures and delayed responses slowed its investigation. It granted no reduction from the base penalty. Treasury described the combined enforcement action as its third-largest penalty and the OCC’s largest. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. The FinCEN settlement requires the bank to engage a third party to review past transactions for suspicious activity that went undetected and to undergo independent reviews of its monitoring and customer due diligence programmes.

title: Yemen government says it raised Houthis’ alleged use of Chinese tech with Beijing
description: A report says the group is trying to produce advanced missiles, and shipping documents listing a Chinese supplier were found with some parts.
content: The Yemeni government has spoken with Beijing about the Houthis’ alleged attempts to utilise Chinese-made technology for weapons, a Yemeni minister said on Wednesday, as the two sides’ long-running civil war escalates. “The Chinese are partners and we have discussed with them about, you know, the use of dual products,” Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba said in response to an Agence France-Presse question about reports the Iran-backed group was trying to secure Chinese components to help manufacture weapons. “They were very keen for any sort of information so they can investigate it. Their support to the Yemeni government is clear,” Zouba added. The minister spoke to journalists via a virtual press conference to address the war in Yemen, which has also drawn in the government’s main backer, Saudi Arabia. The comments came after a recent report by the Conflict Armament Research group (CAR) alleged that the Houthis were attempting to produce advanced medium-range ballistic missiles. CAR also suggested the group was “expanding its supply chains beyond Iran-linked supply networks, with several purpose-built missile components found alongside shipping documents that listed a Chinese supplier”. AFP has been unable to independently verify the allegations made in the report. The Houthis have used their arsenal of drones and ballistic and cruise missiles to target Yemeni government forces and civilian infrastructure in neighbouring Saudi Arabia to deadly effect as fighting flares following the collapse of a truce in July. The Houthis boasted of hitting Saudi oil giant Aramco’s facilities overnight, as well as recent attacks targeting the Riyadh airport, which have killed at least 18 people since October 7. Houthi attacks have also targeted oil tankers in the Red Sea – Saudi Arabia’s alternative export route following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the wider Middle East war. China has long been one of the largest buyers of Saudi crude. A Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen’s government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a civil war that has created a dire humanitarian crisis in the impoverished country.

title: Sally Rooney books can’t be sold in UK amid Palestine Action ban, publisher says
description: The Irish writer is a supporter of the activists, who have been put on the same ‘terrorist’ blacklist as militants like Hamas and Hezbollah.
content: Irish author Sally Rooney can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for the activist group Palestine Action, her publisher Faber said on Wednesday. Rooney has previously expressed her support for the group, which was banned as a “terrorist” organisation by the UK government in July 2025. It is not banned in Ireland, where Rooney lives. The proscription, which the organisation is appealing against, puts Palestine Action on the same blacklist as militant groups Hamas and Hezbollah, making it illegal in the UK to be part of, support or finance it. “Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher,” Faber said in a statement on its website. “As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format,” the British publisher said, adding that it would continue to sell her work in other countries and regions. The bestselling author of Normal People and Intermezzo previously said she would donate earnings to Palestine Action and told the High Court in London that the proscription would have an impact on freedom of expression. “As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence,” Rooney said in a statement. “After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK,” the author said, adding she was prepared to “accept the consequences” of her beliefs. Britain’s Supreme Court is set to hear an appeal against the ban from the group’s co-founder Huda Ammori next month. Thousands of people have protested against the ban and been detained in the process, while rights groups and some public figures have condemned the ban as criminalising dissent. Palestine Action’s stated goal on its website is to end “global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime”. Its proscription came after a series of high-profile stunts protesting the war in Gaza, including targeting weapons factories, especially those belonging to Israeli arms group Elbit.

title: EU leaders to ‘urgently’ call for new trade weapons to tackle China shock
description: Brussels plans new measures to confront trade imbalances even after a surprise deal with Beijing to limit Chinese hybrid car imports.
content: Leaders of the EU’s 27 member states will instruct Brussels to “urgently” come up with new weapons to counter the imbalances they believe are caused by China’s economic policies, at a meeting in the Belgian capital on Thursday. The instruction – part of a draft statement being negotiated ahead of this week’s European Council summit – comes after the European Union and China reached a surprise deal in Beijing last week that will cap the number of Chinese hybrid cars imported to the bloc at 350,000 per year. While the deal dampened the immediate threat of a trade war, officials and diplomats in Brussels made clear on Wednesday that it was not enough and that the EU intends to keep the pressure on China to moderate its exports in other sectors. “One swallow does not make a summer, but it’s a first result and the start of a process to get China to moderate its exports,” said a senior diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity. The text does not directly name Beijing, as the bloc looks to avoid head-on confrontation with the world’s second largest economy, but uses language often used to describe the perceived damage China’s industrial might has caused to the EU economy. “The European Council took stock of global macroeconomic imbalances, and invites the commission to continue to engage in results-oriented dialogues, to make effective use of the EU’s instruments, and to urgently enhance the EU toolbox with new instruments to better address these imbalances,” read the statement, which was seen by the South China Morning Post and could change before Thursday’s summit. Leaders will discuss these imbalances over lunch and are expected to ask the European Commission, which manages trade policy for the 27 member states and which has taken the steer on negotiations with China, to create new instruments by the end of the year. Two of these have already been announced: a diversification tool to compel companies to broaden their pool of suppliers and a “solidarity mechanism” to compensate firms hurt by Chinese retaliation. But diplomatic sources expect many leaders to back a Franco-German proposal for a kill switch that would quickly kick countries and firms out of the EU market if they used coercive behaviour. While there has been speculation that last week’s surprise agreement on hybrid cars will dampen appetite to take action among EU members, sources have been assured that this is not the case. Multiple well-placed sources said the deal showed that the “two-track” model of talking with China and working behind the scenes on new trade weapons works. The fact that Germany came on board with strong action might have been a game-changer, several people said. “We might be a bit more optimistic than we thought initially. It goes hand in hand – in order to have a credible dialogue, we need to be seen to have instruments that allow us to take action when needed,” a second diplomat said. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Wednesday that “we will no longer stand idly by when other states harm our economy through high subsidies, artificially devalued currencies, overcapacity and aggressive pricing”. “Anyone who seeks a trade conflict with us will find that we are now prepared to fight back – and with appropriate responses,” Merz was reported as saying by Bloomberg.

title: Hong Kong extends smart fire alarm scheme to another 6,000 old buildings
description: Fire service says no installations have been completed so far although the policy was rolled out over five months ago for 3,600 blocks.
content: Hong Kong’s Fire Services Department has extended a scheme allowing property owners to install smart fire alarm systems rather than traditional safety equipment to another 6,000 old buildings, but conceded that no installations had been completed although the policy was rolled out over five months ago for 3,600 blocks. Lai Kin-mo, acting deputy chief fire officer for building improvement, said on Wednesday that while 300 buildings had expressed interest in installing the system, which can send alerts within 10 seconds of detecting smoke, owners were still trying to reach a consensus on related issues. “Different service providers will provide different installation plans that involve work fees. I think it’s mostly prices that they are negotiating as the technology is already there and space is not a concern,” Lai said. The department previously authorised 3,600 old buildings of six storeys or under that were built or submitted building plans before March 1987 to install the system from April 30 this year. To expand the scheme, 6,000 composite and residential buildings of seven floors and above built or with building plans submitted before March 1987 would be authorised to install an alarm system starting this month to satisfy fire safety requirements, Lai said. The system uses Internet of Things (IoT) technology to connect smoke and carbon monoxide detectors installed inside a building to a central monitoring system operated by a service provider, which then alerts authorities to fires. Lai said the detectors’ signal could be transmitted to the service provider within 10 seconds. “With this new fire alarm system installed, when a fire breaks out, the system will be able to automatically detect the hazard and alert authorities for us to respond within a shorter time,” Lai said. For newly eligible buildings of seven to 12 storeys, installing the system means these buildings would no longer have to rely on hosepipe reels or manual fire alarms that are triggered by a person breaking a glass panel or pulling a handle to activate a detector. However, these buildings would need to place two 5kg (11lbs) powder extinguishers on each floor and ensure a dry riser was functional inside the building. Eligible buildings of 13 storeys or above would need to install IoT detectors on existing fire safety pumps and water tanks, in addition to removing any existing manual fire safety systems. Lai estimated that installing the smart system would take two to four weeks, compared with one to two years for hosepipe reel and manual systems. The cost would be between HK$500,000 (US$64,000) and HK$2 million, as opposed to a range from HK$1.3 million to HK$2.6 million for conventional works. In addition to expanding the eligibility for the smart system, the department will also authorise up to 900 eligible old commercial and industrial buildings to install an improvised sprinkler system with a direct pumping design instead of a water tank. Lai said the department had noticed limited space in these buildings for a tank, structural concerns over the additional weight and difficulties in gathering owners to agree to start works. This improvised system would take three to five years to install, less than the six to eight years required for traditional sprinkler systems with a tank. With sprinklers connected directly to the public water supply, the Water Supplies Department would notify the fire service when locations with buildings using the system faced water shortages for emergency planning, Lai said. “We will ramp up our deployment of vehicles and manpower to deploy more resources should a fire break out in that area,” he said.

title: ASML’s chip equipment sales to China soar 109% despite US export curb push
description: The Dutch firm expects China to account for 20 per cent of its total sales this year, even as the US pushes for tighter export restrictions.
content: Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML expects China to account for about 20 per cent of its total sales this year, after seeing shipments to the market more than double during the previous quarter despite mounting US pressure for tighter export restrictions on less advanced chipmaking machinery. The company’s sales to China surged 109 per cent in the third quarter compared with the previous three months, according to financial results released on Wednesday. That took China’s share of ASML’s machine sales to 23 per cent, up from 14 per cent in the second quarter. The revenue jump comes as Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten faces pressure from Washington to tighten restrictions on sales of chipmaking machines to China. Last month, Jetten expressed confidence in a Bloomberg interview that the Netherlands would reach an agreement with the United States regarding Washington’s proposed Match Act, which aims to further restrict ASML’s ability to export less advanced lithography machines to China. Sources familiar with the matter previously told the South China Morning Post that Jetten was scheduled to visit China next spring. ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet stressed during an investor call that Chinese customers were not highly motivated to develop domestic alternative equipment as long as they had continued access to the company’s products. He added that China still had a “very, very long way to go” to match ASML’s technology. The firm expected demand from China to remain strong for 2027 and beyond, given the country’s chip capacity build up, said Roger Dassen, the group’s chief financial officer. Despite the geopolitical headwinds, ASML raised the lower end of its full-year 2026 sales guidance to €44 billion (US$49.25 billion) and pinned its gross margin forecast at around 56 per cent, the upper end of its earlier range, accompanied by further capacity expansion plans. Revenue in the fourth quarter was expected to reach “between €14.2 and €15.2 billion”, Dassen said, adding that sales momentum was “really very, very strongly building up”. We are looking at ways, especially in 2028 and beyond, to further extend our capacity Christophe Fouquet, ASML The strong 2026 revenue – which is expected to grow by 36 per cent – is mainly being driven by robust demand for ASML’s advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) machines, sales of which are set to rise by over 45 per cent this year. Non-EUV business revenue is expected to expand by 20 per cent, with installed base business revenue rising 50 per cent, according to Dassen. With growth momentum expected to continue into 2027 and 2028, ASML said its planned 30 per cent capacity expansion in low-NA EUV systems for the next two years would not be enough to meet demand. “We have to do more and we are looking basically at ways, especially in 2028 and beyond, to further extend our capacity,” said Fouquet, adding that ASML’s customers were also planning further capacity expansions for the coming years. “A lot of our discussions with our customers now are shifting in fact beyond 2027. A lot of order intake for 2028. But also some strong interest to already place orders for 2029 and sometimes even 2030.” ASML shares were up by more than 1 per cent in Amsterdam at around noon local time following the announcement.

title: Regulator expects Man City to face January showdown over breaches of Premier League rules
description: The club have repeatedly maintained they are innocent of the charges, and currently sit top of the table with six wins out of six.
content: The chair of English football’s independent regulator has said he expects Manchester City’s appeal after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules to be heard by January. City, who have repeatedly maintained they are innocent of the charges, are currently top of the Premier League table with six wins out of six following their 3-0 win over Liverpool last weekend. No sanction has yet been announced, but City could face a heavy points deduction leading to relegation and there has even been speculation they could be stripped of the three Premier League titles they won between 2009 and 2018. “The Premier League have said that they want to get this resolved within [this] season, and actually, of course, it’s not the Premier League, it’s an independent commission that’s actually going to hear this, made of three retired either judges or lawyers,” Independent Football Regulator (IFR) chair David Kogan told Times Radio on Wednesday. “My understanding is that there is a prescribed process, which is 12 weeks, and so people are assuming this will actually be heard by the middle or the end of January. “But as I say, it’s not our process, it’s that of the Premier League’s independent commission. What I don’t think we can do is take any judgment until we’re quite clear.” Kogan said on Tuesday he would resign if there was political interference in any future IFR investigations of City. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for his comments saying he would be “really concerned” if City’s Abu Dhabi owners left the club following the verdict. Downing Street subsequently had to backtrack, insisting no one was “above the rules”. Burnham, who was mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 to June 2026, has since published all of his dealings with the City hierarchy. “We’ve had absolutely no interference from anybody since we created the regulator a year ago,” Kogan said. “We cannot, when regulating football, be subject to political interference on decisions we make about owners, directors or anything else.” He added: “And I won’t actually be prepared to run an organisation which is subject to that degree of interference.” Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca said last week he “completely trusts” the club and believes it will win its appeal.

title: How a new US Army unit could challenge the PLA’s area-denial strategy in a Taiwan conflict
description: A fourth specialised American task force has been established to counter Chinese efforts to keep enemy warships and aircraft at bay.
content: The United States Army has launched a new task force aimed at countering Chinese efforts to block American and allied warships and aircraft in a potential conflict. The 4th Multi-Domain Task Force (MDTF) – established at Fort Carson, Colorado on October 8 – is the latest addition to a series of specialised formations developed for operations in the western Pacific. Those formations were earlier activated in Washington state, Germany and Hawaii. The new unit includes nearly 2,100 soldiers and reports to the 7th Infantry Division, also known as Multi-Domain Command – Pacific, which was established in June. A 2024 US Army plan envisages five MDTFs worldwide, three of them assigned to the US Army Pacific. Pacific-focused MDTFs are designed to deploy elements to forward positions across the Indo-Pacific, where their mobile, land-based capabilities could pose a threat to Chinese military assets. While the latest announcement gave no timetable for deploying elements of the fourth MDTF to the region – or details on whether it has received systems such as the Typhon missile system – the Pacific-focused task forces share a clear strategic purpose. The aim is to challenge what Western military analysts describe as Beijing’s anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) approach – a strategy aimed at keeping enemy forces at bay and preventing foreign intervention. At the heart of this approach, analysts say, is a network combining Chinese long-range missiles, advanced radar, satellites, surveillance systems and military communications that could be used to detect and target opposing forces, potentially making outside intervention more difficult and costly for American and allied forces confronting the People’s Liberation Army (PLA). MDTFs are specifically tailored to counter this defensive shield. By integrating long-range precision weapons with intelligence, cyber, space and electronic warfare capabilities, these units aim to identify targets, disrupt enemy systems and launch strikes from dispersed positions on land. Major General Bernard J. Harrington, commander of Multi-Domain Command – Pacific, described how the US Army was developing this approach, saying in June that his command intended to use unmanned vessels, long-range attack drones and other capabilities to penetrate an adversary’s A2/AD network. “Every radar that emits, every node that transmits, every headquarters that commands, we aim to hold continuously at risk alongside our joint partners and allies,” he said. Chinese radars and satellites could detect approaching US warships and aircraft, allowing commanders to direct missile attacks against them. MDTFs would aim to disrupt this process by locating Chinese radars, command facilities and missile launchers, interfering with their communications through cyber and electronic warfare, and striking key targets with land-based missiles. If successful, such attacks could make it harder for Chinese forces to track and strike American and allied ships and aircraft, giving them greater freedom to operate in the region. The US missile launchers behind such attacks could themselves be difficult to find, requiring the PLA to “expend considerable effort to locate and track enemy forces”, said Timothy Heath, a China expert and head of defence consultancy Perceptum. He said mobile missile launchers could be concealed in vegetation or built-up areas, whereas warships were easier to detect at sea. Beijing would also have to remain alert to the possibility that “a hidden unit may launch a surprise attack”. Earlier formations have already tested some of the concept’s elements in the region. During the Valiant Shield exercises in Palau in June 2024, the Hawaii-based 3rd MDTF joined other US Army personnel in firing Precision Strike Missiles from an unmanned launcher at a moving maritime target. The 1st MDTF deployed the Typhon mid-range missile system to the Philippines in 2024. This year, the 3rd MDTF sent Typhon launchers and Himars rocket artillery to Japan’s Kanoya Air Base for exercises. Beijing has strongly opposed such deployments. In May, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun called Typhon a “strategic offensive weapon” and warned that deploying it to Japan would increase the risk of military confrontation and an arms race in the region. Japan could be especially important to the US Army’s plans. Its southwestern islands stretch towards Taiwan, potentially offering positions for mobile missiles and sensors, while the Philippines provides possible locations to the island’s south. Yet, unlike warships operating in international waters, land-based missile units depended on host-country permission and were constrained by their deployment locations, Heath said. He warned that their presence in Japan or the Philippines could lead PLA planners to consider strikes on allied territory, potentially widening a Taiwan conflict. Michael M. Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said Japan’s willingness to allow US missile operations would depend on the circumstances of a Taiwan conflict and Tokyo’s legal and political constraints. He said the “largest political hurdle” would be declaring one of Japan’s legally defined security situations – “something that has never been done before” – and that the allies should agree on operational requirements and exercise their plans beforehand. The US Army’s 2024 plan said some MDTF elements, including long-range strike units, could eventually be based permanently in allied countries, though no such arrangement has yet been announced for the newly activated task force. Those uncertainties matter because the formations are designed to act early in a crisis. Lieutenant Colonel Ben Blane and two fellow US Army officers warned in a March analysis for West Point’s Modern War Institute that MDTFs needed forward positions, intelligence networks, host-nation relationships and logistical support established before conflict erupted – arrangements that could not be rushed into place from the United States. For Beijing, the activation of another MDTF points to a growing American effort to threaten Chinese military assets from land as well as sea and air. But whether the new formation could influence a Taiwan conflict will depend on getting its capabilities into position. Without forces positioned to influence a Taiwan conflict from the outset, “the army risks becoming a spectator in the Indo-Pacific’s most consequential fight”, Blane and his co-authors warned.

title: Nord Stream trial: Russia used pipelines as ‘weapon’, defence says
description: Sergiy Kuznietsov is accused of leading a Ukrainian team of divers and an explosives expert to bomb the facility in 2022.
content: A lawyer for a Ukrainian accused of blowing up the Nord Stream pipelines supplying Russian gas to western Europe said on Wednesday that Moscow used the network to exert political and economic pressure, as the former military officer’s trial opened in Germany. Sergiy Kuznietsov is the first person to go on trial over the 2022 sabotage. The 50-year-old is accused of leading a Ukrainian team of divers and an explosives expert to bomb Nord Stream, seven months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. At the start of proceedings in Hamburg, prosecutor Stefan Schmidt said Kuznietsov, acting on behalf of the Ukrainian state, had committed a war crime by “using military means” to hit civilian targets. He is also charged with attacking civilian infrastructure and causing an explosion. Defence lawyer Nicola Canestrini told the court there was no clear evidence linking the former special forces officer to the sabotage. He also accused Russia of using the pipelines as a political and economic “weapon”. Russia had exerted immense pressure on Germany at the time, and gas markets went haywire before Moscow turned off the tap. “In September 2022, the pipelines were not supplying anyone with heat,” Canestrini said. “They were a means of exerting pressure in a war,” added the lawyer, who said Russia was guilty of committing war crimes, rather than his client. Three out of four pipelines were seriously damaged by the blasts under the Baltic Sea in September 2022. Before the sabotage rendered them inoperable, Russia had steadily reduced gas supplies through the pipelines to Europe in apparent retaliation for sanctions imposed over its invasion. While some in the West were quick to accuse Russia of sabotaging its own export route, German investigators identified a cell of Ukrainians they say were the alleged perpetrators. According to the indictment, Kuznietsov entered Germany in early September 2022 using a forged Ukrainian passport and, together with the rest of the sabotage team, boarded a rented yacht in the German Baltic Sea port city of Rostock. The yacht was allegedly loaded with large quantities of military-grade explosives and set sail for a spot where the pipelines ran under the Baltic Sea near the Danish island of Bornholm. Divers then allegedly planted explosive charges equipped with timers on the pipelines, which blew up several days later. Prosecutor Schmidt said the bombing aimed to ensure deliveries via the pipelines would be “permanently halted”, so Russia could no longer use revenues from gas sales to finance its war efforts. The defendant will not testify during the trial, with his lawyers saying confidentiality rules prevent former Ukrainian special forces personnel from speaking publicly about their activities. The pipelines were built and owned by a corporate consortium led by Russian energy giant Gazprom. At the time of the blasts, none were in operation. Moscow had already suspended gas deliveries to western Europe through Nord Stream 1, comprising two pipelines. Nord Stream 2, also made up of two pipelines, had only just been completed and never entered service. Kyiv has consistently denied orchestrating the sabotage, but has made no secret of its satisfaction with the results. Another suspect, partially identified as Volodymyr Z., was arrested in Croatia in August and is accused of taking part in the sabotage as a diver. A Croatian court has approved his extradition to Germany, although he is appealing against the decision. According to media reports, Volodymyr Z. was advising the makers of a Hollywood film inspired by the sabotage, with Oscar-winning actor Adrien Brody tapped to portray the leader of the sabotage unit. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Germany has become Kyiv’s leading military backer and regularly accuses Russia of sabotage and espionage on its soil. The investigation into the Nord Stream sabotage has proved awkward for diplomatic ties, but German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul noted on Wednesday that President Volodymyr Zelensky had said Ukraine was not responsible. “I am waiting for the outcome of these proceedings, and then the government will take a position,” he said. Ukraine’s supporters in Germany have also been unhappy with the trial however, and a small group protested outside the Hamburg trial on Wednesday. They held placards saying: “Russia is a terrorist” and “What are war crimes? A blown-up pipeline? Or the bombing of buildings and the killing of people?”

title: China’s Li Qiang vows more high-value imports as trade surplus faces scrutiny
description: Speaking at the Canton Fair’s 70th anniversary, the premier defended China’s role in global trade and invited foreign firms to invest in the country.
content: Premier Li Qiang said on Wednesday that China stands ready to import more high-quality goods, particularly high-value-added products, as part of efforts to promote more balanced trade. Li made the pledge at an opening ceremony for the autumn session of the biannual Canton Fair, China’s largest foreign trade exhibition. The nearly three-week-long event officially opens on Thursday, with more than 32,000 exhibitors and 210,000 overseas buyers registered in advance. “International trade is not merely figures on a ledger, but a voluntary choice to enhance well-being,” Li said during the keynote speech, according to a readout from state news agency Xinhua. “As both a ‘super seller’ and a ‘super buyer’, China delivers predominantly ‘neighbour-benefiting’ and ‘neighbour-enriching’ positive spillovers to all partners,” he added. His remarks came as the fair marks its 70th anniversary and China’s growing trade surplus faces heightened scrutiny from Western nations, whose officials have warned about the risk of deindustrialisation in pillar sectors. Li said market connectivity should not be treated as a “bargaining chip” in geopolitical contests, but as an effective way to generate economic growth. Beijing would continue to pursue high-quality development, expand high-level opening-up and inject greater momentum into the global economy through practical measures, he added. The premier also met about 70 business leaders from 30 countries and regions at a business round table held on the sidelines of the trade fair on Wednesday. He said ties between China and overseas companies were expanding beyond trade to include innovation, investment and supply-chain cooperation, creating new opportunities for businesses to benefit from the country’s development and strengthen global economic links. China would accelerate the development of a modern industrial system, including new power grids, computing networks and next-generation communications networks, Li said. He welcomed global companies to invest in China, expand their presence in the country and deepen practical cooperation across supply chains to create more open and resilient global supply chains. Exporters at the Canton Fair are expected to showcase emerging technologies including AI-guided medical capsules, service robotics and high-displacement motorcycles. The event is also using AI-powered maps to guide buyers to specific booths. Total outbound shipments from China rose 36.3 per cent year on year to US$447.18 billion in September, customs data showed on Wednesday. Imports grew by 31 per cent to US$313.65 billion. Export growth was supported by demand for hi-tech gear such as chips and electronic components amid a global boom in AI computing power and electricity infrastructure, according to the General Administration of Customs. Beijing and Washington recently agreed to US$30 billion in mutual tariff cuts on goods including appliances, toys and agricultural products. China’s exports to the United States also rose last month from a low base last year, growing 39.56 per cent. Chinese exporters are also facing tighter European rules on carbon tariffs and hybrid vehicles. While Chinese shipments to the European Union rose 25.25 per cent in September, the two sides reached a surprise deal on Friday that will impose strict quotas on Chinese hybrid car exports to Europe, among other measures.

title: Trump claims ‘massive’ resource exploration set to begin in Greenland
description: Recent Arctic pact grants the US no extraction rights in Danish territory, where harsh climate and geology have stymied past efforts.
content: US President Donald Trump said that “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in “our new and beautiful Greenland”, though it was not clear what developments he was referring to on an island where resource extraction has stymied companies for decades. Despite Trump’s optimism, the harsh climate of Greenland – a self-governing territory of Denmark, rather than a part of the United States – as well as a lack of infrastructure have foiled all previous attempts to extract so-called rare earth minerals, as well as oil and gas. No efforts have ever progressed beyond the exploratory stage, and a moratorium on new gas and oil permits has been in place for several years. “Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform following a campaign event Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska. Trump was stumping for Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan, who is seeking a third term to represent the state in an election against Democratic former congresswoman Mary Peltola. Rising energy prices – a direct result of the Iran war, which began on February 28 after the US and Israel launched joint strikes – are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for working class Americans before the midterm elections next month. Trump’s comments are likely aimed at addressing voters’ concerns before Election Day on November 3. Last month, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, following months of tensions with Nato allies over the US president’s repeated demands to take control of the semi-autonomous Danish territory. It doesn’t grant the US any special exploration rights, but does place some limits on investments by non-Nato countries in strategic sectors. The deal also paved the way for more US bases in Greenland and eased tensions over Trump’s repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States. The agreement would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence. Trump has expressed his desire to acquire Greenland since 2019 and, during his second term, issued threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a Nato ally. The Danish Foreign Ministry said in a statement that “the agreement does not grant investors from the US any preferential treatment compared with investors from other Nato countries, EU countries and Nato partners when it comes to access to natural resources in Greenland”. The Greenlandic prime minister’s office declined to comment on Trump’s statement. However, Jorgen Hammeken-Holm, Greenland’s deputy mining minister, acknowledged to CNN that there was activity by US companies. “We are very far away from ‘massive’ exploration,” Hammeken-Holm told the network, adding that while many smaller exploration projects are under way, it could take “years” before they become operational. Naaja H. Nathanielsen, who represents Greenland in Denmark’s parliament, told Associated Press on Wednesday that she wasn’t very surprised – or concerned – following Trump’s post. “This is just the way the president decides to engage,” she said. “I think we have all come to expect something like that.” Greenland has large deposits of the rare earth minerals that are needed to make everything from computers and smartphones to the batteries, solar and wind technologies that will power the transition away from fossil fuels. China currently dominates the world’s supply of these critical minerals and the Trump administration is seeking to break Beijing’s chokehold on them. The US Geological Survey has also identified major potential offshore deposits of oil and natural gas. But tapping these resources could be prohibitively difficult: the rare earth minerals are encased in rock, and the offshore oil and natural gas deposits are covered by Arctic ice. And in 2021, Greenlandic lawmakers said the island would not issue any new oil and gas permits because of the environmental impacts of oil extraction, and a desire to avoid further worsening of the global climate crisis. Trump’s Truth Social post also touted Greenland’s strategic location, saying that “from a Security Purpose in the Defense and Offense of both the United States of America, and Europe”, the island is “second to none”. “Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived,” he wrote. “It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!” The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the US military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defence and space surveillance operations for the US and Nato Trump said last month that the US would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” including “building two very major military bases”. Additional reporting by Reuters and dpa

title: In US-China rivalry, middle powers urged to be ‘indispensable’ chokepoints
description: By embedding deeply into supply chains, smaller countries that fear being squeezed out of global decision-making can offer a ‘best’ dish.
content: Middle powers should become “indispensable” chokepoints to safeguard strategic autonomy and survive the power rivalry between the US and China, former leaders and top diplomats said at a forum in India on Wednesday. The assessment comes as smaller and middle-tier countries seek to protect themselves from mounting geopolitical uncertainties arising from the tariff war launched by US President Donald Trump. The trade conflict has hit America’s allies and foes alike and grown complicated amid volatility in the global energy market brought on by the US-Israel war on Iran, now in its eighth month with no sign of ending soon. Changing dynamics between Beijing and Washington have also loomed since Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met last month in Washington, raising concerns among countries in between that they risk being squeezed out of global decision-making. “Whilst these middle powers can’t operate at the scale of the big ones, what they can do is make themselves indispensable,” former British prime minister Rishi Sunak said at a panel discussion at the annual Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Wednesday. Sunak, who stepped down in 2024 after 20 months in office, also cited the examples of non-superpower countries that have embedded themselves deeply into global supply chains to achieve strategic leverage. Dutch company ASML is the world’s sole producer of EUV photolithography machines, for example, while Germany produces ultra-precise, atomically smooth optical components, both essential to manufacturing the world’s most advanced computer chips to enable AI development. Meanwhile, South Korea leads global memory chip manufacturing, and Japan controls the supply of the high-purity chemicals used in silicon wafer fabrication. “You don’t have to provide the whole buffet,” Sunak said. “You just need the one dish that is the best.” Supporting the idea of building “strategic stocks” in energy, AI and critical minerals, Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand argued that countries should use their advantages constructively. Anand said the question being put to middle powers was whether “we want to be passive observers, or are we going to shape the international order?” Canada is locked in a bitter trade war with the US following Trump’s threats to impose 50 per cent tariffs on about US$20 billion worth of imports from its northern neighbour. In a highly publicised address to the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called on middle powers to band together to protect themselves from a decline in global order. Anand, who is on a two-day visit to India, said Ottawa sought to double its non-US trade over the next decade through bilateral and multilateral trade agreements. “It’s for us, for Canada. It’s not just about working with middle powers,” she added. “It’s also about furthering our domestic economic resilience. It’s also about diversifying trade relationships, and so working with middle powers is part of a broader foreign policy package.” Addressing the forum, Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar described current shifts as an expansion of global leadership. “What we are now moving towards is a different kind of order,” India’s top diplomat said. “The shareholding is changing. The board of directors is expanding.” “In our case, we were not members of an alliance, so we’ve always sort of learned to be in the rain without an umbrella,” Jaishankar added, noting India’s long-standing foreign policy of non-alignment. India should not be called a “middle power”, he continued, saying such labelling would be “limiting itself” and that, in fact, India was the “power in the middle”. Touching on the Xi-Trump summit in Washington in September, former Australian prime minister Kevin Rudd downplayed fears that the event signalled a new era of superpower co-management. Rudd, a former Australian ambassador to the US, called the likelihood of a functional “G2” agreement between China and the US “close to zero”, citing the countries’ deep-seated strategic rivalry. Still, diplomats cautioned that middle powers needed to prioritise building domestic resilience, making it a long-term imperative driven by broader structural shifts in global geopolitics rather than the actions of individual figures like Trump. “If you look at US foreign policy pre-Trump 2.0, you will notice that under [former US president Joe] Biden as well, there was increased protectionism,” Anand said.

title: Philippine law targeting foreign agents spurs fears of free speech curbs
description: Officials calling for the law worry foreign agents could support pro-China candidates in the 2028 Philippine presidential election.
content: Philippine officials want a new anti-foreign interference law ahead of the 2028 presidential election, as a raid on a suspected online scam centre near the country’s military headquarters and reports of Chinese-linked money transfers to a company tied to Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio’s family fuel national security concerns. On Monday, immigration and military operatives arrested 76 foreigners at a facility in Quezon City suspected of being linked to Philippine offshore gaming operators (Pogos), whose online gambling businesses flourished when former president Rodrigo Duterte was in power. Authorities have long suspected that Pogos were covertly used for illicit activities, including espionage. The group comprised 74 Chinese nationals and two from Myanmar. The facility in Barangay Socorro was located down the street from Camp Aguinaldo, the sprawling complex housing the Armed Forces of the Philippines’ headquarters and the Department of National Defence. On the suspected activities at the facility, retired rear-admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, a military spokesman for West Philippine Sea-related matters, told reporters: “The appropriate government agencies must look into this. This will have very serious national security implications.” Trinidad said the military’s recent shift towards external defence had brought new security challenges, including attempts to influence public opinion through information campaigns. Philippine officials have warned about possible foreign interference in the run-up to the 2028 election, including fears that outside actors could seek to boost candidates seen as friendly towards China. Such concerns have taken on added significance following reports that Cale88 Foods, co-founded by Duterte-Carpio’s husband, Manases Carpio, received money from Chinese mainland and Hong Kong corporations, which prompted a security investigation. Beijing has denied it is seeking to interfere in Philippine elections.
