In April 2025, the Chinese embassy in Manila said China had “no interest in interfering in elections in the Philippines”, accusing some Philippine politicians of using such allegations against Beijing for political gain. Retired Supreme Court associate justice Antonio Carpio has urged Congress to speed up passage of the proposed Foreign Influence and Interference Act, an enhancement of the current Foreign Agents Act, which requires foreign agents to register and disclose their foreign source, compensation and activities. A working group will consolidate eight new measures into one bill to be presented in the House of Representatives. The proposed legislation would extend to online influence operations, including so-called troll farms and foreign or local agents acting on behalf of foreign persons or entities to manipulate public opinion for political ends. Offenders could face prison terms and fines of up to 20 million pesos (US$318,000) for activities including helping political candidates through financial contributions. Trinidad said malignant foreign actors were involved in actions and messages designed to distort public perception. “The objective is not even for us to believe them. The objective is for us not to believe anybody,” he said, warning that they were aiming to undermine trust in government and its institutions. At a media briefing in September, Trinidad said foreign influence tactics had shifted towards focusing on domestic issues, including the impeachment proceedings against Duterte-Carpio and the flood-control scandals. He said the use of Filipino-language content made such activity “more difficult to detect”. Weaponised against legitimate dissent? Local government secretary Jonvic Remulla cited Philippine intelligence reports on a talk show last month that indicated an unnamed superpower had “under its payroll more than 40,000 bloggers and influencers and commentators to spread fake news about the Philippines”. He did not identify the country nor provide details to substantiate the figure. Meanwhile, the National Security Council has said it would investigate the reported 319 million pesos in transfers from Chinese and Hong Kong corporations to Cale88 Foods, where Manases Carpio was president and chairman of the board when the remittances occurred. Anti-Money-Laundering Council director Ronel Buenaventura last week testified during the vice-president’s impeachment proceedings that the transfers were flagged because they appeared to have no justifiable purpose. Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr has called for a “thorough investigation into the matter … due to serious implications to our national security”. President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr said on October 7 that he found the matter “most disturbing” and that, if proven true, it would represent “a threat at the highest level to the Republic”. In response, Duterte-Carpio said on Monday: “Are we forbidden from doing business with China? Because it is a national security risk?” She also accused the Marcos administration of “becoming the troublemaker of Southeast Asia”. On October 6, the Chinese embassy in Manila condemned what it called a “false narrative alleging that China had funnelled funds to a particular political faction in the Philippines”, describing the allegation as “malicious”, saying it would take measures to protect China’s “legitimate interests and dignity”. Critics warn that legislation intended to counter foreign interference could also threaten to curb legitimate political expression. Carlos Nazareno, a digital rights advocate at Democracy.Net.PH, said the proposed law could affect foreign organisations such as the Konrad Adenauer Stiftung and Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which fund local initiatives on democracy and disinformation-fighting. Dominic Ligot, founder of advocacy group Data and AI Ethics PH, said the threat from China was real but warned that combining the proposed law with anti-disinformation bills could create “a slippery slope because these laws can be weaponised against legitimate dissent”. Enrico Gloria, an assistant professor of political science at the University of the Philippines, said the bill should clarify the boundaries of acceptable activities for people connected to foreign countries, while offering protection against unfounded accusations. Referring to his contributions to commentaries and analysis on the South China Sea issue, the recent graduate of a doctorate degree in social science from Tsinghua University said that “I would be worried about what I say or what I write … because of the stigma.”

title: What does the historic Bank of America fine mean for US-China capital streams?
description: Analysts say penalties signal tighter scrutiny over cross-border financial flows.
content: As the US Treasury imposed historic fines on Bank of America over compliance failures involving Chinese money-laundering networks, analysts see the action as a signal that could prompt Western banks to tighten scrutiny of Chinese clients and cross-border transactions. The penalties, announced on Tuesday and totalling more than US$1.21 billion, included what the US Treasury described as its third-largest penalty on record and the largest in the history of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. Bank of America had failed to report more than US$5 billion in suspicious transactions in a timely manner, including more than US$1 billion involving national security-related and other priority risks such as “suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese money-laundering networks, fraud and potential trade-based money-laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border”, according to a Treasury statement. The bank had also processed millions of dollars in payments “in apparent violation of sanctions programmes”, including those targeting Russia, Iran and narcotics and global terrorism networks, the Treasury added. Rui Meng, a finance professor at the China Europe International Business School, said that the fines “sent a signal to the market”. “US scrutiny of cross-border financial flows involving China will continue to intensify, and US banks are likely to raise compliance requirements for China-related transactions,” he said. “But this will not lead to a complete shutdown of US-China financial channels.” Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at French investment bank Natixis, said US – and even European – banks would need to tighten scrutiny of Chinese clients’ activities, particularly those involving “grey activities” or sanctions. “For the Chinese side, they will have to be extra careful, because there can be reverberations,” she said. “It’s a warning note that there is no such thing as strategic stability ... between China and the US. This is another sign out of the many we have already seen.” Following the US Treasury announcement, Bank of America’s shares fell by more than 2 per cent in after-hours trading on Tuesday. In a written statement to the South China Morning Post, a spokesperson for the bank said it had worked with regulators to resolve issues related to the penalties and was committed to addressing the issues identified by regulators. “Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” the spokesperson said. “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators.” Separately, Bank of America dropped out of the running for a role in Moonshot AI’s Hong Kong initial public offering, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter. The penalties against Bank of America came as Washington is stepping up efforts to disrupt illicit finance and sanctions evasion, including targeting networks that help countries, such as Iran, circumvent US restrictions. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the Tuesday announcement that financial institutions are “on the front lines of protecting our economic and national security”. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” he said. However, Xu Tianchen, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said the action was part of a broader US effort to address financial sector compliance failures, rather than being explicitly directed at China. “I don’t think it explicitly targets China, but rather targets specific activities involving Chinese entities,” he said.

title: AI risks could repeat China shock that cost jobs, former US commerce chief Raimondo warns
description: US warned to prepare for economic and labour market disruption from AI, similar to when Chinese import surge led to manufacturing job losses.
content: The rapid and unbridled development of artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to disrupt the US economy in a way that is comparable to the “China shock” that displaced American workers, former US commerce secretary Gina Raimondo warns. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Tuesday, she drew parallels between AI’s potential disruption to American jobs and the past impact of Chinese manufacturing competition on the US labour market. “In America, we’ve seen what happens when we move through an economic transition without planning it … [the] so-called China shock left millions of Americans out of work and it destabilised our country,” Raimondo said. The former commerce secretary, who served under former US president Joe Biden, made the point when suggesting that one of the challenges brought by AI advancement was to “prepare our people” for a technology that could put them out of work. The term China shock refers to the economic and labour market disruption in the US caused by a massive surge of cheap Chinese imports that led to manufacturing job losses across US factories. Raimondo blamed that for being the root of the divisive politics that “was still destabilising our country and the fuel firing populism on the left and on the right”, highlighting her concerns over the potential upheaval unfettered AI could bring to the US. Her warning came as discussions of the emerging technology took centre stage on Tuesday, the first day of the 2026 edition of the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, a three-day event held in the Indian capital. While Raimondo emphasised the risks associated with AI, other speakers argued that AI could prove a force in reshaping the global economy. Jonathan Gray, president and chief operating officer of US investment giant Blackstone, said technological advances would fundamentally transform how consumers, businesses and governments operate. Gray compared the emerging AI revolution to the industrial transformation of the US in the late 19th century, arguing that the spread of increasingly capable AI would have far-reaching consequences for economies and societies. “We’re moving from a place like we did in the US … with the industrial revolution that when you bring this super intelligence to the entire world it’s going to profoundly change how we live, how consumers live, how businesses are [being] impacted and how governments oversee societies,” Gray said. The scale of investment required to develop AI was another recurring theme at the forum, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into data centres, computing infrastructure and electricity generation to support increasingly sophisticated AI models and growing AI adoption. Blackstone’s Gray said the firm had a positive view on electricity as everything involved -including technology, data centres, autonomous vehicles and robots – used electricity. “So AI is gonna move from the desktop to the physical world that’ll demand more electricity. Obviously, the digital infrastructure is hugely important,” he said. US Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller warned in a separate forum discussion that the investment boom was already contributing to inflationary pressures. As hyperscalers race to build out bigger and more data centres to power AI models, they were bidding up the prices of semiconductors of all types with a spillover effect to impact anyone else using the same products. “That’s what we’re starting to see in the US. We’re starting to see AI [inducing] inflation because it’s just increasing demand in other areas,” Waller said. He also cautioned that AI’s economic benefits would take time to materialise, as companies were still figuring out how to use the technology to boost productivity. “There’s a lot of trial and error and a lot of experimentation,” Waller said.

title: Huang Qifan, China’s political tumbler, falls after a decade of close corruption calls
description: Until this week, Huang had appeared to weather scandals that had ripped through Chongqing over the years.
content: For a decade, former Chongqing mayor Huang Qifan stood out as a political survivor while colleague after close colleague fell in China’s far-reaching anti-corruption campaign. Throughout that time, including his seven years as the megacity’s mayor from 2009 to 2016, Huang was seen as a “tumbler” in Chinese politics – a weighted doll that wobbles but never falls over. The nickname was well-deserved – he served under six municipal Communist Party secretaries, watching two of them – Bo Xilai and Sun Zhengcai – jailed for corruption. Bo and Sun were both members of the Politburo, the pinnacle of the party’s power, and their downfalls were two of the biggest political earthquakes the country has seen in recent decades. Yet Huang survived. Huang, 74, was also very visible after he left public service in 2018. Rather than retreat to retired obscurity, Huang kept up a busy schedule of interviews and conferences across the country, firing hot takes on China’s economic issues. So when news of the corruption investigation into Huang finally came on Tuesday, it was a surprise to many – not only because it involved one of China’s most celebrated economic technocrats, but also because it came so long after the political tremors around him appeared to have stopped. “Subjecting someone like Huang, who had emerged from many previous rounds, to a formal corruption investigation, before the fifth plenum sends a very serious message to the whole party: corrupt officials should not harbour any illusions of escaping detection,” said a Beijing-based political scientist, who declined to be named due to sensitivity of the matter. “There is no political ‘tumbler’ and no safe landing for corrupt officials in the anti-corruption fight.” The fifth plenum is a party meeting scheduled for October 26-29 in Beijing at which the organisation’s inner circle will discuss and adopt a landmark document to “deepening party self-governance”. The event is expected to focus on tackling systemic corruption, tightening internal political oversight, and eliminating organisational loopholes across the bureaucracy and state sectors. While many anti-corruption investigations into retired senior officials go unnoticed and unannounced, Huang’s unusually heavy speaking schedule made his downfall difficult to hide from the public. The South China Morning Post understands that Huang was originally scheduled to deliver a keynote speech in Beijing on October 25 and another in Hangzhou the next day. Before Tuesday’s announcement, word got out that he would miss the Hangzhou event. An employee at AIA Group – the organiser of the October 25 speech in Beijing – said they had not been able to reach Huang or his secretary since Monday. Huang’s reputation as a tumbler goes back to his relationship with Bo, the charismatic and swashbuckling Politburo member who ran Chongqing from 2007 to 2012. As Bo rolled out his ideologically charged “singing red songs and smashing the dark forces” campaign, Huang was the administrative and economic brain behind the policies that became known as the “Chongqing model”. The model combines state-led capitalism, aggressive public-welfare provision, and foreign direct investment with a populist revival of revolutionary Maoist culture and a heavy-handed public security crackdown. Positioned as an alternative developmental path to China’s coastal, market-driven consensus, the model gained national and international attention as a potential blueprint for addressing rising wealth inequality, regional imbalances and social stratification. The two men projected an image of an unshakeable governing duo. During the national parliamentary “two sessions” in Beijing in March 2010, Huang famously described his working relationship with Bo as “like a duck to water”. He was also a magnet for reporters at the annual meetings, readily answering questions about the economy and Chongqing. That alliance faced a critical test in February 2012, when Bo’s estranged police chief, Wang Lijun, fled to the US consulate in Chengdu, triggering one of China’s biggest political scandals in decades. Following the diplomatic stand-off, Bo was removed from the party’s leadership. He was later sentenced to life in prison on charges of bribery, embezzlement and abuse of power. The aftershocks hit many of Bo’s subordinates in Chongqing, as the municipality’s new leadership headed by caretaker party chief Zhang Dejiang, repeatedly pledged to “eradicate” Bo’s “toxic influence”. Despite the chaos, Huang remained in position. In November 2012, Sun took over from Zhang, becoming Huang’s new partner and direct supervisor. Like Bo before his fall, Sun was also seen as a political rising star. He relied on Huang to maintain the city’s administrative machinery and drive double-digit economic growth. Huang, it seemed, had weathered the Bo saga unaffected, and was among six regional officials to be part of President Xi Jinping’s delegation to the United States in 2015. The political ground shook beneath Chongqing again in 2017, just months after Huang stepped down as the city’s mayor. Sun was rounded up in anti-corruption investigation during a trip to Beijing for a top-level meeting, and ultimately sentenced to life imprisonment on corruption charges. The southwestern metropolis again pledged to clean up the negative influence of a disgraced party boss and again Huang appeared to sail through the controversy. Huang stayed on in his semi-retired role in the national legislature as vice-chairman of the National People’s Congress Financial and Economic Affairs Committee, finally stepping down in March 2018. Even after his retirement, Huang, respected as a capable economic manager, remained an influential intellectual heavyweight. Affiliated with prestigious platforms including the China Centre for International Economic Exchanges, the China Finance 40 Forum and Fudan University, he had a towering media profile, offering perspectives on a wide range of economic issues. In 2021, he warned that the business models of Chinese internet firms would no longer work in the coming decade, slamming them as “taking advantage of weaknesses in human nature to entice purchases”. In 2022, Huang warned that China’s property market had reached a turning point, questioning whether the country could sustain its decades-long construction boom. As recently as May this year, he described China’s record US$1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025 as “shocking”, urging Beijing to rebalance trade through a combination of gradual yuan appreciation, tariff cuts and improved benefits for workers. He is known among various lecture organisers as exceptionally proactive and eager to take the podium, and is said to have told organisers that he is willing to talk on any issue. He is also believed to be in good health for his age, with a fondness for steak and cigars. His confidence was built on decades of economic policy experience. Born in Zhuji in Zhejiang province in 1952, Huang rose through Shanghai’s industrial bureaucracy. Entering the municipal party and government apparatus in 1983, he was deeply involved in the early development and opening of the Pudong New Area. In October 2001, he was transferred to Chongqing as a vice-mayor, overseeing the city’s industrial policy, state-owned assets, taxation and financial sectors before becoming mayor in January 2010 – a post he held for nearly seven years. Under his stewardship, Chongqing logged consecutive years of double-digit GDP growth, routinely outpacing the rest of the country. Huang promoted the Chongqing-Xinjiang-Europe freight railway, and attracted Hewlett-Packard and Foxconn to build an electronics manufacturing hub in the city. He also pioneered the municipal investment vehicle modelled on Singapore’s state fund Temasek and kept runaway property speculation in check through strict land-supply management and an expansive public rental housing programme. Huang’s downfall follows a smaller earthquake in Chongqing. Since 2022, the anti-corruption drive has sped up, targeting more and more senior officials across the country. Chongqing was hit hard, with seven other high-ranking provincial officials coming under investigation since then. The most senior of the seven was then-mayor Hu Henghua, who came under the microscope in March, triggering another shake-up across the administration. The investigation into Huang comes less than two weeks before the party’s fifth plenum, which brings together the hundreds of full and alternate members of the Central Committee. The Central Committee’s ranks have been thinned by the anti-corruption campaign, with 34 of its 205 full members under investigation or stripped of their status as deputies to the National People’s Congress. The Beijing-based political scientist said Chongqing had been the epicentre of China’s most disruptive political tremors over the past two decades and the investigation of Huang nearly a decade after retirement showed Beijing’s resolve to clean up Chongqing’s factional legacy, allowing no perceived seniority to impede its continued organisational housecleaning. Not all are that surprised by Huang’s fall. His family’s commercial dealings cast a persistent shadow over his administration. In Chongqing, the extensive business footprint of his son was “an open secret” among political and business circles, according to sources familiar with the situation. “Many in Chongqing’s government and financial circles know his son very well, as Huang Qifan is widely regarded as the ‘godfather’ of Chongqing’s state-driven financial vehicles, which can mobilise a lot of resources,” said a source who worked with Huang. The source said the younger Huang quickly immersed himself in China’s capital market deals.

title: Culprits found, say sorry after sparking flashpoint during WTT China Smash final
description: Japan’s eventual winner Sora Matsushima exonerated after being criticised for abruptly interrupting play to complain about a camera flash.
content: A table tennis team from Chinese Taipei have issued a formal apology on Wednesday after video footage confirmed two of their junior players accidentally triggered a camera flash that disrupted the men’s singles final at the WTT China Smash in Beijing. The incident had initially drawn heavy scrutiny on Japan’s newly crowned world No 1 Sora Matsushima, who was penalised with a yellow card for abruptly interrupting play to complain about the flash and subsequently accused by fans of using gamesmanship to secure victory over Chinese Taipei’s Lin Yun-ju. Although the tournament concluded on Sunday, the controversy surrounding the flash incident at a crucial juncture of the final continued to reverberate through the week. With Lin trailing 9-10 in the deciding game, Matsushima abruptly shouted out and pointed towards the stands to signal a camera flash just as his opponent tossed the ball to serve. Penalised with a yellow card for halting play without permission, Matsushima regrouped on the re-serve to seal an 11-9 victory and deny Lin the title. The sequence sparked fierce online debate, with critics arguing Matsushima deliberately stalled to disrupt Lin’s rhythm and should have been docked a point. The narrative shifted on Tuesday when Matsushima’s mother reposted a fan video confirming that a camera flash had indeed illuminated the stands three times. “Sora’s fans helped me find it! It’s wonderful to find the proof, Sora didn’t lie!!” Matsushima’s mother, Yumi Matsushima, said. “I hope a solution can be found so that players are no longer distracted by such things and can compete in peace!!” Footage clearly showed a flash appearing behind Lin after the score reached 10-7 to the Japanese in the final game. A second flash occurred as Lin served, triggering Matsushima’s complaint amid audible confusion across the stands. A third flash appeared at 10-9. According to media in Chinese Taipei, the flashes were caused by two junior players who were in Beijing to compete in the youth tournament. Their club, the Songshan-Chengzheng team, explained that the players were merely attempting to record match footage on their phones and accidentally activated the flash, and had no intention of disrupting play. 輝空のファンが探してくれた！ 証拠が見つかって良かった😌 輝空は嘘ついてない‼️ 選手がこんな事に気を取られる事なく試合ができるよう、この問題をなんとか解決してほしいです‼️ — 松島由美 (@soratoamikuaira) October 13, 2026 On Wednesday, the Songshan-Chengzheng table tennis team released a formal statement offering an unreserved apology. “Regarding the disruption and impact caused by the use of a camera flash during the 2026 Beijing Smash men’s singles final, our team extends our most sincere apologies,” the statement read. “We are deeply sorry to the athletes, coaches and on-site personnel who were affected.” Emphasising their long-standing focus on student character and sportsmanship, the team said they would guide students to understand that beyond their own performance, they had to respect competition rules and safeguard the rights of every competitor. “Facing this incident, our team will uphold an educational and guiding role, directing students to face the issue, reflect deeply and learn to take responsibility for their behaviour,” the statement said, pledging to reinforce these concepts in daily life and future events to prevent any recurrence. The team concluded: “Our team will take this as a lesson to continuously implement character education and sports ethics, hoping that all participants can jointly maintain a healthy competitive atmosphere in an environment of mutual respect, fairness and justice.”

title: Hesai launches 3D spatial camera as Chinese lidar maker expands into physical AI
description: The launch marks the latest step in the firm’s push to broaden its business beyond vehicles and establish a foothold in the emerging physical AI industry.
content: Hesai Group, the world’s largest maker of lidar sensors for vehicles, has launched a 3D spatial camera as it expands into physical artificial intelligence in search of new growth opportunities. The handheld device, called Kosmo, is described by Hesai as a “physical AI eye” and converts real-world environments into detailed, editable 3D models. The company said it was designed to standardise the digitisation of complex spaces such as campuses and factories. “Our interesting new products, which represent an extension of our innovative capabilities, will lead to some new business patterns,” David Li Yifan, CEO of Hesai, told reporters in a media briefing on Wednesday. “Hesai has some other product series in the pipeline that can contribute to the development of the infrastructure for the entire physical AI industry.” Kosmo is supported by an intelligent platform that integrates AI algorithms, digital 3D models and cloud services. The company said the device could help filmmakers, video game developers and cultural service providers convert physical environments into production-ready 3D content more quickly. Li said Hesai envisioned building a Kosmo platform to help train robots as embodied AI develops. The company has partnered with Pixar Animation Studios’ Renderman software unit to develop Kosmo-related technologies. The CEO said Hesai aimed to evolve into a broader technology company as the AI industry grows, adding that its technologies and products could eventually be supplied to businesses such as humanoid robot makers. In August, Andrew Fan, chief financial officer of the Shanghai-based firm, told the South China Morning Post that the company was more than an automotive supplier, pointing to its push into AI-related products. In April, Hesai unveiled its “6D” full-colour platform, saying it would enable lidar sensors to measure distances and identify small objects with industry-leading performance. It describes the technology as 6D because of the sensors’ ability to detect the X, Y and Z coordinates of an object, plus its reflectivity, velocity and colour. The lidar sensors are powered by Hesai’s self-developed Picasso chip and have not yet been delivered to customers. Hesai’s push into AI comes as Beijing seeks to make China a global leader in robotics, backed by a strong supply chain for the industry. China is already the world’s largest market for industrial robots and a leading developer of humanoids. In 2024, it accounted for 54 per cent of the world’s industrial robot installations, ­according to data released by the International Federation of Robotics in September 2025. Hesai’s lidar sensors help intelligent vehicles map their surroundings. The company supplies products to China’s 10 largest automotive groups. The company reported net income of 70.6 million yuan (US$10.4 million) for the three months ended June, up 60 per cent from a year earlier. Revenue grew 21 per cent to 860.8 million yuan, it said.

title: Beijing warns Taiwanese not to be ‘two-faced’ after Kevin Tsai attends DPP rally
description: The TV host has drawn ire after attending an event for a Taipei mayoral candidate whom Beijing calls a ‘diehard separatist’.
content: Beijing has warned Taiwanese people against acting “two-faced” on the issue of “Taiwan independence” after television host Kevin Tsai Kang-yong attended a campaign rally for a Taipei mayoral candidate labelled a separatist by Beijing. The episode underscores the political risks facing Taiwanese entertainers working on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. “No individual or force may act as a ‘two-faced person’ – reaping the benefits of the mainland’s development while simultaneously colluding with ‘Taiwan independence’ separatist forces,” Chen Binhua, spokesman for the mainland’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO), said on Wednesday. “We have always respected and protected the legitimate rights of Taiwan compatriots to freedom of speech and expression, but there is no room for ambiguity on questions of fundamental principle.” Chen was responding to Tsai’s appearance at the opening rally for Puma Shen Pao-yang’s campaign headquarters on October 4. Shen, a lawmaker from Taiwan’s independence-leaning Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), is running in Taipei’s November mayoral election. Tsai, a well-known television host and writer, has built a following on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. He came to prominence co-hosting the Taiwanese talk show Kangsi Coming, which attracted mainland Chinese audiences, before appearing on the mainland-produced debate programme I Can I BB from 2014 to 2021. His books on communication have also attracted mainland readers. Tsai said he attended the rally to hear different views, according to Taiwanese broadcaster TVBS. He also said it would be “great” if he could interview both main candidates, referring to Shen and incumbent Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an of the Kuomintang, who is seeking re-election. Tsai’s agent said his attendance at the rally was not an endorsement of Shen, TVBS reported. On Wednesday, Chen said “the actions of ‘Taiwan independence’ diehard Shen Pao-yang are well known to all”. Shen was added to Beijing’s list of “diehard Taiwan independence separatists” in October 2024. The TAO accused him of propagating “separatist fallacies” through his role in founding Kuma Academy, a civil defence organisation. In October 2025, mainland police announced an investigation into Shen on suspicion of secession-related crimes, accusing him of establishing Kuma Academy as a separatist organisation. On Wednesday, the TAO also announced sanctions against VWAY, a company linked to Shen’s father, prohibiting it from doing business with mainland Chinese entities. Chen said Shen’s father had used VWAY to evade June 2025 sanctions placed on Sicuens International Co Ltd, which he headed. “The mainland will never allow companies linked to ‘Taiwan independence’ hardliners to profit from the mainland,” Chen said. Tsai’s appearance at Shen’s rally sparked criticism on mainland Chinese social media, with some users questioning his motives. Many comments expressed disappointment over his attendance at the rally and his posts on the platform were flooded with comments saying Taiwan is part of China. Leapmotor, a Hangzhou-headquartered electric vehicle maker that had previously featured Tsai in its promotional content, said on October 4 that it had taken down all content involving him. It also pledged to strengthen its vetting of business partners’ backgrounds and positions. Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council chief Chiu Chui-cheng said on October 6 that participation in Taiwan’s “free and democratic way of life” and its “fair and open elections” did not require Beijing’s consent. He urged Beijing to respect Taiwan’s democratic system and refrain from interfering in its elections. This is not the first time that a Taiwanese celebrity has fallen foul of cross-strait sensitivities. In August 2025, the MAC said some Taiwanese entertainers had reposted mainland state media content that it said undermined the sovereignty of the Republic of China, the island’s official name. The council said such conduct crossed a red line and could amount to violations of relevant laws. On Wednesday, Chen praised Taiwanese entertainer Nicky Wu Qilong, who recently shared a video online of himself waving a Chinese flag on Tiananmen Square. Chen said it was “only natural for Taiwan compatriots to express their patriotic feelings spontaneously”. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Exhibition of pioneering Hong Kong school for national talent in early 1940s opens
description: Showcase of Ta Teh Institute and its legacy will be presented at Hong Kong Museum of History from Wednesday to February 15 next year.
content: A new exhibition about a pioneering school that nurtured talent for the country has opened at a Hong Kong history museum as part of the government’s efforts to promote national education, with many exhibits shown in the city for the first time. “National Development and Achievements Series: Cultivation and Renewal – The Education Legacy of Hong Kong’s Ta Teh Institute”, a free exhibition presented by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, will run at the Hong Kong Museum of History in Tsim Sha Tsui from Wednesday to February 15 next year. Ta Teh Institute was a liberal arts university established in Tuen Mun in 1946 during the Chinese Civil War. It was the second university to be established in the city after the University of Hong Kong. The institute closed down in 1949. It was founded by the leadership of the Guangdong District Committee of the Communist Party of China, a historical party organisation active between 1945 and 1948, through cooperation between the Communist Party and patriotic democrats in Hong Kong. Communist Party leaders at the time, including Zhou Enlai, called for the school’s founding to resettle important people fleeing south during the war, as well as to cultivate young talent for the country. The institute brought together many renowned academics and cultural figures at that time, including historian Jian Bozan, literary figures Guo Moruo and Mao Dun, and politician Qiao Guanhua, who later served as China’s Foreign Minister from 1974 to 1976. Despite being banned by the colonial government in February 1949 after less than three years in operation, the school groomed over 800 promising young people, many of whom later took up posts in finance and politics across the country and played leading roles in national development. To mark the 80th anniversary of the establishment of Ta Teh Institute, the exhibition features more than 60 sets of artefacts related to the institute and its alumni, as well as around 125 historical photographs and supplementary exhibits, of which half are being displayed in Hong Kong for the first time. Selected exhibits include minutes of meetings of the institute’s affairs committee, student cards and lecture outlines delivered by renowned professors. The exhibition also recreates the arch, school buildings, a dormitory and a classroom, allowing visitors to experience campus life at the time. Connie Cheung, the museum’s curator of exhibition and research, said Hong Kong’s role stood out clearly in the institute’s history. “Hong Kong is a place for gathering outstanding cultural scholars and young people who want to learn,” she said. “This nurturing and cultivation of talents is the main core of our exhibition. Hong Kong has the soil of culture and nurturing talents for the development of our country.” Cheung added that although not many Hongkongers knew about Ta Teh, its place in the city’s history was significant. “We would like to let visitors and Hong Kong people know more about this institute, which ran for only two and a half years, but its influence is very great and lasts until today.” Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said in his policy address in September that the government would establish a National Development and Achievements Museum in Kwu Tung North, showcasing the country’s achievements in science, technology, culture and sports.

title: China approves Alibaba AI models for use in iPhone Duo and other Apple handsets
description: Apple confirms it will finally launch Apple Intelligence in China in October after years of regulatory delays.
content: China has granted approval for Alibaba Group Holding’s artificial intelligence models to be integrated into several Apple handsets, including the new iPhone Duo, in the Chinese market, clearing a key regulatory hurdle for the long-delayed launch of Apple Intelligence in the country. Updated network access permits for the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and several earlier Apple models from China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology now include three approved AI systems: Apple Intelligence alongside Alibaba’s Tongyi Qianwen and Tongyi Wanxiang. Tongyi Qianwen, also known as Qwen, is a family of large language models developed by Alibaba Cloud, while Tongyi Wanxiang specialises in AI text-to-image and video generation. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Tim Cook, executive chairman of Apple, said during a visit to Shanghai on Thursday that the company would release a beta version of Apple Intelligence for the mainland market in late October, but the firm’s revamped Siri AI would not be included in the update, according to a report by Chinese media outlet Jiemian. Apple said in a statement on Thursday that the firm was “excited to have received approval for bringing the original, core set of Apple Intelligence features like live translation, Clean Up in photos and writing tools to our users in China, and we look forward to making them available in an upcoming beta later this month”. The regulatory filing provides more clarity on the capabilities of the iPhone Duo – Apple’s first foldable smartphone – ahead of its scheduled release next week in China, where local regulations require stringent security evaluations and algorithm filings before any public AI deployment. Apple has yet to roll out Apple Intelligence on the Chinese mainland, despite receiving regulatory clearance from Beijing in July. The service has already been deployed across other major markets, launching in the United States in 2024 and Europe last year. Core Apple Intelligence features, such as writing and image editing tools, are available in Hong Kong. In July, the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) confirmed the licence for Apple Intelligence – which powers features such as email summarisation, report drafting and image editing – exclusively on iPhones. An Alibaba representative said at the time that its Qwen model would “be integrated into Apple Intelligence experiences within iOS, iPadOS, macOS and visionOS for users in China” to enable text and image generation capabilities. Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. While Apple relies on partnerships with Google and OpenAI to support its Intelligence feature in international markets, Beijing’s stringent oversight has pushed Apple to collaborate with local tech firms, including Alibaba. An Apple Intelligence roll-out is critical for Apple as it leans on AI features to stave off fierce domestic competition in China, the world’s largest smartphone market. Local players including Huawei Technologies have been pushing aggressively in the premium tier as the broader industry struggles with surging component costs. China’s overall smartphone shipments plunged 15 per cent in the third quarter, with Huawei the only player among the top brands to record an uptick in sales, according to an IDC report released on Tuesday. Huawei led the market with a 21 per cent share, with shipments up 17 per cent year on year following the launch of its new trifold handset and flagship Mate 90 series in September. Apple ranked second with a nearly 18 per cent share of the Chinese market, though its shipment volume was down 4 per cent year on year. The initial response to Apple’s recently launched iPhone 18 Pro series in China has shown positive signs. The company sold more Pro models in the first three days after launch in China last month than it did in an entire week following the release of the iPhone 17 Pro line-up last year, according to a report by Counterpoint Research. That strong start propelled Apple to reclaim the top spot in China by smartphone sales for the week of September 14 to 20, with the company capturing a 33 per cent share of the market. Additional reporting by Ann Cao

title: Taiwan turns to US drone boats to track rising mainland Chinese sea activity
description: High-speed Devil Ray T24 autonomous vessels to join coastguard fleet in major expansion of island’s maritime reconnaissance tools.
content: Taiwan’s coastguard is buying US-designed uncrewed surface vessels for its first dedicated drone-boat programme to strengthen its ability to detect and track the growing presence of mainland Chinese vessels operating around the island. Florida-based Maritime Tactical Systems (Martac) announced on Tuesday that the deal covered an undisclosed number of its Devil Ray T24 autonomous boats, with production planned for both the United States and Taiwan. Martac described the deal as “one of the most significant international purchases” of US-made uncrewed surface vessels, while James Lee, chief executive of Confucian, Martac’s Taiwanese partner, described it as the coastguard agency’s “first unmanned surface vessel programme”. The procurement follows a sharp increase in mainland Chinese maritime activity around Taiwan, with coastguard, research and other government vessel sightings reaching record levels in June, July and August, according to Taiwanese defence ministry figures analysed by the South China Morning Post. Beijing has also expanded its coastguard operations east of Taiwan, maintaining regular patrols in the area since June and describing them as routine law enforcement. The drone deal builds on a 2025 partnership between Martac, Confucian and Taiwan’s National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST), which Taiwanese media identified as the main contractor for a wider coastguard programme to acquire 25 uncrewed surface vessels. The partnership between Martac and NCSIST also encompasses technologies including AI-assisted target tracking, autonomous interception and coordinated operations involving multiple unmanned vessels, although Taiwan has not said whether those capabilities would be incorporated into its coastguard T24s. According to Martac, the Devil Ray T24 is 8.4 metres (27.5 feet) long and capable of burst speeds exceeding 50 knots. Its modular design allows it to carry different equipment for maritime surveillance and a host of military activities, such as electronic warfare, mine countermeasures and anti-submarine reconnaissance. Taiwan’s coastguard director general Chang Chung-lung said the T24s, along with aerial drones, would be used mainly for “long-range search and reconnaissance, investigation and remote rescue”, extending the coastguard’s operational reach. The agency said these assets would eventually operate alongside its cutters, forming a network for coordinated operations and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. The coastguard’s planned cooperation between its vessels and unmanned systems is noteworthy given Taiwan’s long-standing preparations for the agency to take on military duties, although it remains a civilian body in peacetime. The island’s National Defence Act allows the government to bring the coastguard into the military order of battle during a conflict. The agency’s Anping-class cutters illustrate this approach. Designed to be fitted with Hsiung Feng II and III anti-ship missiles upon wartime mobilisation, vessels in the class have conducted missile-firing exercises since 2022. The latest involved the Qijin, which launched a Hsiung Feng III supersonic anti-ship missile in September. The T24 itself has also shown a strike capability, launching an exercise torpedo during US Navy-backed trials in Sweden in December 2024. Taipei, however, has not said whether the T24s would eventually be armed. In an analysis last month, Cathy Fang of Taiwan’s Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology said the coastguard’s uncrewed maritime systems could extend surveillance coverage and improve evidence gathering while reducing the risks faced by crews. She cautioned that they would need to be integrated with existing command networks and coastguard operations to be effective. Beijing sees Taiwan as a breakaway province to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Chinese memory giant YMTC to grow revenue 6 times faster than peers as IPO nears: report
description: Country’s top NAND maker bets on enterprise SSDs and AI infrastructure to drive next phase of growth, Counterpoint says.
content: Yangtze Memory Technologies Corporation (YMTC), China’s leading flash-memory maker, is set to grow revenue six times faster than its industry peers this year as it expands into server-related business ahead of a planned initial public offering (IPO), according to Counterpoint Research. The company’s server-related revenue was effectively zero in 2024, but could account for nearly 39 per cent of its revenue by 2028, according to the market intelligence firm on Tuesday. Much of the momentum is tied to a growing role for enterprise solid-state drives (SSDs), which are widely used in data centres. The shift would broaden YMTC’s business beyond storage products for smartphones and personal computers. The expansion comes as the company’s parent, CCSH Corporation, seeks to raise 33 billion yuan (US$4.9 billion) through a listing on Shanghai’s Star Market. Its revenue grew 40 per cent year on year to 63 billion yuan in 2025, according to the prospectus. Counterpoint said YMTC’s strategy involved expanding partnerships with controller suppliers including Phison, Silicon Motion and Alibaba Group Holding’s T-Head, alongside a key enterprise relationship with Huawei Technologies. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. “The bigger question is whether YMTC can convert this into design wins with customers outside China, not just domestic hyperscalers,” said MS Hwang, research director at Counterpoint, referring to securing places in customers’ products. The challenge is to turn manufacturing scale into a stronger position in higher-value storage markets. In an earlier report, Counterpoint ranked YMTC – China’s only NAND flash maker operating at commercial scale – third globally by NAND shipment volume in the second quarter, behind Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, but ahead of Japan’s Kioxia and US-based Micron Technology. YMTC, which is based in Wuhan in central China’s Hubei province, ranked only fifth by revenue, reflecting its heavier exposure to consumer products. NAND, which retains data when power is switched off, is a core component of SSDs. In artificial intelligence infrastructure, those drives store training datasets, model files and other information that computing systems need to retrieve quickly. Enterprise SSDs accounted for 48 per cent of global NAND bits shipped in the second quarter, up from 26 per cent a year earlier, according to Counterpoint’s August assessment. The research firm attributed the shift to growing demand for AI inference, the process of running trained models to generate responses. Morgan Stanley said in an August report that Chinese memory manufacturers could reshape competition through scale and domestic demand even before matching global leaders in the most advanced products. Broader enterprise SSD qualification for YMTC would bring the company into more direct competition for the industry’s higher-value business, the bank said. YMTC’s expansion continues to face equipment constraints. Washington added the company to its Entity List in December 2022, imposing licence requirements on exports, re-exports and transfers of items subject to US export rules, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment and technology. Counterpoint also said YMTC was researching DRAM, the working memory used in phones, computers and servers, as it sought to expand beyond NAND. Its mobile memory development includes a newer design intended for eventual mass production, while an earlier version remains in research and testing.

title: Japan farm minister submits resignation in first scandal blow for PM Takaichi
description: Kazuo Yana steps down after vote-buying claims, marking the first cabinet exit for Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi since taking power.
content: Japanese Agriculture Minister Kazuo Yana said he tendered his resignation following allegations of possible vote-buying, lining him up to become the first minister in Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government to quit over a scandal. “I apologise for causing such a huge inconvenience to those involved,” Yana said to reporters after submitting his resignation on Wednesday. He said he made the move out of concern for holding up parliament and his ministerial duties. Yana declined to comment on how Takaichi had responded. The prime minister had resisted earlier calls to have Yana step down over reports he claimed to have cut roadworks funding to municipalities that did not support him in February’s general election. The tide turned after allegations surfaced that he may also have infringed Japan’s strict electoral laws by arranging free transport to an election kick-off rally, a move some media suggested was tantamount to vote-buying. Yana has denied breaking the law, saying that the transport was arranged as a venue cost and did not constitute a donation. But in recent days Takaichi appeared to be gradually cutting him loose. “If it looks likely there was illegality, and if I come to a conclusion that there may have been unlawfulness or a breach of the law, then I will not hesitate to make a personnel decision,” Takaichi said in parliament earlier in the day. “I myself cannot say with certainty at this point that it was illegal,” she added. Yana’s resignation would make him the first minister to step down over a scandal in Takaichi’s year-old government. The prime minister has appeared keen to ensure her cabinet does not succumb to the kind of sequence of cabinet resignations that has plagued her predecessors. Takaichi’s administration continues to receive relatively high public support and it is not clear whether Yana’s exit would reflect badly on her. The latest opinion poll by national broadcaster NHK puts her public support at 51 per cent, a fraction down from last month, but still above recent prime ministers. To date, Takaichi’s cabinet has withstood reports of scandal. In March, a tabloid reported that then Education Minister Yohei Matsumoto had an extramarital affair and had met his mistress at his office. Takaichi defended Matsumoto, and he continued in his role until September, when Takaichi reshuffled her cabinet. Tabloids have also alleged that Economic Security Minister Kimi Onoda and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama circumvented election rules, but those allegations have not made waves in the same way the reports concerning Yana have. It remains to be seen if Yana’s resignation will be viewed by the public as an isolated case that Takaichi responded to swiftly and appropriately or if it will have a domino effect that unsettles her cabinet. Either way, the allegations involving election campaign tactics and threats of retribution could pose a headwind for Takaichi’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party ahead of next spring’s local elections, when voters will choose local leaders and council members. While it was the allegations of vote-buying that made Yana indefensible, the reports that Yana had claimed to single out certain localities in his district that had not given him sufficient support for a February election and cut their road infrastructure funding could have been what hit a nerve for rural areas that have long been a stronghold of support for the ruling party. One of the localities allegedly targeted by Yana passed a motion on Wednesday strongly criticising his comments, saying that road funding is crucial in responding to natural disasters and protecting the lives of local residents. In a change of tune from last week when she said she wanted to see Yana stay on in her cabinet, Takaichi described his comments on cutting funding as “really uncool” on Tuesday, in one of the first signs she was distancing herself from the embattled minister. Yana retracted his comments about the road funding and apologised. “It was very inappropriate and I am deeply remorseful,” he told reporters last week. He denied that he had urged the Infrastructure Ministry to cut funding to the localities. An official at the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism said at a press conference on Tuesday that there had been no pressure from Yana over budget allocations.

title: ‘Pure fate’: China newlyweds share identical names, face endless glitches in life situations
description: Social media users even suggest that the couple name their future child ‘Congcong,’ a clever combination of their names.
content: A newlywed Chinese couple has gone viral on social media because they share exactly the same name, written with the same Chinese characters, and work in the same industry. The coincidence has caused a few practical complications, but many people see it as pure fate. On October 6, the groom, 33, and the bride, 28, both named Zhu Xiaocong, held their wedding in Zhejiang province, eastern China. Someone shared their wedding poster online, which showed that the couple had exactly the same name, written with the same Chinese characters. The bride said some relatives who did not know her husband thought the wedding planner had made a mistake. When they learned it was not a mistake but a coincidence, they said the couple were “completely meant to be.” The couple not only share the same name and come from Zhejiang province, but also work in the civil aviation industry. The wife is a flight attendant, while the husband is an aviation safety officer. They both attended the same job fair in 2016. They recalled that when an interviewer called out “Zhu Xiaocong,” they both stood up. At the time, they simply noted that someone else had the same name and considered it a minor incident. Later, the husband’s colleague, who was also the wife’s classmate, noticed the coincidence and introduced them. They began dating in 2019. The couple have had some amusing difficulties because of their identical names. When they registered their marriage in May and applied for a property ownership certificate, the computer could not automatically process their information, so staff had to take time to enter their records manually. The wife also shared on her account that they once accidentally swapped boarding passes during a leisure trip. Because the passes did not show their gender, security staff had to check their identities. The wife told the SCMP that they both used to respond when friends called “Xiaocong.” They later came up with a system: the husband is “Da Cong,” meaning “older Cong,” and the wife is “Xiao Cong,” meaning “younger Cong.” Social media users found the coincidence amusing, with some suggesting that the couple name their future child “Zhu Xiaocong” or “Congcong,” combining their names. Another user said the story was like Japanese director Shunji Iwai’s famous romance film Love Letter, in which the two characters who share an unspoken adolescent crush are both named Itsuki Fujii.

title: Meet Shane Gillis’ ex, Grace Brassel, who’s speaking out over his sexist SNL jokes
description: Several celebrities, including Schitt’s Creek’s Dan Levy, have criticised Gillis’ monologue about women’s gym attire, with his influencer ex-girlfriend also chiming in.
content: American comedian Shane Gillis has come under fire for his Saturday Night Live opening monologue during which he made a sexist comment about how women dress in the gym. “I haven’t been to the gym in so long – I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” he said. “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial bait-coloured [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look! You’re not allowed to look.” The 38-year-old, who had been invited to host the show on October 10, has received widespread backlash from the internet as well as from celebrities such as Schitt’s Creek’s Dan Levy, who slammed Gillis in an Instagram reel saying: “I’m speechless that something like that can exist on live national television. And to be perfectly honest, more men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it’s complacency that has created the environment in which women are sexually assaulted and it’s a ‘conversation’ as opposed to a ‘crime’.” Gillis’ ex-girlfriend, Grace Brassel, also seemed put off by his comments and responded by sharing a workout reel which she captioned “full body workout for the h*es”. Here’s everything you need to know about Shane Gillis’ ex-girlfriend, Grace Brassel. What does Grace Brassel do? Grace Brassel graduated from the University of Delaware in 2021 with a degree in communication and media studies, per her LinkedIn profile. With over 123,000 followers on her Instagram and an even more impressive fan base on TikTok, Brassel is an influencer and has been posting content since 2019. She is also currently working as a self-employed social media manager. Previously, Brassel was a social media platform and influencer strategist at DIFF Eyewear from 2023-2024. In 2023, Brassel appeared on the Dr Phil show to speak about the dangers of vaping after she was hospitalised with a collapsed lung in 2022. How long did she date Shane Gillis? Brassel and Gillis were first connected in July 2024 when they were photographed attending Miss Universe Olivia Culpo’s wedding to NFL player Christian McCaffrey. One particular snap of Brassel posing with her hand on Gillis’ chest went viral. The couple confirmed their romance in July that same year and were spotted attending several sporting events together. Brassel also regularly shared couple photos on her Instagram and had supported the comedian at his various gigs, including when he hosted SNL in March 2025. In November 2025, a source told People that the couple had officially split. What has Grace Brassel said about Gillis? Just days ahead of Gillis’ controversial SNL stint, Brassel had shared a reel on her social media showing footage of herself crying. In the caption, she seemed to be talking about her relationship with Gillis, saying: “Last year I was in a relationship that fully stripped me of who I am. I’ve been so terrified to even talk about what I went through, especially after relentless bullying from his fan base (for no reason). “I want to share this to let women know IT GETS BETTER!! And you can do it! I had it on level hard mode and I survived! And I’ve never been happier,” she added.

title: Disney+ K-drama The Remarried Empress: Shin Min-a reigns in lavish royal romance fantasy
description: Royal intrigue, romance and betrayal are wrapped in lavish sets and opulent costumes in the Disney+ adaptation of a popular webtoon.
content: Lead cast: Shin Min-a, Ju Ji-hoon, Lee Jong-suk, Lee Se-young Shin Min-a is, for all intents and purposes, Korea’s first Disney Princess as she plays the titular royal in the lavish new K-drama The Remarried Empress. Adapted from Alphatart’s web novel of the same name, this star-studded romantic fairy tale tells the story of Navier Ellie Trovi (Shin), whose position in the mythical Eastern Empire is threatened when her once-faithful husband, Emperor Sovieshu (Ju Ji-hoon), takes a mistress: Rashta (Lee Se-young), a runaway slave he has rescued. Directed by Jo Soo-won (Pinocchio, My Happy Ending), the series unfolds amid extravagant finery and sprawling palaces that feel part Palace of Versailles, part theme park. It may only be a matter of time before Navier joins Cinderella and Elsa in Disneyland’s famous parades. The first three episodes premiered earlier this week at the Busan International Film Festival, ahead of the series’ Disney+ debut next month. The title, The Remarried Empress, gives away more than is covered in the three episodes released so far. Navier and Sovieshu appear to be the perfect royal couple: elegant and composed in public, and doting and compassionate in private. Navier oversees the Eastern Empire’s daily affairs, including preparations for an extravagant New Year’s celebration that will bring dignitaries from near and far to the palace. The only cloud over their apparently idyllic marriage is that she is yet to provide Sovieshu with an heir. The throne has come under threat in the past from questionable members of his extended family, and only a child of their own can secure its future. While hunting one day, Sovieshu encounters a gang of armed men pursuing a beautiful commoner. He intervenes, arrests them as would-be assassins and is immediately captivated by the young woman, Rashta, whom he brings back to the palace. Covered in scars and fresh wounds, Rashta is revealed to be a runaway slave owned by the sadistic Viscount Lotteshu (Park Ho-san). Sovieshu is smitten with the helpless maiden and steals a kiss. He punishes Lotteshu, destroys Rashta’s certificate of ownership and, breaking his earlier promises, declares that he will take her as his mistress. Navier, meanwhile, is an accomplished archer and horse rider who has a unique bond with the creatures of the forest. Her skills don’t protect her from an attack by an aggressive, wormlike beast that burrows beneath the ground. Back at the palace, Navier sends for the royal doctor, only to learn that he is tending to her husband’s new guest. Navier also encounters an enchanted bird that later appears in her private garden. A note attached to its ankle reads, “Wouldn’t you agree that our meeting was fate?” She sends a message in response, and so begins a playful, flirtatious back-and-forth between the empress and the bird’s presumed owner. The bird is actually Prince Heinrey of the Western Kingdom (Lee Jong-suk), a dashing swordsman with a taste for adventure and a scandalous reputation who can transform into the feathered creature at will. Sovieshu’s decision sends shock waves through the court, not least for the empress, who is blindsided by the unprovoked betrayal. The scheming Lady Albani (Jung Young-joo), wife of the emperor’s imprisoned uncle, sees an opportunity to advance her own designs on the crown. As a commoner, Rashta cannot bear a recognised heir. But if she were to be formally adopted by Albani, her baby would be next in line to the throne. Consequently, Rashta moves into the palace, bringing her into direct contact with Navier. Tensions come to a head on the night of the New Year’s celebration, in front of the land’s wealthiest and most powerful figures. Sovieshu snubs his wife by choosing Rashta for the first dance, only for Prince Heinrey to stride across the room and proposition Navier in front of the emperor and his subjects. Although the empress has yet to remarry, the series is already brimming with romance, betrayal, palace intrigue and humour, played out in sweeping strokes of softly lit melodrama. Hints suggest the kingdom is also imbued with magic and monsters, although these elements have so far remained on the periphery. Fans of the web novel will know where the story is headed and should delight in the scale and opulence of the adaptation. For the uninitiated, The Remarried Empress glides effortlessly into the realm of Beauty and the Beast or Frozen, with a smattering of Princess Mononoke-style fantasy for good measure. It lacks only musical numbers to feel like a full-blown Disney property in its own right. The Remarried Empress starts streaming on Disney+ on November 4.

title: US holds ‘unusual’ civil-military meeting in Tokyo ahead of Trump’s China trip
description: Diplomatic, administrative and military officials said to have exchanged intelligence and aligned Asia-Pacific priorities and messaging.
content: Senior American diplomats, administration officials and Indo-Pacific military commanders met in Tokyo earlier this month in what one source called an “unusual” gathering ahead of US President Donald Trump’s planned visit to China in November. People familiar with the meeting said it represented an evolution of a long-standing practice in which US ambassadors stationed across Asia and the Pacific gathered to exchange intelligence, coordinate diplomatic reporting and align regional priorities. The Tokyo gathering brought a broad mix of diplomatic, administrative and military officials into the process, suggesting a formalised and elevated-level approach to regional coordination on the US side. The roster included the de facto American envoy to Taiwan, while the programme featured a visit to the US naval base in Yokosuka, Japan. The group also held a 30-minute courtesy phone call with Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi and a meeting with Vice-Foreign Minister Takehiro Funakoshi. US ambassador to Japan George Glass hosted the closed-door sessions that ran from October 7 to 9, which he called an “inaugural Indo-Pacific ambassadorial summit”, although the event was not an international gathering in scope. Multiple sources said the meeting brought together officials involved in planning Trump’s next Asia trip, providing a forum to discuss Washington’s regional strategy and coordinate diplomatic messaging ahead of a series of high-level engagements. One person familiar with the gathering described the Tokyo sessions as “unusual” and “important”, saying they were used to lay out a “master plan” for the next six weeks – including Trump’s Asia swing – and for all to get on the “same page”. Another source said discussions were understood to have focused on Washington’s regional priorities and the coordination of diplomatic messaging as the US president prepares to meet his counterparts from the Philippines, China, Japan, India and Australia. Possible talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and a potential encounter with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un are also on the table. Along with Glass and US ambassador to China David Perdue, Tokyo’s attendees included the US ambassadors to South Korea, the Philippines, Australia, New Zealand, Thailand and Vietnam, as well as the US ambassador to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). Raymond Greene, director of the American Institute in Taiwan, attended as well. At Yokosuka, Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of US Indo-Pacific Command, briefed the ambassadors and senior State Department officials, including Allison Hooker, undersecretary of state for political affairs, and counsellor Daniel Holler. Rear Admiral Kyle Gantt, deputy commander of the US Seventh Fleet, also attended. Paparo was closely attuned to Chinese activities in the Indo-Pacific and North Korea’s reported assistance to Russia in its war against Ukraine, a source said. Some in Washington have also raised concerns about reported Chinese and Russian assistance to Iran. However, Trump on Tuesday said such assistance was at a “very low level” and that it was not happening “at all”. Another source said the discussions were also understood to have covered the issue of denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula and regional maritime and economic cooperation. The gathering came amid reported unease among American allies over Trump’s approach to China and his commitment to what Washington and its partners have described as a “free and open” Indo-Pacific. Trump has repeatedly referred to Chinese President Xi Jinping as a “friend” while criticising American allies, adding to questions about how his administration intends to balance engagement with Beijing against its regional security commitments. Trump has described a pending US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan as a “negotiating chip” and hosted Xi for a full state visit in September that reinforced a G2-style framing of US-China relations. During the September summit in Washington, Trump called the US and China “allies in World War II”, using language that echoed Beijing’s wartime narrative against Japan. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. The remarks and optics from Tokyo emerged as China-Japan relations remained strained over Taiwan and maritime issues, while the confrontations between Beijing and Manila over territorial disputes in the South China Sea have persisted. In South Korea, Trump has ordered cuts to joint military exercises and said he “may” meet the North Korean leader, citing their personal rapport. The Tokyo meeting also came as the administration was preparing for a series of high-level engagements across Asia. Before heading to China, Trump is expected to stop in Manila to meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr. He is also expected to meet Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the Asean summit. US envoy to India and Trump ally Sergio Gor was notably absent from the Tokyo gathering. Trump is set to attend the Asean summit in Manila on November 16 before travelling to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting on November 18–19, as the South China Morning Post previously reported. In China, he could also meet Putin, who has confirmed his attendance at the Apec summit. Trump has expressed interest in meeting Kim, though neither Pyongyang nor the White House has confirmed such a meeting. In September, the SCMP exclusively reported that Beijing was willing to help arrange a fourth meeting between Trump and Kim. The two leaders met three times during Trump’s first term to discuss denuclearisation, but none of the meetings produced a breakthrough. After the Tokyo gathering, US ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said in a social media post that the American commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific “could not be clearer”.

title: Bali tipping row: call for Indonesian tourists to pay up triggers backlash
description: Told they bargain too much, domestic visitors ask why Bali fawns over foreign tourists while treating locals like second-class citizens.
content: A debate over tipping culture has erupted across the Indonesian resort island of Bali and beyond, triggered by a politician’s unfavourable comparison of domestic and foreign tourists. In a social media video, I Gusti Arya Wedakarna urged domestic tourists to “normalise giving tips in touristy places”, which he said was part of the island’s “ethics”. “Perhaps that’s the psychological reason why Balinese people are more excited about serving foreigners,” said Wedakarna, an Indonesian Regional Representative Council senator from Bali, in the clip that went viral earlier this month. “I’ve noticed that some of my local friends never leave tips,” he said. “They even bargain, perhaps too much, and they also want a lot [from the workers].” He added that all tourists who came to Bali “must be protected” and there should be “no discrimination as we need all of them”. Bali received about 16.3 million tourists last year, comprising 9.3 million Indonesians and 7.05 million other nationalities, according to data from the Bali provincial government. A survey done by the Balinese tourism agency in 2019 found that foreign tourists spent around US$145 per day, or more than 2 million rupiah at the prevailing exchange rate. Domestic visitors, by comparison, spent just 530,000 rupiah. Wedakarna’s comments have reignited a long-standing accusation that businesses and hospitality staff on the Hindu island discriminate against Indonesian visitors in favour of higher-spending foreigners. In July, many Indonesians complained about being treated like second-class citizens in their own country after a running club in Bali, set up by two Dutch nationals, allegedly excluded locals from their membership and events. “We should try going to East Nusa Tenggara or Sumba, the scenery is really beautiful and we help their economy. Bali is already too overconfident, they’re no longer appreciating local tourists,” one social media user quipped in response to Wedakarna’s comments. The discussion has also centred on whether tipping should be the norm in Bali, or whether it would shift the financial burden of employee welfare from business owners to consumers. “Tipping culture is foolish,” another online commenter argued. “If implemented in Indonesia, business owners would be like those in the United States, where employees are paid below minimum wage because they’re assumed to get big tips.” Ni Luh Djelantik, a fellow Indonesian Regional Representative Council member from Bali, said customers already paid “service charges” at most businesses, which was akin to tips for workers. “Local tourists shop, stay, rent [accommodation] or [pay for] transportation and eat, all using rupiah,” Djelantik said in a social media post last week. “In Bali, many poor foreigners live in boarding houses, buy takeaway meals, wait in line with locals, and at cafes, they only order water but hang out for hours, or even bring in lots of food from outside. Many of them work illegally.” ‘We never ask for tips’ Residents of Bali such as Ngurah Saka fear the controversy could damage the island’s appeal to Indonesian travellers and tarnish the reputation of local hospitality workers. “My concern is that people will increasingly discredit Bali, and we, as residents, will be the ones in trouble,” said Ngurah Saka, 33, a civil servant in Denpasar. “As civil servants, we know that we are heavily dependent on the tourism industry. We receive levies, revenue and the regional budget from tourism. For us, there is no difference between domestic and foreign tourists, absolutely no difference.” Last year, Bali received 176 trillion rupiah (US$9.8 billion) from tourism-driven economic activity, almost half of the nation’s total tourism revenue, according to the island’s government data. Accepting tips was not the “main purpose for us in doing hospitality”, Ngurah Saka said. “When we install the internet, there’s always a warning not to tip. In hospitality, it’s actually the same. Although it’s not written down, we never ask for tips. My friends in the tourism sector also never ask for tips.” I Putu Winastra, chairman of the Bali Regional Executive Board of the Indonesian Travel Agencies Association, also rejected the stereotype that domestic visitors were less generous than their overseas counterparts. “We cannot generalise all 10 million domestic tourists. Not a few domestic tourists also give tips, sometimes even more than foreign tourists,” Putu Winastra said. “When we deliver service with heart, of course, guests can understand and appreciate that.” He also insisted that Bali businesses “never discriminate” against Indonesian tourists as “everyone is equal”. “In Indonesia in general, we must compete to provide good service to tourists from anywhere, so that they will see the extent of our professionalism as a local operator,” Putu Winastra said. Tipping culture should be stopped I Wayan Suyadnya, sociology lecturer I Wayan Suyadnya, a sociology lecturer from the University of Brawijaya, said employers should ensure the welfare of their employees so that they would not have to rely on the generosity of customers. “Local workers face immense pressure. On one hand, they must use their income to preserve their culture and traditions, but on the other, they must support their families and survive on very, very low wages,” he said. Asking for tips was “not part of Balinese culture” as it “gives the impression that we are beggars”, Wayan Suyadnya said. “For me, the Balinese are people who are fully aware of their responsibilities. They receive salaries and they are paid, so they rarely expect tips.” He added: “Tipping culture should be stopped. We must return to the philosophy that everything related to services should be paid by the company through fair wages.”

title: Nearly 1 in 3 unattended dogs captured in Hong Kong euthanised this year
description: The Environment and Ecology Bureau says 617 unattended dogs have been euthanised since 2021, while fewer captured dogs are being reclaimed or rehomed.
content: Roughly one in three unattended dogs captured by Hong Kong authorities had been euthanised as of May this year, a sharp rise from 18 per cent in 2021, according to the latest legislative documents. The proportion of captured unattended dogs later reclaimed by their owners or transferred to animal welfare groups for rehoming has also fallen over the past five years, the Environment and Ecology Bureau told lawmakers on Wednesday. In a written response to the Legislative Council, Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan said 617 unattended dogs had been euthanised between 2021 and May this year.
