The euthanasia rate nearly doubled from 18 per cent in 2021 to 37 per cent in 2024, before easing to about 31 per cent in 2025. About 30 per cent, or 55 dogs, had been euthanised as of May this year. Transfers to animal welfare groups for rehoming also fell from about 45.6 per cent of captured unattended dogs in 2021 to around 36 per cent in 2025. Around 32 per cent, or 57 dogs, had been transferred as of May this year. Meanwhile, fewer owners are reclaiming their lost dogs. The reclaim rate fell steadily from about 29 per cent in 2021 to 20 per cent last year. Around 22 per cent, or 40 dogs, had been reclaimed by owners as of May this year. The response noted that unattended dogs reclaimed by their owners, rehomed or euthanised in a given year might not have been captured in that same year. The bureau said the three animal rehoming centres partnering with the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department, which falls under its purview, could accommodate a total of about 450 animals, including stray dogs. A fourth rehoming centre is targeted for completion by the end of 2027. The response added that existing laws do not allow a dog microchip to be registered on another person’s behalf. The department is considering clearer wording in the dog licence application form to remind keepers of their responsibility to properly control their dogs. Tse reiterated that the government was conducting a comprehensive review of existing dog-control legislation and would consult the legislature on proposed amendments by the end of this year, with the aim of amending the laws in 2027. He acknowledged that current penalties for abandoning animals and failing to keep dogs under control were “not sufficiently deterrent”, and vowed to study increasing the penalties for such offences. Under the Dangerous Dogs Regulation, “fighting dogs” currently include pit bull terriers, Japanese Tosas, Dogo Argentinos and Fila Brasileiros, as well as any crossbreeds of these four types. Asked whether the definitions should be updated, Tse said the government was “listening to the views of different stakeholders” and would refer to practices in other countries and regions when formulating a proposal. Hong Kong’s animal welfare laws – namely the Protection of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance and Dangerous Dogs Regulations – have come under intense public scrutiny following a spate of dog attacks, including the suspected fatal mauling of a woman in Yuen Long in September, with legal experts calling for long-delayed reform. Animal welfare advocates also urged the government to close a legal loophole that made it difficult to prosecute owners who failed to microchip or properly secure their animals. The issue of unattended dogs, many of them free-roaming warehouse guard dogs, has been thrust into the media spotlight since the attacks, although authorities have not publicly confirmed which specific animals were responsible. Many animal welfare activists earlier told the SCMP that they would forge ahead with microchipping stray dogs despite heightened legal risks, arguing that charging dog rescuers was counterproductive. They also renewed calls for a comprehensive “trap, neuter, release” programme as an alternative to euthanasia.

title: Cloudy outlook? How haze crisis is testing Singapore’s events economy
description: While the F1 race weathered the haze, observers say the recurring disruption could weaken Singapore’s appeal as a global events hub.
content: When Daniela Cruz arrived in Singapore last week, hazy skies obscured the picture-perfect sights she had seen on social media, offering a different view of the city state from the one she had expected. The 27-year-old bank associate had travelled from Australia for the Formula One Singapore Grand Prix, but the smoky weather dampened her experience. “The buildings we saw on social media were covered in haze, and it made conditions extremely hot and humid,” she said. The haze blanketing Singapore’s skies over the three-day event raised fears of disruption. On Thursday, a day before racing began, motorsport governing body FIA said the conditions could potentially restrict entertainment acts and outdoor activities. This was not the first time the marquee event had faced uncertainty due to haze. In 2015 and 2019, organisers introduced precautionary measures, including health advisories and the sale of N95 masks, while both editions of the night race proceeded without major disruption, as did last weekend’s event. The poor weather did little to diminish the novelty of the night race, which drew a crowd of more than 300,000 this year. But while Singapore managed to keep one of its flagship events running, the recurrence of haze could weaken the city state’s appeal as an international events hub, observers said. Smaller events have also faced cancellations as air quality deteriorated, with conditions showing little sign of improving. The stakes are significant for a city that has invested heavily in attracting international visitors and major events. From its debut in 2008 until 2024, the Singapore Grand Prix generated more than S$2.2 billion (US$1.72 billion) in incremental tourism receipts, with the figure for 2025 still being calculated, Trade and Industry Minister Gan Kim Yong said in February. Singapore’s meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (MICE) sector is another important contributor to its visitor economy, with tourism receipts from the segment reaching S$2.3 billion last year, a 35 per cent increase from S$1.7 billion in 2024. Dedicated sports fans were unlikely to be deterred from future editions of the Singapore Grand Prix, one of the most distinctive events on the F1 calendar, said Guy Llewellyn, an assistant professor and academic director for Asia-Pacific at EHL Hospitality Business School. “A single hazy weekend is unlikely to outweigh its unique atmosphere, entertainment line-up, and broader appeal as a destination,” he added. But first-time and leisure travellers who viewed the event as part of a wider holiday experience could be discouraged from revisiting the night race and Singapore, Llewellyn said. For Cruz, the smooth traffic flow and multitude of activities during the grand prix set a high bar for future races. But she gave the concerts, which featured American singer Lana Del Rey and Swedish pop star Zara Larsson, a miss to avoid having to walk long distances in the heat and haze. “Regarding the haze, we can tolerate a level similar to the weekend’s, but a worse level would lead to us reconsidering visiting again.” Foggy road ahead In recent weeks, air quality in Singapore has deteriorated amid an increase in hotspots in neighbouring Indonesia and unfavourable weather, raising concerns over outdoor activities across the city state. While the F1 race avoided disruption, some domestic events have been cancelled or suspended. The fate of coming activities remains uncertain as the government prepares contingency measures for worsening pollution. Air quality in recent weeks has stayed primarily in the “unhealthy” range, with the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) reading staying between 101 and 200. The city state recorded its highest reading this year of 192 on the opening day of the grand prix on Friday. Singapore recorded its highest PM2.5 reading this year – which reflects the average concentration of fine particles in the air – on Wednesday, peaking at 288 in the western region. As at 5pm on Wednesday, the PSI reading remained in the “unhealthy” range, rising to 175 in the west. Some Singaporeans have chosen to stay indoors, with others donning masks outdoors. Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu on Saturday said the government had contingency plans in place across different air quality levels, and would distribute masks to eligible Singaporeans, such as the elderly or those in lower-income brackets, when the PSI exceeded 200 – deemed to be in the “very unhealthy” range. Several public sports centres shut their doors on Wednesday, and the city state’s health promotion agency, which organises workout sessions and nature walks, has cancelled all outdoor activities since Saturday. A number of running events have been suspended in recent weeks, including a ticketed 5km run at Sentosa on Sunday. In 2015, thick haze led to the cancellation of the first night of finals at the FINA World Cup. PSI levels entered the “hazardous” range of above 300 that year. Organisers with events slated for October told This Week in Asia they were prepared to suspend activities if the situation worsened and would heed advisories and regulations set out by authorities. The National Environment Agency advises the public to avoid prolonged strenuous outdoor physical activities if air quality is in the “very unhealthy” range, while those with lung conditions are asked to refrain from being outdoors altogether. Singapore’s sports agency advises organisers to consider suspending or modifying outdoor activities, and review the risks of conducting events in air-conditioned settings, when air quality levels enter the “very unhealthy” range. Decisions on cancelling or modifying the Garmin Run Marathon Series on October 25, which 6,000 had signed up for, would be made a day before the race, a spokesperson said. Garmin Run Club has cancelled multiple practices due to the haze in recent weeks and advised runners to adjust their training plans depending on the day’s haze levels. Local club JRT Volleyball Academy cancelled training sessions on Saturday after forecasts showed air quality could deteriorate into the “very unhealthy” range. Coaches were tasked with monitoring air quality and readings before and during sessions, said director Jerry Teo. Observers urged event organisers to prioritise safety over commercial viability. According to Llewellyn, destinations that adapt and manage health risks effectively are better placed to protect their reputation in the long run. “Contingency planning can no longer be treated as an occasional disruption. It needs to become part of standard event management,” he said. Zilmiyah Kamble, senior lecturer in hospitality and tourism management at James Cook University Singapore, said while the haze created “considerable uncertainty” for outdoor events, the city state was likely to remain an “attractive choice” as organisers were also assessing “the destination’s broader capacity to manage health, safety and operational disruption”.

title: A place in university the next goal for Chinese athlete Chen Yujie, Asia’s fastest woman
description: The 17-year-old Asian Games champion is balancing elite training for the world championships with gaokao preparations next year.
content: Fresh from a dominant showing at the Asian Games, teenage track star Chen Yujie is balancing professional training for next year’s world championships with preparations for the national college entrance examinations, setting her sights on a local university. At the recently concluded 20th Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, the 17-year-old bagged four medals before returning home to resume life in the final year of high school. Chen won gold medals in the 100m and two relays, and a silver in the 200m. Earlier this week, Chen returned to the track at Ningbo Sports School, completing her first post-Games training session under coach Wu Yacun. Yet Chen has never compromised on her academic performance. Having maintained a daily commuter-training routine since taking up athletics, she views education and sport as mutually nourishing. “I’ve always felt that learning stays with you for a lifetime,” Chen told a CCTV interview programme. “The knowledge I gain helps me understand the technical moves and requirements in my training faster and more thoroughly, so they mutually reinforce each other.” For Chen, academics and athletics are equally indispensable. She believes that while race times from one’s teens and twenties inevitably fade as age advances and the hair turns grey, navigating society ultimately relies on the knowledge and character cultivated in youth. “Out of 1.4 billion people, only a rare few can make it to the Asian Games, and even fewer actually win a gold medal,” she said. “[But] a gold medal is not the sole benchmark of an athlete.” Her coach shares that philosophy, fully endorsing her dual commitment to track and the classroom. “Throughout a person’s life, knowledge elevates understanding and allows them to comprehend broader domains,” Wu said. “In this process, while we strive for excellence in sports, academic performance must not fall behind either.” Born into an athletic family in Ningbo, Chen’s parents are both former track-and-field athletes. However, they deliberately avoid interfering with her training, leaving technical matters entirely to her coach while focusing primarily on her academic studies. Chen said she juggled her studies and training on a strict schedule. Outside of closed training camps, she attends classes at Ningbo Xiaoshi High School, completing morning academic lessons before heading to Ningbo Sports School at noon for track sessions, followed by recovery and physiotherapy at the clinic or sports science institute. She then returns to school for evening self-study, where teachers are arranged to tutor her on missed coursework until she heads home at 9.30pm. Her schedule is jointly coordinated by the high school and the sports school. Now in her final year of high school, Chen has repeatedly stated her intention to prepare thoroughly for next year’s gaokao, aiming for admission to her preferred university. Her recent stint in the spotlight has not disrupted her routine. Returning home after the Asian Games, she said she had little time to relax, immediately working to catch up on lessons missed during her competition preparations. Balancing elite training with gaokao preparations, Chen said: “Whether entering university through a sports waiver or by taking the exam, you ultimately still have to study. I believe you have to examine yourself every single day.” Regarding her university goals, Chen noted that while her parents did not impose restrictions, she preferred to stay local. “Ideally, I wouldn’t leave the province or the city, mostly because I want to stay close to my parents,” she said. “They focus more on my personal growth. Whatever personality I develop, they only gently prune around the edges, without interfering with my overall direction.” Chen revealed that after completing a period of recovery training in Ningbo, she will report to the national team later this month to begin winter training.

title: 3 Hong Kong taxi drivers banned for 3 months under demerit points system
description: In a first, transport chief reveals number of taxi drivers disqualified since points system took effect two years ago.
content: Three Hong Kong taxi drivers have been disqualified from driving cabs for three months after accumulating 15 demerit points or more under a penalty system in place for two years, the transport chief has said, disclosing such figures for the first time. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said on Wednesday that since the mechanism took effect in September 2024, 229 taxi drivers had incurred demerit points as of October 2, with 125 cases involving a refusal to accept a hire. In a reply to a question from lawmaker Chris Ip Ngo-tung, Chan said the three drivers had been disqualified for three months after incurring 15 demerit points or more on the Taxi-Driver-Offence points system - the first time authorities revealed this figure. Under the system, taxi drivers will receive three, five or 10 demerit points for each of the 11 types of misconduct and can be disqualified from driving a taxi for three months if they accumulate 15 points or more within two years. Repeat offenders face a six-month suspension. Overcharging passengers, refusing or neglecting to accept a hire, refusing or neglecting to drive to a location indicated, and defacing, damaging or altering the meter, incur the maximum 10 demerit points. Those who accumulate 10 points or more have to complete an improvement course. As of August this year, the Transport Department received 5,944 complaints about taxi drivers, including 605 that involved “refusing a hire”, 860 concerning overcharging and 874 about taking an indirect route. Amid concerns that New Territories residents struggle to find green taxis during peak hours and face repeated refusals when switching to urban, or red, taxis, Chan pledged to review green taxis’ service arrangements such as providing more taxi ranks in the Northern Metropolis megaproject and at port areas. Hong Kong has 18,163 taxis, including 2,838 green New Territories ones. “In the future, we will continue to optimise the operational arrangements for New Territories taxis,” Chan said. “The government will conduct timely reviews on the permitted operating areas of New Territories taxis. For example, operating areas of green taxis have been expanded to cover the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge Hong Kong Port and the Hong Kong Port Area of the recently commissioned new Huanggang Port.” Chau Kwok-keung, chairman of the Hong Kong Taxi and Public Light Bus Association, said the three disqualifications proved that the penalty system had a deterrent effect and that drivers should behave. “Cabbies should be mindful that if they misbehave, they risk losing their job, even for a short period of time and it’s not worth it,” he said.

title: IMF head urges US and rich nations to rein in deficits as global debt soars
description: High interest rates and fiscal indiscipline in major economies are squeezing low-income countries forced to prioritise repayments over aid.
content: The head of the International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday that the US and other wealthy nations needed to urgently tackle mounting global debt levels that were weighing heaviest on low-income countries and straining the global financial system. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said that while US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other US leaders recognised that the federal deficit and national debt had grown too high, just trying to grow the US economy out of its more than US$40 trillion in national debt would not suffice. “At the fund, we believe that, growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments,” Georgieva said at the autumn meeting of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok. “There is no magic,” she said, noting some other measures would be needed. “You have to go in a direction of tightening that, bringing it down, bringing the deficit down.” Rising debt levels and global inflation, partly resulting from high energy costs due to the Iran war, have pushed interest rates to multidecade highs, adding to the burdens of the world’s poorest nations. Efforts to bring debt under control with what Georgieva and other experts call “fiscal consolidation” have suffered setbacks from heavy spending during the Covid-19 pandemic and since. “Fiscal risks are rising, and a proper reaction is largely absent in many countries,” said Rodrigo Valdes, director of the IMF’s Fiscal Affairs Department. “And in major advanced economies, the effect of fiscal indiscipline does not stop at the border. It travels to the rest of the world.” “Among the world’s poorest countries, interest payments have reached historic highs relative to revenue, and declining amounts of aid are creating gaps that some countries have been unable to finance,” the IMF’s latest Fiscal Monitor said. That is forcing countries to make hard choices between supporting their most vulnerable people and meeting their debt repayment obligations. “We know that today the median developing country is going to pay, is actually today paying three times more on their interest repayments than developed countries,” Alexander De Croo, former Belgian prime minister and the administrator of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), said in an interview. On average nearly 10 per cent of government spending is going to repay debt, and the combination of high prices for fuel, fertiliser and other needs, the impact of the El Nino weather phenomenon and higher borrowing costs has left many low-income countries with little opportunity to recover. “I mean, we don’t see really a light at the end of the tunnel,” De Croo said. Generating jobs, especially at a time when increasing use of artificial intelligence threatens to make many traditional occupations obsolete, is another top priority. More than 1.2 billion young people are expected to enter the global workforce in the next decade or so, while forecasts suggest a net creation of only 400 million new jobs. The UNDP announced this week a “Jobs for Prosperity” initiative that will work with governments, development banks such as the World Bank and private businesses to encourage investment in key job creating areas such as tourism, healthcare and food processing. The initiative and other efforts would focus on helping countries attract investment by improving their governance and policies, while creating pipelines of “investible projects”, De Croo said. “These are things that are feasible. It’s been proven that you can do it in many places of the world.”

title: Hong Kong police hunt suspect who stole HK$80,000 necklace from jewellery store
description: Man in his forties asked to try on necklace at Chow Sang Sang store before snatching it and making quick getaway on an airport-bound bus.
content: Hong Kong police are searching for a man who stole a gold necklace worth nearly HK$80,000 (US$10,193) from a Chow Sang Sang jewellery store in Tai Po on Wednesday afternoon. According to a source, the suspect, described as a man in his forties, entered the shop on Kwong Fuk Road around 3.10pm. After asking to try on the necklace, which weighed more than a tael (37.5 grams or 1.3 ounces), he snatched it, fled towards Kwong Fuk Lane and boarded an airport-bound bus. Initial investigations revealed that the suspect did not appear to be armed, and no property was damaged during the incident. Officers have cordoned off the scene to collect evidence and review surveillance camera footage from nearby premises. A search across the district is under way.

title: China’s Liaoning carrier heads to the Pacific as US, Japan prepare for missile drills
description: Timing of PLA naval training in western Pacific could overlap with expanded Keen Sword exercise near Taiwan involving 57,000 troops.
content: The PLA Navy’s Liaoning aircraft carrier has started its second drill series in the western Pacific this year, with the training likely to coincide with an expanded US-Japan military exercise that could have implications for a Taiwan contingency. The Liaoning carrier group was carrying out the drill in “relevant waters” of the western Pacific Ocean as part of the navy’s annual training plan, China’s defence ministry said on Wednesday. While it did not disclose the exact location of the drill, the ministry said it was meant to “test and improve the troops’ combat-oriented training level” and complied with international law and practice, targeting no specific country or objective. The ministry also did not specify how long the drill would take, but such carrier exercises generally run for weeks. The Liaoning’s first training session in the western Pacific this year lasted 35 days from May to June. In June last year, it conducted training with the Shandong aircraft carrier for about 20 days. This suggests the Liaoning’s drill could overlap with that of Keen Sword 27, a biennial military exercise involving the US and Japan. Keen Sword will be conducted from October 19 to 29 across Japan and its surrounding waters, including Japan’s southwestern island chain near Taiwan. It will involve about 45,000 Japanese personnel, 6,100 vehicles, 40 ships and 260 aircraft, up from about 33,000 personnel, 30 ships and 250 aircraft in 2024. About 12,000 US troops are reportedly expected to take part. An activity planned for Yonaguni Island, just over 100km (62 miles) from Taiwan, is the exercise’s clearest link to a potential Taiwan contingency. For the first time, the US will deploy two of its newest missile systems to Yonaguni, including its Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) anti-ship missile platform and its Marine Air Defence Integrated System (MADIS), according to Stars and Stripes. Japan will temporarily deploy Type 88 surface-to-ship missiles and Type 03 medium-range air-defence systems alongside the US missile systems. The training and exercises come amid growing tension between Beijing and Tokyo since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made remarks regarding Taiwan in November last year, drawing criticism from Beijing. In December, the Liaoning’s training east of the Miyako Strait led to a stand-off between Chinese warplanes and Japanese fighter jets that had approached to monitor the activity. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to reunify it with the mainland. Japan, like most countries, does not recognise the island as independent but opposes any attempt to take it by force and Washington has committed to supplying Taiwan with weapons.

title: India jails ‘cockroach’ leaders over protests against alleged voter roll manipulation
description: The crackdown on the youth movement activists has sparked a wider outcry over democratic freedom and rights to peaceful assembly.
content: Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were remanded in custody for five days on Wednesday, as police ratcheted up efforts to clamp down on anti-election commission protests. CJP activists and opposition parties have defied a security crackdown to demand the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, accusing the poll body of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party. The commission, which oversees voting in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing. Delhi Police said CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka, 30, and Saurav Das, 27, were taken into custody for their “alleged repeated attempts to disturb public peace and violate the law”. At the end of the five-day remand period, they could have their detention extended, be granted bail or be released. On Tuesday, the pair jumped security barricades to wave the national flag at Jantar Mantar, a decades-old protest site that police have barred people from using. “Their alleged attempts to instigate others through social media to engage in similar unlawful activities were also taken into consideration,” police added. Parliamentary opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, from the Congress party, backed the men, who were detained after entering the site. Jantar Mantar, in the heart of the capital, has been sealed off for days with yellow metal barricades and guarded by security personnel. Delhi Police said on Monday it had removed the site from its list of designated protest venues. “Waving the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime,” Gandhi said in a post on social media. “Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice.” The Congress and CJP have both protested over the voter roll revision. Gandhi said on Wednesday that “all protests are one”. “Different banners, one cause,” he said. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke praised the men, saying they “knew they could be thrown behind bars” but went ahead to wave the national flag. “They’ve shown the entire country that the only way to stand up to a bully like Modi is to never bow down, no matter the consequences,” he said in a post on social media. Das has worked as a journalist, while Ranka, an engineer, studied at the prestigious Indian Institute of Technology and the London School of Economics. Rights advocates and critics say Modi’s government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents – allegations the government rejects. Human Rights Watch said on Wednesday the Indian government must uphold the right of citizens to protest peacefully. “The Modi government should stop throwing young protesters in jail and instead engage with them to address concerns over the right to vote and fairness of elections,” it said in a statement. Journalists in New Delhi marched on Tuesday to protest the detention of reporters during demonstrations. The Press Club of India said attacks on journalists doing their jobs were “unacceptable”. The electoral list revision, which began last year, has led to more than 133 million names being removed from electoral rolls, according to media reports. Critics say the exercise has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. Election authorities say the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries. Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls. Home Minister Amit Shah, Modi’s powerful right-hand man, dismissed the protests as localised and accused Gandhi of pursuing an “action plan to protect infiltrators”. “The people of India are not going to fall for your deception,” he said, predicting a “resounding majority” for government in the next general election, due in 2029.

title: Hong Kong urged to add online safety briefings, penalise no-shows at public gyms
description: Industry leader and lawmaker propose solutions after ombudsman probe reveals severe shortages in mandatory briefing sessions.
content: Hong Kong should make better use of its public gyms by allowing online safety briefings and penalising no-shows, an industry leader and a lawmaker have urged after the ombudsman identified management loopholes. The Office of the Ombudsman launched the inquiry into public gym management on Tuesday, noting that rigid mandatory training requirements combined with a severe shortage of places were creating significant barriers to public participation and leaving facilities underused. The watchdog also flagged booking loopholes for monthly ticket holders, including late cancellations and the absence of penalties for no-shows. Gordon Yau Yick-chung, chairman of the Hong Kong Fitness Guide, on Wednesday described the briefing and training requirements as outdated. “A few decades ago, such practices were necessary because gym workouts were less common and safety was a concern,” Yau told a radio programme. “Nowadays, many young people could learn that basic knowledge by watching videos, or their secondary schools are already equipped with fitness rooms … with that rule in place, it is not easy for people to use public gym rooms.” There are currently 87 public gyms operated by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department (LCSD). Users must attend a three-hour briefing and pass a written test, or complete a 12-hour training course with an attendance rate of at least 80 per cent. Only those holding qualifications recognised by the Physical Fitness Association of Hong Kong, China, are exempted. A preliminary inquiry by the ombudsman found a severe shortage of places for both the briefing sessions and training courses. In 2025, the LCSD received 377,000 applications for the briefing sessions, but offered only 25,000 places across 1,000 sessions. For the training course, it received 257,000 applications for 58,500 places across 2,500 courses. To improve accessibility, Yau suggested allowing users to complete training and tests online, while expanding exemptions for holders of commercial fitness licences or relevant degrees. He acknowledged, however, that removing the test as a control on numbers could leave public gyms overwhelmed by demand. Yau also said users had little incentive to cancel bookings or use all their time slots because there were no consequences for failing to do so. He added that it was often impossible for anyone else to take over a slot cancelled at the last minute. Yau believed financial penalties could help to prevent such behaviour and improve gym utilisation, although implementing them might take time. Lawmaker Leung Tsz-wing suggested that the government introduce flexible, short-term class options such as those run on a monthly basis, to allow more people to obtain certification. Unlike Yau, Leung believed the briefing or course remained necessary to ensure safety, noting that weight equipment could pose risks if used incorrectly. The LCSD should instead make better use of fitness trainers and its 87 venues to provide more places, he said. He also suggested the LCSD sell packages of 10 or 20 entries rather than unlimited monthly passes, and impose penalties on no-shows to ensure the efficient use of public funds. To further increase usage, he said the government could consider subcontracting gym operations to the private sector and explore the feasibility of 24-hour operations.

title: China chip exports jump 136% to US$45b as AI frenzy jacks up prices
description: ICs among the fastest-growing categories in September, underlining country’s growing influence in semiconductor supply chain.
content: China’s integrated circuit (IC) exports surged 136 per cent year on year in September to US$45 billion, exceeding the 108 per cent growth rate in the first nine months of the year in a sign of the country’s rising influence in the global semiconductor supply chain. In September, China exported 32.7 billion units of ICs, according to customs data released on Wednesday, a 1 per cent year-on-year increase in volume. But higher prices fuelled the 136 per cent jump in value amid a memory chip shortage stemming from the global building spree in artificial intelligence infrastructure. The first three quarters as a whole saw exports of 275.2 billion IC units worth nearly US$302 billion, according to the General Administration of Customs. The growth in semiconductor exports far outpaced overall export growth from China, which rose 36.3 per cent year on year to US$447.18 billion last month. The data shows how Chinese chipmakers remain deeply entrenched in the global tech supply chain despite not producing the most advanced hardware given their limited access to top-of-the-line manufacturing equipment. “The booming development of AI has accelerated global investment in computing power, expanding the demand for terminal equipment and intermediate manufacturing products,” said Wang Jun, spokesman and vice-minister of the customs authority, in a news briefing on Wednesday. The operation of massive computing facilities has simultaneously driven up global demand for electricity equipment, prompting a surge in Chinese power-related exports across generation, transmission and energy storage, he added. Beyond chips, other hardware products also saw higher shipments. Exports of computer parts grew 2.1 times year on year during the nine-month period, exports of memory components like solid-state drives increased 1.3 times and exports of data-processing equipment – such as servers – rose by 7.2 per cent, Wang said. Chinese-made AI glasses and robots are also continuously entering international markets as they “enrich global AI application scenarios”, Wang said, without disclosing exact trade figures. Meanwhile, semiconductor imports have also been growing quickly owing to China’s heavy investment in digital and AI infrastructure. Memory imports grew 150 per cent year on year in the first nine months of the year, while IC imports rose 56.6 per cent, Wang said.

title: Opinion | In Hong Kong, accountability must be more than a slogan
description: The Anderson Road, One Stanley and Queen Mary Hospital cases suggest that the city remains better at talking about accountability than ensuring it.
content: When news broke last week that three newly completed housing blocks were to be demolished without ever having been occupied, I suffered an immediate attack of deja vu. In early 1974, I was in the first wave of recruits to the Operations Department of the newly established Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC). As luck would have it, my first posting was to the team dealing with the old Public Works Department. That was my introduction to the wide world of corruption and shoddy work in the local construction industry. The terrible thing is that some practices seem to have hardly changed at all despite half a century of efforts to eradicate them. Common problems we found in those days were foundations not dug deeply enough or concrete not up to strength. There seemed to be a particular issue with steel reinforcement bars: there were not enough of them, or they were too short, too thin or in the wrong place. Sometimes they were deficient in all four aspects. The Anderson Road project is a classic example of the genre. A CK Asset subsidiary was successful in the tender for a residential site in Kwun Tong. There were to be six blocks comprising 2,930 flats for starter homes, at least 1,000 of which were to be sold at a significant discount to eligible buyers as required by the Housing Bureau. In the event, steel bars in all six blocks were found to be inadequate and work stopped two years ago. An announcement last week said three of the blocks were salvageable and remedial work was in hand; demolition and new construction was the most cost-effective solution for the other three. The news broke just days after a similar report that the government was investigating allegations of insufficient steel bars at a new luxury residential project at One Stanley, some 24 of which had been sold in the last six months. It was just last month that we learned that full commissioning of a new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) medical block at Queen Mary Hospital had been delayed as all 28 lifts were found to be defective and only four of them could be made operational quickly with minor repairs. There have also been questions about the building materials in the construction of the Tung Chung East MTR station. The relevant authorities have not been idle in the face of these events. There have been investigations by the ICAC leading to arrests and prosecutions in the Anderson Road and Queen Mary Hospital cases. The Stanley developer, K&K Property, has offered an additional warranty. However, such measures are essentially closing the stable door after the horse has bolted. Society at large has suffered other costs from these cases. Starter homes that should have been available for occupation now will not be ready for months or even years, leaving the intended occupants inadequately housed for longer. Hong Kong’s reputation as a world-class city has been damaged among the buyers of luxury homes, some of whom are from overseas. The whole community has been denied the benefit of the new medical facilities in Pok Fu Lam while remedial works are performed. What is disturbing in all these cases is the lack of integrity and professionalism. The projects all have safeguards built into execution. There are regular inspections, tests on materials and checks of quality, but somehow these serious lapses still find their way through. Far too many of our professionals, including public servants, are doing the minimum necessary rather than exerting themselves to their full capacity. This is a cultural problem, and quality leadership must be part of the solution. All of this is by way of introduction to the concept of accountability, which we have been promised in all these and similar cases. Frankly, we have become very good at talking about accountability and rather less impressive in actual performance. We have introduced a system to deny rank and file officers salary increases in some circumstances, and we are introducing a new arrangement for accountability applying to heads of departments. In theory, we have had a system of ministerial accountability since 2002, but we seem to have forgotten about it. It has been a long time since I last heard references to it. This is odd as accountability applies at all levels, but it should start at the top, not the bottom. It is vital that we get this right given that the results of an investigation into the Tai Po fire – the worst disaster in a generation, with 168 lives lost – are expected to be released soon. The committee of inquiry’s hearings revealed shortcomings in the performance of several departments and bureaus. Accountability must be the basis on which we take follow-up action, not just a slogan.

title: Malaysia’s Najib loses bid to suspend 15-year 1MDB sentence on medical grounds
description: According to his defence’s arguments, he faces 14 health issues, including heart disease, high blood pressure, stomach ulcers and glaucoma.
content: A Malaysian court on Wednesday rejected Najib Razak’s bid to suspend his 15-year jail sentence in the 1MDB scandal pending the jailed former prime minister’s appeals, ruling that his health and other grounds did not justify a stay. The decision means his sentence is set to begin after his current prison term ends in August 2028. Najib, 73, received a conditional royal pardon last month allowing him to serve that separate sentence in the SRC International case at home, but he must first pay a 50 million ringgit (US$12.25 million) fine. SRC was a subsidiary of 1Malaysia Development Berhad, a state investment fund established to spur economic development that became embroiled in an international corruption scandal. Kuala Lumpur High Court judge Noor Ruwena Md Nurdin said the seriousness of the offences was an important public interest consideration, finding that Najib had failed to establish the “special circumstances” needed to suspend his punishment. “Therefore, I find no merit in this application, and it is accordingly dismissed,” she told the court. Najib was convicted on December 26 last year of abusing his power and laundering about 2.3 billion ringgit from 1MDB. He was prime minister and finance minister at the time of the offences and chaired the fund’s board of advisers. The court sentenced him to 15 years in jail and fined him about 11.4 billion ringgit, rejecting his defence that he had been duped into accepting stolen funds. A further financial penalty of 2.08 billion ringgit brought the total to 13.47 billion ringgit. Ruwena said the size of those penalties did not justify suspending the conviction and punishment, noting that payment was not currently required while his appeal remained unresolved. She also declined to assess the defence’s arguments about its prospects on appeal, saying “this Court is not a forum to decide on the correctness of the convictions”. Najib’s party, the United Malays National Organisation (Umno), launched a public collection to help pay the fine in the SRC case. Party president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said on September 27 that it had raised 9.25 million ringgit, less than a fifth of the target. “The 50 million [ringgit] is being raised,” Najib’s lawyer Muhammad Shafee Abdullah told the court on Wednesday, saying preparations for house arrest were continuing. Shafee spent more than an hour arguing for the stay, citing Najib’s health, delays in preparing his appeal and legal findings the defence intended to challenge. He said the appeal record remained unavailable as of October 7, more than nine months after the conviction. The next case management was scheduled for December 16, with no hearing date fixed and about 91 grounds of appeal identified. Shafee also disputed the prosecution’s description of Najib as a repeat offender, saying the conduct underlying both cases occurred before either conviction. “So for the prosecution to take a broad brush and to say this is a repeat offender in this case is wrong,” he said. Ruwena, however, said Najib could no longer be considered a first offender because his SRC conviction had been upheld by both the Court of Appeal and the Federal Court. Health arguments The defence’s written arguments, obtained by This Week in Asia, cited a prison medical report listing Najib’s 14 health issues, including heart disease, high blood pressure, stomach ulcers, knee osteoarthritis and glaucoma. Najib takes 14 medications daily, with allergies and complications restricting his treatment options, according to the submission. His lawyers argued that his age and illnesses put him at risk of irreversible deterioration before his appeals were decided. Deputy public prosecutor Ahmad Akram Gharib opposed the application, describing Najib’s prospects on appeal as a “50-50 situation” and arguing that the seriousness of the offences should carry greater weight. In his written judgment released to the public in June, trial judge Collin Lawrence Sequerah rejected Najib’s claim that fugitive financier Low Taek Jho, better known as Jho Low, and senior 1MDB executives had conspired to deceive him. Such an account would “stretch the imagination into the realms of pure fantasy”, Sequerah said, finding that Low had acted on Najib’s behalf. He described financial plunder that “made Attila the Hun look like a choirboy in comparison”. Low, who remains at large, is wanted by authorities in Malaysia, the United States and Singapore. Najib maintains his innocence and has appealed against all four abuse-of-power convictions and 21 money-laundering convictions. He has been imprisoned since August 2022 for misappropriating 42 million ringgit from SRC. A royal pardon in 2024 halved his original 12-year sentence and reduced his fine from 210 million ringgit to 50 million ringgit. Shafee has previously said Najib cannot raise the money himself because his bank accounts remain frozen. Under the latest pardon’s terms, any breach of his house arrest conditions would require him to return to prison.

title: Where a Melbourne-raised wellness entrepreneur goes in Hong Kong for coffee and dim sum
description: Shroommate’s Vivien Wong believes dining well is about more than good food. She shares her favourite spots in Hong Kong, London and Paris.
content: Vivien Wong is the co-founder of wellness brand Shroommate, offering mushroom-infused coffee and matcha. She spoke to Andrew Sun. I’m not the kind of person who eats on autopilot. I am a fussy eater – well, in spirit more than practice. But I do try to eat with intention. For me, dining well is not merely good food. Who you are eating with also matters. Then there is the rest of the experience: how you are greeted, the decoration, the service. Growing up in Melbourne, Australia, cafe culture is everyday life. In Hong Kong, I found EN Coffee (Shop B, LG/F, 6-10 Shin Hing Street, Central. Tel: 9504 4817) tucked away in an alley, like a secret you don’t want to share. I love the restrained simplicity: Zen-like space, warm wood textures, small green plants and, most importantly, single-origin coffees presented with details that feel thoughtful rather than performative. Each cup comes with provenance and tasting notes, as if introducing the beans properly. Ralph’s Coffee (three locations including Shop M12, Landmark Prince’s, 10 Chater Road, Central. Tel: 2325 4473) somehow reminds me of my best Melbourne coffee moments. The custom blends, roasted in-house, carry a confidence that feels crafted and familiar. The cafe is lavish in an old-world way: dark woods, green tiles, classic checks and an art deco atmosphere. It feels like you have stepped into a Ralph Lauren photo shoot, where everything looks effortless. When friends visit, I don’t just want them to eat. I want them to feel the city. For dim sum, I always take people to Lin Heung Lau (249-253 Des Voeux Road Central, Sheung Wan. Tel: 2116 0670). It is not only about traditional plates arriving with confidence. It is the old decoration and the vibe that make you sit a little longer, talk a little louder and appreciate the ritual. It is hospitality you can taste. For something more elevated, Ho Lee Fook (3-5 Elgin Street, Central. Tel: 2810 0860) has a distinct Hong Kong pulse. Executive chef ArChan Chan sets the tone for an evening that feels opulent. It is the kind of restaurant that understands night-out energy: bold, polished and alive. When I travel, I follow famous chefs – not because celebrity is the point, but because I believe a restaurant is a reflection of the person behind it. My favourite Paris experience is three-Michelin-star Arpège (84 Rue De Varenne, Paris. Tel: +33 1 47 05 09 06). Chef Alain Passard’s cuisine is shaped by precision and belief. It is not just about taste, but also timing. Reservations can involve a six-month waiting list, which means planning becomes part of the journey. But once inside, you not only appreciate his vegan dishes; you also get access to his private music and art collection. It is dining as immersion. In the UK, The Brasserie of Light (400 Oxford Street, Duke Street, London. Tel: +44 20 3940 9600) is my must-go place. The moment you walk in, you are transported to a world where art, architecture and culinary craftsmanship are inseparable. They are all one mood. Designed by Martin Brudnizki, one of the UK’s most celebrated interior designers, the space features Damien Hirst’s iconic Pegasus artwork. You almost forget you are there to eat. Food becomes almost secondary but it never disappoints.

title: China’s EV industry faces double blow from EU export quota, VAT rebate cut
description: China’s carmakers have relied on booming exports to ride out a domestic sales slump, meaning new export curbs will hit hard.
content: China’s electric vehicle (EV) makers have been hit with a double blow as both Beijing and Brussels introduce measures that will affect their exports, leading analysts to revise down their earnings forecasts for the industry. The twin measures – combined with a sales decline in China’s domestic market – could create a “do-or-die moment” for some of the country’s 50-odd EV makers, ramping up financial pressure on the companies, according to industry officials. On Friday, China and the European Union reached an “understanding” on trade that will see Brussels impose a quota on imports of Chinese-made hybrid vehicles – part of a wider effort by Europe to reduce its trade deficit with China. That was followed by an announcement from Beijing on Monday that it would slash a value-added tax (VAT) rebate for exports of electric cars from 13 per cent to 9 per cent from April next year. The policies are set to have a direct impact on Chinese carmakers’ earnings from exports – a setback for an industry that has relied on booming overseas shipments to offset a slump in domestic sales over the past year. The four-percentage-point cut in China’s export VAT rebate “is poised to act as a direct margin headwind for Chinese new-energy vehicle exporters … which could materially weigh on their international profitability”, Deutsche Bank said in a note on Monday. BYD, the world’s biggest EV maker, could see its net profit per car exported to the EU fall by about 5,000 yuan (US$747) as a result, according to the bank. Europe is the major growth market for Chinese-made EVs, and an export quota is nothing less than a barrier for companies like BYD to pursue high growth there Eric Han, Suolei Meanwhile, Chinese carmakers will see their hybrid vehicle exports to the EU market fall by “several million cars” over the next four years due to the export quota, according to EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic. Bloomberg reported that the European Commission was likely to cap Chinese-made hybrid vehicle imports at 350,000 per year initially, with the quota increasing by 6 per cent annually over the next four years. China shipped a total of 452,000 hybrid cars to the EU in the first half of 2026 alone, according to data from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association. BYD alone would see its European sales decline by about 80,000 cars due to the quota, Deutsche Bank said, putting a drag on its export growth in the future. The bank said it had revised down its profit forecast for BYD in 2027 by 21 per cent. “Europe is the major growth market for Chinese-made EVs, and an export quota is nothing less than a barrier for companies like BYD to pursue high growth there,” said Eric Han, a senior manager at Shanghai-based consultancy Suolei. “They are encouraged to move up the value chain to build expensive, premium models to attract European customers.” Chinese carmakers have pivoted to hybrid cars in the European market over the past two years, after the EU placed tariffs of up to 35.3 per cent on pure electric cars from China. Buoyant overseas sales have offered China’s automotive industry a cushion against a weak domestic market, with car sales plunging 21.7 per cent year on year in the first nine months of 2026 to 13.3 million. China’s vehicle exports are forecast to surge to 12 million this year, up 44 per cent from last year’s 8.3 million, according to the China Passenger Car Association. Despite their growing popularity overseas, some of China’s EV makers are facing financial pressure as sluggish sales contribute to a fierce price war in the domestic market. Among the nearly 30 Chinese carmakers that focus solely on EVs, only three generated a profit in the first half of the year: BYD, Stellantis-backed Leapmotor and premium EV assembler Nio. Another 20 or so manufacturers make both EVs and petrol-powered cars. Morgan Stanley said in a report on Monday that auto manufacturing facilities in the EU could be highly sought after by Chinese carmakers as they increasingly localised production to avoid tariffs and the new export quota. Underutilised plants and contract manufacturers could gain pricing power as late entrants seek access, while Chinese battery and component suppliers with European capacity are likely to follow assemblies built by Chinese carmakers to expand capacity, it said.

title: Chinese business visit to Russia-held Kuril Islands prompts protest from Japan
description: The trip to Etorofu aimed at identifying joint Russia-China investment opportunities in the disputed southernmost part of the archipelago.
content: A business delegation from northeastern China has visited a Russian-controlled, Japanese-claimed island off Hokkaido to explore joint economic projects, prompting protests from Tokyo. Officials and business leaders from Heilongjiang province, which borders Russia’s far east, travelled to Etorofu – known to Russians as Iturup – to survey potential investment opportunities, according to the Sakhalin Oblast government, which oversees the island. Etorofu is the largest island in a disputed archipelago that Moscow administers as the Southern Kurils and Tokyo claims as the Northern Territories, situated off Hokkaido in northern Japan. The delegation explored opportunities in aquaculture, seafood processing and tourism development, the announcement on Tuesday said. The visitors showed particular interest in cultivating sea urchins and sea cucumbers, it added. Tokyo and Moscow have long-standing territorial disputes over the four southernmost islands of the archipelago – called Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai islets by Japan – which were seized by Soviet forces after Japan’s World War II surrender. Japan renounced claims to the Kuril Islands and southern Sakhalin in the 1951 San Francisco Peace Treaty, which the Soviet Union did not sign. Tokyo maintains that the four southern islands were never part of that territory. A joint declaration between Japan and the Soviet Union in 1956 that ended the state of war and restored diplomatic relations did not resolve the territorial dispute over all four islands. Tokyo strictly rejects third-country investments or visits conducted under Russian regulatory procedures, a position underlined on Wednesday by Toshimitsu Motegi, the Japanese foreign minister. Japan had conveyed its position to both China and Russia through diplomatic channels and strongly urged them to respond properly, Motegi added. When asked about the Japanese government’s response, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on Wednesday that the victorious outcome of the anti-fascist war should be “respected and safeguarded”. She added that she had no comment on the business activities conducted by private companies during the visit. The Chinese visit follows Russian President Vladimir Putin’s trip to Etorofu in August, on his first inspection of the disputed islands since assuming the presidency in 2000. He reviewed deep-sea fish processing operations and met municipal administrators. Tokyo condemned Putin’s visit to the island as “absolutely unacceptable” and summoned Russian ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to issue a formal protest. The latest development may deepen Tokyo’s concerns that Beijing and Moscow are coordinating efforts to solidify Russian control over the islands, presenting Japan with an increasingly unified Sino-Russian front. Japan’s relations with both China and Russia are strained. Ties with Beijing soured after Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in November that a conflict over Taiwan could pose an existential threat to Japan, triggering a diplomatic impasse. Meanwhile, Japan-Russia relations collapsed after Tokyo joined Western sanctions over the war in Ukraine, prompting Moscow to suspend peace negotiations and suspend visa-free visits for former Japanese residents of the disputed Kuril Islands. Opposition politicians voiced stronger objections over the Chinese visit. Yuichiro Tamaki, leader of the Democratic Party for the People, called it an unacceptable step towards normalising Russian control. “We absolutely cannot tolerate China openly entering the area on the premise of Russia’s illegal occupation,” Tamaki wrote on social media. “Prime Minister Takaichi must promptly lodge protests with both China and Russia.” China’s interest may be driven by Russia’s 2022 creation of a special economic zone for the Kuril Islands, established after Western and Japanese sanctions over Ukraine. The framework offers domestic and foreign investors a 20-year exemption from corporate income tax, transport, land and real estate taxes as part of Moscow’s push to develop its far east.

title: 13 children die after overloaded boat capsizes in India
description: ‘A few families have lost all their children’, one villager said. The boat was bound for a Hindu festival when it sank.
content: Rescuers dragged 13 dead children out of India’s Ganges River after an overloaded boat capsized en route to a Hindu festival, officials said on Wednesday, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressing grief over the “deeply painful” tragedy. The boat overturned late on Tuesday in Vaishali district in eastern Bihar state, with locals rushing to pull people out of the water in the dark using mobile phones to find the bodies. “It was dark when we suddenly heard children screaming and crying for help as the boat capsized,” said Ravi Yadav, a young villager who joined the rescue effort. “We managed to rescue only three children, using the light from mobile phones and torches, because it was dark.” Villager Ramlakhan Rai said the boat was “small” and “not in good condition”, adding that people were crammed onto a vessel that was suitable for only a handful. “It is devastating – a few families have lost all their children,” he said. Six people were pulled out alive, including two children reported to be in critical condition. Nirmal Kumar, from the local health centre, said four children and two adults were sent to the district hospital. “We tried our best to revive them … but 13 were already dead,” Kumar said. Vaishali district magistrate Varsha Singh said that 13 bodies had been recovered. “The loss of lives in the boat capsizing incident in Vaishali, Bihar is deeply painful,” Modi said in a statement on Wednesday, announcing compensation for their families. “My thoughts are with the bereaved families in this difficult time.” Boat accidents are common on Indian waterways, often blamed on overcrowding, poor enforcement of safety norms and inadequate life-saving equipment.

title: China’s carmakers eye record sales, luxury model hits regulatory bump: 7 EV reads
description: From a Huawei-backed brand’s safety failure to US bans causing ‘severe self-harm’, here are seven EV stories you may have missed.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage on electric and new energy vehicles from the past two weeks to help you stay informed. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. China carmakers eye record 12 million global sales in 2026 as EV demand surges Chinese automotive groups have cause to celebrate their go-global strategy amid breakneck export growth in recent years, with deliveries in 2026 expected to beat expectations already buoyed by an international energy shock caused by conflict in the Middle East. 2. Brake-pedal failures in luxury Chinese EV draw regulatory spotlight A safety failure spotted in tests of a Chinese electric vehicle (EV) made by a Huawei Technologies-backed luxury brand has raised doubts about the cars many consumers view as a source of national pride, and prompted regulators to step up policing of quality and reliability. 3. Booming EV fleet drives China’s highway charging demand to all-time holiday high China’s EV charging volume on its highways hit a new high on the first day of the seven-day National Day holiday, as the country’s rapidly expanding electric vehicle fleet drives up demand for charging infrastructure. 4. China’s BYD considering lithium battery plant in Argentina, foreign minister says BYD is studying whether to manufacture lithium batteries in Argentina, Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said on Thursday after meeting Stella Li, the Chinese electric vehicle maker’s executive vice-president. 5. Why US bans on Chinese EVs are ‘severe self-harm’ for American carmakers The United States should engage with Chinese carmakers and battery manufacturers “strategically”, using targeted safeguards instead of the current “wholesale restrictions”, which could lead US carmakers to lose global market share, according to experts. 6. As import curbs loom, Chinese carmakers hard to miss at Paris Motor Show No Chinese carmakers were represented at a dinner on Sunday attended by French President Emmanuel Macron and around 60 European automotive industry players, but they were hard to miss when he visited the Paris Motor Show the next day. 7. Renault’s plan to build Chinese EV motors in French town sparks job loss fears As EU-China trade talks neared, the Renault plant shows the hard reality of creating jobs in a shrinking industry, even with Chinese partners.

title: Complaints of nuisance behaviour on Hong Kong public transport hit 3-year high
description: Noisy and inconsiderate passengers who play loud music or put feet up on seats in the spotlight as government cites jump in complaints since 2023.
content: Complaints about noisy and inconsiderate passengers on Hong Kong’s public transport have more than doubled over three years, with authorities recording a surge in reports of people playing loud music and putting their feet on seats. The Transport Department and Environmental Protection Department received 66 complaints about noise nuisance and improper or unhygienic behaviour in 2025, up from 31 in 2023, according to figures released by the government on Wednesday. “[Passengers] should be considerate and maintain mutual respect towards other passengers when using public transport services,” Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said in a written reply to lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung. Noise complaints, including those involving passengers playing audio at high volume on electronic devices, rose from 10 in 2023 to 11 in 2024, and then to 24 last year. Complaints about improper or unhygienic conduct, such as placing feet on seats, also doubled from 21 in 2023 to 42 last year, with 33 recorded in 2024. Chong had asked whether the government would consider explicitly outlawing playing audio through loudspeakers and placing feet on seats, as well as increasing penalties for nuisance behaviour. He also cited measures adopted in mainland Chinese cities, Japan, Singapore and London to curb such behaviour, and suggested installing more warning signs and making regular reminder announcements. Chan said existing legislation governing the MTR, franchised buses and other public transport services already contained provisions regulating improper passenger conduct, with corresponding penalties. “The operators have also put in place guidelines to assist frontline staff members in handling situations relating to passenger conduct in an appropriate manner based on the actual circumstances,” she said. These included verbal advice, follow-up action and referrals to law enforcement authorities when necessary. The government did not directly address whether it would introduce new offences or increase penalties. On proposals to introduce quiet compartments, Chan said all MTR heavy rail trains equipped with televisions already had designated quiet cars, where the screens were muted. High-speed rail services also had quiet cars, where passengers were required to silence their phones, use headphones and move to either end of the compartment when making calls. “When considering the introduction of ‘quiet zones [or] compartments’, operators need to prudently consider their mode of operation, operational arrangements such as space and design of the compartment as well as the impact on overall carrying capacity in order to strike a proper balance,” she said. The government would continue working with operators to promote considerate behaviour through publicity and education, she added.

title: ‘I bathe, wash dishes, apply make-up’: Japan’s PM says busier than men who came before
description: A self-described workaholic, Sanae Takaichi has previously said she sleeps for just two to four hours a night.
content: Japan’s prime minister said on Wednesday she probably spent “three or four more hours” than her male predecessors tackling household duties on top of her already packed daily schedule. “In the morning, I bathe, fix breakfast and then wash dishes, not to mention apply make-up,” Sanae Takaichi, elected last year as Japan’s first woman prime minister, told parliament. “I feel like I’m spending three or four more hours than male prime ministers doing these things.” A self-described workaholic, Takaichi has previously said she sleeps just two to four hours a night and sometimes scheduled 3am staff meetings. Gender roles are rigid in Japan and women are chronically under-represented in politics, with just 68 women lawmakers elected out of 465 seats up for grabs at the last Lower House election in February. Discussions about Takaichi’s time management came up when a ruling coalition member asked her about the marathon hours Japanese prime ministers customarily spend attending parliamentary sessions. It is common for Japanese leaders to devote five to seven hours a day being grilled by opposition lawmakers or otherwise just sitting in parliament. Citing a study, lawmaker Fumitake Fujita of the Japan Innovation Party said that, in 2022, Japan’s prime minister attended parliamentary sessions for 72 days, vs 50 days in Britain and 13 in Germany. While acknowledging the importance of legislative discussions, Fujita said: “The fact that our leader is confined for such long hours to parliament isn’t in line with the global standards.” Takaichi said in a post on social media in July that she was “getting consumed until dawn with poring over documents brought home from work and those related to parliamentary questioning”. “I do enjoy reading these piles of documents at midnight that I took home,” she said on Wednesday. “But it is difficult for me to squeeze out time to buckle down and think with a clear head” about “the future direction of this country or my grand vision for it”, she said.

title: Will South China Sea’s code of conduct remain elusive as deadline looms?
description: The proposed code can only succeed if it sets clear rules to prevent clashes at sea rather than to resolve territorial claims, analysts say.
content: A long-awaited code of conduct (COC) for the South China Sea risks becoming a toothless agreement, analysts have warned, as Beijing and Southeast Asian nations scramble to hammer out a deal by the end of 2026. More than three decades since it was mooted, the proposed pact has remained gridlocked over how to balance competing territorial claims among China and four rival claimant states – Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei and the Philippines. Maritime experts speaking at a conference in Kuala Lumpur this week agreed that the code was not meant to settle sovereignty disputes and were divided on whether it could keep the peace. “If anything involves clarifying maritime rights, not only China but also the Philippines and Vietnam will not accept a binding COC,” Ding Duo, a researcher at China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies, told This Week in Asia on the sidelines of the Maritime Institute of Malaysia’s 9th South China Sea Conference on Tuesday. Ding said the biggest obstacle was the COC’s scope, arguing that it should focus on maritime states managing their activities and preventing confrontations rather than settling territorial differences. Claimant states held differing positions on which activities should be permitted or restricted under the agreement, including operations involving external powers, he added. “Such differences should be settled within the COC platform,” he said, adding that disputes should not be resolved elsewhere. Asean has repeatedly called for restraint and clear rules under the COC, which was first proposed in 1992, to manage disputes in the contested waterway. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations and China exchanged draft proposals in 2000 but failed to reach an agreement on such a code. Instead, they signed a non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties (DOC) in 2002. Consultations on the code resumed in 2013, and negotiators began working on its draft text in 2018. The code was intended to set operational rules for parties in the disputed waterway to ensure that incidents at sea would not escalate into conflict, said Sumathy Perumal, acting director of research and senior fellow at the Maritime Institute of Malaysia. “I don’t think [the] COC will impact maritime rights or maritime claims,” Sumathy said. However, continued confrontations in the South China Sea had complicated negotiations and made it harder for parties to reach consensus on the code, she noted. “The incidents on the ground [are] probably delaying [negotiations], and a lot more details [need] to be agreed upon by those intending to sign the COC,” she said, explaining that a mutually accepted framework was important to help China and Asean preserve peace in the waterway. Questions persisted over whether the claimant states would accept legally binding rules that could restrict their activities in the waters. “The fact a COC has not been realised until today is reflective of the fact that nobody seems to really want it. If they had wanted it, they would have really made it happen,” said Nazery Khalid, a maritime security expert and senior fellow at the Maritime Institute of Malaysia. He said claimant states were reluctant to surrender their freedom to pursue competing maritime claims because binding rules could restrict activities currently permitted under the 2002 declaration. “With a legally binding Code of Conduct, there are certain things that you cannot do any more, which you can do under the DOC,” Nazery said. Reality at sea On the water, maritime tensions – between several Asean claimant states and China, and among the Southeast Asian neighbours – have continued to flare over fishing grounds, offshore energy resources and disputed maritime zones. Disputes between Malaysia and the Philippines have persisted over their overlapping claims in the waters off Sabah. In June 2024, the Philippines submitted a claim to the United Nations to extend its continental shelf 350 nautical miles from Palawan, prompting Malaysia to file an objection over Manila’s move. Tensions grew after Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr signed two maritime laws in November 2024 that Malaysia said infringed on its territory. Malaysia also lodged two separate diplomatic protests in February and July ahead of Manila’s presentation of its continental shelf submission to a UN commission in July. Malaysia and Vietnam also hold overlapping continental shelf claims in the South China Sea, despite having jointly submitted a claim to the UN in 2006. In December 2019, Malaysia separately filed a submission to extend its continental shelf northwards into the waters around the Spratly Islands, prompting Vietnam to lodge its objections that the submission overlapped with its maritime entitlements. Confrontations involving China have also been frequent across the region. In January, a Chinese coastguard vessel entered Malaysia’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ) – the 200-nautical-mile band in which a coastal state holds special rights to marine resources – near the South Luconia Shoals off Sarawak on Borneo. The Royal Malaysian Navy’s offshore patrol vessel KD Kelantan had shadowed the Chinese ship since December 2025. According to local media reports, Chinese vessels have maintained a near-continuous presence north and south of the shoals since 2014. In October 2021, Malaysia’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Chinese ambassador to protest the presence and activities of Chinese ships, including survey vessels, in Malaysia’s EEZ. While Beijing did not respond to the protest then, it claims the shoals as part of its Nansha Islands – known internationally as the Spratlys – and maintains that its coastguard patrols in the area are lawful operations within waters under Chinese jurisdiction, even as it prefers dialogue with Putrajaya to manage differences. Philippine and Chinese vessels have also clashed in the disputed waters, with tensions rising in recent weeks despite a 2024 provisional bilateral arrangement meant to calm waters around the Second Thomas Shoal. Last week, Manila accused a Chinese coastguard vessel of firing a water cannon and carrying out dangerous manoeuvres to delay the medical evacuation of an ailing Philippine Navy sailor from its grounded warship at the shoal by nearly 10 hours. Beijing countered that it had allowed the evacuation on humanitarian grounds after prior notification, accusing Philippine vessels of using the mission to cause “infringements and provocations”. That stand-off followed an incident in September in which Manila accused Chinese warships and coastguard cutters of blocking a Philippine resupply run to the same outpost – the first reported interception there since the 2024 arrangement was reached. Chinese coastguard spokesman Jiang Lue accused Manila of breaking its commitments by conducting an unapproved mission. Philippine officials, however, maintained that the bilateral provisional understanding did not require Beijing’s prior consent. In October 2024, Hanoi accused Chinese law enforcement personnel of assaulting Vietnamese fishers near the archipelago. China disputed the account and maintained that its authorities had taken lawful steps to stop Vietnamese boats from fishing illegally in waters claimed by Beijing. China asserts sweeping claims across the South China Sea based on an 11-dash line drawn on a Chinese map in 1947, which it later reduced to a nine-dash line in the early 1950s. In 2016, an arbitral tribunal in The Hague ruled that Beijing had no legal basis to claim historic rights over resources within the nine-dash line, which exceeded its maritime entitlements under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos). Beijing rejected the ruling, maintaining that the tribunal lacked jurisdiction over the dispute. In July, China’s Foreign Ministry reiterated its opposition, insisting that the decision would not affect its territorial sovereignty or maritime rights in the South China Sea. “The so-called ‘award’ is nothing but a worthless piece of paper that is illegal, null and void, and has no binding force,” China’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement in response to the 10th anniversary of the ruling. Nazery said the stakes in the South China Sea were high because it sat astride one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes and had become a focal point of great-power rivalry between Washington and Beijing. “The last thing we need in Asean is to be adversely affected by the so-called great-power rivalry,” he said, warning that Malaysia must navigate differences carefully while maintaining its long-standing policy of neutrality and non-alignment. While the fundamental question for Putrajaya was whether parties would respect existing international law, particularly Unclos, it must also maintain sufficient naval and surveillance capabilities at sea to protect its EEZ, Nazery said. “You can talk all you want about safeguarding your maritime sovereignty, but typically you need the assets to back it up.”

title: Domestic helper charged with murdering 93-year-old employer in Hong Kong
description: Indonesian Kharsina, 52, remanded in custody after being charged, four days after elderly woman in her care was found unconscious in Kai Tak flat.
content: An Indonesian domestic helper in Hong Kong has been remanded in custody after being charged with killing her 93-year-old employer at the weekend. Kharsina, 52, was brought to the Kwun Tong Court on Wednesday to face a count of murder. Police arrested her in the early hours of Monday after her 93-year-old employer was found unresponsive in her flat at Long Yiu House in Kai Tak’s Tak Long Estate on Sunday. Paramedics rushed the elderly woman to hospital after administering emergency treatment at the scene, but she was pronounced dead shortly after. Officers arrested Kharsina on suspicion of murder after further investigation. The defendant appeared in court on Wednesday morning to hear the charge against her, which was translated for her by an interpreter. The prosecution asked for a 12-week adjournment for further investigation, including obtaining an autopsy report. The request was granted by Magistrate Eric Yao Kwok-sun, who set the next hearing for January 6 next year.

title: Hong Kong’s San Tin tech hub operator vows affordable land to lure tenants
description: Hub operator also considers redeveloping fish ponds near Lok Ma Chau for a client needing more than 20 hectares.
content: The operator of Hong Kong’s flagship San Tin Technopole has pledged to offer affordable land to attract tenants, while revealing plans to reclaim and redevelop fish ponds near the Shenzhen border to accommodate a client requiring substantial premises. Sunny Chai Ngai-chiu, chairman of San Tin Technopole Company Limited (STTCL), on Wednesday also welcomed the proposed funding of HK$10 billion (US$1.27 billion) for the government-owned entity overseeing the technology cluster next to the mainland Chinese border. He also praised flexible measures designed to expedite development in the area.
