Speaking at a summit organised by the government-backed Logistics and Supply Chain Multi-Tech R&D Centre, Chai recalled that when the government granted land in Tseung Kwan O to the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation a few years ago, the premium was 10 times higher than that of an innovation park bordering Shenzhen and Shanwei in Guangdong province. “For an advanced manufacturing company wanting to come to Hong Kong, this could be an obstacle,” said Chai, who chaired the science park company before taking up his current role in July. “But the Sandy Ridge project set a very good milestone, because it is less than two times the land cost [on the mainland],” he said, referring to the planned supercomputing hub in the Northern Metropolis. “San Tin will follow a similar [approach],” he added. In March, the government granted an 11.6-hectare (28.6 acres) site at Sandy Ridge to a mainland company for HK$581 million under a 50-year lease to develop a large-scale data centre. In a Legislative Council paper released on Tuesday, the Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau (ITIB) sought HK$10 billion in funding for the San Tin Technopole. The government would also inject land assets into the company to reduce its start-up costs. The company would be allowed to contribute land as capital when co-developing or co-investing in projects with other firms. Of the total, HK$3 billion would be earmarked for forming 210 hectares of innovation and technology land, while HK$6 billion would fund infrastructure on an initial 20-hectare batch. The remaining HK$1 billion would cover the technology park’s initial operating expenditure. Land development at the site would adopt a multipronged approach, under which the company could “flexibly select suitable land parcels to directly participate in land development works”, taking into account its development plans, business and investment attraction efforts and available resources. On Wednesday, Chai said this meant the company could take the initiative and contract private-sector operators to carry out land development, rather than relying on the Civil Engineering and Development Department. In response to an inquiry from the South China Morning Post, Chai welcomed the proposed budget and land development measures. “The government and ITIB have been removing barriers and easing restrictions to streamline administrative procedures, providing STTCL with the necessary flexibility to make strategic decisions based on our development plan and investment promotion priorities,” he said. He added the scale of the San Tin Technopole – with 210 hectares designated for innovation and technology, about 17 times the size of the Hong Kong Science and Technology Park in Tai Po – would make it ideal for companies requiring large areas for manufacturing and research. “Hong Kong has outstanding basic research achievements, but often lacks pilot-scale facilities, making it difficult to localise and industrialise them,” he said. “As Hong Kong’s largest industrial base, building on the Loop’s research and development capabilities and extending to prototyping, pilot production and manufacturing, San Tin Technopole can accelerate the ‘1 to 100’ process.” He also told the summit that the company was considering developing fish ponds near the decommissioned Lok Ma Chau control point to provide land for a client needing an area larger than the 20 hectares in the first phase. Chai said the Lands Department was working to resume the fish ponds and the company would take the lead in developing the site. He did not disclose the site’s size or a development timeline. In a separate paper submitted to the Legislative Council on Tuesday, the government said more than 45 mainland and overseas enterprises had expressed “a clear interest” in establishing operations or facilities in the Northern Metropolis. Authorities said the firms came from a range of sectors, including education, innovation and technology, industrial manufacturing, tourism, advanced construction, pharmaceuticals and logistics supply chains. Speaking at a meeting of Legco’s subcommittee on the Northern Metropolis on Wednesday, Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said the government had been discussing a preferential policy package with the companies. The package, proposed in last year’s policy address, is intended to facilitate negotiations between Hong Kong’s investment promotion agencies and target firms. Potential incentives include land grants, tax reductions and co-investment with the government.

title: As US pursues mine deals, Xi warns African resources are not tools for ‘rivalry’
description: The long-term viability of China-Africa ties relies on the continent gaining more value from its resources, analysts say.
content: Africa’s resources should not be used as a tool for geopolitical rivalry, Chinese President Xi Jinping has warned, as the US challenges Chinese dominance of critical minerals on the continent. “Africa’s resources belong to Africa,” Xi told Botswanan President Duma Boko in Beijing on Tuesday, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua. He said it was a “historical injustice” that an unfair international division of labour had left the continent at the bottom of industrial and value chains, and China would contribute to plans for greater added value for Africa’s mining sector, according to state broadcaster CCTV. Xi said China would be glad to see other parties providing genuine support for Africa’s development, and would work to create more favourable conditions for business investment and operation, Xinhua reported. “A fair and open cooperation environment is crucial. Africa’s resources should not be used for geopolitical rivalry,” Xi said. The Chinese president also proposed affordable, sustainable financing and the development of supportive logistics corridors, along with a promise to transfer green technology, create local jobs and train workers. Kai Xue, a Beijing-based corporate lawyer who advises on foreign direct investment and cross-border financing, said Xi’s proposals reflected China’s interest in ensuring Africa remained a leading destination for its mining investment. “That depends on African countries gaining more value from their resources,” he said. Chinese companies hold major mining stakes across Africa, including copper and cobalt mines in the Democratic Republic of Congo, copper mines in Zambia, lithium operations in Zimbabwe and bauxite mines in Guinea. They also have stakes in Guinea’s vast Simandou iron ore project, which is designed to produce up to 120 million tonnes (132 million tons) a year. Africa was a major focus at last month’s China Mining Conference and Exhibition 2026 in Tianjin, Xue said. “We want to keep it that way, and the long-term viability of the relationship depends on Africa gaining more value from its resources,” Xue said. “That goes beyond refining.” He said presenters during the conference placed strong emphasis on geological surveys, showing that Chinese miners were also looking to expand their extraction efforts. Xi’s remarks come as Washington seeks a larger share of Africa’s critical minerals. In 2024, the Biden administration lobbied Congo to block the sale of Chemaf, a distressed copper and cobalt mining firm, to a mining subsidiary of China’s state-backed Norinco. In December last year, the US signed an agreement with the country giving American investors first right of offer on designated mining projects. After Congolese state miner Gecamines withheld approval for the Chemaf deal, US firm Virtus Minerals acquired the company’s assets earlier this year. The US push extends beyond Congo. The US signed a mining investment framework with Nigeria in September, and a US-backed consortium has been in talks over Tanzania’s Kabanga nickel project. Xi’s call for higher-value industry echoes a push already under way in many African mining countries. Namibia banned exports of unprocessed lithium and other critical minerals in 2023. Zimbabwe banned raw lithium ore exports in 2022 and suspended lithium concentrate exports in February this year. Harare later set out quotas for concentrate shipments, with commitments to build local processing plants among the conditions. A broader ban on concentrate exports is planned for January 2027. In Zimbabwe, China’s Huayou Cobalt has built a US$400 million plant that turns lithium concentrate into lithium sulphate, and shipped its first consignment in April. The sulphate still needs further refining to become battery-grade material. Other Chinese miners have announced plans for similar plants. During their talks in Beijing, Xi and Boko upgraded China-Botswana ties to a comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership and singled out the Khoemacau copper mine among the projects they wanted to pursue together. Chinese miner MMG bought the mine for US$1.9 billion and began expansion in February, including a new processing plant. MMG aims to raise capacity to 130,000 tonnes of copper in concentrate a year by 2028.

title: Who is Arthur Saint Bleick? Meet Selma Blair’s teen son as the actress faces assault charges
description: Following her recent airport arrest in New York, the Legally Blonde actress posted an Instagram reel featuring her 15-year-old son – what do we know about him?
content: Selma Blair made headlines this week after she was arrested at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York for allegedly assaulting two Delta Air Lines flight attendants. According to reports, the Legally Blonde actress punched and bit the flight crew members, and even tried to open the plane door mid-flight. Upon landing, the 54-year-old was taken into custody and transported to hospital, during which the actress allegedly attacked a police officer and a nurse. She has been charged with two counts of second-degree assault and has pleaded not guilty on both charges. Her publicist later told the press that Blair had “experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct”. Blair, who was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018, was released on bail and her next hearing has been scheduled for January 19, 2027, according to CBS. Since the incident, Blair has shared a reel on Instagram on October 12, which features some selfies, snaps with friends and a photo of her son Arthur, whom she shares with her ex-boyfriend, fashion designer Jason Bleick. The comment section under the post was flooded with supportive words from fans following her arrest. “Sending you love right now. Those of us with chronic illness get it. You don’t have to explain it to us ... We just want you to feel better,” one fan wrote. “Nobody can understand what you’re going through and the debilitating pain you endure. Don’t listen to the haters. You are loved,” another chimed in. This is not the first time Blair has been involved in an in-flight incident. In 2016, while on her way to a family holiday in Cancun with Arthur, the actress reportedly had a “drunken outburst” and had to be subdued by two nurses. She later apologised for her behaviour and explained that she had mixed her medication with alcohol. But what do we know about Selma Blair’s only son, 15-year-old Arthur Saint Bleick – whom the actress once described as having given her hope? Who is Arthur Saint Bleick’s dad? Blair shares Arthur with her ex Jason Bleick, a fashion designer. The pair dated between 2010 and 2012, according to People magazine. Although they are no longer together, they seem to have an amicable relationship and work together to co-parent their son. Blair has described her ex as a “super dad” in one of her Instagram posts. “Jason is a huge part of Arthur’s life. He’s shown up in a big way,” Blair said, speaking to People about their parenting situation. “I’m really proud of us.” He was born weeks after his due date On Arthur’s eighth birthday, Blair shared in a since-deleted Instagram post that her son was “weeks late” when he was born, and that she’d had to endure a painful induced labour. “The inducing was horrific and no dilation. Full labour with non-dilation for 37 hours,” she wrote, according to The Independent. “I finally asked for an epidural. I was so at their mercy. And I had to protect him.” The actress welcomed her son with the help of Dr Paul Crane, a Beverly Hills obstetrician and gynaecologist known for his celebrity clientele including Kim Kardashian, Beyoncé and Kris Jenner. He gave his mum hope In a tearful appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show in 2022, the Hellboy actress talked about experiencing sexual abuse as a child and dealing with alcohol addiction. “I didn’t know I had hope until I saw my son, and I love him more than anything,” she told Barrymore. In her 2022 book Mean Baby: A Memoir of Growing Up, Blair also revealed she started drinking from as early as age seven. Arthur Saint Bleick is proud of his mum Blair took part in the 31st season of Dancing with the Stars and Arthur, who was frequently seen cheering his mum on from backstage, expressed his pride when she made her debut performance on the show in September 2022. “I’m really proud of her. It’s just wonderful that she does this stuff and moves around and all of it,” he told Access Hollywood. Unfortunately, Blair had to withdraw from the show early because of her health and MS. They celebrated Blair’s 54th birthday together Blair turned 54 in June this year and shared a photo featuring her and Arthur with a birthday cake, and her leaning in to give him a kiss. “Love in all its forms. Cake, my Arthur, lovely people,” the caption reads. Arthur wore a simple beige pullover with the ends of his hair slightly bleached.

title: China and North Korea to open border bridge after unexplained 12-year delay
description: The New Yalu River Bridge, which was completed in 2014, will be officially opened amid warming relations between the two countries.
content: A bridge between China and North Korea that was completed 12 years ago will finally open on Thursday. The two countries will hold an opening ceremony to mark the official opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Wednesday morning. Last week, signs that the bridge would soon open were spotted, including vehicles crossing and traffic lights and bridge indicators being activated, according to South Korean newspaper The Chosun Daily. The bridge links the Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju and is expected to become a major trade route between the two countries. It was originally scheduled to open in October 2014, but this was stalled for a decade with no official explanation. Currently, traffic between the two cities must pass through the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, an ageing bottleneck that cannot support trucks weighing more than 20 tonnes and has only a single lane. The new four-lane crossing is expected to become China’s largest economic and trade gateway with North Korea. State-run China News Service reported in 2014 that it would handle up to 80 per cent of trade between the two countries. The delayed opening was caused by incomplete road connections, customs and logistics facilities on the North Korean side, compounded by strained relations and Covid-related border closures, according to The Chosun Daily. However, diplomatic ties between Beijing and Pyongyang have warmed in recent years, with passenger rail services and direct commercial flights between Beijing and Pyongyang resuming. Chinese President Xi Jinping also visited North Korea in June following a visit by North Korean leader Kim Jong-un to Beijing in September last year. “The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge will further facilitate economic trade and people exchanges between the two countries and deliver greater benefit to the two peoples,” Mao Ning, a spokeswoman for the Chinese foreign ministry, said on Wednesday. The opening of the bridge coincides with Pyongyang’s rapid expansion of land connections with Russia. Last month, North Korea and Russia held an opening ceremony for their first road bridge over the Tunmen River, which connects the cities of Rason and Khasan. The two bridges could allow the North to deepen economic integration with its neighbours, Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies, told The Korea Herald last month. Lim said that establishing major overland corridors allowed Pyongyang to capitalise on strategic competition between Beijing and Moscow and maximise its own economic gains.

title: Hong Kong tennis star Coleman Wong wins big at the Asian Games
description: Not only is he the first from the city to win tennis gold at the Asian Games, but he now also has a spot at the 2028 Olympics.
content:
Tennis player Coleman Wong Chak-lam won his historic men’s singles title at the Asian Games earlier this month.
The 22-year-old Hongkonger was facing China’s Wu Yibing, who is ranked No 111 in the world. Winning would also come with a place at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
Wong’s triumph at Higashiyama Park Tennis Centre suggests the 99 players ranked above him should worry.
His gold was the eighth the city’s athletes had won in Japan. Within the city’s overall medal count of 54 is a record 11 golds. This was three more than in 2023.
“Before the Games started, I was just hoping to win a medal, regardless of the colour,” Wong said. “But honestly, now reaching this point, winning this medal, you can call it unlocking an achievement.”
Wong also explained the role his family played in getting him to this stage of his tennis career.
“Since I was young, my family always had the mindset of, ‘OK, if you want to do it, just go for it’,” Wong said. “I went abroad ... to try at a very young age.”
He hopes his success can convince other families in the city to take a leap of faith in sports.

title: Hopes for stock support rise in China ahead of CSRC head Wu Qing’s speech
description: Possible measures include state buying, IPO slowdown and encouragement for buy-backs and long-term capital, asset manager says.
content: Chinese investors are gearing up for a speech next week by the chief of the securities watchdog for clues on how Beijing will ramp up support for the country’s stock market after its latest efforts did little to bolster sentiment. Wu Qing, chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), is due to deliver a keynote speech at the Financial Street Forum in Beijing on Monday. Other top financial regulators including central bank governor Pan Gongsheng will also address the four-day conference. Investors will closely scrutinise Wu’s speech after the CSRC’s recent efforts to talk up stocks fell short of reviving confidence. Speculation is rife that regulators will come up with more measures to prop up stocks if sentiment worsens. The CSRC convened a symposium with market participants over the weekend, with Wu signalling market-stabilising measures and touting the resilience of China’s economy. Possible measures on the table included direct state buying, encouragement of more buy-backs by listed companies, guidance for entry of long-term capital and slower approvals of initial public offerings (IPOs), according to investors including Huichen Asset Management. “The CSRC will very probably do more to put a floor under the stock market, should stocks fall further,” said Dai Ming, a fund manager at the Shanghai-based asset-management firm. “The most direct way to intervene is state buying, and slowing the pace of IPOs is possible as well.” Mainland equities have taken a pounding amid deteriorating sentiment on global technology stocks and China’s weak domestic demand. This week, the CSI 300 Index traded close to its lowest level in 14 months, and a gauge of the 50 biggest stocks on the chip-centric Star Market fell to a nadir not seen since April. The latest state intervention dates back to July, when China’s two state buyers bought at least 60 billion yuan (US$9 billion) of stocks to arrest a decline triggered by a rout on artificial intelligence bets globally. Stocks stabilised afterwards alongside more evidence of strong demand for AI buildout. The recent sell-offs were more related to positioning and an uptick in global longer-dated bonds than to the domestic economic fundamentals, according to Li Xuewei, a fund manager at HSBC Jintrust Fund Management. He pointed to the gains in utilities, banks and other dividend stocks as evidence that the decline was not caused by a systemic risk. “The pullback in Chinese technology stocks is more about changes of sentiment and positioning,” Li said. “We may see a repair window after sentiment calms and the positioning reaches a rebalance.” Shiva Capital Group, one of China’s biggest hedge fund firms with at least 10 billion yuan of assets under management, lambasted domestic insurers for causing the market swings. In a recent letter to clients, founder Liang Hong accused big insurance firms of massively cutting holdings of technology stocks last month to minimise losses after chasing the AI bets in July. Meanwhile, deleveraging was still under way, putting further restraint on stocks. The outstanding balance of stocks bought with borrowed money on the mainland’s exchanges dropped 5 per cent over the past two months to 2.52 trillion yuan on Monday, according to the data from China Securities Finance. The CSRC’s persistent push for market-stabilising mechanisms would eventually override these challenges, according to Chasing Securities. The combined value of buy-backs and dividend payouts by listed companies exceeded 7 trillion yuan since the State Council issued a high-stakes document outlining a long-term blueprint for the capital market in 2024, it said. “The market is subject to the fallout of sentiment and even speculation in the short term,” said Yuan Chuang, an analyst at the brokerage. “But in the long run, it will reflect companies’ intrinsic values. Investors should stick to value investing against the backdrop of bigger volatility.”

title: Abby Choi’s ex-mother-in-law urged delay in calling police until ransom from ‘kidnappers’, court hears
description: Choi’s partner, Chris Tam, tells Hong Kong High Court that Jenny Li tried to paint the model’s disappearance as an abduction.
content: The former mother-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung tried to prevent her family from reporting her disappearance to police by suggesting that they wait for her “kidnappers” to issue their demands, a court has heard. Choi’s partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, told the High Court on Wednesday that Jenny Li Sui-heung had tried to paint the influencer’s disappearance as an abduction, saying he should delay calling police until after the perpetrators contacted him. “Li Sui-heung said to me: ‘Maybe they just want money. They still haven’t called you. If you report to police now, how can they extort money from you?’” Tam said on the second day of his testimony. The 28-year-old model was last seen alive on February 21, 2023, before parts of her dismembered remains were discovered at a flat in Tai Po’s Lung Mei Village three days later. Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and his elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are on trial after pleading not guilty to a joint count of murder. Li is not a defendant in the trial. The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the burial of Choi’s body, an offence to which his two sons pleaded guilty before the trial began last month. Prosecutors argued the murder arose from a family feud over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.2 million) flat at the upscale Kadooria development in Ho Man Tin. Kwong Kau, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the flat and enlisted his two sons to help kill the influencer so he could keep it for himself. Tam said his partner became unreachable by phone after she sent him the last message at 2.06pm on February 21. He initially thought her phone was malfunctioning, but later found it unusual that it appeared to have been turned on and off when location data suggested the device was in Tai Po. Tam said the Kwong brothers and their mother appeared calm and unconcerned by Choi’s disappearance when he visited them at the Kadooria flat that evening. The court heard Tam and Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, filed a missing-person report at Cheung Sha Wan Police Station later that night. Cheung also called the Kwong brothers to ask about her daughter’s whereabouts but ended up quarrelling with them, Tam said. The next day, Tam asked Anthony Kwong, who was serving as Choi’s stand-in chauffeur at the time, to show him where he dropped off the socialite in Tai Po the previous day. The witness said Kwong, whom he also referred to as Damon, “beat around the bush” and claimed that Choi got off “around the area of Tai Po centre”, suggesting that she might have gone into one of the many shopping centres in the district. Choi’s former brother-in-law also allegedly put on an act by driving Tam to Tai Po on February 23 to help him look for Choi, before a police officer called Tam that afternoon saying the force suspected the Kwong family was linked to the model’s disappearance. Tam said Anthony Kwong subsequently met police ostensibly to offer help before he was arrested in the early hours of the following day. The witness appeared emotional as he lamented his failure to realise sooner that those close to him could have been behind the crime. “So when I look back at the conversations, it turns out that you were taking me in another direction, and all along you were just lying to me and deceiving me,” he added, addressing Kwong. In cross-examination, Tam revealed that he and Choi used to have a close relationship with Kwong, and that they would often hang out and travel to Macau and mainland China for fun. He said the couple would bear almost 85 per cent of their expenses on food, whereas Kwong paid for the remaining 15 per cent. Tam acknowledged that he once borrowed HK$5 million to gamble in Macau during a trip with Choi and Kwong in August 2021. As a result of his failure to repay the loan, he noticed what appeared to be a group of debt collectors lurking around their home in Kowloon Tong in early 2022. Kwong’s legal counsel, Trevor Beel, suggested that his client gave Choi HK$600,000 to help her settle the debt, but Tam said he had no idea and had never heard anyone saying that. Tam also rejected Beel’s contention that Choi saw Kwong differently when she suggested that they should sever ties with the family following a bitter row in mid-2022. “She might have told me that Damon was OK, but after all he belongs to the Kwong family. Whatever happened, they would cover up for each other,” he added. Beel immediately followed up: “So they were guilty by association?” Tam explained that he was only saying Anthony Kwong would often stand by his mother, Jenny Li, whenever an argument arose between her and Choi. Tam said that Li, who lived with the two children Choi had with Alex Kwong at the Kadooria flat, had allowed them to visit Kwong Kau during the Chinese New Year holiday in January 2023. Choi was reportedly furious because she had barred Kwong Kau from making contact with his grandchildren. When Choi tried to contact the children by phone, Anthony Kwong and the rest of his family appeared evasive and refused to let her know that they had gone to see their grandfather, Tam added. Asked why Choi did not arrange for the two children to live with her and their stepfather, Tam said she was concerned that the arrangement might not be acceptable to the children’s paternal grandparents. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: C919 set to lead way as Chinese aircraft forecast to secure 5% of world market in 20 years
description: Cirium’s aircraft fleet outlook says Airbus and Boeing will continue to dominate despite ‘gradual shift’ to emerging players like Comac.
content: China’s chief civilian aircraft builder will command 5 per cent of the world’s fleet allocation by 2045 as global demand for narrowbody jets and the domestic order book look strong, an aviation analytics firm has forecast. Airbus would have 47 per cent of the passenger fleet allocation and Boeing 39 per cent, both leading state-owned Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (Comac), analytics firm Cirium forecast on Tuesday. It said Embraer would take 3 per cent and ATR 2 per cent. Comac has a roughly 1 per cent share of today’s world fleet allocation, independent aviation analyst Li Hanming said. In a summary of its annual aircraft fleet outlook, Cirium said the forecast allocations would “illustrate the persistence of the Airbus and Boeing concentration alongside the gradual shift” towards emerging manufacturers. Shanghai-based Comac is trying to expand its world market share through sales of its C909 regional jet and narrowbody C919. The C919, which debuted commercially in 2023, has received more than 1,000 orders from Chinese airlines, but Comac delivered just 15 last year, below a target of 75, and only three in the first quarter of this year. Comac is still seeking certification to enable C919 flights in the European Union, while the United States is reportedly restricting shipments of American-made aircraft engines and other parts to China, delaying the company’s production plans. China would account for 18 per cent of the world’s aircraft fleet allocation by 2045, Cirium’s report said, with narrowbody jets leading other larger variants because of their “greater seat capacity and unit cost efficiency”. Narrowbody planes represent 76 per cent of the modelled passenger fleet allocation, compared with just 3 per cent for regional jets. The single-aisle C919 is comparable to the Airbus A320 and Boeing 737 models. Cirium said the global passenger fleet was expected to see compound annual growth of 3.2 per cent in the years to 2045, slightly below the growth rate it forecast last year. It said global supply chain bottlenecks, cost pressures and “geopolitical uncertainty” were limiting the pace of added capacity. It forecast that about 43,000 new passenger jets, freighter jets and turboprop aircraft would be delivered globally between 2026 and 2045 – with an estimated total value of US$3.2 trillion in today’s dollars – and that more than 50,000 passenger aircraft would be in use by 2045.

title: Hong Kong bus operators seek fare increases of up to 17.7% amid fuel price surge
description: Citybus asks for 17.7 per cent increase, while KMB seeks 16 per cent, with the government saying it will take public affordability into account.
content: Four Hong Kong franchised bus operators have applied to raise fares by up to 17.7 per cent, citing “significant financial pressure” from soaring fuel prices driven by the Middle East conflict. Citybus has sought the steepest increase, at 17.7 per cent, followed by KMB at 16 per cent. Long Win Bus and New Lantao Bus have applied for rises of 8.1 per cent and 9.8 per cent respectively, according to a paper the Transport and Logistics Bureau submitted to the Legislative Council on Wednesday. The bureau said the sharp rise in diesel pump prices triggered by turmoil in the region had imposed an additional burden on the operators, creating “significant financial pressure and operational difficulties”. It noted that the four companies’ fuel purchase prices jumped by about 75 to 134 per cent in March compared with January, pushing fuel expenditure up by 85 to 132 per cent over the same period. Oil prices were expected to remain high amid uncertainty over the trajectory of the Middle East war, the bureau added. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan pledged that the government would act as a diligent gatekeeper when assessing the applications and would take public affordability into account. “We attach great importance to the service reliability and financial sustainability of the bus companies. At the same time, we are equally concerned about affordability for the public. We will certainly perform our gatekeeping role well,” Chan told reporters after attending the legislature’s meeting on Wednesday. “We will take various factors into account. In particular, we will examine the franchised bus companies’ coming operating situation, cost and revenue projections, long-term financial outlook, and the impact on services.” According to the paper, the four companies recorded profits ranging from HK$7.92 million to HK$369 million in 2025. However, all four are estimated to have recorded a substantial decline in profit in the first half of this year. KMB carried an average of 2.53 million passengers a day this year and recorded a post-tax profit of HK$369.32 million in 2025. But it estimated a 55 per cent drop in profit for the first half of this year. New Lantao Bus and Long Win Bus, which carried 110,000 and 140,000 passengers a day respectively, recorded post-tax profits of HK$7.92 million and HK$46.44 million last year. Their profits were estimated to have fallen by 129 per cent and 31 per cent respectively as of June this year. In response to media queries, KMB and Long Win Bus said the sharp surge in fuel costs has “severely impacted” their operating finances. “Refined oil prices remain persistently high and subject to extreme volatility,” the companies said in a joint statement. Without government subsidies, they said their operational conditions had been affected despite implementing cost-control measures. Citybus, which carried an average of 890,000 passengers a day, made a post-tax profit of HK$39.02 million last year, but estimated a 52 per cent fall for the first half of this year. Citybus said that its application for a fare increase has been “carefully considered” to balance public demand and the company’s financial sustainability, due to a significant surge in fuel prices and rising operating costs over the past two years. Justifying its proposed increase, Citybus said the fluctuations in international refined oil prices caused by the Middle East situation were “far greater” than those in crude oil prices, resulting in a more direct impact on franchised bus companies. “Experts estimate that international refined oil prices are unlikely to return to pre-conflict levels in the short term,” it said. The bureau said in the paper that the operating environment of the firms was expected to remain challenging, owing to factors such as competition from other public transport modes, continuously rising operating costs and wages, and persistently high oil prices due to disruptions to the fuel supply chain. “Furthermore, franchised bus operators need to continue making long-term capital investments, such as introducing new energy buses and the associated facilities, to enhance service quality,” it said. “It is necessary for franchised bus operators to further strengthen their financial positions and long-term financial sustainability so as to continue providing proper and efficient bus services.” The bureau said the government would consider all relevant factors when scrutinising the applications, including oil prices as a component of operating costs. It stressed that future changes in fuel prices would be fully taken into account in subsequent applications. Legislator Ben Chan Han-pan said the proposed increases were “exceptionally high” and called for scrutiny by the Executive Council when looking at the applications. He said that the fare increases would “undoubtedly place a heavy financial burden” on the public and disrupt their daily lives. If the government did not reintroduce subsidies for the operators, it might be “difficult to suppress” the final approved fare increases, Chan said. “This could force companies to cut service frequencies, impacting citizens’ daily commutes,” he said. Ex-lawmaker Michael Tien Puk-sun, a former chairman of the Kowloon-Canton Railway Corporation, said franchised buses’ fare adjustments should be linked to an annual, transparent mechanism similar to the MTR Corporation’s fare adjustment formula based on a basket of indicators such as inflation, wage changes and a productivity factor. “This formula provides the best approach, avoiding the current process where the Executive Council reviews applications and triggers multi-year debates,” he said. In 2024, KMB and New Lantao Bus both applied to raise fares by 6.5 per cent, while Citybus was seeking an increase of nearly 9.5 per cent for most of its routes. Last January, the Executive Council gave KMB the green light to raise fares by 4.3 per cent, and New Lantao Bus and Citybus by 6.5 per cent and 7.5 per cent, respectively. The Legco transport panel will discuss the fare-increase proposals on Friday. After soliciting the views of lawmakers and the Transport Advisory Committee, the government will submit its recommendations to the Executive Council for final approval.

title: Small acts, shared dreams: students find purpose in helping children in need
description: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalists Dream Compassioneers help young people discover their potential through volunteer work supporting children.
content: About 300 Hong Kong students applied this year for roughly 30 places on an overseas programme to help children in need, up from about 50 applicants last year. Dream Compassioneers co-founder Chan Yik-yeung said the response also showed what students could achieve when trusted with responsibility. Founded in 2020, the organisation runs local and overseas service programmes and is a member of the International Association for Volunteer Effort. Its recent projects have taken volunteers to Cambodia, the Philippines and Nepal. Contacts made at an international volunteer conference in South Korea also led to exchanges with organisations in Zambia. Participants can begin in junior committee roles before taking on responsibilities in event planning and fundraising, and eventually move into executive positions. “We hope to serve the world and let more people understand those who need help, but nurturing young people is also an important part of what we do,” Chan said. Co-founder and executive director Ice Or Ka-ying balances running her own start-up with what amounts to a full-time role at Dream Compassioneers, despite the organisation having no paid staff. Its network includes advisers, board members, executive committee members and school-based service clubs. For Or, this embodies the “Hong Kong spirit”. “Everyone contributes what they can, and we work towards the same goal,” she said. Before sending larger groups overseas, the organisation sends smaller teams to visit potential partners and assess arrangements. It also maintains contact with government bodies, Chinese diplomatic missions and local organisations. During a recent programme in Nepal, participants visited four institutions serving children in difficult circumstances. Or said many students wanted to take part again after returning to Hong Kong. Chan recalled how children at one institution remembered volunteers from the previous year and asked about them by name. Students also brought donated stationery and other supplies, while the group sought to identify needs that Hong Kong organisations could help meet. In Cambodia, Dream Compassioneers has established the Trabaek Community Dream Compassioneers Preschool, which provides education and daily meals for children in rural communities. Volunteering has also shaped some members’ study choices. Adelin Lin Ho-yan, a first-year social work student at the University of Hong Kong and a vice-president of the group’s 2026-27 executive committee, said three years of service activities had helped persuade her to study social work. She previously served as president of the group’s club at Yan Chai Hospital Law Chan Chor Si College. A trip to South Korea was particularly memorable for Lin. “I saw that there were many people from different places who shared the same commitment to serving people in need,” she said. Fellow vice-president Sophia Yau Yuet-sum, a first-year hotel and tourism management student at Chinese University, joined the group in Form Three. She progressed from learning to organise activities to chairing one edition of its debate competition. The executive committee is led by president Charlene Fong Hoi-tung, a first-year mental health nursing student at Hong Kong Metropolitan University. Another vice-president, Yanna Wong Yu-hei, a Form Six student at St Paul’s Convent School, joined after discovering the group’s Chinese New Year fair and debate competition on social media. “Young people may sometimes underestimate what they can do,” Or said. “But when we come together as a team, we can achieve far more than we might expect.” The Spirit of Hong Kong Awards were established in 2013 to recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention.

title: Russia batters Ukraine’s power facilities amid Kyiv’s growing strain with US
description: Zelensky blasts Moscow for ignoring Trump’s truce, as Kyiv cites missing early warnings and throttled Starlink access.
content: Ukraine on Wednesday accused Russia of wilfully flouting Donald Trump’s purported “energy ceasefire” and passing up an opportunity to ease hostilities, after a renewed wave of deadly strikes across the country that also hit vital power supplies. Kyiv in particular faced a barrage of powerful ballistic missiles and attack drones targeting energy facilities and critical infrastructure, despite the US president’s surprise weekend announcement. Four people were killed in the city and power to at least 600,000 people was cut after significant damage was reported to power facilities and equipment. Power plants also came under ballistic missile attack in the eastern Kharkiv region, hitting electricity and heating infrastructure, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said. Zelensky blasted the latest attack as “entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale”, adding: “Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect towards the United States”. “Russia does not consider the American President’s statements strong,” he wrote on X. Trump blindsided both Kyiv and Moscow on Sunday by unilaterally announcing an “energy ceasefire”, two days after enraging Ukraine’s Western allies with news of a deal with heavily sanctioned Russia to supply diesel fuel. The US leader has repeatedly lashed out at Zelensky – and even said he should be replaced as president – for Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. A senior Ukrainian official confirmed to Agence France-Presse reports in recent days that Washington threatened to pull intelligence-sharing with Kyiv that it relies on to detect incoming attacks. The renewed signs of strain with Trump have cast doubt on those arrangements, as air raid sirens warning of approaching drones or missiles failed to sound on Monday night and Tuesday night before explosions were heard. That has occurred only rarely in the past. Ukrainian officials attributed the issue to the Russian military’s use of hard-to-detect missiles or potential technical issues. But Zelensky on Tuesday evening said Ukraine had received “no early warning from our partners” about ballistic missile launches, calling it “absolutely unjust”. An aide to Zelensky meanwhile said the operation of some Starlink internet terminals also appeared to have been restricted overnight, disrupting “a number of missions” by Ukrainian defence forces. “Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,” said Sergiy Beskrestnov. A senior Ukrainian official said that Starlink speeds had been “throttled”, suggesting that it was done to Russia’s advantage. “What is important is that this has been ongoing since last night. Some restrictions were already being reported yesterday evening, so, in effect, it is happening in sync with this morning’s Russian ballistic attack,” they added. Zelensky has said Ukraine is prepared to hold off from striking Russian energy infrastructure, but accused the Kremlin of having “squandered the opportunity for de-escalation” in the nearly five-year conflict. Russia has previously targeted Ukraine’s power stations and heating infrastructure, crippling supplies before winter, when temperatures can plummet to as low as -20C. Ukraine has been pushing its allies for more military support as Kyiv increasingly comes under attack, particularly the supply of advanced interceptor systems to shoot down missiles and fast, jet-powered drones. Russian ballistic missile attacks were also reported in the eastern region of Kharkiv and Zhytomyr in the northwest, and other strikes hit Sumy in the northeast and Chernigiv in the north. Two people were killed in the central Dnipropetrovsk region and a further person in Zaporizhzhia in the southeast, the authorities said. The governor of Russia’s southwestern Saratov region, citing preliminary estimates, said a Ukrainian drone strike had killed one person in the city of Balakovo. Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin said air defence forces had downed nearly 500 drones flying towards the Russian capital overnight. Russian authorities said around 160 more were brought down over the Rostov region, while others targeted Moscow.

title: South Korean FA condemns ‘personal attacks, criticism’ of players as attempt to sow discord
description: Latest firestorm follows public outrage over behaviour of footballers who earned exemptions from mandatory military service after Asian Games.
content: South Korea’s football association has told fans to stop “excessive personal attacks”, warning of the “psychological burden” they could inflict on national team players in the crosshairs since their World Cup flop. Hong Myung-bo quit as coach after the team failed to advance past the group stage in North America, and Spanish interim manager Robert Moreno is awaiting word on a possible extension. With the Asian Cup scheduled to take place in January in Saudi Arabia, the national side are engulfed by claims of internal divisions. Local media reports say some younger players feel held back by senior members of the squad, including long-time captain Son Heung-min. In a lengthy statement, the Korea Football Association (KFA) condemned what it called attempts to sow discord. “Unverified information and speculative claims about national football team players have recently been spreading on social media and online forums, with some players facing excessive criticism and personal attacks,” the KFA said on Tuesday. “Such behaviour goes beyond the bounds of legitimate criticism and can place a severe psychological burden on individual players,” it said, urging fans to refrain from “making assumptions about internal team dynamics and fuelling divisions within the squad”. Speculation about discord emerged after Bayern Munich defender Kim Min-jae threw his boots in anger after being substituted in the second half of the disappointing home 0-0 draw with Venezuela this month. Kim said afterwards that “every player needs to put their head down and give it their all”, fuelling talk of divisions within the squad. The latest firestorm follows public outrage over the behaviour of some players who earned exemptions from mandatory military service after winning gold at the Asian Games. The controversy erupted after Asian Games football captain Lee Gi-hyuk proclaimed with a smile “I’m not going to the military” after beating hosts Japan in the men’s final this month. He said he would have had to report for duty just nine days later had his team lost, interrupting a lucrative career at its peak. A video of Newcastle United’s 19-year-old Park Seung-soo wearing a military discharge cap tilted to one side and giving a smiling salute further fuelled the outcry. Both players later apologised. Their post-match celebrations, seen as suggesting that military exemptions had been their main motivation, sparked a backlash and prompted Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul to pledge to scale back the benefit. South Korea requires most able-bodied men to perform between 18 and 21 months of military service, but under a system introduced in 1973, athletes who win an Olympic medal of any colour or an Asian Games gold are eligible for an exemption for “enhancing national prestige and promoting culture”.

title: China tests a Dune-like iron-harvesting crawler robot in the Taklamakan Desert
description: Device based on rare earth magnets traverses the sands to extract iron in real-world echo of Frank Herbert’s sci-fi classic.
content: Chinese researchers have built a self-propelled crawler robot that harvests iron from sand and have tested the device in the dunes of the vast Taklamakan Desert – an area the size of Germany – in northwestern China’s Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. In Frank Herbert’s classic science fiction novel Dune, mobile factories traverse the sands of the fictional planet Arrakis to extract the drug melange, also known as “spice”. The real-world device similarly travels across the desert, extracting valuable resources. The rare earth-magnet-based separator, developed by researchers from Tarim University in Xinjiang, filters ferromagnetic materials from sand using dry magnetic separation. According to the team’s study published in the Chinese-language journal Metal Mine, the Taklamakan contains “vast quantities of ferromagnetic materials”, with previous research estimating iron content in its sands of about 6 per cent. “However, their scattered distribution and the difficulty of collection have hindered the effective recovery and utilisation of these resources,” the team said in the paper published on October 8. Testing in the Taklamakan – the world’s second-largest shifting sand desert and the largest desert in China – showed the prototype extracted an average yield of 0.46 per cent magnetic material from the raw sands, the paper said. The average total iron content of the harvested magnetic material was about 28 per cent, indicating the device “is capable of recovering and preliminarily concentrating iron-bearing magnetic materials from desert sand”. The device offers a low-power solution to extracting minerals from the desert, with the prototype operating on the equivalent of a large phone power bank, according to the researchers. Relying on a battery with a capacity of 20,000 milliampere-hours, the 4.3kg (9lb) crawler operated continuously for 12.5 hours at an average speed of 1.5cm per second, maintaining stability while navigating 20-degree slopes. The device also has a mounted solar panel that could further extend its operational range, they said. Iron is one of the world’s most abundant and widely used resources. According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS), China ranks fourth globally in crude iron ore reserves at 17 billion tonnes, after Australia with 59 billion tonnes, Russia with 35 billion tonnes and Brazil with 34 billion tonnes. This year’s USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries report also ranked China at No 4 – after Australia, Brazil and India – in usable ore production in 2025. Despite China’s significant iron ore reserves, imports still account for most of the country’s consumption of the resource. According to the Chinese paper, the country’s iron ore resources are characterised by complex compositions and low grades, which lead to low recovery rates and less efficient utilisation. The team said preliminary surveys had indicated the existence of iron-bearing magnetic components in the sands of the Taklamakan Desert, with previous research indicating the iron content in the desert was around 6 per cent. The Taklamakan Desert covers 337,600 sq km (130,350 square miles), about the size of Germany. One way to extract those scattered minerals is through magnetic separation, which sorts materials based on differences in their magnetic properties. The team said that traditional manual separation techniques such as magnetic attraction, visual sorting and gravity washing were “ill-suited to the extreme conditions of the desert environment”. To take on these challenges, they designed a dry magnetic separator that relies on a ring of neodymium iron boron (NdFeB) permanent magnets to sort through the sand and pull out magnetic particles. China dominates production of NdFeB permanent magnets, the strongest commercially available rare earth magnets which play a critical role in the production of electric vehicles and aerospace components. At the end of 2023, China banned the export of rare earth processing technologies, including those needed for making neodymium iron boron permanent magnets. China has also imposed strict export controls on certain types of NdFeB magnets. Relying on a tracked chassis to move across the sand, the device uses a rotating feeding mechanism that scoops up sand in buckets and dumps it into a feed inlet leading to the magnetic separator, according to the paper. Inside, the NdFeB permanent magnet array attracts magnetic materials to the surface of a central drum. As the drum rotates, iron and other materials move into a magnet-free zone before dropping into a discharge chute. Meanwhile, any non-magnetic materials fall out of a separate sand discharge outlet. In June 2025, the team carried out a prototype performance test of the device, evaluating its climbing ability and energy consumption, and found it could cover a distance of 18.2 metres (60 feet) for every 3 per cent of battery consumed. A study of the separated magnetic material showed total iron content of around 24 per cent and 32 per cent in two representative samples. The researchers said the iron content of the enriched samples was “significantly higher” than ordinary silica sand samples and was accompanied by elements such as titanium and manganese. “Overall, the magnetic separator designed in this study is capable of the preliminary recovery and enrichment of iron-bearing magnetic materials from desert sand,” the team said. They noted that some fluctuations still occurred between tests, which could be due to the uneven distribution of ferromagnetic components in the sand as well as varying terrain. However, “overall trends remained consistent, indicating fundamental stability in the prototype’s separation process”, they said. Passionate about science? title: No rush to T+1: Hong Kong exchange won’t hurry settlement-time change, sources say
description: Market players support the change to keep up with global peers, but many worry the fourth quarter of 2027 would be too soon, sources say.
content: Participants in Hong Kong’s stock market may need to wait longer for shorter transaction settlement times, as market participants want more time to prepare for the change, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) said in a consultation paper in April that it aimed to implement a so-called T+1 system – under which trades would be settled one day after transactions – in the fourth quarter of 2027, replacing the existing T+2 cycle. Conclusions from the consultation process would be revealed soon, but HKEX could extend the timeline after many participants said they wanted more time for training before the change, a source told the South China Morning Post. “While many brokers and other market participants generally agree on the benefits of following the international trend to shorten the settlement cycle, some expressed worry that implementing the change in the fourth quarter of 2027 was too soon,” the source said. The source said large institutional investors worried about the chance more than local brokerages because time differences meant they would often have less than a day for settlement. “Cross-border settlement involves a lot of money transfers and stock transfers,” the source said. “It would be better for HKEX to arrange more testing and workshops next year to let brokers and banks get ready.” The fourth quarter of 2027 was always a tentative target, and the bourse operator had consistently indicated it would only make the change when market players were ready, one of the sources said. The new target would be in 2028, as the bourse would allow time for system testing and educational workshops for brokers, banks and investors before even confirming a launch date, the source added. An HKEX spokesman said the bourse operator received feedback from many stakeholders during the consultation period that ended in May. If Hong Kong fails to keep up with markets like the US and Australia … it risks losing its competitive edge globally Paul Pong Po-lam, Pegasus Fund Managers “Their feedback will help facilitate a smooth and orderly transition of Hong Kong’s securities market to a T+1 settlement cycle,” the spokesman said. “We are preparing our consultation conclusions; further details will be announced in due course.” The US and Canada shifted to T+1 in May 2024, while the UK and Europe were exploring the same option, according to HKEX CEO Bonnie Chan Yiting. Mainland China has long operated under a T+1 cycle. Robert Lee Wai-wang, a lawmaker for the financial services sector and chairman of Grand Finance Group, said he also heard feedback from larger financial institutions that may require more time to handle T+1. “It is not fundamentally a matter of rejecting the change to T+1, but needing more time due to complex operational arrangements that need to be changed,” Lee said. “The core issue is the compressed time frame caused by time zone differences,” said a global fund manager, who was not authorised to speak publicly and requested anonymity. Overseas operations teams could be left with just a few hours to complete settlement workflows, significantly increasing the risk of settlement failures and penalties, the person said. Custodians and foreign funds would be expected to absorb higher operating costs by expanding headcount, shifting coverage hours and automating settlement workflows, the manager added. Paul Pong Po-lam, managing director of Pegasus Fund Managers, said moving to a T+1 was an inevitable global trend. “If Hong Kong fails to keep up with markets like the US and Australia, which have already adopted or plan to adopt T+1, it risks losing its competitive edge globally,” he said. Regulators should closely assess the readiness of market players, especially smaller firms and mainland-backed institutions with limited resources, to help them overcome their operational challenges, he added.

title: Malaysian turtle conservation heroes in Sabah unite to fight poachers
description: A group of volunteers is monitoring poachers to help stop the illegal trade of protected turtles and protect the state’s rich ocean biodiversity.
content:
Roziah Jelali knows what you need to catch a turtle poacher: a pair of binoculars and patience in spades. The 36-year-old Malaysian volunteer ranger once spent three months in Sabah, a Malaysian state in the north of the island of Borneo, tracking a man she suspected of illegally capturing protected turtles.
Once a reptile that thrived in the azure seas of Omadal Island, part of Sabah, many turtles have been hunted, killed and sold for their meat, according to conservation experts.
Recounting the 2023 incident, Roziah said she patrolled the beach from dawn daily to keep an eye on the poacher. She would scribble detailed notes on her target’s movements at her stilted home, backed by tips from her network of part-time conservationists on nearby islands.
“Every day after my patrol, I would sit near my house with my binoculars and watch him. He was initially operating on Bum Bum Island, then he came to Omadal,” Roziah told South China Morning Post. “He would kill the turtle at sea, then when he returned, he would cut it open and cook it on the boat.”
Her careful surveillance led to the rescue of a live turtle and a crackdown against an illicit ring selling turtle meat in the waters of Omadal and the town of Semporna. Using Roziah’s information, wildlife officials caught the poacher and an accomplice. They were accused of illegally catching five turtles, four of which were butchered for their meat.
Roziah did not learn the anti-poaching skills on her own. She received training from Sabah’s Wildlife Department and WWF-Malaysia while learning more about the rich biodiversity off the state’s east coast, such as the seagrass, sea grapes and green turtles.
She and four other women are part of a volunteer watchdog committed to protecting the marine life that once thrived around Omadal Island but has been threatened with extinction due to poaching.
They are also adept at craftwork, regularly weaving pandan leaves into mats and baskets. Their husbands also have strong ties to the sea, as sustainability is crucial to their jobs as fishers.
As volunteers with the Women’s Association of Omadal Island (WAPO), the women would share findings with their peers.
According to WAPO chairwoman Sitti Rasah Haji Abdul, the association has not recorded any turtle landings on Omadal and other nearby islands since last year. In the past, turtles would lay their eggs in guarded hatcheries, and this would help prevent attacks by predators like monitor lizards or theft by villagers.
While Sitti is disappointed about the disappearance of nesting turtles, she is determined to do her part to bring about their safe return.
Sea turtles have been a fully protected species under Sabah’s wildlife conservation laws since 1997. According to marine life experts, the presence of these turtles is a key sign of a healthy marine environment.
Through their grazing, green turtles contribute to the growth of seagrass meadows, which store carbon that is biologically essential for fish and shellfish. Nesting turtles also help move nutrients from the sea onto beaches and keep jellyfish populations in check.
But the threat of illegal turtle trading extends beyond Malaysia’s Borneo shores.
The waters surrounding Sabah form part of the trafficking corridor spanning the Sulu-Celebes Seas between Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia, according to the wildlife trade monitoring group Traffic.
Turtle eggs are particularly prized by poachers, according to Elizabeth John, Traffic’s communications manager.
The Sulu-Celebes Seas accounted for most of the illicit wildlife trade activities involving turtles between June 2003 and September 2021, according to the latest available data in a Traffic report released in 2023.
“Our records from that study period showed cases of stockpiled dead green sea turtles, the discovery of live hawksbill turtles with missing scutes in the north of Sabah and other turtle parts seized several times in the Semporna district,” John said.
While Sabah’s law enforcement agencies have been active, the state continues to be a hotspot for illegal turtle trade.
“The seizure cases in Semporna district included people from island communities instructed by middlemen to poach turtles at turtle foraging grounds,” John said.
In November last year, police and wildlife authorities raided premises in Semporna and seized 570 hawksbill turtle scutes weighing 17.8kg and valued at US$3,450 (HK$105,550), believed to be destined for the black market.
They arrested two people, including a foreign national.
Between eastern Sabah and the southern Philippines, the Celebes-Sulu Sea provides ready cover for wildlife criminal gangs to hide among fishers, cargo and passenger boats, said Ramli Dollah, a lecturer and maritime security expert at the Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities at Universiti Malaysia Sabah.
“The same boats, operators, routes, landing points and intermediaries can move people or different types of goods,” said Dollah, who referred to their system of “co-riding and camouflage”.
The vast area in Sabah and beyond poses a formidable challenge for enforcement agencies to catch poachers and smugglers, according to Dollah.
Maritime security specialist Nazery Khalid, an adjunct professor at the University of Malaysia, Terengganu, said the vast Sulu-Celebes Seas were difficult for poorly resourced Malaysian and Philippine authorities to patrol.
“There may be cooperation among them in areas such as intelligence sharing, but without maintaining boots on the ground in the form of operationally fit vessels, traffickers can operate with impunity or outmanoeuvre the enforcement agencies’ vessels,” he said.
Sitti and Roziah consider their roles complementary to those of the enforcement agencies as they pursue the common goals of boosting Malaysia’s turtle population and conservation of other species.
“If not me, then who will do it for the generations to come?” Sitti said. “As long as I am still able to carry out conservation work, I will continue.”
Sitti added that she and the volunteers faced constant risks of potential confrontation with turtle poachers and stormy weather when they were out on boat patrol.
These challenges do not faze Roziah. “We must have courage and determination. That is the most important thing,” she said.

title: Asia must guard against repeat of 1997 financial crisis: Philippine central bank chief
description: The pre-crash boom of the 1990s ‘wasn’t really a miracle’, Eli Remolona says, urging Asean to prepare for fresh shocks.
content: Asian countries must remind themselves about what happened during the region’s financial crisis in the late 1990s and guard against a recurrence of such shocks, the head of the Philippine central bank said ‌on Wednesday. Before the Asian financial crisis started in 1997, regional economies saw huge capital inflows that prompted the World Bank to describe it as the “East Asian miracle”, Eli Remolona, governor of the central bank, said in an International Monetary Fund panel on the outlook for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. “Investment poured into Asia and then you had the crisis because it wasn’t really a miracle. I think we have to remind ourselves about that. We have to guard against that kind of crisis,” ⁠he said. “We have not really been making a lot of effort looking at that kind of crisis.” It wasn’t really a miracle. I think we have to remind ourselves about that Eli Remolona, Philippine central bank governor The remarks came at the ‌annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank being held in Bangkok, Thailand, which was an epicentre of the Asian financial crisis. Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF’s Asia and Pacific Department, pushed back against the ‌view, arguing in the panel discussion that the IMF had made progress assessing financial vulnerabilities and potential spillovers among ⁠each economy. “We have taken [the ⁠crisis] to heart, and we’ve dealt with a framework to talk about how should countries deal with volatile capital flows in terms … such as when should they intervene ‌in foreign exchange markets and so on,” Srinivasan said. Srinivasan also said while Asean economies had weathered the trade tensions caused by US tariffs fairly well, their energy intensity could be ‌among risks ‌to the outlook as some countries rely heavily on oil and gas imports. Atsushi Mimura, Japan’s vice finance minister for international affairs, ‌also cited the energy shock from the Middle East conflict, as well as rising inflation, as among short-term risks to the region’s outlook. “Of ⁠course, we all know that it [fiscal support] should be ‘triple T’ – targeted, tailored and temporary,” Mimura said on how economies should exercise discipline ⁠in delivering spending to cushion the blow to households and firms from the energy shock. As many countries face competitive pressure from China, Asean members should focus on further strengthening investment to diversify supply chains in critical minerals and energy, Mimura said, ‌a drive Japan was willing ‌to support. “All Asean countries should definitely further invest so that they can always catch up with AI and innovation,” Mimura told the panel. “At the same time, I think Asean countries are really well positioned in the supply chain for digitalisation because they’re producing critical minerals.” The 11-member Asean bloc comprises Brunei, Cambodia, East Timor, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

title: Global deforestation fell in 2025, but Congo Basin losses surged
description: Worldwide destruction dropped 15 per cent, though impending super El Nino threatens 2030 targets.
content: Deforestation slowed worldwide last year, but the improvement is unlikely to last as the situation deteriorates in Central Africa and an exceptionally strong El Nino weather pattern intensifies, a new study said on Wednesday. Seven million hectares of forest – roughly the size of the Republic of Ireland – were permanently destroyed in 2025, a 15 per cent drop from the previous year, according to the annual Forest Declaration Assessment. The slowdown, however, is not enough to keep the world from missing a pledge to end deforestation by 2030, according to the report, which was drafted by a coalition of research groups and non-governmental organisations. The 2025 figure is “encouraging but so far it’s the exception, not a new trajectory”, Erin Matson, the study’s co-author and lead consultant at advisory group Climate Focus, said in a media briefing. To meet the target, agreed at the United Nations’ Cop26 climate talks in 2021, deforestation would have to fall by around 1 million hectares per year. Clearing forests for agriculture or mining operations remains the leading drivers of deforestation. Last year’s improvement was due in part to progress in Latin America, with a 33 per cent drop in what has historically been the world’s deforestation “hotspot”, according to the study. The authors pointed particularly to Brazil’s deforestation action plan and increased enforcement in the country’s Amazon. Progress in the region, however, “rests heavily on the choices of a small number of governments and remains highly vulnerable” to recent and coming elections across the Amazon basin. Brazil’s left-wing leader, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva – who has vowed to end illegal deforestation by 2030 – faces populist right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in a run-off presidential election on October 25. Deforestation had surged under the administration of Bolsonaro’s father, far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro. Progress could also be threatened in Colombia and Peru, where hard-right presidents were recently elected, according to the experts. Across the Atlantic in Africa, the situation deteriorated in the Congo Basin, where rainforest loss reached 2.4 million hectares – near the same level of deforestation as the Amazon for the first time. The Congo Basin, a region larger than India that stretches across 12 African nations from Cross River in Nigeria to the Rift Valley in East Africa, is the world’s second-biggest tropical forest area and its biggest tropical carbon sink. Its vegetation absorbs millions of tonnes of planet-warming carbon dioxide a year. It ranks among the world’s most-biodiverse areas, boasting 10,000 plant species and forests that provide homes for four species of great apes, as well as forest elephants and okapis – an endangered relative of the giraffe. “Losing such a size of forest every year is a disaster,” said Sam Nguiffo, a lawyer and founder of the Centre for Environment and Development in Cameroon. “As humanity, we clearly cannot afford that because it will be totally irreversible,” he said. El Nino, the warming phase of a natural climate cycle, also threatens progress because its effects include droughts, creating conditions for wildfires. The current El Nino event, which emerged in June, is expected to peak later this year but is already shaping up to be the strongest ever observed. El Nino has been associated with strong drought in Indonesia, where tracts of forest and plantations have been burning in biodiverse Borneo and South Sumatra for months. “If projections of the historically strong 2026-27 El Nino materialise, drought and fire risks will intensify further across tropical forest regions,” the deforestation report said. Matson, of Climate Focus, noted that there was a “huge spike” in tree cover loss during the last “super” El Nino event in 2015-2016. “We can’t fully predict the future but it’s unlikely, I would say, that in 2026 we’ll see the same kind of reductions (in deforestation) that we saw last year,” she said. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: 13 years in prison for former care home warden who raped intellectually disabled woman
description: Hong Kong judge slams former carer’s ‘extremely despicable’ crimes, saying defendant had not only abused his power but also displayed no remorse.
content: A Hong Kong court has sentenced a former assistant warden at a care home for people with intellectual disabilities to 13 years in prison for raping a female resident five times, with the judge condemning the assaults as “extremely despicable”. High Court Judge Douglas Yau Tak-hong on Wednesday sentenced Chung Pui-kei, 38, who was found guilty of five counts of raping the 23-year-old resident at Hong Chi Pinehill Integrated Vocational Training Centre Kwong Fuk Hostel in Tai Po. “The defendant’s crime is extremely despicable and he is at risk of reoffending,” Yau said. “Even the psychiatrist or psychologist found no remorse in [him]. That is appalling.” The judge chastised Chung for “abusing his power” as the victim’s carer and betraying the trust his employer and the victim’s family had placed in him. He noted that the 13-year sentence reflected the gravity of Chung’s crimes. Prosecutors had proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Chung had assaulted the resident three times in a male staff room and twice in her room between July 13 and August 9, 2024. The victim’s intellectual developmental disorder means she has the mental capacity of a nine-year-old. The defendant’s decision to plead not guilty had resulted in the victim being called to testify in court and having to recall her ordeal, the judge said. During her testimony, the victim said she had refused Chung’s advances and expressed discomfort during the assaults, but had not dared to speak out for fear of being scolded by the defendant. Chung told the jury at trial that the reason a DNA test found his semen on the victim’s bedsheet was that he had sat on her bed in his sleepwear, and that his sweat had caused the semen to be transferred through his shorts onto the bed. The judge said the jury’s verdict clearly rejected the defendant’s absurd arguments. “This explanation was absolutely ridiculous – a total waste of the court’s and the jury’s time,” he said. Yau said the assaults were premeditated, citing evidence that showed Chung had intentionally groomed the woman to develop feelings for him. As the victim’s carer at the time, Chung told her they could be together in a romantic relationship once their circumstances changed. Yau said the defendant clearly knew the victim had the mental capacity of a child and behaved like one, and was unable to push back against an adult in a position of authority. The court noted that Chung, a psychology graduate, had told a case psychiatrist that he had a difficult time in custody and once hit his own head against a wall in distress. But after a medical assessment, correctional officers reported him to be psychologically healthy. Chung did not submit any mitigation to the court. His relatives had submitted statements praising him as a “dutiful” son. Hong Chi Association, the city’s largest NGO serving people with intellectual disabilities, said on Wednesday it was deeply saddened by what had happened, adding that justice had been served by the court’s ruling. In August 2024, it appointed an independent committee headed by a former Law Society president to review oversight at its facility.

title: Submerged to save Bangkok: rural Thais bear brunt of capital’s flood defences
description: Thailand deliberately funnels monsoon floodwaters into villages north of Bangkok, leaving some homes submerged for months on end.
content: Stilt houses in villages north of Bangkok are no longer high enough to stay dry as Thai authorities deliberately flood riverside communities to spare the capital. Inside the home of Kamonchanok Sathaphonamonwut, raised more than three metres (10 feet) above the ground in Ayutthaya province, her family of three sleeps on makeshift platforms and cannot use the waterlogged toilet. Her village has been flooded six years in a row, pushing some to move away, while others have raised their houses higher. “Our area simply cannot cope with this much water any more,” said the 34-year-old, wading through her soaked home. But while authorities prioritise protecting Bangkok and other business hubs from floods, “when it comes to our residential communities, they neglect us”, she said. Thailand experiences flooding every year during the monsoon season and scientists say human-made climate change has made heavy rain and floods more frequent and severe. After devastating floods in 2011, the government expanded embankments, water gates and other infrastructure to direct water away from Bangkok, the historic city of Ayutthaya and industrial zones along the Chao Phraya River, which flows through the capital. The defences have largely kept commercial centres safe, but residents of other areas have been left to fend for themselves. Around 20km (12 miles) from Ayutthaya’s centuries-old temple ruins, a Unesco heritage site, residents say floods that once reached their knees now rise above their heads in some areas and can take several months to recede. Office worker Kamonchanok has been forced to commute by boat and hoist her household appliances and other belongings above the waterline. “All we can do is deal with the consequences,” she said. “There’s only so much we can do to adapt.” Thai irrigation department spokesman Thanet Somboon said climate change, low-lying geography and recently built embankments that altered the natural flow of the Chao Phraya had contributed to more severe flooding of downstream communities. “Even when water is released from the Chao Phraya Dam at the same rate as before, the impact is greater than it used to be,” Thanet said. And after irrigation channels were completely full of diverted water, he said authorities had “no choice but to discharge the remaining water downstream”. But Thanet acknowledged that officials may need to review infrastructure to “ensure floodwater can be kept within the intended limits”. Environmental conservationist Sasin Chalermlarp said the government had done “an excellent job” managing floods across the central plains, but added that its efforts were “cruel” to those bearing the brunt of the flooding. In low-lying riverside districts that serve as flood retention zones, whole stretches of villages could be seen underwater this month, with some homes abandoned and others submerged up to their roofs. Sasin said floodwater that once spread across much of Ayutthaya was now concentrated in just “5 to 10 per cent” of the province. As flooding in hard-hit districts has become more severe, many who remain have paid to lift their stilt houses higher and keep their living space dry. Kamonchanok’s family raised their home twice in the 1990s, the second time by 1.5 metres. But floodwaters reached their house in 2011 and again for the past six consecutive years. Raising a house can cost between 100,000 and 1 million baht (US$3,000 to US$30,000), depending on its size and height, residents say. Some families have lifted their homes twice in just a few years, exhausting their savings and borrowing just to get by.
