Despite spending more than 1 million baht raising her home, Sawong Raksri, 87, is unfazed. “It floods like this every year recently. What’s the point of complaining?” she said. Sasin acknowledged that the area’s low-lying land made it a natural route for floodwaters. “But the villagers have no choice. They are being forced to make sacrifices,” he said. Sasin, who lives in a protected part of Ayutthaya, has proposed a “flood-free tax” on those who benefit from the defences, to help affected families raise their homes and repair damage. Thanet from the irrigation department said the idea warranted further study to determine “how to support people who sacrifice their land to accommodate floodwater”. The government’s flagship fix is a US$780-million flood diversion canal, designed to carry 1,200 cubic metres of water – around half the volume of an Olympic-size swimming pool – per second around the bottleneck where the Chao Phraya narrows through Ayutthaya. It is expected to be completed by 2030. Until then, Kamonchanok said her community was not even demanding an end to intentional flooding, but rather a cap on water levels and financial support for those whose homes sit below the flood line. “All we’re asking for is to be able to live comfortably in our own homes,” she said. “Why can’t they give us that?”

title: Tai Fung Lau at 65: Hong Kong restaurant’s Lu cuisine legacy, Bruce Lee ties and more
description: The history and cultural legacy of Tai Fung Lau can be seen in its interiors and staff, and tasted in its hearty dishes rooted in Lu cuisine.
content: Ask any regular at Tai Fung Lau Peking Restaurant in Hong Kong’s Tsim Sha Tsui district what keeps them coming back, and they are likely to mention its down-to-earth dishes, generous portions and value for money. This year, as the restaurant marks its 65th anniversary, second-generation owner Steven Wan Kwok-keung remains committed to preserving both the hearty portions and the flavours of his father’s kitchen. That determination begins with a subtle distinction many diners might miss until Wan points it out. Tai Fung Lau is often described as a Beijing restaurant, but its culinary roots lie in an older northern tradition from eastern China’s Shandong province. “We are Shandong people; our tradition is Lu cuisine,” Wan explains. “Beijing cuisine is diverse, but a big element of it comes from Lu cuisine.” For Wan, the difference lies in the spirit of the food. “Lu cuisine is hearty: big portions and good value,” he says. “Haipai is more refined.” Haipai refers to the Shanghai-influenced style that reached Beijing from Jiangnan as travel and trade became easier. Tai Fung Lau has never been rigid with its offerings; the Shanghai influences on its menu are evident, but its underlying sensibility remains unmistakably Lu – robust, unfussy and made to satisfy. Steeped in history Tai Fung Lau’s history is not only preserved in its recipes, but also in the stories of the people who have gathered here. In the 1960s and early 70s, painters, calligraphers and writers met at Tai Fung Lau for bihui – bat wui in Cantonese – or brush societies. They ate and drank, exchanged ideas and, once the conversation had set the mood, began to paint and write. One notable visitor was Zhang Daqian, the modern Chinese painter and calligrapher celebrated for his mastery of traditional landscape painting and splashed-ink works. After dining at Tai Fung Lau, Zhang wrote the restaurant’s name in his signature calligraphy. The connection is remarkable; Zhang’s works are highly sought after – in 2022, his Landscape after Wang Ximeng (1948) sold for HK$370 million (US$47 million) at Sotheby’s Hong Kong, setting an auction record for the artist. Zhang’s original brushwork is now kept at Wan’s home, out of public view. A replica, however, has become the restaurant’s logo and signage. Making money from tour groups Wan’s family history begins far from Tsim Sha Tsui. His father, Wan Chi-fun, was from Penglai, in Yantai, Shandong, and moved to Shanghai as a young man. There, he worked around old opera troupes and their masters while training as a chef. After arriving in Hong Kong in the early 1950s, he worked for others before opening a teahouse in Tin Wan, Aberdeen. It was a hard business: fishermen returning from night work ate first, followed by farmers from the surrounding area. The teahouse was a lesson in the fragile economics of the trade. After his HK$10 share of a year-end gift from a supplier – known as pao jin in Mandarin and pao gum in Cantonese, and shared among staff – went missing after someone else collected it, Wan’s father left the teahouse and opened Tai Fung Lau in Tsim Sha Tsui in 1961. The restaurant’s first premises stood near the present-day Hong Kong Jockey Club site on Prat Avenue, in an area dense with northern restaurants. Tai Fung Lau initially served local diners before shifting its focus to Japanese tour groups. There was one problem, however: coaches could not enter the narrow street. Patrons had to walk more than 200 steps from Chatham Road South, the nearest main road, and pickpocketing was common. “They wore suits and drove Mercedes to steal from people,” Wan recalls. When the old premises were demolished for redevelopment, the restaurant moved to its current address around 1979. The walk shrank to about 40 steps, which was shorter, safer and better suited to tour groups. The influx of visitors could turn an ordinary service job into a path to prosperity. At the time, a husband-and-wife team maintained Tai Fung Lau’s bathrooms and handed out towels. Japanese visitors often tipped 100 yen at a time; they were so many that, according to Wan, the couple earned enough to buy a flat within two years. Wan also recalls that Tai Fung Lau was a popular meeting place for Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan fan clubs. Lee, he says, performed at the restaurant more than once during the tour-group era. Members of the Jackie Chan fan club would arrive in groups of up to 600, eat in two swift sittings, then head to the Hong Kong Coliseum in Hung Hom for a show. Little physical evidence of that period remains. “We have no photographs,” Wan laments. “Back then, it was not fashionable to take photos like that.” Preserving the old ways Perhaps the clearest testament to the restaurant’s enduring legacy is 76-year-old waiter Lai Kam-yau, who began working for Wan’s father when he was just 11. Lai came from a boat-dwelling fishing family in Aberdeen. He started out carrying trays and selling buns at the old teahouse, then moved with the family to Tai Fung Lau’s current location. When Wan’s father died, Lai made a promise: “As long as you need me for one more day, I will work for one more day.” More than six decades later, he has not missed a day at the restaurant. That loyalty is reflected in the kitchen. Tai Fung Lau still makes its Peking-duck pancakes by hand each day, beginning at about 5pm, so they can be served fresh. Wan once considered buying ready-made pancakes, but found they hardened almost as soon as the duck was carved. The restaurant instead uses fresh dough without preservatives, and its soup dumplings and boiled dumplings are wrapped to order. “We don’t like pre-made food,” Wan says. “We would not want to eat it ourselves.” Tai Fung Lau’s generous portions of Peking duck are a contrast to many of the city’s fine-dining restaurants, where the emphasis is on the crispiness of the skin. Here, generous pieces of meat are paired with the usual cucumber, leek, hoisin sauce and pancakes, which are about the thickness of flatbread but fluffier. This stays true to the tradition of Lu cuisine described by Wan, where the Peking duck is served as a main course, not an appetiser. Questions about the future Some of Tai Fung Lau’s classic comfort dishes have fallen out of favour because they use offcuts such as intestines and aorta. Yet, these ingredients can be delicious. The stir-fried aorta with chives is fragrant with sesame oil and satisfyingly crunchy, while the deep-fried intestine with peppers is spicy and moreish. The combination of wok hei and seasoning makes these dishes a masterclass in texture. They also reflect an era when scarcity meant using every part of the animal, and a good chef knew how to make each one shine. Dumplings are a staple of Beijing cuisine, and Tai Fung Lau serves three varieties. The restaurant can also accommodate bespoke requests and special dietary needs, provided they are ordered in advance. What troubles Wan about the future is whether anyone will remain to make the food this way. Most of Tai Fung Lau’s staff are over 65, and mastering dough work, northern noodles and Beijing techniques takes years of apprenticeship. In an industry where young cooks can leave as soon as they acquire the skills, finding and retaining the next generation is difficult. Some of the richer traditional dishes have already disappeared as customers gravitate towards lighter food, and experienced masters become increasingly difficult to find and hire. Wan is unsure whether his children, who have strong ties to Australia, will carry on the family business. The challenge is not simply passing down a name; it is building a kitchen capable of sustaining its traditions. “I’m afraid they would not be able to manage it,” he says. “I can’t find chefs.” Tai Fung Lau Peking Restaurant, Windsor Mansion, 29-31 Chatham Road South, Tsim Sha Tsui.

title: Young Malaysians’ US$1.3bn short-term credit spree sparks warning over bad debt
description: Consumers aged 30 and below drove a third of ‘buy now, pay later’ purchases, prompting caution over ‘excessive’ borrowing.
content: Malaysians aged 30 and below bought some 5.4 billion ringgit (US$1.32 billion) worth of goods and services on short-term credit in the first half of this year, the country’s Finance Ministry has revealed. The ministry said it had recorded 65.9 million “buy now, pay later” (BNPL) purchases among younger consumers in the first six months of 2026 – equivalent to more than one in three, or 37.9 per cent, of total purchases nationwide. As of June 30, the outstanding BNPL financing balance among this age group stood at 2.4 billion ringgit, it said. Some 96.8 million ringgit, or 4 per cent of the outstanding balance, was classified as non-performing or unpaid. The ministry said that industry regulator the Consumer Credit Commission strictly required BNPL providers to conduct creditworthiness checks and affordability assessments before extending lines of credit to young customers. “These assessments must take into account the consumer’s overall financial commitments, including existing credit facilities from both bank and non-bank providers, as well as any new facilities being applied for,” the ministry said in a written reply published on parliament’s website on Tuesday evening. Thorough checks were crucial to ensure loans aligned with young people’s ability to repay, it said. “Excessive and uncontrolled use of multiple BNPL facilities simultaneously could lead to high repayment commitments and severely impact consumers’ financial standing,” the ministry warned. BNPL services are currently regulated under Malaysia’s Consumer Credit Act 2025, which mandates compliance with fair and responsible lending standards set by the Consumer Credit Commission. The ministry was responding to a question from Alias Razak, a Perikatan Nasional lawmaker for Kuala Nerus, regarding the commission’s measures to safeguard young people from falling into excessive debt. In a separate written reply to Howard Lee, a Pakatan Harapan lawmaker for Ipoh Timur, the ministry said BNPL providers were not legally required to freeze payment demands and late fees while investigations into unauthorised transaction disputes were ongoing. “Disputed transactions must first be investigated to determine whether unauthorised activity occurred,” it explained, adding that providers were nonetheless required to resolve complaints fairly, transparently and promptly. To safeguard users, the commission’s standards call for robust security controls, including mandatory identity verification and a “kill switch” feature that enables consumers to immediately freeze their accounts if they suspect fraud or identity theft. The ministry added that consumers would not be held liable for losses from unauthorised transactions if the breach was caused by systemic failures or security oversights on the provider’s end. This article was first published by The Star

title: Unexpected path, lasting impact: hearing loss setback leads to decades of teaching
description: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist Ivan Fung overcame job setbacks linked to his hearing impairment to help others across generations.
content: Hearing loss made it difficult for Ivan Fung Wing-hong to find work in Hong Kong’s construction industry after graduation. Nearly three decades later, that early setback has led to a teaching career spanning young children, postgraduate students and elderly people. Born with a hearing impairment, Fung struggled with language subjects at school because he could not always hear clearly. He was stronger in maths and art, which eventually led him to study building-related subjects at what was then City Polytechnic of Hong Kong. The institution became City University of Hong Kong (CityU) in 1994. After graduating in 1995, he applied for a job on a sewage treatment project, but the employer was concerned that his hearing impairment could pose a safety risk on a construction site. His other job applications were also unsuccessful. His father suggested teaching, but his initial applications to secondary schools came to nothing. A former lecturer eventually encouraged him to take up a junior academic role at the institution where he had studied. “Step by step,” Fung recalled of what followed. He went on to spend 20 years teaching at CityU, where he later supervised postgraduate students. His work has earned him a place among the finalists for the Spirit of Nurturing Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Fung’s teaching has since extended far beyond the university. He said he had helped at his wife’s tutorial centre, where some pupils came from single-parent families, and taught younger children art and other subjects. He has also taught postgraduate engineering students in mainland China and given lessons and talks to professionals and elderly people. In its nomination, Paradise Home Foundation described his philosophy as receiving help, helping oneself and then helping others. That approach also guides his community work with the foundation and its Chinese culture education centre. His recent activities range from Chinese cultural education to digital literacy. Fung said programmes included hanfu design activities for students and older participants, as well as projects in which primary and secondary pupils used artificial intelligence to create short videos. He has also helped elderly people understand the risks posed by AI, explaining how AI-generated images, videos and cloned voices can be used in scams. He urged them to verify suspicious messages or calls, even when they appeared to come from relatives or friends. Paradise Home Foundation said his academic background helped him explain both the uses and risks of AI in terms older people could understand. For Fung, the nomination offers reassurance that his unexpected career path has been worthwhile. “It gives me a sense of recognition and tells me that the path I chose was the right one,” he said. The Spirit of Hong Kong Awards were established in 2013 to recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention.

title: Sluggish Chinese demand weighs on LVMH, as Louis Vuitton’s Molly Tea case casts a shadow
description: Luxury giant takes a painful hit from slowing sales in Asia due to macro-led deterioration in China and lawsuit against local tea company.
content: LVMH, the world’s largest luxury goods group, has attributed an Asia sales drop in the third quarter – the only regional decline the company reported – to, in part, a slowdown in Chinese demand. The Louis Vuitton, Dior, Bulgari and Fendi parent group said Asia took a hit from a sharp macro-led deterioration in Chinese consumer sentiment, with tangible impact on discretionary expenses, the group said during an earnings call session on Monday. The fall in demand coincided with a string of trademark lawsuits Louis Vuitton has filed in China. In one case, local tea chain Molly Tea was ordered by a Chinese court to pay 10.3 million yuan (US$1.5 million) in restitution in July over its use of a logo similar to the French brand’s four-petaled flower. The initial ruling, despite the appeal, sparked heated online debate and drew public sympathy for the Chinese company. “On Molly, (it’s) very difficult to size a precise impact, but it’s probably fair to say that it had a negative impact, at least at the beginning of the quarter,” said Cecile Cabanis, chief financial officer of LVMH, during the earnings call. “The news flow has not been particularly good in China in the summer, so this has really weighed on the feel-good factor and created a short-term subdued Chinese backdrop. We hope it will subside. We need to do more, but we have not stopped investing in China,” Cabanis added. The group said the quarter was marked by a challenging, macro-driven consumer backdrop among its Chinese clientele, leading to a mid-single-digit decline in Asia, with a more tangible impact on fashion and leather goods. “Louis Vuitton’s lawsuit against Molly Tea caused a notable hit to its performance, as it was against Chinese consumers’ sentiment by suing the young tea brand and seeking hefty damages,” said Fu Yifu, a special research fellow at Su Merchants Bank in Nanjing, capital of eastern China’s Jiangsu province. “When international luxury brands operate in China, respect for local cultural sentiment comes first. For high-impact brands, proactive goodwill and restraint protect their long-term brand equity better than stressing legal correctness,” Fu said. In Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan, the group’s business performance did not change much compared with the previous quarter. For the Chinese cluster, offshore sales declined by mid-single digits in the third quarter. For the first nine months, the group posted revenue of €57.1 billion (US$63.9 billion), up 2 per cent year on year, with solid growth in the US, Europe and Japan. Mainland China’s personal luxury goods market contracted by 3 per cent to 5 per cent in 2025, a report by Bain & Company said earlier this year.

title: Chinese team finds 11,700 new viruses in world’s biggest seabed metal deposit
description: Research into a marine area with vast metallic deposits uncovers a wealth of viral lineages and genetic resources.
content: Up to 6,000 metres (19,700 feet) beneath the surface of the Pacific Ocean between Mexico and Hawaii, billions of potato-shaped metallic nodules are scattered across the seabed. The Clarion-Clipperton zone’s reserves of vital metals such as nickel, cobalt and manganese could surpass the total known reserves on land, according to some estimates. While no commercial mining has yet taken place on the underwater plain, the International Seabed Authority has issued 17 exploration contracts for the area, five of which are held by China. But a recent in-depth study of the zone by a Chinese research team has shown that future deep-sea miners will discover more than mineral wealth – they will encounter countless mysterious viruses. The researchers examined samples of sediment from the zone and identified 11,742 different viruses. Over 99 per cent of the viruses – 11,662 in total – were new discoveries. “These findings provide insights into the ecological roles of viruses in the polymetallic nodule province, establishing a vital pre-mining baseline of microbial ecosystem for future environmental impact assessments,” first author Hou Bowen wrote in the paper, which was published in Nature Communications late last month. Hou is a joint doctoral student at Chongqing University and the Second Institute of Oceanography under China’s Ministry of Natural Resources. The 60 samples used in the study were collected in 2023 and 2024 by one of the Chinese entities that holds an exploration contract, the China Ocean Mineral Resources R&D Association. Using protein-sharing networks, the scientists compared the viruses with data on viruses previously found in seawater, trenches and hydrothermal environments. Only about 4 per cent of the protein clusters of the viruses found in the zone were shared with at least one external data set. This means that the area is home to viral lineages and genetic resources that have not yet been recorded by scientists. The viruses in the region are likely to have unique characteristics that reflect the unusual environment in which they have evolved, which is rich in heavy metals while being extremely deficient in available nutrients. The vast majority of the viruses the team discovered belong to the Caudoviricetes class, which has a tail structure that can inject genetic material into bacteria like a syringe. Viruses in this class are present in various ecosystems, including the ocean, land and even the human gut. These viruses are not generally dangerous to humans; they can only target and destroy bacteria. Indeed, human activity is likely to pose a bigger risk to the viruses than the other way round. Once mining disturbs the sediment, the viruses may not be able to perform their role in the seabed ecosystem, such as breaking down organic matter and releasing nutrients into the environment.

title: Letters | Mind Hong Kong’s dorm boom today doesn’t become tomorrow’s oversupply
description: Readers discuss demographic trends that should drive the city’s housing plans, seniors’ digital capabilities, and how Trump might finally win a Nobel Peace Prize.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Hong Kong has become a sought-after regional education hub, drawing mainland and foreign students to its universities. Rising international enrolment has intensified demand for student housing, with on-campus places insufficient and rents near university districts buoyant. Some hotels are becoming dormitories, universities are expanding stock and new campuses are being built in the New Territories. Today’s headlines highlight this immediate demand but it should not drive long-term planning. The government and universities must look beyond current accommodation shortages and make strategic forecasts. Should student inflows slow in three to five years, today’s expansion could leave a surplus of purpose-built housing, inflicting lasting damage on Hong Kong’s property market. Policymakers should assess how durable the city’s appeal truly is: what drives non-local students to choose Hong Kong, and can graduates build careers and settle here? Advances in connectivity and the rise of satellite cities give graduates more work options, so Hong Kong must weigh its strengths when it comes to retaining talent. If student numbers show sustained growth, housing supply can be calibrated accordingly; otherwise, oversupply would depress rental and housing markets. Demographic trends add further complexity. Hong Kong, mainland China and other places face ageing populations, and youth inflows are no longer as strong. Yet an ageing world also presents an opportunity. Hong Kong already has comprehensive health and medical facilities; by enhancing and actively promoting them, the government could attract affluent elderly people to retire here. Their high-end spending – on health and medical care, property, investment assets – would diversify the city’s sources of demand. Hong Kong must not treat these as piecemeal projects. The government should nurture an ecosystem: non-local students gain an education here, some graduate into the city’s medical, health and tech sectors, where Hong Kong’s strengths in turn attract affluent overseas retirees to settle here. One element reinforces another, so the ecosystem must be planned and grown as one. Property also remains a key vehicle for investment. Weak returns could prompt capital outflows, undermining competitiveness. We must factor in global, not only domestic, trends when deciding how many student homes to build, and avoid deepening the K-shaped divide. Tseung Cheuk-yee, Sai Ying Pun Hong Kong’s elderly are capable of going digital I am writing in response to the letter, “Major football matches should have cash ticket booths” (October 3). During the pandemic in mainland China, there was a strict contact tracing policy according to which people needed to scan a QR code wherever they went. I was particularly surprised on the first day I landed in Guangzhou amid the pandemic to see elderly persons, even those in their 80s or 90s, managing to use their smartphones to scan QR codes and access public services. I talked to some of them, who told me they had no choice but to embrace digitalisation. Basically, if you didn’t learn how to use it, you were effectively grounded. Even in my hometown, a village, the elderly are able to use their smartphones to purchase groceries online or chat with friends or family living far away. We should not underestimate the elderly people of Hong Kong. They are quite capable of learning to embrace technology. Instead of viewing digitalisation as a hurdle, we should think of ways to help the elderly embrace it. A. Chan, Guangzhou Imagine no arms exports Maybe I went to the wrong business school. I was told that our democracies operate in a free world economy, where the fittest survive. Right after the second world war, our streets in Austria and Germany were packed with enormous made-in-Detroit cars, while Germany was still manufacturing three-wheelers. At that time it looked to me like American industrial overcapacity. Restricting industrial capacity seems to be a very difficult subject; where to start? Does it include military equipment? This would actually have the biggest impact by far worldwide. Imagine countries – not only G20 (Group of 20) members – limiting their production of arms to their own capacity and needs. No exports. This would be enormous progress for humanity – and it might make Donald Trump more eligible for a Nobel Peace Prize. Roland Guettler, Lai Chi Kok

title: Indonesia’s Bali hit by fuel crisis as huge queues form at petrol stations
description: Bali’s governor insists supplies are ample and points the finger at panic buying, even as fuel deliveries fail to keep pace with demand.
content: Motorists have been left queuing for hours at petrol stations across Indonesia’s resort island of Bali in recent days amid reports of a crippling fuel shortage. Long queues have been spotted all around the island, including in the capital Denpasar, Badung and Tabana, according to the Bali Post. On Tuesday, Bali Governor I Wayan Koster stressed that there was enough fuel to go around, suggesting that panic buying might have caused the shortages at the pumps. “People need to be patient because the depots have more than enough fuel to meet demand,” he said, as quoted by the Jakarta Globe, adding: “The rate at which fuel flows to gas stations is not keeping pace with demand.” The crisis was not only hurting local businesses but also disrupting the plans of thousands of Australian holidaymakers, Yahoo News reported. “This morning, my wife lined up at 4.30am and waited for 2½ hours before finally being able to refuel. It’s crazy,” one tourist said, as quoted by Australian news outlet 7news. Earlier, local politician I Made Rai Warsa had pointed the finger at Pertamina, telling the Bali Post that the state-owned oil giant “must be sensitive to the situation on the ground”. “Be honest about fuel availability,” the member of the provincial-level parliament was quoted as saying on Monday. Government official Ida Bagus Setiawan, head of Bali’s Manpower and Energy and Mineral Resources Agency, responded that Pertamina was doing what it could to ensure a steady and uninterrupted supply. He further urged the public to use fuel wisely, given the current “global geopolitical situation”, and told the Bali Post that the local government was also encouraging the use of electric vehicles. Governor Koster on Tuesday said he expected the shortages to ease by Wednesday, urging residents to remain calm and also calling on Pertamina to ensure there was enough fuel. The company had initially allocated 2.2 million litres (581,000 gallons) of fuel per day to Bali, he told the Jakarta Globe. Pertamina confirmed to the Bali Post that it was closely monitoring fuel stocks, with a spokesman pointing to the recent arrival of a ship carrying 18 million litres (4.8 million gallons) of government-subsidised RON90 petrol known as “Pertalite” as well as 2.5 million litres of “Pertamax” – a higher octane, non-subsidised petrol – “to meet the need of the Balinese people”. Globally, oil prices have been rising again in recent weeks amid a flare-up in attacks in the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran. Benchmark Brent crude climbed above US$106 barrel after dipping slightly on Tuesday, Bloomberg reported, while West Texas Intermediate advanced towards US$95. Brent has surged in price by more than 70 per cent this year amid conflict in the Middle East, which has roiled energy markets and throttled exports from the Gulf – a key oil producing region.

title: This Singaporean grandma, 73, couldn’t walk without pain. Today, she deadlifts 67.5kg
description: Singaporean mother of six, Rosemina Hamzah, overcame chronic pain and diabetes after training with her daughter at the gym and deadlifting.
content: When 73-year-old Rosemina Hamzah stepped up to the hex bar at Singapore’s Mbold Seniors Hex Bar Deadlift Challenge in August, she was not just attempting her first deadlift competition ­– she was rewriting what ageing looks like. Latching onto 67.5kg (149lbs), more than her own body weight of 64kg, the novice lifter pulled it with ease – a personal best to win her category. It was a remarkable feat for a woman who, just over a year ago, could hardly walk and was constantly in pain. Before August 2025, Hamzah had seldom exercised. The 1.44-metre-tall (four-foot-nine) Singaporean retiree had cycled to and from her work as a cook occasionally when she was younger and carried groceries home from the market every week, but beyond that, physical fitness had never really factored into her life. Today, Hamzah – a mother of six children aged 30 to 50, and affectionately known as Cik Rose (“Aunty Rose” in Malay) – is a regular at her local gym in the eastern part of Singapore. There she is often seen training alongside her daughter, Maryam Rahman, a 33-year-old personal trainer. Hamzah has a workout routine that someone even half her age might find challenging – a mix of strength, cardio, and balance and coordination exercises, done three or four times a week. These exercises include deadlifts, gorilla rows, squats, chest presses, hip thrusts and more. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Maryam Rahman (@gymbaddiesg) Guidance from her daughter What triggered the change in Hamzah? “I couldn’t tolerate how I felt any more,” she says. “My joints were hurting all the time – a problem that started after I suffered a fall in 2023 – and I noticed that I was always fatigued. I also had high blood pressure, elevated cholesterol levels and diabetes, health issues that began in my sixties.” Concerned for her mother’s health, Rahman suggested that she start working out with her at the gym she trained at, to help strengthen her leg muscles and address her lack of energy. She bought Hamzah a membership and reassured her that she would guide her through her fitness journey. Rahman understood the stakes better than most. In 2023, she survived a serious traffic accident that required multiple surgeries and left her bedridden and in a wheelchair for months. Doctors credited her existing muscle mass with saving her life – a revelation that fuelled her determination to rebuild her strength during her hospital stay by doing light weights and rehabilitative exercises at home after her discharge. Before long, she was walking again, well before the doctors predicted she would. “I started to believe that there was a purpose for everything that happens to us,” says Rahman, who received her PT certification in 2022. “So with the knowledge and experience that I have, I decided I wanted to change lives.” Starting with her mother. “My mum wasn’t thrilled when she found out that I was going to start training her, but I had already signed her up and told her that she couldn’t waste my money,” jokes Rahman, a single mother of four. “She pretty much pushed me to start working out,” Hamzah says. “Despite her reluctance, Mum showed up anyway,” Rahman continues. “At first, her goal was just to strengthen her lower body so that she could walk without being in pain.” From nervous at the gym to inspiring others Hamzah had no expectations before her first workout, but remembers feeling nervous and afraid. “I thought the gym was only for younger people and I was worried I’d hurt myself,” she says. “The weights looked intimidating and I wasn’t sure if I’d be able to lift them.” Lift them, she did, although it took some time. Rahman notes that her mother used to need adjustments to her workout routine because of her joint pain, but not any more. “Mum’s improved so much … she has more energy now and can walk longer and faster without getting breathless,” Rahman says. “I’ve noticed that she’s more cheerful and mentally alert, too.” Hamzah feels much better now, she says, having got her cholesterol and blood pressure levels and diabetes under control. She can keep up with her grandchildren, walk and cycle to pick them up from school and, to her surprise, perform her prayers close to the ground with her legs folded under her body (the prostration position in Islamic prayer). This was something she was unable to do for a long time. “After just six weeks of working out regularly, I could pray with ease,” she says. “Before, I couldn’t even bend my knees 90 degrees.” Hamzah is somewhat of a social media celebrity these days, since Rahman began posting about her on her Instagram account, @gymbaddiesg, and on TikTok. The videos featuring Hamzah are among the most-watched of Rahman’s content. Hamzah has inspired many Singaporean seniors who have contacted Rahman for help to get active and healthy. This June, Rahman invited them to join her and Hamzah on a 3km (1.86-mile) morning walk. The new walking club, Moving with Ma-Chics, was open to men and women of all ages and saw all available slots snapped up. Rahman plans to organise more such events, to encourage more seniors to get physically active. “Strength training becomes more important as we get older because our bone density and muscle mass decrease with age,” Rahman explains. “Strength training not only preserves muscle and bone; it also improves balance and mobility, protects joints, supports heart and metabolic health, boosts cognitive function, reduces the risk of falls – which also increases as we age – and helps us maintain our independence and quality of life.” ‘Nothing short of enjoyable’ Rahman now trains mostly women who want to age healthily and move better or lose weight but don’t know how. Before starting any type of workout, she advises people to consult their doctor, especially if they have health issues. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Rahayu Mahzam (@rahayumahzam) Hamzah is proud of Rahman, saying that she is a testament to her daughter’s determination and commitment to be the best trainer she can be. “I didn’t expect my fitness journey to be smooth because of my age and medical conditions,” she says, “but from day one, Maryam reassured me that I’d be OK, and the experience has so far been nothing short of enjoyable.” The mother and daughter have always been close – Hamzah cared for Rahman’s children when she was bedridden – but training together has strengthened their bond even more. They are focused on taking part in a Hyrox doubles event together in Singapore at the end of November and are currently training for it. Rahman says: “Mum’s my biggest inspiration. She’s been through a lot in life, yet she handles many things independently and always with lots of patience and a smile. I admire her resilience, and it makes me happy to see her in such good health and enjoying all these new challenges.” Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: China’s exports surge by 36% in September, riding wave of tech demand
description: The country is on track for another all-time high trade surplus this year as imports and exports blow past forecasts in September.
content: China’s trade momentum gained pace in September – driven by strong global tech demand and a pre-holiday shipping rush ahead of the “golden week” break – logging a monthly high for its trade surplus in 2026 and putting the country on course for another record gap this year. Outbound shipments rose 36.3 per cent year on year to US$447.18 billion last month, customs data showed on Wednesday. The figure exceeded a forecast of 25.7 per cent growth from economists polled by financial data provider Wind, and was higher than the previous figure of 25 per cent in August. China also saw imports grow by 31 per cent last month to US$313.65 billion, above the Wind poll’s projections of 23.79 per cent growth. This brought China’s September trade surplus to US$133.53 billion, up from the US$119.1 billion reported in August. Total trade for the January-September period rose 23.8 per cent year on year. “Foreign trade growth in the first three quarters was the fastest in the past five years,” said Wang Jun, vice-minister of the General Administration of Customs, at a press conference in Beijing on Wednesday. The growth in exports was driven by products in the technology sector, such as chips and electronic components, amid growing global demand for artificial intelligence computing power and electricity infrastructure, Wang said. China is on track to post another record annual trade surplus this year, after last year’s US$1.2 trillion imbalance drew heightened scrutiny from Western trading partners. Its cumulative surplus had already reached US$938.11 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up about 7.2 per cent from the same period last year, customs data showed. With last month’s high surplus, Xing Zhaopeng, a senior China strategist at ANZ Research, said he expected the full-year surplus to exceed the previous full-year high from 2025. “Looking ahead, sustained AI demand and easing China-EU trade tensions should remain supportive of exports, while oil price uncertainty remains a key wild card for imports,” Xing added. Exports to the US continued to rise against a low base last year, growing 39.56 per cent in September. President Xi Jinping met with US President Donald Trump in Washington late last month, where the leaders agreed to an artificial intelligence dialogue and recommended tariff cuts on US$30 billion in goods from each side. Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, said that an extension of the trade truce through to January 2027, combined with tariff cuts on products such as toys, Christmas decorations and kitchenware, “should keep this recovery trajectory intact for the remainder of the year”. Meanwhile, Chinese exports to the European Union rose 25.25 per cent in September. Song noted this figure reached a seven-month high, pushing year-to-date export growth to the bloc to 16.4 per cent. Beijing and Brussels met for talks late last week, reaching an agreement to cap Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the bloc and facilitate approval of rare earth export licences for European businesses. Tensions with the European Union have risen in the past year over China’s trade imbalance. Last week, France and Germany called for a new trade weapon that would cut off access to the EU market when third countries cause severe distortions. Exports to members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, China’s largest trading partner by bloc, surged 52.26 per cent year on year. By product, exports of integrated circuits rose just 1 per cent year on year in volume terms last month but surged by 136 per cent in value terms, driven by higher prices amid a memory chip shortage fuelled by a global AI infrastructure buildout. “As China moves up the value-added ladder, the fastest growing export products are increasingly in higher margin goods, while low-end manufacturing begins to move elsewhere,” Song said. China’s rare earth exports rose 6.74 per cent year on year by volume in September, customs data showed, even as Beijing continued to exert tight control over shipments of the minerals, essential components in a range of hi-tech products. The customs data release on Wednesday did not provide a country-by-country breakdown by product categories, which is expected to be released on Tuesday.

title: Helper’s arrest over death of elderly woman sparks calls for carer support
description: Calls come after police arrest 52-year-old helper on suspicion of assaulting and murdering 93-year-old woman on Sunday.
content: The arrest of a domestic helper over the suspected murder of an elderly woman has dominated Hong Kong headlines, with police investigations revealing that the 93-year-old had been assaulted repeatedly in the hours before her death on Sunday. Citing surveillance footage, police said on Monday the 52-year-old Indonesian helper hit the widow, surnamed Kwan, on the head, face and neck, stepped on her abdomen and moved her body in a “rough and violent manner”. The helper appeared to be Kwan’s primary carer. The 93-year-old, who had no children, suffered a stroke more than two years ago and required long-term medication and regular medical checks. The helper was arranged by a relative of Kwan and began work in January 2023. Preliminary investigations found that friction between the two had built up over time because the helper was overworked, with minor assaults occurring intermittently every day over the past fortnight. The helper was later charged with murder and appeared in court on Wednesday morning. She remained in custody. The tragedy has prompted calls to include carers looking after isolated seniors in a government database to strengthen support and monitoring. Foreign domestic helpers have become key carers amid Hong Kong’s rapidly ageing population, particularly as the government promotes “ageing in place” so elderly residents can remain in familiar surroundings for as long as possible. While stressing that physical abuse was unacceptable, social welfare observers and a migrant workers’ group said on Tuesday that domestic helpers often shouldered much of the caregiving burden and needed adequate rest and support. An employer group and an employment agency representative also suggested installing surveillance cameras, regularly reviewing footage and seeking third-party mediation as ways to deter and prevent potential abuse. Lawmaker Grace Chan Man-yee, who represents the social welfare sector, said the tragedy highlighted the risks faced by domestic workers who served as sole carers for isolated seniors under the same roof. She urged the government to include such helpers in its database of carers for the elderly and disabled. Set up in July last year, the database links data from different government departments to build a community support network for carers. As of the end of last month, community care teams had contacted more than 36,300 high-risk households and made more than 4,200 welfare service referrals. “Regular home visits, as well as encouraging them to visit community centres, can help ease carers’ pressure and allow a third party to identify potential problems,” she said. “It is important to note that hiring a domestic helper does not mean that an elderly person no longer needs any social services … Social services can help release the helpers from their round-the-clock caretaking duties.” She added that training efforts for domestic helpers should also be stepped up, including caretaking skills, stress management and awareness of abuse and legal consequences. Dicky Chow Ka-chun, an assistant research director at think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, echoed calls to include domestic helpers in the database. He suggested focusing on helpers who acted as primary carers, as well as first-time employers of domestic workers, as both situations could indicate greater care needs. “This tragedy has shed light on what can make a carer high-risk: when one person shoulders a large share of the caregiving duties. It is not only about households encountering financial difficulties, medical issues or social service needs,” he said. While acknowledging that the government increasingly recognised the heavier responsibilities placed on domestic helpers, he said authorities should also improve their access to support. He said support should be provided in the helpers’ mother tongue, with more resources and manpower deployed, including respite care services to give them a break. Chow also urged the government to strengthen monitoring of its pilot scheme to import foreign carers for elderly people, which is due to be rolled out next year. The initiative, announced in the latest policy address, will offer accredited helpers a salary 10 to 20 per cent higher than standard rates. The Asian Migrants’ Coordinating Body said it would not comment on individual cases, while noting that the responsibility of caring for the elderly often fell solely on domestic workers, which was “not fair and not easy”. The group emphasised that caring for a sick, paralysed elderly person single-handedly alongside general household chores was an “immense burden”. It called for establishing mandatory rest hours for domestic workers and a broader review of the multitasking demands placed on helpers. Betty Yung Ma Shan-yee, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Employers of Domestic Helpers Association, suggested employers install surveillance cameras and review footage regularly to monitor conditions at home. She added that family members should remain actively involved and help mediate conflicts. Speaking on a radio programme, Thomas Chan Tung-fung, chairman of the Hong Kong Union of Employment Agencies, advised employers and helpers to turn to agencies for help if tensions arose. He said agencies would warn helpers involved in physical clashes with employers and report obvious injuries to police, while also helping mediate verbal disputes. He added that some agencies had translators and staff from the same backgrounds as the helpers, which could help resolve tensions.

title: Police in Germany seize robot after teen girl is allegedly groped
description: Investigators probe whether machine was controlled in real time as two teens face scrutiny for live-streaming incident.
content: German authorities opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment after a robot controlled by two young men touched the buttocks of a 16-year-old girl and made thrusting movements toward her, police said. Police in the western city of Cologne responded after the incident overnight Saturday to Sunday in which the robot’s suspected 16-year-old owner and a 19-year-old companion were said to have filmed the alleged assault. They were said to have streamed the incident and commentated on it online. Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel said the two male teenagers have not been charged but are considered suspects, and investigators were examining whether the robot’s movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time. Police were unfamiliar with this type of incident, he said. “We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far,” Bermel told Associated Press, saying it was “new territory for us”. Emergency teams that were dispatched to the scene near a fast-food restaurant found the robot in the trunk of a vehicle, Cologne police said in a statement on Monday. The robot and the two young men’s mobile phones were confiscated. North Rhine Westphalia Police Cologne, on Facebook, posted an image of the red-and-gold robot lying on the ground. The robot, said to be 120cm tall, was dressed in a white tank top, black sweatpants and wearing a gold chain and sunglasses. It also had what appears to be a fake mustache. Videos circulated on the internet show two young men escorting the robot towards a group of women, bumping into one and hugging others, on a lively nighttime street. One of the men repeatedly shouts at the robot and pulls it backward after it makes sexual gestures, prompting laughter among people in the area. On the police’s Facebook account on Tuesday, officers criticised inappropriate comments and warned that sharing or joking about such incidents can worsen the impact on any victim.

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: mental health advocate who saved suicidal teen
description: Minal Mahtani, founder of OCD & Anxiety Support Hong Kong, says a stronger referral system is needed to provide better community services.
content: Hongkongers can be struggling with severe mental health problems but still not be considered urgent cases, according to mental health advocate Minal Mahtani, who wants community groups to play a bigger role before individual cases reach crisis point. Mahtani, founder of OCD & Anxiety Support Hong Kong, said better referrals between hospitals, community mental health services and specialist charities could help people receive timely support while they wait for formal treatment. Her work has earned her a place among the finalists in the community category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. People assessed as stable can face long waits for psychiatric care, while district community mental health centres providing valuable general emotional support may not have the specialist techniques needed for conditions such as obsessive-compulsive disorder and anxiety, she said. She wants a two-way referral system in which hospitals and community centres can direct suitable patients to organisations such as hers, while charities can refer people back when medication, housing or financial support is needed. OCD & Anxiety Support Hong Kong runs monthly peer-support groups and affordable counselling, as well as yoga, art therapy and sound healing. Mahtani said she wanted those services to be more readily available to Hong Kong people, regardless of race, income, language, sexual orientation, religion or other background. Hong Kong was her home, she said, and the charity was intended to offer a safe, confidential and non-judgmental space where people could feel understood rather than alone. She likened the support provided by her organisation to a “warm hug” given at a difficult time, with people leaving sessions feeling more hopeful and better equipped to cope with anxiety, stress, OCD or depression. Mahtani started support group meetings in 2014 after losing a cousin to suicide. She became concerned about how difficult it was for people in Asian families to talk openly about mental health issues. Only two people attended the first meetings. Twelve years later, she said around 30,000 people have sought help from her charity, including many who joined online during the Covid-19 pandemic from Hong Kong and overseas. The stigma of mental health problems remained a barrier, she said, as those with such conditions were still sometimes associated with being unstable, dangerous or “crazy”. Despite the challenges, Mahtani is pleased to see greater openness. When she first handed out green ribbons in Central for World Mental Health Day in 2015, some people returned them because they feared being associated with mental illness. But the annual campaign now draws 40 to 50 volunteers, while passers-by more readily stop to ask about support for themselves or loved ones. Her work has also brought her into contact with people in acute distress. About four years ago, she received a call from the mother of a 14-year-old boy who was threatening to take his own life. Mahtani stayed on the phone with him while rushing to the scene and later persuaded the child to step away from the ledge. He is now at university in the UK and still sends her updates. “We need to look out for each other when people are going through hard times,” Mahtani said. “Everybody needs to keep sharing, because that’s when we can truly heal. If we don’t share, nobody knows.” Launched in 2013, the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards honour individuals and groups whose work might otherwise go unnoticed.

title: Growth in China’s factory-gate prices accelerates, but consumer inflation subdued
description: Statistician attributes producer price index growth to higher commodities prices, boost to demand from AI-related infrastructure.
content: Growth in Chinese factory-gate prices continued to accelerate last month, while consumer price growth remained subdued despite Beijing’s efforts to shore up domestic demand and support the economy in meeting its annual growth target. The producer price index (PPI) rose 5 per cent year on year in September, the highest rate since mid-2022, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday. It rose by 3.8 per cent in August. The reading beat a projection of 4.3 per cent from economists polled by financial data provider Wind. Meanwhile, China’s consumer price index, a crucial gauge of inflation, rose 0.9 per cent year on year in September, compared with 0.8 per cent in August. Wind projected a 1.02 per cent rise. Dong Lijuan, a senior statistician at the bureau, attributed the accelerated PPI growth to higher prices of commodities such as crude oil and non-ferrous metals in international markets. She also said accelerating development in areas such as artificial intelligence and AI-related computing infrastructure had boosted demand and pushed up prices in some industries. China’s factory-gate prices have risen since March, marking a reversal from a 41-month deflationary streak, with higher energy prices amid the US-Iran conflict adding to external inflation pressures. In its latest projection, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday that oil prices would reach US$130 a barrel from the fourth quarter of this year to the first quarter of next year. On the consumption front, weak domestic demand remains a key challenge as Chinese policymakers seek to lift inflation towards the annual target of around 2 per cent. With the year drawing to a close, Beijing has stepped up efforts to shore up domestic demand and support its annual economic growth target of 4.5 to 5 per cent. Earlier this month, the Ministry of Finance approved an additional 550 billion yuan (US$82.18 billion) local government bond issuance quota, vowing to boost local investment. That came after Beijing announced measures late last month that included interest rate cuts for policy banks and the country’s first interest subsidy programme for commercial mortgages. The government has also unveiled guidelines to promote spending in areas including sports events, recreational vehicles and smart home products. Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said the data showed that China’s domestic demand remained weak, while inflationary pressure persisted on the supply side. “The market is waiting for a signal of any potential policy shift in the fourth quarter to boost the economy and achieve the growth target for this year.” Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 1 per cent year on year in September, unchanged from August. Consumer goods prices were up 1 per cent, while service prices rose 0.8 per cent. Food prices were down 1.7 per cent.

title: China ‘robot trainers’ fold clothes, wash dishes 200 times a day for up to US$900 a month
description: Some view this as deeply ironic: humans are teaching robots to work, yet these machines will one day replace their trainers.
content: Across China, a new breed of freelance “robot trainers” are wearing motion-capture gear to turn everyday household chores – picking up cups, opening bottle caps and washing dishes – into data that will teach tomorrow’s machines. The data is later converted into training sets to help robots work in settings ranging from kitchens and factories to supermarkets. Such roles are increasingly advertised on mainland social media and job platforms. They reportedly pay trainers between 4,000 yuan and 6,000 yuan (US$600 and US$900) a month and attract unemployed workers and young people seeking flexible jobs. Liu Yun, 40, entered the field after losing her job in the automotive industry and struggling to find new work because of her age. At a Beijing studio, she wore a sensor bracelet and finger-mounted chips, following instructions on a computer screen as she repeated movements such as moving cups and scrubbing surfaces. “Rather than training robots, it feels more like teaching a two-year-old child,” Liu told Jizhou Studio, a mainland media outlet. Her every movement was monitored. Large screens ranked workers by productivity and accuracy. The daily quota was 160 samples, while top performers completed more than 260. For Liu, the repetitive work quickly became exhausting. Washing dishes and wiping tables 200 times a day was already her limit. Sun, 22, a student from Shanxi province in northern China, took the job during his summer break while looking for an internship. His assignments included folding clothes, sweeping floors, and recording standardised movements for robot training. The work paid 120 yuan (US$18) for a day shift and 135 yuan for a night shift, but turnover was high, with many workers leaving after just a few weeks. Sun found the income insufficient to make up for the physical and mental strain of repetitive work. For others, the job offers flexibility. Guo Hongjuan, from Jiangsu province in eastern China, works from home for about six hours a day, collecting data through tasks such as arranging books, wiping tables and moving objects. She earns around 4,000 yuan a month and says the arrangement allows her to work while caring for her child. The collection of human labour data is also moving beyond household tasks. In August, Shenzhen-based technology company Physen AI partnered with a sanitation company to equip street cleaners with data-collection devices. As the workers swept roads and responded to disruptions, such as passing electric bicycles, their movements were captured to help robots better understand real-world environments. The rise of robot trainers has drawn mixed reactions online. Some users have jokingly called it a “cyber assembly line”, while others describe it as “home-based migrant labour”. One middle-aged worker shared that after three months of low-paid robot-training work, he had at least learned how to do household chores. Another online user noted: “It is deeply ironic. Humans are teaching robots to work, yet those machines will one day replace the very workers who trained them.”

title: IMF warns higher borrowing costs are straining public finances worldwide
description: Higher bond yields raise debt-servicing costs and increase fiscal pressure across advanced and emerging economies, global lender says.
content: Rising sovereign debt and borrowing costs have prompted a fresh warning from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) about risks to the fiscal health of member countries, with 24-year highs in US Treasury yields expected to become one of the focal topics for central bankers and finance ministers gathering in Bangkok this week. The average yield on 10-year government bonds across the Group of Seven economies increased by more than 1 percentage point between February and September this year, reaching its highest level in nearly two decades, according to an IMF blog post on Wednesday. The US, France, Japan and other advanced economies have drawn attention in recent weeks as government bond yields climbed to multi-year highs, fuelling concerns about rising debt and spillover effects on emerging markets, a theme likely to feature at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings. “Higher borrowing costs are adding to fiscal pressures at a time of high debt, making credible consolidation more urgent,” wrote Rodrigo Valdes, chief of the IMF’s fiscal affairs department, and deputy head Era Dabla-Norris. Government bond yields are widely regarded as benchmarks for funding costs. Higher yields could attract capital into advanced economies, potentially raising the funding costs for emerging markets as well. “In an increasing number of economies, interest rates paid for new debt now exceed expected nominal growth rates,” the IMF economists said. “Governments therefore need stronger primary balances to keep debt ratios from rising.” The Washington-based lender was expected to release the latest edition of its Fiscal Monitor report on Wednesday, providing a fresh assessment of public finances across member economies, including debt-to-gross domestic product ratios, a critical measure of fiscal risk. Emerging market economies should reduce fiscal vulnerabilities and strengthen debt management IMF economists Oil price shocks, persistent inflation, stronger investment demand and expectations that artificial intelligence could boost future economic growth had contributed to the rise in yields, according to the blog post. While advanced economies had greater capacity to manage rising debt burdens, a trend had emerged in which governments around the world were spending an increasing share of tax revenue on servicing debt, it added. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in a recent interview with US media, outlined plans to reduce federal debt after US government liabilities topped US$41 trillion. Emerging economies were projected to spend almost 11 per cent of their tax revenue on servicing debt over the next five years, up from about 7 per cent between 2011 and 2019, according to the IMF. For advanced economies, the number was expected to exceed 9 per cent, compared with around 6 per cent during the earlier period. The global primary deficit, the difference between a government’s revenue and expenses before interest payments, stood at about 3.3 per cent of GDP this year and was expected to widen further, the economists added. “Emerging market economies should reduce fiscal vulnerabilities and strengthen debt management,” they said. “For low-income countries where external financing is already tighter, strengthening tax systems and improving spending efficiency are essential to preserve priority spending.”

title: Style Edit: Shiatzy Chen draws inspiration from orchids for SS27 at Paris Fashion Week
description: Sheer layers, sculptural collars and vivid colour bring an orchid-inspired twist to Shiatzy Chen’s spring/summer 2027 collection.
content: Florals don’t have to mean full bloom. For spring/summer 2027, Shiatzy Chen takes the orchid but looks beyond its purely decorative appeal to the proportions, movement and resilience of the plant. Presented at Paris Fashion Week on October 5, the new collection translates that botanical inspiration into a thoughtful line-up where fluidity and structure come together. The season forms part of the house’s year-long exploration of the Four Gentlemen of Eastern culture. Following on from the Resort collection’s focus on bamboo, the orchid offers a different approach to thinking about how clothes should unfold around the body. Petals, leaves and roots inform elongated silhouettes, while layered shirts, jackets and skirts give the whole wardrobe a sense of movement. The clearest expression appears around the shoulders and neckline, where sculptural collars recall orchid petals. A-line hems and slender shapes preserve definition without sacrificing lightness, while soft fabrics introduce a relaxed touch. Rather than relying solely on decoration and floral motifs, the collection lets its botanical inspiration emerge through cut, surfaces and layered pieces. Fabric treatments accentuate that approach. Digital denim prints applied to sheer materials create overlapping washes that remind one of Eastern freehand ink painting, bringing the familiar appearance of denim into a more elevated register. Concealed jacquard patterns, cutwork cotton and translucent embossing add texture to the collection, while “Orchid Archive” prints, sequin fringes and laser perforation cleverly echo the plant’s freely extending aerial roots. Although restraint is a key note of the collection, colour is assertive. Cobalt blue, peach pink, crimson, burnt orange and botanical green appear in layered combinations, with orchid motifs subtly worked into checks. Menswear develops a similar balance through cropped jackets worn over longer shirts, transparent fabrics, large botanical prints and dimensional floral shirts. Knitted textures soften the tailoring. Accessories offer more tangible references to the natural world. Straw bucket hats sit alongside elongated baguette bags with bamboo-joint handles and stylish jade details. Leather floral sandals, cut-out uppers and clasps modelled after bamboo and orchid stems extend the theme and echo the collection’s central concept: a botanical idea can be expressed through more than flowers alone.

title: MTR Corp ordered to submit report after 2 disruptions at Lam Tin station in 15 hours
description: A fire and overheating wires separately disrupted services, as Hong Kong’s rail operator apologises and says it will discuss compensation with the government.
content: Hong Kong’s MTR Corporation has been ordered to submit a report to the government within a month following two separate service disruptions at Lam Tin station within 15 hours, with the railway operator apologising to passengers for the inconvenience caused. Services on the Kwun Tong line were disrupted at about 8am on Wednesday when wires overheated in an electrical room on the station platform, prompting trains to skip the stop. Services resumed by 10am. The previous evening at around 5.30pm, train services between Kwun Tong and Tiu Keng Leng stations were suspended after an insulating rubber component in a track turnout at Lam Tin station caught fire. Services resumed about an hour later. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said the government was “highly concerned about the consecutive incidents”. She said the government had directed the MTR Corp to conduct a comprehensive review and submit a report within a month. “I hope they will comprehensively review every piece of equipment and every single component to determine what circumstances led to this incident, covering inspection, maintenance, and manpower allocation across every single detail,” she said. Some residents voiced their grievances on social media. “The fire alarm went off at Lam Tin station this morning and there was another serious incident,” one Threads user said. “Last night, I couldn’t get home after work, and today I couldn’t get to work.” Another user, who witnessed the incident at 9am, said he had to consider how to get back to work. Lee Kim-hung, deputy director of operations engineering maintenance, said the corporation would investigate the causes of the two incidents and whether they were linked, with independent experts invited to join the inquiry. He said the insulating rubber component and related parts damaged in Tuesday’s fire had been replaced. Staff would inspect the remaining 30 components across the city outside operating hours. The MTR Corp will also deploy additional engineering staff at Lam Tin station to closely monitor its electrical system and facilities. Lee said the rubber component had been replaced in March and inspected in September. Such malfunctions were rare, he added, and the company would follow up with the supplier. The wires in the electrical room involved in Wednesday’s incident were last inspected in February, with no irregularities detected, he said. He added that the corporation had complied with maintenance and inspection requirements for both facilities. Cheris Lee Yuen-ling, deputy director of operating and metro segment, apologised to passengers and said the corporation would discuss compensation with the government under the established service performance arrangement. She said the MTR Corp had deployed an additional 210 staff to help passengers at affected stations and provided 120 shuttle buses to cover the affected routes. Describing Wednesday’s incident, she said the latest disruption began when a fire alarm went off in the electrical room. The stationmaster immediately sent staff to the room, where they found that the fire-extinguishing system had been activated and equipment was emitting smoke. The operator activated its emergency response procedures and evacuated passengers from the station. Firefighters later arrived and extinguished the fire. Cheris Lee said staff began emergency repairs and safety checks once the equipment had cooled. She added that Tuesday’s fire was caused by a short circuit in an insulating rubber component. Meanwhile, Chan also suggested that the MTR Corp make greater use of technology. “I suggested that the MTR leverage technology more, for instance, using [technologies] that monitor component temperatures so as to anticipate issues earlier and prevent them from occurring,” she said. Michael Tien Puk-sun, former chairman of the Kowloon-Canton Railway Corporation, said the core problem lay in the MTR’s use of two earthing systems for its power supply, which could easily cause a fire. “The MTR powers train carriages through overhead cables using direct current [DC], while other station facilities use alternating current [AC]. Both systems need earthing to direct current safely into the ground,” he said. “If the voltages differ, current will flow from one side to the other. If there are flammable materials underground, this can create sparks and cause a fire.” Lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung said the MTR Corp needed to conduct a thorough investigation to identify the cause of the repeated incidents within such a short period. Smart Transportation Alliance executive director and former lawmaker Gary Zhang Xinyu, a former MTR Corp engineer, said the two disruptions had little technical connection, as the first was caused by a signal system fault and the latest by a power supply issue. “Such incidents are common in daily operations, but it is a bit suspicious that they happened at the same station within a short period of time,” he said. Under the MTR Corp’s service performance rebate arrangement, the rail operator sets aside between HK$1 million and HK$40 million for each disruption lasting 31 minutes or more that is caused by factors within its control. The amount rises by 20 per cent if the disruption occurs during peak hours – from 8am to 9am and 6pm to 7pm on weekdays, excluding public holidays. The peak-hour uplift does not apply to the Airport Express. Once the fund reaches HK$25 million, it is returned to passengers as discounted fares on a designated Saturday or Sunday. Additional reporting by Cannix Yau

title: Aramco complex hit as Houthis and Saudi coalition trade strikes
description: Fire reported at Dhahran office tower, while intercepted missile debris wounds four and damages 15 homes in Riyadh.
content: An administrative building belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran was attacked, causing a limited fire, the Energy Ministry said in a statement on Wednesday as fighting between Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified. Authorities responded to the incident late on Tuesday and took necessary measures, the ministry said, adding that there were no injuries or deaths. A company source told Reuters earlier that a ballistic missile hit the Aramco headquarters complex in Dhahran. The source said ‌an office tower in the complex was struck and that its top three floors were damaged. The source and two other people with knowledge of the matter said the building was on fire. The complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals. The Houthis have for a week been firing ballistic missiles and drones at key Saudi sites in retaliation for the kingdom’s backing of government forces in Yemen’s reignited civil war. Riyadh’s international airport has received four strikes, including one on Saturday that killed 13 people. Saturday’s ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country. Earlier, six sources told Reuters they heard loud booms near the ⁠Aramco complex. The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of a missile that it had intercepted and destroyed in Dhahran had fallen on a residential area, without providing further details. Authorities also reported that drones and missiles were intercepted ‌and destroyed in the capital, Riyadh, and the country’s southern region. Four people were injured in Riyadh after fragments from two Houthi missiles fell following their interception and destruction, Saudi Civil Defence said on Wednesday. The debris caused limited damage to 15 homes in the capital, the Civil Defence spokesperson said, adding that the injured were two women, ‌a man and a child. The Houthis had threatened a “harsh and painful” response to Saudi-led strikes on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the ⁠Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil ⁠refinery in Riyadh. The group has warned oil workers in Saudi Arabia to stay away from sites that could be targets. The Houthis earlier on Tuesday said Saudi Arabia was attacking Sanaa, and the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on ‌the city’s outskirts. Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company’s Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa. The coalition said in a statement on Tuesday evening that it attacked the station and other sites in an ‌operation aimed ‌at “neutralising the capabilities of Houthis” to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen and international waterways. The Saudi cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement on Tuesday before the strike on Saudi ‌Aramco saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom. Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the ⁠Houthis’ sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for ⁠Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean. While a government offensive that began a week ago pushed the Houthis from the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains around the city of Taiz this ‌month. Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from ‌allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks. Washington, Saudi Arabia’s strongest ally and long-time security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis. However, the deadly strike on Riyadh’s airport on Saturday prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the group. He wrote on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday that “the Houthis are behaving very badly,” accusing them of acting “probably at the behest of Iran”. “I’ll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!” he wrote, referring to next month’s midterms. The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on February 28. Iran, Saudi Arabia’s long-time regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Opinion | Does Hong Kong’s economy serve the people or profit?
description: While mainland China might not have a Nobel Prize-winning economist, its lifting of millions out of poverty offers an example worth reflecting on.
content: China has lifted nearly 800 million people out of extreme poverty, arguably the greatest achievement in poverty reduction in human history. Even so, no mainland Chinese economist has won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. Across the Pacific, the United States has produced about 75 per cent of Nobel economics laureates, even as its economy staggers under mounting public debt, chronic fiscal deficits, and recurring financial crises and government shutdowns. Of the 99 economics laureates ever awarded, only two are from Asia. Amartya Sen was honoured for his contribution to welfare economics and Abhijit Banerjee for his work in alleviating global poverty. Both are from India, not China. Why such an anomaly? The short answer strikes at the heart of the matter: economics in the West and economics in China serve different purposes and recognise different kinds of achievements. Western economics serves capital and the capitalist system, emphasising market forces, efficiency, productivity and gross domestic product (GDP) growth. The Nobel economics tradition, which is rooted in Western academic institutions, has largely recognised contributions developed within that intellectual framework. In China, economics is proudly ideology-driven. It integrates the planned economy with the socialist market economy, where state enterprises and private enterprises compete and complement one another. For Hong Kong, practising a capitalist economy under the “one country, two systems” framework and increasingly integrating its development with national development, the anomaly raises a question more consequential than who wins a Nobel: what is Hong Kong’s economy ultimately for, and whom does it serve? Consider electricity, which is an essential service. Hong Kong’s two power companies operate under government-negotiated schemes of control, which permit a return of 8 per cent on their average net fixed assets. The larger the asset base, the greater the permitted return. All other factors – such as inflation rates, wage movements, general economic conditions and household affordability – don’t even enter the equation. Even fuel cost risks are passed on to consumers through fuel cost adjustments. It is a profit-guaranteed scheme based on a single variable: capital assets. This is the purest form of economic policy serving capital rather than the people. Many would argue that economics shouldn’t be viewed through the dichotomy of lifting GDP or lifting livelihood. The benefits of GDP growth will trickle down to the people, they say. If only it were that simple. Hong Kong is extraordinarily wealthy on paper.
