The UBS Global Wealth Report 2026 places Hong Kong’s average wealth per adult at just under US$650,000 (HK$5.1 million), the fourth highest in the world. By that measure, an average two-adult household would hold more than HK$10 million in wealth. Hong Kong should be overflowing with prosperity and happiness. Averages can conceal more than they reveal, though. Put a multimillionaire and a struggling tenant together, and their average wealth looks impressive. As a study from June noted, Hong Kong is the world’s most unequal society in terms of wealth distribution. That explains the gulf between statistical prosperity and the everyday hardships Hong Kong people experience. Picture a familiar Hong Kong summer scene. Why are our shopping centres always so crowded, particularly in summer, even when people are not shopping? The answer is that many people living in cramped accommodation are reluctant to turn on the air conditioner because of the high electricity bills, so they stroll through air-conditioned malls, enjoying free air conditioning while clocking up their 10,000 steps. Comfort, exercise, thrift – all in one outing. This is our Lion Rock spirit: finding happiness amid hardship. However, this celebrated Hong Kong spirit is no excuse for policymakers to leave our citizens struggling in hardship. Housing offers another telling example. We are told that property prices are determined by supply and demand, and Hong Kong’s land shortage makes exorbitant prices inevitable. Is land really the issue? Roughly three-quarters of Hong Kong’s land remains undeveloped. Singapore has about only two-thirds of Hong Kong’s land area and roughly four-fifths of our population, yet close to 80 per cent of households live in government housing that is more spacious and affordable than Hong Kong’s dwellings. The difference between Singapore and Hong Kong is not land but government policy. Hong Kong’s history makes this clear. When property prices plunged amid the Asian financial crisis, the government suspended scheduled land sales and halted new Home Ownership Scheme sales to prop up property prices. Such resolute policy is rarely seen in Hong Kong, and it worked. Property prices rebounded. But even when property prices returned to reasonable levels, the city government did not interfere and instead chose to let property prices keep rising until they were beyond the reach of most. The real issue is that government policies – on land, housing and many other aspects – serve capital, not people. The same question of whom economic policies serve illuminates the contrast between Chinese and Western approaches to development. China’s high-speed rail network delivers public benefits through connectivity, mobility, productivity and national development. The US has abundant capital and technological expertise, yet it hasn’t built a comparable network. US capital flows to AI companies in the hope of ever-greater profits. It does not flow to infrastructure, the huge benefits of which would diffuse across the community rather than to investors. China does not need a Nobel Prize to validate its economic miracle. However, the Hong Kong government seems to need a Nobel laureate economist to remind it that markets are tools rather than masters, that GDP measures output instead of human well-being and that the economy exists to serve the people, not the other way round.

title: 2 Taiwanese executives arrested over mainland components in military drones
description: Investigation into Jiin Ming Industry is the second in two months over prohibited mainland gear in military drones.
content: Two Taiwanese executives have been arrested for allegedly using mainland Chinese-made components in drones supplied to the island’s military. It is the second time in two months that a Taiwanese drone supplier has been investigated by the island’s authorities over the alleged use of prohibited mainland components. The case has intensified opposition scrutiny of the government’s efforts to build a “drone team” based on a “non-red” supply chain that excludes components and technology from mainland China. Prosecutors in the northern city of Taoyuan said on Monday that Jiin Ming Industry and its subsidiary were suspected of installing mainland-made chips and camera lenses in military drones. The companies allegedly submitted false certificates of origin when the drones were presented to the military for inspection, according to the Taoyuan District Prosecutors Office. Jiin Ming vice-chairman Chien Hao-ting and business manager Chen Yang-cheng were arrested after prosecutors searched multiple locations on October 8. A court ordered the two detained for two months and held incommunicado on “suspicion of violating the National Security Act and committing offences including document forgery and aggravated fraud”. Jiin Ming, a hardware manufacturer which started making drones several years ago, said it would cooperate with the investigation and had activated contingency measures, with chairman Tsai Hsiang-feng temporarily assuming Chien’s duties. Taiwanese Defence Minister Wellington Koo Li-hsiung said on Tuesday that the suspected irregularities involved small-value purchases of Jiin Ming drones by individual military units rather than larger procurement programmes. He acknowledged that such purchases – sometimes involving only two or four drones – had not previously been subjected to more detailed inspections in which units are dismantled. Koo said the ministry would now require even small batches to be dismantled and inspected to prevent prohibited “red” components from being concealed inside the aircraft. “We will enforce this strictly,” he said. The opposition Taiwan People’s Party said the case exposed weaknesses in the government’s efforts at boosting supply chain security. It also questioned Jiin Ming’s links with companies that it described as being close to the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and accused the government of failing to adequately scrutinise military contractors. “Jiin Ming was selected as a member of the national drone team, but was found to have allegedly used mainland Chinese-made components. Does no one in the DPP government need to take responsibility?” TPP chairman Huang Kuo-chang said on Tuesday. The controversy comes two months after Taiwan’s first case of a military drone supplier being investigated for suspected violations of the island’s security law and attempted fraud. In August, Hang Jian Technology was accused of using mainland Chinese-packaged chips and mainland-made flight-control boards in drones supplied to the island’s Eighth Army Corps. The company won a NT$2.9 million (US$92,000) contract to supply 180 drones. The army discovered the suspected mainland components during acceptance inspections, withheld payment and referred the case to prosecutors. Company head Chang Tung-lin was subsequently detained and held incommunicado. Prosecutors described it as “the first military drone procurement case involving suspected violations of the National Security Act”. Legislator Ma Wen-chun, from the opposition Kuomintang party, said after the August case that Hang Jian had faced controversies over mainland Chinese components and origin labelling as early as 2019 and 2020 but had continued to receive government contracts and subsidies. She said scrutiny needed to extend beyond major contractors to the entire supply chain, including chips, flight-control systems, communications modules and lower-tier suppliers. “If contracts repeatedly stipulate that mainland Chinese-made components are prohibited, but violations are still only discovered during acceptance inspections after delivery, what exactly has all that vetting prevented?” Ma said. The defence ministry later said the Eighth Army Corps had withheld payment after discovering the suspected mainland components and was taking steps to suspend the supplier from government procurement, terminate the contract and pursue liability for breach of contract. Analysts warned that the risks went beyond procurement compliance, with mainland Chinese electronics potentially creating operational and information-security vulnerabilities. “If Chinese electronics or related equipment are used, is it possible that this electromagnetic spectrum information could be obtained by the Communist Party more quickly?” said Lin Ying-yu, a strategic studies professor at Tamkang University in New Taipei City. “I think that would certainly pose a major threat to our drone operations.” Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any unilateral change to the cross-strait status quo by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: In Focus | Why did Hong Kong’s 11 Skies fail and can the megaproject be rescued?
description: As New World Development returns control of the struggling project to the Airport Authority, experts examine the legal and economic ramifications.
content: The roar of plane engines and the hustle and bustle at Hong Kong International Airport’s Terminal 2 present a stark contrast to the pin-drop silence at the adjacent 11 Skies commercial complex. A South China Morning Post reporter who travelled between the two places in early October found minimal footfall at the shopping centre, with the bright and airy environment of the airport terminal replaced by dim, stuffy and boarded-up corridors, and poor air conditioning amid the simmering outdoor heat. Occupying a gross floor area of 3.8 million square feet, 11 Skies is a mammoth project at the airport. Seventy per cent of the space was originally earmarked for a mall with 800 stores and 120 food and drink concepts, and the rest equally divided between experiential entertainment facilities and grade A office spaces. But only one of its three office towers currently houses some companies running businesses at the airport. The rest of the space sits in gloomy darkness. After months of market speculation, the fate of 11 Skies was decided in early October when Hong Kong’s Airport Authority and developer New World Development signed an agreement to end the latter’s nearly 50-year contract for the project. With the authority back at the helm, the mall’s management plans to tear down the existing 11 Skies signature logo, reconfigure the retail space into an entertainment hub, bring in tenants and investors, and relaunch the project under a new name and identity. New World, which has been mired in a debt crisis since 2023, relinquished its control of the property and paid a HK$2.3 billion (US$293 million) break-up fee. It will spend an additional HK$1.05 billion on works and services before handing operations over to the authority by April next year. The majority shareholder, the Cheng family’s private investment vehicle Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, will grant the authority an option to buy New World shares. Although the call option gives the authority the right to buy 750 million shares at HK$3 each from Chow Tai Fook Enterprises within the next three years, it comes with conditions that call its feasibility into question. This rare break-up in Hong Kong’s public works sector raises questions of moral hazard and the risks of setting a precedent. Wei Lai, head of Lingnan University’s department of finance, said the surrender appeared to be a negotiated restructuring involving a substantial termination payment, asset transfer and other contractual obligations. “On the question of moral hazard, I would be cautious about characterising the arrangement as allowing a private developer to return a project ‘at will’,” Wei said, stressing that the arrangement was different from an unconditional exit option. “From an economic perspective, the more relevant moral-hazard question is whether this arrangement changes the ex ante incentives of developers in future projects.” Debt-ridden partner in an ambitious project New World’s exit had been under discussion for months. As a key step in taking over, the authority set up a new subsidiary, IEC Holdings, to spearhead the Skytopia project, a HK$100 billion megadevelopment that will turn the airport into a destination for yachting, shopping, dining, wellness, culture and entertainment. The 11 Skies project is part of it. The authority’s executive director for commercial, Cissy Chan Ching-sze, became CEO of IEC on October 1. “We will soon rename 11 Skies and change its style in a cost-effective way to reflect a new identity so that we can go recruiting for tenants and investors,” Chan said shortly after New World announced the deal on September 30. On the same day, the developer’s financial results and debt levels were also a focal point. In 2023, signs of New World’s financial distress prompted it to seek ways to reduce or refinance its debts to boost liquidity. The 11 Skies project was also a factor in the debt crisis. Under the original terms of the contract, the developer was required to pay a guaranteed rent or a revenue rent representing 20 per cent of the gross revenue from the project, whichever was higher. New World was due to pay the rent from 2027 until the end of the contract in 2066. The early termination allowed the developer to shed the contract’s financial obligations. As of June 30, the developer’s total debt stood at HK$143.3 billion. Net debt amounted to HK$126.3 billion, an increase of HK$6.2 billion during the financial year. To ease its financial burden, the developer implemented seven measures to reduce debt, including asset disposals, capital expenditure optimisation and a decade-long suspension of dividend payments that ended last year. Julian Lee Pui-hang, the authority’s executive director for finance, conceded that it had to bring forward the 11 Skies project by parting with the “debt-ridden partner”. “How can we work with a debt-ridden partner as we need to bring forward the project?” he said. “The deal represents the best efforts of the controlling shareholder.” Exit deal triggers moral hazard? Wei of Lingnan University said she did not think the existence of one exceptional and costly exit mechanism by itself established an expectation for developers to bid more aggressively or take greater risks. “Where difficulties arise partly from unusually adverse market conditions rather than simply from poor project execution, an orderly restructuring may in some circumstances preserve more economic value than allowing the situation to deteriorate further,” she said. Market financing introduced an additional layer of market discipline because lenders and institutional investors would assess the financial position, risk exposure and expected returns of the authority. “That market discipline can reduce, though not eliminate, governance and moral-hazard concerns,” Wei said. Ervi Liusman, senior lecturer at the hotel and tourism management school at the Chinese University of Hong Kong Business School, said allowing a private developer to surrender a contracted commercial property would theoretically constitute a moral hazard if the developer could avoid the commercial risks it originally agreed to bear without facing a penalty. “Allowing a developer to exit at will without penalty will encourage aggressive bids, knowing that there is an exit option if the market conditions deteriorate,” she said. Liusman said that, based on what was revealed to the public, the developer had to bear significant financial losses upon returning 11 Skies, which meant the project was not surrendered at will and therefore did not constitute a moral hazard or set a bad precedent. The surrender of the infrastructure, the break-up fee and other related expenses dealt a blow to New World’s balance sheet. It resulted in HK$18.32 billion in net impairment losses and provisions relating to 11 Skies in the year ending June 30, contributing to New World’s HK$26.8 billion net loss. The net loss widened from HK$16.35 billion a year ago. “Because the Airport Authority remains accountable to lenders and investors, it has strong incentives to ensure that any decision to take back the development is commercially justified and capable of generating long-term value,” Liusman said. If the developer incurred substantial losses and contractual penalties, the focus shifted from who absorbed the loss to which party was best placed to unlock the future value of the asset, she explained. “The Airport Authority’s intervention may then be seen as a realistic restructuring of a strategically important asset rather than a transfer of risk from private sector to the public sector,” Liusman said. Despite being wholly owned by the government, the authority has primarily funded its infrastructure, such as the HK$141.5 billion three-runway system, through issuing debt, charging departure taxes and drawing on internal resources. The authority also retained the dividend payments the government agreed to forgo for a decade until last year. It rarely directly taps the public coffers. Ken Ip Man-hon, associate director of Saint Francis University’s Innovative Incubation Centre, said whether private developers should be allowed to exit large public-facing projects when commercial assumptions deteriorated was a legitimate policy question. “The bigger lesson is that long-term projects need both accountability and flexibility,” Ip said. He said a long-term project could not realistically be based on the assumption that its original business model would remain optimal for decades. The project was tendered in 2018, a record year for tourist arrivals in the city before unexpected disruptions arose amid the social unrest of 2019 and the Covid-19 pandemic between 2020 and 2023. After the borders reopened, another unexpected trend emerged, with mainland Chinese visitors – the city’s largest group of inbound travellers – spending less and Hongkongers choosing to cross the border for leisure spending. Chan of the authority said her team would reposition and reconfigure the 11 Skies retail space into an entertainment hub, offer more unique experiences for visitors and bring in new features from overseas. Win-win arrangement? Ip said the authority was moving in the right direction by expanding the project beyond conventional retail to include aviation activities, arts and culture, tourism and experiential entertainment. “The more important question remains – that is, what activities benefit most from being next to an international airport?” Tourism and entertainment were part of the answer, but Ip suggested that the site could also include higher education, executive education, professional training, research and innovation. “If 11 Skies can become a mixed-use international gateway rather than simply a better shopping and entertainment complex, the new strategy could give the project a much stronger foundation,” he said. Li King-king, a professor at Hang Seng University of Hong Kong’s department of economics and finance, said the early termination was a very special case and was potentially a win-win arrangement. The break-up was driven by factors such as location, airport design, trends in the Hong Kong retail market, changes in consumer behaviour due to the internet and residents travelling to the mainland for leisure, he said. “The focus is whether the whole of society, the entire Airport Authority, the whole of Hong Kong, benefits from this agreement,” Li said. Delaying the project could incur costs and affect overall airport planning, and the parties had to make a choice, taking society’s overall interests into consideration, he added. The authority is now racing to reconfigure and relaunch the 11 Skies complex in 2028, with plans to align the project with the ambitious Skytopia megadevelopment at the airport. Skytopia is a strategic blueprint that aims to create a new landmark for Hong Kong that will serve as a major growth engine for the economy. The ecosystem will include a 20,000-seat arena for world-class performances at AsiaWorld-Expo next to the airport, a yacht bay providing 500 berths, a water recreation area, art galleries and storage facilities. It will also feature a promenade with leisure facilities and an autonomous transport system connecting Skytopia, the Hong Kong border crossing of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge and Tung Chung railway station. “We expect the entertainment hub to serve as a platform for mainland companies to market their products to an international audience, and for international businesses to make inroads into the mainland market,” Chan of the authority said. The authority aims to recruit top-notch entertainment operators and business partners globally to be a part of major Skytopia components in the 2028-29 financial year. “It will be an attraction for locals, transit passengers and visitors,” she said. Additional reporting by Lo Hoi-ying and Denise Tsang

title: Hong Kong racing superstar Vincent Ho on his fightback from brain bleed, world-class quest
description: Named one of the city’s Ten Outstanding Young Persons, the 36-year-old is consumed by his desire to join the planet’s elite jockeys.
content: Explaining his aversion to socialising, Vincent Ho Chak-yiu was suitably succinct. “When I have to talk, it’s a lot of effort,” he told the South China Morning Post. “Harder than riding a horse, for sure.” It is logical that one of Hong Kong’s greatest jockeys feels most contented on horseback. When Ho begins speaking, though, the personal takes and tales roll off his tongue. He relives the day in New Zealand that he “felt completely dead” after riding 39 horses, explains how he bounced back last year from the traumatic brain injury that knocked him out for four days, issues a rebuke to the anonymous critics who “can’t even sit on a horse” and relates how hugging trees helps him manage a life of incessant scrutiny and judgment. On the sacrifice and temperance that are built into his every day, Ho said: “I don’t like to go partying, because it’s noisy. I’m sensitive to alcohol, and I don’t like to drink. “I don’t feel like I’m missing out on anything.” No, Ho’s days are consumed with pursuing “my goal of becoming a world-class jockey”. “My coach says I never switch off,” he said. In school, Ho would lapse into daydreams about “jumping on horses”. After his focus switched to the flat, he would “visualise every day, even when I was in the shower” of ways in which he could refine his craft. The strength, fortitude, drive and modesty that Ho has exhibited in the 20 years since he was accepted into The Hong Kong Jockey Club’s (HKJC) Apprentice Jockeys’ School were recognised last week, when the 36-year-old was named among the recipients of the city’s Ten Outstanding Young Persons award. “It’s a great honour, but it’s for the whole Hong Kong racing community,” Ho said. “My dad always told me that it was important to be respected, and to give back. “I have to do well in my career, or I’ll have done nothing to inspire anyone, nor be able to give back to society.” Ho was 13 when “the story started”, after his father spied a Pokfulam Public Riding School advertisement for budding equestrians. “I always loved animals and, living in a concrete city, getting to ride horses was really special,” he said. Among other activities, Ho had played badminton, table tennis and football, and practised martial arts, as well as trying the piano and Chinese painting. “I wasn’t as good at any of them as I was at riding,” he said. “My parents always let me try lots of things; they wanted to find my passion and talent.” Ho reckons that passion, coupled with his latent ability, set him apart when HKJC whittled 1,000 candidates down to around 12, after his eagle-eyed dad also spotted the opportunity to apply for their apprentice jockeys’ school. The “great resources, coaches and horses” supplied by the club hastened Ho’s development, along with the help of “my really great mentor”, the champion trainer, Caspar Fownes. Still, before he could compete on home turf, Ho had to undergo an overseas rite of passage. “We can’t just start riding straight off, because the gap with the experienced jockeys here would be massive,” he said. After around six months in Australia, where the native staff would “support their own people first”, Ho asked to transfer elsewhere, which was how he ended up in Matamata on New Zealand’s North Island. “In winter, it went down to minus 6 degrees [21.2 degrees Fahrenheit], which toughens you up,” Ho said. “You have to stay strong, adapt and be resilient.” The 39-horse day entailed riding 10 on the gallops, before his agent drove him to Cambridge trials to mount 29 more. “I felt absolutely dead,” Ho said. He recalls times when he would “travel in the truck with the horse for four hours, set it up, ride it, take off the saddle, wash and walk the horse, then travel back with it.” All the while, he told himself: “I have to do my best and be back in Hong Kong as soon as possible.” “I never thought about giving up,” Ho said. “I love riding horses, the feeling of winning and of overcoming obstacles. I like riding horses that other people can’t perform on, or make the horse listen to what they want to do, and I can.” He recorded 44 winners during 12 months that, in hindsight, were “fun and essential”. “In Hong Kong, we’re very privileged with all the staff who help us,” he said. “HKJC provides us with an incredible support network and facilities.” There was a neat symmetry with his back-breaking New Zealand day when Ho managed 39 wins in 2010-11 to be crowned Hong Kong Champion Apprentice. Nonetheless, it was his partnership with Golden Sixty, the horse with whom he will forever be inextricably linked,that propelled Ho to stardom. His 26 wins on the horse, from 31 rides between 2019 and 2024, included 10 Group 1 victories. “In his first trial, he accelerated through a gap without hesitation when I asked,” Ho said. “Not many horses are that brave ... They don’t have that turn of foot.” It was to Golden Sixty that Ho turned as he recuperated last year from his fourth brutal fall in little more than 18 months. A July 2023 tumble in Japan resulted in a fractured T5 vertebrae, whiplash and pneumothorax. In January 2024, a spill at Sha Tin left him with four fractures to the vertebrae in his neck, and a broken finger. At the same racecourse 11 months later, Ho was concussed after being dislodged from Super Win Dragon. When he came off Oldtown, again at Sha Tin, on February 9 last year, Ho sustained a brain bleed and brain contusion, along with shoulder and neck fractures. Ho remembers nothing of the following four days in an intensive care unit. During his seven-month rehabilitation, he was sensitive to noise and bright lights, as well as noticing a change in his ordinarily level temperament. “I had an amazing medical team, the HKJC found my sports doctor in Switzerland [at the Swiss Olympic Medical Centre] and they were confident after seeing the scans that I would get back with no problems,” Ho said, adding that the “amazing” plant-based diet he has followed for the past eight years, along with endless days devoted to riding, physiotherapy and the gym, gave him further confidence that he would successfully return. “I never wanted to quit,” he said. “For me, riding horses is like drinking water and eating.” Still, when it was time to literally get back on the horse, Ho went to “the only one I fully trusted”, visiting Golden Sixty at his retirement stables in Hokkaido, Japan. “We know each other inside out, and I knew I wouldn’t get injured on him,” Ho said. Back in Hong Kong, Ho managed “fearful thoughts” with the aid of a sports psychologist. “Sometimes, in Asian culture, we think seeing a psychologist always means you’re ill,” Ho said. “But it helps you perform, and helps in everyday life.” Ho has no residual issues and, with nine wins from 74 mounts this season, he is back up and running. At the outset of his career, Ho would “get really angry” after a disappointing race, and “not be able to focus on the next one”. “I learned that the next race is also important,” he said. “You put your life on it, and owners and trainers put their heart into training the horse.” Equally, Ho has grown to ignore online critique. “If you’ve done your best, it’s fine,” he said. “It’s like telling [Lionel] Messi or [Cristiano] Ronaldo how to kick a ball: ‘shut up’. “Those comments come from people who can’t even sit on a horse.” As a high-profile figure in what he views as “the number one sport in Hong Kong”, Ho “prefers not to go to malls or walk around Central”. “Coming back from my injury last year, I demanded so much from myself that sometimes I got overwhelmed,” he said. “Now, I have one half-day completely off every week. I go into nature, do some grounding meditation, or go for a hike,” he said. “Sit in the park hugging a tree. Some weird stuff.” Regardless of the achievements that led to him becoming the first jockey honoured in the outstanding young persons’ 54-year history, Ho said he was “not even halfway” towards the world-class status he craves. “There’s lots to improve and it won’t be easy, but I’ll do my best,” he said. Wise words from a man who does not like the sound of his own voice.

title: Henderson banks on tenant ‘FOMO’ to fill US$8b Central Yards project
description: The developer says demand is strong for remaining offices in Central Yards, as Hong Kong tenants gravitate to premium new-build projects.
content: Henderson Land Development is banking on demand for premium offices to support its HK$63 billion (US$8.03 billion) Central Yards project, as tenants gravitate towards top-tier buildings even while much of Hong Kong’s office market remains weak. Jane Street’s decision last year to take about 70 per cent of the office space in the first phase of the project has helped draw interest from other potential tenants, according to Tom Andrews, director and head of leasing and operations at Central Site 3 Management Limited, a subsidiary of Henderson Land that manages the Central Yards project. “It’s helped us massively,” Andrews said in an interview on Friday, adding that the Jane Street deal had given Central Yards “a real seal of approval from a great anchor client”. Andrews said he was seeing demand for the remaining 30 per cent of available office space coming from a mix of quantitative trading firms, multinational companies, private equity funds and wealth managers. The pattern reflects a widening divide in Hong Kong’s office market, where demand has concentrated in newer, high-quality buildings while older offices continue to face pressure over vacancies and rents. “You basically have a split or bifurcated market,” Andrews said. “People want top-quality, premium-grade assets.” Although demand had strengthened, the market had not yet reached the stage where tenants were fighting over space, he noted. However, with the best buildings filling up, some tenants were beginning to feel a “fear of missing out” on top-tier offices, he added. Occupancy rates remain high in some of Central’s leading office buildings, with One and Two International Finance Centre effectively full and The Henderson exceeding 95 per cent occupancy. Henderson paid HK$50.8 billion for the waterfront site where Central Yards is now located in November 2021 – a record price for a land purchase at the time, which came just before Hong Kong’s office market fell into a prolonged downturn. Central Yards has more than 1.6 million square feet of planned gross floor area, with roughly 40 per cent allocated to offices and 54 per cent to retail, according to project figures. Retail presents a different challenge for Henderson. Hong Kong’s tourism recovery has not consistently translated into stronger consumer spending, putting pressure on landlords and retailers. For Andrews, the solution is “giving people excitement”. “Hong Kong is an incredible city,” he said. “People always like something new … something that represents both Hong Kong and the global stage.” The developer on Tuesday announced that Kim Jones, the new fashion label from the British designer of the same name, would become the first retail anchor at the waterfront project. The label will open its inaugural global flagship store, spanning about 4,000 square feet across two floors, in 2027. Central Yards’ first-phase retail section spans about 300,000 square feet and is expected to open in 2027. Henderson plans to bring about 100 brands and concepts to the development, including fashion, lifestyle and dining businesses. At the launch event on Tuesday, Henderson Land chairman Martin Lee Ka-shing said Central Yards “isn’t just a development to us; it’s a love letter to Hong Kong”. His wife, Cathy Chui Lee, joined Jones for a fireside chat about the designer’s new label and his connection to the city. Jones said Hong Kong’s mix of cultures and blend of old and new had drawn him back throughout his career. “You see things that you’ll never see anywhere else.” For now, leasing director Andrews said his team was scouting the world for retail concepts, travelling to markets including mainland China, Europe, Japan and South Korea, while monitoring trends and tapping contacts across Henderson. He said the project’s success would ultimately be judged by investment returns, visitor traffic and its ability to generate lasting interest.

title: Why younger Japanese now fear Trump’s US more than China
description: A survey reveals under-50s see the US as the world’s top threat – driven by growing horror at its foreign policy, analysts say.
content: A growing number of Japanese regard the United States as the greatest threat to world peace ahead of traditional rival China, according to a new survey. The annual poll, released by the Japan Press Research Institute on Saturday, found 26.8 per cent of respondents named the US as the biggest threat to global peace. That was up 9.3 percentage points on last year and far above the 6.6 per cent recorded in 2024. Russia came top of the list in 2025 but slipped to third place this year, with 18.3 per cent of the total vote. China rose 8.2 percentage points to first place, cited by 32.5 per cent of the 5,000 people polled in July and August. Analysts attribute the shift in sentiment to the actions of one man. This is all about Trump, Trump, Trump Stephen Nagy, international-relations professor “This is all about Trump, Trump, Trump,” said Stephen Nagy, a professor of international relations at Tokyo’s International Christian University. “For the last two years, Japanese people have looked on with growing horror at Trump’s erratic behaviour, his lack of knowledge and his lack of interest in so many things.” The results of the survey are more of a referendum on the US president than an accurate reflection of Japanese attitudes towards the US military or ordinary American people, according to Nagy. “It is obvious that the war in Iran was not necessary and is not going well,” he said, adding that Japanese people were “alarmed” by Trump’s flattery of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and “the lack of positive takeaways” from his recent meeting with China’s Xi Jinping. “This has all punched a huge hole in the US’ reputation,” Nagy said. North Korea and Iran rounded out the top five in the latest threat perceptions survey, which also canvassed opinions on Israel, Ukraine and Japan itself. Trump was named as the primary cause of recent global problems, with more than eight in 10 respondents saying he was having a negative impact on the world while only 13.2 per cent called him a positive force. Women of all ages and respondents of both sexes were most concerned about the US. Some 32.1 per cent of women named it as the greatest threat, compared with 26.7 per cent who named China. Men and women aged 20 to 49 also put the US ahead of China, while the order was reversed among those aged 50 and older. Nagy suggested that part of the reason for this was that older people might still fondly remember the US’ victory over the Soviet Union during the Cold War. “Young people, on the other hand, have grown up with 9/11, the Iraq war, the US retreat from Afghanistan, Trump’s love-hate relationship with Ukraine and the general cringeyness of the Trump administration.” Broken trust Sumie Kawakami, a lecturer at Yamanashi Gakuin University in Japan and author of a book on gender issues, said Japanese people had broadly “lost trust” in the US president. In addition to starting trade and actual wars during his second term, Trump has also sanctioned the International Criminal Court (ICC) and its president, Japanese judge Tomoko Akane, and hosted Xi at a summit in the US where he characterised China as a World War II ally against Japan. “No one knows when he is just going to flip the script,” Kawakami said, adding this unpredictability had put Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in a “difficult position”. Takaichi had pledged her support for the ICC “because the court is a key part of Japan’s position on the need for the rule of law internationally” and the Japanese public also backed this position, Kawakami said. “But she cannot go so far as to strain the relationship with Trump because of the need for US security support in the region.” Other Japanese prime ministers have had to show what Kawakami calls “pragmatism” in their dealings with Washington, but walking that tightrope has been harder for Takaichi than for any of her predecessors. Ken Kato, a conservative-leaning Tokyo businessman and former firm Trump supporter, said he was now having reservations about the US president – but still believed “China is a far larger and more immediate threat to Japan”. “Trump should certainly have been more forceful with Xi and I fear that by welcoming him with a red carpet in Washington that he has sent the Chinese the wrong message,” he added. Nagy said he suspected that “the favourability of the US among the Japanese will return” under a different president, after Trump had left the White House for good and the relationship had stabilised “once more”. “That is exactly what the government in Japan, and the governments in … the rest of East Asia also want,” he said. “They just want ‘normal’.”

title: Gulf sporting events face risks amid escalating regional conflicts
description: Security threats could jeopardise major tournaments and economic investments in the region.
content:
When 60,000 football fans gathered in Jeddah for the Arabian Gulf Cup earlier this month, they also inadvertently highlighted another issue: the vulnerability of major sports events hosted by Gulf monarchies to the ongoing wars in the region.
Although the two-week football tournament proceeded as scheduled, persistent risks were underscored when a Houthi air strike on Riyadh’s international airport resulted in three fatalities on October 9.
Following this, there was a significant escalation in the Yemen war, with Riyadh continuing its military support for the internationally recognised government against the Iran-backed Houthis.
Analysts warn that the threats posed by the Houthis and Iranian air strikes against Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states – Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman – could have negative implications for the region’s ambitious sporting calendar.
If these conflicts continue, the uncertainty could jeopardise upcoming major events. These include the 2030 Asian Games in Qatar and the 2034 Fifa World Cup and Asian Games in Saudi Arabia.
Regional instability is not exclusive to the Gulf region; however, it significantly influences host countries’ decisions. This perspective comes from Guy Burton, the co-host of The FootPol Podcast, which explores the intersection of football and politics.
Security considerations are built into every major event bid, but West Asia presents particular challenges.
“What is distinctive in this context is the volatility,” Burton said, noting how difficult it was to predict whether threats would escalate or subside.
The risks extend beyond just security concerns. Gulf monarchies have significantly invested in sports to diversify their economies away from reliance on oil and gas revenues.
If conflicts disrupt these events, the tens of billions of dollars invested in stadiums, hotels, airports and airlines could appear wasted, along with the economic policies underpinning them.
To emphasise the situation, the Bahrain and Saudi Formula One Grand Prix races originally scheduled for April were postponed and moved to Malaysia, resulting in an estimated loss of US$200 million (HK$1.5 billion). This followed the cancellation of the Finalissima football match in March, which was set to take place in Qatar between Spain and Argentina.
Similarly, the Esports World Cup was moved from Saudi Arabia to France in August, casting a shadow over the Public Investment Fund’s (PIF) US$55 billion (HK$431 billion) leveraged buyout of EA Sports – the largest transaction of its kind.
According to Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, fellow for the Middle East at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy, “the next big test” would be the AFC Asian Cup across Saudi Arabia in early 2027.
“That experience will be closely studied for what it may portend for future large-scale events in the Gulf,” said Ulrichsen, including the Fiba Basketball World Cup in Qatar later that year.

title: Meet architect and designer Steve Leung, whose work spans from Hong Kong to Hokkaido
description: Beyond high-profile projects like the Swim Club at the Kimpton Tsim Sha Tsui hotel, Leung designed his own cosy holiday home in Niseko.
content: One of Hong Kong’s most prominent architects and interior designers, Steve Leung has been in the business for four decades and counting. In 1997, Leung restructured his architecture business and established two firms: Steve Leung Architects and Steve Leung Designers. Leung’s business has since grown to include brands like Steve Leung Hospitality, and he is now best known for both interior design and being an avid restaurateur. Ask any Hong Kong resident and they’ve probably, perhaps unknowingly, set foot inside an establishment designed by Leung’s group – from the Mango Tree flagship inside Elements shopping mall to, more recently, the Swim Club at the Kimpton Tsim Sha Tsui hotel. The crown jewel of the Kimpton Tsim Sha Tsui, which opened its doors last year, the Swim Club very much exemplifies the experience-driven approach to design that has come to define most projects across the Steve Leung Design Group portfolio. Perched on the 50th floor of the hotel, the space feels at once vintage and modern, taking cues from the retro-style pool clubs of Southern California as well as the glistening skyscrapers that make up the Hong Kong skyline. At the entrance, shimmering blue mosaic walls and a rippled glass ceiling along with bubblelike spherical lights create the illusion of being underwater, while an archway frames the view of Victoria Harbour and terracotta-coloured poolside sun loungers. The result is an urban oasis away from the hustle and bustle of the city yet still deeply integrated into its environment. Circular bar stools, table lamps and floor lamps with spherical touches, custom-made by Steve Leung Hospitality, also point to another core tenet of the design philosophy – “less over-design, more human-centric thinking” – which Leung himself says has come to define not only his own practice but also the wider evolution of interior design in Hong Kong over the years. In a city built for efficiency, ideating spaces where every detail is carefully considered and designed to make people feel at home is paramount for Leung and his team. That objective also informs Leung’s projects further afield, including his very own holiday home OOAK Niseko, located in the snowy hillsides of Hokkaido, Japan. Wooden ceilings, floor-to-ceiling windows and a relatively muted yet cosy colour palette blend seamlessly in with the surroundings, while the distinctly Japanese minimalism of the space gives off the sense of endless calm and inner peace. It certainly lives up to its name, OOAK, which stands for One of a Kind. Besides his documented love for food, it’s no surprise then that one other key passion informs Leung’s love for quality, lived-in design: family. OOAK Lamma, a picturesque home built with timber reclaimed from an old fishing boat on Hong Kong’s Lamma Island, now serves as a private kitchen run by Leung’s daughter Stefanie. Accessible only by boat, it comprises two former village houses – the buildings lovingly restored to be a safe haven for a select number of lucky guests. “Hong Kong is a small city with big challenges,” Leung says of continuing to push the boundaries of design in the region, whether through commercial or personal projects. “These constraints push us to turn challenges into opportunities.” Despite the rising influence of AI and technology, he believes the humanity of design will always win out. Citing Hong Kong’s “openness to the world” and “new ideas, materials and ways of living” as reasons why the city’s design scene will continue to thrive, Leung writes, “The next generation can shape not just better spaces, but a better way of living ... The future of Hong Kong design is about finding our own voice and creating a language of our own, one that reflects who we are and how we want to live.”

title: 10 mouth-watering English adjectives and idioms to describe food
description: Whether it’s bursting with flavour or making your stomach turn, here are some common terms and phrases to use for your next meal.
content:
The world boasts a wide range of cuisines and dishes. Some of them might be to your liking, while other times, the execution might not be up to grade. Upgrade your vocabulary with these English terms and phrases that are perfect for describing your next meal, whether you love or hate it.
Meaning: describes food that looks or smells so good it makes you hungry and eager to eat Example: She posted a mouth-watering photo of a gooey chocolate lava cake on Instagram.
Meaning: tender and full of juice, almost exclusively used to describe meat or fruit Example: The steak was so succulent that I did not even need sauce.
Meaning: describes food that looks or smells attractive, making you hungry Example: The roasted vegetables were arranged so beautifully on the plate; they looked incredibly appetising.
Meaning: when something is exactly what you needed or wanted at that moment – especially satisfying hunger, thirst or a craving. It implies perfect timing and complete satisfaction. Example: I was craving something warm and cheesy, and this pizza absolutely hit the spot.
Meaning: packed with intense, vibrant and concentrated taste
Example: The chef’s signature curry was bursting with flavour, with layers of spice that lingered on my tongue.
Meaning: a meal or dish that provides a rich, varied and exciting sensory experience, often in taste, texture, temperature and aroma Example: Each dish at the new Thai restaurant was a feast for the taste buds, combining sweet, sour, salty and spicy in every bite.
Meaning: having almost no taste, lacking flavour; bland and dull Example: Despite looking promising, the chicken breast was dry and insipid – completely forgettable.
Meaning: extremely unpleasant, disgusting or nauseating. This is a very strong word for food that is outright offensive to your senses. Example: The combination of canned tuna and chocolate sauce was revolting.
Meaning: so overly sweet, rich or sugary that it becomes sickening and unpleasant. It is often used for desserts, drinks or sauces. Example: The cheap maple syrup had a cloying, artificial sweetness that coated my tongue in a bad way.
Meaning: to cause a strong feeling of disgust or nausea Example: Watching him mix ketchup with his ice cream was enough to make my stomach turn.

title: US fines Bank of America US$1.2 billion, says it violated money laundering, sanctions laws
description: The bank failed to mitigate and report ‘priority national security risks’, including Chinese money-laundering networks, the US Treasury says.
content: The US Treasury Department said on Tuesday that it was imposing US$1.2 billion in fines on Bank of America for allegedly violating anti-money-laundering and sanctions laws. The fines on America’s second-biggest bank amount to the third-largest in the department’s history. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law.” Treasury said Bank of America also reached a US$11.6 million settlement with the department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control over “apparent violations of numerous sanctions programmes, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism”. In a statement, Treasury said its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network assessed the US$1.2 billion penalty for Bank of America’s “failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border”. The penalty includes US$750 million that will go to the US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine ever imposed by that federal bank regulatory agency. Treasury said that Bank of America “admits that it wilfully violated” the 1970 Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to help the government detect and prevent money laundering. The latest action is the third-largest penalty ever issued by the Treasury Department, behind a roughly US$4 billion settlement in 2023 with Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and an around US$3 billion settlement with Canada-based TD Bank the following year. Both those historic actions happened as part of the Biden administration’s focus on anti-money laundering and efforts to promote compliance with the then-emerging virtual currency industry. Months later, Binance founder and CEO Changpeng Zhao, was sentenced to four months in prison over charges that he looked the other way as criminals used his platform to move money connected to child sex abuse, drug trafficking and terrorism.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong’s hosting of Apec finance ministers’ meeting a deliberate choice
description: The city must use the occasion to showcase not only its achievements as a global financial centre but also how it can serve the nation, the region and the world.
content: When finance ministers and senior officials from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum’s 21 member economies gather next week, Hong Kong will host the event for the first time. The choice of venue is no accident. China holds the Apec chair this year, and Beijing picked the city for a key ministerial summit. Sending the finance ministers to Hong Kong is a deliberate statement: the city remains the nation’s pre-eminent international financial centre, and the central government wants the world to see it. The pattern this year is telling. In June, Macau hosted the 13th Apec Tourism Ministerial Meeting, drawing more than 200 delegates to discuss smart tourism and travel facilitation. Tourism for Macau, finance for Hong Kong: each special administrative region has been given a stage suited to its strengths, and in Macau’s case a timely reminder that its future must extend beyond gaming tables. Both meetings serve as curtain-raisers for the Apec leaders’ summit in Shenzhen next month. Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu called the hosting a sign of Beijing’s recognition of Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre. The numbers amply support his claim. According to KPMG, some 116 initial public offerings raised more than HK$388 billion (US$49 billion) up to the end of September while whole-year proceeds are projected to hit a record half a trillion. Nearly 70 per cent came from A+H listings by mainland firms seeking international capital. Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (Swift) data shows the city handled about 76 per cent of the world’s renminbi payments as of August. Offshore yuan lending reached a record 935 billion yuan (US$140 billion) last year. This is what integrating and serving the country looks like in practice: Hong Kong as the channel through which mainland enterprises reach global investors and the renminbi reaches the wider world while the city itself prospers. The Apec meeting’s agenda plays to these strengths. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po has outlined four priorities for Hong Kong: fiscal policies that support livelihoods, financing for digital infrastructure, inclusive finance and nurturing young financial talent. He notes that about US$38 billion in green and sustainable bonds was issued in Hong Kong last year, leading the Asian market for the eighth consecutive year, and that the city will showcase its insurance-linked securities services, captive insurance (a kind of self-insurance by businesses) and catastrophe bonds as tools for regional climate resilience. Some will point to the likely absence in Hong Kong of US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who is expected to send a deputy in his place while he prepares for President Donald Trump’s visit to Shenzhen next month. It would be a mistake to read this as a snub. US Treasury secretaries have attended only four Apec finance ministers’ meetings held overseas since 2000; Janet Yellen attended once in four years, when Washington was host. Two trans-Pacific trips in under four weeks make little sense when Bessent is expected to meet Vice-Premier He Lifeng in Shenzhen ahead of the summit, with the trade truce due to expire on January 10. Indeed, the priority Washington attaches to the Shenzhen summit is itself encouraging. It signals that the world’s two largest economies are serious about converting a fragile truce into something durable. For Hong Kong, whose fortunes depend on open markets and stable great-power relations, that matters. Still, hosting is not an end in itself. A well-run conference showcases capabilities; it does not create them. Hong Kong’s lasting appeal depends on deep and liquid markets, a convertible currency, transparent regulation and the professional expertise global investors expect, all reinforced by steady and predictable policymaking, and the rule of law. Those must be guarded as carefully as the meeting’s logistics. Hong Kong has been handed a valuable and highly visible platform. It should use the occasion not merely to display its achievements but to deepen genuine connections and partnerships with fellow Apec economies, proving that a city which serves the nation can also serve the region and the world.

title: London wine club’s Shanghai outpost to offer Chinese drinkers a ‘sweet spot’
description: 67 Pall Mall founder Grant Ashton says club’s 6,000-label list, including 1,000 Chinese wines, reflects a shift towards drinking less but better.
content: London-based private members’ wine club 67 Pall Mall is scheduled to open its first mainland China outpost in December, in Shanghai’s former French Concession. Founder Grant Ashton says the move reflects a global shift away from spirits – which can reach 40 per cent alcohol by volume (ABV) – towards wine, typically 12 to 14 per cent ABV. “Wine is halfway down to zero,” he says, mapping out the spectrum from spirits to non-alcoholic drinks. “If you’re starting from spirits, wine is your sweet spot. A lot of the younger generation is starting from wine as being their naughty place and going back lower than that.” Alcohol consumption among young adults has been declining. According to the Annals of Internal Medicine, alcohol use among Gen Z adults aged 18 to 29 fell by more than 5 per cent between 2022 and 2024. In China, baijiu sales softened, particularly among younger consumers, who increasingly see the 40 to 60 per cent ABV spirit as their parents’ drink. Ashton says younger people are drinking less overall. For those who do drink, however, he sees wine occupying a middle ground: it has less alcohol than spirits and, he says, is more interesting than beer. The emphasis, he adds, is on drinking better, not more. “I suspect you’ll see the same thing in China,” he says. “When you get to trust your sommelier and they serve you something slightly different, over time, people expand their horizons.” In Shanghai, the wine club will occupy Grand Mansion on Donghu Road, a century-old French Renaissance-style building. Storytelling and heritage are central to Ashton’s approach, from the London and Singapore clubs to the new Shanghai outpost. A happy accident in London The London club opened in 2015, but its beginnings were more happy accident than carefully laid business plan. Ashton, then a hedge fund manager and wine collector, had more wine than space in his cellar. Ashton and his friends wanted to open a wine bar where they could store their collections and hang out. They found a beautiful old bank building in St James’s that had been empty for 15 years. Restaurateurs had looked at it and walked away. The building, which formerly housed Hambros Bank, had only one entrance and exit, no kitchen door and no obvious way to manage staff or deliveries. “I wasn’t a restaurateur,” Ashton says. “So I looked at this building going, ‘Oh yeah, it’s great.’ All the other restaurant operators went, ‘There’s no kitchen door. How are you going to get your staff in and out?’ I didn’t think about that.” Local authorities then told them they could open a club there, but not a restaurant. After signing the lease, Ashton discovered an underground network of tunnels that had once served as the bank’s vaults, providing a back-of-house route. It was pure luck. The building’s long history became part of the club’s identity. Ashton hired an archivist and an architect to research the site. Its walls now display photographs of every building that has stood there since 1720. Heritage and history around the world In Singapore, the club occupies the former penthouse of film mogul Runme Shaw. Ashton borrowed original movie posters from the Shaw family archives, installed a spotlight from their old cinema warehouse and placed vintage Shaw cinema seats in the corners. The space pays tribute to Singapore’s cinematic history. “An empty concrete shell is pretty boring,” Ashton says. “These are scheduled monuments. There is a story there.” Shanghai’s Grand Mansion will follow the same philosophy. Built in 1925 by a British financier, the building served as the Japanese Ordnance Department headquarters and has hosted Russian and American commercial offices. It also served as a government reception venue, where US president Richard Nixon and Philippine president Gloria Macapagal Arroyo met Chinese leaders. The site was a restaurant until 2015, then sat empty for years before Ashton took the lease. He even found a cellar underground for members to store their own bottles. The Shanghai club will showcase Chinese wines alongside international labels, with local wineries among its shareholders. The model follows that of other 67 Pall Mall locations, where regional producers invest in the clubs. Its wine list is set to feature 6,000 wines from 45 countries, including 1,000 Chinese labels. Coravin technology – which stops oxidisation by letting you pour wine without pulling the cork – will allow the club to offer 1,000 wines by the glass. “If I put a glass in front of you and say, ‘This is 200 yuan [US$30],’ you might take a risk on it,” Ashton says. “But if I put a bottle on the table that you don’t know, you’re not going to drink that.” Ashton has seen a similar shift from high-alcohol spirits towards wine in India, where whisky accounts for nearly half the market. “If that segment for wine goes from 5 per cent to 10 per cent, you’re talking about 1.4 billion people,” he says. “If you double wine consumption in India, it’s millions. Same in China.”

title: HKEX completes pilot green trading schemes with mainland China exchanges
description: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing’s Core Climate platform allows 15 firms to buy Green Electricity Certificates via Guangzhou Power Exchange.
content: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) has completed the first cross-border trading of green products under two separate pilot programmes with exchanges in Guangzhou and Shenzhen, according to an executive. The exchange’s Core Climate platform has enabled 15 companies, including Airport Authority, China Power International Development, Bank of China (Hong Kong) and others, to purchase Green Electricity Certificates (GECs) through the Guangzhou Power Exchange Centre with a total volume of about 100,000 GECs, said Paul Chow Koon-ying, group chief sustainability officer at HKEX in an interview with the South China Morning Post on Tuesday. GECs are the nationally recognised energy attribute certificates in mainland China, with each certificate representing one megawatt-hour of renewable electricity. Companies can trade the certificates to meet their renewable electricity commitments. Launched in 2022, Core Climate is Hong Kong’s international green marketplace for international firms to trade carbon credits, while the new pilot programme is the first time GECs have been added to the platform. The platform enables companies, investors and project owners to access transparent and certified environmental instruments and forms part of HKEX’s broader commitment to advancing Hong Kong’s role as a leading sustainable finance centre, Chow said. “These pilots are important steps in strengthening green energy and carbon market connectivity across the Greater Bay Area,” Chow said. He added: “We will work towards commercialising GECs in Hong Kong, with the aim of making them available through Core Climate, while strengthening collaboration with our partners to develop transparent, efficient and connected sustainable finance infrastructure across the region.” In another pilot programme, the Core Climate platform is used to settle Shenzhen Emission Allowance transactions with the Shenzhen Green Exchange, the HKEX said on Wednesday. “The pilot marks the first cross-boundary settlement between onshore and offshore carbon exchanges, strengthening carbon market connectivity between Hong Kong and the Chinese mainland,” Chow said. Chow said these pilot programmes supported the nation’s dual carbon goals and responded to policy priorities in the Chinese mainland and Hong Kong to explore cross-border carbon trading and settlement, providing practical experience to support the continued development of the region’s carbon markets. Globally, there has been an increase in demand for green financing since the US-Israel war on Iran started in late February, which has driven up oil prices and prompted global companies to seek cheaper, more stable energy supplies, according to Julian Wentzel, chief sustainability officer at HSBC in an interview with the SCMP last month. Companies and governments would need to raise funds to finance up to US$20 trillion in global expenditure over the next five to eight years to establish or upgrade their facilities to use renewable energy or other clean energy, Wentzel said.

title: Public comments flood US government websites over proposed H-1B, OPT fee hikes
description: Chinese students and other graduates voice concerns over steep new costs that could threaten their prospects of working in America.
content: Kana Liu, a Chinese Canadian living in the US on a work visa, felt compelled to speak up. Faced with a Department of Homeland Security proposal to charge up to US$100,000 in fees for international students to work in the US after graduation under Optional Practical Training (OPT), she rushed to the government’s public comment portal. “I firmly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee,” she wrote on the federal comment site on October 12. “They create undue barriers for legitimate students and educational institutions while failing to effectively address the stated goals of preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers.” Liu is among thousands weighing in on two contentious proposals that could sharply raise fees for international students and employers of skilled foreign workers, fuelling debate and adding uncertainty for those hoping to study, work or remain in the US. Nearly 62,000 Chinese students took part in OPT in the 2024-2025 academic year, according to the Institute of International Education’s Open Doors report. The OPT proposal, published on October 8, has drawn more than 2,000 comments since its publication. It would charge US$70,000 for a student’s first OPT authorisation and US$30,000 for each subsequent one. Schools would pay the fees but could pass the costs on to students or employers, according to DHS. The comment period runs until November 9. Another proposal concerning H-1B visas for skilled foreign workers has drawn about 11,700 comments. Unveiled in late August, the proposal would charge employers US$103,265 for each new H-1B petition subject to the annual cap of 85,000 visas. The comment period has closed, and a final decision is pending. Public comments can influence a final rule by requiring agencies to address concerns, but agencies are not obliged to adopt commenters’ recommendations. How much weight DHS will give the feedback remains unclear. Both proposals have sparked debate worldwide over their potential impact on international students. OPT generally allows graduates to work in the US for up to a year, with extensions available for those in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields. Many later seek H-1B visas, which can provide a pathway to permanent residency. The proposals come amid the Trump administration’s broader immigration crackdown. Last year, President Donald Trump ordered a US$100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, causing widespread uncertainty. Federal judges have since struck down versions of the measure. DHS’s proposed US$103,265 fee would instead be introduced through formal rule making by the agency. Last week, Vice-President J.D. Vance also announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud at nine universities, including Harvard, Yale, Stanford and MIT. DHS defended the OPT proposal in response to the South China Morning Post, saying the new fees would strengthen oversight and combat fraud and abuse. “With an increase in the number of F-1 [student visa holders] being recommended for OPT, DHS has encountered more schools, employers, and students engaged in schemes to exploit current regulations for fraudulent purposes,” a DHS spokesperson said. Official data shows that OPT authorisations rose from about 99,000 in 2015 to nearly 195,000 in 2024, while STEM OPT authorisations increased from about 27,000 to more than 95,000. DHS is also proposing to require officers to review each application to extend work visa status, including H-1B, rather than generally defer to previous approvals, according to a Federal Register document scheduled for publication on Wednesday. Speaking up Liu was on OPT but said she had to switch in August to a work visa available to Canadian citizens to maintain her legal status in the US. Many of her Chinese friends ended up on O-1 visas and are struggling to find work or maintain legal status. “It really sucks,” she told the SCMP in Mandarin. “As international students, we really have to band together, speak up for this group and voice our concerns.” The proposal could significantly affect Chinese students, who make up one of the largest groups of international students in the US. Many commenters on the OPT proposal have Chinese surnames, though their nationalities are not always clear. “Fraud should be addressed through investigations, employer verification and enforcement against actual offenders, not by imposing collective financial penalties on law-abiding graduates,” a commenter named Hang Deng wrote on October 9. The proposals have drawn divided responses. Professional groups have raised concerns, including the American Hospital Association, which asked DHS to exempt healthcare workers from the proposed H-1B fee. Others support the fee, arguing it would protect American workers. Among them is the US Society of Software Engineers, which describes itself as an organisation dedicated to protecting American jobs. The group said it did not seek to eliminate skilled immigration but wanted reforms to ensure “the best minds get to work for American companies without causing wage pressure and lay-offs for Americans”. The US$103,265 fee was a “positive step” towards that goal, it said. “We believe that H-1B is ripe with fraud and employers seek to drive down wages,” the group said. Larissa Liao, a Chinese student who graduated with a master’s degree at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor this summer, is now looking for a job on OPT. She called both proposals ridiculous and said they left her speechless, but she was more hopeful that they would never become reality. “It feels like a mind game that leaves international students and employers overwhelmed,” she said in Mandarin, “but I don’t actually believe it will really come into effect.”

title: Russia detains Japanese journalist suspected of spying
description: Tokyo calls for fair treatment of Hokkaido Shimbun correspondent detained in Russia’s far eastern Sakhalin region.
content: Russia’s FSB security agency said on Tuesday it had detained a Japanese journalist for alleged espionage, and Moscow’s Foreign Ministry said it regretted that Tokyo was using correspondents to carry out spying. In a statement on its website, the FSB said the Hokkaido Shimbun journalist was detained in the far eastern Sakhalin region on the day before he planned to leave Russia. It did not specify when this was. Russia and Japan, ‌which never signed a formal World War II peace treaty, have seen their diplomatic relations deteriorate since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, though Japan relies on Russia for supplies of liquefied natural gas. In a statement, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova identified the journalist as Imai Yuki, according to the Russian transliteration of his name, and said his detention cast a new pall on relations with Tokyo. Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said on Wednesday that Japan’s embassy in Moscow and consulate-general in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk had asked Russian authorities for information and called for fair treatment and humanitarian consideration for the Japanese national. Motegi did not confirm the identity of the person detained. Tokyo planned to summon Russia’s ambassador and lodge a protest over the arrest, TV Asahi reported. The Hokkaido ⁠Shimbun said it was still confirming the details. “We will respond with the reporter’s safety as our top priority,” the publisher said in a statement, declining to comment further. In a Russian state ‌television video report on the case, three masked men in black uniforms could be seen handcuffing a man lying on the ground as a voice off camera said he was suspected of spying. The video showed the man being accompanied by two FSB servicemen onto a plane, then in a cage ‌in a Moscow court, which ordered him detained for nearly two months. The agency “thwarted the illegal activity” of the journalist, the FSB said. “As a result of ⁠intelligence operations, it was established that he ⁠gathered and stored information related to the country’s defence capabilities in order to pass it on for national intelligence purposes to be used against the security of the Russian Federation,” the statement said. “Tokyo’s attempts to use its correspondents ‌in Russia with the status of foreign journalists to gather information for undermining our state’s security are regrettable,” said Zakharova, the foreign ministry spokeswoman. Japan had adopted an anti-Russian position during Russia’s military campaign in Ukraine and refused to consider Moscow’s concerns ‌about ‌Tokyo’s “remilitarisation”, she said. “We have to note that what has occurred will become an additional factor clouding the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations,” Zakharova said. Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it joined Western ‌sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine. Russia and Japan have a territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Russian President Vladimir Putin visited ⁠one of the disputed islands in August, causing an uproar in Japan. A delegation from China’s Heilongjiang province also visited the island on Tuesday, amid strained relations between Beijing and Tokyo. Japan has ⁠said it will continue implementing sanctions against Russia and supporting Ukraine. This month, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s cabinet approved additional sanctions against Russia, including expanded export bans and asset freezes targeting individuals affiliated with the Russian military. Asked whether improving US-Russia relations and Japan’s reliance on energy imports from Russia made it difficult for Tokyo to ‌take countermeasures, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said: “It ‌is true that there are many issues between Japan and Russia.” “From Japan’s perspective, despite the difficult situation in Japan-Russia relations, Japan has taken resolute measures based on its position,” he said. “At the same time, Russia is a neighbouring country to Japan, and communication is necessary to resolve these issues.” One of the most prominent cases of a foreign journalist arrested in Russia was the detention of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich in 2023. He was found guilty of espionage by a Russian court, sentenced to 16 years and then freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024.⁠

title: Trump’s ‘golden age’ push hands top science honours to big tech. Will it work?
description: Top medals for big tech chiefs like Musk and Huang signal shift to market-driven research but Chinese analysts doubt viability of model.
content: The White House’s bid for a US “golden age” of science should put China on alert, Chinese analysts have warned, but they remain sceptical as to whether President Donald Trump’s alliance with Silicon Valley billionaires can pull it off. This comes as Trump, in another arguably unconventional move, handed the country’s highest science and engineering awards to top American tech bosses. Elon Musk, head of electric-vehicle maker Tesla and aerospace manufacturer SpaceX, received the National Medal of Science, the US’ top scientific honour. Joining him in receiving the award at the “Science: A New Golden Age Summit” in Washington on Thursday were leading chipmaking chiefs Jensen Huang of Nvidia and Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices, as well as Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Personal computer tycoon Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, the US’ most prestigious award for the category. While entrepreneurs have previously won these awards, observers noted that it was unprecedented for tech executives to be honoured on such a scale – particularly given that the National Medal of Science had long prioritised scientists and researchers. The award was established by Congress in 1959, while the technology medal was introduced in 1980. All of this year’s recipients have close ties with the White House. Musk is widely considered a Trump ally despite their months-long public feud last year, while Huang, Su, Brin and Dell are all members of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. The companies they lead have also deepened their commercial ties with the Pentagon to varying degrees. With artificial intelligence (AI) emerging as a major arena of the China-US tech rivalry, those enterprises are also critical players in the supply chain. At Trump’s state dinner last month for Chinese President Xi Jinping, Musk, Huang and Su were seated at the same table as the two leaders. Sun Zhanqing, a special researcher at the South China University of Technology’s Institute of Public Policy, said the line-up of awardees showed that a “new type of power relationship” was taking shape in the US. “Tech entrepreneurs’ standing in [shaping] resource allocation, technological road maps and the national science narrative is rising,” Sun wrote in a note on the think tank’s social media channel on Friday. Still, he cautioned against conflating US tech executives’ growing influence over scientific research with scientists’ actual “capacity to create knowledge”. “The Trump administration’s science awards may create a cycle that warrants vigilance,” warned Sun, who is also deputy director of the government-affiliated Guangzhou Academy of Social Sciences’ Urban Culture Research Institute. Tech bosses’ resource advantages yielded more visible results, he said, earning them higher honours that in turn could reinforce their policy influence and ability to secure more resources. “Ultimately, people may attribute the advantages created by this cycle to the idea that a certain group of people is inherently more creative,” he warned. “A golden age of science cannot be judged solely by how glamorous the people standing on the podium are.” An analysis by Xinzhi Observatory, a technology-focused channel owned by Shanghai-based news portal Guancha, also struck a sceptical note on last week’s US science summit. Even as the Trump White House continued to cut routine federal funding for basic science, it was trying to tap the massive computing power and capital of private giants to rebuild US global leadership in research through so-called superintelligence, the piece noted, using Trump’s new preferred moniker for AI. With entrepreneurs increasingly steering research, the purity of scientific inquiry and the public interest could face an “unprecedented test,” it cautioned. “Whether reliance on the patronage of tech oligarchs can truly open a new, enduring golden age of science remains a highly contested unknown.” However, China could ill afford to let its guard down, the observers cautioned. “The award ceremony was not merely a ‘symbolic arrangement’,” Sun said. “Big tech companies are taking part in national tech competition as technology developers.” He cited the more than US$6 billion in science and technology investments announced by the Trump administration at Thursday’s event. This includes US$2.4 billion in contributions from 11 companies, including Nvidia, AMD, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, to provide AI “science tools and compute credits” for researchers. Xinzhi Observatory said the investment plans announced at the summit might reveal a blueprint for “stockpiling talent reserves for future industrial competition” – by pushing advanced computing capacity directly to the local level to spur broader basic innovation. Thursday’s event built on “Science: A New Golden Age”, a report by White House Office of Science and Technology Policy director Michael Kratsios released in July. It outlines a major overhaul of the framework for American science, whose foundations were laid by the 1945 report “Science, the Endless Frontier”, written by Vannevar Bush, director of the US Office of Scientific Research and Development during the second world war, while positioning itself as the 21st century successor to it.
