Kratsios’ report argues that the post-war “linear model” of technological progress – flowing in sequence from university-based basic research funded through slow, consensus-driven peer review, to applied research, then to technological development and industry – no longer held in many fields. It said US private companies dominated research spending, bureaucratic and funding structures were burdening scientists, and the fruits of American science often ended up helping rivals build their advantage due to decades of industrial offshoring. It proposed prioritising funding for risk-taking individual scientists over “legacy institutions” and expanding the Genesis Mission – launched by the Trump administration in November to use AI to accelerate scientific discovery. However, Kratsios’ report has drawn criticism at home, including over its ostensible aim to shift vast resources away from traditional academia towards big tech, effectively turning national research into a venture-capital model. But Chinese observers say it could pose a challenge to Beijing, by shifting the gravity of US-China tech competition away from individual breakthroughs to how well each side governs its innovation system. The report identified China as the first “peer-level competitor” to the US in research and development spending – driven by Beijing’s “all-of-society approach” to partnerships across sectors. Strategically, the White House report was a “direct response” to China’s whole-of-nation approach to scientific research, said Zhu Yanmei, dean’s adviser at the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute. She warned in a July post that regardless of future administrative shifts, its core propositions – that science must serve national competitiveness, that federal funding must pursue quantifiable gains in technological sovereignty, and that AI must be treated as national infrastructure – had probably become consensus in US strategic circles. She also cautioned that the problems highlighted in the US report – bureaucracy, conservatism and inefficiency – mirrored chronic flaws in China’s own research system. “What China needs is not simple benchmarking or a reflexive response but a profound reflection on its innovation paradigm. In criticising America’s own ailments, the report has inadvertently held up a mirror for China,” she wrote. “For China, the report’s biggest takeaway may be this: a true science and innovation power is measured not by the number of papers or the scale of funding but by whether its institutions can keep generating ‘crazy ideas’ and turn them into ‘world-changing forces’.” Beijing is also moving to streamline its research system. Guidelines issued last Friday on developing new productive forces called for boosting the role of companies as the main force in scientific and technological innovation, and for supporting capable private firms to lead major national technology projects. In April, Xi called for an open, inclusive innovation environment that tolerated failure and placed greater weight on AI-enabled basic research.

title: Review | Outrigger Phi Phi Island Resort offers a tranquil escape with sustainability in mind
description: Despite its secluded location, the resort is just a short boat ride from popular sightseeing spots like Maya Bay, made famous by a 2000 Leonardo DiCaprio-led film.
content: Considering the number of tourists who visit every year, there aren’t many luxury hotels on Thailand’s Phi Phi Islands, possibly the result of stringent measures put in place in recent years to prevent overtourism. Outrigger Phi Phi Island Resort is thus a welcome new addition to the scene. Located on the northern tip of Phi Phi Don Island, the main island in the Phi Phi archipelago, this laid-back, unpretentious resort sits on the quiet shores of Laem Tong Beach, within a protected national park, with easy access by long-tail boat to the busier tourist attractions around Monkey Beach and Maya Bay. Away from the crowded resorts and beaches of nearby Phuket, the Phi Phi Islands are renowned for their more isolated nature and crystal-clear aquamarine waters, popular for snorkelling and paddleboarding, among other water sports. The islands suit Outrigger, a Honolulu-based hospitality chain that champions barefoot luxury, easy access to adventure tourism, and fuss-free, family-friendly service, and also operates outposts in popular beach destinations like Fiji and the Maldives. The resort’s 63 spacious suites and villas feature humble but homely furnishings; traditional Thai drums serve as wall decor in my oceanfront villa and as chairs in the lobby reception area. Designed by acclaimed Bangkok-based creative studio Opendesigner, the interiors use Southern Thai textiles, natural textures and wood and rattan materials liberally to achieve the effect of being one with, if not exactly living in, the outdoors. The main attractions, though, are all outdoors. The resort offers live music and film nights, placing as much emphasis on communal activities as on individual R&R. After a long day traversing the surrounding Andaman Sea, I unwind with evening cocktails at Edgewater, the resort’s main bar and grill, set against a cotton-candy sunset fresh after the rain. F&B offerings here are spearheaded by Chef Satya Beeknoo, former winner of the reality show Iron Chef Thailand, who specialises in what he calls Thai creole cuisine. The menu is heavy on Thai flavours infused with Mediterranean influences, and the fresh seafood is a real highlight, with a variety of grilled dishes like squid, red snapper and sea bass on offer in the evenings. After the resort’s soft opening, another on-site restaurant, Mala Kitchen, is set to serve more Thai classics and international dishes. Over at the Zeavola Spa, I relax completely with an aromatherapy massage, followed by hot tea and dried apricots and dates. I leave feeling as Zen as the wild long-tailed macaques I saw roaming around the aforementioned Monkey Beach – best observed from a distance, as they can attack when provoked. It’s a stark contrast to where I was just hours earlier, swimming with fish and, unfortunately, seeing the occasional piece of plastic rubbish float by. Like several other luxury resorts in the area, Outrigger Phi Phi takes pride in its sustainability efforts, minimising the use of “imported” materials in its construction and largely eschewing single-use plastics across the property. Though luxury hospitality can never be truly sustainable, those gestures feel all the more meaningful when you return to the resort’s quietude, with its butterflies and hermit crabs, after escaping the hordes of tourists at Maya Bay, made famous by the 2000 Leonardo DiCaprio-led film The Beach. If tourism as an industry is here to stay, I would hope more resort experiences feel this way, as connected to and respectful of the surrounding nature as possible. I leave Outrigger Phi Phi the same way I arrived. The only way to and from Phuket is by boat, but this time I’m wearing some extra hardware: a handmade bead bracelet given to me as a welcome present, inspired by the rituals of the indigenous Urak Lawoi community. It’s a physical reminder of the resort’s values – peaceful rest, cultural preservation and authenticity – and something I will wear for years to come. The author stayed as a guest of the Outrigger Phi Phi Island Resort

title: Opinion | Smart economics: tackle climate change and air pollution together
description: While air pollution has often been treated as an inevitable price of rapid economic growth, polluted air itself imposes many enormous costs.
content: Indonesia continues to battle some of its worst wildfires in years, spreading toxic haze to Malaysia and Singapore. Floods have devastated communities in Thailand, India and Nepal. Kathmandu is also seeking climate justice after a catastrophic collapse of rock and glacier ice near its border with China. Another environmental tragedy unfolds without such dramatic images. Across the world, millions of lives are lost each year to polluted air. Many more people live with debilitating illnesses that strain household finances, overwhelm health services and keep them from working. Governments that plan and budget for climate change and air pollution separately miss opportunities to protect health and strengthen their economies through the same investment. We recently co-chaired an assessment for the UN Environment Programme and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) that puts a value on those opportunities. We estimate that outdoor and household air pollution caused about 8.4 million premature deaths worldwide in 2025. Outdoor fine-particle pollution was also associated with 5.5 million new cases of childhood asthma, 2 million new cases of dementia and millions of cases of other serious illnesses. Our assessment is the first to quantify the combined economic value of climate and clean-air action within a single, internally consistent framework. A key innovation is its fuller accounting of pollution-related illness, or morbidity, including healthcare costs and lost productivity that conventional analyses have often undervalued. Air pollution has often been treated as an inevitable price of rapid economic growth, but polluted air itself imposes many enormous costs. Those losses should count whenever a government considers whether cleaner energy or transport is too expensive. At the same time, there is reason for optimism. Wider adoption of electric vehicles and renewable power can help improve local air quality and reduce long-term global warming. Work on our report began last year in Beijing, whose improvements in air quality demonstrate what sustained policy action can achieve. Our assessment evaluates 25 measures across energy systems, industry, transport, agriculture, residential heating and cooking, and waste management. Complementing long-term decarbonisation, action on super pollutants – including methane, black carbon and hydrofluorocarbons – can help slow warming. Measures targeting methane and black carbon also improve air quality. Methane contributes to ground-level ozone, which damages health and crop yields. Black carbon, a component of health-harming soot, warms the atmosphere and accelerates melting when deposited on snow and glaciers. If the full package of measures is implemented, every US$1 invested could generate around US$4 in market benefits, including lower healthcare spending, higher productivity and avoided climate damage. Including the broader economic value of longer, healthier lives raises the benefits to US$15. Some health and economic gains can become apparent within a single term of government. For governments seeking faster growth and balanced budgets, the US$4 market benefit figure deserves particular attention. Fewer illnesses mean fewer working days lost and less pressure on health services. Reduced heat exposure protects workers’ health and productivity. These gains help strengthen economies and ease pressure on public finances, even though they do not all accrue directly to the government. Finance ministries should assess investments against these combined benefits. Each year of delay in implementing the package forfeits more than US$1.5 trillion in benefits we cannot recover. Full implementation of these measures could prevent an estimated 144 million premature deaths from air pollution cumulatively by 2050. Compared with the report’s baseline scenario, it could also avoid around 0.34 degrees Celsius of warming by mid-century – a significant contribution to limiting the extent and consequences of an overshoot beyond the 1.5 degree warming threshold. Governments need not finance every investment themselves. Clear legislation, predictable standards and credible enforcement can encourage private businesses to act. Rules on methane leakage, vehicle emissions and refrigerants can create demand for cleaner technologies. Better coordination between ministries can reduce delays and implementation costs. Delivering these gains also requires attention to who can afford to change. Families need reliable access to cleaner cooking and affordable, energy-efficient cooling. Farmers need practical alternatives to burning crop residues. Targeted public support and access to affordable finance should be built into implementation from the start. Pollution crosses borders, so neighbouring countries have much to gain from coordinating their efforts. International financial support also remains essential for countries unable to cover necessary upfront investments. These priorities belong at the centre of the CCAC Annual Meeting in Bangkok this week and the COP31 UN climate change conference in Antalya, Turkey, this November. Governments need not wait for a breakthrough in international negotiations. They can remove barriers and set investment in motion now. From smoke-filled and flooded cities to retreating glaciers, Asia has much to gain from tackling air pollution and climate change together. Investments made today can improve health quickly and deliver economic benefits for generations. Every budget that postpones them leaves families and economies paying the price.

title: Cornell suspends frat parties after alleged gang rape
description: The Ivy League school is facing accusations that it failed to properly punish the men involved in the high-profile 2024 incident.
content: Cornell University on Tuesday suspended fraternities’ parties and social events for the remaining academic year following outcry over an alleged gang rape at one of the elite college’s all-male clubs. The 2024 incident, as alleged in a graphic lawsuit filed last month, has drawn accusations that the Ivy League institution in New York state failed to properly punish the men involved. The accuser claimed that she was pressured to take ketamine, assaulted and raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity – one of several “Greek life” organisations common across US colleges. Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said the suspension “will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue”. “I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” he added, referring to the accuser’s pseudonym. Following her initial allegations, Cornell shut down the fraternity and temporarily suspended the accused male students, two of whom were later expelled. But critics have said the university’s response was too lenient, prompting it to launch an independent review. Thousands of students and faculty members rallied at Cornell this month to demand justice for the accuser, displaying signs reading “Hold them accountable” and “Protect survivors”. Protesters have also gathered in New York, Boston and other US cities to show support for the accuser, while social media users have shared the hashtag #IAmJaneDoe. Cornell has named a former top US prosecutor, Sally Yates, to assess the university’s response to the rape allegations. But, addressing the Cornell community, Kotlikoff said on Tuesday “it is clear that we cannot wait for these findings to take action”. He said the suspension on fraternity social events was effective immediately and there would be “zero tolerance” for any violations. “Any fraternity holding an in-house party or social event will receive an immediate emergency suspension,” Kotlikoff said. He announced other measures including the appointment of a dedicated staff member to support individuals reporting sexual misconduct, and inviting specialised New York State Police detectives to probe future sexual assault allegations. Meanwhile, prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the alleged gang rape, with Governor Kathy Hochul appointing state Attorney General Letitia James to lead the case. That came after local authorities said they declined to prosecute in 2024 because the complainant’s testimony did not establish a lack of consent. In the US, one in four female undergraduates experienced forced sexual contact or sexual contact for which they could not consent, according to a 2020 study of 33 institutions by the Association of American Universities. Mental health non-profit the Jed Foundation has reported that men in fraternities – which are routinely criticised for shielding sexism – are more likely to commit sexual violence.

title: Trump press secretary Katie Zacharia says she passed bar exam in China, raising eyebrows
description: Katie Zacharia worked at a Beijing law firm and calls herself a lawyer, but reporters found no record of her admission to practise in the US.
content: Katie Zacharia, US President Donald Trump’s newly appointed White House press secretary, faces questions about her legal credentials after telling reporters on Tuesday that she passed a bar exam “when I moved to China”, without identifying the jurisdiction. Zacharia, who has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer, made the remark after her first official White House press briefing. According to her LinkedIn profile, she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm, one of China’s largest, in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. A review by the South China Morning Post of attorney registration records in New York, the District of Columbia, California, Texas and Florida found no listing for Zacharia. Independent journalist Judd Legum separately reported finding no evidence that she had been admitted to practise law in any of the 50 US states or Washington, DC. Passing a bar examination and being admitted to practise law are separate steps. The searches do not establish whether Zacharia passed an examination. The White House did not immediately respond to SCMP’s request for comment, including a question about which jurisdiction had admitted Zacharia to practise. A White House official did not directly answer when NBC News asked whether Zacharia had passed a bar exam. The official said she had moved to China with her husband after law school because of his job at an American private equity firm, and had worked on international transaction law there before the couple returned to the United States. Zacharia told NewsNation she had practised with “all the appropriate credentials”, without specifying a jurisdiction. Her reference to China leaves unclear whether she was describing when she passed an examination or where she qualified. Eligibility rules for China’s national judicial examination in 2011, when Zacharia reportedly began working in Beijing, required candidates to hold Chinese nationality. Foreign nationals were therefore ineligible to take the examination, a step towards qualification to practise mainland Chinese law. Employment at a Chinese law firm does not, by itself, establish that someone holds a licence to practise Chinese law. SCMP has asked Zhong Lun to clarify Zacharia’s role and qualifications. The firm did not immediately respond. Zacharia received her law degree from Pepperdine University and was named press secretary last week. She previously served as a spokeswoman at the Department of Homeland Security and as a senior communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group.

title: Peru governor touts Chinese interest in deep-water port pitched as Chancay alternative
description: Scaled back to US$844 million from a US$7 billion plan, Corio terminal in Arequipa has yet to secure an investor or operator.
content: A planned US$844 million port in southern Peru has drawn interest from several foreign investors, including Chinese companies, a regional governor said on Monday, as the government began promoting the project abroad. “Several companies have approached us. We have investors from the US, China and India who are very interested,” Rohel Sanchez, the governor of Arequipa, told reporters after signing an agreement with the state investment agency Proinversion. He said firms from Turkey and the Netherlands had also been in touch, as had South Korean investors interested in technology for a logistics park to be built alongside the terminal. Proinversion president Luis del Carpio said Corio would likely handle general cargo and containers but could also be used to export copper from the region to Asia. Regional officials have long promoted the deep water off Punta de Bombon, in Islay province, which they put at between 20 and 28 metres (66 to 92 feet). Chancay, the port north of Lima that China’s Cosco Shipping Ports has run since November 2024, has a maximum depth of about 18 metres. Smaller master plan For years, Arequipa’s government described Corio as a US$7 billion hub with room for 100 million tonnes of cargo a year, more than Peru’s public ports currently handle in total. The master plan approved by the National Port Authority in September is far more modest: a multipurpose terminal of around US$800 million developed in three phases. Its capacity would be close to 2 million tonnes a year, industry sources told the news site Infobae. Proinversion now has to draw up tender rules and find an operator willing to finance, build and run the terminal, the Lima-based magazine Revista Economia reported in September. A demand study commissioned by the port authority had not been finished, and specialists quoted by the magazine estimated that operations could begin in five or six years at the earliest. Chinese interest Sanchez, who leaves office in December, has also spoken of Chinese suitors before. In September 2024, he said business delegations from China, South Korea, Portugal and the US had visited Arequipa to look at the project. Julio Caceres, president of the Arequipa chamber of commerce, went further during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Lima two months later, telling the broadcaster RPP he had “confidential information” that four Chinese companies had approached the regional government. No names have emerged since. Peruvian officials have also used Corio to court American capital. Bloomberg reported in June 2024 that the government was pitching the port to US investors as a counterweight to China’s role in the country’s shipping. A report on Peru’s port sector published in August by Shanghai Maritime University, on a Shanghai government platform that advises companies investing overseas, did not discuss Corio. It recommended that Chinese firms enter the Peruvian market through equipment, engineering and logistics contracts and warned against port investments justified only by cargo forecasts or memorandums of understanding. Two Chinese-backed port projects are already under way in Peru. In September the government said Jinzhao, a mining company owned by China’s Zhongrong Xinda Group, would start construction in 2027 of a US$405 million port at Marcona, in the Ica region, once a land agreement with Shougang Hierro Peru had removed the last major obstacle. Transport minister Jose Tangherlini said the first phase would take about two years and cost US$200 million. Most of the cargo will come from Jinzhao’s own Pampa de Pongo iron ore mine, a US$1.78 billion project. Cosco, meanwhile, has spent most of this year fighting Peru’s transport regulator Ositran over its power to supervise Chancay. The US State Department called the port’s Chinese owners “predatory” in February, after a lower court ruled in Cosco’s favour. An appeal court sided with Ositran in July, and Cosco said last month it would keep up its challenge. Las Bambas, the largest Chinese-controlled copper mine in southern Peru, already exports through Matarani, a port in the same province as Corio. The mine, run by MMG with partners Guoxin and Citic, moves its concentrate there by truck and rail and has its own berth and storage shed at the terminal. The idea of a port at Corio dates back to 2000. The port authority rejected a private proposal in 2019, and a consortium led by a retired navy admiral, Cesar Zelada, has continued to pursue its own plans for the site, saying a US company is among its investors.

title: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer after surgery to remove part of his lung
description: Vatican says 71-year-old pontiff spent a peaceful night after 90-minute operation was completed without complications.
content: Pope Leo XIV spent a peaceful night in Rome’s Gemelli hospital after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung and confirmed he has cancer, the Vatican said on Wednesday. The surgery confirmed that the pope had the most common type of lung cancer, known as lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin late on Tuesday. The Vatican said doctors were waiting for the results of further tests before deciding on a course of treatment. The press office pointed to the medical statement’s mention of the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors took out all suspect tissue in hopes of removing any lingering traces of the cancer. Experts said some of Leo’s lymph nodes also would have been removed and tested to determine if the cancer had spread. There was no word yet on those test results. If the cancer had spread, more tests would be needed to determine what kind of therapy to pursue, said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Centre. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy or targeted therapy, which involves oral pills for specific cancers. “Adenocarcinoma is the most common [type of lung cancer], also with the most favourable prognosis,” said Liu, who is not involved in the pope’s care. “While we know the diagnosis, we now need to know the stage.” He added: “We now need to know how big it is, how many spots in the lung are involved. Is it just one nodule, or more than one, and the lymph nodes, are they cancerous?” For now, the implications for the pope’s long-term health remain unclear. The Vatican said more information would be provided later in the day. The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the nodule, or growth, on his lung during his Sunday noon prayer. The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about three hours, the Vatican statement said on Tuesday. The surgery itself lasted around 90 minutes. “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said, adding that the pope later returned to his room. The right lung has three sections or lobes, while the left has two. After one lobe is removed, the rest of the lung can gradually compensate, especially in otherwise healthy and physically active people. Leo is known to be sporty, with weekly tennis games and swimming. Before the surgery, Leo walked into the Gemelli hospital through the main entrance and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery was performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora. Oncologists said before the operation that even if the nodule turned out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis would be “excellent” since it would have been removed at an early stage. While Gemelli has a specific papal flat that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo is staying in a nearby room since the flat is undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office. The Vatican on Monday cancelled all Leo’s audiences through October 20. But there was no word on whether he would be able to keep his planned trip to South America next month. Oncology surgeons often advise patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery – which would give the pope just enough time to make his planned November 6–17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. But whether he can go will depend on his recovery. The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 31,000km (19,000 miles) on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru. “If it is stage 1, he can complete these trips. If more treatment is needed, I would likely advise against the trips,” said Liu.

title: Tupac Shakur murder: ex-gang leader sentenced to 40 years to life in prison
description: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis was convicted of masterminding the drive-by shooting that shaped the golden age of rap music.
content: A former gang leader was sentenced to 40 years to life in prison on Tuesday for orchestrating the 1996 drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas, capping the prosecution of a long-unsolved murder that shaped the golden age of rap music. Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, found guilty of first-degree murder in August, received the penalty during ‌a hearing in a Las Vegas courtroom. Until Davis’ 2023 arrest, the killing of Shakur, shot dead in the passenger seat of an SUV driven by his record executive, Marion “Suge” Knight, had stood for nearly three decades as one of America’s most notorious cold cases. The murder, which silenced one of rap’s most commercially successful and influential artists, heightened the image of violence permeating 1990s hip-hop culture while stoking the infamous East Coast-West Coast “gangsta” rap feud of the era. Despite Davis’ conviction, the question of who pulled the trigger in the fatal shooting of the 25-year-old rap legend has never been conclusively decided. Davis was tried and convicted for ⁠masterminding the murder to avenge the beating of his nephew by Shakur and members of the rapper’s entourage inside the MGM Grand casino on the Las Vegas Strip on ‌September 7, 1996. Davis has said he would appeal against his conviction. The clash at the casino stemmed from hostility between two Los Angeles-area street gangs – the South Side Compton Crips, of which Davis was the self-described leader, and Mob Piru, ‌which was associated with Shakur, Knight, and their music label, Death Row Records. Members of both groups were in Las Vegas to see a ⁠world heavyweight title boxing match that night ⁠between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon. Within hours of the casino brawl, Davis ushered his nephew and two other associates into a white Cadillac and went looking for Shakur and Knight, determined to settle scores, according ‌to an account Davis later gave police in an unrelated investigation and that prosecutors cited during his murder trial. Davis said he passed a gun to the two men seated behind him in the Cadillac, one of whom opened ‌fire ‌through the window when they caught up with and pulled alongside Knight and Shakur’s vehicle in traffic. Shakur was struck four times and died in a hospital ‌six days later. Knight, who suffered a minor injury from a bullet fragment that grazed his head, is now serving a 28-year prison term on an unrelated voluntary manslaughter conviction. Authorities ⁠said they long believed Davis was involved in Shakur’s killing but lacked sufficient evidence to charge him. That changed when he went public with his story in media appearances ⁠and a memoir that, along with tapes of his secret meetings with investigators, formed the bulk of the prosecution’s murder case. In his book, Compton Street Legend, Davis himself wrote that he was considered a suspect in the murders of both Shakur and Christopher Wallace, a rival rapper. Wallace, who performed as ‌the Notorious B.I.G. under the New York-based Bad ‌Boy Entertainment label, was shot dead in Los Angeles in March 1997. Although the Wallace killing remains unsolved, there has long been speculation that he was gunned down in retaliation for Shakur’s killing months earlier. While Davis was never accused of actually firing the shots that killed Shakur – Nevada law allows someone to be charged with murder as a participant in the crime – prosecutors have never named a suspected gunman. All three other men in the Cadillac with Davis that night have since died.

title: Six Flags closes US rides after man flung to his death from roller coaster
description: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was ejected from the ride, struck other patrons and fell beneath the attraction at the park in Georgia, Atlanta.
content: Six Flags Entertainment Corp said it would temporarily close 10 rides at its theme parks, including the Goliath ride that was involved in a fatal accident on Monday, amid a string of incidents at its facilities. “Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily closed similar attractions across our parks,” the company said in a statement. “The safety of our guests and team members is our highest priority.” The attractions paused are located at seven resorts including Kings Island in Ohio and Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey. There is no immediate timeline for them reopening. Shares of Six Flags, which bills itself as the largest owner of regional theme parks in the US, fell as much as 17.28 per cent on Tuesday to their lowest level since the Covid-19 epidemic closed resorts worldwide. A 42-year-old man was killed in a roller coaster incident on Monday at the Six Flags Over Georgia park. Officers working at the park responded to reports of an event involving a guest at around 3.58pm. Preliminary information indicates that Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was ejected from the ride, struck other patrons and fell beneath the attraction, according to a statement from the Cobb County Police Department. Six Flags said last month that it would permanently close the X2 coaster at its Magic Mountain Park in Valencia, California. The Dordick Law Corp said three of its clients sued the company after allegedly suffering catastrophic brain injuries as a result of the X2 ride. The firm said it has retained more than 100 clients who have claimed injury. Six Flags said the X2 ride passed a multitude of safety tests. Six Flags Over Georgia is located about 19km (12 miles) west of Atlanta. In its statement, Six Flags said its staff and local authorities responded immediately, and that it is cooperating fully with the authorities as they complete their investigation of Monday’s incident.

title: New Trump spokeswoman makes White House debut, takes only 3 questions
description: Katie Zacharia opened her first press briefing by reading – very slowly – a long list of what she said were the US president’s achievements.
content: New White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia made her briefing room debut on Tuesday by taking remarkably few questions from journalists while leaving no doubt who she believes has all the answers – US President Donald Trump. “I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people,” she said, describing her vision for the job. Zacharia, a 41-year-old devotee of Trump’s hard-right Maga movement, is taking over the White House communications role just as Republicans face warnings of heavy defeat in coming midterm elections. She is also replacing the combative but skilled former press secretary Karoline Leavitt at a time when polls show the 80-year-old president becoming ever more unpopular. Little known to the general public, Zacharia opened her first session at the famous briefing room podium by reading – at a notably slow pace – a lengthy list of what she said were achievements under the “energetic” leader. These types of initial round-ups, dubbed “toppers” in White House press lingo, are usually followed by a long question and answer session in the packed room – often extending to dozens of questions. But Zacharia took questions from just three reporters, starting with right-wing website Breitbart, an outlet frequently accused of spreading conspiracy theories. The next questions went to Fox News, one of the key pillars of Trump’s media support, and to the Daily Mail tabloid website. With that, after just 15 minutes, Zacharia declared the briefing finished and walked out, pursued by the sound of reporters shouting unanswered questions. “I thought she was very good,” Trump, known to enjoy watching his staff’s performances on television, later told reporters. Up to now, Zacharia has been working as a commentator on Fox News and right-wing Newsmax, as well as advising Trump Media and Technology – the group behind the president’s Truth Social platform. She did not indicate whether she would aggressively pursue Trump’s unprecedented attempts to punish US media outlets that he does not like. Most recently, the administration has plunged into a legal dispute with CNN, MS Now and Politico over attempts to bar them from the White House. White House’s communications director Steven Cheung praised Zacharia’s performance, saying she “commanded the room” and reminded Americans of Trump’s “great work”. But liberal commentator Brian Krassenstein predicted she will “be a disaster”. The New York Post tabloid described her as “visibly nervous”. Zacharia did make one piece of news, announcing that Trump had sacked his ambassador to Greece after a bribery scandal. The bulk of her messaging, however, solely aimed at polishing the image of the Republican leader, who, nearly halfway through his term, faces plummeting opinion polls over his war against Iran, economic hardship and a long list of domestic controversies. “This is a president and administration that is looking out for you, the American people,” she said, declaring herself “thrilled to officially be part of this incredible journey”. Asked if the demanding job would affect her personal life, Zacharia described how her family of four children was adapting. But she slipped up, triggering ripples of laughter, when she referred to “my president, excuse me, my husband”.

title: Trump ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as ambassador to Greece amid misconduct claims
description: Kimberly Guilfoyle insists accusations are false after reported conduct prompts the White House to demand her exit.
content: The White House publicly asked for US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle’s resignation on Tuesday as she faced mounting accusations of improper conduct, and she announced within two hours that she was quitting, ending days of talk and speculation about her professional fate. Guilfoyle insisted that she would “vigorously defend” herself. President Donald Trump’s administration had said earlier Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. That revelation came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle “has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well”. “She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” Trump said just after Guilfoyle’s resignation, which was posted on her X account. He said he had not spoken to her but “she will not be there”. Guilfoyle’s departure comes after its possibility was previewed to Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior US official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were “extremely p***** off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct. In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill. Guilfoyle addressed the accusations directly in her resignation post on X, saying: “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity”. “I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she said. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.” In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle’s lawyers denied that she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services - public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination - that had not been paid. The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle’s travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations”. After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here”. But after another report appeared later, Rubio - speaking Thursday before leaving Athens - berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them. “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on. A second US official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied. The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation. There was no immediate response to Zacharia’s statement from the Greek government or Cabinet members. Ahead of Tuesday’s announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. “This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity,” Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated “the same way as every other ambassador” and argued that an official summons had not been necessary. Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president’s daughter-in-law, accompanied by Dua Lipa’s “Dance the Night”, from the 2023 soundtrack of the movie Barbie. Greece has taken on an increasingly important and influential role because of its geographic location in Southeastern Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly on energy issues as the war with Iran has spiked global oil prices. Besides the vast number of Greek-registered oil tankers that regularly ply the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, Greece is well positioned to be a pipeline conduit for liquefied natural gas imports into the Balkans and beyond. As the US ambassador to Greece, Guilfoyle had put an emphasis on energy issues, although her close association with executives in that sector was part of what got her into trouble. Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the United States could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported - citing text messages- that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a US$100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did. The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives. Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behaviour appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece. Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was married to Democrat Gavin Newsom when he was San Francisco’s mayor, before he became California’s governor. She later was engaged to Trump’s son Donald Trump Jnr.

title: Is this the best time for US strategists to push for abandoning ambiguity on Taiwan?
description: Trump’s quiet approach to Taiwan opens door for debate on ending decades-old US policy of strategic ambiguity.
content: For nearly five decades, the United States’ Taiwan policy has centred on strategic ambiguity by not declaring whether it would intervene militarily in a potential Taiwan conflict. This policy – designed to deter Beijing from using force while preventing Taipei from formally declaring independence – is being challenged by realist US strategists amid a broader debate over America’s role in the world, growing constraints on US military might and a shifting regional balance of power driven by China’s military rise. A small group of realist US strategists is pushing for the US to rule out military intervention over Taiwan to avoid the possibility of a catastrophic war between mainland China and the US. Experts said this idea, despite still being a minority view, was at least opening debate on the long-standing one-sided policy. “When US officials first adopted strategic ambiguity over Taiwan, China’s military was no match for that of the US. This is no longer the case,” wrote Jennifer Kavanagh, director of military analysis at the Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, in an opinion piece late last month. “At the same time, the American military suddenly seems fragile, lacking the advanced munitions and naval forces it would need for a major power conflict and facing serious vulnerabilities in its basing infrastructure. “Simply put, the US military remains the strongest in the world, but its ability to outlast China in a war over Taiwan is now in question.” Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not formally recognise the island as independent, although Washington is committed to supplying it with defensive weapons and opposes any forcible takeover. Kavanagh told the South China Morning Post on October 8 that of her many modelling efforts looking at what would be required to break through a blockade of Taiwan, the bottom line was that neither Beijing nor Washington could defeat the other side. “The conflict would start with some kind of intense war. [In the modelling, the] US typically runs out of air-defence missiles and offensive missiles before China does, even if China depletes stockpiles,” she said. “My assumption is that China blockades Taiwan and just bleeds it out. And there’s not so much the US can do.” In a research report published on September 10, Kavanagh not only proposed ending strategic ambiguity over Taiwan but also argued for replacing US mutual defence treaties with Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Australia with narrower security partnerships. The report also said the US should move most forces away from positions near mainland China in the first island chain – a string of US-led chokepoints along an arc of islands extending from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines – towards a smaller presence centred farther east around the second island chain, stretching from Japan through Guam to Papua New Guinea. Her proposal drew strong pushback within US national security circles, was called a “bombshell” and “radical”, and was deemed to be Communist Party “talking points”. “When I started arguing this, I was trying to be careful how I phrased what I was saying in the way that would make it clear that I was arguing for something that I thought was in US interests,” said Kavanagh, explaining how her position had become more direct since she first made the argument earlier last year. “The US foreign policy is in a period of flux. And people are debating what the US role in the world should be. “Being clear and direct about alternatives and options that the US has, and making a strong case for why this is in the US’ interest contributes to the debate.” Kavanagh belongs to a school of foreign policy that rejects military interventionism in favour of military restraint, narrow national interests and a focus on domestic strength. Since last year, she has written several reports and published opinion pieces proposing a Taiwan non-intervention policy. From the late 1990s until recently, a group of US foreign policy scholars and analysts has advocated restraint and argued that Taiwan’s importance does not justify risking a war with Beijing. In 1998, Ted Galen Carpenter, now a senior fellow at the Randolph Bourne Institute and the Libertarian Institute, advocated continued arms sales but explicitly ruled out military intervention in a policy paper he wrote while at the Cato Institute, a Washington-based libertarian think tank. Doug Bandow, a Cato senior fellow, made a similar case in 2024. In a 2015 paper, Charles L. Glaser, now a senior fellow at MIT’s security studies programme, proposed that Washington end its commitment to defend Taiwan in exchange for Beijing peacefully settling its maritime disputes and accepting a continued US military role in East Asia. More recently, Kavanagh and Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow in the Carnegie Endowment’s American statecraft programme, argued in Foreign Affairs in February 2025 that Washington should prepare to stay out of a Taiwan conflict if the People’s Liberation Army did not attack US bases or warships. In September 2025, Michael Swaine, a senior research fellow at the Quincy Institute, proposed a gradual transition to explicit non-intervention, emphasising the reassurance of allies and Beijing. Swaine said that maintaining the possibility of the US intervening militarily would become increasingly dangerous and would risk a major war with China under a worsening strategic rivalry between the two powers. He said there was an increasing tendency in Washington to regard Taiwan as a vital strategic location that, by implication, must be kept from Beijing. Alongside this, Beijing was steadily increasing its military capabilities regarding Taiwan. “These two trends are increasing the likelihood of one or both sides taking what they view as deterrent actions that cross red lines, leading to a major crisis and possible conflict,” Swaine said. “If these trends do not change, the US must consider just how vital Taiwan is to the US. Since I believe that it is in fact not a vital enough interest to justify risking a major war with China.” Xin Qiang, deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University, said the basis of strategic ambiguity stemmed from the extremely strong US military capability and its deterrent power, but the policy had become meaningless with the rise of Chinese military power. But he said it would be difficult for this argument, which was still proposed by a minority voice, to become a mainstream view due to policy inertia. “They’re actively debating it and it’s no longer just a one-sided policy position that leaves no room for discussion. The fact that this is happening is a good thing in itself, regardless of whether it will ultimately succeed,” Xin said. The argument for policy change comes as US foreign policy is in a period of flux, with US President Donald Trump’s administration pushing the boundaries of what has long been status quo foreign policy. Taiwan was among the most closely watched issues at the two summits between presidents Trump and Xi Jinping this year. While former US president Joe Biden repeatedly said the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a potential conflict, Trump has declined to say whether he would do so. After the first summit in May, the US paused a US$14 billion arms sale to Taiwan, which is still on hold. And the US is considering postponing the announcement of major arms sales to Taiwan until after November’s Apec summit in Shenzhen, the SCMP reported last month. While he was silent on the Taiwan issue during the second summit last month, Trump raised the question after the meeting in Beijing in May of whether it would make sense for US forces to travel 9,500 miles (15,300km) to fight a war. .

title: Philippines rejects China’s calls for direct contact amid ‘miscalculation’ warnings
description: Manila says the channels failed to improve trust and were used by Beijing as a ‘smokescreen’ to mask ‘aggressive actions’ at sea.
content: The Philippine military has rejected calls to restore direct communication channels with its Chinese counterpart, despite warnings from Beijing that their absence risks “miscalculation” during confrontations and could further escalate tensions in the South China Sea. On Tuesday, the Armed Forces of the Philippines said it would not communicate with its Chinese counterpart in advance of its maritime operations, arguing that such channels were ineffective without mutual respect for international law. Retired Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, spokesman for the military’s operations in waters the Philippines considered its territory, said the channels had failed to improve trust, accusing Beijing of using them as a “smokescreen” for what Manila regarded as coercive and aggressive conduct. He also said the Philippine military supported Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro’s decision to suspend direct communication channels with China. The Chinese embassy in Manila had called for such channels to reopen in a Facebook post on Monday, arguing that communication was essential to prevent misunderstandings and keep tensions from escalating. “Everyone knows that no matter how difficult bilateral relations become, communication channels should remain open to avoid miscalculation and prevent tensions from escalating,” it said. The embassy accused Teodoro of suspending military-to-military communication for what it called “political self-interest”, saying such a move “fuels mistrust, narrows the space for crisis management, and pushes frontline personnel closer to confrontation”. The Philippine Department of National Defence (DND) responded on Tuesday by reposting a 2024 statement from Teodoro, in which he said he had barred contact between the department and the Chinese embassy since July 2023. The statement followed the embassy’s claim that the armed forces’ Western Command had agreed with China on a “new model” for managing the situation at the disputed Second Thomas Shoal, including arrangements for resupply missions. The embassy said Teodoro and other key Philippine officials had approved the arrangement. Teodoro denied the DND was involved in any such deal, saying there was no discussion of a “gentleman’s agreement” or a “new model” during a courtesy call by then Chinese ambassador Huang Xilian shortly after Teodoro took office. “I reiterate that I have disallowed any contact between the DND and the Chinese embassy since the courtesy call of Ambassador Huang Xilian, a few days after I assumed office in July of last year,” Teodoro said in the statement. “During the said courtesy call, there was no discussion or briefing on any ‘gentleman’s agreement’ or ‘new model’, which is contrary to the Chinese embassy’s pronouncements.” Trinidad said the military supported suspending direct communication channels because dialogue could not be effective without trust and respect for international law. “Bilateral dialogue will be effective if the messages match the actions on sea, air, and ground. Unfortunately, this has not been the case,” he said. He rejected the suggestion that the absence of direct communication could increase the risk of miscalculation and further escalate tensions. “The miscalculations happen when you are not following international regulations and international law,” he said, referring to incidents involving Chinese vessels that the Philippines says have entered waters it claims and attempted to prevent resupply missions to the BRP Sierra Madre. The ageing warship, grounded at Second Thomas Shoal in the South China Sea, serves as a Philippine military outpost on the disputed maritime feature. Trinidad said the Philippine navy and coastguard had the legal right to challenge the presence of Chinese vessels in waters claimed by Manila, arguing that such encounters served as warnings to the ships involved. “So, don’t take it literally that they are not being warned, they are not being challenged,” he said. He maintained that China’s “coercive and aggressive actions”, rather than the absence of a direct communication channel, were the main source of miscalculation. The dispute over maritime activities in the South China Sea is rooted in competing claims and sharply different interpretations of international law. In 2016, an arbitral tribunal established under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea ruled that China’s historic-rights claims within the nine-dash line had no legal basis insofar as they exceeded the maritime entitlements permitted under the convention. Beijing rejected the ruling, arguing that the tribunal had no jurisdiction and that the award was null and void. The ruling did not determine sovereignty over all disputed islands and reefs. Competing accounts The evacuation of a Philippine marine from the BRP Sierra Madre on October 8, after he suffered a medical emergency involving a nearly ruptured appendix, became the latest flashpoint in the disputed waters, with Manila and Beijing offering different accounts of how the operation unfolded. Navy Captain Marissa Andres-Martinez said the Philippines would not seek China’s permission to conduct maritime operations in waters it claimed. “Nothing was communicated to the Chinese coastguard,” she said of Manila’s response to the emergency. Andres-Martinez said the navy would continue operations to sustain the soldiers aboard the vessel without seeking China’s permission. The armed forces’ public affairs chief Colonel Xerxes Trinidad said other seafarers should also recognise the urgency of medical evacuations. “The moment you call for a medical evacuation, it is something of concern that all. I think, a proper Navy or any seafarer would do to give way to that.” His remarks came amid Philippine Coast Guard accusations that Chinese vessels had used water cannons against Philippine ships responding to the medical emergency. China offered a different account of the incident. On Friday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said the Philippine coastguard had “intruded the adjacent waters of Ren’ai Jiao, Nansha Qundao of China”, referring to Beijing’s names for Second Thomas Shoal and the Spratly Islands. “The China Coast Guard took legitimate and reasonable measures to handle the situation in accordance with laws and regulations,” Mao said. China had allowed the evacuation on humanitarian grounds after communication between the two sides but “individual Philippine officials have distorted facts and wrongfully accused China without showing the whole picture to the public”, Mao added. The Chinese embassy in Manila on Monday urged the Philippines to tow away the “illegally grounded” warship and evacuate its personnel to end their exposure to risk. On the same day as the medical evacuation, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr called for a binding code of conduct in the South China Sea during a speech at the 24th Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore. Marcos said an agreement between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations was “absolutely necessary” to reduce the risk of further confrontations.

title: Taiwanese finance minister plans to join Apec meeting in Hong Kong
description: Taiwan’s Chuang Tsui-yun says she intends to take part in meeting, where Chinese finance chief is due to deliver opening speech.
content: Taiwanese Finance Minister Chuang Tsui-yun plans to attend the Apec meeting in Hong Kong, where the Chinese finance chief is due to deliver the opening speech. Chuang’s ministry told Reuters on Tuesday she would attend the meeting “as is customary”. Hong Kong is hosting the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting on October 20 and 21, while the Economic Leaders’ Summit will take place in Shenzhen next month. China is the summit host for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum this year. In response to queries from the South China Morning Post, the Financial and Treasury Services Bureau, which is organising the event next week, said China’s Ministry of Finance was handling the registration and accreditation. The bureau did not directly confirm Chuang’s participation, saying the Hong Kong government would continue to maintain close cooperation with the Chinese Ministry of Finance as the registration process for delegates was being completed. Under Apec guidelines, the ministry would provide all delegations from member economies with “necessary arrangements” and support in respect of accommodation, transport, reception and hospitality arrangements, it said. “The [Hong Kong] government welcomes delegates from all Apec member economies to Hong Kong and will render full support to the … [work of the Ministry of Finance] with a view to ensuring a high-quality experience for participating delegations,” a bureau spokesman said. Taiwan participates in Apec under the name “Chinese Taipei”, and Apec is one of the few international bodies that includes the self-ruled island. Chuang, who has been the finance minister since 2023, will be the second high-level Taiwanese official in William Lai Ching-te’s administration to take part in this year’s Apec summit. Taiwanese labour minister Hung Sun-han visited Nanjing last month to attend the Apec ministerial meeting to discuss employment, vocational training, social security and the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs. He said at the time his delegation was not subjected to any “downgrading” and was granted the same rights as other members. Beijing has accused Lai of “stubbornly clinging” to a “separatist mindset” and playing up the alleged “mainland threat”, rejecting his repeated offers of talks. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. The SCMP earlier reported that China’s finance minister, Lan Foan, will deliver a keynote speech at the meeting, which will be held at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. So far, expected attendees include Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers, South Korean Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyoung-il and Singaporean Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance Jeffrey Siow Chen Siang. Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said that Taiwanese officials taking part in an Apec meeting, even if it was held in Hong Kong or on mainland China, was not a “novel phenomenon” and “not surprising.” “I therefore will not attach much importance to Taiwanese officials’ attendance at Apec ministerial meetings,” he said. Lau said cross-strait relations were still at a “low ebb”, pointing to Lai’s continuing political provocations. He said the participation of Taiwanese officials showed that Beijing and Hong Kong followed the rules of international organisations to which they belonged. “In short, don’t read too much into the arrival of Taiwanese officials at an Apec ministerial meeting held in Hong Kong,” he said. Hong Kong finance chief Paul Chan Mo-po said the meeting would focus on fiscal policies that supported livelihoods, financing for digital infrastructure, inclusive finance and young financial talent. Last week, the SCMP reported that United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent might skip the Hong Kong meeting to focus on preparing for US President Donald Trump’s historic visit to Shenzhen in November.

title: China basketball chief Guo warns national team, domestic league entering critical time
description: New season features a notable increase in regular-season and play-off fixtures, alongside an upgraded developmental league for younger players.
content: Chinese Basketball Association president Guo Zhenming addressed the national team’s struggles on Monday afternoon, warning that the domestic league had reached a critical juncture in its bid to improve standards in the country. Speaking at the season launch press conference, Guo placed the burden of accountability squarely on the domestic competition as he discussed the state of the national squad. “We must clearly recognise that Chinese basketball is at a critical juncture of climbing a slope and crossing a hurdle, where falling behind is inevitable if we do not advance,” Guo said. “There remains a clear gap between the national team’s results and the expectations of the public.” He said the national team’s results are the most direct external test of the league’s value, saying the two “share a common destiny”. “This assessment places the responsibility squarely on the league itself, if the competitive quality of the league fails to rise, the foundation of the national team is out of the question.” Guo highlighted that the new campaign would feature a notable increase in regular-season and play-off fixtures, alongside an upgraded developmental league to provide younger talent with essential match exposure. “In the new season, I hope all members of the CBA [Chinese Basketball Association] will unite, uphold the sporting spirit, and deliver exciting and civilised games to fans nationwide, using the high-quality development of the league to help Chinese basketball continually climb,” Guo added. “Let us work together with the mindset of ‘success does not need to be in my name, but success will certainly involve my contribution’ ... and contribute more basketball strength to building a sports powerhouse.” The 2026-27 CBA campaign is scheduled to tip off on Friday, with defending champions Shanghai Sharks hosting Shenzhen Leopards following an opening ceremony featuring the raising of the 2025-26 championship banner and the presentation of championship rings. CBA Company chairman Yang Yang outlined the technical overhauls heading into the season, chief among them the reintroduction of promotion and relegation. Under the new format, promotion and relegation play-offs will be held in April 2027. The 19th and 20th placed teams from the CBA regular season will face the runner-up and champion of the second-tier National Basketball League (NBL) in home-and-away ties. Winning on the court, however, will not automatically guarantee promotion. Winners of the play-off must pass strict salary cap compliance and governance reviews before gaining eligibility for top-flight entry assessment. The move ends a 20-year absence of relegation, which was abolished ahead of the 2004-05 season in favour of an entry assessment model. The prolonged lack of relegation pressure had long been blamed for eroding competitive urgency at the bottom of the table. Yang said the league aimed to enhance openness, competition and standardised governance to drive “survival of the fittest”. Beyond the shake-up at the bottom of the table, the CBA regular season will expand back to 46 rounds comprising 460 matches, four rounds more than last season, while the play-offs will adopt a 3-5-5-7 series format. Under this format, the post-season expands progressively at each stage, running as a best-of-three opening first round, best-of-five quarter-finals and semi-finals, and a best-of-seven championship final series. Roster regulations have also been adjusted to balance minutes between domestic and overseas players. For the 2026-27 season, clubs will be permitted to register up to three foreign players simultaneously, reduced from four last season, with a seasonal cap of six player registrations per club, down from eight. The announcements prompted immediate debate across mainland social media. While a minority accepted the structural changes as a pragmatic step forward, with one user noting, “Although ... but fine, it’s better than nothing,” the prevailing response was heavily sceptical. Many fans dismissed the administrative rhetoric as empty platitudes. “This bureaucratic talk is just for show,” one commenter wrote. Others questioned the league’s modest schedule: “The schedule is still too short, and there are still too few teams. What happened to the earlier plan to expand to 22 teams?” Debate was also equally divided over the tightened foreign player rules. People backing greater domestic reliance argued that fewer imports would force local athletes to develop composure under pressure. “Four quarters, four appearances for foreign players is plenty; that way domestic players get tested in crunch time and know how to play when they join the national team,” one fan wrote. “Right now, domestic players are just blue-collar role players in clutch moments.” Conversely, others insisted that shielding local players from overseas competition was counterproductive: “Open it up to foreign players! That is the only way domestic players can improve.”

title: China is working on a submarine tank that can operate underwater for 2 hours
description: Scientists’ concept includes module operating 50 metres (164 feet) under water for amphibious landing operations.
content: A Chinese research team has proposed four types of equipment that could rapidly switch between wartime environments, including operating deep under water for long periods, as multi-domain combat is set to develop in the coming decades. The “heterogeneous” equipment is designed to exceed conventional armoured vehicles by rapidly reconfiguring physical modules and functions within seconds for missions across land, water, air and electromagnetic contest grounds, according to the scientists. The researchers said their designs had advanced towards engineering application and “combat-oriented validation” after prototypes and field tests proved their feasibility. A paper written by researchers from the Inner Mongolia First Machinery Group – a company involved in China’s tank and armoured vehicle development – and the Beijing Institute of Technology, was published by the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Acta Armamentarii on August 6. The study places the concept within the projected development of armoured vehicles between 2030 and 2050, when the researchers expect military operations will require closer coordination between platforms and systems across multiple domains. The research reflects a broader vision of future armoured warfare in which vehicles can adapt more quickly to changing threats and coordinate with systems such as drones. The authors argue that conventional armoured vehicles, whose capabilities are tied to fixed physical modules, could take more than 45 seconds to transition from reconnaissance to striking a target. They also said that conventional vehicles’ effectiveness in intercepting multiple targets could fall from 89 per cent to 38.6 per cent in a 10-second drone attack. For vehicles built around their new approach, the researchers set a target of reducing the observe-orient-decide-act (OODA) decision cycle to 9 seconds, which they described as a fivefold improvement over current performance. The design also aimed to keep fluctuations in the power supplied to high-energy payloads within plus or minus 3 per cent, while allowing different vehicle configurations to be tailored to specific missions. In tests, the team reported an average module-connection time of 8.7 seconds and a success rate of 98.3 per cent across 1,000 trials conducted at temperatures ranging from 50 degrees Celsius to minus 20 (122 to minus 4 Fahrenheit) under strong electromagnetic interference and in muddy terrain. Among the capabilities, the researchers proposed a dedicated water module capable of operating under water up to 50 metres (164 feet) deep for two hours, with the transition between operating environments designed to take as little as 12 minutes. However, their tests did not establish underwater performance and the paper did not provide underwater speed or range figures. The concept is intended to give armoured units greater flexibility in amphibious operations, allowing a vehicle to approach through water before switching to its land configuration for operations ashore. The researchers proposed combining underwater manoeuvres with drone-assisted obstacle clearance, projecting that the system could clear 30 obstacles per minute and reduce the time required for a landing operation by 60 per cent. The land-based core module could reach speeds of at least 70km/h (43mph) on roads and 40km/h off-road, with a range of at least 600km (373 miles) using hybrid power, according to the paper. The authors said the concept could improve performance across five key areas compared with existing modular armoured vehicles, such as Germany’s Boxer, estimating it would cut whole-life costs by around 40 per cent. The South China Morning Post has contacted corresponding author Ren Xuan for comment.

title: MI5 chief warns Iran is targeting military sites in UK as hostile state threats surge
description: The security agency has established a specialised assessment centre after intelligence head outlines rising hybrid warfare risks.
content: Iran is trying to hit military sites in the UK and the suspected plot to attack a US-run military airbase in September was “not unique”, the head of Britain’s MI5 spy agency said on Tuesday. Ken McCallum, who leads the UK’s domestic security service, said Tehran was seeking to intensify its attacks in Britain beyond the traditional targets of Iranians opposed to the country’s Islamic authorities. That has included arson and sabotage attacks on Jewish sites that Britain says were carried out by Iranian proxies. McCallum said another “major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites”. The incident at RAF Fairford “is not unique. There have been other examples, not just in the UK but around the world”, McCallum said. McCallum delivered a speech outlining major threats to the UK as detectives investigate a suspected terror plot against the US-run base in western England, which has been used to bomb Iran during this year’s war. Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base on September 27 as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant – petrol – in three vans at the site, but no explosives. British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which led the US to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. Seven men in their twenties have been arrested and released on bail under investigation. Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. In a stark speech, McCallum argued that the UK faced a “new era of national security” and was at a turning point equivalent to the September 11 attacks a quarter century ago. He said his agency’s work countering state threats – chiefly from Russia, Iran and China – had quadrupled in the past decade, and claimed that both Russia and Iran were expanding their hybrid warfare campaigns against the UK. Meanwhile, technology was racing ahead, with artificial intelligence “supercharging” the cybersecurity battle between attackers and defenders, he said. McCallum said terror plotters had used artificial intelligence for reconnaissance and attacks, including AI-enabled drones. Even more concerning, he said, was “AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons”. He said terror groups “would dearly love” to have chemical, biological or radiological weapons, but these were hard to obtain. “One risk is that AI could enable dangerous knowledge to get into the hands of people we would all rather didn’t have that knowledge,” he said. “A second and different risk … is the possibility that AI could generate novel pathogens not previously seen.” McCallum said MI5 had set up a new AI Threat Assessment Centre to try to keep ahead of the risks. “Human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are. It is capable of outthinking us. This is genuinely novel, and deserves the serious attention it is getting, including in MI5,” he said.

title: Hong Kong renews TV station licences with push for ‘telling good stories’
description: Licences will run until 2039 for HK Television Entertainment and TVB, and until 2040 for i-Cable Hoy.
content: Hong Kong authorities have renewed the free-to-air licences of the city’s television broadcasters with conditions to boost local production of English-language national education shows and programmes aimed at “telling good stories” of the city. The Executive Council, the city’s top decision-making body, approved the renewal on Tuesday, extending 12-year licences to all three broadcasters. These licences will run until 2039 for HK Television Entertainment (HKTVE) and TVB, and until 2040 for i-Cable Hoy. A government spokesman said the approvals, alongside various relaxation measures and enhancement requirements, aim to “foster the sustainable development of the local broadcasting industry and provide more diversified and quality television programmes”. “The Chief Executive in Council’s decision to renew the free television licences, along with the timely regulatory updates, has demonstrated the government’s commitment to cultivating a more favourable business environment,” a Commerce and Economic Development Bureau spokesman said. The spokesman added that such an environment would enable the broadcasting industry to thrive, capitalise on the strength of the city’s brand and reinforce Hong Kong’s position as Asia’s world city. The council accepted the Communications Authority’s recommendations, including investment proposals of HK$2.3 billion (US$293.07 million) for HKTVE, HK$6.2 billion for TVB and HK$950 million for i-Cable Hoy for the first six years of the renewed licences. The council also supported relaxation measures including allowing more flexibility in airing non-designated language programmes for both integrated Chinese and English channels and reducing airtime for designated programmes. Under the updated licence conditions, broadcasters must “increase local production and broadcast of English programmes on telling good stories of Hong Kong and national education-related programmes”. Other requirements include enhancing subtitling requirements and adding a cap on simulcast content. The authority has also implemented measures to streamline administrative requirements and complaint handling procedures to reduce compliance costs.
