City leader John Lee Ka-chiu said in his policy address last month that the government would remove barriers and ease restrictions for the broadcasting industry, ensuring the regulatory regime keeps pace with the times. Following a review and public consultation by the authority, an amended version of the Generic Codes of Practice for Television will be proposed before the end of the year, with implementation targeted for mid-2027. TVB welcomed the licence renewal and pledged to continue to invest in producing more “high-quality programmes” to create diverse entertainment for Chinese-speaking audiences worldwide, while telling good stories of mainland China and Hong Kong. “We look forward to the swift implementation of a series of deregulation measures to ensure fair competition between internet media and free-to-air television, enabling the free-to-air television industry to continue providing the public with high-quality … programmes,” a spokesman said. HKTVE, which operates ViuTV, also welcomed the approval, saying that the renewal laid a solid foundation for the station’s long-term development, enabling it to continue providing high-quality free-to-air television programme services. “The station will continue to fulfil its responsibilities as a licensed broadcaster by producing high-quality and diverse original programmes, whilst continually enhancing the standard of its content and production,” a spokesman said. i-Cable Hoy said the new measures would boost scheduling flexibility and operational adaptability, helping it allocate resources more effectively amid a rapidly changing media landscape while delivering a high-quality entertainment experience.

title: China sentences 3 more Myanmar crime bosses to death in scam centre crackdown
description: Trio among 61 members sentenced from family-run Wei syndicate – one of the notorious ‘four families’ of northern Myanmar.
content: Courts in China have sentenced three key figures of a notorious Myanmar crime syndicate to death for operating large-scale cross-border telecoms fraud networks and causing the deaths of four Chinese nationals. The Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court and the Nanan City People’s Court in southeastern Fujian province handed down the rulings against syndicate head Wei Huairen, his nephew Chen Dawei and accomplice Liao Jingfang on Tuesday, following a trial held in May, state broadcaster CCTV reported. They are among 61 members of the family-run Wei syndicate convicted of running massive cyber scam centres as well as illegal detention and extortion rings out of northern Myanmar targeting victims across China. Three other key defendants – Wei Qingtao, Kang Min and Xiong Hengxing – were sentenced to life in prison, while 55 accomplices received fixed prison terms ranging from 39 months to 24 years. The courts – designated by central authorities to lead the prosecution – also ordered extensive asset confiscations, heavy fines and deportations where applicable. The ruling marks China’s latest high-profile legal milestone in systematically dismantling the violent transnational scam empires that once operated with near-total impunity along its southwestern border with Myanmar. According to the verdict, the syndicate was spearheaded by Wei Huairen, a former border guard militia commander and head of the Wei clan – one of northern Myanmar’s infamous “four families” of Kokang. He also headed the family’s Henry Group conglomerate. The Wei family leveraged its political and military influence in Kokang to set up multiple criminal compounds in Laukkai, the region’s capital. The syndicate harboured and provided armed protection to fraudulent “investors”, running industrial-scale telecoms scams, operating illegal casinos, trafficking narcotics, extorting victims and organising cross-border human smuggling, the courts heard. Investigators found that the illicit gambling and fraud operations processed more than 12.2 billion yuan (US$1.7 billion) in criminal funds since 2019. Wei Huairen, the family’s third eldest brother, served as chairman of the 1006 Border Battalion Supervision Committee of Kokang. This enabled him to weaponise state-authorised military forces for private criminal ends, the CCTV report said. Court documents detailed violence inside the scam compounds, revealing that the syndicate colluded with fraud operators to murder two Chinese citizens who disobeyed internal rules. Meanwhile, Chen Dawei, groomed as the clan’s second-generation armed enforcer, used private militias to carry out killings, including those of two other Chinese nationals. A documentary aired by CCTV last week revealed that Chen admitted to randomly murdering a victim as a “ritual sacrifice” to prove loyalty while forging ties with fraud compound financiers. The Wei family “uniquely” abused institutional authority, the documentary said. While ostensibly drawing government salaries to protect the border, clan leaders co-opted the state apparatus for private gain, it noted. “By intertwining official border guard units with private militias, the family pioneered a violent model of armed military control over telecoms scam compounds” and casino hubs in Laukkai, the narrator said. Kokang was long carved up among the “four families” – the Wei, Bai, Liu and Ming clans – who ran vast compounds where tens of thousands of trafficked workers faced torture, beatings and forced labour to carry out online scams. Jurisdiction was a key obstacle to China’s efforts to combat cross-border scam operations, the CCTV documentary revealed. After China issued arrest warrants, the Myanmar authorities initially argued that the syndicate bosses held Myanmar nationality and should therefore face trial and serve any sentence locally before extradition could be considered. Beijing countered that it held full legal jurisdiction because the syndicates mainly targeted Chinese citizens. Domestic prosecution in China was crucial for “thoroughly uncovering the full scope of crimes and deterring future syndicates”, the authorities argued, according to the documentary. “The ‘four families’ in northern Myanmar had reached a stage where they simply had to be eliminated,” Niu Jiawei, deputy director of the Asean division at the Ministry of Public Security’s international cooperation bureau, said in the broadcast. “If the heads of Kokang’s ‘four families’ were not brought to justice, the Chinese police would not accept it, Chinese law would not accept it and the Chinese people certainly would not accept it.” The impasse was finally resolved through a consensus on regional security, leading Myanmar authorities to detain and hand over the fugitive bosses, according to the documentary. In late 2023, Beijing launched an aggressive cross-border law enforcement campaign that saw regional authorities hand over fugitive syndicate leaders and repatriate nearly 60,000 Chinese fraud suspects. The latest judgment follows sweeping executions handed down to rival Kokang kingpins. In January, 11 members of the Ming crime family were executed following sentencing by a court in eastern Zhejiang province, while syndicate founder Ming Xuechang died by suicide before he could be arrested. The following month, four core members of the Bai family were executed after being sentenced in Shenzhen, southern China. The Fujian courts convicted Wei, Chen and their co-defendants on seven criminal counts, including intentional homicide and fraud, citing the grave harm their armed network inflicted on society.

title: Slain model Abby Choi called ‘birthing machine’ by ex-father-in-law, court hears
description: Choi’s partner Chris Tam takes stand for first time in murder trial, describing day that led to breakdown in model’s relations with ex-in-laws.
content: The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung called her a “birthing machine” and tried to assault her before he allegedly plotted with his two sons to kill her three years ago, a court has heard. Choi’s partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, recounted on Tuesday a bitter argument between the influencer and her former in-laws in what he said was a watershed moment leading to a breakdown in the relationship in mid-2022. Choi was previously married to Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, who is standing trial on a joint count of murder alongside his brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, and his father Kwong Kau, 68. Testifying for the first time in the High Court, Tam also said Choi had given his family a false impression that her former in-laws were leading a good life, because she feared her two children from her previous marriage would be disparaged in their new home due to their background. Tam said he was not surprised initially to find out that Kwong Kau was the registered owner of a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin, before she told him the flat was in fact bought using her money. “When I saw the Kadooria flat was in Kwong Kau’s name, I did not deliberately ask [Choi] about it because she had been telling me all along that this family was doing OK,” Tam said. Kwong allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the upscale property and enlisted his two sons to help kill the 28-year-old on February 21, 2023. Prosecutors argued the flat was only registered in his name to avoid paying HK$9 million in double stamp duty. The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the burial of Choi’s body, an offence to which his two sons pleaded guilty before the trial began last month. Tam said his family’s wealth grew significantly after his father, who founded the popular restaurant chain TamJai Yunnan Mixian, received part of the profit from selling the brand to a Japanese company for HK$1 billion. He said he first met Choi around the end of 2013 and early 2014, when he briefly returned from Australia during a break in his studies to meet up with her then-husband Alex Kwong, his former classmate. He said Alex Kwong “totally disappeared” after one day in 2015, the same year he began the process to divorce Choi and absconded from criminal proceedings arising from his alleged involvement in a HK$6.3 million theft case. Tam said he did not probe further after Choi said her then-partner was safe, because he thought she had somehow managed to find a way to contact him. “I came out very often with Abby afterwards. We took care of her children together, and love grew between us as time went by,” he added. The court heard Tam and Choi formally started dating in December 2015 and held a wedding banquet a year later, although they never registered their marriage. The model gave birth to their daughter in September 2016, and their son was born three years later. Choi lived with her partner’s family at a luxurious residence on Begonia Road in Kowloon Tong and received up to HK$300,000 monthly from Tam’s father to cover the couple’s expenses. Tam said the two children Choi had with Alex Kwong lived separately with two domestic helpers initially at a flat in the Laguna Verde estate in Hung Hom, before the socialite decided to move them to the Kadooria development in 2019 because it was closer to her Kowloon Tong home. The witness highlighted a heated argument between Choi and her former mother-in-law, Jenny Li Sui-heung, on a day when the influencer’s elder daughter had a fever at the Kadooria home in June or July 2022. According to Tam, the model was angry at Li for telling Alex Kwong to stay away from the child because she could infect him. “My understanding is that Abby was at that time accusing Li Sui-heung of preferring sons to daughters,” he said. Kwong Kau, who joined the row, reportedly lunged at Choi and hurled curses at her after he accused the influencer of assaulting his wife. “And then Kwong Kau said: ‘Who do you think you are? You’re just a birthing machine’,” Tam continued. Tam said the elder Kwong attempted to attack Choi a second time, but he intervened to prevent the former police officer from hitting the model. He said Choi then barred Kwong Kau from visiting the residence. She also told Tam they needed to cut ties with the Kwong family, whom she described as horrible and ungrateful. Defence lawyers also grilled a police officer helping to lead the investigation of the case. Detective Constable Ko Yan-ki, who was originally not expected to take the witness box, was cross-examined over his text conversations with Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, in the months preceding the trial. The messaging logs were produced as evidence after the officer contacted Cheung while she was giving evidence last week about her purported ownership of a flat at Whampoa Garden. She later clarified that she did not own the property. Ko rejected the prosecution’s suggestion that he should have avoided contact with Cheung while her testimony was ongoing, saying he needed to make prompt inquiries on new information regarding her property ownership. The messaging records also showed that Cheung had a monetary dispute with a friend she met at a mahjong parlour earlier this year. Cheung said she was alleged to have owed HK$1.6 million, but she insisted the debt was settled seven years ago. She also revealed that she once lost “a few tens of millions of dollars” while gambling at a mahjong parlour in Jordan. Ko said Cheung’s alleged debts did not catch his attention when he investigated the case, adding that he could not ascertain whether her claims about gambling millions of dollars away were true or exaggerated. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: Review | From Jumbo Floating Restaurant to neon, nostalgia aplenty at Hong Kong art-tech show
description: Hong Kong Performing Arts Expo’s opening showcase evoked the city’s vanishing heritage but couldn’t tie them together.
content: When Hong Kong’s Jumbo Floating Restaurant capsized and sank in the South China Sea in 2022, social media users lamented the loss of a culinary icon. Some tongue-in-cheek proposals called for it to be transformed into an underwater restaurant or diving sanctuary. No salvage operation or documentary project has materialised, leaving the fate of the wreck a lingering mystery. That sense of loss, nostalgia and imagination surrounding Hong Kong’s vanished and disappearing landmarks anchored City Reverie, the opening performance of the second Hong Kong Performing Arts Expo (HKPAX), which ran from October 9 to 13. The 50-minute interdisciplinary performance was staged on October 8 and 9 at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre’s Studio Theatre in Tsim Sha Tsui, while Objectopia, an interactive installation in the nearby Salisbury Garden, will be on view until October 22. City Reverie is neither the most technically advanced nor the most visually spectacular production. Still, it stands out as an affectionate tribute to Hong Kong. Before the contemporary music concert begins, audiences enter an immersive underwater realm with projections simulating the sunken Jumbo Floating Restaurant. Two divers holding gaming controllers provide a humorous reminder that the audience is stepping into an artificial, fictional world. The scene recalls British artist Damien Hirst’s 2017 satirical archaeological exhibition “Treasures from the Wreck of the Unbelievable”, which included mockumentary footage of divers discovering statues of Mickey Mouse and modern pop icons. Unlike Hirst’s sardonic critique of art-market provenance, however, this sequence uses ambient lighting, soothing melodies and imaginative visuals to invite viewers to revisit a Hong Kong landmark. The rest of the performance feels overwhelming at times. Divided into five chapters, its score moves between soothing, nostalgic and futuristic contemporary pieces, performed on grand pianos and synthesisers by composer Lam Fung and pianist Jerold Chu. The music accompanies a video collage of familiar urban Hong Kong motifs: archival footage of traditional palanquins, bygone neon-lit streets, vintage Cathay Pacific planes flying low over Kowloon City. Gradually, the images disintegrate into blurred digital noise and cascading computer code reminiscent of The Matrix. Before the performance, audience members are given wristbands supplied by technology firm Upmood. The devices record biometric data, including heart rate variability, pulse, stress levels and emotional states, as participants watch a short video featuring poetic lines dedicated to Hong Kong. The readings are then incorporated into the final chapter, where the creators integrate the audience’s emotions into the live musical performance and screen visuals displaying words such as “calm”, “sad”, “tense” and “aroused”. Interactive elements can encourage audience engagement, but here they feel only loosely connected to the broader narrative. The video is too brief to prompt meaningful reflection, while the display of emotional metrics lacks imagery specifically tied to Hong Kong. According to the organisers, City Reverie is designed to prompt audiences to encounter the city “as memory, rhythm and future possibility”. But the project offers little resolution and does not explain how biometric tracking deepens the audience’s connection to the city. The accompanying installation, Objectopia, suffers from a similar narrative limitation. An interactive LED display featuring a map of Hong Kong, it invites visitors to scan a QR code and access a web platform where they can choose from 88 digital icons of the city – from egg tarts and aeroplane olives to Bruce Lee – to be projected onto a large screen. The installation is playful, accessible and eye-catching, but offers little historical context. Younger visitors or tourists unfamiliar with traditional street delicacies may come away with little cultural or historical insight. Overall, City Reverie is a nostalgic attempt to use art tech to revisit Hong Kong’s vanishing heritage, offering a refreshing departure from conventional classical productions, such as the concurrent stagings of Cavalleria Rusticana and Pagliacci at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre. But, despite its inventive score and visual ambition, the production needs greater conceptual coherence to rise above a superficial collage of urban nostalgia. City Reverie was performed on October 8 and 9 at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre Studio Theatre; Objectopia runs until October 22 in Salisbury Garden, Tsim Sha Tsui.

title: Schools urged not to make pupils with special educational needs repeat grades
description: ‘Repeating a grade will only aggravate their social and emotional adjustment difficulties and increase mental health risks,’ updated guide says.
content: Hong Kong schools should not require students with special educational needs (SEN) or severe mental illness to repeat a grade, under revised education authorities’ guidance that warns the practice could worsen their adjustment difficulties. The latest version of the Education Bureau’s School Administration Guide requires subsidised schools considering grade retention for pupils with special educational needs (SEN) to consult parents through a team of professionals, including an educational psychologist. “Repeating a grade will only aggravate their social and emotional adjustment difficulties and increase mental health risks,” according to the guide, which was updated in August and came to the attention of the media on Tuesday. The team should also include the school’s student support team and teachers, as well as psychiatrists when necessary, it said. Schools should also provide support measures suited to the individual SEN student’s needs as an alternative to repeating a grade. In its update, the bureau said schools should avoid repeated grade retention because it could reduce students’ interest in learning, damage their self-image, increase their risk of dropping out and heighten mental health risks. When deciding whether a student should repeat a grade, schools should review the child’s overall circumstances, including academic performance, conduct, learning attitude, performance in extracurricular activities, other learning needs and the wishes of both the student and their parents. “Schools should not regard grade repetition as the sole method to assist student learning, nor should it be used to punish students,” the guide said. The bureau also urged schools not to arrange for a large number of students at a particular level to repeat a grade. Under the guide, a primary school’s overall repetition rate should not exceed 3 per cent of total enrolment, while the rate for secondary schools should not exceed 5 per cent. Students may repeat a grade only once during their six years of primary school and may not repeat Primary Six. Principals told the South China Morning Post on Tuesday that grade retention was a serious decision requiring a holistic assessment of each student’s circumstances and suitability, adding that the guidelines urged educators to think “more cautiously” about the matter. Lee Yi-ying, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Subsidised Secondary Schools Council, said the learning needs of SEN students varied widely, and each potential case of grade retention should be assessed holistically according to the child’s needs and suitability. “The guidelines are meant to ask us to be more cautious, especially for SEN students. Our concern is that more formulaic assessment [for retention] isn’t ideal,” Lee said. The secondary school principal said she believed the guidelines did not impose a total ban on repeating a grade for SEN students, but required schools to take additional steps to assess their circumstances more holistically. Lee said that even under existing practices, students with and without special needs required counselling when repeating a grade to ensure they did not see the measure as a sign of personal failure. Schools would also evaluate whether a student needed to repeat a grade with a variety of factors besides performance, including the number of days in attendance. Lee said that for some schools, a low rate of attendance suggested an incomplete immersion in campus life and could foster decisions for grade retention. She added that repeating a grade could help some students who needed more time to master their learning, while others might benefit from dropping elective subjects or switching to another subject. Langton Cheung Yung-pong, honorary chairman of the Hong Kong Aided Primary School Heads Association, said the updated guidelines were a step in the right direction. Cheung said his school already consulted a multidisciplinary team of professionals when deciding whether a student should repeat a grade. “The new guidelines are a response to actual needs,” Cheung said. For students with intellectual disabilities, he added, additional time was not the key to improving their grades, making repeating a year an unsuitable measure for them. Primary school repeater numbers in Hong Kong fell from 1,610 in 2015 to a 10-year low of 1,205 in 2025. The repeaters accounted for only 0.38 per cent of all primary students last year. For secondary schools, while the number of repeaters decreased from 11,560 in 2015 to 9,273 in 2025, they still accounted for 2.67 per cent of the total secondary student body, according to the bureau’s statistics. The bureau said the number of students with special education needs enrolled in public schools was 67,870 in the 2024-25 school year. Additional reporting by William Yiu

title: Huawei, once hobbled by US sanctions, passes 100 million Kirin chip milestone
description: The Chinese tech giant is also testing a next-generation processor and expanding its presence in the domestic AI chip market.
content: Huawei Technologies has shipped more than 100 million devices powered by its Kirin processors since 2023, when it returned to the smartphone market with a new generation of premium handsets. The company says testing of its next-generation Kirin 2027 chip is also progressing in line with expectations. The company disclosed the figure on Tuesday as it unveiled new details about its flagship Kirin 9050 series, the first mass-produced chip using its proprietary LogicFolding architecture, developed under a framework it calls the Tau Scaling Law. Huawei said the new chip design integrates more than 50 million hybrid bonds and improves transistor density by 53.5 per cent. “The Kirin 9050 series has successfully achieved mass production with the support of China’s domestic electronics supply chain,” the company said. Chinese media outlet Yicai reported on Tuesday that Huawei had also begun testing its next-generation Kirin 2027 processor, with preliminary results meeting the company’s targets. The report cited Xu Songyu, a director responsible for wireless device chips at Huawei’s semiconductor business. Speaking at a press briefing on Tuesday in Shanghai, Xu said progress on LogicFolding had surpassed Huawei’s expectations despite early uncertainty over whether the technology could be manufactured at scale while maintaining production yields, according to Yicai. The company did not immediately respond to the South China Morning Post’s request for comment. LogicFolding is a technique under Huawei’s Tau Scaling Law, which was announced in May. The approach proposes a major shift in semiconductor development by improving how quickly data moves between parts of a chip and across a computing system. The strategy aims to extract more computing power through optimised semiconductor designs without relying on the most advanced chipmaking equipment, particularly the world’s cutting-edge lithography tools blocked by US-led export controls. Huawei is also expanding its business in semiconductors used to power artificial intelligence systems, with its Ascend AI chips gaining ground in the Chinese market as Washington’s restrictions limit access to the most advanced American processors. The company shipped 572,000 AI accelerators in the first half of 2026, ‌up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, capturing a 28 per cent share of China’s data centre AI chip market, according to research firm IDC data reported by Reuters. AI accelerators are specialised processors used to train and run AI models. Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China over the same period, giving it 34 per cent of the market, down from 44 per cent a year ago, Reuters reported, citing IDC, which declined to comment on the data. Huawei’s chip ambitions suffered a setback in 2020 when tighter US sanctions barred the company from using the foundry services of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. The company returned with its home-grown Kirin 9000s processor in 2023, which powered its Mate 60 Pro smartphone.

title: Could Pakistan’s Chinese-made weapons help protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks?
description: Islamabad, which reportedly sent JF-17 jets and an HQ-9 system to Saudi Arabia, has vowed cooperation with Riyadh ‘in every possible way’.
content: Chinese-Pakistani fighter jets and a China-made air-defence system reportedly deployed to Saudi Arabia could be brought into action following Pakistan’s renewed pledge to defend the kingdom after deadly Houthi attacks on Riyadh. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said on Sunday that Islamabad would cooperate with Riyadh “in every possible way” under their defence agreements, after Houthi strikes on the Saudi capital’s main airport the previous day killed at least 13 people and wounded hundreds. A further attack on Sunday killed a Pakistani national and injured 11 others, Saudi authorities said. Sharif’s pledge follows an October 5 emergency meeting in Riyadh, where Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey agreed to implement their collective-defence commitments and prepare for the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities to the kingdom. A joint statement released after that meeting did not specify troop numbers or weapons. The military commitments stem from the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed in August, under which an armed attack on one alliance member is considered an attack on all three. The pact builds on an earlier bilateral defence agreement signed between Islamabad and Riyadh in September last year. A Reuters report in May citing security and government sources said that Pakistan had deployed around 16 aircraft, mostly JF-17 fighters jointly developed with China, and a Chinese-made HQ-9 surface-to-air missile system to Saudi Arabia. It remains unclear whether the systems would be used to counter further Houthi attacks. But if brought into action, they could provide another opportunity to assess the performance of Chinese-origin military equipment under combat conditions, following Pakistan’s use of Chinese-made J-10CE fighters and related weapons during its May 2025 conflict with India. The sources quoted by Reuters said the JF-17s were dispatched in early April and that the deployment also included around 8,000 troops, while two security officials also reported two drone squadrons. While Pakistani personnel handle the operation of the equipment, its deployment is reportedly funded by Riyadh. Neither government responded to requests for comment from Reuters at the time, and there is currently no public evidence that either the JF-17s or HQ-9 have been used against the Houthis. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is investigating why its air defences failed to stop the airport attacks, in which multiple drones were reportedly launched first to pave the way for cruise and ballistic missiles. Associated Press reported in September that the kingdom had sought air-defence support from Pakistan and other countries as interceptor stocks dwindled. But any role for Pakistan’s HQ-9 would raise questions about how effectively it could operate alongside Saudi Arabia’s existing air defences. Pakistan’s Dawn newspaper reported last week that there was no public evidence of arrangements allowing Pakistani or Turkish sensors to routinely “cue” Saudi weapons – passing information about a detected threat to help another system track or engage it. Although the HQ-9 can operate using its own radar, sharing such information could help the allies coordinate interceptions. Yet, having additional weapons available does not necessarily mean they can operate as a single defensive force. That coordination challenge is particularly relevant because Saudi Arabia still relies heavily on American military systems. An analysis in August by the think tank Arab Centre Washington DC said US weapons, intelligence and integrated air-defence systems remained central to the kingdom’s military capabilities, even as Pakistani-operated Chinese equipment helped diversify its defences. Pakistan has described its role as defensive, saying that it was providing support including reconnaissance while Saudi forces conducted combat operations. Islamabad has also denied reports of Pakistani jets striking the Houthis in Yemen. Experts say closer defence cooperation between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia could create opportunities for Chinese arms manufacturers. The ChinaMed Project cited Liu Zongyi of the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies as saying that Pakistan could connect Chinese weapons suppliers with Middle Eastern buyers – giving Beijing a potential route to expand sales without joining the Mecca alliance.

title: Plan to live-stream US execution tests Southeast Asia’s content curbs
description: Analysts urge regulators to step up efforts to limit resharing and improve detection tools to reduce harm to the public.
content: The US government’s plan to live-stream the execution of a former Army member convicted in a deadly 2009 mass shooting is raising questions about how effectively Southeast Asian governments can restrict graphic online content. Analysts say while authorities may have powers to restrict access to the live stream, containing clips and altered copies of the killing posted to social media could prove far more difficult. The issue gained fresh urgency on Tuesday, after Australia’s Environment Minister Murray Watts condemned the proposed broadcast as “disgusting”. Australia’s online regulator, eSafety, told Agence France Presse it lacked the power to prevent the live stream, but stressed that online services had a responsibility to protect users from harmful content. New Zealand’s Classification Office had earlier said it could not classify a live stream while it was taking place and lacked the authority to block access to such an event. Nidal Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base in Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be live-streamed, and the Pentagon subsequently confirmed the plan. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had not made a final decision on whether the execution would be live-streamed, despite his comments a day earlier approving the broadcast, leaving the plan’s current status uncertain. Details of how the broadcast will be distributed also remain unclear. In Southeast Asia, existing rules provide potential avenues for restricting access, but analysts say whether authorities invoke them depends on their assessment of the broadcast, how it is presented and where it appears. Benjamin Ang, head of the Centre of Excellence for National Security at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said regulators would first need to determine whether the broadcast warranted restrictions. “Regulators and platforms would then need to coordinate to pre-identify when and where the live stream will take place so they can effectively detect the live stream and block access to it in their countries,” he said. Powers to restrict In Singapore, the Internet Code of Practice requires licensed providers to comply with rules on prohibited material. For websites, internet access providers meet their obligations by denying access to sites notified by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) as containing such material. The code considers whether content depicts “detailed or relished acts of extreme violence or cruelty”, alongside any intrinsic medical, scientific, artistic or educational value. These are assessment criteria, rather than an automatic requirement for blocking an execution broadcast. Malaysia’s Online Safety Act provides for the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) to order licensed platforms or network providers to restrict access. This follows MCMC’s assessing a user report and determining on reasonable grounds that the content is harmful. The law covers material that may incite violence or terrorism, promote public hostility or disturb public tranquillity, but does not specifically list execution live streams. Indonesia’s Ministerial Regulation No. 5 of 2020 on Private Electronic-System Operators, amended in 2021, requires operators to prevent the distribution of prohibited material, including content that relevant authorities classify as unsettling the public and disrupting public order. Operators must comply with takedown orders within 24 hours of receipt. In urgent cases, they must act without delay, and no later than four hours after receiving a warning. Failure to comply can lead to access blocking, including through internet service providers. These deadlines, however, do not shield viewers from a short live event. This Week In Asia has reached out to IMDA, MCMC and Indonesia’s Communications and Digital Ministry for comment. Beyond the original stream Even if access to the original broadcast were restricted, recordings and excerpts could spread elsewhere, creating a separate challenge for regulators and platforms. Drawing on lessons from Islamic State beheadings and the Christchurch terrorist massacre, Ang said regulators should work across platforms to limit resharing, while services should use machine learning to detect altered copies of the footage. Platforms must also “downgrade related search terms, and de-monetise and disable offending accounts”, he said. Benjamin Y.H. Loh, a communications and media scholar at Monash University Malaysia, said containing reposted footage could become “a cat-and-mouse game”, with social media users uploading clips of the event to spoof platforms’ detection efforts. He also pointed to the Christchurch attack, where redistribution of footage on the massacre became a major content-moderation challenge. Clips were altered with music, sped up or mirrored before being uploaded in attempts to evade platform moderators and automated detection tools. However, advance notice would allow platforms to prepare for the broadcast, Loh said. “You need to have a lot of human moderators on standby to handle the incoming reports.” He said moderators could also monitor retransmission of footage, citing how illegal live streams of World Cup matches in June and July were quickly discovered and blocked or banned. “It’s not going to be instantaneous, of course,” he said. “There will definitely be a few that will go through the cracks.” Loh also cautioned that a broadcast showing the execution directly versus an indirect account of proceedings would raise different questions. “The platforms’ decisions really depend on the material and how they apply their own Terms of Service,” he said. Propaganda tool The risks of broadcasting or live-streaming Hasan’s execution could extend beyond exposure to graphic imagery, as experts warn the footage could also be used to promote extremist narratives. “Some of the accounts that clip or repost the original live stream may do so to advocate violence or incite hate against certain races or religions,” Ang said, adding that community and religious leaders and educators could help raise public awareness of the dangers of such content. But for political scientist Bilveer Singh, live-streaming the execution would simply reinforce anti-West or anti-American views among extremist actors and susceptible audiences in Southeast Asia. “It will also complicate ongoing deradicalisation efforts that Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia have been pursuing, because if this execution goes through, it provides extremists with material to exploit,” he said. Analysts warn that extremist sympathisers could also portray Hasan as a martyr, regardless of his crimes. “Therein lies a radicalisation toolkit for these people,” Bilveer said. For Ang, the practical objective is reducing harm rather than promising complete containment. “It may be impossible to stop every instance of the livestream, but countries can do as much as they can to reduce the harm to their populations,” Ang said.

title: As I see it | US cosplays WTO against China while paralysing the real global body
description: By stymying the WTO’s appellate body and citing treaties it has not ratified, Washington proves the rules-based order is actually a rules-for-thee order.
content: The French have a phrase for the urge to leap from a high place without any wish to die: “l’appel du vide” (the call of the void). The World Trade Organization, based in French-speaking Geneva, has put it to poetic bureaucratic use. In its French texts, a losing party’s appeal to a court that cannot hear it is “faire appel dans le vide”, or appealing into the void. Americans should take the credit. The WTO’s Appellate Body has had no sitting judges since Washington began blocking new appointments in 2019. Under WTO rules, an appeal suspends adoption of the panel ruling. So the loser simply appeals, the ruling is frozen and compliance is postponed indefinitely at no cost. More than 30 panel rulings have gone “into the void”. A court with no judges is not a court. It is a very expensive waiting room. Consider a recent hearing convened by the Office of the US Trade Representative to review China’s compliance with its WTO commitments. Terry McCartin, assistant US trade representative for China, Mongolia and Taiwan affairs, said that after 25 years of membership China “still embraces a non-market economic system” and now targets entire industrial sectors for global dominance. Maybe so. Why not take the case to the WTO? We know why. The US has disabled the court of appeal. So Washington plays prosecutor, convenes its own jury and borrows the authority of a global body it has deliberately kneecapped. That is cosplay: the costume of multilateralism with none of the institutions inside. Remind me, who has been waging a global tariff war that upended the entire trading system? Imagine a defendant who not only commits his crimes but demolishes the courthouse, then turns up in a judge’s robe to try others for stealing from him. The defence, I suppose, will be that the WTO was already flawed and Washington is merely forcing reform. The US has long accused the Appellate Body of overreach, creating law rather than interpreting it. And China’s state-heavy economy does strain a rule book written for a different era; it is, however, not the only one doing it. But a reformer proposes fixes and bargains for them. Washington has simply wielded a veto for years and then complained that nobody enforces the rules. It could have aired its grievances in a proper forum, where it has won its share of cases. But wait, no such forum exists any more; the US makes sure of that. This is how Washington treats international law generally: embrace it as a weapon, shun it as a constraint. Take the International Criminal Court. US President Bill Clinton signed the Rome Statute but never sent it to the Senate, partly fearing politically motivated prosecutions of US personnel. That position was at least debatable. The Trump administration has now gone much further, sanctioning the entire court. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced in July a campaign to isolate it, urging other countries to withdraw. That is not scepticism about a court but a call to dismantle it. Or take the law of the sea. The US never ratified the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Yet Washington is delighted to wave the convention at China in the South China Sea, while claiming its own 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone under customary law. Rights à la carte, obligations off the menu. Then there is the law of the sea as practised. Operation Southern Spear, the US military campaign against alleged drug boats, has by recent tallies killed at least 238 people. A UN report this September concluded that the strikes breach international, maritime and human rights law, and may amount to extrajudicial killings. The administration claims it is in an “armed conflict” with cartels. Human Rights Watch and many legal experts counter that lethal force is lawful only against an imminent threat to life. A suspected smuggler is entitled to arrest and trial, not a missile. When rules bind others, Washington is a stern sheriff. When they bind Washington, it is a sovereign nation with a veto, an unratified treaty or a sanctions list. The rules-based order, it turns out, is a rules-for-thee order. Beijing is hardly a saint, and its trade practices deserve scrutiny. But scrutiny needs a credible venue and a credible prosecutor. Washington has sabotaged the first and disqualified itself from the second. Standing at the edge of the global legal system, the Americans feel the call of the void. As they look down, they are pushing everyone else off the ledge, then lecturing the survivors on compliance.

title: Hong Kong Premier League club suspend player over racially sensitive social media message
description: Tai Po also issue strongly-worded statement and give teenager Gabriel Mesquita a formal written warning after he responds to netizen.
content: Tai Po have hauled Gabriel Mesquita over the coals after he posted a racially sensitive message on social media, issuing the teenage midfielder with a formal written warning and indefinitely suspending him from first-team training and matches. Brazilian Mesquita, who joined the local Premier League club as a free agent this summer, aggressively bit back after a Threads user wrote “Gweilo will always be Gweilo” in response to the player posting an image of his Hong Kong identity card application form. Privately messaging the offending poster on Sunday, Mesquita said he was here to “take money out of” Hong Kong, and called the Chinese “a bunch of ugly dudes with tiny d****”. Previously with Macanese club Ka I, Mesquita has twice appeared for Tai Po this season, his only start coming in a shock 2-1 home defeat by Football Club last month. In a statement issued on their social media channels, Tai Po said they had “immediately issued a formal written warning to the player and imposed disciplinary measures, including an immediate suspension from all first-team training and matches”. Strongly hinting that the episode had not run its course, the statement continued: “The Disciplinary Committee will continue to investigate the matter and reserves all rights to take further action in accordance with [Mesquita’s] contract.” Mesquita has scored twice in two outings for Tai Po’s under-22s. He would have been unlikely to figure in the club’s Asian Champions League 2 match with Lion City Sailors on Thursday, regardless of his suspension, having not been in the squad for their opening fixture, a 3-0 loss away to Adelaide United four weeks ago. “The remarks in question were made solely in a personal capacity by the player,” the Tai Po statement added. “They bear no direct relation to the club and in no way reflect our official stance. “The club firmly reiterates its zero-tolerance policy towards racism and insulting language, and strongly rejects any behaviour that shows disrespect to fans or the public. “The club extends its sincere apologies to all fans and members of the public affected by this incident, and will continuously strengthen player conduct and professional ethics management.” Lee Chi-kin, the Tai Po head coach, will speak at a press conference on Wednesday to preview the match against Singapore’s Lion City at Mong Kok Stadium.

title: How Nobel laureate Michael Woodford’s research shaped policy at China’s central bank
description: In a 2005 speech in Beijing, Woodford said China needed stronger economic research and better economic training.
content: Two decades before winning this year’s Nobel Prize in economics, US-born economist Michael Woodford was influential in shaping policy at the People’s Bank of China through his landmark models on economic downturns. In 2005, Woodford delivered a speech titled “Economic Literacy, Central Bank Communication, and Macroeconomic Stability” at a forum in Beijing, with tickets highly sought after, according to a report by state-owned China News Service at the time. Xie Ping, a professor at the Graduate School of the PBOC at that time, chaired the session, which was attended by economic-administration officials and other participants. At the time of the Beijing speech, state broadcaster China Central Television reported that Woodford believed greater scope and sophistication in US and UK central banks’ communications with the public had fostered more knowledgeable and well-informed participants in economic markets. “For China to achieve this, it needs stronger economic research and better economic training,” he suggested at the time. Eight years later, in its second quarter 2013 Monetary Policy Implementation Report, the PBOC showed that it had taken note. “As Columbia University professor Michael Woodford put it, once rates hit the lower bound and nominal interest rates remain flat for an extended stretch, public expectations materially shape economic outcomes, making central bank guidance far more important,” according to the 2013 report. On Monday, Woodford and Robert E. Hall were awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalise stabilisation policy. Working independently, the two economists examined factors beyond standard macroeconomic variables such as inflation, output and consumption. They illustrated how households and businesses shape the economy according to their expectations of the future, said the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which presented the award. Their research highlighted why clear communication of policy plans by central banks and governments matter. Such messaging could “influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction” during downturns, the academy said. Hall, the other Nobel laureate, is a professor at Stanford University. His co-written textbook Macroeconomics with John B. Taylor was translated into Chinese and has long been widely used in undergraduate and graduate economics courses across Chinese universities. “The PBOC has in recent years laid out priorities to build out its policy-rate framework, improve monetary transmission efficiency and better anchor market expectations,” said Sun Lijian, director of Fudan University’s Financial Research Center in Shanghai. “[Its] approaches align closely with the New Keynesian framework – a result of the two economists’ research.” In a year when artificial intelligence and the digital economy are dominating mainstream attention, the Nobel Prize was awarded to two “old-school” macroeconomic theorists. Sun called this year’s Nobel award a “long-overdue catch-up lesson” amid a “major inflation test”. “It’s not a reward for innovation. Woodford’s magnum opus was published 23 years ago, while for Hall, it has been 48 years,” he said. “The prize shows their work remains highly relevant for the current times, amid inflation and doubts over policy credibility.”

title: Spanish royals visit Ceuta to back enclave amid border migration strain with Morocco
description: The royal couple are visiting Ceuta as local communities face ongoing migration pressures and heightened diplomatic frustration with Rabat.
content: King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia kicked off their first visit to Ceuta on Tuesday in a show of solidarity with residents of the Spanish city in North Africa as they grapple with a migration crisis that has strained relations with Morocco. The royal couple will then travel to Melilla, Spain’s other North African exclave, on Wednesday. It will be the first visit by a Spanish monarch to the two cities since Felipe’s father, Juan Carlos I, toured them in 2007. Their visit comes after about 80,000 migrants crossed Ceuta’s border in July, with more than 140 people dying. While most of the people who pushed across the frontier quickly returned, thousands still remain in the Spanish city of 84,000 residents perched on the Mediterranean Sea. It’s unknown how many remain, though the mayor has estimated that there are still as many as 15,000. Their presence has become a source of social tension in Ceuta and a political issue across Spain, where opposition parties hope to use migration concerns to unseat the progressive government in elections next month. Some migrants have come forward with abuse allegations, which the Spanish government is investigating following the publication of an Amnesty International report that detailed allegations of mistreatment and torture by Spanish soldiers. One migrant said soldiers beat him so badly that he needed staples in his head for his injuries. Residents of the city, meanwhile, have felt abandoned by national authorities, as the crisis remains visible on their streets. The official royal agenda says that the king and queen will “show the support of the Crown for Ceuta’s institutions and society”. Large crowds of people lined up to greet the royals and shake their hands. As Felipe met them, some broke into the familiar sports chant, “I am Spanish, Spanish, Spanish”. The royals will also meet with local officials and visit a school located “in a multicultural setting that respects different religions”. Ceuta had been a place of religious coexistence, but the border crisis has strained its Christian-Muslim fault lines. The royals will also visit a cemetery to show their respects to the people who died in the attempted crossings on July 30 and 31. Dozens of unidentified migrants who died in the crossing were buried there. The border fences separating Ceuta and Melilla are under constant pressure by migrants both from Morocco and sub-Saharan countries who see the Spanish cities as a key step towards their ultimate hope of making it to mainland Europe. Morocco does not recognise Spain’s sovereign claim on the specks of land that have been under Spanish control for centuries, and diplomatic watchers in Spain will be keen to see if Morocco reacts to Felipe’s visit. While Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has defended Morocco’s role in helping resolve the crisis, many in Spain have questioned whether Rabat could have done more to impede the mass crossing.

title: Investigators probe cockpit control movement in fatal cargo plane runway crash
description: Sound spectrum analysis and flight simulations will seek to determine whether Boeing freighter’s thrust lever moved mechanically or was forced forward.
content: Aviation investigators in Hong Kong are working to determine why a cockpit control on a Boeing cargo freighter moved forward during landing last year, killing two security personnel after the plane veered off a runway and into the sea. The Air Accident Investigation Authority (AAIA), an independent body under the Transport and Logistics Bureau, provided an update on Tuesday on the fatal incident involving the Boeing freighter, owned by Turkish cargo airline ACT Airlines and operated on behalf of Emirates SkyCargo. The aircraft veered off the tarmac at Hong Kong International Airport in October 2025, colliding with a ground security patrol vehicle before plunging into the sea, killing two people in the vehicle. According to an interim statement, a key focus of the investigation was the forward movement of an engine thrust lever, which caused the aircraft to turn left during the landing roll and veer off the runway. The AAIA said it would conduct specialist sound spectrum analysis to determine whether the lever’s forward movement was “driven mechanically or caused by external forces”. “To date, technical examinations of the relevant aircraft components have not revealed any mechanical failure related to the accident,” it said. “The investigation team will also arrange flight simulation trials to reconstruct the circumstances of the runway excursion on the day of the accident, and will review the accident history of aircraft of the same type.” An AAIA spokesman said the authority had proactively expedited the investigation, which is expected to be completed by the end of this year. The Transport and Logistics Bureau said the accident was complex and that some work had to be carried out overseas by relevant authorities. It said the AAIA had also been required to undertake extensive coordination with accredited representatives and technical advisers from parties including the United States National Transportation Safety Board, Boeing and aircraft component manufacturers, as well as verify and confirm relevant information. The bureau said it was highly concerned about the accident and had asked the AAIA to press ahead with the investigation, with the aim of concluding all work by the end of 2026. “Should any evidence of suspected unlawful acts come to light during the investigation, it will be referred to the relevant law enforcement agencies for follow-up without delay,” it said.

title: Average loss for elderly Hongkongers to investment scams jumps 33% to HK$1.08m
description: Hong Kong recorded 29,670 scam cases in the first eight months of this year, a 5 per cent increase over the same period in 2025.
content: The average loss suffered by elderly victims of investment scams in Hong Kong rose by a third year on year to HK$1.08 million (US$137,600) in 2026, the city’s police chief has said, calling for greater community vigilance against syndicates preying on retirees. Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming on Tuesday also warned of a recent surge in scams involving fraudsters posing as customer service officers, with such cases nearly doubling from last year. Speaking at the launch of “Anti-fraud Cinema” organised by Standard Chartered Bank, Chow said Hong Kong recorded 29,670 scam cases in the first eight months of this year, a 5 per cent increase over the same period in 2025, accounting for half of all crimes in the city. He added that 5,119 scams were recorded in August alone, a monthly record high. Total losses from scam cases reached HK$5.2 billion as of August, a 4 per cent rise from the same period last year. Investment scams accounted for HK$2.33 billion of those losses. Chow said the average amount lost by seniors in such cases had jumped from HK$810,000 last year to HK$1.08 million this year, an increase of 33 per cent. “Quite a number of elderly people or those who have just retired plan to invest their savings and pensions, and hope to enjoy their later years,” Chow said. “Unfortunately, some encountered impostor investment experts online and ended up losing everything.” In one case, he said, a retiree joined a WhatsApp investment group after getting to know a purported investment expert. She was told to download a counterfeit investment app and transferred large sums to multiple bank accounts. The victim later realised she could not withdraw her investment and lost HK$1.8 million over two weeks. Chow also highlighted a rise in scams in which fraudsters posed as customer service officers and deceived victims with claims such as flight cancellations or damaged parcels. He reminded the public that airlines and courier companies would never ask customers for bank account details or demand fund transfers. As of July, all 28 retail banks in the city had joined FINEST, a joint data-sharing platform launched by police, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, and the Hong Kong Association of Banks to track and block suspicious accounts. Chow said the force “regularly review crime trends and adjust the strategies for combating fraud”. “Anti-fraud work is a prolonged battle that requires joint efforts from all sectors of society,” he said. “By raising public awareness and their defence capability, we aim to intercept scams at the source.”

title: Hong Kong star Angela Yuen details harassment, sparking writer’s apology
description: Golden Horse nominee details years of verbal and physical harassment in show business, calling out deep-rooted misogyny.
content: Hong Kong actress Angela Yuen Lai-lam has detailed her experiences with sexual harassment over years in the entertainment industry, including an incident where an actor planted an unscripted kiss on her cheek during filming. The revelations by the film star – a two-time Golden Horse Award nominee, including a nod for next month’s ceremony – sparked heated discussion online and swift fallout. On Tuesday, culture editor and writer Wong Wing-leung, known by his pen name “Red Eye”, issued an apology after Yuen recounted how he once likened interviewing her to “sitting in a nightclub”. In a 3,000-word social media essay in Chinese titled “Those Apologies That Would Never Come”, the actress recounted being repeatedly demeaned, sexualised and subjected to verbal harassment by industry figures since entering show business. She said that on one occasion, a veteran male actor unexpectedly planted an unscripted kiss on her cheek during filming and “he never communicated afterwards about the kiss without prior consent”. Yuen, who turns 33 later this month, said that in another incident, a male film director scrutinised her physical appearance, telling her: “You’re the type people don’t want to sleep with – just be genuine friends with.” She also recalled a drunk male emcee asking her in Japanese whether she liked his genitals. Yuen said that while attending an interview to promote her 2025 film Gamer Girls, a male reporter sat down and said, “I feel like I am sitting in a nightclub”. According to Yuen, although the man appeared to realise his remarks were inappropriate, he did not offer an apology but excused himself by claiming that he felt like an escort. The actress said that even though she immediately pointed out that his comment was inappropriate, the man still failed to apologise. “I finished, the vibe went silent for half a second, and the interview continued as normal as if nothing had happened. Apology? It did not come, of course, and I had to handle the embarrassment that I caused,” she said. For Yuen, this was not an isolated incident but a snapshot of misogyny in the industry. “When the culture reporter made his ‘nightclub’ remarks, it was not a slip of tongue. Instead, the cultural atmosphere that we live in has condoned or even encouraged such ‘jokes’ that place women in a position to be gazed at and consumed,” she said. Culture editor and writer Wong admitted on social media on Tuesday that he was the reporter identified by Yuen. Expressing shame over what he termed a “slip of the tongue,” Wong admitted “mishandling” the situation by failing to apologise and recognise the distress he had caused. “I am fully aware that I made an inappropriate joke that ruined the interview at the time, and this is something I have kept in my mind ever since. I wish to offer my sincere and solemn apologies,” he said. Wong was formerly the editor-in-chief of the magazine As Artistic As You. In a social media statement released on Tuesday, the publication noted that it had terminated its contract with the writer last year. In her post, Yuen also highlighted how an online environment prone to victim-blaming perpetuated misogyny. “We have strong myths of the ‘perfect victim’ and impose a much more stringent moral inspection on the victims than the predators,” she said, adding that this had led to a “chilling effect” where victims were forced to stay silent out of fear for privacy breaches and reputational damage. “True change begins when we stop treating such offences as ‘isolated incidents’ and instead see the deep-rooted, systemic denial behind them – a denial of women’s autonomy, a denial that their professionalism should be taken seriously, and a denial of their right to define what constitutes respect and what constitutes offence.”

title: South Korea shopping centre stabbing leaves 8 injured
description: The Justice Ministry has apologised after the Incheon suspect met his probation officer hours before the shopping centre rampage.
content: A 59-year-old man stabbed at least eight people on Tuesday at a shopping centre in the South Korean city of Incheon, police and fire officials said. One victim was in life-threatening condition and received surgery at a nearby hospital. The suspect attacked shoppers as he moved through the shopping centre before business owners and bystanders subdued him, according to local police and witnesses. The man has a history of violent offences and mental illness and was required to wear an electronic monitoring anklet, according to South Korea’s Justice Ministry. The man’s name was not released, in keeping with South Korean practice for most criminal suspects. Witnesses told South Korean media that the attacker appeared to have knives tied to both hands and stabbed people in different parts of the shopping centre while moving up and down the floors on an escalator. Nah Hyun-joon, who helped subdue the attacker using chairs with several other people, said he saw the man attack about four people in the second-floor food court before moving up to the third floor, where he stabbed at least one woman. Nah said the attacker then headed towards a cinema on the fourth floor but was blocked by several people holding chairs at the top of the escalator. Nah said he and others trapped the man from below and eventually subdued him near the escalator’s third-floor entrance, pushing him down with chairs and removing his knives, before police arrived. “He just went around stabbing people,” Nah told local television. “He didn’t even say anything. He just stabbed whoever he saw.” The injured were taken to nearby hospitals, including one woman in her twenties who underwent surgery after arriving in cardiac arrest, Incheon’s fire department said. The department did not provide details on the severity of the other injuries. The suspect was sentenced to four years in prison for attempted murder in 2015, according to South Korea’s Yonhap news agency. He was placed under electronic monitoring in 2019 and had committed no repeat offences while under supervision, the Justice Ministry said. The suspect was booked last month on suspicion of carrying a weapon after using a kitchen knife to puncture a protest sign outside a hospital where he had a dispute, and was receiving treatment for alcohol dependence and unspecified mental illnesses, according to the ministry. Earlier on the day of the attack, the suspect attended a counselling session from 10 to 11am and then met his probation officer from 11.20am to 11.55am, the ministry said. The attack began at 1.40pm. The officer confirmed that the suspect had taken his medication and had lunch with him until 12.30pm. Authorities detected no attempts to destroy his monitoring device, the ministry said. “We sincerely apologise over the great public concern caused by the knife attack by an individual under electronic monitoring,” the ministry said in a statement, adding that it would review both the supervision of the suspect and broader electronic monitoring procedures.

title: India to gain? Trump’s Russian diesel deal offers New Delhi leverage
description: Washington’s climbdown on Russian fuel undermines US sanctions pressure and clears a path for India’s Ukraine diplomacy, analysts say.
content: US President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports and allow fresh supplies to reach global markets could give India greater leverage in its own dispute with Washington over discounted crude purchases, analysts said. Beyond the energy dispute, they said the move could also open up diplomatic opportunities for New Delhi, from pressing for more consistent treatment by Washington to building on its efforts to help negotiate an end to the Russia-Ukraine war. Under the deal Trump announced on Friday, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Trump said a further 3 million tonnes would follow “within a short period of time”, subject to the condition of Russian refineries. The US Treasury has also issued a temporary licence easing sanctions on Russian diesel shipments. The announcement came weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which directs the US president to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported from the leading buyers of Russian oil or natural gas, subject to an exception for certain countries. India is among the countries that could be affected by the measures. Ukrainian and EU officials have criticised Trump’s diesel deal, arguing that it could help finance Moscow’s war effort. However, analysts told This Week in Asia that the move could give Delhi greater room to defend its Russian oil purchases, particularly amid soaring energy prices linked to the US-Iran conflict. “India should be firm in citing the deal reached with the US in bilateral talks,” said Srikumar Menon, a former Indian diplomat. “While doing so, India should demand consistent treatment or even waivers under sanctions laws, further diversify its supplies and leverage exports of refined-products.” India has become a key supplier of refined petroleum products to Russia in recent months, as Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries have contributed to domestic fuel shortages. At the same time, Indian refiners were already cutting purchases of Russian crude amid the threat of punitive US tariffs. Russia’s share of India’s crude imports fell to about 35 per cent in September from as high as 56 per cent in July, according to data from global commodities tracking platform Kpler. “It is clear that Trump’s diesel deal exposes US double standards, just as America prioritises its energy needs while pressuring India,” Menon said. “The US move highlights selective application of principles; it certainly helps reduce the moral and political weight of Western criticism. India can continue its strategic autonomy between Russia and the West with greater confidence and negotiating leverage.” The Russia-Ukraine war has tested India’s policy of strategic autonomy and multi-alignment, with Delhi seeking to preserve ties with Moscow while maintaining relationships with Western allies. Trump has also sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has disrupted global energy supplies. “Trump’s decision weakens Washington’s moral and political case for penalising India over Russian oil purchases. If US energy security justifies buying Russian diesel, it is difficult to deny India the same line of argumentation,” said Uday Chandra, a professor of politics at Ashoka University in India. Washington’s sanctions framework targeting major buyers of Russian oil, including India and China, remained in place – leaving India exposed to the threat of steep US tariffs despite the recent change in policy, Chandra said. “India is better off using this opening [from the US diesel deal] pragmatically rather than accusing Washington of hypocrisy,” he said. “It can seek exemptions from American sanctions and greater predictability in its energy trade.” India’s peace proposal India could also use its diplomatic ties with both Russia and Ukraine to pursue a broader role in efforts to end the war, Chandra said. “Delhi can build on its recent peace initiative for Ukraine by helping negotiate practical arrangements concerning energy infrastructure, shipping and trade,” he said. “The real opportunity here is to turn India’s strategic autonomy into diplomatic capital beyond insisting on its right to buy Russian oil.” A three-part truce framework recently put forward by Delhi was described by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha as the “most comprehensive” among recent international proposals to end the war. The core pillars of India’s proposal reportedly include easing intense naval and aerial fighting in the Black Sea to allow the uninterrupted passage of Ukrainian agricultural products, grain and energy exports to global markets. Trump announced an immediate “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday. However, both warring parties have disputed that any such agreement actually exists. Benchmark Brent crude oil was trading at around US$105 per barrel on Tuesday, a slight pullback after prices spiked on Monday following a spate of attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi militants. The diesel deal showed that Washington was prepared to sacrifice principles for pragmatism when domestic affordability became a political priority, said Srinivaasan Balakrishnan, an analyst with Indic Researchers Forum, a Delhi-based think tank. “[But] the larger lesson is that strategic autonomy must translate into economic resilience,” he said.

title: As import curbs loom, Chinese carmakers make a stand at Paris Motor Show
description: Chinese executive says EU cap could trigger worrying “stampede” as manufacturers relocate production lines.
content: No Chinese carmakers were represented at a dinner on Sunday attended by French President Emmanuel Macron and around 60 European automotive industry players, but they were hard to miss when he visited the Paris Motor Show the next day. Allianz Trade said in a report that Chinese marques comprised half the exhibitors at this year’s show, even as they dealt with the fallout from a China-EU agreement to curb the growth of China’s hybrid and plug-in hybrid automotive exports to the bloc. Against the backdrop of the agreement, they are increasingly learning to speak the language of European politicians by showcasing their commitment to investing in Europe and creating jobs. A Chinese auto sector executive at the show said that if the shipment cap was strictly carried out on a first-come, first-served basis, it was likely to trigger a worrying “stampede”. A senior EU official said that was likely to be the model. Brussels was planning to launch a safeguard measure from the start of December – if the 27 member states approved the arrangement – the official said, adding that it would cap annual imports at 350,000 units to start. The official said the controls, in place for four years, were designed to cut China’s 12 per cent share of the EU hybrid market by half. Leading Chinese brands such as BYD, Chery, SAIC and Geely are likely to feel an impact, given their heavy footprint in the continent’s hybrid and plug-in market. The cap was described by a Chinese executive in Europe as “a band-tightening spell”, intended to push Chinese companies to relocate production chains to Europe. That relocation effort was visible at the Paris show, with Chinese carmakers using the occasion to showcase their expanding production and hiring efforts in Europe. Automotive investment is inherently long-term … [requiring] substantial capital and many years of planning Fang Dongkui, China Chamber of Commerce to the EU “Production is our biggest bottleneck in Europe,” said Xpeng CEO He Xiaopeng. The Guangzhou-based firm, which produces four models at Canadian company Magna’s factory in Austria, was discussing the expansion of production in Europe with various countries and companies, he said. Alex Tang, Xpeng’s vice-president of international business, said its accumulated sales overseas had passed 100,000 this year and it was aiming to see that figure exceed 1 million by 2030, when 60 per cent of the cars it sold outside China would be locally produced. He declined to provide a specific percentage for EU production. BYD executive vice-president Stella Li told Bloomberg TV the company was looking to hire 40,000 people in Europe by 2030, a threefold increase from its current level, and planned to absorb talent displaced by industry lay-offs in Europe. She told French channel BFM Business that BYD was looking to open two more factories in Europe, on top of a factory in Hungary that is set to open this year, with France on the location shortlist. Chongqing-based Changan Automobile announced plans to produce 180,000 cars in Europe in 2028 and 350,000 by 2030. As the investment plans mount, the China Chamber of Commerce to the EU has emphasised the importance of a transparent, predictable and consistent regulatory environment. “Automotive investment is inherently long-term,” said chamber secretary general Fang Dongkui. “A battery plant, vehicle manufacturing facility, testing centre or R&D project requires substantial capital and many years of planning.” In a report released on Monday, Morgan Stanley analysts said the destination of Chinese carmakers’ products was not changing – only the route. “Global growth shifts from exporting vehicles into Europe to producing them locally, from price-led market share gains to margin-led positioning, and from a single export channel to a multimarket footprint,” the analysts said. “Such a development would favour Chinese [electric vehicle] leaders with the scale, balance sheets and European manufacturing plans already in motion to pivot quickly.”

title: Meet Lulu Tenney, the model spotted with The Social Reckoning’s Jeremy Allen White
description: The Bear actor, who was divorced in 2023, was spotted in New York City with Tenney – she has modelled for brands like Dior, Chanel, Ralph Lauren, Prada and Valentino.
content: The Bear star Jeremy Allen White may have a new woman in his life. On October 7, the 35-year-old stepped out for a walk in New York City, hand in hand with 25-year-old model Lulu Tenney. The pair was photographed looking cosy as they chatted on a bench, according to TMZ. Neither White nor Tenney has commented on their rumoured romance. Exclusive: Jeremy Allen White and model Lulu Tenney holding hands on a date in NYC 💞 🎥: The Image Direct pic.twitter.com/sppjIwDCPO — TMZ (@TMZ) October 8, 2026 White, who divorced Addison Timlin – the mother of his two daughters, Ezer, seven, and Dolores, five – in 2023, has previously been linked to actress Molly Gordon, singer Rosalía and model Ashley Moore. Over the weekend, his new film, The Social Reckoning, a sequel to The Social Network (2010), opened with a disappointing US$5.5 million at the North American box office. So, just who is Lulu Tenney? What is Lulu Tenney’s background? Tenney was born and raised in Brooklyn, per Elle. She attended the Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music and Art and Performing Arts – which counts Timothée Chalamet and Al Pacino among its notable alumni – and got into theatre at a young age. The model hoped to become a “rock star/cast member of Saturday Night Live/stand-up comedian/singer/dancer/actress”, she told Elle, before adding that her long-term goal is to “live upstate, have chickens, make honey, and have a little restaurant in town”. As of this January, Tenney is based in Paris. How did she get into modelling? Tenney started modelling early in life. According to Elle, she appeared in a Baby Gap advertisement as a toddler after being spotted at a playground. At 13, a modelling agent scouted her while she was out with friends in SoHo, Manhattan. After three test shoots, photographer Steven Meisel contacted her and placed her on the 2016 cover of Vogue Italia, leading to her runway debut at Calvin Klein’s spring/summer 2017 showcase by Raf Simons. Tenney has since worked with brands like Ralph Lauren, Givenchy, Chanel, Dior, Prada and Valentino. She’s an aspiring actress Tenney has always been passionate about acting. “I grew up doing theatre, and I think that’s why I love modelling: because I love acting,” she told Elle. Tenney starred in the music video for The XX’s “I Dare You” and has appeared in short films like The Clock (2019) and Jungle Red (2021). She is also actively trying to break into the acting industry through auditions and self-tapes.

title: India’s ‘cockroach’ movement leaders arrested again as voter roll dispute grows
description: The youth movement leaders jumped barricades at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi after authorities revoked the venue’s designated protest status.
content: Leaders of India’s “cockroach” protest movement were detained again on Tuesday, their second detention in days, as a stand-off with authorities deepened over a contentious overhaul of voter rolls. Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, two prominent faces of the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party, were taken into custody with other members after jumping barricades to enter Jantar Mantar, historically one of New Delhi’s main protest venues. Delhi police on Monday removed Jantar Mantar’s designation as a protest site and named three alternative venues elsewhere in the city. The move drew criticism from the CJP and other protesters, as they had been trying to demonstrate there since the weekend. The CJP, a pressure group, and major opposition parties have staged planned and impromptu protests in the capital for days over alleged electoral manipulation. Their main demands include the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and a halt to the voter-roll revisions. Authorities have responded by detaining protesters, barricading roads and closing metro stations – measures critics say are aimed at stifling dissent. The Indian National Congress-led opposition filed a petition in the Supreme Court on Monday after thousands of protesters marched through Delhi.
