Ju-ae’s presence at the museum’s opening was meant to impress upon North Koreans that Kim’s achievements would endure for generations, Yang said. Ri’s presence, meanwhile, projected the image of a normal state, he said. Lim agreed about the symbolism of the family’s attendance, adding that the museum was also meant to burnish national pride and cohesion. “By emphasising that North Korea has built what it describes as the world’s most powerful defence industry despite economic hardship, the regime seeks to offset public fatigue caused by prolonged economic difficulties, reinforce the perceived necessity of defending the system and strengthen loyalty to the leadership,” he said. The museum opened as both Koreas continue to expand their military capabilities. On Monday, North Korea test-fired at least one tactical ballistic missile state media said was meant “to confirm the success in the research for the technical upgrading of an important core element”. The official Korea Central News Agency called the upgrade a “big success” that heralded “an important change” in the performance of the country’s offensive weapons systems, without providing further details. The test came four days after South Korea had announced the first successful launch of a domestically developed hypersonic glide vehicle, a type of warhead for ballistic missiles that can manoeuvre and glide at hypersonic speeds.

title: Lessons for life: Hong Kong educator looks beyond exams and interviews
description: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist Christine Ma-Lau helps children recognise their strengths, respect others and understand how they can contribute to society.
content: For Hong Kong educator Christine Ma-Lau, preparing children for exams or school interviews is only part of the job – helping them understand who they are, how to treat others and what they can contribute to society matters just as much. Ma-Lau founded JEMS Character Academy in 2009 after concluding that many imported character education programmes did not fully meet Hong Kong’s needs. She developed her own curriculum around three areas: identity, relationships and community. Her work has earned her a place among the finalists for the Spirit of Nurturing Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Ma-Lau said she did not want children to learn good behaviour simply to perform well in a school interview. “The goal is not simply to teach a child to say good morning. It is to help them develop genuine respect for other people,” she said, emphasising that behaviour should flow naturally from the attitude behind it. The same approach guides JEMS’ community service work. According to Ma-Lau, the academy has supported more than 15 local non-profit groups and raised more than HK$1 million (US$127,423) for children’s charities. Children are prepared for visits to disadvantaged communities and encouraged to reflect afterwards, she said. The aim is not to make them feel sorry for people in difficult circumstances but to develop empathy and respect. She recalled asking children after the visits to consider the experiences and contributions of the people they had met, rather than seeing them simply as recipients of help. Ma-Lau believes the impact of those lessons may only become clear years later. One participant, she said, later helped establish an initiative that supports Hong Kong students from less privileged backgrounds in applying to top UK universities. At the initiative’s 10th anniversary event, the participant’s mother thanked Ma-Lau for teaching her daughter to care about others when she was 11. Another former student, who had struggled to sit still as a young child but had a natural gift for communication, contacted Ma-Lau after starting his first job. He told her that lessons on time management, handling pressure and teamwork had finally made sense in the workplace. Ma-Lau said helping children recognise their strengths was especially important because not everyone thrived under the same approach to learning. “You need to understand your own strengths and what you can contribute. That’s an important part of working well with others,” she said. Her work with children extends beyond JEMS. Ma-Lau founded and chairs the Character Education Foundation. She also sits on the board of Mother’s Choice and co-chairs its services committee, and is an adjunct professor at the Education University of Hong Kong. She said children’s causes remained particularly close to her heart. She also serves on the board of LEAP, which promotes healthy choices and drug prevention among young people. Through the Character Education Foundation, Ma-Lau has brought character education into schools and the wider community through programmes such as Character Day and the Children’s Character Festival. The next festival, in 2027, will focus on resilience, encouraging children to talk about facing setbacks, trying again and recovering with help from others.

title: Chinese star Zheng Qinwen ‘delighted’ to make debut at Hong Kong Tennis Open
description: The 24-year-old will be joined by Venus Williams and Alexandra Eala, and be hoping to keep her resurgent form going after winning China Open.
content: Freshly crowned China Open champion Zheng Qinwen will be hoping to keep her renaissance on the court going when she makes her debut at the Prudential Hong Kong Tennis Open in November. Zheng will be joined by Venus Williams, who is returning for the third time, and Alexandra Eala. The 24-year-old became the first Chinese player to clinch the Beijing title on Sunday and also made it to the US Open quarter-finals, losing to eventual champion Elena Rybakina in September. “I am delighted to be playing in front of the fans in Hong Kong for the very first time,” Zheng said. “I have heard many great things about the Prudential Hong Kong Tennis Open and I am looking forward to finishing the China season and my 2026 season there. It has been a tough 18 months, but I am very pleased with my recovery journey and hope to compete well at Victoria Park.” An Olympic gold medallist in Paris 2024 and a former world No 4, Zheng underwent elbow surgery last year and missed nearly eight months of action. She dropped to world No 160 earlier this year, but after her win in China, Zheng was ranked world No 23. Despite dropping down the rankings this year, Zheng’s slump in form did not really affect her brand value. In August, Forbes released its list of highest-earning tennis stars, topped by Jannik Sinner’s US$58 million and followed by Carlos Alcaraz, who earned US$53.7 million. Serena Williams rounded out the top three with US$40.1 million. Zheng ranked seventh on the list and was the only Chinese player in the top 10, earning US$22.6 million over the past 12 months. Her on-court winnings, though, were just US$600,000 – meaning over 97 per cent of her earnings were off the court. Even with her drop in form, Zheng’s 14 long-term sponsors stood by her. Chinese sports marketing expert Zhang Qing said he was not surprised by the decisions of those brands. “Investing in an athlete is essentially investing in the expected value she may bring in the future,” he said. Zhang added that the results on the court matter, yet it was not all for those sponsors because Zheng’s age, her current competitive level, her performance in adversity and her potential future position all determine that the brands will not measure her solely by short-term rankings. Zhang also said it was now also critical to see if a brand could still maintain contact with their customer when there were no competitions for their sponsored athlete. “It’s a testament to the corporate’s patience and execution capabilities,” he said. “Moving forward, can the two parties create something new together, such as exclusive products, product lines, or even ultimately, jointly owned brand assets?” Zheng’s appeal was highlighted by television viewership during her win in Beijing. Her straight-sets victory over Mirra Andreeva in the final attracted a television rating with a 19 per cent market share, nearly double that of the second-ranked broadcast. Last October, Chinese-style tea drink Chagee promoted Zheng to its global brand ambassador and moments after her win, the company announced a nationwide “buy-one-get-one-free” promotion for the following day. The campaign surged to the top of social media trending lists, but an overwhelming amount of traffic crashed the system on Monday morning, leaving users unable to access the page. In June, Beats launched a Studio Pro colourway exclusively for Zheng, and even incorporated elements of her zodiac animal, the Horse, into the packaging – the same month her ranking dropped to 160. Tennis brand Wilson released her signature racquet last year and she partnered with Turkish Airlines this year. After winning the China Open, Zheng opted to withdraw from Wuhan this week, citing “extreme fatigue in my body” after playing in New York, the Billie Jean King Cup in Shenzhen and in Beijing over the past six weeks. Promising fans to return to Wuhan “in my best shape next year”, Zheng was listed for the Japan Open, which runs from October 19 to 25 in Osaka. The Hubei native will compete in Hong Kong at Victoria Park from November 2 to 8. Ahead of her return to Hong Kong, Williams said: “I am really excited to be returning to compete at the Prudential Hong Kong Tennis Open and finishing my 2026 season in this beautiful city. I have such fond memories of Hong Kong when I played there a decade ago.” Wang Xinyu, Diana Shnaider, Jasmine Paolini, Paula Badosa, Maria Sakkari and Sorana Cirstea have also confirmed their participation at the event.

title: Chinese billionaire featured in ‘American Factory’ shares lesson for firms going global
description: Fuyao Glass founder Cao Dewang urges Chinese companies expanding abroad to respect local laws, culture and workers.
content: Chinese billionaire Cao Dewang, whose glass-making empire was featured in the Oscar-winning documentary American Factory, has urged Chinese investors expanding overseas to respect local laws, regulations and culture, drawing on decades of experience building a global manufacturing business amid shifting US-China relations. Speaking at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) on Monday, the founder of Fuyao Glass said the approach had been central to the firm’s success in the US and warned against simply transplanting Chinese practices overseas. “When I go to America, I use American people and American resources,” he said, adding that Fuyao’s US operations employed between 6,000 and 7,000 people, with fewer than 200 staff sent from China. Cao, 80, known as “China’s glass king”, founded Fuyao in 1987 and transformed it into the world’s largest automotive glass manufacturer. The company’s US expansion became the subject of American Factory, which won an Academy Award for best documentary feature in 2020 and explored the cultural and labour tensions surrounding its Ohio plant. Fuyao’s US operations have since become a case study in both the opportunities and challenges facing Chinese manufacturers going global, particularly as trade tensions and tariffs complicate investment decisions between the world’s two largest economies. Cao stepped down as chairman of Fuyao last year, handing the position to his son, Cao Hui, in a generational transition at one of China’s most prominent privately owned manufacturers. He has since turned his attention to education and philanthropy, particularly Fuyao University of Science and Technology, a non-profit institution he established in southeastern China’s Fujian province to cultivate engineering talent and explore new approaches to higher education. “I have already announced my retirement,” Cao said at the HKU event. He added that Fuyao University of Science and Technology was not about personal recognition or simply creating another educational institution, but rather about exploring reforms to mainland China’s private university model. He said he had pledged 10 billion yuan (US$1.7 billion) to the university, of which less than half had been spent, and expressed confidence in its long-term sustainability. What should be passed on is wisdom. Wisdom, knowledge and character are more valuable than wealth Cao Dewang, Fuyao Glass On succession, Cao said passing on a family business required long-term planning rather than acting only in a founder’s final years. He added that Fuyao had begun preparing for succession as early as 1995, including by establishing a board structure designed to balance the influence of major shareholders and professional managers. Asked what entrepreneurs should pass on to the next generation beyond wealth, Cao said the answer was not simply money. “What should be passed on is wisdom,” he said. “Wisdom, knowledge and character are more valuable than wealth.”

title: Philippines drops 3 impeachment charges against Sara Duterte despite evidence
description: Prosecutors said the allegations of unexplained wealth will be the sole remaining count against the vice-president.
content: The Philippine Senate, sitting as an impeachment ⁠court, approved the ⁠prosecution’s withdrawal of most of ⁠the charges against Vice-President Sara Duterte on Tuesday, in a trial that could kill her hopes to run for president in 2028. Prosecutors have been presenting evidence against ‌Duterte since July on charges that she betrayed public trust, amassed unexplained wealth, violated the constitution and committed corruption, bribery and other high crimes. Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro told the court on Tuesday that they sought to withdraw three of the four charges and ⁠leave the allegations of unexplained wealth as the sole remaining issue for senators to ‌rule on. Luistro said the evidence presented by prosecutors was already “substantial and compelling” to remove Duterte from office. The ‌prosecution withdrew charges accusing her of misusing confidential funds, bribery and ⁠alleged threats ⁠against President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, the first lady and a former House speaker. Focusing on a ‌single charge would substantially narrow the issues before the court, offering practical benefits for the Senate, ‌the respondent ‌and the public, Luistro said. Duterte’s office did not immediately ‌respond to a request for comment. Duterte’s lawyer argued it was unfair, ⁠saying their side would be unable to present its case on the ⁠allegations that have been withdrawn. The impeachment court earlier ruled that only senator-judges capable of taking part in the trial would be counted in ‌the vote for ‌conviction, making it easier to reach the two-thirds majority needed to secure a guilty verdict. If convicted, Duterte may be disqualified from running for public office, including the presidency in 2028.

title: Fiji’s justice minister resigns after intimate video goes viral online
description: Siromi Turaga will continue as an MP and a member of Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s People’s Alliance party.
content: Fiji’s Justice Minister Siromi Turaga stepped down from cabinet on Tuesday after an intimate video of him went viral online – the second such scandal to rock the Pacific island nation’s government. Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, who previously sought credible “proof” before taking action against Turaga, said he accepted his colleague’s resignation. “You mentioned him? Go ahead and report him to me and the Online Safety Commissioner, and I will get proof from that authority with you making the allegations,” Rabuka said on Monday, as reported by the Fiji Sun. Rabuka earlier said he had not seen the video that showed up on Turaga’s social media page last Saturday before it was taken down. Turaga, who is also the acting attorney general, will continue as an MP and a member of Rabuka’s People’s Alliance party. Turaga was abroad when the video began circulating on social media, prompting a warning from the Online Safety Commission against posting and sharing intimate images or videos of people without their permission. He has yet to publicly address the saga. The prime minister has sought advice from the Solicitor General’s Office on appointing a replacement for Turaga’s positions. Before Turaga’s departure, a letter sent to Rabuka’s office urged him to apply rules without gender distinction, pointing to a female minister who was removed from cabinet last year after getting embroiled in a similar controversy. “Fairness and consistency are what our people deserve,” the letter said. A video showing Lynda Tabuya dancing naked was leaked online and went viral in 2024. She was dismissed from her position as minister for women, children and social protection. Tabuya eventually returned to the government after Rabuka appointed her as the information minister in August last year. He defended the decision that also earned a rebuke from former prime minister Mahendra Chaudhry. “She is well-suited to spearhead the government’s public relations machinery through the Ministry of Information,” Rabuka said. “Is Rabuka merely forgetful or is he just plain fickle?” Chaudhry said in a social media post. Tabuya said the private clip, meant for her ex-husband, was hacked from her stolen mobile phone, public broadcaster Radio NZ reported.

title: British fashion designer Kim Jones announces eponymous label with Hong Kong flagship
description: The eponymous label from Jones, who designed for Dior, Louis Vuitton and Fendi, will launch in 2027 at Hong Kong’s Central Yards complex.
content: British fashion designer Kim Jones, who spent more than two decades working at some of the world’s most prestigious luxury houses, including Dior, Fendi and Louis Vuitton, has announced the launch of his new eponymous label, selecting Hong Kong for its flagship destination. He is joined in the venture by his long-time deputy, design director Lucy Beeden. Jones describes his label, which focuses on menswear and tailoring with genderless, versatile designs, as “unrestricted by traditional categories”. The inaugural collection is predominantly crafted in Japan, with leather goods produced in Italy. The label is scheduled to debut for autumn/winter 2027. Kim Jones will roll out from mid-2027 through its proprietary e-commerce platform and will open its first flagship store at Central Yards, an upcoming large commercial development on Hong Kong’s New Central Harbourfront, in October 2027. The brand also has plans to expand across Asia and beyond. Jones launched his first clothing label in 2003 after graduating with a master of arts in fashion from Central Saint Martins College of Art in London. The label was paused when he was appointed creative director at Dunhill in 2008. In 2011, he became the style director of the men’s ready-to-wear division at Louis Vuitton, where he redefined luxury menswear by integrating travel aesthetics, technical precision and street culture – punctuated by the seminal 2017 Supreme collaboration. In 2018, he transitioned to Dior Homme, elevating the brand through contemporary art partnerships. In 2020, he simultaneously assumed artistic direction for Fendi womenswear, overseeing haute couture, ready-to-wear and fur collections until 2024. Jones concluded his seven-year tenure at Dior in early 2025, wrapping up a 15-year chapter at the helm of major European luxury houses. In 2025, Jones expanded his presence in Asia as creative director of Areal, a hi-tech luxury outerwear line owned by Chinese performance apparel giant Bosideng. Jones’ decision to establish his flagship at Central Yards in Hong Kong signals a strong commitment to Asia as a primary market for his independent venture. Speaking at a panel talk at Central Yards on October 13, Jones says: “Hong Kong is the crossroads of different types of people. I love coming here to shop. Having my first store here seems like a lot of sense. “I learned a lot of my craft in Hong Kong,” he says of the city he has visited several times a year during his time with Dunhill. In a separate press statement, Jones said: “After many years working with incredible houses and collaborators, it feels like the right moment to do something under my own name again. “This brings together the things I’ve always been interested in – fashion, art and design – and gives me the space to work with people I admire and explore new ideas. I’m excited about what comes next.” Stay tuned for SCMP Lifestyle’s exclusive interview with Jones this week.

title: Hong Kong police arrest 20 over prostitution syndicate that trapped women in debt
description: Police say women from Southeast Asia had to provide unpaid sexual services to repay travel and accommodation costs before sharing earnings with the syndicate.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested 20 people in connection with a cross-border prostitution syndicate that allegedly recruited women from Southeast Asia and required them to provide unpaid sexual services to repay travel debts. Police said on Tuesday that the syndicate paid for the women’s travel and accommodation but required them to provide sexual services 30 to 45 times without payment before they could earn money from prostitution. The women then had to hand over half their earnings. “This method left the women completely under the group’s control when they first arrived in Hong Kong, while allowing the syndicate to make huge profits,” Senior Inspector Lam Wa-yan of the special duties squad said. Police began investigating in June after noticing that several women arrested during prostitution raids held passports from Southeast Asian countries and had similar backgrounds, travel patterns and areas of activity. Investigators later identified syndicate members who had lived in Hong Kong for years and allegedly used their networks and language skills to recruit women in Southeast Asia. The syndicate rented three flats in Sham Shui Po and Tsuen Wan and divided them into cubicles used as brothels. Police said the women were required to place all or half of their cash earnings in envelopes and leave them at designated locations for members to collect. After learning that the syndicate planned to bring more women to Hong Kong on October 10, officers carried out surveillance and saw core members take them from the airport to the group’s brothels. Police then raided premises in Sham Shui Po, Tsuen Wan, Tuen Mun, Yuen Long and Sha Tin. The 20 suspects – one man and 19 women aged 20 to 86 – included the alleged ringleader, core members and 16 sex workers. Four held Hong Kong identity cards, two held recognisance forms and 14 held passports issued by Southeast Asian countries. Police said one suspect had a triad background. Two alleged core members appeared in West Kowloon Court on Tuesday, charged with trafficking people into or out of Hong Kong and living off the earnings of prostitution. Police said 16 other suspects would be charged with breaching their conditions of stay and would appear in court on Wednesday. The remaining two were to be released on bail pending further investigation. Officers also seized about HK$100,000 (US$12,742) in cash, as well as phones, account books, condoms and lubricants. Police froze more than HK$10 million in suspected crime proceeds and believe accounts linked to the syndicate were used to launder more than HK$10 million over several years. The investigation is continuing and police have not ruled out further arrests.

title: Marcos on South China Sea row; anger in Thailand over iron cage beds: 7 Asia highlights
description: From US stealth jets in Indian drills to Luckin Coffee’s Singapore expansion, here are a few highlights from SCMP’s recent Asia reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from the SCMP’s coverage of Asia over the past week that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Marcos says Philippines ‘resigned’ to managing South China Sea dispute The Philippines is “resigned” to managing its long-standing dispute with Beijing in the South China Sea and avoiding dangerous escalations, President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr said. 2. ‘A show of strength’: US F-35 stealth jets join Indian air drills US F-35 stealth fighters have joined Indian warplanes for military exercises near the Pakistan border in recent days, marking the first time America’s most advanced multirole combat aircraft has taken part in joint drills in India. 3. Iron cage beds at Thai elderly home fuel anger, owner defends ‘innovation’ A care scandal has erupted in Thailand after a nursing home was exposed for confining old and sick residents in beds covered by iron cages with barely a foot of space above their heads. 4. Why Malaysian doctors are turning down permanent posts in Borneo On Facebook, public hospitals in Malaysia’s Bornean states have been rolling out “Selamat Datang” [welcome] banner posts to embrace medical staff reporting for duty. 5. How Singapore’s local cafes compete with Chinese coffee giant Luckin When Chinese coffee giant Luckin Coffee moved into the unit next to his neighbourhood cafe in Singapore, Folk Yard owner Chew Yit Shan grew nervous. Luckin launched with an aggressive promotional deal of S$1 (78 US cents) per cup, served in just two minutes. In the first few months following its arrival, Chew saw sales at his independent cafe drop by 15 per cent. 6. To retire or not to retire? Malaysia divided over working past 60 Chew Kin Wah spent seven seasons gracing Malaysian television screens as “Kee Tat” in the hit sitcom Kopitiam in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Now 61, the Malaysian actor is still working, albeit more selectively, taking projects when the right offers land on his table. 7. The hidden heartbreak of losing a pet in Singapore and Malaysia Growing up in a Malay family in Singapore, Hafeez Hassan feared dogs. He never expected to mourn one like a sibling. “Maybe that is what I have been grieving all along … The experience of loving something that I was taught I was not supposed to love,” he said.

title: Nasa’s Perseverance rover on Mars breaks record for off-planet driving
description: Perseverance surpasses Opportunity’s 45km milestone after 5½ years, with engineers aiming to top 100km.
content: Nasa’s robotic Perseverance rover has now driven farther than any other vehicle on the surface of any world other than Earth, racking up 45.2km (28.1 miles) since arriving on Mars in 2021, the US space agency said on Tuesday. The car-sized, six-wheeled rover reached the milestone 5½ years into its mission to explore if conditions conducive to microbial life ever existed on Earth’s neighbour. In doing so, it is visiting some of the ‌most ancient terrain ever encountered in the solar system. “Perseverance’s engineering hardware and instruments are in excellent shape with all redundant systems still available,” Steven Lee of Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, said. “A recent assessment of all systems concluded that they are capable of operating well into the 2030s, likely beyond,” added Lee, the project manager for Nasa’s two Mars rovers, Perseverance and Curiosity. Perseverance has exceeded the previous figure of 45km driven on the Martian surface by Nasa’s Opportunity rover from 2004 to 2018. Both also exceeded the driving distances of any lunar rover. Perseverance, with its suite of scientific instruments, has focused on the ⁠Jezero Crater, a region in the northern hemisphere of Mars believed to have been flooded with water and home to a lake basin billions of years ago. The rover set ‌the milestone in a journey towards an area called Idubi, through the region off the crater’s western rim nicknamed Lac de Charmes. Its companion rover, Curiosity, rolls along in the Gale Crater near the Martian equator. Perseverance is showing no signs of slowing down, Lee added. Its ‌mobility system mechanisms are being tested to show it can drive 100km or more, he said, with the hardware to be tested ⁠to the equivalent of 150km ⁠to 300km in the effort. Nasa attributed a major role in Perseverance’s success to its self-driving capability, an autonomous navigation system called AutoNav. Lee said 90 per cent of its drives are done autonomously, with ‌no human intervention. “Perseverance takes stereo images of the terrain ahead, generates a 3D software map, and selects the safest path towards a drive goal,” he said. Another key component is the Vision Compute Element, a fast co-processor computer that ‌allows the ‌rover to process images and run its self-driving software very quickly, almost continuously during drives, Lee added. That contrasts with previous rovers, which needed to pause to “think” before each drive ‌segment, he said. The rover’s original mission envisaged just 20km of driving. The rover’s plutonium-based power system is performing as expected, Lee said, adding it has “many years of useful energy still available”.

title: Review | Good Trip review: Nick Cheung, Chung Suet-ying play father and daughter in road comedy
description: Nick Cheung plays a terminally ill father who is taken on a road trip by his daughter, played by Chung Suet-ying, in heartwarming comedy.
content: 3.5/5 stars In Good Trip, a father and daughter’s impromptu final excursion unfolds as a deceptively playful comedy road movie. It tackles one of the most agonising subjects a family can face – the impending death of a parent – with surprising, life-affirming levity. Co-directed by Norris Wong Yee-lam (The Lyricist Wannabe) – who also wrote the screenplay – and Wong Hoi (Let It Ghost), and produced by the acclaimed filmmaker Mabel Cheung Yuen-ting, the film avoids unbearable sentimentality; it is instead anchored by the relaxed, lived-in charm of its two leads. Good Trip opens with an intriguing wuxia scene, which we soon realise is the daydream of Keung (Nick Cheung Ka-fai), a former film extra and cancer patient, gazing at a television screen from his hospital bed. Keung’s cinematic devotion has clearly rubbed off on his daughter, Shan (Chung Suet-ying), an underappreciated art assistant labouring on a gritty film shoot. But their routine is abruptly shattered when Keung is notified that pneumonia complications have left him with barely two weeks to live. That very night, Shan is instructed to retrieve a gigantic prop bowl from a remote warehouse for the following morning’s shoot. Keung insists on sneaking out to join her. What begins as a modest nocturnal drive swiftly snowballs into a pan-Asian odyssey occurring miraculously over a single day. By morning, they are winning in a Macau casino alongside Keung’s estranged friend, Hong (Philip Keung Ho-man). Now a cleaner, Hong once crippled Keung financially in a failed business venture, indirectly ruining his marriage. This chapter also serves as a wistful homage to the classic gambling films of Cheung’s early career. The duo then impulsively flies to Japan to surprise Keung’s wife, Fong (Yoyo Mung Ka-wai in her second film since 2007). Having left Keung and Shan seven years ago to run her father’s business in Okinawa, Fong affords her hapless husband a parting opportunity to seek absolution. Yet an air of unreality persists throughout. Why do Keung and Shan have their passports? Why can they speak Japanese? Why do passing strangers bear an uncanny resemblance to Keung’s doctor (Mirror member Stanley Yau Sze-chun) and nurse (Yeung Nga-man)? Surely everything aligns far too smoothly to be tethered to waking life? Anchoring this dreamy spontaneity is Cheung. Evolving well beyond his wacky roots in the late 1990s, he wields masterful timing – and plenty of dad jokes – to craft an adorably frustrating patriarch. His delicate tonal balance transforms a man who failed his family into a deeply sympathetic comic creation. For all its leaps in logic, the film remains a delightful watch – even if a cruel final twist recasts the journey through an enormously poignant new lens. By blending naturalistic performances with heartwarming humour, Good Trip delivers a meditation on mortality that is almost too tender to be true. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook.

title: Hong Kong watchdog freezes US$590m of assets over alleged IPO fraud schemes
description: The SFC has also suspended 65 listing applications so far this year, as regulator looks to strengthen market quality in the city.
content: Hong Kong’s securities watchdog has moved against two syndicates suspected of being involved in three alleged initial public offering fraud schemes involving assets worth HK$4.6 billion (US$590 million), according to a statement released on Tuesday. The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) also announced on the same day that it had suspended 65 listing applications in the first nine months of this year due to the poor quality of their listing sponsors’ work, in what analysts viewed as an effort to strengthen the city’s market quality. The SFC has frozen the HK$4.6 billion of assets related to the three alleged IPO fraud cases, according to the statement. The cases involved listed companies allegedly signing agreements with the syndicates to divert part of their IPO proceeds away from the companies under the guise of “financial product investments”, the regulator said. Chinese bubble-tea maker Sichuan Baicha Baidao Industrial, also known as Chabaidao, was suspended from trading by the SFC before the market opened on Tuesday, under a rule that can be invoked when companies issue false or misleading information or an intervention is needed to maintain orderly and fair trading. Two other firms – biotechnology firm Cloudbreak and data analytics provider Tianju Dihe Technology – were also suspended using the same rule on September 10, 2026 and April 1, 2025, respectively. “We believe that the actions taken to date have significantly disrupted two suspected syndicates which may have been involved in IPO-rigging cases,” said Michael Duignan, the SFC’s executive director of enforcement. For the first syndicate – suspected of being involved in the Chabaidao and Cloudbreak IPO fraud schemes – the SFC issued restriction notices to six brokers, freezing up to HK$4.379 billion across nine entity bank accounts – a record for a case of this kind in the regulator’s history. The accounts belonged to Sun Ran, the alleged mastermind behind the syndicate and a licensed representative of Harvest Global Capital Investments Limited, and eight companies registered in the British Virgin Islands, Seychelles and Samoa. For the second group – allegedly involved in the Tianju Dihe listing – the SFC placed restrictions on HK$285 million across accounts belonging to the investor Liu Haoran and two local companies via 29 brokerages. The SFC said parties involved in the cases might be ordered to compensate affected investors through a restitution process in the future. It stressed that the brokers receiving restriction notices were not subjects of its investigations. “We maintain a zero-tolerance policy towards any form of IPO rigging, price manipulation or the creation of a false market,” said Julia Leung Fung-yee, CEO of the SFC. In January, Leung issued letters to investment banks pushing them to improve their work as financial market gatekeepers, as some firms were chasing deals rather than focusing on quality. The SFC said in a circular on Tuesday that the quality of sponsor work had improved overall this year, but that more needed to be done to raise standards. “The SFC noted deficiencies persisted in some listing application documents,” the regulator said, adding that it had suspended the vetting processes for 65 listing applications over the first nine months of the year due to quality issues related to documents prepared by sponsors. “It is reasonable to expect continued vigilance and potentially further interventions where the SFC identifies conduct that may undermine market integrity, particularly around IPO allocation, trading patterns, disclosure or attempts to create a false impression of demand,” said Kenny How Sze-ming, a council member of the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Professionals Association. The action was in line with the SFC’s broader effort to police IPOs, he added. As the suspension mechanism used by the SFC freezes investors’ capital for a long time, the regulator is working to streamline resumption procedures. It has also introduced targeted post-listing requirements as an alternative means of combating misconduct. The new rules are expected to take effect in the first quarter of next year. Chabaidao, based in Chengdu in southwest China’s Sichuan province, is the country’s third-largest maker of fresh tea drinks by sales value. It raised HK$2.46 billion (US$313 million) in its IPO in April 2024, with China International Capital Corporation as the sponsor. Chabaidao’s shares dropped 27 per cent on their first day of trading and have lost about 77 per cent from the offer price of HK$17.50. The stock closed at HK$4.035 on Monday.

title: China, Russia deepen maritime and Arctic logistics ties to secure energy supply
description: Top Chinese diplomat Wang Yi says Beijing stands ready to work with Moscow and ensure passage of key global corridors.
content: Beijing and Moscow vowed deeper maritime and logistical cooperation to protect shipping lanes and energy supplies, as China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi met Nikolai Patrushev, chairman of the Russian Maritime Board in the Chinese capital on Monday. “China stands ready to work with Russia to align maritime strategies and leverage their complementary strengths to protect each other’s legitimate maritime interests,” Wang said, according to a foreign ministry statement released late on Monday. The two sides should “safeguard maritime security in the Asia-Pacific and ensure the passage of key global corridors”, he added, noting the need to maintain stable energy and resources supplies. Patrushev, who is a presidential aide to Russian leader Vladimir Putin, agreed with Wang and also emphasised shipping safety during the meeting, according to a statement released by the maritime board on the same day. The growing trade and energy cooperation between the two countries required reliable and resilient transport routes, Patrushev said, while stressing joint efforts to ensure the safety of navigation. Global oil transit through the Strait of Hormuz has remained severely disrupted since the US and Israeli air strikes on Iran in February. As recurrent negotiations between Washington and Tehran yield little tangible progress, a protracted tug of war over control of the strategic waterway continues. With no immediate prospect of a return to normal shipping, coupled with Western sanctions against Russia, global energy supplies are facing immense strain. Arctic shipping was also discussed during the meeting, with Wang noting that China’s development of the “Polar Silk Road” aligned with Russia’s push to advance routes through the frozen region. “Both sides should expand exchanges in maritime and Arctic affairs to activate a ‘blue engine’ for the development of China-Russia relations,” Wang said, while Patrushev noted “particular significance in the joint development of strategic logistical initiatives”. “Pursuing these initiatives, our countries are able to reshape the global geoeconomic map, making maritime trade cheaper, more accessible and secure against any risks, including military escalation, piracy and sanctions,” Patrushev said. In the Chinese foreign ministry statement, Patrushev was quoted as echoing his remarks, made days earlier in Shanghai during visits to the Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding yard and Yangshan Port. Moscow was willing to strengthen cooperation with Beijing in areas such as construction of a “trans-Arctic transport corridor” and multilateral ocean governance, and draw on China’s experience in shipbuilding, logistics and maritime trade, he said. In recent years, Russia has actively sought to unleash the economic potential of its northern regions by developing Arctic shipping. Beyond promoting the Northern Sea Route, Moscow aims to turn its Arctic coastline into the backbone of an integrated transport network, linking railways, river systems, ports and industrial projects across the country’s far north, Siberia and far east regions. China, which views the Arctic shipping lane as a vital alternative to established maritime routes, is widely seen as a key partner in this effort. In August, shipping company Sea Legend launched the first regular Chinese container service to Europe via the Arctic. While in Beijing, Patrushev also met Liu Wei, the transport minister, and discussed joint development of new strategic maritime and river communications, mainly polar ones, according to a separate maritime board statement released on Monday. The meeting statements did not mention Putin’s expected visit to Shenzhen next month for the Apec summit – an event closely watched for a potential trilateral meeting of Chinese, Russian and US leaders. However, Wang emphasised that President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart were in close communication and the two countries had stronger strategic mutual trust and more resilient cooperation across various fields, as well as closer multilateral coordination. Patrushev added that the close interactions between the two heads of state served as “the best guarantee for a dynamic, pragmatic and forward-looking bilateral relationship”, according to the ministry’s statement. Amid today’s turbulent international landscape, the Russia-China comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination for a new era “is more important than ever”, he said.

title: Ex-Cyberport department head, 5 others, charged over HK$20 million tech subsidy fraud
description: Former entrepreneurship head Alice So allegedly took bribes, including plane tickets and luxury gifts, in return for pushing subsidies for AI start-up.
content: A former department head of Hong Kong’s fintech hub Cyberport has been granted bail after being charged with accepting bribes to help an artificial intelligence (AI) start-up secure HK$20 million (US$2.25 million) in funding from a government-subsidised programme. Alice So Nga-lai, 59, former head of entrepreneurship of the Hong Kong Cyberport Management Company, was accused of receiving advantages such as flight tickets, one handbag, two tote bags, one coin purse and a mobile phone between October 2023 and December 2025. The bribery charges allege she was given several tickets for round-trip flights between Hong Kong, Thailand and Japan. On Monday, she appeared at Eastern Court to face a count of a public servant accepting advantages. The charge was filed by the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC). The corruption watchdog’s operation, codenamed “Thunderclap,” was launched early this year. The ICAC alleged that Viola Lam Yuen-lee, 39, director and shareholder of Find Solution AI Limited, offered the gifts to So as a reward for giving the company preferential treatment in its application for subsidies under the Digital Transformation Support Pilot Programme. ICAC said its investigations showed So had accepted bribes to expedite subsidy releases and curtail probes into complaints lodged by applicants against Find Solution. Cyberport served as the secretariat for the programme, which was launched to provide local small and medium enterprises in the IT industry with subsidies. The government launched the programme in January 2024 with a fund of HK$500 million. Under the scheme, participating companies paid half the digital solution cost, while government subsidies covered the remainder, capped at HK$50,000 per applicant. Cyberport is the government-backed public technology incubator, innovation hub and flagship digital tech community. At the time of the alleged offence, So managed all secretariat matters concerning the programme, including reviewing subsidy application documents and disbursing funding, according to the ICAC. The agency also charged three other individuals – Daniel Lee, 40; Chan Hoi-tsun, 31; and Tsang Wai-ping, 52 – who were the downline vendors who allegedly urged Cyberport to approve the subsidy applications by falsely claiming that they had engaged Find Solution AI to provide services and had already paid half the fee for those services. The trio faced a joint count of conspiracy to defraud along with Viola Lam and Paul Lam Kin-ho, 35, Find Solution AI’s secretary. The ICAC said in a press release on Monday that its investigation revealed the present case involved at least 400 applications totalling about HK$20 million in subsidies. The six defendants were not required to enter a plea at Monday’s hearing as the prosecution sought an adjournment for further investigation. They each paid a cash bail ranging from HK$20,000 to HK$100,000 and agreed to comply with the conditions, which included remaining in Hong Kong. Magistrate Edward Wong Ching-yu set the next hearing for January 4 next year. Additional reporting by Danny Mok

title: Hong Kong group aims to cultivate a lasting future for rural Lantau communities
description: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist Good Old Soil brings farmers, craftspeople and young people together to build a rural economy that can outlast short-term funding.
content: Many rural projects in Hong Kong start with funding, run for a year or two, then disappear when the money runs out. Good Old Soil, a community organisation, is trying to take a different approach on Lantau. Supported by the non-profit Land Education Foundation, the organisation works with farmers, young people, restaurants, craftspeople and businesses to build a local economy that can sustain itself after individual grants end. Founded in 2022, Good Old Soil opened a shop in Mui Wo that same year. Its work ranges from farm-to-table activities and local food products to apprenticeships and support for small rural ventures. That approach has earned it a nomination in the sustainability category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Miffy Ng of Good Old Soil said the challenge was to make rural conservation financially sustainable as well as environmentally sound. She added that many community projects relied heavily on government or charitable funding and when the money ran out, organisers left, giving villagers little reason to trust the next group that arrived. “If you really want to establish a relationship with a community, you cannot come for one or two years and then disappear,” she said. “The economic side has to work as well.” One of Good Old Soil’s earliest projects linked Mui Wo farms with nearby restaurants. Ng said transporting small quantities of vegetables off Lantau could be expensive, so the group instead encouraged customers to visit the farms and eat meals prepared with local produce. The model has since expanded. The community organisation’s Mui Wo shop now sells products made with local ingredients, including seasonal produce boxes, frozen foods and a beer made with chicken-heart wampee. It also stocks products from Lantau growers and community makers, including pineapple gift boxes, tea and handmade goods. Building those relationships takes time. One farmer took years to be convinced. He had previously sold wampee fruit through shops in the city but became frustrated when customers questioned the quality of his produce. He eventually stopped selling outside Lantau, preferring to keep the fruit on his farm. Good Old Soil spent three to four years getting to know him before he agreed to work with the group. “He had to see that we were not going to come in for a short project and then leave,” Ng said. The relationship later led to volunteer harvests and products that introduced his fruit to more consumers. During the short harvest season, volunteers help pick the crop before it spoils. The community organisation also seeks to pass on rural knowledge to a younger generation. Its “Made in Lantau” apprenticeship programme has brought about 170 participants to learn directly from farmers and other local producers. Some returned to Lantau at weekends for months, while others maintained ties with the community afterwards or started projects of their own. It also helps small rural ventures develop product ideas, build their brands, pitch to the media and apply for funding. Some draw on inherited food traditions, while others use local materials or agricultural produce. For Good Old Soil, the goal is not simply to sell more local vegetables but to preserve enough of rural Hong Kong to give future generations a choice of how to live and work. “In Hong Kong, there should be more than one way to live and work,” Ng said. “If we can keep this environment and this community going, then when the next generation wants to try something of its own, there will still be a place for it.” Launched in 2013, the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards honour individuals and groups whose work might otherwise go unnoticed.

title: China proposes streamlined export rules for ‘low-risk’ avionics in boost to industry
description: The proposed rules aim to reduce paperwork and shorten supply times for aircraft parts to help international expansion of the industry.
content: China is seeking public comments on draft rules that would streamline procedures for “low-risk” exports of aviation components such as engines and inertial navigation systems to give the industry a competitive boost. Such avionics currently are classified by Chinese authorities as “dual-use” items, which can serve both civilian and military purposes, and are subject to strict export licensing requirements. If implemented, “this will reduce compliance costs for an industry with extensive international operations and create a more convenient business environment” for aviation firms, said independent aviation analyst Li Hanming. The draft rules, published by the Ministry of Commerce on Tuesday, would allow eligible aviation companies – including airlines, maintenance firms and manufacturers – to export these components for repairs, maintenance and replacement purposes without applying for individual export licences for each shipment. Instead, companies would register relevant information and automatically receive export certificates, allowing them to proceed with shipments, according to the draft, which is open for public comment for one month. According to a commerce ministry statement, the proposed rules aimed to reduce paperwork and shorten supply times for aircraft parts, helping support aviation safety and international expansion of China’s aviation industry. If implemented, the rules would “put into practice for the first time the export certification system provided for under the [2024] regulations, allowing exports to be managed according to different risk levels and circumstances and improving regulatory effectiveness”, the ministry said. Under export measures introduced in 2006, companies can obtain annual licences for civil aviation components sent overseas for certain activities such as repairing and leasing, allowing multiple customs clearances during the licence’s validity period. The system needed updating following the introduction of China’s new dual-use export control regulations in December 2024, which provide for export certificates to be issued after companies register required information for certain activities, including sending civil aircraft components overseas for repair, the ministry said. To prevent abuse, companies would be required to report how export certificates are used and retain relevant documents. Authorities could request additional information about questionable exports or revoke certificates in certain cases.

title: Why Haidilao’s US$14.9 million credit line to founder is fuelling China tax speculation
description: Hotpot chain says funds are for personal financial arrangements, but the loan comes ahead of Beijing’s offshore trust tax deadline.
content: Haidilao International Holding has agreed to provide its founder, Zhang Yong, with a one-month loan of up to the Hong Kong dollar equivalent of 100 million yuan (US$14.9 million), a move that has raised market speculation as investors closely watch Beijing’s October 22 deadline for offshore trust taxation. The Hong Kong-listed hotpot chain said in a stock exchange filing on Monday night that it would fund the loan from internal resources and charge interest at 0.6 percentage points above the one-month Hong Kong interbank offered rate. The principal amount translates to around HK$117.2 million. Zhang, the company’s controlling shareholder, chairman and CEO, could use the money only for “personal financial arrangements”, the filing said. The funds could not be used to finance purchases of Haidilao shares, loans or guarantees to third parties, or any purpose that breached listing rules or regulatory requirements, it added. Haidilao also said it reserved the right to monitor how the money was used. It said the group had ample funds and that the loan would not “affect daily operations or business development”. The interest income would also benefit the group and its shareholders, it added. The filing did not elaborate on the purpose of the loan or mention any tax-related considerations. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The deadline stems from rules Beijing announced on July 24, requiring Chinese tax residents to pay a 20 per cent individual income tax on gains from assets held in offshore trusts and on income generated by those trusts. Owners of existing trusts had 90 days from the announcement to declare and pay outstanding taxes without a incurring late-payment surcharge, according to an official notice. Company filings showed Zhang and his wife, Shu Ping, controlled about half of Haidilao through discretionary trusts and holding companies. Both were Singapore citizens, Chinese media had reported, citing Haidilao’s 2018 listing prospectus. But those with foreign nationality could still be treated as Chinese tax residents if their main economic interests remained in China – a phrase law firms said the new rules left undefined. Mainland China accounted for about 96 per cent of Haidilao’s revenue as of the end of June, according to its interim report. On September 8, SP NP, a holding company controlled by a trust established by Shu, sold 259 million shares, or 4.65 per cent of Haidilao, at HK$10.62 each, raising about HK$2.75 billion, according to a stock exchange filing. The couple’s stake now stands at about 45.51 per cent. Although Haidilao said the sale was a personal matter for the shareholder and unrelated to its business, investors linked the disposal to the new tax rules. The stock dropped about 10 per cent over the following two trading days, according to a South China Morning Post report. In a September research note cited by international media, Morgan Stanley described the stake sale as a market “surprise”, warning that tax-related concerns would continue to weigh on sentiment until investors gained confidence in Haidilao’s earnings outlook and were assured there would be no further disposals. Shares of Haidilao fell 3 per cent to HK$9.30 on Tuesday.

title: China-US astronomy team may have found possible relic of a recent ‘gold factory’
description: Mystery glow seen in the Milky Way could be the result of a violent collision between two orbiting neutron stars, according to scientists.
content: A mysterious glow of high-energy light in our Milky Way galaxy could be the remains of an extremely rare cosmic “gold factory”, according to a new study by Chinese and US researchers. The collision of two orbiting neutron stars – dead stars so dense that a teaspoon of their matter would weigh a billion tonnes – may have shone as brightly as Jupiter in the sky, they wrote in a paper posted last week on the preprint server arXiv, which has yet to be peer-reviewed. The violent smash spewed out atoms and a flood of neutrons, which the atoms soaked up to form some of the universe’s heaviest elements, such as gold, platinum and uranium, while the wreckage collapsed into a black hole. The blast probably happened less than 1,000 years ago, as the glowing cloud it left behind is still small and bright, signs of a young remnant, wrote the researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing and the University of Notre Dame in Indiana. However, no one seems to have recorded it – not even Chinese astronomers, who kept some of the world’s most careful sky records from the Song dynasty onwards and famously noted the 1054 “guest star”, a supernova that left behind what is known today as the Crab Nebula. The team, led by Prantik Sarmah, of the Institute of High Energy Physics under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, noted that the flash was probably very brief and faded within days. Although the researchers noted such an event “would, in principle, have been readily visible to the naked eye”, it sat so far south in the sky that it would have been hard to see from China, Japan, Europe and other places that kept detailed records of the night sky at the time. Though bright, the blast would have posed no danger to people on Earth. A 2024 study led by US scientists found that such a collision would need to happen within about 36 light-years to threaten life, and this one would have been many thousands of light years away. Neutron star collisions are believed to happen in a galaxy like the Milky Way only once every tens of thousands of years. If confirmed, the glow would be the first known remains of such a collision within our galaxy. First spotted by the High Energy Stereoscopic System (HESS) gamma-ray telescopes in Namibia, it has puzzled astronomers for years. Most such sources lie along the flat disc of the Milky Way, where stars are born and die. This one sits well below it. Scientists have blamed it on either a spinning dead star known as a pulsar or the debris of an ordinary exploding star. But no pulsar has been found nearby and there is no sign of the shell-shaped cloud a supernova leaves behind, the team wrote. A neutron star collision would solve that puzzle, they proposed. The explosions that create neutron stars can kick a pair out of the galaxy’s crowded disc and it can drift for millions of years before the two finally merge far from where they started. The team said the idea can be tested. The heavy elements made in the collision are radioactive and as they decay, they should still give off a faint glow of gamma rays. Current telescopes are not sensitive enough to see it, but future ones, such as a proposed Chinese space telescope called the MeV Gamma-Ray Observatory, could. Astronomers could also look for light from the original flash that bounced off dust and is only now reaching Earth. Big telescopes in the southern hemisphere, such as the US-funded Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, should be able to spot it, they wrote, letting scientists see the flash and look for signs of the heavy elements it made.

title: Fifa president Infantino could pull off ‘Houdini’ act as critics struggle for candidate
description: The Swiss, though, is not safe yet as the opposition have mounted legal challenges in the US and filed official complaints with Fifa committees.
content: Gianni Infantino could survive weeks of criticism and secure re-election as Fifa president in the absence of a heavy hitter to challenge him, observers have said. The 56-year-old Swiss has lost the support of many associations in his bid to be re-elected to a fourth and final term since he launched and then hastily shelved his plan to allow private investment into the World Cup. Infantino, though, does crucially retain his core support in Africa and South America. His Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan, which came to light in July just after the hugely successful World Cup, would have created a commercial subsidiary to run Fifa’s biggest events, such as the World Cup. However, with two of his fiercest critics, Aleksander Ceferin and reportedly Victor Montagliani, opting to run for re-election as heads of European governing body Uefa and North American grouping Concacaf respectively, the opposition to Infantino is desperately seeking a viable candidate to challenge him in the election next March. Candidates have to declare by November 18. Terrence Burns, who was marketing strategist for two successful World Cup hosting bids, said Infantino was always in the box seat. “He holds all the cards and always has,” he said. “Any prospective challenger at this point feels either performative or strategic to cut deals.” Former International Olympic Committee (IOC) marketing chief Michael Payne said “everyone is surprised” that no serious candidate has come forward to challenge Infantino. “If he is re-elected, which is looking increasingly likely, it will redefine the term Houdini,” Payne said. Long-time Infantino critic Lise Klaveness, the head of the Norwegian Football Federation, has impressed many but has ruled out running. However, even if Klaveness changed her mind, she would face a huge challenge in becoming the first woman to run world football and emulate Kirsty Coventry, who last year became the first woman elected as IOC president. “People within the IOC administration were working towards the goal of Coventry being elected, as [her predecessor] Thomas Bach’s wish was for her to be president,” a source close to the world of football governance, who asked not to be identified, said. “Lise faces exactly the opposite. Fifa staff would be working to stop her being elected.” Infantino, though, is not safe yet as the opposition have mounted legal challenges in the US and filed official complaints with Fifa committees. Klaveness and the Norwegian federation have highlighted three issues, with the common thread being Infantino’s friendship with US President Donald Trump. The venture capital firm of Josh Kushner, the brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared, was to be the major investor in FFE. However, the same source warned “there is no certainty that the complaints will be looked into. Even if they were to consider them, they would take their time. “The fear in the Infantino camp is the Norwegians could take them to CAS [Court of Arbitration for Sport] if dissatisfied with the decision”. Burns, though, believes the greatest risk to Infantino comes from the legal challenges launched by Uefa in the US courts to gain access to the papers pertaining to FFE. Fifa are strongly contesting the case. “This point is a fly in the ointment,” Burns said. “If the FFE was just a case of misguided process and communications strategy, why hide its specifics? “That lack of transparency is a rock in Infantino’s shoe that will not fade away.” Payne believes the lack of support for Infantino from leading football nations such as Spain, France and England could be damaging. “Running a global sports federation requires unity – Fifa will be on the brink of civil war, and this is totally new territory for a sports governing body,” he said. Burns, though, thinks the opposition will reluctantly make peace with Infantino. He said football’s governing bodies would rather avoid division “unless of course there is overwhelming criminal activity to justify it – which there is not”. The other point that could tip the balance is if there is a “financial upside” for the federations by removing Infantino. On that point, he said, “again, there isn’t”. Burns believes that the process is likely to “result in even greater consolidation of power and influence for Infantino when it is all over”.

title: Singapore’s 3-Michelin-star neo-Nordic Restaurant Zen reopens with a local touch
description: Bjorn Frantzen talks about changes at his fine-dining restaurant after its renovation, and his ‘extremely important’ Singaporean head chef.
content: Singapore’s three-Michelin-star Restaurant Zen reopened in August 2026 after a three-month refurbishment – with a medley of changes that mark its new chapter. Founded in 2018 by Swedish chef Bjorn Frantzen, Zen inhabits a three-storey shophouse along the buzzing Bukit Pasoh Road in Chinatown. The renewed interior swaps the previous living-room setting on the ground floor for a 16-seat stone counter, in a look more reminiscent of Frantzen’s eponymous restaurant in Stockholm and FZN in Dubai. “I wanted to even out the time you spend on each floor and showcase the skills of the chef with the kitchen counter,” says 49-year-old Frantzen, currently the only chef in the world to simultaneously run a trio of three-Michelin-star restaurants. Kicking off the evening at a lively, high-octane pace, chefs whip up seven moreish, well-balanced canapés, ranging from a raraka, Zen’s refined take on the Swedish potato classic, to a beignet brimming with pig trotters, garlic and horseradish. Final flourishes are delivered with panache right in front of guests, such as the generous shaving of truffles on top of Zen’s scene-stealing French toast. Alongside Zen’s spatial evolution is a subtler, less-reported change: Singaporean head chef Kelvin Ng’s role has expanded with the reopening; he now handles everything related to the restaurant. “Today I run the restaurant as a whole, be it maintenance, recruitment or produce sourcing,” the 31-year-old says. “It’s a big jump.” The last few years at Zen have seen notable shuffles at the top – chef Tristin Farmer left in 2024 while co-executive chefs Toraik Chua and Martin Ofner left in mid-2025 and early 2026, respectively – but Ng, who first joined Zen in 2020 and was promoted to chef de cuisine in September 2025, seems poised to steer the ship to steadier waters. “To have a local head chef is extremely important to me,” Frantzen says. “There has never been so little drama or problems when Kelvin is in charge, because every country has their own kind of hidden language.” He is my boots on the ground, and has the know-how of the city Bjorn Frantzen on Kelvin Ng From hawker stall to haute cuisine The recipe to Ng’s success – besides his smiley, easy-going demeanour – lies in an indefatigable spirit shaped by humble beginnings. His affinity with food began to take shape at just 10 years old, when his parents opened a bak chor mee (minced meat noodles) stall at a coffee shop beneath their public housing flat in the Hougang neighbourhood of Singapore. “It began as a joke when I said I could wash the dishes to help them out,” Ng says with a chuckle. “But it turned out to be true. I would help out at the stall during the weekends and school holidays with small prep work, serving and taking orders.” While some chefs pinpoint a single extraordinary meal that set them on their career path, Ng says his interest in cooking was kindled within the crammed, quotidian confines of a hawker stall. “Whenever I saw my parents cooking a bowl of bak chor mee for their customers, and saw them eat the same dish every day, it would never fail to put a smile on my face,” he says. Ng’s parents, however, were less zealous about their son joining the food industry. “They have witnessed a lot of hardship and didn’t want to see me suffer,” Ng says. Undeterred, he enrolled in a culinary and catering management course at Singapore’s Temasek Polytechnic – without telling them. But that was not the only hurdle Ng had to overcome. He was unfamiliar with the world of ingredients and techniques beyond Singaporean cuisine. “I only knew how to cook local food,” he says. “I didn’t even know what thyme was, let alone more obscure Western herbs.” Once again, Ng pushed on. He knuckled down and expanded his repertoire. An internship in Provence, France, and a series of culinary competitions sharpened his skills. He later earned a bachelor’s degree in food business management from the Culinary Institute of America and spent a year as a chef de partie at New York’s two-Michelin-star The Modern. Working in New York was a lifelong dream for Ng, but the Covid-19 pandemic cut the experience short and forced Ng to return to Singapore in 2020. But this setback opened another door: he joined Zen as a chef de partie that year and subsequently rose to sous chef. In 2023, he once again moved to the United States, where he worked at two-Michelin-star Pineapple and Pearls in Washington, before returning to his position at Zen in 2024. Nordic flavours with a Singaporean touch One of Ng’s defining duties now as chef de cuisine has been shaping Zen’s neo-Nordic cuisine around Asia’s best produce. While the menu, as with that of FZN in Dubai, is still largely conceptualised in Stockholm, Ng plays a significant role in finessing flavours and adapting dishes to the region’s seasons and rhythms. Over the past year, Ng has extended Zen’s sourcing to include China, introducing songrong, or matsutake mushrooms, from Yunnan province, to the new menu. “We actually serve it in its purest form,” Ng says. “All we do is clean it and slice it thinly.” The pine-needle fragrance, elegant sweetness and earthy undertones of the mushrooms are paired with Scottish scallop, miso sabayon, chicken dashi and roasted garlic. Marron from the cold, pristine waters of Western Australia is another Zen speciality. The crustacean’s sweet, succulent meat is complemented by vin jaune, brown butter and caviar, and finished off with walnuts for a contrasting crunch. Saltiness and acidity are the hallmarks of Swedish cooking – fermentation and pickling are some of Frantzen’s trademark techniques – which means Ng’s task is to fine-tune the flavours to suit local palates. His nuanced touch as a home-grown Singaporean chef has not gone unnoticed. “He is my boots on the ground, and has the know-how of the city,” Frantzen says of Ng. “He’s so secure in himself, humble, serious and professional. And he comes in on time.” Those qualities, it turns out, are not accidental, but the values instilled in Ng by his parents – who continue to work in hospitality since closing their hawker stall at the end of 2023. “They always tell me, ‘Be on time and never be late,’” Ng says. “They wake at 3am and start work at 4am. They are only off from work once a month. I’ve seen their dedication and hard work, and it has inspired me to do the same.” From washing dishes and slinging noodles at a hawker stall to leading the charge at what is purportedly Singapore’s most expensive restaurant, Ng’s career has covered all bases, but his dedication and discipline have remained the same.

title: Hong Kong’s Huanggang Port handles 79,500 travellers, 8,000 vehicles on opening day
description: Immigration clearance and public transport connections operated smoothly and met government’s expectations, Hong Kong transport chief says.
content: Hong Kong’s new Huanggang Port handled 79,500 passengers and 8,000 vehicles on its first day of operations, as transport officials prepared for heavier flows over the coming holiday weekend. Statistics from the Shenzhen General Station of Exit and Entry Frontier Inspection showed 41,300 people entered Hong Kong through the rebuilt checkpoint between Hong Kong and mainland China on Monday, while 38,200 departed the city. The figures track total border crossings, rather than unique travellers. “The overall operation of immigration clearance and public transport connections was smooth, meeting our expectations,” Transport Secretary Mable Chan told a radio programme on Tuesday, adding that transport operators were boosting staff and service frequencies to manage higher volumes over the coming Chung Yeung holiday weekend. Chan said signs at the public transport interchange showed passengers how to connect to buses and other services, while staff were on hand to provide directions. The government would strengthen publicity to help familiarise travellers with the new arrangements. KMB, the city’s largest franchised bus operator, said its two routes serving the checkpoint – B10 and B11 – carried about 25,000 passengers on Monday. The company added that it had recorded 70 trips at Tai Lam Tunnel interchange and Tsing Yi station for the B10, and about 70 B11 trips in Yuen Long. During the peak periods over the holiday weekend, the daytime routes could run as frequently as every five minutes, KMB operations director Kelvin Yeung Chun-wai said. “We ran extra trips throughout the day because it was the first day of operations and we didn’t have much data,” he said. Yeung added that KMB would study whether to extend the operating hours of the existing overnight NB73, which serves Sheung Shui, Fanling, Tai Po and Sha Tin. The new connection has already significantly reduced travel times for some students from the mainland. Wong Kin Ho, principal of Tin Shui Wai’s Yuen Yuen Institute MFBM Nei Ming Chan Lui Chung Tak Memorial College, said the school had about 120 cross-border pupils and had interviewed around 20 who used the port on Monday. “I spoke to one student yesterday, and he said the difference in travel time was quite significant – he saved 60 minutes,” Wong said. “Previously, it could take him one hour and 45 minutes to get to school via Shenzhen Bay or even Lo Wu. Yesterday, he went through Huanggang and took a KMB bus to Tin Shui Wai and on to school in about 45 minutes, so it was much more convenient,” Wong said. But he added the change was not suited for every pupil as the B11 stop was some distance from the school and required another connection. The school would need more time and data before deciding whether to arrange a dedicated service, Wong said. Legislator Jeff Yiu Ming, who visited the checkpoint, praised the clear signs and efficient passenger clearance. “It took only about a dozen seconds to clear immigration,” he said. But he saw queues of more than 10 people for taxis, including travellers with luggage heading to the airport, and noted that some eventually took buses instead. He also flagged a potential traffic bottleneck around San Tin caused by ongoing roadworks and heavy vehicles, and suggested authorities review signal timings and the taxi queuing area. KMB expects passenger numbers on its border routes to rise by 10 to 20 per cent over the holiday period compared with a normal weekend and has allocated extra resources to bolster services.

title: Systems to counter missiles and drones take centre stage at US defence expo
description: Emphasis on air and missile defence at AUSA exhibition reflects concern over aerial threats as conflicts in Ukraine and Middle East drag on.
content: As missiles and drones take a bigger role in modern warfare, major defence contractors gathered in Washington this week to showcase their latest advances in the technologies – and systems to counter them. The three-day Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition, which opened on Monday, is one of the largest ground-based weapons shows in the US. This year there was a strong emphasis on air and missile defence systems, reflecting growing concern about how to counter aerial threats as conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East rage on, and following reports that the US military’s missile stockpiles have been badly depleted by its war on Iran. Lockheed Martin, one of the world’s largest defence contractors, had its latest advanced missile systems on show – the Extended-Range Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System (ER GMLRS) and Precision Strike Missile (PrSM), launched from its High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (Himars), a light multiple rocket launcher. But the main focus was its air and missile defence systems, with the latest PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) and Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) on show – used for short- and long-range air defence, respectively. The company also had its new PAC-3 Edge next-generation missile interceptor on show for the first time after it unveiled the programme on Friday. The PAC-3 Edge is an upgrade of the PAC-3 MSE currently in operation in Ukraine, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific region. It incorporates a new seeker, upgraded flight controls and a multi-pulse rocket motor supplied by Northrop Grumman, which Lockheed Martin says enhance the interceptor’s ability to counter advanced threats, including hypersonic missiles, ‌at ⁠longer ranges and higher altitudes. During the ceremony at the AUSA expo on Monday, Tim Cahill, president of missiles and fire control for Lockheed Martin, said the PAC-3 Edge would “fly further, faster and higher” than its predecessor, with more manoeuvrability, thrust and sensitivity. It is expected to begin testing by 2027 to be ready for deployment in 2031. “We’re looking forward. We’re asking ourselves, what are our adversaries going to be doing in three or four or five or 10 years from now? And we’re preparing for that,” Cahill said. “We’re going to make sure that the adversaries have nowhere to hide. It doesn’t matter what they do. It doesn’t matter what they try. This missile is going to take them out.” It comes as the ongoing war in Iran has exposed the importance of munitions stockpiles and defence against low-cost drone swarms in modern warfare. According to an April report by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, the US military may have used more than half of its pre-war inventory for four key munitions – PrSM, SM-3, THAAD and Patriot missiles – and more than 1,000 rounds of Tomahawk and Joint Air-to-Surface Stand-off missiles during the first 39 days of its war with Iran, which began on February 28. That situation could be “critical” for a potential western Pacific conflict, the report said, as it would take up to four years to return stockpiles to pre-war levels, which were already deemed insufficient for a war against a peer. “Building stockpiles to levels adequate for a war with China will take additional time,” it added. In contrast, Iran has heavily relied on its low-cost, one-way attack drones – such as the Shahed-136 “kamikaze” drone – that were used to swarm and overwhelm the air defences of US military bases in the region. The US and Gulf states have consumed and depleted multimillion-dollar air and missile defence rounds to combat the cheap drones, prompting calls for more efficient solutions. These drone warfare tactics are also projected to be critical in the Indo-Pacific flashpoints – particularly the Taiwan Strait, where both the US and China have been building up their drone fleets in preparation for a potential armed conflict. A satellite imagery analysis suggests that the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has stationed over 200 obsolete 1960s-era J-6 supersonic fighter jets – converted into attack and cruise-missile-like drones – across six airbases near the Taiwan Strait. In response, the US has introduced the “hellscape” concept into its Taiwan Strait strategy, aimed at deploying a massive fleet of autonomous drone swarms, loitering munition systems and marine drones to disrupt PLA amphibious invasion forces in any contingencies. It also requested US$54 billion for “autonomous and remotely operated systems across air, land, and above and below the sea” in the 2027 budget request, according to the Pentagon’s budget overview book. To counter short-range drone swarms and incoming missiles, General Dynamics, one of the largest American land-based arms contractors, showcased its two latest air defence systems – the Leonidas Ground Vehicle (GV) and the Manoeuvre-Short Range Air Defence (M-SHORAD) Increment 4. The Leonidas GV is a mobile high-power microwave counter-drone defence system developed as a collaborative initiative by the defence tech company Epirus and General Dynamics.
