Scott Taylor, director of US growth at General Dynamics, said the Leonidas GV was developed with “drone swarm defeat” in mind and aimed to solve the “prolific problem” of being unable to use electronic warfare interruption against fibre-optically controlled drones by using weaponised electromagnetic interference technology. In this way, the Leonidas GV could overload the internal electronics, navigation and communication systems of multiple hostile drones at once, causing them to drop from the sky simultaneously. “One of the things that’s been very clear in a lot of the studies that are publicly discussed out there, particularly in Southwest Asia, is that the enemy can start flying enough drones at you that it overwhelms an electronic warfare or a kinetic machine gun capability,” Taylor said. “So the Epirus-based vehicle – the Leonidas over there – that one uses electromagnetic interference to weaponise, and it can drop 50 drones at one time, single pulse, no bullets, no fratricide risk.” Also on display, the M-SHORAD anti-aircraft weapon system uses a self-loading equipment dock mounted on light, tactical and utility vehicles to provide air defence against short-range drone and missile threats for light infantry brigades. Taylor said it had “powerful short-range air defence and counter-drone capability integrated in one”. It is equipped with Iron Wasp suicide drones that intercept incoming enemy drone attacks, as well as a 30-calibre machine gun. “With what’s going on in Ukraine, what’s happening in the Persian Gulf in the Strait of Hormuz, there’s a lot of people talking about the challenges with drone defeat,” he said. “Now they’re having US$30,000 drones destroying multimillion-dollar vehicles, and so trust me, we’re being approached all of the time by our allied nations as well.” The need to counter drone attacks – and a desire to reduce American casualties on the battlefield – has accelerated the integration of autonomous systems into US Army operations. At the expo, GM Defence showcased its prototype of a “commercially derived” Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV) concept, with a design based on Chevrolet’s Silverado to demonstrate potential future drive-by-wire controls, camera-based sensing and modular payload capabilities for support missions like logistics and casualty evacuation. Pete Johnson, vice-president of integrated vehicle solutions at GM Defence, said the UGV was a “direct reflection” of how his company listened to the US Army and paid attention to the changing character of warfare. “We’re watching closely the developments in Ukraine and the Middle East, and how the army is organising the campaign in the Indo-Pacific,” Johnson said. “And all of those observations are pointing to a very clear need: more robotic and autonomous capability to deliver operational effect and to reduce risk for our soldiers.”

title: King Fook expands with US$34 million Admiralty lease despite slow luxury sales: analysts
description: The planned boutique in Pacific Place is set to open in 2028, with analysts divided over whether luxury watch sales can cover costs.
content: King Fook Jewellery Group’s decision to lease a 550 square metre (about 5,920 square feet) retail space at Pacific Place Phase II in Admiralty signals confidence in Hong Kong’s retail market, despite slowing demand for luxury goods, analysts said. The six-year lease for the shop in Hong Kong’s prime business district carries total base rent of about HK$268.5 million (US$34.2 million), or about HK$3.73 million a month, according to a company announcement filed with Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing on Monday. The lease is tentatively scheduled to commence on February 1, 2028. Stanley Poon Chi-ming, managing director at Centaline Commercial, said the number of visitors to Hong Kong had risen steadily this year, supporting growth in retail sales, particularly in the jewellery and watch sectors. “Thus many retailers in this industry have been expanding their store networks, creating a ripple effect among competitors,” he added. “King Fook, which has not expanded its store count for some time, is now seizing this opportunity to open new locations.” Poon said the average rent was reasonable for an upscale shopping centre such as Pacific Place. “One advantage of renting space at Pacific Place is the concentration of numerous luxury brands and chain jewellery stores within the mall, creating a strong commercial draw,” he said. Financial commentator and academic Simon Lee Siu-po said total retail sales in Hong Kong’s jewellery, watches, clocks and valuable gifts category totalled HK$52.32 billion last year, averaging about HK$143 million per day. “The daily rent for King Fook’s newly leased store is around HK$120,000, a cost that is presumably still affordable for the company,” he added. “It’s not too difficult to absorb the rent as retail shop rent has dropped significantly.” However, Terence Chong Tai-leung, executive director of Lau Chor Tak Institute of Global Economics and Finance at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, offered a more cautious assessment, saying it would “not be easy” for the company to generate enough revenue from luxury watch sales to cover the rent. “King Fook must sell roughly 10 watches per day just to cover the rent,” he added. “The global demand for luxury goods, such as jewellery and watches, is declining, particularly given the slowdown in mainland China’s economic growth.” Data released by China’s National Bureau of Statistics in September showed that total retail sales of consumer goods rose by 1.1 per cent year on year in the January-August period, while the core consumer price index rose by 1 per cent in August. Hong Kong presented a more positive picture. Sales of jewellery, watches, clocks and valuable gifts increased by 11.9 per cent in August from a year earlier, according to figures released by the Hong Kong government in October. Visitor arrivals in Hong Kong reached 5.46 million in August, up 6 per cent year on year and marking a new post-pandemic monthly high. Mainland Chinese visitor arrivals during this year’s “Golden Week” totalled about 1.6 million, up about 6.37 per cent from the same period last year, according to government data. King Fook said the new premises would operate as a single-brand watch boutique.

title: China gives green light to Visa for local clearing organisation after years-long wait
description: People’s Bank of China will allow the US card payment giant to set up a local entity to process domestic transactions within its network.
content: The People’s Bank of China on Tuesday gave its approval to Visa to make preparations for a locally registered bank card clearing organisation, calling the move a major step in the country’s financial opening up in an online statement. The US card payment giant will have one year to finish its advance arrangements, after which it may submit an application to begin operations, the central bank added. With a local clearing organisation, Visa would be able to settle domestic yuan transactions directly with its own network. Historically, these transactions were dominated by China’s state-owned service UnionPay, while overseas providers could process foreign currency payments for multicurrency cards. In recent years, the establishment of joint ventures allowed for the handling of some domestic transfers by foreign service providers. Visa competitor American Express received a clearing licence for its joint venture in 2020, followed by Mastercard in 2023. However, Visa’s local branch would be permitted to do so as a wholly foreign-owned enterprise. The PBOC’s announcement, coming weeks after President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States, marks a continuation of China’s pledge to open its financial sector. During the trade negotiations ahead of the trip, both sides reached “a consensus in principle” in the field of financial services, according to China’s Ministry of Commerce, including the approval of applications from American financial institutions to establish local Chinese branches. Visa CEO Ryan McInerney said in a press release that the approval marked “a significant step forward in Visa’s long-standing commitment to China. “For more than 40 years, Visa has been an active contributor to China’s dynamic payments landscape. We look forward to taking the necessary steps in the process, pursuant to the PBOC’s regulations, to begin operating domestically in China,” he said. Visa’s entry could also foster greater competition and diversification in China’s bank card clearing market Su Yue, Economist Intelligence Unit McInerney added that “we greatly appreciate the important role of the leaders of the United States and China in pursuing a constructive and strategically stable relationship between the world’s largest economies.” McInerney was also part of the delegation of CEOs who joined US President Donald Trump on his state visit to Beijing in May. On Tuesday, Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng held a meeting with a delegation from the National Committee on US-China Relations, saying that both sides should inject greater certainty and stability into bilateral economic cooperation, as well as the global economy. Visa first submitted its application to the PBOC in July 2017. In 2019, an official from the central bank confirmed to Chinese media that Visa had voluntarily withdrawn its application materials in January 2018, submitted a revised application three months later, and had entered an ongoing review process. Su Yue, principal economist for China at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said the PBOC’s move represented a meaningful step forward in China’s measured financial opening up, and sent a positive signal to US firms following the Xi–Trump meetings. “Visa’s entry could also foster greater competition and diversification in China’s bank card clearing market and expand payment options for foreign individuals and businesses,” she said. However, she added, this should not be interpreted as a broader institutional shift or an acceleration of market access approvals for other firms. “Visa stands to benefit from greater access to China’s market, but it will continue to face intense competition from domestic players and the rapidly evolving digital payments ecosystem,” Su said.

title: China to tighten leash on futures quant trading to contain risks amid stock slump
description: Country’s five futures bourses propose rules to define specific violations, punishments as top policymakers emphasise market stability.
content: China’s futures exchanges will intensify a crackdown on malfeasance linked to programme trading by defining specific violations, as Beijing seeks to contain any cross-asset risk that could place additional strain on the nation’s already struggling stock markets. Participants who failed to report and inspect clients’ programme trading, also known as quantitative trading, in compliance with the rules would be subject to disciplinary action, according to separate statements on the websites of China’s five futures bourses including the China Financial Futures Exchange and the Shanghai Futures Exchange. Those who caused risks by failing to establish efficient internal controls or risk management would also be penalised, with a permanent market ban as the most severe punishment. The exchanges are soliciting public comment on revisions to the rules and punishments until Monday. The announcements came just days after the China Securities Regulatory Commission convened a meeting with market participants, signalling possible stabilisation measures if stocks fell further. Top policymakers have placed great emphasis on financial stability this year, as the capital markets are a critical part of Beijing’s tech self-reliance drive, given their ability to generate funding for home-grown companies. Stocks in China and the US have been on diverging paths recently. US equity benchmarks are trading near record highs, withstanding elevated Treasury yields, while China’s key gauges have suffered extended declines. The CSI 300 Index fell 0.3 per cent on Tuesday, closing at its lowest in 14 months, and the chip-heavy Star Market 50 gauge finished little changed, hovering near a level not seen since April. Some investors attributed the underperformance to China’s weak economic domestic demand and Beijing’s reluctance to introduce more forceful stimulus measures. Meanwhile a top Chinese hedge fund blamed the decline on big insurers cutting holdings of technology stocks. High-frequency programme trading was also highlighted as one of the factors contributing to the perennial underperformance of Chinese stocks. The Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges rolled out measures in 2024 to curb such trading, as retail investors complained it gave an unfair edge to those who used it. “The significance of stabilising markets is not only to manage short-term volatility but also to create a stable market environment for funds’ long-term allocations, listing companies’ financing and the industry transition by stabilising expectations,” said Xu Chi, an analyst at Zhongtai Securities. The futures exchanges said they would punish participants that failed to follow rules and take appropriate measures in the event of emergencies, the statements said. Violators could face warnings, reprimands, restrictions on opening new positions for up to 12 months, cancellations of relevant memberships or fines of as much as 500,000 yuan (US$74,684). The China Financial Futures Exchange is the sole place in mainland China offering trading of financial derivatives. It provides futures contracts and options linked to the CSI 300 Index as well as contracts tied to government bonds across maturities. The Shanghai Futures Exchange focuses on commodity trading, covering 25 items ranging from copper and aluminium to crude oil and rubber.

title: Letters | The hidden costs of China’s energy security
description: Readers discuss the impact of rising diesel prices on coal miners, and blood clot risk faced by women.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. In early October, driven by a sharp deterioration in geopolitical conditions, China’s major oil refineries reportedly suspended refined petroleum exports to all regions except Hong Kong and Macau. According to data from commodities analytics firm Kpler, the country’s commercial diesel inventories have plummeted by around 20 million barrels compared to pre-conflict levels. With the spillover of the Middle East geopolitical conflict and the deep restructuring of international energy supply chains, the global refined petroleum market is facing unprecedented supply disruption and price turbulence. While China’s defensive measure is entirely necessary to safeguard against global energy shocks and imported inflation, regional coal miners are nonetheless experiencing severe cost pressure from rising diesel prices at the bottom of the supply chain. The most direct manifestation is the steeply rising price of No 0 diesel. Coal mining relies heavily on No 0 diesel as its core power source. Currently, the retail guidance prices for No 0 diesel in Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia, two of China’s primary coal-producing autonomous regions, have climbed to around 8.04 and 8.14 yuan per litre, respectively. Driven by geopolitical tensions and persistent constraints on domestic and global energy supplies, fuel and logistics costs are poised to surge further. Consequently, small and medium-sized coal enterprises across China, particularly in Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia, are experiencing a severe structural squeeze: their operational inputs (diesel) are dictated by soaring, market-driven international prices, while their outputs (coal) often face rigid domestic price expectations. Suspending operations would be the rational way to stem losses, yet supply-security obligations make a prolonged shutdown difficult. Administrative mandates have entirely severed these companies’ market-driven avenues for risk management. Where strict energy-security directives are enforced, unauthorised production halts by mining enterprises are strictly prohibited, with non-compliance facing severe penalties. This compulsory production arrangement requires miners to internalise security costs that should inherently be shared by the broader macroeconomic system, at the direct expense of their own deteriorating balance sheets. Ultimately, what is affected is not merely local employment and the tax base, but also the regional business environment and the confidence of investors. To maintain long-term energy security without eroding micro-level resilience, targeted support mechanisms could prove essential in helping regional miners navigate these troubled waters. Grace Chai, energy analyst, Kaisun Holdings Limited Let’s talk about blood clot risk World Thrombosis Day falls on October 13. It is a good moment to talk about a risk most women are never told about clearly. A clot in the deep veins of the leg, called deep vein thrombosis, can break off and lodge in the lungs as a pulmonary embolism, which can be fatal. It is less common in Asian than in Western populations, but reported rates across Asia have risen. For women, the risk rises at specific, predictable points in life. The first is contraception. Combined pills containing oestrogen raise the risk of a clot roughly three-fold. For a healthy young woman, the absolute risk remains small, so this is no reason to stop the pill. It is a reason for a proper conversation before starting it. The second is pregnancy. Overall the risk is about four times higher than usual, and it peaks in the six weeks after birth. In Britain, blood clots are the leading cause of maternal death. The third is menopause. Hormone therapy taken as tablets carries a raised clot risk; evidence suggests skin patches and gels do not carry the same risk. At every stage the risk is raised further by a previous clot, a close relative who has had one, obesity, smoking, cancer, surgery or long periods of immobility such as a long-haul flight. None of this should frighten women away from contraception, pregnancy or hormone therapy. It should prompt three things. Tell your doctor about any personal or family history of clots before starting hormones or when you become pregnant. Keep moving after childbirth or surgery and on long journeys. And know the warning signs: swelling, pain, warmth or redness in one leg; sudden breathlessness; chest pain that is worse on breathing in; coughing up blood. A swollen, painful leg needs a doctor the same day. Breathlessness or chest pain is an emergency. These symptoms are too easily dismissed, in pregnancy especially, as normal swelling or tiredness. A clot found early is very treatable. A clot missed can be fatal. Dr Andrew Choong, vascular, endovascular and aortic surgeon

title: Hong Kong police ramp up investigation into Anita Mui’s missing ashes with unit upgrade
description: Police say case, originally handled by Lantau district crime squad, now being handled by higher-level New Territories South regional crime unit.
content: Hong Kong police have stepped up their investigation into the disappearance of the ashes of late Cantopop diva Anita Mui Yim-fong by committing more resources and manpower to the case. Mui’s family had revealed over the weekend that the urn containing the singer’s remains was discovered to be missing from Po Lin Monastery on Lantau Island three months ago, complaining that police had made “no progress” in their investigation and that the incident had caused “immense distress”. A police spokesman said on Tuesday that the case, classified as a “request for police assistance” and originally handled by Lantau district crime squad, was now being handled by the New Territories South regional crime unit. No one has been arrested so far. Police said they would continue to maintain contact with the family and relevant parties and update them accordingly. A police region is the highest geographical administrative level in the Hong Kong Police Force. A police district is secondary to a police region. Lantau district is under the New Territories South region. It is understood that the escalation will ensure that more manpower and resources are allocated to the case. Mui’s family made a public appeal for information on the whereabouts of the ashes in a statement issued on Saturday, Mui’s birthday. The singer, who died in 2003 aged 40, would have turned 63. The statement revealed that a fan first discovered that the urn had gone missing from a columbarium at the monastery on July 18, while paying tribute to Mui. The monastery is located on the Ngong Ping plateau and is the site of the famous Tian Tan Buddha or Big Buddha. The fan discovered that the screws on the door panel of the niche housing Mui’s ashes had come loose, and the urn inside was missing. The fan notified Mui’s family, who made a police report.

title: How a detour saved a Malaysian trekker from jaws of deadly Nepal floods
description: Low Hock Meng, the only one among the 55 Malaysians reported missing in Nepal who has returned home so far, recalls his harrowing survival.
content: It was a detour that saved his life. Malaysian Low Hock Meng, a 71-year-old veteran trekker, had set off on his own in Nepal. He wanted to explore the Tamang trail, Langtang Valley and Gosaikunda. Along his journey, he made the decision to visit the Nagathali viewpoint for a glimpse of Tibet on August 25. Low then made his way down towards Thuman en route to Lingling in Nepal’s Bagmati province on August 26. That is when he realised that something was seriously wrong. When he looked at Syapru Besi, a downstream town, from his vantage point, he saw signs of a major flood, although the waters had begun to recede. “Bridges along my intended route to Lingling had been washed away, electricity was disrupted and I could not get through to anyone by phone. All the guest houses were closed,” he said. Low declined to have his photo published. When he reached Thuman, helicopters circled overhead, bridges were no longer there and floodwaters were rushing through the village. His change of direction had left him unaware of the deadly floods that had just swept through the region, washing away villages and killing and injuring people across Nepal and neighbouring Tibet. Low had narrowly escaped the August 26 tragedy. “Otherwise, I would have been exactly in the path of the flash floods,” he said. Low is the only one among the 55 Malaysians reported missing in Nepal who has returned home so far. Having visited Nepal several times, including completing the Annapurna base camp trek twice and reaching Everest base camp on multiple occasions, Low is no stranger to the country’s mountainous terrain. This trip, however, would turn out to be unlike any of his previous adventures. “When I asked the locals, they told me there was a big problem and that I could not proceed to Lingling,” he said. That was when he learned about the floods that left more than 1,400 people dead, while thousands remain missing. With nowhere to go, Low approached a young boy and asked if there was somewhere he could rest. The boy’s family offered him shelter. By that evening, the human toll of the disaster had become ­painfully clear. “Later that evening, people started coming in and crying. It was shocking.” He was then asked by the boy’s family to follow them to their ­village five hours away on foot. Along the way, Low then came across a Nepali man, who had previously worked in Malaysia and learned of an alternative mountain pass leading to another village, where he could find transport to Kathmandu or Pokhara. He continued through the mountains, eventually reaching Tipling on September 3, where he managed to contact his family and let them know he was safe. From then on, he kept in touch whenever internet access was available. “All this time, I still did not know what exactly happened and was piecing together information.” Low only reached Kathmandu on September 11, but he decided he could not leave Nepal immediately, especially after watching ­videos of the devastation and experiencing the hospitality of the Nepali people. “I knew that I couldn’t just leave at a time when these people needed support the most,” he said. He then tried another trek towards Langtang Valley via an alternative route, hoping to support local communities. But the journey brought further challenges: he was caught in a snowstorm at Gosaikunda and was stranded for three days. He also encountered landslide-hit areas and had to navigate stretches where established trails had disappeared. “I had to follow the trails made by the locals when passing through. Whenever there were footsteps, I would follow them to get by,” he said. Food was scarce, both for the locals and for him. Dal bhat – a meal of rice, vegetables and pickles – and eggs were his main sources of sustenance. “Across the various villages I stayed at, I would hear that they lost someone or that a loved one was missing. “They grieved in private but when they greeted you, they gave you their best,” he said. After returning to Kathmandu, Low checked in with the Malaysian embassy on October 1. “They were surprised but they knew who I was and had my particulars.” Low is now safely back in Malaysia and reunited with his family. His family is happy, but the kin of 54 other missing Malaysians can only hope that their loved ones will somehow return unscathed. This story was first published by The Star

title: Crowd chaos ruins student sandwich record bid
description: More than 1,400 people, including 700 students involved in world-record bid, attended the event, with some claiming overcrowding nearly triggered stampede.
content:
The Garden Company, one of Hong Kong’s oldest makers of bread and biscuits, has apologised and pledged to review its crowd-management procedures after a world-record attempt involving more than 700 students making sandwiches descended into chaos.
The incident occurred on Sunday at SKH Tang Shiu Kin Secondary School in Wan Chai, when the company tried to set a record for the “largest sandwich-making lesson” to mark its coming 100th anniversary.
More than 700 primary school pupils were involved and some attendees estimated that at least 1,400 people, including parents, attended the event, causing overcrowding at the venue.
Some attendees posted about the situation on social media, claiming that people forcing their way through the doors had nearly triggered a stampede. They accused the organiser of poor crowd management.
In a social media post on Monday night, the Garden Company apologised and said: “We attach the utmost importance to the safety and experience of every participant, and have proactively contacted all parents to gather their feedback.”
“In light of the shortcomings in the organisation of this event, the Garden team is conducting a thorough review, and we humbly accept the criticism. We will examine our procedures and relevant measures to ensure that such incidents do not occur again.”
The company also acknowledged the extended wait times at the end of the event.
“We sincerely apologise to the affected parents and children,” it said.
It stressed in the evening statement that there was no “stampede” or “fighting” as rumoured, adding that no one was injured.
Videos circulating online showed paper towels scattered across the floor of the hall and many children standing in the corridors waiting to leave amid scenes of chaotic jostling.
Some attendees complained on the social media platform Threads that as the event drew to a close, groups of parents frantically forced their way through the doors to get inside, “completely ignoring instructions on-site to the point where even the doors were broken”.
Some parents also complained on social media that the instructions given that day were unclear, while the venue was small and had only one tiny door as an exit.
“One moment, the staff told people to wait at the entrance; the next, at the playground; and then suddenly, to walk into the hall,” an attendee said.
The attendee recalled that many parents became agitated because they were worried about whether they would be able to pick up their children.

title: Therapy dogs in high demand: Hong Kong programme booked out until February 2027
description: Animals Asia’s Dr Dog volunteers are finalists in the teamwork category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards.
content: A Hong Kong therapy-dog programme run by one staff member and 65 volunteers with their dogs is fully booked until February 2027, as demand from schools, hospitals and elderly homes continues to outstrip the available visiting slots. Animals Asia’s Dr Dog and Professor Paws programmes rely on volunteers who give up their time, shoulder much of the cost of transporting their dogs and return regularly to venues across the city. “None of it would be possible without the volunteers,” said Karina O’Carroll, Animals Asia’s animal welfare education manager. “There would be no programmes.” The volunteer team has been named a finalist in the teamwork category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Dr Dog began in Hong Kong in 1991, when Animals Asia founder Jill Robinson began visiting people with her golden retriever, Max. The programme now brings suitable dogs into hospitals, elderly homes, schools and other venues, while Professor Paws teaches schoolchildren about responsible animal guardianship and how to interact safely with dogs. The dogs are not trained specifically for the programme. Instead, Animals Asia assesses their temperament and behaviour, applying strict entry requirements to ensure that both the animals and the people they meet are comfortable and safe. For volunteer Jacqueline Kwan, the rewards often emerge gradually. She recalled children who were frightened during their first encounter with a visiting dog but began touching and interacting with it on later visits. By the third or fourth meeting, some could remember individual dogs by name. At one Christmas gathering, a young child asked staff where George, one of Kwan’s dogs, was. “They’re always thinking about it, and they’re so happy when they see the dog,” she said. “That brings me joy.” Fellow volunteer Connie Tsoi, who brings Chestnut, a poodle, said the children’s reactions were among the most rewarding parts of the visits. Kwan was also accompanied by Freddie, her Shih Tzu. Both volunteers have spent years taking part in Dr Dog and Professor Paws activities. The work also carries less visible costs. Because dogs face restrictions on much of Hong Kong’s public transport, volunteers often rely on taxis to reach venues. O’Carroll said volunteers spent about HK$40,000 transporting their dogs in 2025, of which the organisation reimbursed HK$28,000. The programmes receive frequent requests from companies seeking corporate volunteering opportunities, but O’Carroll said regular involvement is more useful than large one-off groups because of venue space constraints, required human training and other factors. A visit may require extensive coordination between the dog’s guardian, venue staff and the people receiving the visit, while privacy and consent requirements can limit the number of outside volunteers who can attend. “Teamwork is the volunteers, the dogs, the venue, the staff,” she said. “It is a real team effort to conduct these visits successfully, with both human and animal welfare as the top priorities.” The visible joy, along with the known physiological and psychological benefits of spending time with companion animals, was enough to motivate everyone involved, keep the programmes going and bring volunteers back, she added. Demand has left little room for expansion for now. O’Carroll said she remains the only staff member running the two Hong Kong programmes, although continued demand may require greater capacity in the years ahead. She also wants Professor Paws to continue teaching children that animals are sentient beings that require care, time, effort and responsibility. “Hong Kong is a small community. We have to learn how to share space and coexist responsibly.” Launched in 2013, the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards recognise individuals and organisations whose work contributes to Hong Kong and its communities.

title: Chinese great-grandfather, 101, defies ageing with daily diet of Coke, Sprite, seafood
description: Nanny who cares for Lu says he has a fantastic appetite, regularly finishing half a bowl of rice and a whole plate of crabs in a single meal.
content: A Chinese centenarian leads a happy, healthy life despite a habit generally considered “unhealthy”, prompting curious reactions online. A 101-year-old great-grandfather in eastern China’s Zhejiang province recently went viral for his love of drinking large amounts of Coca-Cola and Sprite. While young people in China embrace healthy lifestyles – eating foods inspired by traditional Chinese medicine, following low-sugar diets and taking daily footbaths – Lu Shizeng defies these practices yet remains hale and hearty at his ripe old age. Lu is especially particular about food. Living in the countryside, he takes a rickshaw to the town market every five days to buy seafood, including fish, shrimp and crabs, as well as pork and vegetables. Until last year, Lu reportedly still rode his own tricycle into town. But after a fall, he began moving more slowly, and his family forbade him from riding again. Lu said he spends most of his savings on food. His two sons – one living in Beijing and the other running a factory nearby – hired a nanny to look after him. The nanny said Lu has a great appetite, finishing half a bowl of rice and a whole plate of crabs in one meal. He also stocks up on carbonated drinks such as Coca-Cola and Sprite. Lu especially likes chilled Sprite with a few drops of white wine in it. He also enjoys sweet fruits such as watermelon, pears and mandarins. Lu maintains a regular daily routine. He goes to rest after dinner, which he finishes at 5pm, and falls asleep around 8pm. He usually wakes at 4am and spends another two hours leisurely stretching in bed before finally getting up at 6am. He also takes a nap every day at noon. Lu is very proud of his good health. “Some elderly people may have a stroke after a fall, but I’m totally fine. I can also remember things from my youth quite well,” he said. He added that he rarely catches a cold and has relatively low blood pressure. Furthermore, Lu said he is satisfied with the monthly old-age allowance he receives. In Zhejiang province, centenarians receive 800 yuan (US$120) a month. In comparison, people aged 90 to 99 receive only 100 yuan per month. “Living to 101 while drinking Coke – some experts might be unhappy now,” one online observer commented. “A good mood and a regular sleep schedule are the most important reasons behind his longevity,” another said. A third commented: “Some people are born this way. Their lifestyle is only a minor factor in their longevity, which is something that more than 99.9 per cent of people can only dream of.”

title: Style Edit: Rolex unveils the Perpetual Padellone with moonphase disc in 3 models
description: Drawing inspiration from the Swiss watchmaker’s vintage Ref. 8171, the complete calendar watch expands the Perpetual collection first launched in 2023.
content: When it comes to crafting watches with a satisfying vintage aesthetic, Rolex has just about the most captivating archive imaginable to draw on. That archive is the inspiration for the continual evolution of the Perpetual collection, the latest iteration of which was launched in 2023. The first model in that collection was the 1908, a dressy, retro-styled wristwatch that drew on designs from the early 20th century. For 2026, the collection has taken a major step forward in terms of complexity, adding a watch that combines an annual calendar with a moonphase: the Perpetual Padellone. Here, the inspiration is a Rolex classic first introduced in 1949: the Ref. 8171. But the Perpetual Padellone updates that watch with complications of rare sophistication. Powered by the new Calibre 7190, based on the 7135 movement at the heart of 2025’s dressy Land-Dweller sports watch, the Perpetual Padellone displays the time, day, date, month and moonphase on its dial. The day, date and month change instantly at midnight, with the day and month displayed next to each other between 11 and 1 o’clock, and the days of the month laid out around the edge of the dial, indicated by a blue hand with a crescent moon on it. Rolex’s Haplos system means that the watch can tell which months are 30 days long and which are 31, so it only needs to be adjusted once a year, at the end of February. The moonphase is a blue enamelled disc that rotates every 29.53 days, a full lunar month. Instead of doing what most moonphases do – obscuring an image of the moon some of the time – it displays both a full moon and a new moon, made from meteorite, which take it in turns to align with a triangular indicator at the top. The moonphase and calendar indications can all be set independently, using four correctors on the middle case that can be adjusted using a correction stylus. The Perpetual Padellone comes in three versions, each with a 39mm case. Two of them come with cases in the brand’s own Everose gold, paired with a white dial with a grained finish: one with a metallic Settimo bracelet, with its rows of seven polished links; and the other with a brown alligator leather strap. A matt black alligator leather strap can be found on the third version, where it complements a 950 platinum case and an ice blue dial, also with a grained finish.

title: IMF revises China GDP projection down this year, cautions on export reliance
description: The latest World Economic Outlook report warns export strength cannot bolster persistent property crisis, sluggish consumption.
content: The International Monetary Fund has trimmed its projection of China’s economic growth in 2026 by 0.1 percentage point to 4.5 per cent, cautioning that resilient exports are no longer sufficient to fully offset persistent weakness in domestic demand. The revised projection sits at the lower end of Beijing’s annual growth target for this year, down from the previous forecast of 4.6 per cent in July, according to the organisation’s latest World Economic Outlook, released on Tuesday. “Sluggishness in domestic consumption and weakening investment amid continued property sector strains were only partly offset by robust export performance,” the IMF said. “Higher global oil prices, together with protracted uncertainty and structural headwinds, are expected to weigh on activity,” it said, adding that policy support by Beijing was expected to prevent a “sharper slowdown”. The IMF projected oil prices would reach US$130 a barrel from the fourth quarter of 2026 to the first quarter of 2027, with limited scope for further inventory drawdown. Consequently, oil prices are projected to be 17 and 40 per cent higher on average in 2026 and 2027, respectively. In response to the IMF’s revised projection, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Tuesday that the country’s economic fundamentals remained solid and that Beijing was confident in its economic prospects. The world’s second-largest economy had set its target for gross domestic product growth at “4.5 to 5 per cent” for 2026, a shift from the “around 5 per cent” goal set in recent years, as the economy grapples with weak domestic demand, a prolonged property downturn and rising external risks. In the second quarter, China’s GDP grew by 4.3 per cent, missing market expectations and marking the lowest growth rate recorded since the end of 2022. Exports have provided a key source of support for growth this year as domestic demand remains subdued, with China’s exports rising 25 per cent year on year to US$401.44 billion in August. Meanwhile, its cumulative trade surplus reached US$805.51 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up about 3 per cent from the same period last year, customs data showed. The latest trade figures are due on Wednesday. The IMF said in its latest report that China’s trade surplus could widen further in 2026, following a record US$1.2 trillion surplus last year. But strong exports have yet to translate into a broader recovery in domestic demand, as the increasingly capital-intensive nature of export growth had limited its benefits for employment and household income, according to a Morgan Stanley report on Monday, produced by a team led by Robin Xing, chief China economist at the investment bank. Facing pressure to meet its annual growth rate target, Beijing has been ramping up policy support in recent weeks, including cutting interest rates for policy banks, offering mortgage interest subsidies for homebuyers and unlocking 550 billion yuan (US$82.2 billion) in local debt quotas to boost investment. Morgan Stanley expected Beijing’s targeted easing measures to underpin a modest growth rebound in the fourth quarter. Domestic demand is likely to remain under pressure into 2027 amid local debt strains, a weak property market and subdued consumer confidence. In an early October report, J.P. Morgan analysts noted that while weak consumption calls for further infrastructure spending and incremental stimulus, upcoming political milestones – including the fifth plenary session in late October and the run-up to the “two sessions” legislative meetings in March – could make local officials more risk-averse, thereby delaying project approvals. The IMF said it now expected China’s economic growth to slow further to 4 per cent in 2027, down from 4.1 per cent in its July projection.

title: Mainland Chinese traders boost Hong Kong stock buying for fourth month as AI bets surge
description: Southbound buying surges in September, with technology shares attracting the largest inflows.
content: Mainland Chinese investors bought more Hong Kong stocks than they sold for a fourth consecutive month in September, with purchases accelerating despite persistent headwinds from elevated US Treasury yields and oil prices. Onshore traders poured a net HK$60.8 billion (US$7.7 billion) into Hong Kong’s stocks via the Stock Connect programme last month, up from HK$10.4 billion in August, according to financial data provider Wind. Net buying reached HK$134.1 billion in the third quarter. Mainland investors concentrated on technology stocks, particularly artificial intelligence model developers, while healthcare shares recorded the heaviest selling. The inflows underscored mainland investors’ enthusiasm for Hong Kong stocks, particularly companies unavailable on China’s onshore markets, which remain more exposed to AI hardware makers. The buying frenzy helped Hong Kong stocks to relatively hold up last month, with the Hang Seng Index falling 3.7 per cent despite concerns about rising capital costs and heightened expectations of further US rate increases. China’s CSI 300 Index dropped nearly 6 per cent in September. Among the most-bought stocks in September, Chinese AI model developer Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, attracted inflows of HK$6.94 billion, while Baidu, the search engine operator behind large language model Ernie Bot, drew almost HK$6 billion, Wind data showed. Social media giant Tencent Holdings pulled in HK$3 billion. The strength of a rebound in Hong Kong stocks is building up after two months of corrections Kenneth Wu, ICBC International Conversely, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (SMIC), China’s biggest chipmaker, suffered net selling of HK$6.4 billion. Z.ai slumped 46 per cent in September, Baidu fell 11 per cent and SMIC retreated 14 per cent. By sector, the technology industry drew HK$22.6 billion of inflows, followed by industrial companies with HK$10.2 billion and financial firms with HK$9.9 billion. The healthcare industry recorded the largest outflows at HK$4.4 billion. “The strength of a rebound in Hong Kong stocks is building up after two months of corrections,” said Kenneth Wu, an analyst at ICBC International. “But the risk factors include an escalation of military actions in the event of a breakdown in US-Iran talks and China’s weak data on consumption and investment. So allocations should focus on growth tech stocks and dividend stocks.” Hong Kong stocks could face challenges in the fourth quarter amid China’s piecemeal stimulus efforts, tighter monetary policies in the US and a shifting narrative around the AI trade, according to investment banks. The Hang Seng Index could trade between 22,500 and 26,000 in the fourth quarter, with risks skewed to the downside, according to CCB International. The benchmark gauge rose 0.3 per cent to 24,345.22 on Tuesday.

title: Style Edit: How Richard Mille and Ferrari fuse horological artistry with Formula One precision
description: The collaboration between the Swiss watchmaker and the Italian sports carmaker has brought collectors two distinctive timepieces – the RM 43-01 and RM UP-01.
content: The fascination with Ferrari reaches well beyond what leaves the factory gates. It encompasses not only engineering and design, but also the culture of connoisseurship and collecting that has grown around the marque. Richard Mille speaks to much the same audience. Their partnership consequently reads not as an exercise in co-branding, but as the convergence of two distinct worlds connected by performance, craftsmanship and collectibility. When the two brands announced their multi-year partnership in 2021, they found common ground in an appetite for technology, innovation and uncompromising performance. The relationship reaches across Ferrari’s racing universe, from Formula One and endurance racing to the Ferrari Challenge and Driver Academy, creating a connection that extends well beyond the watch itself. That broader world is central to Richard Mille’s approach to luxury. The brand has always understood that its watches appeal to consumers who want more than technical specifications. They are objects with a strong sense of identity, often tied to the worlds of sport, motorsport, art and adventure. Ferrari brings another powerful dimension to that proposition: an established culture of enthusiasts and collectors, stretching from its loyal tifosi to owners of historic and contemporary Ferraris. For affluent consumers today, this kind of cultural connection is increasingly important. Luxury is no longer defined solely by rarity or craftsmanship; it is also about access, experience and the communities that form around the things people choose to collect. A Ferrari provides entry into a particular lifestyle of driving, design and competition. Richard Mille does something similar within contemporary watchmaking. Together, they create a proposition that speaks directly to collectors who see ownership as an extension of their interests and identity. Introduced last year, the RM 43-01 brings Ferrari’s design language directly to the wrist. Developed with Ferrari’s Centro Stile, its case, crown, pushers and strap borrow cues from the marque’s supercars, including the Purosangue, SF90 Stradale and Daytona SP3. Inside, the industrial theme continues. Textured surfaces evoke cast engine parts, while microblasted bridges, angular structures and X-shaped supports give the movement the appearance of a miniature power-train. Its tourbillon split-seconds chronograph has also been engineered for performance. Richard Mille refined the mechanism through extensive testing to improve efficiency and maintain steady torque throughout the watch’s power reserve. The partnership’s first major expression was the RM UP-01 Ferrari. Rather than translating Ferrari’s aesthetic literally onto a watch, Richard Mille approached the collaboration through the shared pursuit of performance. Measuring just 1.75mm thick, the watch required more than 6,000 hours of development and testing, while its 1.18mm movement was engineered to withstand accelerations of more than 5,000g. Its construction is equally revealing. Titanium was chosen for its combination of lightness and resistance, while the movement architecture was reworked almost entirely to achieve the extreme proportions. Even the winding system was reconsidered, with two integrated crowns replacing the conventional winding stem. The result is a watch in which engineering dictates the aesthetic rather than the other way round. Limited to 150 pieces, the RM UP-01 Ferrari also enters the territory of modern collecting, where scarcity is only one part of the appeal. Its significance comes from the story behind it: a highly unusual piece of watchmaking born from an exchange between Ferrari’s engineers and designers and Richard Mille’s technical team. That is perhaps the most compelling aspect of the partnership. Richard Mille does not need to recreate Ferrari on the wrist. Instead, it draws on the values and culture surrounding the marque – the pursuit of speed, the fascination with engineering, the pleasure of collecting and the emotional connection to performance. Ferrari, in turn, gains a partner whose watches occupy a similarly rarefied space in contemporary luxury. The appeal lies in that shared world. For a new generation of affluent collectors, the most desirable luxury experiences increasingly connect an exceptional object to a larger story. The Richard Mille-Ferrari partnership offers precisely that: a meeting of two cultures where craftsmanship is inseparable from performance, and ownership becomes a way of participating in something larger than the object itself.

title: Can Singapore engineer love on dating apps? From public service to private romance
description: FirstDate is being piloted among government employees aged 21 to 35 amid Singapore’s efforts to raise its fertility rate.
content: For Singaporean civil servant Clare*, finding a suitable lifelong partner has been an uphill battle. Swiping on dating apps soon became a chore after multiple unsuccessful first dates, so when the government launched its own platform, the 32-year-old was all for it. “It’s like: ‘Why not?’, and I think it does have a few screening procedures so it might save you some trouble like having to deal with impersonators or people who do not match with their advertised profiles,” she said. Singapore launched dating platform FirstDate last month, as the city state grapples with a record-low fertility rate. While the platform has drawn some criticism online for its limited range of eligibility, observers also say it is a good way to encourage first meetings for potential couples. FirstDate is being piloted among government employees aged 21 to 35 by GovTech, which told local media there was no decision yet to expand the initiative beyond the public sector. The government agency has not provided figures on how many users in the sector meet its present criteria for the app. Singapore’s public service workforce is about 158,000-strong as of March this year, according to the government job portal. App users answer a survey about their interests and values, and the platform uses a Nobel Prize-winning algorithm to generate recommended pairings based on participants’ preferences and compatibility. The first round of sign-ups closed on October 5 after emails on the platform were sent to public officers a week before. A matching cycle lasts about a month, according to local media reports. Public reaction to the app has been mixed, with some online commentators arguing that limiting it to civil servants is elitist and that having an age limit implies an expiration date for relationships. Many also pointed out that dating was not a top priority for young Singaporeans facing rising living costs. If life was cheaper, people would “go out more often, go dating and have kids”, one social media user wrote. The FirstDate platform, which matches participants to one partner at a time, can still be effective for those who are serious about finding love, according to Norman Li, a psychology professor at the Singapore Management University. “Today, people are overwhelmed with perceived choices, many of which are not even real choices, which makes it psychologically hard to settle down and stay with any one person,” he said. But he noted that the agency faced the challenge of getting enough sign-ups to broaden the dating pool and increase users’ chances of perceiving potential matches as suitable and attractive partners. “A major problem today is that people’s standards are too high for the market to clear, due to constant exposure to celebrities, internet and movie stars and dating app choices,” Li said. For Jean Liu, an associate professor of psychology at the Singapore Institute of Technology, restricting matches is a positive as it helps prevent dating fatigue and being overwhelmed by choices. “You won’t have a few highly popular individuals flooded with attention, as you might on a typical app,” she said. The platform launch comes amid the city state’s battle to raise its fertility rate, which sank to a low of 0.87 last year. The government has rolled out new measures, including increasing childcare leave and lowering childcare fees, and set up an inter-agency work group to tackle the trend. Li said that FirstDate likely had similar goals of boosting marriage and fertility. The platform – powered by an algorithm that earned one of its creators a Nobel memorial prize in economic sciences in 2012 – is the latest in a series of Singaporean initiatives aimed at matching singles. In 1984, the government launched the Social Development Unit (SDU), which organised events for university graduates to meet up. In a speech a year earlier, Singapore’s founding father Lee Kuan Yew had warned that graduates were marrying late and having fewer children than the less educated. A separate body, the Social Development Section (SDN), was created in 1985 for those with only secondary school qualifications. In 2009, both units were merged and renamed the Social Development Network to widen the dating pool and create more opportunities for singles to meet and eventually marry. Li predicted FirstDate would be more successful than its predecessors. “The goals are the same as before, but SDU and SDN were event-based, which apparently didn’t attract too many people,” he said. “This time, a systematic dating app has been thoughtfully designed to create matches.” Liu, however, said the initiatives were fundamentally different. FirstDate sprouted from a GovTech “hackathon”, she said, and should be best viewed as a government product trial that borrowed the agile and experimental approach of private tech. She urged users to refrain from dismissing the platform because it was a government project. “When others step in, whether the government or our own family members, it can feel orchestrated and ‘unromantic’,” she said. “However, if we look across history and in many parts of the world, relationships have often been arranged or brokered by families or communities.” Daniel Goh, an associate professor of sociology at the National University of Singapore, agreed that it was premature to pass judgment on the platform since it was still in its pilot phase. “I would be shocked if the government does not open the platform to citizens if it is proven successful,” he said. “The question is: what is the threshold for success?” Other Asian countries, faced with a similarly dipping birth rate, have also tried to play Cupid. In 2024, Japan launched a government-backed dating app that required users to prove they were committed to marriage, verify their income and undergo an interview with the app operator. As of June this year, 16,000 people had registered on the app, 760 couples were in “serious relationships” and 265 couples had tied the knot, according to Japanese government data. Also in 2024, authorities in South Korea launched a dating programme for participants in Seoul to mingle through curated activities, such as outdoor dining by the Han River. Some 126 couples were matched during that event, prompting the city government to roll-out the second edition last month, which was heavily oversubscribed with more than 2,300 singles aged 25 to 45 registering for just 100 slots. According to a survey by pollster YouGov, one in four Singaporeans used dating apps in 2024, with Gen Zs and millennials more likely than older generations to have done so. Out of those who have swiped for love online, 59 per cent used Tinder – making it the most popular platform – and 46 per cent took to Coffee Meets Bagel. Civil servant Clare, meanwhile, is keeping her hopes up despite not finding a match after the first round of pairings concluded on FirstDate. “I’m slightly bummed, but I’ll wait for the next cycle to start to try again.” *Full name withheld at interviewee’s request

title: Thailand’s deepening labour shortage roils harvest as unpicked fruits rot
description: ‘We have to choose which fruit to harvest and leave the lower-priced fruit to rot on the trees,’ a farmer says.
content: Ripe mangosteen and rambutan hang unpicked from trees in eastern Thailand, where a shortage of migrant workers is forcing growers to decide which crops are valuable enough to harvest and which will be left to rot. For Jomsak Putirattana, who also grows durian in Chanthaburi province, the departure of his five Cambodian workers after a border dispute disrupted crossings has intensified competition for labour. Daily wages have more than doubled in some cases, from about 350 baht to 400 baht (US$10 to US$12) to as much as 800 baht to 1,000 baht, he said, making some lower-value crops too costly to harvest. “We have to choose which fruit to harvest and leave the lower-priced fruit to rot on the trees,” Jomsak said. His hope of keeping more of the crop from going to waste “is dimming every day”, he added. The dearth of workers highlights Thailand’s growing dependence on migrant labour as an ageing population shrinks its domestic workforce. Migrants account for roughly a 10th of the nation’s labour force. Workers from neighbouring Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos have long filled jobs on farms, construction sites and factory floors that employers struggle to recruit Thais to do. Increasingly, they are also behind shop counters, serving tables at restaurants and bars, and filling other service jobs across Bangkok and major cities. Geopolitical pressures are reducing the nation’s migrant pool. The country’s border dispute with Cambodia prompted many Cambodians to leave Thailand, while political turmoil and recruitment restrictions in Myanmar are making hiring more migrant workers a slower and more difficult process. Recruitment in Myanmar now takes six to eight months, according to Myat Thu, managing director of recruitment agency Kaung Myat San Thu. Complaints over wages, subcontracting and worker protections have also made some Thai construction jobs less attractive to workers in Myanmar. So Thailand is looking further afield with plans to recruit workers from Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh for the first time, according to Labour Minister Julapun Amornvivat. The shift could put Thailand in greater competition for migrant labour with Singapore and Malaysia, which already draw workers from South Asia. “We need to build resilience and flexibility, rather than depend too heavily on any one source,” Julapun said in an interview. The first Sri Lankan workers are expected to arrive in January, primarily for construction projects. Thailand has discussed an initial pilot of about 10,000 workers, while labour agreements with Nepal and Bangladesh are expected next year. The search for new workers is particularly urgent for Thailand’s construction industry, where migrants account for 60 to 70 per cent of a workforce of about 4.2 million to 4.5 million people, according to Liza Ngamtrakulpanit, president of the Thai Contractors Association. Employers warn that shortages could delay major infrastructure projects and private construction while squeezing contractors’ cash flow as developments are held up. The government is also preparing a broader registration programme to more quickly renew migrant worker permits and bring undocumented migrants already in Thailand into the legal workforce, potentially covering millions of people, the labour minister said. For Jomsak, longer-term reforms may come too late for the next harvest. Eastern Thailand produces fruit valued at about 200 billion baht annually by his estimate, with the primary season compressed into four or five months beginning in late April. While some businesses are moving workers from other parts of Thailand to fill the gaps, Jomsak sees that as a temporary relief. “What we’re doing is giving a painkiller to treat the wound,” he said. “The problem is still there.”

title: Opinion | Apec a chance for Hong Kong to earn its place in China’s tourism boom
description: As Beijing makes visits easier for overseas travellers, Hong Kong must learn what it takes to be included in their itineraries.
content: Over the coming weeks, Hong Kong and Shenzhen will host two major gatherings of Asia-Pacific decision-makers. Hong Kong’s first Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting takes place on October 20-21, with around 500 visitors expected, while Shenzhen hosts the Apec Economic Leaders’ Week next month. These Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum meetings will bring international visitors to two neighbouring cities at the centre of China’s Apec year. For Hong Kong’s tourism industry, they offer a timely opportunity to turn that attention into longer stays in the city and encourage visitors to explore more of China. There is a question we need to answer first. As overseas travellers find it easier to visit mainland cities directly, what would persuade them to include Hong Kong in that journey? The central government’s latest plans make the question timely. Last month, Vice-Minister of Culture and Tourism Wang Jianhua outlined further improvements to inbound travel services, covering visas, payments, accommodation and transport. He also described plans for experiences combining traditional culture with contemporary Chinese life. The mainland recorded 154 million inbound tourist trips last year, up 17.1 per cent, with visitor spending exceeding US$130 billion. Its tourism development plan sets goals of 190 million inbound visits and more than US$150 billion in annual spending by 2030. This creates a growing market in which Hong Kong businesses can compete for customers. Hong Kong can combine its international connections and established visitor services with convenient access to mainland destinations. For visitors uncertain about planning a China holiday, that combination could offer a manageable introduction. Our tourism businesses have an opportunity to connect the two, helping customers choose experiences on the mainland and providing dependable support throughout their journey. Multi-destination tourism provides a foundation. Hong Kong’s Tourism Board already offers “Hong Kong+GBA” and “Hong Kong+Chinese mainland” products for European travellers to combine visits to Hong Kong with the Greater Bay Area and other mainland destinations in a single trip. It has also worked with partners in North America and Europe to promote travel across destinations. The offers should also reflect differences between visitor markets. There were 12.1 million non-mainland visitors to Hong Kong last year, about 24 per cent of total arrivals; overnight visitors stayed an average of 3.1 nights. Operators could develop a straightforward Greater Bay Area extension for first-time visitors and more specialised food or cultural itineraries for returning travellers. This would give the Tourism Board and the travel trade a clearer basis for promoting products to different audiences. Turning this opportunity into business requires coordinated action. Local tour operators and destination management companies can build bookable itineraries around interests such as food, culture, golf or contemporary urban life. They can bring together Hong Kong and mainland experiences, arrange transport and accommodation, and give visitors a clear point of contact throughout the trip. The Tourism Board can help these products reach visitors while they are planning their journeys. Working with overseas travel trade, airlines, event organisers and mainland tourism partners, it can promote itineraries that give Hong Kong a meaningful place in a China holiday. The meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (MICE) sector gives this proposal stronger commercial footing. Hong Kong welcomed 2.51 million MICE visitors last year; 1.43 million stayed overnight, generating about HK$10.7 billion (US$1.36 billion) in spending. Business events already bring overnight stays and substantial spending to the city. Tourism operators can build on this by offering delegates and accompanying visitors extensions that combine Hong Kong with destinations across the Greater Bay Area. Hotels have a direct commercial stake. Hong Kong hotel associations can help members work with tour operators and mainland partners to offer extensions before or after a Hong Kong stay, with clear referral arrangements. Restaurants, guides and attractions can be included in those packages, giving visitors a reason to set aside time for the city. The city government can also help bring Hong Kong and mainland authorities together to address cross-boundary barriers that individual operators cannot resolve, including gaps in ticketing arrangements and coordination between tourism services. This would give businesses a more workable basis for building and selling multi-destination packages. The commercial concern is real: time spent elsewhere may mean fewer nights or less spending in Hong Kong. The test is whether these partnerships bring visitors, stays and spending the city would otherwise miss. Operators and tourism bodies should track those results, alongside repeat bookings, to see which itineraries create lasting value for Hong Kong. Delivering such a journey requires attention to unfamiliar details. Visitors need accurate guidance on entry requirements, realistic transport arrangements and help when plans change. Notably, Hong Kong’s four ports connected to the mainland – including West Kowloon Station and the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge port – joined its 240-hour visa-free transit scheme last November. Eligibility still needs to be checked against nationality and itinerary. The coming Apec meetings offer an occasion to test a small selection of extensions with delegates and accompanying visitors. Their questions and booking decisions could help operators understand what makes an offer useful. The lessons could shape packages for subsequent conferences and exhibitions. Success would be measured through additional Hong Kong nights, local spending and repeat bookings. Operators would also need to establish whether their offers attract customers who would otherwise have chosen another route or destination. As mainland China becomes easier to explore, Hong Kong will need to earn its place in visitors’ itineraries. Our businesses can do so by making the city a rewarding part of the holiday and helping travellers experience what lies beyond it. A well-organised first journey could begin a customer relationship that brings further visits and business to Hong Kong.

title: Chinese stocks an undervalued opportunity, says Charlie Munger disciple
description: Value-investing adherent Li Lu of Himalaya Capital says excellent firms are trading at low prices relative to their competitiveness.
content: Shares in Chinese companies present better opportunities today than at other times, a disciple of legendary investor Charlie Munger said in a rare reflection on the world’s second-largest economy amid tensions with the US and the ongoing artificial intelligence race. The comments by Li Lu, Chinese-American founder and chairman of Seattle-based value investment firm Himalaya Capital, came amid divergence between the markets on opposite sides of the Pacific. While stock markets in China and Hong Kong have been struggling despite China’s economic growth, supply chain dominance and fast technology advances, US stocks have defied high inflation, government debt concerns and two-decade-high Treasuries yields to hit new highs. “If you are rational investors and look at the whole picture, you might take a different perspective,” said Li, who was close to Munger, the late partner of Warren Buffett in Berkshire Hathaway. “In today’s market, you probably find better opportunities than you would find in different times.” Li shared his views during an event at Columbia Business School in New York last week, returning to his alma mater for an in-depth dialogue with Columbia professor Tano Santos. Acknowledging the impact of China’s property downturn and 10 years of stagnation in the country’s financial markets, the veteran investor said he also saw bright spots in the Chinese economy: its manufacturing prowess was advancing, as were its technological self-reliance and competitiveness. Some excellent Chinese firms were being traded at relatively low prices, Li said. The veteran adherent to Buffett’s value investing principles – which also attract many Chinese followers – highlighted the mutual dependency of a single global market, though he added that the fast economic rise of China had reshaped the world order and triggered the tension with the US. “Everybody is competing fearlessly, all believing time is on their side,” Li said. China aimed to achieve semiconductor self-sufficiency, while the US hoped for an AI breakthrough, and other countries had their own calculations, he said. “But it all highlights that peaceful stability is of strategic importance, and the largest countries really do have the responsibility and the desire to keep it that way,” he added. The current market bifurcation offered rational investors a better opportunity set than other periods, according to Li. Staying rational, which was difficult during a major technological wave, could dramatically expand investment possibilities, and as a result, the market’s speculative side became far more active. “At a given time, one doesn’t really create an enormous amount of new capital,” he said. “If capital is overwhelmingly driven to the top, that means the market can easily bifurcate, with a whole bunch of otherwise wonderful businesses trading at very low prices. This holds true in the US, China or any other place.” As an investor applying value investing globally, one insight is that “wealth in the end is really the percentage of ownership of global purchasing power”, Li said. “And the way we express that is by buying great businesses in the most dynamic economies at advantageous prices and waiting long enough for the value to preserve and grow over time.” Turning to AI, Li said the technology was enormously helpful and transformative, yet also extraordinarily dangerous. Society needed to establish a firm red line so that humans would always remain in the loop, he said. AI presented a more complex challenge than earlier technologies, he added. “This technology will always have incremental costs associated with it, and this is fundamentally different from the internet or a bunch of previous technologies, where you make a one-time investment and can advertise for a long time,” he said. “So you have four or five layers of consideration for the pacing and development.”

title: China Mobile triples capacity at mega Inner Mongolia computing hub amid nation’s AI push
description: The US$403 million expansion covers 44,500 square metres, equivalent to six soccer fields, and boasts a total power capacity of 120 megawatts.
content: China Mobile, one of the country’s state-backed telecoms giants, has tripled the capacity of its largest intelligent computing hub in northern Inner Mongolia, amid Beijing’s push to boost digital infrastructure to power the country’s artificial intelligence ambitions. The expansion of its data centre in Hohhot was recently completed, with total processing capacity increased to 20,100 petaflops, according to a report by Inner Mongolia Daily on Monday. That was triple its previous capacity of 6,700 petaflops, according to data from a 2024 report by the state-run People’s Posts and Telecommunications News. A petaflop is a measurement of a computer’s speed and is equal to a quadrillion operations per second. Of that total, 16,700 petaflops were dedicated to artificial intelligence and smart computing tasks, the Monday report said. The project, the world’s largest single-site intelligent computing centre run by a telecoms operator, would funnel 90 per cent of the computing power to the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei economic zone, according to the report. The 2.7 billion yuan (US$403 million) expansion project covers roughly 44,500 square metres, equivalent to six soccer fields, and boasts a total power capacity of 120 megawatts. The megaproject cements the role of the computing hub – which began operations in 2024 and deploys around 20,000 AI accelerator cards. It also underscores Beijing’s broader drive for tech self-reliance, with the northern Chinese region seen as a critical node in its “Eastern Data, Western Computing” strategy. The National Development and Reform Commission, China’s top economic planner, said a total of 4 trillion yuan would be invested in national computing network buildout during the 15th five-year plan. Launched in 2022, the Eastern Data, Western Computing initiative aims to move data processing from the country’s densely populated, power-hungry eastern seaboard to its energy-rich western provinces. Hohhot, the capital of Inner Mongolia, and Ulanqab, another major city in the autonomous region, have emerged as a key link in this massive infrastructure network. Ulanqab, historically known for potato farming, is now dubbed “Grassland Silicon Valley” because it has attracted tech heavyweights like Huawei Technologies, ByteDance and DeepSeek, as well as some US tech giants. In 2013, Huawei began working with the Ulanqab municipal government to expand its data centre presence there. Five years later, US tech giant Apple announced plans to host its iCloud service on data centres in the city, the same year Chinese cloud platform UCloud began building its own facility in Ulanqab. ByteDance had been in preliminary talks with local data centre vendors to add between five and six gigawatts’ worth of compute in Ulanqab over the next two years, the South China Morning Post reported in September. The China Mobile Hohhot intelligent computing project also touts a high percentage of green energy adoption, reflecting Beijing’s efforts to align the rapid expansion of AI with national carbon goals. Green electricity powers 88 per cent of the facility, according to the Monday report.

title: Exclusive | China keeps extending the Shenzhen Apec deadline. Why are US execs so unenthused?
description: Some American CEOs are said to be skipping the gathering because of poor communication about the summit schedule and planned events.
content: Some senior American executives are lukewarm about attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and related business events in Shenzhen next month, according to people familiar with the matter. They cited limited scheduling details, few expected breakthroughs and a lack of opportunity for meaningful engagement. Beijing has invited multiple US business leaders – particularly those who joined President Donald Trump’s May trip to China and later attended the White House state dinner for Xi Jinping in September, the sources said. But some CEOs have decided not to attend the event because of a lack of concrete details about the schedule and planned meetings. It comes just weeks after a group of Chinese executives were not able to attend the state dinner for Xi in Washington, despite being in the US capital at the time. Some of America’s biggest tycoons – including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Goldman Sachs’ David Solomon – joined Trump’s business delegation in Beijing and were among the 130 high-profile guests at the White House during Xi’s visit. One source said Beijing viewed those who attended both events as top-tier guests who represented the most advanced industries in the United States. Executives from American companies with operations in China were also said to be on the invitation list for the Shenzhen gathering, as well as those from leading businesses in other Apec countries. However, two separate sources said that a few US business leaders had dropped out due to a lack of communication from Beijing about the summit schedule and planned events. According to them, some of the CEOs have moved on to other commitments and begun scheduling alternative engagements. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the matter publicly. One of the sources said China had extended the deadline for companies to register for the summit several times, suggesting that interest so far had been lukewarm and that Beijing was not addressing the reasons behind the muted response. The source added that if China was committed to attracting CEOs to Apec, it would release the schedule and coordinate their itineraries and meetings. The person also said that Apec offered limited opportunities for meaningful engagement for many CEOs, making attendance optional. Another source said there appeared to be a disconnect between the two sides regarding the agenda and meetings. The Apec CEO summit will be held from November 17 to 18 in Shenzhen and will be followed by the leaders’ summit from November 18 to 19, when 21 economies – including the US, Russia, Japan and South Korea – will meet to discuss regional economic cooperation and trade issues. Trump and Xi will meet on the sidelines of the summit – their third meeting in seven months. Xi is also expected to travel to Miami in December for the Group of 20 summit, which the US is hosting this year. Xi is expected to hold bilateral talks with other counterparts on the sidelines of Apec, including Russian President Vladimir Putin, and there is speculation that there could be a trilateral meeting between Xi, Putin and Trump. One source said Beijing’s focus on inviting those who attended the White House dinner suggested an approach that ignored Washington’s resistance to Chinese investment and the limited scope for outcomes at a multilateral forum like Apec. The issue of business leaders accompanying top officials on such trips has been in the spotlight after a group of Chinese business leaders were excluded from the White House guest list last month at the last minute, despite being in Washington at the time. The South China Morning Post earlier reported that they were left out due to poor communication between Beijing and Washington, the two sides’ differing views on reciprocity and the White House’s unclear attitude towards Chinese investments in the United States. Additional reporting by Dewey Sim

title: ‘Everyone wants to make history’: revamped Huanggang Port opens to brisk business
description: Travel agencies launch special tours as retailers welcome more customers at the 24-hour border checkpoint.
