content: Hong Kong travel agencies and border shops have capitalised on the opening of the revamped Huanggang Port as thousands of visitors poured through the control point, with special tours on offer and shopkeepers reporting brisk business. Agents said the port’s 24-hour joint clearance arrangements could give cross-border tourism a major boost, although crowd control measures dampened trade at the checkpoint entrance. Tour groups organised by Hong Kong travel agency Big Line Holiday were among the first visitors at the upgraded checkpoint on Monday morning. Chan Yin-ping, the agency’s chairwoman, said about 1,000 people had joined the tours, with 20 groups scheduled between 10am and 1pm. Plans for further tours had yet to be decided, pending a smooth first few days of operation. The agency staggered the tours across different time slots to avoid putting too much pressure on the new checkpoint. “But we still decided to organise the tours because today is the first day and everyone wants to make history,” she said. Chan was confident the port would give tourism a boost. “The port is open 24 hours and Shenzhen is just across the border from the New Territories, unlike the round-the-clock crossing at the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge, which involves a much longer journey,” she said. “You can have supper, watch a movie and still make it back to Hong Kong, or even stay for breakfast. Joint clearance is more convenient too.” The tour costs HK$299 (US$38) and includes a buffet lunch and a visit to Honghuashan Park in Shenzhen. Among the participants were retirees Thomas Li and Wendy Sung, both in their sixties. Li, who lives in Ma On Shan, said the new port made it easier to reach Shenzhen without having to transfer to the East Rail line. “The port is sure to bring more visitors to Ma On Shan, since there is a direct bus route connecting the two places,” he said. Sung said she wanted to take pictures of the port’s eye-shaped observation deck. “I am looking forward to experiencing the joint clearance arrangements I read about in the news,” she said. The revamped Huanggang Port officially opened on Monday after six years of redevelopment, becoming the first Hong Kong-mainland China border checkpoint to adopt a “joint clearance” immigration system. Located next to the Futian checkpoint, the new port replaces the old Huanggang facility, which served residents arriving by shuttle bus from San Tin or by private car via Lok Ma Chau. With immigration procedures for both Hong Kong and Shenzhen handled inside the same building, authorities said clearance times would be cut from 30 minutes to five minutes for travellers on foot, and from 10 minutes to two minutes for drivers. According to the Security Bureau, the new control point had handled 20,201 incoming and 22,011 departing travellers by 5pm. The 42,212 passenger trips recorded represented a 181 per cent increase compared with average Monday traffic last month at the previous control point. The new port also handled 2,713 incoming and 2,995 outgoing vehicles. The number of vehicle trips was 12 per cent more than the average recorded on Mondays last month. Businesses around the port reported an increase in customers, with some rolling out promotions to mark the opening. Nana Xue, owner of Tiger Teochew, a restaurant serving Chiu Chow dishes, said the eatery was offering a 12 per cent discount from Monday until the end of the month, and that business had exceeded expectations. “We have around 60 per cent more customers than average, 30 per cent more than we expected,” she said. Zhou Qunhui, manager of a 7-Eleven convenience store at Huanggang Checkpoint station, said customer numbers were double the usual average, although crowd control measures meant she saw fewer people than she had hoped. Railings had been set up in front of her store to channel passengers towards the checkpoint, diverting footfall away from the shop. “I hope the railings can be removed later. Around 200 customers came in the afternoon, but I expected more on the opening day,” she said. Hongkongers were exploring the nearby shopping areas, although some said the surroundings still felt sparse. Yoyo Chen, 50, said she was still familiarising herself with the area and had not spent anything yet. “The old Huanggang Port nearby was quite quiet, and I have not seen many shops around the new port. Other ports, such as Futian, have more businesses and are more vibrant,” she said. Another visitor, surnamed Chan and in his sixties, said he had lunch at a nearby restaurant. “We did not set a spending budget; we are just wandering around, but so far nothing special,” he said.

title: Not just about tax: why Australia’s tech entrepreneurs are moving to Singapore
description: Singapore’s start-up ecosystem, commitment to innovation and proximity to Australia are among pull factors, industry players note.
content: Investor Ben Lindsay relocated from Sydney to Singapore in March, with wife and dog in tow – his sights set on growing venture capital firm Investible from an Australian outfit into an Asia-Pacific one. Lindsay is among a growing number of investors, businessmen and tech founders from down under who are setting up bases and relocating to Singapore, Dubai and San Francisco to expand their company’s reach. For example, Australian billionaire Adrian Portelli, founder of savings and rewards platform LMCT+, announced on social media in August that he was moving to Dubai. But for Lindsay, Singapore, with its start-up ecosystem and proximity to Australia, stood out among the possible destinations. Earlier this month, Fred Schebesta, co-founder of Australian comparison website Finder, also relocated to the Southeast Asian country, becoming the latest high-profile entrepreneur to leave Australia, citing zero capital gains tax and a more favourable business climate. The trend follows Canberra’s announcement in May of major tax reforms that were deeply unpopular among business owners and investors. The new rules centre on the government’s plan to replace the current 50 per cent capital gains tax discount with one based on the actual rate of inflation. Come July 1, 2027, a minimum 30 per cent tax on gains will be introduced. Schebesta told Yahoo Finance last week that the government’s capital gains tax overhaul was the “nail in the coffin” for Australia. He also cited an accumulation of anti-business regulations, compliance costs and red tape that made scaling difficult. For Lindsay, Singapore’s pull factors were just as important, if not more so. “Honestly, tax was never the driver for me,” he told This Week in Asia, noting the appeal of the city state’s business and investment community. “Whether it’s the education system, or the way Singapore has turned very limited natural resources into a global powerhouse, there’s something special here. I felt I’d learn more from the people living and working in Singapore than I would back home.” His relocation aligned with the company’s strategy to expand across the Asia-Pacific region, and Singapore felt like the natural next chapter, he added. The city state’s commitment to research and its role as a regional hub made it an ideal base for his company handling investments in climate and deep tech, Lindsay said. Singapore has pledged S$37 billion (US$28.9 billion) to boost research, innovation and enterprise over five years, starting in April this year. “That’s a government putting serious money behind turning research into companies, which is exactly what deep tech founders need,” Lindsay said. Roy Green, a professor emeritus and special innovation adviser at the University of Technology Sydney, is quick to point out that Australian entrepreneurs moving elsewhere “is not a new phenomenon”, saying the country still has a vibrant start-up community thanks to investors and international students setting up shop there. “The Australian government is now looking for the right balance between tax concessions, targeted grants and equity stakes for early-stage ventures and businesses growing into global markets and value chains,” he said. Green said he expected to see a more settled incentive framework by the time of the next federal budget in May 2027. Still, growing interest from Australian entrepreneurs and small and medium-sized enterprises eyeing Singapore as a base for regional growth has not escaped the attention of industry players. “Singapore remains an important gateway for Australian businesses looking to engage Southeast Asia, while Australian expertise and capability continue to support collaboration across priority sectors including technology, the digital economy and the green transition,” Australian High Commissioner to Singapore Robyn Mudie told This Week in Asia. Batya Shulman, president of the Australian Chamber of Commerce Singapore, cites Singapore’s stability, connectivity and pro-business environment as “strong drawcards” that make the city state “an ideal launch pad into the region”. The chamber was building on this through initiatives offering practical support and real connections in the wider Australia-Singapore business relationship, Shulman said. Amelia Walsh, senior trade and investment commissioner at the Australian Trade and Investment Commission Singapore, agreed that Australian tech firms could use the city state as a hub to meet customers, build partnerships and better understand market opportunities across the region. Corporate service providers told This Week in Asia that tax increases were not the sole reason for the growing Australian interest over the past year. Ray Tay, director of Vivos, said his company handled an average of 12 inquiries per month across August and September, compared with two per month last year. “The founders who do well here are moving for the market, not just the tax rate,” he said. “They are building a regional business with real customers, staff and investors in Asia. Singapore increasingly expects that substance too, in both its work pass and tax rules.” Beatrice Lim, head of client relations at corporate service provider Margin Wheeler, similarly noted that Australia-linked inquiries during the first nine months of this year were about 150 per cent higher than over the same period last year. Lim said the increase was visible before Australia’s tax reforms were announced in May, and unlikely to be tax-driven as none of the inquiries specifically cited this as the reason. “For Australian founders, Singapore’s position as a gateway to Southeast Asia, its English-speaking business environment, established legal and regulatory framework, access to professional and financial services, and relative ease of establishing and operating a company can all form part of that attraction,” Lim said. Lindsay also encouraged Australian entrepreneurs not to move for tax reasons alone. “Australia and Singapore have always been close partners,” he said. “I’d love to see more Australian founders treat Singapore as a second home base, not a departure lounge or second thought to the US or Europe.”

title: Hong Kong athletics team face make-or-break period after 0 medals at Asian Games
description: Failing to win a world championship medal next year, or not qualifying for the Olympics, could see the sport lose its Tier A status at HKSI.
content: There were many reasons for Hong Kong to celebrate the recent Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. From the most golds won to bringing home a record-breaking number of medals, the city generally fared well at the multi-sport event. Whether it was the 11 golds or the 54 medals from the city’s athletes playing in 14 sports, some sports, notably sailing, were the biggest winners of all, with four golds and 10 medals overall. Fencing, swimming, cycling, karate and squash all won their fair share of medals, followed by wushu and rowing. But there were also sports that yielded no results. Three years after Tiffany Yue Nga-yan saved their skin – in terms of elite athletes’ support – with a women’s long jump bronze medal in Hangzhou, the city’s 38 athletes returned home empty-handed from Japan, after athletics barely reached the Paris Olympic Games via the Universality rule. Failing to win a world championship medal next year, or being unable to have one athlete qualify for the Olympic Games in Los Angeles on their own merits, could see the sport lose its Tier A status at the Hong Kong Sports Institute (HKSI). Senior executives of the sport had told the South China Morning Post before the regional games that there was “always pressure to win a medal”, and admitted they must now secure a ticket to the City of Angels on their own, something they last managed at the Tokyo Games. “We need to be event-oriented or athlete-oriented, and study where we have better chances of success,” Simon Yeung Sai-mo, senior vice-chairman of the Hong Kong, China Association of Athletics Affiliates (HKAAA), said. “We will then focus our resources on that event, and support those athletes the best we can. “Long-distance running is prosperous in Hong Kong, and the women’s marathon looks realistic not only because of the larger participation pool. “Virginia Lo Ying-chiu could finish a half marathon in one hour and 12 minutes. You double that, plus six more minutes. If she can finish a full marathon around that time, it would give quite some ranking points.” With entry standards counting in only performances achieved in competitions of category C and above, Yeung added that athletes may need to participate in more contests “here and there” to amass points. “The association is also studying how to slightly postpone next year’s national championships so that it falls within the Los Angeles Olympics’ qualification window, and ensure the 2028 edition is also within that period,” he said. “That would give us a chance to earn double points and every country is doing the same.” The “very high” entry standards to the world championships and the Olympics, however, were not helping Hong Kong’s case. The benchmarks for the 44 individual events – men’s and women’s – were all significantly ahead of the city’s records, leaving Yeung to concede that reaching the Olympics via world rankings remained “the most practical path” not only for Hong Kong but “most of the Asian countries”. “World Athletics’ standards are really high, but it’s a commercial world out there after all,” he said. “We need to find our ways to get it done. “Qualifying through rankings means we need to find the right tournaments to participate in, and athletes could be exposed to being overtaken by rivals behind, but it’s reality.” Equestrian, whose last Asian Games medals came in 2023 in Hangzhou, faced a similar challenge after the sport also missed out on the Paris Games two years ago. There was also no gold medal at the National Games last year, or medals of any colour at the FEI World Championships in August. The Hong Kong Equestrian Federation acknowledged “we’re facing difficulties staying in Tier A”, regardless of whether they qualify for the next Olympics. The federation declined to comment, suggesting that funding and evaluation matters were not something that “we are in a position to discuss publicly at this stage”. By the letter of the law, any sport has to fulfil one of the four criteria – Olympic qualification, Asian Games medal, world championships medal or National Games gold medal – on top of scoring 10 or more Elite Vote Support Scheme points under the HKSI during the two-year review cycle. Badminton also has yet to produce any medals at the required events in recent years, but its streak of consistently sending athletes to the Olympics since the 1992 Games in Barcelona should spare it from any trouble. In a written reply to the SCMP, a HKSI spokesman declined to confirm the status of individual sports, suggesting that it is “subject to the Elite Sports Commission and Sports Commission” to make the final call. There was also encouraging news for the city’s athletes in those weeks in Japan. Tennis was serving an “observation period” before the Asian Games, but they saved themselves in style. Coleman Wong Chak-lam’s men’s singles gold medal not only fulfilled the criteria and secured the sport’s elite status for four more years, but it also earned him a spot at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Gymnastics also managed to get off the hook after Ng Ka-ki took bronze in men’s vault, behind Carlos Yulo of the Philippines and Mahdi Olfati of Iran. It was the typical case of one athlete saving the entire sport. Former gymnast Stone Shek Wai-hung, who now coaches the city’s women’s team, has done it a few times for his sport by winning back-to-back gold medals at the 2014 and 2018 Asian Games, and qualifying for the 2024 Olympics. But for gymnastics – which only regained its status in 2011 after an exile at the institute since the start of the millennium – why it is still considered an elite sport after producing only two athletes capable of winning a medal at the regional games in 15 years, is a legitimate question. “Questions regarding the development of gymnastics in Hong Kong are for our head coach, who is at the world championship now and will be back in November,” Albert Ng Tsz-kin, executive director of the Gymnastics Association of Hong Kong, China, said. “We executives at the association couldn’t really answer the question.”

title: Environmental concerns see China fall 3 places in global ‘trade sustainability’ ranking
description: Hinrich-IMD Sustainable Trade Index ranks mainland 19th out of 30 major economies – 15 places behind Hong Kong.
content: Mainland China fell three places this year on a global ranking for trade sustainability, tracking what the compilers of the index described as declines in economic and environmental metrics. The Hinrich-IMD Sustainable Trade Index, which was released on Tuesday, ranked the mainland 19th out of 30 major economies. The United Kingdom ranked first, Singapore second, New Zealand third and Hong Kong fourth. The 30 economies covered by the annual index are evaluated on their ability to grow economically through international trade – with multilateral trade deal participation a major criterion – as well as for environmental soundness, which includes natural resource management and per-capita emissions. A third pillar is societal factors covering education and labour standards. The mainland fell primarily because of “modest declines in its economic and environmental performance” compared with other economies in the index, said Jia Hui Tee, senior trade policy analyst at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, adding that “weaker performance” in macroeconomic indicators such as real gross domestic product growth per capita had weighed on the ranking. The foundation, a philanthropic organisation focused on trade, first published the index in 2016 and now releases annual rankings together with the IMD World Competitiveness Centre at the IMD Business School in Switzerland. The mainland’s economic output grew by 4.7 per cent year on year in the first half of this year, lower than the growth figure recorded for all of last year and tracking soft domestic consumption. The economies climbing this year are the ones that stopped treating sustainability as the price to pay for achieving competitiveness Hinrich-IMD Sustainable Trade Index report The mainland ranked seventh out of 30 on economic strengths, the compilers said, down from fifth last year. However, it remained the “top performer” in gross fixed capital formation, the foundation and the centre said in a summary of their findings, which also noted its “persistent” strength in exports. China’s environmental ranking fell by four places, Tee said, driven in part by “weaker performance on energy intensity” and higher dependence on natural resource-based trade. Energy intensity measures the amount of energy used to produce a single unit of economic output. Economic and environmental concerns might be “competing for attention, and attention is a choice”, the compilers said, calling out China as well as the United States. “The economies climbing this year are the ones that stopped treating sustainability as the price to pay for achieving competitiveness,” they said in a summary of their findings. Hong Kong saw “improved performance” on gender non-discrimination in hiring and on forced and child labour, it said, and was also the top performer in “energy intensity”.

title: Meet Arthur Tang, founder of Artta Concept Studio
description: Partner to key Hong Kong developers like HKR International and Chinachem, Artta aims for ‘high-end global aesthetics with spatial refinement’.
content: “Method acting” usually refers to the technique used by actors on stage or screen, but to Artta Concept Studio and its founder Arthur Tang, it’s the most accurate way to describe their interior design practice. Trusted partners of prominent Hong Kong developers like HKR International and Chinachem, the designers at Artta Concept Studio have been focused since the firm’s founding in 2010 on creating immersive environments for different target audiences of specific spaces, rather than following a singular style across all projects. “Hong Kong residents lead high-octane, hyper-globalised lives, driven by a unique demographic DNA,” Tang writes, which means the city’s interior designers and the projects they work on must answer to varied needs. Tang says Hong Kong interior design was historically driven by one dominant trend at a time, but he believes that’s changed entirely over the past decade. “Moving away from loud, high-key extravagances and commercial aesthetics” to “a far more personal approach” means adopting a thoughtful, practical style, and an overall more culturally refined feel, he writes, adding that contemporary spaces are now “prioritising functional longevity over superficial spectacle”. Many Artta-designed spaces aim for a timeless visual identity, focusing not on certain aesthetics but rather using high-end materials and features that will never go out of style. The Peony Chinese Restaurant in Discovery Bay, for instance, avoids the classic hallmarks of a typical Chinese eatery, using modern bronze metallic partitions to give the air of a high-end establishment. It still incorporates nods to heritage, with accents across the space that also lean on the deep red of the Buckeye Belle, a much-loved variety of peony. Artta was established on the principle of “design for impact”, and that idea inspired some of the restaurant’s most technically ambitious and visually impressive features, including the flower-shaped ceiling installation also modelled on the same peony. Even with its client-driven commercial impact, the studio doesn’t lack its own creative identity. Some projects, such as the Sienna One Sales Gallery and Clubhouse in China’s Zhejiang province or the Toscana Sales Gallery, also in Hong Kong’s Discovery Bay, look more futuristic than others. But all – especially those made for Hong Kong’s most well-heeled and well-travelled clients – are designed to be forward-thinking, using what Tang describes as “architectural intelligence”. “For years, [Hong Kong’s] rapid ‘design metabolism’ meant interiors were overhauled every decade to chase fleeting trends,” he writes, adding that the city has since undergone a “maturity shift” by rewarding spaces with “intuitive spatial flow” and an amalgamation of various “international, multidisciplinary design languages”. Putting all that in “a localised framework”, he says, is what makes Hong Kong’s design scene truly incomparable, a blend of “high-end global aesthetics with spatial refinement”. Tang believes “the city’s design trajectory is shifting towards integrating multiple coexisting trends rather than a singular style,” which he sees being led by Artta Concept Studio. “[In] a city that never slows down, yet deeply craves stillness,” he writes, you have to find your own niche “to create spaces that truly possess a soul”.

title: From fishing boats to Michelin stars: Vietnam’s CoCo Dining turns the humble into haute cuisine
description: ‘Top Chef Vietnam’ winner Vo Thanh Vuong spent years trying to cook like someone else. Now, his kitchen is a reflection of the sea he grew up on – and the story behind his Michelin star.
content: “You know the phrase ‘fish out of water’? Well, that’s me in the city,” chef Vo Thanh Vuong laughs. “Now, I’m back on the water.” It’s just past dawn; we’re on a fishing boat off the coast of Vung Tau, roughly 100km (62 miles) southeast of Vietnam’s largest city, Ho Chi Minh. Vung Tau is the port that supplies Ho Chi Minh City’s best restaurants, but by the fleet’s clock, it’s already late; most of the other vessels have already unloaded their catch. Vuong is showing me how to hold a fishing rod. His hands seem to know the motion better than his mind does. Vuong grew up in Phan Thiet, about 160km (100 miles) north along the coast, where his family’s livelihood depended on what the South China Sea had to offer. Vung Tau is where his family’s boat went down in 2000, when he was 11 years old, 40km (25 miles) off its coast. Losing the watercraft cost them dearly, and suddenly, every pair of hands mattered – including his. Vuong was fishing full-time until he was 20, long enough to know the fishing life was not for him. So, he left for Ho Chi Minh City, also known as Saigon. Now, almost two decades later, he is back on the water – not because he has to be, but because he wants to be. By mid-morning, we have caught almost nothing. Vuong shrugs. He tells me this is what most trips are like: long stretches of nothing punctuated by work. Because “the sea gave you very little entertainment, you learned to be comfortable with silence”. Back on shore, we head to a local fish market in Vung Tau to pick up something for lunch. Everything is laid out at knee-height. Vuong moves through the displays like he’s reading a familiar book. He picks up a big fish with one hand and turns it over. He doesn’t wince or fidget the way many people do when handling something slippery and cold. He checks the gills, the eyes, the firmness and sets it back down – or keeps it, and moves on. “When an ingredient is truly good, you don’t need to do much to it. Sometimes, the best thing a cook can do is step out of the way.” In Vung Tau, he cooks a meal from the catch of the day. “Do you want to see the fisherman or the chef cook today,” he asks. He explains that the fisherman cooks fast, because at sea, speed is survival: you cook to eat and move on. But the chef cooks slower, because he has learned to enjoy the process – the prepping, the seasoning, the tasting, the small adjustments. We tell him we want both. He laughs and gets to work. His preparation is simple, and he hums as he cooks – the way he did as the youngest boy in his family, with two brothers and a sister. Several gas stoves are burning at once. He chops the garnishes with precision and seasons the braising liquid, gauging measurements by eye. He steams a mix of flower crabs and three-spot swimming crabs with beer. He sets a hotpot going with tamarind, pineapple and tomato, and portions the cobia into chunks. He treats the oriental trumpeter whiting like a ceviche: sliced thin, cured in lime juice for 15 minutes, then tossed with a home-made sweet-spicy sauce, raw onion and herbs – the way he used to make it on the boats. On those trips, food was whatever the sea and the hold allowed. Rice and instant noodles were the foundation, and they carried mam (fermented-seafood paste), nuoc mam (fish sauce), dried fish and squid, pickled vegetables, eggs and water. A good meal might be muc com – baby squid with its roe – with sour fish soup and pickles. “We would spend the whole day catching fish for other people,” he recalls. “At night, we’d sit together and argue about which fish was best for ourselves.” Some nights, the swells were heavy enough that seawater splashed into their rice bowls; the rice would turn salty, but they would look at each other, laugh and keep eating. “You didn’t complain,” he says. “You were hungry, and you were at sea.” And the night the power died and the charcoal got too wet to burn, they ate a freshly caught grouper raw on deck – bled, sliced thin, with wild lime and sea salt, similar to what he prepares for us. He serves the food the way he always does: everyone else first, himself last. It’s what he calls a staff meal, the food he makes for his team at CoCo Dining – his one-Michelin-star Vietnamese restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City, opened in 2021 – after service. What he has prepared for us today is not, by his own admission, the food that made his name – that food was French. When Vuong left fishing behind and enrolled in culinary school in Ho Chi Minh City, he didn’t go in with a plan. He had no kitchen training and no technique. He also had no language for what he was learning. What he did have was nine years at sea. At the time, that felt like something to hide. “I didn’t want to expose my past,” he says, recalling his inexperience. “I had self-esteem issues.” Vuong didn’t finish Grade 6 and, later, quit culinary school. He became a chef by observing the people around him, figuring things out along the way. He spent eight years training under French-Cambodian culinarian Sakal Phoeung and learned to cook in the French tradition. In Vietnam, that still carries a particular weight: post-colonisation, French cuisine remains the benchmark for fine dining. For a Vietnamese chef with no pedigree, no formal training and a past aboard fishing boats, French haute cuisine was how Vuong proved he belonged. “I simply didn’t see [Vietnamese cuisine] as something I needed to learn,” he recalls. “It was everyday food, so I didn’t think about it as a cuisine I could build a career around.” So, Vuong learned to cook French, well enough to find success with it. For years, that was his identity in the kitchen. It even won him the first prize on the televised cooking competition Top Chef Vietnam in 2019. From 2021 to 2023, he was changing the menu at CoCo Dining twice a year, working mainly with modern gastronomy and fermentation. Eventually, he felt like he was running out of ideas. One night, towards the end of 2023, he and Daniel Dang Hung Minh – CoCo Dining’s managing director – were drinking together, unwinding after another week of trying to solve a menu that wouldn’t come together. Vuong started cooking just for the two of them, preparing the kind of Vietnamese drinking food he would naturally make for himself. After tasting it, Dang said: “This tastes much more like you; this is where you’re strongest. Why don’t you just be honest with your cooking?” Vuong resisted. He thought, “No, this can’t be the direction of a fine-dining restaurant.” He had spent years learning modern techniques and developing himself as a chef. Going back to familiar food almost felt like going backwards. But what Dang had said stayed with him, so Vuong started experimenting secretly at home. “Maybe I had been trying too hard to become the chef I thought I was supposed to be,” he says, “instead of being honest about the chef I actually was.” In 2024, CoCo Dining served a menu called Ra Khoi – meaning “to set sail” – but for Vuong, it signified “a return to the source”, as the first tasting menu he designed after deciding to lean into his fishing heritage. His first version of the menu pulled together fragments of memories: the mam muc (fermented-squid paste) he used to eat on the boat became stuffed baby squid with fermented-squid sauce. A wind-dried prawn reminded him of how his family preserved seafood, so he worked with tiger prawn. A simple crab salad became blue crab with mustard greens. Never before had Vuong put his childhood on a plate on purpose. Last year, the restaurant earned its Michelin star. It turns out, the fisherman and the chef could coexist after all. “I wasn’t sitting there thinking to myself, ‘I’m going to make a menu about my childhood.’ I was just following one memory into another, and suddenly, there was a menu,” he says. Back in Ho Chi Minh City, Vuong brings out his oldest jar of mam chao (fermented fish) from the fermentation room at CoCo Dining. A whiff of it brings us back to the market of Vung Tau. The fermented fish is threadfin bream, sun-dried for five days in Phan Thiet by his family, who have been fishing and making mam for generations. At the restaurant, he and his team mix it with a starter made from sticky rice, layer it in a jar and seal it tightly. Usually, it’s ready after a month, but he lets his develop for at least two. “We learned not to waste anything,” he says. “Even the fish that wasn’t going to be sold had a purpose.” Vuong believes his role is to bring the ingredients to life again: “In a museum, you put an artefact behind glass to stop it from changing. In my kitchen, the things I want to preserve are alive: they ferment, they age, they dry and they continue to change.” It’s what makes his “archive” different from a museum’s. Recipes can be written down and “collected” and remain the same for generations, but his fermentations live and breathe. “You can’t treat each batch exactly the same,” he says. “You have to observe it, smell it, taste it and understand how it is developing.” At CoCo Dining, Vuong balances the deep umami of his fermented seafood with ginger and other aromatics. In his signature dish, baby squid is stuffed with squid trimmings and pork, then glazed with a sauce made from squid ink and a spoonful of the mam muc. If diners are curious, he brings out a jar so they can taste the fermented-squid paste as it is. “For me, that’s the heart of my ‘Living Archive’. If you put something in a box and never touch it, eventually, it becomes history. If you cook it, share it and pass it to someone else, it continues to live,” he explains. His menu, Luu Tich (“Living Archive”), arrives at a moment when what deserves to be preserved and presented as part of Vietnamese culinary heritage is under debate. Vietnam is bidding to become the next global gastronomy hub, with a pitch built on “luxury” through authenticity rather than European-style fine dining. Vuong is cautious about the language. He has spent too long on the other side of the word “authentic” to trust it easily. Real necessity informed those techniques, he says. “Coming from a fishing boat off Phan Thiet, the word ‘luxury’ felt very far from my life. But there was a lot of knowledge in those practices.” “Vietnam doesn’t need to borrow someone else’s definition of luxury” Vo Thanh Vuong For him, that knowledge of salt, patience and time is its own form of wealth. “Vietnam doesn’t need to borrow someone else’s definition of luxury,” Vuong says. He thinks that luxury today can be the time and attention we give to something that was once simply part of daily life, “not taking something humble and making it expensive just because we put it on a fine-dining plate”. But that doesn’t mean he cooks the same way his grandmother did. In Vuong’s eyes, French technique is merely another set of tools – just as sorting and scaling fish is part of a fisherman’s toolkit. Both, he says, come from the same place: trying to understand an ingredient and bring out the best in it. But does that make a dish less Vietnamese? “If authenticity means following a recipe strictly without any changes, maybe some will feel that what we do is not authentic enough,” he says. “I’m not trying to recreate the past exactly. A dish doesn’t become inauthentic because it evolves. It becomes inauthentic only when you lose sight of where it came from.” If he were to curate a museum piece for people 100 years from now to understand where he came from, he would choose a thung leu, the wooden barrel used to make fish sauce in Phan Thiet. His grandfather used to make fish sauce at home, and the whole area of Phan Thiet, Vuong remembers, smelled like fish sauce. “Now, Phan Thiet is much more modern; that smell has mostly disappeared,” he says. “Not many households make fish sauce at home any more, so something that was once part of everyday life has become much less visible.” In the museum, the label for the exhibit would read: “Thung Leu, Phan Thiet, Vietnam – a wooden vessel for making nuoc mam. For one boy from the coast, it was simply part of home. Inside it are fish, salt and time. Around it is the knowledge of generations who learned how to live with the sea.”

title: Nato ‘ready to fight tonight’ if attacked, top commander says
description: General Alexus Grynkewich outlines ‘theory of victory’ in Warsaw amid European warnings of escalating Russian sabotage.
content: Nato’s top military commander said the alliance is “ready to fight tonight” if it is attacked, as European officials warn Russia could test Nato’s defences with increased covert attacks or a limited military incursion. European nations have in recent months faced an escalation of covert Russian activity, including an arson attack on an Estonian defence company and a failed attempt to attack a Ukrainian aircraft at a German airport. If Russia decides to attack Nato, the alliance will respond by using sensors, autonomous systems and military force to stop any assault, Nato’s Supreme Allied Commander US General Alexus Grynkewich said in Warsaw on Monday. Grynkewich spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum to set out what he called Nato’s “Theory of Victory”. The Nato commander said he does not believe that a conflict is imminent or inevitable and that the most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war and to maintain open lines of communication to “resolve misunderstandings”. Grynkewich provided no specific details about what kind of attack Nato is preparing for, nor where, nor with what kind of forces. But outlining what a response to a Russian attack could look like, Grynkewich said Nato’s combined land, sea and air forces will move to stop Moscow seizing territory and deny Russia the ability to hold ground. “My theory of victory is simple,” he told the Warsaw conference. “We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational war-fighting system arrayed against us.” That includes not just the attacking force but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls it, he said. In recent weeks, senior European officials and intelligence services have warned that Russia may be planning to test the Nato alliance with increased covert attacks or even an incursion after a spate of sabotage incidents across the continent. Denmark’s defence intelligence service specifically warned Russia could use such tactics to split the Nato alliance. But, at the same time, US President Donald Trump has also sent shock waves through Europe by agreeing to a deal to buy diesel from Russia in a bid to try to lower prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections. Earlier this year, Trump said he was pulling American troops from Europe and his war with Iran has led to critical shortages of advanced air defence missiles in Europe. “Ultimately it’s a political decision” as to where troops are deployed but “no one should question the US commitment to the alliance”, Grynkewich said. It is important, Grynkewich said, that alliance members coordinate a “coherent” response to Russian activity to make it clear to Moscow “where our red lines are”. The response to increased Russian malign activity and sabotage, he said, should be to double down on support for Ukraine. While Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia is planning to escalate with drone or rocket strikes on European allies supporting Ukraine, other countries have called for calm. Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Agency said there is a “low but growing risk” that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several Nato countries bordering Russia. Nato does not seek war with anyone but will see a military attack coming and “is unlikely to be caught by surprise”, Grynkewich said. Although Grynkewich said Nato would defend against any attack by Russia using a network of sensors and autonomous systems, some Nato nations have previously struggled to perform in exercises simulating drone warfare. They have also faced challenges detecting and responding to incursions of drones which have entered their airspace. Multiple attack drones have crashed in Nato countries bordering Russia, Ukraine and Belarus. And in May, residents in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius were told to seek shelter after a drone strayed into Lithuanian airspace. When asked if Nato could deter Russia in the way Grynkewich described, his spokesman, Colonel Martin O’Donnell said Nato nations are increasingly deploying ground sensors and other technology to detect and counter drones. The network that connects systems to shoot down drones and sensors is in the process of being established, although they have not yet taken down any drones, he said. In September, Germany accused Russia of being behind a plot at Leipzig airport to use a drone laden with explosives to attack a Ukrainian aircraft. British officials also said they thwarted a Russian plot to target a drone facility outside London while Estonian officials said Russia was behind a fire at a defence company. The incidents are among at least 211 blamed on Russia by Western officials since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine and tracked by Associated Press. In its assessment released earlier in September, Denmark’s defence intelligence service suggested Russia could try to acquire Ukrainian drones and use them to attack Europe to obfuscate any Russian involvement. Tusk suggested Russia is likely to pretend any attacks are “accidental” in a bid to “paralyse or at least weaken the motivation of Nato countries” to rush to the defence of a member state coming under attack. The Danish service said the aim of any such attack would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine and sow division in Nato. But both the Danish service and O’Donnell said while Russia is fighting in Ukraine, it would be difficult to launch an outright attack on Nato.

title: Editorial | Huanggang Port upgrade a showcase of Hong Kong’s gateway role
description: As the revamped checkpoint expedites cross-border travel and integration, attention must be paid to software in addition to hardware.
content: The revamped Huanggang Port has opened to a promising start. Thousands of passengers passed through it on the first day of operations, which officials described as satisfactory. Considering its significance amid intensifying cross-border integration under the strategic national drive for Greater Bay Area development, this is a welcome beginning. The new facility, along with its upgraded systems and transport links, will be put to further tests in the coming long weekend and the weeks and months beyond as it draws more daily commuters, holiday crowds and business travellers. More than 5,000 travellers passed through the crossing during first two hours of operation on Monday, a 60 per cent increase compared with the average weekday usage before renovation. Some early users described the new terminal as bright, spacious and more efficient. But some found the multi-storey complex overwhelming and called for clearer signage and support for navigation. Designed to transform a decades-old land crossing into a modern gateway, the six-year-long redevelopment is redefining travel convenience under the new phase of “one country, two systems”. The new complex operates around the clock for passengers and vehicles, with a designed capacity of 200,000 passenger trips a day – potentially rising to 300,000 during peak periods. This is a significant rise when the old crossing handled an average of 40,000 travellers a day and a peak flow of 65,000 people, and a daily average throughput of 9,000 vehicles and a peak of 12,000. What sets the new site further apart is the “collaborative inspection and joint clearance” model, under which travellers queue once and clear both Hong Kong and mainland immigration in a single automated channel. The process, officials say, will cut the procedure from about 30 minutes to roughly five minutes. No fewer than 160,000 people have registered to use the e-channel for joint clearance. For a checkpoint with heavy footfall and vehicle flow, the saving of time matters. The new terminal is a showcase of what a makeover can do to expedite cross-border travel and integration. But there is more to the convenience than just applying biometric verification, automated channels and co-located clearance around the clock. The hardware upgrade must also be backed by improvement in software, including better transport connectivity and contingency measures. The new crossing is essentially an integrated ecosystem of transport links, immigration and customs procedures and emergency arrangements. Thanks to intensive drills and preparation by the authorities on both sides in the run-up to the opening, the operation was by and large smooth on Monday. The coming long weekend will provide a more stringent test. In addition to the usual northbound exodus for leisure, the Chinese tradition of paying tribute to one’s ancestors on Chung Yeung Festival is expected to boost border crossings. The pressure must not be underestimated. The timing of the opening adds another layer of significance as Shenzhen and Hong Kong gear up for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings and related events in the coming weeks. The revamped checkpoint will provide first-hand experience of Greater Bay Area integration as visiting delegates, business leaders and international guests shuttle between the sister cities. A smooth and seamless crossing will reinforce Hong Kong’s role as the gateway to the Greater Bay Area and the region. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has rightly described the project as a “critical milestone” for Greater Bay Area connectivity. Coming after the release of the city’s first five-year plan, Lee said the opening of the revamped checkpoint represented an explicit action for Hong Kong to align with the national development strategy and deeply engage in the construction of the Greater Bay Area. Indeed, Huanggang will become even more strategically significant as the city strives to fast track the mega Northern Metropolis development. This was also recognised by Guangdong’s top official, Huang Kunming, who called on Shenzhen last week to use the upgraded checkpoint to better align with the metropolis project. Hopefully, the revamped crossing will further boost closer cross-border integration under one country, two systems.

title: How Hong Kong’s post-war tattoo scene fused sailor art with Chinese imagery
description: A photobook by Jimmy Shy and Yu Chang traces Hong Kong’s distinctive post-war tattoo style, while challenging the triad stereotype.
content: When Taiwan-based tattoo artist Jimmy Shy and street-film photographer Yu Chang decided to travel to Hong Kong to document the city’s fading post-war tattoo history, they agreed on one criterion: they would find their subjects only on the street. “We relied entirely on instinct,” Shy says of the project, which started in 2023 but began life as casual phone photos years earlier. “A lot of tattoos were hidden under clothing, so whenever we had a feeling that someone might have the kind of tattoo we were looking for, we first had to convince them to show us.” The encounters were unpredictable. One construction worker demanded they help him carry cement before agreeing to be photographed. Another refused until Shy, 40, and Chang, 37, showed their own tattoos – triggering something akin to a competition. “He lifted his shirt and said, ‘Mine is bigger than yours!’” Shy remembers. “He had a huge old eagle tattoo on his body, and it was beautiful. “Sometimes we can look at these people and their tattoos without knowing anything about them, and somehow still feel a glimpse of their spirit and the lives they have lived.” The results of Shy and Chang’s collaboration were released earlier this year as the photobook Hong Kong Traditional Tattoo. The title prompts the question: what exactly makes these tattoos traditional, and what makes them uniquely Hong Kong? More than just a triad marker The first image that comes to mind may be a scene taken from one of the many golden-era kung fu or crime films, with the bold, graphic ink worn as a badge of triad identity and street status. But Shy argues that the history of Hong Kong tattoos is more layered than it appears. “Without looking more deeply into it, most people would never realise that some images now commonly perceived as gang-related did not actually originate from gang culture at all,” he says. Shy, who is the co-founder of Hello Tattoo Studio in Taipei, has spent years tracing an overlooked chapter of tattoo history he calls “Asian sailor tattooing” – a tradition that took shape across the post-war port cities of Asia, with Hong Kong as one of its most important crossroads. Before World War II, tattooing across East and Southeast Asia was either defined by indigenous spiritual traditions or strict government prohibitions and deep social stigma, historically associated with penal branding of criminals. In pre-war Chinese port cities, commercial tattoo shops were almost non-existent because body modification was viewed unfavourably by mainstream society. Between the late 1940s and mid-70s, Western naval forces and merchant mariners began using ports in places in Asia including Hong Kong and the Philippines as primary logistics hubs and entertainment quarters for the US Navy and Allied forces. Tattoo parlours quickly opened near naval bases and docks in Wan Chai and Tsim Sha Tsui to service the influx of foreign sailors, offering tattoos that symbolised deployment, rites of passage and protective talismans for life at sea. These included Hong Kong’s first official commercial shop, Rose Tattoo Studio, opened in 1946 by James Ho. Western techniques, Eastern imagery This subculture created a distinct “fusion” style bridging Western techniques and traditions with Eastern imagery and art. “Getting tattooed could also become a special souvenir of someone’s time in Asia,” Shy says. “I’ve always been deeply drawn to that kind of craftsmanship – the ability to bring two very different cultures together and make them coexist naturally within the same visual language.” What emerged from this collision was something unprecedented. Tattooers took familiar Western sailor motifs – anchors, ships, bald eagles – and reworked them with Chinese dragons, tigers and pin-up girls in high-slit cheongsams. At the heart of this story is Pinky Yun, a defining Hong Kong tattoo artist often regarded as the godfather of the Oriental style and whose influence rippled across the Pacific and into the work of American tattoo legends like Sailor Jerry, also known as Norman Collins, and Don Ed Hardy. Yun’s own journey followed the sailors who were his clients. His career took him through Japan, Taiwan, Macau and Europe before he settled in the United States in the early 70s – where he continued working within the sailor tattoo tradition and exchanging drawings, machines and ideas with American tattoo artists. “Some of Sailor Jerry’s pin-up drawings from the 1960s were adapted from designs by Pinky,” Shy reveals. “This kind of exchange continued even after Pinky opened his shop in the United States.” His influence travelled on skin across the world, and Shy names two flash designs – pre-made drawings by the tattoo artist that clients can choose from – that best represent that era: Neptune and Suzie Wong. The Neptune design, based on the Roman god of the sea, merged this protector of sailors with the Chinese dragon; the bearded sea god holding a trident is shown wrapped in or riding a coiled, scaled Chinese dragon amid East Asian clouds and wave swirls. Suzie Wong drew from the 1960 film The World of Suzie Wong, a major Hollywood romance hit that was actually filmed in the Neptune Bar downstairs from Yun’s Wan Chai shop. The qipao-clad character, played by Nancy Kwan, became the alternative to the classic “pin-up girl” American staple. The tattoo boom The business of tattooing during that time was shaped by the peculiar circumstances of military life. Ships would arrive with thousands of sailors, their shore leave often lasting only hours, and tattooing was sometimes prohibited by the military over disease concerns, forcing tattoo artists to work secretly in small rooms with modified machines. “Everything had to be extremely efficient,” Shy says. “As soon as a serviceman walked into the shop, he needed to choose a design almost immediately. The walls would be covered with pre-drawn flash designs.” The economic opportunity was staggering. Yun’s nephew once told Shy that as a 15-year-old, his biggest dream was to become a police officer – but he could make more in monthly tips helping Yun at the tattoo shop than a policeman’s salary. “There were so many customers that they desperately needed extra hands,” Shy recalls. “Even though he barely knew how to tattoo, he was put to work anyway.” As the wars wound down and foreign servicemen returned home, Hong Kong’s tattoo culture shifted dramatically. Without the sailor clientele, tattoos became increasingly associated with gang identity as the primary local trade shifted to bouncers, street youths and members of triad societies – a perception reinforced by the popularity of the city’s gangster films from the 80s. “Images of intimidating characters with a dragon on one side and a tiger on the other left a strong impression on audiences,” Shy explains, referencing the Chinese idiom long hu xiang bo (“a dragon and tiger fighting each other”) – lung fu soeng bok in Cantonese. “Many older tattoo designs were absorbed into that same stereotype.” Crossing boundaries For Shy, understanding this history has reshaped how he views tattooing itself. “Tattoo history is less like a straight line and more like an interconnected web,” he says. “We tend to divide tattooing into categories like American traditional, Japanese and so on,” Shy reflects. “These labels are useful, but they can also create the impression that every style has a clear boundary and a single origin. When we look back, we can see that those boundaries were actually being crossed all the time. “No one was really trying to define or categorise what they were doing as a particular ‘style’. It was simply part of everyday life.” He draws a parallel to music. “The same piece can be played again and again across different generations,” he says. “Understanding this history has made me realise that tradition has always survived through reinterpretation.” And ultimately, Shy believes, what endures is emotion. “Across different eras, our instinctive responses to beauty, fierceness, cuteness, happiness, or sadness probably haven’t changed all that much,” he says. “Everyone may have a different reason for liking a particular image, but before we understand its history or meaning, we are usually moved by the image itself.”

title: Exclusive | China’s finance minister to deliver opening speech at Apec meeting in Hong Kong
description: Draft agenda shows Lan Foan will address finance ministers at the meeting as IMF, World Bank and Asian development lenders present economic outlooks and policy proposals.
content: China’s finance minister, Lan Foan, will deliver a keynote speech, while presentations by three prominent financial institutions will be among the highlights of next week’s Apec meeting in Hong Kong, the South China Morning Post has learned. A draft agenda obtained by the SCMP on Monday listed a series of programmes for finance ministers from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation’s 21 member economies on October 20 and 21 at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. Sources said major economies were finalising their representatives for the gathering. So far, expected attendees include Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers, South Korea’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyoung-il and Singapore’s Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance Jeffrey Siow Chen Siang. Last week, the SCMP reported that United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent might skip the Hong Kong meeting to focus on preparing for US President Donald Trump’s historic visit to Shenzhen in November. Shenzhen will host the Apec leaders’ meeting on November 18 and 19, marking the third time China has hosted the event, after Beijing in 2014 and Shanghai in 2001. Preparations for the finance ministers’ gathering are under way, with insiders saying security arrangements will be equivalent to those for a state-level event. About 500 guests are expected to attend the annual meeting. “Security will be extremely tight. Even delegates may not be able to sit in the same room as their ministers during the conference,” one source said. According to the agenda, some key officials will arrive a day before the meeting, on October 19. That day will be devoted to drafting the finance ministers’ joint statement, regarded as the most significant outcome of the gathering. The meeting proper begins on October 20 with a finance ministers’ retreat at 10am, followed by a working lunch. A focal point will come at 2pm, when Lan is scheduled to deliver five-minute opening remarks. Chen Xu, chair of the Apec 2026 senior officials’ meeting, will then provide an update on Apec 2026’s key priorities and developments. A group photo session is expected at 2.10pm, followed by three discussion sessions between 4pm and 6pm. In the first session, the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and Asian Development Bank will present their global and regional economic and financial outlooks. In the second, the World Bank will present a fiscal policy report on supporting households and investing in human capital, after which ministers and heads of delegation will be invited to share their views. In the final session, China’s Ministry of Finance will present a policy statement on enhancing cooperation in digital infrastructure financing across the Apec region. The meeting will conclude on the morning of October 21, with discussions focusing on financial access and opportunities for all, as well as young financial talent. It will wrap up with the announcement of the joint statement before lunchtime. Sources said senior leaders, delegates and their spouses would be offered tours of major attractions or landmarks in the city on October 19 and 21. Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said in an exclusive interview with the SCMP that he hoped dignitaries attending the meeting would experience the city’s latest vibrancy for themselves. According to the agenda, the October 20 dinner will be held at Cloud 39, the city’s latest all-glass rooftop venue, atop the Henderson office tower in Central. Chan said earlier that Hong Kong’s role as host reflected Beijing’s strong support and underscored the city’s status as an important international financial centre in the region. Vietnam will host the Apec meetings in 2027.

title: Hong Kong investors are warming to US Treasury bonds as yields hit 20-year high
description: Strong demand was seen at a US$22 billion auction of US government bonds last week, following the fast rise of Treasury yields.
content: US Treasuries are looking increasingly attractive to Hong Kong investors after a prolonged sell-off pushed yields to multi-decade highs, prompting some strategists and wealth managers to recommend buying while others warned that further losses may lie ahead. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield surged above 5.36 per cent on Wednesday, its highest in 24 years, before retreating to around 5.23 per cent on Thursday following strong demand at a US$22 billion auction of 30-year government bonds. Higher yields, which move inversely to bond prices, offer investors an opportunity to lock in attractive income and potentially benefit from capital gains if yields retreat, but the prospect of further tightening Federal Reserve policies, persistent inflation and heavy US government borrowing could keep yields elevated, according to strategists. Standard Chartered has turned more bullish, recommending an opportunistic long position in 10-year Treasuries after yields climbed above 5 per cent. The bank expects the 10-year yield to retreat towards 4.75 to 5 per cent over the next six to 12 months, citing expectations of moderating inflation and a shallower Federal Reserve tightening cycle than markets anticipate. “We view the risk/reward for the US 10-year government bond after the recent yield spike as compelling and we are initiating a long opportunistic idea at the current yield,” authors led by Jonathan Liang, chief investment officer for fixed income and FX at Standard Chartered, said in a September 28 report. Cusson Leung, CIO of international wealth management at KGI, also sees an opportunity to lock in high yields, although he cautioned that the market might not have reached its bottom. “We might not get the absolute bottom yet. Practically it is almost impossible to get an absolute bottom,” Leung said, recommending that investors gradually build positions during the fourth quarter. Unlike investors favouring shorter maturities, Leung prefers 10- to 30-year Treasuries, expecting inflationary pressures to ease by the end of the first quarter of 2027 and potentially revive expectations of Fed rate cuts. Others remain wary of taking on excessive duration risk. Jason Chan, senior investment strategist at Bank of East Asia, favours three- to five-year Treasuries, which he said offer sufficient income to cushion against further yield increases while limiting exposure to price volatility. He advised avoiding longer-dated bonds, citing persistent inflation, fiscal deficits and the potential crowding-out effect of artificial intelligence-related capital expenditure. Louis Wong, executive director at Phillip Capital Management, also favours the middle of the yield curve, particularly five- to 10-year Treasuries. “A 10-year yield near 5.25 per cent is high against the past decade but the next move in yields can still be up,” Wong said. He added that the elevated yields are drawing the attention of Hong Kong and mainland investors, as the assets offering returns of around 5 per cent compete with local bank deposits and dividend-paying stocks. While Hong Kong’s currency peg to the US dollar limits exchange-rate risks, mainland investors funding their purchases in yuan face greater currency uncertainty, he said. Further Fed tightening could also leave bondholders facing capital losses before they have earned enough income to offset them, he added. Wong suggested investors focus on two- to 10-year Treasuries or short-term Treasury funds, while managing currency exposure to avoid exchange-rate movements eroding their returns.

title: RJ Mitte, Breaking Bad star and disability rights advocate, dies at 34
description: Bryan Cranston voices ‘deep despair’ over on-screen son who brought authenticity and barrier-breaking visibility to Hollywood.
content: Actor RJ Mitte, whose personal experience living with cerebral palsy informed his role as Walter White Jnr, the physically disabled son of a methamphetamine kingpin in the landmark television series Breaking Bad, died on Monday at age 34. News of Mitte’s death in Brownsville, Texas, was announced in a statement released through his talent management agency. A publicist for the actor later confirmed news reports that Mitte took his own life. No further ‌details about the circumstances were given. “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” the initial statement said. Breaking Bad star Bryan Cranston voiced his “deep despair” over the death of his “sweet son” on social media. Mitte was best known for his breakout role on the AMC cable TV series Breaking Bad, playing the only son of Cranston’s lead character, Walter White, a terminally ill high school teacher who descends into a secret life of crime cooking crystal meth. The acclaimed show, often cited by critics as one of the best television dramas of all time, ran from 2008 to 2013, garnering 16 Emmy Awards, including two ⁠for best drama series. Mitte was 14 when cast for the pilot episode, which began shooting in 2007, Cranston said. Drawing on his real-life struggle with cerebral palsy, a chronic muscle-control disorder, ‌Mitte brought a rare measure of authenticity to a television character whose physical disability was portrayed as largely incidental to the storyline. His performance as Walter “Flynn” White Jnr, who walked with crutches and spoke with a slur, gained early attention from fans who dubbed him “the breakfast king” for his ‌recurring appearances in scenes around the family breakfast table. But his role grew in prominence as the story arc of the series progressed. He starts out ⁠as a carefree teenager who admires his ⁠father, then is forced to reckon with the family’s disintegration as the truth about Walter White’s meth-making “Heisenberg” alter ego emerges. In a statement posted to Instagram on Monday night, Cranston paid tribute to Mitte, saying he was a “fine ‌actor” and “vocal advocate for performers with disabilities”. “It is especially devastating to hear that he took his own life,” Cranston wrote, adding he and Mitte “were texting each other just a few weeks ago” about possibly meeting for lunch. “I don’t know if ‌that lunch ‌would have changed his future,” Cranston wrote. “But I do know that I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight ‌on Breaking Bad dimmed. I’ll miss you, son.” Despite his disability, Mitte “never – ever – allowed that challenge to be an excuse for anything” during the show’s production, Cranston recalled. “He met the demanding ⁠shooting schedule head on with great determination”. Mitte later played a stand-up comedian with cerebral palsy in the 2019 romantic comedy film Standing Up for Sunny and a high school wrestler with CP ⁠in the 2021 coming-of-age film Triumph. Mitte, whose credits also include the films The Recall and The Oak Room, had been working to promote a new movie, Talking to Strangers, appearing as a podcast guest to discuss the film in recent days, according to Hollywood trade publication Variety. Off screen, Mitte served as a Screen Actors Guild spokesman for ‌performers with disabilities, and was a celebrity ‌ambassador for the United Cerebral Palsy foundation. Born in Jackson, Mississippi, Mitte suffered brain damage at birth, was adopted as an infant and was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at age 3. He was fitted with leg braces and crutches for much of his childhood, but through athletics and exercise eventually outgrew his need for walking devices. According to Wikipedia, Mitte was raised by his adoptive mother following his parents’ separation and assumed financial responsibility for a younger sister and his mother at age 13, after she became paralysed. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel pummel Mexico, leaving 5 dead
description: Five people remain missing as twin storms along the Pacific coast and Baja California trigger emergency rescues.
content: Rains and flooding along Mexico’s Pacific Coast from Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel have left five people dead, authorities said Monday. The El Nino phenomenon, characterised by rising water temperatures in the Pacific, is fuelling a more intense hurricanes this season in the region. Simon claimed the life of a 71-year-old man who “died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo” in the southern state of Guerrero, Governor Evelyn Salgado said during the daily presidential press conference. Tropical Storm Rachel is blamed for the deaths of four members of one family, including two children, whose bodies were found on the outskirts of the city of Ensenada in Baja California, the state’s prosecutor’s office reported. Five more people remain missing, while security forces used helicopters to rescue 32 people, prosecutors said. Simon did not make landfall and, after weakening to Category 2 on the five-point Saffir-Simpson scale, was moving away from the coast, authorities said, adding that a rain alert remained in place. Officials warned waves of up to five metres high were still expected in some coastal areas. Flooding and landslides had already hit communities close to rivers and streams in the states of Michoacan and Colima. Simon will approach Mexico’s west-central coast between Wednesday and Thursday, according to the US National Hurricane Centre (NHC). The latest official report from Mexican authorities indicates that “it will hit Mazatlan, Sinaloa, as a Category 1 hurricane,” said national civil protection coordinator Laura Velazquez. The tourist gem of Puerto Vallarta, which had been bracing for extreme weather, awoke Monday to clear skies and a rainbow.

title: In Focus | From laser shields to iPhone detectors: inside China’s booming secrecy industry
description: Manufacturers race to capture market amid tech advances, rising espionage fears and Beijing’s tightening national security requirements.
content: A group of Chinese officials are in the middle of a highly sensitive meeting involving critical decisions yet to be made behind closed doors, with documents stamped “classified” spread across the table. Suddenly, an invisible laser beams into the room, sweeping across a glass window and allowing the contents of the meeting to be transmitted elsewhere. China’s Ministry of State Security laid out this seemingly futuristic scenario six months ago, warning government departments and other entities against a new form of laser-based eavesdropping potentially conducted by foreign spies. Sophisticated contactless surveillance technology like this relies on detecting vibrations in glass windows caused by sound waves inside a room. By directing an invisible laser beam at a window, receiving the reflected signal and analysing it, an operator can reconstruct speech from within the room, according to the ministry. Dramatic and distant as that scenario may seem, solutions to these risks exist. Amid heightened fears of foreign espionage and data leaks, Chinese manufacturers are paying keen attention to client needs and racing to capture the skyrocketing market. To fulfil the need to protect official secrets, they offer devices designed specifically to detect such laser eavesdropping tactics, as well as a growing list of devices and training to meet the mounting national security requirements in one of the world’s largest bureaucratic systems. The boom coincides with technological advances, rising espionage fears and Beijing’s tightening national security requirements, creating new opportunities for manufacturers of secrecy-protection equipment. As demand spreads from national authorities to local governments, companies are diversifying their products and services while seeking growth overseas, particularly in countries with close security ties to Beijing. Lasers, curtains and Apple products Any outsider would be surprised at the immense range of devices and technologies to maintain information secrecy available in the Chinese market. Product catalogues from several secrecy-protection equipment companies obtained by the South China Morning Post showcase diverse products meant to address a host of espionage threats. In the laser intrusion example, a monitoring system is capable of detecting and issuing alerts over incoming laser beams while identifying the direction from which the laser originates. Another product uses laser-protection film that absorbs lasers of particular wavelengths while maintaining window transparency. Then there are specialised curtains made from electromagnetic-shielding fabric that can block electronic signals and electromagnetic interference while providing protection against infrared thermal-imaging surveillance. An insider said the products currently seeing the strongest demand were systems capable of detecting and blocking unidentified signals, including Wi-fi and Bluetooth signals from devices that are not on China’s approved whitelist for official use. “Many advanced eavesdropping or covert surveillance systems are capable of wireless control via Wi-fi or Bluetooth from distances exceeding 100 metres (328 feet) – a range that may well extend beyond the defensive perimeter of physical security measures like on-site security scanners,” the insider said. “As a result, systems designed to counter unidentified Bluetooth, Wi-fi and other signals have become a popular requirement.” Among these unidentified-signal detection systems is another notable category: equipment that searches for signals emitted by foreign-made devices, particularly Apple devices, according to the catalogues. Citing national security concerns, some Chinese government ministries and agencies have since 2023 required employees to stop using iPhones in the workplace. Beijing has long restricted the use of foreign-made electronic devices and vehicles in certain areas of government compounds on national security grounds. In 2021, Beijing barred vehicles made by US electric car manufacturer Tesla from entering government facilities and military compounds because of concerns about espionage. The insider said covert anti-recording equipment was another growth area as companies updated and developed their products, with such devices mainly used when setting up secure meeting rooms and during overseas activities involving Chinese personnel. While most devices sold by these Chinese companies are made domestically – product catalogues show that at least one also imports Russian-made anti-recording jammers to sell to Chinese customers. Skyrocketing demand According to an employee at a Chinese counter-espionage equipment manufacturer, the industry has existed for years but demand for its products surged around 2023. “The company has been making secrecy-protection equipment for 20 years, and business had been neither particularly strong nor weak,” the employee said. “But since [2023], the value of orders has increased substantially year after year, and customers have become much easier to find.” The company now has an annual output value of about 100 million yuan (US$14.9 million), according to the employee, who requested anonymity citing the sensitivity of the matter. With brighter prospects for the sector, the company had also become more willing to invest in the development of more advanced secrecy-protection equipment designed to respond to emerging technologies, the employee added. It is not entirely clear what drove the jump in demand in 2023, but it coincided with a series of major counter-espionage and data security developments in China. In August that year, the Ministry of State Security set up an official account on WeChat, the country’s largest social media platform, churning out daily posts about espionage risks to the public. Set up just one month after a new counter-espionage law came into effect, the account publishes weekly updates on typical cases of espionage and information theft to warn the public and officials of threats. The ministry has also called for society as a whole to “jointly build a line of defence for secrecy protection and engage those in counter-espionage”. Also in 2023, China passed major amendments to its 2014 anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage activities and the investigative powers of national security law enforcement agencies. The ministry has repeatedly warned Chinese officials, students and tourists against recruitment traps and foreign intelligence operatives. The message comes against a backdrop of intense competition between Beijing and Washington, alongside its Western partners. In July 2023, in a rare public comment, then-CIA director William Burns said the American agency was making “progress” in rebuilding its spy network in China after severe setbacks a decade earlier. Beijing responded by declaring it would take “all necessary” countermeasures. A year later, in 2024, China updated its Law on Guarding State Secrets, the first major change to the law since 2010. Explaining the amendments, state news agency Xinhua said the revised law “makes clear that the state encourages and supports research and application of science and technology for secrecy protection … and fosters the secrecy-protection technology industry”. The law also explicitly places secrecy protection within President Xi Jinping’s “holistic approach to national security”. As a retired official from a local government secrecy-protection department noted: “Over the past decade, national security has gradually evolved from a relatively narrow and specialised field into a key principle within China’s economic, administrative and social governance.” “China has made a series of adjustments to its policies, regulations and the way government departments operate to promote this shift,” said the retired official, who also requested anonymity citing the sensitivity of the matter. Since 2024, the US Central Intelligence Agency has released Chinese-language online videos that explicitly seek to recruit informants from within China’s government and military. Dennis Wilder, a former senior US intelligence official and policymaker, said the rapid growth of China’s counter-espionage industry stemmed “in part [from the fact] that both offensive and defensive intelligence collected remotely is growing in sophistication as AI comes into play”. “China’s security system has always been massive,” Wilder said. “The technology of espionage and counter-espionage is advancing. It’s a predictable reaction to have new tools.” Who buys the equipment and what they want The industry insider said China had about 10 sizeable companies specialising in secrecy-protection equipment, many of which had some degree of connection to the defence industry. The main clients of Chinese secrecy-protection equipment are military units, government departments at the provincial level or above, and state-owned enterprises dealing with state secrets, according to the insider, who noted particularly strong demand from companies in the defence sector. The insider told the SCMP that the business was expanding into some local government departments where “construction of their secrecy-protection systems is still only at an early stage”. Such ventures could already be accelerating. The 2024 revision to the state secrets law stipulated that “governments at or above the county level shall strengthen secrecy-protection infrastructure and support the development and application of key secrecy-protection technical products”. The law further required governments at or above the county level to include secrecy-protection work in their budgets.
