According to the former official, “As secrecy protection develops into a mature industry backed by government regulations and procurement budgets, this is expected to create a self-reinforcing cycle in which security requirements and the market for protective technologies continue to expand.” Anti-espionage training support Besides the sales of devices, some secrecy-protection equipment companies help train officials travelling overseas in counter-surveillance and anti-eavesdropping techniques, according to another source familiar with the matter. The source said companies were required to set up a room containing concealed surveillance devices, allowing officials to practise counter-surveillance skills and ultimately locate the hidden equipment. “We teach the trainees how to use different types of portable counter-surveillance equipment, as well as the possible types and locations of eavesdropping devices. The training normally lasts one or two weeks and involves several rounds of assessment.” “Sometimes the surveillance device they need to find is a stone inside a flowerpot. Sometimes it’s a piece of decoration attached to a dome light. They can be very well concealed,” the source added. In January, China’s National Administration of State Secrets Protection published an article calling for stronger supervision, management and security-awareness training for personnel sent overseas on official assignments. Eyeing growth overseas Counting successes within China’s own borders, these secrecy-protection equipment companies are looking to expand their business overseas. “Overseas sales of secrecy-protection equipment mainly involve government departments in Central Asian and African countries, particularly countries in those regions participating in the Belt and Road Initiative, including Tajikistan and Kazakhstan,” the source said. Secrecy-protection equipment was generally not expensive, the source added, with a complete system typically priced at between 100,000 and 200,000 yuan (about US$15,000 to US$30,000), making it easily affordable for government agencies in developing countries. A secrecy-protection equipment firm, which asked not to be identified, told the SCMP that its systems could be provided with support for local languages, including Russian, and that the company also offered comprehensive training on how to use the equipment. Beijing has meanwhile continued to expand security cooperation with Central Asian and African countries, including exchanges and training programmes.

title: Opinion | Don’t leave Asia’s ageing debate until it’s too late
description: As the global gap between healthspan and lifespan widens to almost a decade, an ageing Asia’s health question is increasingly a business one.
content: Last month, Japan’s internal affairs ministry released its yearly data ahead of Respect for the Aged Day. People aged 65 and over now make up a record 29.6 per cent of the population. But the figure I keep coming back to was this: 9.43 million Japanese workers were 65 or older last year, about 13.8 per cent of everyone with a job. Members of Japan’s older population are not simply retired. A large part are still at work and some of those people are the ones businesses depend on. The Asia-Pacific Regional Conference on Population Ageing is set to be held in Hangzhou, China, later this month. The organisers – HelpAge International, the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) and the China National Committee on Ageing – point out that ageing is reshaping labour markets and public finances across the region. But we also need to consider what happens to a family or a company when the person holding it together gets sick at 45. I can answer that one. At 37, after building companies across three countries, I ended up in intensive care. That experience is why I now spend my working life on prevention. What happened to me is common enough to show up in global data. Researchers at the Mayo Clinic looked at World Health Organization figures for 183 countries and found that the gap between how long people live and how long they stay healthy widened over two decades, reaching 9.6 years by 2019. That is nearly 10 years, on average, of living with illness or disability. The authors tied the gap to noncommunicable diseases, which tend to build quietly through midlife and get noticed late. I live in Bangkok, and Thailand is a good place to watch this happen quickly. The World Bank projects that people aged 65 and over will go from 13 per cent of Thailand’s population in 2020 to 31 per cent in 2060. Over the same period, the working-age share is set to fall from 71 per cent to 56 per cent, a drop of nearly 30 per cent in the working-age population and the third-largest decline in East Asia and the Pacific, after South Korea and Japan. For the Asia-Pacific, UNFPA expects one person in four to be over 60 by 2050. Put those numbers side by side and the health question becomes a business one. Each worker counts for more when there are fewer of them, and a nine-year stretch of poor health is expensive whoever ends up paying for it. Our hospitals were built for a different moment. They are very good once something has gone wrong. They are not so well equipped to sit down with a healthy 45-year-old and work out what that person’s blood results might look like at 60, so it rarely happens. Companies and family businesses can act on this sooner than any ministry. Start with the board. Family offices in this region spend months on succession documents and trust structures, and almost no time asking whether the principal will be well enough to run things in 10 years. Key-person health belongs on the same risk register as succession. Then change what a check-up is for. A yearly report filed in a drawer does very little. A proper baseline in midlife, read by a doctor and repeated over time, gives people something to act on while the fixes are still small. And stop treating prevention as a perk for people who are already burned out. If Japan is any guide, many people in Asia will keep working well past 65. They will need to be fit enough to do so. Governments will still carry the cost of people who are ill, and that cost is going up. Yet, every healthy year someone keeps in their 50s is a year nobody has to pay for later, and a year their company doesn’t have to run without them. I got my warning at 37. Many people get theirs much later, when there is less they can do about it. If the delegates in Hangzhou want one practical idea to take home, it should be to start the conversation about ageing at 40.

title: Carney makes case for Canadian unity as Alberta referendum nears
description: The country’s fourth-largest province will hold a nonbinding vote on October 19 on pursuing formal independence.
content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Monday urged Alberta to remain in Canada, warning that a vote next week on whether to hold a referendum on leaving Canada would begin a “long and uncertain process” at a dangerous time for the country. “This year, Thanksgiving is a bit different,” Carney said in a holiday message to Canadians. “A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future, whether to remain part of Canada or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.” Canada celebrates Thanksgiving in October, unlike the United States, where it falls in late November. The October 19 vote asks Albertans whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the process of holding a referendum on separation. Alberta’s independence movement has grown after years of organising. Some of its leaders emerged from the 2022 “Freedom Convoy”, which began as a protest against the Covid-19 vaccine mandate for cross-border truckers and grew into weeks of demonstrations against pandemic restrictions and then-prime minister Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government. The vote comes as US President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to Canada’s sovereignty have badly strained relations between the long-time allies. Trump has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st US state. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who called the vote, supports remaining in Canada. She has said recent polling put support for separation at roughly 22 per cent, a level she called “still too high for my liking.” Keith Wilson, a leader of the independence movement, urged Albertans to back a path towards a separation referendum, arguing the province needs “leverage and lasting change” in its dealings with Ottawa. “What protects us when Ottawa turns against Alberta again?” he wrote on social media. Carney, who grew up in Alberta’s capital Edmonton, pointed to a proposed West Coast pipeline from oil-rich Alberta as an example of what the province can achieve within Canada. The project is intended to open new markets and help Canada diversify its oil exports beyond the United States. He also cited new housing and high-speed rail as he argued that Canada is building major projects again and that division would make that harder. “Canada is working,” Carney said. “Truth is, we can’t achieve any of this if we’re divided. You can’t build big things on fault lines.” Carney said Canada faces “real threats to our economy, to our security, to our way of life”, adding: “We have to be strong and we are stronger together.” “Generations of Albertans helped build this country,” Carney said. “It’s yours. It’s ours. And it’s worth fighting for.” Even a vote for separation in a future referendum would not automatically make Alberta independent. A 1998 Supreme Court ruling found that provinces cannot secede unilaterally and negotiations with the federal government would have to follow.

title: Catholic US soldiers should not join Nidal Hasan firing squad, archbishop says
description: Armed forces ⁠archbishop objects to planned live-stream of Fort Hood shooter’s execution, slams ‘barbarically killing’ adversaries.
content: Catholics serving in the US Army should not take part in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to live stream on December 3, a prominent US archbishop said on Monday. In an unusually strongly worded statement, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of ‌Catholic members of the US armed forces, raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree. Broglio said he presided at the funeral of one of Hasan’s victims and lamented the shooting. But the Ohio-born archbishop asked whether the US wanted to “imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries”. “I oblige any Catholics assigned to ⁠the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the church,” Broglio said. US Army regulations do ‌allow for soldiers to request religious exemptions or accommodations and the army has yet to say how it intends to select members of the firing squad. US Defence Secretary Pete ‌Hegseth announced plans to live-stream the shooting last week, triggering a backlash among Republicans in Congress, religious leaders and ⁠international observers. US President Donald ⁠Trump approved Hasan’s execution by firing squad but has said he is still deciding whether to allow the live streaming to proceed. The event would be extraordinary, even for ‌a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or live-streamed, according to death penalty experts, and the US military has not executed anyone ‌by ‌firing squad since 1945. Hasan, now 56, requires a wheelchair, having been shot by police during his arrest. Hegseth said last week he ‌wants US soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and location of Hasan’s shooting spree. Hegseth has argued ⁠that making the event public will help serve as a deterrent. Broglio questioned whether the effect of a live-streamed execution on young viewers ⁠had been considered. He said the US military had a good reputation and asked if there was “really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man ‌in a wheelchair to the whole world”. Broglio’s ‌statement was issued soon after he met Pope Leo in Rome on Monday. Leo has clashed with Trump and his Pentagon over issues including the Iran war. Leo on Saturday condemned the death penalty, without mentioning the Hasan case specifically. US Vice-President J.D. Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has said that if it does ultimately get live-streamed, he would not watch it.

title: US actress Selma Blair arrested after incident on flight, accused of assault
description: Judge sets US$20,000 bail as defence lawyer cites medical emergency for actions on New York-bound plane.
content: Actress Selma Blair was arrested after she was accused of injuring two flight attendants on a trip from Los Angeles to New York. She was also accused of kicking a police officer taking her to the hospital and kicking a nurse once she got there. She pleaded not guilty Monday night to two counts of assault for state charges involving the officer and the nurse. And she faces separate federal charges based on what happened on the flight, which her representatives say was brought on by a severe medical emergency. Blair, 54, was detained by police at around 11pm Sunday after the Delta Air Lines jet parked at the gate at John F. Kennedy International Airport, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said in a statement. Blair and one of the flight attendants were taken to a hospital for evaluation, the Port Authority said. A police officer taking her to Jamaica Hospital Medical Centre said in charging documents that while she was securing Blair to a stretcher, Blair pulled a leg from the straps and kicked her repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling. Later, a nurse moving Blair said the actor kicked her in the chest, causing substantial pain. She was arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault late Monday at a court in Queens, where her lawyer entered a not guilty plea on her behalf. She appeared to cry as she stood in court in handcuffs, wearing jeans and a white hooded sweatshirt. Her lawyer Shawn Barnes told a judge her actions were not intentional. He said the actor, who has multiple sclerosis, missed several doses of “a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms”, according to the New York Daily News and New York Post. He said she had got on the flight in Los Angeles after a heavy workload, and hit her head during the flight. He said these factors along with the altitude led to “a state of severe confusion and disorientation”. The judge set her bail at US$20,000 cash or US$60,000 bond and set the next hearing for January. She left court with her lawyers. Details of what happened aboard the aircraft weren’t immediately disclosed by the airline, police or the FBI, which was investigating, but Delta said in a statement it “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behaviour, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first”. In air traffic communications, the Delta pilot asked the tower to have medical personnel waiting at the gate to treat bite marks and a bloody nose, but said ambulances were not necessary. “It sounds like the disruptive passenger also bashed her head on the bulkhead or something like that,” the pilot told the tower, according to audio posted on the ATC app. “So we’ll obviously have to get her potentially checked out as well as involved with law enforcement.” The FBI also issued Blair a notice charging her with assault related to her actions aboard the aircraft, according to a federal law enforcement official who spoke to Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak publicly about the matter. Those charges will be handled through the petty violations court in federal court in Brooklyn. No date has been set for Blair’s appearance. It’s not the first time Blair has had issues aboard a plane. In 2016, Blair apologised for making statements she later regretted during a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles. She said she had mixed alcohol with medication, causing her to black out. Blair had major roles in films including 1999’s Cruel Intentions, 2001’s Legally Blonde and 2004’s Hellboy. In recent years, she has advocated for disability rights after getting her multiple sclerosis diagnosis in 2018. In 2023, she joined President Joe Biden at the White House to celebrate the anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act.

title: Ukraine clears key hurdle in EU membership bid
description: Parliament approves minority rights law, prompting the bloc to open new negotiation clusters.
content: The European Union will on Tuesday open new negotiation chapters with Ukraine, an essential step in Kyiv’s long path to join the bloc. Ukrainian lawmakers on Monday passed legislation protecting the rights of national minorities, which removes a major hurdle in Kyiv’s bid for membership. The status of the Hungarian-speaking minority in western Ukraine had long caused tensions with Budapest and Hungary had blocked Ukraine’s EU membership bid, officially submitted days after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. European Council President Antonio Costa on Monday said he welcomed “today’s decision by EU Member States to open two further negotiation clusters with Ukraine and Moldova”. “We look forward to opening all remaining clusters as soon as possible,” he said, adding: “Your future lies in the EU. Let’s keep up the momentum!” Aspiring members will have to carry out sweeping reforms in their countries to comply with EU norms ranging from environmental policy to agriculture. Thirty-five negotiation chapters have to be completed and then a unanimous decision by the 27 member states to accept a new member is necessary to join the bloc. The ratification by each member state can be through parliamentary approval or a referendum. In addition to Ukraine and Moldova, the Western Balkan countries of Montenegro, Albania, Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, North Macedonia and Kosovo are also striving to join the EU. Montenegro is the furthest along in the EU admission process. The country, which has a population of only about 620,000, was recently certified as being capable of concluding its accession negotiations by the end of 2026, provided it maintains its pace of reform. On Thursday evening, the topic of EU enlargement is also due to be discussed at an EU leaders summit in Brussels. Additional reporting by dpa

title: Burnham says Iran’s IRGC likely behind UK airbase incident
description: Tehran denies involvement, demands evidence from London after recent security scare at RAF Fairford.
content: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford airbase in Britain was “highly likely” to have been coordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The RAF Fairford base in southwest England, which had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, became the focal point for a major ‌security response after five British men were arrested nearby in the early hours of September 27 on suspected terrorism and explosive offences. US officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to launch a drone attack and last week US President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted a decision to withdraw the bombers from the base. “I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard,” Burnham told parliament. Iran has rejected any connection with the Fairford incident. “Tehran has had no involvement in ⁠this matter, and if the British government possesses any documents or evidence to support its claims, it should present them,” said Iran’s ambassador to Britain, Seyed Ali Mousavi, according ‌to Iran’s state news agency IRNA. Details around the suspected plot remain thin. The five detained men were later released without charge on police bail “under stringent conditions”, and two other arrested men, including a British-Iranian national, have also been released. Detectives have ‌said petrol but no viable explosive had been found in vans seized along with the five men. However, both police and Burnham have pointed ⁠towards the involvement of a foreign state. UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told Parliament a known individual, whom she did not name, who was based in Iran was believed to be behind what had happened. “We will not tolerate these threats on our ‌soil,” Burnham said. “We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and ‌the ‌IRGC to do us harm.” Foreign ministries from almost 30 countries including the US, Canada, France and Germany issued a statement condemning “Iran’s use of violent attacks, including ‌the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyberattacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners”. “The UK has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project ⁠hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors,” the statement said. The British authorities have for a number of years accused Iran of being involved in ⁠numerous plots and attempted assassinations in Britain using criminal networks and proxies, accusations Tehran has repeatedly denied. Last year Britain said there had been 20 credible Iranian-backed threats to kill or kidnap individuals based in the UK. In July, Britain used new powers to ban support for the IRGC and a linked group, ‌Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which had claimed responsibility ‌for seven attacks earlier this year at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities, and Persian-language media. Ed Miliband, Britain’s foreign minister, said he had summoned the Iranian ambassador while the ministry announced two Iranian nationals had been sanctioned. The two men were Ruhollah Bazghandi, who Britain said was the IRGC’s head of counter-espionage operations, and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, a facilitator for the already sanctioned Zindashti criminal network which is accused of involvement in several plots against Iranian dissidents.

title: Elon Musk becomes biggest known donor in US midterms to boost Republicans
description: World’s richest man has spent US$276 million to help Trump’s party defend control of Congress.
content: Elon Musk, the world’s only trillionaire, has quietly become the biggest known donor in this year’s midterm elections, doling out more than US$276 million since July to try to save Republican majorities in Congress. The numbers, first reported by The New York Times ahead of this week’s federal filing deadline, were confirmed by Andrew Romeo, a spokesman for Musk’s super PAC (Political Action Committee). The money includes US$158 million given to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates, one of the largest known political donations in American history, according to the Times. Another US$76 million went to America PAC, a Musk super PAC, which has once again built out a major turnout operation like the one it used to help elect US President Donald Trump by knocking on doors in 2024. Musk also provided US$10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group that supports the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas, Ken Paxton. The race has been a major focus of Musk’s efforts. It is a dramatic turnaround since last May, when Musk said he intended to cut back on future political spending. “I think I’ve done enough,” he said at the time. Despite the cash infusion, Musk has generally kept a lower profile than in 2024, when he appeared on stage next to Trump at rallies, and in the early days of the president’s second term, when he led the Department of Government Efficiency. He had a falling out with Trump while leaving his government post, but the two have since reconciled. Trump presented Musk with the National Medal of Science last week. Musk’s net worth has fluctuated around the trillion-dollar line this year based on changes in stock prices, but he topped US$1 trillion again last week according to Forbes magazine. Republicans have a gaping financial advantage over their Democratic counterparts – a disparity that has been a rare bright spot for a party that is bracing for major potential losses amid deep voter frustration over the president’s performance, stubbornly high prices and the unpopular war with Iran. They have been using the money to blanket the airwaves in the race’s final stretch. “These robust investments have allowed the [Republican] apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” Romeo told the Times. Democrats responded to the news by accusing Republicans of using vast amounts of cash to mask their shortcomings. “Republicans are hoping to buy these elections, injecting tens of millions into races to try and outrun their unpopular candidates, unpopular president and unpopular economy,” said Lauren French, a spokeswoman for Democrats’ Senate Majority PAC.

title: Hong Kong can boost regional prosperity through ‘soft connectivity’, adviser says
description: Hong Kong is transforming itself into the region’s institutional ‘harbour’, a key adviser to the city’s leader tells forum.
content: Hong Kong’s institutional advantages and close ties with mainland China and the wider world can contribute to the Asia-Pacific region’s prosperity, a key adviser to the city’s leader has told a conference. Stephen Wong Yuen-shan, head of the Chief Executive’s Policy Unit, said on Monday that Hong Kong was transforming itself into the region’s institutional “harbour” – where trade from regional markets could converge and take advantage of the city’s “soft connectivity” advantages. He said such “soft connectivity” could help transform Hong Kong’s unique advantages under the “one country, two systems” principle into effective regional governance by embedding Chinese standards into the process of sharing prosperity across the region. Wong delivered a keynote address at the Asia-Pacific Think Tank Forum in neighbouring Shenzhen, stressing Hong Kong’s intention to develop regional “soft connectivity”, including digital trade agreements, carbon markets and cross-border logistics policies. “What crosses a border today is no longer just a container. It may also be a rule, a data set, a verified figure or a certificate,” Wong told the forum. “Under our unique institutional advantage of one country, two systems, different legal, monetary, customs, and regulatory arrangements operate within one country. “And Hong Kong has accumulated valuable experience in connecting different systems and making cross-border exchanges work in practice.” Wong added: “The Asia-Pacific has achieved an extraordinary expansion of physical connectivity over recent decades. “As trade becomes more digital, services-intensive and environmentally accountable, soft connectivity may become an increasingly important part of the region’s next phase of development. “Hong Kong’s contribution may therefore lie in helping to build that connectivity.” Monday’s forum was convened by the Shenzhen Academy of Social Sciences and Shenzhen University to mark the mainland Chinese city’s hosting of the Apec leaders’ meeting next month. China is the host of Apec 2026, whose theme is “Building an Asia-Pacific community to prosper together”. “A community, in the end, is a set of mutual recognitions of each other’s contracts, certificates, data and, ultimately, each other,” Wong added. Hong Kong will host the finance ministers’ meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum next week.

title: US agents search home of Democratic lawmaker Ilhan Omar in criminal probe
description: Minnesota Democrat decries ‘political intimidation’ as party leaders question search timing weeks before midterms.
content: Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic US congresswoman Ilhan Omar, a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed focus to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her re-election bid. The search of the Minnesota congresswoman’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by top Democrats in Congress, who raised questions about the timing given long-standing Justice Department protocol to avoid overt investigative steps involving political candidates in the direct run-up to an election. Omar, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, said she was being targeted as one of the Republican’s “political enemies”. The scope of the investigation was unclear, though Trump and officials in his administration have repeatedly referred in recent months to the existence of an inquiry into Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the US and left-wing views have drawn scrutiny from the White House and other Republicans. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last month cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork. “Something’s going to happen,” he said in a potential foreshadowing of the search. In a statement on X on Monday, Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement”. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.” At a political rally in Ohio later Monday, Trump attacked Omar’s Somali origins, saying: “She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet”. The crowd responded by shouting: “Deport”. Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election. Top Democrats seized on the timing as the latest instance in what they said was the “continued corrupt weaponisation” against Trump’s perceived adversaries. “For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” said a joint statement from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.” The search was carried out by agents with Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security. A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Justice Department, which said in a statement that HSI agents had executed a judicially authorised search warrant in the Washington DC area related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details. The street around Omar’s home was blocked off Monday morning as some HSI agents removed boxes labelled “Seized Property Evidence”. The operation came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor” and suggested that Vice-President J.D. Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it’s “really up to the DOJ”. Trump suggested he didn’t know what was happening with the investigation even as he seemed to suggest that Omar was engaged in suspect behaviour. Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud, an allegation she has denied, and has said the administration was looking for pathways to investigate her. Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress. When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks. In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced to 14 months in prison. Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress. According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in the 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family”. Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies” and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive”.

title: Israel pupil, 15, killed, over 20 hurt, after suspected leftover bomb detonates
description: The explosive, likely from a round of fighting with Hezbollah militants three years ago, went off as a student picked it up, police said.
content: An Israeli teenager was killed and more than 20 other people injured Monday by a suspected leftover Hezbollah bomb as they hiked near the Lebanese border, officials said. The Israeli military, which dispatched helicopters to the scene, said an initial review showed the explosion was likely caused by an unexploded munition from Lebanese militant group Hezbollah. The explosive, which was likely a cluster bomb from a round of fighting three years ago, went off in the hands of a pupil who picked it up, Israeli police said. Police said that school authorities had received the go-ahead for the outdoor excursion in the region, which Hezbollah has hit in successive rounds of fighting as Israel pounds the Iran-backed group. “I share in the heavy grief of the family of the boy who was killed in the explosion during the trip near the northern border, and I wish a swift and full recovery to all the injured,” Defence Minister Israel Katz posted on social media, adding that the incident was being investigated. Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the victim was a 15-year-old who had gone on an annual school trip. In addition to the one dead, more than 20 others were wounded, Northern Command police chief Meir Eliyahu said. The northern city of Haifa took in three teenagers with moderate injuries and a 61-year-old with severe injuries, Rambam hospital spokesman David Ratner said. The incident injured both students and staff from a religious high school as they were on an outing, the municipality of the northern city of Maalot-Tarshiha said. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu scrapped plans and was holding assessments over the “severe incident”, his office said. “The Prime Minister asked to ensure that the injured are being evacuated as quickly as possible to hospitals and is continuing to hold ongoing assessments,” Netanyahu’s office said in a statement. The incident comes ahead of October 27 elections in which Netanyahu is facing a tough race for a new term. The opposition is accusing him of not doing enough to ensure Israelis’ security after three years of war, despite recent quiet from Gaza, which Israel has devastated since the October 7, 2023 attacks by Hamas. Gadi Eisenkot, who is the principal challenger in the elections, said he was “praying together with all Israelis for the swift recovery of the wounded” and wished strength to rescue teams. Yair Golan, head of the centre-left Democrats party, said three years of periodic fighting with Hezbollah had left Israel’s northern border area with “dangers that cannot be ignored”. He called for “a thorough and comprehensive inspection of the hiking areas in the north”, including removing unexploded ordnance. Earlier this year, Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war with rocket fire at Israel in solidarity with its backer Iran, which was attacked by Israel and the United States. Israel responded with air strikes and a ground invasion into Lebanon, where authorities say more than 4,300 people have been killed since March. Israel and Lebanon agreed to a framework deal that involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region. Violence in the border area has since decreased. Israel last month carried out a massive explosion in Lebanon to destroy a tunnel complex where it said Hezbollah kept weapons and fighters.

title: Eala stunned in Wuhan by No 217; Zverev ends year at No 1 after Alcaraz loses in Shanghai
description: Philippine star loses to Chinese qualifier Shi Han, while Zverev becomes first German to finish season as ATP’s top-ranked player.
content: Filipino star Alexandra Eala suffered a shock 4-6, 6-3, 6-3 first-round defeat against 217th-ranked Chinese qualifier Shi Han at the Wuhan Open on Monday, while seven-time grand slam champion Carlos Alcaraz ⁠lost ⁠7-5, 7-6 to ⁠unseeded Belgian Zizou Bergs in the Shanghai Masters. The result in Shanghai also confirmed Alexander Zverev as the ATP’s year-end world No 1. Eala, the 13th seed, missed last week’s China Open to compete in the Asian Games in Japan, where she claimed a bronze medal for the Philippines. Her return to the tour did not go as planned. Just one week separates Eala and Shi in age and despite the gulf in their experience, very little separated the two 21-year-olds on Monday. Eala is ranked 19 in the world, a title winner on the WTA Tour and a former semi-finalist at the WTA 1000 level. Shi, meanwhile, is ranked outside the top 200 and entered the clash with just two tour-level victories under her belt. For large stretches of their showdown though, their contrasting positions were completely unnoticeable. Eala shook off trouble on her own serve and converted her first break point opportunity of the match to scoop the opening set in 54 minutes. The second set followed a similar pattern but this time Shi utilised her powerful backhand to break Eala for a 4-3 advantage and she soon drew level to force a decider. Riding a wave of momentum, Shi grabbed a seventh game in a row to leap to a 3-0 lead in the final set as Eala faded. Shi finished the job to claim the first tour-level top-100 victory of her career and book a second-round date with former US Open finalist Leylah Fernandez. Earlier in Shanghai, and fresh from defending his Japan Open title with a victory over Czech Jiri Lehecka, Alcaraz never found his rhythm in a scrappy two-hour, two-minute contest with Bergs. The second-seeded Spaniard, who was ⁠sidelined for almost five months before returning at the US Open ‌in late August and reaching the quarter-finals, joined 24-time grand slam champion Novak Djokovic and US Open ‌runner-up Ben Shelton among the casualties at the ⁠ATP Masters ⁠1000 event. Bergs produced a composed all-court performance, thriving in the quick conditions as the 27-year-old broke Alcaraz’s serve three times to clinch the biggest victory of his career. Bergs had lost their only previous meeting, falling to Alcaraz in the last 16 of last year’s Japan Open, but showed no signs of intimidation ⁠as he outplayed the 23-year-old in key moments. The upset also ensured that French Open and US Open champion Zverev, ‌29, will finish the season as the world No 1, becoming the ‌first ‌German to achieve the feat and the oldest player to achieve it for the first time. “It’s been a fantastic season for me winning in Paris and New York and knowing that I will finish the year on top of the rankings is just a dream come true,” said Zverev, who will face Kazakhstan’s 19th seed Alexander Bublik in the round of 16 in Shanghai. “So much work and effort have been put into achieving this goal, especially after coming back from the ankle injury [at the 2022 French Open semi-finals]. “I look forward to finishing the season in style.” Zverev’s route to the top spot ‌opened after Italian Jannik Sinner had not played since beating ⁠him in the Wimbledon final on July 12 due to a ⁠knee injury. The 25-year-old missed the North American hard-court swing, the US Open and the ongoing Asian swing. The five-time ‌major winner will ‌also sit out the European indoor season and the ATP Finals in Turin, where he has lifted the trophy in each of the past two years.

title: Garden Company apologises after crowd chaos mars student sandwich record bid
description: More than 1,400 people, including over 700 pupils involved in world-record bid, jostle to leave as overcrowding nearly triggers stampede.
content: One of Hong Kong’s oldest makers of bread and biscuits, the Garden Company, has apologised and pledged to review its crowd-management procedures after a world-record attempt involving more than 700 students making sandwiches descended into chaos. The incident occurred on Sunday at SKH Tang Shiu Kin Secondary School in Wan Chai, when the company tried to set a record for the “largest sandwich-making lesson” to mark its coming 100th anniversary. More than 700 primary school pupils were involved and some attendees estimated that at least 1,400 people, including parents, attended the event, causing overcrowding at the venue. Some attendees posted about the situation on social media, claiming that people forcing their way through the doors had nearly triggered a stampede. They accused the organiser of poor crowd management. In a social media post on Monday night, the Garden Company apologised and said: “We attach the utmost importance to the safety and experience of every participant, and have proactively contacted all parents to gather their feedback. “In light of the shortcomings in the organisation of this event, the Garden team is conducting a thorough review, and we humbly accept the criticism. We will examine our procedures and relevant measures to ensure that such incidents do not occur again.” The company also acknowledged the extended wait times at the end of the event. “We sincerely apologise to the affected parents and children,” it said. It stressed in the evening statement that there was no “stampede” or “fighting” as rumoured, adding that no one was injured. Videos circulating online showed paper towels scattered across the floor of the hall and many children standing in the corridors waiting to leave amid scenes of chaotic jostling. Some attendees complained on the social media platform Threads that as the event drew to a close, groups of parents frantically forced their way through the doors to get inside, “completely ignoring instructions on-site to the point where even the doors were broken”. Some parents also complained on social media that the instructions given that day were unclear, while the venue was small and had only one tiny door as an exit. “One moment, the staff told people to wait at the entrance; the next, at the playground; and then suddenly, to walk into the hall,” an attendee said. The attendee recalled that many parents became agitated because they were worried about whether they would be able to pick up their children.

title: Dog shelter worker awarded HK$89,000 over canine attack despite volunteer claim
description: District Court rules employment relationship existed despite lack of formal contract as victim was paid and directed by shelter staff.
content: A Hong Kong court has awarded more than HK$89,000 (US$11,340) to a worker at a dog shelter who was seriously injured in a canine attack, rejecting her employer’s argument that she was a volunteer. District Judge Harold Leong Kwok-on said on Monday that the employment relationship between Kelly Animals Shelter in Lau Fau Shan and the victim had been established despite no contract being signed, noting she was paid, allocated work by staff and did not manage the business or shoulder profits or risks. The employee was attacked at about 3pm on November 16, 2022, while attempting to herd dogs at the shelter back into their kennels. She sustained multiple injuries and was taken to Tin Shui Wai Hospital’s accident and emergency department. She was then transferred to the orthopaedic ward at Tuen Mun Hospital for treatment. After being discharged, she continued to receive orthopaedic treatment, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and psychiatric care, having been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder. The employee sustained wounds to her face and both hands, including a 3cm cut above her left eyebrow, two deeper wounds on her left hand and a near-fracture of her right little finger. Her hospital treatment included stitches, shots for rabies and tetanus, and surgery to insert screws to stabilise the site of the fracture. Her front tooth was also knocked out by the dog, and she received treatment at the oral and maxillofacial surgery and dental departments at Tuen Mun Hospital. The court ordered compensation of HK$89,359.27, taking into consideration the medical bills and her income at the time of the accident.

title: Review | Netflix drama Did Someone Happen to Mention Me? review: Koji Yakusho leads amnesia comedy
description: Koji Yakusho plays a famous Japanese actor who is suddenly forgotten by his nation as a vaccine’s side effect.
content: 3.5/5 stars Lead cast: Koji Yakusho, Kento Kaku, Kenichi Matsuyama In Netflix’s new comedy series Did Someone Happen to Mention Me?, Koji Yakusho stars as a world-famous Japanese actor who discovers that almost the whole of Japan has forgotten him. Playful and lighthearted, the eight-episode series follows the veteran performer as he loses his celebrity status overnight and is forced to reassess his character and relationships while rebuilding his life and career. Created by acclaimed actor-writer-director Kankuro Kudo (Go, Ping Pong, Extremely Inappropriate!), the series is packed with big-name cameos and industry in-jokes that help distract from the flimsy mechanics of its high-concept premise. Gen Takasegawa (Yakusho) is a second-generation Japanese celebrity whose career hits new heights when he is cast as King Lear in a historic production at London’s iconic Globe Theatre. While he is away, Japan is hit by a pandemic. Upon his return, Gen discovers to his horror that anyone who took the new vaccine has no memory of him. His credit cards are cancelled, his social media presence vanishes and even his estranged wife, Machiko (Noriko Eguchi), and their young son don’t recognise him. Homeless and destitute, Gen takes a job at a sauna under its formidable manager, Chijimi (Maki Sakai), to make ends meet. Although nobody believes his story, colleague Tetsu (Kento Kaku) – an aspiring playwright – helps him secure work as an extra on a late-night television drama. Not only does this bring Gen back into the orbit of his first wife and manager, Yoko (Yoh Yoshida), and his long-time screen rival Daiya (Masatoshi Hamada) – neither of whom remembers him – but it also gives him an opportunity to rebuild his career and, hopefully, find a modicum of humility. The more we learn about Gen, the more we discover what a train wreck his life was. His wealth and fame were offset by two failed marriages, a series of salacious affairs chronicled in the tabloids, and a tearaway daughter, Ema (Yumi Kawai), who now works in a concept cafe dating sugar daddies. Gen begrudgingly acknowledges how his pampered and privileged existence has made him selfish, arrogant and heartless. Along the way, he encounters struggling assistant director Kazuki (Kenichi Matsuyama) and a troupe of small-time stage performers, including Hayato Isomura and Chisato Nakai. There is even an appearance by Sean Holmes, the associate artistic director of Shakespeare’s Globe. Kudo’s script introduces Maslow’s hierarchy of needs as Gen’s primary guide towards a better life. The psychological theory prioritises food, shelter, clothing and sleep as humanity’s primary survival needs before expanding to include “safety and security”, “love and belonging” and so on. Perhaps more interesting is how Kudo frequently compares Gen’s fall from grace with King Lear’s physical and psychological collapse. The first episode sees Gen perform Lear’s famous “Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks” monologue on stage, and Kudo returns to Shakespeare’s words throughout the series, equating the mad old king’s violent tirade to Gen’s metaphorical death and rebirth. Beyond the show’s ambitious dramatic underpinnings, Did Someone Happen to Mention Me? has a lot of fun at the expense of its protagonist, Yakusho’s indisputable star power and Japan’s struggling film industry in general. The script laments the waning popularity of grandiose period samurai films that employ large crews of skilled craftsmen, while trashy romantic dramas are hastily thrown together to meet the huge demand created by streaming services. The show also pokes fun at the disruptive nature of big-name day players who arrive on set half-drunk and ill-prepared, even as every episode hosts a procession of eye-catching cameos that Netflix would prefer remained under wraps. At its best when charting the wild and unpredictable life of a jobbing thespian – from amateur stage performer to background actor, and top-flight movie star to celebrity endorser – Did Someone Happen to Mention Me? is built upon a fantastical premise that cannot withstand the slightest amount of scrutiny. The public’s collective amnesia apparently stems from the second dose of a vaccine taken by close to 90 per cent of the Japanese population, but that never suitably explains why Gen’s online presence also vanishes, or why he cannot simply point to his decades of past work as definitive proof. Kudo swings for a more fantastical, Capra-esque tone that audiences must simply accept without question if they are to proceed. Those willing to take this leap of faith will be treated to a wonderful showcase for Yakusho’s range as a performer and a whimsical rumination on status, arrogance, complacency and the acting profession itself. It is hardly Shakespeare, but it puts on a good show. Did Someone Happen to Mention Me? starts streaming on Netflix on October 22.

title: Teenager shoots headmaster and teacher with a hunting gun at French school
description: A member of staff at the school, near Marseille, is said to have disarmed the boy. Prosecutors said he hid the weapon in a guitar case.
content: A 14-year-old boy opened fire with a hunting gun at a school in France on Monday, wounding the headmaster and a teacher before being disarmed by a member of staff, local authorities said. The shooting took place at Joseph-Lakanal middle school in the southern town of Aubagne, near Marseille, where a third person was grazed by gunfire, police said. Authorities said there did not appear to be a link with high school protests that have rocked France in recent weeks. “The middle school was not affected by the high school students’ protest,” police told Agence France-Presse. The suspect “came in carrying a bag which was a guitar case. He clearly removed a weapon from this guitar case – a long gun,” said Marseille’s deputy public prosecutor Audrey Jouaneton. He fired at least four shots, including inside a classroom occupied by teachers and pupils, leaving a mark on a blackboard, she said. The headmaster, 53, and teacher, 37, were not in critical condition, according to authorities. “The suspect, for reasons as yet unknown, fired at the head teacher, who was hit by a shower of pellets in the thighs and lower back,” said Jacques Witkowski, prefect of the wider Bouches-du-Rhone region. He then fired at a second teacher, who was hit by buckshot in the thigh before a member of staff disarmed him, he said. The suspect “is not known for any history of delinquency or radicalisation”, Witkowski added. Sarah, a pupil at the school, told Agence France-Presse she heard the fire alarm go off during her Spanish lesson and went into the corridor, where she and her classmates “bumped into” the gunman. “He started shooting and said: ‘I’ve only come for the teachers, not for the pupils,’” she said. An investigation into attempted murder has been opened. French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who visited the scene, said the suspect’s father had been taken into custody. Investigators were “trying to understand how this young person ended up in a position with this gun”, Nunez told reporters. French President Emmanuel Macron on social media praised the teaching staff for their quick reaction. “I commend the composure and exemplary response of the teaching staff, which helped to prevent the worst from happening,” he said. Education Minister Edouard Geffray, who also went to the scene on Monday, called for action against such violence. “All this seems to sit within a global social phenomenon,” he said. “We have to provide a societal response … Schools can’t do everything, schools cannot treat major violence.” There has been a spate of violent incidents at French schools in recent months, prompting bag checks on entry in some establishments. In February, a 14-year-old stabbed an art teacher in southern France at least three times, leaving the 60-year-old in critical condition. A 14-year-old pupil in June last year fatally stabbed a teaching assistant in eastern France. In another, a pupil carried out a stabbing spree in several classrooms in April last year, wounding a girl and three other pupils.

title: Huanggang Port praised for ‘light speed’ checks, but some find layout huge
description: More than 42,000 travellers use new border-crossing facility by 5pm on first day, as authorities prepare for surge over coming long weekend.
content: More than 42,000 travellers and 5,700 vehicles passed through the revamped Huanggang Port on Monday under a “smooth” first-day run of the new “joint clearance” system to cross between Hong Kong and mainland China, as officials braced for larger crowds over the coming long weekend. Early bird travellers and residents simply curious to see how the new system worked were the first to pass through the facility when it opened at 6.30am, with some calling the clearance process “light speed”. Many travellers said they approved of the new approach, by which travellers heading in either direction need only show one identification document. Others also said they were impressed with the architecture of the building, which took six years to construct. But others found the facility mazelike and simply too huge to cross quickly, which undercut the appeal of the new clearance process. Speaking to the press after inspecting the new 24-hour checkpoint’s operation on Monday, No 2 city official Eric Chan Kwok-ki said he was pleased with the “smooth” operation. “There’s a reason we chose [Monday] to open. The National Day ‘golden week’ holiday has just ended,” he said. “We believe there will be fewer visitors. So everyone has time to get familiar with the operations. “We hope our colleagues will quickly familiarise themselves with the operation over the next few days so they can handle the bigger challenges during the peak on Saturday and Sunday when there will be more people,” the chief secretary said. Chan also said that if the new “collaborative inspection and joint immigration clearance” model worked well, the government would consider extending it to other checkpoints. Officials said clearance at Huanggang could be cut to five minutes, from about 30 minutes needed at the previous facility. Hong Kong residents who hold a valid mainland travel permit can use their Hong Kong ID cards interchangeably at the joint clearance channel for both outbound and inbound trips. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said a joint command centre had been set up with Shenzhen authorities to ensure operations went smoothly on both sides of the border. “It will be in operation as long as necessary, especially during peak times, like weekends or during the Apec conference,” Tang said. Shenzhen is hosting the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in mid-November, while the bloc’s finance ministers will gather in Hong Kong later this month. Traffic at the crossing is expected to surge on the coming long weekend, as Monday is a public holiday following the Chung Yeung Festival on Sunday. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said contingency plans were in place to ensure sufficient public transport for the anticipated rush. “We will not underestimate the challenge to be brought about in the coming long weekend,” Chan said. According to the Security Bureau, the new control point had handled 20,201 incoming and 22,011 departing travellers by 5pm. The 42,212 passenger trips recorded represented a 181 per cent increase compared with average Monday traffic last month at the previous control point. The new port also handled 2,713 incoming and 2,995 outgoing vehicles. The number of vehicle trips was 12 per cent more than the average recorded on Mondays last month. Among the first travellers using the new facility was a Shenzhen resident, surnamed Liao, who crossed into Hong Kong at around 6.30am and returned to the mainland shortly before 7am. “The clearance was done in a minute,” he said, adding praise for the architecture of the building, which he likened to a modern airport. Another mainland visitor, surnamed Wen, also praised the speed of the clearance process. “It was light speed,” Wen said. Dey Wu, a Shenzhen resident who holds an American passport, agreed the clearance was efficient. “The process took less than a minute,” she said, adding that officials told her she was the first foreigner to cross. “I used to come [to Hong Kong] once a month. Now, I would be happy to come twice a week.” But on the Shenzhen side, a 70-year-old Hong Kong traveller who uses a cane to walk, Helen Ho, said the building was too big. “I did not feel it was actually much faster as the building is so big and I had to take many lifts, and I had not been guided enough along my way,” Ho said. A Tung Chung resident also said a technical glitch prevented him from using facial recognition clearance although he had registered for the option in advance. He ended up using his Hong Kong ID card to pass the gate. Cheerful members of a mainland tour group held up signs with slogans such as “New Huanggang, first in line” as they arrived. One traveller, 52, and 11 of her family members spent five hours taking a high-speed train from Hunan province to Shenzhen. “It is great. It is modernised and service is great,” said the woman, surnamed Kuang, adding they would continue their journey to Hong Kong. Hong Kong authorities said 30 tour groups used the crossing to head south into the city. Timothy Chui Ting-pong, executive director of the Hong Kong Tourism Association, said he expected more local travel agencies to launch tours themed around the crossing in the near future. He added that some visiting mainland tour groups had already switched to the facility for their departure. Visitors also drove to cross the border, but some said the time they spent waiting for their turn was more than double compared with the previous checkpoint as drivers were not familiar with the new procedures. But celebrity feng shui master Mak Ling-ling, who also drove across, said it took her one minute for clearance. “The facility is new, it is quite natural drivers may take some time to familiarise themselves with the new procedures,” she said. “Overall, the new port has more lanes so the process was in general faster.” The crossing is expected to be able to handle up to 300,000 travellers a day. The Immigration Department said it expected about 100,000 people to use Huanggang Port daily during initial operations. It can also handle 15,000 vehicles a day. The previous facility began 24-hour clearance in 2003, becoming the country’s first land crossing to provide round-the-clock clearance for both travellers and cargo. It handled an average of 40,000 visitors a day and a peak flow of 65,000 people. On average, 9,000 vehicles used the crossing. Additional reporting by Kristen Cheung

title: Why China is likely to be cautious about recent Trump-Putin diesel deal
description: The US may still try to target major buyers of Russian energy despite the deal aimed at cutting American fuel prices, analysts warn.
content: China is likely to view the latest US dealings with Russia as “transactional”, according to observers, who said Beijing was likely to wait and see what the longer-term impact would be given the possibility that Donald Trump might abruptly change course again. The US president announced that under a deal with Vladimir Putin, Russia would “immediately” supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets. He wrote on social media that another 500,000 tonnes would follow in November, with a further 1 million tonnes “within a short period of time”. “Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump added. Analysts said it was too soon to say if this was a temporary fix driven by domestic political concerns or the first step in a wider push to dismantle Western sanctions. The agreement marked a sharp reversal from the United States, coming just three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which allows him to penalise major buyers of Russian energy. It was also struck less than a month before the midterm elections on November 3, where soaring fuel prices threaten the Republicans’ hold on Congress. The Kremlin said the deal was made during a “very substantive and friendly” call focused on the war in Ukraine. On Sunday, Trump also said both sides had agreed an “energy ceasefire” “effective immediately” but Ukraine said it knew nothing about it and Russia continued to strike power plants. Asked about the diesel deal on Monday, foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said China’s position on Ukraine was clear and consistent, and that it believed dialogue was the only way to resolve the crisis. Cui Hongjian, head of European Union studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, said China would watch how the deal developed. He said Ukraine and Europe were hoping it would be an emergency “stopgap” rather than a “first step that sets off a domino effect” on sanctions. He added that China’s view would be shaped by whether Russia used the deal as a springboard to “pry loose the West’s entire set of energy sanctions against it”. “So China’s approach right now, in my view, will still be to wait and see which direction things develop in,” Cui said. He also said it was likely to have little impact on China’s energy trade with Russia, as Moscow still needed to sell to its largest buyer. “The question is to what extent will [the deal] actually affect China’s energy security or whether China can protect its interests in the overall energy market,” he said. “I don’t think China will be too concerned at the moment about what major direct impact this might have. It still requires a period of observation and assessment.” Zhang Chi, a senior researcher at the University of Hong Kong’s Centre on Contemporary China and the World, said the diesel deal was “self-contradictory” and reflected the “selective” nature of the US approach. But he said the Graham Act could be used as a bargaining chip in talks with Russia, China and India. “Even as the US pursues Russian energy for its own benefit, the secondary tariff or secondary sanctions mechanism under the Graham Act could still be triggered to target other major importers,” Zhang said. Beijing would also need to closely monitor the sunset provisions of the Graham Act and how the resolution of the Russia-Ukraine war might affect its implementation, Zhang added. Ma Bo, an associate professor of international relations at Nanjing University, said Trump was hoping the deal would help limit Republican losses in next month’s elections. “Therefore, I think this is a very transactional matter, perhaps a one-time offer, and it may be adjusted after the midterm elections,” he said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticised the deal, saying any easing of sanctions on Russia without a lasting de-escalation agreement was “an obvious weakness”. Ukraine, which Trump asked to stop “knocking out diesel fuel in Russia”, continued to target Russian refineries after the diesel deal was announced, prompting the US leader to call on Saturday for Zelensky to be replaced. Ma said Beijing would have to wait and see if these latest developments had any impact, and that China and other Asian importers should not take Trump’s deal with Putin as “a clear indicator of future tariff decisions or cooperation with Russia”. “If countries adjust their strategic planning or expect a permanent US policy shift [on secondary sanctions], that could backfire when the midterm election results are in,” he added. Zhang said the diesel deal would be a fresh test case for the evolving US-China relationship. “How the US uses and adjusts its sanctions system based on the new strategic positioning of US-China ties is a new observation point to verify the progress of improvement in US-China relations,” he said.

title: Hackers heat fridges at major French supermarkets, spoiling food
description: Authorities launch probe after chillers were cranked to 50 degrees Celsius, causing tens of millions of euros in losses.
content: Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit) overnight, causing fires and spoiling food. The Paris prosecutor’s office said on Monday that a “large-scale” attack was “affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France”, leading to food losses and fires. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a person in his office said. France was coordinating with European ‌counterparts because other countries could also be affected, the person said, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk. Felix Aime, a senior cyber threat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected. Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were hit, while Monoprix, which operates about 490 stores in France, said 5 per cent of its stores were affected. Les Mousquetaires, owner of retailer Intermarche, said fridges at around 150 of its stores were heated up to 50 degrees for six hours overnight. A spokesperson said all affected food had been discarded to eliminate health risks. Paris resident Geert de Clercq witnessed staff at an Intermarche in central Paris throwing cartfuls of defrosted frozen foods ⁠into a giant trash container, with molten ice cream sloshing out of broken tubs on the street. Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket group had also been targeted. “Targeting equipment essential to ‌the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he wrote on X. There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV ‌the “unprecedented” attack would represent losses amounting to “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day”. Christel Delberghe, director general at European retail association Eurocommerce, said: “This incident underlines ⁠the importance of resilience across the entire supply ⁠chain”. Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control panels that manage an entire store’s fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere. The source close to Lecornu said ‌ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss. Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”. The affected units “were running outdated firmware”, Danfoss said, adding that it had “long advised customers to keep supported systems ‌updated ‌with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions”. On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty’s Team82 published research detailing vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller. According to the report, software ‌updates issued by Danfoss addressed issues that could have allowed attackers to bypass authentication controls and execute code on compromised devices. The attacks resemble disruptions reported at about a dozen US military commissaries in late August ⁠that led to food losses after fridges were affected. In a statement, French retail association Federation du Commerce et de la Distribution called for “full transparency” from Danfoss about the incident. It said supermarkets aimed ⁠to protect consumers and return to normal operations as soon as possible. The FCD said some impacted stores were already back up and running. Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Netherlands’ largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has major operations in the US, said it was dealing with a “security issue” on its network and had taken several ‌systems offline as a precaution. A message on the retailer’s ‌smartphone app said it was unable to deliver groceries because of a “cybersecurity incident”. Online orders account for about 10 per cent of Albert Heijn sales. Physical stores remained open, while Dutch news agency ANP reported that rival retailers had seen a surge in delivery orders. Ahold Delhaize said there was no reason to see a link between the incidents in France and its supermarkets. Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US. Websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion chains displayed notices saying “site temporarily down”. It was unclear whether other operations had been affected.

title: Selfies, queues and confusion, but Huanggang Port’s wow factor shines through
description: Motorists using checkpoint said border clearance took longer than expected, while building’s spaciousness and design impressed travellers.
content: The much-anticipated opening of the revamped Huanggang Port border crossing between Hong Kong and Shenzhen on Monday was marked by excitement, eagerness and confusion. At around 8am, 1½ hours after the control point opened, many private vehicles were neatly lining up for immigration clearance. The use of new technology, a new location and a new facility meant that extra time and patience were needed. Visitors, mostly tourists and retirees travelling on foot, had a wow moment inside the modern facility, prompting plenty of selfies. Vehicles queued at a temporary traffic buffer zone on San Sham Road in the morning before making their way to the new facility, where police cordoned off roads and directed traffic towards the building. Driver Ho Shun-ping, in his sixties, waited 25 minutes in the buffer zone and another 30 minutes at the “integrated information collection device” before finally crossing the border into mainland China by car. “It actually took a long time because many drivers were using the device from the car for the first time,” he said. “They parked a bit far from the device and had to jump out of the car to check. The staff inside the booth then had to help manually one by one.” Ho said the process had reversed the usual pattern at the old crossing: cars used to wait for passengers crossing on foot, but on Monday it was the other way round. “The overall process took longer than expected compared with my usual experience at the old crossing,” he said, adding that he used to spend only 10 to 20 minutes crossing at the old checkpoint, “even waiting for five to 10 minutes would have been long enough in the past”. The opening of the facility marked the end of the 37-year run of the Lok Ma Chau/Huanggang control point, which began operating in 1989. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Sunday called the revamped port “a critical milestone” for connectivity in the Greater Bay Area, saying the landmark project would allow the city to better integrate into and serve the overall development of the country. He described it as the most important 24-hour passenger land boundary checkpoint, with a designed daily capacity of 200,000 passenger trips. The border crossing has introduced a new “collaborative inspection and joint clearance” model, which is designed to cut clearance time from about 30 minutes to around five. Eligible passengers can complete both departure and entry clearance procedures by presenting one identity document and passing through an automated channel with three gates. Ringo Lee Yiu-pui, honorary life president of the Hong Kong, China Automobile Association, urged Shenzhen authorities to update electronic maps and road signs. He said unclear signs had caused confusion among Hong Kong motorists. “Some drivers spent at least 10 minutes around the Shenzhen side of the border and could not tell the road signs for the new or old border [crossing],” Lee said. Three retirees – a couple surnamed Liu and their friend surnamed Lam – set off from Sheung Shui to visit the crossing as a tourist attraction. They spent almost 30 minutes crossing the border. That included a bathroom break, photo-taking at every opportunity, connecting to the free Wi-fi, and asking an immigration officer how to register for the “joint clearance” channel. The actual time they spent crossing through the “joint clearance” channel was less than a minute. The spaciousness and the fluid design of the checkpoint building made it a popular photo spot for travellers. The Liu couple took photos on the escalators leading to the departure hall on level 5, while Lam stopped to photograph a vast glass wall overlooking Shenzhen as he passed the arrival hall on level 4. “It has high ceilings. The environment’s great, the air quality’s great. It’s very comfortable,” Mr Liu, 80, said. Shortly after 1pm, queues of about 20 people had formed at each of the “joint clearance” lanes in operation. The three retirees had waited for 12 minutes. Five minutes into the wait, Lam said he wished authorities would open all the clearance lanes. While most of the automated lanes were in use, about five were cordoned off at the first gate. “They should open all the lanes so we don’t have to queue. If they had expected many people to come, then they should open up more lanes,” Lam said. All three retirees said they preferred the Heung Yuen Wai checkpoint, which they could reach with a HK$2 fare from their homes in Sheung Shui. The fare to the revamped Huanggang checkpoint was HK$4.10 as they first had to take a minibus to the San Tin interchange before switching to a bus. “We have already retired, so we like to save every penny we can,” Lam said. “I’d come here if I needed to, but not for the sake of it again.”

title: OpenAI’s GPT-6 may lead to robotics breakthrough  as soon as next year: Unitree founder
description: Wang Xingxing says OpenAI’s latest advances have accelerated prospects for a ‘ChatGPT moment’ in embodied intelligence.
content: US start-up OpenAI’s latest advances in artificial intelligence may be a tipping point that leads to a breakthrough for the robotics industry as soon as next year, according to the founder of Chinese giant Unitree Robotics. Wang Xingxing, also the CEO of the Hangzhou-based company, said on Monday that OpenAI’s recently released GPT-6 model prompted expectations that a breakthrough could happen “within one or two years”. “It’s possible that, say, a GPT-7 model released next year could directly crack the problems of embodied intelligence,” he said at an industry event in Shanghai. In August, before GPT-6’s release, Wang said the industry could take two to three years at its fastest pace, or as long as a decade, to reach its “ChatGPT moment” – a critical threshold of technological maturity. He defined that moment as robots being able to complete around 80 per cent of tasks in 80 per cent of unfamiliar environments using voice or text commands. Wang’s latest comments came after OpenAI unveiled its flagship GPT-6 Astra model in September, demonstrating powerful capabilities in robotic manipulation. Unitree had also tested the new model on its own robots and got “good results”, he said. “The whole embodied intelligence industry has been shaken up after the release of GPT-6,” he said on the opening day of the 26th China International Industry Fair in Shanghai. “The biggest mistake I’ve made over the past decade or so is that I didn’t believe in AI enough.” As head of China’s leading humanoid robot maker, Wang’s public remarks are closely watched by investors and analysts as a bellwether of the state of the domestic robotics industry. He had previously sought to temper growing investor frenzy over China’s humanoid robot sector, warning that hardware development was progressing faster than the software needed to make robots genuinely “intelligent” and useful in real-world settings. While the physical capabilities of China’s humanoid robots have continued to impress – including the setting of several speed records at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing in August – their limited autonomy and “intelligence” have continued to raise questions about their commercialisation prospects. Previously focused on hardware, Unitree is also increasing investment in developing the “brains” of its robots. The company earlier said it planned to allocate around half of the proceeds from its recent initial public offering to research and development on robotic models. Wang said on Monday that Unitree was carrying out trials in factories, although the efficiency and ability of its robots still needed “further improvement”.

title: Review | Opera Hong Kong’s Cavalleria Rusticana and Pagliacci double bill lights up the stage
description: Cav/Pag captivates with vibrant staging and stellar performances, showcasing verismo pairing’s raw emotion, gripping tales.
content: Opera Hong Kong’s first fully staged production of Pietro Mascagni’s 1890 Cavalleria Rusticana and Ruggero Leoncavallo’s 1892 Pagliacci does justice to the classic double bill. Familiarly known as Cav/Pag, the production features lively staging, strong performances in the leading roles and splendid work by the Opera Hong Kong Chorus. Since 1893, the two operas have often been performed together for obvious reasons. Both are set in the rural Italian south and both explore themes of jealousy, betrayal and revenge that culminate in violent death. They are also outstanding examples of the verismo school of opera: gritty, realistic stories about ordinary people, abandoning traditional recitative for sung dialogue, and stripping ornamentation from the singing to focus on melody and the direct expression of emotion.
