Cavalleria Rusticana, or Rustic Chivalry, takes place in a Sicilian village at Easter. Turiddu returns from army service to find his sweetheart, Lola, married to the carter, Alfio. Attempting to forget her, he seduces the innocent Santuzza. However, this only rekindles Lola’s interest, and the two embark on an affair. Humiliated and distraught when Turiddu refuses to leave Lola, Santuzza reveals the betrayal to Alfio. Intent on vengeance, Alfio challenges Turiddu to a fight to the death. Pagliacci is set in Calabria and the clowns of the title are a travelling troupe performing commedia dell’arte, the ancient form of improvised theatre. The troupe’s leader, Canio, is jealously possessive of his young wife, Nedda. Becoming afraid of him, she agrees to run away with her secret lover, Silvio. One of the actors, Tonio, who had been cruelly rejected by Nedda, discovers her plan and tells Canio. As they perform the roles of a cuckolded husband and unfaithful wife on stage that night, Canio’s rage overcomes him – he stabs Nedda to death and when Silvio tries to save her, kills him, too. Director and designer Enrico Castiglione sets both operas in the same Sicilian square and prefaces them with video projections of lava flowing from Sicily’s volcano, Etna, as a metaphor for the way the burning passions of the characters erupt. Cavalleria Rusticana comes off best, not least because it is in many ways the better opera. The story is told with stark power and simplicity and momentum builds inexorably to the tragic denouement. It is also packed with gorgeous music, from Turiddu’s plaintive opening serenade to Lola – neatly presented with the singer in the auditorium, through two rousing, rollicking set pieces, Alfio’s “Il cavallo scalpita” (“The horse paws the ground”) and Turiddu’s “Viva, il vino spumeggiante” (“Hail to the sparkling wine”) to the varied, exquisite choruses. Pagliacci is more problematic, with an unwieldy structure, some longueurs in the music and characters with whom it is hard to sympathise. Where Mascagni and his librettists focus on driving the story forward, Leoncavallo (who was librettist as well as composer) combines a similarly melodramatic tale with more sophisticated elements – the play within a play, the idea that actors are human beings with real emotions – which can distract from the narrative flow. An excellent beginning has Tonio’s prologue performed in the auditorium with the singer walking around communicating directly with the audience and it was a good choice to have the most famous last line in all opera, “La commedia è finita!” (“The comedy is over!”) delivered by Tonio, as Leoncavallo originally intended, rather than Canio. This bookends the prologue and reflects Tonio’s role as the manipulator of events – the show’s director, in fact. However, overall Castiglione does not manage to achieve the pace and focus that he does in Cavalleria Rusticana. While the addition of a large group of clowns adds movement and colour, it is hard to believe that they would be part of such a small, down-at-heel commedia dell’arte troupe. In keeping with tradition, the roles of Turiddu and Canio, Alfio and Tonio are performed by the same tenor and baritone, here giving two exceptional artists the chance to showcase their dramatic range and fine singing. Leonardo Capalbo’s forceful, dark-toned tenor is perfectly suited to this style of music, he moves extremely well and his acting has both the realism and the emotional intensity these roles demand. He was outstanding as Turiddu, making the character’s changing moods and dilemmas convincingly real and brought plenty of passion to Canio, although there were moments when a little less might have been more. Alberto Gazale was superb in both operas – blessed with an elegant, ringing baritone, his confident, virile Alfio was skilfully contrasted with the devious Tonio, whose hunchback Gazale cleverly suggested through his posture, and he held the audience spellbound in the prologue. On the women’s side, Kate Jackman took the vocal honours – Santuzza can easily become strident, something Jackman’s warm, full mezzo smoothly avoided and she gave a heartfelt performance. Bing Bing Wang’s ultra-sexy Nedda made it easy to see why three men were all enamoured of her. Her singing suffered a few lapses but her acting was excellent, not holding back on the character’s mean side and neatly managing the physical elements required by the staging, including stylised moves and expressions when Nedda plays Colombina. Two local singers shone in supporting roles – Dominique Chan was believable and moving as Turiddu’s mother while Chen Yong was a lively Peppe in Pagliacci with an appealing rendition of Arlecchino’s charming serenade to Colombina. A special word for the Opera Hong Kong Chorus, whose singing brought out the full beauty and complexity of the music – especially impressive in Cavalleria Rusticana, which makes huge demands on the chorus, with music that ranges from lyrical to holy to upbeat. Equally impressive was their detailed acting and assured movement on stage. All the members are part-timers who must fit their commitment to Opera Hong Kong into busy lives, yet their performance was of truly professional calibre. Much praise goes to the chorus members and to chorus director Alex Tam for the passion and dedication that have enabled them to reach such a high level – it has been a pleasure to watch them evolve over the years. Roberto Gianola’s authoritative conducting brought out the best in the score and the Hong Kong Philharmonic. “Opera Hong Kong: Cavalleria Rusticana & Pagliacci”, Hong Kong Cultural Centre Grand Theatre. Reviewed: October 9.

title: Financial, mental health issues pushing women footballers towards early retirement
description: Extensive review by players’ trade union highlights the gulf between the sport’s rapid growth and conditions for most players.
content: Almost half of women’s footballers are considering leaving the game early, with financial pressures and mental health struggles the main reasons, according to a Fifpro report highlighting the gulf between the sport’s rapid growth and conditions for most players. The 2026 Fifpro Global Employment Report “Working Conditions in Women’s Football”, billed by the global players’ union as the most extensive review of working conditions in the women’s game in a decade, interviewed 800 players worldwide and found stark disparities. Some 49 per cent of players ‌surveyed said they were considering leaving football earlier than planned. Of those, 59 per cent cited their financial situation as a reason and 46 per cent pointed to psychological stress. “The women’s football industry has come a long way,” Fifpro director of women’s football Alex Culvin said. “[But] for 95 per cent [of players], the rest of the industry, there is a hell of a long way to go.” While inflation-adjusted average monthly club wages have tripled since Fifpro’s previous global study in 2017 to US$2,601, the median is substantially lower at US$1,669, illustrating what the report describes as “uneven and fragmented” growth. In 10 Eastern European countries analysed, average salaries remain below the national minimum wage. Even in western Europe and Asia/Oceania, which include some of the game’s bigger markets, ⁠average pay is not significantly higher than national minimum wages, according to Fifpro. “The professionalisation of women’s football is accelerating in some parts of the world and revenues are increasing; however, the progress ‌and benefits are not evenly distributed among players across the world,” Culvin said. The report found only 56 per cent of players have an employment contract, while 13 per cent receive a club pension and 47 per cent said their clubs do not have sufficient staff. Average contract length has risen from 12 months in 2017 to ‌19 months, while the proportion of players with agents has climbed sharply from 14 per cent to 41 per cent. “Whether a player has a written contract, a pension, medical cover ⁠or parental leave often depends less on her ⁠ability” than the country she lives in and the club she plays for, according to the report. Conditions have improved at the top Culvin said conditions have improved dramatically for a small group of about 5 per cent at the top, but many ‌players are being asked to meet professional demands without being given professional environments in which to work. “There is a recurring theme of precarity and fragile conditions,” she said. “Not only in terms of treatment and fair remuneration, but also just generally the expectations ‌that are ‌put on these players – professional expectations that don’t operate in professional circumstances because the conditions that are provided to them are suboptimal.” Mental health emerged as another significant concern, with 57 per cent of ‌players saying they had struggled with their mental health. Half of those players had not been provided with support by their clubs. Fifpro is calling for enforceable minimum standards covering areas including pay, facilities, ⁠staffing and healthcare to be written into employment agreements at the national level. Only eight of the 30 national women’s leagues analysed have a collective agreement with players through their unions. Fifpro wants psychological ⁠support to be mandatory. It pointed to the National Women’s Soccer League in the US, where mental health practitioners work alongside club staff and players have a right to six months of mental health leave. One area in which the global union said regulation had produced clear progress was maternity protection. Since Fifa introduced global minimum maternity ‌standards in 2021, the proportion of players considering leaving ‌football to have a family has fallen to 19 per cent, compared with 47 per cent in 2017. Culvin said women’s football had reached a point where rapid commercial expansion should be matched by greater protection for the players driving that growth. “There doesn’t need to be a choice for us between commercial growth and player protection,” she said. “Those two things need to go hand in hand and work in tandem.” For players with relatively short careers, she added, ambition cannot come solely from those on the pitch. “It can’t just be the player’s ambition,” she said. “It has to be matched by the club’s ambition, and not only ambition, resources to that ambition.”

title: Ivanka Trump’s Guo Pei dress for Xi visit sparks interest in Chinese haute couture
description: Guo, one of China’s best-known couturiers, has also designed outfits for celebrities including pop star Rihanna.
content: Ivanka Trump’s appearance in a blue embroidered couture outfit during the welcome ceremony for President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last month has drawn attention to its designer and the growing international profile of Chinese bespoke fashion. The outfit was designed by Guo Pei, one of China’s best-known couturiers, who also created the spectacular yellow embroidered cape with a long train and fur trim worn by pop star Rihanna at the 2015 Met Gala. Guo told the South China Morning Post that Trump’s outfit was not created specifically for the diplomatic occasion, but its design and colour were carefully considered. She said blue was chosen to convey calm and a shared aspiration for peace. The outfit was originally intended for a trip to China that US President Donald Trump’s eldest daughter had expected to make with her father. Guo said she and Ivanka Trump discussed its design and colour at the beginning of the year. Ultimately, Ivanka Trump did not make the journey to Beijing in May. But she had a front-row seat at the White House welcome ceremony for Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on September 24 at the start of a state visit aimed at stabilising a relationship tested by trade, technology and national security disputes. “Green is often associated with peace, but I felt blue could convey a more natural sense of calm,” Guo said. “I recommended blue, and Ivanka liked it too. She called the shade robin’s-egg blue.” Guo said she believed the colour had a serene quality that could express a shared desire for world peace. Bespoke clothing offers a level of fit and perfection that ready-to-wear simply cannot match Guo Pei, fashion designer The jacket featured silver-thread embroidery in a scrolling vine pattern, which Guo said “symbolised cultural common ground” because similar motifs appear in both Eastern and Western artistic traditions. Its wide, flared sleeves were designed to symbolise openness and acceptance, while the fitted inner dress was made longer than a normal day dress to convey the formality and respect befitting an occasion attended by national leaders, she said. Chinese-inspired clothing featured prominently throughout Xi’s visit. Xi wore a black Mao suit, a style with folded collars popularised by revolutionary leader Sun Yat-sen, while senior Chinese officials also donned dark Chinese-style attire to the White House state dinner. Peng, meanwhile, showcased four looks: a dove-grey, loose-fitting dress; a navy dress incorporating qipao elements; a red, floor-length V-neck gown for the state dinner; and a purple midi dress with a Hanfu-style collar. Guo said she believed Peng’s clothing had been tailor-made. As China’s first lady, her clothes “do not rely on complicated details; instead, they highlight her poise and the formality appropriate to her position”, Guo said. Chinese bespoke fashion has gained popularity both at home and abroad, despite weak domestic consumption and the high prices of custom-made luxury clothing. China’s haute couture market was valued at US$13.42 billion last year and is projected to reach US$31.86 billion by 2034, according to HTF Market Intelligence. The market research firm said “rising disposable incomes among affluent consumers, increasing demand for exclusivity, growing luxury consumption, and expanding influence of international fashion trends” would drive the growth. Guo, a guest member of the Federation de la Haute Couture et de la Mode, French high-end fashion’s governing body, said more than 60 per cent of her brand’s pieces were priced above €20,000 (US$22,406), with demand coming primarily from international markets. While overall demand had remained “relatively stable”, Guo said she had noticed more younger clients turning to haute couture for special occasions, such as weddings and high-end events. “Bespoke clothing offers a level of fit and perfection that ready-to-wear simply cannot match,” she said. Guo said she was optimistic about the market’s prospects in China, where consumers increasingly valued aesthetics, quality and craftsmanship over simply meeting basic needs. “People are increasingly choosing things for their beauty and fine craftsmanship, and because they genuinely love them,” she said. “I believe this trend will bode well for the market.”

title: India’s opposition marches on Supreme Court as ‘cockroach’ protests gain ground
description: India’s opposition alliance is harnessing the youth-led protests, testing whether their anger can build real political momentum against Modi.
content: Indian opposition leaders and student activists marched on the Supreme Court on Monday to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over alleged voter roll manipulation, as authorities erected heavy barricades and shut six metro stations across New Delhi. The rally went ahead after the Chief Justice of India turned down a meeting request from an opposition delegation, urging them instead to file a formal petition. Mainstream opposition parties have sought to harness a groundswell of public anger generated by the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which has spearheaded weeks of protests against alleged electoral roll manipulation. Tensions boiled over during the weekend when Delhi police detained dozens of student activists and blocked planned rallies, handing the opposition fresh political momentum for Monday’s march. Among those held was CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who was picked up by police on Saturday ahead of a demonstration that authorities said lacked official clearance due to law-and-order concerns. Dipke was released the following day alongside other activists. The CJP was founded in May after India’s chief justice Chief Justice Surya Kant referred to people with fake or bogus degrees as “cockroaches”, remarks widely interpreted as a swipe at young Indians facing problems with education and employment. Embracing the slight, Dipke launched the group as a satirical online platform that quickly morphed into a formidable street-level movement. Although Dipke has repeatedly said the CJP is not a registered political party – describing it as a Gen Z-led pressure movement aimed at strengthening democracy – its growing momentum has led observers to speculate it could eventually enter electoral politics. Opposition parties and student supporters have taken to the streets almost daily this month, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over a recent electoral roll update known as the Special Intensive Revision. Critics and opposition leaders say the process led to the deletion of around 130 million names from draft rolls, alleging that millions of genuine voters were wrongly removed to benefit the ruling party. The Election Commission has strongly denied the allegations, defending the removals as a routine clean-up of deceased, relocated and duplicate registrations. In response to the weekend crackdown, the Supreme Court ruled on Sunday that peaceful, unarmed protesters in Delhi could not be detained except in accordance with legal procedures. The court also directed authorities to ensure metro and railway services operated normally – a directive swiftly tested on Monday when police closed six stations citing security concerns ahead of the march. Local media reports said Rahul Gandhi, leader of the multiparty INDIA opposition alliance, had filed a petition in the Supreme Court against Kumar over alleged “vote theft”. Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay, an independent political commentator, said clamping down on the protests could prove counterproductive for the Bharatiya Janata Party-led (BJP) federal coalition government. “It seems the government has not been able to come up with any counterstrategy,” Mukhopadhyay said. “They are creating a certain public mood. There is a strong possibility that the CJP could take to the electoral path.” Parallel demonstrations have broken out in major cities like Mumbai, Bengaluru and Kolkata, alongside reports of police detentions across Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and West Bengal. “The movement is escalating and becoming far more widespread than initially thought,” said Kingshuk Nag, an author and political commentator. “It is led by students and their line of thinking is unconventional. Now, opposition parties have jumped into the fray.” Nag added that while the BJP was adept at countering the main opposition Congress party, it would need a new playbook to handle student leaders. He drew comparisons to Arvind Kejriwal, founder of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), who launched his political career following a major 2011 anti-corruption movement. Nag said the CJP could potentially become a comparable – or even larger – political force. However, other analysts urge caution regarding the movement’s long-term impact. Praveen Rai, a political analyst at the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies, pointed out that Congress previously ran a campaign centred on allegations of vote theft during state elections in West Bengal without gaining traction. “The ongoing street protest by Congress is a manifestation of deep political frustration arising out of several electoral defeats,” Rai said, adding that the demand for the election chief’s resignation was “politically immature” and lacked credible evidence. Nonetheless, Rai said the youth movement had galvanised the opposition to demand administrative accountability. “CJP can play an important role as a stakeholder. Elected governments tend to lose momentum and start taking things for granted if there are no active opposition parties or pressure groups.” While India’s history has seen youth-led protests capable of toppling governments – such as the 1990 student movement over caste reservations that destabilised the VP Singh administration – Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government does not appear to be in immediate danger. The next general election is not due until 2029. However, elections in key states including Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Punjab will offer an early test of whether this youth-driven momentum can pose a genuine threat to the BJP’s dominance.

title: Hong Kong electronics fairs to showcase 120 robots as firms aim to expand AI use
description: Hong Kong Electronics Fair and electronicAsia will bring together more than 3,200 exhibitors from 15 countries and regions.
content: More than 120 robots, including humanoid machines designed for factory work and elderly care, will be showcased at two major Hong Kong electronics fairs, as mainland Chinese manufacturers seek to expand the commercial applications of AI and tap overseas markets. The Hong Kong Electronics Fair (Autumn Edition) and electronicAsia will open on Tuesday at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai, bringing together more than 3,200 exhibitors from 15 countries and regions for four days. Leo Yang, Asia-Pacific director of mainland Chinese firm Booster Robotics, said that the company was developing affordable robots capable of competing with leading American manufacturers, which he acknowledged had an edge in technology. “China and the US are the top two in this industry,” Yang said at a media preview on Monday. “The top ones [in the US] are the best ones in terms of hardware and software. But pricing is an issue, a problem. So what we are doing is developing practical, affordable and reliable robotics to compete in the market.” The company is showcasing its latest humanoid robot, the Booster T2, which was launched in August and is making its Hong Kong debut. Equipped with artificial intelligence (AI) chips and a maximum dual-arm payload of 10kg, the robot is designed to perform tasks such as grasping objects, transporting goods and sorting materials. Yang said the robot had computing power of 2,000 trillion operations per second and supported open development tools, allowing researchers and businesses to customise its functions. While its current applications largely focus on education and research, the company plans to introduce more commercial uses from late this year into 2027. These include deploying robots as security guards, factory workers and assistants capable of caring for children and the elderly. Another mainland exhibitor, Neucity, is showcasing a multifunctional service robot designed for use in hotels, hospitals and retail outlets. It can handle tasks ranging from guest reception and guided tours to delivering medicine and monitoring patients. Zhang Tao, a research and development engineer at the company, said one of its robots was already working as a lobby manager at a hotel in Guangzhou. In hospitals, the robot can deliver medication, conduct remote ward inspections and use facial recognition to verify patients’ identities before releasing medicine, while nurses can monitor its activities through smartwatches or computers. “If a nurse needs to deliver medicine to a patient in bed 30, the robot will first verify whether it is the correct patient,” Zhang said. “Only then will it open the compartment and allow the patient to collect the medicine.” Zhang said the company hoped to expand overseas, arguing that its technology offered an advantage over robots designed for a single purpose. “Many robots on the market only perform one function, such as simple deliveries,” he said. “Ours combines multiple functions with AI capabilities.” Beyond robotics, exhibitors are also developing AI-powered consumer products tailored to different overseas markets. Shenzhen-based L’Atitude 52°N is introducing its Departure Collection smart sunglasses, which offer AI-powered travel guides, real-time translation and voice-activated assistance. Hardware product manager Robin Wang said the glasses, launched in August, were already being sold in Europe and North America but were not available in mainland China. He attributed the decision to differences in consumer habits, noting that mainland consumers often preferred umbrellas for sun protection, while sunglasses were more widely worn overseas. “We noticed significant differences in consumer behaviour between the domestic and overseas markets,” Wang said. “We believe there are greater opportunities in overseas markets for outdoor travel products, so we decided to start there.” The company expects to sell several thousand pairs this year and is exploring partnerships with overseas telecoms operators and distributors. Wang said Hong Kong provided opportunities to connect with international businesses and technology suppliers as the company pursued further expansion into markets including Japan, Taiwan and Australia. The two fairs, organised by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council, will also feature a new Future Industries Zone and dedicated showcases for smart wellness and entertainment technologies, alongside business-matching activities aimed at helping mainland enterprises expand overseas.

title: Opinion | Manchester City scandal a test of Britain’s commitment to rule of law
description: After backlash to Burnham’s response, unravelling the tangled web of this sorry affair is no longer just a question of sporting integrity.
content: The visit by star-studded Manchester City, the most successful English football team of recent times, was a highlight of Hong Kong’s football festival this summer. Supporters, sporting the club’s colours, flocked to Kai Tak Stadium, turning it into a sea of blue. Now, the club has plumbed the depths, found guilty by an independent tribunal of systematic breaches of the English Premier League’s financial rules over almost a decade. The affair has, with justification, been described as one of the biggest sporting scandals ever. But it transcends football. The controversy has diplomatic and economic implications for the United Kingdom – and has become a problem for Prime Minister Andy Burnham. City are appealing against the decision and strenuously deny any wrongdoing. The club has been majority owned, since 2008, by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, an Emirati royal and vice-president of the United Arab Emirates. The UAE is an important economic partner and ally of the UK. There have been reports that UAE officials, in response to the proceedings against City, have threatened to withdraw billions of pounds in investment from the UK and warned of damage to the bilateral relationship. Concerns have been raised that there will be political interference in the disciplinary process. The stakes are high. City were found guilty by the Premier League’s disciplinary commission of 114 charges involving sweeping breaches of financial rules and failures to cooperate with the investigation. “Sham” contracts were used as part of a disguised funding scheme that inflated revenue and understated costs by more than £900 million (US$1.19 billion), the panel found. This gave the club a huge advantage over its rivals, allowing it to spend more on players. It has, effectively, been found to have built its success by cheating. The offences are so serious a heavy penalty is expected, should the club’s appeal fail. It could even be expelled from the Premier League. A confidential hearing spanned 12 weeks in 2024. The tribunal’s scathing ruling, when published last month, prompted widespread public condemnation of City. But the initial response from Burnham, in a BBC interview, struck a different tone. He began by suggesting the club might have been unfairly treated and went on to say he would be concerned if its Abu Dhabi owners sold it. The prime minister, while promising not to intervene in the process, spoke of the valuable contribution the owners had made to the redevelopment of Manchester during his time as the city’s mayor. His comments sparked an instant backlash and a swift climbdown. He had, uncharacteristically, misjudged the public mood. Burnham’s remarks have also prompted scrutiny of his relationship with the owners. This is not surprising. The regeneration of Manchester has been a driving force for Burnham’s political career, helping propel him to 10 Downing Street. As mayor of the city, he joined a delegation from the club visiting Shenzhen in September 2018, welcoming the opening of its second mainland office there. This, Burnham said, showed City’s commitment to China. “I can’t help but be impressed by how football in the country is undergoing a revolution,” he added, declaring that the club’s ambition “matches that of the football authorities in China – it’s a perfect partnership”. Three months later, the Premier League investigation began. There is a need for the disciplinary process, which has already taken far too long, to be swiftly concluded, to provide clarity and certainty. Only then will the Premier League be able to move on. The league is arguably Britain’s biggest cultural export and its integrity and reputation are at stake. It is difficult, in light of the guilty verdicts, to imagine City being presented with the Premier League trophy at the end of the season, although this remains a possibility. Many believe the process will drag on. The club’s chairman, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, who among many other roles acts as the UAE’s special envoy to China, said in a defiant open letter to supporters that it still has a long way to run. The best outcome would be for the club to admit to wrongdoing, take the punishment and start to rebuild its reputation, perhaps in the unfamiliar setting of the lower leagues. At least it could then look ahead with a clear conscience. There is not the slightest indication that will happen. The game has moved into extra time. And City, at least, believe there is still much to play for. However long it takes, justice must be done and be seen to be done. Unravelling the tangled web woven by this sorry affair is not just a question of sporting integrity, it is a test of Britain’s commitment to the rule of law.

title: Saudi Arabia faces more drone, missile attacks after Houthi’s fatal airport strikes
description: A Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis says it has intercepted weapons including in areas where there are key oil and gas facilities.
content: Saudi Arabia said it was dealing with new drone and cruise missile attacks on Monday, posing fresh security threats to the kingdom following the weekend’s deadly strikes on Riyadh airport. “We have detected and are monitoring a threat involving drones and cruise missiles against the kingdom and the threat is being dealt with,” the state-run Saudi Press Agency reported. It cited Defence Ministry spokesman Turki al-Maliki on behalf of a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis. The coalition said earlier it had intercepted missiles and drones aimed at the kingdom overnight, including areas that are home to some of Saudi Arabia’s key oil and gas facilities. Saudi authorities on Monday extended a suspension of operations at the King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, where two separate attacks over the weekend killed at least 14 people and wounded more than 300, many critically. King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was targeted separately. Meanwhile, air strikes on two districts in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa killed one person and wounded 12 others, according to the Houthis. Their media centre blamed Saudi Arabia for the strikes. The weekend’s events mark the deadliest strikes for Saudi Arabia since the Iran war began and come a week after Saudi-led forces in Yemen launched a campaign to retake areas held by Houthi militia, including the Bab el-Mandeb strait and “eliminate” the group. As the violence stretched into Monday, the coalition vowed a “decisive” response. There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix. We come out of the ashes all the time and every time Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Against that backdrop, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, one of the most senior Saudi officials to speak publicly in the wake of the strikes, sought to project resilience, telling oil industry executives that the kingdom remained committed to providing energy security. “There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix. We come out of the ashes all the time and every time,” Prince Abdulaziz said at an energy event on Sunday. At the World Petroleum Congress (WPC) on Monday, he called for a serious response to events of recent weeks, while noting the country should remain focused on economic diversification and investment. The WPC gathering has been disrupted by the hostilities, with some executives who had been scheduled to attend, including the chief executives of BP Plc and Shell Plc, withdrawing. Riyadh has been in conflict with Houthi militants ever since they took control over the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in 2014 and forced the internationally recognised government backed by Saudi Arabia to resign the following year. US President Donald Trump said over the weekend he was considering joining in the fight against the Iran-backed militant group. “The attack last night is very emblematic. A very advanced, sophisticated ballistic missile, very accurate, targeting a commercial airport and now a number of civilian casualties,” former White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk told Bloomberg Television. “It’s an act of terrorism. I think there has to be a response.” A senior United Arab Emirates official, meanwhile, urged a revival of regional security arrangements. “It has become evident that we are all targets and that our security is indivisible,” Anwar Gargash, senior adviser to the UAE president, said on X. Brent crude extended gains to above US$105 a barrel on Monday following the weekend strikes. Traders weighed resilient Middle East flows against rising regional tensions and a US claim that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a so-called energy ceasefire. The Saudi civil aviation authority said one person died and 11 were injured after an unknown projectile hit the main airport in Riyadh on Sunday. That followed a strike on King Khalid airport on Saturday. The attacks brought travel at the Riyadh airport to a near-standstill. They also forced the capital’s financial hub to shift to remote work and schools to do remote learning. The FAA on Sunday issued a warning to all US airlines to exercise caution flying to or over parts of Saudi Arabia “at all altitudes”. Authorities have indicated the 25th World Petroleum Congress and associated events, scheduled to run until Wednesday, will continue. Riyadh is also scheduled to host the Future Investment Initiative (FII), its flagship investor gathering, later this month. The two events draw industry heavyweights and thousands of delegates. “Comprehensive security measures will be in place at Riyadh’s airports, our conference venues and official hotels, with coordinated arrangements for participants’ transportation and movements,” the FII’s Chief Executive Officer, Maha Al Saud, said in a statement. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: ‘Inconvenient truth’: Man City case spotlights realities of UK-UAE ties
description: Analysts point to a much deeper network of high-stakes diplomacy and geopolitical economics between London and Abu Dhabi.
content: When Liverpool fans greeted Manchester City at Anfield on Sunday with jeers and banners demanding the Abu Dhabi-owned football club be relegated, they took aim at what critics have long dubbed “sportswashing” – the practice of using high-profile sports investments to launder a tarnished international reputation. Focusing solely on public relations, however, obscures a much deeper network of high-stakes diplomacy and geopolitical economics between London and Abu Dhabi. The reality behind the United Arab Emirates’ acquisition of the club is an “inconvenient truth” rather than a mere branding exercise, according to Simon Chadwick, a leading sports business expert and co-editor of The Geopolitical Economy of Football: Where Power Meets Politics and Business. Rather than buying influence through sport, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan’s 2008 takeover was the result of “intense diplomacy” that subsequently helped London navigate the global financial crisis that struck later that year, Chadwick said. An emergency £7 billion bailout of Barclays Bank organised by Sheikh Mansour, involving Emirati and Qatari sovereign wealth funds, spared cash-strapped British taxpayers from footing the bill. However, it later transpired that Barclays misled shareholders about the mechanism of the UAE’s £3.25 billion share of the bailout. They were given the impression that Sheikh Mansour had invested in his personal capacity, rather than through Abu Dhabi’s International Petroleum Investment Company, triggering a lengthy legal battle with British firm PCP Capital Group. It ended in 2021 with a British court finding Barclays guilty of “serious deceit”. Nevertheless, the City acquisition remained “part of a diplomatic landscape that saw Britain and the UAE drawing closer together”, said Chadwick, a professor of Afro-Eurasian Sport at the Emlyon Business School in France. This was evident during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Britain in 2015. Rather than touring Anfield or Old Trafford, home of Manchester United, Xi went to City, where he was prominently photographed alongside then British prime minister David Cameron and Chancellor of the Exchequer George Osborne. Chadwick, himself a generational fan of Championship team Middlesbrough, said it was “inappropriate” to describe the City case as sportswashing. “This is not sportswashing, it’s sport diplomacy,” he said. “The British government was part of this and now, of course, through this diplomatic activity, we’ve got a level of interconnectedness between the UAE and Britain the realities of which are proving to be unpalatable to a lot of people.” These realities are reflected by the £30 billion of investments in Britain made by UAE sovereign wealth funds and state-owned enterprises over the last five years. Alongside the much-vaunted urban renewal of Manchester as part of Sheikh Mansour’s strategic investment in the Blues, these injections into Britain’s defence, technology, life sciences and connectivity infrastructure have been a welcome boost after the Covid pandemic wreaked economic havoc – much like the Barclays bailout in 2008. As mayor of Manchester during the Emirati-funded renewal of Britain’s second biggest city, Prime Minister Andy Burnham now finds himself trying to pull off a diplomatic rescue act to avert retaliation by the UAE. Downing Street has made no secret of its worries that action by independent football regulators against City’s Emirati owners could have serious economic consequences. Burnham, therefore, appears prepared to weather the domestic political storm, telling the BBC in an October 1 interview that he would be “really concerned to lose them” given that the UAE had been “such a huge partner” in building modern Manchester and turning City into a global force. The prime minister’s initial response to the independent commission’s verdicts – which found the club’s leadership deliberately obstructive and evasive – was thus “tone deaf”, according to Guy Burton, a Brussels-based international relations researcher and co-host of The FootPol Podcast, a sports show focusing on the intersection of football and politics. British newspapers have also noted that the Prime Minister’s Office, when approached for comment, has not disputed their reports that the UAE could freeze its investments in the country if independent regulators deem Sheikh Mansour’s ownership of City not “fit and proper”. Shortly after taking office in July, Burnham called four Gulf leaders, including Mansour’s elder brother UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, to reiterate British support for their defence against Iranian air strikes being carried out in response to attacks by the US and Israel. Their discussion further included ideas to “step up collaboration on technology and AI”, a Downing Street spokesman said in a statement. The UAE is investing tens of billions of dollars in data centres, AI and other collaborations with US and European firms as part of a strategic drive to become a global leader in the field. In addition to Burnham’s experience as Manchester mayor, his expectations of further UAE investment were fuelled by the free-trade pact Britain agreed with the six Gulf Cooperation Council states – the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman – in May. London hopes the deal, the first free-trade agreement between the GCC and a G7 country, could boost the UK economy by an estimated £3.7 billion (US$4.9 billion) a year and increase wages by £1.9 billion annually in the long run. The UAE is Britain’s biggest economic partner in the GCC, accounting for £25 billion of the £53 billion in bilateral trade in 2025. It is home to about two-thirds of the roughly 300,000 British nationals living in the Gulf monarchies, with most clustered in Dubai, the country’s commercial centre, and more than 5,000 British-owned businesses. With City’s appeal against the verdicts and further deliberations pending, any Premier League sanctions are unlikely to be unveiled until after the end of the season in May. Burton also predicted additional fallout from other clubs “who feel they missed out on financial opportunities because of City’s financial doping”, much of which would play out during and after May, and “for years to come”. “There are a lot of twists and turns still to come in this story, much as there are in the wider instability in the region,” Burton said. With so much at stake, Burnham’s vow not to politically interfere in the case may ultimately prove to be hollow. City’s case, the governance and application of rules within the Premier League, and the thriving relationship between Britain and the UAE “are embedded within a very dense network of interconnections between the two countries”, Chadwick said. That means “it is an inconvenient truth for many people” that the City case might not result in the strict application and enforcement of rules through a “set of draconian sanctions”. Instead, the outcome could be a “negotiated diplomatic settlement”, Chadwick said. “But it’s not sportswashing,” he added.

title: China’s top diplomat to visit Azerbaijan, Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria to boost ties
description: Wang Yi’s four-nation tour comes amid Beijing’s push to shore up its trade corridors and geopolitical influence.
content: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi will visit Azerbaijan and three Balkan countries amid Beijing’s push to shore up its trade corridors and geopolitical influence in the regions. Wang will attend the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku, Azerbaijan, on Thursday “as special representative of President Xi Jinping”, according to China’s foreign ministry. Aside from Azerbaijan, Beijing’s top diplomat will visit Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria, it said, for a four-nation trip running from October 14 to 20. This will mark Wang’s first visit to Azerbaijan in seven years. His trip to Montenegro will be the first-ever official visit by a Chinese foreign minister since the country gained independence 20 years ago. Wang last visited Bulgaria as foreign minister in 2015. According to foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning, China hopes to engage in full dialogue with all parties at the CICA summit, uphold multilateralism and work to improve governance in Asia. “As the current international and regional landscape is becoming more complex and volatile, Asian countries have a stronger wish to safeguard peace and tranquillity and promote economic growth,” she said at a press conference on Monday. Mao added that Wang on his trip would meet with the countries’ foreign ministers and hold in-depth exchanges with their leaders. His itinerary spans important logistics hubs and Balkan infrastructure partners along the Middle Corridor, also known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route. This transport link connects China to European markets by passing through Kazakhstan, crossing the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, continuing through Georgia and Turkey, and bypassing Russia. The countries Wang will visit have also engaged with Beijing through the Belt and Road Initiative, a China-centred global trade and infrastructure scheme. Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria are important partners for Beijing in southeastern Europe, Mao said, adding that China has had significant cooperation with the countries in trade, investment, tourism and infrastructure. This year marks the 20th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Montenegro, and the two countries have jointly delivered flagship cooperation projects, including Montenegro’s North-South highway, she added. Mao said the Peljesac Bridge in Croatia, built by a Chinese company, had become a symbol of China-Croatia and China-Europe cooperation. China hoped Wang’s visit would “strengthen the alignment of development strategies with Croatia, expand practical cooperation, and ensure that bilateral relations enjoy steady and sustained growth”, the spokeswoman added. Bulgaria became one of the early European members of the Belt and Road Initiative when it signed a memorandum of understanding in 2015. It has cooperated with China in science and technology innovation, finance, green initiatives, environmental protection, agriculture, energy, forestry and health.

title: US turns to low-cost Blackbeard hypersonic missiles to overwhelm Chinese defences
description: At US$385,000 per unit, the carrier-launched weapons are being developed with an emphasis on affordability and mass production.
content: The US Navy aims to field a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile on its carrier-based fighters, a weapon that could pose a new challenge to the air defences protecting Chinese warships and coastal military installations, experts said. California-based defence company Castelion’s Blackbeard is designed to fly at more than five times the speed of sound and strike ships and land targets. Unlike more expensive hypersonic weapons, it is being developed with an emphasis on affordability and mass production. In May, the Pentagon sought congressional authorisation and funding to buy more than 12,000 Blackbeard missiles for deployment across the armed services over five years. US Navy projections put the average gross unit cost at about US$385,000 in the financial years 2028-31. In contrast, the cost of Lockheed Martin’s larger Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile (LRASM) is estimated in US Air Force budget figures for the 2024 financial year to be about US$3.25 million. The price difference could allow US forces to build much larger stockpiles and launch repeated attacks against Chinese warships, forcing them to expend defensive interceptors and potentially making it easier for larger, more powerful anti-ship missiles to hit their targets, experts say. The Blackbeard could also threaten Chinese coastal anti-ship missile batteries and air-defence systems, although experts differed over whether American carrier-based aircraft could get close enough to strike such targets. According to the US Naval Institute (USNI), the navy ordered 50 pre-production missiles in June and a further 444 in September and is seeking early operational capability this year – though budget projections and a Castelion announcement in April pointed to 2027. USNI News reported that an F/A-18E/F Super Hornet showed in September that it could carry two Blackbeard missiles. The US Navy is planning to equip each Super Hornet to carry up to four missiles, it said. The push for larger inventories reflects concerns about how quickly American forces could run short of long-range precision weapons in a conflict involving Taiwan, a continuing point of friction between Beijing and Washington. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. In war games published in 2023, the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that US forces exhausted their simulated LRASM stocks within the first week in every iteration of a hypothetical attack on the island. Meanwhile, Chinese military researchers have examined the various ways they could counter potential large-scale US precision strikes, according to Christopher Sharman, director of the US Naval War College’s China Maritime Studies Institute (CMSI). Sharman pointed to a 2023 article published by the People’s Liberation Army journal Air Force Military Studies that examined more than a dozen conflicts involving US and allied long-range strikes. CMSI published an English translation in August. The PLA authors recommended attacking US forces before they launched their weapons, jamming satellite navigation signals and coordinating drones, fighters and air-defence systems, Sharman said. However, publicly available information did not establish whether the PLA had adopted those recommendations, he added. The bigger question was not just “whether individual warships can intercept incoming missiles”, but whether the Chinese navy could “maintain an effective, integrated defence across the fleet” during a coordinated attack. Sharman stressed that he was speaking in a personal capacity and his comments did not necessarily reflect the views of the US government, Defence Department or the Naval War College. Peter Jones, a retired Australian vice-admiral and adjunct professor at UNSW Canberra, said hypersonic missiles forced defending forces to “detect, track, assign weapons about five or more times quicker” than against conventional subsonic anti-ship missiles. A “layered defence” that would draw on the networked capabilities of ships and aircraft in a task group offered the best chance of countering such attacks, according to Jones. “Whether the latest Chinese destroyers can engage these missiles is unclear,” he noted. Much would depend on the Blackbeard’s flight path and radar signature, as well as the effectiveness of Chinese radars, defensive weapons and electronic warfare systems, Jones said. Another uncertainty is how much damage a Blackbeard strike could cause. The US Navy’s requirements specified a desired payload of about 34kg (75lb), although the missile’s actual warhead weight remains unconfirmed. Timothy Heath, China expert and founder of security research firm Perceptum, said Blackbeard could be useful for “striking sensors such as radars that support anti-air missiles”. Damaging those radars could make it easier for larger, more powerful anti-ship missiles used alongside Blackbeard to hit their targets, he suggested. While Heath emphasises the missile’s supporting role, Lyle Goldstein, director of the Asia Programme at Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, sees greater potential for Blackbeard to disable a warship on its own. Calling it “a significant leap in US Navy capability”, Goldstein argued that the force of a high-speed impact could be “just as or more important than the warhead”. Even one strike could cause “mission kill”, leaving a ship unable to fight and forcing it to return for repairs, he said. Goldstein also argued that combining lighter and heavier missiles with long-range attack drones could make defending warships “especially challenging”. Yet both Goldstein and Heath identified a major obstacle to employing the Blackbeard near Taiwan: the vulnerability of US carriers and carrier-based aircraft. “The main limitation is the launch platform,” Heath said, noting that manned carrier-based strike aircraft were “expensive and vulnerable”. Beijing’s attacks could force US carriers farther from Taiwan, potentially beyond the missile’s effective range, he added. Goldstein was more cautious, expecting US carriers to “operate on the margins of any conflict in the western Pacific”, potentially putting mainland Chinese targets beyond the reach of the Blackbeard. But he predicted a possible role for the missile against PLA Navy warships operating farther into the Pacific Ocean and potentially threatening American logistics around Guam. In contrast, Heath saw greater potential for attacks on Chinese coastal missile and air-defence systems, arguing that launching Blackbeard from carrier-based aircraft would “dramatically expand the flexibility and range with which the missile can be used”. The Blackbeard’s effective range and ability to strike moving warships have yet to be publicly shown.

title: Kimi Antonelli dares to dream of historic Formula 1 title after Singapore GP podium
description: Mercedes driver could become the youngest-ever champion at next race in Texas after finishing third behind Max Verstappen in city state.
content: Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli said he was allowing himself to dream about a historic ⁠world title, which is within reach ⁠at the next race in Austin, Texas, after the ⁠20-year-old sealed his 14th podium finish of the season at Sunday’s Singapore Grand Prix. The title would make Antonelli Formula 1’s youngest-ever champion and Italy’s first since 1953. Antonelli’s third place in a Singapore GP that was controlled from start to finish by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen was scrappy, as he flirted with a penalty for testing ‌the track’s limits. But it was enough to extend his lead over teammate George Russell to 102 points and when asked if he dared to dream of clinching the title in Austin later this month on the long journey home he said: “For sure. “But at the same time, I know it’s very close, I know it’s there, but I just need to make sure that I keep doing the best I can. The mindset is always the same, to go out there and win. “I think this ⁠weekend I haven’t particularly driven that well … but I feel confident that, [with] a week to reset, I’m really looking forward to being ‌back in Austin. “If I don’t do my job well, then the result won’t come. So in order to achieve what I want, I need to perform at 100 per cent.” Sooner or later Antonelli could mathematically win the championship in ‌Austin on the assumption that there were still five races to come, with the fate of the Grands Prix ⁠in Qatar and Abu Dhabi ⁠in the air because of the conflict in the Middle East. However, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff was refusing to tempt fate. “I remind myself that this is motor racing ‌and crazy things have happened,” Wolff said. “It probably needs the other two [contenders], George and Lewis [Hamilton], to retire and him winning. So this is not a likely scenario,” he added, while ‌recognising that ‌the title was within reach and maybe inevitable. “It’s going to come towards him, whether that’s in Mexico or Brazil, or far down ‌the line.” Verstappen finally conquers Singapore Verstappen’s victory came ‌in the 250th Grand Prix start for the 29-year-old Dutchman. It was his 73rd career victory and ‌first at Singapore in 10 attempts. Verstappen, who also won the sprint race on Saturday, ⁠has now won ⁠every race that appears on the 2026 schedule except the Spanish Grand Prix at ‌The Madring in Madrid, which ran its inaugural event this year. “It’s taken a ‌while, but ‌I think this race was very good,” Verstappen said after ‌the victory. “It worked out, so of course I’m very happy ⁠to win here.” Russell, who worked his way up from the back of the starting grid due to engine penalties, finished a respectable ninth ⁠at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, where overtaking is notoriously tricky. Wolff said both drivers would probably be running in Austin on an upgraded ⁠car as some, but not all, of its teething problems had been ironed out in Singapore. “I think that this new car needs a very different set-up philosophy than the previous car,” he said. “Does it have the performance that we were ‌hoping the upgrade would bring? I don’t ‌think so yet, but it was a step in the right direction.” Antonelli narrowly avoided a five-second penalty, hitting the maximum limit of breaches of the track boundaries. However, Wolff praised his driving and joked about how he could boost the diminutive driver higher for a better view of the track edges. “I have a good strategy. I’m going to put a pillow from the hotel under his a***, so he can actually see the road.”

title: China, EU take a breath after surprise deal brings temporary halt to trade tussle
description: Agreement, praised on both sides, features controls on Chinese EV shipments and tariff reductions, helping to cool tensions – for now.
content: Weeks of high-wire negotiations between China and the EU culminated in a surprise trade deal that will, among other measures, impose strict quotas on Chinese hybrid car exports to the bloc and slash Chinese tariffs on a variety of European goods. The deal, unveiled on Friday, takes some of the heat out of searing bilateral trade tensions and temporarily averts the prospect of a bruising trade war – a cooldown augmented by Beijing’s subsequent reduction of value-added tax (VAT) export rebates on certain goods, which could help curb outbound shipments further. China’s Ministry of Commerce described the deal as an “upward arrangement” based on the country’s outbound shipments of hybrid cars in 2025, adding the agreement would ensure further room for the “stable growth” of Chinese companies’ exports. French President Emmanuel Macron hailed the agreement during a visit to the Paris Motor Show on Monday, saying that it would help Europe better protect its market from “disloyal competition”. Under the terms of the deal, Brussels will cap imports of Chinese hybrid cars at 350,000 units per year, rising at 6 per cent annually. This will leave exports at less than half the 800,000 vehicles the EU has projected will be shipped in 2026. After the bloc’s 27 member states consent to the arrangement, the bloc will use a technical safeguard instrument to moderate the import of Chinese hybrid cars, likely to be in place from December 1. Once 350,000 units have been imported, others will be turned away at EU ports. “No measure will specifically target Chinese products, still less treat Chinese companies in a discriminatory manner. The quota China receives will be no lower than that of any other source of EU imports,” the commerce ministry said in a statement on Monday. [The deal] is like a band-tightening spell on Chinese firms ... We would of course prefer to not have it, but we have to take one for the team Chinese executive, Europe The agreement, which will be in place for a four-year period, aims to halve China’s share of the EU hybrid market from the current 12 per cent. Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the EU almost tripled from 2024 to 2025, rising from around 107,000 to around 302,000, according to the ministry, which cited the European Commission’s statistical office. “[The deal] is like a band-tightening spell on Chinese firms,” said a Chinese executive in Europe who requested anonymity to speak freely. “We would of course prefer to not have it, but we have to take one for the team.” Brussels’ goal was to push Chinese firms to bring their production chains to Europe, the executive said, estimating the move would increase production costs by 30 to 50 per cent. Asked on Monday how Beijing grew to accept the concessions – after Chinese officials spent weeks rejecting the prospect of voluntarily limiting auto shipments – Brussels framed its position with a time-worn business maxim: “The customer is always right.” A senior EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, referenced the saying when discussing the deal. “In business, there is a saying that the customer is always right. So, as a customer, we have made the point very clearly that we are hurting, and that we will remain a customer. But the volumes and the surge that we have seen are unsustainable.” The agreement would comply with World Trade Organization rules, the Chinese commerce ministry said, adding Beijing reserved all its rights under the WTO framework, including “recourse to dispute settlement and seeking trade compensation”. With petrol prices high due in large part to the US-Israel war on Iran, European customers have been making the switch to electric vehicles in greater numbers. Hybrid and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) made up 46.6 per cent of the European car market during the first eight months of this year, according to data from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA). PHEV demand is booming in some of Europe’s biggest markets, with registrations in the first eight months of the year up 77.6 per cent in Italy, 33.9 per cent in Spain and 15.6 per cent in Germany, according to the ACEA. The European Union market grew by 30,720 vehicles in August, per ACEA data – a year-on-year increase of 4.5 per cent – with Chinese carmakers BYD, Chery, Leapmotor and SAIC accounting for about 92 per cent of the growth. Chinese brands are expected to have an outsize presence at the auto show in Paris, which opened on Monday. According to a report from Allianz Trade, the country’s carmakers will take up a 50 per cent share of exhibitors, as the share of European marques drops to 40 per cent. Separately, in a bid to address growing concerns from the West over trade imbalances, Beijing will cut the VAT export rebate rate for new energy vehicles from 13 per cent to 9 per cent from April 1, according to a notice issued jointly on Monday by the Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration. Tax rebates on e-cigarette exports will also be cancelled, per the notice.

title: Hong Kong steps up Russia arrival checks after Siberian lab worker’s death
description: Health officials order expanded surveillance at airport after researcher at anti-plague institute in Siberia dies from pneumonia of unknown origin.
content: Hong Kong will step up health surveillance measures for arrivals after a laboratory worker at an anti-plague research institute in Russia died from pneumonia, but authorities have stressed the risk to residents remains low. According to World Health Organization (WHO) information provided by Russian authorities, there was no evidence of ongoing transmission, the Centre for Health Protection (CHP) said on Monday. Russian authorities previously stated ‌that the worker at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute in Siberia had died from pneumonia, but that the origin of the infection ⁠had yet to ⁠be determined. The centre said it had not received any reports of residents or travellers arriving in Hong Kong from Russia with cases of pneumonia of unknown origin in recent months. “The CHP assesses that the immediate public health impact to Hong Kong is low. For the sake of prudence, the CHP has implemented a series of control and prevention measures to guard against imported cases,” a spokesman said. These included arranging for Port Health Division officers to conduct temperature checks for passengers arriving on flights from Russia, as well as conducting health assessments for arrivals exhibiting symptoms and transferring them to public hospitals for further testing. The department will also display signage and broadcast announcements in the airport arrival area and through airlines to urge passengers who have visited Irkutsk Oblast in Siberia within the past 14 days to declare their travel history. It will also provide the Airport Authority and airlines with the latest information regarding the case, and urge airlines to remind their flight crews to strictly enforce established prevention and control measures if they identify suspected cases on their flights. The centre will also send letters to all doctors and hospitals in Hong Kong, reminding them to remain highly vigilant and to strengthen surveillance. Any patient who has visited the area within 14 days before the onset of symptoms and has developed pneumonia of an undetermined origin must immediately report to the centre for further testing. “The CHP will continue to closely monitor the latest developments, respond swiftly and strictly guard against imported cases to safeguard public health,” the spokesman said. Russian media reported earlier this month that the 28-year-old laboratory technician working for the institute had died of pneumonic plague that could have come from a broken test tube. But Russian officials stressed that postmortem tests had not detected the disease. Pneumonic plague, which spreads between people and causes severe lung infections, is highly treatable if detected early. The centre said that according to the latest information from the WHO, citing data provided by Russian authorities, no plague cases had been recorded recently in Irkutsk Oblast, testing of the deceased’s contacts found no high-threat pathogens, and there were no further cases of severe pneumonia linked to this case. The Russian authorities reported that no biosecurity incidents had occurred at the laboratory, and quarantine measures were instituted in hospital where the patient was treated, according to the centre.
